Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Older People's Exercise intervention in Residential and nursing Accommodation (OPERA)
Abstract: This is a joint proposal between the Centre for Health Sciences at Queen Mary University of London (QMUL) and the Clinical Trials Unit at Warwick Medical School. Design: Cluster randomised clinical effectiveness trial, preceded by a pilot study, with simultaneous process evaluation and cost utility analysis, and a secondary costs and consequences analysis based in residential and nursing homes (RNHs) Setting: 77 private and public sector RNHs (+ 3 pilot homes) in two localities: NE London & central England. We have active support for this project from our lead PCT in each locality. We will seek consent from the RNH's management, as guardians of the cluster, to take part in the randomised study, consent from individual residents to participate in the evaluation and separate consent from residents to participate in the exercise class component of the intervention. Target population: ALL people aged 65 or over living in residential or nursing homes except those identified by RNH staff to have a very limited life expectancy or another condition which would make participation difficult or inappropriate will be invited to participate in the study. Our exclusion criteria will be severe cognitive impairment (score of 10 or less on the Mini-Mental State Examination [MMSE]) and inability to communicate in English. All eligible residents will be invited to take part in study assessments. All residents, except those unable to transfer (with assistance from one person) from a wheelchair to chair will be invited to participate in the exercise classes; this includes residents who are not participating in the evaluation. Since mortality in this population is substantial we will have an ongoing programme of screening new residents to join the study. Health technology being assessed: Experienced physiotherapists will deliver: (1) a rolling educational programme for RNH staff to help provide an environment where residents can safely increase their physical activity, complemented by (2) a twice-weekly exercise classes for residents in each RNH, with a strong emphasis on the aerobic and social aspects of group exercise. Classes will include some residents who are not depressed; this will serve to improve the group dynamic, ensure a representative range of motivation and match how such a programme would work in 'real life'. Informed by the MRC framework for testing complex interventions, and specifically our previous work modelling a complex intervention for falls prevention, we will decide on the final components of the intervention in the pilot stage; we will then develop and refine the intervention package. The intervention builds on our previous experience of group exercise interventions and primary care staff training for musculoskeletal pain and falls prevention. Previous studies of exercise classes for depression in this group that have not included education for RNH staff have had equivocal results, and indicate that a brief intervention is likely to lose its effect in the long term. Our ongoing regular 'whole RNH' programme will maximise the possibility of demonstrating beneficial effects. Such an intervention will be built into the year-round routine of RNHs. Thus, participants recruited at baseline will be able to continue in the class for one year. In both the intervention and control RNHs we will run a rolling staff training programme, delivered by our research nurses in the control RNHs, promoting 'best usual care' around depression, i.e facilitating recognition and onward referral of depressed residents to conventional services. Measurement of costs and outcomes: We will collect outcome data on both depressed and non-depressed participants. Our primary effectiveness analyses will be based on the Geriatric Depression Scale-15 (GDS-15). Our three primary outcomes are: 1) The prevalence of depression in the nursing homes (amongst residents able to complete assessment) twelve months after randomisation. 2) The proportion of residents identified with depression at baseline who are in remission at six months. 3) The change in the severity of depressive symptoms in residents identified with depression at baseline at twelve months.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: SHIFT. Self-Harm Intervention, Family Therapy: a randomised controlled trial of family therapy vs. treatment as usual for young people seen after second or subsequent episodes of self-harm
Abstract: The SHIFT Trial has been designed as a pragmatic, individually-randomised, controlled trial comparing Family Therapy (FT) with Treatment as Usual (TAU) for adolescents aged 11 - 17 years who have engaged in at least one previous episode of self-harm. The trial aims to recruit 832 participants from centres in Yorkshire, Greater Manchester and London. Family therapy will be delivered by qualified family therapists using a modified version of the Leeds Family Therapy & Research Centre Systemic Family Therapy Manual (LFTRC Manual), the development of which was funded by the MRC to support trials of FT. The primary outcome is rate of repetition of self-harm leading to hospital attendance 18 months after randomisation. Secondary outcomes include rate of repetition at 12 months, cost-effectiveness, quality of life, and predictive / process measures.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Clinical and cost-effectiveness of technologies for testing and treating sexual partners of people with sexually transmitted infections: Evidence synthesis and mathematical modelling study
Abstract: Design: Evidence synthesis (ES): mathematical modelling study, cost-effectiveness analysis Search Strategy 1) Existing data, a) updateof NICE rapid review of effectiveness of partner notification to December 2007 (full access, Low is PI), b) distribution by clinical setting for sexually transmitted infections from Avon System for Surveillance of Sexually Transmitted Infections in Avon and Brent (full access, Low is PI), c) risk behaviour while care seeking from Patient Access to care for Sexually Transmitted Infections project (full access, Cassell is PI); d) community-wide impact on partner treatment and re-infection rates of patient-delivered partner therapy for chlamydia and gonorrhoea from randomised controlled trial in USA (access to data from Matthew Golden, PI, project collaborator); 2) Planned data collection, a) new rapid reviews of Medline, Embase, Cinahl, Cochrane Library, Jan 1990-Dec 2007 for data about sexually transmitted infection co-infection rates, partner treatment, complication and transmission rates, health-related quality of life of complications of sexually transmitted infection, b) practices for sexual partner testing and treatment from Genitourinary Medicine and Primary Care Sexually Transmitted Infections Services project (full access, Mercer is PI), c) health state valuation of complications of chlamydia using the Peninsula Medical School Value of Health Panel using the preferred methodological approach of NICE (full access, Green is co-applicant). 3) Existing individual-based transmission dynamic network mathematical models, a) Chlamydia Screening Studies (ClaSS) project model (full access, Barton, Low and Roberts are authors), b) Health Protection Agency model of chalmydia transmission (full access, Edmunds and Turner are authors), c) Imperial College model of chlamydia and gonorrhoea transmission (full access, Garnett and White are authors). Review strategy and evidence synthesis 1) We will use NICE-recommended methods for rapid quality assessment and data extraction for literature reviews and determine best available estimates by consensus. We will collate and document sources for all other parameter values. 2) Mathematical modelling: Using data collected from literature searches and existing studies we will parameterise and program each of the three mathematical models to be able to provide the required outputs for each infection. We will then examine the model outputs for each partner management strategy (epidemiological treatment with testing - base case, partner treatment without testing, partner treatment after test results known, partner testing for index infection only). The most plausible estimates for each infection and strategy will be derived from iterative comparison and programming, which reveal sources of uncertainty and allow the robustness of inferences to be assessed. 3) Cost-effectiveness analysis: This will be from the health service perspective using current NICE recommendations for the discounting of future costs and outcomes. We will use model data for the numbers of infections averted, cases of infertility and HIV averted by adopting different partner testing strategies. As above, we plan to collect data on HRQL for female reproductive tract complications of chlamydia. We will apply the preference weights to health states in models to derive quality adjusted life years (QALYs).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: FiCTION - Filling Children's Teeth: Indicated Or Not?
Abstract: Dental decay is the most common disease of childhood, with a large health and economic impact. Although conventional clinical opinion is that carious primary (baby) teeth should be restored (filled), the majority of cavities in young children are unrestored. There is, as yet, no conclusive evidence for the most effective approach to managing decay in baby teeth. The results of this multi-centre randomised control clinical trial will provide evidence on the clinical and cost-effectiveness of three treatment approaches. Consenting children, attending for regular dental care, will be randomly assigned to one of the three treatment groups; with 'conventional fillings' (using dental drills and local anaesthetic injections to cut away decay, then filling the cavity), 'intermediate fillings' (sealing decay into teeth with filling materials, generally without using dental drills or injections), or 'no fillings'. They will then be reviewed yearly (and at any extra dental visits) for episodes of dental pain, and abscess formation. In addition, the impact of the disease, and its treatment, on their quality of life will be assessed. The follow up period is for 4 years in the first instance. Specific objectives are: 1. to compare the effectiveness, in terms of clinical and patient-centred outcomes, of three treatment approaches to the management of decay in primary teeth i.e. conventional fillings, intermediate treatment and no fillings. Specifically: (i) to compare the incidence of pain and sepsis that occur with the three treatment approaches; (ii) to compare the incidence and pattern of new decay in both primary and permanent teeth, quality of life issues, and the cost-effectiveness of the three treatment approaches; and 2. to examine patient, parent and dentist preferences for the three treatment approaches. The results of this study will have important implications for individual care for children with dental caries and, as dental caries is such a common disease, there will be implications for service management. In order to ensure the results are widely applicable, the study will be conducted in Primary Care, where most children's dentistry is carried out, and will run in practices which have varying local factors; inner-city London, the North of England, Wales and Scotland. The research will be led from the University of Dundee (in collaboration with others from the Universities of Cardiff, Glasgow, Leeds, London, Newcastle and Sheffield) but a strong multi-disciplinary research team has been established to work alongside a UK-wide team of specialist paediatric, and Primary Care dentists, ensuring that whilst the trial design and conduct is of the highest standard, it remains practical and pragmatic.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Seal or Varnish? A randomised trial to determine the relative cost and effectiveness of pit and fissure sealants and fluoride varnish in preventing dental decay
Abstract: Dental caries (tooth decay) remains a significant source of morbidity in children, particularly those from deprived backgrounds where levels of decay are three times higher than in better off areas. In the worst affected areas 69% of 12 year olds have decay in their permanent teeth. The majority of this (84%) is located on the biting surface of the first molars which erupt at age six. We know that the application of pit and fissure sealants to the biting surface is effective in preventing tooth decay. This treatment consists of a plastic coating that occludes the rough biting surface which harbour decay-causing bacteria. The application at six-monthly intervals of fluoride varnish, containing high levels of fluoride is also known to prevent decay. This works by strengthening the tooth enamel making it more decay resistant. What is not known is which of these two modes of treatment works best and which is the most cost-effective. It is also not know which of these treatments are most acceptable from the perspective of children and their parents. Fissure sealant application requires an involved dental intervention (use of rotary brush, tooth surface preparation to make the sealant stick, use of a sucker to keep the tooth dry). Varnish application simply involves painting the tooth surface. This trial will examine the relative clinical and cost effectiveness of these treatments and investigate their acceptability to children and their parents. The study will take the form of a randomised trial in which children will receive either fissure sealants on their first permanent molars or fluoride varnish. We will determine the success of the study, by comparing the proportion of children who receive the alternative treatments who are caries-free in their first molar teeth after three years. We will also look at the cost effectiveness and patient acceptability of the treatments. The findings from this study will be applicable across the NHS, particularly in areas of high need with greatest health inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Using evidence to reduce risk of healthcare acquired infection following primary hip replacement
Abstract: Aim: to assess the cost-effectiveness of competing strategies that reduce risk of infection following hip replacement in an NHS hospital? Design: Decision analytic cost-effectiveness model informed by existing evidence. Target population: Patients undergoing primary hip replacement in NHS hospitals. Setting: NHS acute and community care services. Methods: State transition Markov models will be developed and updated with data that describe relevant parameters. Systematic reviews will be undertaken and the results meta-analysed. Other sources of evidence, such as surgical registers, will be assessed for quality and used to update model parameters. Uncertainties will be assessed by (i) probabilistic interpretation of parameter uncertainty (ii) important sources of variability will be considered. A Bayesian approach will allow external prior information (e.g. expert opinion) to be incorporated into the analysis. Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) re-sampling will be undertaken from each parameter distribution, in the WinBugs environment. The result will be a joint distribution of cost and QALY outcomes. These points describe the joint uncertainty among model parameters. Net monetary benefits will be calculated and described and interpreted for the purpose of decision making. Expected output of research: A comprehensive policy for the management of infection risk among patients undergoing primary hip replacement in NHS hospitals. The policy will depend on the cost-effectiveness criterion. There will be intermediate outcomes as we progress toward this goal: estimates of the clinical effects of risk reducing interventions; estimates of the changes to economic cost outcomes; and, estimates of the changes to health benefits. We will identify the efficient level of investment in infection control programmes, and identify the best strategies to implement. If the decision is highly uncertain, we will estimate the value of perfect information to inform future research efforts

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Getting the benefit from electronic patient information that crosses organisational boundaries
Abstract: This is a study of the organisation and management of patient information sharing across and between organisations. The PCTs in this project are each involved in a variety of initiatives to share information with other organisations. These initiatives are broadly of two kinds. They are part of national initiatives, such as within NPfIT, where technological platforms are being created that enable electronic patient records to be shared by many organisations. They are also engaged in local initiatives (e.g. community nursing) and the tailoring of NPfIT subsystems in support of local needs. This is a theory driven, empirically based, action research. There are two aims: 1) An examination of the implications and possibilities of sharing of e-Health records across organisational boundaries for improved clinical care and the better management of healthcare; 2) To identify the factors in the design, implementation and subsequent evolution of these systems to facilitate inter-organisational uptake of the systems. The theoretical framework will combine concepts of organisational contingency with complexity theory to analyse emergent practices and behaviour commonly associated with e-systems. The organisational context for the research is primary care and the role of the Primary Care Trust. The study is based on a comparative case study of two PCTs in the Midlands (Northants and Walsall). These are both implementing and planning to introduce innovative e-health solutions and systems. Both can be characterised as being on the forefront of e-health developments within the NHS and developing solutions to cross-boundary sharing of patient information. The methodology is mixed-methods and longitudinal. It combines interviews with mapping usage data from computer logs alongside questionnaire survey and document analysis. As action research, it will engage project staff, management as well as patient and carer groups from an early stage. The objectives of the study are as follows: 1. To explore by longitudinal study the barriers/facilitators in the development of e-health systems and the outcomes achieved when they are used across organisational boundaries in two PCTs. 2. To explore, for each PCT, the differences between systems created as a result of national and local strategies to produce platform-independent electronic systems and those that are locally developed as a result of inter-organisational initiatives. 3. To examine whether an action research framework in which usage reports are provided every three months, alongside feedback sessions to managers and end users, can promote effective take-up by providing an evidence base of benefits and barriers. 4. To synthesise the results with other studies of inter-organisational healthcare systems and similar systems outside healthcare, in order to produce guidance on the development and evolution of successful systems.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: NHS Commissioning Practice and Health System Governance
Abstract: Few questions are more important to the NHS than how its commissioners can exercise governance over local health economies and service providers, and how much governance to exercise. A more strongly evidence-based programme theory of PCT commissioning would strengthen commissioners' managerial practice through a stronger understanding of how to select and apply different commissioning practices, how these modes of commissioning work and when to desist from attempting to (over-)manage providers of NHS services. The proposed study compares NHS modes of commissioning with selected examples of commissioning in the Netherlands and in the German health systems. This research therefore aims to explore which practices for commissioning health services are most effective for different contexts, producing evidence-based recommendations to improve NHS commissioning practice. It also aims to explore what NHS commissioners can learn from commissioning in two other European health systems and, should personal health budgets materialise, describe their implications for commissioning within the English NHS. To achieve these aims we will make a realistic evaluation, describing and comparing commissioning cycles across: (1) Three different care groups (acute, long-term, health promotion); (2) Four different PCTs in England; (3) Three health systems (England, Germany, Netherlands). For each of these settings we will describe the cycle of deciding service objectives, selecting health care providers, negotiating contracts (or the equivalent), monitoring compliance with the contracts, and obtaining any redress or adjustments necessary. By comparing these cases we will explore what implications the use of different health care 'technologies' has for commissioning, what implications the differences between PCT organisational structures and management practices have, and what the implications of different legal and regulatory systems, and units of payment, are.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Health and social care services for older adults in prison
Abstract: Prisoners aged 60 and over are the fastest-growing age group in the England and Wales prison system. It has been established that they have much more complex health and social needs than younger prisoners, and that these are often unmet. The cost of housing older prisoners has been estimated at six times that of younger prisoners. Despite this, there is no national strategy for the care and management of older prisoners, and few prisons provide any specialist services for their different needs. Transition in and out of prison is particularly difficult for older people, in particular the provision of relevant services for their increased health and social needs. This project aims to determine what health and social services are currently available for older prisoners; to explore the main issues of entering and leaving prison; and to design a new system of assessment and care planning for older people newly received into custody. Policy states that prison health services should be equivalent in scope and quality to those available in the community. However, social services departments rarely provide any input to prisons, meaning many older prisoners' mobility and functional needs are not addressed. We will establish, by questionnaire, current specialist service provision for older people at all prisons in England and Wales; examine the integration between health and social services in each; and, by qualitative interview, establish factors that promote and inhibit effective integration. Transitions between health services and other institutions are problematic for older people, and this is particularly true for older people entering prison. We will conduct qualitative interviews with approximately 70 people aged 60+ admitted at two prisons to explore the difficulties faced by this group, and what may improve their care. We will also review their clinical records to determine what contact they have with the various prison agencies and departments. There is currently no specialist assessment for older people on reception to prison, which means that many of their health and social needs are not routinely identified or addressed. We will facilitate an action learning group to design, implement and evaluate a new system of assessment and care planning in one prison, based on principles of the Single Assessment Process already established in the community. The needs of older people on discharge from prison have yet to be established. We will conduct qualitative interviews with around 60 prisoners immediately before release, and again in the community. These will cover what problems they expected upon release, and how these were dealt with in the community. All qualitative interviews will be examined using constant comparative methods of thematic analysis, while quantitative data will be reported using standard descriptive statistics. This project will build on the existing continuity of care literature both in prison and community environment. This group of older adults has specific and complex needs not currently addressed by existing service provision. The proposed research will directly improve the care of older people entering prison, and provide useful data on which to base future interventions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The effectiveness and cost effectiveness of telephone triage of patients requesting same day consultations in general practice: a cluster randomised controlled trial comparing nurse-led and GP-led management systems. - The ESTEEM trial
Abstract: A growing workload and increasing demands on UK primary health care suggest a need to explore news ways of providing care for patients. This study will investigate the effectiveness of telephone triage as one method of primary care provision. Many practices currently operate GP or nurse-led triage systems of different types as a way of providing fast access to care for patients and in order to manage practice workload, despite uncertainty about the benefits and costs. UK based trials of primary care telephone consultation and triage to date have been conducted in relatively small populations and/or in limited numbers of practice settings, and without the use of computerised interactive decision support. Moreover, there is currently little robust evidence of the effectiveness of telephone triage for patients requesting same day consultations in the context of in-hours general practice. This important agenda will be addressed in a large scale pragmatic cluster randomised controlled trial of two forms of triage currently being promoted by the NHS for use in UK Primary Care. The trial will compare the clinical and cost effectiveness of GP-led telephone triage versus nurse-led computer-supported telephone triage for patients requesting same day consultations in primary care. The principal outcomes assessed will be cost, primary care workload, patient safety, patient health status and patient experience of care. A nested process evaluation will examine the acceptability of the systems to patients and practice staff. The research will be conducted in 42 GP practices from Devon, Warwick, Bristol and Southampton, with individual practices randomly allocated to usual care, nurse-led triage or GP-led triage arms.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Optimal strategies for monitoring kidney disease in diabetes: properties of monitoring tests, progression of renal dysfunction and impact of treatment
Abstract: "People with diabetes have regular urine and blood tests for detection of early signs of kidney disease to guide treatment changes to prevent. However, there is no clear evidence about how often people should be tested and with what combination of tests. We will systematically review the literature and obtain the best available data to inform parameters for a computer model to identify optimal monitoring strategies. We will obtain individual patient data from large, long-term cohorts of patients with both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. We will review these data-sets in detail before deciding which will provide the best estimates of the within-person variation in tests, trends over time and variation by individual characteristics including age, gender, treatment and ethnicity. We will then combine these estimates, with the best available data from published evidence about other parameters, in a computer model to calculate the best strategies and the optimal intervals for testing. We will judge the outcomes of different ways of screening and monitoring by the extent to which a test accurately judges the need for a change in treatment (a ""true-positive"" test). Costs and estimates of the quality of life associated with these outcomes can be used to compare the overall costs and benefits of different ways of screening and monitoring. The study will provide data that will inform both the patient level decisions (for example
Status: too frequent testing may lead to a low true-positive rate where patients may be given unnecessary and potentially harmful treatment) and wider decisions about the optimal strategies to be incorporated into clinical guidance."

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: NHS Bristol, North Somerset and South Gloucestershire Integrated Care Board
Award_Title: The FAST (First-aid Advice & Safety Training) Parents programme for the prevention of recurrent unintentional home injuries in preschool children
Abstract: Design: (1) theoretical phase and development of the parenting programme (2) a multi-centre feasibility study of the programme using a cluster randomised controlled trial. The theoretical phase will include two systematic reviews: (i) a Cochrane review of parenting programmes to prevent injury undertaken by two co-applicants will be updated (ii) a new qualitative review of the barriers and facilitators to parent engagement in parenting programmes. Setting: Children’s Centres in Bristol and Nottingham Target population for feasibility study: (1) Children’s Centres: those ranked highest for the number of children aged 0-4 years in their catchment area who have attended the local Children’s A&E department during the previous year will be invited to participate (2) Parents/carers: of children aged under 5 years who have sustained an unintentional physical injury or ingestion in the home that resulted in seeking medical attention during the recruitment period Health technology: In depth discussions with Parenting UK, a national parenting programme development organisation, have established a collaboration to develop the parenting programme. The programme will combine first aid & safety training with components of existing programmes that have a theoretical likelihood of reducing child injury (e.g. enhancement of parental self-efficacy, communication, positive discipline), and will be age and development specific. Programme development will be informed by the systematic reviews, by a parent advisory group and by the experience of NHS and voluntary sector practitioners who deliver first aid training to parents. For planning, this First Aid and Safety Training for Parents (‘FAST Parents’) programme is speculated to be delivered weekly over 8 weeks. The feasibility study will be a multi-centre cluster randomised controlled trial with allocation at the level of Children's Centres (CCs). Eight CCs will be recruited from those with high numbers of preschool children having medically attended injuries, 4 CCs in Bristol and 4 CCs in Nottingham will be randomly allocated to one of two treatment arms using a remote automated system available through the Bristol Randomised Trials Collaboration: (1) Intervention: ‘normal care’ plus the FAST Parents programme (2) Control; ‘normal care’ only. ‘Normal care’ in both cities includes the options available to HVTs following routine notification of children with injuries, i.e. telephone contact, face-to-face contact, referral to services, or no action. Recruitment of parents will be prospective and use the existing routine process of the HVT being notified of children who have sustained an injury. In Bristol and Nottingham around 60-100 eligible children are notified to each CC area each year. We plan to recruit a minimum of 64 parents; 32 in each city with 16 in each treatment arm, i.e. 8 per CC area. A researcher will obtain consent, baseline and post intervention measures. The FAST Parents programme will be delivered by a Health Visitor supported by HVTs in each intervention CC and observed by a researcher. (continued)

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: INCLUSIVE trial: Initiating change locally in bullying and aggression through the school environment
Abstract: There is growing concern about the level of aggression and violence in UK schools. INCLUSIVE is a new multi-component intervention based upon international school environment interventions and restorative justice (RJ) approaches. This study is a pilot trial which aims to examine the feasibility and acceptability of the planning and delivery of the INCLUSIVE intervention and trial methods to inform a full-scale trial. The INCLUSIVE intervention consists of provision of an external expert facilitator, funding and a needs assessment survey. These enable schools to convene an action team and nominate staff to receive training. These in turn lead to and/or enable various outputs including 1) revised policies and school rules; 2) use of restorative justice approaches including circle time and restorative conferencing; and 3) revised peer mediation schemes to promote a safe school environment; as well as 4) a student curriculum. The intervention will also allow some tailoring of what outputs are delivered in each school, according to student need, informed by our survey. This balancing of standardisation and flexibility is common practice in school-environmental interventions. This study involves a total of 8 schools in south-east England, randomly distributed to intervention and control conditions. A total of 1,200 students aged 12/13 (approx. 600 per condition) will complete baseline surveys at the beginning of the school year and follow-up surveys approximately nine months later. In addition, school-level data and teacher surveys will contribute to the intervention evaluation. The primary outcome will be aggressive behaviour as measured by student self-report. Secondary outcome measures include teacher-reported classroom level aggression and violence, school exclusions and disciplinary proceedings related to aggression, student substance use, risky sexual behaviour, emotional well-being, quality of life and NHS use due to accidents and injuries. The study also includes a process evaluation examining intervention planning, delivery and receipt; assess feasibility, fidelity, coverage, acceptability and contextual influences; and explore intervention logic model and causal pathways. To this end interviews and focus-group discussions with intervention facilitators, action-team members, school staff and students. Additionally, a cost-benefit analysis will be conducted to examine the economic feasibility of the intervention. Data from this pilot will be used to plan a full cluster-randomised trial of the INCLUSIVE intervention.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: A randomised controlled trial of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and/or aspirin for colorectal adenoma (or polyp) prevention during colonoscopic surveillance in the NHS Bowel Cancer Screening Programme: The seAFOod polyp prevention trial
Abstract: Research design: A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2 x 2 factorial trial integrated into the screening and surveillance phases of the National Bowel Cancer Screening Programme (BCSP). Study population: BCSP patients stratified as 'high risk' (>/=5 small adenomas or >3 adenomas with at least one >10 mm in diameter) after adenoma clearance at screening colonoscopy. Exclusion criteria to include regular aspirin use, aspirin/fish hypersensitivity, peptic ulcer disease and colorectal resection. Planned interventions: Enteric-coated eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) free fatty acid 2 g daily po or placebo (medium-chain triglyceride Migyol 810™) AND enteric-coated aspirin 300 mg daily po or placebo, for 12 months until scheduled BCSP ‘high risk’ surveillance colonoscopy. Proposed outcome measures: Primary efficacy end-point; the number of patients with at least one adenoma detected at BCSP surveillance colonoscopy at 12 months. Secondary end-points; the number of patients with at least one ‘advanced’ (>10 mm diameter, high-grade dysplasia or villous component) adenoma; the total number of adenomas per patient; the number of patients re-classified as 'intermediate risk' (for subsequent three year BCSP surveillance colonoscopy); adverse events (AE) including clinically significant bleeding episodes; erythrocyte and mucosal PUFA incorporation; production of EPA- and aspirin-dependent eicosanoids including prostaglandin E3, 18R-HEPE and resolvin (Rv) E1; analysis of resected adenoma tissue. Assessment and follow up: Compliance and AE monitoring, as well as blood/tissue sampling, all integrated into the BCSP with only one extra visit at 6 months. Colonoscopy and polypectomy complications monitored by the BCSP. Colonoscopic outcomes post-intervention available via the BCSP database. Proposed sample size: 678 individuals randomised equally to the four treatment arms for 80% power, with 5% two-sided significance, to detect a minimum 18% relative reduction in adenoma recurrence (from 60% to 49%) in each two-arm comparison. This is less than the EPA effect observed in a familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) RCT and below the reduction in polyp number at one year (38%) in previous aspirin polyp prevention trials. Assuming 40% ineligibility (including 20% aspirin use) and a 15% drop-out rate, 1400 'high risk' individuals need to be identified at screening colonoscopy. Statistical analysis: ITT analysis using an ‘at the margins’ approach and direct estimation of relative risk by Poisson regression (with robust standard errors), including treatment arm as an explanatory variable. Predictive value of EPA and eicosanoid biomarkers for adenoma outcomes determined by multiple logistic regression with known clinical factors (eg. adenoma characteristics) as independent variables. Project timetable: 50 'high risk' patients will be identified in each of 15 BCSP Centres per year. Accrual to be completed in 2 years with full primary outcome data available 3 years from the start of randomisation. Six months set-up and six months for clinical and biomarker data analysis are integrated into the four year project.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: The medium-term sustainability of organisational innovations in the National Health Service
Abstract: The research consists of a follow-up study, building on a recently completed evaluation of organisational innovations in NHS genetics. This study will include further empirical research in a subsample of four of the case studies in the evaluation, each of which was initially successful in establishing itself following pilot funding. By conducting secondary analysis of the original dataset, and then revisiting these sites around 24 months after the completion of the original project, a rich, longitudinal dataset will be created, allowing nuanced understanding of what has helped and hindered medium-term sustainability of these services, accounting for differences of context, mechanism and outcome between the sites. The four sites are theoretically sampled according to key variables known from the literature to be important in determining initial sustainability, so that the four sites converge and differ in terms of these criteria, with points of commonality and divergence (Eisenhardt 1989). Key variables include sector of provision (primary v hospital care) and whether the innovation was locally designed or based on a national model (see project description for more detail on sampling). The overall setting of genetics services is chosen as typical of many areas of NHS provision that are relatively marginal in political terms, and thus which must rely on locally led change rather than top-down change initiatives. A literature review, and secondary analysis of data from the original evaluation, focusing on issues around sustainability, will inform fieldwork in each of the four sites, encompassing interviews, observation of meetings and document collection and analysis.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Research use and knowledge mobilisation in the commission and planning of public health services - what helps and hinders - a study in the co-creation of knowledge.
Abstract: Methods Five strands of work will address the RQs. Six in-depth case studies (43): i) In-depth qualitative interviews with those carrying out commissioning (JP) (managers, commissioners), as well key stakeholders to explore RU, challenges and perceived impact. Repeat interviews after milestones events (Circa: 60-70 per site – 180-210 in total). Observation of commissioning (JP) meetings. to explore RU (Circa: 8-10 meetings per site). Documentary analysis of commissioning (JP)documents e.g. minutes; commissioning (JP) agreements; job descriptions. ii) In-depth qualitative interviews with RU role holders (CKOs 44) role perceptions: barriers and facilitators; organisational support; changes. C.5-10 interviews per case – 30-60 in total. Analysis: Longitudinal thematic analysis and narrative analysis (45). iii) RU – impact on organisational performance: Routinely collected datasets laid alongside case study findings: (RU and performance measures: e.g. DoH PCT WCC assurance process; public service agreements (PSA): RU and ‘better commissioning decisions’: e.g. QoF; patient reported outcomes (PROMS), etc. (NB: In Scotland corresponding measures will be collected). Analysis: Descriptive statistics using SPSS. iv) National survey: of RU role holders to explore the applicability and transferability of the emerging findings across the UK. v) An interactive national workshop: to both disseminate and road-test substantive findings and discuss transferability.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The clinical and cost effectiveness of diversion and aftercare programmes for offenders using class A drugs - a systematic review and economic model
Abstract: This study aims to assess the clinical and cost effectiveness of diversion and after care programmes for offenders using class A drugs. Two systematic reviews will be undertaken (1) assessing the usefulness of diversion and aftercare programmes for offenders using Class A drugs and (2) assessing the economic impact of these programmes. The reviews will use a combination of search terms relating to offenders, substance abuse, aftercare, interventions and diversion. The systematic reviews will be performed and appropriate studies selected. A summary will be provided explaining in detail the findings from each of the included studies. This will include descriptions of the interventions being evaluated, target populations, outcomes and results. Data will be extracted from the studies followed by data analysis. Data from different studies will be pooled if appropriate for a larger meta-analysis. The main findings will be summarised, including the strength of evidence for each outcome and any potential limitations (including biased reporting). It is anticipated that there will be insufficient data from existing published literature to complete a full economic model, examining the cost effectiveness of diversion programmes. This study will therefore in addition to the findings from the systematic review, utilise anonomysed case linked data from the National Drug Treatment Monitoring System, Drug Treatment Outcomes Research Study, Drug Data Warehouse and Medical Research Council Addiction Cluster to assess the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of diversion and aftercare programmes for criminal offenders using Class A drugs. This part of the study will also identify pathways through and within the treatment, after care and criminal justice systems and the relationship between staying in treatment, relapse and outcome in terms of self-reported and recorded offending. The study will then establish an economic model to combine clinical and economic data from the systematic reviews and datasets. The economic model will establish the resource use and costs of diversion and after care. To check that the model is valid and relevant, researchers will consult with relevant experts in offender health research, offenders who use drugs, drug treatment and after care services, forensic mental health and service users to ensure it is an accurate representation of practice. The economic model will be used to separately estimate the cost effectiveness of diversion and after care.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A randomised trial of nicotine patch preloading for smoking cessation
Abstract: Background: Standard smoking cessation support advises smokers not to use nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) whilst still smoking before their quit day. However this could be beneficial for a number of reasons. For example, it may decondition the link between smoking and associated environmental cues, it may familiarise smokers with NRT so they use it most effectively post-quit, and/or it may cause aversion, and therefore may make smoking less desirable. Evidence for the beneficial effect of nicotine preloading has proved inconclusive. Design/Methods: We will conduct a multi-centre, pragmatic, randomised controlled trial of four week nicotine patch treatment pre-quit day, alongside standard NHS stop smoking service (SSS), versus standard NHS SSS support without pre-quit patch. Participants will be recruited through GP practices and through an existing smoking cessation clinic. Support will be in the form of one-to-one clinic visits, and the standard support will be provided by the NHS. Outcomes/Follow-up: Follow-ups will take place 1 week, 4 weeks, 6 months and 12 months after each participant’s quit day. The primary outcome will be six month validated prolonged abstinence. Additional abstinence outcomes will be 4 week and 12 month prolonged abstinence, and point prevalence 4 week, 6 month and 12 month abstinence. Markers of potential mediators, such as changes in carbon monoxide and cigarettes per day, aversion, dependence, smoking reward, urges to smoke, confidence in quitting and motivation to change will also be measured. A health economic analysis will be carried out.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Evaluating Long-term Outcomes of NHS Stop Smoking Services (ELONS)
Abstract: Design: Observational study including: 1. Secondary analysis of routine data collected by SSSs using the North51 database 2. Prospective study of service clients from 9 PCTs Follow up at 4 weeks & 12 months. Gold standard NHS SSS client satisfaction questionnaire. Setting: NHS SSSs in England Target population: Smokers who make contact with NHS SSSs Health technologies: Treatment provided by SSSs – a combination of behavioural support and medication. We will focus on evaluating outcomes for smokers who receive one of the 5 main forms of behavioural support (intervention types) provided. These are: closed groups, rolling groups, one to one drop in, one to one appointments with a specialist adviser, one to one appointments with a sessional adviser (usually a pharmacist or practice nurse). Measurement of costs and outcomes: Primary outcome is prolonged abstinence at 12 months. We will also assess abstinence at 4 weeks. Measurement will follow the Russell Standard (intention to treat and biochemically validated). We will measure uptake by assessing what proportion of their smoking population SSSs reach and we will explore the reasons for and timing of relapse amongst smokers who do not remain abstinent. We will also assess client satisfaction with NHS stop smoking services. Sample size: Secondary analysis: All smokers who set a quit date with an SSS who uses the North 51 database during the period Jan-Dec 2010. Prospective study: 3000 smokers using NHS stop smoking services in 9 PCTs, with representation from each intervention type. Project timetable: Start October 1st 2011. Secondary analysis October 2011-February 2012. Four week follow-up May 2012-February 2013. Client satisfaction survey May 2012-February 2013. Satisfaction survey and short term follow up analysis June - September 2013. Twelve month follow-up April 2013 - February 2014. Analysis, write-up, dissemination to services Febraury - September 2014.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Responsiveness of primary care services: development of a patient-report measure
Abstract: Stage 1: A literature review will be undertaken focusing on indicators of responsiveness and the measurement of responsiveness. We will interview a diverse sample of up to 50 patients and up to 20 providers in 12 primary care organisations to explore the variety of needs and preferences of patients, and of the way practices have been successful or obstructive to getting these needs met. Interview data will be analysed using a thematic framework, and feedback on findings gained from patients, service providers, and patient participation groups. We will develop an approach to sampling users, which will enable access to the views of diverse groups. Stage 2: We will develop an instrument to measure primary care service responsiveness based on the findings of stage 1, and investigate different approaches to administering the instrument to optimise accessibility. The instrument will undergo two rounds of piloting, each involving 150 patients in three organisations, to check acceptability, face validity, comprehensibility, and feasibility of use. Cognitive interview techniques and will be used to identify problems with questions; face validity and acceptability will be assessed through patient interviews and by inspecting completion rates and distribution of responses to questions. Stage 3: To assess the reliability, validity, acceptability to patients, and feasibility of use of the instrument, a large scale pilot will be undertaken involving up to 3000 users in 20 primary care organisations. Test-retest reliability will be assessed by administering the instrument again to a random sample of 200 responders after 2 weeks. Construct validity will be assessed by comparing results from the instrument with external indicators including adherence to agreed standards on responsiveness (NHS Primary Care Contracting 2009). Feedback will be gained from service providers about the feasibility of using the instrument with the local population, and the value of the data to them.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Predictive risk stratification: impact on care for people with or at risk of chronic conditions
Abstract: New approaches to the management of chronic conditions are needed in order to shift the balance of care from the acute to primary and community sectors and improve services locally. The Welsh Assembly Government (WAG) has commissioned the development of a predictive risk stratification model (PRISM) for Wales to stratify people into one of four risk strata based on having an emergency admission in the following year. PRISM has the capacity to tailor care at individual patient level to patient need. Questions remain however about how the model will be adopted by potential users at each risk strata. The aim of the proposed study is to describe the processes of introducing PRISM in Wales and to estimate the effects on the delivery of care both to patients living with or at risk of developing a chronic condition, and to those with no perceived risk. A mixed-method ‘before, during and after’ quasi-experimental cohort study will be conducted with Intervention sites and Control sites. Changes following the implementation of PRISM and its acceptability will be measured within the Intervention and Control sites. The Client Service Receipt Inventory questionnaires and routine data from the PRISM dataset will be used to compare services delivered to patients both before and after implementation. Costs of system implementation and of changes in processes of care delivery will be assessed. Focus groups and semi-structured interviews with service providers, commissioners and policy makers will explore the individual and organisational processes of change and judge how well PRISM works in supporting better patient care and service planning. The acceptability to patients of the predictive risk stratification approach will be assessed using the Quality of Care Monitor. SF-12 data will be collected at each time point in order to inform the design of a subsequent study to evaluate the effect of implementing PRISM on patient outcomes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Contracting with General Dental Services
Abstract: A multi-method, multi-stage design is proposed, integrating qualitative and quantitative methods. Phase 1 of the study is a scoping phase which includes a literature review and interviews with key informants which together will define tracer issues to be examined in Phase 2. Phase 2 involves case studies of 3 types of dental practice (fully NHS; part NHS/part private; and fully private) and medical practices in the same PCT. Case studies will involve interviews, documentary analysis, and non-participant observation of contract negotiations and reviews. Emerging themes will be tested using a questionnaire to a wider number of GDPs and telephone interviews with PCT commissioners (Phase 3). This will broaden the empirical base of our work and build a more generalisable picture. A purposive sample of 6 PCTs within North West England will be undertaken, based on pilot data collected previously in questionnaires to GDPs where their perceived relationship with the PCT was explored. Three PCTs will be chosen where relationships were very good or good and 3 where 3 where relationships were poor or very poor. In each PCT, 3 dental practices and 1 medical practice will be studied in Phase 2, (i.e. a total of 24 case studies will be undertaken). Case studies will be undertaken longitudinally (over 12 months) to capture the lived, experience and personal knowledge of GDPs, GMPs and dental commissioners, using qualitative tools focusing on language and dialogue collected over a period of time. Qualitative data will be analysed using a constant comparison method to generate codes and themes. In Phase 3 questionnaires will be sent to all GDPs in the 6 PCTs involved in the case studies and also in a further 8 PCTs randomly selected from a list of the l52 PCTs in England. Telephone interviews will be undertaken with commissioners in all 14 of these PCTs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Integration and continuity of primary care: polyclinics and alternatives
Abstract: Research design: Multiple nested case studies with systematic cross-sectional comparison between sites. As study sites we will sample one instance of each type of governance structure listed under 'Background' in the detailed research proposal (theoretically-informed sampling). In each site we will make a nested case study describing the linkages between the clinical practices and the governance structures involved in coordinating services for patients needing services from multiple organisations. In each site data collection and analysis will start by describing the coordination (or not) of services at clinical practice level and the factors reported to aid or impede coordination. Working 'upwards' and 'outwards' from clinical practice, a wider case study will then trace and describe how the organisational or other contextual causes produce these facilitating or constraining factors. The process will then be repeated, connecting the organisational level to its local health system context. The sequence will in each study site produce three nested case studies, together describing the interactions between: (1) the clinical care level; (2) provider organisation or 'service' level; and (3) health system level (interactions between whole organisations). In this way we propose to expose more precisely than in previous studies the links mediating governance structures and clinical practice. Findings for each site will then be systematically compared across study sites by applying across them all a standard analytic framework. This will expose similarities and differences between sites, i.e. between governance structures, in the relationships between governance structures and the coordination of complex care, and enable us to make theoretical generalisations from the findings. As a tracer group we select frail elderly people since they make heavy use of complex (multi-provider) care. Data will be collected by interviews of patients, professionals and other key informants; content analysis of policy and management documents; and re-analysis of secondary data.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Equity of access to cardiac and mental health services in England.
Abstract: The project focuses on the ecological analysis of quantitative data drawn from a variety of sources including, crucially, small area estimation data derived from the modelling of the clinical needs of organisationally- and geographically-defined populations. The analysis will cover the whole of England and the primary units of analysis will be the General Practice and the Middle Layer Output Area (MSOA). Following an initial period of systematic review and synthesis of clinical guideline and health care literature – resulting in the formalisation of our ‘pathways to care’ conceptual framework and the definition of detailed modelling and analytical objectives – the project comprises two substantive phases of research. The first focuses on the production of condition-specific estimates of clinical need for all practices and MSOAs in England. This rests on a) the use of data drawn from major epidemiological surveys (principally the Health Survey for England and recent Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys), to construct, using a Bayesian approach, multilevel models which describe the risk that different types of person living in different areas will experience particular cardiac or metal health conditions, and b) the application of the resulting model parameters to microsimulated estimates of the socio-demographic characteristics all individuals in practice and MSOA populations in order to derive local probabilistic estimates of the burden of health care needs in those populations. Having generated need estimates which capture both expressed and unexpressed need at practice and MSOA level, the second substantive phase of research concerns relating those estimates to the subsequent utilisation of health services by those populations. This will draw, in particular, on Quality Outcome Framework (QOF) data on primary care activity, Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) data on Inpatient and Outpatient activity, and ‘prescribing analyses and cost’ (PACT) data on prescribing activity. Additional mental health data will be drawn from the Mental Health Minimum Dataset (MHMDS) and ‘Improving Access to Psychological Therapies’ (IAPT) data with respect to the treatment of people suffering from depression and anxiety disorders. The goal here is to establish a sound evidential basis upon which to test whether the various use:need ratios vary significantly at practice, PCT, MSOA or LA level and, if so, to model the extent to which inequalities in the uptake of service can be explained with reference to systematic demand- or supply-side factors. Dissemination plans include the a) delivery of estimate 'toolkits' & the underlying methodology via the Public Health Observatory website, b) journal & conference papers to academic and practitioner audiences, and c) a proactive exploration in the south west of how local estimates of cardiac and mental illness can be used to inform local public health and commissioning processes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: Intensive Care National Audit & Research Centre
Award_Title: Ensuring comparisons of health-care providers are fair: risk modelling for quality improvement in the critically ill.
Abstract: Objective 1. To improve current risk prediction models for critically ill patients Detailed statistical analysis plans will be developed, with input from the Expert Group (see: Team Expertise), to address each of the specific points detailed above (or other aspects of modelling identified as important by the Expert Group). Model improvements will be assessed both visually (e.g. by calibration plots) and using a panel of measures of model performance to encompass discrimination (c index or area under the ROC curve), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test), and overall fit (Brier's score, Shapiro's Q, R-squared) using bootstrap methods to adjust these measures for overfitting to the data. Objective 2. To develop new risk prediction models for critically ill patients Learning from Objective 1 of the project will feed into the methods used for development of new models. Clinicians in the relevant fields will be consulted for their input into the design of the risk prediction models. Models will be developed to maximise predictive performance while considering ease of use. Objective 3. Immediate translation of research results into practice Risk models developed through this project will immediately be implemented into the routine comparative reporting for both the CMP and NCAA. Results will be presented at the Annual Meetings for both the CMP and NCAA for participating units/hospitals, supported by regular data collection training for both audits, and to academic and policy audiences throught the joint Health Services Research Network/NIHR SDO Programme meetings. Enthusiasm suggests that new audits will be established, on a cost-recovery basis, for new areas (e.g. cardiothoracic critical care). Timeline: Jan 2011-Dec 2011 - Objective 1 (Expert group meetings- Mar 2011, Sep 2011) Jan 2012-Oct 2012 - Objective 2 (Expert group meetings- Mar 2012, Sep 2012) Apr 2012 - Objective 3: Presentation of results of Objective 1 at the Annual Meeting of the CMP Nov 2012-Dec 2012 - Objective 3: Completion of final report and wider dissemination of results

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Implications for the NHS of inward and outward Medical Tourism
Abstract: *Stream 1 (Economic) estimates the economic impact of medical tourism to the NHS from four elements of trade flow:(i) inward flows of foreign nationals seeking NHS care (ii) inward flows for private care, but with follow-on/complications picked up by the NHS (iii) outward flows of patients who then return with complications which are picked up by NHS (iv) outward flows of patients who then provide system benefits (e.g. relieving pressure for NHS treatments). Primary data collection entails survey and interviews with 6 key groups in the UK and one overseas: a) Patients who have sought and experienced care overseas, encompassing good and bad experiences. We have already a cohort of UK Indian residents who have provided information for a current project, and will supplement this with 4 other groups. Semi-structured interviews collect a mix of quantitative and qualitative information. It would be desirable to do a similar survey of those foreign nationals seeking care within the UK. b) Health providers and purchasers, to identify the indicative magnitude and key issues surrounding follow-up care to those who have undertaken medical tourism from the UK, and to those foreign nationals who have experienced care within the UK. Again, a small cohort London has contributed to a current project, and we would seek to re-interview them and expand the network to cover other areas (again, a mix of quantitative and qualitative data). c) Foreign health providers to UK patients. Professor Smith has good relationships with institutions in India and Thailand, both of whom experience UK patient inflows of 100,000 annually. These institutions collect basic data on patients treated and will allow use of aggregated data for this project. In addition, interviews with key members of these institutions will highlight foreign care provider perspectives of UK medical tourism (inward but also outward). Secondary data analysis provides information on the number of patient movements, inward and outward, and any associated economic flows. * Streams 2 & 3 (Decision-making and Quality): draw on data from the patient interviews (5 UK-based groups) outlined in Stream 1. (Streams 1, 2 & 3 share data sources). * Stream 4 (Industry): data from professionals and industry stakeholders: 15 professionals (BAPRAS, BDA, BMA, Picker); 15 from Medical Tourism industry (marketers, brokers, insurers, providers). * CASE STUDIES: data contributes towards 5 depth industry case studies of inward and outward flows (from across dental, elective, cosmetic and IVF). Each case includes: 10 patient interviews to illuminate decision-making and treatment experiences; website/ analysis; and interview data from industry and clinical interests.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Facilitating knowledge exchange between health care sectors, organisations and professions: studying ‘boundary spanning’ processes and their impact on health care quality
Abstract: We will use an in-depth longitudinal, case study approach. Our case study is a project designed to improve services through collaboration between general practitioners, community services, voluntary groups and acute specialists over an 18 month period in the Southall area of London. The project includes the development of a network of leaders across organisational and community boundaries to facilitate knowledge creation and exchange, and is directly linked with a programme of ‘whole system’ stakeholder conferences to create organisational learning and change, together with community development. Fieldwork will be undertaken in the three specific topic areas in which boundary spanning activities will be undertaken as part of the case study: (a) Dementia, (b) Child & Family Health, and (c) Depression & anxiety in people from black and ethnic minority backgrounds. In seeking to test our research hypothesis we will: provide a rich ethnographic account of the boundary spanning processes (horizontal and vertical) that occur within each of the three topic areas throughout the duration of the overall project (by means of non-participant observation, 360 degree interviews centred on individuals in the boundary spanning groups, participant (boundary spanning individual) diaries, and ongoing review of project documentation); monitor a range of routine datasets and quality indicators pertaining to the three topic areas across the whole PCT, making comparisons between the 26 general practices in Southall and practices from the remainder of the PCT; undertake a 'before and after' Knowledge, Attitudes and Practice questionnaire survey of a stratified, random sample of named staff in (a) each of the 26 general practices in Southall, (b) practices elsewhere in NHS Ealing, and (c) practices in neighbouring PCTs in West London; and conduct 'before and after' focus groups with patients & carers in each of the three topic areas as to their experiences of care and treatment .

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Oxfordshire & Buckinghamshire Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A randomised controlled cluster trial comparing the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of a school-based cognitive–behaviour therapy programme (FRIENDS) in the reduction of anxiety and improvement in mood in children aged 9/10
Abstract: DESIGN: Randomised controlled cluster trial comparing FRIENDS (delivered by health professional or school) vs. treatment as usual for the reduction and prevention of anxiety symptoms and low mood (i.e. reduced symptoms of depression) in children aged 9/10. SETTING: 45-54 junior schools in Bath and North East Somerset and Wiltshire. INTERVENTION BEING EVALUATED: FRIENDS is a manualised cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) programme designed to improve children's mental health. Each child has a workbook and group leaders a comprehensive manual detailing the content and structure of each session. FRIENDS involves 10, 60-minute weekly sessions delivered to whole classes as part of the school PSHE programme. FRIENDS teaches children practical skills to identify their feelings; to learn to relax; to identify unhelpful thoughts and to replace them with more helpful thoughts; and how to face and overcome their problems and challenges. Initial training and regular supervision of leaders will be provided by a specialist CBT expert. An additional session for parents/carers is provided at the start of FRIENDS to provide an overview of the programme, the CBT rationale and the skills the children will be taught. Parents will receive a sheet at the end of each session summarising what the children have discussed and the ideas they will be practicing each week so that they can reinforce and encourage their use at home. MEASUREMENT OF OUTCOMES AND DURATION OF FOLLOW-UP: (a). Psychological functioning: The primary outcomes will be reduced levels of anxiety and improved mood (i.e. reduced symptoms of depression) as assessed on continuous measures at 6 & 12 months. Secondary outcomes are improved self-esteem, and reductions in bullying. Assessments at 3 different times: • Time 1, baseline; • Time 2, post FRIENDS (6 months); • Time 3, 12 month. Parents will complete a behavioural screening questionnaire at all 3 time points. (b). Acceptability: Children will rate FRIENDS on 10 dimensions e.g. enjoyment, acquisition and use of new skills, etc. (c). Delivery: Leaders will assess FRIENDS on factors such as child engagement, school support, etc. (d). Treatment fidelity will be assessed by observing a random selection of 10% of FRIENDS sessions and assessing whether learning points and exercises were covered. (e). Parent Interviews at baseline and 6 months: For the economic evaluation, a purposeful sample of carers/parents of 300 children, 100 from each condition, will complete the Client Receipt of Services Questionnaire about their child’s use of health, social and educational services. Qualitative interviews with 20 parents from the FRIENDS group to assess how and why the intervention might benefit children e.g. changes in friendships; family relationships; educational progress and engagement in out of school social and recreational activity. (f). Cost and cost-effectiveness: an analysis comparing the two versions of FRIENDS vs. treatment as usual. The cost-effectiveness analysis will be based on the primary outcome measures. Both the cost analysis and the cost-effectiveness analysis will be from the joint perspective of the health (NHS) and education/social services sector. The research will identify, measure and value the resource consequences of each alternative (applying opportunity cost as the main principle for valuation. PLANNED ANALYSIS: Analysis and presentation of data will be in accordance with CONSORT guidelines. The primary comparative analyses will be on an intention-to-treat (ITT) basis with due emphasis placed on confidence intervals for the between-arm comparisons. Descriptive student- and class-level statistics will be used to ascertain any marked imbalance between the arms at baseline. The primary analysis will employ a mixed effect linear regression model to compare the active CBT interventions versus treatment as usual, adjusting for stratification variables and baseline score, and taking appropriate account of the hierarchical nature of the data (repeated measures, students, classes and schools). Sensitivity analyses making different assumptions will be conducted to investigate the potential effects of missing data. Secondary analyses will include: 1) repeating the primary analysis adjusting for any variables exhibiting marked imbalance at baseline to examine whether this influences the findings; 2) comparison of children who score high and low on anxiety and mood questionnaires at baseline to examine who most benefits form these interventions; 3) similar analyses for other secondary outcomes (using appropriate multi-level models and adjusting p-values for multiple testing); 4) investigation of process measures such as number of sessions attended. PROJECT TIMETABLE: Mth 1-2: Recruitment, establish project infra-structure. Mth 3-6: School recruitment; recruit FRIENDS leaders. Mth 7-8; Randomisation; prepare assessments. Mth 9; Training; consent. Mth 10-12: Baseline assessments; deliver interventions. Mth 13-15: data entry, cleaning and checking. Mth 16-18: Baseline analysis & 6 month assessments. Mth 19-21: 6 month data entry, cleaning and checking. Mth 22-24: analysis and 12 month follow-up. Mth 25-27: 12 month data entry, cleaning and checking. Mth 28-30: analysis. Mth 31-36: Project write up and dissemination. RECRUITMENT RATES: Local pilot work in 30 junior schools indicates that less than 1% of children opt out of FRIENDS and that approximately 90% complete baseline and follow-up assessments. Conservatively, we predict 90% of the eligible population will participate and of these 80% will complete follow-ups.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Does the Royal Horticultural Society Campaign for School Gardening increase intake of fruit and vegetables in children?
Abstract: This study will undertake two linked randomised controlled trials. 1) Schools in the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Campaign for School Gardening will be randomised to receive an intensive or less intensive gardening intervention. 2) Schools not originally part of the RHS Campaign will be randomised to receive the less intensive gardening intervention or no intervention (comparison group). The RHS Campaign for School Gardening promotes school gardening and growing of fruit and vegetables. The Campaign provides resources to help teachers set up and make the most of their school garden, teach the National Curriculum outdoors and inspire their pupils to live healthier lifestyles. There are two levels of intervention: more intensive involving hands on support from a regional advisor (10 schools per region) “partner schools” and less intensive “associate schools” where schools can undertake twilight training and receive support from schools involved in the intensive intervention arm. The RHS plan to deliver their Campaign to schools in the London region starting in the spring of 2010. In study 1, we will select 26 schools who have undertaken the RHS benchmarking scheme and have indicated their interest to be involved with the Campaign. We will randomly allocate 10 schools to receive the intensive intervention and 16 schools to receive the less intensive intervention. It will not be possible to randomise schools to receive no intervention at all since the RHS is committed to providing support to all schools who register an interest in the Scheme. Due to this, we will recruit a second set of schools into a linked trial. We will contact the remaining schools in the region who have not signed up to the RHS Campaign. We anticipate that this will be about 400 schools in London and we aim to recruit 32 schools. Of these schools, 16 will be randomly allocated to sign up to the RHS Campaign and to receive the less intensive intervention and 16 schools will act as comparison schools. All schools will have baseline measures taken and then followed for 2 years and outcomes measured. Children included in the study will be at key stage 2 (ages 7-10) in years 3 and 4 at baseline. The key outcome to be assessed will be change in fruit and vegetable consumption. Secondary outcomes relate to the effect of the intervention on other food intake and nutrient intake. The RHS Campaign will be evaluated over two growing seasons. We plan to measure baseline food and nutrient intakes using a previously validated tool (CADET) prior to involvement in the scheme and then again after two years, allowing for two growing seasons. The project will allow us to determine whether support for gardening in schools can affect fruit and vegetable intake in primary school children.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: The effects of schools and school-environment interventions on health: evidence mapping and syntheses
Abstract: Methods The review will involve 3 stages: 1) a descriptive map of available evidence, plus a preliminary synthesis of intervention logic models and theories of school-level effects on health; 2) in-depth reviews and syntheses of evidence addressing our research questions; and 3) drafting of final report and other dissemination. Target population and setting Students, staff, parents and/or the local community of schools catering for those aged 4-18. Intervention being evaluated School environment (SE) interventions aiming to change the physical, social or cultural environment within schools to promote health. Search strategy In stage 1, we will include studies pertinent to our research questions: (RQ1) literature describing/explaining the theories and conceptual frameworks that are used to inform SE interventions or explain school-level influences on health; (RQ2) evaluation studies reporting on SE intervention effects on health, as well as cost, economic and econometric studies examining the costs of SE interventions; (RQ3) process evaluations of SE interventions; (RQ4) multi-level and ecological (school) studies of school-level influences on health; and (RQ5) qualitative studies exploring the processes by which school-level factors might influence health. We will search bibliographic databases and specialist registers; hand-search relevant websites and approximately five selected journals; consult with key education and child/adolescent health researchers; track citations and check reference lists of found reports; and incorporate found keywords into revised searches.
