Award_Title: Environmentally Sustainable Health Services: Scoping Review
Abstract: RESEARCH DESIGN The scoping review would combine a literature and policy review with a structured stakeholder consultation involving qualitative interviews and a prioritisation exercise based on the Delphi method. CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK Conceptual frameworks for sustainable development recognise three interdependent elements - economic development, social development and environmental protection - referred to as the triple bottom line. The proposed scoping review would focus on the environmental element of sustainability, but would also explicitly and actively make the connection with the economic element by asking how a focus on environmental sustainability can be aligned with solutions to the productivity challenge facing the NHS. RESEARCH METHODS, TIMEPLAN & OUTPUTS STAGE 1: Literature and policy review (Jan-Feb 2011) Academic literature on the environmental sustainability of health services will be identified by searching bibliographic databases covering health and environmental research; seeking recommendations from experts in the field; and using citation indices. We will draw on the experience of our Information and Library Services team in developing the search strategy. Academic literature will be supplemented with grey literature taken from the websites of key organisations. The literature review will include a review of the business and management literature, to explore how other sectors are aligning sustainability and productivity. Relevant policy documents will also be reviewed in order to identify the key policies and levers driving sustainable practices within the NHS, and the research needs arising from these. Studies of all methodological types will be included in the review, but brief editorial pieces will be excluded. A qualitative data extraction framework will be developed and used to summarise the content of each article in terms of what is known about developing sustainable health services, what is not known, and what research needs are indicated. STAGE 2: Qualitative interviews (Mar-Apr 2011) Interviews will be conducted with approximately 15 representatives of key stakeholder groups including organisations active in the field of sustainable health care at the level of policy, research and practice (including voluntary sector organisations and sustainability consultants currently working with the NHS and other large organisations); members of the NHS management community; clinicians; and patient groups. The interviews will build on stage one by testing the research needs emerging from the literature and policy review, and will explore stakeholders' perceptions of (1) how the delivery of health services will need to change in the transition to a sustainable society and (2) what research is needed to underpin this. The interviews will be analysed qualitatively using a thematic coding technique, with the aid of analytical software (NVivo). STAGE 3: Delphi exercise (May-Jun 2011) The research needs identified in the first two stages will be prioritised by means of an online Delphi exercise. Participants in the Delphi exercise will include interviewees from stage two plus additional experts identified during the research. We would aim to recruit around 30 participants for this exercise, but would accept greater numbers if available. The Delphi method is a systematic means of consulting expert opinion which allows a consensus position to be built iteratively without being imposed by more powerful or influential groups. The process will involve participants completing a series of short online questionnaires in approximately 3 rounds. In each round, participants will rank and provide comments on the suggested research areas, as well as adding any further research gaps. Scores and anonymised comments are then fed back to participants before repeating the exercise in the next round. As the rounds progress, participants tend to converge towards a consensus position. If convergence does not occur, this will be reported and discussed in our report to the SDO. STAGE 4: Synthesis, writing up & dissemination (Jul 2011) In producing the final report we will synthesise material from all 3 stages of data collection. The report will include: • An overview of existing knowledge and research on developing environmentally sustainable health services (primarily based on the literature review) • A prioritised list of areas in which further research is needed (from the Delphi exercise) • Expanded detail on priority research areas (based on interview data and literature review) • An analysis of the connections between the sustainability and productivity agendas (based on interview data and literature review) In addition to the report to the SDO, we would publish a King’s Fund report and hold a conference or seminar to support dissemination (see ‘contribution to collective research effort’ section).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: How can frontline expertise and new models of care best contribute to safely reducing avoidable acute admissions?
Abstract: The design comprises a case-study design of four acute admission sites, using primarily qualitative and additional quantitative methods, in two periods of data collection, with a mid project stakeholders conference and learning sets between these phases. The study incorporates: - Ethnographic qualitative methods (observation, interview and documentation analysis) - Up to 6 mini case studies of patient journeys in each of the four case sites - Quantitative analysis of key processes of care using an adapted Value Stream Mapping (VSM) approach. - An embedded study of cost. - A parallel learning set to encourage exchange of ideas and learning across sites The mixed methods design incorporates a sequential process. Qualitative research will map out the issues. Then quantitative methods will assess the extent to which key processes occur and how costs compare. In addition, data will be summarised into predictor outcome matrices to identify key mechanisms for reducing avoidable admissions. Table one (in detailed project description) relates data type to research question. The research is underpinned by two complementary theory driven frameworks. Realistic Evaluation (Pawson and Tilley, 1997; Anderson 2008) will be used to determine key processes of change within a system, how these relate to outcomes, resource use, cost and context. ‘Theories of Change’ (Weiss et al, 1996), will be used to develop theories about how interventions achieve their aims. Our approach uses ethnographic methods within a subtle realist framework (Hammersley, 2002). Following piloting, data collection will take place as follows: 1. System-level cases Setting and sample: The organisational case study design comprises a comparative analysis of four South West acute admission sites, three with innovative ways of providing experienced clinician input early in the pathway, and one traditional model. Systematic comparison of sites is shown in Table 2 Data collection: To describe decision making roles and input, and to identify ways in which organisational pathways, spaces and resources affect decision making: 1) Formal Interviews (6-8 per organisation) with key informants (RQ 1,3 & 4); Interviews will explore experience of acute care settings and decision making processes. 2) Participant observation of organisational processes, team make up and function (RQ1,3,4). 3) Documentary analysis of financial and business planning, governance, and implementation of process change (RQ1,3,4,) 4) Data on costs and admissions; staffing costs (RQ3). Phase two data collection will follow a similar pattern but focus on testing the provisional theories developed in phase one. 2. Mini case studies - the patient journey Setting and sample: Detailed study of 6-10 patient journeys per site will permit comparison of decision making, patient level clinical and patient pathway variation. Individual patient cases will be selected from ED and AA settings on the basis of being potentially avoidable (Table 3). Data collection in phase one: 1) Participant observation of acute admissions location (RQ1, RQ2). 2) Individual interviews with up to10 patients, practitioners and family members at key points (RQ1, RQ3). 3) Analysis of medical and nursing records. 4) Quality of admissions decisions will be analysed using peer-review and consensus by external/internal clinicians modeled on the National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) methodology. 3. Measuring key processes of care: Value stream mapping To quantify differences in acute admissions processes between the four participating NHS trusts, and estimate the extent these occur across the NHS, we will map patient pathways for predetermined core common tracer symptoms studied in 2 above using value stream mapping - structured diagrams documenting the steps and activities in the care process, a lean management method for improving patient flow and pathway efficiency across departmental boundaries (Graban 2009, Ng et al 2009). For each site a minimum of 30 patients’ movements will be mapped, recording timing, place, type, length and seniority of professional contacts. 4. An embedded health economic study Comparison of resource use and cost implications between the four sites for the core conditions and pathways will be defined mainly through the Value Stream Maps of the sampled patient journeys, using data on staffing costs and resource allocation to patients with potentially avoidable admissions, and the feasibility of estimating the opportunity cost of these resources. Resource implications of the hypothesised key mechanisms driving the outcomes of the different models of care will be explored, and a generic modelling framework developed (RQ4). 5. A parallel learning set to encourage exchange of ideas across sites and learning from clinicians and managers will be set up at each site. Interaction and systems changes will be encouraged between sessions. The learning sets will be based on action learning methodology to promote self-awareness, critical enquiry, ideas generation, active reflection and solution finding.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Do higher primary care practice performance scores predict lower rates of emergency admissions for persons with serious mental illness? An analysis of secondary panel data
Abstract: Design and theoretical/conceptual framework: Effective primary care can have an important preventive role, and should therefore be associated with lower emergency admission rates. Quality indicators for mental health have been routinely measured in English primary care over a number of years as part of the Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF). Our null hypothesis is that there is no association between QOF performance and emergency hospital admissions for people with mental illness either for mental or physical conditions. We will test for an association between changes in practices’ mental health QOF indicators and changes in their rates of emergency admission using data on all practices in England over the period 2004/05 to 2009/10. Our analysis will also estimate the impact of potential improvements in the QOF on subsequent mental health expenditure on secondary care. Sampling: We will construct a national dataset covering around 8000 English GP practices by drawing together routinely available secondary data. To examine the impact of the QOF on hospital expenditure, we will merge this national dataset with the costs of all 1.2 million patients who use specialist psychiatric hospital or community care in a given year. Our analysis will therefore be representative and produce generalisable results. Setting/context: We will use Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) data on emergency admissions for mental health patients from general practices for both physical and mental conditions over the period 2001/02 to 2009/10 in England. QOF data is available from 2004/05 to 2009/10. We will merge a number of data sources at practice level to create a panel which will provide statistical power and precision to the econometric analysis. To examine the relationship between the QOF and subsequent mental health expenditure we will use individual level cost data in the Mental Health Minimum Dataset (MHMDS) which has been derived from Reference Costs and is available for 2007/08 and 2008/09 covering care by specialist psychiatric teams in hospital or in the community. Data collection: We will use the following data: QOF Indicators: The Quality Management Analysis System (QMAS) provides QOF achievement and prevalence data at practice level. Some QOF indicators have remained constant, others have been modified, dropped or introduced. This represents a ‘natural experiment’ that allows variations in admissions between practices to be investigated. Covariates: Local population characteristics: Neighbourhood Statistics (ONS) socio-economic and demographic data will be attributed to GP practices using the Attribution Data Set which contains information on the number of patients in each practice resident in each Lower Super Output Area. The socio-economic data are very rich and include measures of deprivation, education, morbidity, ethnicity, rurality and small area characteristics. GP Practice variables: General Medical Statistics (GMS) data on GP and practice characteristics, and MHMDS data which will be aggregated to practice level. Mental Health Services Mapping Data will be used to construct supply variables. Hospital variables: hospital characteristics and quality indicators. Data analysis: We will estimate both cross-sectional and panel data models for the period 2004/05 to 2009/10 to examine the association between QOF and admissions over time. Examining the within practice temporal variation will remove the risk of unobserved factors which might affect both practice emergency admissions and quality. We will estimate both random and fixed effects multiple regression and count data models. All models will include year indicators to allow for temporal trends, and a rich set of relevant local population and practice covariates [1]. Random effects panel data models will include the average admissions for a practice over the period 2001/02 to 2003/04. This pre-sample ‘baseline’ will pick up unobserved practice and patient confounding characteristics which are time-invariant [2]. We will also include lags of QOF to allow for delayed effects of quality. We will carry out a variety of robustness checks. For ease of presentation the scores for all variables will be reported as incidence rate ratios (IRR). Our models for examining the association between QOF and subsequent hospital costs will include both OLS cross-sectional and random and fixed effects panel data models where we control for practice fixed effects and year dummies. We will regress costs in 2007/08 and 2008/09 on QOF scores from 2004/05 up to 2008/09. Given the positive skewness of costs we will also estimate transformed OLS and generalised linear models (GLM). We will use two-part models to test if better quality scores have an effect on average patients by reducing the probability of admission and/or by reducing costs once admitted. Possible lagged quality effects on costs will be captured by modelling ‘baseline’ quality from 2004/05 to 2006/07 on patient expenditure in 2007/08 and 2008/09. [1] Dusheiko M, Doran T, Gravelle H, Fullwood C, Roland M. Does higher quality of diabetes management in family practice reduce unplanned hospital admissions? Health Services Research 2011; 46:27-46. [2] Blundell R, Griffith R, Windmeijer F. Individual Effects and Dynamics in Count Data Models. Journal of Econometrics 2002; 108:113-31.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of community based services for older people: a secondary analysis to inform service delivery.
Abstract: CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK: Our conceptual framework aligns closely with a modified Donabedian framework proposed by Lilford et al (2010), which, examines the relationships between structures, processes and outcomes, but which separates the processes into three further subcategories: clinical processes, (involving the actual treatment, such as the processes of the rehabilitation, medication); targeted processes (designed to improve clinical processes through training in the use of a device); and generic processes (such as skill mix or staffing models adopted by an organisation). SAMPLING: This secondary analysis draws on two established datasets that includes approximately 7900 patients admitted to older peoples' intermediate care services in England. SETTING / CONTEXT: The setting for the research is older peoples' community based intermediate care services. DATA COLLECTION: This project involves the merging and re-analysis of two datasets which have collected prospective data from 33 community based older peoples' teams (SDO 08/1519/95; SDO 08/1819/214; Projects 1 and 2) between 2006 and March 2011. The datasets include comparable, detailed descriptive, longitudinal data about each team; staff and patients. The first dataset is complete (Project 1), and includes data from 1913 patients and 325 staff from 20 teams between 2006 and 2008. The second dataset (Project 2) will be complete in March 2011. It already has 5800 complete patient records from 13 teams and based on current return rates, we expect this to exceed 6000 by 1st March 2011, resulting in a total database of over 7900 patients and approximately 800 staff, forming the largest dataset of IC in the UK. Each dataset includes detailed information about the team, the patients and the staff. More detail about each of the outcome measures is provided in Appendix 1. DATA ANALYSES: These are described in detail in the full proposal attached. However our study involves multivariate analysis, specifically multilevel mixed-effects linear regression or multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression in which patients are treated as clusters within team. The comparative cost effectiveness of each model of care (Q7) will be derived using the team level staffing data from the service proforma to develop a cost of each service, which will be compared against the Quality Adjusted Life Year (QALY) gains adjusted for patient dependency at admission (33). This approach replicates the economic analyses used in Project 1 (7). We will utilise costing data from the NHS and Social Service perspective which is recommended by the National Institute for Clinical Excellence for its technology appraisals (34). Preliminary analyses will be descriptive in nature. Mean resource use, costs and QALYs per patient will be reported for each team. Following this, multivariate analyses will be undertaken to examine the relationship between skills mix and costs. ost-effectiveness involves the simultaneous examination of costs and outcomes. A separate set of analyses will be undertaken to look at this issue. Firstly, mean costs and QALYs gained will be plotted for each team on the cost-effectiveness plane to highlight which teams are the most cost-effective. Secondly, the correlation of skills-mix variables with average cost-effectiveness ratios will be estimated. Finally, the simple multivariate analyses examining skills mix, costs and outcomes, will be extended to include the impact of workforce cohesion on the costs and outcomes for services and users. The additional explanatory variables will include staff autonomy, integration, quality and team working. These will be measured by the mean team scores on these domains, and will be treated as having fixed effects within the models. For all regression analyses, the team characteristics are incorporated within the multivariate analysis using a random effects model in STATA. To address Objective 3 we will analyse descriptive longitudinal data from 8 teams taken at 3 time points to assess trends over time in relation to team size, skill mix, team management and service context. The data will be merged in Microsoft Excel for ease of comparison of numeric and string data. All 45 variables will be examined across the three time points for each team to examine trends or changes. We will then compare (qualitatively) the changes that have taken place across all teams. For instance, we will explore variations in the numbers of referrals to the teams; changes in the host organisation; alterations to the number and types of staff employed; and changes to management structure. The output of this work package will be a longitudinal description of IC since 2005. A previous, similar study by Martin et al (35) provides a useful basis for comparison to earlier studies and framework for reporting. Objective 4 will be addressed through a synthesis of the findings from questions 1 - 7, and further analysis in consultation with the literature. The results of the above research will be used to develop a service tool kit, which will provide vital evidence based guidance for both commissioners and providers of intermediate care on: how best to configure services and staff; in what conditions a referral to IC is most appropriate; the best treatment models for specific patient groups; and, how best to measure IC services to allow meaningful comparison of process and outcomes data. We will consult with our partners and stakeholder groups to determine the best way of presenting and disseminating these data. The toolkit will include normative data around each of the research questions (including service structure, staffing models, the characteristics of patients admitted to IC, and the patient and service characteristics associated with specific outcomes), which services can use as a basis for comparison and benchmarking.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Assessing the effectiveness of support for breastfeeding mothers: updating the Cochrane review - Additional work
Abstract: The aim of this study is to update the existing Cochrane review on support for breastfeeding women. This updating will: - Integrate the more recent UK and international data related to breastfeeding interventions - Strengthen the evidence related to specific components of interventions (those that work as well as those that do not) - Provide new evidence from international studies to allow for the exploration of effectiveness of interventions in sub-groups such as low income, young, white women, and minority ethnic groups where rates of exclusive breastfeeding are low. It will also support exploration of the differentiation of the evidence for impact on duration of any breastfeeding and exclusive breastfeeding, and allow the opportunity to explore issues of generalisability in different settings - Provide the clinical and public health evidence to inform the development of an economic model - The review will be modified to address key issues. In particular, we will: - Remove all studies of sick mothers and infants to ensure the review focuses on healthy mothers and infants only. - Add a new analysis to examine the way in which the support is provided, ie whether it is pro-active (offered to women) or reactive (expects women to request it). The design is based on the current Cochrane review, updated to follow the revised Cochrane handbook methods. The search strategy has already been conducted using the methods of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group. 34 studies are currently included in the review; all of these need to be re-appraised for risk of bias, in line with Cochrane's updated methodology. Previously excluded studies (n=14) will need to be reassessed for the same reason. We have identified 31 new studies that need to be assessed and if eligible for inclusion, added to the existing studies.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The cost-effectiveness of testing strategies for type 2 diabetes
Abstract: The overall aim is to compare the cost effectiveness of fasting plasma glucose (FPG) and glycated haemoglobin (HbA1c) in testing for diabetes in people as part of the NHS Health Check Programme. This will include evaluation of the impact of using risk stratification tools and random blood glucose (RBG) measurement to determine which individuals should have further tests. A secondary aim will be to assess the relative values of these tests in detecting individuals at high risk of developing both diabetes and vascular disease in the future. We will review the evidence on the sensitivity, specificity and FPG, HbA1c and RPG for detecting undiagnosed diabetes based on published literature and analysis of data from screened populations cohorts. We will then model the outcomes of screening using alternative tests, taking account of uptake rates. Uptake is an important consideration because some HbA1c tests can be done at any time whereas FPG tests can only be done after someone has not eaten for eight hours. We will also review the evidence on the relative effectiveness of FPG and HbA1c for estimating vascular disease risk. Since cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the main cause of mortality in people with type 2 diabetes, vascular risk is likely to be an important determinant of cost-effectiveness. We will develop a refined economic model based on existing models used to inform previous reports on cost-effectiveness of screening for type 2 diabetes and prevention of diabetes. This model will be used to compare the lifetime cost-effectiveness of screening FPG versus HbA1c-based screening strategies incorporating evidence on diagnostic performance of the tests.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Determining the Impact of Smoking Point of Sale Legislation Among Youth (DISPLAY) Study
Abstract: Aim: The aim of the study is to assess the impact of the TPMS (Scotland) Act 2010 (that bans of point of sale (POS) advertising) on young people’s exposure to tobacco advertising, their attitudes towards smoking and their smoking behaviour. Design & Setting: We propose a before and after study of four communities with data collection at baseline before implementation of legislation in April 2013 and longitudinal follow-up for four years. Data collected in early 2015 will also provide baseline data to assess the impact of full implementation in all retail outlets. Community is defined as the catchment areas of schools selected for study. Schools will be purposively selected to reflect two levels of urbanisation (urban vs. small town) and two levels of social deprivation (high vs. medium, low). There are four main components to the study. In each community there will be: 1. An annual mapping study of tobacco retail outlets: Data for all outlets selling tobacco in each of the study communities will be extracted annually from the Register of Tobacco Retailers established under the Tobacco and Primary Medical Services (Scotland) Act. In Geographical Information Systems (GIS), the geo-coded outlet data will be combined with data from the marketing audit study (see below) and then analysed to provide an assessment of changes in tobacco vending and advertising over the study period. Further, tobacco retailing exposure measures will be constructed for each of the study participants at each time point. 2. An annual tobacco advertising and marketing audit of: i) A Panel of tobacco retailers (overt): A panel of 7 retailers per community will be recruited to monitor point of sale displays and related marketing activity. Data collected will include: visibility/placement of tobacco products; external and internal promotions; variety of/most prominent brands and pack sizes available; visibility of pricing information and price of key brands: tobacco control signage. Photographs of the interior will be taken and depth interviews will be conducted with retail managers/owners. ii) Tobacco retail outlets most used by young people (covert): All outlets identified in the mapping exercise will be visited by interviewers trained in covert observation. Data will be collected using an abbreviated version of the form used with the retailer panel. There will be additional data collection for both i) and ii), in May 2013 to assess compliance in supermarkets, and in May 2015 to assess compliance in all retail outlets 3. An annual school survey: This will have repeat cross-sectional design, in two phases. In phase 1 (2013-14), data will be collected from a sample of S2 and S4 pupils to explore the impact of partial implementation in supermarkets alone on awareness and attitudes. In phase 2 (2015-17), the survey will be repeated with a whole school sample (S1-S6), which will be of sufficient size to explore the impact of a complete ban in all retail outlets on both intermediate outcomes and longer term smoking behaviour outcomes. 4. Annual Focus groups: These will be conducted with school survey participants, purposively selected to include young people who are most at risk of becoming adult smokers. The topic guide will cover: local smoking behaviours and cultures; access to tobacco products including direct, indirect/proxy and black-market; awareness of and views on tobacco promotion including point of sale, other direct marketing methods, packaging, branding; awareness and perceptions of the impact of the legislation; views about preventing youth smoking. Outcomes: Using available evidence we have developed a logic model, which classifies outcomes according to the time-frame within which we expect them to occur. Short-term outcomes (within 6 months) include: Prevalence and density of POS advertising in tobacco retail outlets (mapping and audit studies). Intermediate outcomes (within 1 year) include: Awareness of point of sale advertising; Cigarette brand awareness; Perceived ease of access to cigarettes; Attempts to purchase cigarettes; Perceived youth smoking prevalence; Pro-tobacco attitudes (from the school surveys). Long-term outcomes (within 3 years) include: Incidence and prevalence of smoking (from the school surveys). Qualitative data will be collected via focus group interviews. Additionally the study will assess any unintended or adverse consequences associated with the legislation including: increase in purchases from black market sources or proxy purchases; and introduction of new strategies by retailers or tobacco industry to circumvent the regulations. Planned Analyses: Data from study components 1 to 3 will be integrated into 1 dataset. The primary analyses around implementation in supermarkets will focus on estimating the change in POS advertising between baseline (T0) and T1b and its relationship with intermediate attitudinal outcomes. In addition to the above, the primary analyses around implementation in small shops will also examine the impact of full implementation on behavioural outcomes. Specifically, we will: i) Examine change in exposure to tobacco advertising, access to tobacco products and attitudes towards smoking between T2 (baseline) and T3a-c for total sample – with sub-group analyses; ii) Examine change in incidence of regular smoking and smoking prevalence between baseline at T2 and T3b and T3c ; and iii) Assess if there is a of a dose-response relationship between changes in POS advertising or changes in availability of cigarettes and other study outcomes. Qualitative data will provide contextual data within which to interpret quantitative data and enable us to understand the mechanisms by which the legislation works. Using GIS we will develop methods of depicting data from across the study components using spacial analytical techniques. Figure 1 in attached pdf provides an overview of the study design, flow of study participants and timetable, together with a logic model, power calculation and project milestones.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Outreach programmes for health improvement of traveller communities: A pluralistic synthesis of evidence
Abstract: Methods: There are several systematic reviewing synthesis options, i.e., meta-analysis, narrative synthesis or realist synthesis. In order to guarantee that maximum utility can be made of the available evidence, we propose a dual track of evidence synthesis. Such methodological pluralism will enable maximum learning to be achieved, regardless of the type and diversity of the evidence accessed. Target populations and settings: Gypsies, Roma Gypsies, Roma, Scottish, Welsh, Irish and New Travellers, Boat Travellers, Showpeople, Circus people. Location: for the narrative synthesis, which looks at studies from a descriptive synthesis level, including studies from non-European settings might fail to add clarity to the issues of effectiveness and cost effectiveness. If this is the case the data retrieved could be reported separately the realist synthesis strand will examine the underlying principles of outreach, wherever they are applied. Intervention being evaluated: Outreach (interventions which take place beyond usual limits of the delivering organisation) aimed at Traveller Communities; Outreach interventions with an explicit health improvement aim; one to one or group interventions, as long as it involves at least one person going to places where Traveller Communities live at least once. Search strategy: Searches will be made by two reviewers for existing relevant systematic reviews using Cochrane, Campbell, CRD/DARE and EPI-Centre databases, in addition to searches for primary studies. Our initial scoping review suggests that the formal literature base (i.e. from peer-reviewed journals) on outreach programmes for Traveller Communities is relatively small. However, there does appear to be a substantial amount of ‘grey’ literature on this subject and therefore we will access as much of this as possible using a variety of search strategies, including: Searches of electronic databases, open access resources, specific websites, reference lists of relevant studies, Science Citation Index, and Social Science Citation Index; additional information from authors. Review process: The review strategy will use a dual track of evidence synthesis, using in parallel either a meta-analysis with analysis of cost effectiveness or (in negotiation with commissioners), a narrative synthesis with analysis of likely cost effectiveness, with a realist synthesis. Expected output of research: The research design features iterative consultations with the commissioners so that formative outputs are produced, as well as a final report. In addition, dissemination though conferences, academic and professional journals will be undertaken. Project timetables: 06/11 - 9/11: Primary literature search and consultation with commissioners and steering group members. 10/11 - 04/13: Dual track evidence synthesis. Expert hearings will be organised to inform the realist synthesis track at regular intervals, as dictated by the emerging evidence. There will be a minimum of two expert hearings in the course of the analytical phase. 04/13 - 07/13: Reporting Steering group meetings will be held approximately six monthly, to coincide with key research phases.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Evaluating the efficacy of the Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies (PATHS) curriculum in promoting social and emotional wellbeing among children in primary school: a cluster randomised controlled trial
Abstract: DESIGN: Cluster randomized controlled trial SETTING: Primary schools in England TARGET POPULATION: Children in primary school aged 7-11 INTERVENTION: Promoting Alternative Thinking Strategies (PATHS) (see section C) HYPOTHESES: (1) Children in primary schools implementing PATHS over a two-year period will demonstrate significant improvements in social and emotional competence (1a), health-related quality of life (1b), exclusions (reduction) (1c), attendance (1d) and academic attainment (1e), when compared to those attending control schools. (2) The effects outlined in H1 will be sustained at two-year post-intervention follow-up. (3) Children in primary schools implementing PATHS over a two-year period will demonstrate significantly better psychosocial adjustment upon transfer to secondary school, when compared to those attending control schools. (4) Quality of implementation will be associated with improved outcomes in school implementing PATHS. (5) Proximal changes in social and emotional competence and the learning environment will be associated with distal improvements in motivation to learn, psychological wellbeing and (reduced) internalising and externalising difficulties, which in turn will impact upon attendance, academic attainment and exclusions. (6) The PATHS intervention will demonstrate cost-effectiveness. PRIMARY OUTCOME MEASURE*: Social and emotional competence - the Social Skills Improvement System (SSIS)/Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) (50,51) SECONDARY OUTCOME MEASURES*: Health-related quality of life - the Kidscreen-27 (KS27) (55); attendance (% half-days of unauthorized absence), and attainment (end of Key Stage 2 Points Scores for Maths and English)** - school data; psychosocial adjustment to secondary school (KS27 school environment, peers/social support, and psychological wellbeing subscales) CONTROL/BACKGROUND MEASURES: At cluster level, we will survey schools' usual practice (e.g. involvement and implementation status for related initiatives, such as Social and Emotional Aspects of Learning, Targeted Mental Health in Schools, Circle Time, Nurture Groups) plus their salient characteristics (e.g. size, urbanicity, OFSTED ratings), and collect data on PATHS implementation processes (e.g. fidelity, dosage). At participant level, school data on sex, age, ethnicity, free school meal eligibility (FSM) and special educational needs (SEN) (primary need and stage of provision) will be sought. SAMPLE SIZE: Based upon previous evaluations of PATHS and a recent meta-analysis of SEL interventions (16), an effect size of at least d=0.2 is anticipated for the primary outcome measure. With Power = 0.8, Alpha = 0.05(60), taking into account an average of N=75 per cluster (school) (3 classes x 25 pupils per class) and an estimated ICC of no more than 0.05 (57,58), 50 clusters are needed (25 in each arm of the trial). This yields a total sample of 75 x 50, N = 3,750 (see SD1 CONSORT diagram) ANALYSIS: Hierarchical linear modelling (HLM)*** to evaluate the efficacy of the intervention on the primary and secondary outcome measures (H1a-e, H2, H3) and to investigate impact on health inequalities for key sub-groups; path analysis to evaluate the association between fidelity to treatment model and outcomes (H4), and the underlying SEL change theory (H5); cost-effectiveness analysis to determine the ratio of implementation costs relative to the improvements in measured outcomes, and indicative cost-benefit analysis to determine the ratio of implementation costs to monetary savings caused by reductions in exclusions and increases in attendance and attainment (H6). TIMESCALE: Start Jan 2012, End March 2017 (63 months). LEAD-IN PHASE (01-08/2012). Key tasks to include recruitment of project staff, formation of funders' network and public advisory group (see section G), development and piloting of online survey system for outcome measures, recruitment of schools (and initial PATHS training for staff), ethical approval and random allocation procedure. MAIN TRIAL PHASE (09/2012- 08/2014). Schools randomly allocated to the treatment arm of the trial will implement PATHS with support and technical assistance from the implementation team (see section C), with children in three classes (Years 3, 4, and 5). Schools in the control arm of the trial to continue usual practice. At the beginning (Time 1 - 09/2012), mid-point (Time 2 - 09/2013) and end (Time 3 - 07/2014) of this period, the research team will administer our primary and secondary outcome measures. Control/background measures will be taken at Times 1 and 3. We will visit each intervention school on a half-termly basis and conduct structured observations of sessions and interviews with key stakeholders to develop a rich picture of the intervention process. FOLLOW-UP PHASE (09/2014 - 08/2016). We will follow-up and continue to take outcome measures for the children from the main trial (N=1,250) who have transferred to secondary school. This will follow the same pattern established in the main trial, with measures at the beginning (T3), mid-point (T4) and end (T5) of the phase. WRITING-UP/DISSEMINATION PHASE (09/2016 - 03/2017). We will complete all analyses, prepare and submit journal articles, and disseminate our findings at academic and practitioner conferences. *To maximise validity, we will use multi-informant (child, teacher and/or parent, as appropriate) sources for the SSIS, SDQ and KS27. **Measure applies to sub-sample of participants (N=1,250) who transfer to secondary school at the end of the main trial. ***HLM also allows analysis of differential impact by gender, ethnicity, FSM, and SEN (health inequalities).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A cluster randomised controlled trial evaluation and cost-effectiveness analysis of the Roots of Empathy schools-based programme for improving social and emotional wellbeing outcomes among 8-9 year olds in Northern Ireland
Abstract: DESIGN: Cluster randomised controlled trial. SETTING: Primary schools in the Belfast Health and Social Care (HSC) Trust, South Eastern HSC Trust, Southern HSC Trust and Western HSC Trust areas in Northern Ireland. TARGET POPULATION: All primary schools (in the four HSC Trust areas) not already implementing the Roots of Empathy (ROE) programme will be eligible to take part, with the exception of Special Schools and schools with less than 10 children in Year 5 (aged 8-9 years). All children who are entering Year 5 in 2011/12 in eligible schools at baseline will be eligible to participate in the trial. RANDOM ALLOCATION: 70 schools will be recruited for the trial (20 in Belfast HSC Trust; 20 in South Eastern HSC Trust; 30 in Southern and Western HSC Trusts combined) and will be randomly assigned to either the intervention (n=35) or control group (n=35). Where there are parallel classes, one Year 5 class will be randomly selected within each school. The intervention group will receive the ROE programme in their selected Year 5 class for one academic year (2011/12). The control group will not receive the ROE programme but will continue with usual classroom activity. The control group will be placed on a waiting list to receive the programme the following year, but on the understanding that it is not delivered to their current Year 5 cohort as they progress through Years 6 and 7. INTERVENTION: The ROE programme is a universal, classroom-based social and emotional competence promotion programme for primary age pupils. It is a 27 lesson programme that runs for one school year and is based around a monthly classroom visit by an infant and parent whom the class 'adopts' at the start of the school year. During these monthly visits children learn about the baby’s growth and development via interactions and observations with the baby. Each month a trained ROE instructor, who is not the class teacher, visits the classroom 3 times for: a pre-family visit; the visit of the parent and infant; and a post-family visit. Each ROE lesson provides opportunities to discuss and learn about the different dimensions of empathy, namely: emotion identification and explanation; perspective-taking; and emotional sensitivity. The parent-infant visit thus serves as a springboard for these discussions about understanding feelings and infant development and effective parenting practices. The total cost to implement the programme in 35 schools (including start up and in-kind costs) is approx. £105,000. These costs for 2011/12 will be underwritten by the NI Public Health Agency (see accompanying letter). CHILD OUTCOMES: PRIMARY: 1) increased prosocial behaviour; 2) reduced behavioural difficulties. SECONDARY: 3) increased understanding of infant crying; 4) increased ability to recognise emotions; 5) increased empathy; 6) increased ability to regulate emotions; 7) improved educational outcomes; and 8) improved quality of life. DATA COLLECTION: Parental and pupil consent will be sought prior to participation in the trial. Pupils in both the intervention and control groups will be tested on the outcome measures at baseline (pre-test), at the end of the intervention and then annually for the next three years, using the same measures, and until children are at the end of their first year in secondary school. Data will also be collected on programme delivery and fidelity across all 35 intervention schools as well as data on activities undertaken across the 35 control schools. In addition, qualitative case studies will be conducted in 6 schools to track the experiences and perspectives of the children, parents and teachers and to study the actual implementation of the programme. SAMPLE SIZE: Existing meta-analyses suggest typical effect sizes for programmes like ROE of a magnitude in the range of d=.22 to .57. Children's behaviour (Outcomes 5 and 6 above) represent the primary outcomes for this trial. Typical ICCs for the behavioural measure to be used (SDQ) have been found typically to range from .05 to .15. With the inclusion of pre-test covariates, it is reasonable to assume that the multilevel models to be used in the analysis will account for at least 20% of the variation in post-test outcome scores. With these assumptions, it is estimated that a total sample size of 1,260 children will be required to detect the lower bound anticipated effect size (.22) with 85% power (for ICC=.05) and 60% power (for ICC=.15). The average class size for the schools in the proposed trial is estimated to be 33. With an anticipated recruitment rate of 75% and an 8% attrition rate per year, this will result in a final sample at the final data sweep of 18 children per school on average. With 70 classes in the trial, this meets the total sample size of 1,260 children. ANALYSIS: Baseline characteristics will be summarised by school and described by group allocation. The difference in outcomes will be described at each follow up point. Data will be analysed by intention to treat using multilevel modelling with pupils (level 1) clustered within classrooms/schools (level 3). As there is only one classroom per school then it is not possible to distinguish the effects of classrooms and schools. The introduction of interaction effects into the models will enable the exploration of potential subgroup effects by gender and socio-economic status. An economic evaluation in the form of a cost-effectiveness analysis will be undertaken alongside the trial. The costs and outcomes of ROE and usual education will be compared to assess the cost-effectiveness of ROE in preventing cases of aggressive behaviour and increasing prosocial behaviour among school aged children. A broad societal perspective will be adopted capturing resource use data related to each child’s contact with the National Health Service, Personal Social Services, educational services and judicial service directly as a result of their aggressive behaviour. Additional data on out-of-pocket costs incurred by the child’s family because of the child’s antisocial behaviour will also be collected. Uncertainty surrounding the estimate will be summarised in a cost effectiveness acceptability curve. PROJECT TIMETABLE: Project set up (Aug 11); Pretests (Sep 11); Intervention implementation (Oct 11 - Jun 12); Qualitative case studies (Oct 11 - Jun 12); Post tests (Jun 12); Analysis and write up of trial and case study data (Jul - Nov 12); Submission of first interim report of findings (Dec 12); 12 mth follow-up (Jun 13); second interim report (Sep 13); 24 mth follow-up (Jun 14); third interim report (Sep 14); 36 month follow-up (Jun 2015); final analysis and write up (Jul - Dec 2015); Final report (Dec 2015).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The effectiveness and cost effectiveness of the Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management programme in primary school children: a cluster randomised controlled trial, with parallel economic and process evaluations
Abstract: Design: A cluster randomised controlled trial with recruitment staggered over three years. The unit of randomisation is the school, and randomisation will be stratified to ensure balance on the following school characteristics: level of deprivation; rural/urban location; involvement in other emotional enrichment programmes. One teacher per school will participate. Setting: 80 primary schools in Devon, Torbay and Plymouth. Target population: Primary school age children from Reception and Years 1-4 in the class of the one teacher per school recruited to the trial. Teachers with mixed year groups, fewer than 15 children in their class, or in the classroom fewer than four days per week will be excluded. Intervention being evaluated: The IY TCM course; a manualised six-day course delivered to groups of up to 10 teachers. Control teachers will receive the intervention in the following academic year, which is a prerequisite for schools agreeing to participate. Schools will be randomised to intervention (TCM training) or control (teaching as usual). Measurement of outcome and duration of follow up: The primary outcome will be the children’s socio-emotional well-being assessed using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ; 22) completed by teachers and parents. The SDQ is a well-validated and widely used measure of behaviour, emotions, pro-social behaviour, peer relationships, and hyperactivity. The secondary outcome will be children’s academic attainment using teachers’ routine assessment of national curriculum levels (23), checked against the Wechsler Individual Achievement Test in a sub-sample (24). For economic evaluation, parent-completed Child and Adolescent Service Use Schedule (25, 26, 27) will report the use of health, education and social services, plus criminal justice sector resources. Responses will be supplemented by interview with a sub-sample of parents and reports from school about education-based services. Structured direct observation of teacher-child interaction using the Teacher Pupil Outcome Tool among a sub-sample of children will assess if TCM changes teachers behaviour (28). Teachers will also complete the Sense of Efficacy Scale (29), Maslach Burnout Inventory (30) and Everyday Feeling Questionnaire (31) to assess the impact on their well-being and efficacy. Our Feasibility Studies include the completed validation of a child-completed measure to assess how happy they feel about their school (32) and the planned validation of the EQ-5D-Y (33; a youth version of the EuroQol measure recommended for 7-19 year olds) among 4-7 year olds, as well as delivering four TCM courses. As illustrated in Appendix 2, we plan to recruit 15 schools in the pilot phase and 65 schools over the two subsequent years. The pilot phase will use the same methodology as the main phase, but will test acceptability of the study for parents, teachers and children, recruitment and data collection procedures, and provide qualitative information to improve recruitment and retention in the main phase. Progression from pilot phase to main phase will depend on being able to recruit at least 14 schools, achieving a 66% response rate among parents and retaining 80% of teachers and parents at first follow up (T1). Data collection for both groups will occur at the beginning (October, T0) and end (June, T1) of the academic year of recruitment, and TCM training will be delivered to the intervention group between these data collection points (See Appendix 3). Further follow up will occur annually in the spring term in the following two academic years (T2 and T3). The teachers and children will separate at the end of the first academic year (between T1 and T2), allowing the control teachers to access TCM without breaking the trial design in relation to the child well-being measures. A parallel process evaluation will use qualitative methods to build on work from the Feasibility Studies. In the pilot phase the process evaluation will seek to refine the research processes, and in the main phase it will investigate factors that influence the uptake of TCM strategies. We will use semi-structured interviews and focus groups with teachers, SENCos and head teachers to elucidate the experiences and perceptions of the TCM course. This will provide a multi-dimensional assessment of how TCM was implemented and received, identifying barriers and facilitators to TCM across participating schools. We will also examine access to other sources of support for teachers, and whether other teachers working in study schools but not selected to attend the TCM course, take up TCM strategies in the classroom. Sample size: 40 schools will be randomised to each of the intervention and control arms; the number of children per arm at final follow-up is expected to be 760 per arm (i.e. 19 per school) assuming that: each class contains 30 pupils; a recruitment rate of 71% was achieved among parents in a current trial using the SDQ (34) and a 10% loss to follow-up by T3. The sample size allows for clustering assuming an intra-cluster correlation coefficient for the SDQ total score to be 0.15, estimated using data from Sayal et al 2009 (35). This provides 85% power at the 5% level of significance to detect a difference in the mean SDQ score between trial arms equivalent to an effect size of 0.3 of a standard deviation or to a difference of 2 points on the SDQ scale. A two-point reduction would reduce the percentage of children classified in the borderline/abnormal range from 20% to 14% where borderline /abnormal is defined as those scoring 12 and above out of 40 on the SDQ scale (36). Planned analyses: Random effects linear regression models will be fitted to compare means for continuous outcomes between the trial arms according to the “intention to treat” principle, allowing for the correlation between outcomes of children from the same school using school as a random effect. A cost-utility analysis will be use the EQ-5D-Y should the measure prove valid and reliable; if not, we will assess cost-effectiveness using the SDQ. We will take a broad perspective including the health, social, education and criminal justice sectors; although results will be broken down to allow assessment of alternative perspectives. Timetable: As illustrated in Appendix 4, the study will last a total of five years with a two month setting up period, one-year pilot phase, two further years to recruit to the main phase, and two years of follow up for each school. This leaves the final six months for analysis, writing up and dissemination. Recruitment rate is dictated by the school year and will be 15, 30 and 35 schools in Years 1, 2 and 3 respectively.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Cluster randomised controlled trial, economic and process evaluation to determine the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of a novel intervention (Healthy Lifestyles Programme, HeLP) to prevent obesity in school children
Abstract: DESIGN: Cluster randomised controlled trial with economic and process evaluation. Schools will be stratified by % of children eligible for free school meals and number of Year 5 classes and randomised within strata to intervention and control groups, by an independent statistician from the Clinical Trials Unit. The unit of randomisation will be schools rather than individual children and multi-level modelling will be applied during analysis to account for this. SETTING: State Junior/Primary schools in Devon and Plymouth; sample weighted towards schools from wards with highest indices of deprivation. TARGET POPULATION: Children aged 9-10 years, their parents and schools. INTERVENTION BEING EVALUATED: HeLP is a multi-component 4 phase Programme that seeks to create a receptive environment, targeting all children and their families, to enable the development and support of healthy lifestyle behaviours. The overarching concept emphasises achievable, sustainable behaviour change, concentrating on moving towards a healthy energy balance. Three key behaviours are emphasized and these are framed within the concept we label ‘80/20’, suggesting we should aim to maintain healthy behaviours 80% of the time. Phase 1 focuses on 'Creating a Supportive Context' for the school, child and family and involves a variety of delivery methods (assembly, activity workshops, parent’s evenings, and newsletter articles) to establish information, raise awareness, bolster motivation and build relationships. This takes place in the autumn term of Year 5. Phase 2, which takes place in the spring term, is the intensive 'Healthy Lifestyles Week' using education sessions in the morning delivered by the class teacher which link into drama workshops in the afternoon, delivered by a local theatre company, to increase motivation, knowledge and self efficacy and develop a number of skills to enable behaviour change. Phase 3 is 'Personal Goal Setting and Parental Support' and aims to develop planning skills, increase self awareness and increase parental support. Phase 4 is Reinforcement Activities” (assemblies, drama and education session, 1-to-1 goal review meetings and newsletter articles) which aims to develop monitoring and coping skills as well as consolidating parental support (see Table 1, section 3 detailed description). MEASUREMENT OF COST AND OUTCOMES: Height will be measured using a SECA stadiometer; weight and body fat will be measured using the Tanita Body Composition Analyser SC-330. Physical activity will be measured using accelerometry and food intake using the Food Intake Questionnaire (44). Mediating variables will be measured at 12 months, using a questionnaire assessing knowledge, attitudes, perceived norms behavioural intentions and diet and physical activity (see section 7 in the detailed description). The 18 and 24 month anthropometric measurements will be made by an independent assessor, blind to allocation. Resource use and costs associated with delivery of the intervention will be identified and measured within the trial. PROCESS EVALUATION: A process evaluation will be conducted to provide insight into the way HeLP works in terms of uptake, delivery and experience. This will include collection of quantitative and qualitative data to assess participation, engagement and experience of children, parents and teachers. PLANNED ANALYSES: The primary effectiveness analysis will be based on intention-to-treat and take account of clustering by schools and adjusting for relevant child and school level covariates and baseline scores. Results will be presented as between-group differences, at 18 and 24 months, with appropriate 95% confidence intervals. Framework analysis will be used to analyse the qualitative data. Cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA) will involve a within-trial economic analysis and the development of an economic model, with evidence synthesis, to assess the longer-term cost-effectiveness of HeLP. Within-trial analyses will provide a robust estimate of the costs associated with delivery of the HeLP intervention, presenting a mean incremental cost per school / per child. CEA will relate incremental costs to incremental health outcomes (e.g. cost per unit of BMI change, cost per change in proportion of overweight/obese). Modelling will link effectiveness outcomes to weight status over time (child to adult), and the impact of weight status on health outcomes (eg prevention of adult overweight/obesity, diabetes, CHD), with costs and QALYs for health outcomes over time informing the CEA in a policy-relevant way (eg cost per life-year, cost per QALY). Modelling will build on existing studies in this area (45-47), although further development of the modelling framework will be undertaken using available observational and epidemiological data (48, 49). SAMPLE SIZE: To have 90% power, and 2-sided 5% significance level, to detect a between-group difference in BMI SDS of 0.25 units at 24 months, assuming a standard deviation of 1.3, an ICC of 0.02, allowing for an attrition rate of 20% and adjusting for baseline BMI SDS, requires 952 children to be recruited (36). Also, allowing for possible attrition of schools, we will aim to recruit 32 schools to ensure we have 28 schools including 980 children and their families, (based on an average of 35 children per school). A difference of 0.25 units in BMI SDS has been shown to be a meaningful change impacting on improvement in adiposity and metabolic health (37). The mean between-group difference in BMI SDS of ~-0.2 units (95% CI -0.5 to 0.1) at 24 months in our exploratory trial demonstrates such an effect size to be plausible (23). Whilst, we had an 8% attrition rate in our exploratory trial, we have allowed for a conservative attrition rate of 20% in our sample size calculation. PROJECT TIMETABLES: Months 1-5 Agree final protocol; secure ethical and research governance approval, attend regional association of primary head teachers meetings, agree standard operating procedures with the CTU. Months 3-10 Recruit and train trial staff, recruit schools and children to trial, randomise schools, gain consent, collect baseline measures; allocation revealed Months 11-46 Deliver intervention, collect 12, 18 and 24 month outcome and process data Months 47-56: Check, clean and analyse data; write report, feedback results to participants, consider policy and roll-out implications

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: BIBS: Benefits of Incentives for Breastfeeding and Smoking cessation: A platform study for a trial
Abstract: Our definition of incentives includes financial (positive or negative) and non financial tangible incentives or rewards. Recipients may be women, families and/or NHS or non-NHS service providers at local, regional or national level. Setting: Primary and secondary health and community (including pharmacy) care at three sites: Aberdeen, where there are no incentive schemes; Lancashire, which has incentive schemes to promote breastfeeding and Glasgow, which is about to start a research trial of financial incentives for stopping smoking in pregnancy. Stage 1. We will synthesize the evidence for incentives delivered to women, families and NHS or non NHS providers and their associated theories of behaviour change, using focused research questions to inform the design of a trial. This will produce: i) evidence synthesis reports ii) a taxonomy of incentive characteristics, behaviour change theory, mechanisms of action and the barriers/facilitators to stopping smoking in pregnancy and breastfeeding iii) a short list of promising incentives. Stage 2. For the incentive short-list we will investigate recipient, provider and public acceptability and any unintended effects. Mixed method data will refine the incentive characteristics, timing, quantity, delivery processes, recipient monitoring, organisational, environmental and contextual factors that are likely to increase effectiveness. Stage 3. A DCE survey will refine the most promising intervention(s) to trial. The DCE will identify the relative probabilities of behaviour change for different types and level of incentive intervention and inform effect sizes. If probabilities vary across individuals with different characteristics, and affect outcomes, then a range of incentives may be more effective than a ‘one-size-fits-all’ approach. Combining all aspects of this study will enable us to define a trial intervention, recruitment and delivery strategies, provide a sample size calculation, model effect sizes and define outcome measurements. This will inform the design of a trial.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Screening for psychological and mental health difficulties of young people who offend: An integrated evidence synthesis and value of information analysis
Abstract: Design: We will use an integrated evidence syntheses (systematic review, decision modelling, value of information analysis). Search strategy: We will search a wide range of published-literature databases, grey-literature databases and relevant websites among other strategies (e.g., hand-search of reference lists, reverse-citation search). Review strategy: Five linked phases, with each one designed to answer one of the five objectives. Phase 1: Systematic review of the prevalence of mental health problems identified by the screening measures and the diagnostic/psychometric characteristics of those measures. Phases 2: Assessment of the clinical effectiveness of screening strategies in this population, and in the likely absence of information on this, a broader assessment of the clinical effectiveness of interventions for mental health problems in young offenders. Phase 3: An assessment of the cost-effectiveness of screening strategies in this population. Again, in the absence of information, we will broaden this to examine the cost-effectiveness of interventions for mental health problems in this or similar populations. On the basis of the anticipated limited literature we will construct a decision model informed by the results of phases 1 to 3. In the absence of inputs from phases 1 to 3, we will use inputs from a range of experts, including stakeholders. Phase 4: This phase will use value of information analysis to identify research priorities and the value of developing future research into screening strategies for young offenders with mental health problems. Phase 5: Benchmark current screening practice in the UK against minimum criteria laid down by the National Screening Committee. Expected output of research: 1. We expect that each phase of the evidence synthesis will lead to a review meeting each of the objectives given above and overall will make a substantial contribution to the literature in this area. 2. Our review will help establish the value of further research and help to prioritise areas to focus on. 3. We will disseminate the results of the review widely in a number of ways (HTA report, peer-reviewed publications, academic and professional conferences). We will consult with stakeholders to identify the most suitable methods for disseminating the results to relevant practitioner and policy forums. Expertise in the team: Our research team combines the necessary methodological (e.g., systematic reviews, value of information analysis) and content expertise (e.g., young offenders, mental health interventions) to answer this important but complex question. We also have specific expertise in the planning and implementation of dissemination strategies. For further details of expertise, please see next section. Project timetable: Literature search (months 1-3), phases 1-3 review (months 3-12), decision modelling and value of information analysis (months 12-15), write up and dissemination (months 15-18)

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: A trial to evaluate an extended rehabilitation service for stroke patients(EXTRAS)
Abstract: Development of longer term stroke rehabilitation services are limited by lack of evidence of effectiveness for specific interventions and service models. This study will evaluate a new extended stroke rehabilitation service which will commence when Early Supported Discharge (ESD) ends. Study design: Multicentre randomised controlled trial with health economic and process evaluations. Setting: Twelve or more NHS stroke services. Participants: Adults with a new stroke (and carer if appropriate) being discharged from hospital under the care of an ESD team. Study intervention treatment: An extended stroke rehabilitation service provided following completion of ESD. A senior ESD team member will undertake a structured assessment and goal setting focussing upon extended activities of daily living at 1, 3, 6, 12 and 18 months. Assessments will usually be undertaken by telephone. Study control treatment: Usual care post ESD. Usual care may involve referral of patients to a range of rehabilitation services upon completion of ESD in accordance with local clinical practice. Randomisation: Central independent web based service. Primary outcome: Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living Scale at 24 months post randomisation. Secondary outcomes: For patients: health status (Oxford Handicap Scale), quality of life (Euroqol EQ-5D), mood (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale), experience of services and resource use (adaptation of the Client Service Receipt Inventory) at 12 and 24 months post randomisation. For carers: quality of life (Euroqol EQ-5D), carer stress (Caregiver Strain Index) and experience of services at 12 and 24 months post randomisation. Blinding: Outcomes by blinded assessor. Process evaluation: Semi-structured interviews with a subsample of study participants and staff to gain insight into their perceptions and experience of study treatments. Sample size: Allowing for 25% attrition, 510 participants are needed to provide 90% power to detect a difference in mean Nottingham EADL score of 6 with a 5% significance level.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Programme of centrally-managed pregnancy & childbirth systematic reviews of priority to the NHS and users of the NHS.
Abstract: Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth reviews are extensively used to provide evidence for influential national clinical guidelines produced by NICE. Future prioritisation was determined formally at a meeting in 2010 involving representatives of NHS and consumer organisations using a modified group technique (with guidance from the James Lind Alliance). Of the agreed high priority list, 23 topics were covered by recently published reviews, or reviews currently in the editorial process. In addition some review topics fell under other review groups. Drug misuse in pregnancy (Drugs and Alcohol Group), Epilepsy in pregnancy (Epilepsy Group). Ways of providing information for helping parents make decisions about prenatal testing (Consumers and Communications Group). This left, in total, 16 priority topics that required new reviews and 30 priority topics that needed updating of existing reviews - these are the deliverables in this project.

Award_Title: Effective Practice and Organisation of Care in the NHS
Abstract: The systematic review topics that will be supported by this programme grant are listed below and are categorised by the priority areas set out in the Operating Framework for NHS England 2010/11: Quality improvement 1.
