Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: A Programme of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Reviews and of Updates of Intervention Reviews in Dementia
Abstract: The personal, social and economic burden of dementia is huge. It accounts for more years lived with disability than any other condition. Through its rigorous methods, The Cochrane Collaboration has improved the quality of primary research into clinical interventions for dementia. Through a programme of Cochrane DTA reviews we now have a similar opportunity to tighten the intellectual framework for the evaluation of diagnostic tests in dementia. The scope of the programme is twofold. A series of Diagnostic Test Accuracy (DTA) reviews will cover the full range of important imaging and laboratory biomarkers, and of simple clinical tests. A series of updates will focus on interventions, both pharmacological and non-pharmacological, which are currently in clinical use in the NHS. In addition to the publication of high quality reviews in the Cochrane Collaboration database, a strong emphasis will be put on integrating the results of the reviews in digested reports for policy development, health technology appraisal and commissioning in the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group
Award_Title: Exercise for improving balance in older people
Abstract: Scientific/policy justification for review/review update: Decline in the ability to maintain balance is common in older people and, as well as being a risk factor of falls, can also seriously restrict activities of daily living and social participation. In particular, falls often result in injury, loss of independence and early death. This review, first published in 2007, examines the effects on balance of various exercises, such as walking, balance training, muscle strengthening, tai chi and dance. Based on evidence from 34 trials, the review found some weak evidence of short-term benefits of exercise but noted a lack of evidence to determine any lasting effects. This review was the 10th most downloaded full text review in 2008 and the most cited review for the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group for 2009. The contact author still receives regular requests for reprints. It is a priority review for updating. A search update in June 2010 has identified 74 eligible trials of which 36 are now confirmed for inclusion and 38 await classification. Thus this will be a substantial update. Together with the implementation of new review methodology, the work involved is equivalent to a new review.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Exercise for preventing and treating osteoporosis in postmenopausal women
Abstract: Scientific/policy justification for review/review update: Osteoporosis is a major public health problem the projected global burden of osteoporotic hip fractures is expected to exceed six million by 2050 and the economic burden of osteoporosis is comparable to that of other major chronic diseases. The current review of 18 studies (up to 2000) did not determine the long-term effects of the varied exercises or specific exercises. However, exercise is commonly prescribed as part of rehabilitation packages for patients; it is low cost and typically involves home exercise. This reflects the policy shift from acute to community services. Furthermore, surveys have found that the knowledge base of healthcare professionals is poor in the management of the disorder, highlighting the need for information. It is therefore necessary that clinicians and patients are aware of evidence based exercise strategies that may help in the management of the disorder. It is anticipated that the findings the proposed review will be incorporated into updates of Clinical guidelines, e.g. SIGN. There are over 200 member societies listed on the International Osteoporosis Foundation’s website. We anticipate that we would engage with a number of these organisations in the development of the update. A key word search of PubMed for ‘exercise and osteoporosis’ limited to 2000- present gave 1050 hits.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Supported self-management for patients with moderate to severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD): an evidence synthesis and economic analysis
Abstract: Despite the presence of a number of trials and systematic reviews about self-management for COPD, there remain many unanswered questions. The available published studies have been diverse in terms of the patient group, composition of self-management intervention, nature of delivery (for example lay person vs health professional; setting; group vs individual), and although the evidence suggests that overall self-management is beneficial in improving quality of life and reducing hospital admissions, the effect on other outcomes is not clear and further work is needed to establish which particular features and elements are most effective. There are a number of trials published (or in progress) since these systematic reviews, and therefore it is timely to evaluate these questions in more detail. In addition, although there are likely to be few studies, there is no systematic review of the effects of self-management delivered post-discharge. The aim of this proposal therefore is to evaluate the current state of the evidence for the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of self-management interventions delivered post-discharge, and using the wider literature to unpick which elements of /approaches to self-management interventions in general are the most effective and cost-effective in improving patient outcomes. Interventions are likely to be complex and multi-component, and specific elements may not be directly trialled head-to-head. Therefore more complex analysis techniques such as meta-regression and mixed treatment comparison meta-analysis methods (incorporating indirect comparisons) are likely to be required.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A Randomised Controlled Trial of the Effectiveness of PDSAFE to prevent Falls among People with Parkinson's Disease
Abstract: DESIGN: Multi-centred, individually randomised two-group controlled trial proceeded by 3-months monitoring of individual fall rate and a pilot study. A qualitative study of personal insights and an economic evaluation will run in parallel and be integrated with the main RCT. SETTING: Participants for the main trial will be identified from four areas in the south of England. We will work with the members of the DeNDRoN network as well as PD nurses and PD specialists to recruit participants. We will also approach Parkinson’s UK local support groups, primary care consortia and outpatient services. TARGET POPULATION: People with a confirmed diagnosis of PD, live at home, have experienced at least one fall in the previous 12 months and can understand and follow instructions will be eligible for recruitment to the trial. RANDOMISATION: We will recruit 600 to the pre-randomisation falls collection period, we estimate with drop outs approximately 540 will be randomly allocated to one of two groups; intervention or control. Allocation will be stratified by centre and allocated in blocks with random size of 2, 4,6 or 8. The treating therapist will access allocation on the CTU website. HEALTH TECHNOLOGY: All participants will have usual care. The control group will receive a standardised DVD with a relaxation programme. The experimental group will participate in PDSAFE a personalised home-based programme of exercises and strategies for fall prevention to be delivered by physiotherapists with specific training in the intervention and use of DVD and tablet computer technology. The novelty of the treatment lies in both the content (disease specific exercises and strategies for limiting instability, use of motor relearning and cognitive awareness) and delivery (personalised feedback using DVD for adherence and self-management). The programme comprises: a] exercises for balance, gait and muscle weakness, b] strategies for reducing freezing, encouraging stability and gait efficacy, c] feedback model to promote learning and adherence. Personal sessions with required exercises and will be recorded on DVD and returned so information and instructions can be replayed at home; DVD will be developed with the PwPD. The frequency of the intervention sessions will be faded over time, one hour twice a week for a month, once a week for two months followed by once a month for 3 months. The control group will receive usual care and a DVD with a relaxation programme. MEASUREMENT OUTCOME: a] Pre-randomisation fall collection period: Those who meet the inclusion criteria will be asked to prospectively record fall events using a monthly diary sheet for 3 months between recruitment and randomisation. These findings will be used for comparison with post-intervention fall rate. b] The assessments will take place in participants’ homes at baseline, 3, 6 and 12 months post-randomisation and will be completed by the assessor who will be blinded to group allocation. c] Baseline only: At baseline a medical history structured to include co-morbidities will be taken, disease severity, medication and hand grip will be recorded. d] Our primary outcome is risk of repeat falling between 0-6 months. Pre-specified analyses, particularly those related to disease severity, are likely to assume importance in the interpretation of the trial. In the event of not finding a difference in the pooled sample (ie all participants regardless of severity), we will continue with the pre-specified analysis relating to disease severity, and will accept treatment effect in only one of the sub-groups as evidence of effectiveness. e] Secondary outcomes will include risk of repeat falling 6-12 months, rate of falling 0-6 and 6-12 months, injurious falls and near falls (from the fall diary), a measure of balance, turning, mobility and quality of life.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Motivations, mandates and accountability in demand management: A realist synthesis
Abstract: The proposal is for an evidence synthesis and the proposed research strategy is realist synthesis (RS), developed by the chief investigator of this proposal (Pawson, 2002; 2006) as a method of systematic review to manage the intricate and uneven bodies of evidence that accrue in primary research on complex interventions. Demand management is one such complex arena which fails to respond well to primary investigation by randomised controlled trial (RCT) or review by formal meta-analysis. Results from a previous SDO-funded investigation on the use Threshold Assessment Grids to improve mental health referrals (Slade et al 2006) illustrate the typical pitfalls. Control group practices outperformed those practices that had introduced the grid. The explanation for the perverse result was the very uneven implementation of the scheme and the very different conditions in which the practices operated. As the authors note ‘the main weakness is the “black-box” assumption embedded in trial methodology’ (2006: 14). All of the multifarious incarnations of demand management allow for and often encourage adaptive implementation and are heavily constrained by local institutional and management regimes. For this reason we have chosen an approach that concentrates on the theories underlying demand management, seeking to address their problems and pitfalls, and delivering an evidence base which advises on implementation and targeting – what works for whom in what circumstances. RS operates with an iterative study design explained in the detailed project description and summarised here as follows: 1. Identify the review question. The basic unit of analysis in RS is not the intervention but the programme theories that underpin them. The hypotheses that justify the programme and provide the reasons why it might work are also the hypotheses to be investigated in RS. Review thus begins by searching primary materials to identify the justifications, arguments and programme logic of the interventions under review. In a complex intervention like demand management these justifications are many and the first stage of an RS is to prioritise those theories whose further investigation is likely to help improve its implementation and targeting. To inform this process we will also hold a theory building workshop with a project reference group of NHS stakeholders as described in the detailed project description attached. 2. Searching for primary studies. Searching is carried out in two main stages. The first, described above, is the ‘theory search’. Once completed and after the theory to be interrogated has been selected, RS commences an ‘evidence search’, seeking studies that will provide empirical tests of each component of the theory. For instance, if the theory makes assumptions about the expected reactions of different groups of subjects then primary research is sought that captures the behaviour of those sub-groups. If the theory points to crucial steps required for successful outcomes then research is sought comparing whether this has been implemented across different schemes. 3/4. Data extraction and quality appraisal. These phases are combined in RS. Different programme theories require substantiation in divergent bodies of evidence. Hypotheses about the optimal contexts for the intervention are tested in comparative outcome data; claims about the reactions of particular groups of subjects are tested using qualitative data; implementation ideas are tested in process research, and so on. Primary studies thus contribute specific bodies of evidence but each primary study plays a different role in the final synthesis and so each fragment of evidence needs to be appraised, as it is extracted, for both its relevance for theory testing and the rigour with which it has been produced. 5. Synthesis. The role of synthesis in RS is not to offer a verdict, descriptive summary or mean effect calculation on a family of programmes. Outcomes vary considerably according to how and where programmes are implemented. What is synthesised, therefore, are all the conditions and caveats that make for programme success. Many of these opportunities and stumbling blocks will have been anticipated in the original programme theories but after a total immersion in the data, more refined theories emerge as the key point of synthesis. We will discuss and review our synthesis in a further workshop with our project reference group. 6. Dissemination. The purpose of RS is to improve the implementation and targeting of interventions. Accordingly, dissemination will focus on NHS decision makers responsible for designing and implementing DM initiatives and these stakeholders will be involved from the outset of the review. Outputs will include actionable guidance to assist NHS decision makers to target and implement demand management initiatives, as well as a dissemination event, conference presentations and publications in peer reviewed journals, as described the at

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: An evaluation of an eReferral Management & Triage System for Minor Oral Surgery referrals from primary care dentists
Abstract: The 2010 King’s fund report stated a need to address and manage demand for services within dentistry. It concluded that a whole systems approach to service redesign was needed. Consequently, the introduction of intelligent, centralised referral management within oral surgery (and Dentistry as a whole) will be inevitable within the NHS. A pilot study carried out in Greater Manchester has demonstrated the potential for centralised referral management to improve the quality of referrals and reduce oral surgery waiting lists for acute trusts. However the full impact on costs and quality of care are currently unknown. There is therefore a need to carry out a robust evaluation in order for the NHS to understand the risks and benefits of introducing this type of intervention. NHS Sefton currently has no comprehensive referral management system in place for oral surgery, and offers a useful mix of acute trusts: a teaching hospital (University Dental Hospital), a large foundation trust (Aintree Hospital) and a district general (Ormskirk). Sefton is therefore an ideal site in which to conduct a full and comprehensive evaluation of the impact of introducing a new referral management system. Within the outline bid there were five main areas of research described. The first piece is preparatory in nature and involves a diagnostic test accuracy study. The main study is an interrupted time series design and will fully evaluate a new remote, centralised referral management system for Oral Surgery. • How efficient is remote centralised referral assessment and triage? • How does remote centralised referral management (RCRM) impact on GDP referral behaviour and practice? • How does RCRM management impact on secondary care providers? • How does RCRM impact on patients? • How does RCRM impact on the NHS? A mixed methods study (interrupted time series design,combined with qualitative analysis) will be carried over a period of 36 months. This period of time is necessary in order to: a) Year 1; Collect baseline data, taking into account possible seasonal variation in the number of referrals received by secondary care providers b) Year 2; To look at the potential impact of centralised, electronic referral management and triage system and to gather information and intelligence so that appropriate specialist primary care services can be informed and commissioned prior to full implementation c) Year 3; To assess the impact of full implementation of the new intervention

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Information and value based commissioning - Demand Management for Planned Care
Abstract: The growth in planned care post-2002 The challenge to identifying the source of activity growth is that both supply and demand-side factors have been changing in the NHS in England over the period that we will investigate. Our approach is to exploit both the variation within England in the adoption of various supply-side and demand-side factors and variation between Scotland and England, where Scotland often acts as a natural control not having been subject to either Patient Choice or Payment by Results policies. The generic form of the econometric model that we adopt can be expressed as follows. The dependent variable, h, is the level of elective activity in PCT or provider i, in HRG j, in year t. Two vectors Xijt and Ui are observable covariates at PCT or Provider level, such as, population characteristics, financial status (FT or non-FT, surplus or deficit), provider or PCT specific shifts (Fixed Effects) and capacity. Two vectors Wjt and Qj are observable covariates at procedure level, such as, for example, average cost, Length of Stay, HRG specific shifts (Fixed Effects) and policies affecting that procedure. Particular parameterisations of the model will permit the impact of demand-side and supply-side factors on activity to be estimated. For example, consider the impact of ‘patient choice’. ‘Choice’ came into effect in England in 2006, thus a simple modelling of the impact of this factor is to suppose that it affected all HRGs in England after 2006. The relevant variable of Qj takes a value 1 if the activity occurs in 2006 or later and zero otherwise. Herein lies an immediate problem; every activity indicator in England is potentially affected by the adoption of the Choice Agenda from 2006 on. However, this policy was not adopted in Scotland and so for each hijt relating to Scotland the relevant value of the Choice variable is zero. For this policy, and this particular formulation of the inception of the policy, activity in Scotland acts as the control to the policy treatment in England. The equation will be estimated by standard Fixed-Effects and Fixed-effects-dummy-variable regression methods. Model development will be undertaken to consider refinements in terms of modelling specific HRGs, or developing alternative measures of activity. The potential for demand and supply-side factors to be interdependent in affecting activity will be allowed for by including interaction terms in the regression specifications and analysed where they are statistically significant. To implement our approach we will construct a data set that comprises, for the dependent variable, activity measures (number of procedures or procedures per head of population or relative to non-elective activity) for each elective HRG, in each year, aggregated over either each provider or each PCT (equivalently in Scotland – Health Board) area. These measures can be derived from HES and SMR (Scottish Morbidity Record) data for England and Scotland respectively. Similarly, covariates will be constructed either from HES and SMR, or from other publicly accessible health care data sources. Learning from PROMs, HES and other data We seek to describe and explain the difference in health gain performance across CCGs using both simple approaches and also by estimating patient gain models similar to the previous equation. CCGs may perform well/badly due to both the demography of the area and also because the mean performance across all demographic groups is higher in a CCG area, which is captured by a fixed effect. This might reflect patient selection or provider quality. We will extend the model to include pre-operative conditions to establish their relationship to health gain using a flexible parametric form with and without control for patient characteristics. This framework will also allow us to establish variation in patient QALY gain between demographic groups, conditional upon pre-operative conditions. There exists considerable variation in activity between CCGs and we shall explore the impact of activity variation on patient health gain controlling for demographic characteristics that influence patient reported gain. There is informal evidence that patient gain is on average as great in high activity areas as in those with little activity. This will be explored to examine the implications for the capacity to refer and treat patients most able to achieve health gain. Good patient selection depends on finding those who benefit most. By considering CCGs with few treated patients we can identify the characteristics of patients who are not treated when an area offers low activity, and estimate the health loss for restricted patient groups in low activity CCGs. A combination of high health gain with high volume is clearly a good performance and it will be useful to examine these commissioners in order to infer pointers to good performance. Another dimension of performance is consistency. Using similar methods, we shall examine commissioners' consistency across the four procedures in terms of adjusted volume, average health gain, pre-op condition and so on. If demand is to be reduced, the obvious first step is to withhold treatment from patients who gain little from it. Using the individual PROMS data it is possible to uncover the correlates of patients in terms of pre-op condition who experience health gain below some selected level, obviously, negative health gain, and who therefore benefit less from treatment. It may then be possible to offer guidance as to those who should not be treated. Reports of activities and outcomes will be sent to CCGs, outlining evidence for their own population and appropriately compared to other CCG populations, using forms of presentation such as funnel plots for comparative data. In order to maximise accessibility and possible impact, the group will encourage dialogue and opportunity for clarification of data provided as part of the proposed study, and work with the NHS Alliance to build a dialogue with commissioners and patients.

Award_Title: The effectiveness of Community vs. Hospital Eye Service follow-up for patients with neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) with quiescent disease: a virtual trial. (The ECHoES trial)
Abstract: DESIGN: ECHoES is a virtual trial of ophthalmologists’ and optometrists’ decisions about the need for anti-VEGF retreatment in patients with nAMD. It will be based on vignettes consisting of colour fundus and optical coherence tomography (OCT) images with accompanying clinical data. Vignettes will be created using information collected in a national comparative effectiveness trial of anti-VEGF drugs (the IVAN study), to mimic the characteristics of patients judged to be eligible for follow up in the community. Both groups will assess the same vignettes, viewing images and data and submitting their decisions via the internet. SETTING: Ophthalmologists’ decisions will represent the Hospital Eye Service (HES). Optometrists’ decisions will represent the community / primary care setting. TARGET POPULATION: ECHoES aims to inform the provision of anti-VEGF services for patients with nAMD. Participants will be volunteers drawn from among HES ophthalmologists (either senior trainees or consultants) and community ‘high street’ optometrists. HEALTH TECHNOLOGIES BEING ASSESSED: Expertise of community optometrists (‘intervention’ group) and ophthalmologists (‘comparator’ group) in assessing the need for anti-VEGF retreatment in vignettes. The IVAN database will be interrogated to extract image sets, made up of (a) fundus colour images and an OCT classified by the independent Network of Ophthalmic Reading Centres (NetwORC) as fluid free and (b) a subsequent OCT classified by the NetwORC as fluid free or fluid present (1:1 ratio), the latter requiring retreatment. Image pairs will cover a range of clinical presentations. Clinical factors (e.g. age, gender, smoking history, visual acuity at time of first image, time since macula fluid free, visual acuity at time of second image) will vary in a representative manner. Participants’ decisions will be compared to ‘reference’ classifications (need for retreatment based on grading by the NetwORC and medical retina experts). MEASUREMENT OF COSTS AND OUTCOMES: The primary outcome (‘correct’ / ‘wrong’) is the participant’s decision about the need for retreatment (refer to hospital vs. suspicious or inactive categories) compared to the reference classification. Secondary outcomes are similar comparisons about the presence or absence of lesion components, i.e. blood, exudates, sub-retinal fluid, intra-retinal fluid/cysts, pigment epithelial detachment. The primary outcome for the economic evaluation will be the cost per accurate retreatment decision. SAMPLE SIZE: Ophthalmologists and optometrists (each group n=48) will each assess 48 vignettes randomly sampled from the database (total 1152 vignettes). Each vignette will be assessed by two ophthalmologists and two optometrists. This sample size will have at least 90% power to test the hypothesis (with 2.5% 1-sided statistical significance) that the proportion of vignettes correctly identified as “refer for retreatment” by the optometrist group differs by no more than 10%. TIMETABLE: Months 1-4: Create vignette database. Months 2-8: develop web application for presentation of training and final sets of vignettes. Months 4-6: recruit ophthalmologists and optometrists. Months 7-8: train participants. Months 9-12: participants judge vignettes. Months 13-18: analyses and write-up of the results. PROTECTION AGAINST BIAS: Participants (optometrists and ophthalmologists) will be blind to the reference standard classifications. The order of assessment of vignettes by optometrists and ophthalmologists will be randomised. ANALYSES: Conditional logistic regression of correct decisions by ophthalmologists and optometrists, compared to reference standard classifications; other analyses will investigate whether clinical factors influence decisions.

Award_Title: Intervention Now to Eliminate Repeat Unintended Pregnancies in Teenagers
Abstract: Design:Systematic review using mixed methods: To cater for the complexities in the question we propose a pragmatic, highly structured, innovative and iterative approach combining methodological techniques tailored to each element of the review. Search strategy:Searches of the international literature since 1995 (two years previous to the last substantive systematic reviews in the field) using multiple search strategies including thesaurus terms and keywords relating to teenage pregnancy and second or subsequent pregnancies. We will not restrict search terms to “unwanted” or “unplanned” as not all relevant papers include these terms terms. We will refine and test these strategies iteratively to enhance sensitivity and specificity. A separate search excluding the terms for second or subsequent pregnancies but including a filter for systematic reviews will augment the initial searches. Searches will include the bibliographies of included papers and hand-searches of key journals. For published studies we will include : MEDLINE & MEDLINE IN PROCESS, PsycInfo, The Cochrane Library, ERIC (Educational Resource Index and Abstracts), SocAbs (Sociological Abstracts), ASSIA (Applied Social Sciences Abstract & Indexes) and BiblioMap (The EPPI-Centre register of health promotion and public health research), CINAHL (Cumulative Index to Nursing & Allied Health Literature) including the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, DARE (Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects), the HTA Database, NHS EED (NHS Economic Evaluation Database) and EMBASE (The Excerpta Medica database). In contrast to the searches of published literature, the search of grey literature will focus, primarily but not exclusively, on sources within the UK. We will search the electronic databases: Scopus, Sirius, OpenGrey, Social Care Online, the National Research Register Archive, the NIHR portfolio database and the Index to Theses. We will utilise Google, Google Scholar and search the websites of, or make personal contacts with professional networks e.g. Family Planning Association, reproductive health nursing networks, General Practitioners’ fora to identify DoH and third sector policy documents and evaluations. Since the issues surrounding implementation of interventions are a primary focus of this review, qualitative evidence associated with trials is highly relevant. Therefore we will contact the Principal Investigators of effectiveness studies to obtain any associated qualitative/views study outcomes. Review strategy:The overall mixed method review framework is based on a structured, phased, EPPI-Centre approach. After evidence searching and retrieval, it will be screened against inclusion and exclusion criteria and quality appraised. A mapping exercise will organise and describe the evidence and the scope of the review refined focusing on key areas of the topics identified. This process will draw heavily on the advice of the expert advisory group.RCT data will by synthesised with reference to Cochrane guidelines for public health interventions. Qualitative and effectiveness evidence, assessed from a narrative synthesis viewpoint will address facilitators of and barriers to interventions (feasibility), experience (appropriateness), and acceptability (meaningfulness) of interventions. Realist synthesis will identify the mechanisms through which the intervention works or fails. Economic evidence, from a behavioural economics stance will stratify studies by the public health lever mechanism used, paying attention to the perspective of analysis and type of economic evaluation. Outcomes will be fed back to service users to incorporate their perspective in the final report All search results will be imported and managed in bibliographic reference management software (Endnote). Expected outcome of research: A report and further publications (1. Protocol paper, 2. Methodology paper and 3. Outcomes paper) designed to inform policy makers, providers, researchers and service users by identifying and describing: population of young girls at risk of repeat pregnancy, interventions available to prevent repeat pregnancies, effectiveness of the interventions, and barriers and facilitators of these interventions. Stratifying by groups at greatest risk we will report interventions designed to reduce repeat unintended teenage pregnancies; assess the utility, feasibility and costs of those interventions (or elements of complex interventions) and identify barriers and facilitators to implementation and uptake. We will describe the impact of different interventions on access to and uptake of relevant health and social services, subsequent use of contraceptive methods, pregnancy and abortion rates. Where there is little or no evidence of effectiveness, we will identify promising interventions that are worthy of further evaluation. Award_Title: Evaluating the long-term effectiveness, and the cost and consequences of the Family Nurse Partnership parenting support programme in reducing maltreatment in young children
Abstract: Background: In the first of 3 US trials of NFP (US name for FNP), by age 2 there was verified abuse / neglect in 19% of control children compared to 4% in NFP group and 56% relative reduction in emergency department encounters for injuries and ingestions during the second year of life. By age 4, amongst maltreated children, NFP group of children exhibited fewer risks for harm than control group (e.g. fewer attendances with injuries / ingestions, safer home environment). In the 15 years after birth, mothers as perpetrators of abuse were less common in NFP vs control arm (0.29 vs 0.54; p<0.001), an effect even greater for the most vulnerable sub-group (low SES, unmarried; 0.11). Whilst the beneficial impact upon risk of state-verified first-time reports of maltreatment was experienced after age 5, this difference was earlier (age 3) for the most vulnerable sub-group of poor unmarried mothers. Design: Participants will enter this study upon exit from the Building Blocks trial (age 2 of their first born child) and followed until that child is aged 6. Half of the proposed study participants will have been offered FNP at randomisation, the other half would have continued to receive usual health and social care services locally available. Follow-up will be by data abstraction from health and social care records. Baseline and follow-up data from the Building Blocks trial will be incorporated in the proposed follow-up study analysis. Research aims & objectives: We will examine the longer-term impact of the FNP intervention upon child maltreatment (child in need status, referral to Children’s Social Care(CSC)) and associated outcomes of maltreatment (e.g. injuries and ingestions). The impact of theoretical moderators of programme effect and fidelity to programme will be assessed and will use data already collected (e.g. presence of domestic violence, baseline socio-demographics) and data collected prospectively in this study. Conceptual intermediate outcomes of programme effect will be assessed (i.e. subsequent pregnancies). Longer-term cost and consequences of the intervention (health resource usage) will be assessed. Setting & recruitment: Potential participants are currently enrolled in the Building Blocks trial. Sites encompass a mix of deprived urban and rural settings across England. Target population: Women who were aged under 20 when conceiving their first child, who planned to reside within the study area delivering FNP until their child was 2 years old, who had the capacity to consent to trial participation (including conversational English, as FNP remains to be validated for delivery via interpreters). Study sites were those identified as having the organisational capacity to support intervention delivery and a clear social and clinical need (i.e. high levels of health inequality). Intervention: FNP is an intensive parenting support programme delivered by specially trained nurses from the point at which pregnancy is confirmed until the newly born child is 2. A prescribed schedule of up to 30 visits addresses key content areas to promote improved pregnancy outcomes, child health and development and maternal economic self-sufficiency. Skilful programme delivery is facilitated by practitioner training in Motivational Interviewing, local supervision for nurses and centralised support by a Department of Health policy team. Measurement of outcome: Primary outcome: rates of children classified as a child in need. Secondary outcomes: other objective measures of maltreatment (e.g. referral to CSC), associated measures of maltreatment (including accidents and injuries), possible moderators of abuse and programme effect (e.g. domestic violence). Data will be abstracted from medical and social care records. The former will include health visitor, HES and data from the Department of Health. Services will be approached and paid to provide data. Sample size: 1645 women were recruited to the original trial. Following mandatory withdrawals, 1570 remain eligible for follow-up through records. A 10% loss to follow-up would result in 1413 participants. Assuming an underlying rate of 8%, to detect a difference of 4% in Child in Need status would require 1204 children in total (80% power; two-sided 5% alpha). Planned analyses: Analyses will be by intention to treat, comparing the two groups using multilevel modelling to allow for clustering of effect. Modelling the impact of key subgroups and different intervention elements (e.g. dosage) on outcome will be undertaken by extending the primary models and testing for interaction effects. Group differences in profile of maltreatment will be assessed (e.g. timing, category, referral source, perpetrator). Economic evaluation will consider costs and consequences of the FNP over the full time period of trial follow-up. Project timetable: Approval will be requested for data abstraction via the Confidentiality Advisory Group (section 251 approval) in 2014. Data will be abstracted at two timepoints from health and social care records. Data for the main analysis will be received during 2018 with results will be available in 2019. With the support of the funder, the study has now been extended by five months to allow complete collection of data for the youngest children in the study cohort at the critical Key Stage 1 (KS1) assessment point. Stakeholder involvement: We will extend an existing model of stakeholder involvement to advise the research team which will encompass graduates of the FNP programme in England, as well as other local stakeholders.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: An overview of interventions aimed at improving outcomes for children exposed to domestic violence: systematic review, evidence synthesis and research recommendations
Abstract: The aim of our project is to produce recommendations for future research evaluating interventions for children exposed to domestic violence and abuse (DVA). We will do this by synthesising the findings of previous studies, by modeling the cost effectiveness of known interventions and by consulting with survivors of DVA, their children and service providers. Exposure to DVA is an adverse childhood experience that increases the risk of behavioural and mental health problems throughout childhood and into adult life (Chan & Yeung, 2009; Stanley, 2011), as well as the risk of adult DVA perpetration and victimisation (Whitfield 2003; Murrell 2007). The association with these poor outcomes is cumulative in the presence of other adverse childhood experiences, which often co-occur with exposure to domestic abuse (Radford et al., 2011; Finkelhor et al., 2009). Longitudinal research with children exposed to domestic violence and research with perpetrators indicate that change may be difficult to implement or sustain. However, it is plausible that if interventions with children exposed to domestic abuse improve short-term behavioural and mental health outcomes, they will also reduce the risk of adult DVA perpetration and victimisation. Design Phase I: evidence synthesis This will be based on a wide range of evidence sources (listed below). We will distinguish the effectiveness of interventions by age and gender of children exposed to DVA and highlight contextual factors such as agencies delivering the programmes and the communities in which they are based: 1. Controlled studies (international) In a previous systematic review (Feder 2009) we identified 5 studies (4 RCTs) evaluating interventions with children exposed to DVA and the non-abusing parent. We will update this review and quality appraisal, summarising the main findings and pooling the child-centred outcomes if possible. 2. Cohort studies (international) Including longitudinal studies measuring outcomes for children exposed to domestic abuse engaged in intervention programmes or studies measuring protective factors that may be the basis of future intervention. We will summarise the main findings. 3. Qualitative evaluations of interventions (international) Including interview- based and observational studies of children with or without a parent engaged in intervention programmes. We will combine findings through a qualitative synthesis (Feder 2006), identifying promising interventions and research gaps. 4. Project reports (UK) Including any published account that reports outcomes for children exposed to domestic abuse engaged in an intervention programme. We will combine findings, identifying promising interventions and research gaps. We will identify studies potentially fulfilling our inclusion criteria through bibliographic database searches, by scrutinising references and citations, and by contacting topic experts and service providers. Phase II: cost-effectiveness and expected value of information modeling of intervention(s) We will review higher quality epidemiological studies (well powered cross-sectional population studies measuring potential confounding factors or longitudinal studies) that measure the association between childhood exposure to DVA and adverse adult outcomes, including DVA perpetration and victimisation. These will give us a range of effect estimates of childhood exposure. We will then use the effect size of the trials measuring short-term behavioural outcomes of interventions for children exposed to abuse (see phase I) to project the potential long term effect of the interventions into adulthood using a range of assumptions about attenuation/amplification. Our estimates of long-term outcomes will include perpetration and victimisation, mental health, educational achievement, employment, and involvement with criminal justice systems. If cost data for the interventions are available, we propose a cost effectiveness analysis based on the pooled trials or the trial with the highest internal and external (in the UK policy context) validity. Even if cost data are not available, we will be able to estimate these from current UK costs of intervention programmes, allowing us to consider benefits and costs averted up to early middle age. This will allow us to project the potential cost-effectiveness of the intervention in the UK context, and the potential benefit in terms of reducing domestic abuse victimisation and perpetration and other adult outcomes. That model will be the basis for an expected value of partial perfect information analysis which will identify which subsets of parameters are responsible for uncertainty in the optimal policy decision, and will directly inform a recommendation on whether specific interventions should be further tested. If appropriate an expected value of sample information analysis will be performed to identify the optimal design of further research. (Griffin 2010) It is possible that some of the interventions should be implemented without further research. Phase III: consultation We will identify a group of stakeholders, including Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) professionals, 3rd sector organisations and social care agencies delivering programmes for children exposed to domestic abuse, as well as academics in the field of DVA. Meetings will be held with this group to identify which interventions are currently delivered in the UK and which would benefitfrom further evaluation. We will also discuss the findings of phases I and II with this group, feeding their views into the research recommendations. A pre-existing group of young people will also be consulted through Hyndburn and Ribble Valley Domestic Violence Team (HARV ) in East Lancashire. Throughout the synthesis we will consult two patient and public involvement groups consisting of survivors of domestic violence in Bristol and Cardiff, initially established to support PROVIDE (http://www.provide.ac.uk/), an NIHR applied research programme. The groups, each numbering 6-10 women will inform the detailed design of the synthesis, input their views when the findings are interpreted and when the research recommendations are developed and disseminated. Phase IV: Final formulation of research recommendations and dissemination of findings including research design, types of interventions, potential comparators, duration of intervention(s), target population groups, potential outcome measures. Outputs will include reports to funders and relevant agenices. Timetable (18/12) months Phase I: 1-14 Phase II: 12-16 Phase III: 4-16 Phase IV: 14-18

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Development and evaluation of a novel intervention providing insight into the tobacco industry to prevent the uptake of smoking in school-aged children
Abstract: Design: Iterative design, piloting, assessment and refinement of a multi-component intervention, whose effectiveness will then be evaluated in a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Setting: Secondary schools in the East Midlands. Target population: Students aged 11-13, the age group where large numbers of young people begin to experiment with smoking. Intervention: This project will develop and test a new intervention comprising materials for schools and families to prevent the uptake of smoking in young people. We plan to pilot, evaluate and refine a promising novel resource (Operation Smoke Storm) developed by the Hammersmith and Fulham Stop Smoking Service, for teachers delivering Personal, Social, Health and Economic (PSHE) education, in which young people assume the role of secret agents working undercover in the tobacco industry. Operation Smoke Storm is strongly evidence-based and draws heavily on the ideas of the US Truth Campaign. The package combines paper-based, audiovisual and online interactive components, delivered over three hour-long classroom-based sessions, providing conventional information on the health impacts of active and passive smoking in association with content not previously widely used in youth smoking prevention in the UK (including insights into marketing tactics, environmental impacts of the tobacco industry and exploitation of developing country populations). In a small-scale evaluation of acceptability and ease of use in two London schools it has been very positively evaluated and feedback has been used to inform initial refinements. We will pilot the use of Operation Smoke Storm with Year 7 students, and in addition will develop a booster component for use in Year 8 to maintain and strengthen any positive effects of Operation Smoke Storm, as well as a family-based component intended to promote communication about smoking between children and their parents in line with a promising developing body of literature. Qualitative work with students and teachers will inform the development of these materials; their exact nature will be finalised by the end of the first year of the study. In the design of both the booster and family components we will take as a starting point resources proven effective in earlier studies, such as printed materials, videos and online materials, considering the acceptability and practicality of their use in the UK. Measurement of outcomes, duration of follow-up and planned analyses: As our primary outcome in both the development phase and main trial we will measure the proportion of students who are current smokers or susceptible to smoking at the final follow-up point in Year 8 and compare this between those who have and have not received the intervention. In the development phase this comparison will be between the combined proportion of Year 8 students in our two schools reporting current smoking or susceptibility after receiving the intervention with the proportion of Year 8 students from the same two schools reporting these behaviours in a survey we carried out shortly before our research started. We will judge the intervention to be effective if the confidence interval for the difference in prevalence between the two groups excludes the possibility of no change. If this preliminary evidence proves encouraging (for example, with a 7% absolute difference in current or susceptibility to smoking between Year 8 students who have and have not received the intervention, in line with that seen in the ASSIST study, and with schools willing to be involved in further work), we will carry out a cluster-randomised controlled trial over one year, delivering the school and family-based components to students in Years 7 and 8. Our primary comparison here will be between intervention and control schools, using a multilevel model to take into account the clustering of students within form groups and schools, including as covariates baseline smoking behaviour, school stratifying variables, and other demographic variables that are predictors of the smoking outcome to adjust for any baseline differences and to improve power. The work needed to develop the intervention means it will not be possible to undertake a definitive evaluation with longer term follow-up at reasonable cost. Thus, our cluster-randomised controlled trial will form the first stage of a longitudinal study; we intend to apply for funding at a later date to allow us to follow up students to the end of Year 11. The study will estimate the cost-effectiveness of the intervention in line with previous studies. The costs of the programme (materials and staff time) will be estimated using local costs. Potential health care cost savings will also be estimated from the reductions in current smoking and susceptibility to smoking. The reduction in current smoking and susceptibility will be used to model quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gains and combined with the costs to estimate cost per QALY. During the development phase focus groups and depth interviews with students and teachers will be used to map the key components of the intervention, to explore its acceptability and feasibility, and to provide feedback to inform refinements. Work will be carried out with boys and girls separately in each pilot school, with the aim of reaching theme saturation; data will be analysed using the framework method. We will also undertake a process evaluation during the main trial to assess the delivery of the intervention, using staff questionnaires and observations of delivery. Sample size: A cluster randomised trial with 20 schools in each arm (and 150 pupils in Year 7) will provide just over 80% power to detect a 7% absolute difference in combined current smoking and susceptibility to smoking in Year 8 between intervention and control schools (e.g. from 35% to 28%). Project timetable: Months 1-24: Ethics approval; recruit schools; exploratory trial of Operation Smoke Storm in Year 7 with pre-and post-survey evaluation of changes in current smoking and uptake susceptibility; qualitative work to develop resources for use in Year 8 and with families; deliver complete intervention; assess evidence for effectiveness. Months 25-27: ethics approval for main cluster randomised trial; school recruitment. Months 28-43: Cluster randomised trial. Analysis and publication of results.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Reducing binge drinking among disadvantaged men through a brief intervention delivered by mobile phone: a multi-centre randomised controlled trial
Abstract: Design: The study is a four centre parallel group randomised controlled trial. The components of the study were developed and tested in a feasibility study. Target population: Men aged 25-44 years living in areas of high deprivation who have had two or more episodes of binge drinking (>8 units in a single session) in the preceding month. To ensure good coverage of disadvantaged men two recruitment strategies will be used: through primary care and by community outreach. Intervention: The intervention is a series of Short Message Service (SMS) delivered by mobile phone. The intervention is based on effective empirical studies on alcohol and text message interventions. It employs theoretical models of behaviour change particularly the Health Action Process Approach and incorporates techniques from Motivational Interviewing and Communication Theory. The messages were constructed to take advantage of the conventional pattern of heavy weekend drinking: before weekend drinking, after a heavy drinking episode and midweek sobriety. Messages are tailored to the drinking culture of disadvantaged young men and use popular texting terms and abbreviations. Techniques to increase message effectiveness include: use of gain-framed texts; pairing of messages; and inclusion of questions to promote interactivity. The text messages will be sent over a 12 week period and will deliver the behaviour change strategy in four stages. Stage 1 welcomes the men to the study, establishes empathy and increases the salience of the short term harms of binge drinking. Stage 2 creates the intention to reduce binge drinking by highlighting the discrepancy between an individual's drinking habits (becoming drunk) and the intended aims of drinking (having fun and socialising). It will promote engagement with the benefits of moderated drinking and increase self-efficacy for refusing drinks. Stage 3 transforms intention into action by encouraging goal setting and the formation of action plans and coping plans. Stage 4 supports the maintenance of long term behaviour change. Outcome measures and duration of outcome: Outcomes will be assessed at 3 months and 12 months from the end of the intervention. The primary outcome measure is the frequency of binge drinking (consumption of >8 units in a single session) at 12 months. This outcome is particularly suitable for disadvantaged men: the feasibility study showed that most of the participants had regular episodes of binge drinking with periods of complete abstinence in between. The frequency of binge drinking at 3 months will assess the short term impact of the intervention. The Fast Alcohol Screening Test (FAST) will be used to determine the frequency of hazardous drinking. Total consumption of alcohol will be measured to ensure comparability with previous brief intervention trials. Sample size: The sample size is 798 men. The feasibility study showed that 57% of men had 3 or more binge drinking sessions in the previous 30 days. We aim to detect a reduction in the proportion of men drinking in this way from 57% to 46%, a net reduction of 11% (as significance at p=0.05 with a power of 80%). A recent systematic review of conventional brief interventions found an 11% difference in frequency of binge drinking between intervention and control. The sample size allows for a 20% loss to follow-up. We expect that the loss to follow-up will be less than this, as the loss in our three month feasibility study was only 4%. However, as most alcohol brief intervention trials have a loss to follow-up at 12 months of over 20%, it is prudent to make suitable allowance. Planned analyses: The effect size of the primary outcome will be presented as proportions, odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals. The secondary outcomes will be assessed in a similar way. Further analyses will use logistic regression to explore which of the cognitive antecedents of behaviour change predict change in the primary outcome. The analysis will also explore whether the recruitment method (through primary care or community outreach) influences treatment effect. Project timetable: Months 1-2: Trial manager induction. Obtain for ethical permission. Establish the steering committee and register the trial. Months 3-8: Conduct fieldwork for recruitment. Update the text messages, the computer programme for intervention delivery and the questionnaires. Prepare for the economic evaluation. Train research staff. Months 9-18: Screen disadvantaged men to recruit 798 in total. Conduct baseline interviews. Randomise. Deliver the intervention. Months 15-24: Conduct three month post-intervention delivery follow-up interviews. Months 24-33: Conduct twelve month post-intervention follow-up interviews. Months 34-39: Analysis, report preparation and dissemination. Prepare papers for publication.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Cranberries for preventing urinary tract infections
Abstract: "Scientific/policy justification for review/review update UTI is very common throughout life. Around 8% of girls, 2% of boys1 and 60% of women experience an infection2. UTI is also common in the elderly. UTI tends to recur, and occurs in 20-30% in women and 19% in children who have had at least one UTI3. In the spinal injured population the recurrence rate is 1.82 UTI episodes/patient/year4. Cranberry is very widely used to prevent UTI because it is universally available and is perceived as ‘natural’ and free from side effects. This Cochrane review is one of the most highly cited, viewed and downloaded of all Cochrane Reviews, in the past 3 months it has been viewed 955 times5. The review was last updated in September 2007 and included 10 trials enrolling elderly women and men (3), children with neuropathic bladder (1), adult women (3), and adults with spinal cord damage (3). An updated search has identified 25 articles, with a wider spectrum of participants, including men, men with prostate adenocarcinoma, children, pregnant women and patients with multiple sclerosis along with further trials in women and the elderly. An updated review will address the previously unanswered questions of dose, and the spectrum of potential patients who may benefit. References 1.Hellstrom A, Hanson E, Hansson S, Hjalmas K, Jodal U. Association between urinary symptoms at 7 years old and previous urinary tract Infection. Arch. Dis. Child. 1991; 66: 232–4. 2.Nicolle LE (2008). ""Uncomplicated urinary tract infection in adults including uncomplicated pyelonephritis"". Urol Clin North Am 35 (1): 1–12
Award Budget: Williams GJ et al. Antibiotic prophylaxis and recurrent urinary tract infection in children. N. Engl. J. Med. 2009;361: 1748–59. 4.Waites KB

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Services for reducing duration of hospital care for acute stroke patients
Abstract: Scientific/policy justification for review/review update Stroke is the commonest cause of severe acquired adult disability in the UK. Most stroke patients are admitted to hospital where they usually receive their rehabilitation. Services have been developed that offer patients an early discharge from hospital with more rehabilitation at home (early supported discharge, ESD). The original Cochrane Review of 11 trials (1597 patients) suggested that appropriately resourced ESD services provided for a selected group of stroke patients may reduce long term dependency and admission to institutional care as well as reducing the length of hospital stay. These initial observations influenced clinical guidelines and encouraged some development of such services in the UK. However more robust information from a wider range of settings would greatly assist service planning. We are currently aware of at least a further six trials (700 patients) that cover two new countries and five novel service settings (rehabilitation hospitals rather than acute). The inclusion of this additional information should go a long way to clarifying the role of ESD services in the routine NHS setting.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Pandemic Influenza: Population susceptibility, severity and spread. Rapid Research using the Health Survey for England (HSE)
Abstract: Project Title: Pandemic Influenza: Population susceptibility, severity and spread. Rapid Research using the Health Survey for England (HSE) Scientific Abstract: Design. Serial cross sectional serological prevalence surveys with retrospective ascertainment of vaccination and respiratory illness history in conjunction with the National Health Survey for England (HSE). Setting. Community household setting across England. Target population. Households participating in the Health Survey for England (HSE). Technology being assessed. Use of HSE as a rapid means of determining population level immunity, severity and spread through the first two waves of a pandemic. Measurement of outcomes. Antibody response to influenza strain of interest in vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals. Measurement of population rates of clinical influenza-like-illness. National hospitalisation and case fatality rates. Phase 1 - Retrospective Validation of 2010 population level clinical illness rates derived from HSE by comparison with MRC/Wellcome Flu Watch study (March - June 2014). N= 2952 Phase 2 - Pilot of specimen and data collection alongside HSE (already happened October 2012 - April 2013) and the analysis and reporting of the data (July 2013 - March 2014). N=3216 Phase 3 - Holding phase - project ethically approved each year but only triggered in the event of a pandemic. Phase 4 - Real time monitoring through the first two phases of a pandemic - repeat methodology for phase 2 to provide rapid estimates of severity and spread and monitor through the pandemic. N= 4000 Expertise. UCL and National Centre for Social Research - Unparalleled expertise in population survey methodology and large scale serological studies. Impact. Early measures of age specific severity and spread of infection will allow targeting of vaccines, antivirals and non-pharmaceutical interventions and enable response to be proportionate to severity.

Award_Title: Double-blinded randomised controlled trial of early low dose steroids in patients admitted to hospital with influenza infection during a pandemic
Abstract: Design: Pragmatic mutli-centre double-blind randomized trial. Setting: Hospital in-patient services in England, Scotland and Wales Target Population: Adults (> 16 years old) hospitalized with an influenza-like illness during a pandemic. Health Technologies being assessed: Dexmethasone 6 mg once daily for 5 days from the day of hospital admission, given as adjuvant therapy, in addition to standard care. Based on current national guidelines, standard care will be expected to comprise of supportive measures (fluid and oxygen supplementation), antivirals and antibiotics as appropriate. Measurement of outcomes: The choice of primary outcome measure takes account of the need for simplicity in a trial conducted during a pandemic and of how pandemic severity influences clinical priorities. For a high severity pandemic, a high proportion will be admitted to intensive care, and/or die and so in this situation the primary outcome would be the composite measure of death or admission to intensive care. For a low/ moderate severity pandemic, severe adverse outcomes are less likely, and the primary outcome would be length of stay in hospital. Secondary outcomes include length of stay in intensive care unit > 7 days, readmission within 30 days of hospital discharge, GP consultation within 30 days of hospital discharge, death in hospital. Sample size: Our planned sample size of 2,200 patients is based on the range of possible scenarios that might be encountered during a pandemic. With 2,200 patients, the study will have 90% power to detect a 15% relative reduction in the primary outcome (admission to intensive care or death) in a high severity pandemic. A sample size of 1000 patients will have 90% power to detect a 20% relative reduction in length of stay in a low/moderate severity pandemic.
