Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Evaluating and improving communication with the public during a pandemic, using rapid turn around telephone surveys
Abstract: DESIGN: The project has four stages. The first three occur prior to the pandemic, the fourth during the pandemic. Stage 1 consists of meetings with stakeholders and a re-review of existing literature. This will allow us to generate items for a new telephone survey that will assess uptake and predictors of protective behaviours among the general public during a pandemic. Stage 2 consists of three rounds of cognitive interviews which we will use to refine the wording of our new questions. Stage 3 consists of a cross-sectional telephone survey of a randomly selected, demographically representative sample of the British population during a normal flu season, with a one week follow-up of the same sample. Stage 4 consists of weekly telephone surveys conducted during the pandemic, with follow-up of specific samples as required. SETTING: Stages 1 and 2 will take place within King's College London. Telephone surveys in Stages 3 and 4 will recruit representative samples of the general public within Britain. TARGET POPULATION: Members of the general British public, aged 16 or over. HEALTH TECHNOLOGIES BEING ASSESSED: We will assess an improved version of the telephone survey used by the Department of Health to assess uptake and predictors of recommended behaviours among the public during the 2009/10 pandemic. MEASUREMENT OF OUTCOMES: The selection of outcome variables to be measured in our Stage 3 and 4 surveys will be determined as part of our project. We will ask stakeholders from the Department of Health and Health Protection Agency what protective behaviours they are most likely to recommended to members of the public in the next pandemic. Initial consultation suggests that these behaviours are likely to include respiratory and hand hygiene, vaccine uptake (intended and actual) and use of healthcare resources (actual and intended). Secondary outcomes will include the presence of self-reported influenza-like illness among the population. If data concerning these outcomes are to inform policy in real-time during a pandemic, the must pragmatic and robust option is to use a series of telephone surveys to obtain self-report data on performance of these behaviours among the public. SAMPLE SIZE: A total sample size of 30 participants for each round of interviews in Stage Two will allow sufficient opportunity for any obvious difficulties with question wording to emerge. Sample sizes of 1,067 participants for the surveys in Stages Three and Four will provide us with a sample error of plus or minus three percentage points for our prevalence rates. PROJECT TIMETABLE: Our pre-pandemic work will take seven months. Stage 1 will begin on 1 August 2012, Stage 2 on 1 October 2012 and Stage 3 on 1 December 2013 (the first available flu season for this study). We will submit our interim report detailing our new survey template on 1 March 2013. In Stage 4, we propose running surveys for the first six months of the pandemic.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: FRESH - Facilitating Return to work through Early Specialist Health-based interventions
Abstract: Vocational Rehabilitation is defined as ‘whatever helps someone with a health problem return to or remain in work’. It involves helping people find work; helping people who are in work but having difficulties; and supporting career progression in spite of illness or disability. Health based services supporting people with traumatic brain injury in returning to work are rare in the UK. This 3-year research project is a feasibility randomised control trial with a nested qualitative process evaluation across 3 NHS traumatic brain injury referral centres. The purpose of the study is to develop a treatment manual, training package and mentoring model based on the Nottingham model of Early Specialist Traumatic Brain Injury Vocational Rehabilitation and to test the feasibility of delivering it and measuring its effects and costs in three new NHS sites in a multi-centre feasibility randomised control trial. The primary objectives of the feasibility study are: a) To determine whether an Early Specialist Traumatic Brain Injury vocational rehabilitation package (manual, training and mentoring model) based on an existing NHS service in Nottingham can be developed and implemented in 3 different NHS regional traumatic brain injury referral centres with differing service configurations. b) To determine whether we can test the feasibility of delivering early specialist traumatic brain injury vocational rehabilitation (ESTVR) in these referral centres and of measuring its impact and cost effectiveness (compared to usual NHS care) on return to work (finding new work for those unable to return to an existing job) and job retention (return to work with an existing employer) in a multi-centre feasibility randomised control trial. c) To determine whether early specialist traumatic brain injury vocational rehabilitation can be delivered in a way that is acceptable to traumatic brain injury patients, staff and employers when compared to usual NHS rehabilitation. d) To determine whether we can identify primary outcomes of an NHS early specialist traumatic brain injury vocational rehabilitation service important to service users, NHS service providers and professionals. 102 participants, across 3 NHS centres, with a new traumatic brain injury, admitted to hospital for = 48 hours, over 16 years of age and working or in full time education at time of injury. Participants will be randomly allocated to intervention group or control group. Intervention group: early specialist vocational rehabilitation targeted at preventing job loss (up to 6 sessions) delivered by an occupational therapist, supported by a traumatic brain injury case manager (up to 5 sessions) in addition to usual NHS care Control Group: usual NHS care only The duration of treatment will be 12 months for both groups with questionnaires completed at baseline, 3 months, 6 months and 12 months. A nested qualitative study (interviews and focus groups) will investigate participants’ (service users and employers) and service providers’ (staff) beliefs about important outcomes following vocational rehabilitation, their views of the acceptability and usefulness of the early specialist traumatic brain injury vocational rehabilitation package (manual, package and mentoring system) and of the intervention. It will explore implementation barriers and perceived changes in practice resulting from training and the anticipated and actual effects (including costs) of implementation on supporting services. Findings will be used to inform a definitive multi-centre randomised control trial.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: The future of 24/7 care: investigating the links between staffing levels, patient access and inequalities in health outcomes
Abstract: Background The National Health Service (NHS) was founded on fundamental principles of equity, and the current Government’s long-term vision is of an NHS that eliminates discrimination and reduces inequalities in care [Department of Health 2012]. However, patients’ outcomes are strongly dependent on the time that they are admitted to hospital. At night and during weekends staffing levels are lower, clinical support services are unavailable or are functioning on an 'on-request' basis, and senior clinical staff are located off site. Current evidence suggests that patients presenting to health services at these times suffer higher complication and mortality rates than patients admitted at times when services are fully operational. Extending the hours for which the NHS is fully operational therefore has the potential to improve access, increase the use of inputs by health service providers, and improve outcomes for patients. However, extending fully operational hours could also decrease efficiency by raising input costs and providing services that are relatively under-utilised. Research Aims In order to understand how extending fully-operational hours will affect costs and outcomes, research is needed into the relationships between staffing levels, costs, patient outcomes, and quality of care. These relationships are poorly understood because the rich information routinely collected in patient healthcare records is not linked to the data collected by employers on staff inputs and costs. We propose to link these data in an acute Trust – Salford Royal Foundation Trust (SRFT) – that has gradually extended its hours of full operation since 2007, culminating in the implementation of an ‘Emergency Village’ service in 2012, providing consultant-led care from 7am to 11pm, seven days per week. We will link these data to identify, for each patient care episode, the staff available to provide direct patient care and the availability of direct patient care support services. We will exploit the natural variability in staffing composition and levels over time of day, day of week and week of year, to estimate the association between staff inputs and aspects of patient care, including length of stay, in-hospital complications and mortality. We will also identify the effect on patient care and outcomes of service reconfigurations that extend fully-operational hours. This will enable us to answer four key questions: • What is the impact of changes to fully-operational hours on access to services for different population and patient groups? • How do service re-configurations affect quality of care and patient outcomes for different population and patient groups? • How should staff be best deployed to deliver care throughout the week? • What balance of fully-operational hours represents the most cost-effective use of NHS resources? Data Sources SRFT is at the leading-edge of electronic patient record linkage across primary, secondary, and community care. In partnership with Salford Primary Care Trust it has created the Salford Integrated Record (SIR), with 165 million medical records for over 300,000 patients. SRFT has also been routinely collecting staffing information electronically since 2007. These data can be integrated to generate a unique dataset, including information on: • Patient episodes: admission time, diagnosis, procedures and interventions, length of stay. • Patient demographics: age, sex, ethnicity, postcode, general practice. • Quality of care: patient experience, complications, readmissions, mortality. • Staffing data: number, grade, specialty, skill-mix, remuneration and compensation (hourly pay rates, time in lieu). • Primary care provision: general practice working hours, quality of care, practice characteristics (list size, staffing, qualifications, disease prevalence), prescribing. Comparative patient-level data are also available (from the Advancing Quality Initiative) for all 24 Trusts in the North West of England on quality of care for pneumonia, heart failure, acute myocardial infarction, stroke, and for hip or knee replacement surgery. Analytical Approach In the first phases of the study, we will examine whether achievement of process measures for quality of care and patient outcomes vary by time and day of admission. For Salford Royal, we will link these process measures to staffing levels at the relevant times to identify whether staff availability predicts variations in achievement. Staff costs will be decomposed into variations in the volume of staff on duty, and individual-level linked staff information will be used to examine the implications of anti-social working for staff turnover. The estimated models will enable us to compute the additional costs that would be incurred if staffing levels at anti-social times were to be equalised to staffing times in preferred working hours. The linked data from primary care records will allow us to follow individual patients across sectors and over time in order to examine how patient pathways across care interfaces vary by time of day and day of week. For example, we can examine similar entry and exit points with primary care services on weeknights and weekends and determine whether exacerbations of symptoms first treated in primary care are more likely to lead to A&E presentations if they occur out-of-hours compared with in-hours. We will also examine whether health care needs are met in an integrated health system, including the impact of service reconfigurations in one sector – for example the hospital – on service providers in other sectors. Using data on the adoption of extended opening hours by individual general practices, we will also examine how initiatives to extend opening hours in primary care impact on demands placed on the hospital sector. In the third phase, we will extend the study to other hospitals. For all 24 Acute Trusts in the North West of England, we will examine whether achievement of process measures of quality vary by time of admission and day of admission. For at least one Trust in the NHS QUEST Network we will examine in detail the relationships between processes of care and staffing levels, and compare these relationships to results for Salford Royal. Research Impact This research will provide vital information on the costs, benefits and potential unintended consequences of extending the hours of full operation of services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Interventions to promote or maintain physical activity during and after the transition to retirement: evidence synthesis to inform recommendations for policy and practice.
Abstract: Most people over the age of 50 in the UK are sedentary and the vast majority fail to meet current government guidelines on the amount of activity recommended for improving health [4]. Older people may reduce their level of physical activity when they move from paid work into retirement [2,12]. People who are less well off, as well as those who have less choice over whether to retire or not are the most likely to experience a decline in activity at retirement [3]. Although we know that these problems exist in society we know less about what should be done to encourage people to be more active after they retire. Further, the point of retirement presents a risk for widening health inequalities between social classes, and so interventions in this area have the potential to address such inequalities. Currently available review evidence gives some indication that retirement (and the transition to retirement) represents a promising life stage for physical activity interventions [2,13,14,16], but does not shed much light on all the relevant factors; particularly around specific types of interventions, and interventions for different population groups, in different circumstances and states of health, and experiencing very different paths to retirement. In particular, the effectiveness of interventions and the implications of socioeconomic status on their effectiveness have yet to be considered together in one synthesis. In order to address this research gap, we will conduct a meta-synthesis of physical activity interventions for older people not in paid employment part or full time, and those about to leave paid employment. We will consider studies which report on the effectiveness of interventions but also studies which identify how the perceptions of both older people and service deliverers may act as facilitators or obstacles to successful outcomes following intervention. Further we will aim to understand how encouraging physical activity after retirement might potentially contribute to reducing health inequalities. We will generate a critical meta-synthesis of the evidence suitable to inform policy decisions and disseminate to relevant audiences. Systematic searches will be undertaken to identify recently published relevant studies as well as unpublished material (grey literature) where possible. Scoping workshops with key stakeholders will assist with developing the protocol and search strategies. Supplementary search methods such as contacting key authors will also be undertaken. Data will be analysed initially to generate a critical synthesis to answer each research question individually. Subsequently, a meta-synthesis of findings will be generated to combine quantitative intervention effectiveness data with qualitative findings to generate key messages. The meta-synthesis will allow us to examine the effect of the social and cultural issues surrounding intervention effectiveness and acceptability, including the impact on health inequalities. We have successfully implemented meta-synthesis methods in similar topic areas to generate policy relevant messages (e.g. physical activity promotion by GPs [18] and interventions to encourage walking/cycling [19]). Our findings and key messages will be validated and refined through stakeholder workshops to include older people of varying socioeconomic backgrounds, service providers and funders, and topic experts.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Increasing boys’ and girls’ intention to avoid teenage pregnancy: feasibility trial of an interactive video drama based intervention in post-primary schools in Northern Ireland
Abstract: Rationale: The If I Were Jack intervention aims to increase the intention of both boys and girls to avoid teenage pregnancy and addresses gender inequalities in RSE provision by explicitly focusing on young men and teenage pregnancy. The need for gender-sensitive interventions to address teenage pregnancy has been highlighted as a global health need by the World Health Organisation [41,42] and recommended in systematic reviews [14,43,44]. The intervention has been designed specifically for use across the range of schools in NI, but it is based on international research regarding effective RSE interventions. This study will begin a process of robust evaluation which may lead to the roll-out of the intervention across the UK and international applications of the intervention. The research and policy community will benefit because the proposed research process provides a model for an inclusive, collaborative approach to the development of research-based resources that is potentially transferable to other areas of policy and curriculum. Study Aim: To determine the feasibility of conducting an effectiveness trial of the If I were Jack RSE intervention in post-primary schools. Study Objectives: The study will 1) assess the acceptability of the intervention to schools (principals and RSE teachers), pupils and parents; 2) identify optimal delivery structures and systems for the delivery of the resource in the classroom; 3) establish intervention participation rates and reach, including equality of engagement across schools of different socio-economic and religious types; 4) assess trial recruitment and retention rates; 5) ascertain variation in normal RSE practice across the participating schools; 6) develop and refine survey instruments for use in a phase III trial; 7) assess differences in outcomes for male and female pupils; 8) identify potential effect sizes that might be detected in an effectiveness trial and estimate appropriate sample size; and 9) identify the costs of delivering If I were Jack and pilot the methods for economic analysis in a phase III trial. The Intervention: The intervention is a classroom-based RSE resource designed to be delivered by teachers over four weeks, which also involves parents in the RSE process. The development of the intervention was informed by baseline data on adolescent men’s attitudes to unintended pregnancy and the best available evidence regarding the components of effective RSE interventions. It was designed to fit with the RSE curriculum by a team of researchers working with experts from the Department of Health, Social Services and Public Safety, the Public Health Agency, and the Council for the Curriculum, Examinations and Assessment, as well as teacher trainers, teachers, parents and young people. Although produced in Northern Ireland the intervention would have strong cultural resonance for the UK as a whole. It uses an innovative combination of intervention components to address identified deficits in existing RSE interventions: 1) uses a culturally sensitive interactive video drama to immerse young people in a case scenario of an unintended pregnancy; 2) develops this case scenario of an unintended pregnancy from a teenage man's point of view; 3) targets a number of behavioural and sexual psychosocial variables including knowledge; attitudes; perceptions of risk, peer norms and gender norms; self-efficacy in communication; and intention to avoid sexual risk-taking behaviour in order to help boys, as well as girls, build skills to avoid teenage pregnancy; 4) provides comprehensive training and information about teenage pregnancy for teachers/RSE facilitators; and 5) incorporates communication about teenage pregnancy within the classroom as well as with parents/guardians. It is composed of a number of components: I/ The If I Were Jack interactive video drama (IVD) which asks pupils to put themselves in Jack’s shoes and consider how they would feel and what they would do if they were Jack; II/ Classroom materials for teachers containing four detailed lesson plans with specific classroom-based and homework activities which include group discussions, role-plays, worksheets, and a parent-pupil exercise; III/ 60-minute training session for teachers wishing to implement the intervention; IV/ 60-minute information and discussion session for parents/guardians delivered by RSE teachers; and V/ Detailed information brochures and factsheets about the intervention and unintended teenage pregnancy in general for schools, teachers, teacher trainers, young people and parents. Further details on the If I Were Jack resource, including excerpts from the IVD and feedback from end-users regarding the acceptability of the IVD, are available from: www.qub.ac.uk/IfIWereJack Study Design: This is a phase II feasibility trial, with schools as the unit of randomisation, with an embedded process evaluation. Seven schools will participate. Each participating pupil will be in the study for approximately nine months and will be asked to complete a questionnaire three times – at baseline and five and nine months later. The process evaluation will include semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions with a sample of pupils, teachers, and parents regarding the acceptability and feasibility of the questionnaire, the intervention, and participation in the trial. It will also include observations of a sample of lessons and parents’ information sessions. Study Outcomes: In this feasibility study, key outcomes will be the quality of intervention implementation, and recruitment and retention of research participants. The study will also pilot the feasibility and acceptability of collecting demographic information and other sexual-psychosocial data relating to measuring the proposed primary and secondary outcomes in a future phase III trial, so that potential response rates can be determined, optimal data collection identified, and the costs of these data collection methods assessed.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: INCLUSIVE trial: Initiating change locally in bullying and aggression through the school environment
Abstract: We will undertake a cluster-randomised trial to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the INCLUSIVE intervention in reducing aggression and bullying in 40 English secondary schools. Main research question: Is the INCLUSIVE intervention effective and cost-effective in reducing aggression and bullying in 11-15 year olds in English schools Intervention Schools in the intervention arm will implement the INCLUSIVE intervention over 3 years, 2 of which involve external facilitation. INCLUSIVE is a school-led intervention which combines changes to the school environment with the promotion of social and emotional skills and restorative practices through: the formation of a school action group involving students and staff supported by an external facilitator to review local data on needs, determine priorities, and develop and implement an action plan for revising relevant school policies/rules and other actions to improve relationships at school and reduce aggression; staff training in restorative practices; and a new social and emotional skills curriculum. The intervention combines strong fidelity of inputs, processes and core components with the capacity for tailoring non-core components to local needs. Delivery: The intervention will be delivered by schools, through the school action groups, supported by educational facilitators. Funding: We are seeking intervention funding from charities that funded these costs in our pilot trial (Paul Hamlyn Foundation, Big Lottery Fund). NHS components: There are no NHS staff involved in the delivery of this intervention. 1. Participants: 40 state-supported secondary schools in England. INCLUSIVE is designed to affect all students in participating schools, however outcomes will be assessed among students in year 8 in the 1st intervention year, moving through to year 10 in the 3rd year. 2. Comparator: Normal practice. 3. Outcomes Primary: Two primary outcomes at individual student level will be assessed at baseline and at the 36 month follow-up: 1. Aggressive behaviours in school: measured by the Edinburgh Study of Youth Transitions and Crime school misbehaviour subscale (ESYTC) 2. Bullying and victimisation: measured by the Gatehouse Bullying Scale (GBS) Secondary: Student level and teaching staff level secondary outcomes will be assessed at the 24 months and 36 month surveys. School level outcomes will be assessed at 24 and 36 months. a. Student level: Quality of life: Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) Psychological function: Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) Well-being: Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale (SWEMWBS), Health risk behaviours: Smoking, alcohol & illicit drug use, sexual risk behaviours NHS use: Use of categories of NHS services in past year Contact with police: in past year b. Teaching staff level: stress, quality of life, work absences. c. School level: Truancy and exclusion rates. Economic evaluation: Child Health Utility Questionnaire (CHU-9D), staff quality of life, costs. Process: An integral process evaluation will examine intervention delivery and receipt, fidelity, coverage, acceptability and contextual influences; and explore intervention logic model and causal pathways. Impact: A universal intervention that reduces anti-social behaviour and risk behaviours and improves well-being in secondary schools has broad potential to reduce the high costs of anti-social behaviour and reduce inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A randomised controlled trial to examine the efficacy of e-cigarettes compared with nicotine replacement therapy, when used within the UK stop smoking service
Abstract: Background Electronic cigarettes (EC) closely mimic the sensory aspects of smoking while delivering levels of nicotine comparable to that delivered by oral nicotine replacement products [9, 10]. Their use is gaining in popularity [11-13], with smokers using them as a safer alternative to tobacco or for smoking cessation [11, 14, 15]. Nicotine itself is relatively harmless; the risks of smoking are linked to poisonous chemicals contained in the smoke from a burning cigarette. The tobacco control community are divided on their opinions of EC, but there is agreement that more data are urgently needed on whether EC match the efficacy of other existing treatments in helping smokers quit or reduce smoking. Several studies have suggested that EC have a substantial potential as a stop-smoking treatment but no study has compared it to a standard intensive treatment so far. EC are cheaper than nicotine replacement therapy (NRT; and the other prescription non-nicotine smoking cessation medicines), and hold greater appeal to smokers [1, 7]. There are few other smoking cessation treatment improvements on the horizon and EC are the most promising current development awaiting objective scrutiny. Health care commissioners need to know if they are as effective as NRT when used with the support routinely provided by the UK stop-smoking service (SSS). This proposal aims to provide this information. Design Randomized controlled trial. Setting Two SSS that provide evidence-based treatment to smokers who are typically highly dependent and from economically deprived backgrounds. Strategy for research and modelling A straightforward trial comparing EC to no treatment is not ethically acceptable and it will also not clarify the value of EC in the current treatment landscape. Smokers will be randomized to usual care (UC) including standard NRT or EC. Both groups will receive multi-session behavioural support. Target population 886 smokers seeking help who are 18 years or older, not currently pregnant or breast-feeding and can read/write/understand English. Health technologies being assessed EC are battery-powered devices that provide inhaled doses of nicotine by delivering a vaporized liquid nicotine solution in propylene glycol or glycerol. No tobacco, smoke, or combustion is involved in their operation and no clinically significant levels of any harmful chemicals have been detected in EC vapour [5]. We will provide a starter-kit to participants in the EC arm. We have consulted EC users who advise that the flavour and strength of the refill liquid is an important but very personal choice. Therefore we will direct people to select and purchase their own refill liquid. This will (a) ensure that people use a refill liquid they like; (b) reflect what happens in ‘real life’; and (c) avoid giving the EC arm an advantage of free treatment when some people in the UC arm will have to pay a prescription charge. Recruitment Smokers seeking help will be recruited from local SSS and by advertisements in local papers. Procedure Prospective participants will attend a screening session and those eligible will provide informed consent, demographic data and details of smoking history, and be randomised to one of the two study arms. Usual Care (UC) arm Participants will be assisted in selecting NRT of their choice as per usual practice. The NRT will be provided on letter of recommendation to supply (a local scheme for supplying NRT) for up to three months, as per standard practice. Participants will attend 6 weekly support sessions and attend follow-up appointments at 6 and 12 months. EC arm Participants will be given an EC starter-kit. They will be provided with instructions on how to operate the EC. An information sheet written by experienced EC users will also be provided. Participants will be encouraged to try different refill e-liquids and provided with details of suppliers of e-liquids. Support and follow-up contacts will be identical to those in the UC arm. Measurement of outcomes and costs The primary outcome will be abstinence at one year defined as per Russell Standard [8]. Secondary outcomes will include abstinence at 4-weeks and 6 months, smoking reduction in participants who did not achieve full abstinence, ratings of the treatment, adverse events, and the cost-efficacy of the interventions. An intention to treat analysis will be used with participants lost to follow-up included as non-abstainers [8]. Sample size The 12-month validated abstinence rate associated with UC is expected to be 14% [18]. To detect an 8% increase in abstinence rates at 1-year (i.e. 14% to 22%, RR=1.57, power = 85%, alpha = 0.05) a total of 886 participants (443 in each group) are required. Project timetables: Study set up – 6 months, recruitment period – 21 months, completion of follow-ups – 12 months, data analysis and study write-up – 3 months, total 42 months. Recruitment strategy We will recruit smokers via SSS over 21 months. Currently each service treats around 380 smokers per year (approximately 1330 in total over 21 months). If two thirds will be interested in taking part in this study, 886 participants will be recruited over 21 months with no additional recruitment initiatives. We will, however, also conduct additional recruitment by advertising in local papers. This was an effective method of recruitment in our previous trials. However, given the non-traditional nature of EC, we propose to conduct a 6-month internal pilot in the first year to evaluate recruitment rate and study acceptability.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Understanding uptake of Immunisations in Travelling and Gypsy communities (UNITING)
Abstract: AIMS:1. To investigate the barriers and facilitators to acceptability and uptake of immunisations amongst six Traveller communities (comprising five distinct ethnic/cultural groups) across four UK cities; 2. To identify possible interventions to increase uptake of immunisations in diverse Traveller communities, to test in a subsequent feasibility study. DESIGN: This is a 3-linked phase qualitative study. Phase 1: Qualitative individual/group interviews with Travellers. Phase 2: Qualitative individual interviews with health and community workers who work with the Traveller communities. Phase 3: Feedback Workshops with a sub sample of participants from Phases 1 and 2 at which we will refine and produce a prioritised list of potentially feasible and acceptable interventions. This proposed research is the first ‘intervention development’ phase of the MRC framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions. It is framed within a Social Ecological Model which recognises that behaviour is affected by, and effects, multiple levels of influence. SETTING AND TARGET POPULATION: PHASE 1: Travellers from each of six communities (comprising five distinct ethnic/cultural groups) located in four cities: York (English Roma), Bristol (English Gypsies, Eastern European Roma), East London (Irish Travellers), Glasgow (Eastern European Roma, Occupational Travellers). Within each community in each city: Men and women across generations of families including adults eligible for the flu vaccine (pregnant, over 65, with specified long term medical conditions e.g. asthma, bronchitis); pregnant women eligible for the pertussis vaccine, girls aged 13 to 18 years and mothers of pre-school children/women planning families. PHASE 2: Health, community, third sector and advocacy workers with responsibility for local policy making and/or providing services for these Traveller communities. PHASE 3: Sub sample of participants from Phases 1 and 2. HEALTH TECHNOLOGY: We will focus primarily on the UK childhood immunisation schedule. However to better understand issues relating to adult immunisation, we will also explore views on flu and pertussis vaccinations in adults either identified ‘at risk’ of developing serious complications of flu themselves, or in the case of pertussis vaccine, to prevent potentially life threatening infection in their newborn infants. MEASUREMENT OF OUTCOMES: PHASE 1: We will explore Travellers’ views on the intrapersonal, interpersonal, institutional, community and policy influences on their immunisation behaviours and ideas for improving uptake in their community. PHASE 2: We will investigate health and community workers’ perspectives on the barriers and facilitators (across all five levels of influence) to childhood and adult flu/pertussis immunisations for the Traveller communities with whom they work as well as their ideas for appropriate interventions. Vignettes using verbatim quotes from the interviews with Travellers in Phase 1 will be used to trigger discussion. PHASE 3: The findings from Phases 1 and 2 including ideas for interventions will be fed back, discussed and prioritised. With participants’ permission we will digitally record the interviews. The data collected in Phases 1 and 2 will be analysed using the Framework approach. We will use Nominal Group Technique in Phase 3. SAMPLE SIZE: PHASE 1: 24 to 32 participants in each Traveller community (total 144-192). PHASE 2: 6 to 8 health and community workers in each city (total 24-32). PHASE 3: 10 to 12 participants from Phase 1, and 3 to 4 Phase 2 participants for each community (total 78-102). In Bristol and Glasgow we are planning to engage with two Traveller communities and so will run two Workshops in these cities. These sample sizes have been estimated to draw out meaningful comparisons within and across Traveller communities, vaccines (childhood, adult) and professional roles to allow robust conclusions to be made. OUTPUTS:(1) A prioritised list of potentially feasible and acceptable interventions for increasing immunisation uptake for the six Traveller communities. (2) Comprehensive, in-depth findings on the barriers and facilitators to uptake and acceptability of childhood /adult flu and pertussis immunisation both within and across the six Traveller communities. (3) Methodological development in undertaking research with diverse Traveller communities. (4) Development of a multi-disciplinary research team working across multiple locations and links with local Traveller communities in preparation for securing funding and delivering a subsequent feasibility study. PROJECT TIMETABLE AND RECRUITMENT RATES A 26 month project commencing 1 September 2013. Months -3 to -1: Ethics and Research Approvals. WAVE 1: Months 1 to 12: York and Bristol. M1-2 set up, M2-5 Phase 1, M5-8 Phase 2, M6-11 'within-community' analysis, M12 feedback workshops. WAVE 2: Months 8-19: Glasgow and London. M8-9 set up, M9-12 Phase 1, M12-15 Phase 2, M13-18 'within-community'analysis, M19 feedback workshops. M20-23 Cross-community synthesis. M21-26 write report. M25-26 Dissemination. We have allowed four months in each city to engage with communities, gain their trust and do 24-32 interviews per community. To locate and interview 6-8 health and community workers in each location we have allowed 4 months (1 month overlaps with interviews with the Travellers). These estimates are based on the considerable experience within our research team of working with the Traveller communities and recognise the time it takes to gain the trust of communities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Advancing community hospitals and services in the NHS: learning from international experiences
Abstract: Community hospitals form an established component of healthcare provision in England but there is potential for them, and related service delivery models, to assume a more strategic role in local health economies, particularly in meeting the health and social care needs of future populations. The proposed research seeks to: (1) review the existing evidence base on community hospitals and equivalent service delivery models nationally and internationally, examining a range of organisational characteristics as well as outcomes; and (2) draw on experiences in other countries on the contribution of community hospitals to the healthcare system, by assessing equivalent service delivery models. Specifically we seek to understand (1) the nature and scope of service provision models that can be considered under the umbrella term ‘community hospital’ in the UK and other high income countries; (2) the evidence of effectiveness and efficiency of community hospitals and comparable service models in the UK and other high income countries; (3) the wider role and impact of community engagement in community hospital service development and provision; (4) how models that are comparable to community hospitals in England operate and their role within the wider system of service provision in other countries; and (5) the potential for such models to perform an integrative role on the delivery of health and social care in other countries. Evidence synthesis of community hospitals in the UK and other high income countries: We propose undertaking a comprehensive scoping review to understand how community hospital have been conceptualised and defined in the United Kingdom and other high income counties. We will seek to identify the range of organisational models of service delivery that can be broadly subsumed under the heading of a community hospital and what is already known about service provision and their role in the local and wider healthcare economy. Learning from international experience: We will conduct five country reviews to gain a detailed understanding of the nature, scope and distribution of service delivery models that can be considered comparable to community hospitals in England. This will be achieved using: (i) a structured data collection template, reviewed and validated by an expert in each country, and (ii) 8-10 key informant interviews. We will then undertake detailed case studies of community hospital models in a small subset of countries to provide in-depth understanding of particular models that appear innovative and to offer learning to service development in England. The case studies will follow a structured approach and include a local stakeholder mapping, document review, population assessment, interviews and non-participant observation. We will synthesise the evidence and compare and contrast our findings with those of the two complementary studies of community hospitals submitted under this call, which we will use to draw lessons for future strategic planning of health and social care services in England. We believe that this research will provide important insights for clinical commissioning groups into the potential role of community hospitals in the future delivery of health services closer to home.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The effectiveness and cost effectiveness of a brief behavioural intervention to promote regular self weighing to prevent weight regain after weight loss: randomised controlled trial
Abstract: In the UK the rates of obesity have more than doubled in the last 25 years. The costs of obesity place a significant burden on the NHS. There is a need therefore to investigate the effectiveness of pragmatic interventions that can be delivered in the community and reach the high number of people needing to lose weight and sustain this. Although evidence suggests many behavioural weight loss treatments are effective in the short term, long term weight maintenance remains a critical challenge. On average people will regain one third to one half of lost weight within the first year following treatment and will return to baseline weight within 3-5 years. Only a few studies have focused on weight maintenance and reviews have concluded evidence remains equivocal. A review of RCTs of weight maintenance interventions after weight loss identified 34 studies, none of which had been conducted in the UK. Most studies had evaluated interventions such as food supplements, meal replacements or medication. The review identified the greatest need for research was lifestyle interventions that supported people to manage their weight in the longer term. One promising strategy for weight maintenance is regular self weighing, which is a simple instruction for a health professional to give or public health communication to advocate and it is the kind of behaviour that could become habitual in the way that cleaning one’s teeth becomes automatic and self-sustaining. Systematic reviews suggest that self-weighing can prevent weight regain but this was part of an intensive multi-component intervention. Only two RCTs have focussed on self weighing alone as a maintenance strategy; both were small and had methodological shortcomings, but showed evidence that self weighing prevents weight regain. We have also completed a pilot quasi randomised RCT of regular self weighing where we showed such an intervention delivered by non-specialist telephonists prevented weight regain at 12 months. Following our pilot the aim here is to evaluate the longer term effectiveness and cost effectiveness of a 12 week weight maintenance intervention, focussed on encouraging daily self weighing, in adults who have recently lost weight. 560 adults will be randomised to usual care or a theoretically informed weight maintenance intervention, following completion of standard widely available commercial (e.g. Weight Watchers) and NHS weight loss programmes. People who have lost at least 5% of their weight after completing a weight loss programme will be invited to take part. The focus of the intervention is brief regular support telephone calls (5 min) that encourage daily self weighing. Calls will focus on habit formation and implementation intentions, getting people to plan where, when and how they will weigh themselves and then how they will record it. Few people (1:10) are able to recover from even small (1-2kg) lapses in weight regain. Regular weighing could be used as an early warning of the lapse and allow people to implement the strategies they learnt previously when attending their weight loss programme. Participants will receive text messages to remind them to weigh themselves. The intervention will be delivered by non-specialist telephonists from Gateway, a community interest company. The primary outcome will be change in weight (objective) between the groups from baseline to 12 months. The West Midlands is the most overweight region in the EU with a diverse multi ethnic population.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: ‘Helpmedoit!’ a web and text based intervention to facilitate social support to achieve and maintain health related behaviour change
Abstract: DESIGN: Stage 1 Development and piloting Stage 2 Exploratory trial with process evaluation. POPULATION: Adults (BMI 30+) trying to lose weight recruited via advertising, exercise on referral and primary care. STAGE 1: DEVELOPMENT During the development stage, health behaviour change experts and an IT company will work with user representatives to establish the optimal usability and acceptability of the app, website and SMS aspect. It will explore how to engage helpers and what support to helpers might be effective. This essential development and modelling work, and feasibility testing, follows the MRC guidance for the development and evaluation of complex interventions. The Helpmedoit! intervention will have multiple elements: support for goal setting and planning; nominate your helper to identify goal-specific social support group; obtain agreement from nominated helper(s) to provide support; helper-specific advice on providing effective support; track your progress for monitoring behaviour; specific information (including tips and case stories); the SMS, goal updates, support element of the intervention. Participants will be reminded to access the app and website which will provide guidance in setting goals, planning and nominating one or more helpers. The Helpmedoit! programme will contact these helpers via SMS, and invite them to help the individual. Participants will be able to choose not to share certain potentially sensitive bits of information (e.g. weight) with helpers. They will also be able to deselect helpers as well as nominate new helpers. Participants will be able to update their goals, plans and monitoring pages via SMS and smart phones. Helpers will receive guidance via SMS and the option to log onto the website which will give more detail on helping people to achieve health goals. These will be tailored to participants according to age and gender. They will be sent reminders to provide encouragement or commiseration and further support, depending upon progress towards goals. How this support is given is up to the helpers: it could be via SMS, phone call or face-to-face. SMS reminders will be sent to participants and helpers by the system when the goal date is close. Outgoing text messages will be designed to be engaging, according to best practice and will be based on consultation with the development panel. Data collection: We will recruit 10 user representatives to a development panel to provide input into the design and content of the app and website and how it will link with SMS messaging. The developing intervention will then be tested with up to 30 participants in focus groups or interviews. Outcomes in this stage will be analysis of qualitative data using thematic analysis. A report will be produced and submitted to an independent Trial steering Committee (TSC) who will decide whether the study should continue onto the exploratory trial. We will agree progression criteria in advance with the TSC; however, we suggest the following: Criterion 1: Was the software and associated SMS facility developed to a good standard in the timescale available? Did the software company produce the intervention as specified in the detailed design document? (This document will be produced during the development process in collaboration with the company and based on the findings from the focus groups and interviews). Did the software include the appropriate intervention elements to facilitate social support and behaviour change? This will be assessed by tabulating the logic model elements and the software will be compared to this to ensure it includes the key elements and addresses the aims and objectives of the logic model. Criterion 2: Was it feasible to implement the HelpMeDoIt! intervention via the web-based platform, app and SMS? If there were issues with the app, the website or other technical problems were the company responsive and able to provide solutions to any issues? This will be evidenced by the qualitative findings, page usage statistics, records of ‘bug’ reporting on the website and other measures of adherence. Criterion 3: Was the intervention acceptable and did the majority of the development group members find the intervention usable and acceptable? This will be assessed using the results from the usability questionnaire (which assesses ease of use and usefulness), the think-aloud results, the interview and focus group data and an expert heuristic evaluation. At this point, the study will either be terminated, to end at month 12 after a brief write-up period, or the SSC will agree to the progression to stage 2 feasibility testing. In months 9 and 10, the software company will proceed with further development of the programming in anticipation of proceeding to stage 2. STAGE 2: EXPLORATORY TRIAL This phase will test the app, website and SMS service developed in phase 1 and explore how the intervention works and whether it is worth testing in a full trial. The data collection methods will also be assessed for use in a full trial. 120 participants will be recruited and randomised to either complete the Helpmedoit! intervention or to receive a leaflet with information on healthy diet and physical activity. The active phase of the intervention will run for 6 months where we will remind participants/helpers to use the system, after this period they will still be able to access the program. Demographic information will be collected at baseline. Measures collected at baseline and 12 months include physical activity, diet, height, weight, waist circumference, mental health, self-esteem quality of life, NHS resource use and participant borne costs will be assessed. Potential mediators will be assessed including motivation, self-efficacy and social support. At 6 months, we will conduct a brief interview with up to 30 participants and 20 helpers to collect data on: acceptability; patterns of use; help received; barriers and suggested improvements to each of the interventions. We will also explore among the Helpmedoit! group their perception of the helpers experiences and the value of the helpers support as well as data on both positive and negative social support. Participants will be sampled on the basis of age, gender, socio-economic status, intervention usage and we will specifically seek to interview those who did not take up the intervention and reasons for this. We will collect in-depth qualitative data, on social support and on the ways that positive behaviour among helpers can be supported and encouraged. Qualitative data will be analysed using thematic analysis. Quantitative analyses will include descriptive analyses of recruitment rates, intervention use and response rates. Analyses of diet, physical activity and BMI will be carried out using ANCOVA with baseline scores as covariates to explore estimates of likely effect sizes for a larger trial. Secondary analyses will compare intervention and control groups in terms of weight lost, waist circumference, % weight lost, quality of life, self-esteem and mental health. We will conduct exploratory sub-group and mediation analyses. We will obtain estimates of key cost drivers to inform the design of a future cost effectiveness analysis. The Scottish Primary Care Research Network will cover service support costs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Implications for Public Health: Research of Models and Theories of Disability
Abstract: Nearly ten million people in England experience significant difficulty with day-to-day activities linked to disability. Many are living with other chronic conditions. The experience of disability is also strongly age-related. Further, the impact of impairments has a marked social gradient. People with disabilities are disproportionately disadvantaged with respect to the social factors that contribute to health inequalities, such as educational and employment opportunities, poverty and poor housing, and inequitable access to services. These environmental disadvantages are, in turn, disabling and create barriers to social inclusion. Public health research has largely overlooked the experience of disability, having little to say on appropriate study designs and measures (including economic evaluation); or how to actively engage disabled people. Nor does it demonstrate much of an understanding of the different consequences of having lifelong, acquired or fluctuating conditions; or how social disadvantage, gender, ethnicity, sexual orientation and lifecourse mediate experience. Nonetheless, we have some important platforms on which to build, which offer alternative ways of defining and engaging with disability. Our project will scope models and theories of disability and by assessing whether and how existing intervention studies incorporate these approaches, draw out recommendations for improving study designs and outcome measures. Analysis will focus on what works, under what circumstances and with what consequences. To achieve this, we propose a two-stage project. First, we will undertake a scoping review and synthesis of research critiquing models and theories of disability. This review will summarise the range of models and theories; their place within disability studies and social movements of disabled people; and their potential contribution to public health research and policy. Second, we will undertake a review of 60 purposively-selected public health interventions from the Cochrane (international) Library of intervention reviews. Thirty of the reviews (containing data on at least 160 studies) will be where people with disabilities are identified as a key target group and this will enable us to explore the potential for inclusive designs. Thirty will be more generic interventions, which have potential relevance to adults and children with disabilities (and containing data on 160 studies). This will enable us to gain insights into the ability of mainstream research to capture the experience of disability and the possibilities of developing more universal and inclusive designs. Supplementary insights will be gained by sampling reviews identified in databases held by Campbell Collaboration and Joanna Briggs institute. Synthesis will assess the perspectives and methods employed when evaluating public health interventions. We will focus on mapping and offering a critical commentary on: the models and theories of disability underpinning the intervention; the terminology and categorisation of disability used or if no discussion, a consideration of the potential relevance of the intervention to the experience of disabled people; whether a life course perspective is evident; methods of participant and public and involvement; and (inclusive) study designs and outcomes. The project will provide good practice guidelines, sensitive to diverse experience of disability and grounded in an appreciation of current research practice.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Self-Management of Analgesia and Related Treatments at the End of life (SMARTE)
Abstract: Despite there being a good understanding of patient and carer concerns regarding opioid analgesia and related side effects, much less is known about the optimal means of addressing these concerns which is why they have been highlighted by NICE guidance (1). We aim to develop a support tool to improve the management of medications for pain relief, nausea, constipation and drowsiness in patients with significant pain approaching the end of life. Our self- management support tool (SMST) will be developed using a patient centred approach and will be delivered in partnership with health care professionals (HCPs) in two UK regions. Ultimately we aim to establish the acceptability and up-take of our prototype SMST and determine the feasibility of evaluating this intervention within a larger trial. We have interpreted the brief so that we will focus on patients who are treated with, or due to start treatment with, opioids for pain and that experience (or anticipate) adverse effects of these medications. Our objectives are divided into three distinct phases which is in-line with the MRC framework on developing and evaluating complex interventions and NPT(9). [1] Development objectives (Phase I) • Establish a PPI panel • Establish the content of a prototype SMST and a manualisation strategy that includes a protocol to standardise (i) the training of HCP and (ii) the delivery of the intervention by HPCs to patients and carers • Understand self-management needs and capabilities of patients and carers. • Define usual care [2] Modelling objectives (Phase II) • Refine and co-design the prototype SMST and manualisation [3] Feasibility assessment objectives (Phase III) • Assess acceptability and up-take of the SMST in a mixed-methods observational study involving patients, informal carers and HCPs from 4 palliative care services • Assess the feasibility of obtaining outcome data for a larger trial

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Does active design increase walking and cycling? Evaluation of a natural experiment examining whether moving into housing in East Village increases family levels of physical activity, particularly walking and cycling
Abstract: In the UK, the distances walked and cycled by adults and children have declined over recent years, and in particular the number of journeys made by bicycle both to work and to school are much lower than in other European populations. Although the built environment may be an important influence on physical activity patterns, particularly on uptake of walking and cycling to everyday destinations, there is a dearth of longitudinal evidence. The development of East Village (formerly the Olympic Athletes’ Village) offers a unique opportunity for a longitudinal natural experiment to assess the impact of relocation to a purpose designed walkable urban built environment on walking and cycling patterns. The transformation of East Village into affordable and market rent housing has been carried out on a rapid timescale (ready for occupancy from Autumn 2013), and has been specifically designed to create an environment encouraging walking and cycling and public transport use (with secure bicycle spaces allocated for every home, and restriction of car ownership). This is further enhanced by regeneration of the surrounding area (particularly extension of walkways and cycle paths to the Lee Valley, and connection to the London Cycle Network). The accommodation will be offered to families from a range of widely differing social backgrounds. The rapid transformation will facilitate an assessment of changes in physical activity levels (as well as other health behaviours / outcomes) following relocation to the Village compared with control participants who remain in their original housing. This is a unique opportunity as it (i) represents a natural experiment of people from diverse social backgrounds relocating into a new walkable neighbourhood, and (ii) because most new housing developments take up to a decade to complete. With the support of the NPRI, we are already conducting a two year longitudinal study to evaluate the natural experiment provided by the opening of East Village. One adult and one child from each of 2800 families who apply to live in affordable and market rent homes in East Village are being invited to join a cohort before a formal offer of re-housing is made. In all, 1200 families will be recruited, of which approximately half will move into the Village. Participants will be measured in their current place of residence and then measured again, either in East Village (intervention group) or in their original place of residence (control group). Changes in overall physical activity and body composition (measured objectively using accelerometry and bio-electrical impedance respectively) will be compared between intervention and control groups. The study is powered to detect a 5% increase in the number of daily steps walked (and other activity/adiposity outcomes) in both adults and in children; this represents the lower limit of potentially worthwhile increases in physical activity. The present application extends this study by: (i) evaluating whether movement to an environment with ‘active’ design principles at its heart specifically increases walking and cycling activity; and (ii) quantifying and measuring the design components of East Village and establishing their influence on walking and cycling. We propose to use Global Positioning System (GPS) technology to identify patterns and locations of movement among study participants both within the East Village facility and elsewhere, and to link these personal data with fine-grained environmental data operationalized within a Geographic Information System (GIS) on features of neighbourhood environments of participants before and after moving to the East Village that might promote walking and cycling. Combining the novel GPS data with our established accelerometer data collection will allow us to describe both the level and location of physical activity within the physical environment (including identification of walking and cycling patterns in the intervention and control groups and the extent of change associated with moving to the East Village). It will also allow the segmentation of accelerometer data into that recorded indoors and out of doors, and the objective measurement of time spent outside. Time spent outside is a significant and consistent predictor of children’s physical activity, but until now has been measured poorly, generally by self-report or parent/teacher proxy. The use of GPS data allows a precise measure of time outdoors, and the combination with accelerometer data has allowed us to determine that outdoor physical activity is three-fold higher than indoors. Consequently, a built environment within the East Village that promotes greater independent mobility in children (by providing a safer environment) may be expected to increase time outdoors, and would also be expected to substantially increase young peoples physical activity levels. In combination with novel GIS data, this study we will be able to explore associations between specific features of the built environment (such as walkability, and access to transport and recreational destinations; including green space, purpose built ‘hard’ surfaces) and physical activity. In addition, these data will be used to inform qualitative spatial narratives from participants, which will provide adult and child perspectives on reasons for and purpose of travel. The study offers an important opportunity to examine which, if any, active design principles within a newly build development promotes walking and cycling and increases overall physical activity levels, in individuals (adults and children) from widely different socioeconomic backgrounds; and the differential impact of changes in the built environment on the physical activity patterns of different socioeconomic groups. The results have the potential to inform evidence-based urban planning generally and the design of future higher density urban projects and, particularly in the encouragement of healthier lifestyles in families with varying socioeconomic circumstances. Our established links with the Greater London Assembly, London Legacy Development Corporation, local authorities (particularly Newham), the Town and Country Planning Association, housing associations, urban planners and architects, will enhance the scope for translating study results into policy.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Effectiveness and Cost-effectiveness of a Physical Activity Loyalty Card to Maintain Behaviour Change: A Cluster Randomised Controlled Trial
Abstract: In light of evidence of modest, short term effects of physical activity (PA) interventions, particularly in the workplace, there is a need for more innovative approaches. NICE guidance has highlighted the lack of evidence about what helps people maintain behaviour change and about how to make walking an habitual activity. Despite the workplace being an ideal setting to encourage habitual activity, there is limited evidence on effective, maintained PA behaviour change interventions. This study aims to address this gap and help build the necessary evidence base for effective, and cost-effective, workplace interventions. Using the MRC framework for complex interventions we have developed a multi-component intervention aimed at achieving maintained PA behaviour change. The intervention is based on concepts similar to those that underpin high street loyalty cards, whereby repeated behaviour is rewarded with financial incentives. Using sensors placed around the workplace environment to monitor and promote activity, the intervention provides rewards (retail vouchers sponsored by businesses) for activity, feedback and other evidence-based behaviour change techniques (BCTs). The intervention is based on principles of Learning Theory and Social Cognitive Theory; accepted theoretical frameworks for behaviour change. The study will target office-based employees from public sector organisations in Lisburn city centre. Participants will be encouraged to undertake activity within a 2km radius of their workplace utilising opportunities in the workplace neighbourhood. The intervention will be delivered in partnership with the local City Council and Health and Social Care Trust who are responsible for the health and wellbeing of the South East population. Intervention funding is provided by both these organisations and the Public Health Agency. The cluster RCT will recruit 1380 employees from 5 public sector organisations. Participants will be randomly allocated by cluster (the smallest organisational unit) to either the Intervention Group or Control Group. The Intervention Group will participate in the PAL Scheme for 6 months. A pre-intervention phase will involve focus groups with employees and a bespoke Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) to explore the levels of incentive that could optimise behaviour change. The waiting list Control Group will be given the opportunity to participate in the intervention at the end of the study. Both groups will complete all outcome measures. The primary outcome is steps/day recorded using a pedometer for 7 consecutive days at baseline, 6, 12 and 18 months. Questionnaires will measure health, mental wellbeing, quality of life, work absenteeism and presenteeism, and use of healthcare resources at baseline, 6 and 18 months. Focus groups will further explore who the intervention worked for and why. Interviews with retailers will elucidate their views on the sustainability of a public health focused loyalty card scheme. Process evaluations will be undertaken to assess the intervention “dose” delivered using PAL scheme and website usage data, and intervention fidelity. An economic evaluation will be conducted from the NHS and employer perspective advocated by NICE. The study is designed to maximise the potential for roll-out in similar settings, by engaging the public sector and business community in designing and delivering the intervention.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Learning from National Clinical Advisory Team Reviews
Abstract: We will conduct a qualitative content analysis of all the NCAT reviews, over one hundred in total, undertaken from 2007 and 2012. This will be supplemented by a targeted literature review of the themes to emerge from the qualitative analysis. This will enable us to set the themes in the context of the current evidence base in each area. NCAT Review Content analysis - We will develop our coding scheme using a mixture of deductive and inductive reasoning. This coding scheme will operate using a range of units of analysis pertinent to the information being sought. This coding scheme will have clearly defined and mutually understood analytical categories and systematic criteria for selection of data from the review documents into those categories. Once the reviews are coded they will then be analysed by the research team using NVIVO to identify thematic patterns and conclusions emerging from the data. Literature Review - We will undertake a literature review after the NCAT reviews content analysis. The search terms and inclusion and exclusion criteria for the literature review will be determined by the outcome of the qualitative analysis. Information extracted will be documented systematically and synthesised for write up under the themes identified in the review of NCAT submissions. The research team, would then triangulate the original NCAT review, the evidence base, and any relevant underpinning documentation, to gain insight into the NCAT process and its strengths and weaknesses.

Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: University Hospitals Coventry & Warwickshire NHS Trust
Award_Title: Improving the Absorptive Capacity (ACAP) of Commissioning Networks for Critical Review of Evidence to Reduce Unplanned Elderly Care Admissions into Acute Hospitals
Abstract: Problem: We highlight that exploratory interviews with Clinical Commissioning Group (CCG)leads & clinical leads & managers for elderly care provision suggest that the critical review capacity of the existing & intended, new commissioning networks may be relatively weak. For example, CCG leads explain their position as follows: We have the intelligence & strategic intent, but the challenge is how we exploit that intelligence & use it to drive transformation, with the problem of moving resource from hospital-based elderly care to primary care given as an example of such strategic intent. Such a practical conception of the commissioning problem constitutes 'critical review capacity', which, in turn, maps on to the four dimensions of absorptive capacity or ACAP (acquisition, assimilation, transformation & exploitation. We also suggest the challenge of commissioning high quality elderly care in a productive, but preventative, way, is exemplary of a more general challenge of commissioning complex care, which often encompasses more than a single disease pathway & crosses boundaries within & outside the NHS. Conceptual framework: We highlight studies of ACAP in healthcare already published (Berta et al., 2010; Easterby-Smith et al., 2008; Hotho et al., 2012), & seek to extend such studies. We seek to develop a model of knowledge mobilisation focused upon ACAP of healthcare commissioning networks, but one which is transferable more widely across the healthcare system. Research Questions (RQs): Our over-arching empirical RQ is: How can we enhance ACAP of CCG led commissioning networks in healthcare to inform decisions to reduce unplanned elderly care acute hospital admissions? This breaks down over the course of the study into the following RQs: RQ1. What is the ‘state of play’ regarding ACAP of the commissioning networks immediately following their inception? RQ2: How has ACAP of the commissioning networks progressed in the first 12 months? RQ3: How is patient experience knowledge acquired & utilised to enhance ACAP of commissioning networks? RQ4: How can we ensure potential ACAP is realised in commissioning networks? Timeplan & research methods:The 4 RQs link to 7 Work Packages (WPs), carried out over 36 months (beginning 1st June 2013). There is a pre-NIHR funding research stream, consisting of two projects (WP0), which represent co-investment in the NIHR funded study. The first of these is funded £30,000 by NHS Institute for Innovation & Improvement (Oct 12-Mar 13) which examine 5 CCG led commissioning networks, with a focus upon ACAP of the commissioning network pre-authorisation of CCGs. The second of these is funded £50,000 by a Regional Transformation Fund held by a Primary Care Trust Cluster (April 13-September 13), which examines how patient experience constitutes a source of knowledge for service development within CCG led commissioning networks. Within these two studies, we are carrying out literature reviews, & progressed ethics & R&D approvals, so that we can ‘hit the ground running’ with fieldwork at the start of the NIHR funded study we propose. Within our NIHR funded study, there will be 7 Work Packages Ethics: Ethics and R&D are progressed prior to NIHR funding, so 'we hit the ground running'. Research outputs:formative organisational learning events; psychometric self-reflection tool for commissioning networks to develop critical review capacity; other structural & social interventions to enhance critical review capacity of commissioning networks developed through an action plan followed up in WP6; accessible, professional corporate communications aimed at commissioning networks that are web-based & written material; peer-reviewed academic publication in policy, management, health services research, practitioner & academic conference presentations Team expertise: Currie (PI) is a health services organisation & management expert, directed translational research units (CLAHRC NDL), & acted as PI on previous successful NIHR funded resesarch studies. Kiefer (CI) is a psychologist with considerable expertise in the development of psychometric tools for organisational development. Lilford is a world leading medical scientist with expertise in interventionist methods, & has directed translational research (CLAHRC BBC). Redwood & Staniszewska are experts in knowledge mobilisation around the patient experience & PPI. We have named a Research Fellow (Ogilvie, a former nurse, currently working on NHSI funded study of CCGs). Management: Currie manages the research programme, including all WPs apart from WP3 & WP4, & Research Fellow. Kiefer has responsibility for part WP4. Lilford has particular responsibility for dissemination throughout the study, & provides advice about intervention. Redwood and Staniszewska have responsibility for WP3, within which PPI is encompassed. Study Advisory Board (SAB) consisting of NHS Commissioning Board Local Area Team Leads, CCG Chief Operating Officers, patients/carers, academic experts, oversees the study, & meets annually. Costs: Academic (PI & 4 CIs) time, Research Fellow, secretarial support, laptop & recorder, transcription, travel, learning & dissemination events including website

Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Incentives in Diabetic Eye Assessment by Screening (IDEAS) Trial
Abstract: Reducing inequalities in health is a central part of government health policy. Deprived sections of our communities are known to suffer increased levels of significant disease in many areas and are less likely to attend screening opportunities. Evidence from diabetic retinopathy screening programmes in particular supports this (Scanlon et al 2008), highlighting the fact that in areas with the greatest socioeconomic deprivation, diabetic prevalence is highest and attendance is poorest. As a result, screening programmes in general have the potential to exacerbate existing inequalities in outcomes. A challenge for screening programmes therefore is to find effective, simple and inexpensive population wide strategies to recruit hard to reach individuals. One such strategy gaining prominence is finding ways to incentivise these populations to better align their behaviour with underlying intentions. Our interventions will use cutting-edge theory from the interdisciplinary field of behavioural economics to design incentives that encourage people to utilise screening opportunities. Behavioural economics integrates lessons from psychology into the laws of economics (Kahneman 2003). Psychological phenomena from behavioural economics can allow us to design more effective incentive-based interventions. We will employ the following prominent insights into the design of our interventions, because those are the three most established phenomena in behavioural economics embodied in the well-known Prospect Theory, for which Daniel Kahneman was awarded the 2002 Nobel prize in economics (see Kahneman & Tversky 2000): - Reference Points. Offering a very small incentive can get people to pick up their HIV Result, but increasing the value of the incentive has little effect (Thornton 2008). We will offer an incentive of £10 (equivalent to minimal hourly wage for UK workers >21) to assess whether this leads to an increase in participation. - Overweighting of Small Probabilities. People are known to overvalue small probabilities, which explains the popularity of lotteries and insurance (see Kahneman & Tversky 2000). In the review of the effect of incentives on smoking cessation, one of the reasons given for the lack of effectivenes shown is the low level of incentives on offer in most of the programmes (Cahill & Perera 2008). It follows, that if an incentive programme only has limited resources, it may be more effective to offer a lottery based programme rather than smaller individual rewards. We will offer lotteries where the expected value matches the incentive level offered in the other arms. It may be that overweighting of small probabilities will make a lottery offering eg '1% chance for £1000' more attractive than £10 for certain, so the former should be more effective incentive for participation in screening. - Loss Aversion. We dislike financial losses twice as much as we like financial gains of an equivalent amount (Kahneman 1979).
