Incentives may be more powerful where individuals lose a reward rather than gain one for screening. In our intervention, participants will either receive a fake banknote (such as Monopoly money) that can be exchanged for cash at after screening, or a lottery ticket, which expire at the date of the screening. The study proposed is a randomised controlled trial conducted within the Kensington, Chelsea and Westminster Diabetic Eye Screening Programme of London. Patients, aged 16 or older, who were invited to screening the in the last 12 months and failed to attend or contact the screening service to rearrange an appointment will be studied. Study participants will be identified from the Diabetic Eye Screening Programme prior to commencement of the study. Data from the screening programme for the year 01/04/2011 to 31/03/2012 suggests that 12 months worth of screening activity will provide the required study size. All invitees during the study period will be randomised, prior to invitation, between the three study groups: Group 1 – Control Group: subjects will be sent documentation on diabetic eye screening and the standard screening programme invite only. Group 2 – Fixed Incentive: subjects will be sent a £10 fake banknote which they can exchange for cash at the clinic after attending for screening in addition to the documentation on diabetic eye screening and the standard screening programme invite. Group 3 – Probabilistic Incentive: subjects will be sent a lottery ticket offering a 1% chance to win £1000 if they attend for screening in addition to the documentation on diabetic eye screening and the standard screening programme invite. It will be stated on the £10 fake banknote and the lottery ticket that they will lose their value if the patient does not attend the scheduled or the rescheduled screening appointment, which is expected to trigger loss aversion in groups 2 and 3. The incentive schemes were designed in conjunction with patient representatives and a survey of diabetic patients (see the Detailed Project Description for more information). The study group will comprise patients who have never attended for screening, so attendance in the study group should be very low (a nominal 1%). Evidence (Scanlon 2008) and consultation with the Diabetic Eye Screening Service informs us that the study group have the greatest risk of losing their sight, so an increase in attendance of 10% is worthwhile. With 2 intervention groups, each being compared to the control group, for maximum statistical efficiency we should randomise 1.4:1:1. This would give 412 controls and 294 in each of the intervention groups (1000 in total) and the study would have at least 95% power to detect an increase in attendance of 10% from 1% in the control arm to 11% in an intervention arm and 85% power to detect a smaller increase from 1% to 7.5% (should attendance in the control arm turn out to be 5% the study would still have approximately 85% power to detect an increase in attendance of 10% with an intervention to 15%). Demographic data will allow us to explore whether inequalities in screening may be addressed by an incentive scheme. The proposed trial has been discussed at the local Diabetic Eye Screening board meeting and has support. The trial also is aligned with the National agenda to encourage research achieving higher attendance rates at screening.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A multi-centre cluster randomised controlled trial to evaluate the Guide to Action Care Home fall prevention programme in care homes for older people.(FinCH)
Abstract: Design: Multicentre cluster randomised controlled trial Setting: UK care homes Target population 1. Residents of old age care homes who are not terminally ill or receiving short term respite care. 2. Care homes with robust falls recording, willing to implement the GtACH process and who are not already using a structured falls risk assessment and risk reduction programme. Health technology The intervention is the Guide to Action Care Home (GtACH) systematic process delivered to care home residents by care home staff who have been trained i and are supported. GtACH is a systematic falls risk assessment and action process, co designed by care home and NHS staff, based on NICE clinical guidelines. The assessment takes 15 minutes and actions take up to two hours per resident. The control conditions reflect usual practice. Usual practice requires care home staff to be trained sufficiently to meet legal requirements and to write care plans for each resident but this does not include systematic routine training in fall prevention or the routine use of a systematic falls assessment tool or a falls prevention decision support tool. Residents in both groups will be eligible for usual medical and community services. Measurement of costs and outcome Data will be collected from care home records as this was found reliable in a feasibility study, NHS data, residents and care home staff acting as proxy. Researchers collecting and analysing data will be blinded to treatment allocation. Times are from randomisation. Primary • Rate of falls between three and six months Secondary • Rate of falls at 9 and 12 months At 6 and 12 month - • Fall injuries • Days in hospital • Death • Health and Social service use • Physical activity (PAM-RC) • Functional ability (Barthel Index) • Quality of life (DEMQOL-U-5D, DEMQOL-P-4D), • Health (EQ-5D-5L and EQ-5D-5L proxy) • Medication use Economic study: Within trial cost-effectiveness and utility analyses from NHS and personal social service perspective. The choice to use several health measures reflects the fact that the utility value sets, DEMQOL-U and DEMQOL-P-U, have not been widely used or validated but EQ-5D-5L has successfully been used in care homes. Concurrent process evaluation: To explore implementation of the GtACH process 12 staff focus groups and 30 stakeholder interviews, observations and documentary analysis will be completed. Thematic analysis approaches, constant comparison, progressive focusing of field observations, and memo-writing will be used to construct categories and sub-categories. Sample size: 1308 residents from 66 CHs are required to detect a 33% falls rate reduction in the intervention group. This assumes a falls rate of 2.5 falls per year per resident in the control group, 1:1 allocation, 80% power, a two-sided significance level of 5%, an average cluster size of 20 residents, an intra-cluster coefficient of 0.1 and 16% attrition. 6 sites will each recruit 11 CHs. Randomisation: Variable block randomisation at care home level by Norwich Clinical Trials Unit using a web-based randomisation service. Timetable: 3 years: 6 months set-up; 12 months recruitment; 12 months follow up; 6 months analysis, write-up and dissemination. Team expertise: Falls prevention, care home research and management, multicentre clinical trials, health economics, medical statistics, implementation science, concurrent process analysis

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Mass media for public health messages
Abstract: Mass media such as radio, television, newspapers and increasingly digital, social and mobile media, can be used to communicate public health messages at the population level, potentially reaching many more people than other interventions. Communcation through mass media (particularly through digital media) involves not just the receipt of information but also a two way interactive process where change occurs when people choose to engage with, interpret and respond to the public health messages they receive. Previous research has shown that mass media communications can result in positive changes (or prevent negative changes) in health behaviours across a range of populations. However, effectiveness varies depending on the extent, focus, targeting, theoretical basis, content, source and duration of the campaign, the extent to which the campaign is complemented by other behaviour change strategies and policies, and the relationship between the campaign and other available services and programmes. This study will examine and synthesise evidence on the effective uses of mass media to communicate public health messages and change behaviour with a view to informing the use of public health mass media campaigns in local populations in the UK. It will involve secondary research conducted in three stages. First, the development of a logic model drawing on relevant theory of both the mechanisms for health behaviour change and the mechanisms for how mass media may lead to change (see attached Appendix 1 for a demonstration logic model). Secondly, evidence synthesis of the available evidence on a range of public health topics, drawing on the theoretical model developed earlier. Topics include smoking, alcohol, illicit drug use, diet, physical activity, sexual and reproductive health. We will seek existing systematic reviews in the first instance, and synthesise these where they are high quality, up to date and relevant; where suitable reviews cannot be found, primary research will be identified and synthesised. The final stage of the study will involve exploring the applicability and currency of emerging findings. This will include consulting with topic specific experts across different areas of public health and consulting with service providers and other relevant stakeholders to look at relevance and applicability- particularly to local contexts.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Evaluation of the Healthy Start Voucher Scheme in UK: a natural experiment using the Growing Up in Scotland record linkage study and the Infant Feeding Survey
Abstract: The evaluation of a means tested voucher scheme can inform policy aiming to change behaviour, improve health outcomes and reduce inequalities. Interventions to improve outcomes of pregnancy in low socioeconomic status mothers are important for perinatal and child health and also adult health outcomes. The aim is to evaluate the Healthy Start Voucher (HSV) scheme; does it improve the health of pregnant women and mothers and health outcomes of their children and is it cost effective? We are also interested in reasons for uptake and non-uptake of the HSV scheme. The intervention being evaluated is the HSV scheme; a means tested voucher scheme for pregnant women and mothers with children under four. If these women are in receipt of certain means tested benefits then they are eligible for vouchers to be spent on milk, infant formula milk, fruit and vegetables. In addition women receive free vitamins. All mothers under 18 are eligible for the scheme. By targeting families on low incomes and young mothers, HSV is designed to reduce health inequalities. This evaluation of HSV will be able to assess the impact of HSV on reducing inequalities. The impact on health inequalities by area deprivation, maternal education and marital status will be examined. We propose to have two primary outcome measures one relating to the mother during pregnancy and one relating to the child in early infancy. These are important periods of risk and measure different but important aspects of public health. 1) Pregnancy: vitamin use in pregnancy 2) Early infancy: breast feeding initiation and duration Vitamin use during pregnancy is aiming to create a healthy uterine environment which is important for birth outcomes. In early infancy, breast feeding is beneficial for many aspects of child health and morbidity. An increase in both of these outcomes are the aims of the HSV. Several secondary outcomes from survey data and linked data sets are proposed. These relate to child growth, child morbidity, child feeding and maternal health. This analysis of existing data, incorporates a cost effectiveness analysis enhanced by an embedded qualitative study. There are three main parts to this evaluation: 1) secondary analysis of two existing data sets; 2) economic analysis to assess cost effectiveness; 3) qualitative interview study. The evaluation will take a natural experiment approach and use multiple unexposed groups, including those eligible but not claiming the vouchers and additionally those who just miss the eligibility criteria for HSV in terms of income and age, to assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the HSV. We will take a multiple analytical approach making use of propensity matching of exposed and unexposed and regression discontinuity to minimise bias inherent in both the study design (non-random allocation of the intervention) and types of analyses. The cost-effectiveness analysis will be based around relating the estimated cost of the intervention relative to the observed benefits of the programme (changes in the primary and secondary outcomes, resource use impacts). Research to understand the processes involved in the take-up or non take-up of HSV will require the collection of additional qualitative data. We propose to carry out interviews with 20 mothers who claim Healthy Start Vouchers and 20 who are eligible but do not claim, to elicit reasons for and experiences of participating and not participating in HSV.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The Prognosis in Palliative care Study II (PiPS2)
Abstract: Background: PiPS-A [1], Palliative Prognostic Index (PPI) [2] and Palliative Performance Scale (PPS) [3] predict survival in patients with advanced cancer and can be calculated without a blood test. PiPS-B [1], Palliative Prognostic (PaP) score [4, 5] and Feliu Prognostic Nomogram (FPN) [6] require a blood test. The relative accuracy of the models, their acceptability to patients, carers and clinicians, and barriers to implementation are unknown. Primary aim: To validate PiPS-A&B and to compare PIPS-B against clinician predictions of survival (CPS). Secondary aims: (1) To validate PaP, FPN, PPI and PPS (2) To determine the acceptability of all prognostic models to patients, carers and clinicians and to identify potential barriers to use. Design: A mixed method approach including a prospective observational validation study and a qualitative interview study. Patients in the validation study will have prognostic scores and CPS recorded. Blood samples will only be collected from patients with capacity who give consent. Patients without capacity will only be included if carers give assent, and no blood specimen will be obtained from these patients. Survival will be tracked by the NHS Information Centre (NHSIC) and will be calculated from date of study entry. Patients, carers and clinicians in the qualitative study will participate in audio-recorded semi-structured interviews which will be transcribed and subjected to Framework Analysis [7]. Setting: A multi-centre UK study involving inpatient hospice units, hospital palliative care teams and community services. Population: The quantitative validation study will include patients with advanced incurable cancer. The qualitative interview study will include a purposive sample of competent patients (+/- carers), carers of non-competent patients, and a sample of clinicians. Inclusion / Exclusion criteria: Patients with or without capacity to consent will be included. Patients will have advanced incurable cancer and have been recently referred to palliative care services. Health technology being assessed: PiPS (www.pips.sgul.ac.uk), PaP, FPN, PPI and PPS. Choice of outcome measures: A range of prognostic models will be studied. We have selected measures that are suitable for use in patients with or without capacity and for those in whom a blood test would or would not be appropriate. Sample size (quantitative study): The total sample size is 1,361. The validation set for PiPS-A is 560, and the sample size to compare PiPS-B with clinician predictions is 1,267. Numbers do not sum to 1,361 because some subjects are in both data sets. Sample size (qualitative study): The final sample size for the qualitative study of patients and carers will be determined by data saturation. It is anticipated that this will be around 30. For the pragmatic evaluation of prognostic instruments among healthcare professionals approximately 15 interviews will be conducted. Timetable: Months 1 – 3; study set-up. Months 3 – 26; recruitment. Months 27 – 36; follow-up, analysis, writing and dissemination. Expertise: We have expertise managing large multi-centre palliative care studies and in the use of mixed methods. Study management, data analysis and statistical expertise will be provided by PRIMENT. Qualitative expertise will be provided by the University of Manchester. Our team includes service users and international collaborators involved in the development of PaP, FPN and PPS

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A multi-centred RCT of an augmented exercise referral scheme using web-based behavioural support in individuals with metabolic, musculo-skeletal and mental health conditions
Abstract: The NHS routinely offers a service in which a doctor or health care professional refers a patient, with a medical condition that can benefit from exercise, to an exercise referral scheme (ERS). Schemes involve a supervised programme of both aerobic and resistance exercise tailored to individual needs, at an exercise facility or physical activity (PA) counselling support. However, uptake and adherence can be low, and there is an absence of rigorous data to show long-term change in physical activity. We have had extensive input from patients and ERS professionals to suggest that longer-term motivational support is needed beyond the traditional 10-12 week programme. There is rapidly growing interest in new technologies to support health behaviour change, including websites, text messaging, and apps on smart phones. Such support engages a good proportion of patients and provides valued and effective support. The Lifeguide website has provided support that has been appreciated by patients to self-manage various medical conditions, and health behaviours (Williams et al, 2013; Yardley et al, 2010; 2011) but has not been used to support patients concurrently attending an ERS. We propose to refine an existing form of interactive internet-based support (Lifeguide) into something called e-coach which can help patients with common long-term medical conditions, namely obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, osteoarthritis and depression, to be more likely to attend an ERS and help with long-term motivation to do PA and improve health related quality of life. Our e-coach intervention will provide consistent and coherent support that seeks to empower individuals through increased confidence to be physically active, and to be more proactive in self-managing their condition with PA, with types of PA that are most sustainable. The proposed research will compare standard ERS with ERS plus the e-coach intervention, introduced to patients at the point of referral and remaining accessible during and beyond the usual ERS. At the point of referral a nurse will randomly allocate patients who meet certain criteria to receive either usual ERS or ERS plus e-coach. Only those in the intervention will be given log-in details to access e-coach and given facilitator and technician support to use it. The ERS will provide usual support (i.e. structured exercise or PA counselling) to all participants but e-coach will give additional support that is expected to help patients to remain physically active after 12 months. Research will be conducted in ERS in Glasgow, Devon/Cornwall and West Midlands. As our main outcome, we plan to examine if the two groups differ in the proportion of patients who are meeting public health guidelines of at least 150 minutes of moderate or vigorous PA, using the most advanced objective measurement by motion sensors, at 12 months. A range of PA, health-related quality of life, and resource use outcomes will also be assessed at 4 and 12 months to compare the groups. Economic analysis will consider the long-term benefits for the NHS. Process evaluation will examine use of the web-based support and its effects on outcome among the five medical groups, though we expect some patients will have more than one condition.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: At-Risk Registers Integrated into primary care to Stop Asthma crises in the UK (ARRISA-UK): A pragmatic cluster randomised trial with nested economic and process evaluations examining the effects of integrating at-risk asthma registers into primary care with internet-based training and support
Abstract: Design: Pragmatic cluster randomised controlled trial of a complex intervention with nested mixed methods process and economic evaluations. Setting: UK general practices Literature review: A search of Medline with combinations of terms relating to primary care, risk registers and asthma revealed no relevant papers other than our studies (Smith 2012; Noble 2006); furthermore, there are no relevant studies registered in clinical trial databases. Target population: Patients at high risk of asthma exacerbations/death Inclusion/exclusion: 270 primary care practices, excluding practices with existing formal, prospective processes for targeting patients with at-risk asthma. All the patients identified as having at-risk asthma according to a validated algorithm (n=105370) will be included, except those with recorded refusal for use of anonymous data in research. Health technology: At-risk registers will be created using automated electronic searches identifying at-risk criteria. Training will be delivered via web-based eLearning modules and “webinars” to representatives of all categories of practice staff to train them on how to respond to electronic alerts/flags to ensure best practice care. The flags will tag the electronic health records of at-risk patients to alert all staff at all patient-practice interactions. A practice based study lead will receive email reminders at 6 weeks and 6 months. Control: Control practices will continue routine care, including Quality and Outcome Framework driven practice-based annual asthma reviews and patients’ use of routine and emergency primary and secondary care services as required the but not the flagging or training. Measurements: The primary outcome is the difference in the proportion of at-risk patients with an asthma-related crisis event (A&E attendance, hospitalisation or death) over 12 months. Secondary outcomes: time to first crisis event, asthma control, prescribed medications, medication adherence, smoking status, all cause admission and death, health care costs in all and “at-risk” asthma patients. Anonymous routinely-collected clinical data from patients will be captured. Health economic analysis will be from an NHS perspective, where the measure of effectiveness will be based on the primary outcome measure. Routine data on processes of care, and questionnaires from practice staff completed before, during and after the training and after 12 months of the intervention, plus exit focus groups and interviews will contribute to the process evaluation. Sample size: In order to have 90% power to detect a difference in primary outcome from 7% to 5% assuming an average cluster size of 39 (coefficient of variation 0.72), an intra-cluster correlation coefficient of 0.01 and to allow-for 10% drop-out, we will recruit 270 clusters, 10530 patients. Expertise in team: Expertise in patient and public involvement (PPI), primary and secondary care physicians with research and clinical interest in at-risk asthma, health technology assessments, pragmatic cluster randomised controlled trials, statistics, health economics, qualitative research and comprehensive evaluation of complex intervention.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Fuelling health equity? The impact of the Winter Fuel Payment on the health of UK households
Abstract: The use of financial payments to encourage behaviours governments find useful is becoming common. The logic for these payments is that they may encourage small changes in behaviour which have potentially large benefits to the individual and society (e.g. Higgins et al., 2012; Promberger, Dolan, & Marteau, 2012). Policy based on traditional economics has focused on the direct behavioural effects of incentives and the provision of information. Recent insights from behavioural economics suggest that how cash transfers are labelled may affect how this money is spent. This is because people appear to allocate the cash transfer income to a relatively non-fungible mental account that is directly linked to the transfer label. An example of this type of cash transfer policy is the Winter Fuel Payment (WFP). The WFP was initiated to combat fuel poverty and the related excess winter mortality and morbidity among older households in the UK. This winter morbidity is associated with cold indoor climates generally believed to be caused by insufficient heating of the home. The WFP provides households that include a member over the age of 60 years (in the qualifying week of a given year) with a lump sum annual payment in November, with the goal that it will be put towards increased energy use and lead to warmer indoor temperatures. Recent research (Beatty et al., 2011) suggests that recipients spend 41% of the transfer on fuel, much higher than the 3% expected increase if the payment were treated as cash. Although the WFP has the objective of enhancing the health and well-being of the fuel poor, research has not yet evaluated this possibility. The proposed programme of work will treat the WFP as a natural experiment and employ a regression discontinuity design to estimate the potential causal effect of the WFP on household temperature, circulatory (e.g. blood pressure, coronary symptoms) and respiratory (e.g. lung function) health and the presence of infection (e.g. raised C-reactive protein levels.). Health variables which react quickly to cold and can gauge the presence of upper respiratory tract infections have been selected for this study. We also capitalize on the sharp eligibility criteria for the WFP to test whether the payment improves perceptions of physical health and mental health and well-being ratings. To do this, we will utilize three large scale population health databases; the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, the Health Survey for England, and the UK Biobank study. Each of these studies contain rich measures provided by participants sampled consistently throughout the year, making this data ideal for producing comparisons between those who turn 60 before (recipients) and after (non-recipients/comparison group) the eligibility cut-off date for the WFP. The proposed programme of research brings together an interdisciplinary team working in areas of behavioural economics, environmental economics, epidemiology and behavioural medicine who together will build an evidence base for assessing the potential health benefits of the WFP and whether these are located principally amongst those on low incomes. We will estimate the role of the WFP in making homes warmer and attenuating the 'Winter excess' in morbidity. In addition, we will gauge how these potential effects differ by income groups. This research will provide key insights into how the labelling of a key Government transfer may have health effects.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Understanding the impact of tobacco tax increases and tobacco industry pricing on smoking behaviours and inequalities
Abstract: BACKGROUND:Tobacco tax increases are the most effective & cost effective means of reducing tobacco use & inequalities in smoking yet recent work identifies concerns that this study aims to address:the public health impacts of tax increases are being undermined by tobacco industry(TI) pricing strategies;government willingness to increase taxes is constrained by fear that tax increases prompt tax evasion & avoidance. AIM:To evaluate the public health effectiveness of tobacco tax increases in reducing tobacco use & inequalities in tobacco use & the extent to which this is undermined by TI pricing strategies. RESEARCH QUESTIONS 1.To what extent does the TI transfer tobacco tax increases to consumers & does this differ by product/price segment? 2.What impact do tobacco tax increases, moderated by TI pricing,have on smokers’ behaviour(consumption,quitting,switching)? 3.What are the characteristics of smokers using cheap tobacco,what impact do tobacco tax increases & TI pricing have on smoking inequalities& can TI pricing explain widening smoking inequalities? 4.Do cheap tobacco products provide a market entry route for young smokers? 5.What are the trends in & nature of & what impact do tobacco tax increases have on smokers’,particularly disadvantaged smokers’,tax avoiding & evading behaviours? 6.How can we improve the effectiveness of tobacco taxation as a public health intervention? SETTING & TARGET POPULATION:All adult smokers(12.5 million)in the UK. NON-NHS INTERVENTION:Annual tobacco tax increases implemented by HM Treasury & moderated by TI pricing strategies. FUNDING:No intervention funding required. OUTCOME MEASURES:The primary outcome measure is tobacco use measured via:cigarette consumption;quitting;use of cheap legal products(cheap cigarettes,roll-your-own(RYO) tobacco);switching between one price segment & another;tax evasion & avoidance. DATA &SAMPLE SIZES 1.International Tobacco Control(ITC) Survey:longitudinal study of ~2000 UK smokers & recent ex-smokers with f/u since 2002. 8 waves of data (2002-10) already obtained. Waves 9 & 10(2013 & 2014) available for project. 2.Smoking Toolkit Study(STS):monthly repeated cross-sectional survey of ~1800 adults in England,2006-2015. 3.2008-14 Nielsen brand specific tobacco product price & sales data covering 94% of UK sales. Sample sizes have adequate statistical power for our analyses. ANALYSES RQ1:Literature review of TI price segmentation;analysis of Nielsen data to determine current TI pricing of both manufactured cigarettes & RYO tobacco & the extent to which the TI transfers tobacco tax increases to consumers. RQ2:Analysis of ITC data to explore the impact of tobacco tax increases as moderated by TI pricing on smokers’ behaviour & whether behavioural choices differ by previous product/price choice. RQ3:Analysis of ITC data to determine the characteristics of smokers in each product/price segment; whether behavioural responses vary by socio-economic status & whether cheap product use is linked to widening inequalities. RQ4:Analysis of ITC & STS data to determine young people’s brand & product choices over time. RQ5:Analysis of ITC & STS data to examine trends in & the nature of tax evasion & avoidance & relationship with increases in tobacco taxation/price. RQ6:Policy recommendations based on synthesis of 1-5. POTENTIAL IMPACTS:Development of more effective tobacco taxation policy to significantly reduce tobacco use particularly among the least well off

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Electronically-delivered, multi-component interventions to reduce unnecessary antibiotic prescribing in primary care. A cluster randomised trial using electronic health records (eCRT2)
Abstract: Design: Cluster randomised trial using the electronic health records (EHRs) of the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD). Setting: General practices in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Target population: General population of all ages. Inclusion Criteria: All persons currently registered with participating CPRD general practices. Exclusions: none. Health technology being assessed: Control trial arm practices will continue with usual clinical care. Practices in the Intervention trial arm will receive complex multi-component interventions, delivered remotely as follows: i) feedback of each practice’s antibiotic prescribing results in relation to peers, through monthly updated antibiotic prescribing reports estimated from CPRD data; ii) delivery of educational and decision support tools to support policies of no-antibiotic prescribing or delayed prescribing; iii) 'three minute webinars' to explain and promote utilisation of the intervention materials. The intervention will continue for 12 months. Measurement of costs and outcomes: Outcomes will be evaluated from CPRD EHRs. The primary outcome will be the number of antibiotic prescriptions for RTI per 1,000 patient years. Secondary outcomes will be: the RTI consultation rate; the proportion of consultations for respiratory tract infection (RTI) with an antibiotic prescribed; sub-groups of age; different categories of respiratory infections; and quartiles of intervention utilisation. Safety outcomes will be diagnoses of pneumonia and lower respiratory infection, peritonsillar abscess, mastoiditis, skin infections and bacterial infections. Health care utilisation will be estimated from CPRD consultation and referral records. Sample size calculation: Family practice-specific proportions will be included in a cluster-level analysis, adjusting for pre-intervention values. In the recent eCRT study, the mean antibiotic prescribing rate for RTI was 112 per 1,000 (SD 39.8). Using analysis of covariance, with measures over 12 months before- and after- the intervention giving a correlation coefficient of 0.82, if there are 60 practices in each of two trial arms then, with alpha=0.05, there will be more than 80% power to detect an absolute reduction in antibiotic prescription for RTI of 12 per 1,000 registered patient years. The 120 trial practices may include more than 1.2 million individual participants. Project recruitment rate: During the first 12 months, we will obtain research governance approvals; refine the intervention drawing on behaviour-change theory, systematic review evidence, clinical guidelines, qualitative research with non-trial practices, as well as process evaluation data from the eCRT study. General practices will be recruited and allocated. In eCRT, 100 CPRD general practices were recruited over 6 months. During the second year of the project, the intervention will be active. Each month, updated practice-specific prescribing information will be delivered to intervention practices. Prescribing decisions will also be supported by educational and decision-support tools and webinars delivered remotely through practice systems. Expertise in team: The team has multi-disciplinary expertise in epidemiology, medical statistics, health psychology and primary care research. The team has experience in CPRD data analysis, cluster trial design and analysis using CPRD, as well as complex intervention development and implementation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A cluster randomised controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the GoActive programme to increase physical activity among 13-14 year-old adolescents
Abstract: Background: Adolescent physical activity promotion is rarely effective, despite adolescence being critical for preventing a steep physical activity decline. Low adolescent physical activity is likely to last into adulthood, increasing health risks. Intervention development: The GoActive intervention is evidence-based and designed iteratively with adolescent input to ensure appeal for all students. Strategies for effective inclusion of inactive/shy adolescents were developed in collaboration with people with these characteristics. Feasibility/pilot work: We studied the feasibility in 1 school and conducted a subsequent pilot RCT in 3 schools (2 intervention/1 control). Learning from both projects have been incorporated in the current proposal. Design/setting/target population: Secondary school based cluster randomised controlled trial, recruiting all Year 9 students in participating schools. Intervention being evaluated: GoActive aims to increase physical activity through increased peer support, self-efficacy, self-esteem and friendship quality, and is implemented using a tiered-leadership system. Tutor groups choose 2 weekly activities each; mentors (older adolescents in the school) and weekly peer-leaders (2 per class) encourage students try these. Students gain points for trying new activities; points are entered into a between-class competition. GoActive will run for 2 terms: weekly facilitation support from a council-funded health trainer will be offered in term 1, with more distant support in term 2. Evaluation: We aim to recruit 16 schools with socio-economic status representing national variability. Outcomes assessed at (1) baseline, (2) interim (wk6), (3) post intervention (wk14-16), and (4) 10-month follow-up [main outcome]. Primary outcome: Change in daily accelerometer-assessed moderate-to-vigorous physical activity Secondary outcomes: 1. Accelerometer-assessed sedentary, light, overall physical activity during school time, weekday evenings, weekends 2. Self-reported physical activity, self-efficacy, self-esteem, peer support, friendship quality, mood, school-reported absence and academic performance, measured body fat %, BMI 3. Within-trial, long term cost-effectiveness and cost-utility analyses 4. Mixed methods process evaluation assessing a) programme acceptability, uptake, maintenance, and dose; and b) putative moderators/mediators Sample size: We require 1310 adolescents (N=100/school) for 85% power to detect a 5-minute difference in change in MVPA/day (SD:17.8; ICC:0.034). We aim to recruit 150 participants at 16 schools to account for 30-40% attrition and school drop out. Randomisation: Schools will be randomised after baseline measurements; students will be the unit of analysis. Economic evaluation: Within-trial cost-effectiveness will be expressed as incremental costs per incremental change in physical activity (METs). Long term cost-effectiveness will assess whether the intervention is likely to increase length and/or quality of life, and at what cost. Process evaluation: Focus groups and interviews (mentors/teachers/students) will explore programme acceptability, barriers/facilitators, potential mechanisms of effect, population group differences and maintenance. Qualitative data will inform and be integrated with quantitative data (questionnaires/participation logs). Impact: Stakeholder workshops will ensure dissemination of results for optimal public health impact.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Screening programme for pre-eclampsia (SPREE)
Abstract: BACKGROUND. Pre-eclampsia (PE), which affects about 2% of pregnancies, is a major cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. PE can be subdivided into preterm-PE requiring delivery <37 weeks’ gestation and late-PE with delivery >37 weeks. Preterm-PE is associated with a higher incidence of adverse outcomes. There is evidence that the prevalence of PE can potentially be reduced by the prophylactic use of low-dose aspirin started before 16 weeks’ gestation and therefore there is a need for effective early detection of high-risk women that could benefit from aspirin therapy. HYPOTHESIS. We have developed a technique for PE screening, using a novel Bayes-based method, which is likely to be superior to the current method recommended by the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) based on maternal characteristics and medical history (Mat-CH). Our method uses Bayes theorem to combine the prior information from Mat-CH with measurements of mean arterial pressure (MAP), uterine artery pulsatility index (Ut-PI), serum placental growth factor (PLGF) and serum pregnancy associated plasma protein-A (PAPP-A) at 11-13 weeks’ gestation (combined test). The estimated detection rate, for false positive rate of 10%, of the NICE method is about 40% for preterm-PE and 35% for all-PE and the respective values for our proposed combined test are about 75% and 55% and mini combined test (Mat-CH with MAP and PAPP-A) are 60% and 50%. DESIGN. Prospective cohort study in six NHS hospitals. The study will comprise of a multicentre study on the clinical evaluation of the new method and comparison of performance with current practice. This will require training healthcare providers for each component of screening in order to ensure quality. SETTING. Antenatal scan clinics in the UK NHS. POPULATION. Women with singleton pregnancies attending for their routine 11-13 weeks scan. OUTCOME. The primary outcome will be the false positive and true positive frequencies for screening using the Bayes-based method and for screening according to the NICE guidelines. SAMPLE SIZE. 16,000 singleton pregnancies. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS. The primary analysis will be a comparison of detection rates using the Bayes-based method with the NICE guidelines. McNemars test at the one sided 2.5% level will be applied. The analysis will be adjusted for the effects of aspirin treatment, because treatment biases the comparison of screening performance by reducing the incidence of PE in the treated group. We have investigated the properties of this analysis across a range of scenarios to assess effect of bias adjustments on the type I and type II error rates. In the most extreme case the sample size of 16,000 has 99% power demonstrating an increase in detection rate of all-PE from 35% to 50%. TIME TABLE. Protocol, months 1-2; Training, months 1-3; ethics and R&D approval, months 2-5; site initiation, months 5-6; patient recruitment, months 7-16; collection of pregnancy outcomes, months 12-25; analysis and writing of results, months 26-30. ECONOMIC BENEFITS. Effective screening for PE can lead to effective prevention of the condition and reduce the associated costs for the short-term and long-term management of women with PE and their children.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Variation and Determinants of Novel Psychoactive Substance (NPS) Use: Potential Implications for Policy and Practice'
Abstract: Lifetime prevalence estimates of drug use in the UK suggest that one in three adults (aged 18-59 years) report having ever used illicit drugs (Winstock, 2012). Recently there have been significant variations in the range and types of drugs used. In particular, the recent emergence and use of Novel Psychoactive Substances (NPS) often known as ‘legal highs’ in the UK, Europe and internationally (EMCDDA, 2012), has raised prominent challenges in the fields of drug policy, substance use research, public health and service provision. This rapidly changing drug market and the associated harms of NPS are prioritised as areas of concern in regional, national and local drug strategies (ACMD, 2011; EMCDDA, 2012; Home Office, 2012, RC Psych 2014). The speed at which these substances emerge and the fast-changing pace of drug markets hinders the quality of up-to-date research around patterns of NPS use and associated harms. The evidence that is available however, suggests dependence-like symptoms associated with use of NPS and an increase in referrals to some drug services, have been affiliated with increased use of NPS in the UK and elsewhere in Europe (EMCDDA). NPS represent a distinct challenge in the field of drug addiction, but also a fast growing problem from social, cultural, legal and political perspectives (Sigismondi et al 2012). This study aims to examine the use of NPS within a conceptual framework that elucidates the harms of use, in a bid to inform future practice around the prevention, harm reduction and treatment of NPS use. This study will use quantitative and qualitative methods in order to examine and ascertain variation and determinants of NPS use and to delineate typologies of drug use, particularly NPS and the unique risks/harms in an NPS group and a non-NPS group. The study will make use of a nested case-control design using cohort data from sweep 7 of the Belfast Youth Development Study (BYDS) and will address the key issues by (1): novel analysis of existing data on the use of NPS collected in 2010. (2) conducting a number of qualitative narratives with participants from the identified NPS group/non-NPS group from BYDS and service users to elucidate and cross-validate potential outcomes; (3) utilizing a modified Delphi method, knowledge exchange working groups of lay members, service users, professionals and policy makers will be established in order to facilitate knowledge sharing around the most effective means of reducing the use and harm of NPS with the potential to inform a framework to assist practice. This component has the potential to guide the future strategic direction among policy-makers public health initiatives and those involved in the prevention/treatment of NPS use. To date, research around NPS, including pathways into use, determinants of NPS use and the associated harms is exceptionally limited. This study will generate new knowledge in each of these important areas and will add to the literature regarding the relationships between the potential harms of use and the potential pathways of risk.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The Novel Psychoactive Substances in the UK Project (NPS-UK)
Abstract: There are wide-ranging grounds for concern about novel psychoactive substance (NPS) use. The need for evidence has been identified by the UK Government and the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs for some years, and meeting this research need is now a prominent part of the National Drugs Strategy. The overall aim of this proposal is to inform the development of public health intervention research on NPS in the UK by undertaking an investigation of the current evidence-base. On this basis we will address gaps in available evidence and make recommendations on research priorities. The study objectives are as follows: 1. To summarise and evaluate what is known about NPS use in the UK and related harms and responses through the conduct of a systematic review of peer-reviewed and grey literature. 2. To develop a dedicated conceptual framework for a public health approach to NPS use which identifies the scope for interventions based on approaches developed for the use of other legal and illegal drugs, and the concerns of public health and prevention more broadly. 3. To produce a statement of public health intervention research issues for NPS use in the UK that makes recommendations on key evidence gaps and priorities for future research. There are two study components corresponding to the first two study objectives, including one major study component (in relation to objective 1) and one smaller study components (for objective 2). Synergies between these study components are a key feature of this proposal. The conceptual framework is elaborated in order to assist with the narrative synthesis of the data from the NPS systematic review. It will in turn be used to provide a robust assessment of key evidence gaps and research priorities, and articulation of the key issues facing public health intervention research, presented in the final report. There are unusual levels of uncertainty about future trends in NPS use, implications for public health and the NHS, and it is thus important that strategic research efforts are not confined to the current generation of NPS, but are capable of adapting to the new drugs that are expected to emerge in the years to come.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Screening women age 65 or over for abdominal aortic aneurysm: a modelling study and health economic evaluation
Abstract: A one-off ultrasound screening of men at age 65 for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) and subsequent recall of individuals with identified AAA has been shown to reduce AAA-related mortality and to be cost-effective for the NHS. Whether this extends to women is unknown, so at present the national AAA screening programme in the UK is restricted to men. However, 34% of deaths from AAA are now in women, and this proportion is likely to increase in the future. In this project, we will evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of AAA screening in women. This will involve: (a) Adapting a previously validated long-term cost-effectiveness model of AAA screening in men as a more flexible individual simulation model; (b) Obtaining relevant input parameters for women from the literature and/or other data sources; (c) Running the model for women, to estimate AAA-related mortality, all-cause mortality, life-expectancy, costs, and cost-effectiveness in terms of cost per life-year gained, and per quality adjusted life-year (QALY) gained, over both short-term and lifetime horizons. It is recognised that some input parameters will be very uncertain or even unknown for women (in which case parameters for men may initially have to be used). A key component of the research will therefore be to evaluate the uncertainty in conclusions by both probabilistic and deterministic sensitivity analyses. Where unknown parameters are likely to have a major influence on conclusions, the expected value of information (EVI) related to them will be assessed. Aortic diameters are typically smaller in women than men, life-expectancy is greater, and AAA rupture rates are about four times higher for a given AAA diameter. So in addition it is proposed to evaluate some possible departures from the design of the AAA screening programme in men. These include the definition of an AAA (for example an aortic diameter of at least 2.5 cm in women as opposed to the conventional definition of at least 3.0 cm), age at screening (for example age 70 years for women rather 65 years for men), and the AAA diameter threshold for consideration for surgery (for example 5.0 cm for women rather than the conventional 5.5 cm). Within these options we will also consider the choice of surveillance intervals for AAAs in women below the surgical threshold. Another issue to be addressed is whether there are subgroups of women (for example current and ex-smokers, or sisters of men with an AAA) at whom such screening should be targeted. Although this project has a UK focus, its results will have implications for the development of AAA screening programmes internationally, as is evident for example from the recent recommendations on AAA screening from the US Preventive Services Task Force.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: An exploratory study to test STASH, a peer-led intervention to prevent and reduce STI transmission and improve sexual health in secondary schools
Abstract: Rationale: Young people in the UK are at highest risk of STIs and report higher levels of unsafe sex than any other age group. Their elevated risk has been linked to lack of awareness, insufficient knowledge of how to protect themselves, and social norms which denigrate safer sexual behaviour and undermine the quality of intimate relationships. Research suggests that involving peer supporters in intervention delivery is acceptable to students and effective in reducing risk behaviours via ‘diffusion of innovation’, particularly where peer supporters are influential role models, chosen by peers. Interventions in which peer supporters work informally within their social networks offer a useful alternative to peer-led didactic teaching, which has shown limited effects. To date, there have been no UK school-based studies in which peer supporters utilise social media, despite research from elsewhere suggesting their potential. Intervention: Building on learning from ASSIST (an effective peer-led anti-smoking intervention), we will identify and recruit the most influential students in fourth year (S4) of secondary schools (aged 14 to 16) in Scotland. These students will attend a two-day training run by specialist trainers. Over a defined period (between 4 and 10 weeks) they will use social media and face-to-face interaction to diffuse information, norm change and support for healthy sexual behaviour among their peers. They will be supported – through regular meetings and via social media – by the professionals who trained them. Participants and methods: Stage one involves formative evaluation of the intervention, including expert and student panels to advise on intervention design, as well as piloting of the intervention and evaluation instruments in one school. In stage two the revised intervention will be tested via an exploratory study in 6 schools, with staged implementation and comparison with the previous cohort of S4 students (controls). We will undertake a process evaluation in 6 schools based on: structured observation and evaluation of training; web-based questionnaire for peer supporters; interviews and focus groups with peer supporters, student participants, trainers, teachers and parents; and social network analysis. Measures: The main outcome is attainment of progression criteria to a potential subsequent full trial. The primary intervention outcome is frequency of unprotected sex. We will also assess the feasibility and acceptability of linkage to NHS data on STI diagnosis as a longer-term outcome. Secondary outcomes include: self-reported STI diagnosis, testing and symptoms; sexual behaviour; relationship quality; adherence to targeted behavioural norms; perceptions about the behaviour of others; knowledge of STI risk; awareness and use of local sexual health services; STI prevention skills; beliefs about capabilities. Process measures include feasibility, fidelity, acceptability and reach of the intervention, for example the proportion of nominated peer supporters who agreed to participate. We will assess the perceived value of peer supporters among students, the level of exposure to the intervention, and acceptability to teachers. We will also record the key costs of intervention adaptation, implementation and maintenance and we will assess the feasibility of measuring sexual quality of life and information on sexual health related health care resource use.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Feasibility study of how best to engage obese men in narrative SMS (short message system) and incentive interventions for weight loss, to inform a future effectiveness and cost-effectiveness trial
Abstract: IMPORTANCE: In 2013, 26% of UK men were obese and this prevalence is increasing. Systematic reviews suggest that far fewer men than women engage in formal weight loss programmes, but if they do they are less likely to drop out MAIN RESEARCH QUESTIONS: Is a narrative SMS intervention with embedded behaviour change techniques (BCTs) and endowment incentives acceptable and feasible to deliver in a RCT? How can intervention components and delivery processes be optimised to increase reach, engagement and follow up of obese men? Are progression criteria met for a full RCT for one or both interventions? What are the likely recruitment and attrition rates? What would be the sample size for a full trial? AIM: To co-produce with PPI, an acceptable and feasible RCT design with wide reach to test a narrative SMS intervention with embedded BCTs, with and without an endowment incentive, compared to waiting list. This will inform a future pragmatic, full-scale effectiveness and cost-effectiveness trial DESIGN: A two phase feasibility study. Phase 1 will i) build a narrative SMS intervention with embedded BCTs for men using qualitative co-design, and ii) develop an endowment incentive drawing on insights from behavioural economics, existing evidence and men’s preferences for delivery based on survey/DCE evidence. An iterative mixed methods approach will use systematic review evidence, theory and learning from recent UK behaviour change trials to refine the interventions through PPI and user testing. Phase 2 is a 12 month feasibility RCT with 3 arms: SMS only; SMS and incentive; usual practice with waiting list for SMS intervention. Iterative mixed method data collection and analysis will help to refine the intervention parameters, design and processes in preparation for a potential full pragmatic effectiveness and cost-effectiveness RCT SETTING: 2 communities in Scotland with disadvantaged areas; differing in employment, ethnic groups, urban and rural access POPULATION: Obese adult men with BMI 30 or over and/or waist measurement 40 inches (102cm) or over. Recruitment through community venues (50%) and GP obesity registers (50%) (small payment required). Phase 1: a survey/DCE (n=1067 obese men); qualitative interviews/focus groups with 20-30 men and a stakeholder workshop (n=20) to finalise the intervention. Phase 2: 105 men randomised to three groups (n=35 each) and 24-30 qualitative interviews INTERVENTIONS: 1.Narrative SMS with embedded BCTs; 2.The same SMS plus endowment incentives CONTROL: Waiting list for narrative SMS intervention ALL GROUPS A pedometer for PA monitoring PRIMARY OUTCOMES: Acceptability and feasibility of recruitment, retention, intervention components, time points for verifying weight with assessor blinding, identifying core outcomes that are acceptable and matter for obese men SECONDARY OUTCOMES: Differential recruitment, engagement with narrative SMS and incentive components and attrition by socio-economic status and setting. Quality of motivation (intrinsic and extrinsic), satisfaction with weight loss, qualitative experiences, risk of incentive gaming. Meeting progression criteria, calculating the sample size and securing intervention funds for a full trial LIKELY FULL RCT PRIMARY OUTCOME: Weight loss at 1 year. SECONDARY: % weight loss, waist circumference, QALYs, costs IMPACT: A novel theory based intervention ready for a full RCT, with broad reach and with central delivery at scale

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Healthy Dads, Healthy Kids UK: a cultural adaptation and feasibility study of a weight management programme for fathers of younger children
Abstract: DESIGN Two phases informed by the MRC complex interventions framework.[25] PHASE 1: INTERVENTION ADAPTATION The Healthy Dads, Healthy Kids (HDHK) intervention is a 9 session group-based weight management and healthy lifestyle programme for fathers and their children (aged 4-11 years) delivered in community settings.[5,6,27] The intervention will be adapted to an ethnically diverse UK population using principles for adapting behaviour change interventions for multi-ethnic groups[26] and information from focus groups and semi-structured interviews with overweight fathers and their partners from ethnically and socio-economically diverse groups. Manuals and resources for the facilitators and participants will be adapted. PHASE 2: FEASIBILTY STUDY The feasibility aims to test the delivery and acceptability of the adapted programme, recruitment and retention; additional aims will test the feasibility of components of the proposed RCT to determine the feasibility of the protocol. SETTING Birmingham, an ethnically diverse city. Weight management services for adults currently have an under-representation of men (<15%). The service will be funded by the local authority (LA) and group facilitators recruited from Change4Life Champions, teachers and local authority fitness coaches. A further site will be selected from Sandwell or Wolverhampton. STUDY POPULATION: Obese fathers (BMI>=30kg/m2/27.5kg/m2 for minority ethnic groups) of children (aged 4-11) identified through schools, religious organisations, jobcentres and workplaces. DESIGN: Feasibility RCT with 90 fathers randomised (stratified by ethnicity) 2:1 to intervention (described above) or control group (fathers provided with information about local opportunities for physical activity and voucher for a single free attendance for the family at a leisure centre). OUTCOME MEASURES: Intervention acceptability by attendance at programme. Uptake and adherence rates. Interviews and focus groups will be used to explore programme providers, fathers’, children’s and mothers'/partners' views of the programme, and reasons for non-completion. The feasibility of a future definitive trial will be assessed by recruitment rates, willingness to be randomised, follow-up rates at 3 and 12 months and level of questionnaire completion. OUTCOME MEASURES TO INFORM FULL TRIAL at 3 and 12 months to test feasibility of data collection: Fathers’ weight change at 3 and 12 months; % losing 5% or more body mass, self-reported and objectively measured physical activity, self-reported dietary intake and involvement of father in parenting. Children’s BMI z-score change, % body fat, objectively measured physical activity, self-reported dietary intake, attainment data collected from schools. Quality of life measures and costs of taking part to inform future economic study. Fathers, mothers/partners and children will be interviewed at 3 and 12 months to explore their views on intervention acceptability, ability to sustain behaviour change, changes to food purchasing and cooking practices and family relationships. Fidelity of delivery of HDHK programme from observations of sessions and focus groups with facilitators. SAMPLE SIZE: To achieve feasibility objectives and estimate of fathers’ weight change at 6 months and standard deviation to inform sample size of full trial. PROJECT LENGTH: 27 months. 12 months adaptation; 12 months feasibility RCT, 3 months analyses and write-up.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: What are the determinants of variations in emergency readmission rates and one-year mortality in patients hospitalized with heart failure or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
Abstract: Background Heart failure (HF) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) affect around two million people in the UK and are among the commonest reasons for emergency hospitalisation. Both conditions also have high emergency readmission rates. In international comparisons England lags behind other countries on heart failure prevention and treatment. National audits and other studies have documented variations in care processes and outcomes for many patient groups, including those with HF and COPD. To improve patient care, an understanding of the drivers of service use and outcomes is needed. This remains limited. Previous work has focused on aggregate emergency admission rates or on patient factors that predict readmission and mortality. Studies that have explored associations between hospital factors and outcomes have largely been from the USA and may be of limited relevance to the NHS. Studies have generally been cross-sectional in approach and therefore have not considered the patient journey through multiple health service contacts except in a superficial way. To address these shortcomings, we aim to employ the richness of English NHS hospital administrative data, hospital-level characteristics such as beds and staff numbers, and publicly available primary care quality and access scores and hospital staff and patient experience surveys. We will also collect and incorporate basic information on community services and demand management programmes. Aims and objectives The study aims to use existing data to explore patterns and determinants of variations in outcomes by patients hospitalized with HF or COPD. From available data, can we discover which hospitals have the best outcomes and why? We will focus on two outcomes: short-term emergency readmission and one-year mortality. The approach could serve as a template to investigate other long-term conditions. Our research questions are: 1. What are the main factors associated with variation in readmission and mortality rates? 2. Should A&E attendance data be considered alongside readmission metrics when measuring hospital performance in terms of unplanned activity? If so, how? 3. How consistently do hospitals perform across different readmission-type metrics? 4. Are the results for COPD similar to those for HF? Analysis A&E attendance data include time and day of attendance: we will assess the relation between attendance out of hours, particularly at weekends, and during busy times and admission and the relation between attendance and readmission rates. We will use regression to assess the relation between outcomes (readmission and one-year mortality) and various hospital and GP factors including staff and patient experience survey and QOF quality scores. Principal component analysis will be used to reduce the correlated survey variables. Consistency of hospital performance will be assessed by correlation (non-linear if necessary) and funnel plot outliers; hierarchical modelling will be used to estimate the between-hospital variation in outcomes and how this is affected by patient and primary care factors. Benefits and impact of research 1. Understand how hospital, primary care and patient factors relate to outcomes 2. Understand drivers of variations in readmission rates, a key but controversial performance indicator 3. Appreciate the utility for performance monitoring of the A&E component of the key national NHS hospital administrative database

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Learning about and learning from GP Federations in the English NHS – a qualitative investigation
Abstract: GP federations, defined as groups ‘of practices and primary care teams working together, sharing responsibility for developing and delivering high quality, patient focussed services for their local communities’(RCGP Toolkit 2010) are emerging in response to the pressures facing primary care(Kings Fund, 2013: 5). Federations are a supra-practice level of organisation. They vary in scope and organisational form, from loose alliances of a small number of local practices, to much larger publicly limited provider companies.Potential benefits of federations include efficiencies of scale and scope, strengthening capacity to deliver services outside hospital and improving local integration. Federations present many challenges including balancing individual practice ways of working, autonomy and identity with the requirements of more centralised and standardised procedures which federations imply. Federations are substantially different to the traditional partnership model, however,little is known about how federations are working in practice and the implications of different organisational forms for the organisation of primary care. We will explore how GP federations are working in practice. The aims of the research are to: • Provide a wide ranging and in depth exploration of GP federations in England • Strengthen the evidence base on the organisation and management of general practice for the twenty first century. Based on our earlier study of 2 federations, we suggest that it is not possible at this stage to simply measure the impact of changes on health (proxy) outcomes, given the diverse objectives of federations and evolving nature of the organisations concerned. Yet it is important to understand how federations are emerging and operating and produce early lessons to inform their future development. In addition to a mapping exercise to construct a national picture of the types of federations and their locations, this study will involve in-depth qualitative research in three federation and 1 non federation case study sites. We will use qualitative methods to explore the stated aims of federations and the mechanisms by which such aims are intended to be achieved. We will also assess progress against these aims. Other foci will include the mechanisms by which practices are working together within the federation, enabling and constraining factors regarding establishment and operation of the federation and the impact on the constituent practices (in the widest possible sense including practical impacts on their work, impacts on practice identity etc.). In addition, we will explore impacts on patients in our case study sites using interviews. Data collection will include interviews with a range of stakeholders. Our selection of interviewees will in part be guided by the stated aims of the federations involved but as a minimum it will include patients and carers, practice staff, acute and community care providers and representatives of the social care sector. We will also observe relevant meetings and conduct documentary analysis to add to our understanding of what is happening in case study sites. Study outcomes will be • A typology of federations • A national picture of federations, classified according to our typology • An in-depth understanding of how federations are working in a small number of case study sites • Lessons for the wider implementation of new organisational forms in English primary care

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Young people with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in transition from children's services to adult services (Catch-uS): a mixed methods project using national surveillance, qualitative and mapping studies
Abstract: Several qualitative and quantitative studies have illustrated that young people struggle to move between child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) and adult mental health services (AMHS).(1-3) This has been highlighted in a number of government documents and policy guidance;(4,5) however, it was not until 2011 that the government published a mental health outcomes strategy that states how service transition can be improved.(6) Until recently ADHD was controversial as a diagnosis, and then it was conceptualised as a developmental disorder that affected children; therefore, current service configuration cannot accommodate the young people with ADHD who have started to graduate from children’s services.(3,7,8) Poor transition may result in young people with on-going needs disengaging from services,(9,10) which may in turn lead to poorer long-term outcomes such as: academic failure, low occupational status, low self-esteem, substance abuse (tobacco, alcohol or drugs), car accidents, delinquency, and poorer social relationships.(11) Currently, there are no national data on the level of need for the supervision of medication as per NICE guidelines for adults with ADHD. This study focuses on the transfer and transition of young people with ADHD between children’s services and adult services, with particular reference to those requiring medication related to their ADHD as a concrete indication of ongoing service need. The proposed project consists of three streams: a traditional surveillance study of young people with ADHD on medication who are within six months of the age-boundary for discharge from their service, a qualitative study to explore the views and experiences of service users, their carers and providers regarding the barriers to and facilitators of transitions from children’s to adult services and a mapping study that will describe current services delivery. The surveillance stream will run in parallel through the Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Surveillance System (CAPSS) and the British Paediatric Surveillance Unit (BPSU). They provide an established methodology for the study of rare disorders or events that present to consultant child and adolescent psychiatrists and paediatricians practising in the UK and Republic of Ireland (ROI) respectively. A six-month surveillance study will identify all young people with ADHD on medication that require transfer to adult services and referral services. This stream will generate a sampling frame of paediatricians and child psychiatrists to participate in the qualitative stream, through which we will recruit practitioners working with adults who have ADHD. We will interview young people, parents and professionals to explore their views and experiences of the transition between children’s and adult services. We will target three different groups of young people: 1) young people attending children’s services prior to age of maximal drop out from services (14-16 years old), 2) young people who recently successfully transferred directly to adult services, and 3) young adults who dropped-out and re-entered the system in their early to mid-twenties. Young people and parent carers will be recruited from five centres in England: South London and Maudsley NHS trust, Berkshire Healthcare Foundation Trust, Devon Partnership Trust, Coventry & Warwickshire Partnership Trust and Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust. We will combine information about the location and type of care of services for young adults with ADHD from the surveillance study and qualitative study with email / postal surveys of service commissioners, service providers and key service user groups for young adults with ADHD. All will be asked whether their area has a service for adults with ADHD, if so, whether it has staff with dedicated time to work with these young people and what does it offer them? These findings will inform policy and practice for both child and adult services. They will include substantive contributions regarding service needs of young people with ADHD for both children’s and adult services about barriers and facilitators to transition as well as a national estimate of the level of need.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: A systematic review of psychological interventions to improve motivation for self-management in people with type 1 and type 2 diabetes
Abstract: Self-management is the cornerstone of diabetes management yet the majority of patients struggle to achieve national targets for effective glycaemic control. Psychological factors such as depression, eating and weight concerns, diabetes specific fears and worries, acceptance of the diagnosis, coping, health beliefs, family distress and stigma, can reduce the motivation to self-manage. The last systematic reviews of randomised controlled trials (from 1966 to 2003) suggest that motivation is potentially modifiable using brief psychological interventions to address these psychological factors but the quality of most studies had limited validity. In the past decade the number of intervention studies has grown significantly. With the epidemic of type 2 diabetes and the rise in the incidence of type 1 diabetes, increasing awareness of the inequity of mental health services compared to physical health services, the rising costs of new anti-diabetes medications and medical devices, there is a need to develop and evaluate the most effective and cost-effective psychological interventions that optimise diabetes control. We propose to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of randomised and non-randomised controlled trials testing whether brief psychological interventions are effective in improving measures of self-management, glycaemic control and quality of life. The protocol will be based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. We will stratify by type of diabetes, and for type 1 diabetes by children versus adults. We will search MEDLINE, PsychINFO, EMBASE, Cochrane Controlled Trials Database (since 2003-current), Web of Science and the grey literature for eligible studies. Using an a priori standardised format, we will extract qualitative and quantitative data that describe the clinical sample; the potential active ingredients such as theoretical framework, manual, behaviour change techniques, frequency and duration of sessions, format of delivery (face to face or telephone), group versus individual; unit costs; assessment of bias using the Cochrane Handboook checklist; and measures of self-management or behaviour change, glycaemic control and quality of life. We will conduct meta-analyses, individual participant and network meta-analyses, sensitivity and subgroup analyses and statistical assessment of bias. We propose to undertake a cost-effectiveness analysis of the psychological interventions via four components of health economic evaluation related work, namely review of the cost effectiveness literature, costing of the interventions, modelling of cost effectiveness, and Health Economic Decision Modelling Analysis Plan. We will compare our findings with previous reviews to identify any cohort effects or new developments in theory, policy and methodologies. Our findings will inform commissioners developing diabetes pathways and recommendations for primary research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: The Newcastle Upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The NIDUS study: evaluation of efficacy, outcomes and safety of a new infant haemodialysis and ultrafiltration machine in clinical use.
Abstract: Survival of babies in Paediatric Intensive Care (PICU) is only 50-75% for those requiring renal replacement therapy (RRT) for fluid overload or acute kidney failure [1,2]. RRT is supportive until renal recovery but up to 30% may have chronic kidney sequelae. Until this year [16]there were no approved devices for continuous haemofiltration (CVVH) for children under 8kg and many reports of safety concerns. Currently clinicians have to use machines outside recommendations, or use peritoneal dialysis (PD), for approximately 300 infants under 8kg, in UK PICUs, who need RRT each year. RRT in infants is associated with adverse events including haemodynamic instability [3]. The Newcastle infant dialysis and ultrafiltration system (Nidus) is the first device designed for babies 0.8 to 8kg, and has been shown to be efficacious in a pilot study [4]. Further data on efficacy and safety in clinical use outside the development centre are urgently needed. The aim of this study is to compare Nidus with conventional RRT in PICU. Our hypothesis is that fluid balance control and clinical outcomes will be superior in babies treated with the Nidus with good blood clearance and fewer adverse events. We propose a randomised, stepped wedge cluster design: a one-way cross over with each unit acting as their own control. This was chosen over individual patient randomisation because of the strong views of parents, public and professionals regarding feasibility, recruitment, equipoise, ethics, training and safety in this specific PICU situation. The population is babies under 8kg needing continuous RRT for renal impairment or fluid overload in PICU. The intervention is Nidus, compared to current RRT either PD or CVVH (control). The primary outcome is precision of fluid removal. Secondary outcomes include survival, ventilator-free days, renal recovery, biochemical clearances, haemodynamic status (drop in BP requiring intervention) and adverse events such as transfusions, unplanned loss of circuits and access line changes. In addition, and strongly supported by parents, public and professionals, there will be availability of compassionate use for babies under 8kg outside PICU who fail conventional dialysis treatment and for whom there is no other option. Views of staff on acceptability and usability and experience of parents will be sought by questionnaire and a safety profile of the Nidus will be produced.
