Rationale: Our scoping searches identified a plethora of existing systematic reviews (n=85), including meta-analyses. In Warwick, we have undertaken 20 of these relevant systematic reviews as part of the Cochrane heart group. The searches for some of these reviews are outdated and since their publication; numerous additional trials have been published. Purpose: to comprehensively synthesise the evidence on strategies and interventions, including combinations of strategies and interventions, for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in order to develop a hierarchy of interventions and to advise policy makers and health services on how best to target resource to reduce mortality and morbidity from cardiovascular disease in the UK. Setting: All settings. The applicability to UK cultural and health service practice will be assessed. Patient population: Adult populations (=18 years of age) included in population-based studies, which may or may not be targeted at high risk groups (such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes). Health technologies: Any form of intervention aimed at primary prevention of CVD, including but not limited to lipid lowering medications, blood pressure lowering medications, antiplatelet agents, nutritional supplements, dietary interventions, health promotion programmes, physical activity, or structural and policy interventions. Design: The project proposes a series of six inter-related work-streams: Work-stream (WS)1: Evidence harvest and mapping: We will comprehensively search, select and map existing evidence of intervention and policy effectiveness, following standard guidance for integrating existing systematic reviews into new reviews. The mapping stage of the review aims to describe the scale and range of interventions that have been conducted and to categorise the interventions and their components. WS 2: Determining optimal interventions: We will use a two-level hierarchical network meta-analysis (level 1: intervention type, and level 2: intervention class) to borrow strength within the classes of intervention, strengthening inferences and potentially reducing the uncertainty around individual intervention effects. This process will increase our ability to rank these to inform decision-making frameworks. WS 3: Reliability and conclusiveness of evidence: We will calculate the optimal information size required to yield “moderate” and “strong” meta-analytic evidence using trial sequential analysis. The results of each trial sequential analysis will be classified into one of four mutually exclusive categories (superiority, inferiority, futility or inconclusive result). WS 4: Between-study heterogeneity and prevention effects modifiers: We will test effect modification of intervention effectiveness using sub-group analyses and meta-regression analyses. WS 5: Systematic review of economic evaluation and/or economic modelling studies: We will identify, appraise and summarise published models of cost-effectiveness of interventions for the primary prevention of CVD. WS 6: Transferability, Generalisability of interventions and production of lay summaries: We will determine the applicability and generalisability of interventions to the UK NHS setting and we will work with Patient and Public Involvement advisors to produce a summary of effective interventions, ineffective interventions and assessments of where future research effort and public engagement on this topic should be focused.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Stand Up For Health: A Feasibility Cluster Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) Of A Theory Based Intervention To Reduce Sedentary Behaviour In Contact Centres
Abstract: Design: Two armed feasibility cluster randomised controlled trial to test the feasibility and acceptability of a theory based intervention to reduce sedentary behaviour in contact centres (previously known as contact centres). It will include a quantitative assessment of outcomes and the research processes (e.g. retention rates, recruitment rates) in addition to a qualitative evaluation of acceptability and feasibility of processes and the intervention. Population: people who work in contact centres including managers, supervisors and call operators in Scotland and the North of England, areas with the highest rates of contact centre staff. Other areas will be considered. Intervention: Stand Up for Health (SUH), an adaptive theory based complex intervention to reduce sedentary time through four theories of change: organisational, structural, social, and individual. The focus is on fidelity to the theories of change rather than the specific activities. This is a significantly different approach to other interventions, which focus primarily on fidelity to specific activities. It enables the intervention to take account of the context, resources and preferences of the contact centre and those receiving the intervention. Comparator: waiting list control. The control contact centres will all receive the intervention at different time-points. Duration: 3 months of support followed by embedding of the intervention in the contact centre whereby a SUH team (made up of all staff types) will be responsible for ongoing sustainability. The research team will develop a website to give materials and support to the contact centres. Outcome/s: Main outcomes will be feasibility and acceptability of the recruitment, data collection and study design and feasibility of decreasing workplace sedentary activity. The primary outcome in a future trial would be sedentary time in the workplace. Secondary outcomes would be sedentary behaviour outside the workplace, physical activity, musculoskeletal problems, mental health, productivity, absenteeism, presenteeism. Economic evaluation: Intervention-related resource use will be collected and a model for undertaking a full economic evaluation in a future trial will be developed. Process evaluation: We will conduct a process evaluation using the RE-AIM framework to provide insight into the extent to which the intervention was delivered as planned, and the programme theories worked as intended. The intervention will be refined and adapted as necessary. Analysis of outcome data: The statistician will be blind to the allocation of the contact centres. Sedentary time in the workplace and all continuous secondary outcomes will be analysed using linear mixed effects regression analysis; including site and participant as random effects; and adjusting for calendar time since start of study, season (spring, summer, autumn, winter), and an indicator variable for whether the intervention has been implemented or not as fixed effects. Using observed data from all participants, 95% CI of the intervention effect sizes will provide a guide to indicate the likely effect sizes that we will observe in a future study. Sensitivity analyses will be incorporated to explore the effects of missing data and staff turnover to aid the design of a definitive trial. Potential impact: If progression criteria are met we will apply for further funding. Funding: intervention costs are borne by the contact centres.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Whole-school interventions promoting student commitment to school to prevent substance use and violence, and improve educational attainment: a systematic review
Abstract: Background There is increasing interest in whole-school interventions to promote health. We previously synthesised theory and evidence on the effects of schools and school-environment interventions on health. Synthesis of theory drew chiefly on the theory of human functioning and school organisation to propose that interventions promoting commitment to school can promote health by providing students with the autonomy, social support and reasoning ability to avoid risk behaviour. Synthesis of empirical evidence supported the influence of such factors on substance use (tobacco, alcohol and drugs) and violence. However, the review is almost a decade old, drew on a limited body of evidence and was exploratory in scope, with inclusion criteria not informed by a specific theory of change and thus excluding some relevant studies. The review was thus limited in its ability to determine the best ways to promote student commitment and reduce substance use and violence. There has been a recent upsurge in evaluations of whole-school interventions aiming to promote health by increasing student commitment to school. Therefore, we propose a new review using the theory of human functioning and school organisation to focus on whole-school interventions that aim to prevent substance use via: -modifying teaching to increase student engagement in academic learning; -enhancing student-staff relationships; -revising school policies which involves students and/or which goes beyond health or behaviour management policies; -encouraging all students to volunteer in the community; or -involving parents in school life. Research aim and questions To search systematically for, appraise the quality of, and synthesise evidence to answer the following: 1. What whole-school interventions promoting student commitment to school to prevent student substance use and violence have been evaluated, what intervention sub-types are apparent and how closely do these align with the theory of human functioning and school organisation? 2. What factors relating to setting, population and intervention influence the implementation of such interventions? 3. Overall and by intervention sub-type, what are the effects of such interventions on student substance use, violence and educational attainment? 4. What is the cost-effectiveness of such interventions, overall and by intervention sub-type? 5. Are the effects of such interventions on student substance use and violence mediated by student commitment to school, or moderated by setting or population? Design and methods We will follow existing guidelines on the conduct of systematic reviews. We will conduct electronic and other searches, screening references and where appropriate reports for inclusion. We will extract data and assess quality using existing tools. We will synthesise intervention descriptions, theory and process evaluations using narrative and meta-ethnographic approaches. Syntheses of outcome evaluations will narratively and statistically summarise the effects of the intervention overall and intervention sub-types, and synthesise economic evidence. We will undertake mediator and moderator analyses to assess how intervention effects are mediated by increasing student commitment to school, and vary by setting and population. We will consult with policy/practice and community stakeholders on interim and final findings to inform report drafting, dissemination and knowledge exchange.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Evaluating the Home-based Intervention Strategy (HIS-UK) to reduce new chlamydia infection among young men aged 16-25 years by promoting correct and consistent condom use: What is the cost effectiveness of two different delivery models (face-to-face and digital delivery)?
Abstract: The UK Home-Based Intervention Strategy (HIS-UK) is a behaviour change condom promotion intervention for young men designed to enhance enjoyment of condom-protected intercourse, improve attitudes towards condoms, improve the correct and consistent use of condoms, and thereby reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections. HIS-UK is an adapted version of The Kinsey Institute Homework Intervention Strategy® originally developed in the US and which is based on the behavioural therapy directed practice approach most commonly used to treat sexual problems. HIS-UK has two delivery models; digital delivery using an interactive website (eHIS), and face-to-face delivered by a trained health professional (proHIS). This study will build on the previous work of, and lessons learned from, a) the MRC-funded feasibility study of the HIS-UK face-to-face intervention and b) the feasibility and pilot study of the digital version of the intervention. Aim To assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of HIS-UK delivered by proHIS and eHIS to reduce test positivity of Chlamydia among young men aged 16-25 years as compared to usual condom distribution care. Objectives 1) To assess the effectiveness of HIS-UK among young men aged 16-25 years by comparing between the intervention and control arms: • Chlamydia test positivity (6 & 12 months) • episodes of condomless anal and/or vaginal sexual intercourse (1-12 months) • reported condom use errors and problems (1-12 months) • enhanced condom use experiences (1-12months) • positive condom use attitudes (1-12 months) 2) To conduct a process evaluation and mediation analysis to explore the way in which the HIS-UK delivered by proHIS and eHIS may work and the possible mediators and mechanisms of change. 3) To estimate the costs associated with proHIS and eHIS and their cost effectiveness as compared to usual condom distribution care. Methods To compare the effectiveness of HIS-UK delivered by proHIS and eHIS-UK to usual care we propose a randomised, controlled, superiority trial with three-parallel groups (two intervention and one control arm, 1:1:1 allocation), with an internal pilot phase. We will use a repeated measures study design with baseline measurement (T0) and follow-up monthly online questionnaires to 12 months (T1-12) post intervention and three STI screening points (T0,T6,T12) for chlamydia. We will collect health economic data to compare the resource use and cost effectiveness of delivering HIS-UK by the two delivery models to usual condom distribution care. 2231 young men who are ‘at-risk’ of STIs - defined as men, aged 16-25 years, who report condomless penile-vaginal/anal intercourse with casual or new sexual partners during the previous 3 months – will be recruited over 30 months and randomised to either the control or intervention arms. Impact and Dissemination The beneficiaries of this research will be young men who are at risk of STIs; young men's sexual partners; clinicians, youth organisations, Local Authorities and SH service providers; health promotion specialists and SH advisers; policy makers and Local Authority, Public Health and NHS commissioners; condom distributors; the academic community; the public and wider society; and the public purse.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A multicentre cluster randomised controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of KiVa to reduce bullying in primary schools: The UK KiVa Trial
Abstract: Aim: To evaluate the effectiveness & cost-effectiveness of KiVa school-based anti-bullying programme in reducing bullying & victimisation. Design: A two-arm pragmatic multicentre, cluster-randomised controlled trial, with process evaluation, in 116 UK primary schools. Main research question: Is KiVa effective and cost-effective in reducing bullying among 7-11-year olds in UK schools? Intervention: Intervention schools will implement KiVa over one academic year. KiVa, is a whole-school programme, that has a Key Stage 2 (KS2) lesson curriculum, high visibility break time supervision vests, posters & a parent’s guide. All school staff learn about KiVa and its aims. Indicated actions address confirmed bullying incidents. KiVa has yet to be rigorously evaluated in the UK; two small pilot trial in Wales yielded positive findings, however with considerable variation across schools. Delivery: North Wales & Cheshire, the West Midlands, South East & South West England. KS2 teachers will deliver KiVa class lessons. A trained school based KiVa team will address confirmed bullying. Schools are trained by a local KiVa trainer co-ordinated through the Children’s Early Intervention Trust Charity the UK licensed disseminator. Participants: 116 primary schools (12,828 pupils) across England and Wales Comparator: Usual Practice (UP) Outcomes and measures (baseline & 12 month follow-up) Primary outcome: Pupil self-reported bullying and victimisation using the Olweus Bully Victim Questionnaire. Secondary outcomes: Pupil and teaching staff measures. Pupil level: Pupil mental health: Teacher Strengths & Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) Child roles in bullying Child Health Utility 9D (CHU-9D) School well-being (HIFAMS) School attendance Academic attainment Teaching staff level: Self-efficacy in dealing with bullying Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale Maslach Burnout Inventory-Educators Survey Analysis: Intention to treat based on individual pupils, allowing for clustering between pupils within school using robust standard errors. Between-group comparisons will be presented with two-sided 95% CIs. All analyses will control for school level stratification variables & pupil characteristics. ICCs will be reported with 95% CIs. Primary sub-group analyses will investigate intervention by pupil gender & Free School Meal status. Appropriate imputation methods will be applied via sensitivity analyses. Economic evaluation: Bullying incidence, Child Health Utility 9D, Client Service Receipt Inventory, asking for frequency of additional services used by children (e.g. through the school’s Special Educational Needs Co-ordinator/ team) and consultations with school staff regarding bullying; Intervention costs (e.g. staff training, supervision & resources) including data from routine sources. Process evaluation: An integral process evaluation will assess implementation fidelity; identify influences on KiVa implementation including how it interacts with school context; examine intervention mechanisms, including intervention receipt by pupils and parents; describe control schools’ UP in relation to preventing and dealing with bullying. Impact: A universal intervention that reduces bullying is likely to improve children’s mental health and, via improved school connectedness and peer and teacher relationships, reduce the high costs associated with antisocial behaviour, child mental health and inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Evaluating the real-world implementation of the Family Nurse Partnership: a data linkage study
Abstract: Background The Family Nurse Partnership (FNP) is a home visiting programme to improve outcomes of teenage pregnancies. Understanding the context in which FNP is currently delivered and the factors that influence results is key to understanding who might benefit most from FNP and how service delivery may be improved. Our proposal addresses variation in delivery and targeting of FNP by using longitudinal observational data for the whole population eligible for FNP to generate evidence on the real-world implementation of FNP, and the factors that may influence effectiveness (e.g. setting, provider, participants and programme delivery). Research question / Aims and objectives Aim: Generate evidence on the real-world ongoing implementation of FNP in England Research questions 1 Are mothers who are most in need of support receiving FNP? Objectives • Describe variation in delivery of FNP and usual care across LAs • Describe variation in health, education and social care characteristics of families participating in FNP over time and by LA 2 Which families does the real-world implementation of FNP benefit? Objectives • Evaluate the effectiveness of FNP on health, education and social care outcomes for both children and mothers • Determine which families benefit most from FNP • Evaluate outcomes for groups now eligible for FNP but excluded from BB (e.g. mothers up to age 24) 3 What are the contextual factors associated with benefiting from FNP? Objectives • Explore the effect of contextual factors e.g. usual care, nurse characteristics, programme fidelity • Explore individual and LA-level predictors of programme engagement • Determine how FNP differs between LAs and compared with the BB population Methods Design Linked hospital, education and social care records for all mothers aged =24 years, and their children born in England between 2010-2017, plus FNP programme data. Outcomes Children up to age 6: • Child abuse or neglect • Unplanned admissions;A&E visits • Outpatient department referrals • A “good level of development” • Child in care • Child in need status Mothers: • Unplanned admissions;A&E visits • Subsequent pregnancies • Qualifications before versus after birth Analysis We will compare outcomes for mothers ever enrolled in FNP versus those who were never enrolled. Multiple analysis strategies will be used to take account of measured confounders related to both participation in FNP and outcomes, and to explore maternal and programme variables associated with benefiting from FNP. Timeline (months) Pre-award: Finalise data access approvals and recruit study staff 0-6: Data cleaning / preparation for analyses 6-12: Analyses and write up: research question 1 13-18: Analyses and write up: research question 2 19-24: Analyses and write up: research question 3 25-30: Finalise outputs; dissemination. Impact / dissemination We will work with the FNP National Unit (NU) to disseminate results to LAs, policy makers, commissioners, parents and nurses. We will work with parents to co-produce a range of outputs suitable for FNP families and to identify relevant streams of communication. We will publish peer review journal articles and present at conferences. Findings will provide commissioners and policy makers with detailed and up-to-date evidence to aid decision making about the roll out and targeting of FNP. Our findings will inform ongoing adaptations of FNP.

Award_Title: Type A and type B adverse drug reactions with antimicrobials
Abstract: Adverse effects experienced as a result of using antimicrobials are a major health problem. I aim to further investigate the role of host genetics in adverse drug reactions (ADR), focusing on Clostridium difficile infection (Type A) and penicillin allergy (Type B). The project will involve validation of identified biomarkers that can be used to predict either the severity and/or susceptibility of the host. Downstream benefits arising from this work include early identification of patients at-risk of either the ADR or its severity, and thereby personalisation of medical treatment with benefits to patients treated in the NHS.

Award_Title: Experiences of hospital admission in people with diabetes: what can we learn from users and carers to improve unscheduled inpatient care and to prevent unnecessary hospital admissions?
Abstract: Typically, 10-25% of UK hospital beds are occupied by people with diabetes. Patient experience is often poor, length of stay prolonged, emergency readmissions increased and healthcare costs high. This poor experience and unnecessary financial burden is an obvious target for quality improvement byinnovation. My aim is to explore experiences of people with diabetes admitted to hospital in a 6-month period (using taped, semi-structured interviews) to define problems with care, to find innovative solutions for better management and to evaluate effectiveness of theseinnovations. I will consider the whole patient pathway, not just the hospital episode, and I anticipate the remainder of the CAT research will address:1. Pre-hospital: (a) effectiveness of supported self-management; (b) access to timely support during intercurrent episodes; (c) appreciation of alternatives to hospital admission2. In hospital: (a) Diabetes specific issues; (b) generic unscheduled issues; (c) right place, right person; (d) effectiveness and timeliness of discharge3. Post-discharge: support for recovery and to prevent unnecessary emergency readmission.Improving unscheduled care will be invaluable locally and nationally to support QIPP.

Award_Title: Improving communication with the public during a chemical, biological or radiological incident
Abstract: Objectives: Design a questionnaire to assess lay perceptions about chemical, biological or radiological (CBR) threats. Assess whether this predicts CBR-related anxiety and whether perceptions can be altered. Design: 1188 responses from expert and lay participants will inform the questionnaire design. During a future CBR incident, telephone interviews with 250 affected and 1000 non-affected people will test whether perceptions predict anxiety. A randomised controlled trial using vignettes will test whether CBR perceptions can be changed. Outcomes: Guidelines and tools for improving communication during CBR incidents. Benefits: Improved communication by the NHS and other agencies, ameliorating the impact of future CBR events.

Abstract: Objectives: Develop methodology and provide new policy-relevant information on preferences for facilitating delivery of patient-led healthcare reforms around place of death.Design: Use DCE and mixed-methods to investigate methodological issues, conduct empirical analyses, investigate BTA to generalise DCE results, disseminate, and build capacity.Expected outcomes: Refine methods and improve the quality of information that can be used to inform and target resources in the right places; increase policy-relevance of DCE; identify when costly new research studies can be avoided; increase DCE and awareness and competency in the wider research community and NHS.Anticipated benefits: Potential to deliver patient-focused services.

Award_Title: Equitable care for an ageing population: An exploration of care for older adults at the end of life
Abstract: The aim of this programme of work is to explore issues around the funding, organisation and delivery of affordable, equitable care for an ageing population. Four complementary strands of research with older adults at the end-of-life are proposed; An exploration of the influence of living arrangements on experiences; transitions in care settings; the implications of nursing home funding and the formation of social networks. Both qualitative and quantitative research methods will be used. The findings will have direct relevance to the design and delivery of health and social care.

Award_Title: Adiposity risk in pregnancy: identifying cost effective risk prediction measures that can be implemented at scale within NHS maternity services
Abstract: Background: Half of pregnant women in England are overweight (BMI 25-29.9kg/m2) or obese (BMI≥30kg/m2). Guidelines use obese BMI to allocate high-risk antenatal care. However, 49% of obese women (~87,000/year) have uncomplicated pregnancies and don't require high-risk care, whereas 42% of overweight women (~103,000/year) develop complications despite not being judged as high-risk. This is little better than deciding risk by tossing a coin. Ineffective risk-prediction wastes NHS resources and harms women/offspring. Extensive research demonstrates BMI poorly predicts risk compared with adiposity measures of body-fat distribution. Prognostic risk-prediction improves outcomes and cost-effectiveness. Simple prognostic measures are more feasible to implement than complex multivariable prognostic models.Experts at the 2017 World Obesity Federation Obesity in Pregnancy Hot Topic Conference universally agreed the big unanswered question is how to predict risk. There is an urgent need to identify adiposity measures with greater sensitivity and specificity than BMI for targeted high-risk care to improve health of women/offspring and reduce NHS resource waste.Aim: To identify the prognostic performance of single-variable adiposity measures and multivariable models to predict which pregnant women require high-risk NHS maternity care, and cost-effectiveness of implementation at scale.WP1: Prognostic measure/model development (Years 1-2) Aim: to identify the prognostic performance of single-variable adiposity measures and multivariable models to estimate risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes.I carried out a systematic review which identified 58 studies reporting early-pregnancy adiposity measures (n=82,185 births). Individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis will be used to develop and internally validate prognostic adiposity measures and models to predict maternal/offspring health outcomes. Analysis of prognostic performance will involve calibration, discrimination and internal validation.WP2: External validation (Years 2-4) Aim: to validate the prognostic performance of adiposity measures/models in a new population.Generalisability of prognostic measures/models requires evaluation in a new setting before use in clinical practice. Pregnant women (n=1,400) will be recruited from Newcastle NHS Trust to provide early-pregnancy adiposity measures. These will be linked to routine data on clinical outcomes. The prognostic measures/models from WP1 will be applied to the external population data to assess generalisability.WP3: Cost-effectiveness of implementation (Year 5) Aim: to determine the clinical cost-effectiveness of implementing the validated prognostic measures/models to target high-risk maternity care.Economic modelling will be used to estimate cost-effectiveness of using adiposity measures/models to predict risks. The model will describe the pathways of NHS care initiated based on predicted risk from WP2. Costs and consequences include measurement costs (adiposity measurement) and treatment costs (high-risk care). The output will be cumulative costs, probability of event occurring for each prognostic measure/model considered, and incremental cost per event avoided. Deterministic and probabilistic sensitivity analyses will explore the effect of uncertainty surrounding estimates of cost-effectiveness.Anticipated impact and dissemination NHS/patient impact: Scalable implementation of cost-effective risk stratification. Prevention of adverse outcomes for women/offspring. Reduction of resource waste. Career impact: support my transition to being a prominent research leader in my field. Dissemination/impact strategy target audiences: academia; health professionals/organisations; pregnant women/families; maternity managers/commissioners; national/international policy makers; public/media; third sector. Future research: HTA funding for implementation trial.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Vaccination in older adults: understanding how to do it better and knowing when to stop
Abstract: We have an aging population in the UK thus there is a need to focus efforts on how to keep older people fit and well, and given NHS pressures, help them avoid attending primary care and hospital. Vaccination is a primary means of disease prevention used by the NHS, but evidence is lacking in several areas used to inform vaccine policy decisions in older adults. This research aims to enhance vaccination policy for older adults in England, through better evidence and stronger decision-making structures, to ultimately improve the health of older people. The objectives are: (1)To assess the heterogeneity in vaccine uptake in the 65+ population (2)To explore knowledge, attitudes and perceptions of routine vaccines for 65+ year olds and of other programmes that could offer this group protection against infectious diseases (3)To estimate social contacts and mixing patterns in older people (50+ population) (4)Valuing the impact of potentially vaccine preventable disease on health and capability to determine potential gains from vaccination in people aged 65+ years (5)To develop a methodological guideline for reassessing, including withdrawing, routine vaccine programmesStatistical analysis of secondary data (primary care records) will be used in objective 1 (completion 07/2020). Focus groups with the public will be used in objective 2 (completion 06/2022). For objective 3 a survey will be administered to the public and data statistically analysed (completion 10/2020). A longitudinal study will be used in objective 4 with data statistically analysed (completion 06/2022). For objective 5 a methodological guideline will be developed through a process of initial scoping of key questions, literature review, gaining evidence from stakeholders, and consultation (completion 11/2022). Patient and Public involvement (PPI) will be embedded throughout the research with four consultation events with a panel of PPI contributors informing study document design, analysis and interpretation of results, and dissemination plans. Two PPI contributors will also be part of the advisory group, which will also seek to include GPs, and individuals with a national/international profile in vaccine policy, guideline development, qualitative research, and health economics.Research summaries will be shared with participants and GP practices and at wider public engagement events. Results will be published in peer-reviewed journals and at conferences (including at a PPI conference for which an abstract will be co-produced with a PPI representative). The methodological guideline will be sent to organisations with an interest in vaccine policy and delivery (all of whom will be invited to be stakeholders in the guideline development) including the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation, Department of Health, NHS England, Public Health England and patient groups. The findings of the research can be used to improve vaccine uptake and modify vaccine strategies in older adults, reducing ill health (and the requirement of antibiotics to treat infectious disease), pressures on healthcare services and allow scarce resources to be spent in the best possible way. Ultimately the impact of this research will be the improvement of health in older adults through improved decision making around the use of vaccines in this age group.

Award_Title: Pathways to Policy: Charting the alternate courses and outcomes of women through urgent and emergency health care services for their needs arising from intimate partner abuse.
Abstract: The research will address the question of what are the alternate pathways for women though urgent and emergency health care services for needs arising from their intimate partner abuse? Pathways chart case characteristics, interventions and outcomes. A Realistic Evaluation design is used to understand processes, mechanisms and outcomes within and outwith pathways. The pathways are founded on real practice: identified through retrospective medical record review of cases and semi-structured interviews with service users, key stakeholders and policy makers. The findings will provide evidence to inform policy for the urgent and emergency health care service response in cases of female intimate partner abuse in order to support and protect women within the multi-agency network of services.

Award_Title: How are health care organisations dealing with the challenge of providing co-ordinated diabetes care in an increasingly diverse NHS?
Abstract: This study is concerned with the effect of incentives for competition and collaboration on organisations' delivery of co-ordinated services. The research will use theoretical frameworks associated with inter-organisational relationships to inform case study research of two local health systems using qualitative and quantitative methods to explore the way healthcare organisations understand their objectives and negotiate relationships with other organisations to provide co-ordinated diabetic services. The research will increase understanding of how incentives affect delivery of co-ordinated care, including whether they can be combined to improve the co-ordination of care, which will be of use to policy makers and healthcare organisations.

Award_Title: Funding for cancer drugs in 'exceptional circumstances' by Primary Care Trusts - A legal and ethical analysis
Abstract: The aim of this research is to examine how Primary Care Trust’s (PCT's) make decisions regarding the funding of cancer drugs in ‘exceptional circumstances’. In particular, the study will explore how concepts of equity, transparency and consistency relate to decisions made by PCTs. The study will examine the patient experience of applying for funding of cancer drugs on the basis of 'exceptional circumstances' and what mechanisms of decision making maybe viewed as acceptable to a range of stakeholders, including patients and their families. I will review how, if at all, the law should provide recourse in the Courts to those who feel aggrieved by PCT decisions. The interdisciplinary nature of this research, to be conducted through the University of Manchester’s Doctoral Programme in Bioethics and Medical Jurisprudence, will draw upon both quantitative and qualitative research methods; including a survey of PCTs, content analysis of policy documents, doctrinal analysis and qualitative interviews with commissioners, clinicians and patients. The research will establish if an ethical framework could improve the process of resource allocation for cancer drugs in ‘exceptional circumstances’. This research will clarify the basis for PCT decision making as well as provide strategies for the resolution of difficult funding decisions. This research will benefit patients by ensuring that Health Policy is responsive to need, with a sound ethical basis, which may result in less litigation. If the process of decision making by PCTs in ‘exceptional circumstances’ is seen as fair, the outcome is more likely to be accepted by patients. Stimulation of public debate around this area, in a rational and non-emotive fashion, is likely to result in a greater understanding of the issues.

Award_Title: Gender differences in Outcomes for 30,000 Myocardial Infarction Patients: Longitudinal study before and after hospitilisation
Abstract: Historically, data have not been available to investigate coronary disease pathways from onset of initial symptoms in primary care in the months prior to acute events and consequent morbidity/mortality. Using newly-linked electronic records, this study will examine gender differences in initial symptoms, acute events and outcomes, and identify clinical, social and health service factors explaining these differences. This prospective multiple-time-point longitudinal study, with data on 30,000 patients hospitalised for acute coronary syndromes, will improve understanding of gender differences in onset of coronary disease and the quality of care in primary and secondary prevention, thereby identifying specific interventions to improve outcomes.

Award_Title: A mixed methods programme of study for the determinants and health outcomes of home food preparation.
Abstract: Background The UK and wider world are experiencing an obesity epidemic, with lower socio-economic groups disproportionately affected. Estimates indicate that by 2020, more than 70% of UK adults will be overweight or obese(1), thereby increasing annual medical NHS costs by £5.5 billion before 2050(2). This will be mediated through increased cases of cancer, heart disease, type two diabetes and other chronic non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Since body weight results from the balance of energy input and expenditure, diet plays a key role in obesity development. Dietary quality is also socio-economically patterned, with an estimated quarter of observed inequalities in UK mortality due to inequalities in diet(3). Concerns regarding obesity and associated NCDs, and perceived loss of cooking skills, have prompted research into human nutrition and the potential benefits of addressing links between cooking, diet and health outcomes. However, there remains a paucity of evidence regarding the practices and skills for preparing hot or cold foods at home, including combining, mixing and often heating ingredients. In this proposal, I will use 'home cooking' to refer to this combination of actions. Aims and objectives This project will consider the hypothesis that, in view of the universality of eating and biological links between food consumption and obesity, understanding home cooking and modifying behaviour to healthier practices provides an avenue for reducing obesity prevalence and improving dietary quality and related health outcomes. The research will: systematically review current evidence regarding the determinants and health outcomes of home cooking; provide unique insights into home food preparation practices and the rationale for these behaviours; and identify relative nutritional quality and costs of cooking 'from scratch' versus consuming pre-prepared ready meals. Research plan Phase one: A systematic literature review will be undertaken using standard methods to identify, analyse and synthesise relevant information from peer-reviewed publications, grey literature, websites and expert sources. Two sets of studies will be appraised, addressing either the determinants, or outcomes (benefits and disadvantages) of home cooking among adults. Studies will be synthesised narratively or with meta-ethnography. Phase two: Semi-structured interviews will be undertaken with the public, using photograph elicitation, till receipt review, and 24 hour dietary recall, to develop an understanding of how adults cook at home, what factors influence decision making, and barriers to cooking and eating more healthily. Themes ascertained through Framework Analysis(4) will be used to develop and undertake a large scale survey using the electoral roll of Newcastle upon Tyne. This will identify population frequency and socio-demographic patterning of determinants of home cooking. Phase three: The nutritional quality and financial cost of basic supermarket ingredients for cooking a meal 'from scratch', will be compared with equivalent pre-prepared supermarket ready meals. Comparisons will be stratified by household composition (single, couple, family of four) and food class (economy, standard, luxury). Expected outcomes Findings will be integrated using triangulation protocol methods(5) to deliver a systematic and critical analysis of evidence regarding determinants and health outcomes of home cooking. It will develop an understanding of factors influencing home cooking practices, and a detailed evidence base regarding actual cooking behaviour and skills, elicited through semi-structured interviews and large scale postal survey. The research will provide detailed comparisons of the relative costs and nutritional composition of home cooked and pre-prepared ready meals. It will yield at least four peer-reviewed publications, and three conference presentations. BenefitsThe research will inform evidence-based development of tailored interventions to encourage healthy home food preparation. This will facilitate future reductions in population prevalence of obesity and dietary-related health inequalities. Such action is urgently needed to tackle these vast and persistent health challenges, which are amongst the greatest threats to health globally(6).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Palliative Care for Children and Young People with Life-Limiting Conditions: What? When? How?
Abstract: Background Current definitions of palliative care for CYP are broad and non-specific, which provides practical challenges for patients and families, the healthcare professionals caring for them, and those responsible for commissioning services. Palliative care services for CYP around the UK differ between regions, with multiple statutory and voluntary providers involved. The future development of high quality, standardised palliative care services which serve CYP with life-limiting illness and their families, presents a huge challenge for the NHS. Research Questions How do current definitions of palliative care services for CYP concord with service delivery, policy and guidance in the UK? What is the current evidence base for practice and policy related to palliative care service delivery for CYP? What are the experiences and preferences of CYP, and/or their relatives or carers, in relation to the delivery of palliative care services? What are the facilitators and barriers to the delivery of palliative care for CYP, and how might these be overcome? What should an integrated model of palliative care for CYP look like? Objectives To systematically appraise existing policy and guidance and published evidence related to palliative care service delivery for Children and Young People (CYP) with life-limiting illness. To explore and identify common themes around the experiences and preferences of key stakeholders regarding palliative care service design and delivery for CYP with life-limiting conditions, including the perceived facilitators and barriers to these services. Key stakeholders will include (i) CYP with life-limiting conditions, (ii) their relatives or carers, (iii) professionals and (iv) service commissioners. To collate this evidence and use it to inform the design and development of an integrated model of palliative care for CYP with life-limiting conditions, which will inform commissioning and the development of national policy, as well as future research. Design Systematic review of published guidance and policy, and published evidence, related to palliative care service design and delivery for CYP with life-limiting conditions. Qualitative interview study with CYP with life-limiting conditions, their carers, relevant health and social care professionals, and commissioners of services. Development of a new model of care in consultation with local experts, including service users and commissioners, which will be of immediate relevance and practical use in the development and design of sustainable services. Outcomes Published systematic reviews of (i) published guidance and policy and (ii) published evidence related to palliative care service design and delivery for CYP with life-limiting conditions. A comprehensive multi-perspective analysis and metasynthesis of stakeholder experience and expectations of palliative care services for CYP, including the facilitators and barriers to delivering these services. A proposal for a new model of integrated palliative care for CYP with life-limiting conditions, to inform local commissioning and national policy. Benefits Palliative care and care planning in partnership with patients and families allows identification of preferences, better outcomes for families, and can avoid costly hospital admissions. CYP with life-limiting conditions, many of which are highly complex, represent an important population for consideration by the NHS. This in-depth investigation in to the design and delivery of palliative care services for CYP and development of a practical model of care will ultimately provide benefit for patients requiring those services, and their families. The outcomes will contribute to the improvement of integrated care, are highly relevant to the NHS, social care and third sector providers of palliative care for CYP in community, secondary and tertiary care settings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Feasibility of a low-cost, co-produced complex intervention to reduce workplace sitting time in different workplace settings
Abstract: Background Prolonged sitting is associated with health conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, obesity, musculoskeletal problems, as well as early death, independent of physical activity levels.The workplace contributes to prolonged sitting due to the increase in desk-based jobs, which has resulted in desk-based workers sitting for an average of six hours per working day. Therefore, there is a need to develop interventions to reduce workplace sitting, but to encourage a range of organisations/employers to support their use these must be low-cost and not negatively impact staff productivity. Aim To develop, implement and evaluate the feasibility of a low-cost, co-produced complex intervention to reduce sitting time in different workplace settings.Research question What is the feasibility of a low-cost, co-produced complex intervention to reduce workplace sitting time in different workplace settings? Plan of investigation Desk-based workers will be recruited from four organisations to increase generalisability of findings to a range of organisations.Phase 1: A qualitative study Two small focus groups (one with management and one with other employees) will be conducted at each organisation to establish thoughts on the barriers and facilitators to reducing workplace sitting time.Phase 2: Intervention development Findings from Phase 1, intervention development learning from previous work undertaken by the fellow, and literature review findings, will be synthesised using the Behaviour Change Wheel (BCW)/COM-B theoretical framework and then used as the basis for the development of these interventions. Co-production with members of staff at each organisation will ensure the intervention developed for each organisation is specific to the setting and the characteristics of employees' job roles/activities. Although the final content of the interventions is currently unknown, based on previous work by the fellow, it is likely to include: Posters/prompts to remind staff to sit lessEmails with tips of ways to sit lessA social element involving workplace champions or social mediaSupport from management via emails and 'leading by example'Changes in the way the environment is used rather than costly new equipment such as sit-stand desks.Phase 3: Intervention implementation and evaluationParticipants will be randomly recruited to this phase. Co-produced interventions will run in each workplace for 12 weeks. Baseline demographic and lifestyle data will be collected from all participants. The following data will be obtained at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and three and six months post-intervention:Total daily sitting time and physical activity levels (measured using activPal™ and self-reported logs)General health and wellbeing (measured using the Short Form (36) Health Survey)Sickness absence, productivity and presenteeism (measured using relevant items from the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment Questionnaire and WHO Health and Work Performance Questionnaire)Attrition rates.Data to be collected immediately post-intervention will include:Intervention awarenessQualitative data from focus groups to determine participants' views on the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention and its various componentsIntervention costsSafety/adverse events.Information on intervention fidelity will also be collected and assessed as part of the process evaluation. Potential benefits to the public and NHS It is anticipated that the findings from this feasibility study will inform the development of a 'toolkit' for managers to support the development of tailor-made interventions to be utilised in any workplace. If successful, workplace health and safety policy may be updated to include practical recommendations for the adoption of the 'toolkit'.Such policy changes could have long-term health improvements for employees, which could in turn translate into cost savings to the NHS due to the prevention of long-term conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, depression and musculoskeletal problems. Furthermore, improvements in productivity and absenteeism could result in cost-savings to employers and the wider economy.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: Development and feasibility testing of an intervention: To facilitate the inVolvement of OLder patients with muLtimorbidITy in decisION-making about their healthcare during general practice consultations (VOLITION)
Abstract: Development of an intervention (VOLITION): To support older patients with multiple health problems in joint decision-making about their healthcare with a GP. Aim To develop an intervention aimed at supporting older patients, who have more than one health problem, in joint decision-making about their healthcare when visiting a GP. To feasibility test the intervention, with a view to informing the design of a fully-powered clinical trial to assess its effectiveness in routine clinical care. Background In the UK, the number of people aged over 65 years is increasing, with a predicted population in excess of 13.5 million by 2032 compared with 9 million in 2012. Over a third of spending in general practice goes towards care for older patients. Older people see a General Practitioner (GP) more often than younger patients. They are likely to have more than one long-term health problem. This is multimorbidity. It makes a patient's healthcare needs more complex. Older patients with a greater burden of multimorbidity tend to have a poorer quality of life. Patient-centred care, such as sharing in decision-making with a doctor, has positive health outcomes for patients. Outcomes include taking the doctors' advice about treatments, feeling happier about the care received, and having greater trust in the doctor. Both the World Health Organisation and the National Health Service agree that shared decision-making is important. Older patients with multimorbidity prefer sharing in decision-making about their healthcare. However, older patients are currently less often involved in such interactions when compared with younger patients, and this may have negative health effects. Design and methods The study design will consist of three work packages (WP): WP1. We will identify current evidence and relevant theory to outline the core components of a new intervention aimed at supporting older patients with multimorbidity in shared decision-making when consulting with a GP. WP2. A focus group (group discussion) will establish the views of older patients with multimorbidity and the views of GPs to refine the proposed intervention, ahead of testing it. WP3. A feasibility (test) study of the intervention will be carried out. We aim to recruit a sample of six GP practices, with five GPs per practice and fifteen patients per GP recruited. Practices will be randomly allocated to either the new intervention or to usual care. The feasibility study will assess any resource, cost, and recruitment issues for a future larger study, and assess ways to measure the effect of the intervention. Interviews with patients and staff will aim to work out how acceptable the future trial would be and whether they think the intervention would be feasible. Patient and public involvement (PPI) A PPI group has been established, consisting of eight members of the public, aged over 65 years, with varying health care needs and experiences. A PPI workshop helped to inform this application and changes were made to the background section to better describe why this study is needed. PPI members will be involved in project meetings every three months. The group will help in the design of the intervention. They will help develop patient information leaflets and support ethics applications. We plan to train a PPI member to run a patient focus group, allowing the researcher to watch and make notes with less influence on the conversation. The PPI member will be offered free training for this process. The group will discuss findings from the feasibility study and assist in writing summaries of results. They will help with presentations to professionals, providing a powerful way of conveying a patient-centred message. The group will be regularly debriefed and supported. They will review the PPI setup ahead of the future trial. Dissemination Findings will be circulated to patient groups, charities, clinicians, service managers, research funders and relevant royal colleges. We will use national and international conferences, the NIHR research networks and local clinical networks. Public events will be held with GP surgeries, working with our PPI members as well as other interested groups. We will publish academic papers in high quality scientific journals. A key output of this work will be the drafting of a funding bid. We will propose a full-scale, fully-powered clinical trial. The trial will examine the health outcomes, cost-effectiveness and acceptability of the intervention. Any dissemination will describe how to use the intervention to positively impact on patient experiences. We will seek to ensure direct NHS service benefit within a 5 year window.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Understanding pre-diabetes from the patient’s perspective: A mixed-methods study aimed at improving the success of diabetes prevention programmes.
Abstract: Background In people with pre-diabetes, lifestyle programmes can reduce risk of progression to type 2 diabetes in those able and willing to engage in interventions. The evidence base on how people are informed of their pre-diabetes diagnosis and how they react to such information (especially behaviourally) is sparse and theoretically superficial. Socio-cultural and material barriers to lifestyle change may mean that even those willing to change behaviour are unable to.Aims To inform prevention programmes for type 2 diabetes with a richer understanding of how the diagnosis of pre-diabetes affects people's feelings, attitudes and behaviour in different socio-cultural contexts.Objectives Explore clinicians' experiences of conveying the pre-diabetes diagnosis to patients. Explore the meaning of pre-diabetes to people who have been given such a diagnosis, including the impact on their lives and lifestyles. Identify policymakers' priorities for local diabetes prevention programmes, including their evidence needs. Hold preliminary inter-sectoral workshops with a view to refining current diabetes prevention programmes. Research questions How (and in what context) is the diagnosis of pre-diabetes communicated to patients in General Practice? How does this differ in individuals from different cultural groups, those with limited English and those with low health literacy? How do people from different backgrounds internalise and respond to the pre-diabetes categorisation? How do socio-cultural and structural influences affect this response and subsequent action or inaction relating to health behaviours? What opportunities and constraints do local commissioners and policymakers foresee in implementing socio-culturally tailored diabetes prevention policies? How can we align evidence, policymakers and public participation to co-design effective diabetes prevention programmes? Plan of investigation Work Package 1 Focus groups with clinicians who convey the diagnosis of pre-diabetes. Questions will be directed at understanding their perspectives on the pre-diabetes diagnosis, how they make and interpret such a diagnosis and how they communicate results. Emphasis will be placed on discussing 'critical cases' in which practitioners felt the patient had not understood or did not intend to act on the information. Work Package 2 A variety sample of 30 people will be recruited via local GPs from 2-3 different localities whose population is at high risk of developing diabetes. For each individual, a rich case study will be prepared using three different qualitative methods (and using interpreters or bilingual health advocates as required). Narrative interview (the story of how they came to be diagnosed, what they felt about it and what they have done about it) (9); 'Cultural probes' such as camera, scrapbook (to record likes/dislikes, concerns, wishes, maps of relationships or places), diary (to record specific events and reactions to these), postcards or sticky notes (for things that occur spontaneously) (10). 'Go-along interviews' to explore how people interact with their local environment (e.g. green spaces, leisure facilities, shops, cafés etc) (11).Work Package 3 Interviews will be undertaken with commissioners and local policy makers with two objectives: [a] building relationships and creating an appetite for the findings of work package 1 and 2; and [b] gaining an understanding of policymakers' evidence needs and the constraints they are working under.Work Package 4 Two facilitated co-design workshops bringing together stakeholders to discuss the ethnographic case studies from work package 2 along with other local data (visual maps, public health reports, photographs of local features). Potential benefits to patients and the NHSFor people with pre-diabetes: Clinical and policy responses better adapted to their needs. For clinicians: Richer understanding of the lived experience of pre-diabetes and how this diagnosis might best be communicated to patients. For policymakers: Understanding social, cultural and material constraints that affect people's ability and willingness to engage in preventive interventions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: HPV testing in cervical cancer screening: using behavioural science to understand attendance and anxiety
Abstract: Background: The NHS Cervical Screening Programme (NHSCSP) is rolling out human papillomavirus (HPV) testing as the primary test across England, meaning that all women attending screening will soon find out their HPV results. With changes to the protocol for screening, it is extremely important that psychology and behavioural science informs NHSCSP information materials and wording in test results letters. This is to ensure that women understand their results, are not unnecessarily anxious and re-attend their next screening appointment. This is particularly relevant for women who test positive for HPV with normal cytology, as it is anticipated that this will be a complex result to understand and that some women in this group may display heightened anxiety. Women in this group will be recalled to screening at 12 months rather than 3 years, and it is critical that these women re-attend in order for the NHSCSP to achieve sensitivity gains of switching to HPV primary testing.Aims: This DRF will be carried out in the context of HPV primary testing in the NHSCSCP. It aims to identify demographic and psychological predictors of anxiety and of screening re-attendance among women testing positive for HPV with normal cytology.Methods: Four research projects are proposed which will directly inform a fifth applied outputs project. Project 1 will be a systematic review to consider how women react to testing positive for HPV in the context of cervical screening. Project 2 will involve analysis of existing data from a cross-sectional survey (~N= 673) considering differences in anxiety, distress and intention to re-attend between women with different test results in NHSCSP HPV primary screening. Project 3 will be a cross-sectional survey of women testing HPV positive with normal cytology results to consider theoretically driven predictors of anxiety and attendance at screening. Project 4 will be a qualitative study to gain in-depth insights into how women with HPV positive/normal cytology view their results and to understand their information needs. Project 5 will inform and develop NHSCSP information materials and test result letters, guided by results from projects 1-4, PPI and collaborator input.Dissemination and Impact: This DRF will be extremely timely in providing the NHSCSP with evidence which can be used to improve patient outcomes, as HPV primary testing roll-out will start across England in 2019. On completion of this DRF, the NHSCSP will be able to improve existing test result letters and HPV information materials, and incorporate a new leaflet into the programme specifically for women who test HPV positive with normal cytology. All materials resulting from this DRF will help ensure information clarity, reduce unnecessary patient anxiety and maximise patient re-attendance at screening.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Informing the design of a behavioural intervention to decrease sedentary time in older adults
Abstract: Background: Ageing well is now a global health priority given that the population of older adults is expected to double to 22% from 2015 to 2050. Older adults spend an average of 9.4 hours/day being sedentary, placing them at significant risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer and premature mortality. While the impact of sedentary time is attenuated among those who are sufficiently physically active, this applies to a small minority of the population. Furthermore, few interventions have led to sustained increases in physical activity. Consequently, if we could reduce sedentary time, we could potentially improve the health and well-being of older adults, and reduce the current burden on health and social care resources due to these chronic conditions. While many studies have been conducted on the associations between sedentary time and the risk of chronic diseases, very little is known about how best to achieve population-level reductions in sedentary time among older adults. Further, we know little about the potential benefits that these reductions might have on other aspects of health that are particularly important for successful ageing (e.g., functional health and quality of life). Improvements in functional health and quality of life may prove important in successfully motivating older adults to change their sedentary behaviour. Although some studies have attempted to answer these questions, there are key limitations of the research that has been conducted to date. These limitations need to be addressed to improve our understanding of the role of sedentary behaviours in human health and ultimately in improving population health. Aims: To describe change in sedentary time (Study 1) and its correlates among older adults (Study 2) To identify effective components of existing interventions targeting sedentary time (Study 3) To synthesise existing knowledge on the association of sedentary time with quality of life (QoL) and functional health outcomes (Study 4) To quantify associations of change in sedentary time with functional outcomes and QoL (Study 5) Plan: I will perform epidemiological analyses within EPIC-Norfolk (n=3705), a large population-based cohort of older adults in which participants wore hip-mounted accelerometers for 7 days at two health checks separated by six years. I will use multi-level regression models to describe change in sedentary time and its correlates. Correlates will be divided into four domains (socio-demographic, behavioural, physical health and social and physical environment). I will conduct a systematic review of interventions targeting sedentary time in older adults. I will use multi-level modelling in EPIC-Norfolk to quantify associations of change in sedentary time with functional outcomes (grip strength, gait speed, leg strength) and QoL (EQ-5D). I will conduct a systematic review of associations of sedentary time with QoL and functional outcomes. I will synthesise findings to develop recommendations for designing interventions to reduce sedentary time in older adults. Potential Benefit: With an ageing population, prevention and modification of risk factors is more important. This work will inform the design and targeting of interventions to reduce sedentary time. If effective, such interventions could improve health in older adults and reduce NHS and social care cost in an increasingly overburdened NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Award_Title: Using telemedicine to improve access, cost, and quality of secondary care for people in prison: feasibility study
Abstract: BackgroundPeople in prison tend to experience poorer health, poorer access to health care services and poorer health outcomes than general society. The period of incarceration represents a key opportunity for these patients to access relevant health care treatment, given that primary needs such as shelter and food are addressed by the prison environment. However, there are significant barriers associated with prisoners accessing hospital health services and there is an urgent need for research to identify strategies to improve the quality of healthcare for prisoners. This Fellowship concentrates on patient access to secondary care, defined as health care services and treatment provided by acute hospital sites, using telemedicine, defined as remote video consultations between prison patients and secondary healthcare staff. AimsTo determine whether Prison-hospital telemedicine is useable and acceptable, and can mitigate system blockers to secondary care for people in prison, thereby improving access, cost and quality of careTo determine the feasibility of collecting appropriate quantitative, qualitative, clinical and economic outcome data to allow further formal assessment of prison-hospital telemedicine effectiveness Investigation planThis study includes four objectives incorporating qualitative, quantitative and health economics work, which will be combined in a final report to provide feasibility evidence. OBJECTIVE1. To review existing published literature to understand how telemedicine has been used in prison settings previouslyI will undertake a systematic review of literature describing the use of telemedicine in prisons, to develop an understanding of existing or trialled telemedicine models and model effectiveness. OBJECTIVE2. To review local prison health care data to describe admission/outpatient attendance patterns, and to understand which hospital departments are most utilised/hardest to access by people in prison I will seek to describe local prison priority areas for telemedicine using a combination of: epidemiological data, whereby local prison health care records and published national data are described in terms of external attendances at secondary care sites; corporate data, whereby I will conduct semi structured interviews with 10 staff involved in facilitating/prioritising secondary care appointments to understand barriers to commencement/completion of secondary care treatment for PIP and how healthcare issues are prioritised for limited hospital transfers; comparative data, from the systematic review. Current costs of secondary care treatment from priority departments will also be recorded. Epidemiological data and current costs will be used as baseline data for the feasibility study (OBJ4).OBJECTIVE3. Develop telemedicine hospital-prison care pathways with the hospital departments identified by needs assessment, including prison healthcare staff training elementsI will engage secondary care multi-disciplinary teams identified by OBJ2 (2 departments total) in the co-design of telemedicine appropriate care pathways and associated training packages. OBJECTIVE4. To test telemedicine and associated care pathways in prisons (feasibility study) Quantitative data (prison health care records), qualitative data (12 patient, 12 healthcare key informant interviews) and economic data will be collected to assess outcomes, cost benefit and perceived acceptability of the model, to increase access to healthcare, reduce the number of off-site visits to hospital required by people in prison,improve care quality, and to expedite commencement of appropriate care. Outputs from each objective will be incorporated into a report, providing feasibility evidence for a further formal study of effectiveness of local prison-telemedicine models. Potential Benefits to Patients and NHS This Fellowship will draw together evidence of needs, barriers, and data collection feasibility, to enable further development and evaluation of prison-hospital telemedicine models. By providing evidence and tools, I hope to improve access to secondary care for people in prison, contributing to a reduction in inequalities in healthcare access. Reduced need for patient transfer to hospital appointments will also lower overall NHS costs.

Contractor: Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital NHS Trust
Award_Title: Care in Orthopaedics, burdeN of treatmeNt and the Effectiveness of Communication Technology: the CONNECT Project
Abstract: 1. Background a. Clinical backgroundWe have an ageing population frequently affected by life limiting conditions, often of musculoskeletal origin. Specialist orthopaedic care is required but accessing such care is challenging. The NHS five year forward view is based around new models of care with e-health technology identified as one possible innovation to support access to care. Despite positive outcomes from previously conducted telehealth research uptake in clinical practice remains low.Patients attend the Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital (RNOH) for physiotherapy from all over the country. Patients often find the travel challenging and this research aims to design, implement and evaluate a technology supported consultation to enable access to care without the need for repeated face to face attendance. Our previous research (Gilbert et al 2016) found that SKYPE consultations were not acceptable to all patients and the acceptability of this consultation format is multi factorial and warrants further investigation. b. Theoretical background The proposed research utilises three theoretical models; Normalisation Process Theory (NPT) (May 2013) to explain the work of using e-health technology, Burden of Treatment Theory (BoT) (May et al 2014) to explore the work RNOH patients are required to do to participate in tertiary orthopaedic healthcare and Minimally Disruptive Medicine (MDM) (May et al 2009). A 'minimally disruptive' physiotherapy consultation is one that: - has minimum negative impact on the patient's life- offers reduced workload for the patient- healthcare professionals and care are accessible to the patient The proposed research involves the novel integration of sociological and economic methodology to explore this issue. 2. AimTo design, implement and evaluate a 'minimally disruptive' consultation format in an orthopaedic setting. 3. Plan of Investigation Phase 1 (months 1-6) The purpose of phase 1 is to review literature reporting the use of e-health technology in an orthopaedic setting using NPT with a particular focus on: a) What technologies are used in orthopaedic practice to support access to care?b) What is the work that patients and clinicians are required to do to use these technologies? Phase 2 (months 6-12)A taxonomy of work and tasks for both patients and clinicians to engage with these technologies will have been developed in phase 1 and will be used to determine how these tasks affect the patient's treatment burden. This phase will also explore how the introduction of e-health technology affects negative impact for patients. Phase 3 (months 13-21)A Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) will be designed and conducted to ascertain the most important factors determining patient acceptability on the introduction of e-health technology. Phase 4 (months 21-30) [Modified Clinical Practice]Upon completion of the DCE patient preferences surrounding the amount and type of work required to engage in the consultation will have been identified. A minimally disruptive consultation format will then be designed, implemented and evaluated, using semi structured interviews. An important focus will be the determination of whether the modified clinical practice makes it easier for patients to participate in their healthcare. 5. Benefit to patients and the NHSPrevious studies of the introduction of e-health technologies have utilised top down models rarely leading to routine uptake. To our knowledge, no previous work has explored the role of patient preference in technology normalisation processes, and it is postulated that the knowledge of such patient preferences is more likely to lead to successful e-health implementation. This project will focus specifically on orthopaedic physiotherapy appointments but it will have much wider implications for the introduction of e-health technology to other spheres of the NHS. There is the potential to both provide a better patient service and to effect cost savings.
