Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Optimising Structured Medication Reviews for Older People with Severe Frailty and Care Home Residents to Reduce Overprescribing and Associated Inequalities
Abstract: Aim To improve quality and accessibility of Structured Medication Reviews (SMRs) to reduce overprescribing for older people with severe frailty living in the community and care home residents, informed by intersectional characteristics and experiences. Research questions (RQ) 1. Is there evidence for inequity in delivery and inequality in outcomes of SMRs for community-dwelling older people with severe frailty and care home residents as our target groups, taking into account intersectional characteristics and geographical location? 2. Does exposure to high-risk medications and related health and social care outcomes for our target groups vary according to intersectional characteristics? 3. How are SMRs for our target groups being implemented and delivered in practice, and what are the implications for access to and engagement with SMRs taking into account intersectionality? 4. Does experience of SMRs vary according to intersectional characteristics and geographical location? 5. What actionable solutions can be applied at key points to optimise implementation and delivery of SMRs for our target groups, fostering equity in access to and engagement with SMRs? Methods We plan three work packages (WP). WP1: Inequities in delivery and inequalities in outcomes of SMRs (RQ1 & RQ2). We will use Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) and Connected Bradford to investigate inequities/inequalities in SMR delivery/outcomes. Inclusion criteria Aged 65+ with severe frailty/care home residents. Outcomes SMR delivery SMR invitation/decline/receipt. Medication-related Number of medications/high-risk drug groups; Anticholinergic Medication Index (ACMI) score; medication dose. Health/social care Hospital admission; primary care consultations; home care package; time at home; care home admission; mortality. Analysis Multilevel Analysis of Individual Heterogeneity and Discriminatory Accuracy (MAIHDA) will produce estimates of SMR invitation/decline/receipt for intersectional subgroups. Interrupted Time Series will examine medication-related and health/social care outcomes. WP2: Implementation of SMRs/impact on equity of provision Case study approach (four Primary Care Networks (PCNs)). Process tracing will map structural/process elements in SMR implementation/delivery. We will study how diverse groups of older people with severe frailty & care home residents experience SMRs and examine the practitioner/policy perspective, with discourse analysis of documentary/interview data. WP3: Translating findings into actionable solutions Series of workshops and co-production meetings to enable iterative development/piloting of a targeted training package and detailed SMR guidance for PCNs/Integrated Care Systems (ICSs). PPI Our research project has been developed in full partnership with PPI members. Active PPI involvement is integrated throughout, to develop outputs informed through lived experience of overprescribing. Timelines WP1 Month1-10: Data preparation; analysis of SMR delivery. M11-24: Analysis of medication-related and health/social care outcomes. WP2 M6-11: PCN identification/engagement. M11-20: Recruitment, observations, interviews. M17-27: Analysis. WP3 M22-31: Recruitment, co-production workshops. M26-36: Development of training package, PCN/ICS guidance, reporting. Impact We anticipate direct impact on policy and practice to reduce overprescribing for older people with severe frailty living in the community and care home residents.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Waiting times in Emergency Departments: inequalities and impact on health outcomes
Abstract: Crowding and long waits in Emergency Departments (EDs) – previously known as Accident and Emergency (A&E) – are problems for healthcare systems worldwide. In England, there were 25 million attendances in 2019/20 – 17% more than in 2010/11. 28% of patients now wait more than four hours in EDs. We know there is a strong link between deprivation and health. There are more ED attendances in deprived areas. Waiting times for planned operations are longer for patients from deprived areas but we don’t know if the same is true for waiting times for unplanned ED care. We also do not know whether people who wait longer in EDs have worse health outcomes. Equal access to ED care is a priority for the NHS. There are plans to remove the 4-hour waiting time target and replace it with alternative ways of measuring ED performance. This study will provide vital information to ensure ED care is fair and timely. We will: (i) Examine whether there are inequalities in ED waits, by deprivation, age, gender, ethnicity and other factors (ii) Analyse the impact of waiting in EDs on patients' health (iii) Explore whether differences in the organisation of EDs lead to differences in how patients are prioritised and treated For i) and ii) we will use data already collected by the NHS. They will be prepared for us in a way that means we cannot identify the patients. We will cover the years 2018-22 and be careful to consider the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic. We will look first at all health conditions combined, comparing patients who have the same severity (how sick patients are). We will look in detail at conditions that occur most frequently among more deprived populations: heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma. For (iii), we will observe and talk to patients/relatives and staff in four English EDs, three of them in areas of high deprivation. We will track 20 patients in each ED from arrival/initial assessment until they are admitted into hospital or leave and shadow 15 staff members to watch what different members of staff and patients do. Across the sites we will interview up to 40 staff and 40 patients/relatives to understand their experiences. We will make detailed notes about how the EDs are organised and their different work practices and collect data about waiting times and numbers of people waiting. These data will be thematically analysed to explore differences in practices and processes. Members of patient and public (PPI) networks commented that our research questions are relevant for patients and caregivers, and for their perceptions of ED experiences. Our research team includes a PPI co-investigator who will support us throughout the study and will lead a PPI advisory group. We spoke to a variety of people, including ED staff, policymakers and charities, who confirmed the importance of our research questions. Our research team and advisers include emergency health care professionals, senior strategic leaders in NHS England and members of two medical Royal Colleges. We will produce interim summaries, blogs and visual representations to share findings that emerge during the project. We will produce a non-technical summary of findings for patients, a policy brief and articles for professional/academic journals. We will hold a workshop with patients/relatives and healthcare professionals and managers. We will use our links with the Royal Colleges and others to spread our findings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: An Alcohol-Related liver disease Multi-Stakeholder Hub (ARMS-Hub) to enhance research activity in underserved communities in the UK
Abstract: Aims To create a group of patient/carer representatives and experts from different disciplines and organisations that will increase and improve alcohol-related liver disease (ArLD) research in the UK (ArLD multi-stakeholder [ARMS]-Hub). To explore issues of stigma and barriers to taking part in ArLD research and how to overcome them. To develop proposals for new research involving different professions and settings to address these issues. Background Alcohol use is the third leading cause of early death and the main cause of liver disease in the UK. Hospital admissions and mortality from ArLD have been increasing despite recognition that alcohol use is an important public health issue. There is lack of attention to ArLD research likely due to stigma from the public, healthcare sector and industry. Over the last 4 years in the UK only 8 ArLD trials have begun compared to 36 in fatty liver disease (the second most common form of liver disease in the UK). This project will address the urgent unmet need to increase and enhance ArLD research in the UK. Design We will establish ARMS-Hub, a patient/carer group and work to understand how to overcome stigma and barriers to taking part in ArLD research. Through this work, we will develop new priorities for research and design studies to address these. Creation of ARMS-Hub We will identify existing networks of experts in ArLD across disciplines and settings including hospital specialists, scientists, and community and voluntary sector workers and among different professional groups including allied health professionals, nurses and trial designers. Representatives from these groups and patients with lived experience will form ARMS-Hub. Through group meetings, we will address stigma in ArLD research and ways to overcome it, methods to engage less research-active areas/healthcare professionals and under-served communities. We will generate research priorities and develop proposals for new research studies. Patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) A diverse group of 20 people with lived experience of ArLD and their carers will form a PPIE group. We will invite people through existing patient groups, through the British Liver Trust patient forum and through community support workers. The group will meet both virtually and in-person to discuss stigma and barriers to taking part in research. PPIE representatives will feed back findings to the Hub and form part of the Project Steering Group. Building research capacity Workshops run by Hub members will invite healthcare professionals from less research-active sites to address barriers and facilitators to take part in research. Hub members will offer mentoring of researchers to increase their knowledge and ability to take part in ArLD research. Developing ArLD research proposals A one-day research meeting will share the findings of the Hub and working groups will finalise the proposals that were developed earlier in the project. Dissemination The main output from the project will be several study proposals addressing high priority research questions for submission to Part 2 of this funding call. Findings relating to stigma and taking part in research will be shared widely through national conferences and publication in medical journals. We will distribute a lay summary to all involved networks and through the PPIE group to patients and wider liver community.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Understanding the prospective public health impact and social feasibility of Universal Basic Income schemes in the UK: Developing microsimulation of impact on self-rated health and QALYs and public engagement with ‘left behind’ communities to understand ‘willingness to pay’
Abstract: Research questions What are the estimated impacts of three costed UBI schemes on self-rated health and QALYs and what are the attendant economic implications? How do ‘left-behind’ communities evaluate designs and means of funding UBI for public health? Background This work develops long-term, multidisciplinary analysis of UBI and health in combining two leading research teams. Systematic reviews have found cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between income/income disparities and health (Pickett & Wilkinson 2015) and significant health impacts from schemes that resemble UBI (Gibson et al. 2020). Our logic model indicates that UBI may improve health by reducing poverty, increasing security of income/reducing stress and promoting long-term health behaviour (Johnson et al. 2022). We have: modelled tax-welfare distributional effects of three costed UBI schemes for public health impact against comparator policies; asserted income as a primary driver in the association with mental health; modelled UBI impacts on mental health – estimated 29,000-46,000 cases of adolescent anxiety and depression avoided annually depending on scheme; examined public preferences. Aims and objectives Aim: develop capacity to provide policymakers with comprehensive evidence of UBI health impact Objectives: 1) develop Landman health module to microsimulate schemes’ impact on SF-12 self-rated health and cost via QALYs 2) conduct conjoint experimental surveys on public assessment of design, costs and means of funding UBI 3) conduct participatory citizen engagement workshops to explore community-level concerns over implementation Methods 1) Microsimulation We will use a model that examines changes 'within-between' individuals to analyse relationships between incomes and SF-12 Mental and Physical Component Scores across 10 waves of Understanding Society. We will develop a Landman TTM health module to microsimulate whole adult UK population impacts of income changes produced by our modelled schemes on self-rated health and project impacts on QALYs. 2) Conjoint experiment We will conduct conjoint experiments with UK-wide representative samples where participants choose between schemes with different attributes: level of health impact, targeting, overall cost and means of funding. This will allow creation of a ‘public acceptability model’ to examine policy proposals and framings. We will create an online tool to predict acceptability of schemes among groups. 3) Citizen Engagement We will examine implication and implementation concerns through qualitative workshops co-designed with community co-researchers from Jarrow, England, which has high health inequalities and vulnerability to welfare reform. We will explore and categorise concerns, use them to refine our ‘public acceptability model’ and evaluate health policy framings. Impact and Dissemination Impact: Team: development of microsimulation and qualitative research capacity; Knowledge: enhanced understanding of relationships between income, health and public budgets; Policy: increased capacity to assess health, economic and social impact of UBI versus existing welfare schemes. Northumbria University will own any IP. ? 4 Articles analysing: relationship between income, self-rated security and SF-12 scores in Understanding Society; microsimulation of impact on QALYs; ‘public acceptability model’; citizen engagement workshops ? Online public acceptability tool ? Compass project report and launch event

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Health impact, process and economic evaluation of selective licensing schemes for private rented housing in England
Abstract: Research question Can selective licensing (SL) schemes improve England’s private rented housing sector leading to health and social benefits for residents? Background English local authorities can implement SL to help improve conditions and reduce antisocial behaviour (ASB) linked to private rented housing. SL requires private rented landlords to register, purchase a license with various conditions, and allow inspections to ensure housing standards are maintained. A London study of SL found evidence of impacts but a national study is needed. Study Aim To evaluate SL schemes for the private rented housing sector in England. The evaluation will assess health and social impacts, implementation and change mechanisms, and economic consequences. Work package objectives WP1: To assess area and individual level impacts of SL schemes on health and social outcomes. To assess impacts on equity. WP2: To assess SL in terms of the following (i) stakeholder acceptability (ii) pathways to impact, (iii) unintended and systemic consequences; (iv) barriers/facilitators; (v) equity assessment. WP3: To assess whether SL schemes are value for money. WP4: To share and interpret findings with stakeholders. Methods WP1: The proposed impact evaluation has a natural experiment design with matched control. Outcomes: Area level: mental health and wellbeing (SAMHI: primary outcome); hospital admissions (all cause; cardiovascular; respiratory; injuries due to falls or burns); ASB, population turnover, rent. Individual level: self-reported anxiety (primary outcome); wellbeing, general self-reported health, residential stability (ONS Annual Population Survey (APS)). 53 Local Authorities operate SL in 110 localities, of which 95 started after 2011: n=1,814 LSOAs (approx 5.5% of the English population). We estimate that APS includes 1001 participants per year in these LSOAs. Over our 2011 to 2019 sample period we expect to observe around 9,000 individuals in the intervention group. The number of APS participants in the matched comparison LSOAs will be approximately 3000 per year if we match 3 control LSOAs to every intervention LSOA. Average Treatment effect on Treated will be calculated for multiple time periods as difference in differences (DiD) taking into account the SL’s different start dates. WP2: The process evaluation will be primarily qualitative: n= 72 qualitative semi-structured interviews with stakeholders (tenants, landlords, implementers and representatives of stakeholder organisations); a national and a local workshop (n=10 for each); document analysis. Data collection will mostly focus on 4 ‘case’ SL sites. WP3: Cost benefit analysis using subjective wellbeing approach. Anticipated impact and dissemination WP4 will focus on knowledge exchange. The findings will inform decisions to implement (or not) SL - a choice all local authorities must make. Engagement will involve workshops and our policy and practice links, including charities (Shelter, Crisis, Safer Renting), national government, local and regional government, practice and research networks. Timeline and Milestones (see Gantt Chart). 0-2 mths: ethics approval, PPI & AG meetings. 2-6 mths: WP1 update data, submit protocol; WP2 begin recruitment and data collection. 7-17 mths: WP1 Analysis plan and analysis; WP2 data collection; WP3 prepare data 18-22 mths: All WPs: Interpretive workshops; refine and begin write-up 22-26 mths: final analysis and write-up.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Addressing liver disease in persons living with multiple long term conditions (ALPINE)
Abstract: Why is this study needed? Liver disease is increasing as a result of more people living with overweight and obesity, type 2 diabetes, and alcohol misuse. Often people live with more than one of these conditions at the same time, known as living with “multiple long term conditions”. These conditions are more common in more deprived areas, where there are often not enough liver disease studies to help understand how to improve the lives of people in these areas. When a person lives with multiple long term conditions, they are at risk of complications from each condition. In the past, attempts to see which research questions are most important to people living with liver disease has been done without considering these other conditions that are often present. What is ALPINE? ALPINE is a group that brings together people living with, or at risk of liver disease with researchers in universities, hospital doctors, GPs, and patient charities. The majority of the team is based in the North of England with researchers, GPs and hospital specialists in liver disease and related conditions in areas with high levels of liver disease, including Scarborough and the East Coast of Yorkshire, and Liverpool and the North West Coast. What will ALPINE do? 1. Bring together people living with, or at risk of liver disease in these regions, with doctors and university researchers who want to make a difference to people living with liver disease and multiple long term conditions. 2. Support clinical trials to help people living with or at risk of liver disease in the areas where there are no or very few studies, but many people living with liver disease. 3. Work together to understand what questions are important to people living with or at risk of liver disease and other long term conditions, and the doctors looking after them. This will be carried out through a number of workshops, surveys, and group discussions. 4. Work together to develop new studies to help improve the lives of people living with liver disease and multiple long term conditions. How will patients and the public be involved? Patient and public involvement (PPI) is central to the ALPINE group. We will work with existing PPI groups in the early stages of the project but will extend this group to include more people from areas most affected by liver disease. We will make these new contacts through community-based groups including alcohol support and weight management groups. Our PPI members will be involved in every stage of research from study design, to co-producing grant proposals and sharing the findings. Support and training will be provided to both new PPI members and researchers involved in ALPINE in preparation for bids submitted in Stage 2. What will ALPINE produce? At the end of the project, ALPINE will have grown into a coordinated multidisciplinary group. We will have produced information for patients and the public and clinicians about people living with multiple long term conditions and liver disease and about what research questions are most important to these people. Finally, we will submit two applications for further funding for trials that aim to improve the health and long-term outcomes by answering the questions that we have identified.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: INdependenT prEscribinG in community phaRmAcy; whaT works for whom, why and in what circumstancEs (INTEGRATE)
Abstract: Research question How does independent prescribing in community pharmacy work, why does it work, and in what circumstances? Background Making better use of community pharmacy is a key part of the NHS Long Term Plan. Pharmacies offer convenient and accessible sources of healthcare advice for the public, particularly in areas of high deprivation. Pharmacists have extensive knowledge of medicines, however without additional qualifications they are not currently able to prescribe prescription only medicines. It is over 15 years since pharmacists have been able to become independent prescribers, however few pharmacists are active prescribers, particularly in community pharmacy. There are no widespread, or nationally commissioned services in community pharmacy in England, which require prescribing. Despite poor utilisation of prescribing in community pharmacy nationally, there is a need to learn transferable lessons from pharmacists and services that have delivered successful initiatives and overcome barriers to implementation to understand enablers of successful delivery. This is essential now, as workload and workforce pressures in the NHS are significant. Furthermore, new Education and Training Standards will see all pharmacy graduates from 2026 hold prescribing status on registration. Aims and objectives Our aim is to improve understanding of how independent prescribing in community pharmacy works, why it works, and in what circumstances, so we can recommend strategies to maximise implementation and utilisation to meet the needs of patients. (1) To understand how and why independent prescribing in community pharmacy works, or does not work, for which groups of people, and in which circumstances, through a realist synthesis of published literature (2) To synthesise the findings of objective 1 into a realist programme theory of independent prescribing in community pharmacy (3) To co-produce recommendations with an expert stakeholder and PPIE group that support widespread implementation of independent prescribing in community pharmacy. Methods We will conduct a realist synthesis following the accepted Realist And Meta-narrative Evidence Syntheses: Evolving Standards (RAMESES). A stakeholder group consisting of a wide range of healthcare professionals, commissioners, policy makers and PPIE representatives will meet up to 6 times during the project. The realist synthesis will follow an iterative five stage process: (1) Locate existing theories – via initial exploratory searches and development of initial programme theory with stakeholders (2) Search for evidence – a search strategy will be developed by our information specialist to identify published research and grey literature (3) Article section – articles will be screened against inclusion and exclusion criteria (4) Extract and organise data; data for programme theory development will be coded in NVivo software (5) Synthesise evidence and draw conclusions – context-mechanism-outcome configurations will be developed and embedded within a programme theory which will be refined and developed with stakeholder input. Timelines The project will take place over 18 months. Anticipated impact and dissemination We will recommend strategies to maximise widespread implementation and utilisation to meet the needs of the NHS and patients. We will identify areas where current evidence is lacking, providing recommendations for future research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Scottish Hepatology Access Research Partnership (SHARP)
Abstract: People may only realise they have liver disease when they get severe illness as a result of liver failure which may lead to death. The liver can be damaged over a long time before the person with liver disease is aware of anything being wrong. Finding the liver damage early gives the chance to prevent it getting worse and causing severe illness. As much liver disease is for life, it is important to keep an eye on it and monitoring by liver doctors can prevent problems and complications arising. However, many people with liver disease have difficulty getting to see doctors and specialist medical services. This may be due to a bad personal or social situation such as living in poorer deprived areas, or perhaps because they live in places where there are fewer medical services. In some cases it could be both. Isolation due to social reasons or where they live limits the chances of detecting liver problems and also limits the chance to give good care for patients who are known to have liver disease. Scotland has a higher rate of deaths from liver disease than other parts of the UK. Within Scotland there are areas where these rates are even higher. They include more deprived city and town areas such as Lanarkshire and Greater Glasgow & Clyde, but they also include more remote areas such as the Highland region. This project (called the Scottish Hepatology Access Research Partnership, ‘SHARP’) will develop research ideas to understand and improve access to liver services in Scotland. SHARP will include people from all over Scotland. This will include specialists in liver disease and public health, general practitioners, social care services, charities and patient representatives through the British Liver Trust (BLT). There will be a Management group which will develop research ideas and an Advisory group which will review them to make sure they are aimed at helping the care of liver disease for these people who find it difficult to see doctors across Scotland. Research topics may include finding out about people’s experience of making contact with liver services and how it can be made better; finding new ways to detect and monitor liver disease without needing to travel to hospitals; and working out how to care for those who don’t have access to the internet. The BLT represents patients with liver disease from across the UK and is a vital member of SHARP. Their role is not only to give a patient view on the research ideas, but also to help design and deliver the studies. We hope that this partnership will lead to patient-led research that will make a real change. Liver illness varies between different areas of Scotland and is often related to deprived areas and areas far from medical services. However, the links between the health boards and social services are consistent across Scotland, in particular with Alcohol and Drug Partnerships which address the social and addiction issues often linked to liver disease. Scotland also has very good electronic health records, which can be obtained through a secure network of NHS ‘Safe Havens’. These features make Scotland a very good setting to do this sort of research. SHARP aims to start early in 2023 and will spend 15 months developing research ideas for the NIHR project call early in 2024. Although this project is based in Scotland, the work will apply to other areas of the UK which have similar issues with people who can’t easily see liver doctors but who are in need of high quality liver services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Development of a trial application to assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of adult dRug scrEening and brief interventionS in key hEalth, social care and justice setTings: The RESET PROJECT
Abstract: In England and Wales, alcohol and drug-related crime is estimated to cost society £11.4 and £20 billion annually. Identifying effective interventions therefore has the potential to significantly reduce costs relating to substance use as well as increase individual social welfare. We have brought together a team of international experts in drug and alcohol work in various settings who have carried out numerous research projects around the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of alcohol and/or drugs interventions in a variety of settings. Brief substance use interventions are a secondary prevention activity, aimed at those individuals who are using substances in a pattern that is likely to be harmful to health and/or well-being. They have been shown to be effective for alcohol in primary care and there is some evidence in hospital settings. They are typically delivered by practitioners who are not addiction specialists, to non-treatment, opportunistically identified populations. There is less evidence of the effect of drug-targeted brief interventions and most of the work has been carried out outside the UK. We will use a variety of methods to carry out the following objectives. Our work has co-production as a central tenet, working with academics, practitioners, policy makers and the public, particularly those with lived experience. • To establish a research team with appropriate skills and expertise. • Review and analysis of literature of how similar types of SBI tools/interventions might be of use/implemented in the UK context and are already used in other international settings. • Scoping current use of existing drug SBI tools/interventions in UK settings using reviews of the literature to identify learning/best practice examples throughout the course of the award and feed learning into research design. • Conduct a systematic evidence review to identify the most appropriate screening tools across the three settings (health, social care and justice settings in the UK). • Identification and engagement of relevant stakeholders. We will have discussions with specific communities and population groups, policy makers, local drug and alcohol services, practitioners and service users. • Investigations with key stakeholders in each of the three settings with different categories of individuals using focus groups to inform where and how drug SBIs might be targeted within any given setting. • Development of new academic and/or practitioner partnerships to support anticipated drug SBI research. We will include those with research expertise with particular interventions or drugs, within particular settings. • To develop an application to complete a 2-phase evaluation (pilot and feasibility, followed by a trial/s) on the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of targeted drug screening and brief interventions (SBIs) including extended brief interventions in reducing drug use and associated harm in health, social care and justice settings in the UK, including a comparison of effectiveness between settings. The team will be led by Prof Newbury-Birch. It will meet monthly to develop the work and discuss the findings of the objectives ensuring an iterative approach to how we move the work forward. A key component of the work over this one-year project is to go into local communities to identify how they can be involved in the pilot/definitive study in a way that is beneficial to them and the study.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: The Inspirited Minds Adapted Intervention: Feasibility study of a faith-based culturally adapted intervention to promote mental health and well-being in young Muslim women
Abstract: Research question Can we evaluate a faith-based culturally adapted intervention to promote and improve mental health and well-being of young Muslim women in the community? Background Long-term mental health conditions among young people are increasing. Young women have three times higher prevalence than men. The unmet treatment need is greatest in underserved communities, particularly British Muslims, the largest minority religious group. Ethnic minority groups are under-referred to services and show poorer recovery rates linked to inequalities. This can be explained by little tailored support to meet their needs. Culturally tailored interventions could improve mental health and well-being, but limited evidence exists on their effectiveness in this population. This feasibility trial will address the evidence gap through an evaluation of a religiously and culturally adapted peer support group intervention (IM-Adapted) developed by Inspirited Minds (IM) for young Muslim women aged 18-24. Aim: To establish the feasibility of evaluating a faith-based culturally adapted intervention to promote and improve mental health and wellbeing of young Muslim women in community settings. Objectives • Deliver and evaluate the IM-Adapted group intervention compared with usual psychoeducation • Identify the most effective methods to recruit and randomize participants • Examine the feasibility of delivering the interventions in community settings • Explore implementation and fidelity to the intervention protocol • Determine the acceptability of the interventions, study procedures and barriers to engagement • Estimate adherence rates to the intervention by participants • Explore the feasibility of collecting outcome and resource data • Estimate referrals, recruitment and retention rates • Evaluate the safety of the trial • Estimate sample size for a future definitive trial Methods A cluster randomised feasibility trial will be delivered in community sites in East London and Birmingham, with a nested process evaluation. Sixty eligible young women will be randomised to receive either a) the IM-Adapted intervention or b) usual psychoeducation group support. Using depression, mental health and well-being questionnaires at baseline, post-intervention and 24 weeks, outcomes will be tested to identify the most appropriate primary outcome for a future effectiveness trial. Progression criteria include recruitment and retention, participant engagement, acceptability, barriers and facilitators to interventions and training of therapists, data completion including resource use, and sample size for a future trial. Participative approaches with patient and public involvement (PPI) are embedded throughout, and in the development of this proposal, with plans to involve young women with lived experience in collaboration with IM and the public co-applicant. Timelines for delivery: January 2024 for 24 months Anticipated impact and dissemination PPI and stakeholder involvement will be central to dissemination via relevant networks. Results will be published in peer-reviewed journals, conferences, and shared with IM’s networks, and mental health service providers. This study is a pathway to testing effectiveness to inform guidance in routine care and will provide evidence on how to measure and illustrate impact and benefit of culturally tailored approaches. It will illuminate how to increase participation from under-represented groups and address inequity.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: South Western Ambulance Services NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Prehospital Point of Care Testing to Enable Decision-making (PrePoCTED)
Abstract: Research Questions 1. Which characteristics of point of care (POC) tests make them suitable for inclusion in a platform trial of pre-hospital POC testing to modify patient pathways and improve the clinical and cost effectiveness of Emergency Medical (Ambulance) Service care? 2. What are the facilitators and barriers to pre-hospital point of care testing and the resulting pathway changes that will influence the successful delivery of a platform trial? Background Demand on Emergency Medical (Ambulance) Services (EMS) in the United Kingdom continues to increase, with associated pressure to avoid patient conveyance to hospital whenever this is safe and feasible. Point of care (POC) testing by ambulance staff has substantial potential to inform effective decision-making that will support alternatives to ambulance conveyance, facilitate the initiation of correct treatments sooner, ensure patients reach the service best suited to their needs and improve patient pathways, outcomes and experience. There is an urgent need to evaluate pre-hospital POC tests. A platform trial would be an efficient means of evaluating multiple POC testing technologies within one coherent programme. However, prior to testing the feasibility of such a platform trial we must establish the characteristics of POC tests that make them suitable for inclusion, the supporting evidence base and the barriers and facilitators to both the planned research and implementation of POC testing within current care pathways. Aims 1. Establish a reproducible process that will reliably select candidate POC tests for inclusion in a platform trial. 2. Select the tests that will be included and scope an approach to outcome measurement and economic modelling that will used in a subsequent platform trial. 3. Explore facilitators and barriers to the adoption of POC testing by ambulance services, and our planned platform trial. 4. Achieve full stakeholder engagement and submit a Stage 1 application to the linked HTA call. Methods Work Package (WP) 1: Scoping phase to identify the characteristics of POC tests that make them suitable for use in EMS through a multi-modal approach combined with a series of scoping and systematic reviews (funded in parallel by the NIHR ARC West). WP2: Stakeholder engagement to map the clinical pathways associated with the candidate tests identified in WP1 and determine the facilitators and barriers to POC testing and pathway changes. Construction of associated logic models and identification of candidate outcome measures. WP3: Integration of health economic methods alongside WP1 and WP2 to inform and contextualise the costs and consequences of using different POC tests. Health economic modelling to inform assessment of the identified POC tests. WP 4: Multi-criteria decision analysis, using rounds of stakeholder consensus, to identify the POC tests that will be included in the subsequent platform trial. Timeline Set-up: Months 1-2 WP1: Months 2-7 WP2: Months 6-10 WP3: Months 2-10 WP4/Dissemination: Months 7-12 Impact/Dissemination This research will establish a reproducible, evidence-based approach to the identification of POC tests that have the potential to improve pre-hospital care pathways, and which will be evaluated in a subsequent platform trial. Findings will be disseminated via peer-reviewed publications, presentations, infographics, blogs and social media to ensure cross-sector reach and impact, working closely with patient and public partners.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Platform Randomised evaluation of clinical Outcomes using novel TEChnologies to optimise antimicrobial Therapy (PROTECT)
Abstract: THE PROBLEM Antibiotic resistance is where bacteria that cause infections become resistant to antibiotics. It could threaten the lives of millions of people around the world if urgent action is not taken. To prevent this problem the use of antibiotics should be limited to only those patients who absolutely need it. When patients present to emergency care with a suspected infection, it is difficult for healthcare professionals to know if it is caused by bacteria (which needs treating with antibiotics) or a virus (which cannot be treated with antibiotics). There is no quick test which can confirm bacterial infection, and current laboratory tests take 24-48 hours to give results. Healthcare professionals worry about missing a diagnosis of sepsis, which is a common, potentially life-threatening complication of infection. The best treatment for sepsis includes early recognition, and prompt antibiotics and fluids delivered by a drip into a vein. The lack of a perfect test for bacterial infection, and the concern about delaying treatment for possible sepsis, has led to prescribing too many antibiotics. There are new technologies which may help clinicians make decisions about whether to start, stop, or change antibiotics. However, they have never been evaluated in a large trial that allows testing multiple technologies, alone or in combination, wherever patients are seen with suspected infection. This form of study is called a platform trial. The Covid-19 pandemic showed that new treatments can quickly and safely be brought into clinical use by conducting these platform trials. Well-designed platform trials allow faster decisions about which new treatments and tests should be used routinely to improve patient safety. AIM OF THE RESEARCH The aim of this project is to assemble a multidisciplinary team of researchers who can plan and prepare a well-designed platform trial that allows multiple technologies to be evaluated rapidly, and then to be adopted quickly into care to benefit patients. We need to show that these technologies are safe for patients, improve care, and reduce the unnecessary use of antibiotics. WHAT WILL BE DONE? We will spend 12 months preparing the platform trial. We will identify which technologies should be tested, and when they could be best used to guide decisions about antibiotic use. We will also seek views of patients, carers, and healthcare professionals about the acceptability of using these technologies in routine care, and which outcomes matter to them. In November 2023, we will submit a proposal for a platform trial to the research funder. PATIENT AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT We have three public involvement co-applicants, and will seek support from Antibiotic Research UK, who will connect us to a wider PPI group. Our public involvement co-applicants have experience of either themselves or a relative being treated for serious infection, but we will provide further training to them about the technologies and care pathways. As part of preparing for the platform trial, we will engage in a wide consultation on study design, patient acceptability, patient perceptions of antibiotic therapy in management of bacterial infections, and the risks of antibiotic resistance. HOW WILL IT BENEFIT PATIENTS? This project will allow the research team to design the most efficient platform trial to evaluate technologies to guide clinical decisions about antibiotic use, without causing patient harm or additional stress to carers and families.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Multimodal Approach to Preventing Suicide in Schools (MAPSS) project: A regionally based feasibility trial of an integrated response to suicide risk among secondary school pupils
Abstract: Research Question What is the feasibility of a school-based suicide prevention programme comprising universal, selective, and indicated components in reducing suicide risk, improving risk recognition, and changing health service use among young people aged 14-15 in Northwest England? Background Suicide rates among young people are rising, and evidence-based prevention programmes are urgently needed. Schools offer a potentially ideal mode for delivery. Aim To assess the feasibility of conducting a trial of the Multimodal Approach to Preventing Suicide in Schools (MAPSS) programme in English secondary schools, specifically in relation to participant recruitment and retention, and the social validity (feasibility, utility and acceptability) and safety of the intervention for young people. Intervention The MAPSS programme involves delivering a universal suicide literacy workshop (e.g., safeTALK), screening for suicide risk, and delivering an adapted web-based Cognitive Behavioural Therapy program (Reframe IT-UK) to students identified as high-risk for suicide. Teachers and parents also receive suicide prevention training. MAPSS has been trialled in Australia and piloted in the UK. Methods The sample will consist of ~810 adolescent pupils in Year 10 (age 14-15 years), recruited from six mainstream secondary schools across Cheshire and Merseyside. The schools will be randomly assigned to one of two arms as part of a cluster-randomised controlled trial: intervention (n=4) or control arm (n=2). Year 10 pupils in the intervention schools will receive a suicide prevention lesson (n~540 pupils). Pupils who score 21 or above on the Suicidal Ideation Attributes Scale (SIDAS) or who report past month suicidal ideation will receive Reframe IT-UK plus treatment as usual (TAU) in the intervention schools, while those in the control arm will receive TAU (n~270 pupils). We will compare the continuous scores on the SIDAS outcome measure between groups at baseline and follow-ups. A longitudinal qualitative process evaluation will be conducted in 4 case study schools (intervention schools), to explore factors affecting implementation and social validity. Data will be analysed using a thematic framework approach. We will also collect data on resource use and health outcomes to assess the feasibility of conducting a full economic evaluation alongside a definitive trial. Timelines for Delivery Participants will complete online questionnaires in school at 4 timepoints: baseline (T1); 2-4 weeks post-baseline (after the suicide prevention lesson; T2), 12 weeks post-baseline (after Reframe IT-UK; T3); and T4) 1-year post-baseline. The survey system will automatically flag participants who score in the at-risk range for suicidal ideation. Eligible students will either receive the intervention or TAU, based on the trial arm their school is randomised into. Students receiving the Reframe IT-UK intervention will complete the 8 weekly modules between T2 and T3. The study will be conducted over a 2-year period (2024-2026), with 6-9 months for set up across 6 schools, 1-year feasibility study, and 3 months consolidation. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination The long-term goal is to conduct an effectiveness trial to determine whether MAPSS is a cost-effective suicide prevention intervention for use in schools for young people, and whether such a programme reduces the risk of future suicide ideation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Mixed Method Evidence Synthesis for Equity: to identify inclusive education and information interventions for all people managing early-stage chronic kidney disease
Abstract: Background: About 3.5 million people in the UK who have chronic kidney disease (CKD). It is a problem often linked to high blood pressure, diabetes, and heart disease. If not treated quickly, it can cause a kidney to become damaged and stop working. When kidney disease is in its early stages educating people to take care of their kidneys can stop or slow the disease from progressing. Aim: To support improvements in the delivery of information and education for patients with early-stage CKD and their families using evidence synthesis. Research questions: 1. How is information and education currently provided to patients with early-stage CKD and their families and carers in the UK? 2. What is the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of interventions aiming to deliver information and education to patients with early-stage CKD and their families and carers? 3. What are the experiences of patients and their families and carers and health care professionals of receiving and delivering interventions aiming to provide information and education on early-stage CKD? 4. What are the factors that may enhance or limit the successful delivery of interventions aiming to deliver information and education to patients with early-stage CKD and their families and carers? 5. How has EDI been considered and affected the design, intervention, and evaluation of interventions for patients with early-stage CKD and their families and carers? 6. Study Within a Review (SWAR): What are the experiences of researchers of using the PRO-EDI tool to collect and synthesise EDI data and how helpful are the outputs to decision makers? 7. What are the priorities for future research activity to improve delivery of effective education and information to patients with CKD and their families? Methods: • A systematic review of the quantitative evidence evaluating the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of interventions aiming to deliver information and education to patients with early-stage CKD, their families, and carers. As part of this review, we will develop a typology of relevant interventions. • A systematic review of qualitative evidence exploring the experiences and views of patients and their families and carers and health care professionals of receiving and delivering interventions aiming to provide information and education on early-stage CKD. • An overarching synthesis to integrate the results from the two systematic reviews. We will develop a logic model with an EDI focus to better understand how to overcome health inequalities in information and education provision. We will use a multi-method consultation approach (workshops, social media, telephone, and email) to identify and discuss i) current provision of information, and ii) what the findings mean for clinical practice, service provision and the future research agenda. We will also conduct a Study Within a Review (SWAR), to explore the experience of researchers and knowledge users of using a newly developed tool (PRO-EDI). Impact and Dissemination: In addition to publications in peer-reviewed, open access academic journals, we will produce accessible dissemination materials including briefing papers, podcasts, plain language summaries and blogs, shared via pathways developed with our clinical and patient stakeholders. We will use the findings to establish co-produced research priorities to improve the delivery of effective education and information for patients with early-stage CKD and their families.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: The Looking Forward Project: A pragmatic adaptive trial of hope-focused mentoring to improve mental health and social outcomes for young women who are not in education, employment or training in deprived coastal areas
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Young women who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET) are growing significantly in number. They have poorer mental health and social outcomes relative to young women who work and/or study and compared to NEET young men. Gender disparities are compounded in deprived coastal areas, in which NEET young women especially lack self-agency and aspirations. Research by our group and others shows that greater hope reduces the risks of staying NEET and of having mental health problems. We have developed a hope-focused intervention (called HOPEFUL) for this group. HOPEFUL is a flexible modular programme, delivered over 3-12 weeks, for creating a hopeful mindset and learning skills in setting and pursuing personally meaningful goals. Support is provided by a youth-initiated mentor; someone that NEET young women select from their existing network. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES: We aim to generate evidence on the feasibility, effectiveness, and cost-effectiveness of the HOPEFUL intervention. Our specific objectives are to test the feasibility of conducting a randomised controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate HOPEFUL and refine its design, and then conduct a definitive RCT with an economic and process evaluation. RESEARCH QUESTIONS: Our key feasibility research question is, is it feasible to recruit NEET young women and mentors to a trial of HOPEFUL vs. standard support, with a primary outcome of hope? Our key definitive RCT research question is, does HOPEFUL improve hope and secondary outcomes of mental health symptoms, wellbeing, loneliness, and help-seeking of NEET young women in deprived coastal areas at the primary endpoint of 16 weeks and secondary endpoint of 12 months post-randomisation? Secondary research questions pertain to: evaluating intervention cost-effectiveness; how NEET young women and mentors experience HOPEFUL and its safety and acceptability; and mechanisms of proposed intervention effects and contextual moderators. METHODS: NEET young women (16-24 years) will be recruited from young people’s services provided and commissioned by local authorities and the charity and voluntary sector, including employability, and sexual health services. A feasibility trial (N=70) will be followed (assuming warranted) by a definitive RCT (N=248). The trials will compare HOPEFUL plus standard support to standard support alone, with 1:1 randomisation, stratified by local authority area (East Sussex, Brighton & Hove, Kent, Medway, Norfolk) and age (16-18 versus 19-24 years). Feasibility outcomes will be assessed at baseline and post-intervention (16 weeks), and RCT outcomes additionally at longer-term follow-up of 12-months. The RCT includes an economic and a multi-method, multi-perspective process evaluation. TIMELINES: Total duration: 54 months. Months 1-12: feasibility trial. Months 13-14: analysis against pre-specified progression criteria and protocol amendments. Months 15-54: Definitive RCT. ANTICIPATED IMPACTS AND DISSEMINATION: We will disseminate findings using tailored outputs for participants, the public, academic, health and social care professionals. In the short-term, evidence generated through this project will raise the UK profile of youth-initiated mentoring and support local implementation. In the long-term, we anticipate practice impacts through scaled-up access to HOPEFUL; ultimately benefitting the health and social outcomes of NEET young women and their networks, with associated economic and societal gains.

Award_Title: KNOW-PH (Knowledge for Public Health). The NIHR Public Health Knowledge Mobilisation team
Abstract: OUR APPROACH: The aim of KNOW-PH (Knowledge for Public Health) is to develop, design and deliver knowledge mobilisation in local settings for the benefit of public health and to reduce health inequalities. We will do this using non-linear, ‘Mode 2’ models of knowledge mobilisation that are: i) driven by coproduction; ii) responsive to policy and practice need; iii) learning and action oriented; and, iv) evidence and theory informed. Our approach is creative by design, engaging with policymakers, practitioners and communities across the local public health landscape in the UK. THE PROGRAMME: There are two interrelated components with local government and community partnership at its core: 1) Deep coproduction. This component will mobilise knowledge, organised over two cycles of coproduction (16 months each) using creative methods with local authorities and their partners. 2) Responsive knowledge mobilisation. This will include shorter term knowledge mobilisation projects (3-6 months long), focused on NIHR and stakeholder needs where a ‘window of opportunity’ emerges to address timely, high priority topics for local areas. An iterative process for developing topic focus, synthesising evidence form the NIHR portfolio and coproduction activities will be applied and tailored to the specific needs of local partners. This will be achieved in close collaboration with the NIHR PHR programme team and with two main pillars of KNOW-PH: the Local Authority Reference Group and the Public and Community and Engagement panel. Our inputs and outputs will be distinctively creative using methods such as storyboarding, forum theatre, Lego serious play, arts-based methods and many other creative forms. Our work will be evaluated pragmatically and continuously for impact, capacity-building and cross-sectoral learning. We will produce multiple outputs including project-specific knowledge products, training outputs, guidelines for knowledge mobilisation and how to use creative methods with local government. EXPERTISE AND TRACK RECORD: We are an experienced, multidisciplinary team with expertise across public health research, policy and practice as well as knowledge mobilisation, science communication, public engagement and creative design. We have a track record of mobilising knowledge across the public health landscape, including in local government and have pioneered design-led methods. PATHWAYS TO IMPACT: Our coproduction methods offer a promising route to social, policy, practice and behaviour change. Our projects will mobilise knowledge at receptive moments (e.g. when there is engaged public debate) to capture individual, organisational and system interests at the right time. We will build a social media strategy and extend our community of practice work (e.g. the Knowledge Mobilisation Alliance) to deliver longer term goals. Our pathway promotes longer term embedded practice that will create a shift in ways of doing evidence mobilisation, with potentially long-term implications for health inequalities. PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT AND ENGAGEMENT: Our Public and Community Engagement (PACE) group is at the centre of the work of KNOW-PH. Each project will have a small, bespoke Public Involvement and Engagement team advising. With diverse community organisation leadership, PACE will shape the priorities of the team and support timely and meaningful public involvement across the knowledge mobilisation processes ensuring that community interests are properly represented.

Award_Title: Somerset Health Determinants Research Collaboration
Abstract: Background Somerset is the 2nd largest local authority in the country and faces a range of challenges, including low educational attainment, meeting the needs of rural and coastal communities, and an ageing population. As of 1 April 2023, Somerset is now the country’s second largest unitary authority. This is a pivotal moment for Somerset’s developing health, care and government infrastructure. Together with partners we will develop a culture of doing participatory research and being evidence-based in decisions that impact the wider determinants of health. Vision We will develop a research culture that is embedded with our local communities. We will develop the behaviours, skills, and values to create a culture that provides the conditions for multidisciplinary research to be carried out with and by local people, creating impact in their own communities and on decisions made in Somerset and beyond. Objectives 1. Public involvement in research that is inclusive of and responsive to local needs 2. To support research collaborations 3. Create the systems necessary to streamline the design, delivery and use of research 4. Create a culture that supports research and systematically uses evidence in decision-making. 5. Impacts and findings will reach diverse audiences from local to national. Key deliverables Governance structures will be established to oversee the programme. Posts will be created to manage and deliver five workstreams reflecting the objectives of the programme over two phases: Years 1-3 will focus upon capacity building and implementation of the infrastructure to co-produce research with communities. Years 4-5 will mainstream most of the functions into existing council posts to leave a sustainable research infrastructure. Collaborations/Partnerships UWE Bristol will give the Council support to build research and evidence appraisal skills and support the design and conduct of research. Training and development opportunities will build the capacity of the Council to conduct research and appraise evidence. The Research Business and Innovation unit will support collaborative bids for further research and evaluation funding. Spark is Somerset’s community infrastructure organisation. They will co-lead the Public Involvement workstream to involve communities in identifying research needs and opportunities. University College London’s Institute of Health Equity will support Somerset to develop its approach to addressing the wider determinants of health and evidencing the impact. Timelines and milestones for delivery The Gantt chart illustrates how Somerset’s HDRC will develop from Dec 2023 Year 1 to Nov 2028. Milestones and key activities have been identified for the core setup and each workstream respectively. Impact and dissemination The impacts of the HDRC will include a sustained culture of engaging with and co-producing research with diverse communities; a culture of evidence-based decision-making regarding the wider determinants of health; strong research partnerships formed; research communication channels established, from local to national; and ultimately increased confidence in Somerset Council services and functions and reduced health inequalities. This HDRC will put a spotlight on the importance of communities in research, feeding back to communities the impact they have had, whilst the outcomes and outputs of the HDRC will also be amplified by the platform of the UCL Institute of Health Equity.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Cornwall Health Determinants Research Collaboration
Abstract: Background Cornwall Council are committed to addressing health inequalities and making Cornwall a place to start well, live well, and age well. Rural, coastal and peripheral characteristics are not unique to Cornwall but pose a challenge to equitable and effective service delivery. An HDRC will build from collective experience to better understand the causes and consequences of health inequalities that matter most to people in Cornwall. Aims and Objectives To build and embed research culture, capacity and capability to develop effective evidence-led solutions to the causes and consequences of health determinants and inequalities that matter most to people in Cornwall. - Inform practice and decision making by building and embedding research culture and capacity across the council and its partners. - Develop a research collaboration that combines skills, knowledge and expertise from academic, community, and local authority partners to address and drive improvement of determinants of health. - Generate robust, translatable, research outputs that inform practice and decision-making in Cornwall and beyond. Collaborations/Partnerships Cornwall HDRC will grow from strong, strategic partnerships across local authority, academia, VCSE and Cornish residents. It will facilitate a process of shared and multifaceted learning as each partner adds and gains value from the collaboration. Cornwall Council (CC) will bring expertise in population health and opportunities for impact through service delivery and decision making. CC will gain a research-active workforce and ability to shape and drive research activity. Three Universities of Exeter, Falmouth and Plymouth will bring expertise in key research topics, theory and methodologies and will gain understanding of the issues facing Council officers, helping to align research questions with their needs. Cornwall’s VCSE will bring in-depth knowledge of and connections with local communities and will gain skills for effecting innovative methods for evidencing impact. Communities will bring essential expertise borne of experience and will gain skills, experience and genuine influence on research priorities. Timeline and Milestones for delivery Year 1 – Strong from the Start - Recruitment of core research team - Co-creation of the Citizen Research Group - Setting of shared culture and priorities Years 2-3 - Building Core Capacity - Delivery of first three shared learning opportunities - Fit for purpose local authority research infrastructure - Learning shared at national research conference - Active learning through HDRC evaluation activity Years 3-4 - Consolidate and Grow - Collaborative projects - Submission of joint-funding applications - Evidence of research-informed decision making and commissioning - Co-authored publications Years 4-5 - Moving Forward - Recruitment of a Sustainability Programme Lead - Successful acquisition of further funding - Evidence of change in the impact of health determinants in Cornwall Anticipated Impact and Dissemination Impact will be evidenced by a culture shift within the Council; a deeper and more detailed knowledge of health determinants and their place-based context; an active and empowered Citizen Research Group with evidenced contribution to HDRC activity; and a step-change in collaborative capacity to attract, deliver, and translate into practice, research activity addressing health inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Sandwell Health Determinants Research Collaboration - Better Research for Better Health
Abstract: HDRC VISION To undertake evidence-informed, robustly evaluated activities that reflect the needs and values of our diverse local communities. The Sandwell HDRC will align with a borough-wide Levelling Up Programme to improve the wider determinants of health. BACKGROUND Sandwell Metropolitan Borough Council (SMBC) is the 12th most deprived local authority in England and life expectancy is 2-3 years shorter than the national average. Inequalities have been deepened by the pandemic, austerity and climate change, yet Sandwell’s superdiverse communities, industrial heritage and green spaces are key assets. A research needs analysis in 2021 found a strong culture of evidence-based decision making in the Public Health directorate, but less so across the wider Council. Existing structures and collaborations show commitment and potential to be more research active and evidence-informed, but limited capacity to take this forward. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES The HDRC aims to transform SMBC’s research culture and infrastructure to: *Make the best use of empirical evidence to inform decision-making and investment *Robustly evaluate services to ensure quality, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness *Facilitate research activity with partner organisations and local residents *Effectively disseminate research outputs for wider influence This will be achieved by: *Strengthening research and development capacity, resources and infrastructure *Embedding a strong research culture for evidence-informed decision-making *Developing robust systems and partnerships for cultural and knowledge exchange *Creating a community-led research culture KEY DELIVERABLES HDRC objectives will be delivered via four parallel workstreams: *Build capacity and infrastructure through workforce development and training; data science infrastructure for information sharing and evaluation; and research governance structures and processes *Embed research culture and evidence-informed practice by supporting translation of evidence into practice; embedding needs assessment and evaluation; and increasing use of evidence in decision-making *Strengthen systems and partnerships through academic collaborations for research and learning; structures and processes for wider system partnerships; and effective information sharing *Promote community participation through expanding PPIE structures, and widening engagement and representation in research COLLABORATIONS AND PARTNERSHIPS The HDRC will be a core partnership between SMBC, University of Birmingham and the voluntary sector, supported by wider collaboration and engagement. Partnership with Sandwell Council of Voluntary Organisations and Sandwell Consortium will ensure that local residents and community groups are represented and involved. TIMELINE AND MILESTONES The HDRC has a 5-year phased approach. Year 1: programme establishment and planning, setting baselines and training Year 2: full programme commencement Year 3: dissemination, review and growth, including first publications Year 4: review and consolidate learning Year 5: sustainability through designing and implementing an ongoing programme of activity IMPACT AND DISSEMINATION Strengthening evidence-informed decision-making and investment will improve health outcomes for Sandwell residents and reduce health inequalities. HDRC updates and outputs will be shared via local, regional and national forums and events; peer reviewed journals; and the Sandwell Trends website.
