Pre- and post-intervention data will be collected from families receiving more intensive perinatal mental health services, utilising a range of brief, standardised outcome measures of depression, anxiety, and parent-infant bonding. Counterfactual data will involve collection of data from sites not yet implementing SfL; or the use of wait-list controls. A brief cross-sectional survey of breastfeeding service user experience will be carried out in the same LA s. Future value for money evaluation will be supported through the collection of appropriate service-level data and through work with DHSC to put systems in place so that service use data being collected is fit for purpose. Workstream 3 consists of synthesising the data across the workstreams. Service level process data from WS1 will be combined with population impact data from WS2 to identify the configuration of services associated with the most impact, and to elicit best practices that can be applied across the 75 funded areas and beyond. The WS1 service level data will be used to identify the factors that drive and shape service delivery, and WS1 individual/family level data will be used to identify the acceptability of services to families, and stakeholder views regarding factors that affect uptake/impact. Finally, a realist synthesis will be used to test the overall Theory of Change for the SfL programme, drawing on all data sources to explain the observed impacts at programme and strand levels, and addressing synergies between SfL and Family Hubs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Responsible Gambling: a mixed methods analysis to inform public health policy and practice
Abstract: Background: Changes in the scale and nature of gambling in the UK have created growing concerns about its impact on health, especially in already vulnerable groups. An estimated 430,000 adults and 55,000 youths experience problem gambling, with many more deemed to be at risk. Research gap: Existing responses are based on the paradigm of 'Responsible Gambling', seeking to maximise individual freedom to access gambling opportunities while minimising harm. Yet, despite its endorsement by the Government and gambling industry, there are growing calls for a stronger public health response. However, the process by which such a response would be developed, in terms of policy-making and prioritisation of research on gambling is unclear, as are the social determinants of gambling and the interventions that might be effective within a comprehensive public health response. Fellowship proposal: My proposal responds directly to these gaps. I want to understand the socioeconomic determinants of gambling, the measures likely to be effective in alleviating the associated harms, and the scope for implementing them (and the barriers to doing so), both within local authorities and in national policy.To achieve this, I will take a multi-level approach using a range of methods. This will involve: A systematic review of the quantitative and qualitative literature on gambling interventions, building upon previous reviews by using both quantitative and qualitative studies to understand not just what works but how and in what circumstances. Identifying the determinants of gambling consumption using regression analysis of the association between changes in household gambling expenditure and changes in local spending and job loss, and how this differs between socio-economic groups. Identify the influences on the response to gambling regulation within local authorities, considering how this issue reaches the policy agenda, why it is or is not prioritised, and the nature of any responses, including an understanding of factors that support or hinder cross-sectoral working. This will employ semi-structured interviews with stakeholders in public health, licencing and planning departments as well as elected members. Informed by my literature review and understanding of the approaches taken by local government and, in particular, public health departments, undertake a stakeholder analysis and interviews, to identify the positions of key policy actors, employing quantitative and qualitative methods of textual analysis to explore how they frame gambling policy and the influence this has on how they respond to gambling harms. Integrating the research findings to develop, through co-production with stakeholders, a framework for a multi-level public health response and future research agenda in the UK.I will place PPI at the centre of my research, engaging with those affected by gambling to help me frame and refine the questions I ask, of whom, and how I interpret the answers. I will share my findings with key stakeholders, in particular policy-makers, public health researchers and practitioners, using briefing papers, fact sheets, presentations and short films co-produced with affected individuals. My proposed fellowship has been designed to complement other research on gambling currently being undertaken within the UK.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Preventing infection-related cardiovascular disease in primary care
Abstract: Research questions Q1) Which patients are at risk of respiratory infection-related cardiovascular disease? Q2) What are the effects of aspirin on respiratory infection-related cardiovascular disease? And does respiratory infection affect risk of bleeding when taking aspirin? Q3) What are the effects of using influenza immunisation for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in primary care?BackgroundRespiratory infection (chest infections and influenza) can trigger heart attacks and strokes (cardiovascular disease - CVD). Studies estimate respiratory infections cause over ten thousand CVD deaths per year in the UK, but current CVD prevention strategies do not consider infections.If we could identify people at risk of infection-related CVD we might use existing treatments such as aspirin and influenza vaccine, which are currently used for secondary prevention. Currently we can't identify patients at risk, and don't know the effects of these interventions on infection-related CVD. Aspirin works for primary prevention, but the risk of bleeding outweighs the benefit. A short course of aspirin during a chest infection might prevent CVD with a lower bleeding risk. Influenza vaccine works in secondary prevention, so might benefit high-risk patients. AimTo develop new strategies to prevent infection-related cardiovascular events in primary care Objectives One: Develop a prediction model for infection-related cardiovascular diseaseTwo: Externally validate the prediction model for infection-related CVD Three: Estimate the benefits and harms of aspirin in respiratory infections Four: Estimate the impact of expanding influenza vaccine coverage on preventing CVD MethodsData sources: Anonymised, routinely collected medical records from UK primary care linked to hospital data Population: Adult patients registered in primary care Primary outcome: Infection-related CVD events. This composite outcome comprises acute CVD events within the high-risk period following systemic respiratory infection (30 days) Adverse outcomes: Major bleeding, PPI group developed side effects list Sample size: Initial count: 16,000 events Missing data: Multiple imputation Predictors: Cardiovascular risk (QRisk score), patient demographics, chronic disease status, blood results, and preventative medications Statistical analyses: Objectives 1&2: Model building: logistic and Cox regression. Variable selection by a-priori knowledge, supplemented by bootstrapping. Fractional polynomials to model continuous variables. Exploration of 'off the shelf' machine learning algorithms (boosting and support vector machines). Development in CPRD Aurum and validation in CPRD gold/RCGP RSC. Statistical analyses: Objectives 3&4: Classical statistics (regression), instrumental variable methods (physician preference and vaccination effectiveness, with assessment of instrument validity. Doubly robust propensity score methods (inverse probability weighting with adjustment for propensity score). Timelines for delivery Thesis by 60 months. Objective one and two by 18 months, objective three by 36 months and four by 52 months.Anticipated impactObjectives one and two will allow GPs and researchers to identify high-risk patients. In future, a data-enabled trial of aspirin in respiratory infection could change practice. This trial would be based on objective three. Objective four may influence influenza vaccine allocation directly, as observational studies are the basis of vaccine allocation in the UK. Dissemination Three academic papers. Wider patient and public involvement, media, social media engagement. Engagement of clinical practice by implementing automated prediction tools.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Preventable infant deaths: Improving uptake of safe sleep messages in high-risk families
Abstract: 5.1 Research questionHow will an intervention targeted to families most at risk, improve safety for babies during sleep, and reduce Sudden and Unexpected Deaths in Infancy (SUDI)? 5.2 BackgroundAdvice for parents on safe sleep has reduced the incidence of SUDI in the general population over the last 3 decades, but less so for more deprived families. SUDI deaths have always been more common in these groups but now about two-thirds (approximately 200/300) occur in this group. An era of global case control studies has identified risk and protective factors for the infant sleep environment, which if adhered to, could reduce deaths further. Using what I have learned about the factors that influence decision making in high-risk families, I can now start to put this evidence into action in the form of a targeted intervention to reduce risk. 5.3 Aim and objectivesThe aim is to develop and evaluate a targeted intervention for improving uptake of safer sleep practices in families at higher risk for SUDI. In order to meet this aim, five work packages with the following objectives are proposed: Examine the prevalence and population demographics of known risk factors of SUDI deaths in England since 2018 using data from the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD). Investigate the factors influencing decision-making for infant care in high-risk families (including fathers/partners and grandparents). Co-produce the support package with families, health professionals, academics, and health services commissioners. Conduct a Realist Evaluation study of the intervention. Write a protocol and funding application for a feasibility study to test intervention methods for assessing effectiveness and investigate scope for widening the intervention to include other child health related topics. 5.4 MethodsI will conduct comparative analyses of NCMD data to describe the prevalence of known risk factors present in recent unexpected infant deaths and compare those at high risk or normal risk of unexpected infant deaths. I will use qualitative thematic analysis of interviews with families. I will use co-production to develop the intervention, bringing together an intervention development team to work together to produce the content. Realist Evaluation methods will then allow me to explore the context, mechanisms and outcomes associated with the intervention. This will include observations, surveys, interviews and focus groups. Finally, I will investigate the most appropriate methodology for a future study and write a protocol and funding application. 5.5 Timelines for deliveryA paper describing the NCMD data will be published at the end of the first year. A paper with the findings from the mixed methods study on high-risk families and wider caregivers will be published at the end of the second year. Two other papers (one on co-production study and one on evaluation study) will be delivered in the fifth year. 5.6 Anticipated impactThe intervention will have the potential to improve sleep safety for infants in high-risk families and reduce infant deaths. Learning from this work will contribute to understanding the mechanisms of complex interventions for high-risk groups across a range of infant care practices.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Developing tomographic 3-D ultrasound for cardiovascular screening
Abstract: Research question: Can, in combination with patient risk factors, tomographic 3-D ultrasound (tUS) accurately/automatically detect features of plaque instability in asymptomatic carotid disease (CAD), therefore identify patients at increased risk of stroke/cardiovascular events (CVE), be good value-for-money for the NHS by measuring atherosclerotic burden/volume. Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in the Western World; costing the UK economy £29 billion/year. As the long-term effects of CVD are largely preventable, early detection by population screening could massively reduce the frequency and cost of CVE. We know that screening the general population is not cost effective at a stroke rate of below 1.7% but in high-risk groups with greater disease prevalence it may be. CT and MR angiography will never be appropriate for screening because they involve radiation or are not quick. Alternatively, standard duplex ultrasound can quickly detect asymptomatic carotid disease but requires highly trained Vascular Scientists, of which there is a national shortage. Tomographic 3-D ultrasound (tUS) is quicker, requires less skill, and with development, could be deployed in the community. Principally, screening practitioners could be trained within a matter of weeks. However, measuring arterial disease is slow and currently still requires Vascular Scientists. Aims: To develop and understand the potential clinical and cost effectiveness of automating tUS to detect asymptomatic carotid artery disease (CAD) plus measure atherosclerotic burden in the clinical setting to predict patients who are at risk of stroke. Methods: I will measure carotid atherosclerotic burden (Carotid Plaque Volume or CPV) in 2570 high-risk patients from peripheral vascular or abdominal aortic aneurysm clinics. The prevalence of CAD is as high as 25%. Each patient will have tUS imaging of their aorta and carotid arteries to train AI to calculate CPV. CPV measured using artificial intelligence (AI) machine learning techniques will then be validated against manual measures on MRI and tUS imaging. Models able to predict CVE based on CPV and other established risk factors will then be developed. The cost-effectiveness/value-for money of utilising tUS for the NHS will be calculated under supervision from the Manchester Centre for Health Economics. Timelines: The research will take place over 3 years within the world centre of excellence for tUS vascular imaging alongside world leading experts. All patients will be recruited over the first 12 months and then followed up for 2 years before history on CVE is recorded. In project year 2 the measurements of atherosclerotic disease will be performed and automated. A risk prediction model and value-for-money will be calculated in year 3. Impact and dissemination: My project will deliver an automated CVD screening tool ready to be validated within a national screening programme that is proven to be cost-effective for the NHS. It will require little training to be utilised by screening practitioners and identify individual patients at high-risk of stroke. Results will be presented at international vascular conferences and published open access as well as advertised via social media, all with PPI involvement.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Guidance for health economic modellers for incorporating individual and aggregate behaviour into models of Public Health interventions
Abstract: Background Commissioners of Public Health interventions need to decide where best to spend their money in order to maximise health gains and/or reduce health inequalities. Health economic models use evidence from multiple sources to predict all important differences in outcomes between the intervention(s) and current practice, which can inform policy decisions. Health economic models of behaviour-change interventions typically either exclude behaviour from the model, including only risk factors such as cholesterol, or they make simplified assumptions based on limited or no evidence, for example that behaviour remains constant over each individual's lifetime. However, in other disciplines, like psychology, theories have been developed to try to explain how and why an individual's behaviour changes. In other disciplines, like sociology, different types of models are used to predict the behaviour of a group based on understanding the behaviour of individuals and their interaction with their environment. Model predictions could be improved by drawing upon research from these other disciplines, which would decrease the risk of making wrong decisions about how best to spend limited public funds. Aims and objectives The aim of the research is to develop guidance for health economic modellers for incorporating behaviour into models which compare the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of behaviour-change interventions. The guidance will consider modelling of individual behaviours and the impact of social groupings and factors within a person's environment upon their behaviour. This will provide modellers with tools to make better predictions. Specific objectives are: To identify and critically review existing methods for incorporating behaviour within quantitative models (across disciplines). To use an iterative approach to develop a taxonomy of methods for modelling individual and aggregate behaviour within health economic models of behaviour-change interventions, setting out requirements for each method including data, resources and technical skill. To test the taxonomy and methods within case studies assessing the cost-effectiveness of behaviour-change interventions in order to improve them. To extend an existing conceptual modelling framework of Public Health interventions to provide guidance to health economic modellers about incorporating behaviour into a health economic model. To disseminate the research to modellers, decision makers and members of the public.Anticipated impact and dissemination This research has the potential to improve predictions of the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of behaviour-change interventions, and hence improve resource allocation decisions. This would result in improved health and wellbeing of the general public overall. It could also facilitate decisions about targeting specific populations, hence aiming to reduce inequalities. The research findings will be disseminated via a broad range of methods, including presenting at conferences, publishing in high impact peer-reviewed journals, within ScHARR and collaborators' websites, commissioners' forums, and other social media (eg. via existing blogs and twitter accounts). I will connect with relevant commissioning bodies and academic departments throughout the project with the aim of increasing the impact of the research. I will consult with stakeholders, including public representatives, to understand the best approach to dissemination to achieve the biggest impact of the research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Award_Title: Infant feeding in the context of severe mental illness: a mixed-methods study.
Abstract: Background Perinatal severe mental illness (SMI) includes conditions such as psychosis, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and severe depression, during pregnancy and in the first postnatal year. Breastfeeding initiation is a feed from the breast or expressed breastmilk within the first 48hrs of life. In the United Kingdom, 74% of women in the general population initiate breastfeeding, but no published studies describe the prevalence of breastfeeding in women with SMI, or their experiences of infant feeding. Small studies and unpublished data suggest breastfeeding initiation could be considerably lower than in the general population and women with SMI often receive poor infant feeding support. ObjectivesTo: 1a. Investigate if women with SMI are more or less likely to initiate breastfeeding, compared to women who do not have SMI, attending the same maternity service. 1b. Explore potential socio-demographic and clinical factors associated with breastfeeding initiation in women with SMI. 2. Explore the infant feeding experiences and support needs of women with SMI. 3. Develop resources for both staff and women which modify infant feeding information to the context of SMI. Plan of investigation: Work package 1 (objectives 1a & 1b): Study design: Cohort study. Population: Women accessing maternity and mental health services across South London between 2018 and 2021 (n= approx. 30,000). Data will be accessed from the early-LIfe data cross-LInkage in Research (eLIXIR) database. Exposure: SMI Women with a completed pregnancy (did not end in miscarriage, stillbirth or neonatal death) between 2018 and 2021, who were under the care of a secondary mental health service during their pregnancy. Non exposed: Non-SMI Women with a completed pregnancy between 2018 and 2021, not previously or currently under the care of a secondary mental health service. Primary outcome: Breastfeeding initiation. Data analysis: Prevalence of breastfeeding in both groups will be estimated using descriptive statistics. Women's baseline socio-demographic and clinical characteristics will be described both overall and by group. Logistic regression will be used to investigate the association between the primary outcome and SMI status and potential effect modification by socio-demographic and clinical characteristics will also be explored. Logistic regression will also be used to assess potential predictors of breastfeeding, such as psychiatric illness severity, partner status and deprivation scores. Work package 2 (Objective 2):Study design: An exploratory qualitative study. Population: Around 20 women with SMI, up to two years postpartum. Data collection: Semi-structured interviews about women's experiences of infant feeding. Data analysis: Interviews will be recorded and transcribed verbatim and a thematic analysis carried out. Work package 3 (Objective 3):I will host a stakeholder engagement event to share the findings from the research and to facilitate a workshop for service-users and maternity and mental health professionals. The workshop will enable stakeholder input to the content and format of infant feeding resources, individualised for women with SMI. Benefits: This study will highlight women's specific infant feeding support needs in the context of SMI, enabling clinicians to provide individualised information, improving service engagement and having a national impact on infant feeding policy in the long-term.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: The Missing Billion: Using participatory approaches to improve access to healthcare for disabled people in Uganda
Abstract: BackgroundParticipatory Learning and Action (PLA) is a community-led participatory strategy to improve healthcare access. Community groups are established. They meet regularly to identify issues, develop and implement solutions, and evaluate results. PLA for women significantly reduces maternal and neonatal mortality, but its impact in other areas is not clear. The study aims to assess whether the PLA for Disability (PLA-D) can reduce mortality and improve health and healthcare access of disabled people in Uganda. Objectives: To use an evidenced-based approach to co-create PLA-D. To assess the feasibility of PLA-D implementation. To undertake a cluster-based Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) to assess the effectiveness/cost-effectiveness of PLA-D in reducing mortality. To undertake a process evaluation of PLA-D to understand mechanisms for impact and scale-up. To strengthen capacity for informing disability policy and practice through the conduct of high-quality research.MethodPLA adaptation (months 0-24): We will undertake in-depth interviews and analyse existing quantitative data to describe healthcare access and barriers experienced by disabled people in Uganda. We will update relevant systematic reviews and review the PLA literature. A consortium (researchers, implementers, disabled people) will co-create the PLA-D using the formative research. Feasibility of PLA-D will be assessed with 5 groups in Uganda.A two-arm cluster RCT will assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of PLA-D in Luuka district, Uganda (months 24-48). The control arm will receive health system strengthening support (accessibility audit of healthcare facilities; healthcare worker disability training). The intervention arm will additionally receive the PLA-D intervention, with one group established per cluster (village or city block). Groups will target disabled people, but will be open to their family/community members. We will include 64 clusters per arm with approximately 50 disabled people per cluster (Total: 3200 disabled participants per arm). Data collection will occur: 1) pre-randomisation (baseline), 2) after intervention completion (12 months) and 3) endline (24 months post-baseline). Disabled participants will complete a structured questionnaire with a trained researcher covering: healthcare quality and access, morbidity, quality of life, and contextual characteristics (e.g. poverty). Vital status will be recorded at follow-ups and verbal autopsy undertaken for reported deaths. Direct and indirect intervention costs will be collected. A process evaluation will be undertaken to examine the intervention implementation, potential mechanism for action, and consider strategies for scale-up. Ethical procedures will be adhered to throughout. Analysis/dissemination (months 49-60). Intention-to-treat analyses will compare outcomes between control and intervention arms. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratio will be calculated for outcomes. We will disseminate findings to key audiences (communities, disabled people, Ugandan and international policy/programme implementers, academics) through tailored approaches (e.g. policy/evidence briefs, community meetings, individual meetings, journal articles, academic presentations).Anticipated impact PLA-D is anticipated to improve healthcare access and quality for disabled people in the intervention clusters, and thereby reduce morbidity and mortality. Better health will support participation (e.g. education, employment), and so improve quality of life and reduce poverty. If successful, this programme can be scaled in Uganda and other LMICs, extending this impact. Translational research capacity will be strengthened for Professor Kuper and Ugandan partners.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Preventing Healthcare Associated Infection and Antimicrobial Resistance in Africa
Abstract: Research QuestionHow can the WHO Infection Prevention and Control guidelines be optimally adapted to the African context, and iteratively improved by using causal inference to investigate their efficacy and economic modelling to evaluate their cost-effectiveness? BackgroundIPC has yet to be consistently prioritised in LMIC, and the scale of the problem is poorly described. In the African context, the healthcare built environment is often inadequate, cleaners are poorly paid and equipped and there are few facilities to support hand hygiene. We recently observed that 68% of episodes of cephalosporin resistant/locally untreatable gram negative sepsis followed recent health care exposure, indicating health care facilities are highly likely to be a major site for HAI.Aim Through implementing the WHO IPC guidelines, I will investigate the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of an IPC intervention and co-create acceptable, scalable and sustainable interventions to reduce HAI in Africa.Objectives In equitable partnership with a national-level IPC steering group, to reinvigorate local IPC teams in three hospitals in Southern Malawi; Establish clinical and microbiological HAI surveillance, then implement, test and improve the WHO guidelines on IPC, investigating their effectiveness within an implementation science framework; Assess the efficacy of IPC implementation using descriptive epidemiology, high resolution molecular surveillance and causal inference; To estimate the economic burden associated with HAI, and cost-effectiveness of IPC Co-create acceptable, sustainable, and nationally generalisable guidelines, policy and protocols to mitigate HAI in Malawi in partnership with College of Medicine and Public Health Institute of Malawi.Country of work/partnersMalawi: the study will operate at three government hospitals and be based at the Malawi Liverpool Wellcome Programme, running in partnership with the College of Medicine, Ministry of Health and African Institute of Development Policy (AFIDEP). Methods and timelines Implementing IPC strategy (Workstrand 1): I will convene a steering group and reinvigorate existing ministry of health IPC teams, conduct formative research to understand the success or failure of previous IPC strategies and establish an IPC training programme (Y1). Clinical and microbiological surveillance can then be established and multimodal implementation strategies devised and implemented (Y2-4). Mixed-method evaluation of effectiveness of the implementation will be made and fed back to policy makers (Y3-5 & WS4).Causal modelling (Workstrand 2): HAI cohorts will be recruited before and after implementation for key HAI syndromes and characterised using culture and molecular microbiology (Y2-4). Causal modelling will be utilised to predict efficacy of intervention and improve multimodal strategy (Y3-5).Health economics (Workstand 3): We will estimate the economic burden associated with HAI, and evaluate cost-effectiveness of IPC interventions in order to make recommendations about targeting efforts (Y2-4).Policy (Workstrand 4): We will actively involve MoH and CoM throughout the project and work with MoH to develop nationally scalable IPC interventions (Y4-5).Anticipated impact I will describe the effectiveness, efficacy and cost effectiveness of an IPC programme in Africa. Success in Malawi will entail the development of a cadre of IPC professionals that will establish a learning health system capable of sustaining an effective IPC programme.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Arresting the HIV epidemic in rural South Africa: Using innovations in intervention design and evaluation to reduce sexual transmission of HIV in adolescents and youth.
Abstract: Research Question: I will use participatory research with patients and public involvement (PPI) in a HIV prevention programme that is embedded within a population-based longitudinal HIV incidence cohort of ~20,000, 16-29-year olds in rural KwaZulu-Natal to answer:Will risk-differentiated and tailored biosocial interventions developed with, and delivered by young people reduce transmissible HIV in 16-30-year olds? Are interventions cost-effective? Is it feasible to deliver interventions with fidelity? Background: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) through universal test and treat and HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) can substantially reduce HIV-related mortality, morbidity and incidence. However, innovation in HIV prevention has outpaced the ability to implement and thus HIV remains the single largest health problem in South Africa. Effective Individual-level prevention have not translated into population-level impact because this requires high coverage among adolescents and youth who are hard to engage.Aims and objectives: The goal of my fellowship is to stem the HIV epidemic and it's negative impact on young people in SA through effective implementation of advances in HIV prevention. Specific aim one: I will use community based participatory research to optimise risk-differentiated and tailored biosocial HIV prevention for young people in rural KZN Optimise the risk-differentiation (where more vulnerable and at risk individuals receive more support), and the psychosocial components of the intervention delivered by the peer navigators Establish safe clinical pathways to support decentralised PrEP, ART, and sexual health selfcare Use routine service use data to identify groups that need increased supportSpecific aims two: I will use a 4X2 factorial randomised controlled trial and process evaluation to evaluate the effectiveness and scalability of risk-differentiated and tailored biosocial HIV prevention delivered by peers to reduce the prevalence of sexually transmissible HIV among 16-30-year-old men and women Evaluate the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of the risk-differentiated and tailored biosocial HIV prevention delivered by peers to reduce the prevalence of transmissible HIV Conduct a process evaluation of the acceptability, feasibility, and equitable reach of each component of the interventionTimelines:The study will be in phases.Phase one (0-18 months):I will build on ongoing funded formative work to optimise the intervention and refine the theory of change. Phase two (18-48 months): I will use the unique and time-limited opportunity of a Wellcome funded multidisciplinary population research infrastructure and my PrEP implementation programme to test the effectiveness of the optimised intervention in a trial of n=3000 young people aged 16-30.Phase three (48-60 months): I will conduct the analysis and dissemination.Output: Scalable, cost-effective interventions to reduce the negative impact of HIV on youth in South Africa, that is aligned with National and Provincial plans. Robust and sustainable infrastructure and framework for participatory engagement and active PPI for young people to lead on innovations in delivery and new product introductions in rural KZN. A platform to evaluate the population-level effectiveness of longer acting PrEP and other interventions in the pipeline. Build local capacity to conduct innovative adaptive trials and implementation experiments through the KZN clinical trials consortium.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Understanding the causes and clinical implications of blood pressure decline in older age
Abstract: Background Blood pressure(BP) tends to increase through middle into older age, and treating hypertension reduces cardiovascular outcomes and mortality. However, BP in late life is influenced by co-morbidities and changes in physiological functioning, affecting maintenance of homeostasis. BP declines for over 10 years prior to death in approximately two thirds aged over 60 and in older patients with multimorbidity and frailty, lower systolic BPs (eg. Currently we do not understand the causes and mechanisms of longitudinal BP declines, or associations with cardiac function or co-morbidity. Early recognition of BP declines could aid early detection of serious conditions, such as specific cancers or heart failure. I hypothesise that longitudinal BP declines towards hypotensive BPs in previously hypertensive older individuals represent a 'post-hypertension syndrome', which may indicate higher risk of adverse events with continued antihypertensives. Overall Aim To identify the causes, mechanisms and outcomes of longitudinal BP declines in older age and test whether longitudinal BP data could aid early detection of conditions such as heart failure, cancer or dementia or identify those at increased risk of adverse outcomes. Timeline 80% FTE; 75 months Methods DataBuilding on extensive experience, analysis will be performed using world-leading data from UK Biobank (UKB) and Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD), with secondary analysis of the OPTiMISE deprescribing trial. This fellowship is equivalent to 5 years full time, supported by expert mentors and collaborators, with a tailored training plan. UKB includes over 500,000 participants combining detailed baseline measures, genotypes and linked primary and secondary care electronic records, over 12 years of follow-up and MRI in 100,000 of the cohort. CPRD provides up to 20 years of large-scale population representative primary and secondary care data on over 2 million aged over 60. WP1 Model longitudinal BP trajectories in UK Biobank and CPRD and test associations with diagnoses, physiological and imaging measures, analysing conventional and genetic modifiers of risks for dementia, cancer, cardiovascular disease and frailty, as separate studies. Genetics can establish which risk factors and pathways are causally implicated in falling BP. WP2 Test associations between longitudinal BP trajectory and cardiovascular and adverse outcomes, specifically in older people with systolic BP WP3 Test whether longitudinal BP trajectory prior to study baseline modifies the association between antihypertensive prescribing and adverse outcomes, including falls in 1)the OPTiMISE RCT 2) the STRATIFY: antihypertensives study WP4 Test the association between longitudinal BP trajectory and PH, and PH and conventional and genetic cardiovascular modifiers to understand potential risk factors and overlap in phenotype. Collaborative studies (grant bids submitted to NIHR) to test the feasibility and validity of postural BP measurement. This research will provide the first estimates of the mechanisms, causes and outcomes of longitudinal BP decline in older adults. Results will be widely disseminated, including 8 detailed papers. This work could impact on patient safety and inform future targeted trials towards personalised antihypertensive prescribing.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Housing and health: improving understanding of how energy-inefficient housing affects health through novel data linkages with large UK health datasets and economic modelling
Abstract: Background Cold homes are a major public health problem, contributing to a high proportion of the health and mortality impacts of cold weather. People who are vulnerable (e.g. due to age or disability) also tend to spend more time at home. Cold and hard-to-heat homes are an important driver of socioeconomic health inequalities, but their full impact on the development of chronic conditions over many years remains poorly understood and potentially underestimated. Approach My proposed programme of research aims to directly address these gaps, using a range of methods, in order to inform better decision-making and improve public health. This will involve the following work programmes: WP1. A review of the evidence for associations between long-term exposure to energy inefficient or uninsulated homes and/or cold indoor temperatures and chronic health problems, focusing on key health risk factors and new onset or diagnosis of common chronic diseases (cardio and cerebro-vascular disease, asthma and COPD, obesity, diabetes, anxiety, depression, dementia). This review will include epidemiological studies with ≥1 year follow-up, from countries with temperate or continental climates. WP2. A: Anonymised data linkage of the UK Biobank and SAIL Databank to household-level Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) energy efficiency data, which exist for over half of UK homes. These novel linkages will in turn enable detailed investigation of the associations between housing energy inefficiency (a key predictor of both cold indoor temperatures and fuel poverty) and health, as well as enhancing both resources for future research. B: Using linked UK Biobank data, I plan to analyse associations of home energy efficiency with risk factors such as blood pressure, cholesterol levels and BMI. I will then investigate longitudinal associations between exposure to energy inefficient housing and new diagnoses of a range of chronic health conditions. C: Using linked SAIL data, I plan to investigate longitudinal associations between housing energy efficiency and severe health outcomes such as heart attacks, strokes, COPD and asthma exacerbations, and on mortality, using causal inference approaches. WP3. Updating the Health module of the HIDEEM (Health Impact of Domestic Energy Efficiency Measures) model, using WP1 and WP2 findings, which informs national policy and spending decisions. Patient and Public Involvement An NIHR Patient Involvement Fund supported me to involve 12 people with lived experience of difficult-to-heat homes in developing this proposal, and they have shaped it in several ways, including the range of outcomes and use of a new health dataset. My fellowship plans have PPI woven throughout, including through PPI panels who will meet every 3-4 months, and regular involvement of two lay advisors. This will shape each project's methods, and how findings are interpreted and communicated. Dissemination, engagement and impact I have planned a series of dissemination and engagement activities involving policy-makers, charities, advocacy groups and members of the public, and will develop summaries tailored policy briefs, blogs and infographics. This will facilitate translation of the findings into public health benefits, by influencing housing policy and expenditure decisions, minimum housing quality standards, and informing local health-focused warmer housing schemes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Smoking cessation for pregnant women with moderate to severe mental illness: Intervention adaptation and feasibility trial
Abstract: Background Smoking is the leading preventable cause of fetal and childhood morbidity and mortality and the largest cause of health inequality in the UK. Pregnant women with mental illness are more likely to smoke throughout pregnancy than those without mental illness. Birmingham data indicates women with moderate to severe mental illness (MSMI) are three to four times more likely to be smoking at booking and at birth than women without mental illness. There is no known research exploring how best to support pregnant women with MSMI to stop smoking. This research will address this evidence gap. AimsThe overarching aim is to (i) identify and describe components of smoking cessation interventions showing promise or effectiveness in pregnancy ii) explore perceived women's, health professionals' and organisational influences on smoking behaviour of pregnant women with MSMI (iii) co-design and adapt an existing smoking cessation intervention to be tailored for pregnant women with MSMI and (iv) test its feasibility and acceptability for pregnant women with MSMI. Plan of investigation WP1 Intervention Development (Months 0-31) WP1.1 A scoping review will identify and describe intervention components showing promise or effectiveness in supporting pregnant women/people with mental illness in smoking behaviour change. Identification of intervention components will inform the qualitative interview guide for WP1.2 and intervention adaptation in WP1.3. WP1.2 Qualitative interviews guided by the Theoretical Domains Framework will explore influences on smoking behaviour according to pregnant smokers with MSMI and healthcare professionals. Data will be analysed deductively and inductively using the Framework Method. Findings will be mapped on the Capability, Opportunity and Motivation - Behaviour Model which will identify and prioritise behavioural influences which the smoking cessation intervention can target.WP1.3 Co-design workshops with key stakeholders will be used to adapt the content and delivery of an existing smoking cessation intervention for pregnant women with MSMI. Data from WP1.1 and 1.2 will guide discussions on existing interventions in relation to smoking cessation influences. WP2 Feasibility trial (months 32-55) A feasibility trial will determine acceptability and feasibility of the smoking cessation intervention for pregnant women with MSMI and randomised controlled trial (RCT) procedures. WP3 Grant writing (months 56-60) A protocol and grant application will be developed for a definitive RCT. Anticipated impact and dissemination This research will deliver new knowledge, addressing key evidence gaps for a high risk group of women: A new evidence and theory-based, co-produced smoking cessation intervention for pregnant smokers with MSMI will be developed and tested for feasibility and acceptability in a group of women who suffer long term health inequalities. Barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation for pregnant women with MSMI will be identified and key stakeholders brought together to define and analyse research inputs, impacts and outputs and develop the full RCT. The intervention should directly benefit pregnant women with MSMI and their babies resulting in reduced risk of stillbirth, miscarriage, premature birth, poor health in infancy and improved maternal mental health.Findings will be disseminated through publications/reports, press releases, webinars, social media, presentations and workshops.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Funding_Stream: NIHR Population Health Career Scientist Award
Contractor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Improving existing early years services to reduce inequalities in child health and development
Abstract: Research Question How can we make better use of existing early years services to reduce inequalities in childrens' early years outcomes? Background What happens in the early years influences children's health, wellbeing and opportunities for the rest of their life. Socially disadvantaged children have far worse early outcomes compared to their peers. By age 5 children from deprived communities and some ethnic minorities are far more likely to be overweight and have worse developmental outcomes, making them less ready to learn at school. Whilst the causes of these inequalities are well understood, including socio-economic, structural and environmental causes, evidence-based interventions to reduce these inequalities are scarce. Families in England are offered a combination of early years services (e.g. health visiting, nursery and parenting programmes) designed to prevent negative outcomes. However not all families access all services, and the inequalities in outcomes demonstrate that they are not working effectively for disadvantaged children. Aims and Objectives The aim of this programme is to identify how to make better use of existing early years services to reduce inequalities in children's outcomes. I will investigate how to ensure equitable access to services and which combination(s) of early years services reduce inequalities in child outcomes. Methods This research will be undertaken in the young, socially deprived and ethnically diverse inner-city areas of Bradford. The methods have been designed with Local Authority stakeholders and parents and take an assets-based mixed-methods approach. The Born in Bradford's Better Start (BiBBS) interventional cohort (current n=4000) includes information on early years services access, dosage, families' socio-economic circumstances and child outcomes. Multiple regression analyses will examine the cumulative and interactive effects of exposure to, and dosage of, early years services on child outcomes. Qualitative interviews with families will identify their perspectives on the barriers and facilitators to accessing services, and to good child development. Co-production with service providers and families will use these findings to develop adaptations to existing services to improve access, and to identify combinations of services that reduce inequalities in children's outcomes. Timelines for Delivery This is a four year project that combines delivery of the above objectives with in-depth experiential learning and training. Anticipated impact and dissemination This research will reduce inequalities in child outcomes through improved effectiveness of early years services for disadvantaged families. Co-production of adaptations to existing services ensures that they will be acceptable to families, feasible for delivery and based on evidence, and will, therefore be immediately implementable in Bradford Local Authority and translatable to other local authorities nationally. A knowledge translation group will ensure that the research considers key policy context so that the findings resonate with practice. This group will develop a dissemination strategy to ensure that the findings are shared successfully to local and national service providers and policy makers. Communication strategies will be used to share findings with the community in a concise, meaningful and empowering way, using appropriate communication channels.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare public health and preventing premature mortality
Contractor: North Tees and Hartlepool NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Understanding and addressing inequalities in access to palliative care for those with lung disease; does the inverse care law apply? (LungPal-Equity study)
Abstract: Background 'Health inequalities' are differences in health between people in different groups in society. People in lower socio-economic groups experience worse health, but despite having higher healthcare needs, they are paradoxically less likely to receive care (the 'Inverse care law'). Palliative care supports people with life-limiting illness; ameliorating symptoms and empowering them to plan for the future (e.g., avoiding hospital admissions at end-of-life). Palliative care is both a human and legal right; yet, generally, those living in deprived areas are less likely to receive it. Lung diseases (e.g., lung cancer and COPD) are more common in deprived areas; they cause particularly burdensome symptoms proven to benefit from palliative care. This study will examine inequalities in access to palliative care, using lung disease as an exemplar, to identify solutions that can be implemented into policy and practice. Aim: To identify if, and to what extent, inequalities exist in accessing palliative care for those with lung disease and (if present), understand the underlying reasons and potential solutions. Objectives: To identify and synthesise evidence on the association between socio-economic status and access to palliative care for those with lung disease, including evidence of barriers and facilitating factors. To analyse and quantify the association between area-level deprivation and access to end-of-life care for those with lung disease. To explore perspectives of bereaved relatives and healthcare professionals, including barriers and solutions to accessing palliative care. To develop a framework to understand barriers contributing to inequalities in accessing palliative care and develop key practical recommendations to overcome them. Methods: Includes 4 work-packages (WP) with PPI imbedded within each, WP1: Mixed-method systematic review of published (and available unpublished) research. Review question: 'Do those with lung disease face inequalities in accessing palliative care based on socio-economic status (individual and area-level) and what are contributing barriers and facilitators? WP2- Secondary analysis of population-level data to identify if there is variation between healthcare utilisation at end-of-life (including place of death) for those with lung disease according to area-level deprivation. WP3: Qualitative semi-structured interviews: post-bereavement interviews with relatives (approx. 30) and healthcare professionals (approx. 15) on barriers and potential solutions to improving access to palliative care. WP4: Synthesis of findings from WP1-3. Building a framework to understand barriers and develop a 'tool-kit' of recommendations to address inequalities in access, to implement change. Timeline (4 years 0.75WTE)- See Gantt chart for details Preparation: Convening PPI group and completion of Data Access Request Service (DARS) application. Year 1- Complete systematic review (WP1). Identify key themes to 'follow the thread' into WP2. Year 2- Data collection and analysis (WP2). Obtain ethics for interviews. Year 3- Qualitative interviews and analysis (WP3) Year 4- Triangulation and synthesis of findings from WP1-3, write framework and develop tool-kit (WP4), complete thesis. Dissemination/Impact: Wide dissemination of findings is essential to raise awareness of inequalities in access to palliative care and share practical recommendations to influence policy and practice, to 'Level-up' care. Findings will be disseminated after each WP; including patient/carer groups, publication in high-impact journals, presentation at national conferences.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Mitigating health inequalities in Respiratory Syncytial Virus: an OpenSAFELY analysis of RSV burden and impact of potential maternal vaccine programmes
Abstract: Research question What disparities exist in the burden of Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV), and what maternal vaccination strategies could be adopted to mitigate risk factors underlying these disparities? Background RSV is a common virus causing coughs and colds, usually in the winter. RSV-related illnesses generate approximately 450,000 GP appointments, 400,000 prescriptions and 30,000 hospitalisations in children and adolescents. Evidence suggests the burden of RSV is unevenly distributed in the UK. However, such inequalities have not been comprehensively evaluated in large, representative cohorts. A maternal RSV vaccine to prevent severe outcomes from infection in infants has recently shown efficacy in phase III trials and has been submitted for licensure in the UK, it may be recommended by JCVI. However, uptake of existing recommended vaccines in pregnancy (pertussis and influenza) varies, and there is lower uptake among socioeconomically-deprived and ethnic minority groups. Therefore, any unequal burden of RSV, coupled with the potential unequal distribution of the intervention, risks exacerbating possible health inequalities. Determining the magnitude of health inequalities in RSV using representative data is critically important. This project will allow the evaluation of any inequalities and propose mitigations. Aims and objectives All analyses will use OpenSAFELY, a secure research platform with 95% coverage of the England population developed in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. My objectives are to: Quantify socioeconomic and ethnic health disparities in RSV burden Uncover the relative contributions of ethnicity, socioeconomic status and household size/composition toward the risk of RSV Evaluate potential maternal vaccination strategies and estimate the effect on existing RSV inequalities, and identify the best strategy to reduce the burden on minority groups Methods Objective 1: calculate rates of RSV infection/bronchiolitis in different risk groups and analyse differences in rates using survival analysis Objective 2: use causal diagrams and mediation analysis techniques to determine the underlying causal pathways between the exposures (ethnicity, socioeconomic status and household size/composition and the outcomes (RSV infection, bronchiolitis) Objective 3: use transmission models to ascertain the impact of potential maternal vaccination programmes on disparities identified, using the maternal pertussis vaccine uptake as an estimate for uptake of a potential maternal RSV vaccine Timelines for delivery 10/2023 - ethical approval 10/2024 - upgrading seminar 11/2024 - publication 1: descriptive epidemiology 08/2025 - publication 2: causal analysis 05/2026 - publication 3: vaccination modelling 08/2026 - thesis submission Anticipated impact and dissemination This research has the potential to impact minority groups who are at increased risk of poor health outcomes due to RSV by providing evidence of how disparities can be reduced through specific interventions. In addition, by reducing inequalities this research in turn can reduce the overall burden of RSV on the NHS. Papers will be published open access in peer-reviewed publications. Plain English summaries of my results which can be shared on social media and relevant LSHTM web pages. I will present my research findings at academic conferences, as well as to communities with an interest in health equity and a PPIE (Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement) Advisory Panel I have convened.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Funding_Stream: NIHR Population Health Career Scientist Award
Award_Title: Tackling health inequalities through green/blue infrastructure
Abstract: Research question What are the population-scale health inequalities impacts of applying a 'proportionate universalism' approach to green/blue infrastructure policy and management scenarios? Background Green/blue infrastructure - natural features including parks, street trees and waterways - can impact population health positively through multiple use-dependent (e.g. physical activity, stress recovery) and use-independent (e.g. mitigating excess urban heat) pathways. The evidence base on these relationships has been growing, and while lacking robustness in some areas, has started to inform policies, such as the recent Green Infrastructure Standards for England. There is also evidence linking inequalities in the socio-spatial distribution of green/blue infrastructure and health inequalities; firstly that green/blue infrastructure may actually serve to ameliorate health inequalities to some extent, but secondly that there are significant social inequalities in the distribution of green/blue infrastructure. Aim The aim of the research is to evaluate how green/blue infrastructure interventions might tackle health inequalities at population scale. It will examine the socio-spatial distribution of green/blue infrastructure and how related policy and intervention on planning, managing and investing in this infrastructure can impact positively on health inequalities, specifically through application of a 'proportionate universalism' approach (universal intervention, but with a degree of targeting proportionate to need). Methods Work Package (WP) 1 will develop Causal Loop Diagrams, visual representations of our understanding of the complex relationships between different facets of green/blue infrastructure and socio-spatial health inequalities. These will be co-produced based on rapid evidence review combined with working with collaborators from public health and environment authorities and with public involvement. WP1 will also work with collaborators and public partners to prioritise potential policies and interventions to be evaluated. WP2 will link and analyse large-scale spatial data (such as Census, population health and green space mapping) along with survey data on engagement with natural environments. It will explore empirically the relationships theorised in WP1, at national scale and for specific local authority area studies, and with reference to prioritised interventions. WP3 will then use ecosystem service and spatial microsimulation modelling approaches to evaluate the potential population-scale health inequalities impacts of green/blue infrastructure policy and intervention scenarios. Timelines A five-year fellowship programme, with the three Work Packages building on each other sequentially. Anticipated impact and dissemination The research will be used to influence tools and policies (such as Local Plans) to try to ensure that green/blue infrastructure interventions are designed to mitigate, rather than exacerbate, health inequalities. Dissemination via conferences and peer-reviewed journals will be augmented by translation through blog posts, short films, public engagement events, and co-organised dissemination events with the Town and Country Planning Association (a key collaborator with an established network of relevant planning, health and green infrastructure professionals). Translational materials will be co-produced with collaborators, including local and national environment and public health authorities, and with public involvement. We will offer a 'researcher in residence' programme to deliver bespoke, locally-focussed research outputs directly with and for collaborator organisations.
