Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: What are the factors that influence older adults’ engagement in exercise and physical activity? An evidence synthesis of qualitative research and mapping of quantitative reviews
Abstract: Background: Physical activity has well-established benefits for health and well-being. Successful achievement of activity level targets, not well met at any age, declines as people get older. With an ageing population, successfully addressing this lack is increasingly urgent. Qualitative research about older people s experiences and preferences of engagement in physical activity has been conducted across disparate academic disciplines but communication of findings between disciplines is often poor. Similarly, a number of systematic reviews about the effectiveness of interventions to improve physical activity levels have been undertaken, but have not been brought together to give a comprehensive picture of what is known about the field. We will bring this evidence together using methods of systematic review and synthesis to produce a comprehensive picture of the evidence base. Aims: To understand people s experiences and preferences about physical activity and exercise as they get older (aged 50+). We also want to understand how well the tested interventions reflect these interests and concerns of older people, what limitations and uncertainties there are in the evidence base, and what factors commissioners and providers should consider when designing and implementing interventions to support physical activity and to address health inequalities in this population. Research questions: 1) What are people s experiences and preferences in relation to exercise and physical activity as they get older (aged 50+)? 2) What factors help older people to be physically active? 3) What factors prevent older people from being physically active? 4) What is known about the effectiveness of interventions to encourage older people (aged 50+) to be physically active and what are the impacts on physical and mental health and well-being? 5) Are there groups of older people for whom these interventions work better or less well? 6) What gaps and limitations are there in this information? 7) How well do the evaluated interventions map onto the preferences and problems described by older people themselves? 8) What could be done to enhance the ability of all older people to become more physically active, including those who are often marginalised? Plan of investigation: 1) Systematic review and evidence synthesis of qualitative research among older people on their preferences and experiences related to being physically active. 2) Systematic review and mapping of existing systematic reviews about the effectiveness of exercise/physical activity interventions among those aged 50+. 3) Overarching synthesis of 1)&2) to see how well the studied interventions reflect the experiences and preferences of older people and to describe gaps and limitations in this evidence base. By mapping the nature of interventions studied, and what is known about which activities are successful in which populations, we will also identify gaps and limitations in existing research. Methods: Methods will adhere to those described by the Centre for Reviews and Dissemination guidance for systematic reviews. A detailed protocol will be registered with PROSPERO. Potential benefits to patients and the NHS: Qualitative research in this area is dispersed, and has not previously been brought together in a comprehensive synthesis. Through synthesising this evidence, we will collate and emphasise older people s experiences. The map of existing quantitative reviews will allow us to see how well these reflect the concerns of older people, and to identify gaps and limitations in previously studied interventions. We will use the reviews to make recommendations so that future projects can be made more relevant to real life issues identified by older people. It is hoped that better tailored interventions will be more effective, increasing the ability and willingness of older people to be physically active and leading to improved health and well-being and reduced costs to the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: SKIP [Supporting Kids with diabetes In Physical activity]: feasibility of an online multimedia intervention to promote physical activity in children with type 1 diabetes (T1DM)
Abstract: Background: Low levels of physical activity are common in children with type 1 diabetes (T1DM). This has negative implications for diabetes control, physical and psychological health across the lifecourse, and is costly to the NHS. Children, parents and healthcare professionals hold positive attitudes towards physical activity promotion, but highlight barriers to being active which included low self-efficacy (or confidence) for exercise and fear of hyperglycaemia. Children with T1DM are comfortable with and prefer electronic media and parents are receptive to the use of technology as part of diabetes management. However, online resources are not currently used as part of routine care. Clinicians support the introduction of technology-based resources into clinical care, but have identified a lack of evidence-based resources which are condition and age-appropriate. We have developed an online multimedia intervention (SKIP) to promote physical activity in children aged 9-12 with T1DM, which is underpinned by psychological behaviour change theory and best available evidence. We hypothesise that SKIP will increase physical activity through building self-efficacy for exercise and reducing fear of hyperglycaemia. Aim: The main aim of this study is to establish the feasibility of doing a definitive trial to investigate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of SKIP. The definitive trial will be deemed feasible if we can demonstrate that we can successfully identify and recruit patients with T1DM and the proposed study design is deemed acceptable by patients, parents and clinicians. Our objectives include: Assessing the feasibility and acceptability of recruitment strategies, randomisation, methods of data collection and outcome measures to be used in the future trial, Determining rates of adherence and compliance, study retention and drop-out (with reasons) Assess acceptability of SKIP to children, parents and health care professionals Finalise the design of a future randomised controlled trial including revision of SKIP and assessment of long-term delivery costs. Plan of investigation: The procedure is divided into three parts: [1] randomised feasibility study; SKIP consists of education and interactive elements aimed at improving knowledge of exercise and T1DM, and a mechanism for recording and monitoring blood glucose and physical activity. Children will receive wrist-worn motion sensors to support goal setting and monitoring. We will recruit 50 child/parent dyads from two hospital sites over 10 months. 25 will receive SKIP, 25 will receive usual care only. Objective monitoring data will be collected to determine intervention fidelity, participant engagement with the intervention and the research study. We will test collection of measures at baseline, 8 weeks and 6 months. This will include clinical indicators of diabetes control, anthropometric, behavioural, and psychological variables, communication between health care teams, patients and families, and economic outcomes; [2] qualitative evaluation; we will invite SKIP participants (children and parents) and key healthcare professionals involved in their care to participate in qualitative interviews to give feedback and evaluation of intervention content and delivery, and research processes; [3] Trial development; we will finalise SKIP specification and costs, and research procedures, methods and measures based on feasibility and acceptability testing. We will develop and test measures for assessing healthcare communication and economic outcomes in the main trial. Potential benefits to patients/NHS: Improved self-efficacy for exercise and reduced fear of hypoglycaemia will lead to increased physical activity in childhood which can be sustained across the lifecourse. This will lead to better diabetes control. Supporting clinical staff in promoting physical activity may improve communication between healthcare teams, children and their families. Bet

Contractor: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust
Award_Title: Female Aneurysm screening STudy - FAST
Abstract: BACKGROUND: There is an urgent need to determine if the current policy of excluding women from abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) screening is justified or not. AAA rupture causes over 3,000 deaths per annum in England and Wales2. Even though AAA prevalence in women is lower than in men, the relative burden of disease in women is higher due to increased risks of both mortality and morbidity due to AAA rupture, and after surgery to prevent rupture, in females3-6. AAA rupture can be prevented by early detection and monitoring through screening and surveillance, and surgical repair if the AAA enlarges to a size when the risk of rupture outweighs the risk of surgery7-10. Since 2013 the NHS has been offering AAA screening to all men in the year of their 65th birthday. AAA screening in men has been shown to be cost-effective and reduce AAA-mortality11, 12. Women are not included in the NHS AAA Screening Programme, as there is currently no evidence that screening women is effective13. Women may be unfairly disadvantaged by this policy however. In 2013, 31.7% of all deaths due to ruptured AAA were in females2. Between 2000 and 2009, AAA-death rates fell by 5.6% per year in men but only 4.1% in women14. AAA in women are 4-times more likely to rupture than in men7. There is therefore a need to re-examine the screening of women for AAA. The NIHR has directly commissioned an HTA project (HTA 14/179/01) to develop a statistical model of AAA screening effectiveness in women but key missing inputs for this model are screening attendance rates and a contemporaneous estimate of AAA prevalence in women. If these could be provided it is likely that a national policy recommendation regarding AAA screening in women could be made, possibly without recourse to an expensive large-scale randomized clinical trial. AIMS: The primary aims of this study are to assess the feasibility of using routinely collected primary care data to identify women at high-risk of AAA by inviting these women for AAA screening, determine attendance rates, and assess the prevalence of AAA in these women. PLAN OF INVESTIGATION: We will use locally available primary care data to select a cohort of women at high risk of AAA to invite for AAA screening. We have analysed local general practice databases and have established that the risk factors of interest (coronary heart disease, current smoking and ex-smoking) are recorded on an individual patient basis and that there are adequate numbers of women with these risk factors in the proposed study area. We will invite women with these risk factors for AAA for screening and determine the uptake of AAA screening in those invited. We will screen 6612 women for AAA which will enable an accurate estimate of AAA prevalence such that we can be 99% confident that the true population prevalence in this high-risk group is above the prevalence threshold for screening cost-effectiveness of 0.35%. BENEFITS: Patient benefits Reduce the mortality and morbidity caused by AAA in women through the delivery of AAA screening, an intervention that is currently unavailable to women in the NHS. Establish female specific requirements for the provision of information before, during and after participation in screening. NHS benefits Reduce the number of admissions with ruptured AAAs in women (high cost episodes) and AAA related deaths in women. Maximise the cost-efficiency of future screening strategies for AAA by identifying a population at high risk. Establish a mechanism for the identification of women at high risk of AAA that is relevant to the NHS and can be instituted within current NHS informatics infrastructure.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Preventing Post Traumatic Stress Disorder : the Stress and Wellbeing after Childbirth Study (STRAWB)
Abstract: Background Post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after childbirth is major cause of psychological distress postnatally, with 3% of women suffering at full diagnostic levels and 5-9% when sub-diagnostic levels (partial PTSD) are included. It adversely affects women s functioning at a critical time for family relationship development. Women with PTSD experience intrusions, repeatedly reliving the traumatic event with images, thoughts and feelings as if back in the original situation. They try to avoid situations or people that may trigger intrusions thereby restricting their life. Relationships, such as with the partner, are adversely affected as the woman feels irritable and constantly under threat. The developing mother-infant relationship can be compromised with negative effects on the infant s emotional and cognitive development. Experiencing an event as traumatic does not inevitably lead to PTSD. Intrusive experiences can be normal early responses to traumatic events. Where women view these intrusive responses as signs of illness or failure to cope and they attempt to avoid these responses this contributes to traumatic memories not being processed in a normal way. It is the unprocessed memories that lead to the flashbacks and nightmares that are characteristic of PTSD. There is therefore potential to prevent the development of PTSD. We have developed and feasibility tested the following through a one year funded study(RCF 2012-13 07): 1) A simple screening tool for use by community midwives to identify women who have experienced birth as traumatic. 2) Self help material derived from the theoretical mechanisms about how PTSD develops. 3) A brief training programme to enable midwives to implement both screening and provision of self help material. The self help material incorporates: 1) Simple explanations as to why women may experience early distressing responses to normalize these responses and reduce their negative evaluation. 2) Explanation why it is important not to block unpleasant images and thoughts and just allow them to be there without either distracting or dwelling on them with simple guided exercises to achieve this. 3) Explanation of how discussion in a supported context helps memory processing and provides an exercise to identify a suitable person, time and place with whom to do this. 4) An exercise using implementation intentions (evidence-based ways of translating plans into actions). This aims to help women translate their new understandings into actions. Aim To assess whether the introduction of a routine programme of identification of women who have experienced their childbirth as traumatic, and the provision of self help material to prevent PTSD improves outcomes when compared to usual care. If this is confirmed what is the cost per case prevented? Research Plan 2640 women will be screened early postnatally (between 7 and 28 days) by community midwives to assess whether they experienced their birth as traumatic. Data from our external pilot work suggests 25% will screen positive. These women will be randomised, 330 per arm, to receive the self help material or usual care. Women will be followed up with the gold standard assessment for PTSD which will be completed by phone at 6-8 weeks postnatally. Data will be analysed using standard summary statistics and hypothesis tests. A cost per PTSD case prevented analysis will be completed. Benefits to Patients and NHS This project has the potential to provide a simple system to reduce the incidence of full and partial PTSD after childbirth that can be readily incorporated into the current care pathway. This will benefit the mental health of women and the quality of relationships with partner and infant. PTSD once established is chronic and treatment is expensive. The current work if successful can substantially reduce NHS care costs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: REFLECT - Recovery Following Intensive Care Treatment
Abstract: Background: In 2012-13, 9,270 (8.6%) of the 108,261 patients discharged from Intensive Care Units (ICUs) in England and Wales died without leaving hospital (1). This mortality rate is higher than hospitalised groups considered to be at high risk (2–4) and is over five times the annual UK road accident death rate (5). Most of these patients were discharged from ICU with an expectation of survival (6 and ICNARC data). Local audit confirms that around 75% of patients who died in hospital after ICU discharge had aspects of their care which, if improved, may have increased survival. A sequence of national reports (9–14) suggest that changes in care in ward environments could lead to outcome improvements in critically ill patients. Aim: To develop a multi-faceted intervention to reduce in-hospital mortality rates in patients discharged from intensive care. Objectives To identify aspects of care to improve To prioritise aspects of care to be improved To inform the development of the intervention To finalise the intervention. Setting: Three hospitals representing three ICU types: district general, elective surgical, general medico-surgical. Investigation plan: STAGE ONE: Defining areas for improvement Areas will be identified using: interviews focus groups case reviews Interviews will be conducted with patients, relatives and staff to allow emerging themes to be explored across groups. Interviews will use a topic guide, based on completed work and input from patient representatives. We estimate data saturation will occur after ~20 interviews with patients and relatives and 20-30 staff interviews. Focus group topic guides will be developed from interview themes and completed work to encourage reflection on interview findings and allow new issues to arise. 3-4 focus groups will be required. Interviews and focus groups will be transcribed. A modified grounded theory approach will be used to identify emerging themes (65,66). Preliminary coding will be refined using the method of constant comparison (65) to produce a report for each theme. These reports will be analysed with a second researcher (67). Any differences in interpretation or emphasis will be resolved. Retrospective Case Record Review We will use established methods to review the case records of patients interviewed in this project (58,62). We will triangulate issues identified by patients and relatives with those found in the case records. We will compare the problems in care identified with those identified for non-survivors in previous work. STAGE 2 – Modelling the intervention Guided by a human factors researcher, a stakeholder group will prioritise areas for intervention from those identified in the interviews, focus groups and our earlier research. We will then undertake literature searches to check if these prioritised areas have been previously investigated in other hospitalised patient populations. To capture relevant successful methods for change implementation we will review: implementation methods used in the post-ICU hospitalised patient group implementation methods used in studies of our prioritised areas in other hospitalised patient populations Components of the multi-faceted intervention will be examined in a paper modelling exercise (68) to allow exploration of: interdependencies of components different implementation strategies challenges that may be encountered A stakeholder meeting will finalise the intervention. Our programme of work will develop and test a way of improving outcomes for hospitalised patients following intensive care. This project will identify which areas of care can be changed and determine how changes can be introduced. We will publish the outcomes of our qualitative work (interviews and focus groups) and our case review in relevant journals.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: Camden and Islington NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: HAVoC Study:Helping Aged Victims of Crime: determining the psychosocial effects of crime on older people & a pilot randomised controlled trial of a Victim Improvement Package versus Treatment As Usual
Abstract: BackgroundIncreased rates of psychological, physical morbidity and mortality are the damaging consequences of crime perpetrated on older people. Fear of crime is exacerbated and traumatised victims often become housebound. There are also significant economic costs. In the over 65s in North London over 5,000 serious crimes (2005-6) were reported. There is a statutory obligation to provide support to victims of crime through the police, Victim Support and Primary Care Trusts. NICE guidelines for people with significant anxiety, depression and Post Traumatic Stress Disorder recommend Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT), which has not been evaluated in this socially isolated, vulnerable group. The magnitude of and how best to manage this problem requires further research.AimsFollowing Medical Research Council criteria for the development of complex interventions we will use combined research methods on older victims of crime as follows: 1. Quantitative: to determine the prevalence of psychological disorder at 3 months and its effect using standardised measures.2. Qualitative: (a) To explore factors associated with psychological disorder at 3 months and whether these have changed post intervention (b) To examine the experience of receiving our new CBT informed Victim Improvement Package (VIP). We will determine any modifications required to optimize this intervention.3. We will test the feasibility of a pilot randomised controlled trial (RCT) of our Victim Improvement Package (VIP) against Treatment As Usual (TAU).Plan of InvestigationThis is a 2 year study. Victims of crime (n=640)-identified through Victim Support, the police, self and GP referral and neighbourhood teams-who are aged 65 years or over will be screened for significant psychological disorder at 3 months using the K6 questionnaire. Demographic factors will be recorded and a Structured Clinical Interview Diagnosis (SCID) made. Data will be collected to explore predictors of morbidity. Participants (n=40) will be recruited into a pilot RCT of VIP versus TAU. Main outcome: the WHODAS-II. Secondary outcomes: Beck Depression and Anxiety Inventories, Post Traumatic Stress Diagnostic Scale and economic (Client Services Receipt Inventory). Post intervention qualitative interviews in 10 out of 20 participants will inform the further development of the VIP.Potential ImpactActs of violence and theft leave physical and mental scars. Such trauma may produce social withdrawal and isolation. This practical study will be important to the individual, society, social services and the NHS. This study will:1. Raise the profile of the psychiatric impact of crime on older people.2. Provide quantitative and qualitative information about predictors of psychiatric morbidity to inform future interventions.3. Enable us to develop treatment, using recognised methods, to improve quality of life in a socially isolated and vulnerable group.4. Develop a treatment which should reduce the burden placed on carers.5. Generate information to apply for funding for a full scale RCT.6. Provide preliminary recommendations for management of older victims of crime.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Identifying the long-term needs of stroke survivors and developing an innovative model of care
Abstract: BackgroundStroke is a long term condition that can affect motor function, mood, speech, cognition, participation and quality of life. Clinical and service development research has focused on acute needs but stroke is increasingly recognised as a chronic condition. Current service arrangements fail to meet long term needs. [1, 2] Few interventions have aimed to address needs one year or more after stroke. To improve the well being, participation and health outcomes of long term stroke survivors, robust estimates of need are required. Need should also be defined with reference to stroke survivors’ and carers’ own experiences and views. AimsThe aim is to develop and pilot test a method of meeting long term needs of stroke survivors/carers, undertaking the following steps: 1. identify the long term needs (1-year plus) of stroke survivors using outcome data from a population sample;2. identify stroke survivors’ and carers' own perceptions of long term needs, strategies to meet these and identification of needs that remain unmet;3. identify community care providers’ views of long term needs after stroke and components of long term care;4. use findings from 1-3 to develop an innovative model of long term stroke care; 5. conduct a pilot study of the innovative model of care to assess feasibility and user acceptability, to finalise trial components and define a protocol for a definitive RCT.Plan of InvestigationWe will: 1. analyse South London Stroke Register data (1995-2006; 3277 cases) to investigate patterns of need and provision of care across physical, psychological and social domains;2. conduct qualitative interviews with up to 30 stroke survivors/carers at 1 year, 2, 3-5 and 6-11 years post stroke;3. conduct individual and group interviews with community based providers to identify their perceptions of long term need, service gaps and core components of a long term stroke service;4. conduct iterative group discussions with service providers, stroke survivors/carers, using these data to collaboratively develop an innovative model of long term care5. conduct a pilot study of the intervention to assess feasibility and user acceptability, and test outcome measures for a later RCT.Potential ImpactThe study will provide robust estimates of stroke survivors’ long term needs, informed by epidemiological data, patient/carer experiences and provider views. The components of what should be provided as long term stroke care will be clarified, as will the definition of ‘long term’ in relation to stroke. These results will assist commissioners and providers to plan and deliver services. We will use research findings to develop a novel strategy to meet long term needs of stroke survivors. This will be pilot tested. The study will inform national efforts to meet the long term needs of stroke survivors and carers, that we anticipate will be stimulated by the Department of Health’s stroke strategy.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Who cares? Improving the care pathway for heart failure in residential care.
Abstract: BackgroundHeart failure is a common, disabling and progressive illness. In severe heart failure annual mortality is about 50%; in mild cases 5 year mortality may approach 50%. Little is known about its prevalence in residential care, where acute care often takes precedence over prophylactic disease management. Accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment of heart failure can substantially improve quality of life and longevity. However, diagnosis is complicated by ‘silent’ disease development and atypical presentation in older people. Consequently, heart failure is often undiagnosed and mismanaged in this group resulting in important unmet clinical need.AimsTwo research phases will implement a linked pathway of care to promote earlier accurate diagnosis and effective management of heart failure (HF) in residential and care homes.To improve diagnosis, phase I will determine:• Levels of undiagnosed and misdiagnosed HF using portable echocardiography.• The optimal testing strategy from a range of tests, assessing test accuracy, acceptability and feasibility.• Signs, symptoms, functional capacity, quality of life and unmet clinical need.Translating improved diagnosis into improved care, phase II will compare a specialist domiciliary clinic and (routine) primary care. Phase II will determine:• The scope to optimise pharmacological therapy.• The effectiveness and cost effectiveness of care.• Health benefits and participant acceptability.Plan of InvestigationPhase I. A diagnostic study to quantify undiagnosed and misdiagnosed heart failure (HF) in residential and care homes in the north-east of England. All residents of participating homes age ? 65 years will be eligible. This phase will determine the impact and prevalence of HF as well as the optimal testing strategy. Patients with HF will be eligible for phase II.Phase II. An implementation trial will assess the scope for improved treatment. Participants with HF will be randomised to routine care or a specialist-led domiciliary clinic. This phase will assess changes in the optimal use of drug therapy and short term patient outcomes. Using implementation methods, the long term health benefits and cost-effectiveness (cost/QALY) of changes in care will be estimated.Potential ImpactThis study has considerable scope to reduce mortality, morbidity and improve quality-of-life in a vulnerable and under-researched population. Service delivery models for diagnosis (phase I) and management (phase II) will:• Describe health benefits and acceptability to patients of testing and treatment for heart failure.• Estimate the cost-effectiveness of improved diagnosis and management for policy makers.• Provide the NHS with an evidence-base to develop care pathway recommendations for implementation and audit.• Provide a rich description of the impact of heart failure upon those in residential and care homes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Southport and Ormskirk Hospital NHS Trust
Award_Title: A Randomised Control Trial of Extended Brief Interventions for alcohol-dependent patients in an acute care setting.
Abstract: BackgroundAlcohol dependency is an important public health problem in the UK. Most patients present to acute NHS Trusts, where they receive no specific treatment apart from pharmacological detoxification for alcohol withdrawal. Our recent systematic review (annex 4) showed that there is an urgent need for adequately powered RCTs in alcohol-dependent patients that utilize objective outcome measures and reproducible treatment modalities. In a cohort study, we have shown that an extended form of brief intervention (EBI), delivered by a nurse in an acute hospital setting, was effective in reducing measures of alcohol dependence, alcohol consumption and hospital length of stay. The effectiveness of EBI as a treatment modality in an acute hospital setting now needs to be tested in a RCT.AimsOverall aim: To determine whether EBI delivered in an acute hospital setting by an alcohol specialist nurse (ASN) is a clinically effective treatment for alcohol-dependent patients.Objectives: 1. Establish if EBI reduces alcohol consumption. 2. Establish if patients are satisfied with receiving EBI from a nurse in a hospital setting.3. Determine the cost effectiveness of using EBI in alcohol dependence. To achieve these objectives, we have assembled a multi-disciplinary team comprising nurses, physicians, health economist, statistician and qualitative researcher, with input from a patient group. The trial will be run in association with the Liverpool Clinical Trials Centre who will be responsible for randomisation, databases, monitoring and statistical analysis.Plan of InvestigationDesign: Randomised controlled trialSetting: Acute NHS Trust Patients: Consecutive alcohol-related attendances will be screened for alcohol dependence. Eligible patients who consent will be randomised to either the treatment arm or normal clinical care. Treatment: The EBI utilised by the ASN will follow the FRAMES approach. Four interventions (20 minutes duration each) will be delivered by an ASN within a twelve-week period. Measures will be recorded at recruitment,12 weeks and 6 months (Annex 4 S2 Fig 3). Outcome measures: 1. Alcohol Consumption (Quantity / Frequency measures)2. SADQ (Severity of Alcohol Dependence Questionnaire).Sample size: With 90% power at the 5% significance level, with an allowance for an estimated 50% drop out rate,130 patients will be recruited per group.Potential ImpactAlcohol dependence affects about 1 in 20 hospitalised patients– in most cases, they are given pharmacological detoxification, and when stable, discharged into primary care without further treatment or support. Thus the rate of relapse is high. Our cohort study showed that there is a potential to greatly improve the outcomes of alcohol dependent patients through EBI (Annex 4 Sec.3). If this form of treatment can be demonstrated to be clinically and cost effective in an acute hospital setting, it will provide a natural setting to treat these patients. The potential long term positive benefits are immense: reduction in alcohol consumption, hospital admissions and length of stay, together with an improvement in patient experience.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Leeds and York Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The prevalence and importance of unrecognised bipolar disorder among patients prescribed antidepressant medication in UK General Practice
Abstract: BackgroundDepression is a common problem presenting in primary care, often accompanied by anxiety. In that situation, it is typically thought of as having psychosocial origins and is treated without referral - typically with antidepressants and brief counselling. However, recent research from the USA suggests that 21- 26% of those who receive a diagnosis of depressive disorder in primary care actually have bipolar disorder. The studies have methodological problems, and the results may not apply to the UK. If they do, then we need to understand the implications; for example antidepressants alone may not be effective in the depressed phase of bipolar disorder, or they may worsen the course of bipolar disorder. A large number of patients may therefore receive ineffective or harmful treatment.AimsTo answer the following questions:[1] What is the prevalence of undiagnosed bipolar disorder among people being treated in primary care with antidepressants for depressive or anxiety disorder?[2] Do patients with undiagnosed bipolar disorder have more severe illnesses than people being treated for depressive or anxiety disorder who do not have undiagnosed bipolar disorder? [3]What is the accuracy of the Mood Disorder Questionnaire as a means of identifying bipolar disorder in UK primary care?Plan of InvestigationIn a cross-sectional study, we will identify 308 patients aged 16 and over, registered with one of five general practices in West Yorkshire and being prescribed antidepressant medication, excluding certain conditions. Participants will be asked to complete: a brief screening questionnaire for bipolar disorder, the Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ); a standardised psychiatric interview, the Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (SCAN); a Health Related Quality of Life measure (SF-36). Primary and, where relevant, secondary care records will be examined. Analysis will involve standard descriptive and inferential statistics. The accuracy of the screening questionnaire (MDQ) will be examined using the diagnostic interview as the validating criterion.Potential ImpactIf bipolar disorder is frequently misdiagnosed in primary care, and those misdiagnosed fare worse than those correctly diagnosed, this is an important problem. National guidelines should then be revised and recommend routine enquiry about a history of hypomanic or manic symptoms in those presenting with depressive or anxiety disorder. This study will try to find an easy way for GPs exclude bipolar disorder. The need for referral of a large number of patients to secondary care will have implications for the allocation of resources.Alternatively, the hypothesis of an important epidemic of unrecognised bipolar disorder in the UK may be refuted. This may reduce the likelihood of an increase in the referral of possible cases of bipolar disorder to secondary care.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A controlled evaluation of the health benefits of a participative community music programme for older people (Silver Song Clubs)
Abstract: BackgroundThe growth of the older population in the UK represents a considerable use of health and social care services (Department of Health, 2001). In recent years there has been growing interest in the potential value of the arts in addressing social issues (Clift, 2006; Clift and Vella-Burrows, 2003) and several research studies have focused on the impact of arts activities on health (for example Greaves and Farbus, 2006). A smaller number have found positive outcomes from participative group singing for older people (Houston et al., 1998, Cohen et al., 2006, 2007) though these do have design weaknesses. The Sidney De Haan Research Centre for Arts and Health has also recently found health benefits in a formative evaluation of a singing intervention for older people (Silver Song Clubs).AimsThere is a need now to develop a more controlled study to evaluate the health and economic effects of participation in group singing for older people.The general aims of this project are: • To assess the effectiveness for older people of active engagement in community music activities on measures of physical and mental health, social inclusion and the use of health and social care services• To evaluate the cost-effectiveness for older people of active engagement in community singing.Plan of InvestigationThe researchers will work with their third sector partner organisation and groups for older people in a cluster randomised controlled evaluation of a three-month Silver Song Club intervention. Ten groups of 24 individuals each will have baseline measures taken (SF-12, HADS, EQ-5D, Service utilisation). Five groups will undergo 12 weekly Silver Song Club sessions while five continue with usual activities. Measures will be repeated following the intervention and again a further 12 weeks later, along with semi-structured interviews with participants. An intention to treat analysis will be conducted on outcomes gathered at 6 months. Both effectiveness and cost-effectiveness will be evaluated using national guidelines (NICE 2004; NICE 2006).Potential ImpactOur previous research has indicated improvements to older people, through singing, in physical, psychological, social and cognitive wellbeing. Such findings, if replicated, and quantified, will potentially provide opportunities for health service users to choose to engage in an accessible means of health promotion. Further, a cost-effectiveness analysis will explore the potential for such activity to be mainstreamed through support from public sector health and social care services. This will assist planning decisions by service managers within these organizations, many of whom already support the idea and activities of the song clubs. For NHS practitioners, this will provide an alternative mode of health promotion for appropriate categories of patients.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: NHS West Yorkshire Integrated Care Board
Award_Title: Supporting Timely Engagement with Palliative Care (STEP)
Abstract: The aim of this project is to develop and evaluate an intervention to help patients with advanced cancer and their clinicians make informed decisions about palliative care. For patients with advanced cancer, palliative care received at least 3-6 months before death can improve symptoms, reduce hospital admissions, improve quality of life and enable patients to make choices about their care [1-6]. In a UK population of 3,950 patients with advanced cancer, the median duration of palliative care was only 36 days. We have demonstrated in our current study Time4PallCare that this short time is insufficient to maximise the benefits of palliative care. Initiating a conversation about palliative care is challenging for some health professionals and patients often have unmet information needs and misconceptions about the role of palliative care. Of 31 inpatient and outpatient oncology units across 20 hospitals within Yorkshire and Humber only three had information about palliative care available to patients with cancer. In the proposed project we will work closely with patients and clinicians to develop the STEP intervention. STEP will consist of a patient decision aid and clinician training module designed to facilitate a timely and informed conversation about palliative care. The intervention will be developed following the UK Medical Research Council (UKMRC) framework for developing complex interventions [20,21] and the International Patient Decision Aids (IPDAS) guideline [22,23]. The Ottawa Decision Support Framework (ODSF) is the conceptual framework which underpins the proposed study [24-25]. We will test the intervention within routine care in oncology outpatients clinics and GP practices to ensure it is acceptable and feasible. We will evaluate its impact on practice and develop an implementation toolkit to support its implementation and continued evaluation across the NHS. In July 2016 Leeds became a pilot site for Public Health England s Early Supportive Care Initiative [7]. The initiative aims to improve integration of palliative care within cancer services but does not provide mechanisms to overcome existing barriers which include clinicians feeling ill equipped to discuss palliative care and patient misconceptions about its role. This project is aligned with current government policy, is a national clinical priority and has the potential to be used within advanced cancer pathways across the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Feasibility and acceptability of TOOTHPICKS, a behaviour change intervention to support parent-dental practitioner communication about behaviour change to improve oral health in children
Abstract: Background Dental decay is an entirely preventable disease yet 1/4 children have caries on commencing school, and tooth extractions under anaesthetic are the primary reason for paediatric hospital admissions (costing over £36million p.a.). Dental decay severely impacts children s wellbeing and development, and is the greatest cause of disability amongst primary-school children. Routine dental consultations provide important opportunities for early intervention. However current guidance on supporting parents in preventative behaviours (e.g. regular tooth-brushing, reduced sugar consumption, attending check-ups) focuses on advice-giving and fails to capitalise on research which shows that 'identifying and planning for potential barriers' are key mechanisms for successful behaviour change. Evidence indicates dentists avoid conversations about health behaviours as they are uncertain how to help families establish good oral health-related habits without disrupting clinician-patient relationships, or use ineffective behaviour change techniques (information-giving alone or telling scare stories). We have developed an online course for dentists (TOOTHPICKS) that uses psychological theory to show how to have behaviour change conversations in ways patients find helpful. It increases health professionals motivation and skills to help adult patients with issues like smoking and tooth-brushing. Aims To date no intervention directed at improving behaviour change conversations with parents of children has been tested within primary dental care. We will address this gap by 1) refining the intervention for this context and then 2) conduct a feasibility cluster randomised controlled trial to train dental practitioners to use behaviour change techniques to discuss oral health with parents of children at risk of dental decay. Data from the trial and nested qualitative enquiry will answer questions around the processes/resources needed to conduct a future cost-effectiveness trial. Plan of investigation During Phase 1 we will adapt existing training materials to be specific for child-parent dental consultations. We will develop a patient-facing information help-card for use within practice. In Phase 2 we will conduct a cluster randomised-controlled feasibility trial. We will recruit 30 practitioners (dentists, nurses and hygienists) working within 10 practices and randomise half the practices to the TOOTHPICKS training arm. 100 consecutive parents of children (0-9 years) identified as at risk of dental decay will be recruited (50 from intervention and 50 from control practices). Outcomes will comprise routine clinical data (appointment attendance, basic periodontal examination, treatment and referral for extractions). Measures of behavioural determinants and reported health behaviours will be gathered through questionnaires. Referral rates of whole practice populations before and after the study will also be gathered. Acceptability and fidelity of the intervention will be examined through dentists questionnaires, audio-recording of consultations, practitioners and parents interviews (Phase 3). Potential benefits TOOTHPICKS has the potential to increase dentists motivation and capability of initiating and facilitating useful discussions with families with young children about preventing dental decay, and thereby reduce suffering and the need for dental extractions. Oral health is linked to school readiness, literacy, sleep, social development and nutritional status. Hence, although concentrating on oral outcomes, the intervention could improve children s health/wellbeing beyond the dental context and is consistent with Local Authority under 5s metrics.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Bath and North East Somerset PCT
Award_Title: Waste the Waist: Pilot study for a randomised controlled trial of a primary care based intervention to support lifestyle change for people with high cardiovascular risk.
Abstract: BackgroundPrimary Care Trusts in England need to commission services to promote healthy diet and physical activity for thousands of people who will be identified with high cardiovascular (CV) risk by the NHS Health Checks programme. However, they are faced with resource constraints and a lack of good quality research evidence to guide them to cost-effective interventions. In prior work, which arose from and strongly involved our NHS collaborators, the applicants have developed an intervention which a) has evidence that it can produce sustained behaviour change and modify CV risk factors b) can be delivered on a large scale c) has a cost which is acceptable to primary care stakeholders and d) includes intervention components recommended in evidence-based guidelines for supporting behaviour change.AimsTo pilot, prior to a full trial evaluation, a practical, state-of-the-art intervention to promote healthy diet and physical activity for people with high cardiovascular risk, which has been adapted for use in UK primary care. The pilot aims to 1) Assess recruitment, intervention concordance, study retention and measures-completion rates 2) Assess the acceptability of the intervention to participants 3) Assess the acceptability and feasibility of recruitment, measurement, randomisation and intervention delivery procedures which would be used in a future pragmatic randomised controlled trial 4) Estimate the resources and costs needed to deliver the intervention and conduct a full trial 5) Estimate the standard deviation of continuous outcomes (e.g. changes in participants’ weight).Plan of InvestigationWe will conduct a single-blind randomised controlled pilot study using quantitative and qualitative research methods. 100 patients with high cardiovascular risk will be randomised to receive either intervention or brief advice on cardiovascular risk /the benefits of diet and physical activity. Recruitment, intervention concordance (attendance), and measures-completion rates will be recorded, with measures at baseline, 3 months and 12 months (the intended primary outcomes for the future trial are weight and accelerometry-assessed physical activity and secondary measures include cardiovascular risk markers and cost-effectiveness). Qualitative research will investigate the acceptability and feasibility of the recruitment, measurement, randomisation and intervention delivery procedures.Potential ImpactThe proposed intervention has the potential to impact greatly on the health of those at high risk of cardiovascular disease, and on NHS resource use. There is intense interest currently amongst PCTs and primary care clinicians about how to effectively support lifestyle change for cardiovascular risk management. An intervention model that is optimised to effectively deliver lifestyle change, whilst minimising resource use therefore has great potential for NHS use. A cost-effective intervention for this population could also be adapted for people with existing diabetes and CVD. The close involvement of a PCT Director of Public Health and two GPs, and good links with UK clinical and service delivery networks will ensure that the possibilities for translation into practice are maximised.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Leeds and York Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Multicentre Intervention Designed for Self-Harm, using Interpersonal Problem-Solving (MIDSHIPS) trial: A feasibility study
Abstract: BackgroundAround 150,000 people each year attend hospitals in England due to self-harm, many of them more than once [1]. Over 5000 people die by suicide each year in the UK, a quarter of them having attended the general hospital in the previous year because of non-fatal self-harm, so self-harm is the major identifiable risk factor for suicide [2]. People receive a variable standard of care at hospital: many are not assessed for their psychological needs and little psychological therapy is offered [3]. Despite its frequent occurrence, we have no clear research evidence about how to reduce repetition of self-harm [4]. People who have self-harmed show less active ways of solving problems, and brief problem-solving therapies are considered the most promising psychological treatments [5].AimsWe plan a randomised controlled trial to find out whether problem-solving therapy, when added to treatment as usual (TAU), reduces the rate of repeated self-harm over the next year. Problem-solving therapy has proven benefit in depression and is known to reduce hopelessness and suicidal thinking [5]. We are proposing a feasibility study; if we prove successful in recruiting and treating patients, and in following them up to identify repeat episodes of self-harm, we will apply for funding for a large trial. This application is for a study that includes only 80 people but the large trial, if it takes place, will have up to 2800 participants. The feasibility study can provide hard data on which to base assumptions and processes, and thereby position our team ready to run the main trial.Plan of InvestigationProblem-solving therapy can be set out in simple manuals and is readily taught to health professionals with a mental health nursing, social work or counselling background. Patients in the active treatment-plus-TAU limb of the proposed multicentre trial will receive 4-6 one-hour weekly sessions from staff trained in the intervention by the research team and working to a manual of treatment. In the feasibility study we will: prepare the therapy manuals; train 2 therapists in the problem-solving therapy; screen patients attending hospital after self-harm for their eligibility for the trial; and establish the best methods for recruiting and delivering therapy to 60 patients. We will refine our methods for collecting the information we need about follow-up – from surveys and hospital records.Potential ImpactAt present, around the world, therapy is not usually offered to people who have come to hospital because of self-harm because none is known to be effective [4,6]. The absence of effective treatment is one of the main reasons why fewer than half of the people who come to hospitals in the UK as a consequence of self-harm receive an adequate psychosocial assessment of their needs [3]. Current evidence points towards effectiveness from brief problem-solving therapy but, if it is to become a routinely available treatment in the NHS, we will need clear evidence from a large, multicentre, pragmatic trial in the UK and an economic evaluation; this feasibility study paves the way towards badly needed improvement in patients’ experience and outcome after self-harm.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Taunton and Somerset NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: ACTID Follow up: A 3 year follow up of patients who took part in the Early ACTID study
Abstract: BackgroundThe NSF for Diabetes states that patients should receive ’help in adopting and maintaining a healthy lifestyle’. As a result of this, a number of education programs have been set up for patients with type 2 diabetes (T2DM). Although there is some evidence to suggest that in the short term these programs improve diabetes control, there is no evidence as to whether they work in the medium to longer term. We have shown that providing patients with newly diagnosed T2DM with a program that teaches them to either improve their diet or improve both diet and activity levels over 12 months leads to better weight loss and diabetes control than in those who were given usual care. We now need to know whether these skills will continue to be used and whether the benefits continue for the longer term.AimsWe aim to find out what happens over the following 5 years to patients involved in the Early ACTID trial. This will enable us to determine: 1. The size of any beneficial effect of a diet and a diet & activity program on weight, glycaemic control, blood pressure, lipid profiles and the natural history of T2DM as indicated by insulin resistance and medication use, above that produced by usual care in newly diagnosed patients with T2DM at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 yrs after completion of this program.2.Whether these programs improve eating patterns, activity habits and well being above that produced by usual care, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 yrs after completion of this program. 3.Whether if ongoing benefits are seen, these are greater for those in the diet & activity compared to the diet alone program.Plan of InvestigationAll patients who completed the Early ACTID study will be invited to participate. Those that agree will attend a 3 hour yearly visit to have the measures listed below. These visits will occur at 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 years after they left the study. History, current medication and history of recent illness.Clinical measures: blood pressure, weight, height, waist and hip circumference, percentage lean and fat body contentBlood analysis: HbA1c & fasting glucose; Total, HDL and LDL cholesterol, triglycerides; Insulin resistance- calculated by the Homeostatic model method.Physical activity: assessed using an accelerometer worn for 7 days.Well being: Diener’s satisfaction with life, Rosenberg self-esteem, EQ5D.Diet: 4 day food diary together with 45 min interview with a dietitianPotential ImpactEarly ACTID participants received a straightforward behavioural based program early on in their patient journey which reduced weight and insulin resistance, improved glycaemic control, and resulted in less medication use. These programs were nurse led and after modification and staff training could easily be implemented in primary care. Knowing if benefits from these programs continue to work in the long term is of paramount importance for planning future diabetes services, as it will help to determine whether courses need to be continued or whether refresher courses can just be given at certain time intervals. Maintenance of lifestyle changes, even for 1-2 years, may result in significant savings on medication as well as reductions in cardiovascular risk and diabetes complications.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Developing and evaluating a patient-led, electronic incident reporting scheme for renal patients
Abstract: BackgroundPreliminary work through a series of patient focus groups in Renal Services in the Bradford Trust revealed that patients can and wish to discuss both positive or negative aspects of the safety and quality of their care and would value the opportunity of sharing this information with staff. We also established, however, that patients can feel uncertain about providing such information through a formal reporting scheme. Although the literature on patient involvement reflects this view, the results also demonstrate that patient reporting can be a reliable source of information. We will actively collaborate with patients and staff to co-design and evaluate a patient-led reporting scheme for quality and safety concerns embedded in a shared electronic health record (Renal Patient View, RPV) .AimsDetermine the factors that affect quality and safety in renal services and how these are best reported to to staffAgree objectives for a RPV based reporting scheme and develop a taxonomy of contributory factors that impact on quality and safetyAdapt existing RPV technology and local governance processes to accommodate a patient-led reporting scheme, pilot the scheme and collect a range of qualitative data from patients and staff to assess utilisation; corroborate the report data with existing forms of quality/safety dataFollowing analysis of pilot data, implement scheme across the study settings and survey patients and staff on the implementation process, acceptability, feasibility, and sustainability; examine patient experience as a function of the scheme; and report a cost analysisPlan of InvestigationPhase 1: Literature review of patient-inclusive reporting schemes. Collection of qualitative data from patients and staff to determine factors that affect quality/safety, related information flow, and vision for reportingPhase 2: Set and agree objectives for a RPV based reporting scheme from patient and staff data using an expert panel. Co-development of contributory factors affecting quality and safety. Phase 3: Adaptation of existing RPV; pilot reporting scheme in two local renal services using RPV, observational study of utilisation process, compare RPV data to existing quality/safety data Phase 4:Implement adapted scheme across participating services. Summative evaluation of implementation process and patient experience using survey measures. Cost analysis. Final report.Potential ImpactWe will develop a local patient-led electronic reporting scheme for quality and safety concerns for patients with a long term condition, and a taxonomy of factors affecting quality and safety in renal service provision. We will also possess a critical understanding of the barriers and facilitators to adoption, utilisation, and sustainability of RPV as a patient-led reporting tool, in the socio-technical context of patient care in renal services. The concurrent cost analysis will give information on affordability, service costs, and potential for national roll out.The knowledge generated will be shared with key stakeholders: the National Kidney Federation, NHS Diabetes & Kidney Care, the National Renal Information Exchange Group, DH/SHA Long Term Conditions Teams, Connecting for Health.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: "A feasibility study of ""WorkPlan"" - a guided workbook intervention to support work-related goals among cancer survivors"
Abstract: Background Over 100,000 people of working-age receive a diagnosis of cancer each year in the UK. Evidence suggests that cancer survivors are at greater risk of not working, or leaving work life early compared to healthy controls. Work post-cancer treatment is important for reasons other than financial security, as not working is associated with poorer psychological and physical outcomes. Predictors of longer time to return to work include disease and work-related factors. However, greater attention is being given to the importance of psychological factors such as negative beliefs about the consequences of cancer and beliefs about one's ability to control the effects of cancer. The WorkPlan intervention targets known psychological factors within an intervention to improve work-related outcomes among cancer survivors. We anticipate that a guided self-help treatment might be a valuable and cost efficient strategy that would lead to more positive beliefs about illness, quicker return to work, greater satisfaction with work and the return to work process. Undertaking a feasibility study is critical to inform the planning of a larger, fully-powered randomised controlled trial to improve work-related outcomes among cancer survivors. Aims This study aims to evaluate this theoretically-led intervention (based on the self-regulation model and goal-setting theory) in a feasibility study of a randomised controlled trial with a 12 month follow-up. Specifically the aims are to: Aim 1: Trial data collection materials Aim 2: Trial the recruitment process and feasibility of recruiting participants into the study Aim 3: Test the acceptability among participants of the randomisation process Aim 4: Determine retention in control and intervention groups Aim 5: Conduct the ground work necessary to obtain data that will be required in the definitive trial to enable a full cost-effectiveness analysis. Plan of investigation Following recruitment through hospital clinics and an assessment session 60 cancer patients will be randomly assigned to one of two arms of the trial (a guided workbook intervention or usual care). In order to assess the short, medium and longer term impact of the intervention participants will be asked to complete measures (including illness perceptions, mood and workability) at baseline (pre-intervention), following the intervention (or four weeks post-randomisation for the usual care group) and then at 6 and 12-months post-randomisation. In addition quality of life and healthcare utilisation measures will be completed to inform a health economic assessment. Twenty participants in the intervention group will also be asked to undergo a semi-structured interview following the intervention and then again 12 months post-randomisation to explore the randomisation process, the intervention format, how it was delivered and perceived efficacy and general perceptions of the trial. Twenty participants in the usual care group will be asked to undergo an interview at 12 months post-randomisation to explore experiences of the randomisation process, of usual care and support in return to work and general perceptions of the trial. Interviews will be transcribed verbatim and analysed using framework analysis. Benefits to patients and the NHS The study may be the first step in the development of several long-term benefits and may have some immediate benefits for the sample who participate in this feasibility study. The intervention will provide cancer survivors with the skills and confidence to manage their return to work. The intervention may improve long-term job retention among cancer survivors with the potential also to be adapted for other conditions. Furthermore, the intervention may have long-term implications for improving psychological outcomes among cancer survivors through improvements in well-being, mood and physical functioning, all of which could impact on the utilisation of NHS services

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Development and validation of a short family history screening tool for chronic disease prevention in primary care.
Abstract: BackgroundFamily history (FH) is an important and established risk factor for many diseases, representing genetic factors, and environmental and behavioural exposures. Collecting and using FH information presents real challenges in primary care: no simple, validated tools exist for the accurate recording of FH. Arising from previous studies on patient concerns about their FH, we propose to develop a screening tool based on the FH to identify groups at risk of chronic disease and to assess its performance and psychological impact upon primary care patients. Ischaemic heart disease, T2 diabetes, breast and colorectal cancer have been selected as marker conditions as they fulfil screening criteria, and effective interventions and lifestyle strategies exist for their primary and secondary prevention.AimsA long FH questionnaire (FHQ-12) has been developed, informed by a systematic literature review identifying FH predictors of chronic disease, and qualitative studies exploring the patient’s perspective. This project aims to use mixed methods to define a minimum ‘Q’ set (FHQ-n) for self-completion, and assess its performance and impact in a primary care population. The characterization of performance will include determination of the sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values of the tool to identify patients screened in primary care who would be most likely to benefit from detailed pedigree and risk assessment. We also intend to assess the psychosocial impact and acceptability of undergoing FH screening for chronic disease in primary care.Plan of InvestigationWe aim to recruit 1,200 people aged 20 to 50, with an anticipated prevalence of relevant FH of 40%. Genetics-trained researchers will take a 3-generational 'gold standard' pedigree after the FHQ has been completed. Stage 1 will comprise a survey of FHQ-12 performance against gold standard to define the minimum ‘Q’ set FHQ-n. Stage 2 will assess the performance of FHQ-n in another primary care population and will examine the psychosocial impact of FH screening using questionnaires and interviews with participants at both increased and normal/population risk. Analyses will include: ROC curve analyses of the FHQ-n and pedigree data; iterative analyses of qualitiative data informed by grounded theory, and comparisons of measures for psychological impact over time.Potential ImpactIf this short, validated FH screening tool proves to have suitable performance and acceptability without causing significant psychological harm, it will benefit patients by having immediate clinical utility in primary care. The tool will have the potential to support tailored disease prevention across many chronic diseases in primary care by improving identification of individual disease risk, and the application of risk-reducing strategies such as screening or medication. By contributing to a reduction in the substantial public health burden of chronic disease, the tool also provides potential huge benefits to the NHS. In addition, the study will provide key data on prevalence of FH of chronic diseases in primary care.?

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Towards co-ordinated services for complex conditions? An evaluation of service provision for people with ataxia
Abstract: BackgroundIndividuals with ataxia suffer loss of balance and dexterity, speech, swallowing and visual problems. Complex diagnostic investigations may provide an explanation but only rarely do they identify a reversible cause. Individuals are likely to benefit from treatments aimed at maximising physical and social function. In Greater Manchester, individuals with similar degenerative conditions such as motor neurone disease benefit from an integrated multidisciplinary service. However, anecdotal evidence suggests that services for patients with ataxia are variable and un-coordinated. Recently published national ataxia guidelines give minimum service standards that aim to improve patients’ quality of life. However, implementation of these guidelines will have significant impact on health resources.AimsThe study focuses on adults with progressive ataxia based in Greater Manchester and aims to:1. Explore and compare views and experiences of patients, carers and professionals about symptoms and management2. Explore and compare patients’ and professionals’ views about the patient benefits from co- ordinated services for people with progressive ataxia3. Measure service use and cost the clinical pathways currently followed by patients4. Identify the key cost drivers and patterns of resource use required to implement national guidelines for people with progressive ataxia5. Compare healthcare services to national guideline recommendations6. Explore variability in service provision for people with ataxia across EnglandPlan of InvestigationTwo year study comprising: 1) Semi-structured interviews with patients, carers and health professionals and patient diaries to explore the impact of symptoms and past and present experiences of management, including barriers to access, approaches to self-management and the potential benefits from co-ordinated services. 2) Cost analysis to compare the cost of existing care pathways with standardised vignettes describing care pathways meeting national guidelines. 3) Expert panel to assess whether existing care pathways meet with national service guidelines. 4) National survey of health professionals who manage ataxia will identify current service provision and any variation across England. Ethical approval will be sought.Potential ImpactPatients, carers and health professionals’ experiences will be used to understand the desirability, quality and cost implication of introducing a more co-ordinated, patient centred pathway that meets the requirements of national ataxia guidelines. Areas of patient benefit may include: improved co-ordination and continuity in provision across health specialties and social care; improved access to services; development of strategies to maximise efficient use of services and self-management capacity. The results of this study will provide patient-centred evidence for service commissioners on how pathways for patients living with ataxia and other complex neurological conditions should be improved and implemented.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: An Investigation into the Prevalence of Mental Health Disorder and Patterns of Health Service Access in a Probation Population.
Abstract: BackgroundPrisoners are a socially excluded and marginalised group. Research by Singleton et al (1998) famously shows that c.90% of them suffer from mental health problems, substance misuse problems or both, and these findings are supported by other epidemiological research studies (Brooker, Sirdifield and Gojkovic, 2007). Furthermore, there is an inverse relationship between the degree to which prisoners access services and their high level of need. However, very little research examines the prevalence of mental health disorder and/or patterns of service access for offenders on probation, and we cannot assume that these will mirror those of a prison population. This exploratory study aims to fill this gap.Aims1) To determine the prevalence of serious mental illness among offenders on Probation Officers’ caseloads in Lincolnshire2) To investigate what proportion of mentally disordered offenders’ disorders are known to probation staff3) To use probation records and offender self-report data to examine the extent to which offenders are formally engaged with specialist mental health services4) To examine staff and offender views/experiences of service access and highlight any barriers encountered; and thereby demonstrate how to increase offenders’ access to services and reduce health inequalities5) To inform the development of a national assessment template of the prevalence of psychiatric morbidity and patterns of service access in the probation populationPlan of InvestigationThe study will employ a variety of methods including:1) Utilising a short mental disorder screening questionnaire (designed specifically for use with criminal justice populations to indicate symptoms of a mental illness) with a random sample of offenders2) In addition, where relevant, to use further standardised schedules assessing substance misuse, personality disorder, service access and needs arising from mental health disorder3) Analysis of case records to ascertain the proportion of mentally disordered offenders whose disorder is known to staff, and which services they are known to be accessing4) Qualitative interviews with staff and offenders regarding experiences of facilitating access to/trying to access services, and barriers encounteredPotential ImpactThe study will establish the prevalence of mental disorders in a probation population for the first time, which may have implications for the current level of NHS service provision. Additionally, research around barriers to service access may have implications for the way that NHS/probation services are commissioned and/or provided. Demonstrating how to increase offenders' access to services should lead to offenders receiving a better standard of care which should reduce health inequalities and lead to a reduction in reoffending rates. If screening tools used are effective they could be incorporated into future plans for 'specialist' mental health probation staff. Findings will provide crucial groundwork for developing a national assessment template for use in this field.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The efficacy and cost effectiveness of a falling prediction and prevention programme in older patients with rheumatoid arthritis
Abstract: BackgroundRheumatoid arthritis (RA) affects 0.8% of the UK adult population and results in significant morbidity and increased healthcare costs. Older people with RA are uniquely prone to osteoporosis and osteoporotic fractures resulting from falls, which have a sizeable contribution to both morbidity and mortality from the disease. No falling prevention programme that is tailored to the needs of older people with RA has been developed or tested. This study aims to identify risk factors that contribute to falls in RA and develop a care package to reduce the risk of falling in these patients.AimsThe study aims:• To provide the first detailed prospective assessment of fall-related risk factors in older patients with RA;• To develop a falling prevention strategy that is tailored to the needs of older people with RA, taking into account their experiences and self-perceived healthcare needs;• To perform a pilot study in older patients with RA to assess the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention package and refine it;• To design a protocol of randomised control clinical trial (RCT) for the further assessment of the clinical- and cost-effectiveness of the package.Plan of InvestigationThis will be carried out in a cohort of older patients (? 65 years) with RA attending outpatient clinics in Norfolk & Norwich University Hospital (NNUH).1. Longitudinal data on the risk factors and incidence of falls will be collected by questionnaires and postcard surveillance to determine the chief predictors of falls in RA.2. A sample of fallers and non-fallers will undergo a full clinical and neuro-physiological assessment. A qualitative study will explore their experiences and views on falls and the associated preventive measures.3. Based on above findings, a structured falling prevention package will be developed and pilot tested in older patients with RA. The study will produce a protocol for a RCT to assess the clinical- and cost-effectiveness of the care package.Potential ImpactThe objective knowledge of fall-related risk factors in older patients with RA and a tailored intervention package based on these findings will provide unique guidance on falling prevention for these patients. This will be of direct and tangible benefit to older patients with RA for whom the incidence of fractures will be reduced. The results of this study will have the potential to change clinicians’ attitudes towards falling prevention in these patients and lead to better and cost-effective clinical care for those who have the condition. A key output will be a protocol for a RCT.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Royal National Hospital For Rheumatic Diseases NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Contextual Cognitive-Behavioural Therapy (CBT) for the Self-Management of Chronic Pain in the Community: A Feasibility Study
Abstract: BackgroundSignificant chronic pain is experienced by at least 13% of adults and is one of the most costly health conditions in the UK. It has been shown that the most severe and complex chronic pain can be effectively helped by intensive interdisciplinary forms of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), delivered in tertiary care settings. However, most patients are treated in primary or secondary care and do not access these specialist methods. A current challenge is to translate these methods from tertiary care and test them for application to the far larger number of patients in primary care or in the community. To determine if this is feasible, preliminary work must be done to devise a process of delivery for these methods and prepare the best procedures for conducting subsequent randomised trials.AimsThe ultimate aim of this work is to prepare for a randomized controlled clinical trial (RCT) of a new, intensive, cognitive-behavioural approach (called Contextual CBT) to chronic pain in the community. The immediate aim of the current proposed research is to translate treatment methods, develop research methods needed, and pilot test these for this later RCT. The objectives are to (1) incorporate relevant stakeholders in a process of translating an intensive tertiary care treatment approach into a feasible and acceptable form that can be examined for implementation outside of speciality hospital settings closer to where patients live, and (2) pilot test methods, establish recruitment and retention potential, and identify appropriate assessment methods, to inform later investigation.Plan of InvestigationThe 26-month plan for this project will have two phases. First, using qualitative research methods, patients, GPs, and PCT commissioners will be consulted to produce an adapted model of Contextual CBT and a small survey will examine feasibility and acceptability. Second, a small-scale trial will be conducted essentially to pilot test procedures and determine suitable outcomes measures.
