Follow-up data exploration will focus on recruitment and retention rates, completeness of data, and apparent sensitivity of measures.Potential ImpactAlthough psychologically-based methods are called for in treatment guidelines for chronic pain, effective treatments of this type are not available for most chronic pain sufferers outside of specialty care. Likewise, although treatments for chronic pain for highly complex pain sufferers in speciality care are effective, these have never been modified or tested for chronic pain sufferers with difficulties of moderate complexity contacted in primary care or in the community. This study promises to adapt a comprehensive treatment approach to chronic pain from speciality care for broader application, test the viability of this in a community-based setting, and determine a practical course for further investigation and eventual dissemination of this treatment in this important clinical area.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Case-control study to investigate potential role for Influenza and/or Pneumococcal Vaccination in prevention Against Stroke and Transient Ischaemic Attack (IPVASTIA)
Abstract: BackgroundStroke is a major cause of death and long term illness worldwide. About 130 thousand people suffer a new or recurrent stroke each year in the United Kingdom and about 5% of the population are affected. Strokes are common and lead to substantial disability. Many of those who suffer a stroke survive and the social and economic effects are considerable. There is equivocal evidence from case-control studies that influenza vaccination is associated with reduced risk of stroke and therefore insufficient evidence that vaccination either alone or combined with pneumococcal vaccination prevents new or recurrent stroke. We aim to investigate the potential effectiveness of influenza and/or pneumococcal vaccination for the prevention of stroke and transient ischaemic attack.AimsWe aim to investigate the association between influenza vaccination (current, previous, repeated within season vaccination and time since vaccination), pneumococcal vaccination (ever, time since vaccination) or combined influenza and pneumococcal vaccination with stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA) and whether this association is independent of other major cardiovascular risk factors. The main outcomes will be odds ratios of stroke (fatal or nonfatal) and TIA in those with influenza vaccination (within the past year), pneumococcal vaccination (ever) or combined vaccination in cases of stroke and TIA compared with controls and incidence rate ratios of stroke and TIA according to time since vaccination within cases.Plan of InvestigationThis will be a matched case-control and case series study using the General Practice Research Database. Cases will be patients (living or dead) recorded with stroke or TIA (fatal or non-fatal) over 72 months. We will study the effect of influenza and/or pneumococcal vaccination given in the season prior to first stroke occurring between September 2001 to August 2007. We will analyse risk of stroke and transient ischaemic attack from time of influenza or pneumococcal vaccination with four controls to each case, matched for age, sex, calendar time and practice. Cases and controls will be aged 18 years or over. Confounders including major cardiovascular risk factors, vaccine risk groups and consultation rates will be adjusted for.Potential ImpactThis study will seek further evidence of influenza vaccination, pneumococcal vaccination or both as possible protective factors for stroke or TIA. Current vaccination rates nationally are below the seventy per cent target for some high-risk groups and considerably below target rates (90%) in the United States. If there are additional benefits of influenza and pneumococcal vaccination in preventing stroke this would support and encourage vaccination of existing vaccine risk groups but also provide evidence for extending the programme to younger adults at high risk of stroke, for example those with hypertension. Knowledge on potential benefits associated with influenza and pneumococcal vaccination could contribute to policy decisions and patient information on use of these vaccinations.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Enhancing the effectiveness of the Diabetes Manual: modelling a new self-management education intervention for type 2 diabetes
Abstract: BackgroundDiabetes structured education provision for people living with diabetes (PLWD) was recommended by NICE in Jan 2006. For type 2 diabetes, two group-based programmes are recommended by the DOH although a joint DOH/Diabetes UK report in 2006 indicates the need for 1:1 programmes. The Diabetes Manual is a 1:1 programme which has been found to improve diabetes self-care confidence and reduce anxiety in a recent RCT. The RCT findings and the literature indicate that the clinical and psychological effects of the Diabetes Manual (DM) might be strengthened by providing additional behaviour change support to both the practice nurse who delivers the DM and the patient who follows it. In line with MRC complex intervention framework, further phase II study needs to occur to improve the intervention.AimsThe aims of this 2 phase study are to (i) Determine the nature and feasibility of enhanced-support provision from the perspective of the patient, primary care (practice nurse who is also a potential Diabetes Manual Facilitator) and specialist service (diabetes specialist nurse) care providers (ii) Develop and deliver an enhanced-support Diabetes Manual curriculum to practice nurses and the Diabetes Specialist Nurses (DSNs) supporting them (iii) Assess intervention fidelity by practice nurses delivering it and patients using it (iv) identify outcomes which demonstrate the most encouraging effects (v) Assess intervention uptake and delivery (vi) Inform the development of a cluster RCT to assess the dose related effect of enhanced support against the standard Diabetes Manual programmePlan of InvestigationIn phase 1, 12 practice nurses previously trained to deliver the Diabetes Manual within the RCT will be invited to participate in two action research workshops to develop an enhanced-support component to the Diabetes Manual. One focus group of 12 people with diabetes will be held to assess the appropriateness and feasibility of enhanced support provision. Nominal group technique will be used.In phase 2, 10 GP practices in Coventry will be invited and asked to recruit 5 patients per practice (n=50), who have hitherto refused group education in the last 3 years, to participate in the enhanced support Diabetes Manual cohort study. Patient outcomes, including measures of routine QOF data, patient knowledge, psychological state and physical activity, will be assessed at 6 & 12 months.Potential ImpactThe Diabetes Manual (DM) is a 1:1 programme meeting the national standards for structured education. It has demonstrated some patient benefits and it is currently available for use by PCTs. This research would (i) increase our understanding of the dose impact of enhanced-support to patients on clinical and psychological outcomes (ii) identify effective ways of strengthening support to nurses in the delivery of the enhanced-support DM (iii) enable effect sizes and sample sizes to be estimated for a subsequent phase III RCT of its clinical and cost effectiveness.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust
Award_Title: A Self-management Programme of Activity Coping and Education (SPACE) for Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: is it effective in primary care?
Abstract: BackgroundThe NHS Improvement Plan identified long term conditions as one of the top priorities. The plan identified that self management should be facilitated at every stage of the disease allowing individuals to remain independent and lead fulfilling lives. Self management strategies are provided for many long term conditions but not chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The Clinical Strategy for COPD (launch 2009) will recommend that education and self management strategies should be accessible to all patients. However a recent Cochrane review identified the need for more research in this area. Over the last 24 months we have developed a comprehensive self management manual with a focus on symptom management and physical activity.AimsThe aim of the project is to determine the effectiveness of independent standardised self management designed for patients with COPD, managed routinely in primary care. The intent of the manual is to equip patients with the skills to manage their disease effectively, with a focus on maintaining and improving their physical activity and health status thus retaining or restoring their functional independence. We will also explore acceptability and applicability to adopting this model of care for patients and health care professionals. The self management manual would therefore become part of the integrated care package for these individuals. The aim is to test this model of structured independent self management for patients with COPD that can be rolled out across the UK.Plan of InvestigationA prospective randomised controlled trial of the self management manual versus best usual care in a range of patients in primary care with COPD will be conducted. Participants will be randomised to receive the self management manual or usual care. Those offered the manual will be introduced to it using motivational interviewing techniques. Usual care will be provided by the primary care team. There will be ‘nested’ qualitative studies exploring acceptability to the delivery of this intervention in patients and health care professionals. The primary outcome measure will be disease specific health status. Secondary outcome measures include physical activity and exercise performance using sophisticated activity monitors that we have previously validated in patients with COPD.Potential ImpactThe research will provide an evidence base to inform service design and delivery at operational and policy levels. If the trial is successful, the impact will be to provide a structured, standardised method of delivering a self management education programme to patients with COPD, improving health status and physical activity and symptom management, and creating a direct connection between the evidence base and patient care. Currently there is no standardised effective self management strategy. This standardised approach to self management could be replicated and rolled out regionally and nationally across the UK. It will also provide evidence of the requirements for securing engagement of individuals and health care professionals with self management strategies.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The development of a referral decision screening tool to allow the early identification of mental health problems in police custody
Abstract: BackgroundSince 1999 the NHS has worked in partnership with HM Prison Service to improve prison-based healthcare, aiming to increase the quality and scope of services so as to improve the health status of offenders, a socially excluded group. Most recently, the Department of Health (DH) has recognised that prison healthcare is just one part of an individual’s complex pathway through the criminal justice system (CJS). The publication of two important position papers is imminent; one forms an overarching strategy for improving health and social care across all parts of the CJS and the second is an independent review of diversion from custody for people with mental health problems which is likely to recommend radical change to the way in which diversion services are structured and delivered.AimsThis project aims to improve current practices around the identification of mental health problems in people in contact with the police to better identify those in possible need of early diversion into health and social services. Most diversion liaison services based in police custody suites operate during office hours only, and therefore a way of accurately identifying those likely to require mental health assessment out of hours is required. The project will result in the development of a referral decision tool, suitable for use by non-mental health trained police personnel which accurately identifies those who require a full assessment of their mental health. An accompanying training and implementation package will also be developed.Plan of InvestigationWe will conduct an examination of available research evidence, diversion policy and procedure documents and conduct a national survey and individual interviews to establish current practices around screening for mental health problems in police custody. Following identification of key themes, common working practices and examples of apparent good practice, we will undertake a staged consultation exercise using a Delphi approach to inform the development of a structured referral decision tool designed to be administered by police officers to determine whether referral to mental health services is required. In collaboration with service users and professionals associated training and implementation materials will be developed.Potential ImpactUpon completion, the project will have generated a referral decision tool which can be used by non-mental health trained staff to determine whether a detainee in police custody should be referred for further assessment for possible diversion away from the CJS. The use of such a tool would likely increase the chances of a person being able to access health and social care services and prevent unnecessary progress through the criminal justice process, thus improving health status and reducing social exclusion. The use of the tool would extend assessment procedures to all detainees in custody rather than just those detained during the hours of operation of diversion schemes, thus increasing timely access to services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Optimising hearing-Related Communication for care Home Residents with Dementia (ORCHARD): a realist synthesis
Abstract: Both hearing impairment and dementia are common in care homes. Hearing impairment occurs in 70-90% of residents, and dementia in about 75%. Together, the two can be formidable barriers to communication. Managing hearing loss in care homes is complex. Testing hearing in dementia is difficult. Other problems contribute to poor communication: care homes are often noisy, making communication harder for people with poor hearing; aphasia in dementia exacerbates the impact of deafness; residents and care staff often have different backgrounds and some don t speak English as their first language. Hearing aids are often supplied, but problems can arise, e.g. the resident doesn t tolerate the aid or understand what it s for, may be unable to operate it, or may simply destroy it. Care staff may lack knowledge and skills to support hearing aid use, or may not value the effort required to encourage the resident to wear the aid. Hearing aids are frequently mislaid, lost or broken. Families of residents are frequently upset if an aid is not worn, or if it is missing or broken. Residents not using aids cannot readily access auditory stimuli required to communicate. Evidence regarding effective strategies to improve hearing-related communication in care homes is limited. Managing hearing loss in care homes is complex and often co-exists with other problems, e.g. dementia, which can affect staff attitudes and their approach to its management. Realist synthesis (see Figure 1 in appended supplementary file) is a theory-driven explanatory approach for evaluating health and social complex interventions. It utilises a range of different sources of data, thereby maximising the use of all available literature and resources. It is designed to address the questions of what works, how, why, to what extent, for whom and in what circumstances. Therefore it uses a pragmatic approach to assess evidence, and seeks to explain why different outcomes can occur in different contexts. It has not previously been used in hearing loss research. This team, comprising experts in hearing science, dementia care and realist synthesis, will review all forms of relevant information, including grey literature and relevant websites. We will recruit a context expert group of practitioners, care home staff and the public. This group will meet seven times during the project. These facilitated half day meetings will help us develop and refine our explanations about how best practice in hearing management can occur in care homes. We will also interview a small number (3-5) individual care home residents with both hearing and cognitive problems. From the literature, the group will explore how and why the reported outcomes have occurred. An explanation of the interplay between context, mechanisms and outcomes will be sought. From this, we will develop and refine an initial rough realist programme theory to be tested against the data (from the literature and the experience of our context experts) to see how well it can explain the pattern of findings. The realist programme theory will drive further literature searching; thus moving iteratively between the analysis of particular examples, the emerging rough realist programme theory and further exploratory searching. This requires a flexible and evolving search strategy. Both our methods and our reporting will adhere to the RAMESES guidance on realist synthesis. We will test the ideas arising from the evidence and the emerging realist programme theory with the context expert group at subsequent meetings as the research progresses. This will enable us to understand what best practice looks like and what makes it effective. Finally, this study will i) develop national guidelines to ensure best practice, and ii) suggest future research topics to support care homes in managing hearing-related communication.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: East and North Hertfordshire NHS Trust
Award_Title: Facilitation of Self Management in a Haemodialysis Unit: An Evaluation
Abstract: BackgroundHaemodialysis patients must adhere to multiple dietary and fluid restrictions, but find this difficult(1). Failing to comply with these restrictions can cause a host of clinical complications (11). Patients on haemodialysis also commonly experience psychological problems such as depression(2). Self-management facilitation has been shown to reduce similar problems in other chronic illnesses(6,8,23,24,25). Currently, dialysis patients generally only receive a one off educational programme focused on modality choice before initiation of dialysis. The aim of the study is to evaluate the impact of facilitating on-going self management in this group of service users on the service users and staff. Given the complex nature of the intervention planned, an action research approach will be used.AimsThe duration of the proposed study will be 36 months. The aim of the study is to assess the potential benefits for patients being treated in a haemodialysis unit that receives ongoing self-management facilitation. The aims of the project are built round an action research cycle of:- Developing an action plan: working with service users and staff to source resources and develop an intervention- Intervening and observing the intervention: through changes in quantitative measures, interviews and focus groups, documentation of field notes and critical incidents- Evaluation and forward planning: to bring all the materials together, identifying enablers and barriers to self-management, and produce a roadmap for implementation in other centres.Plan of InvestigationThe self-management facilitator will be a nurse who is also the action researcher, supported by a research team. The study will take place in one renal service treating 400 service users. Using an action research paradigm, the research team will draw upon a mixed methodology to implement and evaluate the 3 phases outlined above.The first phase will define practical methods to implement strategies to promote self-management with the support of all involved in care.The second phase will observe implementation of the strategies through: collection of clinical and psychological measures, focus groups and interviews, and field notes.The last phase will bring all the evidence together (triangulation) producing a roadmap and documentation to support implementation in other centres.Potential ImpactChronic Kidney disease is a large and growing problem, placing a large burden on the NHS (21,22).There is evidence that facilitating self-management in chronic illness can empower service users and improve their treatment adherence, as well as their physical and psychological wellbeing (6,8,23,24.25). By demonstrating how self-management can be practically facilitated within a service the study will have a large impact on key indicators of service performance. Through promotion of self-management the study can promote treatment adherence, improving the quality of life and other clinical outcomes, and potentially reduce unnecessary resource use by this group of service users.Finally the study is designed to enable other services to implement similar changes to service.???

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: RCT of a complex intervention by primary care nurses to increase walking in patients aged 60-74 years. (PACE-Lift Pedometer Accelerometer Consultation Evaluation - Lift).
Abstract: BackgroundPhysical activity is important for older peoples’ physical and mental health and for maintaining independence. Guidelines recommend at least 30 minutes daily, 5 days weekly, of at least moderate intensity PA. Less than 20% of UK 60-74 year olds report achieving this. Effective PA behaviour change interventions include cognitive behavioural strategies eg. goal setting, self-monitoring, relapse prevention and the ability for interventions to be incorporated into daily routine, eg. increasing walking. Primary care PA consultations allow individual tailoring of such advice. Pedometers measure step-counts and accelerometers measure PA intensity, feedback on both of these measures could help to increase PA, but no studies have assessed this combination in older people or in primary care. AimsEfficacy of intervention:i) To determine whether or not a pedometer & accelerometer based intervention plus primary care nurse PA consultations, can help 60-74 year olds to increase their PA over 3 months (primary outcome);ii) To determine whether any increases are maintained over 12 months.Components of the intervention & acceptability to population:iii) To assess the fidelity & quality of intervention implementation over time;iv) To explore the reasons for non-participation in the trial;v) To explore the intervention’s acceptability to practice nurses & older people and what intervention components were most & least helpful;vi) To explore the factors enhancing or acting as barriers for older people in increasing their PA.Plan of InvestigationDesign: RCT with intervention & control arms plus process & qualitative evaluations. Target population: 300 people aged 60-74 registered with 3 Oxfordshire PCT practices, who can walk outside and have no contraindications to PA. Intervention: 3 month pedometer & accelerometer based intervention with practice nurse PA consultations. Four consultations based on cognitive behavioural strategies, PA diary, pedometer average daily steps & accelerometer feedback on PA intensity & timing of activities. Individual PA plans based on increasing walking and other existing PA will be produced. Outcomes: change in average daily steps (primary outcome) and average time spent in at least moderate intensity PA weekly (secondary outcome) at 3 months (main outcome) and 12 months (to assess maintenance).Potential ImpactIf the desired outcome of increased PA levels (both daily steps and time spent at moderate intensity PA) occurs and is maintained, there should be direct participant benefits, as increased PA is associated with numerous physical and mental health benefits for older people. Additionally, participants and nurses will master a behaviour change technique that is transferrable to other health behaviours. If this study’s intervention is acceptable and effective, this will justify funding for a larger trial in a representative primary care population, to test the different components separately and to assess cost-effectiveness. The long term aim is to develop an effective primary care PA intervention for older people, which will reduce the huge NHS costs of physical inactivity in this age group.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The Interhospital Telemedicine Pilot Project
Abstract: BackgroundSpecialist advice for District General Hospital (DGH) Emergency department patients is usually sought by telephone. The quality of information available to the specialist depends on the expertise and experience of the DGH clinician, often a trainee. The safest option is often patient transfer but this has risks and costs. Videoconferencing has been used for communication between minor or remote emergency units and major Emergency departments and by single specialist units linked to outlying hospitals. It is being set up between the Horton General Hospital Emergency department (HGHED)and the Oxford Radcliffe Trust in Oxford for stroke care delivery. We have access to the equipment to investigate its potential role in providing all specialist opinions for the Emergency department.Aims1.To determine whether use of real time videoconferencing for all specialist consultations between the HGHED and Oxford results in more appropriate transfer of patients to Oxford.2.To determine whether use of real time videoconferencing allows more patients to be admitted to HGH care after specialist advice has been sought.3.To determine whether use of videoconferencing improves outcomes for patients admitted to HGH from the Emergency department.3.To provide data to inform the design of a larger trial of DGH Emergency department referrals to tertiary centres randomised to audiovisual conferencing or telephone (usual care).4.To assess patient and clinician satisfaction with the use of audiovisual conferencing.Plan of InvestigationProspective observational study comparing outcome for all HGH Emergency department patients in whom a specialist opinion is sought or who are admitted to HGH without specialist opinion in the 6 months before and after introduction of real time videoconferencing.The main outcome studied will be the proportion of inappropriate transfers to Oxford after specialist opinion. Other outcomes will address changes in the patient’s pathway from the Emergency department following consultation, the outcome for patients admitted to HGH both with and without specialist opinion and the relative importance of videoconferencing in different specialities. Most of the data will be collected by research nurses.Potential ImpactEnabling the specialist to speak to the patient, to see all or part of the patient and to view and guide a focussed examination of the patient by the local clinician should allow them to make a better decision on patient management. As a result the patient may not need emergency transfer to Oxford but could be admitted to HGH with specialist advice or have elective care in Oxford. This would avoid the acute disruption to patient care and family support caused by emergency transfer and would reduce the cost of transport and tertiary level emergency care. Ready access to specialist opinion via videoconferencing may also encourage staff in the Emergency department to seek it more often which could improve the overall care and outcomes for patients requiring admission.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: TEST-BP: Trial of the Effectiveness and cost effectiveness of Self-monitoring and Treatment of Blood Pressure in secondary prevention following Stroke or Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA)
Abstract: BackgroundRaised Blood Pressure (BP) is a major risk factor for stroke. People with Transient Ischaemic Attacks (TIA) and stroke are at higher risk of subsequent cardiovascular events compared to the general population, the highest risk being within the first year of the initial event. Reducing BP in this group has been shown to reduce subsequent events in those designated with “normal”, as well as high, BP levels. Good BP control is often difficult to assess and achieve but self-BP monitoring can lead to improved control and is increasingly common, many patients now owning monitors. It is unclear in stroke and TIA patients if self-monitoring with or without patient-led changes in BP therapy will be effective and cost effective compared to standard BP management and acceptable by patients.AimsIn this Blinded End Point Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) of six months duration the hypothesis tested will be that self BP monitoring, with or without supervised self-management of BP therapy, in those with TIA and stroke who require BP therapy will result in significantly better control (with more participants in these groups reaching target BP) compared to matched control group who have standard BP management. The study aims to test this hypothesis and examine the impact of these interventions on (1) BP control and BP target attainment, (2) surrogate marker of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and 10 year estimated CVD risk, (3) cost effectiveness, and (4) feasibility, acceptability and patient satisfaction with the intervention.Plan of InvestigationTIA or stroke patients requiring BP therapy (n=120) will be randomised into 3 groups; (A) standard BP management (no self monitoring), (B) self BP monitoring alone & (C) self monitoring with patient led treatment changes. In group C the study team will have direct access to the BP data (using telemetry), advising the patient on BP self-management using individually tailored treatment algorithms. Groups B & C will self monitor BP for 7 days at 6 weeks, 3 & 5 months. 24 hour ambulatory BP levels will be measured at baseline and at the end of the study (6 month) as the gold standard. The primary outcome measure will be differences in 24 hour BP at 6 months between the groups. Acceptability, CVD markers, 10 year CVD risk, quality of life, and cost-effectiveness will be secondary outcomes.Potential ImpactThe trial will explore whether self-BP monitoring with or without supervised patient led changes in BP therapy, results in better BP control. Good BP control is associated with significant CVD risk reduction including stroke and TIA. Therefore, if the study findings show the intervention to be effective and cost effective, then this can be applied to the clinical setting for immediate patient benefit. As high BP is the major risk factor for stroke and cardiovascular diseases, this method can be applied to a wider population. This will reduce the morbidity, mortality and disease burden associated with cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases and will have potentially large impact for patients, clinicians and the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: CAPE study. Community cAre Pathways at the End of life: mapping the pathways to improve care.
Abstract: BackgroundHalf a million people die in England each year, 35% under the care of GPs. Some receive excellent care from GPs and District Nurses (DNs): many do not: raising the standard of care for all remains a major challenge. Most people approaching the end of life express a preference to die at home, but this is very dependent on adequate support being available. Identification of those for whom home care is more or less likely to be successful would enable a focus on optimising care for all, whatever their place of death.We address the recognised knowledge gaps of measurement of patient experience, economics of care and the adequacy of current pathways of care in meeting the range of patient care needs in the first detailed UK study of Primary Care provision of End of Life Care (EOLC).AimsThe research question is: for whom is home death “good”? Is it possible to characterise:a) Those for whom a “good death” at home is achievable, for whom greater effort is needed to optimise home careb) Those for whom death a “good death” at home is rarely achieved, for whom inpatient care should be planned and optimised?The aims are:1) To characterise the patterns of care need of people approaching the end of life in the community2) To map their current pathways of care provision and place of death3) To clarify and validate these patterns of need and care pathways with carers, GPs and DNs4) To investigate the health costs of these pathways5) To develop a toolkit for Primary Care Teams to review care and better align patient needs to care provisionPlan of InvestigationA diverse group of 20 practices in Cambridgeshire and Peterborough will be recruited. Phase 1: case summaries of 20 deceased patients, validated by GP and DN, will document care in the last six months of life, with health economic analysis of care pathways.Phase 2: focus group discussions with GPs and DNs reviewing five recent deaths, investigating perspectives on care given and pathways identified. Phase 3 (10 practices): interviews with informal carer, GP and DN of deceased patients (1 cancer, 1 non-cancer), triangulating carer and professional views of care. Phase 4: development of toolkit for practitioner care review: carer feedback questionnaire, guidelines for practice death reviews and templates for clinical records.Potential ImpactCharacterisation of patterns of care need and pathways of care provision will identify patient groups for whom “a good death” at home is more or less achievable, with health economic analysis of the care pathways identified. This addition to knowledge will enable practitioners, service providers and commissioners to tailor care to patients’ needs, with optimum use of resources, whatever the place of death. The toolkit will enable practitioners to optimise their care of people near the end of life by receiving carer feedback, developing practice after-death case reviews and using records to review care.The research team’s connections with the developing NHS EOLC Strategy and national charities such as Macmillan and Marie Curie will maximise the national impact of the study.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: Luton and Dunstable University Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Root causes of adverse drug events in nursing home residents with diabetes: enhancing safety in medicines management
Abstract: BackgroundImprovements in patient safety are central to the Quality Innovation Productivity and Prevention (QIPP) project of the NHS. Adverse drug events (ADEs), such as drug prescribing and administration errors, dispensing problems and adverse drug reactions, are a significant and common cause of patient safety incidents in all health and social care settings. Such events carry significant human and financial costs.Diabetes mellitus is an increasingly common high impact health problem in the UK affecting an estimated 2.6 million people and up to 26% of the care home population (Sinclair & Asprey 2009).The evidence base in terms of understanding the incidence, causes and severity of ADEs is stronger in the healthcare setting with less being known about nursing home provision.AimsWith regard to nursing home residents with diabetes and NHS medicines services:- Identify, describe and analyse adverse drug events linked to NHS provision occurring in nursing homes - Conduct a critical analysis of the moderate to potentially severe harm incidents and feed this back to the relevant providers- Combine this data in a meta-root cause analysis constructing a qualitative overview of the identified causes of the errors- Develop risk assessed strategies, solutions and applied learning through which the number and severity of adverse drug events in this patient group can be reduced- Provide a model and guidelines upon which the management of medications between NHS provision and nursing homes can be improved. Plan of Investigation- Recruit participating nursing homes and identify relevant adverse drug events (errors)- Construct a narrative description of those events and risk assess each using the NPSA risk matrix scoring system- Complete an anonymous narrative analysis and summary of the 'low' harm events and feed this back to relevant providers - Complete a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) of each of the 'moderate' to 'extreme' risk events and feed this back to the relevant health and social care providers as individual, confidential reports- Subject the sample of 25 RCAs to a meta root cause analysis- Utilise that data to construct relevant reports and solution development for NHS providers and those delivering nursing home provision -Provide data upon which NHS commissioning decisions can be made.Potential ImpactThere is clear evidence that ADEs are a significant cause of preventable harm to those in social care. The Care Home Use of Medicines study (Barber et al 2009) concluded that two thirds of care home residents were subject to one or more medication errors. Reductions in the number of these errors in the nursing home setting will:1/ Improve the quality and safety of residents with diabetes2/ Improve staff moral and working practices as developments in patient safety improve efficiency and care delivery systems3/ Reduce costs through the improved utilisation of medicines and savings in staff time 4/ Enhance NHS medication management and reconciliation between health and social care sectors5/ Reduce re-admissions to hospital that are due to avoidable medication incidents in nursing homes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Feasibility and Acceptability of Medical Skin Camouflage for Recovery of Women with Self-Harm Scarring in Prison
Abstract: In prison, women prisoners comprise only 5% of the population yet are far more likely to commit suicide or self-harm than women in the community (3;4;5) or male prisoners (6). Health care services have significantly improved the management of acute SH crises within the community and the prison service (7) but there has been little focus on the recovery, psychosocial functioning and quality of life for living with self-harm scarring. Historically, medical skin camouflage clinics treat individuals suffering with disfiguring skin conditions such as burn scars. Evidence suggests that medical skin camouflage can play an important role in improving well being and recovery for these individuals (21;22; 23). However, all available data relates to non-SH scarring and there is little or no evidence about medical skin camouflage interventions with women prisoners in the UK. Primary Aim: To test feasibility and acceptability of medical skin camouflage for self-harm scarring in womenprisoners. Research questions:Is it feasible to deliver medical skin camouflage in a prison environment?What are the potential barriers to recruitment, participation, retention?Is medical skin camouflage acceptable to women recipients and stakeholders in the prison setting?What women, service-centred and research-centred outcomes should be adopted in future RCT? Plan of Investigation: Randomised, wait-list control design in four phases: Phase 1: -Obtain ethics and National Offender Management Service (NOMS) approvals; establish Research Management and Research Steering Group. -Explore likely barriers to introduction of medical skin camouflage in prison with stakeholders to develop strategies to overcome these in Phase 4. -Develop women, service and research-centred outcomes. In order to achieve this, we shall conduct 2 focus groups with women prisoners (including current self-harmers) and prison staff (6-10 in each, potentially mixed constituency group; 12-20 in total). Phase 2: Utilizing the findings from Phase 1, we shall adapt the medical skin camouflage. In particular, we shall address practical aspects of where, when and how treatment will be delivered in the prison. Phase 3: Changing Faces will train six or more long-term women prisoners as medical skin camouflage practitioners. Phase 4: 20 participants will be randomised to receive 6 weeks medical skin camouflage from trained women practitioners; a further 20 women prisoners will be wait-list controls and receive the intervention after study completion. Data collection. Baseline: basic demographics, women, service and research-centred outcomes from Phase I; psychosocial well­being; social functioning; HRQoL, everyday activities, self-harm and related life-events. Six weeks post-intervention: repeat baseline measures (apart from HRQoL); qualitative interviews to evaluate acceptability for participants and from camouflage practitioners on acceptability of training and delivering intervention to fellow prisoners. Three-months post-intervention pilot collection of resource use and HRQoL data, and participant follow-up data. Recruitment, participation, retention and causes of drop-out will also be collected. Prepare publications, conference abstracts, dissemination events and submit final report. Patient and NHS benefitsKey potential patient-benefits include increased self-esteem, quality of life and recovery for women prisoners with self-harm scarring; improved recovery and decreased likelihood of self-harming behaviour. An intervention to improve self-harm recovery may produce significant efficiency savings for prisons and NHS as the cost of treatment for this group will be reduced both within the prison setting and upon release when they continue to be NHS service users. Prisoners may become empowered to participate in work and social activities. Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Individual Placement and Support (IPS) for patients with offending histories - feasibility of an evidence-based approach in forensic mental health settings.
Abstract: Background Individuals who work find employment helps them deal with their mental health problems as well as improving their self-esteem and inspiring optimism 2, 3. Yet, the employment rate of patients with mental disorder, particularly those with offending histories, remains low. The latter group face various barriers to employment, including discrimination among employers and lack of relevant skills, making work much harder to secure4. Individual Placement and Support (IPS) aims to get people who want to work into competitive employment quickly and in accordance with their preferences. Besides benefits counselling, IPS provides tailored support, for the person and their employer, via employment specialists attached to clinical teams, with no time limit. IPS leads to an overall employment rate of 61% compared to 23% for controls 5. Compared to controls, individuals assigned to IPS keep their jobs for longer and work for more hours 6, 7. Several approaches to sustaining employment have been tested in offenders. Those approaches which work best share some of IPS s characteristics. Yet, despite compelling evidence and a favourable policy environment, studies on the implementation of IPS in forensic mental health settings are lacking. Aims To assess the feasibility of conducting a randomised controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate the effectiveness of IPS in forensic-psychiatric populations. Besides implementation of the IPS model in the forensic services, we will collect data on the feasibility of randomisation, recruitment and retention rates to IPS and waiting list controls; determine feasible effect sizes and the sample size required for a full RCT; describe outcomes (employment and educational activities, re-offending, mental health, self-esteem, social functioning and service use) and variation in outcomes in each group. We will evaluate the process of IPS implementation to (i) identify structural, legal, organizational and individual-level barriers and facilitators to implementation; (ii) assess the extent to which the services follow the principles of IPS; and (ii) assess the acceptability and usefulness of IPS amongst patients assigned to IPS. Method Patients aged 18 or over, who are on caseloads within the Community Forensic Services of Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Trust will be eligible to participate. Those who are unable to provide informed consent, not eligible to work in the UK, currently in open employment, or do not wish to work will be excluded. Following the implementation of IPS in the community forensic services, a feasibility study will commence by randomly assigning participants to IPS and waiting list controls. Besides collecting data about socio-demographics, diagnosis and offending history at baseline, employment and educational activities, mental health, social functioning, and service use data will be collected at baseline, 6 and 12 months, and re-offending data at 21 months. We will do a process evaluation by conducting qualitative interviews with staff to identify structural, legal, organizational and individual-level barriers and facilitators to implementation; IPS fidelity reviews to assess the extent to which the services follows the principles of IPS; and qualitative interviews with patients to assess the acceptability of IPS amongst patients assigned to IPS. Analyses We will describe the feasibility criteria for an RCT and describe outcome data using descriptive statistics. Qualitative data will be analysed using thematic analysis. IPS fidelity will be monitored through regular fidelity reviews against which the fidelity of the service to the model will be checked. Outputs In addition to assessing the feasibility of an RCT of IPS, this study will improve employment and psychosocial outcomes for the participants.
