Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Taunton and Somerset NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Supporting adult patients with Type 1 Diabetes (T1DM) to undertake exercise; Developing and piloting an education programme on exercise and Type 1 diabetes.
Abstract: Background Physical activity is an important part of the management plan in patients with T1DM. Regular exercise improves physical fitness and strength, reduces cardiovascular risk factors, mortality and improves well-being in patients with T1DM. Based on this evidence Diabetes UK and the American Diabetes Association recommends people with T1DM should undertake at least 150 min per week of moderate to vigorous aerobic exercise. In spite of these benefits retrospective and prospective studies show that less than 40% of patients with T1DM participate in regular exercise. Common reasons cited are fear of hypoglycaemia and lack of knowledge as to what nutritional and insulin dose changes are required. Studies from our group show that whilst 96% of 652 adults with T1DM felt that being informed about nutritional adjustments for safe exercise was important, only one in five people felt they had received this information. We also found that healthcare professionals feel ill-equipped to educate T1DM patients around exercise. Aims We will develop and pilot an education programme for patients and health care professionals to guide insulin and carbohydrate adjustment for safe and effective exercise. Methods We will follow the revised MRC guidelines for developing a multi-component or complex intervention. Following a literature review, we will develop an outline curriculum. Exercise and diabetes experts, people with T1DM, and experts in developing structured education programmes will inform the content of this curriculum. Accompanying supporting resources will be developed including web-based tools. This will then be tested in a small group of people with T1DM (n=8-10). Using action research methodology, this initial programme will be refined according to structured observation and patient feedback. We will repeat this process three times to ensure we have the best programme. It is anticipated that the contact time for such a programme will be 3-5 hours but this will be informed by the development work. The development phase of the participant programme will also inform both the training required by educators to deliver the intervention effectively and the process to ensure intervention fidelity during the pilot. This will involve production of a training manual, training resources and quality assessment tools. The second phase of the study is a randomised control pilot study in which 80 patients with T1DM will be randomised to receive the education programme or normal care. This will provide data on how many patients with T1DM are eligible and willing to take part in a study of this programme, the likely rates of adherence to the intervention, participant drop-out, the most effective outcome measures and the optimum way of measuring these and how best to recruit, randomise, treat and follow-up patients in a RCT of this programme. This information will enable us to design a definitive RCT to assess the effect of this education programme in people with T1DM. Potential benefits to the patients and the NHS Development of this programme will enable people with type 1 diabetes to acquire the skills, knowledge and confidence to exercise safely at all levels of physical activity, and with a reduced risk or fear of high/ low blood glucose levels. Over time, this could lead to more people with T1DM increasing physical activity levels and improving physical and mental health. Patients involved in the pilot study will see these benefits during the lifetime of their participation. If a following larger RCT work is successful, the programme could be formally commissioned and implemented nationally within a 7-10 year period to benefit all with T1DM.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Surrey and Borders Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Group Mindfulness Based Therapy for distressing persecutory delusions: A pilot study for a randomised controlled trial.
Abstract: Background There is increasing evidence showing the potential benefits of mindfulness for individuals with a diagnosis of Schizophrenia (Chadwick et al, 2005, 2009; Dannahy et al, 2011; Langer et al, 2012). However, research to date has focused on individuals who experience auditory hallucinations, and research is yet to examine the benefit and process of change of mindfulness for people with persecutory delusions. To date there are only 2 single case studies (demonstrating proof of concept) showing initial promise for mindfulness-based therapy (MBT) for reducing depression associated with persecutory delusions (Ellett, 2013). A more methodologically robust investigation of mindfulness for persecutory delusions is required; however, at this stage, a fully-powered RCT would not be a judicious use of public money as the key parameters for such a trial (e.g. effect size, recruitment and retention) are not known. Aims The research question for the full RCT is: Following the intervention, in comparison to participants receiving treatment as usual (TAU), participants receiving mindfulness-based therapy (plus TAU) will report significantly lower depression, better psychological health, significantly lower levels of distress, significantly lower amounts of rumination and significantly greater progress towards recovery. This full trial research question has informed the aims for this proposed pilot study. In order to address this research question in a full trial we first need to have: (a) a reasonable estimate of the between-group effect size on the primary outcome measure (depression), (b) an understanding of rates of recruitment and (c) a strategy to maximise retention - hence the need for this pilot study. Plan of investigation Participants will be randomised to receive either mindfulness-based therapy or treatment as usual. Mindfulness therapy, specifically adapted for people with distressing psychotic experience, will be delivered using our manusalised 12-session group protocol. This is consistent with the approach in other disorders including depression (Segal et al, 2002) and those who experience hearing voices (Chadwick et al, 2009). The primary outcome measure for the study is depression. Other outcomes that will be measured include quality of life, psychotic symptoms and progress towards recovery. In addition to measuring outcomes, we will also measure potential mechanisms of change, that is, the psychological processes that we expect to change more during MBT than during TAU. These will include rumination, avoidance and negative schema. If the pilot reveals a between-group effect size in favour of the mindfulness intervention, an application will then be made to HTA for a full randomised-controlled trial. Group-based mindfulness is a potentially resource-efficient therapy in comparison to individual therapy. Potential Benefits to Patients & the NHS This study will provide information for a full trial that will ascertain if group mindfulness therapy has the potential to reduce depression and distress, and improve psychological health for individuals with distressing persecutory delusions. Therefore, this pilot study and the full trial to follow have the potential to improve the lives of people living with distressing persecutory delusions and their families. The group-based nature of the mindfulness intervention has the potential to incur significant savings for the NHS, as this is a more cost-effective intervention than individual therapy. Our manualised 12-session group protocol is very clear and easy to follow, such that the intervention would be rolled out within the NHS if it is found to be effective.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: “Test n Treat (TnT)”: a cluster randomised feasibility trial of frequent, rapid testing and same day, on-site treatment to reduce rates of chlamydia and gonorrhoea in high risk Further Education College students.
Abstract: Background Young people attending London FE colleges have high rates of chlamydia and gonorrhoea3;5;10. Both infections can lead to serious complications including ectopic pregnancy and infertility. But screening rates are low4;11, and young people usually need to attend a healthcare facility to get tested. Our small pilot in a FE college5 and economic analyses6;9suggested that offering new, rapid, on-site tests each term might be an effective way to reach them, and could reduce transmission rates and save NHS costs. Objective To assess the feasibility of conducting a future trial in FE colleges to investigate if frequent, rapid, on-site testing and treatment (TnT) reduces chlamydia/gonorrhoea rates in sexually active male and female students aged 16-24 years. Design: Cluster-randomised feasibility trial over seven months with parallel qualitative and economic assessments. Study timing is pragmatic: TnT will be offered to intervention colleges in the autumn term (one month after recruitment) and spring term (4m) with outcome assessment (all colleges) in the summer term (7m). Baseline recruitment Randomisation 1 month 4 months 7 months follow up Questionnaire and Sample for storage 3 Control colleges Thank you text Thank you text Questionnaire and Sample for testing. Treat if necessary 3 Intervention colleges Invitation text TnT Invitation text TnT Setting and recruitment Six FE colleges in London. We will recruit 80 sexually active students aged 16-24 from public areas at each site3;5;10. Participants will be asked to provide samples (urines for males, self-taken vaginal swabs for females) at baseline and after 7 months and to complete questionnaires on sexual lifestyle and healthcare use at both time points. (As previously3, all participants will be informed that baseline samples will not be tested for 7 months and advised to get screened separately from the study if they are allocated to the control group.) Colleges will be randomly allocated into intervention (TnT) or control group (no TnT). Intervention colleges: TnT at one and four months One month after recruitment each intervention college will be visited on two consecutive days by the “TnT” team. The 80 participating students in each college will be texted and invited to come for on-site rapid chlamydia/gonorrhoea TnT. As at recruitment they will be invited to provide a sample, but this time the sample will be tested immediately using the 15 minutes Alere iNAAT system. Participants will be encouraged to wait for the result which will be available in 20-30 minutes. Students with positive results will be invited to the college nurse s room for treatment, partner notification, advice and follow up by a visiting nurse health adviser. (Students positive for gonorrhoea will have a confirmatory test and GUM referral.) At four months participants in intervention colleges will again be invited to provide samples for TnT. Control colleges: no TnT Participants from control colleges will receive texts one and four months after recruitment thanking them for being in the study. Outcome assessment at 7 months Participants from both groups will be invited to provide a) repeat questionnaires b) samples for immediate testing, and treatment if necessary. Outcome measures 1. Key values to inform feasibility, sample size and timescales of a trial of TnT in FE colleges: Recruitment rates (at baseline) TnT uptake rates (at one and four months) Follow-up rates (at 7 months) Prevalence of chlamydia/gonorrhoea in participants at each site at baseline and 7 months. 2. A perspective on the acceptability of TnT in FE colleges, emerging from qualitative interviews8 with purposively sampled college staff (n=12) and students (n=30). 3. Estimate of the cost per person screened and treated in TnT versus usual care

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Hertfordshire Partnership University NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A feasibility study of a psychological intervention to address alcohol misuse for people with mild to moderate learning disabilities living in the community
Abstract: Background: Alcohol is the commonest and most widely available psychoactive substance. With most people with learning disabilities living in the community, there is increasing concern about their exposure to alcohol, increased vulnerability to alcohol misuse, and the ability of services to provide adequate support to those who experience psychological and social difficulties as a result of misuse. Brief intervention and extended brief intervention (EBI) are recommended as first line treatments for the general population who have alcohol use disorders (AUD). EBI has been used in secure in-patient settings but to date EBI has not been evaluated in a community based population with learning disabilities. Aims: The aim of this project is to assess the feasibility of evaluating EBI for adults with mild to moderate learning disabilities through a single-blind, randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing EBI as an adjunct to usual care versus usual care. Issues including acceptability of the intervention, suitability of outcome measures, compliance, recruitment and retention, will be explored. Qualitative interviews will also be conducted with service users, carers and service providers to examine their perceptions of the intervention and its acceptability. We intend to use this pilot data to prepare for a definitive RCT, with the intention of applying for funding from the HTA. Methods: Based on the MRC guidelines for complex interventions we propose a three stage design: 1. Development of the precise content of the intervention and related materials based on interventions currently available for the general population and from the literature in learning disabilities. This will be piloted and refined in order to carry out a feasibility trial. 2. Fifty people with mild to moderate learning disabilities and alcohol use disorders (AUD; Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test>8) and their carers, where available, will be recruited to a two-armed RCT and receive either EBI in addition to usual care or usual care only. The EBI, provided by a trained therapist, will involve five half-hour weekly sessions, which will be based on motivational interviewing. A final one hour session, focussed on maintenance, will be delivered at eight weeks. Assessments of the participants and their carers will be conducted at baseline, end of treatment and at 3 months. We will use measures that detect changes in AUD, mental health, physical health status, knowledge and behaviours, and use of services. 3. Service users, carers and service providers (involved in providing usual support to participants, but not involved in providing EBI) will also give their perspectives on the intervention and its acceptability in qualitative interviews at 12 weeks. We will also attempt to conduct interviews with 50% of those who drop out of treatment to ascertain their views and reasons for dropping out. Potential benefits: We will refine the EBI in line with the findings from this study. These materials will be made available to general practices, substance misuse services and learning disabilities services, enabling widespread use by health providers within the NHS. We anticipate that the materials could also be of use to private and third sector providers as they may become involved in delivering treatments to people with mild to moderate learning disabilities within an inclusion agenda. The findings from this study will inform our preparation for a definitive large scale RCT to test the efficacy of EBI in this population. Managing alcohol misuse should lead to improvements in health and quality of life. Costs to the NHS will be reduced through decreased overall service use due to improved health. The programme would also ensure a more equitable service for service users with learning disabilities and fill the current gap in service delivery to this population.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A Feasibility Study of High-intensity Interval Exercise Training before Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Repair (HIT AAA)
Abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a frequently lethal disease affecting 4 to 8% of men aged >65 years. Mechanical intervention (i.e., open surgery using a prosthetic graft to repair the aneurysm or endovascular placement of a stent graft) is the only effective treatment for preventing aneurysm-related rupture and death; however, aneurysm repair itself carries high risk. The 30-day mortality rate associated with elective open repair is higher in the UK than in comparable countries: 7 versus 3.5%. Hence, there is currently a national drive, coordinated through the AAA Quality Improvement Plan, to improve outcomes for AAA repair. Low cardiopulmonary fitness increases the risk of early post-operative complications and death after open AAA repair and other major non-cardiac procedures. Therefore, fitness should be optimised before aneurysm repair. High-intensity interval exercise training (HIT) is a potent, time-efficient and low-cost strategy for enhancing cardiopulmonary fitness. However, the feasibility and effectiveness of HIT in patients awaiting AAA repair is unknown. We are proposing a feasibility study for a definitive randomised controlled trial of a pre-operative HIT intervention to improve post-operative outcomes in patients undergoing elective repair of an AAA. The main aim is to identify the primary outcome and estimated sample size for the subsequent trial. A secondary aim is to investigate the suitability of HIT, primarily in terms of compliance, acceptability, and its impact on cardiopulmonary fitness. This is a two-centre, two-arm, parallel-group randomised trial. A minimum of 50 patients awaiting elective repair of a 5.5 to 7.0 cm infra-renal AAA will be randomised, in a 1:1 ratio of open surgical to endovascular repair, to HIT or usual care control. Patients randomised to HIT will complete three hospital-based exercise sessions per week, for 4 weeks. Each session will include 4 minutes of hard-to-very hard cycling followed by 4 minutes of easy cycling, repeated 4 times. Outcomes to be assessed before randomisation and 24 to 48 hours before aneurysm repair (week 5 where possible) include ventilatory threshold via cardiopulmonary exercise testing, maximum AAA diameter via trans-abdominal ultrasound, and health-related quality of life using the SF-36 and EQ-5D questionnaires. In the post-operative period, we will record destination (ward or critical care unit), organ-specific morbidity using the Post-operative Morbidity Survey Score, mortality, and the durations of critical care and hospital stay. Twelve weeks after discharge, participants will be interviewed via telephone to re-assess quality of life and determine post-discharge healthcare utilisation. The costs associated with the exercise intervention and healthcare utilisation (in-hospital and post-discharge) will be calculated. A definitive randomised trial will be considered feasible if an appropriate primary outcome is identified and if the lower limit of the 90% confidence interval for the proportion of the exercise group complying with the intervention is ≥67%. A patient will be deemed compliant if they complete ≥75% of the scheduled sessions plus all maintenance sessions if surgery is delayed. For the potential primary outcomes of a definitive trial, the likely effect of the exercise intervention will be estimated via standard intervention minus control comparisons. We will examine the disposition of the 90% confidence interval for the observed effect to the minimum clinically important difference for each variable. A prospective economic evaluation will also be rehearsed to develop and refine methods for the subsequent trial. The potential patient benefits of pre-operative HIT include increased cardiopulmonary fitness, reduced rates of early post-operative complications and death, and reduced hospital length of stay. Given the low cost of implementing pre-operative HIT, the potential reduction in healthcare resource utilisation would likely

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Optimising palliative care for older people in the community: development and evaluation of a new short term integrated service
Abstract: Background People are living longer and dying with frailty and, for many, increasingly complex co-morbidities and health needs. Palliative care is advocated for older people to improve the quality of life, but with little evidence of effectiveness 4 5 6. This study intends to work with NHS staff in a community trust to develop and evaluate a new STIPC service for frail older people with complex needs living at home or in a care home. Short-term palliative care could be cost effective and appropriate because it relies on existing communityservices, but with additional shared support from specialist palliative care (SPC) services at points of actual or anticipated decline in wellbeing and uncertain outcome. Aims The study s primary aim is to develop and evaluate the STIPC service for frail older people living at home or in a care home. The service is delivered through integrated professional working (IPW) between SPC services and community nursing teams, and GPs and geriatricians as main providers of care. This is a feasibility study to develop procedures for a full RCT. The secondary aims pertain to: developing the methodology for a full RCT and a model of IPW between generalist and specialist nurses. The project uses two phases: phase I developing the intervention (objectives 1-2); and phase II feasibility of the intervention (objectives 3-5). To develop the new STIPC service using a post-bereavement postal survey to relatives/carers on preferences of care and palliative outcomes for older people by place of death To consult with stakeholders (e.g. recipients and providers/commissioners of care) on the survey findings and identify the STIPC components and outcomes. To develop the methodology for a future full RCT by testing procedures in order to calculate sample size, manage attrition and missing data, and to guide future assessment of the cost-effectiveness of the service. To refine the intervention for the full RCT and a model of IPW, using nested qualitative studies exploring experiences of a) service receipt to attain personal goals and b) barriers and facilitators to IPW. To test the impact of STIPC on the primary outcome of palliative outcomes (POS-8), and secondary outcomes of symptom management (POS -S), carer burden (Zarit Carer Burden Inventory), carer mastery (Lawton caregiver mastery scale), and service use (CSRI). Plan of investigation The research methods follow the MRC guidance to develop and evaluate complex interventions 7. The study uses two phases: Phase 1 intervention development using a post-bereavement survey to model preferences for care, palliative care outcomes and service use by place of death; and a stakeholder consultations on the findings to develop the intervention with 1) older people and their carers, and 2) representatives from service providers, commissioners, and voluntary sector using Transparent Expert Consultation (TEC) of nominal group to generate recommendations and identify divergence, and on-line/postal survey to prioritise the intervention components and outcomes3. Phase 2 feasibility and procedures to develop the methodology for a full RCT with 52participants randomly allocated to receive STIPC or usual care. The primary outcome is the impact on palliative outcomes, and secondary outcomes on symptom management, carer burden and service use assessed at baseline, 6 and 12 weeks. Nested qualitative studies at intervention completion to examine experiences of service receipt (n=12) and barriers and facilitators to IPW (n=16). Potential impact Improving older people access to palliative care services could impact on patients and cares quality of life and reduce NHS costs. This is a feasibility study that if found beneficial will develop procedures for full RCT, and a refine model of integrated professional working, or if negative inform future interventions and service developments.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Adapting and testing a brief intervention to reduce maternal anxiety during pregnancy.
Abstract: There is now a substantial body of evidence from observational cohort studies demonstrating that anxiety in mothers during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of a range of short and long term adverse outcomes in their children (Talge et al, 2007). These include higher rates of preterm delivery (Diego et al, 2009), impaired cognitive functioning (Bergman et al, 2007; Burns et al, in press), difficult temperament (Davis et al, 2007; Field et al, 2004) and behavioural and emotional problems (O Connor et al, 2002). Despite robust evidence for an association between antenatal maternal anxiety and adverse child outcomes, there is no systematic evidence from clinical trials to show whether treating antenatal anxiety in mothers will improve the outcomes of their children. The effects of intervening early in development could be large, because of the enormous cognitive and socio-emotional developments that occur in the foetal period and the first years of life, and the apparent long-lasting effects of exposure to maternal anxiety during pregnancy (Talge et al, 2007). In light of this evidence, it is crucial that the NHS develops and delivers effective and accessible interventions for anxiety during pregnancy. Evidence indicates that the association between antenatal anxiety and subsequent child difficulties is linear (Bergman et al, 2007), suggesting that efforts to reduce anxiety across the population of pregnant women will yield benefits for the greatest number of children. Brief, cost-effective interventions are required to meet this broader population need. In addition, previous studies have highlighted the critical importance of tailoring interventions to meet the specific needs of pregnant women, in terms of both the therapeutic focus and the mode of delivery. One such intervention that has been developed and had positive preliminary evaluation in Australia is the guided self-help intervention Towards Parenthood (Milgrom et al, 2011). In a randomised controlled trial of 143 women significant reductions in maternal anxiety were reported (Cohen s d = 0.58). The key question that will be addressed in the current research is. 1. What is the acceptability and feasibility of delivering a workbook-based parenting intervention integrated within group-based midwife-led care to treat anxiety in women in the antenatal period? Phase one of the research will involve testing the existing “Towards Parenthood” intervention with a small group of pregnant women, which will allow us to test how well the intervention can be integrated into routine antenatal care. As we intend for the intervention to be delivered alongside existing routine NHS antenatal care, we plan to modify the support element for use in a brief group-based format of 3 sessions, rather than offering weekly individual telephone support as was offered in the trial by Milgrom et al (2011). This has strong potential to make the intervention more cost-effective and more robust for delivery within the shifting NHS environment. It will also make the intervention much more widely available for pregnant women affected by anxiety. We will gather feedback from the women and midwives in the test group on the relevance and acceptability of the intervention to pregnant women experiencing anxiety. This will inform the final adaptation of the Towards Parenthood intervention to an NHS context. Phase two will incorporate the further development and testing of the Towards Parenthood intervention. The intervention will be modified in the light of the work undertaken in phase one, and then tested for feasibility and acceptability in a randomised controlled trial. In sum, the proposed research will lead to the development of an effective, cost-effective and acceptable treatment for women with anxiety symptoms which could be made widely available, thereby meeting critical patient and NHS needs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Is my blood pressure high? An investigation of the optimum method of diagnosing and monitoring hypertension in different ethnic groups
Abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular outcomes for people from some minority ethnic groups are worse than those of the White group. This increase in cardiovascular risk is due to an interplay of complex factors that includes genotype, phenotype, environment and inequalities in access to health care. Measurement of risk factors including blood pressure (BP) is assumed to be equivalent between populations but no evidence exists to underpin this assumption which is vital in both the diagnosis and management of hypertension. Should these assumptions be erroneous, subsequent inadequate care maybe partly to blame for the observed outcomes. This research has importance locally where significant proportions of patients are drawn from diverse and disadvantaged minority populations.AimsThis study has three main research questions:1. How often and in what ways does monitoring of blood pressure occur (including professional monitoring, community monitoring and self monitoring) and how does it differ between White and *minority ethnic populations?2. Are the thresholds for diagnosis and management of hypertension comparable for White and minority ethnic populations using different measurement modalities: office blood pressure, ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) and self monitoring?3. What preferences for blood pressure measurement do people from White and minority ethnic populations have?* This includes South Asian (i.e. of Indian, Pakistani or Bangladeshi origin), Black African-Caribbean, and Irish.Plan of InvestigationThe proposed research design consists of a survey followed by a validation study assessing the impact of ethnic group on diagnostic and management thresholds in the management of hypertension. The survey, of 8000 people including representative samples of both ethnic group, and blood pressure range will aim to elucidate current blood pressure monitoring patterns (self, third party (pharmacy etc), health professional), confirm ethnic group and identify participants for the validation study. In the latter, 800 subjects will undergo blood pressure measurements using standard office equipment, ambulatory monitoring and home monitoring with comparison between ethnic minority groups of the difference between the various monitoring modalities in terms of both diagnostic and management thresholds.Potential ImpactThe key impact of this work will be to provide an evidence base for the appropriate measurement of blood pressure in diverse and disadvantaged communities. BP measurement is important in the diagnosis and management of hypertension and both situations will be evaluated. The results will either confirm equivalence of the three measurement modalities in different populations or show clinically important differences. Given that 12% of the adult population of the UK are currently undergoing treatment for hypertension and perhaps another 20% remain undetected, any study showing that different assumptions regarding blood pressure measurement are needed for different populations would be widely applicable and lead to changes in practice within 3-5 years.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Development and evaluation of an information service for people living with long-term conditions
Abstract: BackgroundFollowing user consultation, the White Paper ‘Our Health, Our Care, Our Say’[1] prioritised information provision as key to facilitating self-care. By 2008 everyone with a long-term condition (LTC) and their carers should routinely be able to access information, or be signposted to advice and support, that helps them manage their condition through the issue of an information prescription (IP). Working in collaboration with the UK Parkinson’s Disease Society (PDS), Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust (NHCT) was a pilot site for IPs for Parkinson’s disease (PD), but there is a need to continue to develop and evaluate locally-based information services for all people with LTCs and their carers, in line with Department of Health (DH) policy.AimsBuilding on our work in a national pilot, we will develop and evaluate a personalised information service based in an acute trust for patients and carers managing specified LTCs. We aim to:•Use action research methods to consult stakeholders, design, test and modify the IP process.•Train healthcare professionals to issue IPs, and Trust information services staff and voluntary information support workers to dispense information.•Develop online resources accessible through the Trust website•Examine the delivery, accessibility and use of the service, and ensure replicability.•Examine user satisfaction with the service and the impact of IPs on follow up consultations.•Compare with baseline data to establish the impact of the service on satisfaction with information and impact on coping.Plan of InvestigationUsing action research methods, stakeholders will be consulted in meetings and focus groups to design, develop, evaluate then modify a personalised information service. Health professionals (HPs) will be trained to issue IPs and information managers, volunteer staff and voluntary organisation information support workers to manage and dispense information. A process evaluation, including documentary analysis of minutes of meetings and issuing records, and interviews with service users and staff will identify who has accessed the service, and how, and allow transferability to other acute services. A controlled baseline and follow-up survey will compare satisfaction with the service and its impact. Follow-up interviews with HPs will explore the way IPs have been used in consultations.Potential ImpactPatients and carers will be helped to identify information they need to manage their LTCs, and access and understand the information provided. They will be signposted to appropriate health and social care professionals to talk through information given, and other local services that can help. This project will improve patient, carer and professional satisfaction with information compared with current provision, and support compliance of local Trusts with DH policies[1,2] by integrating advice and support with care planning and facilitating self-care in the management of LTCs. The experience gained, and tools developed, will help to inform the national implementation of IPs, improve local provision, extend IPs to other LTCs and provide an evidence base for this model of care.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Preventable Incidents, Survival and Mortality Study (PRISM)
Abstract: BackgroundImproving safety is a national priority for patients and for the NHS. Estimates of the number of adverse events have been a major drive to improve patient safety. Extrapolation from international case record review studies has led to widely quoted estimates of 25,000-40,000 UK deaths in adults per year caused by adverse events. The validity of these figures has been questioned. Recently the National Audit Office and Public Accounts Committee have expressed concern about the lack of information regarding the number of deaths from adverse events in acute hospitals. Therefore there is a need for a more accurate estimates to inform political and public debate and to identify those areas where interventions to improve safety will have most impact.AimsThe aim of this study is to improve the safety of NHS healthcare services. The objectives are to:•Provide a baseline estimate of the number of deaths in adult patients who die during or soon after hospital admission associated with adverse events•Make judgments as to the contribution of the adverse event to the death of the patient and to determine how many of these events were preventable•Identify factors contributing to adverse events associated with patient deaths •Estimate the length of life lost due to deaths caused by preventable adverse events •Support priority setting for national and local actions to substantially reduce harm from patient safety incidents and improve the quality and efficiency of NHS care•Disseminate findings to the widest possible audiencePlan of InvestigationA stratified random sample of 10 acute NHS hospitals in England will be selected. In each hospital a random sample of 100 case records related to adult patients who have died during the hospital admission or within 30 days of discharge will be reviewed to identify adverse events. The sample size is based on estimates from a similar US study. The review will be use methods developed for one of the largest UK studies of adverse events to date. Case record reviews will be conducted by trained doctors using a structured form. A second review will be undertaken in difficult cases and on a random sample of all reviewed records to check for reliability. Reviewers will be asked to judge which adverse events were preventable and by how much a patient’s life was shortened by the event.Potential ImpactThe study’s findings will fill a hole in our knowledge and understanding of deaths related to safety incidents within hospitals. A robust estimate of the level of fatal and preventable harm will support the identification of priorities for action to reduce preventable mortality and morbidity (locally, nationally and internationally), and support the development of solutions aimed at reducing high impact incidents. This has the potential to achieve major benefits for patients in terms of reduced harm, as well as increased confidence in, and financial savings for, the NHS. A better estimate will provide a baseline against which the completeness of reporting to the NPSA can be gauged and help rebalance public and political debate around risks of death and severe harm.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Variation in waiting times for teenagers and young adults with cancer in England: determining the effect of patient and NHS factors
Abstract: BackgroundThe treatment of teenagers and young adults (TYA) with cancer presents particular challenges. They develop a distinct spectrum of tumours and can be disadvantaged in falling between treatment approaches established for younger or older populations. They also have their illness during a time of rapid physical and psychological change. Delivery of cancer care for TYA varies enormously in the UK which may lead to delays in diagnosis and there is no national picture of their care pathways, including waiting times. We aim to address a crucial knowledge gap by exploiting a national TYA dataset for 15-24 year olds, examining diagnostic delay through waiting times (time from 1st GP referral to diagnosis). Findings will help to improve services and reduce diagnostic delay for this vulnerable group.Aims(i) To identify diagnostic delay for TYA in England, defined as the time from referral to diagnosis using cancer waiting times data for 15-24 year olds diagnosed since 2003.(ii) To determine how much national variation in diagnostic delay is explained by differences in type of care (type of hospital, level of age-appropriate care) and NHS care pathways (cancer networks), allowing for patient casemix (cancer type, age).(iii) To identify demographic factors such as ethnicity and socio-economic circumstances that may be associated with variation in diagnostic delay.(iv) To assess whether longer waiting times from referral to diagnosis are associated with an increased number or length of hospital admissions during and after cancer treatment, allowing for relevant NHS and patient factors.Plan of InvestigationClinical and demographic data, including cancer waiting times and hospital admissions, will be extracted for subjects aged 15-24 years between 2003-2006 (n=5,700) from the new national TYA dataset held by the North West Cancer Intelligence Service, the lead cancer registry for TYA.Length of wait will be summarised by tumour type, age, sex, ethnicity and deprivation level and compared to national comparative data for adults to identify the extent of diagnostic delay. Multilevel Poisson regression modelling will determine the extent of variation in waiting times nationally for TYA and if it can be explained by treatment location and NHS care pathways whilst allowing for patient factors. The effect of waiting time on the frequency and length of admission will be examined.Potential ImpactIdentifying potential bottlenecks in the NHS for TYA cancer referral processes will be a key outcome, and is central to the NICE Improving Outcomes Guidance (IOG) for young people with cancer, currently being implemented nationally. Improvement in the delivery of care for TYA is a key component of the IOG and this work will inform this implementation to minimise delays in diagnosis. Results will be fed back to cancer networks and used to inform Specialist Commissioners involved in improving TYA delivery of care nationally. The work will identify areas of TYA healthcare delivery which require modification to enable patients to be treated more quickly, potentially improving survival and reducing morbidity after cancer.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: IMPROVE-Stroke: IMproving the PRevention Of Vascular Events after Stroke or TIA – a randomised controlled pilot trial of nurse independent prescriber-led care pathway-based risk factor management
Abstract: BackgroundThere is good evidence of a gap between the findings from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that risk factor modification after stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA) prevents further vascular events, and the implementation of those findings in clinical practice. The resulting failure to fully implement the existing evidence jeopardises the large benefits to patients and the NHS that should otherwise accrue, yet evidence to support effective risk factor management strategies in Primary Care after stroke is lacking. One novel approach may be care led by a Nurse Independent Prescriber, and a recent Cochrane review concluded that this form of intervention warrants further evaluation. However, such a novel and complex intervention requires pilot data prior to a definitive RCT.AimsThis pilot trial is an essential preliminary to a definitive RCT assessing the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of a Nurse Independent Prescriber-led care pathway compared to current practice. The purpose of the pilot is to ensure the design and methods of that future trial are sound, practicable and feasible.The aims of the pilot are:1. To test the feasibility, practicality, safety and acceptability of the study design and protocol;2. To resolve practical issues for the conduct of the future RCT such as the reproducibility of the outcome measures, and recruitment and attrition rates;3. To investigate the acceptability of the care pathway to patients and general practitioners (GPs) and to refine it prior to the full RCT;4. To inform the sample size calculation for the full trial.Plan of InvestigationThe pilot study will be a scaled down version of the future RCT, and will run for 24 months. 40 patients with minor stroke or TIA and clinic systolic BP (SBP) above 140 mmHg will be recruited within one month of their event. They will be randomised to usual care (risk factor management in primary care according to local guidelines), or to a 6-month programme of follow-up visits with a Nurse Independent Prescriber, who will manage risk factors according to an incremental care pathway. All participants will then be followed up after a further 6 months of usual care. A nested qualitative study will explore patients’ experiences and GP views of this programme of assertive risk factor management, to improve its acceptability prior to the definitive RCT.Potential ImpactThe burden of stroke in the UK is enormous – 110,000 strokes per year at a total economic cost of over £7bn. One quarter of strokes are recurrences, and BP reduction after stroke or TIA is the most effective intervention to prevent recurrent vascular events. Yet a failure to implement the existing evidence for secondary stroke prevention leaves many patients at high risk of recurrence and fails to realise the full benefits for the NHS. Achieving a SBP reduction similar to that shown to be feasible in younger subjects would yield a greater than 32% reduction in recurrent stroke, preventing over 6000 strokes/year with a saving of over £92m in direct care costs – if achieved, this would represent a far greater health gain than that from thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Norfolk and Waveney Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Cluster randomised controlled trial of the Serious Mental Illness Health Improvement Profile (HIP)
Abstract: BackgroundPeople with serious mental illness (SMI) die up to 25 years younger than the general population. As a population they receive inadequate physical health and this is unacceptable. Modifiable cardiovascular risk factors, rates of respiratory disease, some cancers, and HIV are highly prevalent. Nurses are ideally placed to assess and intervene but current preparation for this work is inadequate. Current 'wellbeing' programmes are complex and costly and focus almost exclusively on modifying cardiovascular risk factors at the expense of other aspects of physical health. The SMI Health Improvement Profile (HIP) is a brief pragmatic tool (competency training takes 6 hours) to enable practitioners to profile patients physical health and promote evidence/guideline based intervention.AimsThe overall aim of this study is to demonstrate the efficacy of the HIP in improving SMI patients physical health. To achieve this we will establish if, compared to treatment as usual (TAU) (at the 52 week study end point) patients who receive the HIP:1. Show improved physical and mental health;2. Modify cardio-vascular risk and lifestyle factors.Additionally we will: 3. Establish the cost effectiveness of the HIP;4. Explore the process experience of using the HIP from the point of view of patients, mental health nurses, psychiatrists and GPs;5. Examine the impact of the HIP on communication between secondary and primary care services;6. Establish the effect of HIP training on nurse attitudes to and knowledge about physical health in SMI patients.Plan of InvestigationA single blind parallel group cluster RCT comparing the HIP with TAU in a sample of 50 nurses and 200 SMI patients in receipt of services provided by the Norfolk Trust (NWMHFT). Nurses will be the unit of randomisation with eligible SMI patients selected at random from their caseload by their locality manager. Nurses in the HIP group will receive 6 hours training to be competent in the HIP. If nurses drop out of the study patients will be transferred to the care of a HIP/non-HIP nurse to ensure continuity of intervention. Measures will be completed at baseline and 52 weeks by an RA blind to treatment allocation.The primary end point will be change in the physical health component sub-scale of the SF-36v2. The trial will strictly adhere to CONSORT standards of reporting cluster RCTs.Potential ImpactIf the results of our trial are positive nurses across the NHS working with SMI patients can use the HIP to identify and plan care and treatment to enhance physical health. Our aim would be that every SMI patient in England completes a HIP every year; leading to evidence based phyiscal health care and treatment, enhanced quality of life and, ultimately increased life expectancy. Achiving this aim is made more likely by the relative brevity of HIP training for nurses and a focus on enhancing communication between primary and secondary care services.

Award_Title: Risks, roles and responsibilities: Evaluating falls in inpatient mental healthcare settings for older people.
Abstract: BackgroundThe publication of the National Service Framework for older people identified fall prevention as one of eight key areas of activity to improve care. Despite advances in fall prevention activities, older people with mental health conditions being cared for in mental health settings appear to have been neglected by practitioners, academics and policy makers. Impaired mental status and treatment with psychotrophic medication are key risk factors for falls. Falls in mental health settings represent a major issue of concern for patients, their families and the NHS. There is a need to evaluate the experience and context of falls in mental health settings as a precursor to the development of an intervention to provide improved care and services which could be tested via an RCT.AimsTo evaluate how falls prevention and management are understood and experienced, in inpatient mental health settings providing care for older people.To analyse current local and national falls policy and guidelines specific to mental health settings. To develop local policy, practice guidelines and patient and carer information which is fit for purpose and relevant to mental health settings for older people, and make recommendations for national policy.Plan of InvestigationThe study is designed as an in depth three phase case study.Phase 1: Exploratory case study. To evaluate how the risks, roles, responsibilities, guidelines and policy for fall prevention are understood and enacted across the Trust at a number of levels from the patient, carer and staff interfaces to managerial and strategic levels.Phase 2: In-depth study of 2 in-patient clinical settings will enable a more detailed explanatory analysis of the experience of older people as they experience falls and care provision.Phase 3: A series of working groups with staff and patient/carer groups, building on the data arising from the study, will lead to a one day stakeholder consensus event to develop relevant guidelines and policy for use locally and to make recommendations for national policyPotential ImpactThe study presents a model of working that has at its centre a local collaboration of older service users and carers, NHS staff and academics to enable us to address an area of mutual concern and enable immediate impact and implementation through local service development. We propose a high quality social research study with a group of people who so far have been neglected within fall research: older people with a concurrent mental health condition, who can be at additional risk of falls, especially when taking certain medications. This project will develop realistic, patient-centred, local and national recomendations for clinical practice and policy, standard setting and audit which is of direct relevance for the care of older people with mental health conditions.

Award_Title: Defining obesity cut-off points for the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer among minority ethnic groups: a prospective cohort study using national linked electronic health records
Abstract: Aim We aim to prospectively identify ethnic-specific obesity BMI cut-off points for the risk of type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, colorectal cancer, postmenopausal breast cancer and all-cause mortality, among adults from minority ethnic groups that are risk equivalent to the current obesity BMI cut-off point set for white populations. Background The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and World Health Organization (WHO) definition of obesity, e.g. body mass index (BMI) ≥ 30 kg/m2 may underestimate risk of chronic disease in non-white adults. Ethnic minority populations have been reported to experience a higher risk of diabetes at lower obesity BMI cut-off points than white populations. NICE does not consider the evidence sufficiently strong to make recommendations on the use of new BMI cut-off points to classify individual minority ethnics groups as obese. Methods We will assemble a cohort of adults, aged ≥18 years and free from diagnosed type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, colorectal cancer, postmenopausal breast cancer at baseline (white, black, South Asian, Chinese, Arab, and mixed ethnic groups) using linked electronic health records covering primary care, hospital admissions, acute coronary syndrome registry and mortality registry (CALIBER platform). Ethnic-specific obesity BMI cut-off points in association with incident type 2 diabetes, incident myocardial infarction, incident ischaemic stroke, incident colorectal cancer, incident postmenopausal breast cancer and all-cause mortality, respectively will be estimated using Poisson regression, adjusting for age and sex. Analyses will be repeated with additional adjustment for smoking status, and practice-level Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) score. Timelines for delivery Precise and statistically stable obesity BMI cut-off points among adults belonging to minority ethnic groups will be available to NHS health professionals in 12 months. Anticipated impact and dissemination Anticipated impact includes: (a) increased identification of obesity among minority ethnic groups to trigger culturally-appropriate action to prevent type 2 diabetes, myocardial infarction, ischaemic stroke, colorectal cancer, postmenopausal breast cancer and death at lower BMI cut-off points than white populations; (b) greater awareness of increased risk of chronic disease at lower BMI cut-off points than adults from white populations; (c) informing Department of Health & Social Care and NICE Guidelines on identification of obesity among adults belonging to minority ethnic groups. After 12 months, the ethnic-specific obesity BMI cut-off points will be disseminated across the NHS (especially primary care) and existing local minority ethnic information networks. We will ensure that dissemination of the study s findings is respectful and avoids stigmatising people living with obesity. Patient and Public Involvement We collaborate with the Ethnic Health Forum (a charity serving the health needs of minority ethnic groups) and their members who are both service users and part of the community. We will have input from a community advisory board. Ethnic Health Forum members will be involved in research, project management and dissemination.

Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Investigating contextual determinants of cardiovascular disease in older adults
Abstract: The aim is to understand how aspects of the neighbourhood where people live (e.g. services, space, crime, price of food) influences their health and explains differences in cardiovascular risk factors between populations. This study will collect data on community determinants of smoking, diet and physical activity influencing older people living in 23 British towns who have been followed up for 7 years. Analysis will use a multilevel framework which permits the effects of factors working on the individual, household and local community to be teased out. The findings will enable better judgments about whether prevention policy should redirect resources to the problems people face because of the places they live rather than only focusing, as at present, on attempting to change individuals’ lifestyles.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Avoiding paradoxical effects of food packaging to achieve health eating: a mixed methods approach
Abstract: Halting or reversing rising rates of obesity requires more healthy food choices. Nutritional labelling and portion sizing of food packaging are promoted as ways to achieve this, yet recent data suggests that these can have paradoxical effects, resulting in increased consumption. Understanding the psychological processes underlying these effects and how to suppress them is important in developing food packaging that will achieve lower consumption of energy dense foods in those who are more, as well as less, socially deprived. This research aims to evaluate the impact upon food consumption of a range of food packages.

Award_Title: Predicting a) risk of onset and of b) psychosis outcomes based on individual genetic and environmental profiles
Abstract: Psychotic disorders are severe illnesses of the mind that cause people to experience thoughts and sensations they would not otherwise experience. People with severe psychotic illnesses such as schizophrenia have difficulty completing every-day tasks; they lose contact with reality and experience a range of symptoms that usually include hallucinations (such as hearing voices) and delusions (false beliefs that are not based on reality and which they are convinced are true). Patients with these illnesses have a shorter life than the general population by up to 20 years. Treatments for these disorders currently cost about £12 billion every year in England alone. There are no one causes of psychotic disorders, but a range of different risk factors (such as childhood adversity, migration, inner city living, illicit drug use) appear to play a role. In other areas of medicine, such as cardiology and cancer, measuring someone's risk for developing an illness is already well established. For example, tools to estimate the risk of having a heart attack are well developed and used routinely by General Practitioners every day in clinics across the UK. The aims of this project are two-fold: To develop a simple method to assess the risk of the onset of psychosis using a questionnaire of between 5 to 10 items; For those patients who have developed psychosis, to develop a method of predicting illness progression in the next 5 years based on their individual profile of environmental and genetic risk factors. The study will draw on information from five large studies from across Europe and the UK, encompassing over 13,000 individuals diagnosed with psychosis with details on their risk factors, including their smoking and drinking habits, whether they take illicit drugs, childhood/adult traumatic experiences, their ethnicity, where they live and a personal genetic risk for schizophrenia. For this fellowship, I propose to use a type of analysis of the data called statistical and machine learning methods. I have chosen these methods because the current methods of data analyses that are widely used are not very reliable at predicting outcomes for patients with psychosis. In contrast, the statistical and machine learning methods that I want to use will allow for more accurate predictions to be made that are specific to an individual. Throughout the study I will involve patients and members of the general public in the study design, methodology and dissemination of my results. I will further discuss with them any ethical issues that I may encounter (such as discussing whether people would want to know that they are at a high risk for developing psychosis). On the basis of this fellowship I hope to be able to identify people who are at highest risk of illness so that prevention and early treatment options can be tailored to the risk status of each individual. Results of this research will be of a special benefit for school and university counselling services as they will highlight which students are more likely to develop psychosis based on pieces of information about their lives. They may also shed some light on why the rates of mental health issues have increased among younger people in the UK. For patients who have already developed psychosis, my results will highlight those with a poor predicted outcome and who would benefit from early treatment in the hope that enhanced intervention would improve their long-term outcome and thus increase their chances of recovery.

Abstract: I Overall aims: We will determine whether community based treatment programs for chronic hepatitis C infection (HCV) can be developed that allow sufficient patients to be treated in order to reduce HCV prevalence and reduce the overall burden from liver disease. We will determine :- (a) The compliance and response rates in injectors treated in a variety of different settings; (b) Factors that may enhance or reduce treatment compliance and engagement in injectors; (c) re-infection rates in injectors that have been successfully treated; (d) the cost effectiveness of treating injectors; (e) the impact of high rates of treatment engagement on community HCV prevalence. II Background: Chronic HCV is a common infection(1), which if left untreated will progressively lead (7-18% within 20 years) to liver disease leading to cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinioma and liver failure(2). Nearly 200,000 people in the UK are infected with chronic HCV(3, 4). Injecting drug use (IDU) is the key risk group for HCV morbidity and transmission(5). Over 85% of chronic infections are due to IDU(3); in many UK cities 40% of injectors are chronically infected with HCV(6, 7). Prevention of HCV transmision in IDUs is critical to HCV prevention and ultimately to slowing the growing burden of liver disease in the population(5, 8). Opiate substitution therapy (OST) and high coverage needle and syringe programmes (NSP) are the key current interventions to prevent HCV transmission(5, 9). Public health guidance nationally and internationally recommends the scale-up NSP and OST(10, 11). Emerging UK data strengthens the previously weak evidence base(12) (figure 1 appendix): suggesting that exposure to high coverage NSP or OST can reduce HCV incidence by over 50%(5). Nonetheless, despite substantial investment in interventions (e.g. OST has doubled(13)) reductions in HCV prevalence have not occurred. Indeed surveillance data suggest that in the last 10 years HCV prevalence has continued to rise, especially among recent injectors(14, 15). While the risk of HIV infection among injectors remains low, additional strategies are required in order to reduce HCV prevalence(16, 17). The reason is most likely due to the combination of:- (a) high back ground prevalence of HCV(18); (b) chronicity of injecting which can persist for 10-30 years(19, 20); (c) length of time exposed to OST or high coverage NSP. Thus, it is difficult both for injectors and local services to sustain for long enough the level of behavior change and intervention coverage required respectively. We illustrate this in the appendix (Figure 2) which shows that even if annually 50% of injectors were exposed to high coverage interventions impact would be less than 10% after 10 years, and only increasing intervention coverage to >80% could reduce HCV prevalence by 20% after 20 years.Effective antiviral therapy for HCV is available (peginterferon alfa+ ribavirin) with a cure, sustained viral response (SVR), rate of 45-80% depending on genotype(21, 22). Treatment is recommended for all patient groups (including injectors)(23, 24). We define “injectors” (in contrast to ex or non-injectors) as those that have a risk of relapse and transmitting HCV to others – which encompasses people who are currently injecting as well as those who have not achieved five years abstinence(19, 25). Treatment of injectors is increasing in the UK, but few centres are treating substantial numbers. There is reluctance by some clinicians, also expressed by clinical bodies, to treat injectors because of concerns over treatment compliance and risk of re-infection(26-29). The available evidence does suggest, however, that injectors especially those in ongoing opiate substitution treatment can achieve similar compliance and SVR rates as ex and non injectors(30-35). Abstract: Workstream 1: Examination of LD health checks using the THIN primary care database The THIN primary care database includes data on consultations with physicians and nurses including diagnoses, interventions, symptoms, and referrals to secondary care, electronically recorded as Read codes, a hierarchical coding system used in UK primary care31. All prescriptions are recorded, as are height, weight, smoking status and laboratory test results, and the Townsend neighbourhood deprivation score. We aim to inform the programme by examining current uptake of England s LD-DES. Given the DES was introduced in 2008 we will not be able to measure its impact on longer term outcomes such as mortality, but aim to develop the methodology to do so in the full programme grant. a. Validation of GP Read codes to identify LD patients When GP practices opt into LD-DES they are provided with a list of LD adults known to social services to align with patients already on their practice LD register. The latter are identified using the Read codes recognised by the Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF)32. We will examine validity of GP LD coding in THIN. Using code lists developed for our recently completed DH funded project we will identify patients with genetic conditions causing LD (e.g. Down syndrome) to explore what proportion have also been given a DES/QOF Read code for LD, and a code to indicate they are on the practice LD register. b. Pilot THIN work shows the code was used from 2008-2009, increasing dramatically in 2009-2010, consistent with introduction of LD-DES. Around 50% of practices used this code in 2009, consistent with reports of DES uptake. This indicates it may be suitable for identifying practices opting into LD-DES, but external validity will be established by comparison with data provided by PCTs or their successor organisations. Abstract: I Overarching aims of the research programme, outlining the research questions that the work will ultimately addressThe overarching aim is to improve the prevention of STI-related morbidity in women by evaluating the impact of Chlamydia trachomatis screening and Mycoplasma genitalium testing on clinical outcomes. Ultimately the work will address two major research questions: 1) What is the observed impact of opportunistic chlamydia screening in primary care on subsequent clinical complications; pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility? Key questions include:- who is being screened for C. trachomatis and who is not?- what is the uptake of regular repeated screening for C. trachomatis? - are there major inequalities in screening uptake?- how are coverage, frequency and result of C. trachomatis screening associated with PID outcomes?- what is the number needed to screen (NNS) to prevent one PID outcome?- 2) What is the natural history of M. genitalium infection in women? - does M. genitalium infection increase the risk of PID (is it “the new chlamydia”)? - what are the implications of introducing M. genitalium testing in clinical care? II Background to the proposed research, including NHS context and relevant literatureThe National Chlamydia Screening Programme (NCSP) was launched in 2003 in England by the Department of Health to reduce the prevalence of genital chlamydia infection and its related health problems, including PID, ectopic pregnancy and infertility, by screening for asymptomatic infection in sexually active women and men under 25. In 2005, the Department of Health appointed the Health Protection Agency to oversee the NCSP, which is delivered locally by 152 PCTs in England. The NCSP has been criticised for lack of attention to the evidence base for chlamydia screening, leading to flawed design and implementation. In 2009, a review by the National Audit Office [1] found that, since the launch of the NCSP, “an estimated £100 million has been spent but the Department [of Health] does not yet know what effect, if any, this has had on reducing the prevalence of the infection”. It went on to conclude that the Department of Health does not have a mechanism in place to measure the impact of the NCSP and that it should develop a plan with a clear timeframe for measuring the NCSP’s impact on chlamydia and health-related problems. A key problem for the current NCSP is the lack of unique identifiers for participants being screened, and the lack of collection of any clinical outcome data to evaluate the screening programme. The proposed research will address major questions about the impact of the NCSP by filling these (and other) key informational gaps, and will evaluate innovative ways of delivering and augmenting the screening programme. III Importance of the proposed research and its relevance to the NHS The NCSP was set up to address a costly problem, both in terms of women's health and the NHS. Chlamydia is the most common curable STI, affecting around 5% of the general population under 25, and 1 in 10 of the women taking part in the NCSP. The cost of treating the complications of chlamydial infection exceed $2 billion in the USA. So far, the NCSP has cost over £100 million. Abstract: Development Grant work plan The proposed programme development work plan consists of four interconnected research projects, spread over 18 months, some of which will be conducted in parallel. The main aim of the development phase of the programme is to work with and learn from the experiences and expertise of key stakeholders to establish a critical mass of evidence to underpin decisions about the proposed model of support, its evaluation, and implementation. We will use this phase to extend channels of communication and dialogue with research partners, including clinical trials specialists, implementation scientists and participants. Project 1 Aim: To complete a review of a critical mass of existing empirical evidence on the effectiveness of strategies to support family caregivers providing palliative and/or end-of-life care for a relative or friend in the community. Method: Relatively little empirical evidence on the potential role of volunteers in supporting family caregivers providing palliative and end-of-life care exists in the published literature. To develop necessary innovations in practice, we must evaluate evidence from analogous fields for transferrable elements. While systematic reviews (e.g. Candy et al, 2011) have effectively assessed existing evidence from randomised controlled trials of supportive interventions (delivered by either health or social care professionals) for family caregivers who provide palliative and/or end of life care in the home. However, detailed information about the exact nature of the intervention and method of delivery is lacking both from the systematic review and the published research articles. Published reports of both health care professional- and volunteer-led approaches provide few if any details of processes of implementation or the experience of stakeholders. In Project 1 we will conduct an initial scoping review of relevant literature. This will be followed, as part of the future Programme Grant research plan, by a more extensive review of empirical evidence in which we will establish direct contact with corresponding authors of RCTs included in Candy et al s (2011) systematic review for the Cochrane Collaboration, and with leading academic in this field to develop an on-going critical dialogue. The majority, if not all, relevant studies were conducted outside the UK. A critical dialogue, therefore, will be conducted by electronic means (e.g. email, Skype, blog posts, or Facebook), following the methods described by Kralik et al (2005). We will also re-run search strategies described in recent systematic reviews of support provided for family caregivers providing palliative and/or end-of-life care both by health care professionals and lay volunteers. Outputs: Project 1 will provide the foundations for a comprehensive review of existing empirical evidence on the effectiveness of strategies to support family caregivers providing palliative and/or end-of-life care for a relative or friend in the community. This will form part of a portfolio of resources to be included in the participatory dialogue with stakeholders in Project 3. Project 2 Aim: To conduct a nationwide survey of current community-based, volunteer-led initiatives to support family caregivers providing palliative and/or end-of-life care in the home. Little is currently known about the number and range of these initiatives in the UK, although informal sources of information indicate there are a great range and variety in existence. This project will bring together information about current community initiatives for family caregivers in palliative and end-of-life care in a single database. Abstract: Workpackage 1 - Intervention development i) Scoping review of chronic care models (months 1-9) We will conduct a scoping review [60,61] to produce a profile of the existing literature on the application of theoretical models to the management of long-term illnesses. A scoping review is used to examine the extent, nature and range of research in a particular area without an in depth analysis of the literature or quality assessment [61]. Data sources will include electronic databases (e.g. Pubmed, MEDLINE, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews) and references of selected articles. The review will be carried out by a research fellow experienced in conducting systematic literature reviews. Studies will be included if they applied a theoretical framework to the care of a long-term illness and include information on patient health, experience or satisfaction with care, quality of care, impact on hospital services or primary care or costs. Award_Title: Safer Delivery of Surgical Services: a Reliable Teamwork Approach
Abstract: Aim: To facilitate the transformation of surgical service delivery into a high-reliability enterprise in which the risks of patient harm from treatment process are greatly reduced. Background: Modern high technology health care can be extremely effective, but can also be dangerous. Internationally, around 10% of hospital inpatients suffer harm due directly to their care. Reduction of this burden would be a major contribution to the nation’s health. Analysis of treatment related harm suggests that problems arise mainly because healthcare systems and the work culture amongst staff have not kept pace with the complexity of the technologies introduced during the last 50 years and their potential dangers.Surgery is a high risk healthcare activity, carrying risks of wrong site surgery, hospital acquired infection, retained foreign bodies, and complications from technically inadequate surgery. Our research has shown the potential of addressing the systems design, teamwork and technology aspects of the problem, but more work is needed to refine methods, study generalisability and find out how these approaches are best combined. Abstract: Aims & Objectives. The main aim of this 5 year programme is to test the hypothesis that our novel Type 2 diabetes (T2DM) prevention programme reduces the risk of T2DM in a high risk Norfolk population. We will use established strategies with limited impact on general practices, in a programme in part delivered by lay trainers with T2DM, and which could be used by NHS commissioners as an ‘off the shelf’ diabetes prevention programme. The programme has been piloted in our NIHR feasibility programme grant (0606-1099) which has provided substantial data on participant recruitment and retention, recruitment of lay trainers, practice engagement, staff training, IT and database creation, study materials, and has Research Ethics and Governance approval. Background. The importance of T2DM is well recognised. Landmark clinical trials have shown diet and lifestyle interventions reduce the risk of developing T2DM by > 50% over 3 years in people with impaired glucose tolerance. Translation of the resources used in these large clinical trials to NHS clinical practice is entirely unaffordable, a point recognised by the researchers. We need a realistic diabetes prevention intervention for a financially constrained NHS, which has limited financial impact on general practices. Cultural changes in the NHS put patients at the centre of health choices and we propose to develop the role of people with T2DM as lay lifestyle trainers (Diabetes Prevention Mentors; DPMs) and will develop and test this new role alongside healthcare professionals known as Diabetes Prevention Facilitators (DPFs).Research Plans: •Project 1: Carry out a high volume (n = 10,000) two year screening programme in participants at higher risk of T2DM, based on age and body mass index (BMI) criteria to identify subjects with impaired fasting glucose (IFG), using piloted recruitment strategies and existing NHS services. •Project 2: A 3 year Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) of our piloted diabetes intervention programme (UEA–IFG) in 390 participants with screen detected IFG (isolated IFG or with IFG + Impaired Glucose Tolerance) with transition to T2DM as the primary end point compared to 170 standard care controls. •Project 3: Evaluate the additional impact of using DPM in the UEA–IFG intervention in a 3 year RCT in a further 390 IFG subjects, with transition to T2DM as the primary end point, compared to the UEA–IFG intervention alone (n=390), and the potential for the DPM to deliver the intervention independently.•Project 4: Evaluate the UEA–IFG intervention (with or without DPM support), in a three - arm RCT in 240 screen detected T2DM patients with the primary end point of glycaemic control compared to standard care over 3 years. •Project 5: Evaluate cost effectiveness of all programme elements with modelling of longer term health costs. •Project 6: Disseminate the programme’s findings to UK national commissioning bodies and policy makers, and develop a marketing strategy with industry. •Project 7: Examine the integration of the new roles of DPMs and DPFs in NHS and international workforce planning.Research team. The research team is an established group of NHS and academic staff that includes clinical epidemiologists experienced in health service research and diabetes modelling (Harvey/Bachmann/Niessen), NHS diabetes specialists with academic interests in obesity and diabetes (Turner/Dhatariya/Wallace/Sampson), expertise in academic and clinical primary care and qualitative methods (Howe/Hadley–Brown), lay diabetes champion (Rea), clinical chemistry and HbA1c standardisation (John), clinical and health psychology of chronic disease (Hobbis/Smith), economic evaluation (Barton), RCT statistical management (Clark), and service delivery at board level (Sethia).
