This interview will explore acceptability of the classes, alongside barriers and facilitators for attending and other psychosocial outcomes (such as improvements in quality of life domains). • A fidelity checklist aligned with OEP principles will be developed as per the training curriculums and one class per instructor will be observed and scored accordingly. • Qualitative interviews will be conducted with instructors and local authority staff involved in the programme to determine implementation factors alongside a brief cost analysis survey. Class attendees will be individuals over the age of 65 who are currently enrolled as new starters in one of the above programmes. We will recruit all instructors who have received Dance and Music OEP training alongside all instructors currently delivering standard OEP in Hampshire. We will also recruit all members of the local authority involved in the development and implementation of this curriculum. Dissemination The PHIRST Light team will work with stakeholders to co-produce an impact and dissemination strategy unique to this project. We will actively engage with the local PPI group, PAG and wider stakeholder group to consider how the evaluation findings are most effectively communicated, alongside formalising a knowledge mobilisation plan.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Evaluation of the Bristol City Council Substance Use Support Team (SUST) Trauma Informed Recovery Pathway (TIRP) (PHIRST LiLaC)
Abstract: The abstract outlines an evaluation of the Trauma Informed Recovery Pathway (TIRP) intervention, being undertaken by PHIRST LiLaC in collaboration with Bristol City Council. Background: Problematic substance use is a public health problem that causes harms to individuals, their families and communities. It causes premature deaths and increased hospital admissions. When people enter treatment, they often have a range of complex issues to deal with that might affect their ability to engage with and complete the treatment. The Trauma Informed Recovery Pathway (TIRP) being delivered by the Bristol Substance Use Support Team (SUST) recognises that most people who use substances have experienced trauma and that these trauma experiences can have a negative effect on how they access services because of difficulties around regulating their emotions and building trusting relationships. The TIRP intervention includes a range of components including a psycho-educational programme, support from SUST workers as well as peer volunteers. An evaluability assessment conducted with local stakeholders in planning this study considered issues such as data availability and explored practice and public interests in an evaluation through a series of meetings and workshops. Aim and methods: The aim is to evaluate the processes and contextual conditions influencing the delivery of TIRP including its underlying mechanisms of change, and to understand client experiences and early impacts. The study also aims to undertake exploratory work to understand the economics of delivering TIRP. The evaluation will include three main components involving both qualitative investigation and analysis of routine data: (i) a qualitative investigation of TIRP’s delivery, contexts and mechanisms of change involving interviews and focus groups with professional stakeholders sampled from local services (e.g. drug and alcohol, housing); (ii) interviews with clients to understand experiences of TIRP and its perceived impacts on people’s lives (iii) an exploratory economic assessment of resources, costs and potential savings associated with TIRP. This third component will be finalised by December 2022 following further assessment of routine data. Public Involvement: Peer volunteers with lived experience of substance use advised on the evaluation plan and will be involved in the delivery of the research. Outputs/impact: This study is intended to inform the current and future delivery of TIRP service provision in Bristol. It will also provide evidence for practice in the UK, as much of the existing evidence around trauma informed interventions for substance use has been produced in the North American context. Initial proposed outputs include peer-reviewed academic publications, accessible briefings and a policy/practice focused report or other output for the local authority. Where resources and time permit, we will co-design more creative outputs with volunteer peers and SUST clients involved with the evaluation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Winter fuel payments/warm home policies
Abstract: The purpose of this briefing is to inform deliberations among policymakers and stakeholders. It summarises the best available evidence regarding the design and implementation of policies for reducing the health impact of cold homes, particularly during UK winter months. Excess winter mortality (EWM) is a long standing UK public health concern. The UK performs comparatively poorly for excess winter mortality with some of the least energy efficient housing in Western Europe. When framed as fuel poverty the problem extends to poor ventilation and lack of air conditioning. The scale and impact of the problem is likely to increase given general rises in fuel costs and, specifically, disruption to supply caused by the Ukraine conflict.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Alcohol licensing
Abstract: International evidence reviews suggest that reducing the availability of alcohol positively impacts both levels of alcohol consumption and associated harms. To understand the impact of recent changes to alcohol licensing and public health in the UK, this review aimed to identify and synthesise quantitative research evidence on the impact of local alcohol licensing decisions on the health and well-being of the community. We searched peer-reviewed articles and grey literature for UK studies. We extracted and tabulated key data from the included papers and appraised study quality. We included topic expert and public consultation to confirm the scope of the evidence synthesis and suggest evidence for inclusion. We synthesised narratively and made recommendations based on our findings. We identified a small volume (seven papers) of evidence regarding the health (and related) impacts of local alcohol licensing decision undertaken in the UK local authorities. The evidence we identified did not demonstrate a consistent or sustained association between local interventions and health or crime outcomes downstream. This was despite relatively sophisticated study designs using a range of available data sources and some longer-term analysis. Given that the impacts of local licensing decisions are currently limited, greater regulatory powers are needed if local licensing interventions are to be an effective public health intervention to reduce alcohol related harms.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Public health implications of extending working lives
Abstract: Background: The extension of working lives is happening at a time when there are considerable changes taking place in the nature of work. The removal of the default retirement age potentially gives employees more choice regarding when to retire however, choice may not be available to those with poor health or in poverty, with the potential for extending work to impact on inequalities in older age and act differentially in population sub-groups. This work has been commissioned to provide an independent review of existing research in this area to establish what is known, where there are clear gaps in the evidence base, and to provide national and local policy makers with the best available evidence on the public health impacts of longer working lives. Aims: The aim is to identify, appraise and synthesise existing research evidence regarding the pathways from longer working lives to public health impacts, including identifying where interventions at an individual worker, employer, government and wider society may be effective and cost-effective to ensure that longer working lives do not have adverse public health outcomes. Scope: We aim that a core focus of this review will be to examine the evidence using a public health lens to explore health enhancing, health neutral, and potentially varying effects on population sub-groups, and explore how longer working lives may impact on health inequalities. Given the potentially extensive and diverse literature relating to working lives, we propose to conduct the review in multiple stages to ensure that the work is deliverable, and that the outputs will be of practical value to stakeholders, including policy makers, research commissioners and communities and other stakeholders. Methods: The first stage will involve a mapping review, supplemented by stakeholder consultation. This mapping process will establish the volume and characteristics of evidence potentially available, and where priorities for focussing may lie. The output from this first stage will be a report which maps the literature available. This will provide information to underpin discussion with stakeholders and the Public Health Review Team commissioners regarding the refining of the review parameters (inclusion and exclusion criteria) for the second stage systematic review. The second stage systematic review will examine available published and grey literature evidence in order to develop a draft logic model setting out outcomes and impacts, levers of change, moderating and mediating factors and potential intervention points relating to the public health effects of extension of working lives. The model will include indicators of pathways between elements (what might lead to what) where the evidence permits, together with an evaluation of the current strength of evidence underpinning each outcome and impact reported. An accompanying report will detail the evidence via a narrative summary, and highlight any implications for particular sub-groups of the population and impacts on health inequalities. A final consultation stage with stakeholders will explore the applicability and validity of the model in order to co-produce a final version. We will use co-production methods to develop versions which are suitable for varying target audiences.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Peer support and community interventions targeting breastfeeding in the UK: Systematic review and equity synthesis of qualitative evidence
Abstract: Background: Breastfeeding and the provision of human milk offers an accessible and cost-effective practice that is health promoting for both the mother and the child. However, in the UK rates of breast feeding and chest feeding among women and birthing people remains low. There are a range of interventions that aim to promote feeding, which include peer support by trained individuals who share key social characteristics with those they are supporting. Peer support may be delivered in clinical and community settings. Other community provision includes professional and non-professional services delivered through local and regional and community networks. Despite an emerging evidence base for peer-led and community intervention, current knowledge is limited by a lack of understanding as to whether the experiences of intervention generate, maintain, exacerbate, or mitigate health inequities between participating groups. We will systematically synthesise evidence from qualitative studies and process evaluations of peer support and community breastfeeding interventions in the UK to address the following questions: 1) What social characteristics are identified as relevant to participants’ experiences and/or views of peer support and community breastfeeding interventions?; and 2) How are participants’ experiences and/or views of peer support and community breastfeeding interventions influenced by different social characteristics? Methods: We will conduct a qualitative synthesis, drawing on Framework Synthesis. We will update the searches of a prior systematic review from 2017 in eight bibliographic databases, combined with hand searches of related syntheses. We will undertake supplementary literature searching as required. Eligible studies must report qualitative evidence from evaluations of peer-led and community interventions in the UK. Data may be from women and birthing people, or other intervention stakeholders if they are reflecting on participants’ experiences. Retrievals will be screened independently and in duplicate. Studies will be appraised with a tool developed for use in prior public health syntheses. Social characteristics will be charted to understand how they are defined. Data will be mapped according to four domains of intervention experience: reach and recruitment; retention; interaction and sustainment. Within each domain, we will generate themes to explain if and how social characteristics give rise to outcome inequities. We will use the GRADE-CERQual tool to assess the certainty of evidence. We will undertake three phases of PPI engagement with breastfeeding women and peer supporters to refine the review scope, interpret the emerging synthesis and develop funder recommendations. Dissemination: The review is an output from the NIHR PHR Reviews Team. It will support the funder in setting research and funding priorities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Increasing the uptake of annual health checks in children and young people aged 14-17 years with learning disability
Abstract: Aims This research is about health checks in children and young people with a learning disability. We want to find out more about how health checks are carried out, whether there are things about them that are easy or difficult for people with a learning disability, and whether they are useful. We also want to find out the best way for health checks to be carried out and how we can make changes to health checks to encourage more children and young people to have one. Background People with a learning disability experience poorer health, and more challenges accessing healthcare, than those without a learning disability. To try to improve this, the NHS wants people aged 14 and older to have a health check every year, at their doctors surgery or where they live. Research shows that these health checks do improve health in people with a learning disability but fewer young people receive a health check compared to adults. Children and young people with a learning disability and parents/carers have told us that seeing a doctor can be difficult because they might not know how to help them. Design/methods Phase 1: We will work with staff at six doctors surgeries to find out more about the way in which they do health checks. We will ask to see any documents they use to help them to do health checks, interview them to collect detailed information, and ask them whether health checks found any new health problems or a need for further tests, that were not known about before. We will also look at national patient data for information about health problems, tests, and treatments. We will collect information from children and young people with a learning disability, and parents and carers, to find out more about their previous experiences of going for a health check. We will run a focus group with people who are trying to improve health checks for children and young people to find out what they are doing and whether it is working. Finally, we will work with parents, special school staff and doctors to pull together all the information collected to design an ‘intervention’ by finding things that could be changed to make health checks better for children and young people with a learning disability. Phase 2: We will ask doctors to run the intervention by making the changes found in Phase 1 to improve health checks. We will collect information from both doctors and family carers on whether these changes are possible to make and whether they improve health checks. Patient/public involvement We have worked with children with a learning disability, parents and carers, schools, and doctors to inform the planned research. Throughout the project we will work with a ‘steering group’ of parents/carers who will help us to make decisions and give us feedback on what we are doing and what the research findings mean. We will also work with a ‘design group’ of parents/carers, school staff and doctors who will look at the information we have gathered in Phase 1 and design the intervention tested in Phase 2. Dissemination As well as scientific papers and presentations, we will work with families and professionals to produce a Guide to share our findings with people who pay for and deliver annual health check services. We will also organise an event for family carers and professionals to share our research findings and launch the Guide.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Impact of food environment policies and food insecurity on less healthy food consumption, obesity and health economic outcomes – a model-based appraisal
Abstract: Aims This research aims to study how new food policies could change people’s eating habits and reduce intake of foods high in fat, salt, and sugar. We want to study how these changes can improve people’s health and wellbeing. This includes to reduce the number of people that are obese. We would also like to study how these changes might affect people without access to enough healthy food. Background Computer tools can be used to test how policies can improve health and to help people who make decisions (policy makers) choose the best options. To make these computer tools as useful as they can be, they need to use the most recent data about how people change their behaviour. At the moment, computer tools do not capture this data very well. As a result, they might not be able to tell us what impact a policy might make. We will create a new tool that uses what we know about how people decide what food to eat and how this is shaped by the places they live in. With this tool, we will work with policy makers to study the effects of policies on people’s health and wellbeing. Design and methods We will gather information about how the places where people live and get their food can affect their food choices and create a new collection of this. This includes things like how many adverts there are for unhealthy foods and how many types of food shops (such as supermarkets and takeaways) there are. We will include other things that affect food intake such as the cost of food and people’s income. We want to see how these are linked to problems like being obese and not having enough healthy food in some places. We will work with people who care about these issues (including policy makers) to make a new computer tool. This tool will represent people who make food choices, change their weight, and can have problems getting access to food. In the tool, we can make changes to the food environment and see how the lives of each person may change. This may be for better or worse, in terms of their health or not having enough food. The people in our tool and the things that happen in their lives are based on all the data we will collect. We will use Greater Manchester as our case study. We will highlight changes to places that could be made to improve people’s health. Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) We are working with a diverse group of people from across the United Kingdom. They already helped us decide to focus on food policies. They suggested that we look at the ways that local places impact food choices. They asked us to look at how people from diverse backgrounds and cultures might experience different effects. We have asked a member from this group to join our team. This person will help us to make sure that the wider group can support the research, that these meetings go well and are not too complex for a member of the public to understand. We will have group meetings where we work with each other to discuss the work and create our tool. We will have to decide what to include in our tool, and we want to make sure that our tool reflects the problems people face in the real world. Later in the study they will help us understand what the findings mean and help to plan how we will let people know about them.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Wider determinants of health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Rose-NET: Manchester-Leeds Collaborative National Evaluation Team
Abstract: Aim(s) of the research Our Rose-NET centre aims to help health and social care evaluate changes to their services across England. Background to the research Health and social care faces challenges in improving people’s health and promoting independent living. To achieve better health and quality of life, we need to find new ways of delivering services that are effective, acceptable to patients, the public and carers, and make the best use of our health and social care funding. New services might involve new health or care workers, delivering care through the internet, or finding better ways to provide joined-up care. The challenges faced by health and social care mean that some of these changes need to happen quickly and across large parts of the country. If we make such changes, we need to be sure they are delivering better care. This means testing those changes as they occur (what we call ‘evaluation’). That way we can continue with changes that work and stop or change those that do not. Design and methods used Doing evaluation of changes across England needs many skills. We need to be able to start evaluations quickly, using the most up-to-date scientific methods. We need to ensure our research takes account of the diversity of the English population and includes people who are often excluded from research. We need to work closely with leaders in health and social care and with patient and public representatives to understand what they need to know, and to give them the information they need, when they need it. We need to remain independent, to make sure we are fair when we evaluate new services. We need to have a diverse, skilled and experienced team. Our Rose-NET national evaluation team brings together researchers from the University of Manchester and University of Leeds, and experts at engaging with the public from Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust. As well as our team, we can draw on other experts we know to make sure we have the skills to deal with a wide range of evaluations. We have experience of doing national evaluations in areas such as diabetes, integrated services for older people, and new types of digital care. Patient and public involvement Our team from Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust has lots of experience of helping patients and the public contribute to research (involvement), and in communicating the results of research (engagement). They will help us engage people who are less often involved in research, and make sure that we communicate in ways that are accessible and impactful. Stakeholder engagement and dissemination National evaluations will involve a range of stakeholders, including NHS England, the Department of Health and Social Care, leaders of Integrated Care Systems, and wider groups of professional and patients (such as Royal Colleges, and charities). To make evaluation effective, we will work closely with these groups to design research which meets their needs and their timescales (co-production). Then we will make sure they have timely access to the evidence they need, continuing to meet with them to make sure our findings are used when they are making decisions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Funding_Stream: LAAF Programme Doctoral Local Authority Fellowship
Award_Title: How can Local Authorities use health economics evidence and adaptive leadership to inform investment in parks?
Abstract: Background Parks are critical for health and wellbeing (HWB). They help people to increase their physical activity, promote better wellbeing and support community cohesion. Local Authorities (LA) are mainly responsible for managing and resourcing them. However, austerity has meant parks' budgets have significantly decreased since 2011 compromising their quality. Robust health economic analysis and adaptive leadership methods are required to help LAs guide resource allocation decisions for these important assets. Birmingham City Council (BCC) is the focus of this research, together with Walsall Metropolitan Borough Council, Plymouth City Council and Coventry City Council. BCC is the largest Local Council in the United Kingdom, with 427 parks. Research question How can LAs use health economics evidence and adaptive leadership to inform investment in parks? Objectives 1: To explore the historical distribution of (dis)investment in parks by geographic region and deprivation across Birmingham and understand how this (dis)investment has impacted on quality of parks over time. 2: To understand how a range of actors within LAs conceptualise the value generated from parks, and to what extent these different notions of 'value' are used to inform (dis)investment decisions. 3: To build on findings from WP1 and WP2 to develop a conceptual model for articulating the value of parks. Methods The research planned uses methods from both health economics and adaptive leadership. Health Economics is concerned with understanding how to prioritise limited resources for improving HWB. Adaptive leadership aims to help organisations implement difficult decisions in a complex environment. The research is divided into three work packages (WPs): WP1: A retrospective quantitative analysis of how BCC budget cuts have impacted on the management of 427 parks in Birmingham over the last 10 years focusing on the costs, together with indicators of quality including police callouts, fly-tipping, and biodiversity. Analysis will include: Descriptive statistics to summarise data according to the size/density of the local population, size of park and deprivation level. Regression analysis to understand the relationship between park investment and fly-tipping as a marker of quality. Comparison with other council run facilities, e.g., leisure centres, which compete for the same LA budget. WP2: A systematic review of the academic and grey literature, together with qualitative research to understand how a range of LA stakeholders conceptualise the value from parks. WP3: Using information from WP1 and WP2, a conceptual model for articulating the value that parks bring to local areas will be developed with the purpose of informing future decisions. Three workshops will be conducted to a) clearly understand and articulate the problem b) test the feasibility/acceptability of the model and c) to finalise the model structure. Anticipated impact and dissemination Research findings will be shared with green space charities, LAs through the Local Government Association and Association for Public Service Excellence, as well as peer reviewed journals and academic presentations. The anticipated impact of this research will be high as it has a practical focus on helping LAs articulate the value that parks bring to communities to help with investment decisions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Contractor: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Driving timely help seeking and reducing disparities in maternal outcomes through improved design and delivery of postnatal red flag information for women experiencing disadvantage.
Abstract: Research Question How can we make information resources more accessible to women experiencing multiple disadvantage? Background The MBRRACE UK report has shown a serious and persistent gap between postnatal morbidity and mortality rates for women from deprived areas and ethnic minority groups, with most women dying in the postnatal period. If symptoms can be recognised in time this enables them to be treated more effectively. There are numerous information resources of varying quality detailing symptoms of potential postnatal complications that inform women s decision to seek care. However, digital poverty and low literacy can constrain women s access to information in a format they can understand and act upon. Women from ethnic minority groups and those experiencing socio-economic deprivation are at particular risk of low health literacy and digital poverty. Women continue to report unmet needs for information and support in the postnatal period, but there is no guidance for health care professionals on how to provide information to support better care for people experiencing disadvantage or who are not confident in English. Aim and objectives To improve accessibility and delivery of information about women's health for women experiencing disadvantage, using postnatal red flags as an exemplar, to support timely help seeking and reduce the risk of serious illness or death. Objectives: 1. To co-produce an accessible information exemplar of postnatal warning signs of serious illness with women experiencing disadvantage. 2. To co-produce a guide for the delivery of accessible information resources with women experiencing disadvantage and test in practice. 3. To distill a checklist of accessible principles for the design of information resources. 4. To support adoption of the resources into practice through a practical dissemination workshop with stakeholders. Method We will use a Participatory Action Research (PAR) design with co-production, a values driven approach based on the principle that those experiencing a problem are best placed to design the solutions. It combines professionals expertise with the lived expertise of service users to develop sustainable solutions. We will work with peer researchers and up to 60 women who have intersecting experience of disadvantage to ensure the outputs benefit women most at risk of serious illness in the maternity system. We will use interactive techniques in our data collection and analysis, recommended for participants with varied levels of literacy to support engagement. Timeline for delivery Ethics application & recruitment July-Nov 2023 Co-production exemplar and guide Nov 2032-March 2024 Consultation & refinement March –July 2024 Distribution & evaluation Sept – Dec 2024 Workshop planning, delivery, follow-up Sept -Feb 2025 Dissemination and write up Dec-Mar 2025 Anticipated impact and dissemination The checklist will be used by NHS and charities to design postnatal information resources in an appropriate and accessible manner for women living with disadvantage. The delivery guidance will stimulate community engagement and conversations among practitioners about accessibility of information. Long term, we anticipate the red flag exemplar to stimulate timely help seeking for women experiencing postnatal complications, with positive financial impact for the NHS and emotionally for families.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare public health
Contractor: HAMPSHIRE AND ISLE OF WIGHT HEALTHCARE NHS FOUNDATION TRUST
Award_Title: Implementing and evaluating a co-designed, tailored intervention to support pressure ulcer prevention behaviours by older patients and their lay carers in community settings: preparing for inclusive and diverse research (CPrUP2)
Abstract: Development work aims: To systematically map the external influencers on pressure ulcer (PU) prevention behaviours in community dwelling older people and their lay carers, To build comprehensive stakeholder and PPIE networks and an expert research team, With them co-produce a PGfAR application. Background PUs are localised injuries to the skin and underlying tissues; risk increases with age. Evidence-based guidance for prevention exists. Over 19% of patients receiving care at home will have a PU resulting in increased morbidity and mortality and decreased quality of life. PU prevention is a priority for patients, carers, health/social care practitioners (HSCPs) and commissioners. Treatment accounts for ~4% of NHS annual budget. The ageing population and finite healthcare resources indicate a need to find new ways to support patient and lay carer adoption of PU prevention measures. Our research (CPrUP1, NIHR201933) has identified barriers to PU prevention for older, community-dwelling patients and their lay carers. We have co-designed theoretically informed, HCP mediated, patient and lay carer actioned interventions to address these barriers. Workplan/Timelines In CPrUP2 we will: Work package 1 (M1-8). Map the involvement of stakeholders in PU prevention. We will i) conduct a national online survey to establish the full range of who is involved in PU prevention and how, ii) conduct interviews with HSCPs involved in PU prevention, resulting in a map of HSCP involvement with patients concerning PUs and a detailed understanding of their perceived roles in PU prevention and barriers to optimal care. Work package 2 (M6-11). Create a comprehensive stakeholder and PPIE network and robust research team. We will recruit professionals from WP1 and existing networks (n~15 ) across employment types, roles and length of experience. Concurrently, we will create a network of PPIE representatives (n~10). CPrUP1 PPIE representatives will be the foundation of this group. Additionally, we will use established links, focusing on accessing seldom heard groups (older/housebound people or those with caring responsibilities, living in less affluent areas and/or from ethnic minorities) who would not generally engage in research. To facilitate participation, we will i) clearly explain what is involved, ii) provide preparation for the role, iii) offer a “step on/step off” approach, iv) offer a range of involvement methods and v) provide enablers. We will build our research team to include a clinical trials unit, a health economist and other members as required. Development of these networks will ensure the right people (i.e. patients, lay carers, HSCPs and specialist researchers) work together from the start of the PGfAR process. Work package 3 (M11-16). Co-produce a relevant, realistic PGfAR application that is most likely to have maximum impact in practice. The coproduction group will include the stakeholder network and PPIE members using in-person and on-line structured events. The PGfAR (CPrUP3) will aim to implement and evaluate the intervention to reduce the incidence of PUs in at-risk, community dwelling older people. This will involve the use of implementation science and knowledge mobilisation techniques. Design of the trial and economic evaluation will depend on the new knowledge developed in CPrUP2.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Contractor: Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: LUSTRUM 2: co-production of digital health interventions to increase sex partner testing within contact tracing for sexually transmitted infections
Abstract: Background: Contact tracing is key to controlling sexually transmitted infections (STIs). It is a complex intervention which aims to contact, test and sometimes treat exposed sex partners of people with diagnosed STIs (index patients). Achieving good outcomes is challenging. Increasingly, sex partner management is provided digitally (online). This proposal follows The LUSTRUM Programme, which focussed on a contact tracing intervention known as Accelerated Partner Therapy (APT). In APT, healthcare professionals conduct telephone assessments with sex partners before providing index patients with STI and Blood Borne Virus (STIBBV) self-sampling kits and antibiotics to deliver to their sex partners for self-management. Our randomised controlled trial (RCT) showed that APT is likely to be cost-saving and might reduce the risk of repeat infection in index patients compared with face-to-face care. However, only half of sex partners who received APT returned self-sampling kits for testing and might have taken antibiotics unnecessarily. Therefore, LUSTRUM recommended research into new ways of encouraging STIBBV testing in sex partners to improve contact tracing interventions. Aim: To co-produce inclusive, culturally-sensitive, tailored, targeted, brief multimodal digital health interventions (DHIs) for use in contact tracing to increase uptake of STIBBV testing by sex partners of people diagnosed with STIs. Specific Objectives (SOs): To determine the social patterning of STIBBV self-sampling amongst sex partners in the LUSTRUM RCT (quantitative data) to inform targeting of the proposed DHIs. To explore modifiable factors affecting sex partner uptake of STIBBV self-sampling within the LUSTRUM RCT (qualitative data) to inform content of the proposed DHIs. To co-produce inclusive, culturally-sensitive, tailored, targeted, brief multimodal DHIs to motivate and support sex partners to undertake STIBBV self-sampling. To critically reflect on and evaluate the co-production process using multi-co-production team perspectives. To create an implementation resource informed by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research to facilitate adoption of the DHIs within sexual health services. Work Plan: Using a sequential mixed methods participatory design: SO1: detailed secondary analyses of the quantitative RCT dataset to describe sociodemographic characteristics of sex partners who did/did not return STIBBV self-samples. SO2: detailed secondary analyses of RCT qualitative process evaluation datasets to develop intervention content, using thematic analyses, Behaviour Change Wheel, Theoretical Domains Framework, Behaviour Change Technique Taxonomy. SO3: co-production methodologies in a staged approach (to be refined/agreed by co-producers) e.g. formation of the group, exploring/refining SO1,SO2 recommendations, conceptualisation, production and refinement of DHIs. SO4: formative exploration of co-producers experiences, expertise and expectations of the process, critical reflexive evaluation of research team s roles, interactions with co-producers and impact. Co-producers experiences of the process and ideas for improvement. SO5: packaging of the DHIs in a usable and adaptable form for sexual health services. Timelines: Secondary data analyses (SO1,SO2): four months, co-production (SO3,SO4): 10 months, towards the end of which we will create the implementation resource (two months, SO5), total duration: 14 months. Impact and dissemination: Ultimately, we aim to improve sex partner testing outcomes within digital self-managed contact tracing. This could improve the control of STIBBVs in the population and contribute to better antibiotic stewardship.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Award_Title: Butterfly Indoor Air Quality: enabling healthy and sustainable hospitals
Abstract: Numerous neurotoxic and carcinogenic pollutants concentrated in hospitals and commercial buildings induce respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, alongside headaches, eye, nose and throat irritation, fatigue and difficulty concentrating. 1/3rd of industrialised country building stock is prone to sick building syndrome (WHO), causing ~4m deaths p.a. (International WELL Building Institute). Multiple policies are driving legislation, including The Clean Air (Human Rights) Bill (hearing stage) requiring building managers to take action. The UK Chief Medical Officer s Annual Report 2022 focused on Air Quality, and the National Engineering Policy Centre report on IAQ will be published in February 2023. Management of indoor air quality is currently a brute force approach, alternating between mechanically ventilating a room to remove CO2 by replacing it with outdoor air or using air purification devices to kill pathogens and VOCs. Flutterlab has developed a unique way of measuring air quality (patented LaminAIR flow technology) which allows constant measurement of free gas around a room, preventing re-circulated/stagnant air corrupting results (an industry-wide limitation). We are working with Rensair to create a unified operating system which allows optimised responses to achieve hospital-grade ventilation with minimal energy expenditure. Our Butterfly monitors have an innovative display, with colour-changing wings to visually show air quality (see fig.1).. Fig.1: Butterfly Following Innovate UK Fast Start funding, we have developed a prototype for controlling existing Rensair HVAC systems (currently deployed within the NHS). We now need to validate the optimisation process to demonstrate that the solution can automatically optimise ventilation volumes based on accurate, live IAQ data: (i) minimising ventilation energy consumption; (ii) delivering excellent indoor air quality. PPI with patients at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust has identified initial barriers and opportunities. PPI is built into the project, ensuring the patient voice is central to development, e.g., understanding how Butterfly monitors can best reassure patients.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Integrated parenting and financial wellbeing support
Abstract: Development work questions (i) How is financial well-being support (FWbS) delivered in Family Hubs (FH)? (ii) Who is best placed to deliver such support to families? (iii) How can parenting support (PS) and FWbS be integrated? (iv) How feasible is it to collect and link routine data on family finances, parents, parenting and child outcomes to evaluate integrated PS+FWbS in FHs? Background Children in poverty have an increased risk of poor physical and mental health outcomes. Improving family income contributes to better child health and development outcomes, especially for families in poverty. However, early intervention services tend to focus on enhancing parent-child relationships and parenting skills. While these can be effective, results are often disappointing or equivocal. One avenue to enhance the effectiveness of such interventions is to concurrently improve families financial and material circumstances. Frontline FWbS targeting parents potentially plays an important role here. However, we know little about its impact on financial/material circumstances, parent health and well-being, parenting or child health and development outcomes, or if/how it can be integrated with PS. The government s Family Hubs programme offer an auspicious context for exploring this. Aims and objectives Our PGfAR aims to understand: how successful different forms of integrated PS+FWbS are as regards implementation outcomes and if they associated with improved parent, parenting and child outcomes; and if integrated PS+FWbS within a programme improves outcomes compared with service-level integration. To achieve this, we first need to address four areas of uncertainty in the PDG. Development workplan First, the varied models that FHs use to provide FWbS to families in England, and how families access this support. We will survey 75 local authorities (LAs) receiving Transformation Funding and conduct interviews (25-30) with FH managers and commissioners. Second, who is best placed to deliver FWbS to families according to family practitioners and debt/welfare advisors, and how to do this. We will conduct focus groups (2-4) with debt/welfare advisors and FH staff who offer PS. Third, how best to integrate PS and FWbS, and the quality and drivers of implementation. We will conduct a rapid review of relevant research published in English since 2000 and hold a focus group involving PS programme developers. Fourth, the feasibility of collecting and linking data on income/finances, parent health/well-being, parenting and child health and development outcomes across FHs and debt/welfare advice organisations. We will survey 75 LAs and complete a case study of one site (Plymouth). Together, these workstreams will inform three PGfAR work-packages: (i) an evaluation of integrated FWbS in FH in terms of key implementation outcomes; (ii) the optimisation of an integrated PS+FWbS intervention; and (iii) its testing in a pilot trial. Anticipated impact and dissemination The project will inform the planned PGfAR and the extent to which FHs and other services for parents integrate FWbS with PS to reduce child health inequalities. We will present research findings in peer-reviewed journals, blogs and presentations at conferences attended by policy-makers, practitioners, and academics. Timeline The project will commence in March 2024 and last 12 months.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Award_Title: Increasing STI Testing Uptake Among African and Caribbean Communities in the UK: Intervention Development Using the ACE Framework
Abstract: Background: STI rates in the UK have increased by 10-15% since 2020 with the highest burden among ethnic minorities (1). For example, chlamydia diagnoses were twice as high and HIV three times higher among people of Black Caribbean descent versus White British counterparts (2). There is a 2-5 times higher HIV acquisition risk with untreated STIs ?(1) and ?late diagnosis propagates the STI epidemic, enabling ongoing transmission among African communities in the UK (2). However, these groups face greater barriers to accessing services, including knowledge gaps, stigma concerns, and underutilization of health resources (3). Lack of early STI detection enables ongoing transmission, worsened outcomes like infertility and cancer risks, and substantial costs estimated at £360,000 per HIV case (4). Evidence-based, tailored interventions addressing recognized disparities in STI testing are urgently needed and represent a policy priority for addressing health equities. Aim: To co-design and pilot a behaviour change intervention to increase sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing uptake among Africans and Caribbeans in the UK using the ACE framework. Objectives: Systematically review existing interventions promoting STI testing uptake among Africans and Caribbeans in high-income countries. Qualitatively explore multi-level facilitators at personal, community, and health systems levels inhibiting testing among AC communities. Co-produce a targeted behaviour change intervention embedding evidence-based techniques to reduce identified barriers through participatory workshops. Evaluate the acceptability and uptake of the resulting intervention in a real-world pilot. Methods: Following the ACE framework, the project involves four studies including: 1) Systematic Review: I will conduct a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines to identify and synthesize interventions that aim to increase testing uptake among marginalized African/Caribbean groups in high-income countries to inform later co-design priorities. 2) Qualitative study of AC community members and Clinicians: I will conduct semi-structured interviews with 25 African/Caribbean community members and 10 clinicians to understand multi-level barriers/enablers influencing testing decisions across socio-ecological levels. This is the first objective in the Agile Co-Production and Evaluation (ACE) framework, to conduct participatory needs assessments. 3) Co-produce Intervention content: This includes a series of 3 iterative co-design workshops engaging approximately 30 stakeholders to collaboratively develop targeted interventions, messages, and outreach strategies addressing identified challenges. 4) Mixed-methods Evaluation of Pilot study: The intervention will be rolled out among 50 people. Mixed methods will be used to explore changes in testing intentions post-intervention exposure and acceptability. Integrating user feedback and metrics aligns with equitable principles in ACE. Timeline: A three-year program involving planning (months 1), a systematic review (months 2-6), qualitative study (months 6-13), intervention development (months 13-18), pilot and evaluation (months 18-26), analysis (months 27-30), dissemination and writing (months 30-36). Impact: This co-designed intervention aims to enhance access to sexual health services for AC communities in the UK, fostering earlier STI detection and treatment. This will inform postdoctoral research to conduct a randomized controlled trial to assess the co-designed program's impact on STI testing and infection reduction among marginalized groups compared to standard care. The ACE framework provides a transferable model for stakeholders engaging minority communities, addressing broader health disparities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare public health and preventing premature mortality
Award_Title: Adverse Drug Events in Ageing Populations (ADDRESS-AP): Who, why and which drugs to stop?
Abstract: Research question Can we use data from routine electronic health records to better understand who is likely to experience adverse drug events, which medications are most problematic and whether deprescribing leads to benefit or harm? Background As individuals age, they often develop multiple health conditions that necessitate the prescription of numerous medications. While this may be appropriate, some individuals are prescribed an excessive number of medications. This is known as 'inappropriate polypharmacy' and is associated with an increased risk of harm, including delirium and falls. Medication-related harm accounts for 1 in 10 hospital admissions. Presently, doctors lack knowledge regarding which patients are most susceptible to experiencing such harms and the most effective preventive measures. One solution is to 'deprescribe' medications that may cause harm. However, deprescribing has not been evaluated widely in clinical trials, and while some practice it as a routine clinical strategy, outcomes remain unclear. Aims and objectives The primary objective of this study is to enhance our understanding of the balance of harms and benefits that can arise from prescription of multiple medications to certain patients. Specifically, the research aims to: Identify which patients are at the highest risk of important adverse drug events Discover which medications are most strongly associated with adverse drug events Explore whether stopping medications is associated with greater benefit or harm in patients at high risk of adverse drug events: focusing on delirium Methods This proposal will utilise anonymised data from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) and involve the following work packages: Work-package 1 will develop and externally validate two clinical prediction models to identify individuals at the highest risk of developing delirium or experiencing falls. Work-package 2 will use the same dataset to examine the association between the top 25 most commonly prescribed medication classes in primary care, and delirium or falls. Analyses will utilise multivariable Cox regression and supervised deep learning models designed to uncover previously unidentified associations between medication changes over time (including different combinations of medications) and delirium/falls. Work-package 3 will examine the effects of medication discontinuation. Analyses will focus on patients undergoing medication reviews in primacy care and outcomes in those who had medications discontinued and those who did not. A large number of medications, outcomes and analytical methods will be explored using a rigorous, pre-specified and transparent approach. Timelines The first year will involve obtaining approvals, curating variables, and managing the data. In years 2-3, I will develop and externally validate two prediction models. From years 2-4, I will examine associations between specific medications and delirium. In years 4-5, I will undertake the large-scale causal inference study examining the effects of medication discontinuation. Anticipated impact and Dissemination The findings of this study will be communicated through scientific journals and conferences, patient summaries, a bespoke website, social media, and community engagement events. All outputs will be made freely available, and tools will be developed for integration into routine electronic health record systems.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: Brief opportunistic Smoking cessation Advice for financially Vulnerable Individuals accessiNG financial Support (SAVINGS): a randomised controlled trial
Abstract: Aim of the research We want to see whether giving someone who smokes help to quit through a financial advice service makes them more likely to quit than someone who does not get any support. Background to the research People with lower incomes are more likely to smoke and less likely to quit than people with higher incomes. This means they are more likely to be ill due to their smoking. Brief advice and support to stop smoking can increase peoples’ chances of success. Giving this help where people with lower incomes seek financial advice could help more people quit smoking. Design and methods used We have worked with groups that provide social housing and financial guidance. They have helped find the best way to give brief advice on stopping smoking and to plan this study. We have also found financial support services who are interested in taking part. Financial support advisors will ask people if they smoke during routine appointments. If the answer is ‘yes’ advisors will explain the study and ask if they want to take part. We will put those who agree into one of two groups at random. One group will not receive guidance on their smoking. The other will be told the best ways to quit. They will also be sent a nicotine vape and given help to access behavioural support, like a smartphone app or counselling from a stop smoking adviser. We will include 1,538 people who smoke in the study. We will contact people 12-weeks and 9-months after they receive financial support. We will ask about changes in their smoking, quality of life, tobacco spending and financial wellbeing. We will interview the people taking part and the people giving support about their experiences in the study. Patient and public involvement We developed study methods by talking to people who smoke with financial difficulties. We also talked to people who give financial guidance. We will ask two people who smoke and have had support with financial problems to join the study team. They will guide us on the best ways to run the study. We will also ask a small group with lived experience for advice on running the study and presenting results. Sharing results We will share study results with everyone who takes part, including financial advisors. We will also create a plan to share results more widely with people who smoke or have smoked, and who have experienced financial problems. We will ask people with lived experience to review materials sharing our findings. We will also talk to people who work in relevant services to decide how to share this information with them. In the past, we have used images, videos and podcasts to explain our results, and may use these approaches again. We will work with Action on Smoking and Health and the National Centre for Smoking Cessation and Training (NCSCT). They will share our results through their contacts. NCSCT will create a training programme and briefing document based on this research that will be shared with their more than 90,000 contacts.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Coastal and Rural Mental Health Realist Study (CARMHRS): what works, for whom, in what circumstances, how and why?
Abstract: Plain English Summary of Research: Aim This research is about solving the problems people in rural and coastal areas face when trying to get mental health support. It will also look at how services are provided. Problems include not enough services, transportation issues, and poor internet connections. People in these areas also have challenges like floods and economic problems that can affect their mental health. This study aims to find ways to make mental health services better. The study will look at different plans being used to improve mental healthcare in three rural and/or coastal areas (Lincolnshire, Cornwall and North East and North Cumbria). We will work with local communities and produce a guide to help other rural and coastal places improve their services. The goal is to make mental healthcare better for everyone, no matter where they live. Design and methods To find out what is happening, we will do qualitative research, which involves talking to local NHS staff and people in communities and understanding their experience of mental health care. We will also look at differences between places and how this affects mental healthcare. Here’s what we’ll do: Month 1. We will set up the study, including approvals and involving patients and the public. Months 2-23. We will collect data about what is happening. We will find out about social, historical, psychological, and geographical features that play a role in mental healthcare. Using this information, we will build ideas about how to improve access. Two researchers will work together. One will look at what is happening in the mental health system (called a Researcher-In-Residence). The other will learn what the community thinks about that (called a Community Researcher). People will meet to learn from each other. Once we have a good idea about what seems to work, we will refine these ideas by talking to more people. The people we will speak to are mental healthcare staff and community members. Our goal is to see if the plans work in real-life situations. Months 24-28. We will bring together everything we’ve learned to create a guide for anyone looking to improve mental healthcare access and quality in rural and coastal areas. Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) Early PPI: To write this application we involved five members from the Peninsula Patient and Public Engagement Group. Listening to their experience of rural and coastal living helped shape the research questions. For instance, they raised ethical concerns about using video calls for therapy, so we’re going to look at how technology is used. PPI in the project: Each area will have a local PPI team who will meet regularly. They will help with research design, data analysis, build community relationships, and decide how we share our learning. We’ll offer training and they’ll be supported by the local researchers. Representatives from each PPI team will take part in national workshops, to help create the guide. The PPI Co-Applicants will use their experience to work with our lead investigator, RJLH, to run the national workshops together. Dissemination This research project aims to create a practical guide for improving mental healthcare in rural and coastal areas. Once the guide is ready, we plan to share it through networks across England and on social media. We've talked about what we want to do with important organisations, and they are looking forward to sharing the research findings and guide.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Integrated models of community service delivery for children and young people in coastal regions of England: A Realist evaluation
Abstract: Background Children and Young People (CYP) in England experience some of the poorest health outcomes and services in Europe. Inequalities in CYPs health are marked between north and south of England, especially within the coastal areas of England where deprivation is high, and social determinants of health such as housing, education , access to services, infrastructure, employment and social mobility play an important part in CYPs lives. There are also uneven numbers of children in care or YP leaving care in some coastal areas. For these CYP, health outcomes are even worse. Studies in the youth literature show the importance of place and geography in relation to CYP health and opportunities growing up in coastal England. By understanding the protective factors and assets within deprived coastal communities, it may be possible to develop models of care and service provision that build on assets and deliver community services to CYP that are timely, preventative and health promoting before the health problems of adult life become more serious requiring extensive and costly interventions. Such models of care already exist in some coastal community services in England (e.g Integrated Neighbourhood Teams in Kent) but little is yet known or understood about how such models impact on the experiences, lives and health consequences for CYP. Aims We want to find out how integrated community service delivery models (ICSMs) in coastal areas across England affect the experiences and health consequences for CYP and their families. We aim to: Understand what different ICSMs exist for CYP in coastal areas and how they work How ICSMs are accessed and attended by CYP, the barriers and facilitators How CYP and their families experience ICSMs What difference being able to access community services in a coastal area makes for CYP health Assess the cost and benefits of ICSMs designed for CYP Our definition of community services includes all community NHS, public health, social care and voluntary sector support within a coastal Integrated Care System (ICS). Involvement of CYP We have had initial consultation with CPY on the research aims and design, as a result we have included primary and urgent care in our definition. We will consult with our CYP and parents lived experience groups throughout the study through two co-ordinators. What we will do Realist evaluation methods provide a way of understanding what coastal community services work for CYP and under what circumstances. We will undertake a scoping review of the existing evidence on community services for CYP. Following ethics approval, we will collect data from up to 4 case study sites from diverse coastal areas of England. As the realist approach is largely qualitative we will use interviews and focus groups with CYP and professional staff as the main source of data, combined with some quantitative data such as surveys, local public health and administrative data analysis. Our analysis will be combined across the study sites and will include description of services in context, how they work (mechanisms) and the consequences (outcomes) for CYP. What difference this will make CYP living in coastal communities experience large variations in health and care outcomes. The findings will help us to understand how ICSMs can help to keep CYP well, improve health and their social care. The work could strengthen ICS decision making in developing ICSMs that support CYP and their families.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: London School of Economics & Political Science
Award_Title: Adult Social Care in rural and coastal areas – the issues, emerging evidence and process mapping models
Abstract: Our focus is adult social care (ASC) in rural and coastal areas. Evidence of health inequalities in rural and coastal areas has been mounting, prompting some improvements in the evidence base for health interventions and policies to address them. In contrast, evidence for ASC in these locales is underdeveloped. Hence, we have little evidence for national and local policy makers, practitioners and communities to organise ASC to support people’s belonging and maximise wellbeing. We, a lived-experience and academic partnership, will explore these ASC issues in 3 rural/coastal areas - Cumbria, Devon, and Herefordshire & Worcestershire (H&W). Each presents characteristics of the issues underpinning this research call, and contrast each other. Cumbria is very highly rural & isolated - there some larger coastal settlements but these have significant areas of deprivation. Devon has cities, with coastal towns facing challenges, and isolated rural areas e.g. the moors. H&W are highly rural; H significantly more so, while W borders the West Midlands Conurbation. The 3 sites present overlapping and different issues for ASC, providing opportunities to compare and contrast contextual issues and those likely to apply across similar locales. We will work through the following work packages to develop outputs, particularly aimed at augmenting the Rural Proofing for Health Toolkit with evidence for ASC to help local and national policy makers plan for balanced health and social care systems. In work package 1 we will do a scoping review of the evidence on ASC in rural and coastal areas, and interviews with national leaders (about 12) with an overview of ASC in rural/coastal areas, setting the context for the next work package. We will complete research ethics and governance procedures. Work package 2 comprises research in our 3 sites. We will commence with data mapping existing evidence from and about the sites relevant to understanding ASC there. We will undertake interviews with local ASC stakeholders from the local authority, independent and third sector organisations, exploring issues and opportunities from their perspectives (about 15 per site). We will hold 6 workshops per site to explore the experiences and ideas of local people with relevant lived experience (e.g. using services, being a carer, being a practitioner). At least one workshop will focus on living with dementia and one on learning disabilities, being inclusive of people with those experiences. We will be as inclusive of local demographics as possible across workshops. We will report evidence from these work packages to guide ASC policy, practice development and research in rural and coastal areas. In work package 2 we will identify promising innovations in each site to evaluate using the process tracing method (our work package 3), which entails developing a detailed description of the intervention and how it is thought to work, i.e. mechanisms that deliver outcomes. We will search for evidence (e.g. local quantitative evidence, stakeholder experience) to test the intervention hypotheses. We will grade hypotheses to produce a picture of how well we can understand the intervention’s operations/impacts. Knowledge mobilisation and public engagement underpin the whole project (work package 4). We will have an advisory group, including 4 people with lived experience, to guide all stages of the work and advise and support on developing a pathway to impact.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Consolidating a digital exclusion typology and stakeholder engagement exercise to inform future evaluation of digital exclusion initiatives
Abstract: Many people in the UK find it difficult to use the internet and technology, making it difficult to access important health information and services. This issue is known as digital exclusion, affects certain groups more than others, such as older adults, people with lower incomes, rural populations, and those with lower levels of education. Digital exclusion happens for many reasons. Some people lack access to devices or the internet, while others find it too expensive. Many lack the necessary skills, literacy, confidence, or trust to use and engage with digital tools and services effectively. The rapid pace of technological means that our understanding of what causes digital exclusion continues to emerge. Current solutions often focus on just one part, like access to devices or training in digital skills, but this may not be enough if we do not consider the broader context. Our proposal aims to understand why some people are digitally excluded, and how solutions can help. We have four main goals: First, we want to understand the theories and concepts that explain the factors causing digital exclusion. Second, we aim to find out which theories support efforts to reduce digital exclusion. Third, we will gather information on existing initiatives designed to tackle digital exclusion and see how they measure their impact on people’s health and wellbeing. Finally, we plan to identify which of these initiatives could be evaluated in future projects. To do this we will complete two main activities. The first activity will consist of a literature review to create a detailed classification system, known as typology, to better understand the drivers of and solutions to digital exclusion. This typology will be developed with the help of experts in the field including two representatives of organisations working with digitally excluded communities (public research partners), this way we will guarantee that the voices of those communities are heard and integrated into our research. The second activity will involve engagement with key organisations and people working in this area to gather information about current initiatives targeting digital exclusion. We are interested in knowing what their focus is, who they intend to help and how they measure the success of these activities. We are particularly interested in knowing if they are measuring their impact on health inequalities. We will consider how well, or not, these activities address the factors across the digital exclusion typology we created to help to identify which interventions are more likely to be successful. Our project will last 12 months and result in a comprehensive guide to support the design and evaluation of digital inclusion initiatives. This resource will be shared with stakeholders across the UK to help ensure that digital solutions contribute to better health and wellbeing outcomes for all. It will also help inform future work to better evaluate and learn what works and why some things are successful and others not. By doing this, we hope to make it easier for everyone, no matter their age, income, or health, to stay connected and healthy. Our goal is to make sure no one is left behind in the digital world.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving wider determinants of health
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Countermarketing (CM) against the products and activities of unhealthy commodity industries
Abstract: Background Almost three quarters of deaths are caused by health problems like cancer and heart disease. These can be caused by our genes, and where we live, but also by unhealthy food, and alcohol and cigarettes, and other products. Many approaches have been used to try to prevent such deaths. For example, warning labels have been added to products. There have also been health campaigns to help us make healthier choices. The activities of companies who sell these products can also harm health. This is known as the ‘commercial determinants of health’, or CDOH. For example, pricing offers are used to tempt us into buying unhealthy products. Certain types of people or communities are targeted with advertising campaigns, and these can harm health by promoting unhealthy products. Such marketing activities can also widen health inequalities – for example between poorer and better off communities. Companies also try to influence politicians to protect their markets, and mislead the public about the harms they cause, and dispute that they encourage unhealthy behaviours. The public is often unaware of these tactics. ‘Countermarketing’ (CM) has been suggested as a way to raise public awareness. It might also reduce public demand for unhealthy products and may increase public support for policies to promote public health. CM does this by drawing attention to the tactics used by businesses. What will our project involve? It will involve two literature reviews. This is a type of study where we carefully search for existing evidence. We will analyse the information on CM. Then we will produce summaries about the impact of CM and how it works. We are particularly interested in whether it helps to reduce health inequalities. In addition to cigarettes, alcohol and unhealthy food, we will also search for information about social media, e-cigarettes (vapes), gambling, infant formula and fossil fuels. All of these products can harm our physical or mental health. We will work with members of the public to get their views of the products, the industries and their tactics. Why will the project findings matter? Overall, our findings will help public health policymakers and others to decide whether CM interventions would be useful to improve health. They will also highlight any gaps in what we know. In this way they will also help us to plan future research. How will the public be involved? We will involve the public throughout the project. This will include workshops to develop our research plans. We will also work with the public on how to interpret our findings, and how to make them widely available. Fog index 10.04. Flesch-Kincaid reading ease score=60.2 (readable by UK 13-15 year old)

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving wider determinants of health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Care of people at the end of their lives in the rural and coastal communities of the South West Peninsula of England: A participatory realist evaluation
Abstract: Background: We will all die at some point; however, the way people and families are supported at the end of life varies significantly. Evidence suggests that people living in rural and coastal areas may find it harder to access the care they want at the end of their lives. End of Life care (EoLC) is defined as the care of people in their last twelve months of life, with a focus on supporting physical, emotional, and spiritual needs. In Devon, Cornwall and Somerset, 78% of people live in rural or coastal locations. These places also have a higher number of older people and people facing social and economic challenges. Whilst we know there are problems in accessing EoLC, there hasn’t been much research into understanding why these problems exist and how we can improve EoLC in these areas. Study aims: This study will look at how people in Devon, Cornwall and Somerset are cared for and supported at the end of their lives, particularly in rural and coastal areas. We will use a method called realist evaluation to understand what works well and what doesn’t in providing support for people and their families. There are four work packages (WP) which will run in parallel over 28 months. WP1 involves case studies in the six geographical areas in Devon Cornwall and Somerset to understand EoLC. We will also undertake case studies on six different populations such as rural farmers, older people and people who are homeless. The case studies will involve observations, focus groups, and interviews with people at the end of life, their families, professionals who care for them, the voluntary sector, and those organising services. WP 2. We will survey people responsible for EoLC across the UK and interview local, regional, and national EoL leaders to understand the challenges rural and coastal areas face in delivering accessible EoLC for everyone. We will host regular online discussions with stakeholders from local, regional, and national groups. WP3. We will use existing NHS data, collected both nationally and locally, to explore and better understand reasons for difference in care during the last 12 months of life. WP4 brings together findings from WP1-3. Our research team, alongside a patient and family stakeholder group and a professional stakeholder group, will meet to help confirm and develop our understanding. Involving people as partners in the study: The importance of this study became clear during the extensive engagement work we did in 2023, where we spoke with 45 health and care professionals and 18 individuals who were nearing the end of life, their carers or bereaved family members. A PPIE (Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement) group has met to support the preparation of this study, and a patient and family stakeholder group will actively support how this study runs, how we understand the results of the research, and how we tell others about the work. Additionally, there are two co-applicants, a family member whose father died, and a care manager representing the voice of care home residents. Both have contributed to the development of this proposal. We will share our findings regularly during the study, directly linking into healthcare practice to reach those responsible for organising, planning, and providing care. We will publish our findings in peer-reviewed journals and take part in policy events. Additionally, we will present our research at relevant conferences both nationally and internationally.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Public Health Intervention Responsive Studies Team: PHIRST Connect
Abstract: Aim(s) of the PHIRST Team PHIRST Connect were originally set up in 2020. They are a research group that works with local authorities, public health departments, and their partners, such as voluntary sector organisations, and the public to evaluate public health activities. These might be services, new policies or campaigns. The aim is to provide evidence that can help improve the health and well-being of people in the UK with a particular focus on those whose health is poorest. How PHIRST Connect work They team up with local partners who can be from any part of the UK, to define the project and decide what kind of evaluation is possible. They create a detailed plan that is made public and get ethical approvals. They carry out the research supported by a range of local partners (e.g. service providers, public health officers) making sure voices from a range of different backgrounds are included. They use online and in-person approaches to suit different needs and give everyone chance to be included. They identify people who can use and share the knowledge gained, so that the findings can make a difference for current and future service users and improve people's health and wellbeing. Timelines for delivery Projects usually take 15-18 months, with up to ten projects planned over five years. Patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) A specially formed Public Involvement in Research group, currently made up of nine people, without academic training is involved in all aspects of the research, including planning, carrying out the work, and sharing results. They help to make sure things that are important to members of the public are considered in research that is for the public good. Local people with relevant life experiences are also included in each project's advisory group and when possible other local people are consulted on the research design, materials and findings. Sharing results and having an impact on health and inequalities PHIRST Connect engages with various groups that they think will find the research useful (e.g. national public health service commissioners’ groups or staff at the Department of Health & Social Care). They create easy-to-understand materials like infographics and briefings and make presentations to share the findings in ways these groups can easily use. They also publish findings in scientific papers. The work has already had an impact.
