Award_Title: Pilot study of a randomised trial of a guided e-learning health promotion intervention for managers based on management standards for the improvement of employee well-being and reduction of sickness absence
Abstract: Design: This pilot study is the precursor of a cluster randomised controlled trial of an organisational level intervention with outcome data measured at the individual level (wellbeing is the primary outcome with common mental disorder being a secondary outcome) and the organisational level (sickness absence is the primary outcome at the organisational level) and cost-benefit of intervention. This preliminary study will test the acceptability of the trial, feasibility of recruitment, optimise the components of the intervention, adherence and likely effectiveness of the intervention. Setting: The e-learning intervention will be undertaken by managers in one large pilot organisation with autonomous departments. Data will be collected from employees in the same workplaces. Target population: Men and women of working age working in an NHS Trust (the Cheshire and Wirral Partnership NHS Trust). Managers and employees from this organisation will be randomised to intervention and control groups. Intervention being evaluated: All managers in the clusters randomised to the intervention, will receive the e-learning package. Rosemary Anderson, the developer of the intervention will train facilitators to guide further implementation. We will identify the managers and groups of employees to be involved in the intervention. The intervention is an e-learning health promotion programme for managers with a focus on the six management standards domains: Change, Control, Demands, Relationship, Role and Support. We will use the Anderson Peak Performance e-learning module for managers (www.andersonpeakperformance.co.uk) based on the HSE management standards and the Management Standards indicator tool. We will pilot this programme in collaboration with Rosemary Anderson. The programme aims to improve managers’ capacity for helping employees improve their wellbeing and deal with stressful working conditions. The intended focus is on improving social support to employees, improving communication, improving organisational justice, increasing information about job change and making sure that employees work is valued. We will also include strategies for changing /adjusting/rescheduling workloads and strategies for improving job autonomy such as working in semi-autonomous teams. The format of the intervention is a series of linked topics with case examples and assessment. It will be presented over a 3 month period. The same intervention will be used for all managers within the intervention organisations. Use of the programme can be monitored to measure uptake of the intervention. Staff will be incentivised to use the intervention, through management ‘buy-in’, publicity and receiving a certificate of completion as part of continuing professional development. We will also provide a ‘certificate of competence’ for managers as an added incentive for participating. We will present the programme in a way that will incentivise middle managers to participate showing that this can improve their working life. Measurement of outcomes: In this pilot study we will measure the recruitment and retention rates to the study, the acceptance of the intervention and attitudes to the different components of the intervention. The pilot study will include both qualitative methods (focus groups and in-depth interviews) and quantitative methods to pilot the likely effectiveness of the outcomes to be used in the main study. In the main study the primary outcomes will be a) Employee wellbeing: pre-post changes in levels of wellbeing will be assessed using the Warwick Edinburgh Wellbeing Scale, a brief 14 item scale assessing aspects of positive mental health, including both hedonic and eudaimonic perspectives; b) Sickness absence: pre-post changes in sickness absence will be monitored using the existing reporting systems of each of the organisations recruited. The outcomes to be assessed include total sickness absence days per 100 person-years. Secondary outcomes include c) self-report sickness absence- short term (< 7 days) and medium-term (7-21 days) absence; the 12-item General Health Questionnaire (GHQ12), which measures psychological distress; e) self-report psychosocial work characteristics will be assessed using the standardised assessment tools for job strain (control & demands) and effort-reward imbalance. We will also pilot the feasibility of undertaking an economic assessment of the intervention at the organisational level. The primary and secondary outcomes will be assessed before the intervention, and then at four months after the start of the intervention. Initial assessment of employee wellbeing will be carried out before the intervention at baseline and at 4 month follow-up. In this pilot study we will test the feasibility of the processes for collecting sickness absence data. Sample size: For the pilot study we will include three intervention clusters and one control cluster. We will recruit 120 employees per cluster to achieve a sample of 100 employees per cluster. The pilot study will provide evidence for the basic assumptions in our sample size calculations that will strengthen our calculations for the main study. Planned analyses: Pilot study analyses will be descriptive. We will estimate the participation rate and retention rate for managers completing the intervention. We will also collect and analyse electronic data on usage of the e-learning program. We will also estimate the participation rate and questionnaire response rate for employees, in both intervention and control groups, analysing the characteristics of non-participants, specifically in terms of gender and job title. We will also examine the baseline sociodemographic data including age, sex, SOC group, manual or non-manual occupation for those who drop out between baseline and follow up. During the pilot study we will also carry out in-depth interviews with key informants (eg CEO or Head of HR) to assess their views of the positive and negative impact of the intervention. We will also carry out three or more focus groups with 6-8 managers after the intervention to assess the acceptability, ease of use and perceived usefulness of the intervention. We will also assess managers' knowledge acquired through use of the programme. Project timetables: The duration of the study is 18 months. Ethical approval for the study will be obtained by month 2. Recruitment of an eligible organisation has taken place but we are also approaching back up organisations and this will be undertaken by month 2 although we will also have approached organisations before the formal start of the grant. Scoping for additional material to add to the intervention will take place in months 1 and 2. Baseline data collection will be carried out between months 4 and 6. The intervention will be carried out between months 7 and 9. Employee self report data at follow up will be collected between months 10 to 13. Focus groups and individual interviews will be carried out between months 11 to 13. Sickness absence data collection will be carried out during the same period as employee self report data. Data will be analysed between months 6 to 8 for baseline data and 11 to 14 for follow up data. The draft final report will be prepared by month 17 and the main paper will be prepared between months 17 to 18. Results will be fed back to participants in months 17 to 18.

Award_Title: Manipulating the appearance of steps and stairs to make them safer for older people to negotiate
Abstract: Research Design: A repeated measures laboratory based study, investigating adaptive gait in independently mobile older people. Setting. The gait and vision laboratory at the University of Bradford. Target population: Subjects will be recruited from a group of 50 retired volunteers who regularly sit as patients in undergraduate clinics at the University’s Eye Clinic and from a group of 200 older people on the mailing list of Bradford Older People’s Forum. Healthy subjects will be recruited using exclusion and inclusion criteria used previously. Intervention being evaluated: Adaptive gait when ascending and descending steps and stairs will be assessed with and without a variety of modifications to the appearance of both single and multiple steps. Measurement of outcomes: In all stepping experiments, three-dimensional lower limb segmental kinematic data of the stepping action will be collected (at 100Hz) using an eight-camera, motion capture system (Vicon MX; Oxford Metrics Ltd, Oxford, UK) with ground reaction forces collected as subjects step from a force platform onto or from a step that is placed directly over an adjacent force platform (OR6-7; AMTI, Boston, MA). We have used this approach successfully in many previous experiments and many other leading gait labs use it. Our own work and that of others has identified gait and stepping parameters that are important for safe stepping in ascent and descent. Parameters analysed will include foot placement before the initial step and foot position on subsequent step treads, any hits or scuffs of the step, maximum foot/toe elevation, vertical and horizontal heel (descent) or toe (ascent) clearance, gait velocity, and dynamic stability.In addition, knee-drop and peak landing force will also be determined for step descent. Analysis will also include intra subject variability of these parameters as increased variability in toe clearance for example can lead to a greater likelihood of the step being hit and a trip occurring. Sample size: One primary outcome measure will be the increase in vertical toe clearance with the H-V illusion compared to without it. Using data from the pilot study and assuming a 50% increase in variance for older subjects compared to younger ones; assuming a minimum effect of importance of 5%, an estimated standard deviation of 7% and using a two-sided alpha of 0.05, for a paired t-test a sample size of 21 would result in a power of 90%. A sample size of 16 would provide 80% power. This sample size is similar to that used in several recent studies investigating gait adaptations in older subjects (N=19) and suggests that the sample size is appropriate and recruitable. Although the main analysis will incorporate a repeated measures design, the effective power is likely to be similar to that using a simple t-test but will depend upon unknown parameters that are difficult to estimate prospectively. Planned analyses: The analysis of step/stair ascent will primarily focus on foot placement relative to the step riser, toe clearance over the step edge, and foot placement on the upper step or raised surface. The analysis of step descent will primarily focus on heel clearance over the edge or nosing, heel placement distance on the lower step’s tread, pre-landing kinematics for the descent phase and the mechanics of landing for the initial contact period. Existing ‘in-house’ analysis software that uses previously developed (and reported) biomechanical modelling approaches will be employed to investigate how gait parameters, toe and heel clearance and landing behaviour are adapted under the visual illusion. In addition, we need to determine whether a mismatch between step height as perceived visually (5-20% higher than actual size) and that perceived via the somatosensory system once the lead-foot has landed on the top of the step, could unsettle postural stability, particularly for the larger increases in visually perceived step height. If this occurred, it could negate any improved safety gains from the increased toe clearance of the step edge. For this reason we intend to also determine the effects of the different illusions on dynamic postural stability, by determining the anterior-posterior (A/P) and medio-lateral (M/L) distance between the lateral malleolus of the leading foot and the centre of mass (COM) and the A/P and M/L COM velocity at the instant of foot contact. It is likely that toe and heel clearance will reduce as subjects ascend and descend the stairs and we need to determine whether this learning effect is changed in any way due to the visual illusion by assessing the effect of trial repetition. Data will be analysed using a random effects population averaged model, using the Stata version 9.2 statistical programme (Stat Corp., College Station, USA). This multivariate model will be obtained using the Generalised Least Squares (GLS) random effects estimator, which produces a matrix-weighted average of between-subjects and within-subjects results. An exchangeable correlation structure was judged to be appropriate, given the experimental design, and due to the exploratory nature of the study no ‘type I’ error adjustment of the alpha level is deemed necessary. Thus level of significance will be set at p<0.05. Factors of interest will be incorporated sequentially and their statistical significance tested using a likelihood ratio test. Factors with a p-value less than 0.10 will be provisionally retained, whereas those above 0.10 will be dropped. The final model adopted will be the most parsimonious one felt to adequately explain the data. Project timetables: A workplan, documenting the project timetable and including significant milestones, is attached to the application (workplan.pdf).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Randomised controlled trial of a pedometer-based walking intervention with and without practice nurse support in primary care patients aged 45-74 years
Abstract: Background Physical activity (PA) is vital for health, yet most adults are inactive and do not achieve the recommended 30 minutes of moderate intensity activity on 5 or more days weekly. Adults' most common PA is walking, light intensity if strolling, moderate if brisker. Pedometers measure step-count and can increase walking, but most trials have had short-term outcomes, have not separated out pedometer effects from other support and have reported only step-counts, not time spent at different PA intensities. Design: Primary care based 3-arm randomized controlled trial with 12 month follow-up and health economic & qualitative evaluations. Participants: 993 inactive patients aged 45-74 years with no contraindications to increasing their moderate intensity PA will be recruited by postal invitation from 6 South West London general practices and randomly allocated into three groups. All participants will have their PA assessed objectively (step-count & time spent at different PA intensities) for 7 days at baseline, 3 months and 12 months by wearing an accelerometer which gives no patient feedback. They will also complete questionnaires and have anthropometric assessments. Intervention: One intervention group (pedometer alone) will be posted out a pedometer diary and written instructions for a 12-week pedometer-based walking programme, based on their own baseline accelerometer step-count. The second intervention group (pedometer plus support) will receive a pedometer and diary and three individually tailored PA consultations with a practice nurse. They will be supported to follow a 12-week pedometer-based walking programme, using strategies such as self-monitoring, goal-setting, boosting motivation and anticipation of set-backs. The control group will continue usual PA. Main outcome measures in all groups after 12 months: 1. Change in average daily step-count (primary outcome) 2. Change in sedentary time and time spent in at least moderate intensity PA weekly 3. Cost-effectiveness. 4. Acceptability of the interventions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Using systematic reviews to guide disinvestment decisions in NHS commissioning
Abstract: Project 1: we will interview health care commissioners who produce commissioning guidelines, and clinicians who apply these guidelines, to identify factors that facilitate or limit the application of evidence. Participants will be interviewed in their professional capacity using a purposive sample of ‘difficult’ and ‘easy’ decisions around diverting funding from health care interventions that are ineffective, or dealing with interventions where there is insufficient evidence supporting their use. Project 2: we will systematically search for published and unpublished documents to identify examples of organisational structures (e.g., commissioning groups employing outside expertise in evidence synthesis) and strategies, or information products, used to promote the uptake of high quality systematic review evidence by commissioners, providers and clinicians. The search will be structured around the examples of review products described by Lavis (2009). (1). Although the scope of this project is primarily on disinvestment decisions, we will attempt to capture examples of information products used for all types of decision-making. Databases will include MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Health Economic Evaluations Database and The Cochrane Library. Project 3: we will survey PCTS to assess the level of support provided by the different strategies (or information products) using a range of examples identified from the UKCC database of interventions that should not be used, should only be used in a research programme or for which there is insufficient evidence of effectiveness. (1) Lavis J N. How can we support the use of systematic reviews in policymaking? Plos Medicine 2009, 6: e1000141. doi: 10.1371/journal.pmed.1000141.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Long-term follow up of a trial of annual mammographic screening from age 40
Abstract: This project involves the long-term follow-up of an individual randomised controlled trial, in which 160,921 women aged 40-41 were randomised in the ratio 2:1 to an intervention arm invited to annual mammographic screening until age 48, and to a control arm receiving usual care. There were 23 participating centres in England, Wales and Scotland. Women in both arms become eligible for screening in the NHS Breast Screening Programme (NHSBSP) from age 50. Mammography in the trial was by two views at first screen, and by single view at subsequent screens unless otherwise indicated. Analogue mammography was used throughout the trial; digital mammography is now being introduced in the NHSBSP, and may potentially improve sensitivity. All women in this trial have been flagged at the NHS central register (NHSCR), and more than 99.9% successfully traced. This provides data on all cancer registrations and deaths, including data and underlying coded cause of death, and also on emigrations. The majority of these data are supplied electronically. The primary outcome measures will be breast cancer mortality, restricted to deaths in cases diagnosed after trial entry, and based on underlying cause of death from the death certificate, and the cumulative incidence of invasive and in situ breast cancer. We will analyse the risk of breast cancer mortality in the intervention arm relative to the control arm, and the reduction in absolute risk. The latter allows the 'number needed to be invited' and 'number need to be screened' to be calculated, and provide a comparison of cost-effectiveness with screening at other ages. The cumulative incidence of breast cancer will allow the extent of over-diagnosis due to screening to be measured, as well as any potential shift from invasive to in-situ disease.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The diagnostic accuracy of hearing tests and cost-effectiveness of school entry hearing screening programmes
Abstract: This project will evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of hearing screening tests and the cost-effectiveness of screening for hearing impairment at school entry. Four related empirical studies will provide data to contribute, together with routine data and existing literature, to the development an existing economic model. (1) We will determine and compare the diagnostic accuracy of two methods of screening for the identification of permanent hearing impairment at or around school entry; the established pure tone sweep test applied under headphones and a new hand-held pure-tone screener. (2) We will assess the yield, referral age and route through assessment to intervention for permanent childhood hearing impairment and measure the costs of referrals for a geographical area which does not employ a routine School Entry Screen (SES). (3) We will collect the same data for an area with a routine SES and compare it with the data from the service with no SES. We will prospectively assess the impact for the child and the family of a positive result from a screen (both true and false positives) resulting in referral for further assessment. We shall address the issue of the impact of a potential false negative result by a comprehensive review of the existing literature. (4) We will determine the resource costs in implementing the two alternative screening methods in primary schools. Throughout the study we will develop an existing SES economic model to provide robust estimates of key parameters beyond accuracy to be assessed in Study 1. In particular the yield and nature of hearing loss detected in a system with no SES; and the yield, consequences and costs of screen positive individuals in an SES system. Based on our findings we will make recommendations regarding the continued implementation of the SES and the form that implementation should take.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Development of a cost-effectiveness model for optimization of the screening interval in diabetic retinopathy screening.
Abstract: Our aims and objectives are to: • Use demographic and routinely collected clinical information from 15000 patients in 85 Gloucestershire GP practices to develop a risk score for each patient and to identify patient groups whose risk of retinopathy progression is low and whose screening interval can be safely extended; • Model what the influence of the grading classification error is on over referrals and under referrals and how that influence changes over time, taking into account sequential grading results and hospital outcome results, comparing screening intervals that vary according to risk score against current standard practice (annual screening intervals for all patients) and other fixed-interval approaches. • Extend our results to multi-ethnic populations • Determine if assigning diabetic patients to differing diabetic retinopathy screening intervals using a risk estimation model is cost-effective when compared to current practice, which is annual screening of all eligible patients with diabetes; • Estimate the economic benefits if personalised screening intervals were to be applied to the National Screening Programme in England. Research Design and Methods: There are 4 project phases: Phase 1: GDRSS risk factor approach Phase 2: Monitoring interval approach Phase 3: Extension to an ethnically diverse population Phase 4 - Cost-effectiveness & cost-utility analysis.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: The cost effectiveness of genetic markers for antibiotic resistance in tuberculosis
Abstract: "This study will investigate the clinical impact and cost effectiveness of the use of genetic markers for identifying multi- or extensively- drug resistant (M/XDR) tuberculosis (TB) using real patient data in the UK. Although the incidence of MDR-TB in the UK is low (˜1%), its impact on the individual, their close contacts, and the health care economy is disproportionably large. This proposal will compare a range of rapid molecular tests for detecting genetic markers of antibiotic resistance with gold standard culture-based drug susceptibility testing. We will first investigate the clinical effectiveness of the molecular tests through a comprehensive systematic review of the available published and ""grey"" literature in medical
Status: scientific and economic databases. Extracted data will be used to parameterise a transmission-dynamic mathematical model. The model will enable us to predict how interventions such as rapid molecular tests can affect MDR TB through prompt diagnosis of cases - leading to appropriate treatment being started earlier and reducing transmission of the infection to others. We will then utilize this information to conduct an economic evaluation of a range of rapid assays in comparison with conventional culture and susceptibility testing for patients with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis and suspected MDRTB/XDRTB. We will use modelling to estimate the clinical effects and costs for these individuals
Funding_and_Awards_Link: and also to estimate potential savings and health benefits from the prevention of onward transmission. We will compare alternative models of service provision (centralised versus disseminated) and assess the value of targeting rapid testing at various high risk subgroups."
Award Budget: Complete

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Transforming Community Health Services for Children and Young People who are Ill:A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation
Abstract: DESIGN AND THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK Interrupted time series (ITS), supported by longitudinal qualitative research and a cost consequence study, to address the research aims outlined above. ITS design is appropriate when randomisation is not feasible, e.g. when evaluating organizational change and when time series data are available e.g. Health Episode Statistics (HES). The design will support quantitative analysis of change over time in outcomes and costs and qualitative analysis of change over time in processes. This mixed methods approach is appropriate when additional information is needed to interpret quantitative measurements, generating understanding of how service redesign has worked, for whom, in what context and at what cost (i.e. providing a ‘realistic evaluation’). There are two main outcomes for the ITS analysis – hospital admission for the most frequently occuring, common childhood conditions presenting for acute, non-elective care, and length of stay for all conditions in children. These outcomes were chosen based on hypotheses derived from existing knowledge (see full proposal). We will also carry out sub-group analysis on childhood conditions associated with the highest average and highest total length of stay in in-patient care ('complex care'). SITES Three health communities (currently PCTs) representing different geographies, deprivation levels, population profiles, commissioning models, and stages of change, where comprehensive children’s community nursing (CCN) coverage is being or has been introduced while redesigning children’s services. We know that point at which these three sites did or will (in 2012) introduce their CCN service, thus making it possible to date the implementation of change and determine the 'before' and 'after' periods for the ITS. METHODS AND ANALYSIS 1. INTERRUPTED TIME SERIES ANALYSIS of HES data will measure the impact of CCN services on the main outcomes, using data for 24 months pre- and 24 months post-implementation of CCN services. A control condition unlikely to be affected by the organizational change will be used to examine threats to internal validity and to enhance the construct validity of any effect (see full proposal). Additional analysis will explore differences between children with and without complex care needs, and the impact of demographic and socio-economic factors. After graphical exploration of the interrupted time series, formal statistical analysis will include an ARIMA analysis and a time series regression. We will identify the most appropriate model to describe the data. The time series regression will estimate the impact of the service redesign, taking into account any underlying trends, time lags and serial correlation. The regression coefficients corresponding to a change in outcome after introducing the service, and to a change in slope will be calculated. A Durbin-Watson test will check for serial correlation. A non-equivalent but conceptually related dependent variable will be used to enhance internal and construct validity. 2. LONGITUDINAL QUALITATIVE RESEARCH, including documentary analysis, observation of key meetings, in-depth interviews with commissioners, providers. primary care professionals, and service user families, and use of service quality tools will track the process and impact of service redesign before, during, and after it happens. The focus will be on known impediments to progress in community service development and recommended actions from Transforming Community Services. We will also track the influence of changed commissioning arrangements on the service redesign. Narrative analysis of documents and data from observation of meetings will provide contextual understanding of the process of service redesign. Framework analysis of data from in-depth interviews with commissioners and providers will identify key issues related to quality, outcomes and costs of CCN services, over time. Framework analysis of data from families will similarly identify issues related to outcomes, and over time. Data from the validated service quality tools will be compared with qualitative accounts of service quality over time. 3. COST CONSEQUENCE STUDY Resource use will be estimated from: a) HES data for all secondary care contacts for frequently occuring, common childhood conditions, length of stay for all children’s conditions. If possible, given the experimental status of HES data for emergency care, A&E attendances for common childhood illnesses may also be explored; b) questionnaires for CCN team staff and existing data sources, covering grade/scale of staff delivering care, number, type and duration of contacts, equipment, travel time and administration, enabling an accurate ‘bottom up’ costing of care; c) family questionnaires to assess contacts with other health professionals, out-of pocket expenses, time lost from work, time spent on informal care and contacts with other public sector agencies; d) interviews with local commissioners and providers (see above) to generate alternative ‘top down’ costing of CCN services. Unit cost estimates will be applied to relevant resource use data to generate a total cost per patient. Outcomes generated from the other two parts of the study will be presented in a descriptive way alongside the costs of the alternative methods of service provision. The primary analysis will estimate the cost of the intervention using the ‘bottom up’ approach. The ‘top down’ approach will be used as a sensitivity analysis. The impact of the intervention on other costs will be presented, disaggregated into costs falling on the health service, other public sector agencies and families. Results of the cost-consequence analysis will be presented in a manner useful for decision makers and will include estimates of the mean incremental costs associated with CCN services and an assessment of the uncertainty around these estimates. Extensive scenario analysis will test the robustness of the results and the generalisability of results to other patient groups will be discussed. TIMETABLE Year 1: set up cost data collection and HES datasets; begin longitudinal qualitative elements. Year 2: continue cost data collection;begin qualitative and service quality tool data analysis. Year 3: HES and cost data analysis, complete other analysis, draft final report.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: How can international evidence on interventions to manage referral from primary to specialist non-emergency care be applied in a UK context? Development of an inclusive systematic review and logic model
Abstract: We plan to use an innovative method, which combines systematic review and logic modelling techniques to develop an evidence-based framework to define links between interventions and health outcomes. The evidence synthesis and accompanying logic model will provide a strategic perspective on the understanding of how international referral management interventions may be applied in the UK context. It will uncover and evaluate assumptions underpinning how interventions may lead to enhanced outcomes and provide a framework for communication and discussion. The work will thus be directly relevant for informing NHS managers and other stakeholders and for developing practice. The synthesis will also provide an overview of the current state of knowledge in the field and indicate where further research is needed. By examining links between interventions and outcomes it will provide valuable insights into the outcome measures currently in use and have the potential to inform the future measurement of effectiveness. The core research team have worked together for over three years as part of the NICE Public Health Collaborating Centre conducting systematic reviews of effectiveness and cost effectiveness of complex interventions on a number of policy directed topics as well as developing innovative methodologies in evidence synthesis. The successful processes of working developed during this time have created a coherent and efficient team capable of undertaking this proposed research. In addition, Andrew Lee, Nick Payne and Martin McShane bring further considerable NHS practice, commissioning and management knowledge, whilst Danuta Kasprzyk and Helena Britt provide international collaboration allowing the team to draw on their knowledge and advice at every stage of the project from bid submission to dissemination.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Smoking Cessation Intervention for Severe Mental Ill Health Trial (SCIMITAR): a definitive randomised evaluation of a bespoke smoking cessation service
Abstract: We have already conducted a successful external pilot of the SCIMITAR trial and we propose a fully-powered trial in this challenging but important area. DESIGN: RCT, with concurrent economic evaluation. SETTING: mental services & primary care; with sites in York, Leeds &Bradford, North Yorkshire and the North East, South Yorkshire, Manchester and the North West, and North London. TARGET POPULATION: Adults with severe and enduring mental illness (SMI) who currently smoke, and are interested in cutting down/quitting. HEALTH TECHNOLOGY: In response to an NIHR commissioning brief we have already developed a manualised 'bespoke smoking cessation service' for people with SMI; delivered by a mental health professional. The Bespoke Smoking Cessation (BSC) service combines evidence-supported interventions (largely NRT & behavioural support), adapted to a patient population with SMI. The intervention has been developed in conjunction with the National Centre for Smoking Cessation Training (NCSCT). There is a strong emphasis on nicotine-supported smoking reduction and eventual quitting. The manualised bespoke service is offered on a 1:1 basis over four months for people with SMI in primary and secondary care settings. Pharmacotherapy is provided by the patients’ usual GP. This package of care has been shown to be acceptable, with good participant engagement in our developmental phase and pilot trial. A key feature is the delivery of manualised smoking cessation delivered by a mental health professional. The comparator technology is usual care (signposting to existing smoking cessation service provided by the patients' own GP practice or local NHS quit smoking services). PRIMARY OUTCOME: smoking cessation measured at 12 months post-randomisation (exhaled carbon monoxideand sustained self reported quitting ‘Russell standard’) – outcome specified by HTA at the commissioning phase of the pilot trial. SECONDARY OUTCOMES: carbon monoxide-verified smoking cessation at 3 and 6 months; Health Related Quality of Life (SF-12); Nicotine dependence, mood (PHQ9); patient satisfaction health, utility (EQ5D) at 3, 6 & 12 months ECONOMIC EVALUATION: the incremental cost per QALY of bespoke smoking cessation programme compared to usual care will be calculated from both the NHS and societal perspective. PROCESS EVALUATION: In our external pilot phase we have already examined acceptability (to patients with SMI and healthcare staff) and barriers and facilitators to the delivery and uptake of bespoke smoking cessations services using qualitative methods. We do not propose any further process evaluation in the definitive trial. SAMPLE SIZE: powered to detect a risk ratio of 1.8 or equivalently a 16% absolute difference in quit rates. To give 90% power (5% two sided sig.) to show a difference we require a sample size of 160 per group or 200 participants per group after allowing for 20% attrition (i.e. 400 in total). PROJECT TIMETABLES INCL. RECRUITMENT RATE: We will obtain ethical approval to continue the SCIMITAR trial following our successful pilot. We will extend recruitment to include five new centres. Months 0-6 site set up and R&D approvals. Months 6-24 recruitment. Month 36 last follow-up. Month 42 final report. There is agreement for excess treatment costs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: Heart of England NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Why do outcomes of hospitalised patients with first out of hospital cardiac arrest from Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) vary in England and Wales?
Abstract: Study design: Retrospective analysis of an existing multi-centre prospective observational cohort study. Data source: We will use the NHS national heart attack registry, the Myocardial Ischaemic National audit Project (MINAP), to identify a subset of patients (about 1.8%, estimated n = 15,000) who had a cardiac arrest recorded out of hospital and were admitted to hospital. Inclusion criteria: • Adults (aged >18 years) • Out of hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) due to an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) • Initial resuscitation attempts successful leading to admission to an NHS hospital Exclusion criteria: • 2nd or subsequent cardiac arrests • In-hospital cardiac arrest only Case identification: Cardiac arrest is defined as an “absence of signs of circulation and/or considered for resuscitation” (1). Careful scrutiny of MINAP definitions (2) shows that ‘first cardiac arrest’ in patients with ACS may be identified using a number of variables and/or combinations of variables. The optimal approach for case identification of OHCA will be ascertained and sensitivity and specificity reported. Primary outcome: All-cause in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes: Time to all-cause mortality and/or neurological outcome. Impact of potentially modifiable predictor variables: • Emergency Medical Services (EMS) transport time (3, 4) • Use of an electrocardiogram (ECG) in ambulance/hospital • The use of an early invasive strategy (including coronary angiography and / or percutaneous coronary intervention)(5) • Time from first collapse to reperfusion • Hospital volume of cases of ACS over study period (6-9) Impact of potentially non-modifiable predictor variables (i.e. a subset of the confounding variables): • OHCA occurring in presence of a trained health professional (including paramedic) • EMS response time (10) • Presence of a trained medic/paramedic during OHCA • Location of OHCA • History of diabetes mellitus • Ethnicity (11) Other potential confounders: co-morbidity, background risk variables, process variables Using the rich data from MINAP, we will adjust for important confounders of survival from OHCA. These will include: age, gender, ethnicity and urban/rural domicile (from postcode), co-morbidity variables (e.g. previous acute myocardial infarction, chronic renal failure, chronic heart failure, diabetes), lifestyle variables (e.g. smoking status), results of investigations (systolic blood pressure, heart rate, raised cardiac troponin concentration), process variables (such as admitting consultant status etc.), core variables known to be important for surviving a cardiac arrest out of hospital (12, 13) and explore standardisation using established MINAP risk scores for stratification of patients with ACS (14-17). Sample size: Within the complete MINAP database of just under one million events, there are an estimated 15,000 cases with OHCA hospitalised alive. Our initial work suggests that a sample of this size has adequate power to detect meaningful differences in the primary outcome, and will allow a detailed investigation of factors which may impact upon survival after OHCA (18). Statistical analysis: We will impute values for the missing observations using multiple imputation via chained equations (14, 19), as has been suggested in the MINAP dataset (14). Sensitivity analyses will be performed to assess the robustness . We will fit multilevel models with a random effect term to test the hypothesis that the key explanatory variables and confounders explain the variability in outcomes. Time schedule: The total time schedule of this study from setup to dissemination of results, with 60% FTE statastician, is 18 months. Outputs and knowledge generation: The project will produce four main outputs linked to the study objectives. 1) Define the epidemiology and outcome of patients who are admitted to NHS hospitals following successful resuscitation from out of hospital cardiac arrest that has been caused by an acute coronary syndrome 2) Report the relative contribution of potentially modifiable factors linked to the in-hospital pathway for these patients 3) Synthesise of the research findings from our team of experienced clinicians, those with responsibility for healthcare policy, patient and public representatives and expert methodologists to produce key recommendations for service organisation. If the data allow we will evaluate potential modifications to health care system design and estimate the likely impact on health outcomes. 4) Prioritised summary of future research needs

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Health Equity Indicators for the English NHS: Longitudinal whole-population study at small area level
Abstract: This project aims to develop useful indicators of change in NHS equity performance, based on time series change in socioeconomic gradients in health care utilisation and outcomes. This research is needed because NHS decision makers have a duty to have regard to the need to reduce inequalities in outcomes and access to services, but do not have any routine equity performance indicators that enable them to discharge this duty effectively. Simple disaggregation of the performance indicators in the NHS Outcomes Framework will not suffice, since this will not tell decision makers how far the NHS is responsible for cross sectional variation in utilisation and outcomes. We will select a manageable number of indicators following investigation of technical feasibility and a stakeholder consultation process. General indicators - for example, all non-emergency hospital admissions and mortality from causes considered amenable to health care - will be supplemented with groups of specific indicators relating to a small number of specific disease areas. Indicators will include both patient level and small area level indicators, and indicators using both primary and secondary care data. Each indicator will be constructed using comprehensive national data, disaggregated to measure patient level or small area level socioeconomic inequality using both absolute and relative inequality measures, and tracked over time to examine time series change in social gradients from 2001/2 to 2014/15. We will allow for observable change in non-NHS determinants of inequality in both small area level and patient level analyses - in area level analyses using data on small area population need (e.g. ONS data on demographic and ethnic mix and QOF data on disease prevalence, smoking and obesity) and in patient level analysis using data on patient risk factors (e.g. HES data on age, sex, ethnicity and diagnoses). We will then attempt to identify NHS determinants of change in social gradients, on the plausible assumption that changes in NHS delivery can have short run effects on social gradients in health care utilisation and outcomes over a period of a few years whereas many wider non-NHS determinants of social gradients change slowly or have long delayed effects over decades rather than years. We will identify NHS effects by first consulting specialist clinicians to identify plausible NHS determinants of change for particular indicators and then (a) comparing patterns of change between different indicators at different points on the patient pathway and (b) using quasi-experimental research designs such as interrupted time series and difference-in-difference studies. We will present our findings to local and national NHS decision makers in the form of equity dashboards that help to pinpoint change in social inequalities in health care utilisation and outcomes in different geographical areas, disease areas and points on the patient pathway.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Can automated Diabetic Retinopathy Image Assessment softwares replace one or more steps of manual imaging grading and is this cost-effective for the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme?
Abstract: DESIGN: An observational study to quantify screening performance, diagnostic accuracy and cost-effectiveness of automated primary grading, in routine English practice. Three automated software programmes will be assessed. Study phase 1 is retrospective: the automated software packages will grade 18,000 screening episodes, which have been manually graded, from patients attending diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening programme. Phase 2 is a prospective implementation study of an additional 6,000 screening episodes from the same clinic. Manual grading will be 2-field-2 step, by human graders who meet English National Screening Programme (ENSPDR) quality assurance standards and is the reference standard for this study. SETTING: Diabetic eye screening service in England compliant with ENSPDRstandards. TARGET POPULATION: Diabetic patients over 12 years of age eligible for DR screening, attending a London PCT screening programme with a wide spectrum of ages and ethnicity(24%South Asian, 17% black African/Carribean and 38%white European) The retrospective study (n=18,000 consecutive screening episodes) will begin 12 months prior to the start of the grant. The prospective study (n=6,000 screening episodes) will begin soon after the grant starts. HEALTH TECHNOLOGIES BEING ASSESSED: Commercially available software with CE mark, or likely to obtain CE mark within 6 months of study: iGrading (Medalytix), Retmarker (Critical-Health), EyeCheck (IDx). All investigators are independent of commercial software development and have no commercial interest or IP in automated DR screening. Uniquely, we already have access and support for all 3 software packages for the study, and exclusive access to the IDx software for evaluation in the UK. MEASUREMENT OF COST AND OUTCOMES: Each software provides a binary output of “no disease” or “disease present”. Cost effectiveness will be evaluated based on the expected cost per true positive case of retinopathy and cost per QALY. Measures of performance of each automated grading system will include sensitivity, false positive rate (1-specificity) and likelihood ratios, using the final manual grade as the reference standard. These measures will be determined for referrable DR overall and for each grade of DR. Diagnostic accuracy will be described by 95% confidence intervals (CI) for each primary outcome. Clinical interpretation of these measures will focus on the lower limit of the 95%CI for the detection of proliferative (R3), pre-proliferative (R2) DR grades and maculopathy (M1). This indicates the potential number of screening episodes missed by the automated systems requiring clinical intervention. The upper CI for false positive rates for DR grades R1(background) and R0 (no DR) will assess the additional number of screening episodes requiring manual grading and the risk of over-diagnosis. Technical failure rate will be determined. Secondary outcomes will measure agreement for automated systems and manual grading against the final clinical decision for a screening episode. Disagreements between the human grader and one or more automated systems will be arbitrated on a subset of images from the 18,000 retrospective screening episodes.by an internationally recognised fundus photographic reading centre, masked to the original gradings. This gives an independent assessment of the relative performance of manual and automated systems, and provides external validity to the project. Emphasis will be placed on arbitrating discrepancies with manual grades R3, R2, M1 and a proportion of R1 and R0 grades. Technical failure rates for automated and manual grading will be compared. (Continued in ‘additional information section)

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Randomised trial of the effectiveness of Group Family Nurse Partnership (gFNP) programme in improving outcomes for high-risk mothers and preventing abuse
Abstract: Study design: The study will comprise a randomised controlled trial in which eligible families will be randomly allocated to one of two arms i) gFNP delivered over 76 weeks; ii) standard care. Setting: Family Nurses employed by the local NHS trust in conjunction with local councils as part of the Family Nurse Partnership team will provide the intervention in local Sure Start Children's Centres. Inclusion criteria: Expectant mothers prior to 16 weeks gestation and with expected delivery dates within 4 to 6 weeks of each other (per site). Eligibility criteria are either: aged under 20, expecting second or subsequent child, no qualifications or maximum 4 GCSEs at Grade C; or aged 20 to 23, expecting first or subsequent child, no educational qualifications or maximum 4 GCSEs at C, and one of: current or history of mental health problems, ever in care of social services, lives in workless household, or never employed. Intervention: Group Family Nurse Partnership (gFNP) - groups of on average 10 women with similar due dates and partners if applicable starting at 16 weeks gestation and extending until infants are one year; comprises 14 2-hour pregnancy sessions and 30 in infancy, all based on materials originally used for the Nurse Family Partnership(NFP) programme. One of the two Family Nurses is also a qualified midwife who provides routine antenatal midwifery care; both FNs provide postnatal routine infant checks. Recruitment (see Figure 1) Parents will, with the support of the midwifery team, be recruited by researchers at or soon after their the booking-in visit. The midwife will identify all eligible women and, with oral agreement, provide their details to the researcher who will then explain the study in more detail including the randomization. They will be given 24 hours to make a decision after which time the researcher will telephone. If verbal consent is given a home visit will be made immediately or as soon as possible to obtain written consent and baseline details. Researchers will telephone the clinical trials unit so that randomization can occur. Consenting participants will be informed about the group to which they have been allocated by the researcher and those receiving the intervention will be contacted by the FNP team, who will be given the details of intervention families by the Trial Manager. Sample The standard deviation (SD) of the short form Child Abuse Potential Inventory in the target population is approximately 6.3 (Ondersma et al., 2005). We propose to recruit sufficient mothers and babies (families) to allow the trial to detect a difference between groups of 0.5 standard deviations, with 90% power at a significance level of 0.05 (2-tailed); this is considered to represent a moderate size of effect . Very conservatively assuming a correlation of 0.4 between pre and post intervention scores we would need 71 families in each arm of the trial to detect this difference. Conservatively, allowing for an expected 30% drop out rate (based on pilot sites) we would therefore need to recruit a minimum of 84 families per arm of the trial. We therefore propose to recruit 100 families per arm. In the intervention arm this will consist of 10 groups of (generally) 10 families, provided in 5 FNP sites (N=100). Allocation to groups: Consenting parents will be randomly allocated to one of two arms. Randomisation will be conducted by the LSHTM Clinical Trials Unit, who will provide a 24 hour telephone contact system. Data collection: The data will comprise a range of self-report questionnaires, and (at 12-13 months) recorded observations of the parent and infant and hospital attendance data from HES. Data will be collected at baseline (before randomisation) for demographic data and all questionnaire outcomes, at 2-3 months (CAP, EPDS; PSI); and immediately post-intervention when the infants are 12 months (all outcomes including the CARE index). Maternal quality of life information (EuroQuol EQ-5D, SF-36) will be collected at 2, 6 and 12 months. Data will be collected in the respondent’s home. Participating families will be given a £20 Boots Gift Vouchers at each data collection point as an acknowledgment of their contribution, and to promote compliance. Methods for protecting against bias: The researcher will be blind to the intervention groups at baseline data collection but from that point will be aware of allocation, which would in any event become evident from participants' responses and conversation. Measurement of outcomes and duration of follow-up: Primary outcomes: The short form of the Child Abuse Potential Inventory (CAP, Milner, 1990), a self-report questionnaire measuring distress, rigidity, family problems, unhappiness, feelings of persecution, financial problems and loneliness, discriminates between abusive and non-abusive parents; and at 12 months maternal sensitivity and infant cooperativeness as identified with the CARE-Index (Crittenden,1974-2004; 1981), an observational measure which identifies relationships and interactions indicative of maltreatment. Secondary outcomes: maternal depression - Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (Cox et al., 1987); parental distress (Parenting Stress Index, Abidin, 1995); contact with social services indicative of child abuse concerns; hospital A&E attendance (injuries, ingestion, poisoning); and maternal health related quality of life (EuroQuol EQ-5D, SF-36). Programme integrity: Compliance with the programme will be assessed during supervision to assess the extent to which a number of key criteria are being met by the practitioners. In addition information from anonymised standardised data forms completed by the nurses will be examined so that it can be determined whether the content of the sessions conforms with the programme objectives for covering the five programme domains: maternal role, maternal health, family and friends, life course, and environmental health. Attendance per group and individual 'dosage' will also be determined from these forms. Process data: Data will be collected about participants who a) refuse to take part in the study; b) drop-out of the intervention/study including quantitative demographic data and qualitative data to explore reasons for non-participation or discontinuation. Qualitative data will be collected to indicate the acceptability of the programme for clients and practitioners, and other local service providers and commissioners. Data analysis: All primary analyses will be carried out according to the principle of intention-to-treat. Every effort will be made to obtain outcome measures on participants, even if some drop out during the course of the group sessions. The data will be analysed by multiple regression modelling, fitting baseline measures of outcomes as covariates, where available. The small groups in which the intervention is delivered will be fitted as a random effect. A small number of secondary analyses based on explicit hypotheses, e.g. subgroup/ explanatory analyses (considering compliance with the interventions), will be specified in advance. Qualitative data will be transcribed and analysed thematically using NVivo 8. Economic evaluation: We will assess the costs of gFNP implementation in each area and assess the extent to which variations in implementation and uptake have an impact on costs. Simple modeling will be used to assess cost changes given differential uptake (service providers, staff training, see section). Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios per unit of improvement will be calculated. Given the plethora of outcome measures across several domains, a separate discrete choice experiment (DCE) will be conducted amongst trial participants at the final point of follow-up. The outputs of the DCE will be combined with cost estimates and changes in relevant outcomes to generate cost-benefit ratios. Research Governance: The proposed research will be conducted in accordance with the Research Governance framework. Ethical committee approval will be obtained from NHS research ethics committee for a multi-centre study and from each local R&D. Project timetable including recruitment rate (see Figure 2): 5/12 to 8/12 gain ethical approval; finalise details of participant interviews; 9/12 to 3/13 recruit and collect baseline data one site in first month and two sites per month for 4 months with the final group in the 6th month to allow for some slippage (total N=200); 3/13 to 6/13, process interviews on recruitment; 6/13 to 12/13 conduct 2-3 month research visits, 35 per month; 10/13 to 4/14 6 month telephone contacts; 3/14 to 6/14, process interviews with professionals; 3/14 to 9/14 conduct 12/13 month observations and interviews. 9/14 to 11/14, acceptability interviews with clients; 10/14 to 11/14 code CARE observations. Data entry, cleaning and preliminary analysis ongoing. 11/14 to 4/15 prepare final report.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: What is the effect of reduced street lighting on crime and road traffic accidents at night? A mixed methods study
Abstract: Objectives: (1) To conduct a nationwide analysis of street-level data for all local authorities (LAs) where street lighting reduction schemes have been introduced by 2012; to quantify (with adequate power and precision) the impact of these schemes on night-time traffic injuries and on all crimes. (2) To use qualitative research methods to identify articulated public views about street lighting reduction schemes and their consequences, and the role these views have played in local decision making. (3) To develop an inventory of all quantified costs and benefits of street lighting reduction schemes and to examine variation in the costs and benefits of schemes. Objective 1 Design: Controlled interrupted time series analysis. Setting: All local authorities of England & Wales. Target population: People who were victims of road traffic collisions or street crime. Intervention being evaluated: Any street lighting reduction schemes implemented by 2012 (to include switching selected street lights off permanently; switching selected street lights off for part of the night; ‘trimming’ the period where lights are switched on; dimming the brightness in the evening and during the early hours of morning). We shall classify each road according to the type of lighting change implemented. Measurement of outcomes and duration of follow up: STATS19 road traffic injury data will be obtained for the period 2000 to 2012. These data include date, time, location of collision, by type of casualty (pedestrian, car occupant, etc.). Crime data will be obtained for the period up to 2012 from police.uk including the month, location and type of crime. Geographical Information System (GIS) methods: We will link data sets to a road segment database including the characteristics of all roads in England & Wales. We will classify each road segment according to road type, type of street lighting reduction scheme (e.g. part-night switch-off; ‘dimming’), the period at night when lighting is reduced, and the Super Output Area in which it is located. Sample size: We propose to assemble and analyse data for all LAs in England & Wales that have implemented sizeable street lighting reduction schemes by 2012. This will enable reasonably precise quantification of the impact of such schemes on road injuries and crimes, even on the assumption that the schemes only affect roads on which 1% of road injuries and crimes occur. For road injuries, we will maximise power by using data for at least 10 years before schemes were implemented; for the more numerous crime events, data may be available for only one year before implementation. We estimate that across all LAs the expected annual number of road injuries at night on roads with reduced lighting will be around 150, yielding study power of 90% to detect an increase of 32% above pre-implementation road casualty levels. For crime, we estimate that across all study areas the expected number of all (day and night-time) crimes on intervention roads will be around 20,000 per year. This number will provide 90% power to detect a 5% increase in all (day and night-time) crimes above pre-intervention levels (equivalent to a 20% increase in night-time crimes alone), and for major sub-categories such as burglary, we will have 90% power to detect increases of about 10% in all (day and night-time) crimes. By obtaining data from a sample of four police forces (one tenth of all forces) we can expect 400 detailed night-time crime events per year. Using data for one year before lighting reduction and one year after, we will have 90% power to detect a 26% increase in crimes above pre-intervention levels. There will be similar power to detect increases of 40% in major sub-categories of crime (e.g. violence against the person). Planned analyses: Analyses will adapt methods previously applied by the applicants to quantify the effect of 20mph zones on road injuries (Grundy et al. 2009; Steinbach et al. 2010). These are based on conditional Poisson models applied to events (road injuries and crimes) for every individual road segment (over 100,000 road segments in total) across study areas. Comparisons will be made of the change in events on roads before and after the street lighting changes, controlling for: (i) changes over time in day-time road injuries and all crimes on the same road segments (i.e. ‘within-roads’ comparisons); and (ii) year-to-year trends in night-time road injuries and all crimes on all other roads of a similar kind (i.e. ‘between-roads’ comparisons). Objective 2 Design: this will utilise elements of ethnographic rapid appraisal, traditionally developed for research with rural populations in low income settings, but increasingly used as a complement to quantitative epidemiological methods in high income urban settings when more focused qualitative data are required on topics for which good quality epidemiological data do not exist (Trotter, 2001). - Rapid appraisal: Using the review of proposed lighting reduction schemes (DeFRA 2011) and our contacts with all LAs of England & Wales (for Objective 1), we will identify a purposive sample of eight LAs to provide a range of rural & part-urban settings across England, with lighting reduction schemes in place, or proposed. The rapid appraisal will generate data from web searches, phone/email interviews and a 2-3 day site visits as follows: - Survey of web and public sources (e.g. LA websites, minutes of committee meetings) to identify LAs where lighting has been or is to be reduced; public consultations on street lighting to identify methods used and the content of concerns expressed; and contact details for key informants in each locality. - Key informant interviews to identify local consultation processes to date; local stakeholders’ views of public concerns; how concerns are incorporated into policy decisions; other factors that influence policy decisions around street lighting. These key informants will help to identify sites for survey interviews with residents and for ethnographic interviews, and to provide data for Objective 3 (below). In each area we aim to include: councillors, local MPs, LA Engineers Departments, Police Community Liaison Officers, and other local actors identified in interviews. - One-to-one interviews with a sample of 20 people in two contrasting sets of affected streets in each area. Interviews will cover views of current street lighting levels, preferences for more/less lighting, impacts of any changes noticed. Using data on area deprivation (in the GIS) the streets will be selected to include contrasting areas of socio-economic status. - Ethnographic interviews and observations using natural groups where possible (e.g. groups encountered in cafés, community meetings suggested by local key informants). These interviews will be used to generate more narrative talk about street lighting and possible reductions, and the impact of this on health and wellbeing. Analysis: Data from key informant interviews will be thematically analysed to identify the range of ways public consultations are incorporated into decision making and how public health evidence (of the type generated in Objective 1) could, or would, be utilised. Resident survey interviews will be analysed using descriptive statistics, comparing views in areas where lighting has been reduced to those changes are proposed, and comparing higher and lower socio-economic settings. Key informant and ethnographic interviews will be analysed thematically, using both deductive methods (i.e. identifying how far issues such as sleep, anxiety, fear of going out after dark are expressed) and a more inductive analysis to identify the meaning and salience of street lighting for residents and other road users in terms of impact on health and wellbeing. Key issues for data analysis will include salience of concerns; comparisons of views before and after changes; comparison of concerns expressed in public consultations, survey interviews and ethnographic interviews. Objective 3 We will assemble evidence from objectives 1 and 2 (above) of all costs and benefits. We will assemble data from local authorities on the costs of providing types of street lighting (i.e. infrastructure cost, maintenance costs, energy consumption). We will also assemble data on the monetary values (i.e. economic and societal costs) of road traffic casualties by level of severity and the economic, and societal costs of crimes by type of crime using Home Office definitions (Home Office, 2005). We will then compare societal costs of street lighting schemes against the societal benefits in a cost-benefit analysis framework. We will assess the impacts of street lighting schemes on inequalities by conducting stratified analyses (e.g. by: area deprivation, resident population density, crime and traffic injury rates pre-implementation of schemes). Using sensitivity analyses we also propose to examine the impact on our results of the uncertainty in our effect estimates (to derive credible limits of the estimated societal costs and benefits of street lighting reduction schemes).

Award_Title: The M74 study: longitudinal follow-up of the health effects of a new urban motorway
Abstract: DESIGN. Mixed-method study, using a combination of quantitative and qualitative research methods to evaluate both individual- and population-level changes in health and health-related behaviour coupled with achieving an in-depth understanding of how these changes are experienced and brought about. The study will comprise three main components: (1) CORE SURVEYS OF LOCAL STUDY AREAS to compare changes in neighbourhood perceptions, travel behaviour, physical activity and wellbeing in the intervention and control areas by means of combined cohort (baseline achieved total n=1322) and repeat cross-sectional (target total n=3000. minimum required total n=1200) follow-up surveys of local residents, coupled with an environmental audit (documentary analysis, interviews and site visits) to ascertain whether the intervention was implemented as originally planned, to elucidate its broader environmental impact and to identify any potential area-level confounders. (2) TWO-TIER IN-DEPTH STUDY of a subsample of core survey participants to quantify differences in neighbourhood-specific physical activity between intervention and control areas (combined accelerometry and GPS measurement, target n=400: 200 intervention + 2x100 control), and to elucidate participants’ experiences of environmental changes and the mechanisms through which these changes influence behaviour (qualitative interviews, target n=60: 30 intervention + 2x15 control). (3) ANALYSIS OF EXISTING NATIONAL POPULATION DATASETS to evaluate the impact of the intervention on road traffic casualties and to describe concurrent regional and national trends in travel behaviour and neighbourhood perceptions. SETTING. Matched intervention (n=1) and control (n=2) deprived urban areas in Glasgow (see sections C2 and C3). TARGET POPULATION. Householders living in areas previously surveyed in 2005 (see sections C3 and C5). Baseline respondents included both more and less affluent groups (e.g. 52% owner-occupiers). INTERVENTION. The new urban section of the M74 motorway and associated changes to the local urban landscape (see section C2 and m74completion.com). OUTCOMES. Changes in three measures of travel behaviour over an eight-year interval from baseline (2005) to follow up (2013): walking for transport (min/day), cycling for transport (min/day) and car use (min/day). Differences between study areas in time spent in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity within the neighbourhood (nMVPA: min/day). Changes in the monthly incidence of killed and seriously injured (KSI) road traffic casualties between 1995 and 2013 and in their distribution by type of road user, class of road and small-area socioeconomic status of location of incidents. Changes in neighbourhood perceptions and SF-8 physical and mental summary scores. Differences between study areas in time spent in overall MVPA (min/day). An understanding of what environmental changes have occurred in practice and how their effects have been mediated and experienced. KEY SAMPLE SIZES. For TRAVEL BEHAVIOUR, a cross-sectional sample of 400 per wave per study area (exceeded at baseline) would be expected to allow the detection with 95% confidence and 80% power of an increase of 5 min/day in walking for transport from baseline to follow-up within one study area, or a cross-sectional difference of 2 min/day in cycling for transport or 5 min/day in walking for transport between intervention and control areas at follow-up. The availability of two control areas, a larger follow-up sample than the minimum of 400 per study area, and the potential to compare longitudinal changes between study areas using a combination of cohort and repeat cross-sectional analyses will increase the power of the study to detect smaller changes. For objective PHYSICAL ACTIVITY measurement, 86 participants per group would be required to detect a difference of 3 min/day in nMVPA between intervention and control areas. Our target total achieved sample of 400 participants in objective monitoring would be more than sufficient to achieve this. For INJURIES, a minimum of 50 time points is recommended for interrupted time-series analysis of the type we intend to use. The STATS19 dataset from 1997 to 2013 contains 204 monthly data points and therefore easily exceeds this minimum recommendation. ANALYSES. Multivariable regression analyses of the effect of exposure to environmental changes on travel behaviour and neighbourhood perceptions; the sociodemographic distribution of those changes; and their relationship with changes in overall physical activity and wellbeing. Merging of accelerometer and GPS data followed by buffering of the combined dataset in a geographic information system (GIS) to identify nMVPA, followed by adjusted multivariable regression analyses of differences in nMVPA between study areas. Mixed-method thematic analysis of qualitative data linked to spatially-referenced activity data. Autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) interrupted time-series analyses of changes in injury rates; multivariable regression analyses to explore changes in sociospatial distribution of injury incidents. Repeat cross-sectional analyses of Scottish Household Survey data. TIMETABLE. Jan-Aug 2013: Refine study design and survey instruments; apply for ethical approval; commence documentary stage of environmental audit; prepare for survey data collection. Sep-Dec 2013: Collect survey data (completed in two months at baseline); complete documentary stage of environmental audit. Jan-Mar 2014: Clean survey data; prepare for objective measurement and qualitative fieldwork. Apr-Dec 2014: Analyse survey data; collect objective measurement data (with an issued sample of 30/wk, as previously achieved in our PHR-funded study 09/3001/06); undertake qualitative environmental audit and interview fieldwork. Jan-Dec 2015: Complete all remaining analyses and write up.
