Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: The impact of home energy efficiency interventions and winter fuel payments on winter- and cold-related mortality and morbidity in England: evaluation of a natural experiment
Abstract: It has been long recognized that the UK has a large and unacceptable burden of excess winter mortality and morbidity (generally upward of 25,000 excess winter deaths each year), which is greater than that of many comparable northern European countries with colder climates. Although part of the winter excess is attributable to influenza and other seasonal infections, time-series studies suggest the major part of the seasonal burden is related to exposure to cold.[1,2] Theoretical considerations and some direct evidence from the UK, New Zealand and elsewhere suggest that housing may play an important role in determining that vulnerability,[3,4] though it is also recognized that exposures to cold through outdoor excursions may also be important. There has therefore been much interest in, and debate about, the contribution that interventions on housing quality may have on winter- and cold-related mortality and morbidity, especially in the context of rapidly worsening UK figures on fuel poverty (caused mainly by recent upward global trends in energy prices) and recent severe winters. Over the next few decades there will be major investments in the housing sector driven in large measure by (i) policies aimed at reducing household energy use and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions to meet legally-binding obligations of the Climate Change Act (2008) and (ii) considerations of health, in particular the assumed benefits of improved insulation and energy efficiency for winter- and cold-related deaths and illness. However, these investments may be very costly, and they have the potential for adverse as well as positive effects on health[5] if energy efficiency is in part achieved through reduced ventilation. The Department of Energy and Climate Change (DECC) have been interested in the modelling the effects of home energy efficiency interventions on health, in part because health impacts are a potentially important element in guiding policy decisions. In synthesizing evidence for such a model a number of crucial evidence gaps became apparent. Among the most important is the lack of direct evidence on cold-related mortality and harder health outcomes such as hospital admission. Much of the scientific literature on home energy efficiency and health is dominated by small-scale, short-term assessments, often inadequately controlled, and using self-reported measures as key outcomes. No study published to date has been able to make a direct assessment of the impact of home energy efficiency on mortality, and only to very limited to degree (mainly focused on specific patient groups) has any study examined emergency hospital admissions. This is mainly because of the extremely large sample sizes needed to test such impacts (remembering that cold-related deaths and hospital admissions are only a small part of all deaths and admissions – and identifiable only through statistical comparisons) such that randomized controlled trials with mortality as the outcome are effectively precluded. This is a major gap in knowledge, not only because of its central relevance to policies aimed at tackling excess winter mortality/morbidity in the UK, but also because the crucial place such evidence has for the major choices needed in housing policies in general given the context of the large investment needed for climate change mitigation strategies. Moreover, we cannot assess the full economic and NHS benefits of such investments because of reliance on old and untested assumptions. However, because of several unique data sources in the UK, it is now possible to attempt an evaluation of mortality and hospital admission impacts through natural experiment. Key is the emerging availability of nationwide data on housing energy efficiency interventions compiled into a national database by the Energy Savings Trust (EST). This database is the Homes Energy Efficiency Database (HEED), which was established to ‘help monitor and target carbon reduction and fuel poverty work’. HEED tracks house-by-house the sustainable energy characteristics of the UK's housing stock using data gathered from a wide range of sources including energy suppliers, government grant managing agents, local authorities, home energy checks as well as EST programmes (examples include EEC/CERT, fuel poverty programmes, Low Carbon Buildings Programme, CIGA, Corgi). HEED includes data on insulation measures, heating systems, appliances and micro-generation installations, along with property survey information. It now covers approximately 50% of the UK's homes (over 13 million homes) with property- and date-specific details of such energy efficiency interventions over the last decade or so. By linking, nationwide, to postcoded mortality and hospital admission statistics, this data base for the first time makes it possible to address the evidence gap on the relationship between home energy efficiency and cold mortality/morbidity through direct measurement in a well-powered empirical study. We believe evidence will be invaluable in providing important new empirical evidence that has bearing on a wide range of policy areas, including health protection, housing policies, and NHS demands and costs; and it will provide evidence on the potential for housing investment/improvement to reduce health inequalities.[6] It has the potential to be a key element in decisions on major areas of policy formulation over coming years. It will be a unique study with an important contribution to the world scientific and policy literature. [1] Wilkinson P et al. Vulnerability to winter mortality in elderly people in Britain. Award_Title: Evaluating possible intended and unintended consequences of the implementation of Minimum Unit Pricing of Alcohol in Scotland: a natural experiment
Abstract: This is a mixed method study with three components: Component 1 is a repeat cross-sectional study of alcohol-related attendances to Emergency Departments (EDs) in 2 Scottish hospitals and 2 North England geographical control EDs at 3 time points. The study methods and tools are based on a previous study by one of the investigators (Drummond) and the experience of the Scottish Emergency Department Alcohol Audit. Baseline data collection will occur as soon as possible if funding is secured. Waves 2 and 3 will take place 6 and 12 months post-intervention. If implementation takes place more than 12 months post baseline, wave 2 will become a 2nd baseline. Patients aged 16 yrs and over (exclusion criteria in project detail) attending EDs will be asked by research staff to complete a short face-to-face interview. An ED attendance database will be maintained during data collection periods to monitor patient recruitment. The interview will include: basic demographic information; amount of alcohol consumed in the past 24 hours; whether the patient has been a victim of violence, problematic alcohol use in the past year (assessed by FAST). A note will be made of the hospital unique identifier for the attendance. Research staff will retrieve additional demographic characteristics, other attendance details, and diagnoses at discharge (ICD-10) from patient records. Based on previous study by CD, we have assumed 50% recruitment of eligible ED attendees. We anticipate from the 4 sites (2 Scotland, 2 England) 940 recruits per week. Recruiting over 3 weeks pre- and post-intervention would provide a total sample size of 5640 (940*6) giving us the power (>80%) to detect a decrease in the proportion of alcohol-related attendances from 30% to 25% with 95% significance. For subgroup analyses by age and deprivation, we would have good power (>80%) to detect changes on the FAST score Component 2 is a repeat cross-sectional questionnaire for patients attending sexual health services to determine changes in drinking patterns, other substance use and source of alcohol. All patients attending 3 sexual health services in Scotland and 3 in North England as geographical controls will be invited to complete a 5 minute anonymous questionnaire by a trained research support worker. Participants will be recruited over the times periods similar to the ED study. The following will be sought from respondents: where alcohol is procured, other substances used, views on alcohol control, FAST score (to quantify problematic drinkers), and basic characteristics (age band, sex, highest educational level). Assuming conservative recruitment of 50% of attendees at SH clinics at 6 sites (3 Scotland, 3 England) we will have about 10,000 recruits over two 3 week periods (an average of 288 per clinic per week). This would give us power of> 80% to detect an increase in the proportion of people using drugs from 30% to 34%. Component 3 is a repeat cross-sectional qualitative study of young binge drinkers aged 18-25 and older heavy drinkers aged 30+ living in disadvantaged circumstances, who evidence suggests are more sensitive to price changes. Focus groups will be conducted approximately 5-6 months prior to and 5-6 months post-implementation in urban-affluent, urban-deprived and rural-deprived communities within the catchment areas of the 2 hospitals in Scotland recruited for component 1. Discussions will focus on: changes in drinking patterns and purchasing habits, alcohol displacement behaviours; social norms and attitudes. A total of 12 single-sex focus groups will be recruited at each wave enabling comparisons between types of drinker and socio-economic status. Purposive sampling will be used to recruit individuals from the two population groups of interest.via licensed premises (off- and on-trade) with the permission of local licensees and via street intercepts. In addition we will undertake 15 -18 semi-structured interviews at each wave with key stakeholders from professional groups who are well positioned to observe impact and the challenges MUP creates within each study community. Data from the interviews will be triangulated with the findings with other components to provide a more vivid and rounded picture of community expectations, the implementation process and the legislation’s short term impact.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Bristol Girls Dance Project: a cluster randomised controlled trial of an after-school dance programme to increase physical activity among 11-12 year old girls
Abstract: Design: School-based cluster randomised controlled trial. Setting: 18 State secondary schools with Year 7 (aged 11-12) girls in the greater Bristol area. Target population: Year 7 girls in the target schools who provide informed parental consent. Intervention being evaluated: Schools randomised to the intervention (N=9; 270 children) will be provided with a 20-week (i.e. 2 school terms) dance intervention. The dance programme will be delivered twice a week at the school site. Each session will last 75 minutes and will be delivered by external dance teachers using a standardised programme. The dance programme focuses on building the girls’ perceived autonomy to be active and perceived dance competence in a social, mutually supportive environment. All outcomes will be assessed at three time points: baseline (time 0), during weeks 19-20 of the intervention period (1st follow-up) and a year after baseline data have been collected (2nd follow-up = time 0 + 52 weeks). The primary comparison is the 2nd follow-up which is designed to ascertain whether any beneficial effect of the intervention remains once the intervention has been removed. The 1st follow-up is designed to yield information on activity levels while the programme is still running. All baseline (time 0) assessments will be conducted prior to school randomisation. The following outcomes will be assessed at each stage: 1) Primary: Accelerometer derived mean minutes of moderate to vigorous intensity physical activity (MVPA) on a weekday will be our primary outcome measure. Secondary outcomes 2) The following accelerometer derived variables will be considered secondary outcomes: a) Mean weekend minutes of MVPA; b) Mean weekday accelerometer counts per minute (which provides an indication of the volume of activity in which the girls engage); c) Mean weekend accelerometer counts per minute. In addition we will also compute mean minutes of sedentary time per weekday (<100 counts per minute). We will also assess self-reported autonomy competence, relatedness, perceived parental support and self esteem which we are hypothesising may function as mediators of behaviour change. 3) Intervention related resource use in the form of time, travel and expenses will be collected through researcher and dance teacher timesheets from a public sector perspective (Local Authorities, NHS). Researchers will record expenses connected with intervention delivery. 4) Process assessments will be undertaken to assess the dose of intervention delivered, intervention fidelity and the potential dissemination of the intervention. Attendance at each session, session duration and session lesson plan compliance will be reported by the dance instructors. The dose of the intervention (i.e., number of planned sessions delivered) will be recorded in each school. Intervention fidelity will be assessed by two methods: a) dance teachers will complete a log-book indicating whether they delivered planned core components of each session either fully, partially or not at all; and b) four randomly selected sessions delivered by each dance teacher will be observed during the 20 week intervention. At the end of these sessions we will also ask all girls to complete a brief perceived exertion and enjoyment questionnaire. 5)Qualitative work to assess potential sustainability and dissemination of the intervention. Exit interviews will be conducted with each of the dance instructors and a member of the school leadership (Headteacher / Year head etc) at each intervention school. We will also conduct two focus groups with six participants at six of the intervention schools. Focus group participants will be purposively sampled to include girls with high and low attendance levels. Sample size: The target difference for this trial is 10 minutes of MVPA per weekday (i.e., 50 minutes per week) between the intervention and control groups. This magnitude of effect is achievable with this intervention based on our pilot study data. The uninflated sample size required for analysis to detect a difference of 10 minutes/day MVPA, assuming a standard deviation of 18 minutes with 90% power and 5% two-sided alpha is n=68 per arm. We estimated the 95% CI for the school-associated ICC in the pilot study to be <0.001 to 0.087. If we assume that 20% of participants will not provide primary outcome data, the mean cluster size for analysis will be 24, resulting in a design effect of 3.0 using the upper 95% confidence limit for ICC. Thus we will recruit a total of 18 schools and 540 children. Randomisation: This is a clustered randomised trial, with allocation of schools and analysis at the level of the individual. Allocation will be performed by a statistician with no other involvement in the study, and balanced according to baseline levels of MVPA. Planned analyses: The analysis and presentation of the trial will be in accordance with CONSORT guidelines, with the primary comparative analyses being conducted on an intention-to-treat basis and due emphasis placed on confidence intervals for the between-arm comparisons. A full analysis plan will be developed prior to completion of data collection and discussed and agreed with the TSC. We will use descriptive statistics to assess balance between the trial arms at baseline for both school and individual participant characteristics. The primary outcome will be analysed by intention to treat without imputation. In order to take appropriate account of the hierarchical nature of the data, we will use multivariable mixed effects linear regression to estimate difference in the primary outcome for intervention group versus control, adjusting for baseline MVPA and randomisation variables. In a secondary analysis, we will further adjust for any variables that were imbalanced between the trial arms at baseline. Similar analyses will be repeated for secondary outcomes. We will conduct sensitivity analyses to assess the potential effect of missing data using multiple imputation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Understanding the Impacts of Care Farms on Health and Well-being: A Pilot study to inform the design of a follow-on study to assess the cost-effectiveness of care farms in improving health and wellbeing and reducing re-offending
Abstract: This pilot study uses quantitative and qualitative methods to understand how best develop a follow-on study to assess the cost-effectiveness of Care Farms (CFs) for offenders serving community orders (COs). In addition to gathering the information required to design the follow-on study, this pilot will also build knowledge of CFs and the mechanism through which they may improve the health and well being of offenders. Participants: Adult (18 and over) offenders serving COs. Sample: 150 offenders serving their CO in a CF and 150 offenders in other CO settings. Inclusion criteria: Any adult 18 years and over serving a CO in a CF or comparator location. Exclusion criteria: None. Offenders who have committed serious offences or have severe mental health issues are not sentenced to COs. Translation will be provided for those who are not comfortable being interviewed in English. The Intervention: Care farming has been defined as the therapeutic use of farming practices. CFs provide health, social or educational care services for vulnerable groups, through supervised, structured programmes of farming-related activities (1). Qualitative and survey evidence points to the positive impacts for CFs on mental health, self-esteem, social interaction and physical health. However, no studies have been conducted to determine the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of CFs. Despite the lack of robust evidence, commissioners are increasingly placing disadvantaged clients such as offenders, young people excluded from school, people with substance misuse issues to be supported and ‘treated’ on CFs. Care farming is a growing movement with over 2,000 CFs across Europe using nature for health, social and/or educational benefits (2). A survey of CFs in the UK (2007) identified 76 CFs seeing on average over 5800 clients per week (3; 40). Of the CFs surveyed 19 took clients from probation Trusts. Recent figures suggest there are now 189 CFs in the UK (personal communication, Care Farming UK). Clients are predominantly from disadvantaged backgrounds and include those with poor mental health, substance misuse issues, social excluded young people and offenders. Offenders serving their COs on CFs are supervised to undertake a range of unpaid work. COs can be up to 300 hours, spread over time as appropriate for the offender. On average they run for 6 months. Depending on the nature of the farm, the activities undertaken include horticulture, livestock care, aquaculture, building, environmental and conservation work. Three CFs in England will participate in this pilot study: one in Yorkshire and one in Shropshire are already confirmed and a third is being finalised. The CFs all provide some form of farming activity as therapy to a range of clients including offenders serving COs. Their work with offenders is commissioned by local Probation Trusts. In general, the NHS is not involved in funding CFs for their work with offenders, however where NHS funded health trainers are available at the CF, these may be used by offenders. The three CFs are selected for this study as they illustrate the wide range of activities and ways of working that can be found in CFs across the UK. This will help in understanding the variation in CFs and the subsequent intra-cluster correlation coefficient which will be needed when calculating the most appropriate sample size for the larger follow-on study. Secondly, CFs are selected who have long-standing relationships and funding from their local Probation Trusts. Comparator sites: Adult offenders serving COs in settings other than a CF in West Yorkshire, Shropshire and one to be assigned. The activities carried out whilst serving COs in these comparator areas include: building work, food handling, painting/decorating, recycling and cleaning. The Probation Trusts in each region take the decision on where to allocate offenders. Initial discussions with Probation Trusts indicate that these decisions are based on: • a risk assessment • their physical ability and mobility • limiting offenders travel time to the location • supervision requirements These factors will be measured and taken into consideration as potential confounders. Outcomes: Primary: Quality of life and well-being derived from the Clinical Outcome in Routine Evaluation–Outcome Measure (CORE-OM). CORE-OM has been validated among offender populations (27; 28) and can be used to derive QALYs (31). The 34 items cover four dimensions: subjective well-being; problems/symptoms; life functioning; and risk/harm (29). Secondary: Re-offending rates over a max 18 month period Mental health derived from Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (WEMWBS) (32). Measures of smoking, alcohol, drug use, diet and physical activity adapted from General Lifestyle Survey/ Health Survey of England. Exploratory estimates of health utility as derived from CORE-OM (29; 30). Exploratory estimates of the cost per re-offending event avoided due to CF. Potential Impact: While this study is a pilot study it has the potential to contribute to the knowledge base on the processes within a CF that facilitate improvements in health and well-being. Furthermore, this more detailed understanding of CFs as an intervention for offenders will provide insights for commissioners in Probation Trusts and potentially on Health and Wellbeing Boards on which clients may benefit from CFs and in what ways. The proposed follow-on study, currently envisaged as a natural experiment, will provide more definitive answers for commissioners on the cost-effectiveness of CFs as an intervention to improve the quality of life, health and well-being of offenders and ultimately reduce re-offending. Such evidence-led commissioning would have the potential to reduce costs due to reduced use of the NHS and social care and reductions in reoffending reducing costs to the criminal justice system and wider society.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: A096 Vaccines for preventing influenza in healthy children
Abstract: Scientific/policy justification for review/review update Efforts to minimise the impact of influenza have mainly centred on the use of vaccines. Influenza vaccines are a global intervention with policies recommending extension of coverage to children of all ages in the USA, Canada and a growing number of countries. Vaccines were the mainstay of protection from the recent influenza pandemic. Despite such widespread policy promotion, recent reviews have suggested poor quality of evidence from field studies supporting vaccination and a considerable degree of uncertainty on the effects of influenza vaccines. Our review was the first to show lack of evidence of the effects of inactivated influenza vaccines in very young children and the limited nature of the evidence in older children. Since 2007 15-20 studies assessing the effects of the increasing coverage in children have been published. Recently, concerns about harms (ranging from febrile convulsions to narcolepsy) have undermined childhood influenza vaccination programmes and caused anxiety in parents and healthcare workers alike. This has leading in some cases (e.g. Australia) to the cancellation of vaccination programmes. Our review is a key piece of research and source of evidence for those assessing childhood influenza vaccination policies and is likely to remain so if updated.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group
Award_Title: Interventions for preventing falls in older people living in the community
Abstract: Scientific/policy justification for review/review update About a third of community-dwelling people over 65 years old fall each year. The annual cost of care for people with fall-related fractures in the UK is estimated to be over £1.8 billion. A NICE Clinical Guideline (no. 21) on the assessment and prevention of falls in older people was published in 2004. This drew extensively on a Cochrane review (2003) containing 62 trials. This review was subsequently split into two reviews, focussing on older people living in the community (review published in 2009: 111 trials) and in institutions (review published in 2010: 41 trials). While the decision for a ‘review of clinical guidance’ is pending (‘July 2011’), we anticipate this will go ahead. This would reflect the intensive research activity in this area and need to inform practice based on updated evidence. To ensure continuity of coverage in this important area of public health, the Group has initiated processes to split up the topic still further. Realistically though this will take some time to deliver. Meanwhile, the discovery of a further 50 or more new trials, several testing interventions not previously included, for inclusion in the community review makes this a priority for updating.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Real-time Modelling of a Pandemic Influenza Outbreak
Abstract: During the 2009 outbreak of pandemic A/H1N1 influenza much attention was devoted to the problem of capturing the epidemic dynamics through real-time modelling. The aim of such modelling was to provide up-to-the-moment assessments of the present and future state of the epidemic based upon continually updated streams of information. In practice, as illustrated by the 2009 outbreak, direct data are seldom available and multiple sources of data exist, each indirectly informing the epidemic development, each subject to possible sources of bias. This calls for more complex epidemic modelling that can synthesise the information held within a range of data sources to compensate for the lack of direct observation of the infection process. As a result of this, real-time modelling of the 2009 A/H1N1 outbreak proved to be more challenging than had been anticipated. A complex model for epidemic assessment was developed in 2009 integrating a multiplicity of epidemic surveillance data within a statistical modelling framework that accounts for the transmission dynamics of the virus and the healthcare seeking behaviours of a population. The Markov chain-Monte Carlo techniques used require that, as new data become available, the model has to be re-run in its entirety, a computationally expensive process. Therefore, as data accumulate, more sophisticated algorithms might prove more efficient than this current approach. We believe the application of such algorithms to the problem of real-time epidemic modelling represents a significant challenge, yet has the potential to make the process of real-time modelling more tractable, permitting the incorporation of larger amounts of data without the attendant computational expense. We propose to build a system which can supply a timely monitoring of any emerging pandemic to policymakers, developing a statistical modelling approach that synthesises a wide range of surveillance data as well as prior beliefs from historical epidemics.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Pandemic Respiratory Infection Emergency System Triage (PRIEST)
Abstract: Objectives: To optimise the triage of people using the emergency care system (111 and 999 calls, ambulance conveyance, or hospital emergency department) with suspected respiratory infections during a pandemic and identify the most accurate triage method for predicting severe illness among patients attending the emergency department with suspected respiratory infection. Design: Prospective observational cohort study. Setting: 40 acute hospital emergency departments and one ambulance service Population: Patients presenting to the emergency department, attended by a 999 ambulance or calling NHS 111 with suspected pandemic respiratory infection. Interventions: Triage methods to predict need for hospital care, including current triage practice, existing triage methods and potential new triage methods. Outcomes: Adverse outcome, defined as death or requiring cardiovascular, respiratory or renal support. Plan of analysis: We will estimate the accuracy of current triage practice and the discriminant value of existing triage methods for predicting adverse events up to 30 days. If data allow we will also use multivariate analysis to develop new triage methods. Sample size: This will ultimately depend upon the size and severity of the pandemic. We have planned for a sample size of 20,000 cases including 200 (1%) with adverse outcome. A sample of 150 with adverse outcome will allow us to estimate a c-statistic of a triage method, clinical variable or test with a standard error of 0.03 (assuming the true c-statistic was 0.8).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Real time refinement and validation of criteria and tools used in primary care to aid hospital referral decisions for patients of all ages in the event of surge during an influenza pandemic.
Abstract: Design: A prospective analysis, linking criteria in a GP's assessment of patients presenting with syndromic respiratory disease (influenza like illness), to immediate management decisions and patient outcomes. Objective: Assessment, refinement and validation of various triage tools to guide GP referral of patients with syndromic respiratory disease (influenza like illness) during a pandemic in readiness for use should widespread illness exceed health care capacity (surge). Method: GPs using EMISWeb / SystmOne will record their assessment and management of patients with syndromic respiratory disease (influenza like illness) which includes COVID-19, in the routine electronic health care systems. These systems automatically offer structured data capture for various clinical presentations. Such a structured page has been prepared for use in the event of an outbreak of any pathogen of public health interest, initially with intent to function for syndromic presentation of a respiratory illness caused by a novel respiratory viral threat such as a novel influenza or coronavirus. High level hospital discharge data are routinely uploaded from secondary care to the eHRs including hospital admission date, discharge date, main disease code, main procedure code and if death in hospital date of that death. EMISWeb / SystmOne will provide the relevant data extract to external researchers on a weekly basis. Where available, a further analysis will be performed against those cases with a proven diagnosis based on point of care tests ( finger prick, swabs) and any diagnostic information that is available at or shortly after the consultation. Analysis: Weekly cumulative analyses are planned. Univariate and multivariate analyses using unconditional logistic regression will be used to investigate the association between triage criteria threshold values and primary outcomes (hospital admission, and death) and secondary outcomes (length of stay and augmented levels of care (high dependency / intensive care)). The threshold values of triage criteria will be refined by comparing the receiver operator characteristics at various thresholds of abnormality (e.g. respiratory rate >30, >35, >40). The discriminatory value of existing and refined triage tools will be compared using logistic regression. Triage tools will be compared for their ability to predict outcomes using Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUROC) comparisons. The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) will be calculated for triage tools using different score thresholds. The virus, human behaviour, and models of health care provision in the community may change in time. Analysis will be reset between pandemic waves and appropriate comparisons made between pandemic waves.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Birmingham and Solihull Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Family and Social Intervention for Young People. A randomised controlled trial of family and social network intervention for young people who misuse alcohol and drugs: a feasibility study [Y-SBNT]
Abstract: Design: (i) Development phase followed by (ii) Pragmatic randomised feasibility study, including economic evaluation. Setting: Two community services for young substance misusers: one delivered by Lifeline in Birmingham in the West Midlands; the other provided by d'n'a services for young people in Newcastle. Target population: Young people aged 14 to 18 referred for drug and/or alcohol problems to the two services involved in the research. Health Technologies Being Assessed Study intervention: Social Behaviour and Network Therapy (SBNT) is an intervention developed in the UK by members of our research group, shown to be effective with harmful drinkers (UKATT research team, BMJ, 2006) and recommended by recent NICE guidance. We believe that SBNT can be adapted to the youth context with great potential as a clinically and cost effective intervention which can be readily implemented in services for young people. We believe that involving young people who have been through drug and alcohol services in the design of the intervention will give us insights into its acceptability and effectiveness. We will also draw on the literature in this field in adapting this intervention. Treatment as usual: Young people in this arm will continue to receive usual care delivered by the two services. Measurement of cost and outcomes We will measure the variability in primary and secondary outcome measures collected to inform the outcomes for a future definitive trial. Measures will be taken by research fellows at baseline, 3 and 12 months follow ups after random allocation. The primary outcome measure will be level of drug and alcohol use, measured through the Timeline Follow-back (TLFB) interview, validated with adolescent populations (Dennis et al., Addiction, 2004). Family-based approaches have the potential to impact on other facets of young people’s lives and we will measure a number of family, psychological and social risk factors as well as therapeutic alliance that has also been linked with retention and outcomes. In order to explore cost-effectiveness in a full trial, intervention costs will be measured using local service costs; QUALY changes will be measured through EQ-5D at baseline, 3 and 12 month follow-up. We will also measure criminal justice involvement and use of social services. Sample size Sixty participants in total, 30 randomised to receive adapted SBNT and 30 treatment as usual. Each site will recruit 30 participants (15 in each condition). This number will allow us to establish rate of consent, engagement in treatment and drop out. All participants will be followed up at 3 and 12 months for qualitative interview and measurement of outcomes. Project staff will also be interviewed.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: ACTIB (Assessing Cognitive behavioural Therapy in Irritable Bowel): A randomized controlled trial of clinical and cost effectiveness of therapist delivered cognitive behavioural therapy and web-based self-management in irritable bowel syndrome.
Abstract: Design: A 3-arm multi-centre RCT. 495 patients with refractory IBS individually randomised to Therapist CBT (TCBT), low intensity behavioural therapy (LIBT) or TAU by an independent randomisation service (CTU) with block randomisation and stratification by centre. Assessors blind to treatment arm. TAU participants will have access to the WCBT website at trial end. A nested qualitative study will explore patients’ experiences of treatments: interviews at 3 and 12 mths with approx. 17 per arm; analysed inductively to identify factors that facilitate or impede adherence to treatment. Setting: Treatment at home via telephone and internet. Therapists based at King’s College London. Target population: Adults (18 yrs or over) with refractory IBS (on-going symptoms, IBS-SSS >75), fulfilling ROME III criteria and unresponsive to first-line therapies (eg anti-spasmodics or anti-depressants) with a continuing symptom profile >12 months. Exclusion: unexplained rectal bleeding or weight loss, IBD, coeliac disease, colorectal carcinoma. Blood tests: FBC, TTG, CRP taken prior to randomisation to exclude important differential diagnoses. Current medications maintained at a stable dose. Recording of: current and past medications, length of symptoms, sub-type of IBS (diarrhoea, constipation or alternating pattern), previous or current psychiatric diagnoses. Health Technologies being assessed: Therapist CBT and Lower intensity CBT (a web-based self-management programme). NICE recommends CBT for refractory IBS but cost is high and availability poor. We will compare 2 formats of CBT (TCBT and LIBT) for IBS against TAU in a high quality trial. The CBT is based on an empirical CB model of IBS (Spence, Moss-Morris. GUT 56,(8),2007). Key differences between arms: therapist contact time and interactive website access. Structured therapy sessions, based on a previous efficacious CBT trial for IBS, consist of education, behavioural and cognitive techniques, aimed at improving bowel habits, developing stable, healthy eating patterns, addressing unhelpful thoughts, managing stress, reducing symptom focussing and preventing relapse. TCBT: patient manual + 6, 60min telephone sessions + homework tasks with a CBT therapist at week 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 and two 1 hr 'booster' CBT sessions at 4 and 8mths. WCBT: An interactive, tailored CBT self-management website developed with substantial patient input (MIBS trial). Participants access 8 online sessions and homework tasks, similar content to TCBT and receive weekly automated email reminders and minimal therapist support: 3, 30 minute telephone support calls at week 1, 3 and 5 and two, 30 min booster sessions at 4 and 8mths. ‘Booster’ sessions are included in both arms to discuss setbacks and to reinforce positive symptom management. Telephone CBT sessions rather than face to face are proposed, as they have similar efficacy, improve accessibility, are efficient, less costly and could be readily delivered across the NHS from a centralised service. Currently, IBS patients have minimal CBT access. Web CBT is effective in depression and recent small trials show promise for IBS but indicate some therapist input is needed. 73% households have internet connections with numbers rising. Therapists receive manuals, training and supervision to ensure quality and adherence to protocol. All sessions are taped to check treatment fidelity, length and number of phone sessions. Patients’ adherence is measured through number of phone sessions and automated count of web sessions accessed. Secure website passwording will ensure non-contamination of treatments. TAU is defined as continuation of current medications, and GP or consultant follow-up with no psychological therapy. All participants receive a standard information sheet on Lifestyle and Diet in IBS based on NICE. Measurement of cost and outcomes: Primary outcomes: IBS symptom Severity Scale (IBS-SSS) and Work and Social adjustment scale (WSAS). IBS SSS is widely used in IBS studies (50 point change from baseline deemed clinically significant). In this resistant symptom group, accounting for 15 point placebo response in TAU, a 35 point difference between groups at 12mths is relevant for less costly, more accessible LIBT compared to TAU. 12mths primary outcome, data collection at 3 and 6mths to assess effect over time. Data will be entered onto an online data entry system at CTU. Intention-to-treat analysis. Group differences will be assessed using mixed linear regression models accounting for repeated measurements. Covariates: baseline IBS-SSS, treatment group, therapist, IBS symptoms type, time and a time by treatment interaction term to extract differences at 3, 6, and 12mths. Therapist effects and treatment effect moderation by important baseline variables (treatment by variable interactions) will be explored. Mixed models account for missing outcome data under the missing at random assumption, the effect checked using sensitivity analyses. Secondary outcomes: Responder based on Subjects Global assessment of relief (SGA),(Qol (EQ-D5), Enablement, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, adverse events, health care utilization - important to measure the wider IBS effects, will be analysed similarly. A complier average causal effect will be estimated if there is appreciable lack of compliance. Cost-effectiveness: Taking a health service and societal perspective. Intervention costs: based on number of therapy/support sessions, combined information on staff time (based on salaries and overheads) and (for web arm) development costs apportioned over estimated number of users. Other service use and lost employment: measured with a study schedule at baseline and each follow-up. Costs calculated by combining these data with national unit cost and average earnings information. Healthcare and societal costs at 12mths will be combined with the primary outcome measure, QALYs and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios computed for the two therapies compared to TAU and each other, indicating the extra cost of a unit-improvement on the IBS SSS, or the cost saved with unit-deterioration (relevant for therapy comparison). QALYs will be derived using area-under the curve methods from the EQ-5D (measured at baseline and each follow-up)- validated for IBS. Uncertainty around ICERs for each two-way comparison will be addressed using cost-effectiveness planes. Interpretation of the QALY-based cost-effectiveness results will use cost-effectiveness acceptability curves, with all 3 arms compared. Sample size: A mean (SD) IBS-SSS in TAU arm of 250(76) (as in MIBS study) was assumed. Based on a two-sided, two-sample t-test, to detect a mean difference of 35 points at 12 months between LIBT and TAU, (effect size 0.46), 90% power, type I error 0.025 (two primary outcomes), needs a sample size of 119 per arm. Accounting for clustering due to therapists, cluster size approx. 17(10 therapists), intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.02, an inflation factor of 1.32 is required; allowing for 20% attrition and a deflation factor of 0.84 for baseline IBS SSS correlation with outcome; a sample size of 495 is required (165 each arm). This is also sufficient to detect an SGA responder difference between LIBT and TAU of 22%, or an odds ratio of 2.9, with 90% power, assuming 20% responders in TAU arm. Project timetable: Pre-study: Ethics. 1-8mths: Complete R&D, register trial, publish protocol, prepare recruitment & assessment materials, update & test website, recruit & train therapists, design data collection forms and study database, set up randomisation service, 9-30mths: Recruitment, screening, intervention delivery, assessment. 31-42mths: Therapy booster sessions, 12mth follow-up assessments. 43-46mths: Data preparation, and analysis. 47-48mths: Final reports, dissemination. Recruitment: 495 participants over 22mths (23 randomised/mth), Approx. 30 NHS GP practices and Hospital based GI services in Hampshire (SUHT ± 500 IBS pts/yr) and London (GSTT, King’s College Hospital, LSL and S. London Healthcare, ± 1000 IBS pts/yr).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation in pregnancy and following childbirth: literature review and qualitative study
Abstract: Maternal smoking in pregnancy causes substantial harm and, while many women in the UK stop smoking before or soon after becoming pregnant, one in four women smoke for part of pregnancy and one in eight smoke continually. This study will explore barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation in pregnancy by reviewing relevant literature, conducting qualitative research and developing proposals for future interventions. A qualitative study design will combine three systematic reviews and three exploratory studies conducted over a two year period, with data from a rapid mapping exercise to identify existing and in-development interventions for cessation in pregnancy. Firstly, a set of three reviews of barriers and facilitators to cessation in pregnancy and following childbirth will be undertaken focusing on pregnant women, partners/family members and professionals respectively. Secondly, a set of three exploratory studies will be undertaken. These will focus on pregnant women, partners/family members and health professionals. The three studies will be undertaken in one study site in Scotland (NHS Lothian) and one in England (NHS North Yorkshire and York). The sample will comprise: • 20 pregnant women who are continuing to smoke during pregnancy (10 in each site) • 20 to 25 household members residing with these pregnant women (10 to 12 in each site) • 20 pregnant women who have recently stopped smoking (10 in each site) • 20 to 25 household members residing with these pregnant women (10 to 12 in each site) • 20 professionals in each site including midwives and midwifery managers, consultant obstetricians, health visitors and cessation advisers. A subsample of 10 women originally interviewed will also be followed up post-partum to identify longer term experiences. Findings from the interviews will identify barriers and facilitators to cessation in pregnancy from the perspective of each group of interviewees. These will be compared and contrasted and brought together with the evidence from the systematic reviews to produce a narrative synthesis of key themes and issues. These findings will inform recommendations for practice and lead to the development of proposals for interventions to address smoking in pregnancy that can be tested in future research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Parental incentives and quasi-mandatory schemes for increasing uptake of vaccinations in preschool children
Abstract: Childhood immunisation programmes form a core component of public health strategies worldwide. Nationally and globally, childhood immunisations have been highly effective in reducing the incidence of, and associated morbidity and mortality from, a range of infectious diseases. The World Health Organization (WHO) has set a goal of 90% coverage for all immunisations, with 95% coverage for measles and diphtheria. In the UK, coverage for pre-school vaccinations ranges from 85-95%. Incentives and quasi-mandatory interventions to increase uptake of pre-school vaccinations have been suggested by the National Institute of Health & Clinical Excellence as interventions worthy of further consideration. These can be thought of as both financial and non-financial gains or losses provided contingent on receipt, or non-receipt, of vaccinations. Examples include higher welfare benefits for families with children who have received all recommended vaccinations; and restricting school entry to children who are vaccinated. In order to explore the effectiveness and acceptability of such interventions we will conduct a series of three linked studies: a systematic review of existing research; focus group interviews with parents and individual interview with relevant professionals (e.g. health visitors, practice nurses, GPs, head teachers); and an internet survey exploring parental preferences for a range of different interventions for increasing vaccination uptake.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Effects of weight management interventions on maternal and fetal outcomes in pregnancy: Individual patient data (IPD) meta analysis of randomised trials and model based economic evaluation
Abstract: DESIGN: Individual patient data (IPD) meta analysis of randomised trials Our IPD meta-analytical approach will follow existing guidelines and our output will comply as a minimum with the PRISMA statement, and adhere to recent reporting guidelines for IPD meta-analysis. Our methods will be as follows: SEARCH STRATEGY: As a first step in the IPD meta-analysis, we will update the literature search to identify new trials since completion of our systematic review (HTA No. 09/27/06) on effects of weight management interventions in pregnancy. The following databases will be searched: MEDLINE, EMBASE, BIOSIS, LILACS, Pascal, Science Citation Index, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (CDSR), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Database of Abstracts of Reviews of Effects (DARE) and Health Technology Assessment Database (HTA). Language restrictions will not be applied to electronic searches. Authors of the included studies from the International Weight management In Pregnancy IPD collaboration (i-WIP) will also be asked to examine the included study list to identify any studies or data that might have been missed. ESTABLISHMENT OF IPD COLLABORATIVE GROUP: We have already established the i-WIP (International Weight Management in Pregnancy) collaborative group that includes representatives from all the groups which have published trials on weight management interventions in pregnancy. We have provisional support to date from 22 study investigators for access to individual patient data for over 4000 women. DATA COLLECTION, ENTRY AND CHECKING AND STUDY QUALITY: All variables recorded, even those not reported in the published studies, will be considered for collection and for planning subgroup analyses with sufficient statistical power. A bespoke database will be set up and authors will be allowed to supply data in whatever way convenient to them. The quality of each trial will be also be assessed at this stage, for example to evaluate the integrity of the randomisation and follow up procedure. DATA SYNTHESIS: -Summarising overall effect of weight management interventions: Meta-analyses of the effectiveness of weight management interventions in pregnancy will be performed for the weight related and critically important pregnancy outcomes identified by the Delphi survey. Then, for each intervention type and outcome separately, we will perform either a one-step or a two-step IPD meta-analysis to obtain the pooled intervention effect. -Examining heterogeneity and potential subgroup effects: To consider the causes of heterogeneity and factors that may modify intervention effect, for each weight management intervention we will perform pre-specified subgroup analyses by BMI, age, parity, ethnicity, underlying risk factors like diabetes and type of intervention. Examination of subgroup effects will be undertaken by extending the one-stage meta-analysis framework to include treatment-covariate interaction terms, which provide the change in intervention effect for a 1-unit change in the covariate. -Examining optimal levels of weight gain in pregnancy that minimises adverse outcomes: For each BMI group separately and each outcome, we will fit a suitable regression model that accounts for clustering of patient within studies and quantifies how each 1-unit increase in weight gain changes the risk of a poor outcome. -Evaluation of predictors of weight change in pregnancy: For all candidate predictors, we will perform separate analyses in each BMI cohort (normal, overweight and obese) and analyse on the whole meta-analysis database, adjusting again for the clustering of patients within studies. -Exploration of sources of bias: unavailable data and publication bias:For each analysis containing 10 or more studies the likelihood of publication bias will be investigated through the construction of contour-enhanced funnel plots and appropriate statistical tests for ‘small-study effects'. HEALTH ECONOMIC AND DECISION ANALYTIC MODELLING: The cost-effectiveness of weight management interventions in pregnancy will be evaluated using effect size estimates for these interventions obtained from the IPD meta analysis to determine the characteristics of the weight management intervention that are most cost-effective. The cost and health-related quality of life implications of the interventions will be assessed using other relevant data in the published literature. In the base case, the outcome measure will be the cost per life year gained, taking into account only the cost of the intervention and health care costs saved as a result of reduced infant and maternal mortality. Value of information analyses will also be conducted in order to identify the most important parameters for further investigation, and the economic value of such research. EXPECTED OUTPUT OF RESEARCH: We currently have access to data from 4000 individual women. This is a work in progress. Thus there is about a 50-fold increase in the sample size for our IPD project compared to the median number, n=81 (smallest n=12; largest n=1000) in the trials and substantially increase the power to detect genuine interactions. This will enable intervention effects to be quantified for clinically relevant groups. It will also allow the magnitude of benefit due to weight change in pregnancy to be quantified for both the mother and baby. This will allow us to implement those weight management interventions that show clear benefit with specific weight gain targets in pregnancy. For a new trial to detect a 30% reduction in composite pregnancy outcome, thousands of patients are required. This will be practically difficult and expensive. In contrast, our IPD meta-analysis provides an efficient way to substantially increase the sample size, without the need for a new trial, to obtain the sufficient numbers required in most of the categories considered. The economic evaluation will determine the characteristics of the weight management intervention that are most cost-effective.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Mixed methods analysis of the London Hyperacute Stroke System: identifying lessons on 24/7 working (METRO-24/7)
Abstract: It has been repeatedly demonstrated across a range of acute settings that outcomes are poorer in secondary healthcare systems in the developed world outside the conventional five day working week (Bell and Redelmeier, 2001, Freemantle et al., 2012). At the same time some studies report equivalent or better outcomes for some patients treated outside the working week (Aylin et al., 2013, Luyt et al., 2007, Concha et al., 2013). While contested, such studies indicate that high quality out of hours care is possible and that changes in organisation of services might address the current performance gap. Several possible causes for an ‘out of hours effect’ are proposed but there are likely to be many relevant factors associated with out of hours working, including reduced staffing levels (Needleman et al., 2011, Freemantle et al., 2012) and reduced access to supporting investigations (Freemantle et al., 2012). Stroke is a leading cause of mortality and the most common cause of disability in the developed world (MacDonald et al., 2000, Geddes et al., 1996). Stroke is defined by the World Health Organisation as an event associated with “rapidly developing clinical signs of focal or global disturbance of cerebral function, lasting more than 24 hours or until death, with no apparent non-vascular cause” (WHO MONICA Project Investigators, 1988). Stroke shares similar pathways with other medical conditions and most specifically with acute cardiac disease (which is itself a leading cause of mortality and functional disability). International research indicates that weekend stroke admissions are associated with higher levels of mortality (Saposnik et al., 2007, Janszky et al., 2007), and lower likelihood of being discharged to same place of residence (Janszky et al., 2007). However, the picture for stroke is complicated by research covering specialist stroke units, which provide round the clock access to thrombolysis for hyperacute stroke. Research from the US, Australia and Israel suggest that such units reduce the disparity between in hours and out of hours care for stroke patients, with studies showing no significant ‘weekend effect’ in stroke patients in terms of such outcomes as length of stay, mortality, and functional outcome (both in hospital and at 90 days) (Albright et al., 2012, Streifler et al., 2012), and another suggesting the only significant ‘out of hours’ effect was on ‘door to needle’ time, but not patient outcomes (Fang et al., 2013). In the United Kingdom in Greater London a complete service change resulted in July 2010 in the opening of eight Hyperacute Stroke Units (HASUs) that were designated to provide comprehensive stroke care for up to the first 72 hours of care for patients presenting with recent stroke. All eight HASUs were set up according to the same designation criteria and provide round the clock access to thrombolysis and stroke nursing care (Fulop et al., 2013a). Since 2010 the majority of these HASUs have been placed in the top quartile and usually at or near the very top of the table for performance according to quality criteria specified in the national audit of stroke care (the Royal College of Physicians-supported Stroke Improvement National Audit Programme (SINAP)). However, HASUs do not provide the same level of access to therapists, consultant opinion or diagnostic investigations out of working hours as they do within hours. The HASU consultants have no contractual obligation to be on site during the evenings and there are no minimum staffing levels for therapists or doctors at weekends. Basic head imaging is expected to be performed for all patients within one hour of admission but there are otherwise no obligations for these services to provide more detailed imaging out of hours. Finally the HASUs work very closely with the Acute Stroke Units (ASUs) and with Community Rehabilitation Services. In general neither the ASUs nor the community teams are contracted to provide a normal service at weekends causing the discharges from the HASU to be funnelled into a weekday discharge pathway. By drawing together a range of qualitative and quantitative data, this research will provide an opportunity to identify lessons about the development, provision, effects and cost of 24/7 stroke care in the London HASU system. Finally, this study will complement an ongoing NIHR-funded evaluation of the reconfiguration of stroke services in London, Greater Manchester and the Midlands and East of England, led by co-investigator Fulop: this research combines quantitative and qualitative methods to analyse the processes by which the reconfigured London model was developed and implemented, the factors influencing these processes, and the impact the reconfiguration has had on service provision, costs and quality of care (Fulop et al., 2013a, Fulop et al., 2013b). The objectives are: 1.To investigate the extent to which evidence based care received by stroke patients differs between IH and OH services in London HASUs. 2.To investigate the extent to which clinical outcomes differ between IH and OH services in the London HASUs. 3.To investigate how IH and OH services are organised and provided in London HASUs. 4.To investigate how these services are perceived by stakeholders (including stroke clinicians, patients and carers). 5.To investigate the costs of acute stroke care in London HASUs on different days and at different times of admission. METHOD This is a mixed methods study, drawing together quantitative and qualitative approaches. The quantitative analysis will examine whether performance on selected clinical process and outcome measures is influenced by day or time of admission, staffing levels and other inputs (objectives 1 and 2); and an economic analysis (objective 5) will examine current service costs during and outside conventional working hours and how much it would cost to extend work shifts to provide more uniform care 24/7. The qualitative analysis (objectives 3 and 4) will use a comparative case study approach to draw together documentary, interview and observation data on how London’s HASUs organise and deliver 24/7 stroke care in practice, how these service patterns have been influenced by workforce and organisational factors, and how stakeholders including staff, patients and carers experience these services. The case study approach allows examination of how efforts to bring about change interact with the context in which they take place (Baker, 2011, Yin, 2009). This study will collect qualitative and quantitative data from all eight London HASUs. The quantitative and economic analyses draw on a range of data sources covering London’s HASUs. Data sources include data submitted to the Sentinel Stroke National Audit Programme (SSNAP), local staffing levels and staffing structures and training programmes covering the period 1/1/2014 – 31/12/2014. We will regress our primary and secondary outcomes against different combinations of series of covariates of interest. Our primary outcomes are in-hospital mortality, mortality at three months post admission and dependency at 6 months. In the economic analysis we will calculate the mean costs per patient receiving IH and OH care from an NHS and personal social services perspective. The time frame will be from admission to the HASU until three months after stroke. The cost components will include length of stay, interventions, therapy and stroke specific treatment. The qualitative analysis will combine deductive elements with generation and testing of theories from the raw data as it emerges. By focusing interviews and observations on measures analysed quantitatively (for example workforce factors, provision of evidence based care, and clinical outcomes in IH and OH periods), it will be possible to examine factors influencing the current provision of services and their effectiveness both in hours and out of hours. In this way, qualitative data will support identification of factors that may explain the results of the quantitative analyses. We will thus provide lessons on how 24/7 care is currently provided in London HASUs and factors influencing this. The focus on contextual issues may permit identification of lessons that may be generalised to 24/7 working beyond the London and stroke care settings. This process will also involve using analytic conferences where the research team will discuss the analysis and interpretation of the findings. This will provide opportunities to clarify conflicting understandings and to facilitate reflexivity (Barry et al., 1999). References ALBRIGHT, K. C. et al. Award_Title: Births and their outcome: analysing the daily, weekly and yearly cycles and their implications for the NHS
Abstract: Analyses since the 1970s have shown that maternity outcomes have differed by day of the year, day of the week and time of day. It is unclear to what extent this reflects differences in characteristics of women giving birth, efforts made to intervene selectively in the onset of labour or in delivery, or in health services’ workforce factors, notably numbers or seniority.(1,2) Previous analyses of data for England and Wales for the years 1970-76(3) and 1979-96(4) were based on aggregated counts and mortality was not disaggregated by cause. Analyses by time of day, method of onset of labour and gestational age were not possible in these analyses, as the relevant data items were not available at a national level for England and Wales. Recent developments in data recording and linkage have changed this. As a by-product of the change to allocation of babies’ NHS Numbers at birth, the time of day of birth is now recorded in national datasets. As a result of a project led by City University London to link birth registration data with this NHS Numbers for Babies dataset, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) now has national data on gestational age and time of day of birth for years from 2005 onwards.(5|) Linkage with Maternity Hospital Episode Statistics (HES) and corresponding data for Wales in a project funded by the MRC means that data are available about the onset of labour and method of delivery for most, although not all deliveries in the years from 2005 to 2007 and the techniques developed in this project can be used to link these data for subsequent years.(6,7) As morbidity in mothers and babies is also a matter of concern, it would therefore be useful to extend this database by linking births to data about subsequent hospital admissions and readmissions of mothers and babies recorded in HES and the Patient Episode Database Wales (PEDW). Aims The overall aim is to describe and analyse daily, weekly and yearly variations in births and their outcome and explore the potential implications of the patterns observed for NHS staffing and for service users. Methods As the data for 2005 to 2007 are already linked, analyses of daily, weekly and annual cycles will start during the first six months of the project, using these data. In parallel with this, files of key data items from linked birth registration / NHS Numbers for Babies records for births in 2008 to 2011 will be sent to the Information Centre for Health and Social Care (IC) and NHS Wales Informatics Service (NWIS)for linkage to data about care at delivery from Maternity HES and National Community Child Health Database (NCCHD) / PEDW, using the techniques developed for births in 2005 to 2007.(6,7) We have continued to renew and extend the Section 251 permission given initially to link data for the years 2005 to 2007. It has now been renewed and extended to cover the years 2008 to 2012. Once the further linkages are completed, the whole file will be combined for analysis during the second six months of the project.A new application for Section 251 permission has been submitted to extend the linkage to records of subsequent hospital care. Once it is obtained, techniques for linkage of records of neonatal care and other postnatal hospital admissions of mothers and babies to birth registration / NHS Numbers for babies records will be piloted on a sample of records and then used for all the births. It is hoped that this will be achieved in time for analyses to start early in the second year of the project. Analysis Individual linked records from birth registration, NHS Numbers for babies, Maternity HES and its Welsh counterparts will be cross-tabulated and aggregated data will be plotted graphically to describe daily, weekly and annual cycles in numbers of births and their outcome in terms of birthweight, gestational age, mortality and morbidity recorded at delivery and any subsequent hospital episodes. Preterm and term births will be analysed separately and subdivided according to whether or not the onset of labour and the method of delivery were spontaneous. Births occurring at home and multiple births will be analysed separately and the main statistical modelling will focus on singleton births in hospital. Appropriate descriptive and inferential statistical techniques(8-12) will be used to analyse daily, weekly, and yearly cycles in births and their relations to outcomes of pregnancy. Patterns of birth will be analysed nationally and, where possible, by hospital or NHS trust and will take account of available staffing and other data. This is challenging because of the many changes in configurations of services. For this reason we have involved BirthchoiceUK which uses data from routine sources to maintain a web site to provide information for the public about maternity services. It is important to attempt this task, as analyses have shown that caesarean section rates show unexplained wide differences even after adjustment for case mix and other local factors.(13) Therefore, if possible, account will be taken of overall levels of obstetric intervention. Analytical work will again be undertaken in the secure environment of the Virtual Microprocessor Laboratory (VML) at the ONS. Potential benefits to the NHS These analyses should provide information about the ways in which numbers of births and their outcome vary throughout the day, week and year both spontaneously and as a consequence of obstetric intervention. Analyses by NHS trust and maternity unit will aim, where possible, to examine associations with midwifery and medical staffing using workforce data from the Information Centre for Health and Social care and Health Statistics Wales and with characteristics of individual units, using data compiled by BirthchoiceUK for its web site. The analyses are innovative in examining the full weekly cycle and the potential for varying selection factors for intervention rather than a simple dichotomy into in and out of ‘hours’. The results will be discussed with key user groups and a multidisciplinary advisory group made up of representatives of relevant professional and user groups and researchers. References 1. Young D. Award_Title: Development of a culturally adapted weight management programme for children of Pakistani and Bangladeshi origin
Abstract: We will undertake two work packages (WPs), informed by the MRC complex interventions framework. WP1 (Theoretical and modelling phase): Development of a children's weight management programme that is culturally adapted for Bangladeshi and Pakistani (BP) families, but is suitable to be delivered in a diverse community encompassing multiple ethnic groups. WP2 (exploratory phase): A feasibility study to evaluate the acceptability of the developed weight management programme and to assess the feasibility of a future definitive trial. The setting for the study is Birmingham; a diverse city with 44% of children from minority ethnic groups (MEGs), and 20% from BP communities. The NHS offers a group-based community weight management programme for parents of children aged 4-11 years (First Steps), targeting all ethnic groups. Parents are invited to attend 7 sessions, with the children attending the first and last sessions. Sessions are interactive and practical covering nutrition education, behaviour change and physical activity promotion. After completion, families are invited to attend quarterly follow up events. Currently, initial uptake of the programme by BP families is high, but completion rates are lower than in other ethnic groups. The programme is delivered by Birmingham Community Healthcare NHS Trust, and is commissioned by Birmingham City Council. This existing infrastructure will be used for the study. WP1 consists of three strands of work to inform development of the culturally adapted children's weight management programme. 1) We will review the existing programme against the current evidence for effective children's weight management interventions and identify common behaviour change techniques included in effective programmes using the CALO-RE taxonomy for behaviour change techniques. 2) We will recruit 3 groups of BP parents to participate in interviews and FGs to explore barriers and facilitators to participation in the existing programme and potential modifications to enhance participation and sustained engagement. These groups will comprise parents/carers who were offered the First Steps programme but declined to attend (n=15), parents/carers who attended but did not complete the programme (n=15), and parents/carers who completed the programme (n=20-30). 3) We will use our previous experience, existing literature and a framework for the adaptation of health promotion interventions for MEGs4 to guide the programme adaptation process. Accompanying manuals will be developed for the adapted programme. Much of the content will be generic but will include tailored content specific to BP families. The tailored content will provide a template for adaptation to other communities, enabling future transferability and tailoring to different populations. In WP2 we will undertake a feasibility study with the primary aim of assessing the proportion of BP families completing the adapted intervention programme. We will also assess the proportion of families of all ethnicities completing the adapted programme. In addition the feasibility study will inform design of a future RCT to determine effectiveness of the modified programme. Study population: Families in Birmingham with an overweight/obese child aged 4-11 years. Families referred to the existing service will be invited to participate. Purposive sampling will be undertaken to achieve over representation of BP families (60% of the study sample) Health technology: The culturally adapted weight management programme for children aged 4-11 years, modified from the existing First Steps programme. Structure, content and delivery will be determined in WP1. The programme will be delivered over 7-8 weeks, followed by post-intervention support. Study design: Families will be randomised to intervention or standard care arms with a 2:1 ratio. The standard care arm will be offered the existing First Steps programme. Outcome measures: For the primary outcome measure we will estimate the proportion of BP families completing the programme in the intervention arm. We will assess intervention acceptability and success of programme adaptation. For each outcome, interviews, FGs and questionnaires will be used to explore the views of programme providers, children and parents in relation to the adapted programme, and reasons for non-completion. Sociodemographic data will be collected and measures taken on children and parents at baseline. Follow up measures will be taken immediately post-intervention and 6 months after the intervention. Data will be collected by researchers through home visits (with interpreters if required). Anthropometric, diet, physical activity and psychosocial outcomes will be collected and compared between the two groups. Methods for collecting cost data on intervention and standard care will be developed to inform a future economic evaluation. Sample size: We will recruit 120 families (60% BP) and randomise to intervention and usual care arms with a 2:1 ratio (n=80 in intervention arm, n=40 in usual care arm). We will stratify randomisation by BP ethnicity (48 and 24 BP families in intervention and usual care arms respectively). The project length will be 30 months in total.
