Award_Title: Feasibility and acceptability of home sampling kits to increase the uptake of HIV testing among black Africans in the United Kingdom: The Haus study.
Abstract: Design: We propose a two stage, mixed-method design. Health technology being assessed: An HIV home sampling kit (HSK) collection device for use with a lab-based screening test for HIV. Stage I Aim: To develop an HSK-based intervention to increase the provision and uptake of HIV testing among black Africans using existing community and healthcare provision. Specific objectives: 1. Clarify barriers and facilitators to provision, access and use of HIV HSK by black Africans, in primary care, pharmacies and community outreach 2. Determine appropriate HSK-based intervention models for different settings 3. Determine control population and robust HIV result management pathways 4. Develop intervention manuals to enable intervention delivery Settings: •London and Glasgow. •Primary care, pharmacies, and community outreach programs. Target populations: •Black African adults. •GPs, pharmacists, and community based organisations in contact with black African communities. •HIV prevention & HIV care service providers, and commissioners. Exclusion criteria •People younger than 18 years •People who cannot give informed consent Methods: Literature review: A systematic review of self-testing for HIV was published in Apr 2013 (review period Jan 2000 to Oct 2012). We will update this review by reviewing studies and practices related to HSK utility, uptake, barriers, implementation, feasibility and acceptability published since October 2012. We will use standard criteria (CONSORT, STROBE and CASP) to assess study quality. Focus Group Discussions: We will conduct focus group discussions (FGD) with stakeholders and the target population to inform the development of interventions. FGD will examine views towards HSK, rationales for selecting potential settings, and key features of implementation. We will conduct six FGD with Black African people (3 per city). Purposive sampling will be used to ensure diversity in age, gender, African region of origin, time in the UK, and service use. Six FGD will be conducted with service providers (primary care staff, Pharmacists and community workers) (3 per city). All participants will be compensated for their time. Thematic analysis of FGD data will inform kit selection and development of HSK distribution procedures (the interventions) to be implemented. It is likely that two intervention models will be proposed for Phase II evaluation in both Glasgow and London. Interviews: Once the interventions are formulated, 8 additional stakeholder interviews will check the acceptability of procedures. HIV specialists will be consulted to ensure result management and linkage to care pathways are robust. Outcome measures: •Acceptability of HSK intervention to potential users and providers by setting. •Barriers to i) uptake of HSK by potential users and ii) offer of HSK by providers. Outputs: An intervention manual that specifies procedures for targeted distribution of HSKs in two community settings, including training, pathways for HIV result management and linkage into specialist care, and strategies for cost evaluation. Stage II Aim: To conduct a phase II evaluation of selected HSK distribution models to assess feasibility, appropriateness of settings and optimal intervention design for future phase III evaluation. Settings: These will be determined through the formative research conducted in Stage I. Ideally two diverse types of settings will be used in London and Glasgow. Target populations: •Black African people without diagnosed HIV, 18 years of age or older, and able to provide informed consent •GPs and/or pharmacists and/or community based services in contact with black African communities as identified in Stage I as suitable for delivery of HIV HSK interventions. Methods: Training & recruitment: Staff will be trained on site by the research team and a nurse specialist to recruit eligible black Africans between March 1st 2015 and 30th July 2015. Informed consent will be obtained from all participants. Sample size: We have assumed a return rate of 50%. Distribution of 400 test kits in each setting will enable a precision rate of ±5%, should the return rate be lower or higher with a fixed sample size the size of the standard error will be smaller and the resulting confidence intervals narrower. As we envisage testing the intervention in two settings in two cities a total of 1600 HSK will be distributed. Data collection: Quantitative and qualitative research will be used to answer the research questions (see subsequent Research plan). The MRC complex intervention guidance will inform our evaluation. Acceptability and feasibility data collection, result management, cost data and process evaluation will be undertaken. Economic analysis: We will collect economic costs and outcomes of HSKs to calculate the cost per HSK distributed and cost per HIV positive result. We will assess the feasibility of developing a life-time decision analytical model to assess the cost-effectiveness of HSK compared to standard care. Outcome measures: Primary outcome: HIV HSK return rate Secondary outcomes: 1.Point of delivery outcomes: •Acceptability of intervention, including rationales for accepting or refusing a HSK •Acceptability and feasibility of intervention among specified service providers 2.Data collection outcomes: •Demonstration that intervention and services incorporates sufficient capacity to successfully record the numbers of: people offered HSK, accepting HSK, and returning HSK •Feasibility of collecting correct contact details enabling follow-up, reminders and communication of results 3.Pathway to care outcome measures: •Proportion of those whose samples are reactive who: a) are informed of results in person and b) who attend for confirmatory testing 4.Overarching outcome measures: •Cost per person kit distributed and cost per HIV diagnosis per setting •Attrition rates and loss to follow up •Confirmatory testing, proportion of those receiving an HIV positive diagnoses, and clinical stage at diagnosis •Feasibility and sensitivity of outcome measures (testing, behavioural and economic) for a definitive trial. Outputs: A report detailing the feasibility of a phase III trial and intervention manual

Award_Title: NAP SACC UK: A feasibility cluster randomised controlled trial in child care settings to increase physical activity and healthy eating in 2-4 year olds
Abstract: Research questions: 1) Can the NAP SACC child care intervention from the US be adapted and developed for use in the UK? 2) Does the child care intervention have the potential to increase healthy eating, increase physical activity and decrease sedentary time among 2-4 year old children in child care provider settings? 3) Is it feasible to conduct a cluster RCT evaluation of NAP SACC in child care providers in the UK and how should such a trial be designed? NAP SACC intervention: The Nutrition and Physical Activity Self Assessment for Child Care (NAP SACC) - http://www.napsacc.org/ - is an intervention delivered in child care centres with the aim of improving policies, practices and the nutrition and physical activity environment, through a process of self-assessment and targeted assistance. NAP SACC is a theory-based programme that employs components of social cognitive theory and socio-ecological framework. Goals of the programme are to improve the nutritional quality of food served, amount and quality of physical activity, staff-child interactions, and centre nutrition and physical activity policy. Proposed NAP SACC UK intervention: NAP SACC will be adapted for use in the UK through the formative work of this study with a particular emphasis on increasing parental involvement and tailoring the intervention for the UK context. The intervention will be delivered in child care providers. The intervention will be delivered in North Somerset by Health Visitors and in Cardiff by Wales Healthy and Sustainable Preschool Scheme Staff. The intervention will be funded by Public Health in North Somerset Council and by Public Health Wales. NHS components: Public Health Wales is part of the NHS in Wales. Wales Healthy and Sustainable Preschool Scheme Staff are employed by Public Health Wales and work in settings such as Local Authorities. Public Health in North Somerset is provided by the Council and Health Visitors in North Somerset are not employed by the NHS (they are employed by a social enterprise: North Somerset Community Partnership). Setting: Eligible settings will be local child care providers (day nurseries, private nursery schools, maintained nursery schools, Children’s Centres with nurseries and pre-schools) which provide lunch in North Somerset and Cardiff. Providers will have a minimum of 20 children aged 2-4 who attend for at least an average of 12 hours per week. Twelve child care providers (6 in each area) will participate in the feasibility trial. Participants: Child care provider managers/staff; children aged 2-4 attending child care an average of 12 hours per week and their parents; NAP SACC Consultants. Comparator: Usual care Research design and outcomes: This proposed project has 2-phases: Intervention adaptation and development and pilot cluster RCT with process evaluation. The intervention will take place over 6 months and data collection will be at baseline and 12 months after baseline. Data collection will include: 1) Environmental audit of the child care provider 2) Child measurements of zBMI, food diary and accelerometry measured physical activity/sedentary time 3) Process evaluation of the feasibility and acceptability of the intervention and trial methods using observations, logs and semi-structured interviews. 4) Costs to the public sector, child care providers and parents, intervention related resource use in the form of time and expenses.

Award_Title: Community pharmacy interventions for public health priorities: a systematic review of community pharmacy delivered smoking, alcohol and weight management interventions
Abstract: Obesity, smoking and excessive alcohol intake are three of the most significant modifiable risk factors for morbidity and mortality in the UK. Conditions which are caused or exacerbated by these risk factors include cardiovascular disease, liver disease, and lung cancer. The way in which society is organised causes inequalities in these conditions, and inequalities in these conditions are major contributors to overall inequalities in health, morbidity and mortality. The government has set a clear agenda for the future of public health in the UK, focused on improving the healthy life expectancy of the population and, where possible, reducing or removing threats to this aim. Community pharmacies could potentially make a significant positive contribution to this agenda. Compared with other healthcare providers (such as GPs and Practice Nurses), community pharmacies offer the advantage that they are widely available and accessible at a time convenient to users; there are over 10,500 in England, distributed across urban and rural areas. A recent report has estimated that 99% of the population can get to a pharmacy from their home within 20 minutes, either by car, by walking, or using public transport. Importantly, this includes the 10% of the population who live in the most deprived areas of the country. Many community pharmacies now offer services, commissioned by local authorities, related to weight management, smoking cessation, and alcohol screening and brief intervention. However, despite substantial commissioning of community pharmacy services, and the significant potential they have (for the reasons outlined above) to provide a useful service to the public and reduce health inequalities, it is not yet clear whether these services are effective. In this systematic review, we will assess the effectiveness of public health interventions delivered by community pharmacists that aim to reduce and prevent overweight and obesity, smoking, and excessive alcohol consumption, and assess whether there are heterogeneity effects for population features such as socioeconomic status. We will highlight any gaps in the evidence base and seek to establish how such public health interventions are organised, implemented and delivered. Methods and design The design of our review is informed by the results of our scoping search, and will be carried out following established criteria for the good conduct of systematic reviews (Higgins & Green, 2011), and guided by a Review Steering Group. Interventions: The review will examine community pharmacy interventions which focus on weight management, smoking cessation and alcohol misuse amongst people of all ages, in any setting (including NHS settings), and in any country. Study designs: A comprehensive literature search will be conducted for all RCTs, NRCTs, CBAs, ITS and repeated measures studies (EPOC inclusion criteria). In addition, given that there is a lack of EPOC level evidence on community pharmacy-based alcohol misuse interventions, we will include (independent) UK evaluations of these interventions. Search strategy: We will run one overarching search to identify studies of relevance for all three topics, and include the following electronic database searches: MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Social Science Citation Index, ASSIA, IBSS, Sociological Abstracts and the NHS Economic Evaluation Database. All databases will be searched from start date to the present. We will not exclude papers on the basis of language or country of origin. We will supplement the electronic database searches with website and grey literature searches, and will search trial registers and websites of funding organisations for ongoing studies. We will handsearch relevant conference abstracts and the bibliographies of all included studies and request relevant information on unpublished and in-progress research from key experts in the field. We will also seek (independent) evaluations on community pharmacy-led interventions related to alcohol from a range of organisations and people in the UK (local councils in the UK; pharmacy local practice forums, an advert in the Pharmaceutical Journal; Google searches). Outcomes: The review will utilise the causal modelling framework proposed by Hardeman et al (2005) to conceptualise behavioural outcome measures, and we will only include studies if they include at least one outcome which fits into one of four categories listed; Determinant of Behaviour, Behaviour outcomes, Physiology and biochemical outcomes, Hardeman outcomes Data on socioeconomic status and context, where available, will be collected to enable us to answer the secondary objectives of the review. Data extraction and quality appraisal: These tasks will be conducted following established criteria for the good conduct of systematic reviews (Higgins & Green, 2011). Analysis and synthesis We will conduct meta-analyses if appropriate, using Stata for regular meta-analyses, and WinBUGS for more complex analyses. If meta-analyses are not conducted, the synthesis will be restricted to a narrative overview and forest plots may be used to illustrate the results. We will also investigate publication bias by using funnel plot and Egger’s test. Those studies included under the primary outcome analysis that also examine socioeconomic status will be included in the health inequalities analysis. If this data is not available for this analysis, we will summarise the best available data (including information reported in evaluations) in a way which is of most use to the users of this review. Our analysis will emphasise explaining heterogeneity of effects, including a moderator analyses for population features such as socio-economic status and ethnicity. If there is sufficient data, we will also take features of the interventions delivered into consideration, as intervention content might be highly heterogeneous.

Award_Title: A comprehensive profile and comparative analysis of the characteristics, patient experience and community value of the ‘classic’ community hospital situated in contrasting contexts and communities
Abstract: The primary aim is to provide a comprehensive profile and comparative analysis of the characteristics, patient experience and community value of the classic community hospital (CH) in contrasting local contexts and in relationship with local communities. There are three core research questions. 1. What is a community hospital? 2. What are patients’ experiences of community hospital care and services? 3. What does the community do for its community hospital, and what does the community hospital do for its community? Research design and data collection: There are a number of inter-dependent elements conducted by us as well as two other reserch teams(Nolte and Young). For the purposes of this application, only those elements we are involved in undertaking are discussed in detail: 1) A mapping exercise reconciling major datasets; classifying CHs; and administering a resource data survey (survey has been developed with the Young team and follow-up support for completion undertaken by us). 2) Through nine comparative case studies sites, examining: patient experience and community value Analysis: - Mapping CH data will follow the Nolte literature review plus location, and provide a typology - Mapping resources data will be analysed to produce a standardised data set of (a) equity of provision, (b) service utilisation, (c) productivity, for CHs across the UK. - Interviews and focus groups will be transcribed and qualitative coding software used to facilitate data storage and retrieval. Analysis will involve a range of conceptual frameworks depending on the research element. External validity and transferability of analysis will be addressed through detailed description and data-triangulation between work-packages. Research outputs: - Plain language executive summary for community stakeholders involved in the study - A UK wide map and comprehensive database of community hospitals - Production of a final report to HS&DR specifications, suitable for peer review - Short document for each case study site, detailing key findings on patient experience and community value, and the place of CHs in the local health and social care context and community, and implications for commissioning. Benefits and impact: - Add to knowledge of local communities, CHs, commissioners and other providers - Demonstrate impact of CH services on individual patients, CH initiatives on the community - Support decision makers to take a whole system approach by demonstrating inter-dependencies of local health and social care services and the current and potential role of CH within the broader architecture of the NHS.

Award_Title: Evaluation of a national surveillance system for mortality alerts
Abstract: The Dr Foster Unit at Imperial has generated monthly mortality alerts since 2007 (based on statistical process control). They are derived from routinely collected hospital administrative data on 122 diagnoses/procedures for English acute, non-specialist NHS hospital trusts. Mortality alerts are sent to trusts without charge and copied to the Care Quality Commission if the mortality rate exceeds a high threshold. This joint mortality surveillance system was pivotal in alerting the then Healthcare Commission to problems at Mid Staffordshire NHS Foundation Trust. Our proposal, in collaboration with the Professor Aneez Esmail from the University of Manchester and supported by CQC, aims to improve understanding of these alerts and to evaluate their impact as an intervention to reduce avoidable mortality within English trusts. Research questions • Do mortality indices reflect anything about avoidable deaths and wider quality of care? • How do trusts respond to mortality alerts? • How can current responses to mortality alerts be improved? Objectives 1. Describe the findings and impact of a national mortality surveillance system as a feedback mechanism for quality improvement. 2. Determine the relationship of alerts to other potential indicators of quality. 3. Determine the temporal patterns of alerts and whether they are associated with subsequent changes in mortality rates at trusts. 4. Describe trusts’ responses to receiving mortality alerts and the impact on safety/quality improvements, including organisational and staff behaviour. 5. Determine whether there are differences in the delivery of care at frequently alerting trusts compared with trusts that alert rarely, for two conditions commonly generating mortality alerts - acute myocardial infarction and septicaemia. 6. Determine at trusts where mortality decreased after alerts whether they were more likely to apply common safety/quality interventions compared with trusts that repeatedly alert. Analysis Workstream 1 will describe trends in mortality alerts and also examine the relationships between these alerts and outcomes following investigation as reported to CQC and other measures of quality of care through statistical analyses of hospital administrative data. Workstream 2 will include two phases of investigation. Phase A will employ comparative institutional case studies for 12 sample trusts alerting for either acute myocardial infarction or septicaemia. This will inform the development of a structured evaluative telephone survey to categorise and quantify organisational behavioural and contextual aspects of the response to alerts in Phase B., and will permit the analysis of whether these are related to changes in mortality after the alerts. Project outputs will include research reports, papers in peer-reviewed academic journals, conference presentations, seminars and guidelines for trusts on how to respond to mortality alerts (a template for action) and recommend how to improve the surveillance system. Benefits and impact of research • Inform service provision policies for the conditions/patient groups investigated • Support national quality improvement initiatives • Improve the joint national surveillance system and public trust in it • Increase understanding of administrative data use (suitability and usability) for mortality monitoring • Learn from trusts that effectively respond to mortality alerts (reduced or consistently low mortality rates

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Home-based health promotion for vulnerable older people
Abstract: Aim: To develop and test feasibility/acceptability of a home-based health promotion intervention for older people with early frailty. Design: Evidence review, in-depth interviews and development, acceptability, feasibility of a complex intervention. Evidence synthesis: We will update systematic reviews of trials and systematically review policy, qualitative and other data, focussing on defining active components and theories in relevant health promotion interventions. We will use methods developed by NICE/SCIE to synthesise heterogeneous literature. Setting: Community (home) based, in London & Hertfordshire. Target population: Older people 65+ years with early frailty in receipt of community health services/visited at home by a health professional in the previous 6 months. Exclusion criteria: Those in care homes, on GP palliative care register, who lack capacity to consent, already case managed (e.g. by community matrons). Qualitative study: We will supplement data from a current qualitative study with 52 older people and stakeholders from NHS, local authority and community groups with up to 10 further interviews with older people with early frailty and 4 focus groups with carers, home care workers, and health professionals. These will explore facilitators and barriers to health promotion and content/delivery of a new intervention. Transcripts will be analysed thematically. Intervention: Using a co-design approach successful in previous work we will convene panels of older people/carers and multi-disciplinary stakeholders/experts to develop the intervention. Using the MRC Complex intervention model we will develop/manualise the intervention, and synthesise evidence from the reviews, theory and qualitative findings. The intervention will be delivered by health professionals at home for older people with early frailty. Feasibility study: General Practices will identify individuals receiving home visits and invite them to take part. Those eligible will be randomised to receive the intervention or treatment as usual. Intervention visits will be recorded and assessed for content/fidelity. Outcomes: A theory-based intervention tested for acceptability/feasibility in community settings. Data on patient recruitment, retention, willingness to be randomised and potential outcomes for an RCT: functioning; quality of life; frailty; well-being; mobility; psychological distress; uptake preventative interventions; CVD risk factors (BP, BMI, smoking, alcohol, exercise); falls; medication use; service utilisation (NHS/social care); costs; QALYs; mortality. Sample size: To test feasibility we will identify 12-13 eligible older people per GP practice, in 4 General practices (50 participants). This was feasible in previous work.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The Best Services Trial (BeST?): Effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the New Orleans Intervention Model for Infant Mental Health
Abstract: The negative effects of child maltreatment on mental and physical health amplify across the lifespan and costs to society are enormous. Regardless of the extent of early life maltreatment, placement in a nurturing family is associated with rapid development of secure attachment and improved mental health – but only if that nurturing placement is achieved early enough in life. The best type of placement is not yet clear: randomised controlled trial (RCT) evidence has shown that placement of maltreated children in substitute family care (i.e. adoption or fostering) is associated with significant developmental catch-up, but other studies suggest that placement within the birth or extended family may be even better than substitute care. Efforts to improve the mental health of maltreated children in birth families or foster placements have had mixed success and researchers have recommended that far more intensive approaches are required. We are conducting a two-arm UK-based RCT of such an intensive approach. The programme we are evaluating, the New Orleans Intervention Model (NIM), is currently the only one that is well evidenced, although only in a US setting. NIM offers families whose child enters care due to maltreatment a structured attachment-based assessment followed by an intensive intervention aiming to improve family functioning and child mental health. If adequate change is achieved a recommendation is made for the child to return home but, if not, the recommendation is for adoption. US pilot research suggests that NIM is associated with a reduction in future maltreatment of both the index child and other siblings as well as improved mental health in middle childhood. Our control intervention, Case Management (CM), comprises standardised social work contact and referral to other services where necessary. In order to translate NIM for the Scottish context, we conducted extensive mapping and modelling in both New Orleans and Glasgow to understand how best to develop NIM to take account of the differing healthcare and legal context. Since beginning our feasibility RCT, in December 2011, we have recruited 65% of all maltreated children aged 6 months to 5 years coming into an episode of care. Preliminary findings suggest that the intervention is acceptable to parents, foster carers, social workers and legal professionals, but this study will not be large enough to say definitively what impact NIM has on the health of the children involved or how much it will cost in the long term. We are currently conducting similar detailed mapping and modelling work in South London, and a NIM team is going to be launched there in 2015. We now want to test whether NIM is clinically and cost-effective in the different legal jurisdictions across England and Scotland. We propose a multi-centre RCT of NIM involving a continuation of our current Glasgow RCT, including a further 2 sites in Scotland and 1 site in London, England. We plan to involve 462 families in total across these sites, including those recruited in our current Glasgow study. This will allow us to test, definitively, whether NIM is clinically effective and cost effective in the UK.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Evaluation of Health in Pregnancy Grants in Scotland
Abstract: The Health in Pregnancy Grant was a universal payment of £190 made to women who had reached the 25th week of pregnancy and had received health advice from a midwife or doctor. The grant was designed to provide additional financial support in the last months of pregnancy towards a healthy lifestyle including diet, and it was suggested that the link to the requirement for pregnant women to seek health advice from a health professional may provide a greater incentive for expectant mothers to seek the recommended health advice at the appropriate time. The grant was introduced for women with a due date on or after 6th April 2009 but was subsequently withdrawn, the last payments being made to women who had reached the 25th week of pregnancy by 1st January 2011. The grant was paid by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) on receipt of a claim form available from and partly completed by the midwife or doctor. Payment was made directly into a bank account, with a telephone helpline available to provide support through the claim process including options for payment in the event of difficulties opening a bank account. Take up of the grant was said to be at about the same level as for child benefit (98-99%; personal communication, HMRC). Advice was offered as normal by doctors and midwives. Payment was made by HMRC. Administration was by HMRC; the cost of the grant was met by the Treasury. The objective is to evaluate the effect and cost-effectiveness of the Health in Pregnancy Grant. We will do this by assessing the difference in birthweight for babies born to those mothers who were eligible for the Health in Pregnancy Grant with babies born before the Health in Pregnancy Grant was introduced or after it was withdrawn. The study will be based in Scotland because of the availability of high quality routinely collected maternal and neonatal data available for a geographical population; our findings will be applicable to the rest of the UK. Specific questions the research project will address are: 1) Were there differential impacts of the intervention for particular subgroups defined by socioeconomic (both area deprivation and individual occupational social class), demographic (marital status, age, maternal height), or obstetric (parity, previous Caesarean section) factors, or for selected combinations of these groups? 2) Was the Health in Pregnancy Grant cost effective? How did cost-effectiveness vary across important subgroups identified as having differential outcomes? We will analyse the effect of the intervention on an intention to treat basis. The eligible participants will be all women who reached the 25th week of pregnancy in Scotland with a due date between 6th April 2009 and and 16th April 2011. The grants will be evaluated using an interrupted time series approach; the comparator will therefore be all births in Scotland with a due date between 1st January 2004 and 28th February 2009 and between 1st June 2011 and 31st March 2013. The primary outcome will be birthweight among singleton live births; secondary outcomes will include gestation at booking, booking by 25 weeks, stillbirths and neonatal deaths, very low (<1500g) and low (<2500g) birthweight, gestational age, preterm (<36 weeks and <32 weeks), weight for dates (standardized and small and large for gestational age), and 5 minute apgar score.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: How far could widespread dissemination of parenting programmes improve child antisocial behaviour and reduce social inequalities? Combining datasets from trials in different communities to establish for whom programmes are effective and cost effective
Abstract: There are compelling public health reasons for investing in parenting interventions. Poor parenting skills are predictive of a wide range of poor health outcomes in the next generation, especially youth antisocial behaviour (Ermisch, 2008; Hoeve et al, 2010). Persistent antisocial behaviour is a major public health issue, because it is the commonest child mental health problem (ONS, 2004), and carries high health burdens into adulthood, including a 5-10 fold risk of alcoholism, drug abuse, criminality, domestic violence, unemployment and early death (Odgers et al., 2007; Piquero et al, 2011). The extra public costs are 10 times that of controls (Scott et al, 2001). As with poor parenting, there is a strong association with social disadvantage, with a 4-5 times the rate of antisocial behaviour in the most disadvantaged groups (ONS, 2004). Parenting interventions potentially form an important public health strategy for preventing antisocial behaviour and other poor outcomes in children, for a number of reasons. Firstly, because of the high public health and financial burden of antisocial behaviour, it provides an excellent opportunity for early preventive intervention. Secondly, systematic reviews of RCTs (Dretzke et al, 2007; Furlong et al, 2012) show clear beneficial effects; NICE found a mean effect-size of 0.6 SD on child problem behaviour, with good long-term effects, an extremely worthwhile effect in public health terms. Furthermore, our modelling study shows good financial returns from investment in parenting programmes. Although high quality parenting interventions are effective for most families and carry the potential to improve public health substantially, most trials have been of modest size and little is known about their ability to bring about change in more disadvantaged groups. The proposed study will address this question, bringing to bear 4 important design features. Firstly, it will analyse randomised trials, thus reducing risk of bias that may arise from observational studies. Secondly, rather than combining data at the trial level as is usual in meta-analysis, it will combine data at an individual participant level, from 13 trials, thus greatly enhancing the opportunity to detect moderating effects of social disadvantage, as well as wider benefits and potential harms of the interventions. This represents a unique opportunity to overcome the problems of low power and reporting bias that beset subgroup analyses in many individual trials and meta-analyses, and hence to enhance our understanding of how parenting interventions may reduce or widen health and social inequalities (Petticrew et al, 2011; Thompson & Higgins, 2005). Thirdly, it will draw upon qualitative research and public involvement, soliciting parents views on factors affecting intervention success, to inform hypotheses for testing. Fourthly, it will apply cost and cost effectiveness approaches to examine potential benefits to public health. The intervention is the Incredible Years (IY) group parenting programme, identified as effective in many systematic reviews (Furlong et al, 2012) for preventing antisocial and conduct problems in children and improving parental mental health. Although developed in the US, it has proven effective in many trials in Europe. It has received Government funding for training in England, Wales and Scotland, and as a result of its widespread dissemination, there have been 7 randomised trials in the UK, in a range of community settings (Sure Start, nurseries, schools NGOs). However, although each trial was powered to detect main effects, they were not powered to conduct secondary analyses testing differential effects on families with different levels of social disadvantage, and from different ethnic groups. Our pooled set of 13 trials would be the largest of its type in the world, comprising all the non-NHS RCTs of IY in Europe (total N, 1729 families), including 7 UK trials, and 6 in other European systems. It will considerably advance our understanding of differential intervention effects, and cost-effectiveness of parenting interventions for families with differing levels of social disadvantage and child risk factors, thus helping to determine whether such programmes are likely to reduce or widen social inequalities. Most importantly, if there are groups for whom programmes work less well, it will stimulate change in working practices to improve availability and effects of these programmes to such groups. The proposed study would address the following three questions: (1) To what extent do parenting interventions benefit the most socially disadvantaged families? Moderator analyses will examine whether the intervention is less or more effective and cost-effective i) for the most disadvantaged families, sub-grouping families by SES, poverty, lone parent status, ii) by ethnicity, and iii) by child factors, including age, gender, and initial severity of behaviour problems. We will examine effects of trial-level contextual factors, and whether any subgroup effects may be better accounted for by family level variables. (2) What are the wider public health benefits and potential harms of parenting interventions? We will examine effects on harsh and positive parenting, parent depression, child co-morbid problems (e.g. ADHD). Consumer satisfaction data will be pooled and analysed by subgroup. We will model potential long-term cost-benefit generated by the intervention. (3) What are the key ingredients (mediators) of the effect of the intervention on child outcome? Study population (see Chart for summary of trials). Our pooled sample of 1729 families, each with a target child aged 1-9, identified by screening or referral as being at risk of antisocial behaviour; most are low income families, but with a wide range of levels of social disadvantage. In 4 UK trials and 2 trials from the Netherlands, a high percent are from ethnic minorities. Primary outcome measures: Child antisocial behaviour/conduct problems: measured by standardised, well validated instruments, including parent self-report; semi-structured parent interview and directly observed child behaviour. Secondary outcomes measuring wider benefits: 1. Parenting behaviour: by standardised parent questionnaire; direct observation. 2. Parent mental health: by standardised parent questionnaire 3. Child ADHD, emotional symptoms 4. Other outcomes: sibling behaviour problems; social support; partner relations, parenting confidence.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Assessing the impact and cost-effectiveness of needle/syringe provision on hepatitis C transmission among people who inject drugs: an analysis of pooled datasets and economic modelling
Abstract: While there is good evidence that needle and syringe programmes (NSP) and opiate substitution treatment (OST) in combination reduce injecting risk behaviours and some evidence to show their impact on HIV incidence, there is little evidence for their impact on hepatitis C (HCV) incidence among people who inject drugs (PWID). There have been no economic evaluations of NSPs undertaken in Western Europe and few have considered the costs saved due to care and treatment averted. All existing studies have relied on weak measures of NSP effectiveness with most using changes in self reported risk behaviour which can be biased. This project will fill a gap in the evidence by providing robust estimates of the efficacy of NSP and OST on reducing an individual’s risk of HCV transmission, and an understanding of the likely impact of existing coverage levels of NSP and changes in the extent of provision. It will also produce the first assessment of the cost-effectiveness of needle/syringe provision in UK and will estimate the costs and incremental cost-effectiveness ratio associated with increasing coverage on HCV transmission among PWID. The project will answer the following research questions: 1. What is the impact of different coverage levels of needle/syringe provision on the incidence of hepatitis C among PWID at the individual level? 2. What are the contribution of other risk factors on HCV incidence and the overall transmission of HCV among PWID? 3. What is the international evidence on the impact of NSPs with and without OST on incidence of hepatitis C among PWID? 4. What are the costs associated with existing NSP provision in three UK settings? 5. What is the impact and cost-effectiveness of existing provision of NSP, compared to no provision, on HCV and HIV transmission and disease burden among PWID in three UK settings? 6. What are the possible strategies for increasing the coverage of NSP provision in three UK settings, and likely impact and cost-effectiveness of these strategies? The participants under study are PWID. The intervention to be evaluated is NSPs and coverage of the intervention will be measured by calculating the total number of needle/syringes received per month by a PWID divided by their frequency of injections. NSPs in England are funded through Drug Action Teams (DATs) and Local Strategic Partnerships – multi-agency bodies involving local government, police, and health services and can be provided through pharmacies, mobile vans or specialist fixed sites. We will compare PWID with different coverage levels of NSP provision. The outcome of interest is new HCV infections, defined as being antibody negative and RNA positive in Polymerase Chain Reaction testing. Three linked data collection activities and analyses will be undertaken: 1. Analysis of pooled data (RQ 1, 2) Data will be collated from the unlinked anonymous monitoring (UAM) survey of PWID (England, Wales and Northern Ireland), the Australian Needle/Syringe Programme Survey (ANSPS), the Needle Exchange Surveillance Initiative (NESI) and studies of community-recruited PWID. All sources contain comparable indicators on intervention use and new cases of HCV, except for UAM, from which 1800 antibody negative dried-blood spots will be tested. Approximately 13,500 observations will be included of which ~6,400 will be anti-HCV negative and ~160 recent infections. We will analyse the pooled data sets using logistic regression to model the odds of recent infection by NSP exposure adjusting for key confounders (injecting duration, gender, crack use and homelessness) and assessing joint effects of NSP and OST. We will explore evidence of a dose-response relationship and linear decrease in the odds of infection with increasing NSP coverage and examine the impact of OST. 2. Systematic Review (RQ3) We will conduct a systematic review, following Cochrane Guidelines, of published studies and unpublished analyses that report on the effect of NSP exposure and/or OST on HCV incidence. We will conduct a meta-analysis to estimate the unadjusted effects of NSP exposure and/or OST on HCV incidence incorporating the pooled analysis results to determine the generalisability of findings to other settings. 3. Modelling Impact and Economic evaluation (RQ 4-6) An existing dynamic deterministic model of HIV and HCV transmission and OST/NSP intervention coverage among PWID will be adapted. Intervention efficacy estimates will come from the pooled analysis. The model will be used to estimate the impact of historical and current NSP coverage levels for reducing HIV and HCV prevalence and disease burden in three UK settings, and future impact of increasing or decreasing NSP coverage levels. The model will also estimate the population attributable fraction of different behavioural risk factors for increasing HCV transmission in these settings. We will estimate the cost-effectiveness of current NSP provision compared to no provision and the potential cost-effectiveness of increasing NSP coverage in each setting compared to maintaining stable coverage. Data on resource use and costs of existing NSP provision will be collected from each setting, including staff time, salaries, training, equipment and overheads, and will be combined with modeled impact estimates. Following a review of the literature, discussions will be held with collaborators and other stakeholders to develop modeling scenarios for strategies that could improve NSP coverage. Costs will be modeled based on the cost data collected from each site and the effect of changes or differences in NSP provision will be obtained from the literature or from settings that have changed attributes of their NSP provision or by comparing between sites with differences in provision.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Decommissioning health care: identifying best practice through primary and secondary research
Abstract: Although decommissioning - defined here as the planned process of removing, reducing or replacing health care services – is at the forefront of NHS policy it remains strikingly under-researched. This project is designed to address this important knowledge-practice gap. Research questions The overall aim of the research is to formulate evidence-informed best practice guidance to enable the effective decommissioning of NHS services. To this end the project will address three key research questions: Q1. What is the international evidence and expert opinion regarding best practice in decommissioning health care services? Q2. How and to what extent are NHS organisations currently decommissioning services? Q3. What factors and processes facilitate the successful implementation of decisions to decommission NHS services? Research design and data collection In order to address each of these questions the research is organised around three distinct but inter-connecting work-packages: Work-package one will synthesise what is already known about implementing decommissioning in health care and other public sector settings (Q1). It combines a narrative synthesis of recent reviews of the literature and empirical evidence with the views of an international expert-panel via a Delphi exercise. Additionally, in order to develop a detailed understanding of the NHS decommissioning context, approximately 20 semi-structured, telephone interviews will be conducted with key informants from a range of health and social care agencies. In addition, five leaders of recent decommissioning projects in the NHS will be interviewed about their experiences and their views on implementing decommissioning policies. Work-package two will establish the current range and extent of decommissioning in the NHS from the perspective of local commissioners (Q2). The online survey tool will collect both quantitative and qualitative data via a national questionnaire. Work-package three will develop our understanding of how NHS organisations are currently implementing decommissioning policies through a prospective, longitudinal investigation of four case studies in the English NHS (Q3). These will be mixed-method and in-depth and a comparative cross-case analysis will enable us to draws lessons and facilitate learning with regard to the factors and processes that influence successful implementation and outcomes (e.g. in terms of service quality and efficiency) of decommissioning. Data analysis and outputs These multiple data sources will provide a rich and broad understanding of decommissioning and enhance both the validity and transferability of the results. Through application of a theoretical framework drawing on the political and organisational science literatures and actor-network theory we will develop new insights into the topic as well as aiding the formulation and implementation of NHS policy and practice. There is a strong international strand to the research and robust mechanisms for respondent validation and service user involvement. Through active and varied dissemination activities we will make substantive contributions to policy and practice in the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: Heart of England NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Do not attempt cardiopulmonary resuscitation (DNACPR) decisions
Abstract: This study will summarise the research evidence around Do Not Attempt Cardiopulmonary Resuscitatio (DNACPR) decisions, explore the reasons why conflict and complaints arise and identify inconsistencies in implementation of national guidelines across the NHS and examples of best practice. We will establish and engage a stakeholder group at the start of the project. The stakeholder group, under the guidance of a lay chair (co-applicant Barry Williams), will include healthcare users, their relatives, healthcare providers, ethicists, legal personnel and policy makers. This group will ensure the research remains focused on the issues that are important to patients and their families, relevant to NHS practice and compliant with ethical and regulatory / legal frameworks. The programme of work will be divided into 5 discrete work packages (see project flow diagram). In brief: Work package (WP) 1 will synthesise existing research evidence for DNACPR decisions through a systematic review of the literature, thematic review and meta-analysis (if possible). WP 2 will identify the themes behind why DNACPR processes fail by examining Coroner Article 43 notices; incidents, serious untoward incidents, complaints and enquiries from NHS providers and a data from a patient / relative helpline. WP 3 will identify current NHS practices through a review of local Trust DNACPR policies and procedures mapped against national guidelines. It will seek examples of best practice alongside looking for evidence of inequality and inconsistencies. WP 4 will obtain health service providers perspectives on current process. We will use a focus groups to identify understanding of current guidelines and the practical difficulties of implementing policy in clinical practice. WP 5 will pull packages 1-4 together to produce and disseminate a final report. This will be facilitated by a consensus conference with the stakeholder group and representatives of policy makers, patient and professional organisations and those responsible for education and development, to consider the how these findings will impact on future policy and research in the UK. Following this we will summarise and disseminate the findings of the project, setting out the recommendations for best use of available evidence to direct policy and practice, highlighting gaps in the evidence base and indicating prioritised future research needs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Effects of a demand led knowledge translation service on the uptake and use of research evidence by NHS commissioners compared with lower intensity untargeted alternatives
Abstract: NHS funding constraints mean that only the most effective, best value health care interventions and service improvements should be made available. The Health and Social Care Act emphasises the need to use research evidence in the design and delivery of local services. To do this well, commissioners need to make more use of research in deciding which interventions and ways of working will deliver more value from the finite NHS resources available. NIHR has invested significantly in the production of research evidence on the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of interventions to inform decisions and choices. However, full uptake of this knowledge to increase efficiency, reduce practice variations and to ensure best use of finite resources within the NHS has yet to be realised. NHS managers and clinical leads in Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs) can play a key role in improving uptake and use of knowledge to inform commissioning and decommissioning of services. However, their ability to recognise and understand valuable research based knowledge is often lacking. We have already developed a briefing and support service tailored to the needs of commissioners and other NHS managers (in a large NIHR research programme focused on West and North Yorkshire). The service identifies, appraises and contextualises existing research evidence to inform the real world issues brought to us by local decision makers. Feedback on this service from our NHS partners has been uniformly positive and we have helped some achieve major cost savings through evidence informed service reconfiguration. Whilst we are confident the service can meet the many needs in the local health economies in which it was developed, we now need to establish whether this service model really does enhance research evidence use by commissioners compared with other approaches. We plan to do this by undertaking a comparative evaluation with organisations responsible for commissioning NHS services in the North of England. At the start of the study we will assess each CCG's current ability to use evidence to support decision-making. We will repeat the evaluation of evidence use at the end of the main study period to identify changes over time in each of our study areas. The study will take 27 months and will evaluate whether a responsive knowledge translation service increases uptake and use of research evidence by NHS managers compared with less intensive and targeted alternatives. The study will be undertaken by a multi-disciplinary team involving researchers at the University of York and Queens University Belfast and colleagues in the NHS. Appropriate ethical and local governance approval will be sought for the study. A research advisory group will ensure that the project is being managed appropriately and will provide advice on research issues at various stages of the project. The proposed research will generate new knowledge of direct relevance and value to the NHS. The findings will help to clarify which elements of the service are effective in promoting use of research evidence. Those involved in NHS commissioning will be able to use the results to inform how best to build the infrastructure they need to acquire, assess, adapt and apply research evidence to their support decision-making, and fulfil their statutory duties under the Health and Social Care Act.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: A realist process evaluation of robotic surgery: integration into routine practice and impacts on communication, collaboration and decision making
Abstract: The aim of this project is to understand how and in what circumstances robotic surgery produces both intended and unintended outcomes. This will be achieved through a process evaluation, running alongside ROLARR (RObotic versus LAparoscopic Resection for Rectal cancer), a randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing laparoscopic and robotic rectal cancer surgery for the curative treatment of rectal cancer. Realist evaluation (Pawson & Tilley, 1997), which is concerned with understanding for whom and in what circumstances complex interventions work and involves building, testing and refining the theories of how the intervention is supposed to work, provides an overall framework for the study. In Phase 1, grey literature will be reviewed to identify theories concerning (i) how robotic surgery becomes embedded into surgical practice; (ii) how robotic surgery impacts on communication, teamwork and decision making in the OT and how this is affected by the process through which the technology is introduced; and (iii) subsequent impacts on outcomes such as operation duration, conversion to open surgery, and complications. These candidate theories will be refined and added to through interviews conducted with staff at different levels of the organisation across ten NHS hospital Trusts that are using robotic surgery for rectal cancer resection (both Trusts that are participating in the trial and those that are not), along with a review of documentation associated with the introduction of robotic surgery. In Phase 2, a multi-site case study will be conducted across four NHS hospital Trusts (three that are participating in the trial and one that is not) to test and refine the candidate theories. Data will be collected using multiple methods. Observation using the structured observation tool OTAS (Observational Teamwork Assessment for Surgery; Undre et al., 2007) and video recordings of operations will be combined with ethnographic observation and interviews. In Phase 3, interviews will be conducted at the four case sites with staff representing a range of surgical disciplines, to assess the extent to which the results of Phase 2 are generalisable and to refine the resulting theories to reflect the experience of a broader range of surgical disciplines. Findings will be fed back to all four case sites in interactive sessions, feedback from which will assist in the production of actionable guidance concerning how to support integration of robotic surgery into surgical practice and how to ensure effective communication and teamwork when undertaking robotic surgery.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Characterising the nature of primary care patient safety incident reports in England and Wales: mixed methods study
Abstract: Primary care poses unique challenges for the design of better quality systems of care delivery. Transferring lessons from advances made from over a decade of patient safety research in specialist care settings may therefore not be without problems. A WHO-commissioned systematic review and Delphi expert consensus study (February 2012) highlighted the paucity of empirical work that explores the relationship between cause (the error) and effect (harm), and the underlying system failures that facilitate this relationship (Panesar et al., in review). In 2003, a major national investment was made to better understand patient safety incidents occurring in England and Wales called the National Reporting and Learning System (NRLS). The NRLS contains a free-text description of the event, perceived causative factors, and any planned actions made locally following the incident. Over 47,000 incident reports exist from primary care in England and Wales and these have never previously been systematically analysed. Such reports permit a retrospective ‘window’ on the healthcare system, providing a means of looking to the future, by identifying weaknesses of the system that are still present and could lead to further incidents involving patients (Vincent 2004). This study aims to understand the nature and range of patient safety incidents in primary care reported to the NRLS. A team comprising primary care doctors, nurses and health services researchers will undertake thematic content analysis of free-text data in reports to describe the incident, identify potential contributory factors, type and severity of harm. A codebook will comprise iterations of existing coding frameworks for primary care patient safety incident description e.g. the LINNEAUS taxonomy (LINNEAUS EURO-PC, http://www.linneaus-pc.eu), type of harm (Vincent et al., 2013) and severity of harm (NRLS, 2004), as well as empirical de novo creation of a potential contributory factors coding framework. Assigning codes requires ‘sense making’ of the reported story and eliciting human factors and organisational issues discussed within it (Reason 1990; Vincent et al. 1998; Henriksen and Kaplan 2003). Incident characteristics will be summarised using descriptive statistics. Modelling will determine the strength of association between types and severity of harm. A map will be generated to demonstrate the relationships between themes and their potential contributory influences. We anticipate the research will benefit patients and the NHS by characterising patient safety incidents that lead to harm in primary care. This is an unexploited area within primary care patient safety, and should serve to demonstrate the value of safety monitoring and frame the benefits of a reporting culture for healthcare professional, managers, leaders and patients in the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: An Evaluation of the Effectiveness of Annual Health Checks and Quality of Health Care for Adults with Learning Disability
Abstract: Background People with learning disability are a vulnerable group who experience high levels of physical morbidity and mortality. There is evidence that people with learning disability receive sub-optimal care and this inequity contributes to poor health outcomes including avoidable mortality. In 2008, an Independent Inquiry into Access to Health Care for People with Learning Disability concluded that people with learning disability receive less effective care leading to avoidable suffering and death. In addition, the report highlighted the paucity of information on NHS health care for people with learning disability. A key focus of National policy is improving the quality of primary care. In 2007, the Disability Rights Commission recommended the introduction of annual health checks which was supported by the Independent Inquiry. In 2009, a national Directed Enhanced Service (DES) was introduced in England. This DES funds practices to provide annual health checks to adults with learning disability and requires that staff receive training. The health check is intended to identify undetected health problems, improve prescribing and coordination with secondary care. A systematic review by the Learning Disability Observatory confirms that health checks are effective in identifying health problems but found a paucity of evidence on their impact on health outcomes. This study is a large sample evaluation of the effectiveness of annual health checks and a comprehensive study of health and healthcare in a national sample of adults with learning disability Aims 1. To evaluate the process and outcome effectiveness of Annual Health Checks for adults with learning disability in primary care. 2. To describe the health, healthcare quality and equity, and NHS costs for adults with learning disability in a National sample Objectives Aim 1 • Determine whether individuals receiving Annual Health Checks experience improvement in healthcare process measures and health problem identification. • Determine whether individuals receiving Annual Health Checks experience improvement in health outcomes • Determine whether practice participation in the Annual Health Check directed enhanced service improves outcomes for people with learning disability • Determine the change in health service costs in the year before and after an Annual Health Check Aim 2 • Quantify primary and secondary care utilisation • Describe and quantify specific health risks for adults with learning disability • Describe the quality of primary care received by adults with learning disability • Determine annual health service costs for people with learning disability compared to the general population Methods Data Source An established anonymised primary care database which includes full individual records of primary care consultation, diagnoses and prescribing with linked hospital admission data. Sample 12000 adults (18 and over) with learning disability registered with general practices in England between April 2007 and March 2013 and age,sex and practice matched controls without learning disability. Design Evaluation of Annual Health Checks will be undertaken at individual and practice level. The individual level analysis will evaluate the effectiveness of health checks as a personal intervention. We will undertake a self-controlled before and after analysis with practice matched general population controls. This will compare the difference in outcomes between the two years before first annual health check and the two years following with the matched controls. Our practice level analysis will compare changes in outcomes for all people with learning disability in practices which offer health checks with changes in outcomes in non-participating practices since introduction of the directed enhanced service. This analysis will complement the individual patient analysis and identify the population benefit of health checks while also controlling for any temporal improvements in health outcomes for people with learning disability. The description of health, healthcare quality and equity will identify prevalence and annual rates for key health outcomes in all adults with learning disability and quality of primary care in comparison to a practice matched general population controls. We will also estimate the annual NHS costs for people with learning disability compared to people without learning disability. Outcomes For evaluation of Annual Health Checks, the main outcome will be emergency hospital admissions. This outcome has been selected as it is hypothesised that improvements in care across a range of health conditions, as a result of Annual Health Checks, will lead to a reduction in this outcome for people with learning disability. Secondary outcomes will include generic and disease specific process and outcome measures of quality of care and total NHS costs. Our description of health will include additional outcomes including disease incidence and prevalence. Benefit for NHS There are barriers to implementation of this Annual Health Checks in primary care including concern over their effectiveness and resources required. Less than 50% of eligible adults received a Health Check by March 2011. Our study will strengthen the evidence base for this intervention. Evidence of clear benefit from health checks would encourage further implementation while limited evidence of benefit would stimulate modifications to achieve greater benefit for people with learning disability including improvements in the NHS response to health problems identified during Annual Health Checks. This study will also address the paucity of information on the health and quality of NHS care for adults with learning disability to enable the NHS to target interventions to maximise health gain.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The effectiveness and cost effectiveness of an employer-led intervention to increase walking during the daily commute: Cluster randomised controlled trial
Abstract: AIM: To examine the effectiveness, cost effectiveness and acceptability of an employer-led intervention to increase walking during the daily commute. INTERVENTION. Walk to Work promoters will be recruited and trained to encourage other employees to increase walking during their commute to and from work. Employees will receive Walk to Work booklets and pedometers, walking routes will be identified and goals set. Encouragement will be given through 4 contacts from the Walk to Work promoter over 10 weeks. Participants living within 2 miles of the workplace will be encouraged to walk to work; those living further away will be encouraged to use public transport plus walking, or park further away from their workplace and walk. Intervention costs will be covered by the DECIPHer collaboration and Living Streets. STUDY DESIGN. Cluster RCT including economic and process evaluations. SAMPLE SIZE CALCULATION. Based on findings from the feasibility study, the sample size for the full-scale trial was based on an average cluster size of 8, an ICC of 0.15, and attrition of 25%. With a total sample size of 678 we have 80% power with a 5% significance level to detect a 15% increase in mean MVPA. [A sample size of 542 is required to detect a 15% increase in mean overall activity (cpm) with 80% power.] SETTING. Workplaces (n=84) will be recruited in Bath, Swansea and South Gloucestershire. The intervention will be implemented in 42 workplaces; 42 similar workplaces will comprise the control arm. Workplace will be matched by size [small (up to 50 employees), medium (51-250 employees), large (250+ employees)], location and type of business. PARTICIPANTS. Employees who do not always cycle or walk to work. OUTCOME EVALUATION. Accelerometers, GPS monitors and travel diaries will be used at baseline(DC1) and one year follow-up(DC3). Behavioural questionnaires will be used at DC1,immediately post intervention(DC2) and DC3. PROCESS EVALUATION. The context, delivery and receipt of the intervention will be examined from the perspectives of employers, Walk to Work promoters and employees using evaluation forms at key stages of the trial, behavioural questionnaires (DC1, DC2, DC3) and post intervention interviews with a purposive sample of employers, Walk to Work promoters and employees. ECONOMIC EVALUATION. Costs of the intervention will be assessed by recording time, materials and expenses used in training the promoters and implementing the intervention with employees. Costs to participants will be assessed by recording journey time, household commuting costs and expenses using travel diaries (DC1, DC3). Presenteeism, absenteeism and health service use will be recorded using questionnaires (DC1,DC3). Overall absentee rates will also be collected from employers. Employee wellbeing will be measured using the ICECAP-A questionnaire. PRIMARY OUTCOME. Daily minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity(MVPA) SECONDARY OUTCOME: Overall levels of physical activity (cpm); daily minutes of sedentary time; modal shift. PROCESS OUTCOMES. Facilitators and barriers to employer-led Walk to Work interventions; Facilitators and barriers to employees walking to work. Physical activity/MVPA due to walking during the journey to/from work. ECONOMIC EVALUATION OUTCOMES. Costs to employers and employees of the Walk to Work intervention; consequences for employers (absenteeism/presenteeism); consequences for employees (commuting costs, wellbeing); health service use.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A multi-centre cluster-randomised controlled trial of screening and brief alcohol intervention to prevent risky drinking in young people aged 14-15 in a high school setting (SIPS JR-HIGH)
Abstract: Early and heavy drinking by younger adolescents is a significant public health problem. The aim of the study is to evaluate the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of alcohol screening and brief intervention to reduce risky drinking in young people aged 14-15 (year 10) in the English high school setting compared to standard alcohol advice/education. The four centre, two-armed randomised controlled trial (RCT) incorporates a control arm of usual practice on alcohol issues and a 30-minute brief intervention arm. Interventions will be delivered by trained school based learning mentors. A qualitative component will explore staff and participants’ experience of the interventions and of delivering, or participating in, the trial. Randomisation will be at participant level at 20 schools - five in each geographical area. All young people in year 10 will be asked to complete a lifestyle questionnaire with the Adolescent - Single Alcohol Questionnaire (A-SAQ) embedded. Young people who score positive and leave their name will be invited to meet with the learning mentor and asked to consent to the study. Training and the intervention will be manualised. Control: Usual practice on alcohol issues as delivered normally by the school as well as a healthy lifestyle leaflet with information on local sources of help for problems including alcohol problemsl, given by the learning mentor to those that consent to the trial. Intervention: In addition to input equivalent to the control arm; the young people who are eligible and consent to participate will take part in a 30-minute personalised interactive worksheet-based session which was developed during the pilot feasibility trial. This will be delivered by the learning mentor (at school) and will contain structured feedback about the individual student’s drinking behaviour and advice about the health and social consequences of continued risky alcohol consumption. Primary (effectiveness) outcome measure: Total alcohol consumed in 28 days, using the 28 day time-line follow-back (TLFB) questionnaire at 12-month follow-up. Secondary (effectiveness) outcome measures: percent days abstinence, drinks per drinking day and days>2units from the 28 day TLFB. Risky drinking using the A-SAQ and Alcohol Use Disorder Identification Test (AUDIT) and TLFB; Smoking behaviour; Alcohol related problems using the Rutgers Alcohol Problems Inventory (RAPI); Emotional wellbeing using the Warwick Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale (WEMWBS) and drinking motives using the Drinking Motives Questionnaire (DMQ). Secondary (health economic) outcome measures: Quality of life and health utility (EQ-5D 5L); National Health Service and social costs using a modified Short Service Use Questionnaire (S-SUQ) and a learning mentor diary sheet developed in the pilot study; incremental cost per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY) gained at 12 months will be calculated. Fidelity to intervention: 20% of randomly selected cases, with a minimum of one per learning mentor, will be audio taped and transcribed and assessed for treatment fidelity by two independent expert raters from the research team using the Behaviour Change Counselling Index (BECCI) rating scale. Qualitative work will explore barriers and facilitators of implementation with staff and young people. Organisational support: We have organisational support from education departments in each of the four geographical areas who will work with us to identify schools for the study. Schools will provide learning mentor time at no cost.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: What Works to Increase Attendance for Diabetic Retinopathy Screening? An Evidence sYnthEsiS (WIDeR-EyeS)
Abstract: DESIGN: An evidence synthesis of published and grey literature to identify: the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of quality improvement (QI) interventions for increasing uptake and ongoing attendance for diabetic retinopathy screening; use of validated taxonomies of behaviour change [11, 12] or process theory [13] to describe the content of the interventions and establish the coherence between the intervention components and the barriers/behaviours associated with screening attendance; cost-consequence analysis of effective interventions to increase attendance using a simple decision-model. SETTING: No restriction on location of care, healthcare system or screening model STRATEGY FOR REVIEWING LITERATURE AND HEALTH ECONOMIC MODELLING: The project will comprise three phases. Phase 1: will systematically review the literature on interventions to increase attendance for diabetic retinopathy screening; behavioural coding of intervention components using a validated taxonomy [12] and exploration of heterogeneity within and between studies using traditional and innovative statistical techniques [14,15]. Phase 2 will identify and code the barriers and facilitators relating to retinopathy screening using established theoretical constructs [11, 13]. Phase 3 will map the ‘active’ components of the interventions against the theoretical domains identified as key barriers to screening attendance and estimate the relative cost-effectiveness of potential BCTs to increase attendance at retinopathy screening. A formal 'Knowledge Exchange' event will be convened to discuss the implication of the study findings for the UK diabetic eye screening service. POPULATION: People with type 1 and type 2 diabetes and healthcare professionals responsible for diabetes care HEALTH TECHNOLOGY BEING ASSESSED: QI interventions to increase the initial uptake and ongoing attendance for diabetic retinopathy screening, whether targeted at the individual, healthcare professional or healthcare system STUDY OUTCOMES: The primary outcomes of the project will be: -the identification of the most effective and cost-effective components of interventions and service models that improve screening uptake and performance -a theoretical understanding of causal mechanisms of poor attendance and identification of links to appropriate behaviour change techniques (BCT) to mediate change in behaviour -to use the outputs from the project in consultation with end users to make recommendations on the design of future screening interventions in areas or population subgroups with low attendance and to make recommendations for future research PROJECT TIMETABLE: Study duration will be 18 months. Funding start 01/09/15; Stakeholder engagement, protocol development, designing and running searches: 01/09/15 to 01/03/16; Grey literature searches: 01/02/16 to 01/08/16; Screening titles, study selection, data extraction, coding of data using BCT taxonomy and conducting meta-analysis: 01/01/16 to 01/11/16; exploration of heterogeneity and health economic modelling: 1/08/16 to 30/02/17. Stakeholder ‘Knowledge Exchange’ event: Jan. 2017; Report writing: 01/10/2016 to 28/02/17; Submission of final report: 28.02.17 TEAM EXPERTISE: The team has expertise in diabetic retinopathy screening, systematic review methodology, behaviour change techniques, health economics and the use of novel methods to exploring heterogeneity in systematic reviews of complex interventions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Helping people cope with temptations to smoke to reduce relapse: A factorial randomised controlled trial
Abstract: Background Extended stop-smoking medicine use can help prevent relapse [2,3] but uptake and long-term use is low [4,5]. New vaporised nicotine products, e.g. e-cigarettes (EC), and other fast acting nicotine products may be more attractive for long-term use and hence useful as relapse prevention interventions (RPI). While several behavioural RPI have been found ineffective [2] recent data show that an online Structured Planning and Prompting Protocol (S3P), started at the beginning of the quit attempt, reduced relapse between 1-26 weeks from 71% to 61% [6]. Design Factorial design with 2 comparisons added to usual care (UC) 1) Pharmacological: Provision of fast-acting nicotine (NIC) product versus no NIC. Participants (Ps) offered a choice from a range of oral NRT/EC products. 2) Behavioural: Provision of S3P versus no S3P. UC is generally 8-12 weeks of medicine (e.g. varenicline or NRT) plus standard counselling provided from the start of the quit attempt. Population 1400 smokers: age 18+, who achieve 4 weeks abstinence while receiving UC. Recruitment 700 UK Ps from local SSS. 700 Australian Ps from Quitlines. Health technologies 1) NIC: Ps will choose a NIC (oral NRT/EC) to use if at risk of relapse, receiving 4-weeks supply initially, then offered another 4-week supply at 8-weeks post quit date (PQD).
