Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Organising general practice for care homes: A multi-method study
Abstract: General practice provides first line medical care to care homes, but in recent years, innovative commissioning and service development have increased the variation in how general practice is organised for care homes. In this study, we will identify areas where commissioners or providers have worked to enhance GP services for care home residents and evaluate the impact of the organisation of GP care on residents, general practice and care home staff. Aim: To identify effective and cost effective ways of organising general practice for care homes and evaluate the impact on residents, general practice and care home staff. Research Questions 1. In what ways is the organisation of general practice for care homes associated with better resident outcomes and experiences? 2. What are the implications of different models of GP involvement for residents’ service use and costs? 3. What are the perspectives of residents and relatives, commissioners and staff in general practice and care homes on different ways of organising general practice for care homes; which are acceptable and associated with positive experiences? Plan of investigation: Multi-method case study approach Prior to the start of the funded project the following will be completed: Email survey of practice managers in case study areas (CCGs) to describe GP service organisation to care homes, cluster (or latent class) analysis to develop a simple typology of service organisation for use in the following analyses. WP1. (Research question 1) Comparative analyses of chronic disease management, patient and system outcomes for care home residents in case study areas. Three sites will be selected; two with innovative, contrasting ways of organising general practice for care homes and one where there has been no systematic change to services (usually multiple GPs for each care home). At each case site, patient level data from GP records in the ResearchOne database will be analysed to compare achievement on selected measures, before and after the introduction of changes to GP organisation in the innovation areas and over similar time period in ‘usual care’ areas. Outcome measures will include: hospital admission and readmission rates, potentially avoidable (ambulatory care sensitive) admissions, measures of prescribing quality, GP and practice nurse contacts (in person and by telephone), measures of relational continuity and chronic disease management. Comparisons will be made within and across case studies, controlling for resident characteristics. WP2.(RQ 2) Economic evaluation – Costs will be assigned to the service utilisation identified in WP1, and comparisons conducted within and between case sites and typologies WP3. (RQ 3) Qualitative research - Individual interviews in the case study sites with residents, relatives, GP and care home staff and commissioners, to explore perceptions of the context, structure and processes of service delivery to care homes, positive and negative consequences of different ways of working for staff and residents. Participants will be drawn from sites with particularly effective care and others where resident data point to worse care. This study will provide empirical evidence to a) inform organisational change in general practice, b) support commissioners and providers to make best use of resources, and c) ultimately help residents, family and staff influence and choose the primary medical care services they would like to receive.

Contractor: Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Pay More Attention: A national mixed methods study to identify the barriers and facilitators to ensuring equal access to high quality hospital care and services for children and young people with and without learning disability and their families
Abstract: Background Amidst evidence of discriminatory and abusive practice towards adults with learning disability in hospital, a Confidential Inquiry into the deaths of this population revealed they are more likely to die from causes that are potentially amenable to change by good quality healthcare than people without learning disability. Included in the review were the deaths of 14 children and young people with learning disability. Despite this inclusion, the focus of subsequent recommendations has been on changing practice in the adult setting. A major uncertainty is at what age health inequalities for patients with learning disability start. Whilst all public sector services now have a legal duty to provide reasonable adjustments for people with learning disability to ensure their equal access to services, a comprehensive review of how well hospital services are meeting the needs of children and young people with learning disability and their families has not been conducted. Qualitative evidence of parental dissatisfaction with the quality, safety and accessibility of hospital care for children and young people with learning disability exists but what is not known is whether children and young people are facing the same, or indeed different, inequalities as adults with learning disability. By drawing comparisons with children and young people without learning disability, we can identify what inequality exists for whom and why. Resources and interventions that prevent inequality can then be developed or improved and targeted to those who need it, when they need it, resulting in a more efficient and effective service that patients and parents are satisfied with. By paying more attention to our most vulnerable patients we can get it right for all children. Overall Aims a) To identify the cross-organisational, organisational and individual factors in NHS hospitals that facilitate children and young people with learning disability and their families receiving equal access to high quality care and services. b) To identify the cross-organisational, organisational and individual factors in NHS hospitals that prevent children and young people with learning disability and their families receiving equal access to high quality care and services. c) To develop guidance for NHS trusts about the implementation for successful and effective measures to promote equal access for children and young people with learning disability and their families. Design A transformative, mixed methods case study design over 4 phases, prioritising the voices of children and young people and their parents. Each case will be represented by NHS specialist children's hospitals and non-specialist hospitals in England. PHASE 1 Aim: To describe the organisational context for healthcare delivery to children and young people with learning disability and their families Setting: 18 hospitals in England Methods: a) Interviews with senior managers b) Content analysis of hospital documents c) Staff questionnaire comparing how equipped they feel to deliver care effectively to children and young people with and without learning disability. PHASE 2 Aim: Case studies to compare the care and experiences of children and young people with and without learning disability and their parents. Setting: 4 hospitals in England (from Phase 1) Methods: CHILDREN AND YOUNG PEOPLE: a) Individually tailored interviews using creative and digital techniques, b) Hospital tour PARENTS: a) Hospital blog allowing for real time data collection without parents being separated from their child b) Recording of parental safety concerns c) Home interviews. STAFF: a) Semi-structured interviews HOSPITAL ACCESS: a) Retrospective mapping of hospital activity b) Community professionals questionnaire PHASE 3 Aim: To compare a) Children and young peoples’ and b) Parents’ satisfaction with hospital care Setting: 4 hospitals in England (as per Phase 2) Methods: Satisfaction Questionnaire given to a) Children and young people with and without learning disability and their parents on discharge from hospital PHASE 4 Aim: To synthesise and disseminate study findings and develop content of a training DVD Setting: 4 hospitals in England (as per Phase 2) Methods: A workshop involving study participants and experts in the field of learning disability. Data analysis A model for mixed methods data analysis will be used within each phase using appropriate methods before merging and connecting them through a period of data synthesis. Qualitative data will be managed and analysed using the Framework approach in conjunction with NVivo and quantitative data will be analysed using parametric and non-parametric descriptive statistics. Dissemination We will disseminate widely to all relevant stakeholders, including using social media. A report will be sent to all participants in a variety of accessible formats, taking into account the needs of those with learning disability. An on-line report will also be made available for lay audiences, including those with learning disability. End of study workshops for participants and known experts will provide a forum for deciding the content of a training DVD/package to guide students and staff about the barriers and facilitators to the delivery of high quality care for children and young people with learning disability and their families. We will disseminate widely to a range of hospital staff through published abstracts/papers and through national and international conference where we will look for opportunities to reach a range of professional groups. Working in partnership with the Foundation for People with Learning Disabilities, the British Institute of Learning Disabilities, Contact a Family and NHS England will strengthen our dissemination strategy, ensuring the findings are shared in a variety of accessible formats and reach a wide range of parents, professionals and children and young people with and without learning disability, helping drive support for change.

Contractor: The Newcastle Upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Pre-Operative Behavioural Intervention to Reduce Drinking before elective orthopaedic Surgery (Pre-Op BIRDS)
Abstract: "Our study has two linked phases: 1. Feasibility work will: assess acceptability of screening and brief intervention aimed at reducing alcohol consumption to patients listed for elective primary hip or knee arthroplasty and to nurses; characterise usual care; and define and manualise a screening and brief alcohol intervention protocol. Adult patients due to have elective primary hip or knee arthroplasty, will be consented to being interviewed by a researcher. Structured by a topic guide, in-depth interviews will explore views on materials and procedures. Sampling will be purposive, seeking to achieve maximum variation in terms of patients’ age, gender, drinking status and socio-economic status (via postcodes); and nurses’ clinical experience. Sample size will be determined by data saturation (ongoing analysis indicating no new themes). We envisage 8-10 patients/4 nurse interviews lasting up to 60 minutes each. Interviews will be audio-recorded and fully transcribed (verbatim) and NVivo software will aid indexing and charting. Thematic analysis will be structured by the Framework approach (recommended for qualitative work linked to quantitative studies) and Normalization Process Theory will help us consider factors affecting intervention delivery. The intervention will be optimised and manualised and training materials developed and behaviour change techniques described to increase replicability. 2: An external pilot RCT will involve a two-arm, three-centre trial of screening and brief alcohol intervention in risky drinkers who are scheduled for joint arthroplasty. Forty patients will be recruited and randomised into each condition with the intention of achieving 30 per arm at 6 month post-intervention. Eligible patients will be =>18 years, listed for elective primary hip/knee arthroplasty and able to give informed consent. Exclusion criteria will be: patients needing sequential bilateral joint replacement; patients displaying current (active) withdrawal from alcohol; patients with severe psychiatric disorder requiring medical therapy and severe cognitive impairment/dementia impacting on ability to interact with intervention and increasing likelihood of postoperative delirium. Screening will occur at the initial orthopaedic assessment by a nurse who will not be involved in subsequent patient interventions. Alcohol consumption will be screened by using the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT). Risky drinking will be defined as scoring =>8 on AUDIT (score range 0-40) plus weekly or daily drinking of 6 or more units in a session (judged by AUDIT item 3). An initial verbal expression of interest at this visit will be confirmed by phone/email contact up to one week after receiving study information. Full written consent will be obtained at the preoperative assessment clinic visit occurring some 6 weeks after the surgical outpatient visit. This will be followed by remote electronic randomisation that allocates either usual care (comparator group) or a brief alcohol intervention (which will include a single 30 minute 1:1 brief intervention based on a customised version of the ""How Much is too Much ?"" programme). In addition
Status: all intervention patients will be given the opportunity to undergo a second intervention at 1-2 weeks before surgery. Maximal follow-up will be 6 months post-assessment. Success criteria will be based on recruitment

Contractor: Avon and Wiltshire Mental Health NHS Partnership Trust
Award_Title: Guided self-help for depression in adults with autism spectrum disorders
Abstract: Background: High rates of common mental health problems, such as anxiety and depression, are reported in adults with Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) (Hofvander et al., 2009). Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT) is recommended in NICE guidelines as the first line of treatment for such problems in the general population. The development of Increasing Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) services have been at the forefront of implementing NICE guidance. It is not known how readily people with ASD access IAPT services or whether these services meet their needs. Good practice guidelines for IAPT services have been developed for people with learning disabilities (PWLD)(2009, NHS) and there have been efforts to implement and evaluate these practice guidelines via pilot studies. On the basis of research to date, it is likely that people with ASD will also require some adaptation of treatments available in IAPT services. There is for example, evidence from several controlled trials that CBT approaches can be effective in ameliorating anxiety problems in young people with ASD (Lang et al., 2010) and adults with ASD and co-morbid OCD (Russell et al., 2013) if adapted for their needs. To our knowledge there has been just 1 study to date investigating group CBT for young people with ASD and depression (Gilleveray and Evert 2014) and no studies investigating the effectiveness of individual CBT for depression in adults with ASD. Treatment as usual (TAU) for mild-moderate depression is ordinarily 'low intensity CBT' (i.e. psycho-education or guided self-help) in a group or individual format. It is thus not known if guided self-help for depression adapted for ASD is acceptable, feasible and effective as a treatment for depression in this group. Aims: To conduct a feasibility study for a large-scale Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of individual guided self-help for depression adapted for adults with ASD. Methods: (1) The intervention i.e. low intensity CBT for mild-moderate depression in adults with ASD will be developed by adapting existing self-help material in line with this group's needs. The principles of intervention will be Psycho-education and Behavioural Activation and will be delivered via 8 individual sessions (2) A feasibility study will be conducted. Adults with ASD and mild-moderate depression (n=70) will be randomised to ASD adapted guided self-help (GSH)or Treatment as Usual (TAU) across 2 NHS sites over 18 months. In addition, qualitative interviews will be conducted to investigate patients, practitioners' and parent/carers' views, experiences and acceptability of the intervention. The feasibility study will also provide estimates about likely recruitment and retention rates, choice of primary outcome measure and method of data collection for a parallel economic evaluation for a larger scale trial. Outcomes: Study outcomes will be ASD specific self-help material, therapist training materials, clarity about outcome measurement of depression symptoms and information about treatment acceptability and feasibility of treatment evaluation across more than one NHS site.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: ERA – Electronic Records in Ambulances to support the shift to out of hospital care: challenges, opportunities and workforce implications
Abstract: Ambulance services have a vital role in the shift towards the delivery of health care out of hospitals, when this is better for patients, by offering alternatives to transfer to the emergency department (ED). For this to happen safely and effectively, ambulance clinicians must be able to decide which patients will benefit from being treated at scene or left at home, and ensure that patient information, including details of 999 assessment and care, is passed to community based care providers. The introduction of information technology (IT) in ambulance services, to electronically capture and store patient data, can support out of hospital care, and has been encouraged by national policy across the UK, but roll-out has proved complex, with major workforce implications. There is considerable variation across services in terms of implementation and the degree to which electronic records are integrated with other IT. We aim to examine how electronic records in ambulance services can support community-based care in a number of ways: by acting as a base to which other electronic resources (e.g. decision support software, referral tools or ‘apps’) are attached; by facilitating transfer of patient information to or from other providers; by allowing services to identify and manage repeat service users; and by making data readily available for research and evaluation. We aim to investigate and describe the opportunities and challenges of implementing electronic records and associated technology in ambulances to support a safe and effective shift to out of hospital care, including the implications for workforce in terms of training, role and clinical decision making skills. Lessons learned from the experience of implementing electronic records so far should inform future development of IT in ambulance services, and help service providers to understand how best to maximise the opportunities offered by electronic records to redesign care. Our study will include a baseline assessment of progress in all UK ambulance services in implementing electronic records and other technologies to support care delivery and decision-making. We will review and build on what is already known about implementation of technology in health care to inform four in-depth case studies of services at different stages of implementation. Across the case studies, we will assess current usage, and examine the role of context and time in shaping implementation and service change. We will take a whole systems approach, looking at the recursive relationship between technology and the ambulance workforce. Our working methods are participatory, built on a close relationship between the research team, ambulance services and other stakeholders, and using research paramedics as field researchers. In the final phase of our research, we will work with all UK ambulance services and other stakeholders to assess the potential for further development of electronic records, electronic decision support and referral tools to maximise their potential to support the shift of care from hospital to community based services. We will develop and build on existing theory about the implementation of IT in health care, developing the research base in the field of pre-hospital care and across care settings, and examining how implementation of electronic records takes place in relation to the implementation of other IT developments to support alternative care pathways.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: What is the effectiveness of varenicline compared with nicotine replacement therapy for long term smoking cessation and clinically important outcomes such as mortality, myocardial infarction and frequency of service use? Evidence from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink
Abstract: Rationale: Although varenicline has been shown to be effective for smoking cessation in randomised controlled trials, there have been few studies of its longer term (>1 year) effectiveness in real world settings or its effects on important clinical outcomes. In this project we will investigate the effects of varenicline compared to nicotine replacement therapies on long-term smoking cessation, and clinically-important outcomes such as rate of attendance to primary and secondary care, all-cause and cause-specific mortality, diagnosis of respiratory illness, myocardial infarction or depression and anxiety using a cohort of patients prescribed these medications from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD). In a related Methodological Bolt-on funded by the Medical Research Council we will provide further validation of the instrumental variable methods we will use during the study: physicians’ prescribing preferences. This methodological bolt-on is broadly applicable to studies of the effects of pharmacotherapies using routine electronic medical records. Objective: To compare the effectiveness of varenicline with nicotine replacement products for long term smoking cessation and the impact of these treatments on health outcomes. Design: Observational cohort study using the CPRD, Cox-regression, propensity score matching and instrumental variable analysis using physicians’ prescribing preferences. Setting: Representative clinical population in the United Kingdom. Participants: Approximately 180,000 individuals from the CPRD who have been prescribed varenicline or nicotine replacement products since 2006. Intervention: Prescriptions of varenicline or nicotine replacement products. Outcomes: Smoking cessation up to nine years post prescription derived from smoking indicators in the CPRD. Health outcomes including: frequency of attendance of primary care, frequency of hospitalisation, all-cause and cause-specific mortality, diagnosis of respiratory illness including Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), diagnosis of myocardial infarction or diagnosis of depression or anxiety.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: How can interventions integrating health and academic education in schools help prevent substance misuse and violence, and reduce health inequalities among young people? Systematic review and evidence synthesis
Abstract: Background Curriculum-based interventions in schools addressing knowledge, skills and peer norms can be effective in reducing alcohol consumption, smoking and drug use (substance use) and violence.[1-5] But delivery of these is limited in English schools by the marginalisation of personal, social and health education (PSHE).[6-10] Schools are beginning to address substance use and violence in mainstream subject lessons but interventions are not evidence-based.[11] The UK can learn from international evidence of effective interventions. No reviews have focused on such interventions, a key gap given these require distinctive approaches from provision in PSHE and may be more effective. We will review theories of change, and process and outcome evaluations to answer the following: RQ1. What types of curriculum interventions delivered within mainstream lessons in schools addressing substance use and violence have been evaluated? RQ2. What theories of change inform these interventions and what do these suggest about potential mechanisms and effects? RQ3. What characteristics of interventions, deliverers, participants and school contexts facilitate or limit successful implementation and receipt of such interventions, and what are the implications of these characteristics for delivery in the UK? RQ4. How effective are such interventions in reducing alcohol consumption, smoking, drug use and violence, and increasing attainment, when compared to usual treatment, no treatment, or other interventions, and does this vary according to students’ socio-demographic characteristics? RQ5. What characteristics of interventions, deliverers, school contexts and students appear to moderate/are necessary and sufficient for the effectiveness of such interventions? Methods We propose a systematic review of theories of change, process and outcome evaluations of school-based curriculum interventions delivered within mainstream lessons (not PSHE) among students age 4-18 years addressing substance use or violence. Included theories of change and process evaluations must be integral/linked to trials. Included studies must address our research questions. Outcome evaluations must be randomised trials. We will search via databases and other methods. References will be screened first on title/abstract and then on full report. Two reviewers will extract data and assess the quality of included studies using existing tools. Syntheses of intervention descriptions, theories of change and process evaluations will employ thematic synthesis to develop: a taxonomy of interventions; potential mechanisms of action; potential barriers and facilitators of implementation and receipt; and an assessment of applicability to the UK. We will narratively synthesise evidence of effectiveness and conduct meta-analyses where possible. We will also analyse the effectiveness of the subset of interventions identified by stakeholders as relevant to the UK. We will use an ‘equity lens’ to examine subgroup effects to assess impacts on health inequalities.[12] We will use meta-regression[13, 14] and/or qualitative comparative analysis[15, 16] to investigate what factors moderate or explain intervention effects.

Award_Title: A two arm feasibility trial of lifestyle information and Slimming World groups to promote weight management and positive lifestyle behaviour in postnatal women from an ethnically diverse inner city population
Abstract: Research question: Is it feasible to conduct a definitive randomised controlled trial (RCT) of lifestyle information and access to Slimming World groups designed to achieve and maintain healthy weight and positive lifestyle behaviour in postnatal women most at risk of weight retention in an inner city population? Study design: Two arm feasibility RCT to inform need, design, processes and outcomes for a definitive RCT. Participants: 190 women aged >18, with a single pregnancy, who can understand English and have not accessed weight management programmes in their current pregnancy. Obese (Body Mass Index (BMI) >30 kg/m²) or overweight(BMI 25–29.9 kg/m² women at antenatal booking and women with normal booking BMI but excessive gestational weight gain (GWG) as defined by the Institute of Medicine will be recruited and randomised at 36 weeks gestation to intervention or standard care only. Intervention: Standard care and positive lifestyle information and postnatal access to Slimming World groups underpinned by relevant evidence. Benefit of group based weight management programmes has been shown in general population studies but has not been previously considered for weight management in postnatal women. How to influence positive lifestyle behaviours has also not been considered in this population. Women will receive a positive lifestyle leaflet at recruitment, the content reflecting current public health guidance on breastfeeding, diet, smoking cessation, alcohol advice and sleep guidance. From 8 weeks postnatally, women can access Slimming World groups for 12 consecutive weeks, with option to commence a group up to 16 weeks after giving birth. Slimming World will waive group membership fees, to promote equity of access in a diverse inner city population. Control women will receive standard care only. Quantitative outcomes to support a definitive RCT powered to detect significant changes in variables related to postnatal weight management will include: proportion eligible who consent/refuse; time to recruit, proportion ineligible; reasons for refusing; contamination rate; retention/adherence; loss to follow up; missing data; potential adverse events. This study will not be powered to detect significant effects of the intervention on change in body weight. Our primary assessment, likely to be used in a definitive trial, is difference between trial arms in weight 12 months postnatally, expressed as percentage change from weight recorded at the woman's first antenatal appointment. Analysis will be by intention to treat (ITT). Pre-planned subgroup analysis will look at primary outcome in different pre-pregnancy BMI categories. Secondary assessments will include: percentages of women meeting weight reduction of 5% and 10%; breastfeeding uptake/duration; smoking status; alcohol use; diet and nutrition; physical activity; mental & physical health; body image; self-esteem; health-related quality of life; and resource impacts. Process evaluation will assess acceptability of study procedures and experience of the intervention by asking women in follow-up questionnaires and semi-structured telephone interventions with a purposive sample of control and intervention group women (n=15-20) and purposive sample of women on completing Slimming World groups (n=10). Variation in characteristics of Slimming World groups attended will be collated and triangulated with data from women to aid interpretation of findings.

Award_Title: A multi-centred Trial of physical Activity assisted Reduction of Smoking (TARS)
Abstract: Study design: A 4 site, parallel, two group RCT, with internal pilot, to compare (i) tailored support to reduce smoking and increase physical activity as an aid to smoking reduction (and possible cessation) with (ii) brief advice to reduce or quit smoking. Setting: Recruitment in primary care including searching electronic health records and mailed invitation. Reviewing literature: A pilot RCT tested the feasibility and acceptability of trial methods and the intervention, and found preliminary evidence for effectiveness. We updated a systematic review on exercise and smoking cessation; no other studies relevant to this bid were identified. The findings from a larger trial could contribute to updates of NICE guidelines for smoking harm reduction. Target group: Adult smokers wishing to reduce smoking but with no immediate plans to quit. Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria: Smokers registered with a GP, aged 18 yrs or over, smoking 10 or more cigarettes per day, able to engage in moderate intensity physical activity. Health technologies being assessed: Access to pharmacological and behavioural support to gradually reduce smoking, and increase physical activity as a reduction aid, delivered in up to 8 client-centred individual motivational support sessions, via phone or in person, for up to 8 weeks. Smokers will also be directed to Stop Smoking Services for support if they wish to quit. Measurement of costs and outcomes: Primary outcome: Carbon monoxide (CO) verified prolonged abstinence at 8 months post baseline. Secondary outcomes: CO verified abstinence at 3 and 15 months post baseline (only contacting those abstinent at 8 months). Surveys mailed at 3 and 8 months to assess cigarettes smoked (and reduction), health related quality of life, physical activity, mental health, cravings, weight, smoking related costs, health service utilisation and costs. Physical activity (accelerometer) assessed at 3 mths in random sample. Those self-reporting abstinence at 3, 8 and 15 mths will have face to face assessment of CO expired air. Embedded mixed methods process evaluation to assess intervention fidelity, behaviour change processes and moderators and mediators of any effects. Sample size: Various assumptions are made about the expected control and intervention abstinence rates, drawing on relevant literature. A sample size of 450 per group would give 90% power to detect an increase in CO confirmed abstinence rate from 5% to 11% (alpha=0.05, 2-sided test) at 8 months post baseline. The main analyses of abstinence rates will be conducted on an intention-to-treat basis, with participants lost to follow up regarded as still smoking. Difference between current and planned care pathways: Usual care will be guided by NICE. Health trainers typically advise smokers to stop or refer smokers to NHS Stop Smoking Services: In the proposed intervention they will support smoking reduction integrated with physical activity promotion. Project timetable: Set up phase (month 1-8), recruitment (month 9-20), final 15 month data collection (mth 35), data cleaning and analysis (month 36-43); final report (month 44). In mth 12 we will assess progression rules (for recruitment and intervention engagement) from internal pilot to full trial. If data analysis (months 29-30) shows no intervention effect then the trial will be stopped with no follow-up at 15 mths, and final report submitted in month 39. We aim to recruit 20 participants per month at each of 4 sites.

Award_Title: A randomised controlled trial to determine the effectiveness of bridging from emergency to regular contraception: The 'Bridge-it' study
Abstract: This trial aims to test whether a pharmacy-based intervention designed to facilitate uptake of effective contraception after emergency contraception (EC); progestogen only pill(POP) plus expedited access to a Sexual and Reproductive Health (SRH) service increases use of effective contraception and reduces unintended pregnancy compared with standard care. Design: A cluster randomised crossover trial Setting: Community pharmacies in 3 cities Strategy for reviewing literature: We did a literature search of published work (Pubmed since 2008 and NIHR library) and contacted UK, European and US organisations/services and the International and European Emergency Contraception Consortia networks. Only 2 papers described interventions designed to increase contraception after EC; one of these was our own published pilot study(1) (of bridging supply of POP with EC). The other study from Jamaica (voucher that offered reduced price of combined contraceptive pill) was not effective. Target population: Women aged 16 and over presenting to a pharmacy for levonorgestrel(LNG)EC. Inclusion/Exclusion Criteria: Women unwilling to participate or unable to give informed consent, contraindications to POP, already using effective contraception, unavailable for follow-up. Health technologies being assessed: Intervention: Three month supply of POP (75 mcg desogestrel) started the day after EC,with expedited access to a local SRH service (drop-in) for advice and immediate provision of contraception particularly long acting reversible contraception (LARC) Standard care: usually comprises verbal advice to visit a doctor, with/without written information but will be characterised by a mystery shopper study undertaken in participating pharmacies before the trial starts. Measurement of costs and outcomes: Important outcomes: (i)Contraceptive method use determined by telephone contact at 4 months (when POP supply will have run out),(ii)abortion rates at 12 months using record linkage from participants to national registries. Secondary outcomes: (i)adverse events following EC and EC/POP (ii) Contraceptive method use determined by telephone contact at 12 months (iii)unintended pregnancies at 12 months (intendedness measured using London Measure of Unintended Pregnancy-self reported)(iv) assessment of the intervention implementation, fidelity and reach (to understand why the intervention works (or doesn't) and to inform future roll out/ implementation) (v) Cost effectiveness. Sample size: 2080 women from 26 pharmacies Project timetable: 30 months Expertise in team: SRH clinicians/researchers, methodologist/statistician, pharmacists (with public health and commissioning expertise), qualitative researcher, health economist, clinical trials unit, service users. Specifically,we conducted the successful pilot study of bridging contraception after EC. We therefore have undertaken much of the development work and bring this experience to the proposed large RCT. The proposed study will also include many of the community pharmacies who participated in the original trial. The health economist (JT) is a global expert on cost effectiveness of contraception and EC.

Award_Title: Accounting for multimorbidity, competing risk and direct treatment disutility in risk prediction tools and model-based cost-effectiveness analysis for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease and osteoporotic fracture
Abstract: Background: Medicines for the primary prevention of disease are taken long-term or for life. Decisions to start such medicines are therefore very important to patients and the NHS. Clinical guidelines increasingly make risk-stratified recommendations, where treatment recommendations vary by baseline risk of the outcome to be prevented (for example, cardiovascular disease (CVD) or osteoporotic fracture). Guideline recommended treatment thresholds are usually informed by model-based cost-effectiveness analysis (CEA), and implementing risk-stratified recommendations requires clinicians to use risk prediction models. These models are therefore increasingly central to both guideline development and clinical decision making. However, existing models are potentially problematic in older people and those with life-limiting multimorbidity. Risk prediction models do not account for competing risks of death from other causes. This means that they are likely to overpredict CVD or fracture risk in people with multimorbidity, who will often die of other causes. Existing cost-effectiveness models do account for average competing risk but average population cost-effectiveness may not apply to people with multimorbidity in whom competing mortality risks are much higher, and additionally the relatively small lifetime QALY gains from primary prevention may be offset by unaccounted for disutility relating to treatment burden. Overall aim: To improve the evidence generated from risk prediction models and model-based CEA to inform decision-making when selecting primary prevention treatments for CVD and osteoporotic fracture in people with multimorbidity. Methods: The study has three elements. (i) Derivation of new models for predicting the risk of incident CVD and fracture using Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) data to model both the targeted outcomes (incident CVD and fracture) and unrelated death (the competing risk), with internal cross-validation in CPRD to examine discrimination and calibration. We will compare the new model with the most widely used existing CVD and fracture risk prediction models (QRisk2 and QFracture) neither of which accounts for competing risks. ii) Elicitation of Direct Treatment Disutilities (DTD) for the general population and for people treated with statins or bisphosphonates, using time-trade off and best-worst scaling, with design informed using systematic literature reviews and semi-structured interviews with 15 patients and clinicians. (iii) Adaptation of the model-based CEA for lipid modification and bisphosphates used by NICE to quantify the impact of accounting for competing risks and/or DTD on relative cost-effectiveness and effectiveness measured by lifetime QALY gain. Expected outputs and impact: Better risk prediction in people with multimorbidity by accounting for competing risks will improve the targeting of preventive medicines to those who are most likely to benefit, and reduce low benefit and potential harmful medicines use. Accounting for variation in effectiveness and cost-effectiveness by appropriate subgroup analysis in model-based CEA to account for competing risks and DTD will ensure that guideline recommendations for preventive medicines are more appropriately nuanced to the important population of people with multimorbidity. We will ensure that the findings are appropriately disseminated to the full range of interested clinical, guideline developer, public and academic audiences.

Award_Title: "Does ""Mellow Babies"" improve the psychosocial health of mothers and their children? The Mellow Babies Trial"
Abstract: We aim to assess the effectiveness of the Mellow Babies (MB) programme in promoting maternal mental health and in improving social and emotional wellbeing among children under 18 months. Setting: Highland region of Scotland, including a range of urban, rural, affluent and deprived communities. Participants will be referred by health visitors, social workers, paediatricians and GPs. Mothers scoring above threshold on the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) when their child is 6 - 18 months old will be invited to participate. We aim to recruit 212 families to ensure evaluable data on 170. If less than 40 participants recruited by month 8, the study will be stopped (stop/go point). Design: randomised controlled trial. MB will be offered to participants in the active arm of the trial, and usual care to both arms. Families will be seen by a research nurse at recruitment and by a research assistant blind to group allocation at 8 months post-randomisation and when children are 30 months old. Intervention: MB addresses maternal wellbeing and parent-infant interaction. It consists of 14 weekly five-hour group sessions plus one reunion: transport, refreshments, and crèche facilities are provided. MB will be delivered by early years workers in community settings. The intervention will be built upon existing services and expertise. Apart from any referrals made by GPs and paediatricians and collection of service use data, NHS staff and premises are not involved. Primary outcome: Maternal HADS total score at 8m post-randomisation and when the child is 30m old. Secondary outcomes at age 30m: children’s social and emotional functioning (Total Difficulties scale of the parent-reported Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ)); SDQ subscale scores; expressive language in the 50-word Sure Start Language Measure (SSLM); Bayley III Scales of Infant and Toddler Development including Behavior Observation Inventory, counts of positive and negative parenting behaviours in mealtime videos, within-trial cost analysis of participants’ service use and out of pocket expenses, cost-consequence analysis. Secondary outcomes at 8m post randomisation: SSLM, BITSEA, and description of participants’ service use and out of pocket expenses. Longer term outcomes will be addressed through use of administrative data and economic modelling. Process evaluation: Quantitative and qualitative research will examine how the intervention is implemented and explore the mechanisms by which it might achieve impact, for whom it seems to work best and contextual factors affecting impact. Timetable: October 2018 to end November 2022 (50 months). Milestones: prefunding: protocol development; research ethics, management approvals; M1-3: study initiation, set up office, assemble team, intervention training. M4-23: recruit 212 participants (11 per month (M8 stop/go point); M16-47 complete follow up to 30 months old; M47-50 close down, analysis and report writing. Expertise: The team has extensive experience of parenting intervention research and of conducting trials with people who may be hard to recruit and retain. We have a strong track record in translating research into policy, conducting robust qualitative evaluations, and long term modelling of outcomes. The trial will be supported by a fully registered UK CRC CTU, with internationally recognised expertise in complex intervention trials.

Award_Title: Qualitative video-stimulated recall study to explore cardiovascular disease risk communication in NHS Health checks using QRISK2 10-year risk and JBS3 lifetime risk calculators
Abstract: DESIGN Qualitative study using Video Stimulated Recall (VSR) for in-depth analysis of risk communication in NHS Health Checks SETTING General practice (West Mids) TARGET POPULATION Patients - adults (40-74 yr), eligible for NHS Health Check Clinicians - staff delivering NHS Health Checks (e.g., practice nurse) INCLUSION CRITERIA Practices - run NHS Health Checks using QRISK2 in the consultation; already or willing to deliver Health Checks in specific clinics to facilitate data collection Patients - NHS Health Check criteria (1) HEALTH TECHNOLOGY QRISK2 and JBS3 risk calculators SAMPLE SIZE • 12 practices sampled for diversity in terms of area socio-demographics, size and ethnic profile of the practice population, to ensure generalisability through studying a range of practices. Assigned randomly to QRISK2 or JBS3 • 240 consultations video-recorded to obtain 144 (72 per group) for qualitative analysis (all 240 for quantitative analysis) • 48 patient VSR interviews, 24 per group (sampled across CVD risk groups) • 18-24 clinician VSR interviews (1-2 per practice) Comparable size to studies of recorded consultations (2) and VSR (3); will provide range of patients; allows for dropout (~50%) and exclusions where CVD risk is not discussed CVD risk (4). PATHWAYS Current: Usual NHS Health Check pathway Study: Current pathway with half of practices using JBS3 following brief training OUTCOMES Detailed insight into: 1. How CVD risk is discussed 2. Patient/clinician perceptions and understanding of CVD risk 3. Advice/treatment discussed in consultations, and patient intentions 4. 1-3 when using QRISK2 or JBS3 5. Underlying mechanisms. PILOT STUDY VSR processes will be developed and tested (e.g., camera position, interview questions/prompts) through PPI. ANALYSIS Video-recorded consultations and audio-recorded VSR interviews will be analysed using thematic analysis (TA (5)) using constant comparison: • deductive for analysis of Health check consultations • inductive for analysis of VSR interviews (codes/themes generated from data). All Health Check consultations will also be quantitatively analysed (e.g., number of CVD risk mentions; time discussing risk) Most analysis will be between groups (to compare QRISK2 and JBS3). Case study analysis will be used in a subsample, where a case is a matched consultation, patient interview, and clinician interview (and quantitative data), to further explore mechanisms by which intentions for health-protective behaviour are elicited. EXPERTISE • Associate Professor, PI of qualitative/quantitative Health Check research and ongoing RCT (CG) • Senior qualitative researchers in primary care health promotion (DC, NE) • GPs with clinical and behavioural expertise (RC, EC) • Health psychology and qualitative research methods (SG) • Statistical expertise (DCC) • Expert advisors in VSR (ZP) and national/policy implications (MK). A Project Advisory Board (or Steering Group) will be chaired by a senior academic with relevant expertise, with academic, clinical and lay members. Award_Title: “The JACK Trial” A multi-site cluster randomised trial of an interactive film-based intervention to reduce teenage pregnancy and promote positive sexual health
Abstract: The need for gender-sensitive interventions, and especially the need to include teenage boys to reduce rates of teenage pregnancy has been highlighted as a global health need by the World Health Organisation [51, 52] and recommended in systematic reviews [18,48,53,77]. The proposed study will provide a robust evaluation of the effectiveness of a gender-sensitive intervention especially targeting boys. This study follows a NIHR-funded feasibility trial which satisfied all criteria to progress to a full effectiveness trial. The Intervention: ‘If I were Jack’ is an evidence-based, theory informed, user endorsed intervention which has been collaboratively developed in the UK between a team of researchers, statutory stakeholders, Relationships and Sexuality Education (RSE) experts, pupils and teachers over the past six years. It is a teacher facilitated 4-week RSE Programme, designed to be delivered to pupils aged 14-15 years. Building implementation capacity has been key to its success to-date and, if found to be effective, can be rolled out in schools across the UK through statutory and non-statutory providers. Aim: To determine the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of the 'If I were Jack' intervention in reducing rates of unprotected sex among teenagers under 16 years of age and to better understand the contextual influences on intervention effectiveness through a process evaluation. Design and Methods: Stage one involves intervention refinement deemed necessary as an outcome of 1) Feasibility trial which occurred in Northern Ireland (NI), and 2) Transferability study to test intervention acceptability in the other countries of the UK. Primary refinements are the production of an ‘English version’ of the interactive video drama using English actors to enhance cultural identification in England/Wales, an updated NI/Scotland version, and minor adjustments to classroom materials. These refinements will be assessed against progression (stop/go) criteria before progressing to Stage two. Stage two involves a cluster RCT in post-primary schools across the UK with embedded process and health economic evaluations. Schools are the unit of randomisation. The primary outcome measure is avoidance of unprotected sex, which is a well-established primary proximate behavioural determinant of teenage pregnancy and represents a commonly measured behavioural outcome in studies examining the impact of RSE on teenage pregnancy [15,17]. We aim to detect a 50% reduction in the incidence of unprotected sex by 15 years of age (from expected rate of 2.8% to 1.4%). To have 80% power to detect a between-group difference of 1.4% at the 12-14 month follow-up, at a 2-sided 5% significance level, assuming an ICC of 0.01 and allowing for attrition, will require 66 schools (33 per arm). Participants across the countries will be pupils with a mean age 14 years at baseline with follow-up data collection 12-14 month post intervention, prior to potentially leaving school. Secondary outcomes measures are impacts on knowledge, attitudes, skills and intentions to avoid teenage pregnancy, as well as on additional behavioural outcomes of engagement in sexual intercourse, contraception use, and sexually transmitted infections. Analysis will be on intention to treat basis. Expected outcomes: A robust evaluation of a gender-sensitive intervention to reduce teenage pregnancy that, if found to be effective, could be rolled out across the UK.

Award_Title: Feasibility and acceptability of a brief routine weight management intervention for postnatal women embedded within the national child immunisation programme in primary care: randomised controlled trial and nested qualitative study
Abstract: Studies have reported that among women who have a healthy BMI prior to pregnancy 30% are overweight one year after giving birth. Of women who are overweight prior to conception, 44% are obese 1 year after giving birth, while 97% of women who are obese prior to pregnancy remain so at 1 year postnatally. On average women gain about 14-15kg during pregnancy and at 1 year after birth 5-9kg is retained. Postnatal weight retention can significantly increase the risk of later obesity and is associated with chronic diseases indicating the need to develop interventions to help women lose weight after giving birth. Reviews show that most trials in this population include small samples and/or evaluate intensive weight loss interventions. These types of interventions cannot be offered to all of the 820,000 women who give birth every year, 520,500 of whom are overweight/obese. Instead, we propose test a simple intervention for maternal weight management into the national child immunisation programme so, if it is feasible, and eventually effective, it can be rolled out to every woman giving birth at little extra cost to the NHS and no cost to women, thereby reaching even the most disadvantaged communities. We will assess the feasibility of an intervention focused on promoting self-monitoring of postnatal weight and signposting to a online weight management programme by practice nurses as part of the child immunisation programme. In this feasibility cluster RCT 80 women will be recruited from 10 practices (clusters) to test recruitment, acceptability and trial procedures. Every 2 weeks Birmingham Women’s Hospital will complete searches of women who are at least 4 weeks post birth registered at participating practices and send a study invitation to them. Interested women will be visited to collect baseline data. Women must be aged 18 years or more, given birth at least 4 weeks previously and not yet attended the first immunisation, with a BMI 25 kg/m2 or more at baseline. In the 1st year babies are immunised at 2, 3, 4 and 12 months of age; we plan to embed the intervention within these pre-existing contacts. This study will run over the first 3 immunisation appointments (2, 3, & 4 months). The intervention occurs when women attend their practice to have their child immunised and involves a brief intervention to encourage regular weighing to promote self-management of weight and a recommendation to enrol in a proven effective online weight management programme (POWeR). Women will be asked to weigh themselves weekly and record this on a record card attached to the child health ‘red book’ or on the online programme. Women will be advised to aim for 0.5-1kg weight loss p/w until achieving their pre-pregnant weight and within the healthy range. At each child immunisation visit the nurse will weigh them to assess progress against this goal. We know that someone who is regularly weighed is more likely to stay focussed on their weight loss. Nurses will not provide any lifestyle counselling; their role is simply to provide regular external accountability and to signpost women to the online weight loss programme, for weight loss support. The comparator group will receive a healthy lifestyle leaflet. Follow up will be at 3 months post baseline. Women and nurses will be interviewed to ascertain their views of the intervention. The primary outcome will be the feasibility of a subsequent phase III trial based on pre-specified progression criteria.

Award_Title: Investigating SOcial Competence and Isolation in children with Autism taking part in LEGO-based therapy clubs In School Environments (I-SOCIALISE)
Abstract: Background: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are especially vulnerable to isolation as they struggle to establish and maintain friendships due to the social and communication impairments characteristic of the disorder. The most common intervention for this is social skills training but studies indicate that while these children may learn to demonstrate appropriate social skills within the setting of the intervention, applying these new skills to their everyday life is often unsuccessful. LEGO-based therapy is a social development program for children and was developed as a means of addressing the limitations of more generic social skills groups through the use of an intrinsically motivating task. Objectives: The primary objective is to examine the clinical effectiveness of LEGO-based therapy groups on the social and emotional competence of children with ASD within the school setting. Secondary objectives are to examine the perceived social isolation, health effects, and cost-effectiveness of LEGO-based therapy on the participating child. Design: The proposed trial is a cluster randomised controlled trial comparing LEGO-based therapy groups and usual care with a control group receiving just usual care. There will be an internal pilot study which will run for 10 months to examine the feasibility of recruitment. At 10 months we expect to have recruited 120 participants, of which one third (n=40) will have reached the primary endpoint. Stop/Go criteria based on 75% of recruitment target and 70% of outcome measures will be used to assess feasibility of continuing the trial. There will be a nested qualitative, acceptability and fidelity components and an economic evaluation. Setting: The intervention will be delivered by an assigned school teaching assistant (TA) trained by a member of the research team within the participants’ schools. Participants: We will recruit 240 participants. Each participating child will have a diagnosis of ASD, will be aged between 7 and 15 years old, and attend a mainstream school. The child’s parent/guardian and associated teacher/TA will also participate to aid in outcome assessment. Interventions: Participating children allocated to the intervention group will be invited to attend a weekly LEGO-based therapy group for a period of 12 weeks and will also access their usual care. Participants allocated to the control group will continue to access their usual care and will not receive the intervention or any extra support services from the research team. Main outcome measures: The primary outcome measure will be the Social Skills Improvement System (SSIS) completed on behalf of the child by the participating teacher/TA. Secondary measures will include the Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support, the Asher Loneliness Scale, the EQ-5D proxy (5L version), the Child Health Utility 9D (CHU-9D) and bespoke resource use and acceptability questionnaires. Analysis: The statistical analysis will use a generalised linear mixed model framework to compare the mean outcome measure in cases and controls adjusted for baseline measurements and other key covariates (such as age and sex). Intention to treat analyses will be conducted on all outcome measures.

Award_Title: Interventions that improve maternity care and access for immigrant women in England: a narrative synthesis systematic review
Abstract: "INTRODUCTION Our systematic review uses a narrative synthesis (NS) approach to identify, appraise and synthesise reports on empirical research focused on access and interventions that improve maternity care for immigrant women. We will review qualitative, quantitative and mixed-methods research evidence. NS a) Facilitates understanding and acknowledges the broader influences of theoretical and contextual variables, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and geographical location; b) Enables understanding of the shaping of differences between reported outcomes as a result of differing study designs and childbearing populations c) Provides results that enable the development and implementation of maternity services and interventions. METHODS Popay et al's NS [1] is 'an approach to the systematic review and synthesis of findings from multiple studies that relies primarily on the use of words and text to summarise and explain the findings of the synthesis"". The emphasis is on an interpretive synthesis of the narrative findings of research rather than on a meta-analysis of the data. All review steps will involve two or more reviewers. NS allows us to embrace cross-disciplinary and methodologically pluralistic research to map access and interventions in maternity care. The major findings of this synthesis are then used to explain how and why maternity care interventions focused on immigrant women have been implemented and how these interventions address access and inequalities experienced by immigrant women.
