Award_Title: Action 3:30: A cluster randomised feasibility study evaluation of a teaching assistant led, extracurricular physical activity intervention for 8 to 10 year olds
Abstract: Design: Feasibility study. Schools randomised to Action 3:30 or usual provision. Participants: 360 Year 4/5 pupils from 12 primary schools. Recruitment: Prior to recruitment we will collect self-reported physical activity data in 8 schools and accelerometer plus self-reported activity in 4 schools. Then, in 6 schools we will employ recruitment method A. In the other 6 schools we will run recruitment method B which will have taster sessions during PE classess as an additional component. To enhance external validity, a second enrolment for intervention children will be offered. Intervention: Intervention schools will receive the Action 3:30 intervention. Action 3:30 is a 5-day programme that trains Teaching Assistants (TAs) in how to deliver physical activity sessions. TAs then deliver 30, 1-hour sessions after-school. Outcomes: Measures will be assessed prior to randomisation (T0) and during the last 6 sessions (T1). Main outcomes will be acceptability of the recruitment and study design and feasibility of increasing boys and girls Weekday MVPA. The primary outcome in a future trial would be weekday MVPA at T1. Economic evaluation: The KIDSCREEN-10 and CHU9D will be piloted as a health-related quality of life outcomes. Intervention-related resource use will be collected and a survey will be completed in all schools to assess after-school club costs. Process evaluation: We will conduct a process evaluation to provide insight into the extent to which the intervention was delivered as planned and facilitate a RE-AIM evaluation of potential population impact. TAs will record session attendance and adherence. Research staff will observe 3 sessions per school to assess fidelity. We will conduct 12 child focus groups in intervention schools, interview all TAs (n = 12) and key contacts (n = 12). We will examine factors that might have affected recruitment, delivery, attendance, enjoyment, anything that could be improved, potential contamination and any inequalities that might affect future delivery and any logistical issues with the opt-out consent process. Analysis: Eligibility, recruitment and follow-up figures will be presented as a CONSORT chart. Participant characteristics (BMI and activity) will be descriptively compared for participants recruited via the two different approaches and children recruited from the second enrolment. Change in mean activity over the intervention period, and the whole follow-up period will be presented with 95% CIs for the intervention and control schools separately, and further divided to present the findings for girls and boys separately within the two study arms. We will conduct a secondary analysis in which we will pilot the use of a complier average casual effect (CACE) analysis in which the data from all potential students in the 4 schools is used to model the effect of receiving Action 3:30 on MVPA. Mean changes and variation in KIDSCREEN and CHU9D health related quality of life scores will be estimated at the school level. Cost data will be analysed to estimate variation in the cost of implementation at the school level in a definitive trial. We will assess all RE-Aim dimensions to estimate the potential population impact of Action 3:30 in a full trial. Potential impact: If progression criteria are met we will apply for further funding. Funding: Intervention costs are funded by South Gloucestershire & North Somerset Councils

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: A participatory mixed-method evaluation on how removing enforcement could affect sex workers' safety, health and access to services, in East London
Abstract: Sex workers are at disproportionate risk of violence, sexual and emotional ill-health harms that are linked to sex work criminalisation. In the UK, indoor female sex workers are 2.6 times more likely to experience recent client violence if they have ever been arrested/in prison, irrespective of work location, migrant status and drug use. Internationally, sex workers with experience of police enforcement are up to 4-5 times more likely to acquire HIV/STI, accept more money for, be pressured into or engage in unprotected sex with clients. Criminalisation, including of sex workers’ clients, exacerbates these health risks by: disrupting access to care, work environments and safety strategies; disproportionately targeting street-based, ethnic minority and transgender sex workers; and reinforcing structural vulnerabilities (e.g. insecure housing). Emerging international data indicate that decriminalisation can significantly improve safety, care access, physical and emotional health. We will evaluate the impact of removing police enforcement sanctions on female, male and transgender sex workers’ health (violence, HIV, STIs, emotional ill-health) and access to health/social care – a question that has not been researched in the UK and to a limited extent elsewhere. Rather than traditional experimental designs, which require randomisation of an intervention and appropriate comparison areas [19], and which do not account for context [18] and complexity, we will use an innovative, theory-driven evaluation design. [21] We will: estimate the impact of removing sanctions on our outcomes, via mathematical modelling (C); measure the effects of varied enforcement on outcomes via longitudinal, linked behavioural/biological survey data (B), to parameterise the model (C) and capture changes over time (e.g. reduced enforcement due to the presence of Open Doors); investigate how enforcement shapes these outcomes, using qualitative methods (A), to develop indicators and a ‘theory of change’ to guide the evaluation (B/C); and identify contextual factors that influence acceptability, feasibility and implementation of non-enforcement, to inform any scale-up (A). Routine enforcement data across study boroughs (D) will be triangulated with (A/B) to refine measures of (non)enforcement and corroborate changes in policing over time. We will collaborate with sex workers on study design, conduct and dissemination. The findings will inform advocacy for evidence-based policy and any scale up of non-enforcement, in the UK and internationally, as a structural intervention to improve sex workers’ health, safety and well-being.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: The Invasive Dentistry – Endocarditis Association Study: The IDEA Study
Abstract: Background: Infective endocarditis (IE), an infection of the lining of the heart – particularly the heart valves, is a serious disease with high morbidity and mortality. Viridans group streptococci (VGS) from the oral cavity are implicated as the cause in 35-45% of cases. It is not clear if, and to what extent, VGS enter the circulation during daily activities such as chewing food and cleaning teeth or as a result of invasive dental procedures (IDP) such as extractions, endodontic treatment and dental scaling. Because of the hypothesised link to IDP, antibiotic prophylaxis (AP) prior to IDP has been the focus of IE prevention for over 60 years and remains the standard of care for individuals at high-risk of IE in most of the world. However, there has never been a randomised clinical trial (RCT) of AP. Because of this, NICE produced a guideline recommending cessation of AP in 2008. However, the UK is the only country in the world where AP is not currently recommended for patients at high-risk of IE. Furthermore, recent research has shown a significant increase in the incidence of IE following introduction of the 2008 NICE guideline. This has raised concerns about the advice not to give AP prior to IDP in the UK. Ethical concerns along with the size, cost and complexity explain why an RCT has not taken place to date and is unlikely to in the near future. Before an RCT would be worthwhile, we need to be certain that there is a link between IDP and episodes of IE and that is the purpose of the IDEA-study. Indeed, such a study could render an RCT unnecessary. Methods: The IDEA-Study will link national data on courses of dental treatment and on hospital admissions for IE to investigate if there is a link between IDP and the development of IE. Incubation period data indicates that nearly all IE cases present within 3 months of a causal bacteraemic event such as an IDP. So we will address the following questions: 1. Is the incidence of IDP higher in the 3 months immediately preceding an IE diagnosis than in earlier 3 month matched control periods (case-crossover design study)? 2. Do courses of dental treatment (CoT) involving an IDP occur more frequently than CoT that do not contain an IDP in the 3 months immediately preceeding an IE diagnosis? 3. If there is an association between IDP and IE, how soon after the IDP is the peak incidence of IE? We will plot Kaplan-Meier survival analysis curves comparing IE free survival following CoT with and without an IDP. 4. We will also investigate if IE occurs more frequently after specific types of IDP (extraction, scaling etc) or in individuals at high-risk of developing IE. Importance: This study is important because there are ~2,000 cases of IE in England annually with ~600 deaths. All require hospitalization and intensive long-term treatment with antibiotics. A high proportion require surgery to replace damaged heart valves and long-term morbidity and mortality is high. The resulting cost to individuals, families, society and the NHS is extremely high. So if there is a link between IDP and IE, there may be substantial financial, personal and societal savings in giving AP. Alternatively, if no link exists, the costs and risks (antimicrobial resistance and adverse drug reactions) of AP can be avoided and prevention re-focussed on improving oral hygiene in those at high-risk of IE. This study will provide important data upon which NICE and other guideline committees around the world can base their guidelines.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The effectiveness of promotional campaigns associated with revised UK drinking guidelines: A prospective evaluation
Abstract: This study aims to evaluate the impact of promoting revised UK lower risk drinking guidelines (DG) on alcohol consumption behaviour. The UK Government’s 2012 Alcohol Strategy emphasised supporting drinkers to make healthier choices. To help achieve this goal, a review of the DG began in 2013 and is on-going. A likely realistic date for publishing new DG is March/April 2016 and Department of Health have stated that revisions to the DG will be made. Despite their national and international prominence, evidence reviews have highlighted a lack of rigorous evaluations of the impact promoting DG has on alcohol-related behaviour or factors theorised to influence behaviour (e.g. motivations). Evaluation opportunities are rare as DG are revised infrequently and, between revisions, promotional activity is typically low-level and insufficiently predictable to permit prospective data collection. The current UK review provides a valuable opportunity as large-scale promotion of revised DG can be anticipated following their publication. A prospective evaluation will be undertaken to estimate the impact of promoting revised DG on alcohol consumption behaviour among adults living in households in England. It will further seek to evidence a clear causal chain for observed effects by documenting news coverage of the revised guidelines, individual-level exposure to that the guidelines, impacts on capability, opportunity and motivation to change behaviour and effects on behaviour itself. Data on individual-level outcome measures will come from the Alcohol Toolkit Study (ATS). The NIHR-funded ATS collects monthly repeat cross-sectional data from nationally-representative samples of approximately 1,800 adults living in private households in England. It began in March 2014 and the analysis will use data up to October 2017, thus covering 24 months pre-intervention and 19 months post intervention. To facilitate secondary analyses aiming to validate findings and strengthen conclusions, new questions will be added to the ATS for 24 consecutive months (Nov 2015-Oct 2017). These will provide additional alcohol consumption measures, data on exposure to DG and measures of capability, opportunity and motivation to change behaviour. The primary analysis will use segmented regression within an interrupted time series design. It will test whether the level or trend of alcohol consumption behaviour (measured using AUDIT-C score) changes post-publication of revised guidelines. Secondary analyses will repeat these analyses using alternative outcome measures and also apply different analytical approaches (e.g. difference-in-difference analysis). Effects will be estimated for the population as a whole and for subgroups defined by age, gender and socioeconomic status. Mechanisms of effect will be examined using pathway analyses. These will test theorised relationships between capability, opportunity and motivation to change behaviour and behaviour itself. The promotion of DG rather than their publication is the active component of the intervention. As no substantial promotional activity is planned, the public will be exposed to the revised guidelines primarily through news media. The project will review news coverage of the revised guidelines to identify the scale and content of this coverage in England before and after the revised guidelines are announced.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Investigating the contribution of the voluntary sector to mental health crisis care in England
Abstract: Background The relationship between the voluntary sector (VS), or third sector, contribution and statutory services and how these might be integrated to provide a whole system response is a contemporary concern (Alcock, 2010). The provision of crisis support to people experiencing a mental health crisis provides an exemplar of this and of particular significance, given the well-publicised weaknesses in the current arrangements in England (Care Quality Commission, 2015). Mental health crises have been conceptualised as a ‘turning point’, with both risks and constructive potential for people experiencing a crisis (Hobbs, 1984). The policy focus has typically framed mental health crises in a biomedical discourse, requiring rapid psychiatric assessment and intervention, although previous research and service users advocate for a wider range of support, including informal community resources (Fenton et al., 2002; Morton, 2009). The Mental Health Crisis Care Concordat, established in 2014 to lever in improvements in access to high quality and effective support, included harnessing the distinctive contribution of the VS to support integrated care pathways (HM Government, 2014). To date, the research endeavour has largely focused on statutory provision, notably in relation to Crisis Resolution Teams (Rhodes, and Giles, 2014; Wheeler et al. 2015) and there are key gaps in the evidence base for effective mental health crisis care (Paton et al., 2016). Studies that have considered the role of VS services have tended to focus on crisis houses, comparing them with standard psychiatric in-patient care and often for women (Howard et al., 2010). There is, therefore, a significant knowledge gap concerning the extent of the VS contribution, including those services not badged as mental health projects but nonetheless providing crisis support, as is the case with VS organisations (VSOs) supporting homeless people, for example. Moreover, little is known about the range of services provided by small VSOs, particularly those operating informally, or about how the division of labour between providers operates on the ground. In addition, variations in the distribution of VS services, and the extent to which their contributions are integrated into local crisis care pathways, are not clear. From previous literature on the VS, there are problems characterised as “voluntary failure” (Salamon, 1987): essentially an inability to match provision with need (Mohan and Breeze, 2016). This suggests that the distribution of VSOs and volunteers will be uneven, raising policy concerns that those experiencing crises may receive more or less support, depending on where they live: something of a “postcode lottery”. Aim and objectives The primary aim of this research is to identify the contribution of the VS to crisis care pathways in mental health and to make policy and practice recommendations to strengthen the crisis care response in mental health. The scope is mental health crisis care in England and the research objectives are to: 1. Identify the different types of VS support being commissioned and provided to respond to the care and support needs of people experiencing a mental health crisis. 2. Develop a taxonomy of the different organisational types of VS support available, service models and populations served. 3. To investigate the experience of different stakeholders and outcomes for service users of the contribution of different types of VS support to the crisis care system. 4. To identify the factors and processes that facilitate the successful contribution of the VS to effective crisis care pathways. 5. To identify the policy and practice recommendations to strengthen the mental health crisis care response. Methods This is a multi-method study involving four work packages (WPs). WP1 scopes the contribution of VSOs to mental health crisis care. A national survey of VSOs will be undertaken to identify the types of mental health crisis support offered by the range of VSOs, supplemented by interviews with national stakeholders (Department of Health, NHS England, professional organisations) and national VSOs to elucidate detail on the different types of organisational forms of VSOs and views on their contribution to the crisis care pathway. The remaining WPs build on WP1 to provide a rich and detailed picture of the VS contribution. WP2 involves detailed mapping of the VSO provision within two regions to develop a taxonomy of crisis care provision thus extending the typology developed from the national survey. This taxonomy will provide a sampling frame to select two case studies per region in order to investigate the contribution of VSO provision to crisis care at both a system (WP3) and individual level (WP4). In the case study sites WP3 will focus on mapping the different elements of the crisis care system at a local level, including capturing small scale community based initiatives. Data on activities, interventions and stakeholder perceptions of the effectiveness of the VS contribution to the crisis care pathway will be collected through a key informant questionnaire, interviews with key stakeholders and focus groups with mental health service users and carers. WP4 will map the crisis care trajectories of 10 service users with experience of different types of VS provision, collecting this data through interviews with mental health service users, carers and statutory providers. Ethical approvals This project will require ethical approval by the Health Research Authority (HRA) and the University of Birmingham Humanities and Social Sciences (HASS) Ethical Review Committee and will be undertaken in compliance with the Data Protection Act and University of Birmingham policies relating to the conduct of research. Analysis The analysis will involve a detailed mapping of the VS contribution, which will be classified to develop a taxonomy of the different organisational forms, populations served and activities provided by VSOs in England. Data from qualitative interviews will be analysed using the Framework method (Gale et al., 2013) and data from the various sources synthesised to address the research questions. Research team The research team brings together expertise in researching VSOs and in mental health, and from a practitioner, commissioner and service user perspective. It combines the nationally recognised expertise of two leading UK research centres, the Health Services Management Centre (HSMC) and the Third Sector Research Centre (TSRC), with the track record of Suresearch, a mental health service user group involved in research. Public and patient involvement People with experience of mental ill-health will be extensively involved in the conduct of research as co-researchers and as members of a Project Reference Group. Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Understanding new models of care in local contexts: a systematic review using frameworks to examine pathways of change, applicability, and generalisability of the international research evidence
Abstract: The NHS has been challenged to adopt new, flexible models of service delivery that are tailored to local populations [NHS England, 2014]. Evidence from the international literature is needed in order to support the development and implementation of these new models of care and to overcome reported potential issues and barriers [Ham & Murray, 2015]. The proposed study aims to support the development of new, flexible models of service delivery by carrying out a systematic review of evidence relating to new models of healthcare. It will combine rigorous and systematic methods for identification of literature together, with innovative methods for synthesis and presentation of evidence. The proposed synthesis methods will address the identified need for: firstly, enhanced understanding of the mechanisms whereby new models of service delivery impact on healthcare and patient outcomes; and secondly, greater understanding of ways that models might work in different contexts. The research team will carry out a systematic search of the international literature on new models of care. We will search electronic databases and use supplementary searching methods such as citation searching and reference list screening. This systematic search will advance understanding by privileging rigour by focusing on formal evaluations and empirical designs. At the same time a UK-centric systematic search, with a more inclusive evidence threshold will identify contextually rich ephemeral materials that will privilege relevance [Torejeson et al., 2015]. In this way both context and outcomes will receive corresponding attention within this bi-partite review for, as Pawson [2006] has stressed, “outcome patterns are contingent on ... assessments of both rigour and relevance”. Evidence identified via these means will be synthesised in two ways. Firstly, the study will use data from included studies to develop an evidence-based logic model. Initially UK-based literature will be used to populate the model, which will set out evidence underpinning the pathway from new models of care to long term and system-wide impact. The logic model will detail: the types of service transformation which have been described; short term outcome measures reported; and longer term evaluation tools used to examine impact. The model will also outline the mechanisms of action (i.e. theory of change) for the pathway from these new models of care to different types of impact, together with factors reported as moderating or mediating elements. Following development of the prototype model we will then scrutinise the international literature, making comparisons and contrasts between this evidence and the UK evidence. The logic model will thereby act as a translation tool between multiple and diverse evidence types, and enable a contextually sensitive analysis. The second method of synthesis in the proposed work will further examine comparisons and contrasts between the UK and international literature in order to develop a framework of factors potentially impacting on generalisability and applicability of the literature. This element of the work will address the need for understanding how particular models might work in different local contexts. The final phase of the study will use consultation with key stakeholder to examine the clarity and resonance of the developed logic model, and also to gain feedback regarding the assessment of generalisability and applicability.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Improving Outcomes for Children and Families affected by PATERNAL Substance Misuse: A Feasibility Study of the PARENTS UNDER PRESSURE(PuP) Programme for Fathers
Abstract: Parental drug misuse is closely associated with poor child development, child maltreatment, and a greater likelihood that children will develop substance misuse problems themselves [7,8]. It is well known that fathers play an important role in child welfare and family functioning [9], and drug problems are far more prevalent in men than women [10]. Failure to involve fathers in family services has been repeatedly highlighted in child abuse inquiries [11]. However, efforts to involve fathers in parenting programmes remains a significant challenge, with services reporting low rates of engagement, especially in regard to fathers with complex needs [12]. Furthermore, there is little data on the effectiveness of mainstream parenting programmes for improving father-child relationships and fathering capacity. Fathers are rarely involved in parenting intervention trials, and where they are, outcomes for fathers are seldom measured or reported [13]. Thus little is known about what kind of interventions specifically for fathers, and services for couples, work best to improve outcomes for children. Only two pilot studies, conducted in the US, have focused solely on substance-using fathers with young children. Lam et al [14], found greater improvements on measures of parenting and child protection involvement when alcohol dependent fathers received a combined parenting and couples approach. Similarly, Stover et al [15] found gains in measures of quality of caregiving in substance-using fathers with a history of interpersonal violence. Notably, this intervention included a focus on quality of the father-child relationship and development of coping skills for impulsive behavior and aggression. In a recent review on parenting interventions which included men as parents or coparents, Panter-Brick et al [13] recommended that future research should prioritise engaging fathers and coparenting couples, examine process and impact data by fathers, mothers, and coparents, and pay greater attention to sustainability, cost, equity, reach and scale-up. Our study is designed to tackle this vital next step in parenting intervention research. Crucially, we will focus on opioid-dependent fathers and their preschool aged children. We propose to undertake a mixed methods feasibility study of the PARENTS UNDER PRESSURE (PuP) programme that has been specifically designed to improve parental emotional regulation and quality of caregiving, thus reducing child abuse in drug-using families. We will recruit 24 families with preschool aged children by targeting fathers in treatment for opioid addiction. PuP is 24 week home-visiting programme that places an emphasis on the quality of the caregiving environment and the parent’s capacity to provide a safe and nurturing environment. PuP moves beyond teaching ‘parenting skills’ to address dysregulated affect through the use of mindfulness exercises and other emotion regulation strategies. PuP will be delivered by eight PuP practitioners employed by two non-NHS agencies. Our innovative study will determine: the potential pool of eligible fathers/families; successful recruitment strategies; acceptability of outcome measures; up-take, retention, completion and follow-up rates; and acceptability of PuP among parents, staff and services involved with the programme. The AIM OF OUR STUDY is to estimate the parameters needed to design a pilot RCT and viable, sufficiently powered full evaluation, including an economic evaluation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Optimising the outputs of National Clinical Audits to support organisations to improve the quality of care and clinical outcomes
Abstract: BACKGROUND. Audit and feedback (A&F) aims to improve patient care by reviewing health care performance against explicit standards. It is widely used to monitor and improve NHS care, including in national clinical audit programmes. Ideally, where a discrepancy is detected, changes are implemented at an individual, team, and/or service level. A&F generally has small to moderate and variable effects on patient care, although potentially substantial population impacts. Yet cumulative meta-analysis of A&F trials indicates that effect sizes stabilised over 10 years ago, suggesting a lack of learning on how to improve effectiveness. We need to improve the effects of A&F. Moreover, how healthcare organisations respond to national audits is highly variable, further limiting the impact of A&F. Building on collaborations with partner national audit programmes, we will develop and evaluate methods to enhance A&F and explore how to routinely embed such work within UK national audits. AIM. To improve patient care by optimising the content, format and delivery of feedback from national clinical audits. OBJECTIVE 1. A consensus panel will prioritise theory and evidence-informed modifications to feedback interventions, drawing upon a state-of-the-science summary of recommendations. 500 individuals drawn from organisations targeted by four national audits will take part in a randomised screening experiment with a fractional factorial design, whereby they receive and respond to different combinations of feedback modifications through a web portal; proxy outcomes include intended enactment, comprehension, user experience, and preferences and engagement. OBJECTIVE 2. A case study will examine how four purposively sampled, linked pairs of healthcare provider and commissioner organisations (two for each of two national audit topics) respond to feedback modifications. We will use both institutional and systems perspectives, the latter guided by a logic model. We will use documentary evidence, observations and interviews with sampled healthcare organisations, board members, clinicians and managers to examine how feedback is delivered, perceived and acted upon. The analysis will exploit diversity sampling, comparing and contrasting findings across localities and audits. Framework and thematic analyses will focus on understanding how and why the intended effects are achieved, or why they are not. OBJECTIVE 3. We will interview 30 purposively sampled national audit staff, A&F researchers, clinicians and managers targeted by feedback to explore understanding, experience and expectations of integrating research within national audit programmes. OUTPUTS. We will (i) identify a set of modifications for national audits which can enhance their impacts and underpin future rigorous evaluations of cost-effectiveness; (ii) develop a training manual, templates and online resources to help organisations optimise the delivery and use of feedback; and (iii) establish the optimal conditions for embedding collaborative trials within national audits. EXPERTISE. Our team combines international expertise in A&F research with experience of designing and delivering national audits.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: How can loneliness and social isolation be reduced among migrant and minority ethnic people? Systematic, participatory review of programme theories, system processes and outcomes
Abstract: This project aims to synthesise available evidence and produce new insight into the range of approaches to addressing social isolation and loneliness in migrant and minority ethnic people, plus the logic, functioning and effects of these interventions. The health risks of loneliness and social isolation are increasingly recognised and various responses have emerged. Earlier evidence reviews have usefully categorised approaches and confirmed that some interventions are effective in reducing social isolation and/or loneliness, particularly group-based and shared interest activities for older people. However, this earlier work has taken a narrow, individually-focused approach, looking exclusively at interventions specifically designed to address loneliness and/or social isolation. It is increasingly recognised that social isolation and loneliness are complex problems, rooted in socio-ecological systems. Determinants operate at individual, family, community and wider societal level and interplay with interventions in complex ways. More holistic research is needed to improve understanding of the causes and solutions in varied settings. This project addresses this need and extends earlier work by: (1) exploring a wide range of interventions (including neighbourhood initiatives and those where isolation/loneliness are secondary outcomes); (2) focusing on migrant and minority ethnic people of all ages (a growing but under-served population with particular risks); and (3) combining effectiveness assessment with detailed examination of intervention logic, system processes and multiple outcomes. We are a multidisciplinary team with population, topic and methodological expertise. We draw on systems thinking and on recent work indicating the value of participatory methods in enhancing reviews of complex, social interventions. We will use an iterative process of desk-based review methods and group modelling workshops with three Consultation Panels (involving lay experts, community workers and beneficiaries in London, Sheffield and Leicester) throughout the 18 month project. We will generate six complementary research products: 1) A typology of interventions (including detailed descriptions of components and resource inputs). 2) An assessment of comparative effectiveness using network meta-analysis, meta-analysis and/or narrative synthesis as appropriate 3) A descriptive synthesis of the costs (and where reported cost effectiveness) of interventions 4) A refined system model (presented visually in causal loop diagrams and in narrative form) 5) A qualitative meta-synthesis of factors supporting/undermining intervention implementation and sustainability 6) A qualitative meta-synthesis of factors that increase/decrease social isolation and loneliness among migrant and minority ethnic people mapped against interventional activity Our study is designed with impact in mind. Close involvement of the Consultation Panels and an Advisory Group means that evidence-users are engaged throughout. We will produce a range of research outputs tailored to varied audiences and use extensive academic, policy-practice and community networks to engage people with the results. Findings will inform future action aiming to tackle social isolation and/or loneliness in ethnically diverse populations. We also anticipate new knowledge on how to identify opportunities within existing public health-related activity to prevent or reduce isolation/loneliness.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: De-implementation in health and care services: what works, for whom, why, and in which contexts? A Realist Synthesis.
Abstract: Where health and care processes are considered to be inefficient or ineffective, managers and organisations equally require guidance about the process of “de-implementation”, an important strategy that is necessary to address current policy of reducing harm, and improving the quality and cost effectiveness across health and care services. Non-evidenced based decisions andpractices that are known to have poor outcomes, cause harm, and are of low value, continue to be in use, but guidance on how to halt them is missing. In the current economic climate, where service practices that don’t need to be provided are in use, this impacts on the quality of care that patients receive, and contributes to the waste of resources. This evidence synthesis will fill a gap in the evidence base by focusing on the use and impact of different processes for de-implementation. Aim: To produce useful programme theory and practical guidance for policy makers, managers and clinicians to help them with de-implementation processes and procedures. Objectives: 1. Generate a concept analysis of de-implementation. 2. Identify and map the range of different de-implementation approaches and/or strategies currently being utilised across health and care, paying attention to ways in which they are assumed to work. 3. Produce a typology of de-implementation types, processes and contexts. 4. Examine and understand the range of anticipated and unanticipated impacts of these approaches and/or strategies across different settings and stakeholders, paying attention to contextual conditions which influence these impacts 5. Generate an evidence-based, realist programme theory that explains the successful processes and impacts of de-implementation 6. Explore, through stakeholder engagement in the review methods, decision-making processes associated with de-implementation 7. Produce recommendations about ways in which different approaches and/or strategies can help managers and service leaders plan and prioritise de-implementation in a systematic and efficient manner 8. Stimulate a wider debate about avoiding and stopping services that are considered wasteful, of low value and non-efficient, for future provision. A realist approach takes into account the recognised complexities in health and care systems, and will be used for this evidence synthesis. The aim will be to develop, test and refine a programme theory about de-implementation. The output generated will be in the form of a programme theory, populated with evidence that describes ‘what works’ about de-implementation strategies and approaches, and the contextual factors that influence their impact on outcomes. We will interview and work with NHS managers to translate this programme theory into actionable recommendations, using practical examples from the evidence. The evidence synthesis will be conducted in 4 phases over 18 months: Phase 1: Concept, and initial programme theory development in consultation with stakeholders Phase 2: Retrieval, review and synthesis of evidence Phase 3: Testing and refining of the initial programme theory/ ies Phase 4: Actionable recommendations and mobilising of knowledge for use in practice Benefits to the NHS: To inform and guide managers and service leaders about how best to conduct de-implementation in order to ensure health and care services are evidence-based, efficient, and to deliver high quality services for patients which are valued by them.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A pilot randomised controlled trial of one to one befriending by volunteers, compared to Usual Care, in reducing symptoms of depression in people with intellectual disability
Abstract: Background: People with intellectual disability (ID) are more likely to experience loneliness, social isolation, have fewer social networks and lower levels of social participation that can lead to low self esteem and increased vulnerability to depression. The aim of befriending is to provide friendship and emotional support, to reduce loneliness and promote social participation. Befriending has been shown to increase social satisfaction in people with ID and to reduce depressive symptoms in other populations, but randomised controlled trials, including pilot studies, have not been carried out in people with ID. Aim: to carry out a pilot randomised controlled trial of the one to one befriending by volunteers for people with ID, compared to Usual Care and a booklet of community resources. We will assess feasibility data on the recruitment rate of individuals with ID and volunteers, the number of successfully matched pairs and the drop-out rate at six and 12 months follow up. We will also examine the effect of befriending on outcome measures, adherence to the trial protocol, and acceptability of the intervention. Intervention: Face to face meetings between the volunteer and the individual once a week over a six month period. The volunteer will provide social support and help the individual to access activities in the community using a booklet of local resources and will be asked to keep a log of their activities. Control arm: Access to booklet of local resources only. Both groups will have access to Usual care, which will include multidisciplinary input from intellectual disability services, pharmacological and psychological treatments and day services. Inclusion criteria: Individuals aged 18 or over with mild or moderate ID, who have a score of 5 or more on the GDS-LD, not attending education/ day service for more than two days a week, will be recruited from referrals to befriending organisations. Exclusion criteria: severe ID, unable to communicate in English or provide consent. Volunteers will be aged 18 and over and will be recruited by the befriending organisations in their usual way. Those with a criminal record will be excluded. Study procedures: 50 participants with ID will be randomised using block randomisation and allocated to either the intervention or control arm. Forty two volunteers will need to be recruited (assuming a drop out rate of 40% before matching). Outcomes: Feasibility data on recruitment and drop out rates; Primary health outcome: symptoms of depression at 12 months; secondary outcomes: self esteem, quality of life, loneliness, social support, social participation, health related quality of life and service use costs. Outcomes will be recorded at baseline, end of the intervention (6 months), and at 12 months. In volunteers, self-esteem, emotional well-being, loneliness and attitudes towards people with ID before matching and at six and 12 months will be measured. A process evaluation using mixed methods will be carried out involving an assessment of adherence to the intervention, the nature and frequency of contacts and qualitative interviews with stake holders to identify aspects of the intervention that were/were not successful. Trial progression criteria: 70% of the target recruitment rate of individuals with ID is met; 70% are matched to a volunteer; there is less than 30% drop-out rate and the intervention is acceptable.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: workH.O.R.S.E: working Health Outcomes Research Simulation Environment
Abstract: BACKGROUND The NHS Health Check Programme (NHS HCP) seeks to identify and manage people at high risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and diabetes. What is the potential for further improvements in health, equity and cost-effectiveness? AIM This project will provide a validated open source/open access, flexible model enabling local commissioners to quantify the potential and cost effectiveness for population health gain of the NHS Health Check Programme, by building on the solid foundation of our existing IMPACTncd model. OBJECTIVES AND RESEARCH PLAN OBJECTIVE 1: Model Development. We will further develop our proven and tested IMPACTncd computer model to include more diseases (heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and kidney disease, dementia, atrial fibrillation; alcohol misuse, cancers and Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease). To support local commissioning, the model will also compare different implementation approaches and support sophisticated scenario specifications. This validated, fully stochastic generic microsimulation model will include a prototype user interface to help commissioners model the implementation of the NHS HCP at local level. OBJECTIVE 2: Updating the evidence base. To inform model development and delivery, we will build on existing evidence-based guidelines and systematic reviews (SRs) and conduct new SRs. Key parameters to reflect programme implementation will include eligibility, annual coverage, uptake, risk profile, treatment prescription and adherence, brief interventions, and referrals to lifestyle services. OBJECTIVE 3: Assess and compare the alternative strategies for the NHS Health Check Programme. As specified in the NIHR call, we will explore the effectiveness of the NHS HCP, and compare cases detected, cases prevented, deaths prevented or postponed, number needed to attend to prevent a case; life expectancy, disease-free life expectancy; and QALYs. Results will be stratified by age, gender, ethnicity and socioeconomic position (to facilitate equity impact analysis). Health economics analysis will include cost utility analysis (cost per QALY), incremental cost-effectiveness ratios and net monetary benefit. We will also conduct extensive probabilistic sensitivity analyses. OBJECTIVE 4: Stakeholder engagement. We will recruit and engage a diverse group of stakeholders. This will powerfully strengthen the user perspective, refine desirable features of the user interface and identify additional, locally relevant scenarios to test. OBJECTIVE 5: Develop a sustainability and implementation plan to deploy workHORSE as a user-friendly web-based decision model. We will ensure open access to the model, refine scalability strategies and provide recommendations for incorporating local data, and designing and implementing local scenarios. This will include piloting a secure cloud-based platform to allow local commissioners to run their own scenarios. IMPORTANT OUTCOMES Our project will deliver an open source, scalable, decision-support model for use with local or national data. Flexible scenario design features to accommodate and assess changes in NHS HCP delivery and eligibility criteria will enable commissioners to explore the potential for increased effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and population health gain. DISSEMINATION We will publicise our findings via diverse stakeholders, organisations, websites, Health Check users, media, conferences and papers in academic and general journals.

Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Rethinking Strategies for Positive Newborn Screening Result Delivery (ReSPoND): a process evaluation of co-designing interventions to minimise impact on parental emotional well-being and stress
Abstract: Background: Annually, circa 10,000 parents of babies born in the United Kingdom (UK) are given a positive newborn screening (NBS+) result 2-8 weeks after birth(1,2). Despite guidance(3), NBS+ results are inconsistently delivered across UK-regions(4-7) and many parents are dissatisfied with how NBS+ results are communicated(5-12). Expansion of UK NBS to include nine conditions means added pressure for a cost effective approach to communication of NBS+ results. As most infants will be asymptomatic when parents receive the NBS+ result(1, 2), it is vital that communication is done carefully to avoid potential negative effects on future concordance with treatment and relationships with health professionals(4,5,11-13). Concordance and trust are important(14) to ensure timely uptake of confirmatory diagnostic testing and instigation of necessary treatment to maximise outcomes for the child(1,2). Poor communication can affect parent-child bonding and ongoing parental and social relationships(5,6,15). As such, family systems theory(16) will be the theoretical basis for this work. Study aim: To co-design, implement and evaluate interventions to improve delivery of NBS+ results to parents. Primary research question: Can parents and staff co-design interventions to improve delivery of NBS+ results to parents that can be successfully implemented into routine practice in a cost effective manner? Secondary research questions: - How are NBS+ results currently delivered to parents for the condition specific groups (CSGs) and what are the perceived benefits? - What are the current experiences of staff delivering, and parents receiving, NBS+ results for the CSGs? - What aspects of the new, co-designed interventions and local approaches to implementation are important in terms of improving the delivery of NBS+ results? - What are the costs associated with the delivery of the new, co-designed interventions and subsequent use of healthcare services and how does this compare with the costs associated with current strategies? - Which outcomes will be important to include in a subsequent evaluation study of the new, co-designed interventions from a stakeholder perspective? Study design: A mixed-methods study underpinned by family systems theory(16) using four phases with defined outputs: Phase 0: Establish project management arrangements and secure ethics and HRA approvals. Phase 1: A national survey using telephone interviews with all NBS-laboratories in England and representatives of clinical teams to explore current approaches for communication of NBS+ results and inform selection of two study sites for phases 2-3. Outputs: (i) description and cost of current communication practices (ii) selection of two study sites for Phases 2-3. Phase 2: Experience-based Co-design(17-23) will be used in the selected study sites to develop interventions for communicating NBS+ results to parents. Output: Interventions for the four CSGs. Phase 3: A parallel process evaluation(24,25), underpinned by Normalisation Process Theory(26,27) and economic analysis of the interventions in the two selected case study sites. Outputs: (i) process evaluation and economic analysis of the interventions in routine practice (ii) information about suitable outcome measures for a future study. Phase 4: Determine final interventions and design of a future evaluation study Outputs: (i) Design of a future evaluation study (ii) list of suitable outcome measures and relevant resource use and cost Dissemination Everyone directly involved in the study will be sent a summary of research findings. Study findings will be disseminated on the blog http://blogs.city.ac.uk/respondnbs/, national NBS websites https://www.gov.uk/topic/population-screening-programmes/newborn-bloodspot,https://www.gov.uk/topic/population-screening-programmes/sickle-cell-thalassaemia). Additionally, findings will be shared via the website of relevant charities and support groups associated with these conditions (CF Trust, Sickle Cell Society, British Thyroid Foundation, National Society for Phenylketonuria, CLIMB). Finally, results will be disseminated by the usual academic routes at relevant national and international conferences and published in relevant international peer reviewed journals (including the NIHR HS&DR journal). Award_Title: Improving the experience of care for people with dementia in hospital: Systematic review of qualitative and quantitative evidence
Abstract: Aim: To use existing evidence to direct change and improvements in the experience of care for people with dementia in hospital, their families and the staff that care for them. Methods: We will conduct 3 systematic reviews, develop a logic model and convene a series of UK regional consensus meetings to discuss findings in the context of existing services resulting in the co-production of plans for service change. Research questions: 1. What is the experience of people with dementia and their families of receiving care in a hospital setting? 2. What is the experience of hospital staff of caring for people with dementia? 3. What evidence is available to inform on the most effective and cost-effective ways to improve the experience of care for people with dementia in hospital? 4. What is the impact of such interventions on the health and wellbeing of the hospital staff and the families and informal carers of those with dementia? 5. Which factors are important in the successful delivery of approaches to improve the experience of care? PREPARATION: Consultation with the PAG to further develop and finalise the protocol before registration with the International Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO). REVIEW: The search strategy will be developed by an Information Specialist (MR) in consultation with the PAG. Sources will include electronic databases and supplementary methods to identify grey literature. Inclusion and exclusion criteria will be applied to the title and abstract of each identified citation independently by 2 reviewers with disagreements being settled by discussion with a third. Population: People with dementia receiving care in a hospital setting, their families & the staff providing care; Intervention(s): Experience of care / interventions to improve experience of care; Comparator: Any; Outcomes: Any outcomes relating to the experience of care as reported by people with dementia, their families & hospital staff providing the care; Setting: Any hospital setting, including the process of transition into and out of hospital; Study design, publication date, language of publication: No restriction. Full texts will be obtained for papers that appear to meet the criteria and a similar process used. Standardised, piloted data extraction forms will be used to collect relevant data from each included paper. Appropriate quality appraisal checklists will be used according to study design. Quality appraisal and data extraction will be performed by one reviewer and checked by a second with disagreements settled through discussion with a third. Synthesis methods will be determined in response to the nature of the findings. INTEGRATION: We will bring together the findings from the three reviews through the development of a logic model. The logic model will be built column by column to map out the conjectured links between different types of intervention and anticipated outcomes, gaps in the evidence and factors that help or hinder intervention success. We will use face-to-face meetings, telephone conferences and email to ensure that the PAG are involved at all stages in contributing to the interpretation of the findings and the development of the logic model. CONSULTATION/PRE-IMPLEMENTATION: We will convene UK regional consensus meetings with providers, commissioners and recipients of services to discuss the findings in the context of existing services and co-produce plans for service change

Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Do Networked Information Technologies Improve Patient Safety? A Realist Synthesis
Abstract: The aim of this study is to establish how and why networked, inter-organisational Health Information Technology (HIT) services improve patient safety, do not do so, or increase safety risks. The objectives of the study are to: 1. Identify initial programme theories, and prioritise theories to review; 2. Search systematically for evidence to test the theories; 3. Undertake quality appraisal, and use included texts to support, refine or reject programme theories; 4. Synthesise the findings; 5. Disseminate the findings to a range of audiences. We will undertake a realist synthesis, in 5 Stages, corresponding to the objectives. Stage 1 focuses on the identification of programme theories. Searches will be designed and conducted to identify relevant government policies and official reports, and articles by opinion leaders. Documents will be reviewed, to identify relevant statements about HITs and patient safety. Leading theories (in key texts) of patient safety will be identified, and statements relevant to the review identified. The findings will be summarised, for presentation to 4 nominal groups - policy makers, NHS implementation leads, frontline clinicians, and our patient and public involvement group. The groups will meet separately, in the order listed. The meetings will be structured, so as to identify leading programme theories for detailed evaluation. Following the first meeting, each subsequent meeting will also be presented with the outputs of the preceding group(s). Stages 2 and 3 involve a series of literature searches, designed to identify and assess evidence for each link (or a series of links) in a chain of reasoning in the programme theories. We will design searches for Ovid databases, including Medline, Embase and HMIC, and also ASSIA, Sociological Abstracts and IEEE Explore. Evidence will be assessed for rigour and relevance, and then used to evaluate the selected programme theories. The theories will be supported, refined or rejected. We will also identify evidence that sheds light on the reasons why the intended effects of programme theories are - or are not - realised in practice. The nominal groups will be re-convened (by email or web-based service) towards the end of Stage 3, to comment on the emerging findings. The groups may lead us to conduct further literature searches. Stage 4 is the synthesis phase of the review, where the findings are interpreted. The nominal groups will be convened again, by email or web-based service, at the end of this Stage, and will comment on our interpretations and provide their own. In Stage 5 we will prepare a number of outputs for dissemination. The review will add value in two ways. First, the underlying mechanisms that link HITs and patient safety are poorly understood. Identifying the chains of reasoning will help us – and practitioners and policy makers - to understand the underlying logic linking the implementation of networked, inter-organisational HITs and their subsequent effects. We will also identify cultural, economic and other reasons why intended effects – represented by the chains of reasoning - are not achieved in practice. Second, we will produce evidence-based guidance for NHS organisations. We will ensure that the guidance is useful to practitioners. Policy makers and practitioners will be involved in the review and will also be involved in the development of the guidance.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Improving the Oral Health of Older People in Care Homes: a Feasibility Study (TOPIC)
Abstract: Poor oral health is an increasingly common problem for older adults (defined as those over 65 years of age). It impacts on their quality of life, their general health and diet. Access to domiciliary services is difficult and hospital admission for dental problems can be distressing and costly. Income-related inequality in oral health of older adults is a major issue. Therefore, effective prevention of oral diseases is paramount. Four per cent of people aged over 65 and one fifth of those aged over 85 live in care homes. Half of all care homes residents have their own natural teeth but their oral health is much worse than their community living peers (e.g. caries prevalence was 73% vs. 40%). With increasing age, the ability to care for their mouth deteriorates, poly-pharmacy leads to dry mouth, and diets can become rich in sugars. All these factors increase the risk of oral disease and directly impact on comorbidities. Strategies for this population are to prevent disease and reduce pain and co-morbidity. However, a Public Health England survey showed current provision and service to be poor. A Priority Setting Partnership led by a co-PI of this project found that maintaining function, dignity and the fear of losing the ability to look after your own teeth were key issues among older adults. The World Health Organisation has focused on healthy ageing and prioritised the designing of health and long-term care systems that are fit for ageing populations. However, the evidence for interventions on promoting oral health among care home residents is weak, with uncertainty about effect size estimates, recruitment, retention, fidelity and appropriate outcome measures. This makes the design of a full trial problematic at this stage. A relevant NICE guideline (NG48) aims to maintain and improve the oral health of care home residents. The aim of this study is to assess the feasibility of promoting oral hygiene and preventing oral diseases in older people in care homes, following the NICE guideline recommendations related to prevention of oral diseases. Work-Stream (WS) 1 will determine whether a pragmatic cluster-randomised controlled trial is feasible. Preventive elements of the NICE guideline (oral health assessment of residents; daily assisted tooth-brushing with 1,500ppm fluoride toothpaste; and a staff training package) will be contrasted to routine practice in eligible dentate residents. WS2 will use semi-structured interviews and focus groups with residents, care home managers and staff to understand the context and explore the intervention’s acceptability and fidelity. WS3 will produce a cost-consequence model that identifies key outcomes relevant to different stakeholders and the potential to reduce these to a core set of indicators. It will also explore issues associated with the valid, reliable and efficient collection and reporting of core indicators. Feasibility study outcome measures will be recruitment, retention, acceptability to residents and treatment fidelity. Potential outcome measures for the definitive trial include: coronal and root caries lesions, dental plaque, quality of life, oral pain and treatment appointments. The research will determine whether the evaluation of the complex intervention (preventive aspects of the NICE guideline for oral health in care homes) is feasible and acceptable. It will also provide valuable information about how best to recruit residents and undertake research in care homes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: An online parenting intervention to prevent affective disorders in high-risk adolescents: The PIPA trial
Abstract: Depression is a leading cause of disease burden in young people in the UK and globally. The incidence of depression rises sharply during adolescence, making early adolescence a particularly opportune time to target preventive efforts. Moreover, there is evidence that preventative strategies can be effective. Whilst many preventative approaches have targeted young people themselves and demonstrated effects up to two years post-intervention, there is evidence that preventative interventions that target parents are effective in the longer term (up to 11 years)(1). Recent policy documents such as the Five Year Forward View for Mental Health and Future in Mind have advocated for public mental health interventions for young people that include parents. Our collaborators in Australia have developed Partners in Parenting (PiP), an evidence-based personalised online parenting intervention, and demonstrated that it can improve depressive symptoms in their adolescent child with early internalising problems. We aim to adapt this well-developed and evidenced-based intervention to a UK setting. We then aim to test the acceptability and effectiveness of the intervention delivered to parents in improving depressive symptoms in their high-risk offspring, as well as other clinical and non-clinical outcomes in the adolescents, using a RCT design. We propose an initial adaptation phase, which will consist of focus group consultations with parents, teachers and adolescents to make adaptations of the PiP intervention for a UK setting and establish the feasibility and acceptability of the assessment battery. We plan to conduct an internal pilot with a priori stop-go progression criteria based on recruitment and intervention adherence and then a definitive RCT, recruiting 433 families from participating UK schools and direct from the community. We will screen pupils aged 11-15 years with the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire and those scoring highly will be invited to participate in the trial with their parents/caregivers. Parents will be randomly allocated to either the online modular PiP intervention or an online control programme which consists of a standardised package of educational materials about adolescent development and wellbeing. Each intervention is delivered over a 3-month period with assessments completed online by the parent and child at baseline, 6 months later, and 12 months post-intervention (15 months later) including parenting self-efficacy. The primary outcome will be adolescent depressive symptoms measured at 12 months post-intervention using the Short Mood and Feelings Questionnaire. There will be a number of secondary outcomes including anxiety, parenting behaviour, child wellbeing and resilience and parent and adolescent quality of life to measure QALYS and economic utility. To maintain programme adherence, and in line with the Australian protocol, parents will receive weekly check-in phone calls/texts during the intervention period. At the end of the trial, we will be able to demonstrate whether such a tailored online approach is effective and could be rolled out nationally. We will create an exploitation plan based on the results. We will disseminate the findings to national and international audiences including a national launch event with stakeholders from health, education and third sector organisations.
