Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Developing a model for high quality service design for children and young people with common mental health problems
Abstract: The mental health of children and young people (CYP) is a national and international priority, with around 1 in 10 UK CYP having a mental health difficulty. Most of the need lies with CYP experiencing ‘common’ mental health problems (CMHPs). CMHPs are a range of psychological, emotional and behavioural problems that includes anxiety, depression, OCD, self-harm, PTSD, gender identity issues and emerging personality disorders. While health needs for this population group are rising, services across the UK tend to be fragmented, uncoordinated and variable, and most struggle to meet demand. This study aims to develop a model of effective service design for CYP with CMHPs by examining the factors that facilitate access to, and navigation of, services for CYP with CMHPs and the effectiveness and acceptability of those services. CYP with CMHPs typically do not require hospitalisation so the services investigated will be out-of-hospital services providing primarily assessment/triage, early intervention and supported self-care. This evidence-based model will help inform the NHS and assist commissioners and providers in the design and transformation of out-of-hospital services for this population group. The study has 4 work streams. In Stream 1, a series of systematic reviews of the international literature will be conducted, specifically: (a) a descriptive review identifying the range of service models; (b) an effectiveness review that identifies and evaluates those service models where comparative effectiveness data are available; (c) an acceptability review that identifies and evaluates those service models where acceptability data are available; and (d) an economic review that considers provider and user costs/benefits associated with specific service models. The reviews will be synthesised using EPPI-Centre meta-synthesis principles. In Stream 2, a survey and the literature from Stream 1 will be used to map services in England & Wales across a range of different service dimensions (theoretical underpinnings, location, staffing, provider, delivery platform, etc). A typology of service provision for CYP with CMHPs will be derived from Streams 1 and 2. In Stream 3 (a collective case study), 8-10 services will be purposively sampled from Stream 2's service map to reflect the various dimensions of the typology. At each site, in line with the principles of case study research, we will: (a) conduct interviews with key stakeholders, ie providers, managers & users (including those who could not or did not access services); (b) obtain relevant documents; and (c) observe, where possible, key interactions. The three case study data sets will be analysed using Framework. We will also collect economic data (time spent delivering services, equipment costs and user out-of-pocket expenses) in Stream 3 for which bottom-up estimates of costs associated with services will be calculated from NHS and PSSRU sources. In Stream 4, data from Streams 1-3 will be synthesised to elicit a model (or models) of effective and acceptable service design for CYP experiencing CMHPs that integrates all of the factors associated with accessing, navigating and receiving help from services for this population group. Service user & provider perspectives will permeate the entire study via an advisory group (which will include commissioners of services), having an NHS manager & service user group as co-applicants, and via employing young service users as co-researchers.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Nudging healthier dietary habits: evaluation of a supermarket placement strategy in the WRAPPED study
Abstract: Background: Unhealthy diet is a key modifiable risk factor for obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs). The cost of poor diet-related ill health to the NHS is £5.8 billion annually. Supermarkets account for 87% of UK grocery sales. UK government policy supports altering such environments to ‘nudge’ people into making healthier choices. High quality empirical evidence that ‘nudge’ placement initiatives are effective is needed. Testing environmental strategies that help families, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds, to make healthy food choices is necessary to reduce obesity prevalence and improve population health. Aim: This study is the largest supermarket trial internationally and will assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of improving the placement of fresh fruit and vegetables in supermarkets in improving the fresh fruit and vegetable purchasing of women aged 18-60 years. Plan of Investigation: WRAPPED (Women’s Responses to Adjusted Product Placement and its Effects on Diet) is a natural experiment with a prospective matched controlled cluster design. The setting is a UK discount supermarket chain regularly used by many disadvantaged families for their main shop. The intervention involves creation of a new, expanded fresh fruit and vegetable section near the store entrance. Control stores keep the existing layout with a limited range of fresh fruit and vegetables and placement of fresh fruit and vegetables at the back of the store. A pilot phase demonstrated improved diet quality amongst women shopping in intervention stores when compared with those shopping in control stores. An appropriately powered study is required. We will recruit 9 participants from each of 24 intervention and 24 matched control stores through the retailer’s loyalty card scheme (postal letter) and shop floor recruitment, and provide incentives of up to £30 Love2Shop or Amazon vouchers; these methods proved effective during the pilot. Participants will be women aged 18-60 years who shopped at a study store in the 12 weeks before recruitment. This study is unique in its collection of individual level sales data, as well as demographic and dietary information, and is the first to collect outcome data for more than one family member. Participant’s weekly sales data will be obtained through the retailer’s loyalty card scheme and will cover 3 months before refurbishment, plus 0-6 months post intervention. Change in women’s fresh fruit and vegetable purchasing from baseline to 6 months is the primary outcome. Secondary outcome data about women's diets, their young child's diet (2-6 years), food shopping habits, perceptions of supermarket environment, and psychosocial and demographic characteristics will be collected by telephone survey before refurbishment, and 1, 3 and 6 months after. Weekly sales data for study stores will be provided by the retailer. Cost-effectiveness will be assessed from individual, retailer and societal perspectives. Process evaluation will assess intervention implementation, mechanisms of impact and context. Public health benefits: Our study is politically and scientifically important being one of the first field studies of this kind. The findings could provide strong evidence for future public health policy interventions to help address inequalities in diet and NCD risk by supporting development of a healthy store layout that could be adopted more widely in food retail outlets.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Results of a cluster randomised controlled definitive trial of a Peer-Led physical Activity iNtervention for Adolescent girls (PLAN-A)
Abstract: Design: Two-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the PLAN-A intervention. Setting: State secondary schools with Year 9 girls (aged 13-14) in greater Bristol. Target population: Girls in Year 9. School is the unit of randomisation with 20 secondary schools and 1400 pupils recruited. Randomisation will be performed by an independent statistician; 10 schools allocated to the PLAN-A intervention and 10 schools to usual care control. Intervention: The intervention comprises: (a) peer-nomination, (b) peer-supporter training and (c) peer-diffusion. Year 9 girls nominate by questionnaire, the girls in their year who are: good listeners, leaders, trustworthy and respected. The 18% most nominated girls are invited to be peer-supporters, and attend a two-day course (with top up training 5 weeks later) to develop the knowledge and confidence to promote physical activity to their peers. Training is held off-site by external trainers who attend 3 day’s training. Outcomes: Outcomes will be assessed at two time points: baseline (Yr 8 Autumn term) and follow-up (Yr 9 Autumn term, 5-6 months post-intervention). Accelerometer-assessed minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) on weekdays is the primary outcome. The following will be secondary outcomes: (a) Mean weekend minutes of MVPA, (b) Mean weekday sedentary minutes, (c) Mean weekend sedentary minutes, (d) Self-esteem. We will measure potential mediators of any intervention effect, aligned with the intervention’s theoretical basis. Resource use, including intervention materials, venue costs, trainer and pupil time, expenses and administration costs will be collected. Process evaluation: Process evaluation will examine: (a) intervention implementation and fidelity (training observations, questionnaires & interviews with trainers), (b) intervention reciept by pupils (questionnaires & focus groups with peer-supporters & non-peer supporters) and (c) intervention sustainability and roll out (interviews with school contacts & public health commissioners). Sample size: The target between-arm difference is 10 minutes of weekday MVPA (i.e., 50 minutes per week) and the 95% CI from the feasibility study suggests that this is achievable. However, recognising that smaller intervention effects may also lead to meaningful differences in health at a population level, the sample size is calculated to detect a 6-minute difference in weekday MVPA. Based on a cluster size of 70, intra-class correlation and standard deviation of weekday MVPA of 0.01 and 20 minutes respectively, 5% two-sided alpha, 90% power and inflation for 30% loss to follow up we will recruit 20 schools and 1400 pupils. Analysis: Analysis and presentation of results will adhere to CONSORT, the analysis plan will be agreed by the TSC, and registered with ISCTRN before data collection. The primary analysis will be examined on an Intention-to-Treat basis without imputation. To take account of the hierarchical data, multivariable mixed effects linear regression will estimate difference in the primary outcome for intervention vs. control, adjusting for baseline outcome scores and randomisation variables (eg. area). In a secondary analysis, we will further adjust for variables that are imbalanced at baseline. Similar analyses will be repeated for secondary outcomes. Sensitivity analyses will assess any effect of missing data using imputation methods.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: NHS Norfolk and Waveney Clinical Commissioning Group
Award_Title: Feasibility randomised controlled trial of a smoking cessation smartphone app that delivers ‘context aware’ behavioural support in real time
Abstract: Background Three million UK smokers try to quit each year, but over 80% relapse. Any smoking (lapse) early in a quit attempt is associated with a greatly reduced chance of success. Almost half of lapses are due to cravings brought about by a cue from the environment e.g., from learned associations or the presence of other smokers. Few interventions are effective at targeting cue-induced cravings. Smokers are far less likely to lapse when they use a lapse prevention strategy e.g., using self-talk or avoiding other smokers, to avoid or manage cue-induced cravings but few are skilled in applying these. If smokers trying to quit used effective lapse prevention strategies, this would very likely increase their chances of success. With Patient and Public Involvement (PPI), we developed, refined and piloted a theory-guided smartphone app (Quit Sense, formally known as Q Sense) that provides support to help smokers manage environmental cues to smoke as they arise. The app identifies high-risk situations using a learning tool and location sensing. Two pilot studies have shown that Quit Sense can provide ‘in the moment’ support to smokers, including lapse prevention strategies, and that this is engaged with and is acceptable. The next phase of evaluation is to undertake a feasibility randomised controlled trial (RCT) to inform a definitive effectiveness RCT. Research question: Can an RCT of a smoking cessation smartphone app (Quit Sense) be feasibly delivered among an online population of smokers? Aims and objectives 1. Make minor optimisations to Quit Sense to improve the user interface, energy efficiency and method for selecting support message delivery 2. Conduct a feasibility RCT of Quit Sense to inform a definitive effectiveness trial, by estimating: a. Smoking outcome completion b. Usual care arm cessation rate c. Recruitment cost d. Rates of app installation, use and support delivery fidelity e. Completion of health economics-related data f. Participant views of the app (qualitative) g. Intervention effect on smoking behaviour h. Intervention effect on hypothesised mechanisms of action Methods A two arm RCT allocating 160 smokers recruited via online adverts on Google and Facebook to a ‘usual care’ arm (link to NHS SmokeFree website) or a ‘usual care’ plus Quit Sense arm. Enrolment, randomisation and baseline data collection will take place on the study website. Outcomes will be collected at 6 weeks and 6 months follow-up via the study website or telephone, and during app usage. The data will enable us to estimate key feasibility outcomes, the preliminary behavioural impact of Quit Sense, an estimate of cost-effectiveness, in addition to insights on user views of the app through interviews. Timeline M1-4: App optimisation and trial set up; M5-20: Recruitment and follow up; M21-24: Analysis, output completion and dissemination Impact and dissemination This trial will produce essential data to inform a definitive trial of Quit Sense which, if effective, could be offered to smokers outside the NHS to help address a key support gap. Quit Sense is highly scalable, could be combined with most other type of cessation support and could be highly cost-effective. Dissemination via presentations, publications, online articles, press releases, social media and public events will be supported by PPI contributors.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Individually randomised controlled multi-centre trial to determine the clinical and cost effectiveness of an adapted yoga programme for older adults with multimorbidity, including an embedded process evaluation
Abstract: Aim: We will address the NIHR Themed Call on Complex Health and Care Needs in Older People, with a focus on Theme 4: promoting healthy ageing/preventing ill health. We propose a randomised controlled trial in 12 sites across the UK to understand the health effects and cost effectiveness of a 12-week yoga programme adapted for older adults who have complex health needs. NIHR defines complex health needs as the presence of more than one health or social care need (impacting on health) as well as a depth of need in terms of the severity of the conditions or intensity of the needs. The definition of multimorbidity adopted is the existence of two or more chronic health disorders in one individual. The Need: One of the biggest challenges facing healthcare is the presence of complex health needs in the rapidly expanding older population. Research studies have shown that people with complex health needs are more likely to have reduced physical function, quality of life and life expectancy and increased mental health concerns. The more health problems someone has the more likely they are to consult a GP, be prescribed drugs and be admitted to hospital. Treatments associated with long-term health conditions account for 70% of NHS expenditure. Guidelines highlight that further research is needed to identify cost-effective treatments for this patient group. The proposed benefits of regular yoga practice are wide-ranging, including increased strength, flexibility, balance and quality of life, and reduced stress, anxiety and depression. Research suggests that yoga may improve physical function and quality of life in older people, but little work has been done to understand the effects of yoga in older people with complex health needs. Background: A 2016 pilot study of the British Wheel of Yoga (BWY) Gentle Years Yoga© programme was conducted with 52 older adults (average age 75). Adaptations to common yoga poses were developed so that inactive older adults with long-term conditions such as osteoarthritis, high blood pressure and dementia could safely participate in and reap the benefits of chair-based yoga. Recruitment was easy. The study showed that yoga could be a potentially useful treatment for improving mobility as well as mental and social wellbeing. It is simple, cheap, non-invasive, and can benefit several health conditions. Public Involvement: Most of the participants continued in the classes on a self-pay basis after the pilot ended, which confirmed that they found the programme to be of value. They have been actively involved in the proposed trial’s plans and they are committed to continuing their support and help with the project. Methods: The trial will recruit 586 adults aged 65 years or over who have more than one long-term condition. After initial assessments, participants will be allocated either to a group that receives usual care and a 12-week yoga programme (involving weekly group-based sessions and self-managed home practice) or a group that receives usual care only. Participants will complete questionnaires after 3, 6 and 12 months to assess their progress. This will involve assessments of quality of life and mental health. Some participants and yoga tutors will be interviewed to determine their experiences of the programme and study processes. Dissemination: The research findings will be written up in journal publications and evidence briefings, and presented at various forums and conferences.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Strengthening the Implementation and Operationalisation of ‘Open Disclosure’ with Women and Families after Unexpected Harm in NHS Maternity Care
Abstract: Open disclosure [OD], the discussion of harm in healthcare with affected patients or families, is a patient or family entitlement. It may also enhance learning for safety improvement, reduce the distress of those harmed and increase public trust in healthcare. There is often a significant gap between what patients and families want from OD and what clinicians or organisations provide. There are complex barriers to OD: fear of litigation and loss of reputation; lack of skills and effective systems. Despite the legal duty of candour on NHS organisations, disparities in OD between trusts are notable. NHS maternity services are central to policy reform and under public pressure to improve OD. There is limited understanding of how maternity providers can achieve this. This study will examine what improvements are being made, how and their felt effects. AIMS: 1.to generate actionable evidence to inform maternity providers and NHS trusts on how to strengthen Open Disclosure in NHS maternity services; 2. to collaborate in the production of outputs to support improvements in OD for the benefit of women and families, staff teams and quality and safety of maternity care. RESEARCH QUESTION: ‘what are the critical factors that can improve the incidence and quality of Open Disclosure in NHS maternity care?’ METHODOLOGY: a realist evaluation to identify the critical factors that contribute to improvements in OD. Approaching OD improvement as a complex social intervention, the evaluation will explore what assumptions underlie these approaches and examine ‘what works, for whom, in what circumstances, in why respects and why’. This approach will establish a transferable theory of critical factors for improving OD. STUDY PLAN: The 36-month, three-phased research plan is: Phase 1 [Months 1-21] to establish working hypotheses of OD improvement and to refine these hypotheses by realist review of the international literature and telephone interviews with national and regional stakeholders [n=60]; Phase 2 [Months 22-30] construct three ethnographic case studies using the methods of observation; return staff interview (with managers, clinicians, administrators, and women/family representatives [n=48]); and documentary analysis of records of OD improvements in the three purposively selected services, trusts or networks to further refine or revise our hypotheses; Phase 3 [Months 29-36], to include 6 interpretive forums for study participants to make sense of findings and advise on the design of some study outputs, and 1 summative forum for dissemination of initial findings, mutual learning and network building among study participants and policy makers. OUTPUTS: briefing documents and tailored recommendations for service, trust and organisation managers; actionable guidance on OD for staff and women and families (written and video); ongoing lay summaries of study progress and findings; in-depth understanding of process of OD improvement (mechanisms and contexts by which they are effective for different participants and service concerns); academic papers and HS&DR report. Tailored dissemination, supported by stakeholder analysis, will ensure that the study has academic and societal impact. The multi-professional/disciplinary research team have extensive experience of research and quality improvement work in OD and in maternity care. The views and interests of women and families have been, and will be, represented at all study stages.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Supporting survivors of sexual violence: a mixed methods, co-research study of the role, funding and commissioning of specialist services provided by the voluntary sector in England.
Abstract: Background The voluntary sector provides a range of specialist services to survivors of sexual violence. Although national policy increasingly highlights these services as essential in supporting survivors to recover and thrive, there is no high quality evidence to support decisions about what services should be provided to which groups of survivors, and how services should be delivered and commissioned. Sexual violence is increasing year-on-year. Many survivors experience long-term multiple negative effects on their health, wellbeing, employment and social life, with the cost to the public purse estimated at over £8billion a year. This is the first national study on the role of the voluntary sector in supporting survivors. It addresses an existing priority for the NIHR and a significant gap in the evidence. The findings will support local agencies to deliver national policy on providing lifelong support to survivors of sexual violence through the funding of high quality voluntary sector specialist (VSS) services which meet survivors’ needs. Aims and objectives To develop a comprehensive national picture of VSS services for survivors in England, giving voice to survivors’ experiences of services, comparing the range, scope and funding of services, and analysing similarities and differences in how they are delivered and commissioned, in order to make recommendations that will strengthen the service response to survivors. The objectives are to analyse: survivors’ VSS service experiences; the range, scope and funding of services; approaches to service provision; principles underpinning services; referral patterns, pathways and service linkages; commissioning arrangements; to develop a taxonomy of VSS services; and make recommendations for policy and practice. Methods This is a mixed methods research project using an explanatory sequential naturalistic design. It involves survivors as co-researchers with survivors’ experiences embedded throughout. It draws on theory about the distinctive service contribution of the voluntary sector. Stage 1 consists of two national surveys for providers and commissioners. Results will be used to develop a taxonomy of VSS services. This taxonomy will then be used to select four case study sites for stage 2, which involves in-depth qualitative interviews with survivors (n=24-48) and staff (n=68-76). Data will be synthesised to develop a rich picture of each case study site, allowing key features and contextual factors affecting VSS service provision to be identified. Gaps in service and innovative service features will also be identified. Timeline The research will run for two years ten months, with interim stage 1 results published in year 2. Anticipated impact and dissemination The research will generate evidence about what survivors want from and value about services, and new understanding about how VSS services should be commissioned and provided to support survivors to thrive. Commissioners and providers will be able to compare their local services against the national picture in order to configure services optimally. In the longer-term, improvements in survivors’ wellbeing should lead to reductions in service demands and cost. Dissemination includes: stage 1 written report and national workshop; case study site and regional workshops; good practice guides; policy briefing; project report; bite-size findings; webinars; academic articles and conference presentations.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Patient and family involvement in serious incident investigations: Developing and testing national and local guiding processes
Abstract: Aim Co-design processes to guide involvement of patients and families in serious incident investigations at a national, and local level, and to test these processes to understand their impact upon experience, learning and decisions to litigate. Background Reported serious incidents (severe harm, death) are estimated to be 10,000 annually,[1] with enormous, ever increasing costs of litigation.[2] Thus, there is a need to improve learning from serious incidents to reduce incidence, and the fiscal burden of litigation. Reasons why claims are pursued are complex and unclear.[3] NHS Resolution posit that involving patients and families earlier in investigations will reduce costs of administering claims, as well as divert claims pursued for explanation. Other policy and regulatory organisations have proposed greater involvement of patients and families in serious incident investigations, to support better learning. However, there is currently no UK-based evidence to guide organisations to involve patients and families meaningfully in serious incident investigations, to support learning, or reduce the likelihood of litigation. Objectives 1) Explore current involvement of patients and families in serious incident investigations. 2) Explore experiences of patients, families, staff and investigators, who have been involved in a serious incident, or serious incident investigation, what might have influenced decisions to litigate, and views on the potential involvement of patients and families. 3) Identify common principles to involve patients and families in investigations, and use these to co-design local and national processes for involvement. 4) Explore if processes to involve patients and families are feasible and acceptable to all stakeholders and their influence on learning, recommendations, action plans, and decisions to litigate. Methods In Stage 1 (0-6months), a documentary analysis of policies within England will explore how NHS Trusts involve patients and families in serious incident investigations. A scoping review will explore involvement of patients and families in serious incident investigations and decisions to litigate. In Stage 2 (7-15months) we will interview patients, families, investigators and staff (n=60), to support development of the programme theory underpinning the co-designed processes. Data from these stages will be integrated in Stage 2B, to guide co-design. In Stage 3 (16-21months), we will co-design three parallel processes to involve patients and families in investigations, within national (Healthcare Safety Investigation Branch: HSIB), mental health and acute care. In Stage 4 (22-34months), we will implement the prototype guidance and resources in 25 investigations across 5 organisations, conducting an ethnography to assess feasibility, and explore stakeholder experiences, impact on learning, recommendations, actions, and decisions to litigate. In Stage 5 (35-39months), the final guidance and digital platform will be produced. Impact and dissemination Commissioners, regulators and policy makers have all been consulted in preparing this proposal, and have a keen interest in the final research outputs. The HSIB are committed to using the co-designed process, and will role model this usage for the wider NHS. We plan to disseminate widely, to a variety of audiences, through eight academic publications, two policy-facing reports, and the key research output – the co-designed guidance on a digital platform.

Contractor: King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Frame Fit. A randomised controlled trial to determine the acceptability, safety and efficacy of a falls prevention exercise programme for walking frame users.
Abstract: Background Older people often start to use a walking aid as mobility, strength and functional ability declines. This may be related to a specific pathology or to more generalised frailty13. There is evidence that using a walking frame increases the risk of falling more than can be explained by the balance deficits which initiate frame use11. Exercise which include highly challenging balance training for at least 6 months, effectively prevent falls14. However, despite the increased risk associated with frame use, no trials have targeted frame users with a fall prevention exercise intervention addressing the unique challenges facing walking frame users. The frame fit study is a randomised controlled trial investigating the safety, acceptability and efficacy of a home based exercise programme for frame users. The primary outcome measure will be falls in the following year. Method Two hundred and forty participants will be recruited from King's College hospital and local GP practices if they are regular walking frame users, aged over 65 and able to complete the falls dairy and home exercise programme satisfactorily. Baseline demographics, functional ability (Barthel index15) and cognition (Addenbrooke's Cognitive Examination [ACE-R]16) will be measured and assessment of balance (standing balance rating scale 17), strength (grip strength and sit to stand 17), gait (6m walk and timed up and go18), physical activity (IPEC questionnaire19), frailty (frailty index20), fear of falling (iconographical FES-I21) and quality of life (EQ5D22) will be undertaken at baseline and 6-month follow up. In addition to this, participants will keep a diary for 1 year recording any falls and fall related injuries they sustain in that period.Participants will be randomised to either receive the intervention or usual care. The intervention involves a physiotherapist visiting the participant for 7 sessions over a 3 month period with telephone follow up and a final visit at 6 months. The physiotherapist will teach, monitor and progress a programme of home exercises designed to address challenges that frame users experience. Exercises will involve practice manoeuvring the frame, work on safe transfers using the frame and addressing dynamic balance required when it is necessary to let go of the frame. Exercises will be individually tailored and progressive aiming for the participant to carry out the programme 3 times each week. Data analysis After 6-month follow up, differences in the measures of balance, walking, fear of falling, quality of life, physical activity and frailty from baseline to follow up will be compared between the intervention and usual care group using univariate analyses - paired t-tests and Chi square tests for contingency tables. An intention-to-treat approach will be used for all analyses. Significance will be set at P Following completion of the 1 year follow up for falls and injuries, data will be analysed using negative binomial regression analysis to determine differences in fall rates between the intervention and control groups. Health care costs resulting from falls in both groups and costs of delivering the intervention will be collected to conduct economic analysis at a later date. Outputs Findings will be disseminated using academic journals and conference presentations. If the intervention is effective the programme resources will be made available to physiotherapists to enable it to be widely used as part of a tailored approach to falls prevention within the general population.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The impact of malnutrition on patient-centred outcomes and health and social care resources in elderly people accessing healthcare services in the community
Abstract: One million people aged over 65 years are malnourished or at risk of malnutrition1. The vast majority live in the community yet there is a lack of studies evaluating the effects of community-based nutritional interventions2. Malnutrition has widespread adverse effects on the body and in the presence of illness results in delayed recovery, poor quality of life and increased risk of death, yet evaluation of nutrition interventions has tended to focus mainly on achieving weight gain3. Little is known about which other outcomes may be important to nutritionally vulnerable patients and so this project is designed to undertake preliminary work in this area. The aims of this project are: 1. To establish which outcomes are most important to older people accessing healthcare services in the community 2. To design and test the validity of a patient reported outcome measure (PROM) for nutritionally vulnerable individuals who might benefit from nutritional intervention 3. To determine the impact of malnutrition on patient-centred outcomes and health and social care resources in older people accessing healthcare services in the community The project will be conducted using a mixed methods approach including a systematic review and both qualitative and quantitative components. A systematic review will be undertaken to identify valid, reliable and sensitive outcome tools e.g. quality of life questionnaires that might be suitable for use in patients receiving nutritional intervention. A portfolio of tools will be compiled and a series of focus groups will be run for older people accessing healthcare services in the community to identify which outcome tools are most preferred by participants and to identify any other outcomes they consider to be important. Since a significant proportion of the target group are likely to be housebound, data generated during the focus groups will be used to inform the design of a semi-structured interview to be undertaken in a participant's home or over the phone. Data generated by the systematic review and the qualitative studies will be used to design a PROM for use in nutritionally vulnerable individuals requiring nutritional intervention. The construct and content validity of the PROM will be tested by a multi-disciplinary expert group. Face validity will be tested by patients and carers. The predictive validity and reliability of the PROM will be tested as part of a cohort study designed to determine the impact of malnutrition on patient-centred outcomes and health and social care resources. The cohort study will be conducted in 300 community-based older people accessing healthcare services. Participants will be recruited in a number of settings including intermediate care units, GP surgeries and health centres. After giving informed consent (assent will be sought if the person lacks the capacity to give informed consent) data will be collected at baseline and 12 months either in the care unit or in the participant's own home. An interim assessment at 6 months will be conducted over the phone. Data will be collected on nutrition risk status, clinical condition, social and functional status and quality of life. All participants will be asked to consent to data being collected electronically relating to any hospital and A&E admissions, GP visits and health and social care packages they receive during the 12 months of the study. Participants will be categorised at baseline according to their nutrition risk score (high, medium or low risk) and statistical and health economic analyses will be undertaken to determine if there are any significant differences in outcome i.e. health and social care costs, quality of life and mortality, between the low, medium or high nutrition risk categories.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Implementation optimisation and pilot cluster randomised controlled trial of HENRY, a community based programme aimed at preventing obesity in pre-school children
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Rising rates of obesity in preschool children are alarming and emphasise the need for evidence-based approaches to prevent obesity, which can be successfully implemented in communities. Although robust, theory-based prevention programmes exist, it is often a challenge to get parents to attend them and adopt positive behaviour changes in their families. OBJECTIVES: Proposed research consists of two work packages (WP) aiming to 1) optimise the implementation of an obesity prevention programme 'HENRY' via development and testing of a 'Step-up' intervention to support local authorities (LAs) to improve parent engagement (recruitment, attendance) and enhance positive behaviour changes in families; and 2) to determine the practicability of undertaking a full trial to evaluate an optimised 'HENRY' in a pilot RCT with the intent of conducting a definitive trial to test its effectiveness and cost-effectiveness on obesity prevention in future work. HENRY is an 8-week programme currently commissioned across 32 local authorities and delivered in Children's Centres (CCs), combining authoritative parenting skills with practical support to improve family lifestyle behaviours. WP1 DESIGN: Four studies incorporating quantitative and qualitative methodologies utilising routine data. METHODS: Study1: Analysis of existing data from CCs which deliver HENRY to identify those consistently engaging parents and reporting positive family behaviour change (positive deviants) and those failing to engage and support parents. Study 2: Ethnography study, including direct observations of CCs and interviews with stakeholders, to identify barriers and levers to successful implementation.Study 3: Development of the 'Step-up' intervention to optimise the impact of HENRY, underpinned by strong theories of behaviour change. Intervention components may range from provision of support to LAs to improve infrastructure through to providing extra support to parents to attend and successfully make changes to family lifestyle. Study 4: Cluster RCT recruiting 24 LAs and 96 CCs to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the Step-up intervention on improvements to implementation within LAs already running HENRY. LAs will be randomised to Step-up or standard HENRY and routine data on parent recruitment, attendance and child consumption of fruits and vegetables will be used as outcomes. Commissioners will be asked to state their 'willingness-to-pay' for the additional Step-up based on proportional improvements in the programme implementation. WP2 DESIGN: A pilot cluster RCT preceding a definitive trial to test the clinical effectiveness and cost effectiveness of 'HENRY' to prevent preschool obesity. METHODS: CCs with no history of running HENRY will be randomised to receive either HENRY (+ Step-up as appropriate) or continue standard practice (no intervention). Twelve CCs across 2 LAs will be recruited, from which data will be collected by blinded researchers from 120 parents (60/arm). Eligible parents will have at least 1 child aged 1-5 years. Pilot outcomes include: CC and parent recruitment; training competencies; process evaluation; feasibility and acceptability of trial procedures; and sample size for definitive trial. Data will be collected at baseline (pre-randomisation for CC/pre programme initiation for parents) and follow-up (12 months post-parent consent (CC and parents)). Descriptive analysis will provide 95% confidence intervals for estimates. A funding application will be submitted for the definitive trial if indicated by the pilot study. EXPECTED OUTCOMES/ONGOING IMPROVEMENT TO HEALTH If effective, HENRY will offer extensive benefit to health, including reduced preschool obesity, improved nutrition/eating behaviours in children, healthier family lifestyles and enhanced parenting skills; reducing related morbidity and mortality. Proposed research is imperative to the NHS as it will ultimately provide an evidence-based approach to prevent childhood obesity which is attractive to all stakeholders, including parents. This has expressed need, not just for obesity prevention, but also to support costs of a programme that has already incurred much spending.

Award_Title: Unprotected anal sex and HIV negative / untested gay men: A qualitative descriptive study
Abstract: Unprotected Anal Sex (UAS) is common among Men who have Sex with Men (MSM) and carries significant health risks. The objective of this study is to explore HIV negative and untested MSMs experiences of UAS with the aim of generating new understanding of this complex nest of issues at the heart of sexuality, erotic practices and intimacy. By using a systematic review of contemporary academic and gay literature, web-based survey, focus groups and semi-structured interviews the data will be analysed through thematic analysis. The anticipated benefit of this is to significantly contribute to HIV prevention.

Award_Title: The Barkantine Birth Centre (BaBC): an ethnographic study of the philosophy, culture and practice in a freestanding urban midwife-led unit.
Abstract: Objective: To explore the culture, philosophy and practice within a freestanding midwifery-led birth centre. Research Design: Ethnographic study.Expected Outcomes: Evaluation of the impact of the BaBC on service users, families and staff. To explore issues such as: risk, safety, decision making and choice. Shed light on the transfer system and the relationship between the BaBC and the Acute Trust.Anticipated Benefits: It will contribute to the development of midwifery practice and theory. Service users’ choices and experiences will be explored. Health and safety will be enhanced by looking at the accessibility and delivery of care as well as shed light on the system for transferring women, who develop obstetric complications during labour, to the acute unit.In addition commisioners and managers of maternity services will benefit from understanding this new model of care.

Award_Title: Characterisation, determinants, mechanisms and consequences of the long-term effects of COVID-19: providing the evidence base for health care services
Abstract: Long-term health consequences of C-19 (long-COVID) occur frequently. Most infections are not hospitalised; population studies are the place to understand individual and societal challenges of long-COVID. We will address the following questions: How do we define and diagnose the sub-phenotypes of long-COVID? What are the predictors of long-COVID, and what are the mechanisms of the sub-phenotypes? What are the long-term health (physical and mental), and socioeconomic consequences? What factors enhance recovery? What is the level of GP adherence to NICE diagnosis and management guidelines? Can a pop-up tool in medical records enhance adherence? We have an established consortium of experts and platforms uniting linked national primary care registries and population cohorts. The national coverage of primary care registries captures all individuals presenting to their GP, with linked prescribing, consulting, referral and outcome data. Many with long-COVID do not seek care. Population cohorts, with repeat C-19 related questionnaires, overcome this limitation. Further, the standardised pre-pandemic health data enables dissection of the effects of infection versus progression of co-morbidity. Questionnaires will identify long-COVID cases across cohorts. A subgroup of 200 cases will be matched to three sets of controls (C-19 +, long-COVID-), (C-19-, long-COVID+), and (C-19-, long-COVID-). They will wear a device capturing exercise capacity, heart rate and respiration, and complete regular online questionnaires on mental health and cognition. They will attend clinic for imaging to assess target organ damage. Qualitative work with people with long-COVID will inform diagnostic criteria and understanding of the lived experience. Parallel analysis of cohorts and registries will address each question. With NICE, we will quantify adherence to diagnostic and management guidelines in GP records, and pilot a pop-up intervention to enhance adherence. Our findings will enhance diagnostic criteria, identify pathways for bespoke sub-phenotype intervention, and inform plans for health service delivery.

Award_Title: Non-hospitalised Children & young people (CYP) with Long Covid (The CLoCk Study)
Abstract: Uncertainties relate to diagnosis, prevalence, duration and treatment of post-COVID syndrome ( long COVID ) in children and young people (CYP). There is no diagnostic test nor definition for long COVID. We do not know the physical, psychological and social consequences of long COVID and we need to define the clinical phenotype and longer-term physical/physiological/psychological changes to target therapeutic interventions. Risk factors for acute COVID include: obesity, pre-existing co-morbidities, learning and neurological disabilities, mental health (MH) problems, BAME status. The CYP likely to be most at risk of long COVID are teenagers as they represent the majority of CYP pre-COVID with persistent physical and MH symptoms post-viral infection. Ludwigsson (2020) reported five COVID positive CYP with median age 12 yrs with symptoms longer than 6 months. The research questions: To describe the clinical phenotype of post-COVID symptomatology in test-positive CYP, using test-negative comparators Use these data to produce an operational definition of long COVID, necessary for any future epidemiological or interventional study Use this definition to establish the prevalence and natural course of long COVID in CYP to inform NHS services and health policy HYPOTHESIS: the type, prevalence and trajectory of symptoms in COVID positive CYP will differ significantly from the comparator group, allowing us to construct an operational definition of long COVID. We plan a longitudinal cohort study of non-hospitalised CYP aged 11-17 yrs. We will approach 30,000 CYP, half of whom with proven COVID. We expect 6,000 to consent to help us. We will ask them whether they still have physical or mental health problems at 3, 6,12 and 24 months afterwards. The 3,000 CYP with a positive SARS-CoV-2 tests will be compared with 3,000 test-negative controls. DELIVERABLES: we will access large numbers with proven COVID quickly to generate early outputs to inform future intervention studies and health policy.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Understanding the factors that influence why people with dementia make transitions from the community to acute hospital care settings in the last months of life: a retrospective cohort study (Project U-Care)
Abstract: Background Transition from community settings into hospital is common for people with severe dementia, but can have profoundly deleterious physical and cognitive consequences. The concept of 'burdensome transitions' has been introduced to describe potentially harmful transitions between care settings for people with advanced dementia. These are defined as (i) multiple hospitalisations in the last 90 days of life, or (ii) a transition in the last 3 days, or (iii) a lack of continuity between care homes before and after hospitalisation. In the United Kingdom little is known about the frequency of burdensome transitions among people with dementia or the reasons for these, hampering development of effective health policies. Aim To determine the relative individual, illness-related, and environmental factors associated with burdensome transitions for people with dementia in their last year of life, to inform effective public health policies to improve care towards the end of life for this growing population. Methods Study design Retrospective cohort study, with data linkage. Study population People with dementia, aged over 60, who died between 01/01/2001 and 31/12/2013. The population will be identified from the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust (SLAM) Biomedical Research Centre (BRC) Case Register. Data sources The study will use two levels of routinely collected data: a) Individual level data obtained from three sources: the SLAM BRC Case Register, with individual linkage to Office for National Statistics (ONS) mortality data, and Hospital Episodes Statistics (HES) activity for the 12 months preceding death. b) Area-level data including: information on service provision derived from various sources; socio-economic position derived using the Index of Multiple Deprivation (2010); geographic area mapping to determine proximity of patients' place of residence to healthcare facilities. Data analysis Primary outcome - The primary outcome will be burdensome transitions. Explanatory variables - Explanatory variables will be based on a theoretical model informed by the work of Gomes and Higginson (2006). This will include individual, illness-related and environmental factors. Descriptive analysis -h; The number of healthcare transitions during the last year of life (including burdensome transitions, out of hours transitions), hospital bed days, Emergency Department admissions, place of residence, and site of death will be described for the total population. Statistical modelling - Statistical modelling will be used to understand how individual-level and area-level factors interact to contribute to burdensome transitions. Poisson regression will be used to determine Proportion Ratios (PR) for burdensome transitions, which will be modelled as a binary variable. Economic analysis - NHS costs for the last year of life will be described for the whole population using estimates from Healthcare Resource Group codes derived from HES and NHS reference costs. The relationship between burdensome transitions and costs will be explored through univariate and multivariate linear regression modelling. The dependent variable will be total NHS costs in the last 90 days, modelled as a continuous variable. Generalised linear models will be used if the data are skewed. All analyses will be done using Stata. Benefits to patients and NHS Dementia is the commonest cause of death for women in the United Kingdom, and improving care for people with dementia as they approach the end of their life is a national priority. Transitions between health care settings for people with dementia are common towards the end of life, but are associated with morbidity and mortality. Reducing the use of hospital-based care in advanced dementia also has potential economic benefits. This study will provide high quality evidence on the factors associated with transition between healthcare settings for people with dementia, and the associated costs, to inform health policies that aim to improve care for this growing population.
