Award_Title: Improving access to high quality primary care for socio-economically disadvantaged older people in rural areas: a mixed method study
Abstract: Nine million people live in rural areas of England, of whom one in five is over 65 years old. In rural areas, the population of over 85 year olds is the fastest growing age group. Poverty is high in older rural people with a sixth of rural pensioners living below the poverty threshold (below 60% of median income). Access to primary care for rural older people is challenging with one in five living more than 4km from their GP practice and one in three not having access to a car. A review of equality of access to healthcare in the UK found that rural individuals, older people and those in lower socio-economic groups have reduced access to healthcare. There is likely to be a compounding effect when these co-exist. Poor access leads to preventable health inequalities, and increased use of urgent care services including unplanned hospital admissions. The aim of this study is to develop an intervention to improve access to high-quality primary care in socio-economically disadvantaged older people in rural areas and undertake a feasibility study of the intervention. The research questions are: What are the barriers to accessing high-quality primary care for socio-economically disadvantaged older people in rural areas and what are the underlying mechanisms? How and why do patient-side (e.g. social isolation, immobility) and provider-side (e.g. appointment booking system) access barriers interact to affect quality of care and clinical outcomes? What intervention will best improve access to high-quality primary care for socio-economically disadvantaged older people in rural areas? What information is needed to design the definitive RCT for this intervention? Stage 1 aims to understand the barriers, and their interactions, to accessing high-quality primary care in this group (research question 1+2). This will involve a) undertaking a rapid realist review, b) analysing the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing and c) discussing with patients, clinicians and commissioners in focus groups and semi-structured interviews. Evidence gathered from Stage 1 will be synthesised using a realist perspective. Stage 2 will include intervention development (question 3) and a feasibility study, to be called the 'Enhancing Older People's Access to Care (E-OPAC)' study (question 4). From an initial scoping review and patient and public engagement the intervention may involve the following three components, 1) creation of a risk register of older people that may have poor access based on distance, deprivation and healthcare use, 2) two nurse telephone consultations for individuals on the register aiming to re-engage them with primary care, identify problems early, provide solutions and discuss crisis management and 3) a community access advisor focused on supporting individuals with social barriers, such as lack of transport, and providing user feedback to GP practices. The six-month E-OPAC feasibility study will be a cluster randomised controlled trial of eight practices (research question 4). Four will be randomised to the intervention and four to usual care. The feasibility study will test randomisation, recruitment, intervention, implementation and outcome measures. The outcome measures will be based on Maxwell's six quality of care measures and include established quality indicators (primary outcome), number of consultations, patient reported ease of access, unplanned hospital admissions and costs. This research has the potential to improve access to primary care for some of the most vulnerable people in society. Through improving access and engagement with primary care, it is expected that patients will contact primary care at an earlier stage to facilitate early management. This will improve patient health, narrow health inequalities and reduce use of urgent care services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: HPV vaccination in the UK - what next? A model-based exploration and analysis
Abstract: Background Persistent infection with Human Papillomavirus (HPV), a family of > 100 virus types, is a necessary precursor to cervical cancer and a risk factor in other cancers such as orpharyngeal, penile and anal cancers. Two types, HPV-16 and HPV-18, account for >70% of invasive cervical cancer. Since 2008 all 12-13 year old girls (and some older girls and women) in Britain have been offered a 3-dose course of a vaccine which protects against HPV-16 and -18 and, since 2012, the two types that cause most genital warts. HPV vaccination policy in Britain was informed by mathematical and economic modelling, which incorporated uncertainty about the properties of the two licensed vaccines e.g. duration and profile of vaccine protection and the extent of cross-protection against non-vaccine types. Since resultant cost-effectiveness estimates were sensitive to these assumptions, they too were bounded by large uncertainty ranges. Recently additional evidence on the efficacy and cross-protection of existing vaccines has become available, as has new data on UK sexual behaviour and vaccine uptake. Furthermore, a new nine-valent vaccine is currently undergoing phase III clinical trials. These advances in understanding and technology precipitate a continuing review of UK vaccination policy and my overall aim is to develop and use an individual-based model to answer 'second-generation' questions about the impact and cost-effectiveness of HPV vaccination e.g. whether to reduce from a 3-dose to a 2-dose regimen, introduce the new nine-valent vaccine or extend vaccination to boys or older women. Aims and plans 1. Estimate the duration and profile of protection offered by the two licensed HPV vaccines, using novel data from large community-randomised and observational studies and published data from vaccine trial cohorts and immunogenicity studies.2. Develop a type-specific individual-based mathematical model of HPV infection and diseases and fit this to data on sexual behaviour, HPV prevalence and cervical cancer using cutting-edge statistical methods. 3. Use model-based inference techniques to explore a) the extent of vaccine cross-protection and b) the rate of progression of HPV to non-cervical cancers. These are both issues which affect vaccine impact and cost-effectiveness. 4. Use the individual-based model to estimate the potential population-level impact of the nine-valent vaccine, calculating the reduction in incidence of HPV infection (by type), neoplasia and cervical cancer compared with the existing vaccines for different assumptions of vaccine coverage, efficacy and age of vaccination. 5. Conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis to estimate the cost per Quality-Adjusted Life Year gained by using the nine-valent vaccine, compared with current and alternative vaccination policies. 6. Incorporate my findings on duration of vaccine protection, cross-protection and non-cervical cancer progression to investigate alternative UK vaccination strategies. This will include an evaluation of two-dose schedules and the extension of vaccination to boys or older women, comparing the impact and effectiveness of the two licensed vaccines and the forthcoming nine-valent vaccine. Potential benefits This research is concerned with the optimisation of vaccination policy and therefore may potentially bring large-scale benefits to vaccinated individuals and to others through indirect (herd-immunity) protection. Mathematical modelling and economic analyses are used to inform all vaccine-related decisions. Using new data on duration of vaccine protection, sexual behaviour, vaccine coverage and HPV risk, and considering the new nine-valent vaccine, I shall be able to make updated recommendations on optimal strategy for reducing HPV-related cervical and non-cervical disease in the most cost-effective manner.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Improving communication between patients and healthcare staff: Development and feasibility study of a behaviour change intervention
Abstract: BackgroundIncreasing numbers of people live with multimorbidity, including half of those aged 65+. These patients may be prescribed multiple medications, and have unmet needs and difficulties accessing and interacting with healthcare services (Goodwin et al., 2011; Hobbs et al., 2015). Such factors mean older people with multimorbidity are more likely to experience patient safety incidents.Initial findings from a longitudinal, qualitative study suggest many safety incidents arise because of gaps in communication between patients and healthcare staff (Daker-White et al., 2014). Communication issues can leave patients feeling dehumanised and disempowered, and threaten their safety (Coyle, 1999; Rhodes et al., 2016).Street et al. (2005) explored differences in how often patients express concerns and ask questions in consultations. These communication behaviours were found to be predominately patient-initiated, suggesting patient-orientated interventions could empower them to communicate more effectively, and improve safety.A systematic review identified three such interventions for older people (Wetzels et al., 2007). These had positive but inconclusive results, and there continues to be a lack of high-quality research in this area. Furthermore, no such intervention has been developed for older people with multimorbidity (hereinafter referred to as patients), who could benefit most. AimsI intend to address this gap by planning, designing, and developing a brief behaviour change intervention to empower patients to improve their patient safety, by helping them communicate more effectively with staff. I will then carry out a feasibility study to see if a trial of the intervention's effectiveness is possible.I will answer four research questions: What methods of communication are effective for and acceptable to patients, and which effective methods do patients underuse and why? What format and content would be suitable for a behaviour change intervention to empower patients to communicate more effectively with staff? What would enhance the usability and acceptability of this intervention? Would it be feasible to carry out a definitive trial to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of this intervention?Plan of investigationI will follow a theory-, evidence-, and person-based approach to plan, design, develop, and trial an intervention that addresses patients' needs (Yardley et al., 2015). Stage 1: Planning Qualitative synthesis: Use meta-ethnography to synthesise qualitative studies of communication in primary care, and explore what patients' find acceptable and helpful.Qualitative research: Review pre-recorded primary care consultations, and interview 16 patients and 9 staff to explore what effective communication behaviours are underused and why. Analyse data in the context of a framework for understanding behaviour (Michie et al., 2013). Stage 2: Design Define key objectives for the intervention, using data from stage 1.Identify suitable ways and techniques to achieve these objectives, using established methods (Michie et al., 2014).Design the intervention. Stage 3: Development and evaluation of acceptability Think-aloud study: Observe 16 patients and 9 staff using the intervention.Modify the intervention in response to findings to make it more acceptable and useable. Stage 4: Implementation and trialling Feasibility study: Deliver the intervention to 4 general practices and 48 patients to determine whether it is feasible to recruit participants, collect and analyse data, and deliver the intervention in practice.Process evaluation: Interview 16 patients and 9 staff to explore the acceptability of study procedures. Potential benefitsPatients and staff will be consulted throughout the study, and patients will be directly involved in the design and development of the intervention (stages 2 and 3). This will ensure the study is understandable and appealing, and the developed intervention is acceptable and useful.The proposed intervention has the potential to empower patients, improve communication with staff, increase satisfaction with care, and improve patient safety.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: What impact has regulation had on the quality of care in general practice? Lessons from general practice inspections, reports, and ratings.
Abstract: Background: Since October 2014 the Care Quality Commission (CQC) inspects GP practices in England, publishing a report and rating. By April 2017 all GP practices will have been inspected and rated for the first time. Up to 15% (1200) of these will have received an 'inadequate' or 'requires improvement' rating.Regulatory inspections of general practice with public reporting represents a major national policy intervention. It has utilised an estimated £60 million, in CQC and GP practice related costs, but has generated significant resistance. Claims have been made that it is unhelpful to quality improvement, particularly in underperforming practices.However, evidence on the impact of inspections is scarce, and the factors which contribute to their effectiveness or otherwise have not been fully investigated. Current evidence on the relationship between inspections, public reporting and quality improvement in healthcare is largely from hospital settings, which are distinct from GP practices.Aims: I aim to address the following:Q1. What is already known about the role and impact of inspections in general practice organisations; specifically, what works, for whom, in what context, how and why?Q2. Using mixed-methods: Q2a. What GP practice related characteristics are associated with the initial overall CQC rating? Why and how does this association exist in GP practices rated 'inadequate' or 'requires improvement'? Q2b. What GP practice related characteristics are associated with the improvement or otherwise in overall CQC rating on re-inspection? Why and how does this association exist in GP practices rated 'inadequate' or 'requires improvement'? Q2c. Can impacts from CQC inspections, reports and ratings be detected across different measures of quality, and from the perspectives of different stakeholders? Have any impacts detected been sustained? Why and how do these impacts occur in GP practices rated 'inadequate' or 'requires improvement'? Q3. What lessons can be drawn from the answers to Q1 and Q2 for quality assurance and quality improvement in general practice?Plan of investigation: The project will have three work-streams which will produce five peer-reviewed papers, summaries and recommendations for stakeholder groups, and a PhD thesis. There will be patient, public and other stakeholder involvement throughout. This aims to enable collaborative enquiry and reflection, to ensure the ongoing relevance, effective dissemination, and implementation of findings.Work-stream I (Q1) A realist review of the literature using RAMESES guidelines (Paper 1). Work-stream II (Q2a,b&c) Quantitative Bi-variate/multi-variate analyses to identify associations between GP practice characteristics and initial CQC rating in all GP practices (Paper 2). Bi-variate/multi-variate analyses to identify associations between GP practice characteristics and ability to improve or otherwise CQC rating on re-inspection in all GP practices (Paper 2). Interrupted-time-series analyses to identify changes associated with CQC inspection and different measures of quality of care in all GP practices (Paper 3). Qualitative Focus group discussion with patients, GPs, and practice staff at six purposefully selected GP practices rated 'inadequate' or 'requires improvement', and interviews with local GP leaders. (Paper 4). Work-stream III (Q3) Findings from work-streams I and II will be brought together, to provide lessons and recommendations (Paper 5). Anticipated benefits to patients, the public and NHS: Understanding the impact of inspections and public reporting on the quality of general practice, and the factors which enabled quality improvement or otherwise, in particular, in poorly performing practices where patient care is considered at highest risk, is necessary to inform evidence-based policy and practice.Patients will benefit as findings will help improve the quality of care they receive by shaping how quality assurance and quality improvement are undertaken in general practice. The NHS will benefit through the development of more effective mechanisms to quality assure general practice and support quality improvement.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Rapid HIV testing in the dental setting: an acceptability and feasibility study.
Abstract: Title Rapid HIV testing in the dental setting: an acceptability and feasibility study. The Problem In 2014, Public Health England estimated that 103,700 people in the UK were living with HIV. The overall prevalence being 1.9/1000 (Public Health England, 2015). Around 17% of people living with HIV were unaware of their serostatus and around 40% were diagnosed at a late stage when CD4 counts have already dipped below 350. Late diagnosis is particularly problematic in heterosexual groups, older people over the age of 50, and other ethnic minority groups, in particular Black Africans (Centre for Public Health, 2014). If diagnosis is achieved earlier in the course of the condition it can reduce transmission as well as HIV related morbidity and mortality. Rationale Almost 30 million patients attended a dentist in the UK between 2013 and 2015, equivalent to over 55% of the population. NICE (2016) encouraged opportunistic screening in primary and secondary care settings in extremely high HIV prevalence areas (diagnosed adult prevalence of 5/1000); dental settings based in these areas could be ideal locations to implement HIV testing.Existing studies have investigated patient and professional perceptions of the acceptability of HIV testing in dental settings (Greenberg et al, 2012; Blackstock et al, 2010). These studies found that between 55% and 97.6% of participants were willing to undergo HIV testing in a dental setting. Dental professionals were largely accepting of HIV testing in dental settings; willingness to offer the test ranged from 56.7% in the United States to 90% in Vietnam. To date there have been no similar studies focused on HIV testing in the dental setting conducted in the UK.Aim Phase 1 of the study aims to ascertain the acceptability of HIV testing in dental settings from the perspective of dental professionals and service users, especially those from higher risk communities. Phase 2 aims to establish whether point of care HIV testing in dental settings is feasible and acceptable to patients and the wider dental team. Plan The proposed research project is structured into two phases. The initial phase will involve up to 72 participants across seven focus groups to obtain qualitative data on the acceptability of HIV testing in the dental setting as perceived by dentists and service users, particularly those of people from demographics known to be more likely to have undiagnosed HIV or late diagnosis. The second phase of the research project will be the implementation of a non-randomised feasibility study undertaken in urgent care dental clinics and community clinics targeted at marginalised populations including the homeless, vulnerable migrants and people misusing substances. Opt-in HIV testing will be performed using the INSTI™ capillary blood test. All services users over the age of 16 who can provide consent and do not have a known diagnosis of HIV will be offered testing. Service users with a reactive test result will be immediately linked to a sexual health service for confirmatory testing, counselling and treatment cascade as appropriate. The feasibility study will provide essential information as to whether the key components of HIV testing are operable in the dental setting and will collect data on the proportion of patients offered screening, the proportion of those offered who uptake the test, the acceptability of the testing to dental professionals and the public, number of reactive tests, stage of HIV at diagnosis and reasons that patients declined to undergo testing. All those offered the test will be asked to complete an anonymous questionnaire on the acceptability of HIV testing in the dental setting. Process evaluation will be undertaken with dental staff and patients at months six and twelve.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Improving statistical methods for individualised predictions and understanding population variation in survival for colorectal cancer patients.
Abstract: BackgroundColorectal cancer is the fourth most common cancer in the UK for both males and females with approximately 41,000 new cases diagnosed each year. Despite the severity of the disease and the significant efforts that have been made, there is still a strong demand for better understanding of the disease. There is large variation in treatment, prognosis and outcomes following a colorectal cancer diagnosis and further research should focus in investigating the determinants of this variation. Furthermore, there is an emerging need to understand the prognostic factors that affect each patient's prognosis and progress of disease.AimsThe project aims to improve understanding and communication surrounding colorectal cancer by exploring variation in survival with the ultimate aim of improving clinical management by making use of a unique data resource. This will be achieved by developing and applying new statistical methods. The research to be undertaken will investigate colorectal cancer both at the individual and population level. To ensure the use of the findings in practice, a free access webtool will be developed to present results in ways that are easy to understand.Plan of investigationThe project can be summarised into three clinical (C1-C3) and three methodological components (M1-M3) that will help answer these clinical questions.C1 - Develop and validate prognostic models for colorectal cancer patients for use in improving the clinical management, including making treatment decisions and communicating the impact of a diagnosis of cancer. (Individual level)C2 -h; Explore the underlying determinants of inequalities seen across population groups through the extension and development of methods for mediation analysis. (Population level)C3 -h; Communication of results to healthcare professionals, patients, scientists and decision-makers through developing webtools. (Both individual and population level)M1 - Development and evaluation of multiple imputation approaches in the context of time-to-event data to feed into the models developed for C1 and C2.M2 -h; Development and application of standardised (marginal) survival estimates for use in both individual and population predictions (see C1 and C2), including mediation analysis approaches.M3 -h; Further development of methods for the estimation of loss in expectation of life, a measure that will be used both as an output of the prognostic model (C3) and the marginal estimates obtained in the mediation analysis (C2).Patient and NHS benefitThe developed webtool will improve understanding and communication of colorectal cancer prognosis. The prognostic model will make it possible for clinicians and patients to obtain a patient's specific prognosis and to base decisions such as choosing the optimal available treatment around the most appropriate data possible. The findings from the mediation analysis will detect the determinants for the observed inequalities across population groups. Thus, those with the worst prognosis will be targeted and the best policy interventions to alter modifiable factors can be identified and introduced in order to decrease inequalities.The methods developed as part of this proposal will also be applicable in other clinical settings and relevant software will be developed to help their wider application. The available methods will encourage research for other clinical areas and eventually benefit more patients.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Estimating health-related quality of life for people with learning disabilities; an adaptation of the EQ-5D
Abstract: Background: People with LD have poorer health, experience delays in diagnosis and treatment, are more likely to have poorer health outcomes and significantly shorter life expectancy than people without LD. NHS England's response to the Government's mandate of addressing poor outcomes and inequalities has placed transforming healthcare services and reducing inequalities at the centre of their agenda. Integral to an improvement in services is the need for research to accurately reflect the Health-Related Quality of Life (HRQoL) benefits, and thus the cost effectiveness, i.e. value for money, of potential improvements to inform decision making. In LD populations there are challenges collecting data specifically HRQoL for use in economic evaluations. NICE guidance states that the preferred measure of HRQoL for cost-effectiveness analysis in adults is the EQ-5D. However, research shows that people with LD have difficulty completing the measure due to the wording/language and understanding terms used. While proxy completion of EQ-5D has been proposed as a valid method, the ethics and reliability of proxy completions has been questioned. The UK Research Governance Framework and Equality Act 2010, require that, where necessary, reasonable adjustments must be made to provide accessible research materials to enable equity of access. This requirement also applies to the design of reliable and valid measures to record patient reported outcomes. Aim: The aim of this research is to adapt the EQ-5D, a preference based measure of health related quality of life, for people with mild or moderate LD for use in economic evaluation. Plan of investigation: The research utilises a mixed methods approach, across four phases. The first phase will consist of a systematic review of literature on the development or use of quality of life measures in different populations with communication difficulties, cognitive impairment or LD, and the methods used to adapt these measures for different patient groups; this will inform the development of the proposed adaptation. The second phase involves people with LD, carers/supporters of people with LD (e.g. family members or third-sector workers) reviewing both the EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L in individual Think Aloud (TA) sessions and focus groups, with emphasis being placed on the wording/language, domains and structure included in EQ-5D and the mode of its delivery. Results of the systematic review and qualitative research will inform the development of the adapted EQ-5D. The third phase will compare general population values of similar health states using original EQ-5D and adapted EQ-5D in order to assess the extent to which valuations using the adapted EQ-5D correspond to the previously established measure. The final phase will focus on testing the adapted version of EQ-5D in terms of ease of completion, internal consistency and reliability. Potential benefits to patients and the NHS: Service improvements proposed by the current government should be based on robust research evidence. Integral to that is adequately capturing patient-reported health outcomes. The development of a bespoke and robust instrument that allows adults with mild to moderate LD to reflect their opinions on their own health supports these proposals. It is proposed that a more accessible instrument would therefore be a more reliable measure of their own health and could be used in decisions relating to the services and support they receive.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine
Award_Title: Improving the effectiveness and equity of contraception provision in general practice
Abstract: Background Unplanned pregnancies have costs for mother, baby and society. Teenage Pregnancy Strategy, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines on long acting reversible contraception (LARC), and financial incentives for general practitioners (GPs) to give advice to women about LARCs are examples of policy initiatives to prevent unplanned pregnancies and abortions. Assuming most unplanned pregnancies end in abortions, abortion rates have not reduced by much since then, particularly for women in their 20s.We do not know if financial incentives for GPs to give LARC advice had equitable impact on LARC use and reduced abortions. Women at risk of abortions might benefit from early interventions but we do not know how to identify them in general practice. Contraception consultations might not be effective because some women have problems expressing needs and clinicians sometimes make assumptions about what is best for their patients.I will explore how general practice can support women to get the contraception they want and when they need it to prevent unplanned pregnancies.Aim To assess the effectiveness and equity of contraception provision in general practice and explore how best to support women to make informed choices for contraceptive careResearch questions 1.Do financial incentives in general practice to offer LARC advice increase LARC use and reduce abortion rates in the population? 2.Does offering LARC advice reduce risk of abortion in women of reproductive age? 3.Which women registered in general practice are at a higher risk of abortion? 4.How can primary care professionals improve women decision making for contraception, especially for vulnerable women?Plan of investigation I will use Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) which is a database of anonymised medical records from general practice. It has coverage of 6.9% and broadly representative of UK population.Using a before-and-after study design on CPRD, I will measure the impact of financial incentives given to GPs to give LARC advice to women since its introduction in 2009. I will use interrupted time series analysis to examine impact using LARC use and abortion rates, and equity by demographics such as age, deprivation, and practice areas.To examine the effectiveness of LARC advice on LARC use and risk of abortions, I will follow up thee cohorts of women: those eligible for LARC advice if they were using non-LARC contraception, those who attended for emergency contraception; and women not using any contraception who were not eligible for advice which will be the control group. I will analyse effects with regression methods, using LARC advice as predictor variable and risk of abortion as outcome.Using a cohort of women of reproductive age in the CPRD, I will compare women who had abortions with those who didn't, employing regression models to create risk profiles based on age, deprivation, lifestyles, consultation patterns and contraceptive use.Lastly, I will conduct focus group studies of women from different backgrounds to explore their experiences of contraceptive care in general practice, and what support they want to help them choose the right contraception.Potential benefits Unplanned pregnancies and abortions have costs to both the individuals and society, some of these are quantifiable and others not. Switching women from using oral contraception to LARC might save over £100 million for the NHS but many factors affect women's decisions to use a contraceptive method to prevent pregnancies and control their fertility.My proposal will help us understand what works, in whom and where the missed opportunities might be. The findings from the studies will help primary care professionals to support women to make informed choices about contraceptive care that works for them.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Complex Evidence Synthesis using Network Meta-Analysis, IPD and Multiple Outcomes: Application Investigating the Effectiveness of Pragmatic Interventions for Diabetes Prevention and Interventions to Increase the Use of Childhood Accident Prevention Practices in the Home.
Abstract: BackgroundPublic health appraisals usually are informed by simple evidence synthesis methods. These methods do not address some of the key challenges where the interventions are more complex and not as well defined as they are in controlled trials. Interventions that are made up of components are termed as 'complex interventions', for example, interventions to reduce obesity might contain 'diet' and 'exercise' components. Particular combinations of components may be more effective and cost-effective for subgroups of the population. Individual participant data and the simultaneous synthesis of multiple outcomes are rarely used in evidence synthesis but have the potential to reduce the uncertainty in the intervention effect estimates and to help appraisers make better decisions in relation to their effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. Aims The aims of this project are to answer the following research questions:How can complex interventions be assessed to provide better information to decision makers about all possible interventions?How can the evaluation of complex interventions make use of all available data to inform tailored decision making for subgroups of the population?How can the simultaneous evaluation of multiple outcomes for complex interventions improve the evidence base for decision makers? MethodsA search will be undertaken to determine what current methodologies are available for analysing complex interventions. A review of NICE public health appraisals will identify studies where the use of more sophisticated methods may have been appropriate but were not implemented. Evidence synthesis methodology will be developed to include individual participant data into a complex intervention network meta-analysis model and this will be further extended to include multiple outcomes. The performance of the methods will be assessed using simulation studies as well as two case studies in diabetes prevention and increasing the use of childhood accident prevention practices in the home. This will include investigating the value of the added information in relation to individual participant data and multiple outcomes. Anticipated Impact and DisseminationThese methods will have the ability to use all of the information available in evidence synthesis research and improve the precision of the effectiveness estimates of public health interventions. These methods can be translated into a range of clinical and public health evidence synthesis situations where the interventions or treatments are complex. This will provide better information for health intervention appraisers to make better decisions that will improve patient outcomes, improve the efficiency of health appraisal research and enable more efficient allocation of scarce NHS resources. The dissemination plan for this project includes the submission of papers to leading journals with short video abstracts, the involvement of the patient and public group to feedback the results to their clinical and wider networks and presentations at national and international conferences. A multi-stakeholder workshop will be organised in the final year to present the results of the project.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Funding_Stream: NIHR/HEE Healthcare Science Doctoral Research Fellowship
Contractor: Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Reducing Hospital Acquired Infections Due to Antibiotic Resistant Gram Negative Organisms
Abstract: Infections caused by multi drug resistant (MDR) gram negative bacteria lead to poor clinical outcomes and high rates of mortality. They represent an increasing challenge to the current healthcare system by limiting the antibiotics available to treat infections and by placing increasing pressure on the isolation facilities that prevent cross transmission. In order to respond to this clinical need it is essential to be able to judge when cross transmissions have occurred, in order to evaluate containment effectiveness. Current typing methods utilised for this purpose have limited access and are expensive, technically difficult and slow to deliver results. What is needed is a rapid typing technique that can be used responsively to inform infection control practice and to aid in making clinical decisions.This project aims to control the spread of MDR gram negative bacteria by focusing on rapid diagnostic techniques, improving control mechanisms by examining isolation policies and finally identifying factors that lead to poor clinical outcome when colonisation occurs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Understanding the facilitators and barriers that impact on the attendance of electronic cigarette users at NHS stop smoking services: a mixed methods investigation
Abstract: Background CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Tobacco remains the greatest risk factor for avoidable morbidity and mortality in the UK [1]. Some 10 million people still smoke (approximately 20% of the adult population), with strong differences along sociodemographic lines, such as far higher rates in disadvantaged communities [2, 3]. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)E-cigarettes are devices delivering nicotine in vapour form, avoiding the vast majority of toxins released from combusting tobacco [4]. Since 2012, prevalence of use has tripled to an estimated 2.1 million UK smokers, of which approximately 90% also smoke conventional cigarettes [3, 5]. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)When asked about reasons for e-cigarette use, 83% of smokers using them report attempting to quit smoking [6]. Yet the limited evidence to date suggests e-cigarettes may only be moderately effective as quit aids, with a conservative estimate suggesting they may have contributed 0.05% to national reductions in smoking prevalence [7, 8]. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Conversely, consistent evidence has demonstrated considerably greater efficacy for NHS stop smoking services, which are particularly successful in helping disadvantaged smokers [9, 10]. Yet over the period e-cigarette use tripled, attendance at these services showed a sustained (and accelerating) decrease for the first time, falling 11% in 2012/13 and 19% in 2013/14 [11]. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Around 2% of smokers accessing NHS support report e-cigarette use, a proportion ten times lower than the roughly 20% of smokers nationally that report e-cigarette use [3, 12]. Uptake of these services may be affected by sociological barriers amongst smokers, but may also reflect variable policies towards e-cigarettes adopted by local services around the country [13]. Either way, the most effective intervention available for smoking cessation may be being neglected by smokers using e-cigarettes. Given the growing popularity of these new devices, this could have important, unexplored health and inequalities implications [3]. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)No studies undertaken to date with smokers using e-cigarettes have examined factors influencing their intentions of accessing NHS stop smoking services. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Research questions How does intention to access NHS stop smoking services differ between smokers who use e-cigarettes and those who do not? How do smokers' reasons for accessing or not accessing NHS stop smoking services differ between those who use e-cigarettes and those who do not? Do these reasons vary between smokers from different sociodemographic backgrounds, particularly more disadvantaged smokers versus others? How do the local polices which different NHS stop smoking services adopt towards e-cigarette users act as barriers or facilitators to the uptake of such services by this group, and how does this compare to broader factors that influence their attendance? What factors influence the local policies that different NHS stop smoking services adopt towards e-cigarette users? What are the implications for (i) effective provision of services and (ii) inequalities in smoking? Plan of investigation Workstream 1. Using a national survey: Questions will be added to the Smoking Toolkit Study survey (the country's most authoritative source of regular, national smoking data) to: a) Collect nationally representative data on facilitators and barriers to attendance at NHS services amongst smokers who use e-cigarettes versus smokers who do not. b) Compare responses between different sociodemographic groups to assess potential for inequalities in this area. Workstream 2. Using semi-structured interviews: a) Explore with local smokers their perceptions and experiences of their NHS stop smoking service. b) Explore with the local NHS stop smoking staff factors influencing their service's policy towards e-cigarettes. Outputs A clear set of recommendations will be developed, jointly with practitioners and smokers, for how services could be attracting higher numbers of smokers using e-cigarettes. To help address inequalities, this will include different approaches required to attract smokers from different sociodemographic groups. An advisory group with wide expertise will guide the fellowship's pathways to impact.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Award_Title: Medicines Optimisation in Paediatric Patients (MOPPet): A qualitative human factors study on the causes of Drug Related Problems in hospitalised children.
Abstract: Medication safety in children is of great concern with the incidence of paediatric medication error rates estimated at approximately 20%. However, medication errors and adverse drug events (ADEs) are only part of the problem. Drug Related Problems (DRPs) include errors and harms, but also include include sub-optimal use of medicines and those issues with medication that are related to patient acceptability.It is estimated that the incidence of DRPs in children is 40%.This research seeks to understand how DRPs arise in paediatric in-patients. Following the MRC framework for the development of complex interventions, I will use sociotechnical theory and human factors engineering methods to describe medication processes in children's wards, and to use this theoretical understanding to develop recommendations for intervention development. There will be three work packages:WP1 - The current evidence base will be identified. A systematic review of the literature relating to interventions to reduce the incidence of medication error in paediatrics will be undertaken and will also include drug related problems as an outcome. The Cochrane EPOC group's systematic review methodology will be adopted. Appropriate databases will be searched, as will public policy databases and the grey literature. WP2 - a qualitative exploratory study is proposed to develop theoretical understanding of current practice, and to model the systems around medication use in children in hospital. I will use work domain analysis (WDA) to map the medication process in six different hospitals in the north of England. WDA is a cognitive engineering technique that identifies how people, purposes, the environment and tools and technology interact in a task or process. This will also capture how processes are adapted to ensure the task goals are achieved. Multiple data sources will be used to build the WDA: Procedures, policies and guidelines will be used to construct how the process is supposed to function Participant observation will be used to describe and identify how processes are delivered in practice, and also to describe the contextual information surrounding the way people interact with each other, their environment and the tools they are provided with to complete the tasks. In-depth interviews with patients, carers and staff will be used to understand the experience of medication use and the processes and the environment in which they work. Documents, field notes and interview transcripts will be analysed inductively and brought together to form the WDA. The WDA will be validated with a number of focus groups consisting of staff and experts, and a validation focus group specifically for children and young people.WP3 - Recommendations for interventions will be developed in partnership between patients, the public and professionals using the principles of experience-based co-design (EBCD). Experienced facilitators from partner institutions and members of the research team will undertake two consensus workshops. Health professionals, patients and carers will be presented with the findings from WP2 and asked to work together to propose interventions that can then be tested in later studies.This study involves the public in the design of safety interventions, which is novel. By using cognitive engineering theories, interventions that are developed in this study are likely to be more effective than those used previously. The recommendations will then go forward to develop a strategy for medication safety research in paediatric care supported by patient safety collaboratives.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Contractor: Birmingham Community Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Developing an intervention to reduce sedentary behaviour in non-ambulant young people with long-term disabilities.
Abstract: Background: Evidence suggests sedentary behaviour (≤1.5 metabolic equivalents and a sitting/reclining posture (3)), increases risk of all-cause mortality, cardio-metabolic disease and mental health problems. In children, causal links between sedentary time and increased body mass index, reduced fitness and low self esteem have been established (4). These risks occur irrespective of the levels of moderate to vigorous physical activity engaged in (4). Young people with disabilities, who are non-ambulant, are at high risk of experiencing negative health outcomes associated with sedentary time (5-12). An achievable approach to reducing this population's sedentary time is displacing it with light physical activity (LPA) (13, 14). No evidence-based interventions to reduce and break up sedentary time, by encouraging LPA, have been developed for this population. This research will develop and test the feasibility of a digital intervention to resolve this unmet need. Aims and Objectives: 1) To co-create a digital health intervention, in partnership with young people who are non-ambulant and key stakeholders, to reduce and break up sedentary behaviour by promoting LPA. 2) To undertake a feasibility study evaluating acceptability of the intervention and elements of the trial protocol to participants, practitioners and organisations delivering it. 3) To collect sufficient data to allow optimisation of the intervention, provide early evidence of effectiveness and ensure there are no unintended negative effects prior to undertaking a pilot study. Methods: Intervention development will follow the six steps in quality intervention development (6SQuID) method (15), and will be underpinned by relevant models and theories (16-19). Crowdsourcing (an innovative online data collection method, defined by Estellés-Arolas et al., (20)), will be utilised to engage key stakeholders in the intervention development. A mixed methods, single armed feasibility study with 20 participants will be carried out across a minimum of two sites. Data will be collected via individual interviews, the Children's Assessment of Participation and Enjoyment, activity diaries, ActivPAL4 accelerometers and heart rate monitors. A theory based evaluation of the interview transcripts will be undertaken and summary statistics used to describe the quantitative data. Timelines for delivery: Ethical and health research authority approvals will be obtained and the crowdsourcing platforms will open (December 2019). The platforms will close (February 2021) and recruitment for the feasibility study will begin (April 2021). Data collection for the feasibility study will begin when the intervention is complete (September 2021). Data collection will end (January 2022), to allow data analysis and project completion by June 2022. Anticipated impact and Dissemination: The review undertaken within the 6SQuiD, and the feasibility study will be published in relevant scientific journals and conference presentations made. Public and Patient Involvement representatives will produce a video summarising the findings for online dissemination. The crowdsourcing platforms and dissemination of findings will raise awareness amongst families and professionals regarding the implications of sedentary behaviour, and encourage them to address it in clinical practice. Utilisation of technology in research methodology and interventions will be promoted. Potential long-term benefits include implementation of the intervention in the NHS and wider international commercialisation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Award_Title: “The Bigger Picture” How can we make psychological therapy more helpful for people in more deprived areas?
Abstract: Background Mental illness is a major cause of worldwide disease burden, creating annual socio-economic costs of £100 billion in England. Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) is a large-scale government initiative designed to provide effective, evidence based psychological interventions for people with common mental health problems. IAPT treats one million patients annually. Despite efforts to standardise treatments and outcomes, there remains significant variability in effectiveness between IAPT services. A third of referred patients never access treatment, and another third don't complete treatment. Deprivation has well-established links with mental health, and evidence suggests that area-level deprivation predicts poorer treatment access and outcomes, independent of individual socioeconomic status. Current provision models may therefore be maintaining or exacerbating health inequalities. However, the causal mechanisms and relative impact of neighbourhood versus service is unclear. Objectives Quantify the extent of variability in IAPT clinical effectiveness, access, and completion attributable to (a) neighbourhood and (b) service. Determine the extent of this variability explainable by area-level deprivation related variables, after controlling for case-mix. Develop an in-depth qualitative understanding of mechanisms linking deprivation with effectiveness, to inform a theoretical model. Collaborate with stakeholders to identify intervention, policy, and commissioning recommendations, and produce an actionable outcome prediction and benchmarking tool.Plan The research will utilise a mixed-methods sequential design known as ethnographic residual analysis. Work package 1 will comprise a quantitative, cross-classified multilevel analysis of retrospective routine anonymous clinical data from 30-40 IAPT services (estimated 600+ therapists, 12000+ patients). Data will be obtained via the 'iaptus' software provider. All IAPT services collect standardised measures of depression (PHQ-9) and generalised anxiety (GAD-7) symptoms at every appointment. Clinical data will be linked with publicly available area-level socio-demographic and socio-economic data. Multilevel models will partition variance and test variables. The primary outcome is IAPT-defined clinical recovery. Secondary outcomes are treatment access and completion. IAPT uses a stepped-care approach - separate analyses will investigate high intensity provision (psychotherapy/counselling) and low intensity provision (guided self-help). Work package 2 will use a qualitative study of semi-structured interviews to understand causal processes. Patients and stakeholders from two services in deprived areas with poor predicted outcomes will be selected -h; one accurately predicted as under-performing, and one where outcomes are better than expected ('positive deviance'). The estimated sample will include 24-30 patients and 4-8 stakeholders. I will produce an outcome prediction/benchmarking tool with stakeholder involvement, and hold a half-day impact workshop with stakeholders, patients and the public to identify how to implement change. Benefits IAPT is 'fundamental to the implementation and success of the Government's mental health strategy', and research 'to improve [its] efficiency and effectiveness' is a government priority (Department of Health, 2012). Identifying the causal mechanisms by which specific (e.g. deprived) groups or communities find IAPT more or less effective helps us to reduce outcome inequality by a) achieving better engagement with groups at risk of disengagement and poor outcome, b) delivering responsive, targeted interventions congruent to community needs (via IAPT and/or other complementary interventions), and c) improving needs-based service commissioning and psychopolitical validity.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Development and feasibility of a clinically integrated behaviour modification toolkit to promote personalised physical activity routines following recent stroke
Abstract: Background: There are approximately 1.1 million people living with stroke in the UK (Townsend et al., 2012). Increasing physical activity levels improves short and long-term function post-stroke (Saunders et al., 2013), psychological health (Adamson et al., 2004) and modifies cardiovascular risk factors, theoretically improving long-term cardiovascular and metabolic health (Ivey et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2014). Despite the wealth of evidence demonstrating the positive benefits of physical activity post-stroke (Saunders et al., 2013) fewer than 30% of independently mobile stroke survivors undertake even minimal levels of physical activity (Shaughnessy and Resnick, 2009). Stroke leads to complex individual disability creating barriers to physical activity (Nicholson et al., 2013). Current rehabilitation focuses on restoration of function with minimal time and variable levels of health professional expertise in supporting individuals with stroke to be physically active (Mead and Van Wijck, 2011). There is a need to develop and examine the feasibility of interventions to support long-term physical activity specifically tailored to the complex needs of individuals with stroke. Research question: Can physical activity routines be promoted and monitored during the rehabilitation of patients following recent stroke through structured behaviour modification and objective real time feedback? Aims: (1) To review and evaluate current guidelines and services for the delivery of physical activity post-stroke. (2) To explore the use of accelerometers as a tool for motivating physical activity behaviour change in people with stroke. (3) To design and establish the feasibility of a health professional delivery toolkit and matching training for a multifaceted behavioural intervention targeting the introduction and maintenance of physical activity post-stroke. Plan of investigation During Work Package 1 I will review and evaluate current physical activity guidelines and conduct a survey on the current UK delivery of physical activity post-stroke. Work Package 2 will explore the use of accelerometers as a tool to monitor, self-regulate and motivate physical activity post-stroke. The findings of this study and Work Package 1 will inform the design of a set of professional tools and matching training. The tools will enable professionals to assist patients in self-regulating their progress toward achieving PA goals (accelerometer, PA diaries, APP, etc.). The matching online training programme will foster professional motivation and self-efficacy for promoting the safe adoption and maintenance of PA in stroke rehabilitation. Finally the feasibility, acceptability and fidelity of the professional toolkit and training will be assessed in Work Package 3. Potential benefits to patients and NHS: Work Package 1 will inform NHS clinicians and service providers on current physical activity stroke guidelines and UK service delivery. Work Package 2 will establish the feasibility and clinical benefit of using an accelerometer to assist in the self-regulation of physical activity post-stroke. Work Package 2 and 3 will design and establish the feasibility of a professional toolkit and accredited matching online training targeting physical activity post-stroke which will be made freely available to stroke clinicians. The efficacy of the multifaceted intervention developed during Work Package 2 and 3 will be ready for testing in a future multi-centre cluster randomised controlled trial.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: An investigation of the epidemiology of falls, fractures and outcomes among people with psychotic and affective disorders
Abstract: Aims The Lectureship will support a programme of work investigating hospitalised falls/fractures in people with psychotic/affective disorders using data from mental health, acute and primary care services, specifically seeking to: Characterise experiences of falls/fractures and rehabilitation among: 1) people with psychotic/affective disorders; 2) general hospital nursing/therapies staff. Investigate the incidence and predictors of falls/fractures. Investigate outcomes including mortality, duration of hospitalisation, readmission and service use across healthcare sectors, compared to the catchment population. Investigate quality of primary/acute care related to falls/fractures in this patient group, compared to people without mental illness. Background Falls are a leading cause of morbidity, healthcare use and mortality, but little is known about these outcomes in people with mental disorders. People with psychotic and affective disorders have a number of risk factors for osteoporosis and fractures, including diabetes, vitamin-D deficiency, sedentary lifestyle, poor nutritional intake, and hyperprolactinaemia associated with some antipsychotic agents. Recent meta-analyses have found that people with psychosis are 2.5 times more likely to have osteoporosis than controls and are at a 72% increased risk of experiencing fractures. Important gaps in the literature include a paucity of information on the experiences and predictors of falls/fractures in people with mental disorders, an absence of information on outcomes (e.g. duration of hospitalisation) and unclear evidence on targets for intervention. Methods I will conduct initial qualitative interviews with: 1) a purposive sample of people with psychotic/affective disorders who have experienced falls/fractures (supplemented by an in-depth case-note review); 2) focus groups of general hospital nursing/therapies staff. Subsequently, I will utilize a unique network of linked databases to address knowledge gaps: i) the Clinical Record Interactive Search (CRIS) resource containing de-identified mental healthcare EHR data from the South London and Maudsley Trust (SLAM) on over 350,000 patients, containing natural language processing applications enabling extraction of structured data to ascertain pharmacotherapy, physical-health and mental health symptomatology; CRIS linkages to ii) Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), providing national data on hospitalisations and associated diagnoses, iii) national mortality data from the Office of National Statistics (ONS), and iv) local primary care data from Lambeth DataNet (LDN) which currently covers all practices in one of SLaM's four catchment boroughs.Pilot data Preliminary analyses to support the application identified that between 01/2006-12/2012 among 10,988 people with psychosis, 579 and 393 were admitted to an acute hospital following a fall and fracture respectively. The median length of stay was 6.65 (+22.5, total days=6,977) and 12.1 (+32.0, total days 11,327) days for falls and fractures respectively.Project outlineSemi-structured qualitative interviews and case-note review of patients with psychotic/affective disorders who were admitted due to a fall/fracture (n=20) and focus groups with healthcare staff (n=15, Aim-1). Using CRIS, describe the incidence of falls/fractures in psychotic/affective disorders and compare patterns and rates versus standardised age-sex matched local population without mental illness and by common symptom profiles (Aim-2). Investigate predictors of falls/fractures including sociodemographic status (e.g. age, gender, ethnicity, area-level deprivation), medication, psychiatric and physical health comorbidity (Aim-2). Investigate outcomes for falls/fractures among people with psychotic/affective disorders versus catchment population (Aim-3). Investigate quality of care in primary care (LDN) and compare this to people without mental disorders (Aim-4). Outcomes/benefits to NHS Development of a risk prediction tool to identify at risk groups of people with affective/psychotic disorders of falls/fractures to inform: a)New care pathways. b)Platforms for future intervention trials to prevent falls/fractures. 2)Published and disseminated literature (for academic, clinical, service and public audiences) on risks, outcomes and points of inequality.

Award_Title: Mobilising knowledge about ethnic inequalities to improve access, experience and outcomes for Black and Minority Ethnic users of NHS services
Abstract: Training Award

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Mobilising evidence for better health and equity through 'Health in All Policies' (HiAP) in local government
Abstract: This fellowship responds to the urgent need for policy outside of health and social care to address current threats to public health. It addresses the challenge of enduring and causally complex population health problems and inequalities and how knowledge is mobilised in 'whole government' responses. The focus is a family of policies known as Health in All Policies (HiAP). The purpose of the work is to develop this area of KMb conceptually, theoretically and practically to promote the advancement of HiAP and to build an understanding of what and how knowledge can be mobilised. The project will collate, assess and synthesise existing bodies of knowledge mobilisation (KMb) evidence and theory in the field. New KMb theory will be generated on how high-level ideological political processes, governance structures and local ideas, knowledge and practice shape HiAP. This will then inform work to develop, test and refine techniques of KMb of HiAP through co-creation with policy stakeholders. HiAP represent a relatively new approach to public policy and has been interpreted and implemented differently across fields. Success depends on addressing several political and governance challenges. There are a growing number of examples of HiAP and an emergent body of evidence on how such approaches can be successfully implemented and sustained. Alongside this, a rich body of literature in the political sciences on policy processes offers promising, but as yet largely untapped, insight into how knowledge in the field can be mobilised. This fellowship seeks to take this opportunity to assess, synthesise and mobilise these bodies of work. This is mixed methods KMb research that includes: 1) theory synthesis, 2) participatory case studies, 3) co-creative workshops. It has three phases: Phase 1 Preparation (year 1): i) Identification of a series of case examples where HiAP have been developed. The fellow will engage in 3-5 shadowing placements in local and national government settings to 'scope out' how HiAP has been constructed. ii) Systematic scoping review to document the type and volume of literature available on HiAP and articulate its conceptual and theoretical framing. Phase 2 Exploration (years 2-3): i) A full theory synthesis using evidence from the scoping exercise in Phase 1 and a systematic appraisal of theories from political science on how politics and governance interact to influence policy uptake, design and implementation.ii) Case studies involving documentary analysis and interviews with policy actors to examine in detail how HiAP is developed. Phase 3 Analysis, co-creation and evaluation (years 3-4): i) Analysis of case example data ii) Development of KMb frameworks for HiAP with policy partners via workshops with stakeholders to develop guidance for policy makers and stakeholders on how HiAP can be developed, managed and put into place.ii) Development of an on-line forum to disseminate and discuss problems, practice, barriers and enablers in policy-making. This activity sits alongside an extensive training and professional development programme to help the fellow become a knowledge mobilisation expert and develop productive professional networks through which to expand the impact of this expertise.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The Exploratory Map: developing and evaluating a complex intervention to support generalist care of complex needs.
Abstract: This proposal aims to optimise the delivery and evaluation of the Exploratory Map as a complex intervention supporting generalist care for people with complex, chronic illness.General Practice provides holistic care supporting individuals in living their daily lives. A single, disease-focused explanatory framework is inadequate to explain much of the illness needs presented to General Practice; complexity is a function of diversity and uncertainty. Practitioner and patient engage in a dynamic process of shared exploration and interpretation of illness experience. The Exploratory Map describes this process: the integration of biotechnical and biographical knowledge to generate an individualised account of need. However neither the profession, nor the processes of evidence-based practice, have described a framework by which the impact of this activity can be evaluated.This proposal describes 3 steps in the delivery of this complex intervention. An ethnographic longitudinal study explores individual efforts to maintain continuity of daily life in the face of chronic complex illness, including the impact of health care on this creative capacity. Analysis of consultations with patients with complex problems, supported by interviews with both parties, will explore the interpretive process: defining the core components, drivers and barriers to delivery, markers of quality, and impact on patients. Two survey tools will be developed: an outcome measure of creative capacity; and an assessment of consultation type and quality. Tools will be validated within a pilot longitudinal cohort study to assess the impact of an interpretive model of care on patient outcomes.

Award_Title: The Reflective Fostering Programme – improving the wellbeing of Children in Care through a group intervention for foster carers: a randomised controlled trial
Abstract: Research question A pragmatic, randomised controlled trial to evaluate whether the Reflective Fostering Programme (RFP) for foster carers, when offered alongside usual social care support, is more effective in improving the emotional well-being of Children in Care, than usual support alone. Background In 2018 there were 75,420 children in England looked after by the state - 73% of them were in foster care(1). These children are at high risk of poor wellbeing across the lifespan(2). Foster carers have a key influence on the life of children in their care(3). However not enough is known about the best way to support them in their role(4). The Reflective Fostering Programme is a 10-week intervention, delivered jointly by an experienced foster carer and a social worker. It is designed to promote ‘reflective parenting’ among foster and kinship carers. Unlike other programmes for foster carers, it focuses on improving the carer-child relationship, by helping carers to attend to their own state of mind and experiences. A stronger carer-child relationship is associated with greater well-being in children(5). Aims and objectives The aim of this study is to find out whether the RFP alongside usual support is more effective than usual support alone in promoting chid well-being, reducing levels of foster carer stress and burnout; improving the carer’s reflective capacity and the carer-child relationship; and in reducing placement instability. The cost effectiveness of RFP will also be assessed. Before starting the main trial, an internal pilot study will test recruitment and randomisation procedures, examine retention and response rate for the primary outcome at four months, and explore any issues of contamination across the trial arms. An embedded process evaluation within the main trial will examine how the programme was delivered, provide explanation of any unexpected effects and help identify issues related to implementation and scalability. Methods Up to 720 foster carers, caring for children aged 4-13, will be recruited from local authority fostering teams across England and Wales. Carers will be randomly assigned, with those in the intervention arm receiving the RFP alongside usual support. Carers will complete a range of validated measures at 3 time points (baseline, month 4 and month 12). The primary outcome will be child well-being, as assessed by the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) at 12 months. Focus group interviews and observations from four sites will inform the process evaluation. Data related to cost-effectiveness and placement stability will be examined at 12-month follow-up. Timeline for delivery The study is over 57 months, starting in April 2020. Anticipated impact and dissemination Findings will be published in peer-reviewed academic journals and circulated via foster carer networks and within social care forums, and a short film will be co-produced with carers and care leavers that can be used in training and available online. Working with key organisations and our partners in children’s social care we will ensure the availability of training in the RFP to local authority fostering teams nationally. If effective, the RFP could be adopted as an evidence-based approach to improving the well-being of children in care across England and Wales.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Improving outcomes for survivors of human trafficking: evaluating the effectiveness of advocacy interventions in improving mental health and well-being among trafficked people
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Survivors of trafficking report a range of health problems, especially psychological distress. The UK is legally obliged to provide support to promote the recovery of trafficked people and has invested in a national assistance programme based on a model of advocacy support and delivered by non-governmental organisations (NGOs). However, the effectiveness of advocacy interventions in improving the mental health and wellbeing of trafficked people has not been evaluated, either in the UK or elsewhere. AIM: To evaluate the effectiveness of advocacy interventions in improving mental health and wellbeing among people who have been identified as trafficked and have elected to receive NGO support. METHODS: Study Design: Cohort study with assessments before the start of advocacy support (T1), postintervention (T2) and 3-month follow-up (T3), plus mixed methods realist evaluation. Participants: 250 women and men who are aged 18 years or older; are identified as a potential victim of human trafficking following entry into the UK National Referral Mechanism; are no longer being exploited by their traffickers; and elect to receive advocacy support from a participating NGO. Qualitative interviews will be conducted with a subsample of 30 participants, and with 15 NGO staff members. Intervention: Advocacy support as currently provided by NGOs in England. Support varies according to service model (i.e. between NGOs) and to individual need (i.e. between participants). However, common components include: (1) Providing information about rights and support options; (2) Offering encouragement, empathy, and respect; (3) Providing informal counselling and setting goals; (4) Increasing access to community resources and to housing and welfare support; (5) Increasing social support; (6) Skills building and help to access employment. Support is provided for three months (although there may be variation according to individual need). Controls: It is not feasible to recruit a control group. To support the interpretation of any detected change as a causal intervention effect in the absence of a control group we will assess dose-response relationships between change over time and factors describing the intervention experience. Outcomes: Primary outcome is psychological distress at T3 versus T1. Psychological distress will be measured by the Clinical Outcomes in Routine Evaluation-Outcome Measure (CORE-OM). Secondary outcomes are CORE-OM at T2, and health-related quality of life, social support, and unmet needs, and use of health and social care services at T2 and T3. Qualitative interviews will explore service user and staff perspectives on what aspects of support make a difference to mental health and wellbeing, why, and how. ANTICIPATED IMPACT AND DISSEMINATION: This study will inform: 1) interventions to promote recovery and reduce psychological distress among trafficked people; 2) budget allocation, and efficient use of health and other support services resources; 3) development of monitoring and evaluation methods for post-trafficking interventions. Findings will be disseminated through multiple outlets, including scientific journals, academic and practitioner conferences, practice guidance, policy briefing papers, and via social media. DURATION: 36 months.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Football Fans and Betting (FFAB): a feasibility study and randomised pilot trial of a group-based intervention to reduce gambling involvement among male football fans
Abstract: Sports betting is a growth area for the gambling industry. Men are its primary target audience and are at higher risk from the harms of gambling. This study draws on evidence of using sports settings to engage participants in behaviour change interventions (eg Football Fans in Training (FFIT) programme and European Fans in Training (EuroFIT)). These programmes used the social context of the football club to introduce a ‘toolkit’ of behaviour change skills (eg self-monitoring, goal setting) to men in a supportive group setting. Working with experts from gambling treatment/prevention, the Football Fans and Betting (FFAB) programme dhas been carefully developed, drawing on learning from these programmes, to produce a 9 week programme incorporating relevant Behaviour Change Theories, with the aim of reducing sports bettors’ gambling involvement and to improve their wellbeing. This research project is a feasibility study designed to test the following objectives: to refine and test the intervention among a population of sports bettors in football clubs in England; test the feasibility of delivery; pilot the delivery under research conditions; assess research procedures for a potential future RCT of an optimised FFAB programme, and refine our logic model. The study population is regular (at least weekly) male sports bettors, aged 18-55 who want to reduce their involvement in betting in the context of improving health and wellbeing. Potential participants who score up to 14 on the PGSI (Problem Gambling Severity Index) will be eligible for inclusion. This means that men who are already experiencing a low level of gambling harms may be included in the project. Those identified as experiencing more significant harms from gambling however are ineligible and will be signposted for specialist treatment/support services. This research project is carried out over three phases. Phase 1 (months 0-3) involves: refining the FFAB programme, conducting focus groups with sports bettors to test recruitment and development of the smartphone diary app to help record and log gambling behaviour. Phase 2a (months 4-9) is a feasibility pilot conducted in two professional football clubs to test: recruitment and retention (rates monitored to assess this); acceptability of the programme to participants, coaches and clubs (assessed through observations of sessions and post intervention interviews); implementation by coaches (observations and interviews) and feasibility and further development of the app (review of logged data). Phase 2b (months 10-24) is further feasibility study in 2 different football clubs in England. Our study outcomes include refinement of our recruitment and intervention approach (phase 1) and feasibility of the FFAB intervention within clubs (phase 2a and 2b) . Primary outcomes for Phase 1 include qualitative feedback from focus groups on the acceptability of the FFAB programme to our target group, and revision and refinement of the recruitment strategy. Other outcomes from this phase include production of the final FFAB intervention protocol and coach manual, and qualitative feedback from a pilot test of the smartphone app diary data to understand ease of use, frequency of use and quality of data entered. Primary outcomes for Phase 2a and b include assessing the acceptability of the FFAB programme to participants, involving reviewing data on recruitment, retention, participation and drop-out rates, qualitative feedback from participants, and review of smartphone app data. It also includes assessing the acceptability of the FFAB delivery for coaches, based on qualitative data from coaches and team observation of programme sessions. Other outcomes from this phase will be further refinement of the FFAB intervention manual and coaches delivery manual, based on the feedback given above and finalisation of the recruitment and retention strategy. Focus groups with participants and clubs, interviews with non-completers and review of data completeness and data quality for the proposed efficacy outcome measures and the app will assess the FFAB programme process. Using the team’s network and our PPI partners, we will disseminate findings to policy makers, academics, the public and sports stakeholders, highlighting findings from the first robust evaluation of an independent, theoretically informed and systematic intervention for male sports bettors.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: Sheffield Health & Social Care NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A realist synthesis to explain how, for whom and in what circumstances different community mental health crisis services work.
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Mental health crises cause significant disruption to the lives of individuals and families and can be life threatening. The drive for community care alongside large reductions in hospital beds, has led to a proliferation of community crisis services.
