There are known challenges to conducting research in palliative care such as identification and recruitment of populations, but also challenges of poorly established research infrastructure. Having an active, confident, sustainable palliative care research network across North West Coast will spotlight good research practice, build research capacity, and combat barriers to research. OBJECTIVES i)To develop a sustainable palliative care partnership infrastructure across NWC, embedded within existing organisations such as the CRN and ARC, involving strong PPI, as a focus for palliative and end-of-life care research in the region. ii)To work with palliative care providers, patients and the public, and research staff to further understand local barriers and facilitators to palliative and end-of-life care research, and develop and implement solutions to these barriers. iii)To build clinical capacity in palliative and end-of-life care research through the mentorship of emerging research leaders and share academic expertise across organisations. iv)To facilitate the development of high-quality research grant applications that address important clinical research questions that meet the needs of the NWC population (and beyond) focused on the NIHR palliative and end-of-life care calls (NIHR PHR, EME, HS&DR and HTA) in 2022. PARTNERSHIP PLAN a)DEVELOP AND EMBED AN ACTIVE PALLIATIVE CARE PARTNERSHIP NETWORK ACROSS NORTH WEST COAST (to meet objective i) Activities to embed this will be actioned throughout the phased activities below. b)PHASE ONE (0-6 months): RAPID IDENTIFICATION OF CURRENT LOCAL BARRIERS TO RESEARCH AND THEIR SUSTAINABLE SOLUTIONS (to meet objective ii) This will include an online survey and working groups (with providers, research staff, and the public) using nominal group techniques to facilitate a consensus on barriers and solutions to research across NWC. c)PHASE TWO A (7-12 months). PERSONAL MENTORSHIP AND SUPPORT TO CO-DESIGN AND PREPARE RESEARCH GRANT APPLICATIONS (to meet objective iii and iv). This will include peer support and action learning sets, 1:1 mentorship and the buy out of time for emerging research leaders. d)PHASE TWO B (7-18 months). IMPLEMENT IDENTIFIED SOLUTIONS TO ENABLING BETTER PALLIATIVE AND END-OF-LIFE CARE RESEARCH ACROSS NORTH WEST COAST (to meet objectives ii and iv). This will draw from phase one, but may include recruitment training, work on enabling research governance, and further developing our PPI networks. e)PHASE THREE (7-12 months) DEVELOPING AND SUBMITTING HIGH QUALITY CLINICALLY RELEVANT RESEARCH PROPOSALS (to meet objective iv) The outputs of this work will include; high quality applications to forthcoming palliative care calls; a sustainable infrastructure to facilitate excellent research; greater capacity to engage in palliative and end-of-life care research; and developing communities of practice.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: The Mayor and Burgesses of the London Borough of Tower Hamlets
Award_Title: Tower Hamlets Health Determinants and Inequalities Research System (THIRST)
Abstract: Background: Tower Hamlets is a place of diversity, significant deprivation, and rapid growth within a dense urban environment. Wider determinants lead to poor and unequal health outcomes here. Through our partnership with the UKPRP-funded ActEarly consortium and research with community organisations Tower Hamlets has an emerging track record of research collaborations, providing a strong base and fertile ground to strengthen our research system. Vision, Aims and Objectives: Tower Hamlets Health Determinants and Inequalities Research System (THIRST) will make Tower Hamlets a ‘go to’ place to conduct high quality, collaborative, impactful health determinants research, with a strong culture of research-enabled decisions and understanding of the value of contributing to research. THIRST’s five objectives are to: (1) strengthen collaborations between the council, universities, our voluntary and community sector and residents; (2) build infrastructure to facilitate high-quality research; (3) embed a culture of research-informed decisions and prioritisation of research; (4) build capacity across partner organisations and our communities; (5) share our learning widely, to strengthen others’ research systems and evidence-based action on wider determinants. Approach and key deliverables: THIRST will sit at the core of the council’s structure, accountable to the Chief Executive and Tower Hamlets Partnership. Its work will be structured around five workstreams aligned to these objectives. • Workstream 1 will develop research collaborations. It will establish a Collaborative Research Board (CRB), Theme-specific Research Collaborations (TRCs) and a joint business development function linking the council and local universities. Proactive in-reach to the VCS, and co-production work will support public involvement. • Workstream 2 will deliver collaborative infrastructure: accessible, linked data; a streamlined process of approvals; a strengthened cohort of community researchers; and research active settings that engage schools, workplaces and housing associations in research. • Workstream 3 will develop culture and practice. A research strategy aligned to the Tower Hamlets Partnership will set shared priorities for the borough. Proactive support will help decision-makers to appraise and apply research. An independent evaluation will capture the benefit of applied research and of THIRST. • Workstream 4 will focus on capacity building for research among staff, academics and our residents: creating career development pathways and opportunities for two-way collaborative learning. • Workstream 5 will lead dissemination. It will build a Research Collaboration Hub to enable two-way engagement in THIRST, and a proactive plan to share our learning on how to become research-enabled and how to take evidence-based action on similar health determinants. Impact THIRST will improve our understanding of the most cost-effective ways to tackle health determinants. It will create stronger research collaborations and a culture in which policies and practice are informed by research and routinely evaluated and we will share our learning to enable others to do the same. The investment will enable the council and partners to support and use research and build a sustainable model. We will see an increase in strategically aligned collaborative research and research funding around health determinants in Tower Hamlets in which our communities will be fully involved.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Aberdeen Health Determinants Research Collaborative (AHDRC)
Abstract: Vision: Aberdeen City Council is a research active organisation, commissioning and generating research, curating and translating research evidence to support people to be healthy, happy and prosper regardless of their background or where they live. The AHDRC facilitates a supportive and sustainable research environment, enabling the acquisition of skills and training, generating and translating interdisciplinary research to support a post-pandemic recovery, a sustainable and just economic transition, reduce current and prevent future health inequalities, and improve health in the City, Scotland, the UK and internationally. Background: The downturn in oil and gas and the pivot to alternative energy has “shocked” the socio-economic climate in Aberdeen which is transforming ahead of and at a greater pace than other areas. The Council and its partners are working together to manage both opportunities and risks, particularly to mitigate inequalities negatively impacting physical and mental health. We recognise that this needs evidence-based interventions grounded in robust research. Our proposal positions the AHDRC within the existing governance arrangements of the Council and the City’s Community Planning Partnership. The AHDRC cannot be apart from strategies, plans and improvements to which partners and citizens are committed. In this way, there will be a clear pathway for the AHDRC’s work to be informed by the City’s research priorities and to support decision-making through a deeper understanding of health determinants. Aims and objectives: To support improvement in public health outcomes through: Research capacity & leadership; evidence to support decision-making and translation of evidence into practice; an enabling research eco-system; a positive research culture and skills to support confident engagement with research; involvement of stakeholders and the public; and dissemination of learning from the AHDRC. Key Deliverables: A 5 year research programme aligned to the cities priorities; professionals and citizens upskilled in research; evidence reviews available to support decision-making; evaluation embedded into tests of change and service design; engaged and involved stakeholders, communities and citizens; a pipeline of bids to research funders; effective dissemination of learning; accessible and research ready health determinants datasets; a culture which champions the use of research; a knowledge base with libraries of research, data and lived experience narratives. Collaborations/partnerships: The AHDRC will be led by Aberdeen City Council with co-applicants from NHS Grampian; University of Aberdeen, Robert Gordon University as well as community representatives. We have engaged positively, and will develop relationships with, national bodies to deliver collectively of the AHDRC aims and objectives. We will also build on already extensive structures, tools and relationships to ensure continuous and effective stakeholder and community engagement and involvement. Anticipated impact and dissemination: The AHDRC will transform the research culture of ACC, by investing in skills, knowledge, infrastructure and by exploiting the academic and professional capacity which already exists. By building the AHDRC within the Community Planning Partnership, the social, economic and environmental aspect of health determinants and inequalities will be better understood, learning shared, decision making enhanced and health outcomes improved.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: What are the most beneficial models used by community food assets to prevent the need for emergency food aid? A longitudinal qualitative study conducted in two multi-cultural populations in the North and South of England
Abstract: Background: One in five families are food insecure in the UK. Community food assets (CFAs) aim to relieve food insecurity and hunger for citizens in need and have seen rapid growth in recent years, in part fuelled by the COVID pandemic. CFAs can take the form of formal food banks, but are variable in their models/components and many are informal in their approach. Some CFAs offer primary prevention strategies, such as supporting employment opportunities and co-located welfare advice, alongside the provision of food. There is little evidence about what works or is important in being able to reduce/prevent people’s dependence on food aid. Aim: To investigate what approaches used by community food assets are most likely to help prevent the need for emergency food in two multi-cultural populations in the North and South of England and use the research to inform local and national government as to how best to invest in these or other resources. Methods: Three integrated work packages undertaken in Bradford and Tower Hamlets, underpinned by a complex systems approach and delivered alongside community representatives. WP1: Systems mapping using surveys, qualitative interviews and stakeholder workshops to understand and document all CFA models and components across both sites. This will consider interdependencies, relationships, pathways, implementation and sustainability. Actors will be drawn from statutory, voluntary and private sectors and CFA users. Analysis will be both a quantitative (network) and qualitative (thematic). Core outputs will include a systems map and a typology of CFA components. WP2: A longitudinal qualitative study employing three linked and concurrent methods to explore which CFA models and components are most beneficial at reducing food aid dependence and how they interact with the wider system: -Observational research for 12 months based in 5 CFAs via a researcher in residence model. Researchers will work as volunteers at the CFAs and naturalistically meet and talk to CFA staff, volunteers and users. -Repeated go along interviews with ~25 families recruited from the CFAs and ~10 families who experience food insecurity but do not tend to use CFAs. The researchers will spend time with people in order to understand their lives in relation to food insecurity and the roles which different CFAs models/components may or may not play. -A visual/ digital scrapbook study using self-selected photos, video and other media, with the previously described families. Participants will upload visual depictions of what food and food insecurity mean to them. Analysis will be a) descriptive using the pen portrait technique to understand which CFA models/components are most beneficial for whom, when and why, and b) theoretical, using complex systems theory to understand CFAs in relation to the wider context/system. WP3: A pathways to impact strategy runs throughout the whole project, underpinned by the NIHR Adding Value Framework. Core activities include: actionable toolkit, CFA typology, travelling public exhibition, co-creation workshops, feedback loops and policy briefs. Timelines: 32 months. Set up =M<6-3. WP1 =M3–13. WP2 =M10-32. WP3 =<6-32+. See Gantt chart. Impact and dissemination: Delivered as a substantial part of our pathways to impact strategy in WP3. Targeted dissemination to the following audiences: CFA users, CFA workers/volunteers, stakeholders, the public, policy makers, local authorities, academics.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Dragons Voice: Addressing worklessness and promoting mental health well-being in the older migrant community
Abstract: Background This project explores how participation in radio broadcasting can support older workless migrants into secure work and promote good mental health. It builds on the Manchester based radio programme Dragons Voice. Questions 1. What are the barriers faced by older migrants in securing and maintaining sustainable work and what is the impact on their mental health and well-being which will enable them to stay economically active up to and beyond SPA? How can the barriers be overcome? 2. How can radio broadcasting provide training to support older migrants to secure and maintain sustainable work, which in turn can benefit and enhance migrants’ mental health wellbeing? 3. How can community forums like Dragons Voice be used as bridge between the migrant and business communities in order to reduce older migrant joblessness and underemployment? 4. How can community building like Dragons Voice provide a vehicle for marginalised communities like Chinese migrants to support one another into sustainable work? 5. How can participation in community programs like Dragons Voice enhance mental health well-being of older migrants? Aims and objectives This project aims to address problems of worklessness, isolation and poor mental health faced by older migrants. Its objectives are: 1. To understand the experiences, barriers and challenges faced by older unemployed and under-employed migrants in securing and maintaining sustainable work. 2. To identify ways which employers can make use of the skills of older migrants 3. To develop ways to deliver formal, accredited and transferable skills for older migrants 4. To understand how, thorough a medium like Dragons Voice, older migrants can build solidarity within and between communities to address shared barriers to sustainable work 5. To improve and enhance mental health outcomes of older migrants by taking part in the project Development work plan The project will be conducted through co-production workshops involving older migrants, business leaders, community groups and members of the wider BAME community. It will consist of three workpackages (WP)s: 1. Baseline analysis through workshops and rich picturing 2. Mapping of community work to support older jobless migrants through workshops 3. Multi-stakeholder design of a research, policy and practice agenda through a workshop and survey of older Chinese migrants on the relationship between employment and mental health WPs 1-3 will generate qualitative data on the experiences of older Chinese migrants in the job market as well as a co-produced agenda for helping them find and secure sustainable work. WP3 will also produce quantitative data on the link between employment and mental health Timelines for delivery The project will be conducted over a six-month period: 1-2: Assembly of steering group; ethics approval; and rich picturing (WP1) 3-4: Mapping community involvement (WP2); Questionnaire design (WP3) 5-6: Multi-stakeholder research, policy and practice agenda workshops and analysis of survey results Impact and dissemination The aim of this project is to facilitate the coordination of stakeholders (employers, unions, social enterprises) in developing and implementing a research, policy and practice agenda for addressing constraints faced by older Chinese migrants in the Greater Manchester area. Throughout, we will disseminate the project's milestones and outcomes to the wider Chinese migrant community through the Dragons Voice broadcasting.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Plymouth Health Determinants Research Collaboration
Abstract: Background and rationale Plymouth has, like many other coastal cities, high mortality rates. The wider determinants of health contribute to both poor quality of life and inequalities. Plymouth City Council (PCC) recognises that tackling the problems related to employment, housing, food, crime and education requires an innovative approach which is outlined in The Plymouth Plan. An HDRC will build on these strengths to ensure that we better understand what works, why and under which circumstances (financial, contextual and organisational) and share this learning. Aims: 1. Develop the culture and skills to ensure a learning approach informs decision making 2. Produce knowledge for use locally and of value nationally, especially for similar coastal communities Objectives: • Support changes aimed at addressing the wider determinants of health through a cultural change in relation to the use of evidence and evaluation • Carry out specific prioritised research projects related to The Plymouth Plan’s innovations to address the wider determinants of health • Successfully bid for external research funding • Build collaborations for sharing knowledge and carrying out research with other HDRCs and similar coastal communities Methods: We will set up a joint PCC and University of Plymouth (UoP) research team embedded within the council. Researchers in Residence (RiRs) will work with council Research Champions and Public Partners. The team will work alongside those delivering changes designed to address wider determinants of health and collaborate with specialist university researchers. Public Partnership will be developed though links to existing organisations and the engagement of individuals during specific projects. Initial work will focus on culture change and wider skills development. We will focus on helping people understand the shift from commissioning based on monitoring delivery to decision making based on understanding complex interactions. Specific research projects likely to have the most impact locally and nationally will be developed. Informed by a Human Learning Systems philosophy, and building on the existing use of Appreciative Inquiry (AI), the team will use a range of methods suited to understanding complex dynamic systems: evidence synthesis, quantitative analysis of routine data, realist informed observation and interviews and health economics. External funding bids will be developed for calls and based on local priorities and expertise. A Management Board and an Advisory Group will oversee and support the HDRC. Timelines After initial set up and recruitment we will annually prioritise the areas we will be working in. The scale and complexity of the research will grow as our skills and experience do. Within five years we aim to be securing external funding and delivering locally and nationally relevant research. Dissemination and Impact Pathways to impact are built into the Plymouth HDRC Model. Local impact will be achieved through general culture change and staged feedback of the results of specific projects, aided by an understanding of context. Building trusting relationships will be prioritised to ensure engagement with setbacks as well as successes. National impact will be achieved through production of traditional outputs such as reports, research publications, blogs and webinars, as well as using more intensive knowledge mobilisation techniques.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Elucidating the mechaNism of action of behavioural changes on Child tOoth decay in the Randomised controlled CHOICE trial – a role for salivary lactic Acid? (ENCOURAGE)
Abstract: Research question Is the mechanism of action of the Dental-Recur Brief Negotiated Interview (DR-BNI), in children with caries in the CHOICE trial, due to changes in the levels of lactic acid or other carboxylic acids in saliva, and/or alterations in the oral microbiome? Background Child dental caries is a significant problem in the UK, with a high prevalence in deprived communities, reflecting social determinants of health. The DR-BNI intervention has been successful in reducing caries in a hospital setting, and the CHOICE trial is currently testing this intervention in primary dental care practices. In ENCOURAGE we will focus on the mechanistic effects of the DR-BNI in children with caries, by studying the salivary metabolome and microbiome. Aim The aim of this research is to determine if changes in salivary acid levels and changes in the oral microbiome have a role in the mechanism of action of the DR-BNI behavioural intervention in preventing child tooth decay. Primary objective To quantify salivary levels of lactic acid at baseline, and at 6 months follow-up, and determine if change in lactic acid concentration contributes towards the effect of intervention versus control on the caries outcome at 2 years. Secondary objectives (a) To quantify salivary levels of pyruvic acid, citric acid, 2-ketoglutamic acid, succinic acid, malic acid and fumaric acid at baseline, and at 6 months follow up, and determine if changes in these levels contribute towards the effect of intervention versus control on the caries outcome at 2 years. (b) To determine if salivary acid levels correspond with microbiome eubiosis or dysbiosis by studying the oral bacterial microbiome and fungal mycobiome in a subset of 60 children at baseline, and at 6 months follow up. Methods We will obtain saliva samples from children recruited to the CHOICE trial. Saliva samples will be collected at baseline and then again at 6 months following the DR-BNI intervention. A targeted metabolomics approach will be used to determine lactic acid and other carboxylic acids in saliva. The bacterial microbiome and fungal mycobiome will be determined by next generation sequencing in a sub-set of samples. Timeline for delivery The CHOICE trial is currently set up and patient recruitment will commence in autumn 2022. If funded, the EME study will start in October 2022, with a brief set up period of 3 months to develop saliva collection guidelines and update/confirm CHOICE recruitment sites for ENCOURAGE. Another 23 months will be allocated for collection of saliva samples, followed by 8 months for the metabolomics and microbiome analysis of the samples. Final analysis, linkage to the CHOICE trial and reporting will take place in the last 6 months of the project. Anticipated Impact and dissemination This study brings significant added value to the NIHR-funded CHOICE trial. Biological evidence from ENCOURAGE has the potential to improve adoption of and compliance with the DR-BNI intervention in CHOICE, if it is rolled out across the NHS. Understanding the mechanism of DR-BNI in CHOICE, could also guide development of shorter, cost-saving, clinical trials in caries research which is of strategic importance to industry. Findings will be disseminated via conferences, peer-reviewed publications and our extensive PPI network. The outputs of ENCOURAGE will be aligned with CHOICE for dissemination purposes to maximise impact.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: London Borough of Islington Health Determinants Research Collaboration: accelerating evidence-based approaches to challenging inequalities
Abstract: BACKGROUND. Islington is one of the poorest areas of London, and child poverty is high. The council is committed to making the borough fairer for all and reducing poverty. We know that to achieve this, we need to use evidence better. Evidence goes beyond formal research undertaken by a few. It means widening who is involved to include voluntary groups, communities, and residents to understand their needs and listen to and incorporate their experiences, particularly from those we don’t often hear from. We then need to use this evidence to improve the ways in which we design services to better reflect residents’ ambitions and take action on the “wider determinants of health” (such as housing, employment, and the environment), which have such an important impact on our health and wellbeing. VISION. To establish a Centre of Research Excellence in Islington that will transform the way we work. Through this Centre we will have a better understanding of what works to improve residents’ lives. We will use this knowledge to improve health and wellbeing and reduce inequalities. We AIM to: 1. Create an environment, in partnership with residents and communities, which places evidence at the heart of how we work to improve residents’ lives. 2. Strengthen how we generate and use evidence to identify and reduce inequalities in health and wellbeing. 3. Build capacity and participation in creating evidence to drive positive change, ensuring that residents are central to these activities. PLANNED ACTIVITIES focus on three related areas: Building partnerships. We will build stronger partnerships across Islington by improving the ways in which we work and communicate with each other. We will also work more with our residents, particularly those most experiencing hardship or those we don’t usually hear from; charities and other community groups; health and wellbeing leaders across London and beyond; and universities. Create and use evidence. We will improve how we collect, store, join together, and use the information we collect. We will find different ways to use this information to feed into how we make decisions across Islington, focused on improving residents’ lives. Building skills and resources. We will train our staff, councillors, community groups, and residents in the skills needed to create and use evidence so that it can be most effectively captured to achieve change. PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT. Voluntary and community resident groups have shaped our plans. These include creating Citizen Ambassador Panels and a Community Researcher team to review council plans and undertake research locally to feed into these plans. Residents and the voluntary sector will be at the heart of all our activities, ensuring that we continually address residents’ priorities in an organised and coordinated way. KNOWLEDGE SHARING. We will share what we find during this programme widely with different audiences and find new ways to share achievements and challenges. Residents and community groups will be actively involved in how we do this, so that we can maximise impact to those most likely to benefit. IMPACT. Establishing this Research Centre will create the energy, excitement, and capability to improve and change the ways in which we create and use evidence across Islington to transform our residents’ lives. This will help us to realise our ambition of making Islington a more equal place, where everyone who lives in the borough has an equal chance to thrive.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Council of the City of Newcastle Upon Tyne
Award_Title: Levelling up health research in Newcastle City Council: a collaborative approach to tackling health inequalities by addressing the wider determinants of health
Abstract: Public health improvement is a fundamental aspect of what Newcastle City Council does, not least because ours is a city with significant areas of deprivation. As a result, life expectancy and healthy life expectancy are low in Newcastle – many people spend a higher proportion of their shorter lives coping with chronic disease and disability, which affects rates of economic inactivity, physical inactivity, mental health, formal and informal care needs, and preventable mortality. We want research to underpin all our work in support of tackling the wider determinants of health, but we still face challenges in doing so in a coherent, systematic and sustained way. That is why we see the establishment of a Health Determinants Research Collaboration (HDRC) as a crucial opportunity to transform our approach to research and the impact it will have on our city and residents. Research capacity exists in part, but several barriers have been identified which prevent the council being more effective as a research organisation. We aim to establish a comprehensive cross-council research and data infrastructure, with senior leader commitment, that embeds evidence-informed decision making across all service areas, and offers a leading city-wide resource for partners. This will facilitate a deeper understanding of health determinants across the communities we and partners serve, and inform service design, evaluation and improvement. It will be integral to shaping our Council Plan and Local Plan, as well as our Health and Wellbeing Strategy. It will also improve co-creation of research with academic institutions, breaking down systemic organisational barriers so that research is coproduced (including through public involvement) and provides timely results to inform decision making and practice. This will be done through the creation of a number of new, specialist roles to support the council make best use of its data, and to engage in research and analysis to support improved outcomes. Leadership roles in the HDRC will promote a research culture by sharing best practice and helping teams to consider how they plan, carry out, and use research. The HDRC will have a particular focus on reducing socio-economic and place-based health inequalities, whilst recognising the intersectional and compound effects of inequality on already marginalised populations, including those with protected characteristics and vulnerable groups. Factors associated with poverty impact on individuals’ resilience, and resources to access the conditions necessary for a healthy life and/or adopt healthier behaviours, resulting in health inequity. The involvement of service users, decision makers, statutory partners and the public will be principally based on our strong networks and established practice within the local authority. We will also establish roles for public and stakeholder engagement, and dissemination and will host a peer network for sharing and learning from other HDRCs and councils that want to be more research active. Success will be monitored through internal measures to identify the change the HDRC is making to how the council operates, alongside population measures of changed outcomes for the city population. We will disseminate learning through our existing partnerships, mechanisms and public engagement forums.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: An evaluation of an alternative Child Friendly Dental Pathway for Paediatric patients
Abstract: The problem Children in the poorest areas of England have much more tooth decay than those in wealthier areas, and this is a major health inequality. These children are often referred by regular dentists to a Community Dental Service (CDS) for specialist treatment and many are sent on to hospital to have teeth removed while asleep under general anaesthetic. At present, about 15,000 children need teeth removed in hospital each year in England, and this is the commonest reason for children being admitted. Unfortunately waiting times for CDS and hospital referrals have increased during the Covid 19 pandemic. Our proposed solution and study aim During Covid 19, a potential alternative to treating these children was introduced; a special kind of dental practice known as a “Child Friendly Dental Practice” (CFDP). These practices have additional support that allows them the time to manage children with lots of decay and their waiting times are only a few weeks. By seeing these children earlier there is a good chance we can reduce the need to send them to a CDS or to hospital for extractions. This option should reduce demands on hospitals and enable them to focus on those children who have the most urgent complex dental needs. We have some pilot study information which suggests that around 50% of children referred to Child Friendly Dental Practice can be treated there without the need to visit another service. Child Friendly Dental Practices have been developed around a prevention focused and evidence-based model of care that offer benefits of clinical techniques for prevention of decay. The working assumption underpinning the pilot was that the Child Friendly Dental Practices would improve things. We will test that assumption using a 'realist approach' and unravel the mechanisms which could determine how it works. We are therefore going to test these Child Friendly Dental Practices at a much larger scale than our very small pilot study, and we want to do this in a research project that measures all the different aspects of the children, their treatment, whether they ultimately still need teeth taken out under general anaesthetic, and costs and savings. The expected impact of our approach We think that Child Friendly Dental Practices can greatly improve the oral health of children who have severe decay and who are often from the most deprived areas, who may otherwise endure pain and loss of sleep waiting for CDS or hospital referral and likely have multiple teeth extracted at a young age. This approach could reduce the time children wait to be seen for dental problems, the number being treated under general anaesthetic and reduce the costs to the NHS. In addition to published studies supporting the proposed approach, the pilot scheme in Greater Manchester has demonstrated the ability of dentists with some additional training to be able to treat a significant proportion of children referred from regular dentists. Other areas of the UK are already interested in this work and whether Child Friendly Dental Practices would be beneficial for their area. Our work has been brought together by a team involving those working within Child Friendly Dental Practices and CDS, with Commissioners who decide what services to fund and experts who have previously carried out research within child dental health, and with input from members of the public who have used the services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Crisis care for children and young people with mental health problems: national mapping, models of delivery, sustainability and experience (CAMH-Crisis2)
Abstract: There has been a sharp and worrying increase in mental health problems experienced by children and young people. Prior to the pandemic, one in eight 5-19 year olds in England had a probable mental disorder. In 2020, amongst 5-16 year olds this figure had risen to one in six. Amongst those with a mental health difficulty, almost half of older teenagers and a quarter of 11-16 year olds report having self-harmed or attempted suicide. Extreme psychosocial distress, with or without self-harm, is often referred to as a ‘crisis’. Services for young people in crisis are a UK priority, and provision is expanding. However, very little research into crisis services for young people has been undertaken. We therefore do not know what crisis responses currently exist, who uses services, or what works best for children and young people and their families. This project will answer the question: ‘How are mental health crisis responses for children and young people up to the age of 25 sustained, experienced and integrated within their local systems of services’? We will work with a group of young people who advise on research, some of whom have used crisis services, to address the following three objectives: 1. To describe and map NHS, local authority, education and third sector approaches to the implementation and organisation of crisis care for children and young people across England and Wales. 2. To identify eight contrasting case studies in which to evaluate how crisis services have developed and are currently organised, sustained, experienced and integrated within the context of their local systems of services. 3. To compare and contrast these services in the context of the available international evidence, drawing out clear implications for the design and delivery of future crisis responses for children and young people and their families. To help us meet our objectives we will make use of normalisation process theory. This supports studies into what helps, and what hinders, the implementation and sustainability of new approaches to care. We will meet our first objective using a survey, creating a detailed record of crisis responses across England and Wales and how they are organised, implemented and used. To meet our second objective, from the detailed record created in meeting objective one we will identify eight contrasting services selected for variety in terms of: geographic and socioeconomic setting (England/Wales, urban/rural, and relative affluence/poverty); populations served (including ethnic diversity); and service configuration (including third sector and/or social care involvement). Treating each as a case study, we will interview young people and family members who have used the service. We will also interview commissioners, managers and practitioners, including those providing a crisis response and those working in other parts of the local system. We will gather operational policies and related documents, and data on how each service is used and by whom. In our analysis we will focus on understanding how each crisis service is provided, experienced, implemented and sustained. To meet our final objective we will compare and contrast each case study, closing our project by drawing clear, actionable, lessons for the future commissioning and provision of high-quality crisis responses sensitive to the support and access needs of a diverse range of children and young people receiving care from a range of services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Quantifying, Understanding and Enhancing Relational Continuity of Care (QUERCC)
Abstract: Background Relational continuity of care (RCC) is the extent to which patients see the same clinicians over time. It is linked to better health outcomes and patient experience. However, RCC is declining, partly due to increasing practice size, part-time working, staff and patient turnover. Most general practices neither measure nor monitor their own RCC and may be unaware how within-practice policies affect it. In choosing a measure, practices need to consider how it fits their own objectives. The effect of practice-level characteristics - practice size, part-time working, staff and patient turnover - on RCC is unquantified. So we do not know how much changes in these characteristics will change RCC, or if they can be mitigated by within-practice policies. We know some practices have higher RCC than expected, given their characteristics. Learning from them could provide valuable knowledge on optimising RCC. Although health and resource benefits of RCC are well recognised, no economic analysis has evaluated the overall effects on health outcomes and resource use (prescribing, consultations, hospital admissions) or whether the economic case for RCC differs between population groups (e.g. older v younger patients). Most importantly, to optimise RCC, practices need realistic guidance, which is adaptable to their own context. Aim: to understand how to optimise RCC in primary care Objectives: 1. Develop guidance for general practices on measuring RCC 2. Quantify the effects of staff and patient turnover, part-time working and practice size on RCC 3. Understand how some general practices achieve high RCC 4. Develop practical guidance to help general practices optimise RCC 5. Undertake economic analysis of the effects of changing RCC Methods First, in two consensus workshops of patients, primary care clinicians and researchers, we will develop an understanding of RCC and guidance to help practices select measures. Second, in a large primary care database, we will model the association between practice RCC and practice-level characteristics (practice size, staff and patient turnover, part-time working). Having determined predictors of RCC we will identify practices showing higher-than-expected RCC (positive deviants) for investigation as case studies. Third, in depth case studies of positive deviant practices will explore staff and patient experience, trade-offs between access and continuity, and identify practice policies contributing to RCC. Fourth, we will undertake economic analysis of the projected effects of RCC, using linked primary and secondary care data. We will stratify the analysis by age, sex, deprivation and chronic disease status. Fifth, in two workshops of clinicians, researchers and patients, we will co-design empirically-informed practical guidance to improve RCC. This will synthesise findings of our quantitative analyses, case studies, and existing continuity of care research in the UK and internationally. Patient and public involvement (PPI) is embedded in the project, through quarterly consultation with a lay advisory group chaired by our PPI co-applicant. Lay participants will be trained in and contribute to analysis of qualitative data. Timeline 36 months Impact & dissemination Alongside academic dissemination, we will report to NHS England, develop training materials for the RCGP and for our own MSc programme. Following this we will evaluate an intervention to improve RCC as a cluster RCT.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Evaluating the impact of artificial intelligence triage in online consultations to reduce delays in urgent and emergency primary care
Abstract: BACKGROUND GP practices in England provide over 30 million appointments per month, some of which are for medical conditions that require urgent treatment like infections or heart attacks. Delays in urgent care can lead to patient harm including hospital admission or death. A key challenge is to identify which patients require urgent help. Over the past two years, 96% of GP practices in England provided online consultations, which enable patients to request help from their healthcare teams by submitting forms over the internet. Online consultations come to the GP practice unprioritized and can potentially exacerbate delays in providing urgent care. One potential solution is for the online consultation system to automatically detect and highlight urgent and emergency requests as soon as they are submitted as an add-on feature (‘AI Triage’). AIMS AND OBJECTIVES Our overall aim is to evaluate the impact of introducing AI Triage to GP practices already using online consultations on delays in urgent and emergency primary care, healthcare resource use, and explore how these are influenced by organisational context and patient characteristics. Our objectives are to: O1. Implement AI Triage in a representative group of English GP practices. O2. Explore how organisational context influences AI Triage implementation and impact O3. Quantify the usage and accuracy of AI Triage, and its potential and actual influence on triage behaviour O4. Evaluate the impact of AI Triage on urgent and emergency care delays and healthcare resource use at the patient-level METHODS WP1: We will recruit 20 intervention and 20 control GP practices that have used an online consultation system (PATCHS) for at least 12 months. Intervention GP practices will receive an add-on AI Triage intervention (PATCHS+AI Triage). WP2: We will conduct a qualitative process evaluation based on three in-depth case studies, supplemented by interviews with up to 45 staff and 20 patients. WP3: We will conduct a quantitative process evaluation focusing on descriptive analysis of AI Triage implementation (fidelity, dose, and reach), and prediction accuracy. We will examine counterfactual AI Triage predictions, and actual behaviour change, by comparing triage decisions in both control and intervention practices. WP4: We will undertake a controlled interrupted time series analysis evaluating the impact of AI Triage on delays in completing patient requests defined as urgent and emergency by GP practice staff at the patient-level. Secondary analyses will evaluate its impact on the number of online consultations submitted by patients, A&E attendances, and emergency hospital admissions. Sub-group analyses will test for differences in effects for patients with difference characteristics. IMPACT We will implement AI Triage in 40 GP practices, which could be rapidly expanded to all GP practices using PATCHS in England (anticipated to be over 1000 by the time the project starts) and offered to all other GP practices within 5 years. We will create help guides and toolkits on how to use AI Triage safely and effectively for patients and GP practices to be delivered during online consultation deployments.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Evaluating the implementation of the Transforming Children and Young People's Mental Health Provision Green Paper
Abstract: Background The Children and Young People’s (CYP) Mental Health Green Paper Programme is an ambitious implementation programme creating mental health support teams (MHSTs) to provide extra capacity for early intervention and work with school/college staff to promote emotional wellbeing across their setting; funding training to senior mental health leads in schools/colleges to support them in their role; and testing a four-week waiting time for access to specialist mental health services. Aims & Objectives The overall evaluation question is: How is the Programme being implemented at different sites and what are its impacts, user outcomes and costs for different groups of CYP and their families, and different types of education settings and mental health services? The specific objectives are to: 1. Update the Programme’s theory of change as a framework for the evaluation, and identify and/or develop measures to assess Programme impacts and outcomes 2. Understand service models and ways of working and assess the extent of any learning across sites and over time 3. Assess the relationship between Programme workforce, user outcomes and sustainability 4. Compare activity, user experiences, user outcomes and costs between sites and for different CYP sub-groups 5. Explore whether and how the Programme, and MHSTs specifically, are contributing to the development of whole school/college approaches 6. Identify scope for improvement of Programme delivery to improve effectiveness and cost- effectiveness 7. Advise how CYP outcome data beyond 2025 should be collected and analysed at low cost Methods The evaluation combines routine data analysis, quantitative and qualitative data from the Programme’s first five waves (including 287 MHSTs, working in 4,789 education settings, and covering a total pupil population of 2.44 million) and in-depth learning from six purposively selected Programme sites. It is comprised of 8 work packages (WPs): WPs 1-3: Undertaken across all sites WP1: Initial scoping work to update the Programme theory of change and finalise methods WP2: Key informant and education settings surveys WP3: Analysis of routine data from the Mental Health Services Data Set and the National Pupil Database WPs 4-7: Undertaken in six case study sites WP4: Interviews with individuals in strategic, implementation and delivery roles WP5: Capturing experiences and outcomes of direct support from an MHST WP6: Assessing school-level activities and their effects WP7: Comparative costing and cost-effectiveness analysis WP8: Specification of a method for longer-term monitoring of outcomes beyond the study period Timescale The study will start in June 2023, with final data collection in 2025 and a final report in May 2026, plus interim reporting. Impact & Dissemination We will work with our CYP, parent/carer and strategic advisory groups, and collaborators the National Children’s Bureau, to translate the study findings into accessible, usable and high-impact learning for practice. Formative feedback will be provided to those involved in Programme implementation at all levels to support rollout. Dissemination activities will also include: an animated output co-produced with CYP; a consensus event exploring the implications of the findings for decision-makers; infographics, social media, podcasts and blogs; publication in peer reviewed and professional journals; and presentations at conferences, seminars, workshops and meetings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Improving Detection and Management of Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: Creation of a Tees Valley Research Partnership Hub
Abstract: Creating a Research Hub to develop partnerships with professionals and members of the community to increase liver disease research in the Tees Valley Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) is a chronic disease that affects around 1 in 3 people in the UK. If NAFLD is not managed effectively it can progress to advanced scarring of the liver, cirrhosis, and for some, end-stage liver disease. NAFLD is directly linked to obesity and low levels of physical activity, therefore it is considered preventable for most people. The Tees Valley in the North East of England has some of the highest rates of liver disease in England. Darlington, Stockton-on-Tees, and Redcar and Cleveland are ranked 8th, 11th, and 12th for the percentage of adults with overweight or obesity. Darlington, Stockton-on-Tees and Redcar and Cleveland are ranked 7th, 10th, and 13th for death caused by NAFLD in those aged under 75. Hartlepool and Middlesbrough are ranked 4th and 16th for the number of hospital admissions related to NAFLD. Research helps to improve clinical and community services, however there is very little liver disease research in the Tees Valley. Aim: We will create a ‘Tees Valley Research Partnership Hub’. The hub will bring people together with different kinds of expertise to design good quality research projects. These projects will involve researching ways to detect NAFLD earlier and developing services to support people with NAFLD make lifestyle changes. We will increase the amount of research undertaken and provide those involved with training/mentoring to conduct good quality research. Methods: Objective 1: We will work with research partners to agree goals of the hub; what the roles of its members should be; and ensure they receive training to fulfil their roles Objective 2: We will work with our Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement (PPIE) group to review current NAFLD services. We will look at how these services are provided, what type of support they offer; and whether they are suitable for all people with NAFLD. The PPIE group together, the research team and public health and clinical professionals will agree a future service plan Objective 3: We will interview healthcare professionals to find out their training needs to detect NAFLD, and to support people with NAFLD to make lifestyle changes Objective 4: We will work with research hub partners, including members of the public to develop research proposals. Other colleagues from national charities Liver North and Obesity UK; the Research Design Service; the Newcastle Clinical Trials Unit, and the Clinical Research Network have agreed to support us. Timeline: Our research proposal will last 18 months. Objective 1 (months 1-5); Objective 2 (months 5-12); Objective 3 (months 5-12); and objective 4 (months 10-18) Impact and dissemination: We will run four events to engage people with our research hub. We will hold a research hub launch event and agree aims of the hub. We will communicate regularly with research hub partners and communities to provide updates. This will involve presenting our work at local, national, and international meetings and publishing our work in scientific journals. We will also use social media. We will share our work within and beyond the Tees valley. We will create a research partnership hub that has a clear purpose and will live beyond the project timeline.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Combining data to identify families at risk of the harmful health effects of overcrowded housing – a feasibility study
Abstract: Research question: How can we define and identify household overcrowding affecting the wellbeing of families, using publicly available and council-held data? Background Household overcrowding is a growing problem in England and is linked to poorer health. It facilitates the spread of infections and, coupled with poor housing quality, is a risk factor for injuries and poor mental health. For councils to alleviate the effects of overcrowding, new methods are required to identify which houses are overcrowded and how it affects residents. In particular, existing measures are not tailored to particular populations, such as families, where overcrowding limits children’s ability to play and study. Aims and objectives Aim: To develop a method to identify households with families at high risk of overcrowding affecting their wellbeing. Objectives: - Agree a definition of household overcrowding affecting family wellbeing with people that have lived experience of overcrowding - Operationalise this measure in one council, by combining publicly available and council-held data, to identify households with families at risk of the effects of overcrowding on wellbeing - Understand the wider applicability of this measure with other councils and its implications for population-level intervention design Methods A mixed methods design will be used. A resident engagement approach will be taken throughout the project. This considers families with lived experience of overcrowding and community representatives as partners in the project, alongside service professionals and researchers. From discussions with these groups, a description and definition of overcrowding affecting households with families will be produced. Based on this definition, data available to the council will be combined and analysed quantitatively to provide a composite measure of household overcrowding affecting family wellbeing. The methods and illustrative results from one council will be shared with other councils, with a short survey to understand its wider applicability. Timelines for delivery This 12-month project has three overlapping workstreams. Workstream 1: discussions with lived experience partners, representatives and council staff (Feb-Jul 23), with follow up analysis Autumn 23. Workstream 2: data linkage to construct a tailored family measure of overcrowding and analysis (Feb-Oct 23). Workstream 3: draft outputs shared for discussion and feedback with wider council collaborators (Oct-Nov 23), with reporting in January 2024. Anticipated impact and dissemination For councils, the project will provide a feasible method of identifying areas of potential overcrowding affecting the health of families in their area. Longer term, it will enable councils to design and target interventions to alleviate the effects of overcrowding and that may increase the wellbeing of families. Guidance will be produced and disseminated through council and public health networks. For lived experience volunteers, the project should immediately provide the sense of feeling heard. Longer term, their views will have an influence on local and wider policy. Lay summaries in visual forms (e.g. video) will be developed with lived experience partners and disseminated via partner networks. For research, this project will advance our understanding of methods to identify overcrowding affecting specific populations. Findings will be disseminated via peer-reviewed publications and conferences.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: ICANEQUAL: Reducing inequalities for those at risk and those diagnosed with Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC)
Abstract: Liver cancer is the fifth most common cancer in the world. Over the past 10 years the number of people who are diagnosed with liver cancer has increased. At the same time, the number of people dying from liver cancer has increased. Patients do better if they are diagnosed early and get the right treatment at the right time. But, in the UK, some liver cancer patients are diagnosed too late or do not get the best treatments. These patients have poorer quality of life, and lower chances of survival. We think this is because of inequalities in access to timely diagnosis and treatment. We know that these inequalities affect underserved groups such as people who experience social disadvantage or people living in remote and rural areas. But we do not know why. Until we know more about how and why this happen It will be very difficult to reduce current inequalities. This partnership project will build a Community of Expertise for liver cancer. We will work closely with charities, community groups and patient groups such as the British Liver Trust, Egality Health, Can-Survive UK, BME Cancer Communities, Wai Yin Society. The underserved groups who are most affected by the inequalities are also groups who do not usually take part in liver cancer research. This partnership project will include these groups. The partnership project will be designed and planned with our public and patient partners. As will any research that follows. We will run a workshop series. Each workshop will bring 25-30 people together. The people taking part in the workshops will have many different backgrounds and will include people who have been diagnosed with liver cancer, charities, community groups and patient groups, primary care doctors and nurses, surgeons, oncologists, and public health professionals. The people taking part in the workshops will talk about liver cancer diagnosis and treatment, the problems that underserved groups face, and things that can be done to improve inequalities. The workshops will help us to do four things: 1. Build lasting relationships between healthcare professionals, professional bodies, charities, community groups, patient groups and employers. 2. Improve partnerships between researchers working in the fields of cancer, public health, health services research, and implementation science. 3. Increase knowledge and understanding about liver cancer diagnosis and care across the UK, identify the gaps for underserved groups, and find ways to develop research with these groups in mind. 4. Provide the knowledge and partnerships that we need to design and run clinical trials to test ways to increase liver cancer survival. This partnership project will help find out why liver cancer diagnosis and treatment fail underserved groups, and what can be done to reduce inequalities. We will share our results with our workshop participants and partners and through publications in medical journals.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Exploratory research to examine the health impact of scams and fraud and the current knowledge and systems in the police and partner agencies for targeting and delivering victim support services
Abstract: Research Question Exploratory research to examine the health impact of scams and fraud on victims and current knowledge and systems in the police and partner agencies for targeting and delivering support. Background Fraud is growing rapidly and is now the most common crime-type in England and Wales. Victims can suffer considerable impact to their physical and mental health, but there are large gaps in understanding what makes some victims vulnerable and how their needs can be met. As first responders, the police are mainly guided by a law enforcement and crime reduction agenda. Their knowledge and data-capture on victim health needs and the support they offer varies nationally. Aims and Objectives We aim to produce an evidence base around fraud's physical and mental health impacts and examine current systems for supporting victims within two police forces, building on emerging police policies and systems for supporting vulnerable victims. We will: • Analyse the scale, nature and distribution of health impact • Analyse the association between health impact and wider vulnerability (for example, repeat victimisation) • Index current data available to police and other services for assessing health impact • Map current services, resources and capability in the police and support services for addressing health impact Follow-up This project aims to lay the foundation for follow up work to develop robust and evidence-based national frameworks for assessing the health impact of fraud. The follow-up project would involve: • Roundtable events with stakeholders, including victims, to develop the proposed framework • Sourcing local partnerships of police, health and welfare services to trial the framework • Completing process evaluations with practitioners to implement the framework and assess victims' health outcomes • Disseminating findings and learning points nationally Methods This study will use two partnering police forces as case studies. These forces have pioneered a bespoke, multi-disciplinary support system for vulnerable fraud victims, meaning they possess data and expertise most areas lack. The study will employ quantitative and qualitative techniques such as: • Literature review on fraud victimisation, health impact, vulnerability, needs and support systems • Cross-sectional analysis of data from police and other service providers; variables for health impact and wider vulnerability, distribution across victims and crime, and associations with key characteristics of the victim and crime • Semi-structured interviews with local policymakers and practitioners who support victims, including police, social services, victim support and health services, and with national stakeholders with subject matter expertise • Interviews with prior victims who have been assessed as vulnerable and supported by specialists, to gather evidence on their expectations and experiences of this support Anticipated impact and dissemination The Police Foundation will publish a report on its website, disseminate it at a media launch and promote it on its blog, newsletter and social media channels so the research reaches an audience of policymakers and practitioners. A journal article will be published to reach an academic audience. This research seeks to fill substantive gaps in the evidence base and produce a firm foundation for developing more robust and systematic frameworks for identifying and supporting fraud victims with health and welfare needs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: North West England Research Partnership to Improve Early Detection of Liver Disease
Abstract: Liver disease is an epidemic with approximately one in four people in the UK having risk factors that could lead to their liver not working properly. A proportion of people develop scarring within the liver and this is usually not identified until the liver stops doing its job and starts to fail. It is one of the UK’s largest health challenges and is a particular problem in the Northwest of England, which has some of the highest rates of liver disease related deaths in the UK. Research carried out by the Integrated Diagnostics for Early Detection of Liver Disease (ID LIVER) project, led by The University of Manchester and Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust, has allowed us to develop new and improved patient care pathways for the earlier diagnosis and management of liver disease in Manchester. Our approach for this project is to utilise what we have learnt and build on our existing research partnerships with local communities to grow the network into geographical regions with high numbers of deaths related to liver disease but traditionally poor participation in research. To inform our approach, we will listen to and learn from the experiences of community leaders and people from groups at risk of developing liver disease in areas across the Northwest. We will work in partnership with a network of national experts who have experience of working out the economic impact of liver disease in the NHS. These experts will form part of the project network, alongside public, health infrastructure and clinical representatives. Two meetings will be held in Manchester to look at how best to evaluate the economic impact of new clinical pathways in different locations outside of Manchester. We will also hold a workshop halfway through the project to bring together the expertise of public contributors, community and health infrastructure organisations, clinicians, local authorities and researchers to discuss how best to establish new pathways of care in areas identified as most in need of intervention. This workshop will allow us to devise our research question and what evidence is needed to answer it, in preparation for the next stage of NIHR funding to be announced in early 2024. Primary success will be the development of strong research partnerships that enable the sharing of expertise across underserved communities in the North West of England and promote the implementation of new clinical pathways for earlier, more accurate and potentially life-saving identification and management of liver disease.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: A Multidisciplinary national research partnership for early diagnosis of liver disease in alcohol treatment programmes and the role of liver disease biomarker-based behavioural interventions in reducing alcohol-related harm.
Abstract: Alcohol-related liver disease is a major, preventable cause of early death. People develop liver failure because of the build-up of scar tissue in the liver, when extensive it leads to liver failure. Liver disease causes no symptoms in the early stages and by the time people know it is often too late for treatment. People attending community alcohol treatment services are a high-risk group for having liver disease, but most are unaware if they have it. Tests for liver disease(scaring) are available but not used routinely and there is no agreed way how test results should be given to people to avoid false reassurance or causing anxiety. Stopping or reducing drinking is the best way of preventing alcohol related liver disease. Scans and blood tests are now available which can reliably detect liver disease. We do not know if someone knowing they have liver damage reduces their alcohol intake. However, our recent KLIFAD study, which used liver scans and feedback by a standard script and patient video stories designed by people affected by the liver disease indicates that this approach is feasible to be used in alcohol treatment services. Our research aims to build a national research partnership between teams working in alcohol treatment settings, both in communities and hospitals, with researchers who can bring expertise in liver disease diagnosis and interventions to reduce alcohol intake based on those diagnostic tests. We have an existing partnership between two of the largest groups providing alcohol treatments (GCL and NHS alcohol treatment services) and researchers in liver disease. We will use the extensive knowledge and coverage of those alcohol service providers to identify areas with the potential to undertake trials in early liver disease diagnosis. We have details on them and their clients to be able to ensure that factors such as deprivation and ethnicity can be considered so that any research finding will be relevant to the whole of the UK population. We will use the NIHR research targeting tool for liver disease, an online application that helps to identify areas of liver disease burden and how this relates to liver research activities. We can then link the two to decide where best to place research opportunities for staff working in alcohol services to develop their research skills so that they and their clients can participate in later studies. We will meet with the staff from the alcohol treatment providers to identify their research training needs. With the help of the Nottingham Clinical Trial Unit, NIHR clinical research Network, and NIHR academy we will organise training programmes and mentorship opportunities. We will then conduct workshops to strengthen and refine the research questions we need to ask to bid for funding for clinical trials which can answer the key question of how best to diagnose liver disease early and how best to communicate these results to people attending alcohol services to reduce their alcohol intake. We need expert partnerships between alcohol workers, people affected by alcohol use and those suffering from liver disease and patients and the public to refine the feedback on liver scarring tests and expand the collection of alcohol recovery stories. Developing this partnership has the potential to significantly reduce the number of people at risk in alcohol services going on to develop liver disease.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: The Midlands Liver Research Alliance - A partnership to optimise obesity-related liver disease research; targeting areas of high incidence and underserved communities.
Abstract: What is the problem? Over the past 50 years, the number of people dying from liver disease has more than doubled and is going to keep rising. We need to research how to detect liver disease early and how to deal with it as quickly as possible. Right now, early stage liver disease is hard to detect because people don’t normally have symptoms until it is too late. There are different types of liver disease, the most common types are related to: 1) Drinking too much alcohol 2) Being overweight or obese, which makes fat build up in the liver 3) Having hepatitis (from a viral infection or too much alcohol). The number of people with liver disease from having overweight or obesity (obesity-related liver disease) is rising worldwide alongside increasing levels of obesity and type 2 diabetes. Obesity and type 2 diabetes are known to make obesity-related liver disease worse. Over half of people with obesity in Europe are likely to have liver disease without even knowing. Research shows that where you live and your ethnicity can affect your risk of getting liver disease, but we need to do more to look into this. What are we going to do? We will set up an 18-month ‘research partnership’ across the Midlands, bringing together specialists, researchers and the public to deal with obesity-related liver disease and bring in national experts. The partnership will create a ‘patient and public engagement network’ to help include all populations, especially those who don’t normally take-part in research. Who will be involved? The partnership will involve different specialist groups, academic experts, universities, medical doctors, hospitals, charities, industry, patients and public and others across the Midlands. Leicester, Nottingham and Birmingham’s Biomedical Research Centres are leading experts in the area of liver and obesity research and will lead the partnership. What will the partnership do? 1) Professionals and patients will attend group workshops and will work together to decide on the priorities for obesity-related liver disease research. An expert team with mixed expertise will set research questions and plan the best way to answer them using the partnership’s expertise and available resources. 2) Members will attend a group engagement event to work out how to best use and share the knowledge, skills and resources within the partnership to develop and perform the research as well as possible. We will make sure that we share training, mentorship, facilities and resources to help the areas of the partnership with less experience of liver disease research. 3) Patients/service users, carers and the public will have a key role in making sure the partnership performs research to help those who are affected with obesity-related liver disease. We will organise inclusivity and engagement activities to increase awareness about obesity-related liver disease. We will ask for help from patients and the public to design research that targets issues that are important to them. We will also train people who would like to develop their engagement role and become part of future funding application teams. What value will this partnership add? This partnership is bringing together specialists, doctors, universities, patients and the public from across the Midlands and also bringing in expertise from national experts to share knowledge, expertise and resources to make obesity-related liver disease a priority, in research, medical and community settings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: CRASH-4 trial (Clinical Randomisation of an Anti-fibrinolytic in Symptomatic mild Head injury in older adults) Intramuscular tranexamic acid for the treatment of symptomatic mild traumatic brain injury in older adults: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
Abstract: Study question: What are the effects of early intramuscular tranexamic acid on intracranial bleeding, hospital admission, death, disability and dementia in older adults with mild TBI. Background: Mild traumatic brain injury (TBI) can cause death, disability and dementia in older adults. Timely tranexamic acid (TXA) treatment, by preventing or limiting intracranial bleeding, could reduce these risks. The CRASH-4 trial will assess the effects of early intramuscular TXA in about 5,000 older adults with mild TBI. Methods: We are recruiting patients aged 50 years or older if they have a history or signs (laceration, bruise, swelling or pain in head or face) of a head injury; a GCS = 13; any impairment of consciousness and are within 3 hours of injury. We enrol patients at the scene of the injury or in the ambulance. We also enrol patients who present directly to NHS emergency departments. We randomly allocate patients to receive an intramuscular (IM) injection of 500 mg tranexamic acid or matching placebo. We give one 5mL injection (100mg/ml TXA or placebo) or two 2.5mL injections depending on muscle mass. The primary outcome is discharge home from the emergency department within 24 hours. Secondary outcomes include: intracranial bleeding on CT scan, death, disability, vascular occlusive events, seizures, pneumonia, other adverse events, re-admission to hospital within 28 days and any dementia diagnosis at 1 year follow up. Dementia is identified through linkage to routinely collected health-care data. To test the trial procedures and the acceptability of the intervention, we conducted a pilot phase in 500 patients. The pilot confirmed that the study procedures work and that the IM injection is tolerated. Based on the observed recruitment and outcome event rates, we are confident that this trial can be conducted successfully. The trial currently is recruiting. The main phase will run from 1st March 2023 to 1st October 2026 (36 months). There will be a 30-month (March 23 to August 25) recruitment period with six months for data analysis, reporting and closeout. Impact and dissemination: Hundreds of thousands of patients attend emergency departments after mild TBI. The main threat is intracranial bleeding. Timely TXA treatment could prevent this bleeding, but most older patients are seen too late to benefit. In general, mild TBI patients attend emergency departments where they are admitted, observed and discharged but not treated. This worsens hospital crowding with marginal patient benefit. The information from this trial could improve treatment strategies. Rather than being admitted but not treated, mild TBI patients could be treated and (on many occasions) not admitted. An early IM TXA injection at the scene could reduce intracranial bleeding and the need for hospital admission. We will disseminate the trial results via conferences, publications, social media and films. We work with victim organisations and head injury charities who will help ensure timely implementation. Our results will inform NICE head injury guidelines and Joint Royal Colleges Ambulance Liaison Committee (JRCALC) guidelines for pre-hospital care. We have discussed the trial with the JRCALC guidelines’ authors and with the National Ambulance Services Medical Directors' Group and they are strongly supportive. NHS England recognises the urgent need to reduce emergency admissions and improve outcomes. Timely out of hospital TXA treatment could help to achieve this.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Prescribing Antidepressants in Primary care: Ethnic inequalities in tReatment (The PAPER Study)
Abstract: Research question: How can we reduce ethnic disparities in the recognition and treatment of depression? Background: South Asians represent the largest ethnic minority in the UK, but prior research has suggested unequal presentation in primary care and differences in antidepressant prescribing practices for these patients.
