Award_Title: Putting Communities at the heart of Policy: The development of a neighbourhood and community-led research culture and system across Manchester.
Abstract: "The Manchester HDRC places communities at the heart of policy by creating a city-wide co-produced research system, cementing existing collaborations and partnerships by linking the City Council (MCC), the University of Manchester (UoM) and other Higher Education Institutions, community groups, housing providers, voluntary, community, social enterprise and faith sector partners to identify and undertake shared research priorities on the wider determinants of health. Manchester is known for its diversity and strong economic growth over the last two decades. However, it faces challenges in improving health outcomes, promoting inclusion, and addressing inequalities, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The ""Making Manchester Fairer"" (MMF) Action Plan focuses on 8 priority themes to combat poverty and health disparities
Status: establishing multi-agency teams in various neighbourhoods. But there is a need to enhance support for residents and better understand their health and well-being concerns. We will accelerate research
Award Budget: aiming to mainstream evidence-based decision-making across the city to address health inequalities effectively. Aims: Engaging & Empowering Communities: to ensure that residents in geographical and shared interest communities have opportunities to influences policy and services. Embedded Community Researchers will empower local communities and residents to participate in research & use evidence to influence decision making. User-friendly systems will disseminate findings among communities to ensure involvement in findings implementation and measuring impact. Building networks & skills: to embed the findings of bottom-up research into practice by disrupting existing hierarchical structures and creating equitable new systems across organisations and departments. Sustainable training

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Orienting Policy Towards Inequality Minimising Actions (OPTIMA): A systems science approach to 20-minute neighbourhood policy and evaluation
Abstract: BACKGROUND The 20-minute neighbourhood (20MN), access to daily service needs within a walkable/wheelable distance, is being rolled out nationally in Scotland, and locally in other parts of the UK and internationally. It explicitly aims to tackle health inequalities. Yet, the current evidence base is insufficient with potential for unintended harms. Significant investments are being made, and much more will be required for full scale-up. Evidence is required to capture the dynamics, key to measuring changing health inequalities, to avoid suboptimal choices becoming ingrained in sunk costs. AIM To produce timely, effective, actionable evidence on 20MNs and their health inequality implications. OBJECTIVES Four overarching objectives: 1) synthesise the current evidence-base and stakeholders’ lived experience, making current uncertainties explicit; 2) compile service location data and overlay a synthetic population to identify baseline priority clusters of ‘left behind’ areas; 3) adapt an existing agent-based model (ABM) to capture the complex interactions of individuals accessing services, and services responding to their access, to add to our understanding of which 20MN interventions might maximise health inequality benefits; 4) use the early stakeholder engagement via modelling to inform and deliver additional robust real-world evaluation. METHODS The project has four work packages (WPs): WP1 will work iteratively across evidence sources (literature and stakeholders) to inform pathways to health outcomes and behaviour rules of individual and service agents within the system. It will identify uncertainties in this evidence, provide ongoing engagements with decision-makers, and feed co-produced evidence and insights in a timely manner to the WPs that follow. WP2 will collate and analyse novel data linkages which capture the baseline conditions for the 20MN policy, and geographical changes over time. WP2 extends existing work spatially (to the whole of Great Britain) and adds measures of service quality and sociodemographic profile to highlight area-level needs. The linked dataset created will underpin WP3's simulation models. We will apply clustering methods to establish a typology of areas which perform similar with respect to outlined 20MN characteristics (e.g., ‘left behind’ areas). WP3 will use spatially explicit ABMs to bring foresight into (i) which interventions might maximise individual health benefits and (ii) the anticipated impacts of these changes on the local areas (or population groups) for health inequality. For feasibility, we will initially focus on health impacts via active travel and a single Scottish local authority. Iteratively, we will validate and expand pathways and places. The dynamic insights can flexibly examine projected health inequality impacts to mitigate unintended consequences. WP4 will identify opportunities and develop plans for natural experimental evaluation with integrated economic evaluation. IMPACT AND DISSEMINATION The research utilises forward-looking methods, and will progressively output and refine evidence to align with the policy timetable. Since the investments are being planned and managed locally, we expect to be able to have a range of impacts by informing this investment and planning towards minimising health inequality harms (and maximising benefits). We will work closely with our stakeholder advisory group and PPIE group to ensure patient and public benefit and maximal impact.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Monitoring and Evaluating the Impact of Dark Kitchens on the Food Environment: Understanding gaps in the data
Abstract: Research question: How can local authorities monitor, evaluate, control and work with dark kitchens to support population health? Background: Dark kitchens (DKs) have various definitions, but are generally understood to be food preparation kitchens without a storefront, optimised for delivery. However, there is significant variance in the meaning attached to DKs by different people, or groups of people. To the best of our knowledge, there is currently no work being undertaken outside of London and specifically in the North of England around DKs. We do not know if current mechanisms to survey and monitor the food environment, such as the Food Standards Agency Food Hygiene Rating Data adequately capture DKs and the type of foods they provide, therefore we will explore if and how DKs are captured in administrative datasets and look for potential gaps with the current data collection methods to provide a good reflection of what is happening on the ground. Aim: to explore if, and how, we can monitor and assess dark kitchens to understand how they impact on diet (and subsequently health). Methods: We will use mixed-methods to explore DK activity across the North of England. Objective 1) Explore and agree a working definition, or definitions, of DKs; Identify DKs across the North of England using social media (SM) analysis on DK activity (identification of key terms around DKs, use of web scraping techniques across popular SM platforms, and creation of a concept map of frequency of key DK terms). Objective 2) Cross reference SM analysis with existing datasets used to monitor food environments (e.g. FSA Food Hygiene Rating data, planning data and commercial rates data) to explore who is trading as a DK, how this can be identified in existing data, and to demonstrate any gaps. Objective 3) Survey all local authorities in England to explore the monitoring of DK trading; Assess, through workshops, the roles that that planning, local authorities (LAs) and national policy can play in regulating the proliferation of DK establishments. Objective 4) Develop a logic model and feasible future intervention plan. Timelines for delivery Feb 2024: Project start. Feb-Mar 2024: Working definition of DKs in North England agreed. Mar-Apr 2024: SM analysis on DK activity / creation of protocol for SM identification of DKs. May 2024: SM analysis results cross-referenced with existing food environment data. Mar-May 2024: All LAs in England surveyed regarding registration activity of DKs. Apr-May 2024: Hold workshops to discuss roles that planning, LAs and national policy can play in regulating the proliferation of DK establishments. Jun-Jul 2024: Logic model and new intervention plan developed. Jul 2024: Project end. Anticipated impact and dissemination: There is a need for LA multi-disciplinary teams working in the food environment space to have access to a relevant and up to date evidence base on DKs. Working with our national and local collaborators we will ensure findings are disseminated beyond the traditional academic audiences, to policy partners in local and national government with particular attention to colleagues working in public health, planning and environmental health colleagues. Planned outputs include a protocol for SM identification of DKs, a co-authored policy document led by a colleague from the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, an online dissemination event for LA colleagues, a Fuse (www.fuse.ac.uk) brief and podcast.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The 'PANDA' research programme: Primary prevention of maternal ANaemia to avoid preterm Delivery and other Adverse outcomes
Abstract: Research Question Does universal primary prevention of anaemia during pregnancy with oral-iron supplementation have an incremental benefit on reducing adverse maternal and infant outcomes? Background Around a third of UK-women develop anaemia during pregnancy, which is associated with adverse outcomes including maternal and neonatal mortality, haemorrhage, prematurity, and stillbirth. Preventing antenatal anaemia using oral-iron supplementation is a significant opportunity for improving maternal and infant outcomes. There is a need for a pragmatic randomised trial of preventative oral-iron supplementation powered on clinical outcomes. Aims and Objectives This programme aims to improve maternal and infant outcomes by evaluating prevention of anaemia during pregnancy with oral-iron supplementation. The specific objectives are to: 1) identify the barriers and facilitators to the initial decision to take, and ongoing adherence to oral-iron, as a basis for designing a behavioural intervention to improve recruitment and adherence during the definitive trial; 2) identify the optimal preventative oral-iron dose, pilot behavioural intervention, and finalise definitive trial protocol; 3) establish clinical and cost-effectiveness in a definitive trial of oral-iron supplementation with a behavioural intervention; 4) evaluate intervention fidelity and enactment; and 5) explore the impact of anaemia prevention on long-term neurodevelopment and maternal outcomes. Methods Five interlinked workstreams (WS) will be conducted. WS1 includes theory-based semi-structured interviews to understand factors influencing preventative oral-iron use during pregnancy. We will develop a behavioural intervention to target the barriers/enablers to initiating taking oral-iron supplements and ongoing adherence. WS2 will select an optimal dose schedule for oral-iron supplementation and pilot the behavioural intervention, to inform the main trial protocol. 240 women will be randomised to one of three oral-iron schedules: single-daily dose; alternate-daily; and three-times/week, taken up to 28-weeks gestation. Outcomes for WS2 will include intervention acceptability, feasibility, adherence, tolerability and changes in haemoglobin concentration. WS3 is a pragmatic, two-arm, multicentre trial of oral-iron supplementation versus placebo, using the preventative dosage regimen defined in WS2. The behavioural intervention will be delivered to all participating women in both trial arms, to optimise recruitment and oral-iron adherence. A sample of 11020 pregnant women will be enrolled across 20 maternity units. The primary outcome is a composite of pre-term birth, stillbirth, neonatal death and small-for-gestational age. Analysis will apply mixed logistic regression alongside an economic evaluation. A mixed-methods parallel process evaluation (WS4) using observations, interviews and surveys will assess fidelity of intervention delivery, adherence and acceptability. WS5 includes seeking consent from women (participating in WS3) to support future data collection from national databases to evaluate long-term maternal and infant neurodevelopment outcomes. Timelines for delivery The research is planned over 61 months. WS1 and WS2 will be completed by month 27 as the definitive trial starts. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination The findings will address the clinical/cost-effectiveness of a primary prevention strategy of anaemia. If effective, understanding barriers/enablers to adherence will inform subsequent wider-scale implementation, as well as having broader implications for other areas of prevention medicine. Dissemination of findings will target key stakeholders including media, online forums, patient and public involvement and health care professional events, and publications.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Sheffield Health and Social Care NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Supporting Physical and Activity through Co-production in people with Severe Mental Illness (SPACES)
Abstract: 1. Aims and Objectives To co-produce a feasible intervention to increase physical activity among people with severe mental illness (SMI), before testing its clinical and cost effectiveness. Key research questions are: 1. What are the barriers and facilitators to taking part in physical activity for people with SMI and how can behaviour change techniques be utilised in a co-produced intervention to increase physical activity in people with SMI? 2. Is it feasible and acceptable to deliver the intervention for people with SMI via the NHS? 3. Is the intervention clinically- and cost-effective? 4. What are the optimal implementation strategies to embed and deliver the intervention in NHS services? 2. Background and Rationale Life expectancy is reduced by around 15-20 years for people with SMI compared to people without SMI, and this health inequality is increasing. Furthermore, the majority of these early deaths are due to physical health problems which are partly preventable. Increasing physical activity can improve physical health in all sectors of the population including people with SMI. The World Health Organization has said that encouraging people to be more active can have as great an impact as quitting smoking. When compared to people without mental health problems, people with SMI have more sedentary lives and are less physically active. Therefore, supporting people with SMI to increase their levels of physical activity could help to reduce the mortality gap people with SMI currently experience. 3. Research Plan Workstream 1: Development and design of the intervention –Months 1-15 We will co-produce a theory-based intervention; combining existing evidence with new components. Workstream 2: Feasibility study – Months 16-36 The intervention and materials will be piloted and refined to maximise acceptability and impact. A randomised controlled feasibility trial will be conducted to address uncertainties in recruitment, retention, outcome measurement, randomisation, and resource use. Workstream 3: Randomised controlled trial – Months 36-72 The clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the intervention will be assessed relative to usual care. Workstream 4: Process Evaluation & Knowledge Mobilisation – Months 36-72 A process evaluation will be conducted alongside the main trial. This will be guided by core constructs of the Theoretical Domains Framework to identify barriers and facilitators to implementation. A knowledge mobilisation strategy will be developed to increase the prospects of uptake. 4. Anticipated IMPACT & Dissemination The SPACES programme will deliver an intervention aimed at increasing physical activity in people with SMI, with a realistic understanding of its clinical and cost-effectiveness. Based on a logic model, decision makers will understand the resources and outputs required for delivery. The chances of impact will be maximised via an understanding of how this intervention can be implemented. Innovative modes of dissemination include; Service User and third sector networks, Applied Research Collaborations and the UKRI Mental Health Network on inequalities in SMI, which is led by the SPACES consortium. The intervention will directly benefit people with SMI and has potential to save lives and NHS resources, and decrease health inequalities in a vulnerable and disadvantaged population.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Examining Impact of Local Area Coordination as a Preventative Intervention in Adult Social Care
Abstract: The UK government posits prevention as a potential solution to the ASC crisis and key to transforming ASC systems. The transformative potential of preventive interventions lies in their ability to relieve demands and financial strain on formal services, while simultaneously developing more effective systems of support and empowerment for citizens and communities. Currently we lack a detailed understanding of how, why and under what circumstances prevention can improve the lives of ASC service users and reduce the need for statutory services. This proposal addresses this important evidence gap by examining the impact of one particular model of prevention, Local Area Coordination (LAC).This prospective and retrospective study investigates whether and how LAC impacts upon the lives of people who engage with the service and the communities in which it operates. This project is a unique collaboration between academics, LAC managers, frontline staff, voluntary/community organisations and people who participate in LAC services. The research will: Provide the first comparative analysis of well established LAC programmes. Utilise qualitative data from LAC participants to inform the development of a cost consequence framework addressing a significant knowledge gap on the impacts of prevention. Situate its impact by comparing the experiences of those who engage in LAC with those who have disengaged addressing gaps in knowledge around causality and the counter-factual. Embed service user involvement; both through the service user advisory board and through the participatory action research approach to reflect their voices. This project will examine LAC through the integration of participatory action research and nested economic study approaches. The research combines quantitative and qualitative examination of secondary process and LAC system level data, alongside experiential qualitative data gathering on the LAC network in place and on participants' experiences of LAC and the outcomes they perceive it to produce. These data, alongside the review of secondary data sources, are used to develop the cost consequences analysis framework. It is this distinctive combination of methods which will produce a more extensive examination of the effectiveness of LAC; both in terms of its capacity to deliver benefits to the lives of service users (and the communities they live in) and as a preventive intervention. With increased emphasis on preventative ASC approaches and community based programs in the aftermath of COVID-19, this research will provide timely analytical findings to strengthen and inform policy in this field. Our trusted relationships with the National LAC network and broader relationships with both practitioners and national policy makers through both our Enabling Social Action and COVID-19 projects, provide the foundations for ensuring that the findings can have direct impact on decision-making. The findings will provide a stronger evidence base for understanding how, why and under what circumstances LAC can make a difference to ASC provision and create an analytical framework which can be applied to other preventative interventions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The FIRESIDE Study: Optimising Fire and Rescue Service “Safe & Well” visits to support detection and sign-posting for mental health problems in older adults
Abstract: RESEARCH QUESTION Can current “Safe & Well” (S&W) visits delivered by the Fire and Rescue Service be extended to support detection and sign-posting for mental health problems among older people living in the community? BACKGROUND Mental ill-health is a leading cause of disability worldwide. One-in-four older adults experience symptoms of mental ill-health. Anxiety and depression in later life are associated with distressing life events, such as bereavement, loss of meaningful roles, physical function or decline in cognitive capacity. Loneliness and social isolation, experienced by up to 50% of older adults, are associated with depression and suicide. However, fewer than one-in-six older adults consult a healthcare professional about symptoms of a mental health problem. Attitudes and beliefs about mental health prevent older people from seeking and accessing appropriate healthcare, such as: a lack of mental health awareness, perceived stigma, prioritising physical over mental health, and reluctance to add additional burden on NHS resources. Early detection of mental health problems remains a key NHS priority. Thus, “non-traditional” providers of healthcare may provide innovation solutions to support detection and help-seeking among this population. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES The proposed research aims to examine whether and how Fire and Rescue Service S&W visits can be optimized to include detection and sign-posting for mental health problems (anxiety and depression) in older people. Key objectives are set to explore delivery of existing S&W visits, examine acceptability among mixed stakeholder about extending S&W visits to include a mental health component, refine an intervention programme theory, and agree adaptations to S&W visits and new resources. METHODS Multi-method qualitative study designed in two sequential work packages (WPs). WP1 includes: non-participant observation of S&W visits (as currently designed) to better understand delivery processes, interactions and receptiveness among the public; focus groups with Fire and Rescue Service officers to explore acceptability and identify training needs, and; interviews with older people and health and social care stakeholders to establish in-depth contextual understanding of barriers and facilitators to inform design and implementation. WP2 includes a consensus workshop with a diverse range of stakeholders; findings from WP1 will be used to facilitate and inform workshop discussion to agree core components of the extended S&W visit. TIMELINES FOR DELIVERY This is an ambitious 12-month project. WP1 will be completed during months 1-10; WP2 will be completed during months 8-12. At 12 months we will have refined the intervention programme theory for the extended S&W visits, designed a delivery model and protocol for home visits, and developed new training materials. ANTICIPATED IMPACT AND DISSEMINATION A variety of research outputs will be generated to engage a range of different audiences including conference and meeting papers, peer-reviewed publications in high-impact journals and social media content. To maximise reach, we will engage members of our existing networks: National Fire Chiefs Council, Age UK, Primary Care Networks, Public Health England, Royal Colleges of General Practitioners and Psychiatrists, and the Society for Academic Primary Care. Outputs are intended to inform, generate interest in the next stage of testing and promote future scalability.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare public health and preventing premature mortality
Contractor: NHS BRISTOL, NORTH SOMERSET AND SOUTH GLOUCESTERSHIRE INTEGRATED CARE BOARD
Award_Title: Preventing Sudden Unexpected Deaths in Infancy: an assessment and planning tool for families at increased risk
Abstract: Research question How does a risk scoring and planning tool support safer infant sleep during disrupted routines for infants at increased risk of SUDI? Background Advice for parents on safe sleep has reduced the incidence of Sudden Unexpected Death in Infancy (SUDI) in the general population over the last 3 decades, but less so for families living in deprivation. About two-thirds of the deaths (~200/300) occur in this group. Disrupted routines influence decision-making in families at risk, and impact on sleep safety. Incorporating planning for disruption with practical strategies to maintain safety for infants, could save lives. Aims and Objectives The aim of the study is to refine and evaluate a risk scoring and planning tool for improving uptake of safer sleep practices in families at increased risk for SUDI, by: Developing a risk scoring system to quantify the potential risk in different infant sleeping environments. Developing an interface that the target group can use. Conducting a process evaluation study to understand how the tool works in real world conditions. Conducting a scoping exercise to assess the potential for widening this type of tool to other infant safety topics. Writing a protocol for a feasibility study to develop the methodology needed to test the effectiveness of the intervention. Methods We will develop a risk scoring algorithm on distal factors (background characteristics and factors related to birth) and proximal factors (those surrounding the sleeping environment) using existing UK observational data. Distal factors are largely unmodifiable, however the proximal ones are not and can quantify the potential risk in different environments. External validation will be sought using the National Child Mortality Database (NCMD) and from a team collecting similar information in New Zealand. The scoring system and planning tool interface will be embedded in a website being developed and used during a personalised planning activity to maintain safety in different sleeping environments, when routines are disrupted. An infographic of each plan will be sent to recipient s mobile device for sharing with others. A process evaluation involving interviews with families and three health visitor/nursing teams working in deprived areas of Bristol, UK, will investigate the implementation, mechanisms of impact and behavioural outcomes associated with the intervention. We will explore how this approach might be used for other risk-based advice. Finally, we will write a protocol for a feasibility study to develop the methodology needed to test the effectiveness of the tool. Timelines for delivery Months 0-6: develop the algorithm (objective 1), prepare our evaluation protocol, secure ethics, establish research advisory groups. Months 4-7: Develop the user interface for the tool, and guidance about how to use it (objective 2). Months 7-12: Collect and analyse process evaluation data, refine the tool (objective 3). Conduct a scoping exercise for further uses of this type of tool (objective 4). Months 13-15: write the feasibility study protocol (objective 5) and findings for publication. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination This intervention will have the potential to improve uptake of life-saving advice in families with infants most at risk.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Programme: Artificial Intelligence for Multiple Long-Term Conditions
Funding_Stream: Artificial Intelligence for Multiple Long-Term Conditions
Award_Title: Using deep learning approaches to examine serious mental illness and physical multimorbidity across the life-course: from mechanisms towards novel interventions
Abstract: Research question: What are the clinically important clusters of serious mental illness-physical multimorbidity that influence patient outcomes, and the social, environmental, behavioural, clinical and biological correlates of these? Background The prevalence of people living with multimorbidity is increasing globally. Patients with multimorbidity often have complex health needs, live in lower socio-economic circumstances, experience reduced life expectancy and receive fragmented care, due to the dominant single-disease-oriented approach in healthcare. This often leads to incomplete, inefficient, and costly healthcare delivery, and contributes to poor health outcomes in these individuals. Serious mental illness (SMI, defined as severe depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia) combined with physical illness is one of the most common multimorbidity clusters observed across patients, and is associated with substantially lower life expectancy. Improving our understanding of the factors associated with multimorbidity would help inform resource allocation, address healthcare inequities, and inform holistic patient care. Aims and objectives The broad aims of this project are to identify clinically important SMI-physical multimorbidity clusters within nationally representative datasets, and understand the social, environmental, behavioural, clinical and biological correlates of these. Developing a biological and mechanistic understanding of multimorbidity could also help identify new targets for treatment and primary and secondary prevention, and potentially identify the impact of polypharmacy on illness, thus optimising drug treatments for patients. The specific objectives of this development grant are to build a multi-disciplinary collaboration, develop frameworks for data access and governance, and undertake feasibility work to inform our research focus, facilitate future work, and enable the delivery of the aims of the full Research Collaboration. Methods In order to meet our objectives, we will consolidate our multidisciplinary collaboration through workshops to inform detailed research plans for the Research Collaboration. We will also undertake feasibility work, including PPI, risk assessments, and set up of data governance frameworks for large-scale clinical, and genomic data. Our pilot analysis of the UK Biobank data, using state-of-the-art deep learning methods to identify clinically important multi-morbidity clusters, and their correlates will inform the focus of our future work for our full Research Collaboration proposal. Anticipated impact and dissemination Understanding the national social, behavioural, environmental, epidemiological, and spatial correlates of multimorbidity will inform treatment pathways, including the allocation of resources needs across the UK, and public health policy. Our research will help fill key gaps in knowledge about multimorbidity clusters within ethnic minorities in the UK; this may allow targeted social and healthcare interventions within these communities, with patient engagement and education around prevention. Furthermore, prediction algorithms arising from the proposed work will be validated against existing risk scores, and provide clinical decision support through easy-to-use and interpretable web portals. These are expected to directly assist clinical-decision making for people with multi-morbidity, through identification of those at higher risk of poorer outcomes, informing patient management. Our work on understanding the impact of chronic treatments, and polypharmacy on multimorbidity will also help us optimise patient management. Ultimately, this work will inform the provision of more holistic patient care in the context of multi-morbidity.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Contractor: Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Design of an online training programme and support tool for secondary schools to improve response to young people who self-harm (SORTS – SuppOrtive Response To Self-harm).
Abstract: Background: Self-harm among young people (YP) is a serious concern. UK prevalence is at nearly 20% (1) and early reports suggest that the current Covid-19 pandemic will have long-term, negative effects on YP s mental health (MH) (2), potentially increasing rates of self-harm (3). YP who self-harm are at high risk of adverse outcomes, including increased suicide risk (4, 5), yet, most YP who self-harm do not seek or receive professional help (6) There are numerous barriers to YP s help-seeking including fears about negative reactions to discovery or disclosure (5). School staff are well placed to respond to self-harm (7); however they often do not feel equipped to support YP (8). This may result in unhelpful responses that further deter YP from seeking help, or in missed opportunities to intervene. Consequently, there is a substantial, unmet need for an accessible, feasible training programme and support tool for schools to address self-harm among their pupils. Aims and Objectives: To co-produce and test a prototype online training programme and support tool for school staff (SORTS) to improve their response to YP who self-harm. The objectives are to: (i) explore YP s expectations of how schools and staff should respond to self-harm. (ii) co-design a SORTS prototype training programme through interactive workshops with school staff. Methods: Drawing on our systematic review (9) and existing guidelines (10), we will work with a technical provider to develop a SORTS prototype. It will include functional examples of interactive tools and techniques designed to deliver the content and enable users to practice and consolidate new skills. We will conduct online focus groups/interviews with YP to elicit their views about how schools and staff should address self-harm. Co-design workshops with school staff will gather their views on the proposed content and training strategies. Data will be thematically analysed (11) Timelines: The study duration is 15-months. Prototype development (WP1) will start when funding is confirmed and finalised in month 7 (M7). M1-M2: Recruitment and consent. WP2: (M3-M8): M3-M6: Focus groups/interviews with YP; M5-M8: Data analysis; M3-M7: Prototype development WP3: (M6-M14): M6-M7: Recruitment; M8-M14: Participant communication platform; M8-M11: Staff co-design workshops; M10-M13: Data analysis; M12-M15: Design document and final report Anticipated Impact: Impact will necessarily be limited as this is an early phase developmental project. In the medium-term, should SORTS prove effective in further evaluation, we hypothesize that school staff s improved confidence will lead to more appropriate responses that will encourage pupil disclosure and facilitate access to available on-site and external support. This will reduce serious consequences of self-harm, i.e. hospitalisation. Long term, larger-scale benefits will include reduction of societal and healthcare adverse outcomes and costs related to self-harm. Dissemination: Main outputs: (i) prototype SORTS programme; (ii) final design specification for the beta version development (iii) open-access publication on co-design process. In partnership with Charlie Waller Trust, we will engage schools and MH professionals to adopt SORTS. We will explore feasible routes to deliver the programme at scale to end-users at lowest possible cost.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare public health and preventing premature mortality
Contractor: NHS BRISTOL, NORTH SOMERSET AND SOUTH GLOUCESTERSHIRE INTEGRATED CARE BOARD
Award_Title: Increasing parental vaccine confidence and young people’s access to the universal human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme: a co-design study
Abstract: AIM: To co-design with parents who did not provide consent for their adolescent children a multi-component intervention to increase confidence about, and access to, the universal human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination programme. BACKGROUND: Persistent infection with HPV can result in cancers affecting men and, especially, women. In September 2019, the English schools-based HPV vaccination programme, already delivered to young women, was expanded to include young men aged 12 to 13 years. Seeking verbal telephone consent from parents where consent forms are unreturned overcomes some of the barriers to uptake. However, not all parents respond to phone calls. Parents may also provide written refusal due to negative perceptions of need for, safety and effectiveness of vaccination. Increasing parental confidence about, and access to, the universal HPV vaccination programme may help improve uptake. However, the evidence-base for interventions relevant to schools-based programmes is currently lacking. DESIGN AND METHODS: The first study is an exploratory qualitative study to find ways to improve parental confidence about, and adolescents access to, HPV vaccination from the perspectives of key stakeholders and a purposive sample of parents according to their gender, ethnicity, and whether they actively or passively refused vaccination. The findings will be used to inform the co-design of a preliminary plan for a targeted, multicomponent intervention. In the second study, parent working groups will be convened and will work with creative designers to co-design communication materials in multiple languages (as appropriate) aimed at increasing parents confidence in vaccination. A series of workshops will be organised to obtain feedback on the intervention plan and communication materials to ensure they are fit for purpose. These findings will inform a protocol for a future study to test effectiveness of the multi-component intervention at increasing parental vaccine confidence and uptake of the HPV vaccine. PATIENT AND PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT: The proposal was informed by our earlier qualitative research and also discussed with vaccine-eligible young people and groups of parents in Bristol and London. All PPI groups thought better information for parents is needed. PPI groups suggested that a future intervention could include improving access to evidence-based vaccine information through social media outlets or community advocates, and communication training for healthcare professionals. Ongoing PPI with young people and the parent groups will be incorporated at all stages of the study. This will include providing feedback on: (i) strategies to improve recruitment (e.g. accessing hard to reach parents, use of incentives); (ii) the paperwork we use with people who take part (e.g. invitation letters, topic guides); (iii) developing and improving the communication materials, and; (iv) sharing the study findings. DISSEMINATION: We will work with PPI groups to inform our dissemination strategy and co-present our findings with PPI members (e.g. at a community event or through social media). We will summarise the results in multiple languages (as appropriate) to share with parents who took part in the study. We will also share our findings with academics and healthcare professionals through webinars/academic conferences and peer reviewed publications.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Contractor: St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Development and feasibility testing of an intervention to prevent potentially harmful skincare practices during infancy
Abstract: Research question Is it possible to develop an intervention which will reduce infant bathing frequency and then test this in a randomised controlled trial. Background Eczema affects 15% of infants and young children in England and carries the highest global burden of any skin disease. Eczema is the visible manifestation of an impaired skin barrier. A key environmental risk factor for skin barrier damage is bathing. Bathing, even in tap water alone, disrupts skin physiology, increasing naturally acidic skin pH, removing protective lipids from the skin surface and altering enzymatic activity in the upper epidermis. Bathing with wash products such as soaps causes significantly more skin barrier damage than bathing in water alone. Aims and Objectives Work with pregnant women and their families to develop an acceptable intervention which aims to reduce infant bathing frequency and intensity. Undertake a randomised controlled feasibility trial to estimate the proportion of eligible families willing to be randomised to the intervention, their adherence to the intervention and its acceptability. Methods Initial qualitative work will involve the recruitment of at least 20 pregnant women and other family members who will be involved in caring for their infant. Semi-structured interviews will be undertaken. Transcripts will be analysed using thematic analysis to identify the factors influencing infant bathing behaviours, including bathing frequency, duration, temperature and use of wash products. Barriers and facilitators to interventions for reducing infant bathing frequency and intensity will be identified during the interviews; and will be used to determine what form an intervention might need to take. The suitability of such an intervention will be reviewed in a workshop attended by experts and patient representatives. A focus group of pregnant women and their families will then provide feedback on the acceptability of the intervention. Following the qualitative work, we will recruit 125 pregnant women to undertake a feasibility randomised controlled trial of the intervention. Infants will be followed up to six months of age. Lastly, we will invite 20 representative families from the feasibility trial to participate in qualitative interviews identifying views and barriers related to recruitment and adherence to the trial intervention. Timelines for delivery This project is scheduled to last 30 months and commence in March 2022. The initial qualitative work will last 9 months, followed by a 12-month period of recruitment to the feasibility study and follow up to 6 months of age, with trial data analysis, write up and dissemination taking place in the last 3 months of the project. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination A simple intervention that prevents infants developing eczema would be an important advance in population health. If the intervention proves successful, we will proceed in the latter stages of this project with the development of a protocol for a large scale, multi-centre, randomised controlled trial of the intervention with a view to seeking funding for this from the NIHR.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: Informing a research programme to develop, optimise and evaluate a Digital and Remote Support package for Smoking in Pregnancy (DrSSIP)
Abstract: Background: Reducing smoking in pregnancy is a public health priority. The NHS offers effective interpersonal behavioural counselling and nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) to pregnant women; this support is known as the Standard Treatment Programme for Pregnant Women . However, over the last 10 years the numbers of pregnant women engaging with such support have halved. Initially, during this time rates of smoking in pregnancy fell but, these have been static since 2015. Offering additional modes for receiving cessation support could help increase numbers of women engaging with this, ultimately helping more to permanently stop smoking. Digital media can cheaply deliver cessation support to pregnant women but, there are no evidence-based digital cessation interventions for use by pregnant women in the UK. In a future programme grant (PGfAR), we propose translating the Standard Treatment Programme for pregnant smokers, including the provision of NRT, into a digital and remote support package and testing this in an RCT. In this project (PDG), we will complete preparatory work to define PGfAR objectives and hence, optimal research team expertise needed to successfully achieve these. PDG research questions: How do policy and practice experts and, pregnant women who smoke, think NHS smoking cessation care can best be translated into a Digital and remote Support package for Smoking in Pregnancy (DrSSIP) and, how should this influence PGfAR aims? How can we best rationalise a text message cessation support programme, creating space for new NRT-focussed content? Objectives and development work plan: Investigate views of ~40 policy, practice and academic experts on translating the Standard Treatment Programme for pregnant smokers into a DrSSIP, how DrSSIP could successfully support NRT use, and on future implementation pathways. Methods: Qualitative interview and focus group study Investigate pregnant women s views on translation of usual care into a DrSSIP. Methods: Qualitative interview study with ~30 pregnant women recruited online Identify whether or not an existing theory-guided text message cessation support platform: Is effective for those with high nicotine dependence and Whether selected core messages change determinants of smoking behaviour and, whether such changes in determinants mediate intervention effects Methods: Secondary analysis of data from two completed RCTs combined (N=1,409). Findings will help inform scope and breadth of PGfAR objectives and, the resources required in a PGfAR to adapt an existing text support system, retaining effective content and, incorporating new content addressing nicotine dependence An intervention scoping search will identify interventions potentially suitable as DrSSIP components and, potential PGfAR co-applicants. Timelines: Study 1: months 1-10; study 2: months 6-16; study 3: months 1-11; intervention scoping search: months 10-12. Three members of the public will form the PPI panel and will be involved regularly throughout. We aim to submit the stage 1 PGfAR proposal by month 14. Anticipated impact and dissemination: We will gain key understandings to plan a PGfAR for translating the Standard Treatment Programme into a DrSSIP, including the identification of appropriate additional and existing intervention components. Findings will be disseminated to clinical, academic, policy and public groups.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: CITY ST GEORGE'S, UNIVERSITY OF LONDON
Award_Title: Evaluation and co-creation to optimise use and benefits of the Healthy Start scheme
Abstract: Background: The high cost of a healthy diet is an important barrier to eating better. Over the past decade, food insecurity and foodbank use across the UK has increased. To help ease financial constraints, the UK government s Healthy Start (HS) scheme provides vouchers for fruit, vegetables, pulses, plain milk and infant formula to low-income pregnant women and families with young children. However, only half of eligible families in England use it. An in-depth evaluation of the HS scheme is needed to provide insight into the lived experiences of eligible families and the impacts of HS, and identify strategies to improve use and enhance benefits. Aims and Objectives: To: evaluate how HS use influences food purchasing, diet and broader child outcomes; identify factors driving HS use; and co-create strategies to optimise the scheme s impact. Public Involvement: Our project has been developed with families eligible for HS and project partners: Southampton City Council, London Borough of Redbridge, St Mary s (women s and children s) Hospital Manchester, Tommy s charity and the Food Foundation. We have a mother of two children who has lived experience of the HS scheme as a member of our research team and we will recruit a diverse panel of approximately 20 parents eligible for HS vouchers from across England; our public researchers will keep our work relevant to target families. Methods: This 30-month project is structured into five interlinked workpackages (WPs). WP1 provides overarching project co-ordination and governance, overseeing WP linkage and public involvement and coordinating knowledge exchange activities. WP2 will provide qualitative insights into the lived experiences of a diverse range of HS users and eligible non-users, and key stakeholders in three geographically and culturally diverse locations with different rates of HS usage. WP3 will provide quantitative insights into how HS use affects short- and long-term household food purchasing and individual dietary patterns using two datasets: 20 years of Kantar Worldpanel data and primary survey data from a random sample of 1664 HS eligible families. WP4 will provide new quantitative information on the demographic, socioeconomic, psychosocial and contextual factors driving HS use (using the new survey data) and the health and cognitive impact of HS use on recipient children (via secondary analyses on the Hospital Episode Statistics and National Pupil Database). WP5 will identify strategies to improve the HS scheme focusing on policy levers at two levels: local (community systems mapping and priority setting) and national (focusing on eligibility and alternative cut-off criteria). Two workshops will be held in each of our three communities to co-produce strategies for increasing HS use. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination: Locally, high-priority solutions will be identified in our target communities and learnings shared with other local authorities. Nationally, new insights about the HS scheme could identify focal points for targeted interventions. Key deliverables include: i) real-time feedback to policymakers through briefings; ii) presentations and reports to key stakeholders; iii) three community case studies; iv) ~7 academic publications; and v) blogs, infographics or videos co-created with our public researchers to make our results widely accessible.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Understanding the cost-effectiveness of identifying and treating perinatal depression (PND) using secondary data analysis
Abstract: Perinatal depression (PND) occurs during pregnancy or the first year post-childbirth, affecting an estimated 120,000 women annually in England. It remains unidentified by healthcare professionals in 50% of cases. This is a barrier to accessing support. To maximise the sustainability of Specialist Perinatal Mental Health Services within the NHS, they must allocate their finite resources towards cost-effective treatments. This study will answer two important questions about the cost-effectiveness of identifying and treating PND. Question 1: Is selective screening for PND cost-effective? Universal screening for PND is not cost-effective. Some women are at higher risk of PND, therefore it is possible to target screening towards them. Our first aim is to estimate the cost-effectiveness of selective screening for PND. We will build a decision model to explore the costs and benefits of selectively screening high-risk women, using data from a completed observational study of PND in Northern England. Question 2: How can the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) be used to estimate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs)? NICE assess the cost-effectiveness of healthcare treatments/services based on their cost to improve health by one QALY. Not many studies have collected data to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of PND treatments. In contrast, there is ample existing clinical effectiveness data collected using the EPDS. The cost-effectiveness evidence-base can be strengthened by learning how to estimate QALYs from the EPDS. This can be done by mapping between the EPDS and the EQ-5D (NICE s recommended tool for deriving QALYs). Our second aim is to generate a mapping algorithm between the EPDS and the EQ-5D. We will use data from 5 completed studies and follow current best-practice guidelines for mapping. By identifying cost-effective services for PND, more women will be enabled to access support, and services will be able to use their budget more effectively to help more families.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: Co-production of a Caregivers intervention around Responsive Infant feeding Behaviours to prevent childhood obesity (CRIB)
Abstract: Caregiver refers to anyone within the family home who leads an infant feeding encounter, to include, parents, legal guardians, carers. Background Childhood obesity is a global public health challenge. [1] Prevention during the first 1000 days [2] is vital as this is when feeding behaviours are influenced by caregivers.[3] Supportive feeding interactions enable infants to learn how to self-regulate their energy intake and develop feeding autonomy which contribute to lifelong healthy eating behaviours.[4] Obesity prevention interventions that contain information and support for caregivers about responsive infant feeding lead to healthy weight trajectories.[5] NHS Healthcare Professionals (HCPs) offer support to mothers about breastfeeding; [6] there is no universal support to help caregivers who formula or combination feed (breast and formula milk) to learn how to responsively feed. This disproportionately impacts infants living in socially-economically deprived areas, and those from Asian backgrounds, who are more likely to be fed with formula milk [7], [8] and more likely to develop childhood overweight and obesity.[9] We have mapped the barriers and enablers to responsive infant feeding to the Capability, Opportunity and Motivation -model of Behaviour (COM-B) [10] as a basis for intervention development.[11] Aim We aim to co-produce a digital web-based app called a Reusable Learning Object (RLO) with caregivers of infants < 1 year of age accompanied by infographic guidance for HCPs. The RLO will use a mixture of multimedia elements to engage caregivers in interactive learning about responsive feeding through activities and assessments to encourage behaviour change. The HCP infographic will enable them to support caregivers knowledge and skills through supportive discussions. Methods We propose a systematic, stepped approach to intervention development and evaluation through co-production. We will use COM-B methodology [10] and consensus methods, [12] with a diverse group of caregivers (n=7) and HCPs (n-5). Following ethical and governance approval four sequential workshops will be held. We will identify caregiver and non-caregiver behaviours, intervention options and behaviour change techniques.[10] This information will inform the content and interactive elements of the RLO and the HCP infographic. Project Management The project will run from 1st January 2023-30th June 2024. The deliverables are: Medical School Research Ethics Committee, study site approvals (01/03/23) Protocol submitted to HRB Open Research (01/06/23) A report outlining the content, behaviour change techniques and implementation options for the RLO (01/11/23). Specification and prototype RLO (01/02/24) RLO formative evaluation stages 1 and 2 (01/03/24) Final RLO (31/3/24) RLO formative and summative evaluation stages 3 and 4 (31/5/24) Infographic for HCPs (31/5/24) Report on proposed point of contact/care pathway via discussions with local NHS Trusts. (30/5/24) Final paper submitted to International Journal of Obesity (30/06/24). Dissemination We will prepare peer-review publications, open access preprints and conference abstracts. Knowledge exchange and dissemination events will be held virtually with HCPs, caregivers charitable and NHS stakeholders. The PPIE will be supported to present the findings at a conference. We will seek follow-on funding from NIHR RfPB (feasibility study) or HTA schemes (effectiveness trial with embedded feasibility study) to test the intervention within the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: NHS Cambridgeshire and Peterborough Integrated Care Board
Award_Title: Building a community of practice to identify strengths, barriers and prioritise solutions to the right of access to healthcare for Travelling Communities
Abstract: Research question Recent research shows life expectancy of traveller communities (TCs) is 10-12 year less than average, with higher rates of preventable deaths. It is possible that barriers to accessing healthcare are contributing to these health inequalities. They are also replicated in discriminations experienced across employment, education and healthcare.3,4 Improving access to healthcare is the single most effective population intervention for addressing these health inequalities. This project will seek to develop a community of practice, working across TCs, health practitioners and regional and national policy makers to identify barriers to accessing healthcare and to propose relevant solutions to overcome those barriers. Background If barriers to accessing healthcare for TCs are reduced, then health inequalities are also reduced - a direct patient benefit. This project will develop a participatory, “contextual” approach to human rights to address questions of access and to explore how the specific characteristics of TCs are both situated in and impacted by ongoing discrimination and marginalisation6. In addressing this issue we will work directly with a range of stakeholders, including TCs, healthcare practitioners, national policy-makers, local authorities and national and international organisations, and legal experts from the University of Essex Human Rights Centre. This gives the project local, regional, national and international significance. Aims To build a Community of Practice (CoP) to identify existing strengths, barriers and to prioritise solutions to accessing healthcare for TCs. To co-produce policy and practice community-based action plans that enable improved access to healthcare, based on principles of contextualised human rights, advocacy and inclusive involvement. Objectives Work alongside TCs to co-design approaches to a) identify existing strengths, b) identify and explore barriers and c) prioritise and co-produce solutions, Assess, from the perspective of healthcare stakeholders, those TCs identified strengths, barriers and solutions To co-produce, through the application of a Community of Practice methodology (comprising TCs and health and social care practitioners) a set of community-based working practices which will ensure the fundamental right of access to healthcare for TCs is met. These co-produced working practices will inform changes at levels of policy and practice and develop actions plans to tackle ongoing issues of engagement and involvement within TCs communities. Methods This project draws from a range of participatory qualitative methods to co-produce the research outcomes, working directly across TCs and health care practitioners to develop community based action plans for tackling barriers to accessing healthcare. The Community of Practice methodology is an iterative methodology designed to develop deep and detailed discussion of research topics, from a range of vested community perspectives. Timelines for delivery The project comprises 3 work packages of data collection over an 18 month period. Anticipated impact and dissemination This research can impact directly upon health inequalities experienced by TCs at local and national levels, through a range of networks, comprising TCs, health practitioners and policy-makers. Issue specific community based action plans (relevant to other marginalised groups) will be made openly available in written and verbal formats at the end of the project.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Contractor: Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine
Award_Title: TRICORDER: Point-of-Care Cardiovascular Disease Screening With Artificial Intelligence Enabled Stethoscope
Abstract: Research question What is the clinical and health economic impact of deploying an artificial intelligence-enabled stethoscope in primary care for: the detection of heart failure (HF, primary endpoint); the detection of atrial fibrillation (AF) and valvular heart disease (VHD)? Background Heart failure (HF) is a progressive condition affecting over 2% of the population, consuming 4% of the NHS budget1. Although early diagnosis and guideline-recommended treatments are associated with improved quality of life and survival2, over 80% of HF is diagnosed late – following an emergency hospital admission3. Survival following HF diagnosis is worse than many common cancers4, underscoring the urgency of earlier recognition and treatment initiation. We have demonstrated that an artificial intelligence-enabled stethoscope (Eko DUO) can detect HF after only 15 seconds of examination (sensitivity 92%, specificity 80%)5. The expectation that incorporating this technology into routine clinical workflows in primary care will improve community-based detection, health and economic outcomes in HF remains to be proven. This is the aim of this proposal, as a pivotal step towards system-wide deployment. Aims and Objectives The TRICORDER study will measure the impact in primary care of Eko DUO deployment on: Rates of detection of HF Rates of detection of AF and Valvular Heart Disease (also detectable using the Eko DUO, and both causes and consequences of HF) Health economic outcomes Methods 250 GP practices from the NHS North West London Integrated Care System (NWL ICS) and the Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board (BCUH) in Wales will be cluster-randomised to receive Eko DUO or continue usual clinical practice (control) in a 1:1 design. Rates of detection of HF, AF, VHD, and route to HF diagnosis (hospital admission versus community-based) will be determined using linked health and cost data (Discover dataset, NWL ICS, and the BCUH Informatics Hub). GP practices will be followed up for 24 months. Timelines TRICORDER is a 36-month project with 3 overlapping phases: Planning – in partnership with Imperial Clinical Trials Unit Deployment – through established collaboration with NIHR Clinical Research Networks Measurement and reporting – applying statistical and health economic expertise to linked primary-secondary care data assets TRICORDER is designed specifically to lead to multi-sector and national translation through: NICE Medical Technology Guidance Assessment submission NWL ICS follow-on commissioning as a “blueprint” for other ICS regions NHS MedTech Funding Mandate eligibility Impact and Dissemination TRICORDER is expected to prove a substantial benefit to patients and the public through earlier detection of priority cardiovascular disease – underpinned by real-world health economic models that measure savings across the NWL ICS and BCUH. Our previous NIHR AI Award-funded validation study of the Eko DUO (The Lancet Digital Health, 2022)5 successfully studied over 1,000 patients in under three months. Our patient partners now include the UK s largest HF charity, Pumping Marvellous, advocating for the rollout of this technology across the NHS. Guided by our Patient Steering Group, we will continue to present our findings at prestigious national and international conferences6, via high-impact scientific manuscripts5 and through NHS7, social media and broadcast media newsletters8.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare public health and preventing premature mortality
Award_Title: Improving access to cervical screening for physically Disabled people
Abstract: Background Cervical screening is a physically challenging procedure for many people. There is little research exploring the cervical screening experiences of physically Disabled people despite them being less likely to attend screening. Existing research has revealed considerable physical and attitudinal barriers for Disabled people, which are not adequately addressed by installing ramps or referring patients to a facility with a hoist. The recent introduction of human papillomavirus (HPV) primary testing to the screening programme and the associated possibility of self- or clinician-assisted sampling may provide a solution for some but not all Disabled people. Research question This research will explore what barriers exist in current practice, how these might be addressed and the extent to which alternatives to speculum-based sampling might be acceptable to people with a range of physical disabilities. Objectives 1. Identify and describe barriers and facilitators relating to cervical screening for Disabled people that have been identified in international research. 2. Investigate barriers faced by Disabled people in the UK, and acceptability of existing adjustments and alternative screening options. 3. Investigate current practice in primary care, any barriers to making reasonable adjustments that arise from 2, and attitudes towards proposed new solutions. 4. Explore the extent to which GPs, practice nurses, and reception staff have unconscious attitudes and biases regarding Disabled people that may impact on access to screening. 5. Informed by 1-4, co-create recommendations on improving access to cervical screening for Disabled people, and materials to enable Disabled people to self-advocate. Methods and timeline for delivery WP1 (year1): A rapid review following the Cochrane Rapid Review guidance, with the protocol registered with PROSPERO. Inclusion criteria will be participants with any physical disability/impairment, and healthcare professionals. Exclusion criteria will be participants with an intellectual disability and no physical disability/impairment. WP2 (year1-2): An online survey will be conducted with 1500 physically Disabled people or people with a long-term physical impairment or condition that makes cervical screening challenging, to explore barriers and potential facilitators to cervical screening. Telephone/paper-based completion alternatives will be provided. Inclusion criteria will be age 24-64 (cervical screening eligibility), physically disability/impairment, regular, lapsed and non-attenders. Exclusion criteria will be hysterectomy, intellectual disability but no physical impairment. WP3 (year2): An online survey with 500 GPs and practice nurses to explore current practice and attitudes towards proposed solutions. WP4 (year2-3): Thirty qualitative vignette-based interviews with 10 each of GPs, practice nurses and reception staff to explore attitudinal barriers and any issues that arose from WP3. WP5 (year3): Qualitative World-Café event to evaluate co-created recommendations based on WP1-4 as well as patient-facing resources. Anticipated impact and dissemination Several types of patient benefit will arise from this work, including: Awareness raising for patients and healthcare professionals; Patient advocacy; Co-designed patient-facing materials; Co-designed recommendations; Improvements to clinical practice; Improved clinical outcomes, specifically, earlier detection of abnormalities, earlier treatment, and fewer deaths among Disabled people. In addition to WP5 a range of co-created professional-facing (healthcare, academic, policymaker) and patient-facing outputs will also be disseminated throughout the project.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Reducing health and work inequalities and extending working lives
Abstract: Research question: How can policies and interventions, such as occupational health and vocational rehabilitation, increase healthy working life expectancy and reduce inequalities? Background: With pressures to retire later, there is a critical need to monitor healthy working life among adults aged 50-70 and for evidence-based policy and interventions to support extensions to the amount of time that people are healthy and in work. However, longitudinal datasets lack sufficiently large sample sizes for the complex models required to investigate drivers and barriers of Healthy Working Life Expectancy (HWLE). This research will develop a dataset of sufficient sample size and include information on characteristics that will allow analysis of real-world scenarios that can contribute to the development of interventions and policy. Aims: (i) To improve understanding of current and future length of HWLE and the effects of health, lifestyle, workplace, and policy factors that drive this in people with health conditions and (ii) Advance HWLE estimation methods to develop the HWLE indicator for population health surveillance and to inform policy. Methods: The first stage of the research will develop a large dataset (with approximately 700,000 participants (1% of the United Kingdom (UK) population)) using simulated life-courses based on transitions between health, work and vital statuses modelled on survey data (Understanding Society; Labour Force Survey), mortality-linked electronic health record data (Clinical Practice Research Datalink) and trial data (Study of Work and Pain; provides information on the impact of occupational health and vocational rehabilitation). We will work with a Patient Advisory Group (PAG) and government agencies (Department for Work and Pensions, Office for Health Improvements and Disparities and Health and Safety Executive) to link the analysis with real-life scenarios and developing policies. The second stage will use Markov chain multi-state modelling to identify health and work inequalities and then move onto to modelling the impact of policies and interventions, including the role of occupational health provision and health inequalities on the number of years that people are healthy and in work. Consultation with the PAG and government agencies will inform dissemination. Timelines for delivery: Development of the large dataset will be completed by the end of the first year. Analysis of health inequalities and the potential impact of policies and interventions will be completed by the end of the third year. Anticipated impact and dissemination: Outputs will lead to improvements in quality of work participation and wellbeing for people with mental and physical health issues, benefitting policy and real-world stakeholders including government agencies, employers, and health practitioners. The identification of beneficial policies and interventions should lead to an increase in the average number of years that people in the UK are healthy and in work. We will work with government agencies to ensure the findings are considered in ongoing policy development. [AK1]Do you need health before and then health conditions here?

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: Understanding the impact of alcohol calorie labelling on alcohol and calorie selection, purchasing and consumption
Abstract: Background Alcohol use represents one of the largest contributors to premature death and preventable diseases worldwide. Harms from consumption of alcoholic drinks can result directly from the effects of alcohol on body tissues, notably the liver, and by increasing the risk of obesity. Reducing alcohol consumption is therefore a key target for public health policy. Aims To estimate the impact of including calorie information on intended and actual behaviour, with a focus on amount of (a) energy and (b) alcohol selected or consumed To establish attitudes towards, and understanding of, alcohol calorie information To model the long-term impact of alcohol calorie labelling on morbidity, mortality, and costs to health-care services Methods The programme is subdivided into three work packages: WP1: Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTS) in off-trade settings [Aims 1 & 2] WP2: RCTs in on-trade settings [Aims 1 & 2] WP3: Modelling of longer-term impact [Aim 3] RCTs will establish: The most promising design for the alcohol calorie label Effectiveness of this label in different contexts (on-trade vs. off-trade) Responsiveness to this label by demographic groups Potential for unintended consequences as a result of alcohol calorie labelling Attitudes towards, and understanding of, labels Results from WP1 and WP2 studies will inform modelling scenarios for WP3. WP1: Off-trade settings Initial studies will be run in an experimental online supermarket (using large samples representative of the UK) where participants are randomised to conditions which show products with alcohol calorie labels present vs. absent. Participants attitudes and understanding of alcohol calorie labels will also be surveyed. A field study will use an app to record the (a) energy and (b) alcohol content of drinks purchased and consumed over a 4-week period, with participants randomised to seeing calorie labelling or control (no calorie labels) when scanning products. WP2: On-trade settings Two online studies (using UK-representative samples) will examine the effect of calorie labels on intended behaviour in on-trade scenarios: the first drinking in bars, pubs and nightclubs, and the second, purchasing food and drink together (e.g. in a restaurant/pub serving food). A third study will compare actual (a) energy and (b) alcohol ordered and consumed when calorie labelling is present vs. absent in a semi-naturalistic experiment. WP3: Health modelling WP3 will produce modelled results of the long-term implications for health and healthcare costs of alcohol calorie labelling, using standardised methods that provide policymakers with data for direct comparison with other public health initiatives. Timelines for Delivery The project will run for 36 months, with an anticipated start date of March 2023. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination Expected impacts include refinement of policy with regard to alcohol calorie labelling (nationally and elsewhere), alongside further development of public health knowledge. The primary output from the programme will be a report for DHSC colleagues, as well as other policy makers, alcohol and obesity NGOs. Multiple strands of complementary dissemination activities are planned, given this work will also be of significant interest to international academic audiences and members of the public.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Partnership for Black People's Health: involving Black communities in addressing health inequalities
Abstract: The aim of this project is to strengthen an existing, diverse network of clinicians, community organisations, academics, and members of the public to explore methods for involving Black African (BACs) and Black Caribbean (BCCs) communities in addressing health inequalities. We will also extend the network to other partners working on Black People's Health, by which we mean the health of people of Black African and Black Caribbean heritage in the UK. BACs and BCCs suffer a disproportionate burden of health inequalities in all areas of medicine and public health. This is partly due to racism, which compounds other forms of discrimination and other social and economic inequalities (for example those based on economic class, age, gender, immigration status, sexuality, ethnicity or age). Many interventions to improve health fail to reach BACs and BCCs. This is partly because of a lack of effective involvement of members of BACs and BCCs in the development of plans for health care, research and public health. Also, fewer people from BACs and BCCs are employed in research institutions and therefore these communities have less power over how research evidence is produced. This project seeks to address these problems and develop new ways of partnering to involve communities. We will share learning and review our current involvement strategies. We will recruit two project coordinators of Black African and/or Black Caribbean heritage who will support 11 Involvement Leads in our network. Each Involvement Lead will carry out involvement activities with members of different BACs and BCCs (of different age, gender, sexuality, health status, citizenship status) and with staff, volunteers and professionals from community organisations working on Black People's Health. We will strive to include community members that tend to be 'left behind' due to their characteristics or circumstances. We will use a range of approaches to involve community members and test and review what works best for different people in different situations. We will then use what we learn to write applications for funding for research and interventions to address health inequalities. These applications will be co-produced together with members of the partnership, including new members of the public that have become interested in this work after taking part in our involvement activities. Our other outputs will include: a freely available project report on how to build better partnerships; a publication in an academic journal co-authored by the network and available for all to read; social media content on lessons learned and best practice in community involvement for Black People s Health to be disseminated by the partnership; additional visual, audio or textual material produced during the involvement activities to be disseminated on the team s website, led by members of the public taking part in the project.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Contractor: The Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: HEALTH (HarnEssing Artificial intelligence to Lead Transformative Healthcare)
Abstract: Background/rationale Poor air quality is the largest environmental risk to public health, with up to 36,000 UK deaths occurring every year. Exposure to air pollutants can lead to exacerbations of ill health, increased healthcare utilisation (primary care consultations and inpatient hospital admissions), multi-morbidity and mortality. Air pollutants can exert disproportionately large health effects on disadvantaged and vulnerable groups. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), formerly Public Health England, estimated that total costs to the NHS and social care (2017-25) will be £1.6 billion. The Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs have highlighted the need to communicate with the public during air pollution episodes, with UKHSA acknowledging that the use of behavioural interventions, alongside other local and national strategies, can have a synergistic effect. We want to co-produce a personalised intervention that will notify individuals when air pollution levels are likely to increase, thus helping them to make informed decisions on how to reduce their exposure and/or better manage the consequences of exposure. However, this information must be communicated to people in the right way, at the right time, and with the right content. Aim and Objectives To co-produce our communication strategy with disadvantaged and vulnerable groups, tailoring it to their needs and available local infrastructure, and mitigating against digital exclusion. To develop and internally validate a proof of concept risk score to identify those at higher risk and needing intervention. Development work plan We will use existing links with organisations such as NHS North Tyneside Future Case Working Group, Connected Voice, Healthwatch, Age UK, VODA and local community groups to reach target groups. We will specifically include those perceived at high risk of digital exclusion, such as people with disabilities, ethnic minority groups and/or lower income and deprived groups, those living in rural areas and older people. Participants will have the choice of participating in either a semi-structured interview or focus group.
