The topic guide will include questions on what information individuals want to receive about elevated air pollution levels, when, where and how they would like to receive it, and potential benefits and barriers of each, including how we mitigate against digital exclusion. We will co-produce the content of these messages, the range of actionable recommendations (including how local initiatives and infrastructure could help support desired change), and explore any potential unintended consequences. Building on our previous work looking at how different multi-morbidity clusters utilise healthcare, we will also develop a proof of concept risk score to investigate the risk of increased healthcare utilisation and/or acute unplanned admission across different multi-morbidity clusters when air quality is poor. We will use multivariable logistic regression and identify the predictors for high-risk individuals and their associated weights to transform the prediction model into a risk score. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination We enjoy excellent working relationships with relevant leaders in NHS England, DEFRA, WHO Global Air Pollution group, UK charities, UK Faculty of Clinical Informatics, and Integrated Care Systems, and are ideally placed to ensure that our findings reach senior decision-makers.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Contractor: NHS WEST YORKSHIRE INTEGRATED CARE BOARD
Award_Title: Developing and evaluating innovative tailored peer-led Obesity UK support groups to provide support for, and improve research coproduction with, least heard and underserved communities.
Abstract: Development work question: Will innovative tailored Obesity UK peer-led support groups provide support for, and improve research coproduction with, least heard and underserved communities at high risk of obesity? Background: Obesity is a serious chronic disease affecting around a third of all UK adults, and is therefore a government priority. Peer-led support groups have been found to be effective for people living with obesity. Obesity UK run regular well attended peer-led support groups, which have also provided a unique opportunity to engage members in research, and coproduce new research programmes to address issues that are most important to people living with obesity. However, there are some communities who are underrepresented in current Obesity UK groups, and these include South Asian women and members of the LGBTQ+ community who identify as Lesbian and non-binary. These communities are known to be at high risk of obesity and have expressed a desire for tailored support groups. Aim: To codevelop and evaluate innovative tailored peer-led Obesity UK support groups to provide support for, and improve research coproduction with, least heard and underserved communities at high risk of obesity and related co-morbidities. Objectives: Codevelop tailored Obesity UK support groups with two diverse community groups who are currently underrepresented in existing Obesity UK support groups: South Asian women, and members of the LGBTQ+ community who identify as Lesbian or non-binary. Identify and train community peers to run the new support groups. Codevelop a sustainability and implementation plan for the new tailored support groups. Evaluate the innovative codesign approach, implementation and impact of the new support groups in providing required peer-led support and facilitating coproduction activity. Codevelop a toolkit to support the development of further tailored support groups. Codevelop a communications and dissemination plan to share learning from this work. Development plan: Using best practice coproduction principles we will work with target communities to codevelop the tailored support groups and identify peer leaders. The sessions will be evaluated using a codesigned mixed methods approach, which will inform the development of a toolkit to develop further tailored support groups post funding, supported by an implementation and sustainability plan codeveloped with key stakeholders. The new support groups will also provide the required coproduction activity to support a substantive programme grant to develop a new weight and wellbeing registry. Timelines for delivery: April 2023-September 2024: providing 6 months for coproduction, and 12 months to run and evaluate groups, and codevelop a toolkit, implementation and sustainability plan. Anticipated impact and dissemination: This work will lead to new support groups and research within currently underserved communities. Outputs will include an evaluation report, implementation and sustainability plan, and a coproduction toolkit to support the co-development of more tailored Obesity UK support groups. Learning will be shared via conferences, journals, Obesity UK and community networks through social media, films and graphics tailored to community preferences. It will also inform the co-development of a substantive programme grant.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Acceptability, feasibility and pilot study of a culturally sensitive parental and caregiver, community-based intervention using participatory learning and action groups to optimise infant nutrition and feeding practices in children from South Asian families: NEON (Nurture Early for Optimal Nutrition)
Abstract: Despite WHO and NHS recommendations, most infants in the UK are introduced to solids after 5 months; 22% are weaned appropriately at 6 months. This form of suboptimal infant feeding practice is particularly prevalent in the British South Asian (SA) Diaspora who is at high risk of related adverse short-medium term (e.g. childhood obesity) and long-term (e.g. diabetes) consequences.Few interventions exist that are tailored to infants and young children of different ethnic groups and are respectively not sensitive to socio-cultural beliefs in the SA community. The NHS has limited resources with alternative strategies that utilise community assets. The initial NIHR CLAHRC study showed that parents are concerned about the growth and development of their children but do not directly link feeding practices to longer term health problems. It exposed the need for a low-cost community-based culturally sensitive intervention. The Participatory Learning and Action (PLA) Cycle approach is known to be successful in low-income countries and recognised as a low-cost alternative to traditional approaches. The proposed research has the potential to provide a low-cost solution for SA families in the UK, while posing a long-term impact on children's health.The reverse innovation of an adapted PLA model can be translated across the UK and tailored to other high-risk populations. The model has successfully improved maternal and child health outcomes in low-income settings; a meta-analysis of 7 PLA trials showed reductions in maternal, neonatal and under-five mortality, and maternal depression and improved child growth, maternal home-care, and care-seeking practices. Participants of the initial NIHR CLAHRC funded study self-reported changes in infant feeding and care practices at home as the result of the sessions they attended.I will feasibility test and pilot the adapted PLA group model with SA carers of infants ( Finally, generalizable findings from this study will be used to inform a randomised controlled trial to assess effectiveness prior to scale up across the UK. This will be over a longer period of time (8 years) employing the same mechanisms as used in this research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Innovative lifestyle interventions to improve population health
Abstract: Background: More than two thirds of the population are either overweight/obese because of excessive energy intake and/or insufficient physical activity. Based on objective assessment only 6% of men and 4% of women in England achieve 150-min per/week of moderate intensity physical activity in line with guidance. Approximately 6-10% of global mortality associated with non-communicable diseases is due to physical inactivity, yet there is compelling evidence that inactivity and high levels of sitting are both independently associated with disease and mortality. This is of real concern and there is no reason to assume this will improve unless effective population interventions are put in place.Aims and Objectives: This application involves four workstreams to develop and test innovative lifestyle interventions to address the problem of physical inactivity, sedentary behaviours and overweight. It seeks to involve and combine the individual, NHS and environment. The application builds directly on work funded by NIHR and my previous NIHR senior fellowship. There is a particular emphasis on delivering pragmatic evaluations in conjunction with health services, patients and the public. There is a focus on testing interventions that meet the ambition of the NHS to 'make every contact count'. Objective: 1: Develop and test a snacktivity intervention to promote physical activity in the population Objective 2: Obtain public feedback on the usefulness of physical activity calorie equivalent food labelling (PACE) when making food choices and evaluate the usefulness of PACE labelling in real life contexts. PACE is an approach where by the number of calories in food is displayed in the number of minutes of activity required to expend a food/drink item (e.g. this cake requires 45 minutes of running to burn).Objective 3: Investigate the feasibility of implementing a brief weight management programme for postnatal women embedded within the national child immunisation programme.Objective 4: Develop a world class Centre for Public Health Physical Activity Research at Loughborough University. Methods: Programme 1 involves early phase studies to develop a 'snacktivity' intervention, prior to testing in feasibility and effectiveness trials.Programme 2 will investigate feasibility and acceptability of physical activity calorie equivalent (PACE) food labelling in a café/cafeteria environment and whether PACE labelling encourages physical activity. Programme 3 focuses on women who have recently given birth and tests the procedures involved in delivering an intervention where practice nurses routinely promote self-monitoring of weight within the national child immunisation programme/appointments. Programme 4 aims to establish a world class Centre for Public Health Physical Activity Research by working in partnership with patients, health professionals, commissioners, policy makers and industry to ensure our work is relevant to the public and the NHS. Outputs: My ambition is to evaluate lifestyle interventions that can be easily implemented within the NHS and public health settings, to reduce diseases. This award will provide opportunities to develop a large team of researchers and help them become independent researchers in this field. This award will develop my senior research leadership skills and allow me to firmly establish myself as a world expert in physical activity research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Understanding time trends in child and adolescent mental health and the implications for service planning
Abstract: Psychopathology in children and adolescents has a significant impact in terms of economic and social costs, and lost potential. The UK has seen a trend of rising referrals to child and adolescent mental health services as well as an increase in mental health related emergency attendances. However, up-to-date epidemiological data to assess trends in psychopathology in relation to service contact on a population level has been lacking until now. In particular, despite the trend of rising demand for services, there are currently no mandated national datasets available on mental health related contact with services that are available in conjunction with individual level data on psychopathology and socio-economic status. This means that there is a gap in knowledge about trends in service contact in relation to need, and about the evidence for any changes in inequalities of access. Reports also indicate that policy-makers and commissioners are actively hampered in decision making and planning by a lack of data regarding trends and projected changes in prevalence. With the release of the latest 2017 national survey data, this Fellowship represents a new and timely opportunity to study trends using data from the three national child mental health surveys (1999, 2004, 2017), which included identical measures of psychopathology over an 18 year period. In particular, the Fellowship will examine trends in mental health-related service contact in relation to need, exploring contacts not only with specialist services but also with education and primary care, especially significant given the current emphasis on the school's role in mental health. Fellowship aims and methods The two main aims of my research are: 1. To examine trends in psychopathology, impact of psychopathology, and mental health related service contact in children and young people using national survey data 2. To explore the use of such trend data in modelling projections of prevalence and future levels of mental health related service contact This research will include time trends analysis of previously collected data from the national surveys. In collaboration with the survey team, we will also collect three year follow-up data from 2017 participants on psychopathology and mental health related service contact. This will add further value by providing more powerful, detailed and complete estimates of mental health related contacts. The second part of the programme will use insights from commissioners (from qualitative and stakeholder work) along with the trend data to develop models projecting future prevalence of psychopathology and service contact. This work will involve collaborations with Public Health England and modelling specialists. Impact My Fellowship will have an impact on policy and commissioning by contributing to impact assessments, economic and intervention modelling, policy development, and service planning at national and local levels. The findings can help direct funding to address inequalities, workforce planning and training across public sector services as well as target research into prevention and service access. In the longer-term, this Fellowship aims to contribute to better child and adolescent mental health by informing efforts to improve access to the right services at the right time.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: City St George’s, University of London
Award_Title: Engaging migrants in UK primary care to improve vaccine delivery
Abstract: Research question My research will answer a critical question around how best to approach strengthening UK vaccine delivery to under-immunised migrants to lessen their risk of vaccine-preventable diseases. Background Migrants represent an under-immunised group in the UK, with adolescent and adult migrants in particular excluded from initiatives to promote catch-up vaccination on arrival. Ensuring that under-immunised groups receive vaccines is a cornerstone of the UK vaccination system, alongside a need to better define at-risk migrant groups and engage them in the development of acceptable strategies. Aims and objectives The overall aim of this project is to define strategies to engage migrants in the promotion of catch-up vaccination. There are three objectives: Objective 1: Develop and test an innovative catch-up vaccination tool targeting adolescent and adult migrants presenting to UK general practice to align them with the UK vaccine schedule; Objective 2: Do an evidence synthesis to investigate rates and predictors of under-immunisation in migrants, and the relationship between migration and incidence of vaccine-preventable diseases in the UK; and Objective 3: Engage with migrants and healthcare professionals to evaluate the tool and define strategies to improve vaccine uptake. Methods A Project Advisory Group will be set up, including PPI representatives. In Objective 1 I shall develop and test through a prospective exploratory study an innovative catch-up vaccination tool that I have designed with support from Public Health England. This tool will be used when migrants first present to general practice to facilitate data collection on previous vaccinations and deliver catch-up vaccinations required. In Objective 2 I wilI use systematic review methodology to explore the role of migrants in outbreaks, a geospatial analysis using secondary data sources, and a comparative database analysis using data from high quality Danish national registries, linking data on at-risk migrant groups in Denmark with the UK. Synthesising these data will identify key at-risk migrant groups across all parts of the UK, and define the relationship between migration and incidence of disease. Raising awareness among migrants and thus empowering communities is a key step in developing successful public health programmes and is a core focus of Objective 3, where I will engage a migrants and health-care staff through a qualitative interview study to evaluate the tool and explore barriers and facilitators to vaccination, alongside promoting public engagement through a roundtable meeting bringing together at-risk migrant groups.Timelines for delivery I am requesting a 2-year Advanced Fellowship across a 40 month period (0.60%WTE), which includes the recruitment of a nurse (months 1-28 100%WTE) to support Objective 1.Anticipated impact and dissemination This research will have important and impactful consequences in terms of changing practice in UK primary care, guiding PHE in delivering their national immunisation strategy, addressing data gaps, improving knowledge, and raising awareness in migrant communities and among health-care professionals around strategies to delivering catch-up vaccination, aligning with national priorities. A minimum of 4 peer-reviewed publication will be generated alongside a report of the research findings for dissemination, and a roundtable meeting will bring together at-risk migrant groups.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Personalisation of exercise for people with dementia: What works for whom, under what circumstances and why?
Abstract: Research question Personalisation of exercise interventions for people with dementia: what works for whom, under what circumstances and why? Background In the UK, dementia affects over 850,000 people, costing the NHS £4.3 billion and society overall £26.3 billion every year. People with dementia are less active, have a higher risk of falls, and are more dependent compared to age-matched populations. Specific exercise interventions have demonstrable impact on these outcomes, however, dementia symptoms intercede and make participation difficult. A theoretical model is required to understand how to make standard exercises personalised to someone with dementia, thereby making a larger range of exercise interventions more accessible and achievable. Aim and objectives To get more people with dementia to benefit from exercise. The objectives are to: Develop an intervention co-design group Complete a systematic review of the literature on 'personalisation' of exercise for people with dementia Collect and analyse data from an existing exercise study involving 'personalisation' and exercise in people with dementia Model how personalisation of exercise can be used for people with dementia, under what circumstances, and why Develop and preliminary test a 'personalisation' shared decision-making resource in people with dementiaMethods Mixed-methods realist evaluation design. Realist evaluation is an innovative method in healthcare research that is founded in philosophical principles. Distinct work-packages will be conducted, each with specific aims and methods.Work-package 1 will generate a theoretical model of personalisation. A literature review will determine the evidence and provide candidate theories on 'personalisation' of exercise for people with dementia. A co-design group (n=12) will form and periodically meet throughout the project. Work-package 2 will collect retrospective and prospective data from an existing exercise-based cohort of people with dementia to test the proposed model. Data from dyad (n=10) and therapist (n=10) interviews, observations of exercise interventions (n=10), and outcome measures (n=184) will be collected and analyzed. Work-package 3 will synthesis and refine the model through dedicated synthesis and consensus processes. A nominal group technique (n=4 focus groups) will reach consensus on the model and produce a shared decision-making resource ready for feasibility testing in Work-package 4.Work-package 4 will test the feasibility of implementing the model. Implementation methods will initially determine the feasibility of the resource in one community group, before a knowledge transfer activity to start the wider dissemination of findings. Timelines for delivery Three years. A co-design group will initially and immediately be formed and will meet thrice per year to influence focus and findings. A project management group involving named research and clinical supporters and collaborators will meet monthly (virtual and face-to-face). Anticipated impact and dissemination People with dementia and their carers will have improved participation in exercise interventions following this research. Stronger legs, less falls, maintained independence, and improved quality of life will directly impact individuals and indirectly influence the wider social and healthcare services. A clear dissemination plan including academic (rehabilitation journals, international presentations), clinical (knowledge-transfer activity, professional magazines) and patient (Alzheimer's Society leaflets) focus has been developed.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Moorfields Eye Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Improving diabetic retinopathy screening attendance in non-attenders aged ?30 years: mixed methods study
Abstract: Research question: Is there a lack of engagement of people aged ≥30 years and high-risk groups with the NHS Diabetic Retinopathy Screening Programme (DESP) and what are the key factors (barriers/enablers) that influence screening attendance? Background: Despite evidence supporting the effectiveness of diabetic retinopathy screening in reducing the risk of sight loss, attendance for retinopathy screening in particular demographic groups is consistently below recommended levels. Several factors including socioeconomic deprivation, language and ethnicity may influence screening attendance. There is a need to identify modifiable barriers/enablers to inform the development of effective interventions to increase attendance and avoid preventable sight loss. Aims and objectives: To analyse patterns of attendance based on age, and identify barriers/enablers to attending reported by persons with diabetes and healthcare professionals (HCPs). The specific objectives are: To investigate age-related patterns of attendance across the DESP, to quantify screening uptake at the level of the individual, local screening programme and general practice. To identify barriers/enablers to attendance from the perspective of adults aged ≥30 years old with diabetes/ and HCPs. To synthesise research findings and generate evidence-based suggestions for improving screening attendance in this population. To determine the feasibility and acceptability of a candidate intervention to patients with diabetes and HCPs.Methods: This mixed methods study will comprise four phases corresponding to each objective: The EROTES nested study will use the results of the scoping study (EROS study) to conduct a statistical analysis of data to identify patterns of attendance at the level of population based on age (≥30 years), the screening programme and general practice. Semi-structured qualitative interviews (informed by the Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) of behaviour change); explore HCPs' views of barriers/enablers, including suggestions for how practice or processes could be altered to improve attendance in at-risk groups. Synthesis of research findings with input from patients and stakeholders to identify and operationalise strategies to improve screening attendance and a one-day 'knowledge exchange' event with end users to make recommendations on the design of future screening interventions in areas or population subgroups with low attendance. Co-design with stakeholders and conduct a feasibility study of a candidate intervention.Timelines for delivery: Study duration will be 56 months. Ethical approval (months 1-6); statistical analysis (months 7-18); interviews and concurrent analysis (months 19-27); interviews with HCPs (months 28-36); synthesis (months 37-45) and knowledge exchange event (month 45); feasibility study (months 46-55); writing and submission of final report (months 56-60). Anticipated impact and dissemination: There is little UK-based research to understand the perspectives of adults and high-risk groups at risk of low retinopathy screening attendance. Understanding factors influencing attendance in these groups is an important step towards identifying policies and processes to increase attendance and reduce inequity. The results of this study will be disseminated to service providers, professional bodies and patient groups to develop theory-informed and tailored strategies that are directed at the level of the individual with diabetes, the screening programme and general practice.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Award_Title: Removing Erroneous Penicillin Allergy Labels (REPeAL)
Abstract: Background to the research Penicillins are a large group of antibiotics. Therefore, patients with penicillin allergy records have reduced antibiotic options. In addition, penicillin is the preferred antibiotic for many infections. Patients with a penicillin allergy are given 'second choice' antibiotics which can be less effective, more likely to cause side effects, and put people at risk of superbugs. One in ten people have a record of penicillin allergy. Most of these patients can safely take penicillin. This is because the 'allergy' described is not a true allergy but instead a mild side effect, also known as an intolerance or they may have grown out of their allergy. A large number of patients therefore are unnecessarily denied penicillin, often the best antibiotic, and unnecessarily put at risk of the harms associated with 'second choice' antibiotics. The process for assessing patients and removing incorrect penicillin allergy labels is called 'de-labelling.' Patients safe to take penicillin can be identified through taking an 'allergy history'. This involves talking to patients and also checking GP records to find out what happened when they took penicillin. About half of patients with a penicillin allergy record can be identified in this way without the use of penicillin skin testing which is not available to most hospitals. Removing these incorrect allergy records will enable many more patents to safely take penicillin antibiotics instead of the second choice antibiotics which will benefit patients and the NHS. Ward doctors, nurses and pharmacists are able to discuss the benefits of removing the penicillin allergy record with patients if this does not pose a risk to patients. Design, methods and Patient and Public Involvement (PPI) I will review the medical literature to learn how hospitals in other countries have removed incorrect penicillin allergy records from patient medical records. I will look at the effect of this on the amount of penicillin and the amount of second choice antibiotics hospitals used in my hospital as well as patients' infection outcomes and any side effects experienced by patients. Penicillin allergy de-labelling is not currently routine practice in the UK (although it is sporadically undertaken by some healthcare staff in UK hospitals). Asking healthcare workers to work in new ways and patients to accept and act on new advice requires careful thought. I will work with healthcare workers and with patients to identify how to support healthcare workers to incorporate de-labelling into routine practice and also to develop education material that will help patients understand the benefits of de-labelling. Working with patients will ensure the de-labelling process is acceptable to patients and the information and reassurance needed is available at the time of de-labelling. I will monitor patients for any potential harm caused as a consequence of being de-labelled and will measure the success of the study. Dissemination. This work will be shared through publication in medical journals and through the southwest Antimicrobial Pharmacist and Medical Microbiology networks and wider through the national professional networks such as the UK Clinical Pharmacy Association and the British Infection Association, as well as infectious diseases, microbiology and immunology conferences. I will use social media (Twitter and Facebook) to promote the findings of the research I do in this fellowship and link these posts to patient support groups such as Allergy UK. The final phase of my research will be the planning of a multi-centre implementation study to see if this work is replicable in other hospitals in the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Treatment delay in tuberculosis
Abstract: Background Worldwide tuberculosis (TB) is the leading cause of death due to a single infectious agent. Incidence in the United Kingdom is higher than most western European countries. Approximately one-third of pulmonary cases experience treatment delay and this proportion is increasing. Those aged over 65 years are particularly affected by delays and little is known about their experiences of TB. Duration of delay is difficult to measure due to recall bias and insufficient knowledge about the sequence of symptom development. Treatment delay is associated with increased morbidity, mortality, transmission and poor patient experiences. However, the duration after which these consequences occur has not been quantified. Primary care stage of delay is an important contributor and may increase as incidence decreases. Aim and research questions The aim of this project is to address existing gaps in the evidence about TB treatment delay by answering the following questions, using a mixed methods approach: What is the epidemiology of the primary care stage of treatment delay? What is the experience of patients aged over 65 years with TB? What is the optimum diagnostic model to facilitate early referral of patients with TB from primary care? Methods Phase one: Notification data from Public Health England will be linked to the Royal College of General Practitioners Research and Surveillance Centre (RSC) database, Hospital Episode Statistics and mortality data using encrypted NHS numbers. A self-controlled case series approach will be used to evaluate the relative likelihood of developing alert symptoms in the lead up to diagnosis. The first appearance of alert symptoms will be used to re-define the start of treatment delay. Regression techniques will be used to investigate the association of delay with outcomes (death, transmission, duration of treatment and health system use). Phase two: A narrative qualitative study will recruit twelve English and twelve Urdu or Punjabi speaking patients, aged over 65, with TB at any site. After transcribing, a problem-solution approach and levels of narrative approach will be taken to re-story the data and create meta-narratives, respectively. A triangulation protocol will be used to integrate the post-analysis findings from phases one and two. Phase three: I will use logistic regression models to develop a diagnostic prediction tool informing referral of patients from primary care. The tool will be derived from the RSC database and externally validated in The Health Improvement Network database. I will carry out internal validation and calculate performance measures, calibration and discrimination. A decision analysis approach will be used to measure costs and consequences. Patient, public and stakeholder involvement Patients partners have been consulted about the project, the approach for the qualitative work and the development of the plain English summary. Three patient partners will be part of the steering group and will be involved in key decisions in each phase. Impact and dissemination Findings will be disseminated through academic, clinical and public networks and will impact on public and professional facing health messaging. The diagnostic tool will provide a springboard to discussions about improving referral pathways.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: A study of the relationship between inequalities in early child development and subsequent health outcomes in early adolescence to inform policies and interventions to improve health and reduce health inequalities.
Abstract: Background Reducing child health inequalities is a global health priority and evidence suggests that early child development is crucial for future wellbeing. Healthy weight and socio-emotional behaviour in early adolescence are known to be predictive of obesity and mental health in adulthood. However the relationship between inequalities in early child development and these early adolescent health consequences remain poorly understood. This project will identify, and quantify the strength of, causal pathways between inequalities in early child development and body weight and socio-emotional behaviour in adolescence. The findings will inform the development of key policies, of cross-sector relevance, needed to effectively reduce health inequalities and increase wellbeing in early adolescence and throughout the subsequent life course. Research Question What are the mediating pathways between inequality in early child development, and body weight and socio-emotional behaviour in adolescence, and where should we intervene in these pathways to improve outcomes and reduce inequalities for adolescents? Objectives For health outcomes of healthy weight and socio-emotional behaviour in early adolescence: Identify what is already known about the pathways linking early child development to these outcomes. Using the Millennium Cohort Study (MCS), elucidate the mediating pathways between inequalities in early child development and these outcomes Quantify the strength of relationships along each mediating pathway. Quantify the potential effect on adolescent health outcomes of targeting interventions along each mediating pathway Identify targets for intervention and policy implications of the above.Methods A comprehensive participatory systematic review (involving a series of workshops with national and local stakeholders across health and education sectors) will synthesise evidence on and develop a conceptual model of the pathways linking early child development (age 3) to health outcomes, and inequalities in, body weight and socio-emotional behaviour in early adolescence (age 11) (Objective1). This model will be used in causal mediation analysis of MCS data (using structural equation modelling) to identify, and quantify the strength of causal pathways (Objectives 2 &3). Estimates from the causal mediation analyses, combined with effect estimates from controlled trials and systematic reviews, will be used to simulate the effects of intervening on the main mediating pathways (Objective 4). Implications for policy will be explored through a second round of participatory engagement with national and local stakeholders, using a deliberative dialogue approach (Objective 5).Timelines Participatory systematic review submitted for publication by the end of year 1. Longitudinal analysis on the mediating pathways complete and papers submitted for publication by end of year 2 Recommendations for policy produced and disseminated from end of year 3.Anticipated impact and dissemination This research will fill a critical evidence gap by providing a comprehensive synthesis and novel conceptual model of the relationship between inequalities in early years development and later health outcomes in early adolescence. It will identify the mediating pathways susceptible to intervention to mitigate the effect of inequalities in early child development on later health consequences. Working closely with policy stakeholders in health and education, recommendations of cross-sectoral relevance will be generated to inform actionable policies to reduce health inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: ECONOMIC EVALUATION OF MULTI-SECTOR OBESITY POLICY
Abstract: BackgroundObesity is caused by largely preventable risk factors linked to unhealthy diets and physical inactivity. Increasingly, calls have been made for system-wide action with an emphasis on prevention recognizing the multiple determinants of the disease. Policy makers working across different sectors need to allocate scarce resources in a manner that meets efficiency and equity goals. Providing evidence on value-for-money is methodologically challenging as established economic methods that work well within the health sector do not translate well to non-health settings - settings that are crucial for obesity prevention. It is essential that more evidence is generated on (i) knowing which interventions are best value-for-money in terms of obesity prevention and (ii) ensuring that all costs and benefits are properly captured so that an appropriate case can be made for obesity prevention based on evidence.Aims and ObjectivesThis application sets out a research programme for developing methods designed to capture the societal costs and consequences of obesity policy working across five sectors -h; retail, environment, transport, education and workplace. It is methodologically rigorous, timely and co-produced with decision-makers and people living with obesity; ensuring that the research has maximum impact.ObjectivesEach work stream is designed to address different but related determinants of obesity: Environmental: to estimate the cost-effectiveness of interventions that alter local green space. Economic: to measure the value of interventions designed to improve the essential lifestyle skills of young people to improve their chances of sustainable employment. Education: to generate economic evidence on the impact of the national school food standards. Retail: to embed economic evaluation into retail policy; to develop data collection that tracks retail spending; and to use economic insight to shape a food-economy. Transport: to estimate the cost-effectiveness of local active travel policy.Working across these five workstreams we will establish a world-leading Centre for the Economics of Obesity that will deliver high-quality research, liaising closely with policy partners and PPI-members co-producing research.Methods Workstream 1 uses a natural experiment to measure the cost-effectiveness of park refurbishment, capturing health, wellbeing and capability benefits within an economic framework.Workstream 2 addresses the economic determinants of obesity by measuring the value from embedding health and wellbeing training into early-career training schemes.Workstream 3 will apply modelling to extrapolate the costs and benefits associated with the national school food standards.Workstream 4 will map out how economics can shape the retail food economy and understand how vouchers can be designed to promote healthy purchasing behaviour.Workstream 5 uses economic models to estimate the cost-effectiveness of active travel policy incorporating both morbidity and mortality effects. OutputsMy ambition is to build on my existing research programme to develop a coherent, comprehensive research programme that will develop economic methods that can be applied to multi-sector policy and reduce population obesity. I will use this award to establish a strong team of researchers and to contribute to their career development. This award will enable me to become a senior leader and an international expert in the economics of obesity.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: More Robust Evidence to Advance the UK Salt Reduction Programme
Abstract: Salt intake in the UK averages at ~8 g/d; well above the World Health Organization's 5 g/d recommended maximum intake. Via raised blood pressure, high salt intake is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, a leading cause of death and disability. The UK has a salt reduction programme, which is predominantly based on the setting of targets for the salt content of foods to encourage their reformulation. So far, salt targets for 2010, 2012, and 2017 have been set; salt targets for 2023 have been drafted but not yet set. Long viewed as a public health success story, the UK salt reduction programme is now poorly implemented, and no progress in salt reduction has been made since 2014. The overall aim of this research is to provide concrete evidence to strengthen the UK salt reduction programme to reduce population salt intake. Three studies will be conducted, on the (i) salt content of supermarket foods, (ii) salt content of out-of-home foods, and (iii) potential health and economic impact the salt reduction programme, respectively. First, a mixed-methods study (to be completed by December 2022), where changes in the salt content of supermarket foods over time will be assessed, followed by semi-structured interviews with industry and governmental informants on how to overcome barriers to salt reformulation in the supermarket food categories contributing most to salt intake in the UK. Second, the development of a database of the nutritional content and price of out-of-home foods using information available online, with web scraping to be automated from early 2022 and continue thereafter on a weekly basis, so that by 2024 sufficient data will be available to determine whether the 2023 salt targets were effective in lowering salt content in the out-of-home sector. This will be complemented by a cross-sectional survey (to be completed by March 2024) of a representative sample of UK out-of-home businesses on their salt use, the extent to which it is controlled, and existing measures to reduce it. Third, a modelling study (to be completed by September 2024) in which the health and economic impact of achieving all 2023 salt targets in both supermarket and out-of-home foods will be estimated. The number of cardiovascular events and deaths that would be prevented will be obtained by estimating, in consecutive steps, changes in the following parameters: salt content of foods, individuals' salt intake, individuals' blood pressure, and population incidence and mortality rate in ischaemic heart disease and stroke. Cost savings will be estimated using cost figures for the UK salt reduction programme, disease-specific healthcare, and disease-specific productivity losses. Results will be communicated to policymakers, food industry and catering representatives, and the wider public via the advocacy work of Action on Salt, an independent non-profit charitable organisation who will collaborate closely in this research. Reviving and strengthening the UK salt reduction programme would bring enormous benefits in preventing chronic diseases as well as major cost savings. This research will have implications for salt reformulation worldwide as well as for other types of reformulations.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Investigating the effectiveness of pre-surgical ‘health optimisation’ public health interventions for obesity and smoking in elective hip and knee replacement surgery from health service and patient perspectives
Abstract: Research question What impact do pre-surgical health optimisation interventions (for obesity and smoking) in hip and knee replacement patients have on patient outcomes, are they cost effective and do they risk causing health inequalities? Background Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs) have introduced 'health optimisation' interventions (HOIs) that require or support National Health Service (NHS) patients to lose weight and/or stop smoking ahead of surgical referral. The interventions are intended to: Improve clinical outcomes from surgery Reduce the need for surgery Trigger long-term lifestyle changes in patients at a key moment in their lives when they are motivated to improve their healthThere is significant geographical variation in intervention content, reflecting the current inadequate evidence-base for their effects on patients, public health and cost-effectiveness. They also have potential unintended consequences of increasing health inequalities through differential impact on vulnerable sociodemographic groups' access to surgery. Evaluations of existing interventions have not been published. Aims and objectives Investigate the effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and impact on health inequalities of HOIs for body mass index (BMI) and smoking in elective hip and knee replacement surgery from NHS and patient perspectives, using a mixed methodology approach. Methods Complete four Work Packages and a training and development programme through collaboration with clinical, commissioning and research settings and with integral patient and public involvement (PPI): Natural experimental study using existing data centred on the National Joint Registry for England to determine the impact of HOIs on surgery rates, patient clinical and public health outcomes and association with sociodemographic inequality. Data will be analysed using interrupted time series and difference-in-differences analyses to assess the effect of HOI introduction on trends in outcomes before and after the date a HOI was introduced in each CCG area. Extended natural experimental study with an embedded case study of a CCG's new HOI in one of its sub-regions. This will address deficits in existing datasets and evaluations by measuring patient engagement and changes in BMI and smoking status, and the associated costs, alongside the outcomes addressed above. Health economic modelling with use of data from Work Packages 1 and 2 and published literature to estimate the long-term cost-effectiveness of HOIs relating to hip and knee replacement surgery. Qualitative study using interviews with 30 key stakeholders and six citizen focus groups in two contrasting English regions to investigate their views on HOIs and the motivations and barriers to their introduction.Timelines Three-year full-time doctoral fellowship where the Work Packages are completed in parallel including time for reporting and dissemination. Anticipated impact and dissemination I will work with PPI groups and collaborators to use the findings to form and disseminate meaningful recommendations to policy decision-makers and wider stakeholders to enable their evidence-based decisions on the ongoing use or expansion of HOIs. This will have an immediate impact on many thousands of patients. There may be the result of a recommendation of a standard HOI for all CCGs where this would improve outcomes, public health and use of health and care resources.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: No need(le) to worry: Development and feasibility study of a self-help cognitive behavioural therapy resource for children with needle fear
Abstract: TitleNo need(le) to worry: Development and feasibility study of a self-help cognitive behavioural therapy resource for children with needle fear.The problemNeedles are utilised frequently throughout childhood to provide inoculations, to take blood samples to aid investigations, and to administer medications intramuscularly or intravenously. Needle fear is common, affecting up to 50% of the child population. Needle fear can be viewed as a continuum from mild fear to extreme fear and phobia. All children and young people with needle fear will have physiological symptoms and emotional responses to needles and may employ avoidance tactics. However, where there is significant distress and interference to their lives, this would be classed as a phobia.Fear of needles can lead to the delay or even avoidance of necessary healthcare interventions which can result in poorer health and poorer outcomes, including quality of life. It can be a life-long problem, not just for the individual but also for their family. There are limited resources currently available to reduce needle fear in children. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) has been shown to be effective in the treatment of anxiety disorders and specific phobias and recent studies have shown that self-help CBT resources can also be effective in reducing dental anxiety. Despite the acknowledged efficacy of CBT, there is a paucity of evidence related to the use of self-help CBT in managing needle fear. However, given the strong evidence-base for CBT, it is reasonable to assert that an intervention of this nature could be invaluable in helping children manage their fear of needles in many contexts.AimTo develop and undertake a feasibility study of a self-help CBT resource for children with needle fearPlanThe project will comprise two main stages:Stage 1 will involve children aged 11-16 years, their parents, and healthcare providers in the co-design of a self-help CBT resource to reduce children's needle fear. This will involve qualitative interviews with around 20 children with a variety of needle related fears and experiences, and subsequent workshops with children, parents and healthcare providers to co-design the resource. Stage 2 will be an uncontrolled feasibility study focusing on recruitment and retention of participants, acceptability of the resource and testing alternative outcome measures.The feasibility study will address these key uncertainties: a. The most appropriate self-report measure of needle fear, which will be the primary outcome for a future trialb. The perception of key stakeholders, such as phlebotomists, dentists, anaesthetists, research nurses of such a resource, and their willingness to recruit participantsc. Retention and completion ratesd. Acceptability of the developed resource to children and their parents, and their willingness to be recruitedFindings from this feasibility study are essential for the justification and planning of a future randomised controlled trial to reduce needle fear in children, using a self-help CBT approach, with wide impact for paediatric healthcare users and providers.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: “Integrating public health with high street revitalisation: A mixed methods analysis of local initiatives addressing the food environment”
Abstract: Background Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are the leading cause of years of life lost in England. Unhealthy diets are amongst the greatest risk factors for the development of obesity and NCDs, and are known to be determined by the availability, accessibility and affordability of (un)healthy food and beverages. While important, the implementation of local interventions aimed at promoting healthier food retail environments or 'high streets' can be challenging due diverging priorities between promoting health and stimulating economic growth. This has become particularly relevant in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. Aims and objectives This fellowship aims to investigate the integration of public health objectives with efforts to revitalise high streets in England. It will focus on two research gaps: (1) how public health objectives can be achieved and prioritised in the context of increased incentives to support the local retail environment, and (2) how local authority practitioners and policymakers engage with private and third sector stakeholders in decision-making about the local food retail environment. The objective are to: Synthesise existing evidence on the public health impact of initiatives to revitalise the retail environment, and the mechanisms by which initiatives are theorised to impact health and health equity. Understand how the issue of high street revitalisation is framed by stakeholders in the public, private and third sector and the media in England. Undertake comparative case studies of the Childhood Obesity Trailblazer programme in five English local authorities to: Explore local authority objectives, decision-making processes and activities surrounding the food environment and high street revitalisation. Explore the extent to which Trailblazer initiatives integrate with objectives and activities aimed at supporting the high street, and the extent to which public health objectives are prioritised in each local authority context. Identify public, private and third sector stakeholders involved in the Trailblazer programme, and explore their priorities, interests and engagement. Synthesise findings from different research streams and develop a briefing document in collaboration with practitioners and the public.Members of the public will be involved throughout the research project to ensure that the research objectives and activities are relevant to the concerns and priorities of the public in England. Methods The fellowship objectives will be addressed using the following research methods: A mixed methods systematic review of primary research. A mixed methods framing analysis of documents and online materials relevant to the revitalisation of the food retail environment. Qualitative comparative case studies using documentary analysis, stakeholder interviews, stakeholder analysis and focus group discussions. An innovative application of meta-ethnography to synthesise research findings.Anticipated Impact and dissemination The fellowship findings are anticipated to inform and support strategies to create healthy and prosperous retail environments, which is expected to benefit the public's health by making healthier choices more widely available, accessible and affordable. Research outputs will also contribute to greater understanding of the optimal engagement between public, private and other stakeholders in decision-making that impacts health. Findings will be disseminated through co-produced lay summaries, a briefing document sharing best practices, presentations and peer-reviewed publications.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The STADi-HuM study: The interrelationship between receipt of Specialist Treatment for problematic Alcohol or Drug use, Hospitalisation and Mortality in England: A national record linkage and clinical study
Abstract: Background Alcohol and illicit drug-related harm are major public health problems associated with millions of preventable hospital admissions worldwide each year. Both alcohol and drug-related hospital admissions have increased year-on-year for the past decade in England with 1.3 million alcohol-, and 97,000 drug-related admissions in 2018/19. Currently one in every 13 admissions is related to alcohol and/or drugs. Reducing alcohol and drug-related hospitalisation is key priority of the government's public health strategy and several service user groups. We cannot currently accurately predict which people with addiction disorders are at increased risk of repeated hospitalisation and poor health outcomes, and there is limited research on interventions to reduce healthcare/hospital burden among this cohort. In the context of a shrinking addiction treatment system in England, it is increasingly difficult for services to prioritise the limited support available to those most in need. Aims and objectives The overall aim is to advance understanding of interrelationships between addiction treatment, hospitalisation, death and adverse health outcomes. This will be addressed using three work packages (WPs). WP1 will investigate which individual level sociodemographic, diagnostic, clinical and treatment factors predict recurrent hospitalisation, death and poor treatment outcomes among adults presenting to addiction services. Sensitivity analyses will be conducted restricted to hospitalisation and death due to COVID-19. WP2 will derive and validate a clinical 'risk score' to predict which adults presenting to addiction services are most at risk of recurrent hospitalisation. WP3 will design and assess the feasibility of an intervention developed to reduce recurrent hospitalisation among those identified as 'high-risk' by the score developed in WP2.Methods In collaboration with Public Health England (PHE), an existing data linkage between national addiction treatment data (the National Drug Treatment Monitoring System (NDTMS)) and hospitalisation data (Hospital Episode Statistics (HES)) will be expanded to all approved years (2013-2021) and additional datasets (A&E, death certification records), creating the largest addiction database globally (n≈1M). A series of longitudinal cohort studies using survival time analysis with mixed-effects time-to-event models will assess WP1/WP2 objectives.Based on WP1/WP2 findings and the existing literature, a multi-component complex intervention will be developed by Delphi consensus methodology. A feasibility study will evaluate the intervention in a single-site addiction service. Patient and Public InvolvementThis proposal was discussed with the Data Linkage - Service User and Carer Advisory Group and experts with lived experience at PHE. Both groups were very supportive and will continue to be involved throughout the project. I will offer paid work placements for people with lived experience to co-produce and deliver detailed plans to engage with service users, PHE, NHS England, and the wider public. We will run groups and organise discussions to interpret and share findings. Anticipated impact and dissemination Findings will be summarised using accessible and understandable information packs shared widely via social media, and the King's College London and RCPsych press offices. Findings will be published in scientific journals and presented at conferences. Practical recommendations will be developed to influence how we identify 'high-risk' groups and improve support to people with addiction.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Causation in a complex social system: understanding schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, self-harm, and suicide in socially excluded groups
Abstract: Background: Severe mental illness (SMI) including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, self-harm, and suicide contribute a large burden of mortality and morbidity in England. The distribution of SMI is unequal across the population, with elevated rates in socially excluded groups, making it an important public health priority. While research has revealed aetiological clues for SMI, there is limited evidence on the social and environmental causes. These causes exist with a complex system, making estimating the causal associations with SMI challenging. Better understanding of the modifiable social causes of SMI is needed to develop effective public health interventions.Aim: The aim is to explore the causal architecture of SMI in socially excluded populations using recent advances in causal inference, epidemiology, and systems science. By elucidating the causal factors in the social environment for SMI, I will generate evidence to inform public health planning. I will use a range of methods across three workstreams:Workstream 1: Causal analysis of neighbourhood factors and SMI using natural experiments In the absence of randomised trials on neighbourhood factors and SMI, natural experiments create opportunities to explore how factors in the social environment are causally associated with SMI. The Swedish refugee resettlement programme creates a natural experiment as selected refugees are placed into neighbourhoods, emulating a trial-based design. I will estimate the causal effect of neighbourhood factors on SMI, providing important insights. Workstream 2: Microsimulation, agent-based models, and economic evaluation to explore regional inequalities in social exclusion and SMI I will use data from electronic health records, national statistics, and cohort studies to explore how SMI is geographically distributed. Using static and dynamic microsimulation, I will explore the distribution of SMI and model the impact of counterfactual scenarios to estimate the impact that reducing inequality would have on rates SMI. I will develop an agent-based model to estimate the causal association between social exclusion and SMI. I will conduct a cost-effectiveness analysis of interventions which reduce inequalities. I will create an online tool where practitioners can enter details of their local area into the simulation and economic models to estimate the impact that interventions of reducing inequalities might have on rates of SMI.Workstream 3: Predicting suicide clusters to prevent self-harm and suicideWhile suicide prevention is an important public health priority, identifying suicide clusters remains difficult. In this workstream, I will use data from electronic health records, suicide helpline calls, and Google Trends data to predict suicide clusters. I will use agent-based modelling to estimate what early identification of suicide clusters, and resulting timely mental health support, might have on reducing rates of self-harm and suicide. These models will provide proof-of-concept for the use of modelling for public health planning, which could be applied to a wide range of questions to prevent mental illnesses and support outcomes for those with SMI.This fellowship will allow me to apply cutting-edge methods to augment my epidemiological skills. It will allow me to work with members of the public and practitioners, supporting my development as a future research leader.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: CIP-LINC Community pharmacy alcohol-related liver disease risk identification and linkage to care through development of a complex intervention
Abstract: Research Question Can community pharmacy identify people at risk of Alcohol-related Liver Disease (ArLD) and connect them with existing ArLD pathways of care? Background Liver disease is now the 3rd largest cause of premature mortality in the United Kingdom. ArLD causes the majority of these deaths. Mortality from ArLD can be reduced if it is diagnosed earlier.Testing for ArLD in people who drink harmful amounts of alcohol is recommended in national guidance and ArLD pathways exist to facilitate this in primary care. Alcohol identification and brief advice services are already provided by some community pharmacies. There is some evidence that such services can identify harmful alcohol use in people attending the pharmacies but there is no research examining whether these people can be connected to existing ArLD pathways. Methods I will answer the research question through development of the CIP-LINC intervention, a complex intervention that enables community pharmacy to identify people at risk of ArLD and connect them with existing care pathways for ArLD. I will use Medical Research Council guidance on developing complex interventions and Normalisation Process Theory (NPT) to develop and test the intervention in four work packages (WPs) over three years. WP1 - What are the barriers and facilitators to pharmacist-led alcohol identification and brief advice (IBA) in community pharmacy? I will undertake a qualitative evidence synthesis of studies examining barriers and facilitators to implementing IBA in community pharmacy. I will do this according to Cochrane guidance. I will use framework synthesis based on NPT to synthesise the data. WP2 -h; Perspectives of service providers and service users on a role for community pharmacy in ArLD pathways I will undertake a qualitative study of patients with ArLD, pharmacists, pharmacy users and health professionals involved in ArLD pathways to explore their perspectives on a role for community pharmacy in ArLD pathways. I will purposively sample these participants for semi-structured interviews. WP3 -h; Intervention Design I will use the results of WP1 and WP2 to design the complex intervention and training materials. This will be done with key stakeholders in a series of meetings over two months. WP4 -h; Feasibility Study I will undertake a mixed-methods feasibility study of implementing the intervention in community pharmacy. Six pharmacies across Southampton and Portsmouth will be recruited to provide the intervention. I will undertake qualitative interviews with stakeholders to explore the acceptability of the intervention and the feasibility of delivering it. I will collect data that quantifies intervention use and clinical data that could be used to assess effectiveness in a future trial. Impact on NHS/Patients: The intervention has the potential to increase earlier detection of ArLD and thereby decrease morbidity and mortality. The study will develop novel collaborations between community and hospital care, which is in keeping with objectives of the NHS long-term plan. Dissemination strategy: I will publish four journal articles describing my findings and will present my research at academic conferences. I will support a patient with ArLD to write a blog about their involvement in the research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Mapping patterns of viral load emission in exhaled breath over the course of acute respiratory virus infections
Abstract: Background Respiratory viruses such as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) and influenza cause significant morbidity and mortality. The gold standard of diagnosis is nasopharyngeal sampling (NPS). However, many patients can be positive for SARS-CoV-2 by NPS for prolonged periods without being infectious.The NIHR have identified understanding the risk of transmissibility of SARS-CoV-2 and its viability airborne as a research priority. The Barer group (Leicester) has pioneered the use of sampling pathogens in exhaled breath using modified face-masks containing polyvinylalcohol sampling strips (face-mask sampling, FMS). I am first author in a study that is the first in the world to detect and quantify exhaled SARS-CoV-2 using FMS. In this study, we found that viral loads on FMS were highest during early symptom onset and that there was weak, but significant correlation between concomitant FMS and NPS samples. The proposed fellowship was developed with the involvement of 10 patient and public involvement (PPI) representatives who will remain throughout the PhD. Ultimately, the fellowship will determine whether FMS can be used as a tool to rapidly quantify the infectiousness of individuals with respiratory viruses and potential earliar diagnosis. Research questions 1: What is the longitudinal pattern of viral load on FMS during the first two weeks of acute illness for respiratory viruses? 2. How do viral loads on FMS compare with NPS? Methods The project is divided into three work packages. Work package (WP) 1 involves a systematic review and diagnostic test meta-analysis assessing the sensitivity and specificity of existing methods that detect pathogens in exhaled breath, compared to their gold standards (generally, NPS for viruses and sputum for bacteria). WP2 will use five serial face-mask and nasopharyngeal samples from patients infected with the most common respiratory viruses in Leicester (likely SARS-CoV-2 but may also includ influenza if SARS-CoV-2 cases drop) to determine the natural history of emission and its relationship to symptomology and PCR/lateral flow tests on NPS. WP3 will use mathematical modelling to map the viral kinetics from FMS and NPS over the course of acute disease, taking into account data collected from work package 2. Timelines for delivery WP1 will be performed within the first 6 months of starting the PhD. WP 2 and 3 will be performed in parallel to fully map viral load during acute illness, without causing significant participant inconvenience from providing too many samples.Impact and dissemination This work is of public health interest and has the potential to open up new approaches to the understanding and control of respiratory virus infections. Should FMS help to determine the infectiousness of a patient, there would be immediate benefit to the NHS - such as early de-escalation of isolation precautions for infected patients, and early identification of infectious patients at the workplace before symptom onset, and mass testing at big events and travelling abroad. The PPI group will guide dissemination to patients, and results will be presented at national and international conferences to simulate interest and enthusiasm for collaboration into larger, definitive transmission studies.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: INTEGRATE: Using routinely-collected healthcare data to inform clinical guidance and improve population health
Abstract: Background Clear health guidance informed by robust evidence can improve the health of populations. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) is a global leader in developing guidelines for clinical care. However, there are areas of important clinical need where robust randomised evidence to inform guidance does not exist and recommendations for care (what should we do?) are not made. Despite the focus on generating high-quality guidance, at present uptake and impact of guidance is not directly measured (does what we do work?). Not assessing guidance implementation leads to an inability to understand and address disparities by sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic status and region, leading to lost economic benefits from improved health (how can we do better?).The COVID pandemic has created new collaborations and I have worked with partners from NICE over the last year to provide evidence to address urgent research questions. In the INTEGRATE study I will build on this partnership to answer co-produced research questions using cutting-edge epidemiological methods in the unique wealth of routinely-collected data available in England to provide specific and timely evidence to address evidence gaps and inform implementation.Aims and objectives The aim is to determine if evidence generated from routinely-collected data can inform and increase the impact of clinical guidance produced by NICE.The objectives are to: Create early robust evidence where randomised trials are lacking. Assess the extent of implementation of guidance and variations in care. Determine the health and economic impact of implementation or non-uptake. Develop a framework to support NICE in adopting observational evidence into clinical guidance.Methods Workstream A: Using routinely-collected data to inform guideline developmentAfter initial scoping meetings we will complete three cycles of answering distinct research questions using a target-trial approach in primary care data. Shared learning in each cycle will iteratively improve knowledge leading to a framework for incorporation of routine evidence into NICE clinical guidance.Workstream B: Using routinely-collected data to assess and evaluate guideline impactAfter collaborative identification of suitable recent NICE guidance, we will use repeated cross-sectional studies in primary care data to describe changes in individual level-prescribing over time after guideline launch, focusing on disparities in prescribing by sex, ethnicity, socioeconomic status and region. These results will feedback to targeted efforts to improve uptake of guidance in areas of need. We will go on to quantify the health and economic benefits of uptake in a cohort study.Timelines for delivery The learning-systems approach in Workstream A will lead to co-development of knowledge throughout the cycles of research projects, culminating in the final framework for incorporation of routine evidence into NICE guidance in year five. Workstream B will run concurrently over three years.Anticipated impact and dissemination Individual studies will directly inform clinical guidelines as well as producing stand-alone outputs. The ultimate impact will be to improve how NICE will use evidence from routine data for guideline development and implementation, strengthening their work into the future and with potential cost-efficiencies and benefits for the health of the population.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Care Home Evidence-based Interventions to Reduce Infection that are Sustainable and Holistic (CHERISH)
Abstract: Research question: Can a care home research network and data platform enable implementation of effective interventions to reduce/prevent infection in care homes, and address evidence-gaps by facilitating the development and evaluation of new interventions?Background: Our ageing population has led to a focus on prevention to reduce the need for adult social care and support. Many infections could be prevented by implementing existing interventions e.g. vaccination and/or by generating new evidence where none currently exists. Aim: To transform the current reactive model for managing infection in care homes to a proactive, evidence-based approach, which facilitates effective public health intervention and quality improvement; and to demonstrate my approach by delivering exemplar studies on two leading causes of infection: influenza and urinary tract infection (UTI). Methods: The study builds on partnerships with providers and linked data infrastructure established through my VIVALDI (COVID-19 in care homes study) in >300 care homes. Objective 1: Development of a set of 'social care infection indicators' to capture the impact of infection and outbreaks in care homes from multiple perspectives (residents, families, staff, NHS, providers, purchasers). This will include a systematic review of care home surveillance approaches, qualitative interviews with stakeholders and coproduction. Indicators will be used as the basis for infection dashboards for providers and for intervention evaluation in all subsequent studies. Objective 2: Feasibility study to gain insight into whether a rapid diagnostic test for influenza can increase the proportion of influenza cases (residents) who receive antivirals within 48 hours (primary outcome). The intervention will be coproduced with stakeholders and the study will run in 10 care homes. We will undertake a mixed methods process evaluation (focus groups, semi-structured interviews with staff, longitudinal survey).Objective 3: Development and evaluation of interventions to reduce (antibiotic-resistant) UTI. I will link the VIVALDI dataset to national microbiology and prescribing datasets and use it to estimate rates of UTI and UTI-related (gram-negative) bloodstream infections in residents. This will inform the design of my cluster randomised trial of a hydration intervention to prevent UTI in residents, in partnership with NHS England. The primary outcome and evaluation design will be coproduced with stakeholders, informed by the social care infection indicators (Objective 1), and include a health economic analysis and mixed methods process evaluation. Timelines for delivery: Infection indicators in Years 1-2 and deployed the following year. Influenza and UTI studies in Years 2-5. By Year 5, I aim to have obtained further funding to evaluate the influenza intervention, and will partner with NHSE to implement the UTI intervention, if successful, nationally. Dissemination: Knowledge exchange events, conference presentations, journal articles, and infographics. Findings will be shared with policymakers e.g. UKHSA and NHSE. Impact: Infection indicators will support providers and policymakers to monitor infection, and enable targeted public health and quality improvement interventions, improving residents' health and wellbeing. The influenza study will support improved practice in relation to antivirals and influenza testing, reducing outbreaks. Reductions in UTI will benefit residents (wellbeing and health) and the NHS (fewer avoidable admissions and consultations).
