Award_Title: Tackling child health inequality. An interventional epidemiology platform to inform policy
Abstract: Background Addressing health inequalities and improving child health are UK government priorities, but current policies are failing. The UK continues to slip down international rankings for child health in high-income countries. Large and persistent health inequalities, increasing pre-COVID-19, have worsened during the pandemic. Of particular concern are rising mental health problems amongst children and young people. Successful strategies to mitigate these harms will require combinations of public health, welfare, and education interventions. Yet there is insufficient evidence to inform crucial real-world policy changes that can work for all children, equitably. Critical evidence gaps include understanding the best times and targets for policies; which combination of policies will be most cost-effective in a financially constrained system; and the time horizons over which benefits and cost savings will accrue. Research aims: To develop an interventional epidemiology platform to address these evidence gaps. To translate this evidence into policy and practice, informing whole systems change to reduce socioeconomic inequalities in child health.Research questions To what extent do key exposures, for example poor parental mental health and low family income, mediate the association between parental disadvantage and important child health outcomes such as mental health? To what extent do interventions that target these causal pathways from parental disadvantage to child health outcomes improve child health and reduce inequalities? In the context of finite resources, how and when in the life-course should resources be allocated across these causal pathways to reduce inequalities in health, and what are the likely time horizons over which benefits and cost savings will accrue? What are the best ways to embed this evidence into practice sustainably?Methods 1) Causal mediation analysis in longitudinal data; 2) Simulation of trials of interventions and natural policy experiments; 3) Economic evaluation. Work package (WP) 1 will link world leading datasets and cohorts capturing population level data across Europe to develop an agile, efficient research platform for policy evaluation. These include the DANLIFE whole population linked datasets in Denmark (DANLIFE), Wales (SAIL) and NW England (CIPHA), and the EU Child Cohort Network of population based prospective cohort studies. WP2 will assess causal pathways to inequalities in child health and model the effect of different policy scenarios on inequalities in health at the population level, with an initial focus on child mental health.In WP3, I will collaborate with leading economists to apply a dynamic microsimulation model for childhood policy analysis to assess timescales for the return on investment of policies to address child health inequalities. WP4 will translate evidence into policy and practice transformation internationally, working with policymakers and children, young people and families. Anticipated impact and disseminationScientifically robust evidence to drive more effective policies will generate significant population health, economic and social impacts. Working with the WHO, UNICEF and national/local decision-makers, including the Cheshire and Merseyside Integrated Care System, this evidence will be used to design and implement better policies for children. Inequalities are an international problem; solutions will be globally relevant.

Award_Title: Developing a poveRty-informEd learning health and social care system to PRevent mEntal health problemS in disadvantagEd childreN and parenTs: REPRESENT
Abstract: There is growing concern about the prevalence of mental health problems in children, adolescents and parents, particularly in context of poverty and multiple disadvantage. These concerns have been highlighted and exasperated during the COVID-19 pandemic. Children living in family contexts with mental health problems, poverty and social disadvantages have poor public health outcomes which develop in childhood and persist into adulthood and beyond. These problems are often compounded by additional and accumulative stress which interact synergistically. Effective intervention in the early years and childhood is likely to bring about substantial future benefits to health and wellbeing. Yet despite experiencing the greatest mental health and related need, children and families living in poverty rarely have their mental health needs recognised and do not receive effective prevention and treatment. Those interventions that do exist typically focus on individual behavioural determinants or micro-level factors decontextualised from the social determinants of health. This can result in ineffective, stigmatising interventions. Whilst practitioners supporting disadvantaged families recognise the importance of addressing structural drivers of mental health problems, they typically feel powerless to act. This programme of work aims to develop a poverty-informed integrated health and social care system for children and families at risk of mental health problems in the context of multiple disadvantage. The programme of work brings together children and parents/caregivers with lived experience of multiple disadvantage, with leaders from public health, social care and academia to seek solutions and to improve outcomes for vulnerable families. The specific objectives are to: Conduct three interlinked realist syntheses to develop an equity-focused understanding of what works i) to prevent mental health problems in children; ii) to prevent mental health problems in parents and iii) to support children and families living in poverty, programme theories for each separate synthesis (WP1) Draw together the distinct realist syntheses into one overarching meta-synthesis to produce candidate theories for intervening and supporting multiple disadvantaged children and families at risk of mental health problems (WP1) Map the existing formal and informal support received by children and parents who are at risk of mental health problems in the context of poverty and other disadvantage using social network analysis (WP2) Conduct a realistic evaluation of 'valued support' to develop a refined programme theory for a poverty-informed approach to reducing mental health problems in children and parents who experience multiple disadvantage (WP3) Test the programme theory using qualitative comparative analysis (WP3) Examine the preferences and acceptability for the model of poverty-informed mental health care with children, parents and practitioners using a discrete choice experiment (DCE) (WP4) Co-produce an optimum poverty-informed health and social care system for children and families at risk of mental health problems in the context of multiple disadvantage, as part of an overall learning health and social care system (WP5).

Award_Title: PARROT: Penicillin Allergy, Antibiotic Resistance and Patient health OuTcomes
Abstract: BackgroundPatients who have a penicillin allergy (PenA) label are treated with non-penicillin antibiotics, have longer hospital stays, receive repeated courses of antibiotics, and have increased mortality when compared to patients without PenA.Antibiotics used in place of penicillin antibiotics in patients with PenA have a greater tendency to select for antibiotic resistance. This may be contributing to the higher rates of treatment failure and death seen in patients with PenA. Bloodstream infections (BSI) and COVID-19 are serious infections that can cause sepsis. The impact of PenA on AMR and health outcomes in patients treated for BSI and COVID-19 is largely unknown.Aim To understand the associations between PenA, AMR and patient health outcomes in order to inform future antibiotic stewardship policies. ObjectivesThis project will be organised into three workstreams with the following objectives: Workstream-1: To determine the impact of a PenA labels on AMR in patients with bloodstream infections. Workstream-2: To determine the impact of a PenA labels on AMR and patient health outcomes in patients admitted with COVID-19. Workstream-3: To assess if removing incorrect PenA labels will result in a reduction in AMR.MethodsThis fellowship will take advantage of existing big data and collaborate with two NIHR-funded studies: PEACH 'Procalcitonin: Evaluation of Antibiotic use in COVID-19 Hospitalised patients (PEACH)' and ALABAMA 'AntiBiotics, Allergy and Microbial ResistAnce (ALABAMA)' NIHR funded studies.The following methods will be used for each workstream: Worksteam-1: Access the PIONEER Health Data Research Hub, a repository of health data collected as a part of routine NHS care, to identify patients with BSI for a cohort study to explore how PenA impacts AMR and patient health outcomes. PIONEER data are highly detailed with the ability to link BSI diagnoses to AMR and PenA status. Workstream-2: Perform a second cohort study using PEACH Study data to investigate the impact of PenA on AMR, and patient health outcomes in patients admitted with COVID-19. Workstream-3: Undertake a study within the ALABAMA trial, involving longitudinal sampling of ALABAMA participants to investigate whether AMR genes are lost in participants who have had incorrect PenA labels removed.Patient & Public Involvement (PPI)PPI has been embedded since project inception and Jenny Boards (JB), our PPI lead contributor has been involved supporting the project concept, advising on study practicalities, accessibility, and has been invaluable in simplifying the scientific language. JB will continue to advise on this research as a member of Project Management Group. ImpactAMR is predicted to affect 10 million people globally by 2050. Determining the impact PenA has on AMR and health outcomes, ensures this research will have both patient and societal level benefit. It will provide the evidence to support better antibiotic prescribing and in turn mitigate the spread of AMR. Findings from this Fellowship will provide key evidence for the role PenA testing could have on antibiotic stewardship policy to minimise AMR. This research will address a critical research gap expanding our understanding of the mechanism of antibiotic treatment failure in people with PenA.

Award_Title: Alcohol harm reduction in at-risk drinkers in the UK: a mixed-methods approach to increase the number and success of reduction attempts made
Abstract: Research question How can we increase the proportion of at-risk drinkers in the UK making alcohol reduction attempts and the success of these attempts? Background Alcohol consumption is a leading risk factor for early mortality, ill health and disability and is a leading contributor to disease burden in the UK; over 10 million adults in England are at-risk drinkers, meaning they consume alcohol at levels that pose a risk to their health. However, 80% of these drinkers are not attempting to reduce their consumption, and of the 20% that are, only 14% use any evidence-based support. Reducing the harm from alcohol can be achieved at a population-level through small individual reductions in consumption. It is important to incorporate the individuals' drinking goals and needs, and provide evidence-based public health interventions that are easy to access. Aims The overarching aims of this fellowship are to use a mixed-methods approach to increase the: proportion of at-risk drinkers making alcohol reduction attempts; success of these attempts. Methods Work Package (WP) 1: Focus groups to understand alcohol reduction attempts A series of focus groups conducted remotely with members of the public, including under-served groups such as people experiencing homelessness, with a semi-structured discussion on their experiences of alcohol reduction attempts to create a list of co-produced alcohol reduction strategies and desired goals, and an understanding of what might persuade those who have not made an alcohol reduction attempt to do so. WP2: Acceptability of alcohol reduction strategies to drinkers who have not made a reduction attempt An experimental online trial with drinkers who have not previously made an alcohol reduction attempt where participants are randomised to an alcohol reduction strategy and a suggested goal to understand which strategies and goals are most acceptable. WP3: Causal inference methods to evaluate alcohol reduction strategies Population-level data collected on alcohol reduction characteristics from a nationally representative survey of adults in England and causal inference methods used to estimate the total causal effect of alcohol reduction strategies on the success of alcohol reduction attempts. WP4: Interventions to increase the proportion and success of attempts being made A population-level mass media campaign co-designed with members of the public, including those from under-served groups, to increase the proportion of drinkers making alcohol reduction attempts and evaluated using a time series analysis of population-level data. Refinement of the individual-level digital intervention, Drink Less, using the person-based approach to increase the success of attempts being made, and evaluated in a within-app randomised trial. Timelines for delivery WP1 conducted in years 1-2 of the fellowship, WP2 in year 2, WP3 in years 2-4, and WP4 in years 4-5. Anticipated impact and dissemination This fellowship will have a positive impact on population health in the UK by increasing both the proportion of at-risk drinkers making an alcohol reduction attempt and success of these attempts. The research findings will be widely disseminated including via press releases, academic publications, social media, and a stakeholder workshop.

Award_Title: Stories of life and health in an unequal society: how can local government close the health inequalities gap through a better understanding of people’s experiences of resilience, coping, adversity and health in coastal communities?
Abstract: Background Inequalities in health have widened over the last decade, recently being further exacerbated by the Covid pandemic and rise in cost of living. The Chief Medical Officer has highlighted coastal health inequalities and called for research into drivers of poor health and testing of effective solutions. This research focuses on two coastal areas in West Sussex, Wick and Bognor, which are within the 10% most deprived in England. Despite recognition that health inequalities are driven by social inequalities, action to improve health has often focused on individual behaviour change. Greater understanding of how the cultural, social and economic context impacts on health should inform action to reduce inequalities. Researchers have called for prioritisation of listening to communities through ethnographic research, with solutions being developed by and with local people. Research question How can local government close the health inequality gap through a better understanding of people's life stories, their sense of place identity, and their experiences of resilience, coping, adversity and health in two coastal communities? Aims and objectives The research aims to understand how people living in two contrasting coastal communities in Arun experience the place they live and their social context in relation to health, and to engage with local communities to develop solutions to reducing health inequalities which respond to their priorities. The objectives are: To explore people's experience of place identity and understand how this has an impact on their health and wellbeing; To explore how people understand the concepts of resilience, coping, adversity and health through listening to their life stories; To engage with community members to collaboratively develop actions to reduce inequalities which impact on health. Methods The research uses an ethnographic methodology to allow people's experiences and the meaning they make from them to be studied in their social and community context. Methods will include: Systematic review on place identity, resilience, coping, adversity and health; Participant observation and interviews to understand social/cultural context, relationships and what matters to people; Walking interviews in the local neighbourhood to develop a richer understanding of people's place identity; Photo elicitation using participants' images to explore understanding of resilience, coping, adversity and health; Deliberative engagement with local communities to share ideas, generate and explore actions to reduce health inequalities. Timelines for delivery Year 1: Research methods training; establish public involvement group; develop research networks; literature review; ethical approval; research visits; start fieldwork in Wick. Year 2: Complete fieldwork in Wick; fieldwork in Bognor; data analysis and reporting; professional development training. Year 3: Deliberative engagement; stakeholder engagement; write up and dissemination. Anticipated impact and dissemination The research outputs will be shared with local/national stakeholders to increase understanding of how people living in coastal communities experience their social circumstances and their impact on health. Actions developed by local communities to reduce health inequalities will inform local government policy and practice. Learning from the ethnographic and deliberative research methods will be disseminated to inform future research.

Award_Title: CONCOMITANT PRIMARY PREVENTION OF MULTIPLE CHRONIC DISEASES THROUGH DATA-DRIVEN APPROACHES MOBILISING POPULATION-WIDE LONGITUDINAL HEALTH RECORDS
Abstract: WHAT IS THE CLINICAL PROBLEM? Chronic diseases are conditions that last a long time - possibly for a person's whole lifetime. These diseases, which range from diabetes and heart disease through to dementia and cancer, are the leading cause of disability and death worldwide. Around 25% of people in England have been diagnosed with at least one chronic disease, and numbers are rising with our ageing population. Often, people have more than one chronic disease. This is because some of the causes for chronic diseases such as smoking and blood pressure are the same across different diseases. It is far better for people and cheaper for health services to prevent chronic diseases than to treat patients after they become unwell. Knowing about the future risk of chronic disease can help people and health professionals caring for them make decisions about how risk can best be managed through life-style changes and/or medication. At present, a wide array of 'risk prediction tools' are used to predict a persons' future risk of single chronic diseases based on particular risk factors (eg, age, blood pressure) measured at a single point in time. Two opportunities are being missed. First, because these tools target single diseases, the opportunity to identify people who are at risk of multiple chronic diseases is being missed. Second, decisions based on measures at a single time point do not take into account important fluctuations and changes in risk over time. There is an urgent need to combine risk prediction tools and decision making for multiple chronic diseases together, and to extend these tools for monitoring of risk over a patients' lifetime. Using the tools in combination with available electronic health records may support: general practices to prioritise chronic disease risk assessments for people at greatest need; patient and clinician shared-decision making; people to self-monitor their chronic disease risk and their risk factors over time. This could lead to better patient engagement and health for patients and more effective and efficient health services. WHAT ARE THE AIMS OF THIS RESEARCH? The overarching goal of this research is to enhance the prevention of multiple chronic diseases. To achieve this, I aim to: A. develop and evaluate risk prediction tools that monitor a person's risk of multiple chronic diseases over time; B. translate the risk prediction tools into primary prevention strategies to reduce risks of multiple chronic diseases. HOW WILL I DO THE RESEARCH? Computer-learning models will be used with newly-available anonymised electronic health records from 56 million people in England, made accessible for trusted research through NHS Digital and the British Heart Foundation Data Science Centre, and genetic resources. To ensure the risk prediction tools will be suitable for everyone, it will be important to account for: differences in risk factors and chronic disease occurrences across different local and regional areas in England different ways people access health care changes in risk factors and chronic diseases over time I will evaluate the use of the new risk prediction tools in comparison to current clinical practice through simulation models and randomised controlled trials. HOW WILL THIS IMPACT SOCIETY? Adopting optimal strategies for the risk assessment and risk management of chronic diseases will be more cost-effective for health services and also lead to fewer chronic diseases and healthier lives. This aligns with the NHS ambition to 'help prevent over 150,000 heart attacks, strokes and dementia cases over the next 10 years'.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Award_Title: PRecision biomArker Guided MAnagement of TuberculosIs Contacts (PRAGMATIC)
Abstract: Background: There are over 4,000 tuberculosis (TB) cases in England annually. Scale-up of preventative TB treatment represents a cornerstone of the NHS TB action plan. Current tests for latent TB infection (including interferon-gamma release assays; IGRAs) have limited positive predictive value for future TB disease. Hence, we need to treat between 20-100 people with preventative antibiotics to prevent one incident TB case. This results in unnecessary antibiotic exposure and limits treatment uptake, undermining TB prevention efforts. Emerging 'incipient' TB tests aim to detect early stages in the pathogenesis of disease, before symptoms commence. Blood RNA biomarkers can detect incipient TB with high accuracy over a six-month interval and may facilitate more precise targeting of preventative antibiotics towards people at highest risk of progression to symptomatic disease. Aim: To enable more precise use of preventative antimicrobials for TB among contacts and migrants from high transmission countries, by developing the platform for a randomised-controlled trial (RCT) of incipient TB biomarker-stratified treatment. Objectives: To define the optimal incipient TB testing approach. To refine the trial outcome by quantifying the trade-off between incident TB risk and preventative treatment acceptance. To conduct a feasibility RCT. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of the intervention in a preliminary health economic analysis. Methods: (a) A systematic review of the diagnostic accuracy of candidate incipient TB tests. (b) A nested case-control study in biobanked samples from a cohort of 4,400 TB contacts. I will assess the diagnostic accuracy of seven RNA biomarkers, measured using the Nanostring platform, for incipient TB stratified by interval from testing to disease. I will compare the performance of a near-patient cartridge-based RNA assay to the Nanostring reference standard. A discrete choice experiment among patients (n=200) and healthcare workers (n=200) to assess the association between future TB risk and acceptance (or recommendation) of preventative treatment. These results will be used to inform a proposed weighted composite 'net harm' trial outcome incorporating incident TB risk and preventative treatment exposure. A feasibility RCT of IGRA-positive recent TB contacts or migrants (n=100) who do not have baseline evidence of TB. I will randomise to standard care (offering preventative treatment to all) or the intervention arm (using six-monthly incipient TB testing to guide preventative treatment), with 12 months' follow-up for all. Outcomes will include: feasibility of trial recruitment; feasibility and acceptability of the intervention; and the proportion commencing preventative treatment in each arm. Adaptation of an existing health economic dynamic-transmission model by incorporating a decision-tree reflecting the intervention, parameterised from Objectives 1-3. This will inform a preliminary analysis of intervention cost-effectiveness and can subsequently be updated following a definitive trial. Impact: This work will enable refinement of the trial design and will inform a decision on whether to proceed to a definitive trial. The intervention has the potential to transform TB prevention by reducing the burden of unnecessary preventative antibiotics. I will develop skills in clinical trials, discrete choice experiments, health economics and leadership, to continue my path towards being a research leader in respiratory infection.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: To develop an implementation package for general practice to promote evidence-based support for physical activity targeting people with cardio-metabolic risk factors (INSTEP; ImplemeNt phySical acTivity for gEneral Practice)
Abstract: Research question How feasible is an implementation package to support the uptake of physical activity interventions in general practice? Background Regular physical activity has major health and social benefits. However, physical inactivity is common and unequally distributed across society. General practice has a central role in promoting physical activity, especially given high levels of contact and longitudinal relationships with patients. There is growing evidence on the effectiveness of physical activity interventions delivered in general practice. Yet these are generally under-delivered and inconsistently matched to patient needs. Strategies to promote effective and equitable implementation of physical activity interventions need to recognise the constraints and competing priorities of general practice and align with existing roles, routines and resources. Identifying and supporting people with cardiometabolic risk factors (e.g. hypertension, pre-diabetes) is an established activity in general practice. My proposal is concerned with whether general practice can be enabled to provide effective physical activity interventions targeting people with cardiometabolic risk factors. Aim and objectives To develop an implementation package for general practice to promote evidence-based support for physical activity targeting people with cardiometabolic risk factors (INSTEP; ImplemeNt phySical acTivity for gEneral Practice). Objectives: To synthesise current evidence on physical activity support for patients in general practice, including barriers to and enablers of implementation. To develop and refine a multifaceted implementation package (INSTEP) for general practice to promote evidence-based physical activity support for people with cardiometabolic risk factors. To evaluate the adoption of and fidelity to the INSTEP implementation package, including acceptability for healthcare professionals and patients. My overall approach will be consistent with the updated MRC framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions. My planned outcome is an implementation package ready for further evaluation in a feasibility and then definitive randomised trial in general practice. Methods Objective 1 (Months 1-6): Umbrella review to identify and synthesize evidence on (i) effective physical activity interventions that general practice can feasibly offer to patients, (ii) professional and organisational behaviours that an implementation package needs to target and (iii) key determinants of these behaviours. Objective 2 (Months 7-24): Co-design workshops with two stakeholder panels comprising general practice staff and patients respectively from a range of socioeconomic and ethnic backgrounds. Informed by Objective 1, the panels will review available physical activity interventions and implementation interventions according to their affordability, practicability, effectiveness, acceptability, safety and equity in general practice. They will map determinants of professional and organisational behaviours and relevant behaviour change techniques onto implementation interventions to produce a coherent prototype implementation package (INSTEP) suitable for feasibility testing. Objective 3 (Months 25-54): Non-randomised, single arm feasibility study of the implementation of INSTEP in four general practices serving diverse populations, including a process evaluation with nested qualitative interview study. Anticipated impact and dissemination As well as delivering an implementation package to take forward to a feasibility trial, I will generate practical suggestions on how to make effective physical activity support more routine in general practice. I will share these through my policy networks and academic collaborations.
