Award_Title: Improving outcomes in Hypertension and Pregnancy through self-monitoring of blood pressure
Abstract: OVERALL BACKGROUND: high blood pressure is a key risk factor for cardiovascular disease, the greatest cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide and a major marker of the development of pre-eclampsia in pregnancy. Currently the detection and treatment of hypertension is sub-optimal, and pre-eclampsia is a leading cause of mortality in pregnancy. Collaborating with patients in the monitoring of blood pressure has the potential to revolutionise the management of both hypertension and pregnancy. Over the last decade I have undertaken a series of studies developing the evidence base for self-monitoring of blood pressure. The proposed programme aims to build on this through my own research teams, collaborating with others and developing colleagues. SUMMARY: over the five years of the proposed Professorship, I will complete a series of programmes of work, so far funded by over £3m of (largely NIHR) grants, aiming to prevent adverse outcomes by improving the management of raised blood pressure in the areas of essential hypertension and pregnancy. The core research elements will comprise an NIHR self-monitoring programme grant and a new stream of work around self-monitoring of blood pressure in pregnancy (NIHR funded pilot). These are supplemented by a series of new collaborations building on my research including development of a web based self-management intervention, implementation of self-monitoring via a CLAHRC collaboration and an individual patient data meta-analysis. A fourth work stream will include the support and development of both specialist colleagues translating their work in primary care (MRC and RfPB funded) plus development of academic primary care through mentorship of juniors, supervision of PhDs and involvement of students. The key financial requests over and above my salary are for a post doc research fellow and two PhD studentships to both assist in the delivery of and provide added value to this significant programme of work. PROGRAMME 1: OPTIMISING THE DIAGNOSIS AND MANAGEMENT OF HYPERTENSION IN PRIMARY CARE THROUGH SELF-MONITORING. Funded NIHR Programme Grant 2012-17, CI McManus, £2m. Aims and objectives: to assess the role of self-monitoring in screening for hypertension, cardiovascular risk assessment and achieving BP targets, arranged across three work streams and twelve research questions. Background: Hypertension is a key risk factor for cardiovascular disease but primary care currently underperforms in its detection and management: around 13% of adults in the UK appear on hypertension registers but only half are controlled to currently accepted targets and at least as many again are undetected. Self-monitoring of hypertension is under-utilised by primary care despite around a third of patients practicing it, due to both a modest evidence base and a lack of implementation. It has the potential to increase detection of hypertension and improve BP control. Collaboration: the programme is a collaboration of NHS Oxfordshire with Primary Care Departments from Oxford, Birmingham and Cambridge. The co-investigators form a multidisciplinary team including social scientists, clinical academics, patients, administrators and a health service manager. Research Plans: this programme of work will provide the evidence to underpin the integration of self-monitoring of blood pressure (BP) into daily practice in primary care. The major areas of study are set out in 3 work streams (WS): WS1.1 Self-monitoring in the screening of hypertension: currently, although around 10% of the general population have self-monitored their own blood pressure there are very few data evaluating the utility of self-screening in the diagnosis of hypertension. This work stream comprises a systematic review of self- screening in hypertension, a survey of the provision of self-screening (eg in pharmacies and GP practice waiting rooms) with adjunct qualitative work to judge current and future practice. This will be followed by the development of a self-screening intervention and pilot testing of that intervention. At the end of WS1.1 we will be in the position to apply for substantive funding for a trial of self-screening in the diagnosis of hypertension or alternatively to show that such a strategy is not feasible. WS1.2 Statistical and health economic modelling: Our group has a wide range of data from previous blood pressure monitoring projects (TASMINH, TASMINH2 and soon TASMIN-SR, BP Eth and HyBET). These will be utilised along with our expertise in both statistical and health economic modelling to re-calibrate both the Framingham and QRISK cardiovascular (CV) risk equations to use self-monitored blood pressure. The next phase will test this re-calibration in practice (using patients recruited in WS1.1) to assess both its effectiveness and cost effectiveness. Statistical modelling using clinic measured blood pressure to predict future BP forms the last part of this WS - preliminary work from the TASMINH2 study suggests that repeated measurement in a clinic setting may allow prediction of self-monitored blood pressures and may capture at least some of the variability seen between visits. One potential application of this may be the ability to detect masked and white coat hypertension on the basis of clinic BP readings. WS1.3 Self-monitoring in the management of hypertension: this work stream is built around an RCT of the management of hypertension in primary care using self-monitored blood pressure. The trial is in two stages with the main outcome being a comparison of General Practitioners adjusting antihypertensive medication using self-monitoring with adjustment using usual (clinic) measurements in terms of achieved blood pressure. There is a second comparison within the self-monitoring group of telemonitoring compared to self-monitoring without telemonitoring aiming to assess whether the additional cost of telemonitoring brings benefit over and above a simpler system. We have been fortunate to gain significant co-funding from our industrial partners Omron of around £100k. The trial is accompanied by a systematic review to ascertain the most appropriate protocol to use for self-management (in collaboration with colleagues from the National Clinical Guideline Centre). A calibration study will assess whether home monitoring equipment currently in use by patients is sufficiently accurate to be used in both the trial and dailypractice. Health economic and qualitative strands complete the work stream providing data on both cost effectiveness and acceptability of the intervention. I lead this programme of work supported by a programme manager and work stream leads. The first studentship (year 1) will work supporting this programme (WS 1.3) and developing a DPhil proposal in parallel. PROGRAMME 2: SELF_MONITORING IN THE DIAGNOSIS OF PRE-ECLAMPSIA. Developmental. Pilot work leading to Programme grant bid in years 2-3 of Professorship(Funded by NSPCR, £237k). CI McManus Aim: This project aims to undertake the preliminary investigation needed to develop a self-monitoring intervention in pregnancy with the aim of applying for substantive funding to trial the intervention on the basis of these results. Background: Raised blood pressure affects 10% of pregnancies worldwide of which a high proportion develop pre-eclampsia. Around 15% of maternal mortality is due to pre-eclampsia so early detection and prevention is paramount. Pre-eclampsia is defined as a combination of a clinic blood pressure measurement of >140/90 mmHg with a PCR > 0.3mg/mmol. Self-monitoring of blood pressure in pregnancy could improve detection whilst empowering women and reducing screening visits but needs to take into account normal changes occurring through the trimesters and be integrated in standard care. To our knowledge, three small scale studies have suggested that self-monitoring is feasible but have not been operationalised in a way conducive to implementation or testing in a trial. Collaboration: This work builds on a successful partnership between the Departments of Primary Care in Oxford and Birmingham and will develop a new collaboration including PPI representation (Saunders), expertise in Obstetric care and Midwifery and research into the diagnosis of pre-eclampsia from London, Birmingham and Oxford. Research Methods: This work stream is developmental and the aim is to gain programme grant / substantive trial funding midway through the five years of the professorship. We will develop pilot work comprising 4 work streams: 2.1 Systematic Review: this will assess current evidence for patient experience of self-monitoring, schedules for self-monitoring of blood pressure in pregnancy and thresholds for the diagnosis of both pre-eclampsia and gestational hypertension. Standard methods for quantitative and qualitative data extraction and analysis will be used with meta-analysis where appropriate. 2.2 Pilot study: field work will be undertaken with a group of 100 women testing performance of self-monitoring in terms of number of measurements needed to provide an appropriate estimate of underlying blood pressure. This will draw upon evidence from the systematic review as well as previous work by our group outside of pregnancy. Eligible women will be at high risk of pre-eclampsia under NICE guidance as this population requires more extensive monitoring and therefore might be expected to gain the most from any new intervention. 2.3 Qualitative study: participating women and clinicians will be interviewed regarding the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention. Participants will be purposively recruited using maximum variation sampling, to ensure that we have the widest possible representation. Results will be incorporated into a forthcoming “healthtalkonline” module. 2.4 Statistical modelling: based on data from the systematic review, from our previous studies of blood pressure monitors, and from the field work, we will estimate the test performance of home blood pressure monitoring in pregnancy, and how this can be optimised; hence, we will develop a monitoring protocol for later study in a randomised trial proposal. Data from all four strands will inform a subsequent application for substantive trial/programme grant funding. At the time of writing (March 2012), we have just received confirmation of funding (£237k) for this pilot work from NSPCR. The second studentship (year 2) will work supporting the development and delivery of this programme of work. PROGRAMME 3: COLLABORATIONS IN SELF-MONITORING/MANAGEMENT. This programme comprises three collaborations which arise directly from our self-monitoring and management portfolio, namely development of a web based self-management intervention, implementation of self-monitoring under the auspices of the Manchester CLAHRC and finally a collaborative individual patient data meta-analysis. Collaboration: each element of programme 3 entails significant collaborations with national and international colleagues and will build on both my national and international reputations. WS3.1 Integrating self-management into a digital intervention: Pilot funded (NSPCR), Programme Grant Application submitted (Yardley lead, McManus Co-App) [National Collaboration] Background and Aims: The TASMINH2 study was the first major trial to show evidence for the efficacy of self-monitoring of blood pressure with self-titration of antihypertensive medications. Whilst the intervention used telemonitoring, the patient information and data collection was paper based and rather unwieldy. Developing a web-based self-management programme (delivered by PC and/or phone) is an obvious next step. This kind of digital intervention (DI) can potentially improve healthcare efficiency by automating routine aspects of patient education, monitoring and support, while improving provision through convenient, 24 hour access to detailed personalised advice, as well as linking patients and professionals. This work aims to develop and test a DI for self-management. Research Plans: A hypertension DI (pilot work funded, NSPCR, collaborators Yardley, Little, Southampton) will be further developed into a potentially cost effective intervention suitable for use in the NHS which will then be trialled. The hypertension DI allows patients and professionals to log onto a secure website to gain access to a range of tools. These include detailed instructions (with videos) for self-monitoring blood pressure (BP); the ability to send email and text message reminders to self-monitor at patient-selected times; facilitation to help patients set goals for lifestyle changes (e.g. salt restriction, weight loss); support to allow patients to enter data (BP, weight, goal achievement) and create progress charts; the provision of automated personalised feedback based on progress; and access to allow health professionals to remotely monitor patient status, goals, and progress. Initial feasibility work will compare theeffects and cost-effectiveness of different forms and levels of support for the hypertension DI and confirm acceptability and feasibility. A substantive trial will establish the cost-effectiveness of the optimal package of hypertension DI. WS3.2 Implementation of self-monitoring. Funded (CLAHRC & Lloyds Pharmacy). [National collaboration] Background and Aims: In collaboration with Dr Pippa Tyrrell and colleagues in the Manchester CLAHRC, this work stream comprises the implementation of self-monitoring of blood pressure in groups of practices in Wigan and Bury. This directly develops and implements work undertaken by myself. The aim is to engage with practices and to implement self-monitoring of blood pressure using validated monitors (provided via a collaboration with Lloyds pharmacy facilitated by myself) for patients with poorly controlled blood pressure. Research Plans: Unlike the rest of the projects in the proposed programme, this WS is entirely about implementation using PDSA (Plan, Do, Study, Act) cycles to test identified models of care using self-monitoring at an individual practice level, learn from each test and refine the model of care in an iterative process. My role on this is to provide expert advice to the steering group, to provide training to practices and their staff and to assist Dr Tyrell in overseeing the project. This is a new paradigm for me and experience gained from WS3.2 will be utilised in my work to help local development of hypertension monitoring in Oxfordshire (see NHS-HEI Partnership below). WS3.3 Individual patient data meta-analysis for self-monitoring. Funded (NIHR InPractice Fellowship Qamar £107k plus NSPCR project funding £50k (CI)) [International Collaboration] Aim: To undertake an IPD of self-monitoring of BP in order to better understand the effects of self-monitoring. Research Plans: We will undertake an individual patient data analysis including randomised trials that have compared self-monitoring of hypertension(with or without other co-interventions) with a control group. Published and unpublished randomised controlled trials will be eligible where self-monitoring of blood pressure formed part of the intervention. Eligible trials will be identified from an allied Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis undertaken by Qamar (NIHR InPractice fellowship 4.4 below) under my supervision and in collaboration with colleagues from Oxford, Birmingham, Cambridge and Eire. There will be no language restrictions. Standard methods will be employed for data extraction and assessment of methodological quality. A range of data will be requested from included trialists for each trial that meets the inclusion criteria. The primary outcome will be mean difference in systolic and diastolic blood pressure; secondary outcomes will include alternative measures of blood pressure and exploration of causes of heterogeneity including cardiovascular risk profiles of participants, age, sex, persistence with monitoring, measures of health status and anxiety/depression. Authors in the UK and Europe have already agreed to participate and will be invited to contribute to a collaborative meeting to discuss the results and plan the publication in year 1.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Evaluation of the cost-effectiveness of booklet-based self-management of dizziness in primary care, with and without expert telephone support.
Abstract: BackgroundChronic dizziness is a very common condition, affecting 1 in 10 working age adults and 1 in 5 older people. Dizziness can lead to reduced quality of life, anxiety and emotional distress, loss of fitness, unsteadiness and vulnerability to falling. Most dizzy patients are managed in primary care by reassurance and medication to suppress symptoms. LY has carried out trials showing that chronic dizziness can be treated effectively using a self-help booklet to teach patients vestibular rehabilitation exercises that promote neurological adaptation and skill and confidence in balance. However, brief support from a trained nurse was provided in these trials, and this model of managing dizzy patients has not been taken up due to a lack of skills and resources in primary care.AimsTo evaluate the cost-effectiveness of two new models of delivery of vestibular rehabilitation. Our primary aim is to test the hypothesis that provision of the self-help booklet teaching vestibular rehabilitation exercises, with up to one hour of remote telephone support from an expert vestibular therapist, will be more effective than routine care in reducing symptoms (and therefore also disability and handicap) in dizzy patients in primary care. We will also explore the extent to which patients may benefit from provision of the self-help booklet without support. We will determine whether these models of delivery are less costly than routine care of dizzy patients, as they should reduce the number of patients seeking referral to secondary care for unnecessary assessments.Plan of InvestigationIn a single blind two-centre pragmatic controlled trial, we will randomise 330 patients from 30 practices to: a) self-treatment booklet with expert telephone support; b) self-treatment booklet alone; c) routine medical care. Symptoms, disability and handicap will be assessed by validated questionnaires administered by post at baseline, immediately post-treatment (3 months), and at one year follow-up. The study is powered to test our primary hypothesis, that the self-help booklet with telephone support will be more effective than routine care. We will also explore the effectiveness of the booklet alone, and calculate the costs of treatment in each arm, including: costs of the interventions; primary care consultations and treatment; secondary care consultations, assessment and treatment.Potential ImpactIf our study indicates that booklet-based self-management of dizziness is cost-effective, then it can be easily rolled out to relieve the symptoms of the many patients in primary care who currently have chronic, untreated, disabling dizziness. The proposed model of care would further the aims of the NHS Improvement Plan by providing a service based on supported self-management. Demonstration of a cost-effective model for managing dizziness in primary care also has the potential to reduce the cost to the NHS of treating dizziness by reducing demand for referral to secondary care for specialist assessment and treatment. If patients can be treated promptly in primary care they may be less likely to develop psychological and physical sequelae that cause handicap and require treatment.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Implementation of an end of life care pathway in intensive therapy units based in an inner London teaching hospital: does it make a difference?
Abstract: BackgroundDespite high levels of medical intervention, many patients admitted to intensive therapy units (ITU) die. The delivery of high quality end of life care in this setting is therefore fundamental to clinical practice. Research conducted in this area of care is largely USA-based. Evidence suggests that distressing symptoms are often poorly managed and their families do not receive adequate information. Staff may experience stress and poor morale which can result in high sickness and poor retention of staff. Little is known about the situation in UK, particularly in urban settings that are culturally diverse. Care pathways offer a possible means to improve end of life care in the ITU setting but they have not been fully explored, and therefore require further evaluation and possible adaptation. AimsAim: To evaluate and refine an end of life care pathway for use in ITU, based on research into the experience of families and patients, and also the views of ITU and palliative care staff.Objectives 1. To explore and describe the experience of care for families, and where possible patients, in ITU.2. To explore in what ways social factors influence attitudes to and experience of care provided in ITU.3. To explore the views of ITU professionals and of bereaved and surviving families on the content of relevant care pathways for use in ITU. 4. To implement a refined end of life care pathway in two ITUs and observe its effect on the process and quality of care.5. To make recommendations regarding means to improve end of life care and the implementation of care pathways in the future Plan of InvestigationDesign: mixed method phase I and II study (Medical Research Council (MRC) framework for complex interventions) of the development and implementation of a care pathway. Setting: 2 ITUs in south London.Methods: The study has 2 phases:Phase I includes qualitative non-participant observation of ITU activity, qualitative interviews with families, if possible patients, focus groups with professionals to explore experience and refine the current version of an existing pathway (the Liverpool Care Pathway, LCP).In phase 2 we implement the pathway, modified as necessary from the results of phase 1, observe the process of implementation, effects on practice, repeat qualitative interviews and focus groups and survey a wider group.Users are involved in all stages from planning to dissemination. Potential ImpactOur study will gain a better understanding of how families and patients experience end of life care in ITU, and how care may be improved through the use of defined care pathways. The information will immediately be useful to improve care locally, and as dissemination proceeds, nationally and internationally. The results will provide:• A care pathway developed and tested in ITU to improve end of life care• Formal scrutiny of the process of implementing this pathway, to provide guidance on future implementation• An understanding of how to target care and communication in different cultural contexts • Better quality end of life care for patients • Better support for carers, and fewer problems during bereavement • Better supported staff and improved morale

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Medicines reconciliation at the interface: A pilot randomised controlled trial to determine the costs and effects of a pharmacy provided service
Abstract: BackgroundMedicines reconciliation (MR) is the process of ensuring that patients receive the correct medicines when transferring between care settings. Medication errors on admission to hospital have been demonstrated to increase patient morbidity, patient mortality and length of stay. Based on a single randomised controlled trial with errors as the primary outcome measure, NICE/NPSA guidance now recommends that pharmacists should be involved in MR for all hospital admissions. This target is currently being met for 50% of admissions across the Eastern region. The cost and effects associated with expanding this pharmacy service to all admissions are currently unknown. This project is designed to determine the best approach to performing a full scale trial on an expanded pharmacist led MR service.AimsTo determine the design of a randomised controlled trial of an extended pharmacy medicines reconciliation (MR) service in different medical clinical specialities. To estimate the effect of such a service on length of stay (LOS) (primary outcome measure), medication errors, patients’ health-related quality of life, health resource utilisation, post discharge medication errors and re-hospitalisation rate (secondary outcome measures)To determine recruitment and retention ratesTo describe an appropriate approach to recruitmentTo determine which patients potentially receive most benefit from the interventionTo develop an evidence based standard operating procedure for providing an MR servicePlan of InvestigationPhase 1 Trial development (6 months)• Literature search• Health care professional and patient focus groups to agree service and study design• Pilot wards identified via focus groups• Ethical approval sought & obtainedPhase 2 Pilot (9 months)• 200 patients recruited and randomised to intervention or control• Medicines information collected for all patients• Intervention patients receive medicines reconciliation service from pharmacist3 months post discharge Comparison between intervention and control of:• Health-related quality of life & health services resource use• Length of stay• Medication errors Phase 3 Dissemination (6 months)• Health care professional and patient focus groups• Paper preparation & disseminationPotential ImpactThe 50% of patients who currently do not receive MR from a pharmacist on admission are at an increased risk of medication error. The results of this pilot will provide some insight into the value of and need for expanding MR to all hospital admissions. It is necessary to determine the costs and effects of such a service to inform decision making regarding resource allocation.This study will describe how such a service should best be delivered, determine recruitment and retention rates and estimate effect size to enable a larger study to be appropriately powered and designed. The development of an evidence based standard operating procedure will also be useful for dissemination to other hospitals.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The effect of a longer period of exercise in people with Parkinson's disease
Abstract: BackgroundParticipation in exercise is beneficial for health and wellbeing, but the effect over a longer period of time in people with Parkinson’s disease (PD) has not been established. People with PD currently only receive short-term support for exercise therapy interventions funded from NHS services; it is therefore unsurprising that people with PD are observed to have low levels of physical activity that decrease over time. We have evaluated the feasibility of safely supporting exercise in the community for people with long-term neurological conditions. This study sets out to determine the effect of exercise performe over a longer period of time, delivered using community facilities supported from current NHS PD services, on motor and non motor symptoms, health and wellbeing in people with PD.?AimsUsing mixed methodology we will explore the effect of exercise delivered over a longer period of time (six months) in people with PD. We will examine the views of people participating in the programme.Specifically we will:1) Use a randomised controlled trial with one intervention arm and a active comparator control group and blinded assessments to determine the effect of exercise on motor and non motor symptoms, fitness, health and wellbeing in people with PD. 2) Use semi-structured interview techniques to explore participants’ views of the service. We will explore the fidelity of the intervention and determine effect and sample size calculations. The results will be used to design a definitive Phase III Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT).Plan of InvestigationParticipants: Adults with Parkinson’s disease (PD) who are able to walk 100m.Design: Mixed methodology including: a single blind randomised controlled trial with one intervention arm and an active comparator control group with blinded assessments and process monitoring/evaluation using semi-structured interview techniques. Setting: The community of Oxfordshire and ReadingIntervention: A six month community exercise programme delivered by a fitness professional with physiotherapy support. An active comparator control group will perform a hand writing programme.Measures: We will assess at study entry and then at three, six and twelve months.Outcome: We will determine the effect of the exercise programme on motor and non motor PD symptoms, fitness, health and wellbeing.Potential ImpactParkinson's Disease (PD) is one of the commonest neurological conditions to affect older persons. The overall prevalence in the general population is 160 per 100,000 with an annual incidence of 13 per 100,000. It is a frequent cause of falls, fractures, and hospital admission and a costly disease especially in the later stages. Short exercise interventions benefit people with PD. Exercise over a longer period of time has been suggested to improve mobility, health and wellbeing, slow the impact of the disease and thus potentially reduce health care costs in people with PD although this has not been examined. We will provide an evaluation of longer-term exercise supported from current PD services delivered in the community that may be applicable for other neurological conditions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Discharge planning for the homeless, examining The London Pathway. Does a GP led discharge team reduce the in-patient burden and improve quality of care?
Abstract: BackgroundHomeless people are often admitted to hospital and their discharge back to the community may be problematic leading to prolonged hospital stays and/or inappropriate early discharge with a high rate of readmission. The costs of managing homeless people in hospital are very high with above average treatment costs, increased lengths of stay and above average re-admission rates. Pioneering work at University College has developed The London Pathway (a nurse for the homeless combines with a general practitioner to run a homeless discharge planning service). Early work suggests that this may reduce duration of hospital stay and improve care. We will now complete a properly powered examination of this model in a different setting to determine whether this approach can be generally applied.AimsWe will determine whether the London Model of general practitioner led intervention in the discharge planning of homeless people improves the quality of care and reduces health care costs. Specifically we will determine the costs of interventions to improve discharge planning for homeless people and we will examine their benefits in terms of changes to in-patient duration of stay, changes to re-admission rates and improvements in quality of life and patient satisfaction. The aim of this research is to determine whether this novel intervention can be applied in disparate centres and to provide the data necessary for wide spread recommendations regarding the implementation of this approach.Plan of InvestigationWe will examine The London Model of in-patient care for homeless people to determine whether this intervention can be broadly applied. We will study the management of homeless people at The Royal London Hospital over a 12 month period to determine average lengths of stay, readmission rates, mortality, quality of life after discharge and patient satisfaction. We will then introduce our intervention for 12 months. The intervention, ‘The London Model’ will involve a nurse review of all homeless people on admission in association with a local general practitioner with an interest in managing homeless people. The local general practitioner will conduct discharge planning ward rounds and intervene as appropriate. We will examine outcomes with and without the intervention and determine the costPotential ImpactEvaluation of a pilot of this intervention at University College Hospital has shown improved care for patients with more appropriate durations of stay and improved discharge planning and coordination, while producing net savings for the NHS community. Confirmation of these findings and learning from application of the model in another hospital has the potential to drive commissioning and provision of this service at other London hospitals and in major cities across the country. Team working across the primary care/ secondary care barrier for patients with complex needs is equally applicable in a number of clinical settings and has the potential for even broader impact.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: In a general hospital are older people with cognitive impairment managed better in a specialist unit?
Abstract: BackgroundCognitive impairment among older patients on acute hospital wards in the UK is common: we have found a prevalence of 30%. Yet there are concerns that the hospital care of older people with cognitive impairment is poor. NUH NHS Trust has developed a specialist medical and mental health unit (MMHU) aimed at improving care for these patients. The MMHU has been designed to deliver what is current best practice: there has been further staff training, mental health nurses have joined the ward team, working practices with patients and their families have been adapted for their particular needs. Patient outcomes will be evaluated in 2010-2012 by a randomised controlled trial comparing the MMHU to standard care. A comparison of the quality of care on the MMHU to standard care is needed.AimsThe overall aim of this study is to improve the care of people with cognitive impairment in hospital. The objectives of this study will enable us to identify realistic areas in which staff can be trained to improve their care of this patient group. The objective are:1) To compare the patient participants’ experiences on the medical and mental health unit to standard care in terms of:a) mood and engagementb) time spent in active and passive behaviourc) the quality of staff interactions with patients.2) To describe how care is delivered on the MMHU compared to standard care wards.Plan of InvestigationThis study has a mixed methods design. It will take 2 years.1) Participants will be randomly sampled from an ongoing RCT comparing the MMHU to standard care. Experiences of care will be measured using Dementia Care Mapping, a structured observation tool that can produce measures of mood and engagement of participants, their activity, and the quality of staff interactions. 2) Field notes taken during Dementia Care Mapping will be analysed qualitatively to provide a description of how the MMHU differs from standard care and to identify good and poor practice.3) Recommendations for training and management intervention based on the findings will be made.Potential ImpactThis project addresses issues of huge health and economic impact: 30% of older people in hospital have cognitive impairment from dementia or delirium. Whilst it is widely recognised that their care is sub-optimal in terms of a poor experience, there is little research evidence describing the problem, or evaluating ways to improve care. Improving this position is important for many health policies, notably standards 4 (general hospital care) and 7 (mental health) of the National Service Framework for Older People, and objective 8 of the National Dementia Strategy.This study will produce findings that will be immediately implementable both locally in the Trust which provides the study setting and more widely throughout the NHS, leading to rapid improvement in the quality of experience.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The OPIS (On-line Parent Information and Support) project: Meeting mothers' and fathers' information and support needs for home-based management of childhood chronic kidney disease stages 3-5
Abstract: BackgroundChronic kidney disease stage 3-5 (CKD) affects approximately 2400 UK children (0-19 yrs, with a high prevalence among South Asians) all require skilled, home-based care by parents (supported by professionals) often involving older children to promote personal care-giving skills. Parents identify a need for continuously available on-line CKD resources to supplement professional support that may not always be accessible (eg at night). Structured resources tailored to parents' needs are highlighted by the DH as key to optimising care, yet childhood CKD related on-line resource provision is patchy focusing on news/research rather than care-giving with little evidence-base. Involving families in evaluating existing, creating and evaluating new on-line resources should help meet parents’ needsAimsWe aim to (i) explore parent, child/young person, professional views on existing forms of information/support, forms familes prefer and how these would best be delivered to parents (ii) build on findings from (i) and with parents, children/young people, professionals and the voluntary sector collaboratively develop an on-line parent information and support package (OPIS) to facilitate home-based care-giving and empower parents. We will test it with parents to obtain detailed feedback, refine it and define aims and objectives for a subsequent randomised controlled feasability study of OPIS (iii) to assess its impact on the extent to which parents perceive themselves capable of performing home-based, care. We will finalise trial components, defining a protocol for a later definitive trialPlan of InvestigationWe will (i) conduct parent/child/young person/professional focus groups to explore views on existing resources (ii) collaboratively define gaps in provision, identify desirable OPIS components, develop/test resources, define aims and objectives for a feasability study (iii) of usual support vs usual supplemented by OPIS. Eighty parents of children (0-19) with CKD in Manchester will be randomised. Primary outcomes will assess parents’ self efficacy (including sense of empowerment, management styles, ability to understand care-giving information) and assessment of resources, all measured using standardised tools at entry and 24 weeks. Parents' perceptions of OPIS will be explored through semi-structured interviews at 24 weeks, thus testing a range of outcome measures for a later national RCTPotential ImpactBy working with families and professionals to develop and evaluate on-line resources that meet parents, children's and young peoples' identified needs for parental support, we will derive detailed insight into parents’ individual care-giving contributions, experiences of using OPIS and should see improved parental self-efficacy. The research will provide the NHS with an evidence-based, on-line exemplar for parental care-giving that will inform service commissioners' planning and providers' care delivery for growing numbers of children with CKD and potentially other conditions. Significant improvements in scores for measures used would indicate potential for a national RCT, involving greater numbers and longer term follow up of OPIS use, to ensure the trial is sufficiently powered

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Homerton University Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Comparison of short and long term outcome of extremely preterm infants between two tertiary centres utilising different intervention thresholds for management of blood pressure
Abstract: Background: Blood pressure (BP) is routinely monitored in all neonatal units, but the criteria for supporting low blood pressure vary widely. There is a wide range of opinion in neonatal care as to whether blood pressure is a parameter of marked importance, or one which is peripheral to the main aims of therapy. A number of trials have examined the drugs used to support blood pressure, but there have been no studies comparing outcomes in extreme preterm neonates at different blood pressure intervention levels. International review groups have identified this as a priority for research. Aim: The aim of the study is to compare the short term clinical and two year neurodevelopmental outcome of extreme preterm infants (23-28 weeks gestation) those who received two different thresholds of intervention to support BP. Questions to be answered: Primary outcome measures: Death or parenchymal brain abnormality on cerebral ultrasound scan before discharge home. Neurodevelopmental outcome at two years of age. Secondary outcome meaasures: Acquired gastrointestinal pathology (necrotising enterocolitis, perforation or GI surgery) Maximum serum creatinine in the first 2 weeks of life Use of inotropes and duration of their use Mean arterial blood pressure during the first three days after birth Maximum serum potassium level in the first two weeks of life Duration of neonatal care at each BAPM care level (this is the basis for charging for care and a good marker of health service costs) Methods This is a retrospective case notes review study comparing the outcomes of extreme preterm infants in two large tertiary perinatal centres in North East London (Homerton University Hospital and Royal London Hospital) based on the difference in thresholds of intervention to support blood pressure. Inclusion criteria All preterm infants (23-28 weeks gestation) admitted over 4 years from 01/01/07 to 31/12/10. Exclusion criteria Babies admitted after 12 hours of age (ex-utero transfers >12 hours) Babies with major congenital malformation Babies whose intensive care observational charts (to collect BP data) were not traceable Data collection Short term clinical outcome measures; pregnancy complications, condition of the baby at birth, demographics, blood pressure level and management for first 72 hours of life, complications of gastrointestinal tract (e.g. Nectrotising enterocolitits), brain ultrasound scan findings, death or discharge from the neonatal unit and data concerning British Association of Perinatal Medicine (BAPM) levels of care will be collected. Longterm neurodevelopmental outcome; neuromotor function (mobility and hand function), neurology (seizures, presence of shunt), developmental delay, neurosensory impairment (vision, hearing), communication (speech, understanding language), presence and type of cerebral palsy as well as information on respiratory, renal, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal health will be collected. Statistical Analysis Analysis will compare outcomes for the babies treated in the two hospitals according to the different blood pressure management plans. Adjustments will be made for all possible differences in confounders between these two hospitals. The association of the babies blood pressure with outcomes will be examined in order to provide evidence that it is the difference in blood pressure management between the two hospitals rather than other unspecified treatments that are affecting the outcomes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Home or hospital for people with dementia and one or more other multimorbidities: what is the potential to reduce avoidable emergency admissions?
Abstract: Older people with multimorbidities frequently access 999 ambulance services. In cases where a patient s multimorbidities include dementia, the risk of ambulance use, A&E attendance and hospital admission are all increased, even when a condition is treatable in the community. This is particularly important as patients with dementia tend to do poorly in the acute hospital setting and hospital admission can result in adverse outcomes. This study will provide an evidence-based understanding of how older people living with dementia and other multimorbidities are using emergency ambulance services to try to meet their needs. It will also provide evidence of how paramedics make decisions about taking this group of patients to hospital, and what resources would allow them to make more person-focused decisions to enable optimal patient care. This is essential information to inform the formation of the new urgent and emergency care networks described in the Five Year Forward View (e.g. p22 “ambulance services empowered to make more decisions, treating patients and making referrals in a more flexible way”), and the expectation that new care models will be tested and shared. At present the use of Ambulance Services by older people with multimorbidities including dementia (OPMID) is not well understood. However, a review by Buswell et al highlights the issue of inappropriate calls where an ambulance is a last resort or “safety net”. Recent work carried out by members of the applicant team identifies significant challenges faced by paramedics; crews sometimes convey patients to A&E knowing that this course of action is undesirable. This is an area of considerable importance given existing evidence that highlights the likelihood of hospital admission and the resulting potential for adverse social and clinical outcomes for the patient. This study will explore, in three phases, the potential to reduce avoidable emergency admissions for OPMID. This will be achieved by assessing the burden that OPMID place on the ambulance service, investigating the factors influencing paramedic decisions to convey patients to hospital and exploring potential alternatives that could avoid unnecessary A&E attendances and hospital admissions. Phase 1: Retrospective data analysis Quantitative methods will be used to explore how often ambulances are called to OPMID. The issues considered will be: time and resources associated with these calls; who the call was made by; primary and secondary reasons for the 999 call; frequency with which these calls result in OPMID being conveyed to hospital. Phase 2: Observational case studies We will use a phenomenological approach to focus on understanding why OPMID are conveyed to A&E when they have an injury or illness that could be treated at home or in the community. Detailed case studies will be compiled using a combination of observation, interview and documentation analysis, to study the factors influencing the paramedic decision-making process. Phase 3: Needs Analysis We will hold three nominal groups with paramedics to investigate and prioritise the resources that would allow emergency, urgent and out of hours care to be effectively delivered to a OPMID at home or in a community setting, rather than conveyance to A&E with the resulting risk of acute hospital admission. This proposal is part of a clear research trajectory, and builds upon two strands of earlier work by the applicant team. It will answer important questions relevant to improving the care of OPMID by investigating issues specific to the ambulance service that influence the risk of these patients requiring hospital care, instead of being cared for in or close to their own home. The results will inform important downstream investigations and feed into a larger ongoing programme of work to develop and evaluate the alternatives to hospital care.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Healthy Parent Carers programme: feasibility study of a peer-led group-based intervention to improve the health and wellbeing of parent carers of disabled children
Abstract: Background Parent carers of disabled children are at increased risk of mental and physical health problems. They experience specific challenges to maintaining good health that have implications for their wellbeing and their ability to care for their children. In response to these needs, researchers and parent carers have developed the Healthy Parent Carers programme. It is a peer-led, group-based intervention that encourages actions associated with health and wellbeing. Aims This study will test the feasibility of delivering the programme in the community, and the feasibility of evaluating the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the programme in a randomised controlled trial. Plan of investigation We will establish six delivery venues in the South West and identify and train facilitators. We will recruit 96 parent carers of children with special educational needs and disabilities aged up to 25 years to participate in a study comparing ways to improve the health and wellbeing of parent carers. After documenting informed consent and completed baseline measures, we will individually randomise participants, stratified by group delivery site (i.e. 16 to 24 per site), to either take part in a group programme, which includes online materials (intervention), or to receive access to the online materials only (control). The group programme will be delivered by trained parent carers with experience facilitating group interventions. The programme content is organised into 12 modules, which can be delivered over six longer sessions or 12 shorter sessions. Groups will consist of at least eight parent carers. The written materials for the 12 modules will be provided online. Demographics, including children s ages and conditions, will be collected at baseline. Participants will complete measures of mental health, wellbeing, health-related quality of life, health behaviours, patient activation, protective factors such as resilience, social connections, and concrete support, and use of health care, social care and wider societal resources. These data will be collected before randomisation (baseline), 15 weeks after randomisation (i.e. after the intervention arm completes the group programme), and 40 weeks after randomisation. We will monitor recruitment in order to plan for a definitive trial, including the required number of settings, trial duration, and resources. We will assess adherence and dose, and audio-record group sessions to evaluate fidelity of delivery and participant engagement. We will collect participants feedback on the programme content and delivery and the acceptability of the outcome measures. We will conduct interviews with participants in both study arms and facilitators to provide insights into intervention training, delivery and experience. We will report numbers of participants recruited by site, source, and participant characteristics, and the proportion of completed assessments. Standard deviations and the correlation between baseline and follow-up scores on continuous outcomes, and estimates of the level of clustering within delivery groups in the intervention arm will be reported to inform the sample size calculation for the subsequent definitive trial. Qualitative data will be analysed thematically. Summary of potential benefits The intervention aims to improve the health and wellbeing of parent carers, who are at increased risk of psychological and physical health problems. If the programme delivery and evaluation are feasible in this study, we will design a definitive randomised controlled trial to test the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the programme and apply to the NIHR Public Health Research Programme for funding. The intervention delivery strategies are designed to be sustainable outside of research. Hence, if the programme is effective and cost-effective, it can be implemented as part of a public health stra

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Improving employment outcomes for young people with first episode psychosis
Abstract: BackgroundA priority in the treatment of a first episode of psychosis is the restoration of normal social functioning including a return to education and employment. Of the vocational interventions that have been evaluated, Individual Placement and Support (IPS) has been shown to be the most effective, with 50- 60% achieving meaningful vocational activity. However, this still leaves 40%-50% who fail to achieve good vocational outcomes. The reasons for this include loss of confidence, low self-esteem and fears that the stress of work may precipitate a relapse. IPS does not explicitly address motivational issues or try to tackle these sources of ambivalence and the question therefore arises whether a programme that combines IPS with an explicit motivational intervention would bring added benefit.Aimsa. To test an enhancement to the delivery of the IPS approach based on providing the wider clinical team, including the employment specialist, with training in motivational interviewing [1]. This is a technique which aims to equip all staff with the basic skills needed to explore and resolve motivational conflicts regarding the pursuit of vocational activity.b. To collect and analyse data on pathways back to work and education in the First Episode Psychosis (FEP) population and the influence of personal characteristics, motivational factors and structural (service and other external) variables that may facilitate or hinder these outcomes.c. If the new intervention proves effective, to provide a ‘platform’ for a larger, randomised-controlled trial evaluation.Plan of InvestigationWe will compare 12-month employment and education outcomes of 200 patients at 4 FEP clinical teams (ie. 50 patients per team). All teams will be trained to provide IPS with fidelity to research based models [2]. The staff in 2 ‘experimental’ teams will be trained and supported in motivational interviewing (MI) to increase the uptake and success of the IPS provided by Employment Specialists located within the clinical teams. Staff in 2 ‘comparison’ teams will provide only IPS. Training and support in the motivational intervention will be provided by internationally recognised experts and will follow established standards and practice monitoring.Potential ImpactThe intervention has the potential of increasing the numbers of young people who successfully return and remain in work or education. The intervention is developed from two existing ‘technologies’ that are increasingly available in services but which have not previously been combined in the way we propose. The benefits of the research for patients is the enhanced achievement of key learning and/or employment outcomes. In terms of clinical practice, the study aims to contribute to the development of more effective psychosocial interventions and improved patient experience in outcome areas that are central to the government’s social inclusion agenda. This is a key area of current policy.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: How can we improve mental health care of mentally ill mothers in prison and the outcomes for them and their children?
Abstract: BackgroundMental disorder in mothers of infants, particularly if untreated, is associated with very poor outcomes for the mothers health and the childs development in the short and long term. Outcomes are worse in children who also face social disadvantage. Mothers in prison have some of the highest rates of mental illness, mostly unrecognised and untreated, and greatest levels of social disadvantage of any groups in our society. Their healthcare is the responsibility of the NHS, but little is known about the outcomes for them and their children, their service needs or the best ways overcoming barriers to care.This study will investigate health and social outcomes, healthcare experiences, and barriers to care in a unique cohort of women and children recruited whilst in prison 18-40 months ago.AimsTo document:1.The mental health and social outcomes of imprisoned mothers, and the health, social and developmental outcomes of their infants.2.The mental health and social needs of these women and infants during and after imprisonment.3.The extent to which their treatment needs were identified by NHS prison health services, and after their release by local NHS health services.4.The women’s experiences and perceptions of health and social care provision for them and their children in prison and following release.5.Their perceptions of barriers to care and how these might have been overcome by NHS services. 6.A comparison of these findings between mothers who a) were in prison mother and baby units (MBUs) with their infants and b) were separated from their infants whilst in prisonPlan of Investigation134 of 165 mothers recruited in prison 2-4 years ago agreed to be contacted for a follow up, giving us extensive contact information. With their informed consent, researchers will collect data about the mental health and circumstances of these mothers and the development, health and circumstances of the children using semi-structured interviews and reviews of health records. Qualitative interviews will be carried out with a subsample of women who were mentally ill in prison, enquiring about their experiences of the health care provided both in prison and post-release, the barriers to care and the possible solutions to these . This will take place in either the participant’s own homes, or a similar location and in prison if the women have not been released or have returned to prison.Potential ImpactThis study will provide currently unavailable information on the mental health outcomes, care needs and perceived barriers to care in imprisoned mothers of young children, during and after their sentences, and the outcomes for their children. The impact of care on mother and baby units (MBUs) will be examined.The findings will inform strategies to reduce barriers to NHS prison mental health care and improve access to appropriate services for a group with particularly high levels of disorders, which are known to have poor long term outcomes if untreated.In addition to improving acceptability, appropriateness and accessibility of existing provision the findings may lead to the design of new direct interventions, such as specialised perinatal mental health care in prisons/ on prison MBUs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Evaluation of outcomes, costs and benefits of a community pharmacy based cardiovascular risk assessment service
Abstract: BackgroundIncreasing emphasis is being placed by the NHS on prevention of illness with a National Vascular Check service to be introduced from 2009 which will utilise community pharmacies as one of a range of providers. Little is currently known about costs and benefits of pharmacy based checks or how the service will be integrated with general practice. The proposed study will address these issues through a multi-method evaluation of an existing pharmacy based service, “Heart MOT” and will generate robust data on service outcomes, costs and benefits in relation to both public and individual health, working on the interface between community pharmacy and general practice. The study is a partnership between Birmingham PCTs, participating community pharmacies and Keele and Birmingham Universities.AimsThe evaluation aims to address the following research questions: 1. Has the Heart MOT service contributed to improved cardiovascular risk profiles for individuals found to be at moderate and high risk? 2. What is the cost of an opportunistic pharmacy-based service to identify people at moderate and high risk of cardiovascular disease and how does this compare to the benefits identified? 3. Is the Heart MOT service an acceptable choice for patients? 4. Does the Heart MOT service interface with local general practices effectively and efficiently?Plan of InvestigationThe study will be conducted in 12 pharmacies and their local GP practices in two PCTs in Birmingham using a cohort before and after design. The cohort will comprise 400 clients assessed as ‘moderate’ (10-19.9%) or ‘high risk’ (?20% or one or more individual risk factors) of cardiovascular disease using the Framingham equations. Outcome data concerning cardiovascular risk factors and risk score, prescription and life style changes and patient views will be sought from pharmacy and practice records and a survey of clients with six month follow up. The interface between community pharmacy and general practice will be investigated using interviews and focus groups with key stakeholders Documentary analysis of key public documents will be used to provide contextual data for triangulation.Potential ImpactPharmacies are potentially a valuable location for vascular checks as they are convenient and accessible for many people. Little previous evidence is available about efficacy of such pharmacy checks and none for those at the highest risk. Pilot work by our group suggests that pharmacy based vascular risk assessment reaches people (particularly men) who are not regular attenders at their general practice and also a small number who are not registered with a GP. The proposed study will provide robust evidence on the costs and consequences including stakeholder views of a pharmacy based model of cardiovascular risk assessment which will guide service development and assist decision makers involved in future commissioning.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Dentistry Responding In Domestic Violence and Abuse (DRIDVA): Feasibility Study For Cluster Randomised Trial of a Practice-Based Intervention
Abstract: Background Domestic Violence and Abuse (DVA) is a violation of human rights with short and long term damage to physical and mental health. It takes place between individuals in intimate relationships and family members, and may manifest as physical violence, emotional abuse, financial abuse, psychological abuse, and/or controlling behaviour. Although there are dental injuries resulting from domestic violence and abuse, available research shows that dentists and dental care professionals are not actively supporting their patients who present with injuries that might have resulted from DVA. The NICE domestic violence and abuse guidelines recommendation that all healthcare professionals be involved in identifying, supporting and referring to specialist advocacy services people experiencing DVA, have not been implemented in dental services, reflecting the absence of DVA training and referral pathways. Aims The overarching aim of this research is to explore the feasibility of using an evidence-based, cost-effective, and practice-level intervention in improving health and social care outcomes of adult patients with lived experience of domestic violence and abuse utilising primary care dental practices. This study has two aims, which are to: To assess the feasibility of using an adapted practice-based (Identification and Referral to Improve Safety [IRIS]) intervention to aid recognition, appropriate support, and referral of adults utilising primary care dental services presenting with injuries that might have resulted from domestic violence and abuse. To explore the feasibility of a cluster-randomised trial design to evaluate the adapted IRIS intervention in primary care dental services. There are a number of areas of uncertainty relating to achieving the aims of the study. Hence, we will collect information on the following : appropriateness and acceptability of IRIS intervention delivery within primary care dental services recruitment and retention rates, and examine reasons for non-participation and attrition document the types of dental injuries observed as resulting from domestic violence and abuse Plan of Investigation This is a cluster-randomised feasibility study, with a nested qualitative study. General Dental Practices will be the unit of analysis. It is proposed that the duration of the feasibility study will be 24 months. Over a four month period, we will hold series of workshops with key stakeholders to facilitate the development of a dentistry-specific IRIS care pathway. Following the development of the dentistry-specific IRIS care pathway, six general dental practices will be recruited through Greater Manchester Dental Professional Network and randomly allocated to trial arms to explore the feasibility of trialling the adapted IRIS pathway. Three general dental practices will be randomly allocated to the usual practice arm and three general dental practices to the intervention arm. The intervention will involve training staff in general dental practices, installing software in the electronic medical system of dental practices, and establishing a referral pathway to a designated advocate-educator from the collaborating agency (Manchester Women s Aid). A nested qualitative study will also be conducted to explore the acceptability of IRIS intervention within primary care dental practices. Data will also be collected from the electronic medical records of participating practices, referral data from the collaborating agency, and health economics data. Potential benefits to patients/NHS There are approximately 15.4 million incidents of domestic violence and abuse annually in Britain. The total annual monetary cost of DVA in England for the government, the individual (human and emotional suffering), NHS, employers and the criminal justice system is around £23 billion, with an estimated £1.7 billion cost to the NHS. Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: An exploratory mixed method study to identify working conditions and work cultures associated with psychological distress and suicidality among junior doctors working in the NHS
Abstract: Research question. What specific working conditions and contexts are associated with elevated psychological distress and suicidality among junior doctors, as well as potential protective factors. Background. There are currently 55, 000 junior doctors working in the NHS; comprising half the medical workforce. Evidence suggests junior doctors are particularly vulnerable to work-related psychological conditions such as chronic stress, anxiety, depression, or burnout. Some evidence suggests that women doctors may at increased risk of suicidality. Junior doctors face specific pressures related to their professional stage and development which may account for their increased vulnerability to work related stress and distress. No research has examined the association between working conditions/contexts and psychological distress amongst junior doctors. This study will examine and identify specific working conditions and work cultures associated with elevated psychological distress or suicidality amongst junior doctors, including doctors who have attempted suicide. Aims and objectives. Aims To identify specific working conditions and contexts associated with elevated psychological distress and suicidality among junior doctors, as well as potential protective factors and staff preferences for future interventions which could facilitate appropriate support for junior doctors in the future Objectives To identify and explore the psychological, cultural and occupational contexts and patterns associated with reduced psychological wellbeing and suicidality among junior doctors To assess whether specific demographics such as gender are associated with elevated levels of psychological distress or suicidality To explore how junior doctors experience, manage, process and seek support for work-related emotions (i.e. fear, anxiety, guilt, anger, compassion, empathy or shame) To identify potential barriers and facilitators to help-seeking amongst junior doctors who are distressed or mentally unwell and who may be at risk of suicide To identify the value and limitations of current individual, collegial and organisational support, and the care pathways for mental wellbeing currently available to support junior doctors in the workplace To inform guidance and potential improvements e.g. to inductions, handovers, supervisory roles, teamwork and peer support Methods A mixed methods study combining interpretative qualitative methods and a cross-sectional survey with junior doctors working in secondary care Timelines for delivery 16 months Anticipated impact and dissemination Practical recommendations and guidance on accessing appropriate professional support and supporting colleagues experiencing significant stress or distress at work. A better understanding of the association between junior doctors working conditions and their influence on psychological distress and suicidality. This would inform practical recommendations and guidance on how to improve junior doctors working conditions. Academic outputs to fill the knowledge gap on this topic

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Early identification and treatment of young people at high risk of recurrent mood disorders: a feasibility study
Abstract: BackgroundDepression and bipolar disorder are prevalent, recurrent life course disorders that usually begin in adolescence/early adulthood. The introduction of Early Intervention in Psychosis services (EIP) has transformed the NHS approach to schizophrenia, but there is no equivalent strategy to improve early case identification or treatment rates for recurrent mood disorders. Depression is ranked 1st and bipolar disorder 6th (above schizophrenia) in the global burden of diseases study, but fewer than 50% of younger adults with mood disorders access traditional health services and EIP have not reversed this underutilization. Before advocating new services or changes to EIP we first need to clarify our clinical understanding of early onset recurrent mood disorders and barriers to effective treatmentAimsWe will gather quantitative and qualitative data to inform core components of a future programme grant application. This study will:(a) explore the feasibility of identifying young persons at risk of recurrent depression or bipolar disorder currently accessing a range of clinical services (b) examine the utility and acceptability of a psychological intervention specifically targeted at overcoming current problems and reducing the risk of future mood episodes(c) establish stakeholder and young people panels (with input from parents) to help identify barriers to engagement, potential modifications to current services, and through feedback on study findings consider clinical innovations and research prioritiesPlan of InvestigationIn 16-25 year olds, we will:1. Retrospectively assess the number of and presentation of clinically diagnosed cases of mood disorders across a range of NHS settings over the preceeding 2 years2. Prospectively examine the feasibility and acceptibility of using self-rating tools to detect mood episodes and identify those at high risk of recurrences 3. Assess symptoms, quality of life, service use and stability of diagnosis over one year 4. Explore the uptake, acceptability and outcomes of a CBT intervention specifically for individuals at high risk of recurrent mood disorder 5. Develop young people panels to discuss their (and parental) views on acceptable service models We will also establish stakeholder and steering and monitoring groups to review study findingsPotential ImpactThe study will be an important vehicle for developing a dialogue between patients, parents, the public, primary care and NHS services so that all are involved from the outset in openly discussing possible service modifications that might enable providers to respond more effectively to young people at risk of recurrent mood disorders in adulthood.It will raise clinical awareness of the risk of recurrent mood disorders in youth and may increase case recognition and treatment. It will help establish whether screening is acceptable to services and patients; feedback about the therapy and its outcomes will inform modifications to maximize treatment acceptability to our target population.Longer term, the project could generate a more coordinated and effective NHS approach to mood disorders.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Coventry and Warwickshire Partnership NHS Trust
Award_Title: An investigation of the usefulness of Social Firms in promoting vocational recovery for people with mental health problems.
Abstract: BackgroundWork is important for mental health and the lack of it a core part of the social exclusion of the mentally ill. In the UK people with severe mental health problems have very high rates of unemployment though most say they wish to work. Although there has been much recent interest in Individual Placement and Support (IPS) this model is unlikely to be able to meet the vocational needs of all service users. Social firms are businesses which pay open market wages and employ those disadvantaged from the labour market such as people with mental health problems. Thus they represent an important opportunity for improving employment rates in this group. Social Firms in the UK are under researched and there is a lack of empirical evidence about their benefits for people with mental health problems.AimsThe overall purpose of the project is to investigate how NHS mental health services can best use Social Firms as partner agencies to promote the social inclusion of secondary mental health service users and how best this might be achieved to benefit patients. Specific aims are:1. To understand what Social Firms offer people with mental health problems and how they operate to achieve this2. To examine the degree to which people with mental health problems working in Social Firms are typical of service users seen in secondary mental health services.3. To understand from service users', social firm managers' and clinicians' perspectives the scope and effectiveness of Social Firms in offering employment opportunities to people with mental health problems.Plan of InvestigationThe investigation will have three components- A UK national questionnaire survey of Social Firm managers will be conducted in order to answer Aim 1. - To address Aim 2 we will use a cross sectional study of people with mental health problems who are Social Firm employees to investigate the severity of their mental health problems and their level of functional disability.- To answer aim 3 we will interview Social Firms employees with mental health problems, managers of Social Firms and mental health professionals to better understand from their perspectives what this model of employment can offer and how it could be developed to enhance patient benefit.Potential ImpactThis study will provide much more evidence than has previously been available about the contribution that Social Firms can make to tackling the unemployment and social exclusion faced by the severely mentally ill. Understanding what sort of employment opportunities are available, whether people with severe mental health problems and functional disability can sustain these jobs and how they are supported in doing so (with service user employee views integral to the exercise) will allow assessment of how best this model can be used to help mental health service users. This new understanding will be useful to policy makers and service planners in developing new partnerships, with the aim of raising employment rates among mental health service users above their current very low levels.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Increasing physical exercise to preserve beta cell function in adult patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM): a pilot study (ExTOD)
Abstract: BackgroundT1DM results from the destruction of insulin secreting beta cells. The symptoms of T1DM develop and the diagnosis is made when 50-75% of beta cell function has been lost. Preservation of this residual beta cell function will improve diabetes control and reduce the risk of diabetes complications and hypoglycaemia, all endpoints which patients tell us are important. There is now strong evidence from studies of healthy people and those with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) that exercise preserves beta cell function. Barriers to initiation and adherence to exercise have been partially studied in children with T1DM, and one small study has been conducted in North American adults with T1DM, but research is also urgently needed to validate these findings in adult patients with T1D in the UK.AimsOur overarching aim is to encourage newly diagnosed T1DM patients to take up and adhere to a programme of intensive exercise and explore whether this intervention preserves beta cell function. This application is a pilot study to1) identify barriers to the uptake and adherence to an intensive exercise programme which aims to encourage T1DM patients to safely increase and maintain their exercise level to at least 150mins/week.2) determine the percentage of patients with T1DM who would be willing to take part in an exercise study, and define the rates of exercise adherence and drop out3) determine the rate of exercise uptake in the non-intervention arm4) determine the rate of loss of beta cell function (effect size) to enable the power calculations for the definitive trial to be refinedPlan of InvestigationWe will follow the MRC Framework for the design and evaluation of complex interventions. Phase 1: We will assess barriers to initiation and adherence to exercise in 80 patients with T1DM, and their preferences for its form, delivery and supervision. Phase 2: 60 patients newly diagnosed patients with T1DM will be recruited from local research networks and randomised to either conventional treatment or intervention (conventional treatment and exercise). Exercise will be supervised, graded and for a minimum of 150mins/week aiming for 240mins/week for 6 months. Primary outcomes will be recruitment, adherence and loss to follow-up rates. Secondary outcome will be beta cell function.Phase 3: Definitive trial of exercise on beta cell function in T1DM - not the basis of this applicationPotential ImpactExercise will help patients with T1D through improvements in• insulin sensitivity & weight, resulting in lower insulin doses, cholesterol and blood pressure• risks of stroke and heart disease, the commonest cause of T1DM deaths in the UK • well being and mental health. Depression is common in patients with T1DM• reduction in osteoporosis, osteoarthritis and certain cancersDespite this evidence, most patients with T1DM do not undertake the minimum of 150mins per week of exercise currently recommended by the Chief Medical Officer (CMO) in the ‘At least five a week’ report’[1]. Phase 1 will explore barriers to exercise in patients with T1DM. Phase 2 will provide the data to design and power a definitive randomised control study of exercise and preservation of beta cell function.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS/ME) interventions within the Primary Care Setting: Developing resources for support and self-management in primary care.
