Abstract: BackgroundCFS/ME characterised by ? 6 months severe fatigue which impairs function, increases disability, NHS costs and unemployment, & affects 0.2-0.4% people in the UK. NICE guidelines recommend management in primary care with specialist referral when appropriate, requiring confidence in diagnosing and supporting people with CFS/ME. Qualitative work in the MRC FINE trial (ISRCTN 74156610) suggests GPs & Practice Nurses (PNs) receive little formal education/training about CFS/ME. GPs were not confident diagnosing CFS/ME. PNs & GPs feel unsupported in managing these patients, and many GPs are unsure of available resources and referral options. We will develop and evaluate resources and training to help practitioners improve their support and management of people with CFS/ME in primary care.AimsTo develop patient & practitioner resources to improve primary care management of patients with CFS/ME. Within NHS Manchester our pilot will: Develop an education and training intervention for practices; Implement CFS/ME computer-template to assist in diagnosis & management; Develop practice-based CFS/ME register; Develop culturally sensitive patient resources; Develop a clinical CFS/ME facilitator role to support patients & practices; Promote collaboration between CFS/ME service & practices to ensure consistent management; Provide a directory of community/3rd sector resources to promote ‘joined-up’ services; evaluate the intervention acceptability, qualitatively from patient & practitioner perspectives; Generate an HTA proposal for an RCT, powered to evaluate these interventions.Plan of Investigation0-6 months Develop: patient resources (book/diary, DVD); practitioner resources (educational/on-line materials); training package. Identify practices to receive training intervention. Submit Ethics application.7-16 months Implement: training package (patient/practitioner resources & skills training) for practices; service facilitator to support practices & patients, link CFS/ME service & practices & promote collaborative working.17-23 months Evaluate training: semi-structured interviews with people with CFS/ME & primary care practitioners within intervention practices; analysis of referrals to local services; estimate health service use.24-30 months: Analyse data; Refine training package; Disseminate via PCT; Write for peer-review journals & HTA bid.Potential ImpactThis training intervention should result in earlier diagnosis of CFS/ME in primary care, more confident and earlier initial management by primary care practitioners and prompt referral of patients with CFS/ME to appropriate services. When provided with a more confident diagnosis it is likely that patients will play a more active role in self-care and condition management, experience improved outcomes, reducing progression towards the more severe end of the spectrum. Training of primary care practitioners will potentially relieve some pressure on current service providers allowing a focus on more moderate – severe sufferers of CFE/ME who are currently under-served in many areas, whilst patients with milder symptoms can be supported in primary care and self-management facilitated.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Comparing hospital and telephone follow-up for women treated for endometrial cancer (ENDCAT: Endometrial Cancer Telephone follow-up trial)
Abstract: BackgroundOver 7,200 British women are diagnosed a year with endometrial cancer (1). Following treatment, patients attend regular outpatient appointments. However, evidence suggests that routine clinical review has little benefit in terms of survival or detection of recurrent disease (2). Hospital consultations are reassuring for patients but do not always provide the information people need to live well following diagnosis and treatment (3). The National Cancer Survivorship Initiative calls for new models of after care to be evaluated (4). We harness the skills and expertise of specialist nurses to meet the information needs of women treated for endometrial cancer, testing an alternative strategy that aims to provide a quality service to patients while relieving pressure on busy hospital clinics.AimsThis study aims to demonstrate that specialist nurses have the skills and expertise to meet the information needs and concerns of women treated for endometrial cancer, with no physical or psychological detriment, by carrying out a randomised controlled trial comparing traditional hospital follow-up with telephone follow-up by specialist gynaecology oncology nurses. In addition, we aim to explore patient views and experiences of receiving telephone follow-up.Plan of InvestigationThis study is a randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing two forms of service provision: standard hospital outpatient follow-up (control arm) and a telephone intervention administered by specialist gynaecology oncology nurses (intervention arm). Primary outcomes are psychological morbidity and patient satisfaction with information; secondary outcomes are quality of life, patient satisfaction with service, number of referrals, time to detection of recurrent disease and cost effectiveness (efficiency). In addition we will also conduct a qualitative study, using semi-structured interviews, to obtain more in-depth information on patients’ experiences of telephone follow-up and nurse specialist views on positive and negative aspects of delivering the telephone intervention.Potential ImpactThe impact of this study is centred on providing real patient benefit by ensuring patients have the information they need to live well after treatment for cancer within current resource limitations. We aim to provide a high quality service to women treated for endometrial cancer, being responsive to Department of Health initiatives calling for new models of care to empower patients with cancer to manage their condition (4). In 2008-2009 there were over 80,000 gynaecology oncology hospital appointments in England, compared to 10,000 in 2005-2006 (5). If this trend continues it is unlikely that outpatient departments will be able to balance limited resources against demand for services. This study is intended to reduce the burden on NHS hospital clinics without detriment to patient care.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Involving fathers in ante-natal screening for sickle cell disorders: improving informed decision making
Abstract: BackgroundFacilitating informed choice among those at risk of recessive disorders is a key NHS policy objective. In 2001, the Department of Health established the Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme. One of aims of the programme is to provide timely ante-natal sickle cell screening to all couples. If a mother is identified as a carrier, her partner should ideally be offered screening, thereby enabling the couple to make an informed choice on the future of the pregnancy. However, recent NHS trial evidence suggests fathers are tested in less than 6% of cases, when their partent is a known carrier. Little is known about why this is. Not engaging with fathers during ante-natal screening for sickle cell disorders creates local difficulties and threatens a national policy objective.AimsThe study explores fathers’ attitudes and perceptions of the ante-natal screening and identifies potential factors, which could influence uptake of testing. The aims is to: * understand prospective fathers’ attitudes to ante-natal care and screening for recessive disorders, while comparing these views to those of prospective mothers;* examine fathers’ experience and understanding of ante-natal screening for sickle cell, when their partner is a known trait carrier; * explore the role and experiences of health care professionals in engaging fathers in screening; and* disseminate information to communities, third sector organisations, health care providers, commissioners and policy makers, as a means of facilitating a more successful engagement with fathers during ante-natal screening?Plan of InvestigationThis qualitative study will begin by conducting six focus group discussions with prospective fathers and mothers, aged between 18 and 34, to explore their attitudes towards men’s involvement in ante-natal screening. We will then use in-depth, semi-structured interviews to explore thirty fathers’ experience of the ante-natal screening process, when their partner is known to be a carrier. Finally, and to locate our findings within the realities of service delivery we will talk to practitioners and commissioners. The research will provide important evidence on how to facilitate choice among fathers, which will be actively disseminated, using local and national networks, to encourage more sensitive policy and practice.Potential ImpactNHS policy aims to offer sickle cell screening to 90 per cent of mothers by ten weeks gestation. If a mother is identified as a carrier, her partner should be offered screening. The couple is then able to make an informed choice on the future of the pregnancy. However, recent trial evidence suggests fathers are rarely tested. Little is known about why this is and there is no policy or practice guidance on how to engage with fathers during ante-natal care. This research, by providing evidence that explores the attitudes and experiences of fathers, as well as the views of practitioners, will be able to ensure policy and practice is better equipped to engage with fathers, thereby supporting a national (and local) NHS policy objective, which, despite vast investment, is not been met.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Comparison of a new with standard child and family primary care service to reduce the re-occurrence of childhood dental caries (DENTALRECUR Trial)
Abstract: BackgroundDental extraction under General Anaesthetic (GA) is the most frequent reason for planned admission to hospital for children under 11. A minority suffer dental neglect and NICE recognises dental neglect as an indicator of general neglect. Hard-to-reach families may need tailored support as parents whose children develop new decay post-extraction can have low self efficacy. Researchers in US have developed successful parental interventions for childhood dental caries using Motivational Interviewing (MI). We are working with the US team, and families in Salford have informed the study design, the first in the UK, to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of a dental nurse-led intervention of extended MI on parental self efficacy of oral health-related behaviours to reduce recurrence of decay.AimsPrimary Aim:To compare the costs and benefits of a new dental nurse-led service including motivational interviewing with a standard practice-based service in reducing the re-occurrence of dental decay in children who have had a previous primary tooth extraction for dental caries.Secondary Aims:1) To compare the following outcomes of those assigned to the new and standard dental services:• parental self-efficacy to undertake dental health-related behaviours for their child; • parent-reported child behaviours of frequency of sugary foods and drinks and toothbrushing;• parental attitudes to child dental health and value of dental health-related behaviours, preventive or symptomatic use of dental services by the children.2) To investigate the fidelity of the MI interventionPlan of InvestigationParents of children Usual care: appointments sent for preventive care at dental practice New service: by dental nurse• 3 weekly visits one month post-operatively (MI to enhance parental self-efficacy and related to parental Stages of Change for oral health-related behaviours) delivered in the community in Children’s Centres• Follow up in practice with phone/text reinforcement• Fluoride varnish application• Recall 3 monthly in Year 1• Dental examinations by examiner blind to group, at baseline,1 and 2 years post-intervention• Self-efficacy and behaviour measures• Cost-benefit health economic analysis?????Potential ImpactIn 2008/9, the Department of Health (England) reported that over 87,000 children/young people had hospital admissions due to caries, over 50,000 had GAs. Children having primary teeth extracted are significantly more likely to develop further decay and have their first permanent molars extracted. A new dental service that can reduce re-occurrence of dental decay has the potential to result in: reductions in re-attendance in hospital for tooth extraction; reduction of dental pain and lost days from school; improvements in child oral health and oral sepsis; identification of children at risk of neglect. This study addresses the NHS QIPP agenda (Quality, Innovation, Productivity and Prevention) by taking an innovative approach to reduce secondary care costs and oral heath inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Self-management migraine Headache Education (SHE): a pilot trial
Abstract: BackgroundMigraine headache is common, and causes disability and distress for patients. NHS treatment has focussed on medication. Those whose symptoms continue experience decreased participation in work, family and social life. In a review of the literature from around the world we found short courses of relaxation and cognitive behavioural therapy are effective in reducing the frequency and impact of headaches. These approaches work by helping patients address the triggers for their attacks and manage their condition. No such interventions are, however, available in the U.K. We have developed a short, manualised self-management headache intervention (SHE), delivered by a nurse over 5 weeks. We plan to pilot it in the NHS context comparing SHE (plus standard medical care -SMC) to SMC alone.AimsIn line with MRC guidelines (1), a pilot study shall be conducted to address uncertainties that have been identified in the development of SHE and provide design information necessary for a future definitive trial of SHE. The objectives are to:1. Calculate recruitment, consent and follow-up rates.2. Test acceptability of randomisation to participants.3. Describe questionnaire acceptability to participants, and their views of those which represent the most important outcomes. 4. Calculate estimates of the location of the mean and variability around the mean (standard deviation) for the outcome measures. A conservative estimate using the 95% upper confidence limit will be used to inform the sample size calculation of a future RCT.5. Assess treatment fidelity of SHE.Plan of InvestigationWe plan to recruit 80 adults with migraine from Headache Clinics in Lambeth and Southwark, run by Practitioners with Special Interest in Headache. They will be fully informed and invited to participate in a randomised trial. At baseline, 5 weeks and 4 months, information will be collected on headache frequency, impact, disability, anxiety and depression, illness beliefs, health locus of control, quality of life and health service costs. We will invite participants to be interviewed after the intervention, to describe their views of it and the importance they attach to the measures in measuring outcome. Participants randomised to the comparison group will continue to receive SMC and will be offered the manual and relaxation computer disc on study completion.Potential ImpactWe will have information on measures of outcome to estimate how many participants are needed to demonstrate an important change in a particular measure or range of outcomes. We will have qualitative evidence on what participants value in terms of measures of change, and their views of a new approach to self-management education for migraine. Using this evidence we will be able to design a definitive trial. Two user groups have agreed to disseminate the results at meetings, and help us write up and publish our findings in journals targeted at policy makers, service providers and users. If SHE is effective in reducing headache frequency and distress, it will increase capacity for work for people with migraine, and employers, and reduce cost to the health and social services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: South Tyneside and Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Using Specialist Screening Practitioners (SSPs) to increase uptake of the Bowel Scope Screening Programme: a feasibility study of patient navigation within South Tyneside NHS Foundation Trust
Abstract: Background: The new Bowel Scope Screening programme (BSS) offers unprecedented potential to reduce the mortality and incidence of colorectal cancer (CRC) using once-only flexible sigmoidoscopy (FS). However, two of the key criteria against which any screening programme is measured are acceptability and cost-effectiveness, both of which are closely linked with uptake (Wilson & Jungner, 1968). Uptake of the current CRC screening programme using faecal occult blood testing (FOBt) is sub-optimal at 54% (von Wagner et al., 2011). Findings from a meta-analysis and the recent pathfinder sites suggest that uptake of BSS will be at least as low, if not considerably lower than that of FOBt (Littlejohn, Hilton, Macfarlane, & Phull, 2012; Sofianopoulu, Rubin, Richie, Patnick, & Rees, 2012), undermining the potential of the programme. Patient navigation (PN) has been used in the United States (US) and found to increase uptake of cancer screening, particularly among more socially deprived groups (Percac-Lima et al., 2009; Paskett, Harrop, & Wells, 2011; Dietrich et al., 2006; Green et al., 2013). This study will test the feasibility of a PN intervention to increase uptake of BSS in a socially deprived area in the North East of England. Aims: To assess the feasibility of a PN intervention within a UK setting and its subsequent worthiness of further investigation in a large definitive trial. Research questions: The feasibility study will investigate a) the number of people willing to share their contact details with the screening centre, b) barriers to participation in BSS, c) the impact of navigation on uptake, d) the impact of patient navigation on patient knowledge of BSS and informed choice, e) patient satisfaction, f) SSP workload and g) the cost of delivering the intervention, and any associated financial benefits for the NHS. Plan of investigation: Recruitment will occur over a 6-month period within the South Tyneside NHS Foundation Trust. Each individual invited for BSS will concurrently receive a written invitation to this study. The PN intervention will involve non-attenders (i.e. those who confirm an appointment but do not attend, and those who do not respond to the programme s invitation) receiving a phone call from an SSP who will elicit information about the reasons for non-attendance and offer educational, practical and emotional support as needed. If requested by the patient, another appointment for BSS will be arranged. BSS attendance status will be established 8 weeks after the BSS appointment and at this point every participant will receive an End of Study Questionnaire (ESQ) . Interviews with SSPs will elucidate the process of navigation and address workload implications. Potential benefits to patients and NHS: Participation in BSS reduces the chance of developing one of the most common types of cancer. The UK Flexible Sigmoidoscopy trial showed that receiving a single FS had the potential to reduce bowel cancer incidence by 33% and mortality by 43% over an 11-year period (Atkin et al, 2010); an effect that may increase with longer follow-up. The efficacy of FS screening has also been supported in a recent systematic review (Elmunzer et al., 2012). However, the cost-effectiveness of the new programme will largely depend on uptake, as demonstrated by a recent appraisal of options for CRC screening in England (Whyte et al., 2011). Increasing uptake will help reduce the impact of CRC on individuals (e.g. the implications of CRC on quality of life and personal finances) and on the NHS (by reducing the cost of treating CRC). Our expectation is that PN will be a relatively low-cost intervention and may ultimately be cost-saving to the NHS if it prevents CRC cases and thereby reduces treatment costs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Developing a tool to stratify the risk of medication harm in the elderly
Abstract: Medication-related problems (MRP) often lead to increased mortality and morbidity, involving hospitalisation, longer (and costlier) hospital stays. The prevalence of MRP, especially adverse drug reactions (ADR), in older patients (>65 years), lies between 10 and 27% 1, 2 which leads to a significant percentage of older patients requiring hospital care, when compared to other patient groups (16.6% compared to 4.1%). The findings of a recent large UK study showed that 6.5% of hospital admissions were considered to be a direct result of the medicines they were taking.3 The authors estimated the annual financial burden associated with MRP to the NHS as £466m.3 Local data, collected as part of a service review by the Department of Pharmacy, Guy s & St Thomas Hospital, indicates that 2,780 interventions were made by pharmacists across the trust, during a single week. Over 160 of these related to the 3 elderly care wards, with around 40% associated with managing or preventing medication harm.1 This data suggests that the local elderly population in London is at risk of experiencing medication-related problems. Similar data were collected at Brighton & Sussex University Hospital trust in a 7 day period from the 24 January to 30 January 2011 showed that there were 2261 interventions recorded by pharmacy staff. Interventions were classified by 2 pharmacists into 83.2% minor interventions, 11.9% moderate interventions, 4.7% major interventions and 0.13% interventions that prevented catastrophic outcomes. The most common medications causing problems were Warfarin, low molecular weight Heparin, Co-Amoxiclav, Aspirin and Gentamicin. Our study aims to build on existing published evidence and local practice to design a tool to identify elderly patients at greatest risk of experiencing a MRP. The discriminant ability of the tool to stratify the risk of patients will be compared to clinical judgment, made on a medical ward round, at the point of discharge. We hypothesise that the use of a tool to identify patients at risk of experiencing preventable medicines-related problems will better predict MRPs in elderly patients when compared to routine clinical judgment i.e. standard care. This proposal is the initial step in reducing the incidence of medication-related problems in the elderly. The design of a tool which has been demonstrated to better stratify elderly patient s risk of experiencing a MRP will have positive benefit for both patients and staff. For patients it will reduce medication related harm, potentially reduce hospital readmission as well as serving as a method for better informing patients and their carers about how to monitor their medicine more effectively. For staff such a tool would support the care pathway by providing a systematic approach to prioritizing the at risk patients at discharge. This could then be used to communicate important medication related issues to health care staff within both community and secondary care settings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Developing NHS services to meet the needs of an ageing HIV population: the service user’s perspective
Abstract: Background Mortality rates have dramatically improved as a result of increasingly effective antiretroviral treatment. Increased survival, combined with later age at diagnosis, has resulted in a disproportionate growth in the proportion of older individuals accessing care. While complications due to HIV are now rare in treated individuals, diseases not historically associated with HIV, but well recognised as complications of ageing, including cardiovascular disease, bone mineral density loss, cancer, cognitive decline, hepatic and renal dysfunction are increasingly identified and appear to be occurring more frequently and at a younger age than among HIV negative populations. The care of HIV positive individuals has historically been provided within specialist clinics. However, HIV specialists may not have the necessary experience to manage and treat non-HIV and age-related comorbidities and a different model of care may be preferable from a patient perspective. Over recent years, various models of care have evolved to detect and manage comorbidites. Although the Department of Health recommends developing services around the preferences of patients, there is little research in this area. This current project has been designed to quantify patient preferences for the future delivery of HIV healthcare. Aims of the work The overall aim of this study is to identify and quantify the preferences of service users for the future delivery of HIV services, using Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) methodology. Plan of investigation Workpackage 1 will identify which aspects of HIV healthcare services are important to service users. The findings of a systematic review of the literature will inform the discussion guide for a subsequent focus group study. Focus groups will take place in London and Brighton. A sampling strategy will ensure that representation of the groups most affected by HIV in the UK. Participants will be asked about their experiences of HIV healthcare; likes and dislikes of the way services are currently provided and how future services could be provided to meet their needs. Focus group discussions will be recorded and transcribed and data will be analysed using a framework analysis approach. Workpackage 2 will quantify patients preferences for different models of HIV healthcare using a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE). This methodology commonly used by health economists for assessing patients preferences. The data from the systematic review and qualitative analysis will be used to develop a questionnaire (using DCE). The questionnaire will ask participants to choose between different service options. After piloting, the questionnaire will be distributed to people attending specialist HIV clinics in Sussex, Surrey and London. The results will quantify the relative importance to service users of different aspects of healthcare services, and determine whether preferences for the delivery of HIV healthcare differ by service user characteristics, including age, gender, ethnicity and sexual preference. Summary of the potential benefits to patients and the NHS Involving patients in decisions about how their HIV care is provided is likely to increase satisfaction with services, improve attendance and adherence to treatment. Developing improved services may result in better detection and management of comorbidities, prompt and appropriate treatment, fewer medications and a reduced risk of drug-drug interactions, potentially improving quality of life, morbidity and mortality. Good management of chronic illness, including comorbidites, may reduce hospital admissions and medications, benefitting patients and reducing costs for the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Evaluating the benefits of community based aerobic training on the physical health and well-being of people with neuromuscular diseases: a pilot study
Abstract: Background: Historically people with NMDs were told to avoid exercise for fear of exacerbation of the disease process. In recent years, small studies of aerobic exercise have indicated there may be benefit without deterioration in muscle strength and function. Cochrane reviews of exercise in nerve and muscle disease highlighted the small size of these studies and recommended further work with inclusion of a control condition4,5. Exercise to reduce the impact of disease is currently not supported by the evidence to date. The potential beneficial impact on risk factors for diabetes and cardiovascular diseases cannot be under-estimated in a population that has been seen to be under active9,10. Aims: The specific objective of this pilot study is to investigate the effect of aerobic training in two common disabling neuromuscular diseases (NMD): Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) and Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM) for which there is no standard effective treatment. The key difference to previous work in these conditions is the larger sample size, the inclusion of a control group and consideration of the wider effects of exercise in a community setting. The primary aim is to assess if aerobic training gives an improvement in fitness levels compared to a control condition. The data from this study will demonstrate if there is any effect of training on aerobic capacity and can be used to power larger studies of training efficacy. Secondary aims are to ascertain if there are measureable improvement in muscle strength, body composition and functional abilities of participants. In addition, the effects on fatigue, quality of life, activity levels, self efficacy and perceived motivations/barriers to exercise will be explored. The feasibility and acceptability of training people in the community environment will also be ascertained by this study. Safety will be monitored using physiological and patient reported measures. Plan of investigation: Sixty subjects, (30 from each disease group, aged 18 to 80), will be recruited from the established large neuromuscular clinics and patient cohorts at Queen Square and the established Queen Square neuromuscular database. Both disease groups will be investigated concurrently with the same methods but will be viewed and analysed as separate studies. A crossover design will be used with training and control periods. The trial will span three years with each subject participating for a 34 week period. For the training intervention, participants will train in selected local gyms using a bicycle ergometer. Primary outcome measurement for this study is maximum aerobic capacity during exercise testing. Secondary outcome measurement will be muscle strength, lean body mass composition, and activity levels. Importantly, this study will investigate non-motoric effects of exercise such as mood, motivation, sleep and fatigue using questionnaires and interviews. Benefits to patients and the NHS: This study will provide information regarding possible physiological benefits and safety of aerobic training. It will also shed light on whether there any improvements in fitness alter the impact of the disease. A positive outcome will also add to the evidence for the benefits of exercise. It has been our experience that some of our patients have been refused support to exercise by primary care trusts due to lack of evidence of efficacy. It will provide support for people with NMDs to access facilities such as NHS exercise prescription schemes. It is also our experience that people with NMD traditionally access exercise through physiotherapy and rehabilitation services. If this study demonstrates feasibility and acceptability of exercise in community gym facilities, this will remove some of the burden from NHS services. People will be encouraged to self manage and take up exercise on a longer term basis.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: NHS Bristol, North Somerset and South Gloucestershire CCG
Award_Title: Learning from women’s experiences: improving our understanding of the physical, psychological and emotional health impacts of domestic violence and abuse (DVA), help-seeking trajectories and outcomes
Abstract: Background One in four women in the UK experience abuse from a partner or ex-partner at some time in their lives, they are often isolated and find it difficult to access help or support, thereby remaining at risk. Whilst much is known about the prevalence of Domestic Violence and Abuse (DVA) and its health consequences, there are important gaps in the evidence about women s experience of DVA, the barriers, problems and outcomes of help-seeking. Qualitative studies carried out within the UK are lacking. Further research is also needed into setting up education and training of health professionals to understand and detect DVA and refer women for support. Despite Department of Health guidance clinicians often do not ask about abuse nor respond appropriately to disclosure, indicating a need for improved education and training. Aims (i) To increase public and professional awareness of physical, sexual, reproductive and psychological health consequences of DVA based on narrative accounts of women s experiences. (ii) To further our understanding of barriers and challenges facing women in help-seeking and the trajectories, safety and health outcomes for women who do and do not seek help. (iii) To offer a methodology for translating qualitative research data into a resource that is directly relevant and accessible to patients, will inform policy makers and help train health professionals and others involved in their care. The study will be published online as part of the award-winning websitewww.healthtalkonline.orga growing resource that specialises in disseminating qualitative studies of experiences of health and illness. The site currently covers over 70 health conditions and receives over 5 million hits per month. Main research question What are the lived experiences, health problems, information and support needs of women who have experienced DVA, and what are their experiences of help-seeking, both positive and negative. Plan of investigation Qualitative interview – based study of women s experiences of DVA. The strength of this proposal is the emphasis on providing mechanisms for translating qualitative findings into a patient-accessible and educational resource which can be used to influence policy development. We will: 1) collect video and audio recorded interviews with adult women who have experienced DVA 2) use the tried and tested methods of the Oxford health experiences research group and the DIPex charity to prepare a web resource with links to an online forum for peer support and other websites to help survivors 3) conduct a pre-launch formative evaluation of the web resource with potential users 4) prepare a teaching and learning section for health professionals and conduct a post-launch evaluation Working closely with PPI groups and DVA experts, we will interview a diverse sample of 40-60 adult women with current or past experience of DVA. Researchers will write 20-25 analytic summaries to represent the full range of women s experiences from the interviews and to reflect the most important themes. The interview material (including digital and video recordings and the text of the topic summaries) will be processed for the website by the DIPex charity. Video and audio tapes of interviews will be professionally edited to capture 250-300 clips to illustrate the summaries. All data will be entered into a content management system and a draft version of the website prepared for pilot evaluation with potential users. Potential benefit to patients and the NHS Produce a free, non-commercial, website featuring video and audio clips from interviews, an online forum to connect women surviving DVA and teaching and learning materials to help professionals understand the perspectives of women. Pilot the site with women survivors and health professionals in training. Disseminate to local and regional networks and policy-makers.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: What makes older women want to use preventive medications for osteoporosis? A qualitative study of adherence to osteoporosis medication in the 70–85 agegroup.
Abstract: BackgroundOsteoporosis is a major risk factor for fractures, Preventive treatments for those at high risk are improving, but these have to be taken longterm, and can only result in better outcomes if patients are willing to take them on the recommended basis (‘adherence’- voluntary use of medication in prescribed amount at recommended interval). Older women's ability and willingness to use new osteoporosis prevention drugs is crucial to the benefit they can get from these. Studies have shown significant risk reduction in hip fracture in women who are adherent to preventive therapy for osteoporosis: but up to 50% of patients either do not get or do not take the medication. Nonadherence is commoner with age, complicated / multiple drug regimes, problems with mobility, cognition and other illnesses.Aims? to ascertain the perceived factors that influence older women to adhere longterm to preventive medication for fracture risk factors in probable osteoporosis.? give details of key perceptions and motivations to which patients attribute their willingness and ability to adhere to different osteoporosis prevention regimens? establish guidance for clinical staff, pharmacists and manufacturers to maximise the possibility of patient adherence in this patient population.Plan of Investigation30-50 women aged 70-85 recruited through related MRC funded study of screening for fracture risk, sampled purposively across a range of experiences and factors (e.g. age, profile at entry, level of adherence) until a full range of views has been included.. Interviews at 3 and 24 months after initial recommendation to start osteoporosis prevention treatments, to cover understanding purpose of medications; difficulties with medications, including clarity of information given by clinical staff about impacts and use of the medication; motivators & detractors for adherence (e.g. lack of immediate evidence of benefit); views on dosing regimens and formulations; other relevant problems including co-morbidity and “medicalisation” of later life; reasons for and against longterm usage.Potential ImpactEnsuring that older women can make the best possible use of these preventive medications will reduce the major morbidity and mortality of avoidable osteoporotic fractures, and help pharmaceutical companies and clinical staff to organise drug regimes that are acceptable to their older female patients and to the health services who have to deliver them. This evaluation will be in the first years of use of these new drugs and will capture early knowledge about the 'rollout' of their use into the community.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: An evaluation of the feasibility and effectiveness of a supported self management package for relatives of people with recent onset psychosis
Abstract: BackgroundThis study focuses on relatives of people with psychosis. This is an important group of service users who have high levels of need and who are entitled to receive a range of services. Evidence shows that relatives provide a huge amount of care in the community but as a result experience high levels of burden, reduced quality of life, and poor physical health. By offering effective interventions we can reduce these negative outcomes. However, despite this being a government priority, clinical guidelines around services for relatives are not implemented and relatives do not receive the support they need. One reason for this is lack of resources. By developing and evaluating a supported self-management approach we aim to increase dissemination of proven interventions and empower relatives.AimsPhase1 To finalise a cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) orientated self management intervention for relatives of people with recent onset psychosis. Phase2 To determine the acceptability, feasibility and effectiveness of offering this intervention in an NHS Early Intervention Service for psychosis (EIS). To identify service user preferences for mode of delivery and method of use. Phase3 To modify the intervention in light of service user feedback and develop guidelines to disseminate and implement the intervention throughout the NHS.Plan of InvestigationPhase1- Systematic review to highlight key components in existing effective interventions. Focus groups of relatives from participating Trusts to explore experiences of self management, required support, perceived barriers. Development of service user reference group to guide final format of intervention. Phase2- Pilot randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing outcome for relatives receiving either current treatment or current treatment plus supported self management intervention. Participants will be invited to take part in interviews to qualitatively explore experiences of the intervention, focusing on barriers to use and potential solutions. Phase3- Intervention will be modified in light of feedback. A report outlining results and guidelines for implementation will be disseminatedPotential ImpactThis study will produce an evidence based supported self management intervention to meet the needs of relatives in Early Intervention Services (EIS), including detailed information about how to offer this within routine NHS services, and estimates of effectiveness. The intervention provides a clear mechanism by which EIS can empower and meet the needs of relatives within existing resources. The study will provide essential information required for a large scale definitive trial that can evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention on outcome for relatives and for people with psychosis, and can assess cost effectiveness.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: An exploration of patient experiences around diagnosis and treatment of dementia: implications for service development
Abstract: BackgroundOver 700,000 people in the UK have dementia. Early diagnosis and intervention is a key part of the forthcoming Dementia Strategy. There is a growing body of research on patient and carer perspectives of becoming a person with dementia. Although these studies are done in a range of settings it is likely there are elements and themes that transcend culture and context and can inform how clinicians and services respond to patients at this key time of transition. This project will use systematic review methods to establish an evidence base for medical and nursing practice when identifying and supporting people newly diagnosed with dementia. Stakeholder events will be used to develop review parameters and help understand the significance of the findings from a user and service perspective.AimsTo systematically review the international qualitative literature on older people’s and their carer’s experiences of becoming a person with dementiaTo identify key themes from the literature and commonalities and differences across different groups and culturesTo identify barriers and facilitators to early diagnosis and service provisionTo identify the kind of support from primary and secondary care people newly diagnosed with dementia and their carers perceive as helpful and unhelpful To identify common experiences and responses to early signs of dementia and whether these can be used to inform the development of servicesTo explore review findings with key stakeholders and develop recommendations for practicePlan of InvestigationThis study has two phases. A multidisciplinary team, skilled in reviews, qualitative research, and the care of people with dementia, will systematically review qualitative studies on experiences of receiving a diagnosis and the transition to becoming a person with dementia. Review parameters will be refined at a preliminary stakeholder event. A comparative thematic approach will be used to synthesise results and identify barriers and facilitators to early diagnosis and service provision. In the second phase focus groups with service users, carers and health care professionals will be used to ascertain views on the review findings and assist in drafting recommendations and facilitating dissemination. The project will be guided by an advisory group including user representatives.Potential ImpactThis work will contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the types of services people with dementia and their carers find helpful and the barriers and facilitators to early diagnosis and appropriate service provision. Synthesising the literature in this way will avoid duplication of unnecessary research on a sensitive and potentially distressing topic. It will increase understanding of how culture can alter the recognition, help seeking behaviour and experience of patients with dementia and their carers and facilitate identification of key areas for future research. The findings will directly inform clinical practice and education, help inform the development of culturally sensitive services, be a resource for patient representative groups and influence future research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Evaluation of Pilgrims Hospices Rapid Response Community End of Life Service in East Kent
Abstract: BackgroundIn England over 500,000 people die each year. Most people would prefer to die at home, but only 18% do so. The recent Department of Health End of Life Care Strategy [15] advocates a rapid access service with teams providing 24/7 support. Such services support carers and manage the crises that tend to lead to hospital admission and death in hospital. Evaluation of palliative care indicates that some hospital admissions could be avoided if patients had rapid access to services. However the current evidence-base for rapid response is limited to 3 descriptive studies which show the potential benefits but lacked controls, provide no information on carer outcomes and only limited information on costs. The proposed study will substantially strengthen the evidence base for this intervention.AimsThe aim of the study is to contribute to the development of the evidence base on the consequences and costs of rapid response teams.Its objectives are to assess the impact of Pilgrims Hospices rapid response service in East Kent on:• Patients' preference- whether the service enables more patients to exercise their preference about place of death;• Carers' quality of life during and after death;• The relative costs and consequences of a rapid response team compared with normal service of inpatient hospice/hospital care;• A 'good death'.A rigorous trial combining quantitative standardised measures and qualitative analysis based on a natural experiment will evaluate Pilgrims Hospices’ planned 4 phase implementation of a rapid response service in its three operating areas in East Kent.Plan of InvestigationPhase I (months 0-8) Set-up. Collection of baseline information of all patients and carers using current services.Phase II (months 9-14) Introduction of rapid response service in Area 1. Collection of relevant data on all patients and carers eligible for service in Area 1 and collection of equivalent data from controls in Areas 2 and 3. Interviews begin.Phase III (months 15-20) Continuation of rapid response team in Area 1 and introduction in Area 2. Collection of data from all patients and carers eligible in Areas 1 and 2 and collection of equivalent data from controls in Area 3.Phase IV (month 20-29) Rapid response teams operating in all areas, no new patients will be entered into the study, completion of data collection and interviews, analysis and report.Potential ImpactThis study will show if a new rapid response service which Pilgrims Hospices is developing in East Kent increases the choice that people have about where they die, improves the quality of the experience for their families and carers and does so at a reasonable cost. It will contribute to the development of evidence on the impact and costs of rapid response services enabling other localities to improve the quality of service they offer to dying patients. It will also identify the demand for palliative care rapid response services and therefore help policy-makers plan and improve service provision so that it meets patients’ needs. If shown to be successful, the service could provide a template for developing future rapid response services in other areas.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Is there a pathway to recovery through care coordination? Emancipatory action research with mental health service users, carers, and professionals within Northumberland, Tyne and Wear
Abstract: BackgroundUK mental health services have undergone considerable reform in recent years; the advent of managed care manifested in initiatives such as care coordination pathways and CPA have been represented as cost effective, quality-driven systems. They are designed to re-engineer mental health practice to improve patient benefits and aid recovery. However, problems in the design and delivery of such pathways and the reticence of some mental healthcare providers to implement them meaningfully have been noted. Department of Health policy recommends that patients, carers and the public should be involved in all publicly funded research. The proposed project therefore seeks to explore and reach a consensus around quality care coordination through both service user and carers acting as co-researchers.AimsUsing an emancipatory action research approach this project will:1. Explore the experiences of mental health service users, carers and professionals with regards to the delivery of care coordination.2. Explore issues of consensus around good practice and quality care coordination amongst service users, carers and professionals.3. Develop quality measurement tools with mental health service users and carers to be used in the examination of both care coordination and recovery.4. Produce an archive of mental service users and carer narratives.5. Develop a best practice care coordination tool kit including training and other material (inc. the tools devised in aim 3 and the archive in aim 4).6. Provide a collaborative platform for the future cascade of work both locally and nationally.Plan of InvestigationThe project has 3 phases designed around emancipatory action research, which is led by mental health service users and carers at all stages from conception, execution, analysis, and the final ‘action’ stage of the research project.Phase 1: Delphi study of stakeholders in the locality from health and social care in both statutory and voluntary sectors. Development of a quality care coordination tool. The results from the Delphi and tools will be used to develop the focused narratives.Phase 2: Focussed biographical narrative interviews with service users, carers and professionals around good practice in care coordination. Both phases 1 and 2 will feed into the next phase.Phase 3: The development of a tool kit for best practice in care coordination and other dissemination methods.Potential ImpactThis project will generate evidence of best practice in recovery oriented care co ordination:Nationally:1. The best practice tool kit in care coordination developed can be utilised by partnerships of service user/carer organisations and services to develop training and improve economic, social and health benefits.2. The research will support other organisations wishing to work in similar partnerships. This will be achieved through a network of champions of recovery within quality care co ordination.Locally:1. The recognition locally of service user and carer voices in this area will aid the movement towards more empowering mental health services.2. The work will provide insight into the reality of care coordination which can be used in professional training and service development.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Development, effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of a new respiratory and palliative care out-patient breathlessness support service
Abstract: BackgroundBreathlessness is a common, distressing symptom in advanced malignant and non-malignant disease, and impacts significantly on quality of life. Breathlessness in end-stage disease is also responsible for significant healthcare resource usage. Escalante (1996) reported hospital admission rates of 60% in patients presenting to a cancer treatment centre with breathlessness. Preliminary trials of breathlessness clinics with selected groups of patients have been promising, but lack data on their cost effectiveness. The aetiology of breathlessness is multifactorial, and so a multidisciplinary approach is required if all physiological, psychological, social and cultural factors are to be recognised and managed appropriately.AimsThe principal aim of this 2-year research project is to develop and evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of a multidisciplinary out-patient breathlessness support service (BSS) for the palliation of breathlessness, in advanced malignant and non-malignant disease. This is a phase II study to test the hypothesis that a BSS will improve patient mastery over breathlessness and reduce the use of healthcare resources (including GP consultations, accident and emergency attendances, and length of hospital stay) compared with usual best medical care alone (UC), at an acceptable level of cost-effectiveness. The outcomes of this phase II study will also help to determine sample size, develop and test methods for a phase III trial that will follow on from this project.Plan of InvestigationOur methods follow the MRC Framework for the development and evaluation of complex interventions, phase 0-II. We will develop the service based on our findings from literature searches and qualitative interviews already carried out during phases 0-I, and then conduct an exploratory randomised controlled trial with imbedded qualitative interviews (phase II). At baseline we will assess respiratory function and breathlessness mastery and severity using validated scales, and health service usage (using the Client Service Receipt Inventory to calculate formal and informal costs). Individuals will be randomised to the intervention group [IG] (n=55) or UC (n=55). The IG will attend the new out-patient clinical service with multi-professional input. Assessments will be repeated at 4 and 10 weeks.Potential ImpactImprovements in the management and palliation of breathlessness would improve patients’ quality of life, and could reduce NHS costs. If the study suggests that the BSS is more cost effective than UC, this will lead to: methods for a phase III multicentre trial, information about the components that might be most effective (from qualitative interviews) and changes in clinical practice and the development of more appropriate patient centred services. A negative result will help redirect services. The study will also act as a springboard for future studies to investigate the physiological basis of breathlessness in chronic disease, and the impact of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, and will show ways that breathlessness can be better measured and tested.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Mapping Opportunities for earlier detection of Bipolar Disorder – Linking Big Data to Improve Patient Outcomes (MOBILISE)
Abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic and disabling mental illness. There are usually delays of many years between illness onset and diagnosis, meaning that individuals suffer from untreated symptoms. Additionally, prolonged delay is associated with increased disability. However, there is no strategy for improving the early identification and treatment of BD in the NHS. In this project we aim to use large electronic health record databases to identify signs of unrecognised BD and develop a profile of signs of prodromal BD. Work Package (WP) 1 will examine signs of undiagnosed BD and risk factors for, and consequences of, long duration of undiagnosed illness. We will start by identifying all individuals with a diagnosis of BD in the 5 year period between 1/1/2010 and 31/12/2014. Defining onset of BD as first diagnosis of depression or first prescription of antidepressants, we will examine the health records of these individuals after the onset but before diagnosis of BD. This phase of undiagnosed illness is called the “latency period”. We will compare health “events” (eg prescriptions, diagnoses) during this latency period with a control group matched for age, gender general practice and time period but without a diagnosis of BD. Thus we will build a picture of features indicative of unrecognised illness. We will then examine risk factors for long latency and health events in people with long versus short latency periods. WP2 will use information from WP1 to create a health informatics model of how timely diagnosis of BD could alter patient outcomes. This Early Opportunities Mapping will identify different actions that could be taken to close the gap between the optimal and actual care pathways. We can examine, for example, how outcomes might be improved if BD were identified at first opportunity, second opportunity and so on. In WP3 we will examine health events for the year prior to onset of BD (as defined above) to develop a profile of prodromal BD. This group will need to be followed up longitudinally using the electronic health record databases to assess their risk of being diagnosed with BD. This WP therefore lays the groundwork for a future prospective study examining putative signs of undiagnosed and prodromal BD. An Advisory Board, which will include service users, carers, primary and specialist care clinicians, and professionals involved in curriculum development and training of health care professionals, will consider our findings and make recommendations to improve practice, and advise on dissemination. Impact on clinical practice Our research will create a profile of common features indicative of unrecognised BD and adverse outcomes of prolonged duration of untreated illness. This information can be used in the education and training of medical students, GPs, psychiatrists, and other health professionals involved in the provision of MH care. The trajectory to changing medical practice will be accelerated by the inclusion of professionals involved in training GPs and medical students on our Advisory Board. Benefits to patients There are several thousand patients in the UK currently suffering from unrecognised BD. Our research will improve the ability of GPs and other clinicians to identify the illness earlier in its course, thereby reducing the suffering from untreated symptoms, incorrect diagnoses and inappropriate treatment. Earlier recognition and treatment also potentially improve outcomes. Our dissemination strategy could make the public more aware of potential signs of unrecognised BD, enhancing the ability of individuals to seek help earlier. Potential impact on policy Our research can influence policy for improving the early identification and treatment of BD in the NHS, for example by providing evidence for NICE guidelines. The findings may indicate optimal care pathways through Early Opportunities Mapping .

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Supervised pharmacy student led medication review in primary care: A pilot study to ascertain the potential costs and effects
Abstract: BackgroundLevel 3 clinical medication reviews (with patient and notes) are recommended by the Department of Health for specific patient groups. Pharmacy graduates acquire robust therapeutic knowledge and are trained to optimise drug therapy and patient medicine behaviour. Unlike other health care practitioners they have minimal patient contact during training and research has demonstrated a need for improvements in pharmacist consultation skills. To address this issue the current government agenda is to increase patient contact within the pharmacy undergraduate curriculum. Delivery of level 3 medication reviews by pharmacy undergraduates under close supervision has the potential for patient benefit, developing pharmacist consultation skills and providing a potential education model for the future.AimsBy replicating the process of delivering NHS services under clinical supervision, utilised by all undergraduate schools of Optometry and Dentistry within the UK the study aims to• Determine the potential patient benefit arising from supervised pharmacy student led level 3 medication reviews • Determine the effect size of the intervention and its potential cost-effectiveness from an NHS perspective • Develop and describe a novel model for the training and delivery of pharmacy student led medication review clinics utilising consultations with patients with Type 2 Diabetes.Plan of InvestigationPhase 1 DevelopmentLiterature review & stakeholder focus groups undertaken to develop interventionPhase 2 InterventionAppropriately prepared 4th year pharmacy students invited to participatePatients with type II diabetes, identified via their medical practices, recruited and randomised to intervention or controlStudents allocated 2 Intervention patients (IPs) to review, undertake a notes review at medical practice under supervision and discuss with the general practitionerStudent undertakes consultation at a later date with IP to discuss information needs and identify any adherence or safety issuesPatient outcomes measured at baseline and end, and compared to determine effect size and potential cost-effectivenessPhase 3 ReviewFocus groups repeated to review the processPotential ImpactIn addition to meeting a number of current government agendas this project will potentially:Improve both patient knowledge of their medicines and patient adherenceResult in large numbers of medication reviews being undertaken relatively inexpensivelyImprove adherence to national standards for diabetes prescribing and monitoringImprove patient outcomesImprove pharmacist consultation and medication review skillsImprove working relationships between pharmacists and doctorsPositively affect patient opinions of the pharmacist leading to greater future utilisation of this NHS resource

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Incentives, inequalities and influences: an evaluation of a local pay-for-performance scheme for primary care
Abstract: BackgroundThe Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) for UK general practitioners aimed to bring about major improvements in the quality of primary care. This pay-for-performance scheme is based upon the premise that financial incentives improve practice, as measured by a set of indicators, and hence reduce inequalities in the delivery and outcomes of primary care. Whether the benefits of QOF sufficiently outweigh its costs and unintended consequences remains contended. The Darzi NHS Next Stage Review proposed local QOF targets, based upon a national menu, to address local priorities. However, there is debate as to whether such schemes should proceed. NHS Bradford and Airedale established a local QOF in 2008, with locally negotiated indicators, and there is now a key opportunity for evaluation.AimsAim: To evaluate a local pay-for-performance scheme for primary careObjective 1: To examine whether a local pay-for-performance scheme has reduced inequalities in the delivery of clinical care since its introduction.Objective 2: To explore the influences of the local pay-for-performance scheme on practice staff engagement with the stated mission of addressing local health needs.Plan of InvestigationObjective 1: Analysis of data extracted from practice information systems and data on practice population characteristics. We shall evaluate how achievement in meeting targets varies according to area deprivation and whether the gap between the highest and lowest achievers has closed since the scheme began.Objective 2: Interviews with practice staff, purposively sampled based upon practice popualtion characteristics, levels of achievement, and involvement in quality improvement. The interviews will explore perceptions of the scheme and indicators, likely mechanisms of influence on practice, and perceived benefits and harms of the scheme. All interviews will be digitially recorded and transcribed prior to thematic analysis.Potential ImpactThere is a growing literature on QOF in the UK, but we are unaware of any evaluations of locally developed schemes. Our analysis of the impact of a local scheme on inequalities will be generalisable to the wider NHS. Local schemes offer potential advantages over national, e.g. improved engagement by primary care staff which can foster a deeper rather than superficial commitment to improve care and reduce inequalities. They may also have disadvantages, e.g. compromised holistic care, and reduced impact and value-for-money if local indicators lack credibility. This study will elicit the advantages and disadvantages of a local QOF. We will improve understanding of the mechanisms by which the local QOF works (or not), informing other local quality improvement activities in primary care.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A pilot study to promote adherence to two interventions to prevent falls in older people with visual impairment
Abstract: BackgroundVisual impairment (VI) is a risk factor for falls. Interventions to promote home safety and exercise programmes to reduce falls in people aged ?75 years with VI were successful in a study conducted in New Zealand (NZ-VIP). However in NZ-VIP modification of home hazards and adherence to the exercise programme was poor. There is a need, therefore, to understand how to promote adherence to these programmes. This is important since adherence to the exercise programme was strongly associated with reduced falls. We propose to carry out qualitative focus groups then an experimental pilot study which will enhance the intervention for a replication study of NZ-VIP. We will assess the acceptability of the interventions and the feasibility of carrying out a full scale RCT in the NHS.AimsThe long term aim of this pilot study is to identify methods to maximise adherence to the home safety and exercise programmes in order to prevent falls in people aged ?75 years with VI. While patients were consulted in the development of the interventions for the original NZ-VIP study, the results show we need to promote the applicability and adherence to the interventions in the UK. This will increase confidence that the interventions of the main study will be acceptable to UK patients with VI and generate a successful result when introduced in the NHS. Another aim is to estimate parameters required to inform sample size calculations for the main study given that we intend to modify how we engage and support patients. However we will not alter the actual safety or exercise programme.Plan of InvestigationPeople aged ?75 years with VI will be recruited into focus groups with the aim of understanding how to (i) improve the adherence to the two trial interventions and (ii) modify the delivery mode of the interventions to make them acceptable to UK patients. For the RCT, participants will be randomized into one of three groups: i) care as usual and two social visits, ii) a home safety programme, and iii) the home safety and an exercise programme. The primary outcome measures are falls and falls related injuries. Data on falls and adherence to the interventions will be collected daily for six months. Participants will be interviewed after six months to learn how the modifications affected adherence. Analysis will confirm the extent of adherence and the effect size for the main study.Potential ImpactThe potential impact of the pilot study lies in adding confidence to the robustness of the design of the main study; both of which can be completed within 5-6 years. This is because we aim to work out how to deliver the two interventions for the main study more effectively which in turn, will improve the adherence rates and the differences in effect between the intervention groups will be larger. Reduction of falls could have a profound effect on the maintenance of health as those who fall are likely to become disabled and dependent on others. With greater participation the main study and eventual implementation are more likely to realise significant savings to the NHS. The pilot study will also strengthen future full applications to funding agencies including the MRC.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The impact of a bariatric rehabilitation service on weight loss and psychological adjustment.
Abstract: BackgroundBariatric surgery is currently the most effective form of obesity management for those whose BMI is greater than 40 (or 35 with co morbidities), (1, 2). A minority of patients, however, either do not show the desired loss of excess weight or show weight regain by follow up. Research by the present author (3, 4) and discussions with patient support groups (BOSPA; WLSinfo) highlights some of the reasons for this variability, most of which centre on the absence of any psychological support with patients describing how although surgery fixes their body, psychological issues relating to dietary control, self esteem, coping and emotional eating remain neglected.AimsThe study aims to evaluate the impact of a health psychology led bariatric rehabilitation service (BRS) on patient health outcomes and NHS costs. The bariatric rehabilitation service will provide information, support and mentoring pre and post surgery and will address psychological issues such as dietary control, self esteem, coping and emotional eating. The package reflects the rehabilitation services now common place for patients post heart attack and stroke (5) which have been shown to improve patient health outcomes.Plan of InvestigationThe study is a randomised control trial and patients will be allocated to receive either usual care or the bariatric rehabilitation service pre and post bariatric surgery. Follow up measures of weight loss and psychological issues will be taken at baseline (1 week preoperatively), 3, 6 and 12 months postoperatively. The contents of the bariatric service and the follow up measures are based on previous pilot work and have been developed further by the research team working closely with two patient support groups (BOSPA & WLSinfo). St Richard’s Hospital in Chichester offers a NHS based bariatric service for obese patients which is the largest centre in the UK, with 600 patients per year receiving an operation. The study will take 34 months.Potential ImpactIt is predicted that a bariatric rehabilitation service will improve weight loss following surgery and will also facilitate changes in other psychological variables such as quality of life, dietary control, self esteem, coping and emotional eating. This also has costs implications for the NHS as improved effectiveness of bariatric surgery reduces the health costs of obese patients in the longer term. At 30 months a health economist will evaluate the cost effectiveness of the BRS. Results will be fed back to the user support groups involved in the design and published in academic and professional journals.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: A feasibility study to inform the design of a future randomised controlled trial to evaluate a falls prevention intervention in care homes
Abstract: BackgroundIt is estimated that a third of hip fractures in older people in the UK occur in care homes(1). Falls injuries are devastating for residents and costly to the NHS. Rehabilitation reduces falls rates, however these multi-factorial interventions need to be ongoing and rely on patients engaging in their own rehabilitation programme. This is difficult for care home residents as 84% have cognitive impairment. It would seem to be clinically and cost effective for the NHS to train and support care home staff to deliver falls prevention interventions. We have developed, published and tested such an intervention (GtACH)(2) which can be delivered by non professional carers. It includes a falls risk assessment, delivery of evidence-based specific interventions and appropriate referral to services.AimsThe ultimate aim is to evaluate whether the GtACH reduces the rate of falls in care homes. However, we are not in a position to complete a large definitive trial until we have collected further information to inform the design of such a study. This feasibility study will answer pertinent questions to enable a definitive large multi-centre trial as below:We will:• Estimate important parameters that are needed to design the main study• Test the feasibility of completing a randomised controlled trial in care homes• Estimate the proportion of care homes and residents that are likely to take part in the definitive study • Explore whether residents will be able to tolerate the intervention • Make sure we can collect valid and reliable dataPlan of InvestigationA feasibility single-centre cluster randomised controlled study. Six care homes in Nottingham will be recruited with an estimated sample of 68 participants who have fallen. A research assistant (RA) will explain the study, obtain consent and collect baseline data about the home and participants. Homes will be randomised to intervention or control. Staff in intervention homes will be trained by Clinical Falls Specialists to implement the GtACH. The RA will collect outcomes to determine the feasibility, tolerability and acceptability of delivering the intervention, completing the trial and collecting valid and reliable data in this population. Outcomes will be collected from care home records, falls incident books, electronic falls detectors, hospital records and care home staff.Potential ImpactThe findings from this study will be used to inform the design of a definitive multi-centre cluster-randomised controlled trial of a falls prevention intervention for use by care home staff. The findings will have major implications for residents, NHS staff and care home staff. If successful; residents will fall less, so less sufferring less injuries leading to less hopsital admissions and the NHS will be able to effectively target its input into care homes. Care home staff will be trained to assess and treat people to prevent falls but this increase in work will be offset by the reduction in work caused by fractures, injuries and hospital admissions. If the intervention is not successful, NHS and care home staff will not be trained in its use, resources will be used elsewhere.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Birmingham and Solihull Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A pilot study to assess the feasibilty and impact of a motivational intervention on problem drug and alcohol use in adult mental health inpatient units
Abstract: BackgroundSubstance misuse in those with severe mental health problems is common and associated with poor: engagement in treatment, motivation to change, clinical outcomes and increased psychiatric admissions. Estimates vary, but up to 44% of those admitted into psychiatric inpatient facilities have been found to have co-existing substance misuse problems. However, treatment for substance misuse on inpatient units rarely occurs, yet is highlighted as an area of unmet need. A mental health admission can present an unparalleled opportunity for inpatients to re-evaluate their substance use. National guidance recommends psychiatric inpatient staff be trained in the use of simple motivational approaches to address substance misuse amongst this client group, but as yet there is no evidence to guide this.AimsIn order to prepare for a definitive trial of an inpatient focussed intervention for substance misuse within the context of integrated community mental health treatment, this phase II pilot study will aim to:-(1) Test whether engagement in treatment for substance misuse and readiness to change substance use behaviour can be significantly improved by a motivational intervention. (2) Test how feasible and acceptable the motivational intervention is to inpatients and staff as a routine inpatient intervention. (3) Conduct the groundwork for the health economics necessary in the definitive trial to enable a full cost-effectiveness analysis.Plan of InvestigationStaff on each mental health admission unit will be trained to deliver a motivational intervention. New inpatient admissions with severe mental health problems who misuse substances will be invited to take part. Participants will be randomised to: Motivational Intervention (MI) or Treatment as usual (TAU). One-month post-discharge participants in the MI condition will be given a booster session to help: consolidate motivation, transfer the skills from the MI to the community, and engagement with substance misuse treatment routinely integrated within community mental health teams. Participants will be followed up 3-months post-discharge.The primary outcome will be engagement in substance misuse treatment and the secondary outcome readiness to change substance use.Potential ImpactThis pilot study will provide an evidence base for inpatient care of people with co-morbid substance misuse. It will seek to improve readiness to change problematic substance use and lead to improved engagement with community-based treatment services post-discharge for this aspect of their care. The longer-term impact will be that the trial will provide the groundwork for mental health service providers to identify a feasible, cost-effective and easy to implement treatment option that can be readily integrated into standard inpatient and community-based care.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Assessment of a web-based tool for parents of children with Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA) coupled with standard care, versus standard care alone: a randomised controlled trial
Abstract: The diagnosis of a child with a chronic condition produces an emotional crisis for all family members. How well the parents are able to cope with this crisis will affect their ability to participate in their child s treatment'1. Previous research suggests that even in a well-supported service, parents can have difficulties in managing their child s JIA, and tailored information and support is necessary2. This study focuses on the potential of using an online intervention to support parents of children with JIA. Health is one of the most visited areas of the web but website content is unregulated and often not validated.
