Most current websites for JIA are restricted to giving information only, do not provide training in behavioural techniques for dealing with the daily issues in JIA and to the best of our knowledge have not undergone formal evaluation. In response to this the CHARMS JIA Website for Parents has been systematically developed with healthcare professionals and parents of children with JIA. The aim of this trial is to evaluate the benefits to parents and children of having access to this website in combination with standard clinical care when compared to standard care alone. Principal research question: In parents of children newly diagnosed with JIA, does an internet-based intervention that contains information and techniques to manage their child's JIA integrated with the clinical service, when compared with standard care, lead to a reduction in parenting stress? Secondary research questions: a) Does a specially designed online intervention, when offered to parents of children newly diagnosed with JIA in addition to standard clinical care: improve parents' ability to manage their child's arthritis? enhance parents' satisfaction with the healthcare received? improve their child's health-related quality of life? reduce healthcare utilisation? b) Is there a relationship between the level of website usage and these outcomes? Plan of investigation Participants Parents who attend paediatric rheumatology clinics at participation sites and meet the inclusion criteria will be invited to take part in this randomised controlled trial. Inclusion criteria Parents of children aged up to and including 12 years who have been newly diagnosed (within 1 month) with JIA according to internationally agreed criteria3. Parents aged 18 years or over Ability to understand written and spoken English Exclusion criteria Identifiable psychosis or dementia in parents Parents with major literacy problems Procedures Parents will be approached to take part in the trial when they attend a routine rheumatology appointment with their child. Parents who agree to participate will be asked to complete a baseline questionnaire (see Table 1 for a full list of measures). Once the baseline questionnaire is completed participants will be randomised to either the control arm who receive standard care or the intervention arm who are given 12-months access to the website in addition to standard care. Follow Up Evaluations Participants will be asked to complete a follow-up questionnaire at 4 and 12 months post-randomisation (Table 1). Follow-up questionnaires will be sent by the research assistant to the participant s home at 4 and 12 months post randomisation along with a freepost envelope for returning them to the research office. Outcomes: The primary outcome is parenting stress at 4 months post-randomisation. Secondary outcomes include measures of parent mood and self-efficacy to manage their child's JIA, child HRQoL and healthcare utilisation Potential benefits to participants, patients and NHS If the website is effective, it will enhance parents ability to manage their child s JIA which will reduce parenting stress and help to improve their child s HRQoL. This should also result in a reduction in unplanned contacts with health professionals therefore reduce healthcare utili

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Minimising the risks of emergence of antibiotic resistance during therapy by precise regimen individualisation and use of combination therapy (MINIRES)
Abstract: Background of the research Antimicrobial resistance is a major public health and healthcare problem. Resistance has severe implications for patients and communities. As there are few antimicrobials in development, optimal use of existing agents is vital. Intensive Care Units (ICU) provide an environment with high infection rates, high risks of emergence of resistance and are a focus for dissemination of resistance. There has been progressive development and utilisation of pharmacological modelling techniques to optimise patient care and an evolving understanding of the relationship between drug exposure and emergence of antibiotic resistance and clinical cure. Pre clinical models of antibiotic treatment have shown resistance occurs at much higher drug exposures than is possible in man – the implication being even high doses of a single drug may not be sufficient to minimise resistance. However, pre clinically, addition of a second drug has a dramatic reduction in risk of emergence of resistance. The impact of combination antimicrobial therapy on risk of emergence of resistance in man has never been studied and the use of modern pharmacokinetic software to individualise antibiotic dosing to minimise emergence of resistance is also novel. Aims of research The aim is to investigate the feasibility of conductinging a randomised trial to determine whether antibiotic regimen individualisation and combination therapy will reduce the risk of bacterial resistance. This hypothesis will be tested in intubated critically ill patients with Gram negative pulmonary infection. Plan of investigation Determine the impact of antibiotic regimen individualisation performed on days 2 and 4 of antibacterial therapy in addition to combination antimicrobial treatment on emergence of resistance and clinical cure. This will be assessed by a factorial 2x2 design randomised control trial where the four arms are:- Arm A standard care (standard dose piperacillin-tazobactam alone) Arm B personalised (individually optimised) dosing of piperacillin-tazobactam alone based on measurement of serum concentrations and dose modification to meet a pre defined pharmacodynamic index target Arm C standard care (standard doses of piperacillin-tazobactam) in combination with gentamicin dose according to local guidelines Arm D personalised (individually optimised) dosing of piperacillin-tazobactam as for Arm B and also gentamicin in combination, dosed to meet a pre determined pharmacodynamic index target Only patients with culture proven clinically diagnosed Gram negative pulmonary infection will be included. Piperacillin tazobactam will be measured in real time by LC/MS and subsequently dose adjustments made using a non parametric population pharmacokinetic modelling. Antimicrobial resistance will be established using standard methodologies and strains will be typed and the mechanism of resistance established. We will recruit 20 patients into each arm and collect data on a range of clinically relevant therapeutic outcome measures as well as the minimisation of resistance. It is expected patients may receive larger doses of antibiotic than in standard practice so adverse events will be tracked carefully. The objectives of the trial are assessing the feasibility of recruiting patients with Gram negative infection, evaluating if individualisation can be achieved in real-time, determining protocol compliance, provision of estimates of sample sizes for a definitive study, investigating retention and reasons for drop outs, estimating costs and testing data collection systems. Summary of benefits to patients and NHS This research meets the requirements of DH guidance on antibiotic stewardship: providing a mechanism to ensure the right dose is given at the right time. It also ensures the sustained effectiveness of older agents for the future by individualisation and combination. We will help provide proof of principle for ind

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: A multi-centre randomised controlled trial to assess the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of a home-based self-management standing frame programme in people with progressive MS
Abstract: Background MS is an incurable, unpredictable, progressive, life-long, challenging neurological condition that impacts on every part of a person s life. Affecting approximately 100,000 people in the UK, it is the most common cause of neurological disability in young adults, with diagnosis occurring on average at around age thirty. Within 15 years of diagnosis, approximately 50% of people cannot walk without assistance1 and, over time, 25% are dependent on a wheelchair2. At this stage, balance is usually precarious and most people spend the majority of their day sitting down. This immobility has been shown to lead to secondary complications (e.g. pain, pressure areas, muscle wasting, constipation and psychosocial problems such as depression and isolation) which complicate care and delay rehabilitation. The associated high costs are widely acknowledged, both in economic and quality of life terms. Increasing physical activity can minimise these problems, however this is difficult when disability is severe. Usual physiotherapy comprises short intermittent episodes of face-to-face intervention; long-term maintenance therapy is limited due to resource restrictions. Regular supported standing using frames is a self-management option, with some data to support its acceptability, feasibility and efficacy in people severely impaired with progressive MS, both as part of a short3 and longer term4 home-based, health maintenance programme. More robust evidence is required as the studies to date are limited in number and methodological rigor5. Study Aims: We aim to:- 1) Assess the clinical and cost effectiveness of a home-based standing frame programme in improving motor function and quality of life in people severely impaired by progressive MS; 2) Assess the effectiveness of the standing frame intervention in improving balance, muscle strength, joint and muscle range, spasms, respiratory, bladder and bowel function and number of falls; 3) Explore the subjective experience of using a standing frame within the home as part of daily life from the perspective of people with MS and their carers. Study Design and Methods: A pragmatic multi-centred randomised controlled trial with blinded outcome assessment will be adopted. 140 people severely impaired with progressive MS will be recruited from two English regions; Devon/Cornwall and East Anglia. Participants will be randomised to either a home-based standing self-management programme along with their usual care (intervention) or usual care alone (control). Intervention participants will receive two home-based, one-hour therapy sessions, followed by 6 telephone consultations (~15 minutes/call), supported by user-friendly information leaflets and DVD s. They will be encouraged to stand in the frame for 30 minutes, three times per week, over the 20 week period. Throughout this time the Control group will receive “usual care”. In both groups outcomes will be measured at baseline, immediately post-intervention (20 weeks) and at follow-up (16 weeks post-intervention i.e. week 36). Outcomes include: motor function, lower limb muscle and joint range and muscle strength, balance, spasms, respiratory, bladder/bowel function and quality of life. These will be measured using clinically oriented, validated measures. A full economic evaluation will assess the cost effectiveness of this standing programme. The subjective experiences of using a standing frame within the home as part of daily life will be explored qualitatively in a sub-group of 10 intervention participants and 10 carers. This study will provide scientifically robust results regarding the standing frame intervention. If shown to be clinically and cost effective, the evidence provided will be suitable for development of recommendations for a health service delivery model which could be implemented across the UK. Recommendations would include guidance on implementation costs, evaluation tools for m

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Investigating the feasibility of a group self-management programme after stroke
Abstract: Background: Stroke is the commonest cause of long-term disability4. Improvements in survival after acute stroke5 and longer average life expectancy6 are likely to result in increasing numbers of chronic stroke survivors. Care of these individuals often stops after a brief period of community rehabilitation leaving many with unmet needs and feeling abandoned 7,8. Ongoing cuts to NHS funding will inevitably result in further reduction of stroke services, and demand for long-term stroke services will outweigh provision. One solution suggested in the National Clinical Guidelines is to promote self-management for stroke9. Self-management aims to help individuals take control of the medical, behavioural and emotional aspects of their condition. It has been explored in a range of chronic diseases and has successfully improved a number of patient outcome measures10,11. Bridges is a stroke-specific self-management programme (SMP) which can increase an individual s self-efficacy and locus of control (belief in one s ability to achieve goals and perceived control over one s condition)1. It is currently delivered on a one-to-one basis, but the optimum method of SMP delivery remains unclear. Non-stroke SMPs have been delivered in group settings with some success – they are potentially more cost effective and have the added bonus of improved social support. Before a fully powered randomised controlled trial to investigate the efficacy of a group stroke SMP can be conducted, there are still a number of questions about the feasibility of such an approach that need to be answered. Aim:The overall aim of this work therefore, is to investigate the feasibility of a group stroke SMP Plan of Investigation: Participants will be randomised to either the intervention group (group stroke SMP) or the control group (wait-list control group who later receive the intervention). The proposed work will be conducted in six phases over 36 months. At the end of each phase, two meetings will be held: The first with the University College Hospital London Clinical Research Network (UCLH-CRN) patient advisory group to receive feedback on how the study is being run. The second will be with the co-applicants to ensure milestones (see research timetable) have been met. Phase One – Gain ethical approval and design of the group SMP. Phase Two - 60 stroke survivors will be recruited from University College London Hospitals NHS Trust. Each participant will be randomised to condition in order to examine whether it is feasible to randomise participants to wait-list control groups in future RCTs of group stroke SMPs. Phase Three - Involves two focus groups which will investigate acceptability. One made up of stroke survivors and the other made up of carers. These groups will evaluate the programme design, acceptability and participant willingness to be randomised. Phase Four - The wait-list control group will receive the intervention, and two further focus groups will be run, again consisting or either stroke survivors or carers. Phase Five – Analysis of the data will be performed Phase Six – Dissemination and publication of the results Potential Risk: As there are no adverse events associated with either the one-to-one programme or other group SMPs reported in the literature this study is considered minimal risk. Potential Benefits: The findings of this work will impact delivery of long-term stroke services in the NHS in a number of ways. Firstly, if group stroke SMPs are successful there is potential for economic savings through both cost effective implementation of SMPs and reduction of health service utilisation. Secondly, the group stroke SMP has the potential to improve stroke survivor quality of life, self-efficacy and mood and the long-term support for stroke survivors by extending the stroke care pathway beyond community rehabilitation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Enhancing maternal and infant wellbeing: a feasibility study of the Baby Triple P Positive Parenting Programme for mothers with severe mental illness
Abstract: Background The role of the mother as the primary caregiver in the optimal physical and psychological development of her baby is well established. Recent government and other reports call for parents to be supported in their endeavours to raise successful, socially and academically competent children who will reach their full potential13-19. The use of established parenting interventions has been advocated in families without parental mental illness and with older children (aged 2 and above). For infants, the mother s ability to sensitively respond to her baby s needs has received most research attention20-23. Whilst researchers advocate the use of parenting interventions in the treatment of mothers caring for babies24, there are as yet very few studies that have examined the benefits of parenting intervention for mothers with severe mental illness (SMI). Although Mother and Baby Units treat mothers with SMI, they do not yet offer formally evaluated, evidence-based parenting interventions. The extensively researched and effective Triple P Positive Parenting Programme6-11,25-28 has now been expanded to families with babies. Baby Triple P targets three important areas crucial in enhancing maternal and infant wellbeing: 1) positive parenting skills promoting secure attachment, reducing maternal and infant distress; 2) improving partner and social support to increase maternal and overall family wellbeing and 3) increasing maternal coping resources to combat mental illness. Aims The overall aim of this study is to evaluate a recently developed parenting intervention in mothers whose SMI has necessitated admission to a Mother and Baby Unit (MBU) for treatment. This feasibility study aims to evaluate Baby Triple P in a parallel-group, single-blind (outcome assessor) randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing Baby Triple plus Treatment as Usual (TAU) versus TAU alone. This study will also examine the key cost indicators associated with the intervention and its acceptability to mothers and MBU staff through qualitative and quantitative evaluation processes informed by service user involvement. Plan of investigation We plan to recruit 60 mothers with SMI who have been admitted, jointly with their babies, to a Mother and Baby Unit in Manchester or Birmingham. We will randomly allocate mothers to receive either eight sessions of Baby Triple P plus TAU (n=30) or TAU alone (n=30). We will pilot a range of self-report and observer-rated outcome measures at baseline, post-intervention and 6-month-follow up assessments, which will be administered by research assistants blind to allocation. The piloted primary outcome measure will be maternal competence and confidence in caring for her infant. as wellbeing indicator. Secondary measures will assess maternal mood, mental health symptoms and the mother-infant-bond. In addition, data on the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention alongside the costs of delivering this intervention will be collected. We will conduct qualitative interviews with participants and staff to identify the intervention s strengths and weaknesses and any perceived benefits. In preparation for a definitive RCT, we have involved a health economist and the Clinical Trials Unit (CTU). Potential benefits We anticipate that the results of this study will improve understanding of a) the parenting support needs and preferences and b) barriers and solutions to engaging this clinical population. This study is an opportunity to evaluate an intervention combining parenting skills with psychological coping strategies. If found to be clinically and cost effective, it can readily be implemented within existing perinatal outpatient and inpatient NHS services and may be efficacious in less severe maternal mental illness, thereby ensuring a wider population reach. The intervention s focus on ensuring a positive family pathway for child development could potentially reduce the economic as well as personal

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Internet Intervention Supporting Management of Low Back Pain in Primary Care: a feasibility study (Project short name: SUPPORT BACK study)
Abstract: Background The majority of patients who present in primary care with acute low back pain will experience recurrent episodes, and 5-15% will go on to develop chronic conditions. As for other long-term conditions, effective patient self-management underpins the management of low back pain and aims to help patients cope with their condition. Effective self-management may prevent the onset of chronicity, or limit severity and progression where chronic pain is already present. Evidence suggests that whilst clinician-led self-management interventions can be effective, they are resource intensive, and their availability is limited thus restricting access and delaying treatment. We propose developing an internet self-management intervention that can be delivered with or without support, allowing GPs to offer patients an evidenced-based, structured programme at potentially low per-patient costs. The intervention will be designed as a supplementary educational package to be used in conjunction with usual care for low back pain. Aim To develop an internet intervention for low back pain to be used in UK primary care and explore the feasibility of performing a future randomised trial. Plan of investigation Phase I (0-12 months): Intervention development. We will recruit a panel of patients with low back pain to be consulted as part of an iterative process of development and feedback. Qualitative methods will be used to elicit reactions to intervention modules from a diverse sample of patients. The phase will end with a fully tested internet intervention developed. Phase II (13-32 months): Feasibility trial. We will recruit approximately 90 patients (3 groups, 30 in each). Inclusion criteria: patients will have current low back pain and no red flags . Patients will be randomised (stratified by severity using a cut off of 7 on the Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire) to receive either the internet intervention with telephone physiotherapy support plus usual care or unsupported use of the internet intervention plus usual care or usual care alone. We will evaluate feasibility outcomes including uptake/recruitment, adherence, attrition and patient experience. Potential Impact Our intervention will provide patients with convenient access to tailored educational advice and support for self-management. Our project will address both NICE recommendations for encouraging self-management of low back pain, and recommendations for research on education delivery methods. As well as producing an acceptable internet intervention, we will provide information regarding the feasibility of different levels of support as part of the intervention. If effectiveness is demonstrated in a future phase III RCT, the intervention could be rolled out rapidly for use by GPs throughout the country as a first step, low resource use intervention, with the potential to substantially decrease the burden of low back pain.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Getting down to coping' On-line self-management after treatment for prostate cancer: a feasability study
Abstract: Background The consequences for men of prostate cancer diagnosis and treatment can result in sexual, urinary, bowel and/or body-image problems that left unsupported affect quality-of-life and mental health. Previous research shows high levels of unmet needs for these men of which emotional distress is most prevalent. Despite this, men often feel vulnerable and hesitant to ask for support, and health practitioners do not readily identify mild or moderate psychological disorder in this situation. Symptoms of distress that are not addressed early can develop into mental health problems which over time, and with increasing numbers of men surviving prostate cancer, can put greater demands on health care resources, particularly in primary care. These men need psychological and practical support that facilitates involvement and engagement with services. Cognitive-behavioural programmes delivered face-to-face or by telephone have been shown to benefit men with prostate cancer particularly where distress is raised at study entry. Cognitive-behavioural therapy has also been delivered successfully over the internet in mental health but has not to-date been developed on-line for men with prostate cancer. Aim Our overall aim is to improve mental health and quality-of-life for these men by providing easily accessible psychological support within primary care. Our study aim is to assess the feasibility of an on-line self-referral, cognitive-behavioural self-management intervention based within the IAPT framework targeted at men experiencing distress after diagnosis and treatment for prostate cancer. Research Question What is the viability and practicability of the intervention, and what are the key issues to be assessed in subsequent testing of the intervention within primary care? Secondly, what is the prevalence of distress in this group of men and what is the extent of change in their levels of emotional distress over the course of the intervention? Plan of Investigation Our study is a within-participant comparison. Participants will be screened and assessed at baseline before the intervention and followed up for six months after the intervention. 60 men experiencing distress after diagnosis and treatment for prostate cancer will be targeted. Men will self-refer on-line having been given information about the study in GP practices across the NHS West Sussex locality. The intervention will comprise four weekly sessions: men will be able to log-in to each over a week and will start the programme in groups of 15. Assessments will measure distress, cancer and prostate cancer quality-of-life, and service usage. Risk governance assessments throughout the intervention will cover depression, anxiety, work and social adjustment. A preparatory stage of participatory action research carried out by users and the research team, will develop film tools for integration into the intervention as a resource to encourage participant motivation and confidence. Benefit to patients and the NHS This intervention is designed to provide assessable support for men distressed as a result of prostate cancer diagnosis and treatment. There is currently little provision for men at this level, but left unmanaged there is evidence they will use more health services longer-term. This intervention will provide equal access independent of geographical location, and support the planned transition of prostate cancer follow-up into primary care. It will also address under-reached groups, (men on hormone treatment, post-radiotherapy, on watchful waiting or living in rural areas) all of whom have higher needs but less opportunity to access support. Internet use among older men is growing and offers a medium through which a cost-effective and targeted intervention can address individual needs and provide benefit for health care services. The intervention could be offered though GP consortia linked

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Assessment and satisfaction of services for Juvenile Huntington's Disease and modelling alternative methods of service organisation
Abstract: Juvenile Huntington s disease (JHD) is a rare slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder with onset ≤ 20 years. The clinical picture often differs from that of the more usual adult form in that bradykinesia and dystonia are prominent earlier in course of the illness with myoclonus and epilepsy being more common. The condition is rare with the patients widely dispersed. There are no evidenced based guidelines for management but there are recommendations that there should be a multi-disciplinary approach. The problem with this suggestion is that most professionals are caring and supporting a family with JHD for the first time. We will use multi-phase qualitative and quantitative methods to evaluate the current economic costs of providing the current ad hoc service and model the costs of organising care by concentrating expertise in either multidisciplinary clinic(s) or alternatively, delivering this using tele-health technology. In phase 1 we will interview 12 carers and 6 patients and administer the HD quality of life questionnaire. Information from the Framework analysis and HD quality of life instrument will be used to develop a questionnaire which can be sent to patients. In addition carers will be sent the EQ-5D to estimate quality adjusted life years and the EQ-5D proxy version for them to complete on behalf of their child/young adult. This will enable us to evaluate the current care and identify the professionals involved with the family. A web based survey will be developed for all professionals and a subset of different professionals will be asked to participate in a telephone interview. We will enquire about cares and professionals perception of improvements which could be made and their views on concentrating expertise in either a traditional multi-disciplinary clinic(s) or; alternatively, delivering concentration of expertise via tele-health technology. Data merging from qualitative and quantitative data will be achieved through the development of matrices to array and merge the qualitative themes with key quantitative items. Where possible, information will be gathered from routine data collections such as sessions with health professionals. We will gather information on treatments (both pharmacological and non-pharmacological), care home stay, school attendance and carer time away from usual activities. Information obtained from primary carers will be based on questions on the Database Instruments for Resource Use Measurement. Unit cost information will be obtained from standard sources and the EQ-5D proxy version 2 will be used to measure quality of life in order to estimate quality adjusted life years. We will present a cost per quality adjusted life years from an NHS and social care perspective. Decision modelling, using probabilistic sensitivity analysis, will be used to estimate the costs of organising new models of care based on either traditional multidisciplinary clinic(s) or use of tele-health technology to concentrate expertise. At the end of the study we will make firm recommendations for the organisation of care and modelled alternatives. Based on the views of parents/carers as well as the cost benefit analysis, an alternative model can be evaluated in a further study.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Exploring the funding of health care interventions outside service level agreements: an action research study to improve PCT decision-making
Abstract: BackgroundFor many conditions, effective treatments exist that are not automatically funded on the NHS. Primary Care Trusts (PCTs), who face rising demand for healthcare from limited budgets, have established panels to consider individual treatment funding requests (ITFRs). These groups generally work to explicit principles (eg evidence, ethics), but their composition, their decision-making processes, and the judgements produced vary between PCTs (‘the healthcare lottery’). The public, aided by an increasingly vocal mass media, often have strong views on whether PCTs’ decisions on ITFRs are fair and reasonable, and pharmaceutical companies are interested parties. The time is ripe to research the processes by which some people are granted, and others denied, expensive treatments on the NHS.AimsTo explore the decision-making processes for ITFRs in a sample of PCTs with a view to informing the development of information and training materials for PCTs and patient organisations. On completion of this study we hope to have produced • Detailed case studies of the social practices that underpin and inform decisions by PCT panels to fund (or not) particular ITFRs • An account of how the lay perspective influences (or fails to influence) decisions in such groups • A training and development programme for members of ITFR panels • Information for patients and the public to inform their engagement with, and involvement in, ITFR decisions.Plan of Investigation3 overlapping phases: PHASE 1 (fieldwork). We will collect ethnographic and discursive data from a purposive sample of PCTs selected for contrasting approaches to prioritizing ITFRs. We will interview group members, observe meetings, record discussions, and collect written communications and documents. We will also interview other stakeholders e.g. representatives from patient organisations, drug companies. PHASE 2 (analysis). We will draw on discourse methods to analyse and synthesise these data to produce a set of case studies and theoretical insights on the processes of deliberation and decision-making. PHASE 3 (action). We will develop and pilot (a) training materials and methods to support PCTs in addressing ITFRs, and (b) informational materials for patients.Potential Impact‘Rationing’ is one of the hottest topics in healthcare, and is especially key to the patient’s agenda. Both professionals and the public are increasingly committed to engage with debates on how best to spend limited resources. This study will not produce any easy answers, since there are none, but because we plan to move beyond ‘evidence based principles’ (important, but not the whole story) and centrally address the processes of practical reasoning in the policymaking process, we offer the potential to contribute to a fundamental reframing of the ‘rationing’ debate in healthcare. More pragmatically, we plan to produce both training materials and information to support public involvement in this important debate.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Cluster randomised controlled trial to test the effectiveness of an educational intervention to promote hand washing in reducing absenteeism in primary schools
Abstract: BackgroundThe potential for reducing pupil and staff absenteeism in schools through improved hand hygiene in developed countries is well recognised. The effective strategies for achieving this are less clear because of the poor quality of many of the studies evaluating interventions to improve hand hygiene. Three recent systematic reviews all concluded that there is an urgent need for more rigorous trials, and one specifically drew attention to the need for economic assessments with costings relevant to the UK. The Health Protection Agency (HPA) has developed a low cost educational intervention to promote hand washing in primary schools (Hands up for Max!) and while it has been shown to be acceptable to teachers and pupils its effectiveness in reducing absenteeism has yet to be established.AimsThe primary aim of the study is to determine, by means of a cluster randomised trial, whether the Hands up for Max! educational intervention to promote hand washing in primary schools, by reducing the transmission of agents responsible for respiratory and gastrointestinal infections, is effective in reducing absenteeism amongst pupils and school staff. Additional objectives include: (i) assessing the effect of this intervention on pupil knowledge of hand hygiene, confidence in their ability to wash their hands correctly and willingness to use school washrooms (ii) evaluating the impact of this intervention on hand washing behaviour amongst pupils and school staff and (iii) assessing the costs and benefits of this intervention.Plan of Investigation420 primary schools within the South West of England are scheduled to receive the Hands up for Max! intervention. A sample of schools will be invited to participate in our cluster-randomised trial. Those agreeing to do so will be randomised to be an intervention or control school. Intervention schools will receive the Hands up for Max! intervention. Control schools will be asked not to undertake any additional action on hand washing during the trial but will be able to use Hands up for Max! when all follow-up data collection associated with the trial is complete. Primary outcome measures will be the number of half days of pupil absence and staff absence from school. Costs of delivering the intervention and estimation of potential cost saving to education and the NHS will be determined.Potential ImpactChildren are the main reservoir of common cold viruses. Estimates suggest children can expect to suffer 4 to 8 episodes of respiratory infections annually. Infection often occurs at school. The HPA Centre for Infections received 707 outbreak reports of influenza-like illness across England and Wales in the 05/06 season. Of these, 688 were reported in schools. Seventy school outbreaks were confirmed as due to Influenza group B infection and many had co-infections with Norovirus, diarrhoea and vomiting. Improved hand hygiene in schools could lower infection transmission thereby reducing absenteeism and sickness in schools and potentially reducing associated NHS costs. Encouraging regular hand washing in youth may influence long-term behaviour and improve infection control more generally.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Interventions to reduce unplanned hospital admission: a systematic review
Abstract: BackgroundUnplanned admissions to hospital are an increasing source of pressure on the NHS. The increasing age of the population and a growing cohort of patients with multiple morbidity, alongside changes in service provision have increased the focus and drive to reduce hospital admissions. Unplanned admissions represent 36.7% of hospital admissions in England (4.7 million admissions 2006/7). Unplanned hospital admission rates vary between geographical areas from 90 to 139 per 1,000 people. The difference in admission rates between A&E departments is even greater, varying from around 8 to 36 per cent of all A&E attendances. There are a wide range of interventions that aim to reduce emergency hospital admission. There is no existing systematic review of the effectiveness of these interventions.AimsThe overall aim is to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of interventions to reduce unplanned hospital admissions. The objectives are:1. To develop definitions for the terms used to describe unplanned admission. 2 To synthesise the available evidence from randomised and other controlled studies on the effectiveness of interventions: i. directed at the organisation of care ii. directed at access to servicesto reduce the risk of unplanned hospital admissions. 3. To estimate the cost-effectiveness of those interventions identified as beneficial.4. To develop an evidence base for policy and investment in appropriate admission avoidance strategies.5. To inform future research by identifying gaps in the evidence base.Plan of InvestigationSystematic review Study population: Studies that include people of any age living in OECD countries.Types of studies: Randomised controlled trials and controlled studies.Interventions of interest at the individual or area level: organisation of care and access to services.Outcome of interest: Risk of unplanned admission or readmission.Method: Develop definitions. Develop search strategy, include/exclude studies according to criteria, extract data and appraise quality of included studies, statistical analysis and data synthesis, reporting of results of effectiveness and cost-effectiveness analyses. Dissemination of findings and recommendations for policy and practice.Potential ImpactThe average cost of an unplanned admission in 2006/7 in South West of England was £1994. If a modest reduction in avoidable admissions is made as a result of interventions implemented as a result of this work, for example a 1% reduction, then savings to the NHS in England will be in the order of several million pounds a year. Even allowing for the costs of additional services that may be required to avoid an admission, for example extra nursing care in the home, the savings to the NHS are likely to be substantial. It is important that the results of previous evaluations of interventions are systematically and rigourously assessed in order to inform commissioners and clinicians about potentially effective interventions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Development and evaluation of a system to improve communication of test results in primary care
Abstract: BackgroundWe have undertaken a survey of the methods by which test results are relayed to patients in primary care and found enormous variation between practices. Results frequently fail to reach patients. We have also found that no clear guidelines are currently in place, despite the potential for test result communication to affect both patient’s safety and satisfaction with care. A literature review has revealed little existing research on test result communication in primary care. We will research attitudes of patients and staff to current procedures and in consultation with both groups, design an improved system of test result communication using the principles of lean design. Finally we will implement the new system and conduct a pilot study using an action research modelAims1) Determine what patients think are the strengths and weaknesses of the system they have experienced and see how opinions vary among patients and by type of test. 2) Consult with patients and practice staff on how they think the service can be improved and how different patient wishes can be accommodated. Using this feedback and principles of ‘lean’ and Failure Mode Effects Analysis (FMEA), design a prototype system to reduce delay and cost and improve understanding and satisfaction.3) We will iterate with staff and patients to refine the new system prior to its use. 4) Pilot the new system across two practices and further refine it using an action research model.Plan of InvestigationPhase I: From each of four practices, we will seek opinions on current test result communication systems using focus groups consisting separately of patients and staff from each practice.Phase II: Consult with focus groups consisting of patients and staff working together and combined across practices to co-design a new system, seeking to accommodate variability in patient preference and using the principles of ‘lean’ and FMEA. Phase III: The design will be appraised by the above focus groups on an iterative basis thereby improving the design.Phase IV: The new system will be rolled-out across two practices and staff and patients surveyed via questionnaire and focus group to determine effects on an action research modelPotential ImpactThe successful communication of test results can impact positively on the health outcome of the individual. Yet at present there are acknowledged weaknesses in the process of test result communication, including confusion surrounding the relation of the test to the patient’s condition and the failure to relay test results, whether normal or abnormal. Designing a system that provides the patient with the information they want by the means they choose, will not only yield greater patient satisfaction but safe and better care. In addition, when lean thinking has been employed elsewhere in health care in the UK, the increased optimisation of resources has led to a measurable reduction in waste and notable financial savings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Sheffield Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Development, Piloting and Validation of a Questionnaire to Assess Diabetes-Specific Self-Care Behaviours
Abstract: BackgroundIn the 1980s, a Düsseldorf group demonstrated that teaching adults with Type 1 diabetes to eat freely and self-adjust insulin according to carbohydrate intake improved glucose control and reduced hypoglycaemia. The recent DAFNE RCT transformed Type 1 diabetes management, through improvements in glycaemic control and QoL, and showed the feasibility of this approach in the UK. Many people with diabetes find it difficult to sustain this approach. We are currently funded by NIHR to investigate barriers to self-management. Existing measures of diabetes self-care behaviour do not accurately capture diabetes self-management. Such a tool would enable a precise assessment of the contribution of patients to insulin adjustment and self-care and could be used in Type 1 and 2 diabetes.AimsTo develop, pilot and validate a questionnaire assessment tool of diabetes-specific self-care behaviours using a mixed methodological approach. This will incorporate up-to-date recommendations about diabetes self-management that form part of structured education for people with type 1 diabetes but will also have wider application to type 2 diabetes. It will be a generic tool that can be used across different structured education programmes delivered in primary and secondary care.Plan of InvestigationQuestionnaire development will involve an iterative process drawing upon qualitative and quantitative techniques: 1. Identify existing type 1 structured education programmes in UK that fulfill NICE criteria 2. Compare curriculum of these courses to identify core components/teachings [Consensus techniques with diabetes professionals who developed and deliver the courses and the Type 1 Diabetes Education Network] 3. Generate patient-completed, questionnaire items and circulate for comment 4. Pilot questionnaire with users [2-3 focus groups with people who have undergone structured education] 5. Establish validity and reliability [Questionnaire administration to 400 graduates of structured education programmes at different timepoints. Factor analysis]Potential ImpactThe importance of assessing and evaluating structured education programmes in diabetes has been highlighted in the Department of Health/Diabetes UK Improvement Toolkit for Commissioners and Local Diabetes Communities and the NICE guidance for patient education models. Development of a new patient-completed measure of diabetes self-care behaviours would add to this toolkit and give clinicians and people with diabetes, opportunities to identify and explore aspects of diabetes self-management that may require additional input or support from the diabetes team to help initiate or maintain changes in behaviour. Such a tool could also be developed subsequently for insulin-treated individuals with Type 2 diabetes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Investigating patient use and experience of online booking in general practice
Abstract: Research question How do patients use and experience online booking services in general practice? Background Access to general practice is a major public concern, with patients often complaining about difficulty making appointments. Online booking services offer the option of booking a GP appointment 24/7 using the internet, via a website or app. The Government is keen to promote such services. Although many GP practices now offer online booking, recent surveys show that only a relatively small minority of patients use it, but instead continue to book their appointments on the phone. Until now, research to inform policy about online booking services in general practice has been lacking. Aims and Objectives The aims of the project are to compare the characteristics of patients according to their use of online booking, explore how this is related to their experience of care and explore what patients think about online booking in general practice, in order to identify potential ways of appropriately guiding patient-focused implementation and use of online booking. Objectives: To determine the characteristics of those people using online booking compared with those who do not, and examine changes in awareness and use between 2018 and 2019 To explore associations between using online booking, being aware of online booking, and experience and satisfaction with accessing general practice. To explore in depth why patients do and do not use online booking services in general practice, and where they have attempted to register for them and/or use them, their experience in relation to quality, accessibility and future intentions. To synthesise the findings of objectives 1-3 and disseminate the findings to ensure patient benefit. Methods The project will be conducted in three work packages. Work package one addresses objectives 1 and 2 by conducting a secondary analysis of the General Practice Patient Survey, a large national survey sent to 2.2 million adult patients per year. Work package 2 addresses objective 3 via a qualitative semi-structured interview study involving patients with diverse characteristics registered across a broad range of practice settings. Work package 3 synthesises the findings of work packages 1 and 2 using the RE-AIM framework to address objective 4. Patients and the public will be involved throughout. Timelines for delivery This is a 16-month study. Work package 1 will be undertaken between months 1 and 12. Work package 2 will run from months 4 to 14. Work package 3 will run from months 11 to 15. Dissemination will occur in months 15 and 16. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination Our dissemination strategy is focused on ensuring that the implementation of online booking occurs in ways that optimise benefit, with the risk of unintended consequences, such as certain patient groups becoming disadvantaged, being minimised. A stakeholder event will be used to actively refine the findings for the purpose of dissemination. The findings will be disseminated widely, to policymakers professional bodies such as the Royal College of General Practitioners, to GPs, to clinical commissioning groups, researchers, and patients.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Towards a better understanding of the definition, characteristics and health service requirements of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in the UK
Abstract: COPD is a progressive condition that affects 10% of adults aged 40+years worldwide, and costs the NHS between £1-2billion per annum. The natural history of the disease (especially early-stage) is poorly understood and treatments have changed little in the last 20 years. Current diagnosis relies on lung function criteria which tend to over-diagnose in older people and are under debate. I aim to use existing datasets to better understand the characteristics of COPD, evaluate novel diagnostic criteria, describe health service use and assess management of the condition against the latest guidelines. Using these results and a systematic review of the published literature to evaluate whether screening is effective and cost-effective.

Abstract: This research has two aims. The first addresses a substantive question – how can we improve the health of young people looked after by the state? The second is to increase our understanding of effective methods for involving health service users in setting questions for, and participating in the development of, reviews. The study will involve working collaboratively with young people with experience of the care system to produce a systematic review relevant to their health needs. Qualitative methods will be used to capture the extent and nature of their involvement, and the young people’s perceptions of being involved.

Contractor: Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine
Award_Title: Health and economic benefits of active travel in England
Abstract: The focus of my planned translational research programme is on the role of active travel (walking, cycling and public transport) in increasing physical activity levels in England, spanning epidemiology and policy evaluation. This is an important area of research given the inadequate levels of physical activity in the country and consequent impacts on obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular health. The potential contribution of active travel to improving population health and reducing health inequalities in England has been insufficiently documented using nationally representative data. In addition, information about the personal, household and environmental determinants of active travel in English settings and the impact of cross-sectoral policies on active travel is lacking. Aim To determine optimal strategies for increasing active travel and associated health, economic and carbon reduction benefits in England using nationally representative data Objectives 1.To assess the role of environmental, school, family and individual level influences on active travel in adolescents 2.To determine the impact of active travel on cardiovascular and all-cause mortality 3.To assess the health and economic benefits of providing subsidised bus travel to older people 4.To model the impact of different interventions to increase active travel on health and economic outcomes and carbon emissions 5.To assess the patterns and predictors of active travel and associated health, economic and carbon benefits in India 6.To estimate the impact of policies to increase active travel on health inequalities 7.To work closely with policymakers to maximise translation of my research programme Plan of investigation:- Study Area 1: School, family and individual level influences on active travel and associated health benefits in adolescents. This will involve analyses of longitudinal data using two sources; a national study using data from the Understanding Society Survey and a more detailed local study. Study Area 2: The impact of active travel on premature mortality. Using the Office for National Statistics Longitudinal Survey, this study will examine associations between active travel and mortality in England using a very large (~500,000), nationally representative sample. Study Area 3: Health and economic benefits of providing subsidised bus travel in older people in England. This study will evaluate the impact of providing free travel to older people on a range of outcome measures such as physical activity levels, hospital admissions and mortality. This will involve analysing several waves of two existing national surveys and a novel linked dataset. Study Area 4: Modelling the impact of interventions to increase active travel on health outcomes and carbon emissions. The study will use micro-simulation techniques to model the benefits of different policy options (subsidised public transport, investment in cycling networks) to increase active travel on physical activity levels, mortality and carbon emissions. Study Area 5: Assessing the patterns and predictors of active travel and associated health and carbon benefits in India. This study will use a number of routine and purposefully collected data to determine optimal strategies for increasing active travel and associated health, economic and carbon reduction benefits in India. Summary of potential population health benefits: Increasing physical activity has been described as the 'best buy' in public health. The over-arching translational goal of my research programme is to provide policymakers with robust information to support the implementation of strategies to increase active travel in England up to levels seen in leading European countries, namely the Netherlands, Denmark and Germany, to improve population health, through associated increases in physical activity levels, and contribute to a low carbon future.

Award_Title: Developing a novel system of care targetting risk factors for five manifestations of frailty to maintain the independence of older people in hospital and post-discharge.
Abstract: Background Development of manifestations of frailty (MoF) (falls, delirium, incontinence, reduced mobility and loss of function) in hospitalised older people can result in loss of independence and increased care needs following discharge. MoF may be attenuated or prevented through multicomponent interventions. Separate national guidelines advocate these interventions but risk assessments, content and implementation strategies are poorly specified, and duplicative. Aim: To reduce post-discharge loss of independence for older people hospitalised with acute illness through modification of in-patient risk factors for MoF. Research questions relate to identification and modification of risk factors (new risk assessment and care action identification (RACAI) tool); development of a novel system of care; feasibility assessement (delivery, implementation and trial methodology) prior to a multicentre cluster randomised effectiveness trial. Methods Pre-PDG work: We have identified a list of risk factors for the development of the MoF in hospital from the literature. PDG 1 Structured interviews and focus groups to identify key risk factors for development of MoF in hospital, additional to those described in the literature, from the perspective of patients (PDG1a) and staff (PDG1b). Prioritise risk factors for MoF through expert consensus (PDG1c). PDG 2 Systematic literature and graded evidence reviews to identify effective care actions to address risk factors for MoF identified in PDG1 and pre-PDG work. PDG3 Expert group consensus using a modified group technique to agree a list of best practice care actions to target risk factors. Informed by evidence from pre-PDG, PDG1 and PDG2 and input from patient participants. Timelines for delivery - Results and conclusions of PDG1: month 9; PDG2: month 15; PDG3: month 18 Full Programme Grant for Applied Research Workpackage 1 WP1a: Identifying presence of risk factors and specifying care actions WP1b: Development of assessment and care action identification (“RACAI”) tool to identify an individual s risk factors for development of MoF, and a set of appropriate care actions. W1c: Case studies, observations and interviews with key staff in four sites providing acute care for older people. Using positive deviance methods to identify transferrable aspects of high quality patient centred care to inform implementation strategies. W1d: Development of a logic model and intervention implementation framework, informed by W1a, WP1b and WP1c. Workpackage 2 Cluster randomised controlled feasibility study of system of care vs usual care to assess: trial methodology; data collection processes; variation in practices between sites; recruitment and attrition; suitability, utility and feasibility of the intervention, primary outcome measure, and the RACAI tool. Workpackage 3 Multicentre cluster RCT with embedded process and economic evaluations. Evaluation of clinical and cost effectiveness of the system of care on preventing loss of independence post-discharge from hospital (Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living three months post registration). Evaluation of engagement with, implementation and effectiveness of the intervention (process evaluation). Anticipated impact and dissemination (PGfAR) Immediate: improved hospital experience for older people, reduced resource use Within 12 months: improved post discharge outcomes, reduced NHS and social care costs Within 36 months: to inform future guidance documents for acute care of hospitalised older people

What are the care processes and decision processes associated with quality health care and avoidable hospital admissions from care homes in the UK? 4. Between 10% and 30% of care home residents are over 85 (3,4). Those over 85 are the fastest growing segment of the population. The number of nursing home residents admitted to hospital is of particular concern as many of these admissions are considered avoidable and in the best interest of neither the person nor the health services (5). Estimates from studies of avoidable admissions conducted in the US (6) and UK (7) range from 23% to 67% of all admissions. There are 2 broad types of avoidable admissions:1. admissions where, with appropriate knowledge, skills and care practices, facilities and training, the clinical problem (eg urinary infections) could have been managed adequately in the care home setting and crises avoided;2. admissions which are futile given where the person is in the trajectory of their life course.The main focus in this proposal is the first of these categories, ie avoidable admissions for conditions that, if detected and treated earlier, could have been treated in the nursing home. These conditions are often referred to as ambulatory care sensitive conditions (ASCDs) ie conditions which could have been treated in the home. In addition, transfer to hospital disrupts an older person’s pattern of care and relationships. In economic terms, avoidable hospital admissions are costly to the NHS (9). Abstract: (a) Screening Background: Currently data on offenders are routinely collected by Probation Officers on their Offender Assessment System (OASYs), a computerised system managed by the National Offender Management Service (NOMS). This contains information on several criminological and violent characteristics, but also on impulsivity, drug and alcohol use and childhood behavioural problems21. While this contains useful data, it is too cumbersome to use for screening and, in addition, these assessments are carried out on approximately150,000 offenders/annum; the majority of whom would not satisfy the criteria for entry into the Personality Disorder (PD) pathway. Our task is therefore to develop a screening process that will correctly identify the small number of individuals that satisfy entry criteria for the pathway of high risk with severe PD from the large cohort with OASYs data. Pilot work done in preparation for the previous bid and in the London Probation Service22, suggested that identifying this high risk PD offender group was feasible but required further development. The PDG provides this opportunity. Process: To develop the screen, we will select key variables from OASys and apply these to the Prisoner Cohort Study (PCS)17 following standard statistical procedures for developing diagnostic tools and determining their utility through statistical modelling as recommended by Royston and colleagues. Using data from the Prisoner Cohort Study, we will devise a screen that will identify high risk/PD offenders from that database. The calibration tests in our proposal will be the Hosmer-Lemeshow test recommended in Royston s paper. The discriminate statistics will be the area under the receiver operating curve (AUC value) also mentioned in that paper. An important concern in the development of these models is the potential for over fitting, in particular when the model is developed and assessed on the same sample, as mentioned by Royston et al. To overcome this potential problem, we proposed three methods for model validation: (1) leave-one out; (2) split-samples and (3) new sample from the NOMS. Method (1) is a typical internal assessment and a standard procedure within SPSS that is developed particularly for this purpose. Method (2), although an option in our proposal, provides one or several random subsamples that were not used in developing the model but only for testing purpose. However, if Method (1) works well we do not need to use Method (2). This is why we stated leave-one-out OR split samples… will be performed when appropriate in the proposal. The Method (3) was promoted by Royston et al who stated Validation should be done on a different data from that used to develop the model, preferably from patients in other centres . The NOMS administrative dataset is the best resource for this purpose as this will have a sufficient sample size to validate the model. To optimise the performance of the screen, a series of cut-offs of the screen will be assessed for their sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV. Having developed the screen, preliminary testing of the acceptability of different cut-offs will be carried out with our PPI focus group and other relevant stakeholders. The cost implications of the screening programme will be analysed through a detailed examination of the costs of the screen itself in terms of development costs and offender manager time and the potential cost implications of identifying different numbers of PD offenders with differing needs. The cost implications of PPV and NPV will be discussed during the development grant phase but will not be fully analysed due to resource constraints. Our programme grant intends to develop, evaluate and implement best evidence user-involved care planning through the development of a training package. We will assess the clinical and cost effectiveness, feasibility and acceptabtability of this through a cluster randomised controlled trial. If results are positive we will implement our model of training across two NHS sites. To achieve our aim we propose four inter-related work streams which will:1) Develop a user and carer focussed model of involving users and carers in their own care plan. 2) Develop and deliver a training package to mental health professionals which focuses on involving users and carers in their care plan.3) Evaluate the clinical and cost effectivness, feasibility and acceptability of the training package through a cluster randomised controlled trial. 4) Implement the training package across two NHS Mental Health Trusts.II. Background to the proposed research programme, including NHS context and relevant literature.Involving and allowing service users choice in their own care and hence recovery is at the centre of policy initatives aimed at improving quality of care. This principle is enshrined and prioritised in healthcare [1, 2] and particularly mental healthcare policy and guidelines [3, 4]. Current guidance states that the outcome of any assessment will be a care plan developed with the patient, the professional/member of the care team and other appropriate parties, such as family/carer [5, 6]. Mental health nurses, allied health and social care workers provide the majority of care for service users regardless of setting. They have a pivotal role in the development of care planning, particularly as care co-ordinators under the Care Programme Approach (CPA) systems [5, 6]. Despite the rhetoric of involving users and carers in their care this is not reflected in the clinical reality. Abstract: The key outputs will be: Preliminary field work in Site 1 Establish absorptive capacity for co-production at research sites Develop training programme and curriculum Pilot co-production in practice Optimise the logistics for the project Further develop research network Establish second case site Output 1: Preliminary field work in Site 1 We will conduct ethnographic fieldwork with 5 cases, and the ethnographic study of a call centre to gain a better understanding of the types of conditions and problems that people with complex multi-morbidity, and their carers, face day-to-day and the challenges in providing ALTs to support them. Setting This research will be based in Newham, and participants will be recruited via the community care teams at East London NHS Foundation Trust (ELFT). ELFT provides services for older people with memory and mental health issues which are focused on supporting individuals to stay independent in their own home. The services are provided through the Community Mental Health Team for Older People, Community Dementia Care Team, Diagnostic Memory Clinic, Intermediate Care for Older People and a range of In-Patient mental health services. Sample strategy The research will include five older people (index case) and their carers, with different levels of severity in cognitive impairment (including sub-clinical memory loss, mild cognitive impairment and mild, moderate and severe dementia) and a physical or chronic illness. Participants will be purposefully selected to present different health conditions, family settings and ethnic and social backgrounds. As in our previously successful ATHENE study, we will pay meticulous attention to the ethics of informed consent and assent, and follow published guidance for working with people with reduced capacity in this regard. The cases will include people with mild dementia who will give consent or assent directly, as well as those with more severe dementia for whom proxy consent will be sought from the primary carer following standard COREC guidance, according to a protocol previously approved by Harrow Research Ethics Committee for the ATHENE study. Design Qualitative data will be collected longitudinally for each case using ethnographic methods (including semi-structured and narrative interviews, observations, home tours and cultural probes). Each participant will be visited on up to six occasions over a 6 month period. During the first home visit, the purpose of the project will be explained to participants and they will be asked to consider taking part. During the second home visit, semi-structured and narrative interviews will be conducted, used adaptively between participants and carer(s) depending on the index individual s capacity and preferences, and focusing on routines, health, social support networks, technology and problems they experience. At the end of the interview, participants will be provided with cultural probe tools. On the third visit (approximately one week later) the cultural probe materials will be reviewed as part of a longer interview (e.g. we will look at any photographs with the participants and invite them to tell us why they took the pictures). Following the interview, a home tour will be conducted, in which the participants show the researcher different areas of their home to prompt further discussion about what they do and problems they face. Up to three subsequent home visits will take place over a 6 month period (which will be agreed between the volunteer participants and researcher). We will pilot the use of cultural probe materials to capture ethnographic data between these visits. Key objectives are: To check the practicability of data extraction with the different GP systems To check the accuracy of coded data for the primary clinical outcome (proportion of people (≥5yrs) with active asthma who have unscheduled asthma-related healthcare during the year after the trial). Award_Title: COPD in primary care: from case finding to improving patient outcomes
Abstract: BackgroundCOPD is an important health problem, accounting for significant health service and societal costs. However the natural history and factors affecting prognosis are poorly understood and interventions for early disease are limited. There is also considerable underdiagnosis, resulting in potential unmet need. In the UK there is interest in identifying these missing cases with diverse local initiatives, but no evidence of the most efficient approach. This programme comprises 4 workpackages (WP) to address some of these issues. Aims & objectivesThe overall aim is to set up a primary care COPD cohort including the full range of disease severity, as a platform for testing novel health service interventions. Specifically to:1. Ascertain the cost-effectiveness of the addition of active case finding, compared with opportunistic-only case finding for COPD in primary care (WP1)2. Test the validity of existing COPD prognostic indices in a primary care COPD population and develop an improved prognostic index (WP2)3. Identify factors associated with employment, absenteeism and presenteeism among those with COPD of working age (WP3)4. Assess feasibility and benefits of formal occupational health assessment among those with poor work performance (WP3)5. Assess feasibility and acceptability of a pilot intervention to promote home-based exercise among COPD patients with mild dyspnoea and mild/moderate airflow obstruction (WP4)Research plans & outputsWP1 is a randomised controlled trial to compare the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of active versus opportunistic case finding for COPD. This will inform national policy on the most efficient approach to identifying clinically relevant cases, who can benefit from evidence based management.WP2 is the inception of the COPD cohort with 3-yr follow-up to investigate prognosis. New cases identified through WP1 will be invited to participate. In addition, all adults with documented COPD diagnosis from practices will be invited, with the aim of recruiting 2000 in total. Baseline measures will be undertaken with 6-monthly follow up for at least 3 years. A better understanding of factors that determine prognosis, particularly those that are modifiable, is essential for informing patient management decisions, and facilitating doctor patient relationships. Thus a number of prognostic indices have been developed, based on people with more advanced COPD. We will use the data collected for the cohort to examine the validity of these indices in a primary care COPD population and modify or develop a more appropriate index. This will benefit patient management in primary care, where the majority of COPD patients are cared for. The well characterised cohort will also form a platform for other health service related research within this programme and in future.A significant proportion of those with COPD are of working age, but unemployment and absenteeism rates are higher than in the general population. WP3 will use data from the cohort to examine the relationship between COPD severity and employment, occupational performance and productivity. This will inform management of COPD in workplaces, and who should be targeted for workplace interventions. A sample of patients with COPD with poorer work performance will take part in a feasibility study with an occupational health assessment and recommendations aimed at improving performance. This will inform whether such intervention has potential benefit and is feasible.Currently there are relatively few effective interventions for those with mild/moderate CODP. WP4 will focus on this group, conducting an exploratory trial to assess the feasibility and acceptability of increasing physcial activity. This will inform a future definitive trial to assess the effectiveness of the intervention in modifying disease. Abstract: Our aim is to determine if screening for AF is effective and cost effective in reducing stroke and other key outcomes (both harm and benefit) compared to current practice. Our objectives are to: 1. Determine if screening for AF (including paroxysmal AF) is feasible in general practice in people aged 65 and over using a hand-held ECG recorder (Zenicor) 2. Perform an internal pilot cluster randomised controlled trial (RCT) to: -decide whether to proceed to an end-point powered cluster RCT -quantify psychological harms from screening -refine our screening programme 3. Perform a cluster RCT to determine if offering screening for AF (including paroxysmal AF) leads to reduced stroke and to quantify impact on mortality, cardiovascular disease and serious haemorrhage 4. Perform parallel qualitative studies to inform how to optimise screening both in the trial and if implemented nationally 5. Determine whether screening is cost effective Background 10% of ischaemic stroke is associated with newly diagnosed AF and a further 20% of ischaemic strokes are associated with known but untreated or undertreated AF. AF meets many of the classic criteria for screening, but there are weaknesses in the evidence base as identified by the UK Screening Committee. Uptake of anticoagulation is sub-optimal; screen-detected AF may have better prognosis than AF detected through routine clinical practice; and cost-effectiveness analyses (that consistently find that screening is cost-effective) have to make critical assumptions without RCT data on the effect of AF screening on stroke or mortality. An RCT powered to determine the impact of screening on clinical end-points such as stroke and mortality will resolve this controversy. After a one-off screen, participants will be invited to check their heart rhythm using the ECG recorder over a two week period. We will test different recruitment methods (opportunistic; invitation sent by practice; patient invited to contact practice) with the aim of screening up to 400 patients per practice over a six month period. We will record key process criteria: proportion who consent to take part; proportion who complete both one-off and paroxysmal AF screening; proportion with AF identified; and use the results to refine the target population by reporting these in age strata. In an internal pilot, we will randomise larger practices (list size >7000) - 10 to screening and 20 to usual care. Prior to randomisation, we will send an information sheet and consent form to 800 patients in each practice that meet the inclusion criteria. Baseline data will be obtained from the GP electronic medical record in people who give consent. We will flag records with NHS digital for mortality and Hospital Episode Statistics (HES), and link with national stroke and myocardial infarction audits (SSNAP and MINAP). After twelve months, we will obtain data on new diagnoses of AF and use of anticoagulation from the GP electronic medical record. We will send postal questionnaires to a sample of 1,700 participants to assess psychological effects of screening. Key outcomes will be: AF detection rate; anticoagulation uptake rate, stratified by stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc score) and by AF type (paroxysmal or permanent). Parallel qualitative work (see WP3) will be carried out in both the feasibility and internal pilot to inform the design of the screening intervention.
