Test how the public’s views on policies change according to whether people know more about the policies’ impact 7. Use a computer programme – TriplePC (Public Policy Preference Calculator) – to predict the health impact of policies based on work in the other parts of the project 8. Look at whether there is a single way of measuring each part of the model of impact that should be used in research. There are many different questions that measure a person’s health – some give better evidence than others but cost more to use or take too long to answer Patient and public involvement (PPI): Citizen engagement in communities in Tyneside, Bradford, London and Wales have shaped this project, its understanding of how welfare may affect health and what may or may not be acceptable to communities. We will form a PPI Lived Experience Panel to guide experts on what evidence matters to people who are affected by welfare policies. Dissemination: We will produce an accessible visual model, journal articles and an online computer program for use by policymakers and the public. We will hold a conference and meet with our network of policymakers. This includes regional mayors, civil servants, and politicians from all parties.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare public health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Police involvement in interagency crisis mental health first response pathways in England: A realist and cost consequence analysis. PIONEER-MH.
Abstract: Why is this research needed? People experiencing a mental health crisis are highly distressed and need urgent support. The Police have often been relied on to respond, as they respond quickly and can use the Mental Health Act in public places (Section 136) to maintain everyone’s safety. When police and mental health staff respond together, outcomes improve, and people report receiving compassionate responses. Street Triage services are services where the police, mental health services (and sometimes ambulance) respond together. Street triage is delivered in different ways by telephone or response cars, often when a crisis happens in a public place. Resource pressures and doubts about the role of the police in mental health crises has led to police forces in England adopting a new ‘Right Care, Right Person’ policy. This policy limits Police involvement to mental health situations where there is a risk to life or a crime, but may still include Street Triage. It is unclear what impact this new Policing policy will have on crisis services or people in crisis, especially where there are other factors to consider such as living situation, ethnicity, or complex health needs. What is the research aim? The research aims to identify the impact of the new policing policy on the cost of crisis services and explain what works, who it works for and why. What research will be done? The project will be delivered over 32 months in 4 study sites in England, chosen because they involve the police, ambulance, voluntary sector and mental health services in crisis responses in different ways and include individuals with diverse living situations and ethnicity. The research includes a realist evaluation with a cost consequence analysis delivered in 3 workstreams: Workstream 1:A realist analysis will identify initial theories about how and why services work, using interviews and focus groups with 60 people (police, ambulance, mental health staff, people with lived experience) and policy documents. Initial theories will be discussed in 2 workshops with 40 stakeholders. Workstream 2:The initial theories will be tested using routine health and police data collected from NHS, police and the voluntary sector, before and after the introduction of the new policing policy. Interviews or focus groups with 160 people with experience receiving or delivering crisis services will also be conducted. A series of workshops with 40 stakeholders will be used to validate the theories and co-design guidance for service development. Workstream 3: Using service data, the costs and consequences of the new policing policy on crisis services will be calculated for each study site and compared across study sites. How will lived experience (PPI) be involved? A PPI lead with lived experience will coordinate PPI work across all study activity, involving 24 PPI partners and 4 peer researchers. Training and mentorship will be offered, and PPI will be evaluated. Dissemination and impact plans will be co-created and delivered with PPI partners to maximise access to and use of the research findings. What will the research change and how? The findings will inform guidance to people who design and pay for crisis services to ensure services include the best and most affordable aspects of crisis care with the new policing policy. The findings will be shared through academic papers, webinars, social media and lay summaries in different formats such as audio visual and translated versions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare public health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Implementing relational continuity in general practice - understanding who needs it, when, to what extent, how and why: a realist review
Abstract: Aim of our research Relational continuity of care (RCC) means seeing the same clinician over time. Our research will explore why, when and for which groups of patients and clinicians RCC matters. We also want to understand the best ways of delivering RCC within general practice at a time of extreme pressures. What do we know already? Evidence shows many benefits of RCC within general practice. Patients who see the same clinician over time and trust them are more likely to take part in decisions about their care and have better care experiences. RCC is linked to fewer hospital attendances and emergency department visits and a reduced risk of death. Despite such benefits, it is not clear who needs RCC the most and how to make it happen in busy general practice. NHS general practice has been changing. Practices have bigger teams and more patients. They also have fewer qualified general practitioners (GPs) than before. These changes have made seeing the same clinician more difficult. According to the NHS GP survey in 2023, only 16% of patients were able to see their preferred GP most of the time. What will we do? We are going to review the current evidence. We will search journals, public sector reports and policy documents. We will find out how RCC can be achieved, for which patients and which clinicians it matters, and why. We will also get feedback and advice about our research and findings by talking to patients, clinicians and managers. We will hear about what they think we should focus on in our review and whether what we are finding makes sense to them. This information will help us design our research better and help us to create appropriate advice and guidance for patients and the NHS. Patient and public involvement (PPI) Our team includes two PPI colleagues. They helped us shape this proposal. Our PPI group will include eight additional members from different backgrounds and experiences. We will work closely with our PPI group. We will meet with them at least five times throughout the project. We will support and value them. We will give them any training or extra information they need. How will we share our findings? We will work closely with patients, clinicians, managers and decision makers to make sure our findings are relevant and useful. We will talk about our work at healthcare events and conferences. We will employ professionals to produce easy to understand summaries that we can share through social media, with the public and with those who design, deliver and influence GP services. We will publish our study findings in medical journals. We will also hold two events to share the findings with patients, communities, managers and clinicians. Findings from the research will be used to improve services for patients. It will also help people, like government ministers, who make decisions about the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Assessing the potential of a women only, gender- and trauma-informed residential rehabilitation pathway for drug dependent women leaving prison
Abstract: Female prisoners are more likely than male prisoners to use Class A drugs. They frequently commit crimes to support their drug use. When they are sent to prison, they often ask for help with their drug use. But many women leave prison without a plan or the right support to stay off drugs and most do not even have a safe place to live. Women can find drug treatment services that accept both men and women difficult, because of their experiences of trauma and violence. So it is possible that women-only residential rehabilitation (WORR) might work better. WORR can provide special women-centred support, safe housing, and help with other issues like trauma, mental health, and finding a job. We aim to find out if moving women directly from prison to WORR can support their recovery from drug use, helping both them and their children live better lives. This research will look at drug treatment for women in prison and after they have been released. We aim to find out if WORR is the best place to support women after prison. We'll work with drug services and the women who use these services who will do the research with us. As well as long-term recovery from drug use, we'll also look at other ways the women’s lives have got better such as work, relationships with children and their health. First, we need to figure out whether we can do a randomised controlled trial (RCT). In an RCT, women would go to either WORR or to their usual treatment and then we would compare who gets on best out of the two groups. Because we know that RCTs are hard to get right, we are going to do a feasibility study first. This will help us work out whether an RCT is the best way to test whether going from prison to WORR is the most effective way to support women leaving prison and trying to give up drugs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Understanding the intersectional barriers to adopting digital healthcare in rural Scotland
Abstract: We are now being offered the chance to speak to a Doctor, Nurse or Counsellor on our phone and by video, rather than in person. There are also many apps and devices that can support people’s health. This is really useful for people who live a long way from a hospital or GP practice. However, in these remote areas the connection to the internet may not be reliable. In Scotland more than a third of households in rural areas do not have high speed internet. Six percent of households in rural coastal communities do not even have reliable mobile phone coverage. We know that some people living in rural and coastal areas have poorer health than those living in cities meaning that accessing healthcare services is even more important. But, to use digital healthcare services you need to be able to pay for the devices and internet needed and have the skills and confidence to use them. Having the needed skills, confidence and finances is also connected to our wider financial and social circumstances such as ethnicity, employment and age. Charities have stepped in to help people with accessing digital services, but because each individuals and areas circumstances are different many workarounds have been developed. In this research project we will work with people who lack reliable internet access (for any reason). We will work with two charities to help us find and involve these people in the project, who will include Gypsies, Roma and Travellers. First, we will speak with each person to learn about their circumstances and experiences with accessing digital healthcare without reliable internet. We know that this may be upsetting to discuss which is why we want to speak with each person individually. These conversations will help us to understand how barriers to accessing digital services add to or make worse the other barriers people face in life. We will also identify some commonly experienced situations where lack of reliable internet made accessing healthcare difficult. Those experiencing these common situations and the people and organisations (including charities) who support them will be invited to take part in some workshops. During these workshops we will draw out the situation and the workarounds people have been using. There will be 6 of these workshops, some with different groups of people, some with the same people but focusing on different situations. The workshops will take place in the communities without reliable internet access. We will be looking for workarounds that make a difference to people’s health and could help people in similar circumstances in different parts of the UK and world. These workarounds will be the focus of a future research project that we will have developed with the patients, public and stakeholders who took part in this first project. The people and organisations who we will have worked with on the project will form the partnerships for the next research project. From this research project we will help the people developing digital healthcare to understand the combinations of barriers to using their services people experience. We will also map the people and services that are involved with supporting people without reliable internet access to use digital healthcare.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Award_Title: The Digitalisation of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare: Black Women’s Inclusion and Exclusion in Prevention, Services and Care (Midlands and London)
Abstract: The aim of this project is to conduct a widespread community-led scoping exercise on Black women’s intersectional experiences of being included or excluded in the digitalisation of British sexual and reproductive healthcare; including but not limited to sex, maternal health, HIV, menopause, menstruation and puberty. The project aims to contribute to existing research and narratives on health inequalities and digital exclusion amongst disadvantaged groups in the UK. We focus on Black women’s sexual and reproductive healthcare experiences with digital health due to reported inequalities and national calls to action in maternal care. The project directly speaks to the call set by National Healthcare Inequalities Improvement Programme (HiQiP); to mitigate against digital exclusion. This project will use Birmingham and Solihull Sexual and Reproductive Health Strategy 2023-2030 as a tool to identify priority groups of Black women, in marginalised communities. The project will also identify socio-economic determinants impacting transitions to remote healthcare and identify shared common experiences which will offer community-reared interventions to limit barriers to engagement. Black African communities (BACs) and Black Caribbean communities (BCCs) experience some of the worse healthcare outcomes in the UK. The burden of health inequalities experienced by Black people, due to racialised discrimination and prejudice, are disproportionately suffered in all areas of medicine and public health. Reports on Black Maternal Health (2023) and racial disparities within sexual and reproductive health (SRH) amongst Black people living in the UK, has ushered recent attention for further research into racialised health concerns and anti-racist initiatives. Black women experience some of the worst sexual and reproductive health outcomes, and inequalities have widened during the Coronavirus pandemic. Furthermore, people of Black African and Black Caribbean heritage are underrepresented in research institutions and therefore have less power over the way in which research evidence is produced or how digital health interventions are designed (Jenkins et al. 2022). This project seeks to address this problem and develop new ways of partnering and engaging Black communities in addressing the impact digitalisation has on sexual and reproductive healthcare inequalities. Additionally, due to a lack of effective involvement of members of BACs and BCCs in health care, research and public health, many health-related interventions fail to reach BACs and BCCs. Digital interventions are no different. Though scholarship addressing digital health disparities and divide are emerging, little (if any) has Black women’s health experiences, as a priority. Shared experiences of learning and engagement will guide our involvement strategies through evidence and community teaching. Our intention is to inclusively seek members of the community who historically are reluctant to engage in health or social initiatives or ‘hard-to-reach' due to accessibility or circumstances. We will explore a range of methods used to engage with each community group and review best practice. The learning gained from the mapping exercise will support the development of applications for further funding for research and interventions on the impact of the digitalisation of healthcare on health inequalities for Black women more generally.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Contractor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Evaluating the indoor environment, health, carbon emission, and economic outcomes of retrofitting social housing properties to improve energy efficiency in a low-income multi-ethnic population: a quasi-experimental study with process evaluation
Abstract: Why are we doing this research? Housing is important for our health. Homes can be uncomfortable and unhealthy if they are too cold or too hot. If they don’t get enough fresh air they may have problems with damp, mould, and indoor pollution. These problems can increase stress and the risk of lung and heart problems. By improving homes through retrofitting—making them more energy efficient and comfortable—many of these health problems could be prevented. Using less energy also lowers fuel bills and helps cut down on carbon emissions, helping the environment. Housing in the UK is in worse condition compared to many other European countries. The Government is working to retrofit social housing (‘Council housing’, which is one in every five UK homes) to make them more energy efficient in the hope it will help both people’s health and the environment. However, retrofitting could have unexpected effects. For example, making homes too airtight might reduce the amount of fresh air, which could make problems like damp, mould, and indoor pollution worse. We need to understand the pros and cons of retrofitting to help make decisions about whether this is a good thing to do. Our aim is to understand how retrofitting social housing in Bradford affects health, the quality of the indoor environment (for example, warmth or indoor pollution), and whether it is value for money. We will focus on five areas: 1. Indoors: We will use sensors to collect temperature, humidity (air dampness), and indoor pollution in 210 homes that are retrofitted and compare the results to 210 similar homes that are not. This will be done over 18 months, over two winters. We will ask residents about their energy use, comfort levels, and health. 2. Health: We will track health data from GPs and hospitals over five years to see whether residents in 6,500 retrofitted homes have different mental, lung, and heart health compared to those living in non-retrofitted homes. 3. Environment: We will look at how factors such as the age of the building, its type (for example, flat or detached), and residents' behaviour (for example, the temperature they set their thermostat), affect carbon emissions. This will help us figure out which types of homes should be retrofitted first to have the biggest impact on the environment. 4. Value for money: We will compare the costs of retrofitting homes with the potential money saved for the NHS and the economy. This will help us see if retrofitting homes is a good way to spend public money. 5. Community views: We will talk to residents and people involved in retrofitting homes to work out what worked, what didn’t, and any surprises. Their feedback will give us useful insights into the retrofitting process. These findings will help create recommendations for the Government, social housing providers, and housing developers. Our goal is to make sure that retrofitting has the best chance of benefitting both health and the environment. We will share our results through easy-to-understand summaries, reports, meetings, and media coverage. How will we involve the public? Residents will take part as 'co-researchers,' helping us gather information for the study. We will also set up a group of residents to guide us in planning and carrying out the research. This way, the community's views will be at the heart of our work.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Evaluating the impact of major income support policies on health inequalities across the life course: a micro-macro linked modelling study (MicMac)
Abstract: Money has big effects on health. Richer people often live longer and have fewer health problems. Money is a major driver of health inequalities - the poorer health outcomes experienced by disadvantaged social groups. Child poverty is a particularly important disadvantage that has lifelong health impacts. The amount of money people have can be affected by government policies and how the economy is performing, particularly how many jobs are available and changes in the price of essential goods. A nation’s health, economy, and government policies are linked in complex and sometimes unexpected ways. The NIHR previously funded our team to develop a project looking at how new government policies on wages, tax, and benefits can reduce health inequalities. We talked to people experiencing poverty, relevant charities, and people working in government. They gave their views on policies that could reduce health inequalities in the UK. People were interested in policies that give a fixed amount of money regularly (called a Basic Income) and increasing the National Living Wage. That project found broad policy areas to focus on, but specific details are debated. For example, a Basic Income can be paid to everyone at the same level or vary based on need. Such details affect policy costs and benefits. Continuing public and policymaker involvement will decide specific details of policies that we will investigate. New income policies may change the behaviour of individuals and employers in complex ways which cannot be analysed using typical research approaches (like trials). For example, giving people money could cause prices to increase or change how many jobs are available. Computer simulations can be used when trials are not possible. We will use this method to test how policy changes would affect health inequalities and compare the costs and benefits over the long term. Our research team has an existing computer simulation for the short-term health impacts of changes in wages, tax, and benefits for people aged 25 to 64, this is our micro model. This has shown that some policies have the potential to end poverty but are very costly and the health benefits depend heavily on job impacts. To provide a fuller picture, we will extend the model to younger and older age groups and study long-term impacts. This is important as these age groups can be more affected by poverty, so the benefits of policies could be larger and take longer to appear. Reducing child poverty would lead to a healthier and better educated future workforce. Likewise, richer pensioners may need less costly healthcare. We must also think about how policies could change the economy in different parts of the UK. To do this, we will build and test another computer simulation to predict the number of jobs available and level of wages in each region, this is our macro model. We will then link our micro model to the macro model. Doing this will give a fuller picture of the complex ways health and the economy interact and change due to government policies. The linked micro-macro model for the UK will address an evidence gap by comparing the costs and benefits of new policies over the long term. This will help policymakers find ways to improve people’s health by changing their income. Our new models will be freely available to researchers and policymakers, allowing further policies to be explored.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Public Health Intervention Responsive Studies Team: PHIRST REACH
Abstract: Background and aims: ‘PHIRST REACH’ (Responsive Evaluation and Analytics for Community Health) brings together experts in public health, local and national policy and evaluation methods from the Universities of York, Leeds and Bradford Institute of Health Research with public health practitioners and members of the public. As a team we have many years of experience working on local authority evaluations that have positively supported healthy living and environments. Examples include rapid research in school and community services, covid vaccination hesitancy, food insecurity, planning and environment and retail policies. The aim of PHIRST REACH is to deliver high quality, timely evaluations that meet the needs of each local authority and inform decision making around effective use of resources. Importantly, we will use a collaborative, place-based approach, where we engage with each local authority and members of the public throughout the process. Methods: When we receive a project, we will quickly assemble a team of public health and methods specialists and community representatives to lead on the evaluation. Working collaboratively with the local authority, we will assess whether their research question is realistic, before co-developing an evaluation plan involving local community members and relevant local authority team members. As the project could be geographically anywhere, we have made plans to combine face-to-face and remote working. Our experience tells us that rapid evaluation of local services often comes with challenges, including access to data and communities, in addition to ethical and privacy hurdles. We will overcome these through regular and transparent conversations, building relationships and trust with all parties. Public Involvement and Engagement (PIE): We will work with local PIE groups where available to guide our research and outputs. Where these do not exist, we will work with the local authority and our well-established and diverse PIE group local to us to develop new PIE groups and, where needed, provide training and mentoring. Active co-production will be embedded throughout the evaluation, including training members of the public to undertake data collection and help understand and share findings through methods such as ‘citizen science’. All PIE activities are supported by a named and experienced person within our team and we include a member of our core team who is a public representative. Additionally, one of our oversight groups will be public facing. Our approach to involving and engaging local communities will use established principles that we have co-developed to ensure a diverse range of voices are heard via power sharing, welcoming perspectives, respecting lived experience, benefits for all parties, flexible working, building relationships and provision of adequate resources (based on three underlying values of equality, reciprocity and agency). Dissemination and impact: We will produce accessible, timely reports to share findings for each project evaluation. Brief reports and infographics will be provided, but will be accompanied with enough detail to allow for local authorities to make informed evidence-based decisions. We will share targeted outputs in a variety of formats to other audiences, including other policy makers, academics and the general public to maximise the impacts from our learning.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the wider determinants of health
Award_Title: Investigating Access to Health and Social Care and Mental Health in Informal Carers: The Role of Marginalised Socioeconomic Status and Digital Poverty
Abstract: Research questions: What factors impede or support the access of socio-economically disadvantaged informal carers to health and social care services, and how does this access affect carer mental health outcomes? How does digital poverty influence the mental health outcomes of these carers? Background: In 2021-2022, 10.5% of UK citizens were providing unpaid informal care, saving the government £162bn annually. Most carers reside in high-deprivation areas, where access to appropriate health and social care services is more limited. Previous studies indicate that carers are more prone to depression, anxiety, and stress-related physical symptoms, and these negative outcomes may be higher among socio-economically disadvantaged carers. The shift of some health and social care services online, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic and combined with 'digital poverty', may exacerbate difficulties with accessing health and social care support, potentially increasing unmet needs and burden among socioeconomically disadvantaged carers. Aims: The aim is to understand how informal carers with marginalised socioeconomic status (SES) (defined as low/no income or receipt of benefits) access existing health and social care services, and the impact this has on their mental health. The second aim of the project is to explore how potential digital poverty may shape caregiver mental health outcomes. Method: A systematic literature review will identify barriers and facilitators of accessing health and social care by informal caregivers, the impact of access/non-access on mental health, stratified by carer SES and care-recipient's health conditions. This will be followed by a qualitative photovoice study to explore carers' experiences of accessing health and social care and the effects of digital poverty, analysed through critical discourse analysis. The findings obtained from these two studies will inform a survey (N > 300) examining how factors underpinning access to health and social care are related to informal carers' mental health as moderated or mediated by the caregiver SES, caregiver's perceptions of access to health and social care and of digital poverty. Timelines for delivery: The systematic review will be finalised and prepared for publication in the first year. In the second year, the qualitative photovoice study will be completed. The exploratory mixed-method survey will be completed and disseminated in the third year. Anticipated impact and dissemination: We will find out if and how informal carers with a marginalised socioeconomic background access health and social care services. This timely and novel study will give us evidence to identify better ways to support informal carers and address key objectives of the Integrated Care System (ICS), which aims to foster closer cooperation between health and social care services and communities. This study will offer us a unique opportunity to develop an evidence-based health promotion model for these carers showing how to mitigate existing pathways of health inequalities., Through the identification of factors that underpin the access to support services Recommendations will be generated based on key findings and shared with researchers, clinicians, and policymakers via academic publications, conferences, exhibitions of carers' photographs, carer forums with NHS Trust(s), writing blogs, and reaching out to relevant Integrated Care Boards.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Award_Title: Health, socioeconomic, and environmental risk factors for heat-related mortality and hospital admission in England
Abstract: Background Climate change is causing increasingly frequent and intense heat events worldwide. In England, we are already witnessing the impact of extreme heat on population health, with 3,000 excess deaths due to heat in 2022. Our ability to adapt to heat and protect the most vulnerable is impaired by limited understanding of the health, socioeconomic, and environmental risk factors for heat-related adverse outcomes. Aims My research aims to (1) create a dataset linking health, climate, social, and environmental data; (2) identify health, socioeconomic, and environmental risk factors for heat-related mortality and hospital admission, and (3) translate my research into public health interventions. Methods My research will be organised in three work packages: WP1: Linking health, social, environmental, and climate data (Y1-Y2) I will link primary and secondary healthcare data from the NHS for about 57 million people between 2020 and 2024 with socioeconomic data based on the index of multiple deprivation, and occupation from Census 2021; environmental data, including housing and living conditions data from Census 2021, and satellite-derived green space indices; and climate data from the Met Office. Data will be linked by NHS number or residence address within the NHS and Office for National Statistics secure data environments. WP2: Identifying risk factors for heat-related death and hospital admission (Y2-Y4) I will use a case-crossover design and conditional binominal regression to investigate heat-related mortality and hospital admission considering pre-defined thresholds of temperature and humidity. I will conduct subgroup analyses for different health (e.g., chronic diseases, medications), socioeconomic (e.g., occupation, deprivation), and environmental (e.g., accommodation type, proximity to green space) risk factors and their combinations. WP3: Translating my research into public health interventions (Y4-Y5) I will work with my stakeholders to translate my research into practical interventions that protect population health and inform public policy. For instance, I will work with NHS England to enable personalised alerts and advice to be sent via the NHS app to individuals with risk factors for heat-related adverse events; the Met Office and the UK Health Security Agency to update the Adverse Weather Health Plan considering high-risk populations; the Office for National Statistics to develop indicators of health impact to inform national and local climate policy. Impact and dissemination To ensure that my research is implemented, I will reach out to all stakeholders, with whom I have engaged to design my research. My research will benefit the public directly by providing information about risk factors and recommending protective behaviours, and indirectly by helping public health and NHS systems protect the most vulnerable in the population. By enhancing our understanding of health, socioeconomic, and environmental risk factors, my research will help local authorities, voluntary and community sector organisations, and national agencies target their communications and supportive interventions to high-risk individuals. The extensive data linkage developed by my research will enable further research, thus benefiting the scientific community. I will disseminate my findings in scientific publications and conferences and engagement with the public and stakeholders, through newspapers, social media, press releases, workshops, and science festivals.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: PRImary care Streptococcal Management study (PRISM)
Abstract: Rapid streptococcal (strep.) antigen detection tests (RADTs) have the potential to halve antibiotic prescribing for sore throat. The existing diagnostic evidence is limited by spectrum bias (little evidence from typical primary care populations), and sampling bias (simultaneous well taken throat swabs only achieve 85% sensitivity when compared to each other). One alternative to RADTs are clinical decision rules: of the currently available rules the Centor criteria as the simplest and most widely used. The first phase of this study will a)assess the accuracy of available RADTs vs the throat swab in a clinical sample b) estimate sampling bias from in vitro studies. Phase II will compare management using the best RADT defined from phase I with both a clinical scoring rule (Centor criteria or the rule from phase I), and with delayed antibiotic prescribing Objectives: 1) To assess which RADTs is the most accurate in predicting the presence of group A streptococcus by the throat swab in a clinical sample from primary care 2) To estimate the error from sampling bias by performing parallel standardised in vitro studies on the accuracy of the five tests 3) To assess the validity of a scoring system based on the throat swab as the reference standard (such as the Centor criteria) in a UK population 4) To assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of rapid tests when compared to a clinical scoring rule and delayed antibiotic prescription 5) To explore the impact of RADT use on GP prediction accuracy, and treatment decisions

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) in pregnancy - SNAP
Abstract: Maternal smoking during pregnancy is a major public health problem, accounting for around 4,000 foetal deaths in the UK annually. It causes significant postnatal morbidity and mortality through low birth weight, pre-term birth, sudden infant death syndrome and asthma. Maximising the effectiveness of smoking cessation interventions for pregnant smokers is, therefore, important. Current best practice in non-pregnant smokers is to offer behavioural support and either nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) or bupropion. Bupropion is contraindicated in pregnancy, however, and although guidance to health professionals recommends that NRT can be used, the effectiveness of NRT in pregnancy has not been tested in definitive clinical trials. We, therefore, propose this study to determine: i) Whether NRT at conventional doses is effective and cost-effective for smoking cessation in pregnancy. ii) Whether NRT used in pregnancy has any appreciable effect on behavioural and developmental outcomes in subsequent children at two years.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of opportunistic screening and stepped care interventions for older hazardous alcohol users in primary care (AESOPS)
Abstract: The proposed study is a pragmatic randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of opportunistic screening and stepped care interventions for older hazardous alcohol users in primary care. Primary care attendees aged 55 years or over who are consuming alcohol at hazardous levels will be randomised to either minimal intervention or stepped care intervention. Stepped care consists of three successive steps of increasing intensity; behavioural change counselling delivered by a practice nurse, motivational enhancement therapy delivered by a trained therapist and specialist intervention. Progression to successive steps is dependent upon the outcome of each prior step. Outcomes will be measured at baseline, prior to randomisation and then again at 6 and 12 months after randomisation. The primary outcome measure is the quantity of alcohol consumed in standardised drinks, secondary outcome measures include frequency of alcohol consumption, alcohol related problems, quality of life and health utility. Health and social care resource use will be collected at baseline, 6 and twelve months to inform the cost-effectiveness analysis. The sample size of the study requires 500 participants derived from 15 primary care centres in 3 geographical areas of the United Kingdom.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Maximising engagement, motivation and long term change in a structured intensive education programme in diabetes for children, young people and their families: child and adolescent structured competencies approach to diabetes education
Abstract: The intervention is a competency-driven, motivational and patient-centred structured intensive psycho-educational programme specifically designed to improve diabetic control, self-management and quality of life in children and adolescents. CASCADE aims to establish effective delivery and cost effectiveness of a structured intensive education programme using psychological approaches that maximise engagement, motivation and long-term change. A developmentally appropriate curriculum will teach adaptation of insulin dosage, normal eating and management of day to day challenges (e.g. exercise, illness) enabling flexible self management in diverse diabetes regimens. Children and young people (8-16 years) will complete the programme with their families. The primary outcome will be glycosylated haemoglobin (HbA1c) levels 12 months after the intervention. Secondary out-comes will include a 24 month follow up measure of metabolic control in order to evaluate maintenance of the intervention effect, as well as hospital admissions, hypoglycaemic episodes, self-efficacy, diabetes specific quality of life measures, family functioning and measures of emotional and behavioural adjustment 12 and 24 months post intervention. Health economic modelling will establish the cost effectiveness of the intervention and its applicability to the wider NHS. The study will use a multicentre cluster randomised controlled trial with integral process and economic evaluation. The trial and reporting will follow MRC guidelines for clinical trials and CONSORT guidelines. A strong multidisciplinary study team combines the expertise of established clinical and research teams that have a published record in successfully developing clinical research interventions and completion of large scale randomised trials. Our extensive experience in teaching and training will be used to identify the time and resources required to train members of the study centres which will be incorporated into the economic modelling process. The project will use in-post NHS staff to deliver the intervention. Even a small reduction in HbA1c will have an impact on long term risk reduction with potential costs saving to the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: The relative clinical and cost-effectiveness of three contrasting approaches to partner notification for curable sexually transmitted infections (STIs): a cluster randomised trial in primary care
Abstract: "Increasing numbers of patients are diagnosed with sexually transmitted infections (STIs) in their GP surgery. This study is concerned with finding out the best way to enable treatment for the sexual partners of individuals diagnosed with sexually transmited infections (STIs) in their GP practice. This is called ""partner notification"". Treatment of partners is important for two reasons - to protect the original patient from reinfection
Status: and to prevent the further spread of infection by infected partner(s). We will compare three different approaches to partner treatment: (i) PATIENT REFERRAL where patients are simply given information and asked to tell their partner about the problem and the need to be treated. (ii) CONTRACT REFERRAL
Award Budget: in addition to (i)

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Vitamin D and Longevity (ViDAL) trial - randomised feasibility study
Abstract: DESIGN: Cluster randomisation of 20 participating GP practices in 10 matched pairs to inform the design of the main trial (10 to open randomisation between vitamin D3 or no treatment and 10 to double-blind randomisation between vitamin D3 or placebo). Feasibility trial on 1,600 people (average 80 per practice) aged 65-84, with randomisation to 100,000 IU vitamin D3 monthly (equivalent to 3,300 IU/day) of oral vitamin D3 for 2 years (800 subjects), placebo (400 subjects) or no treatment (400 subjects). SETTING: 20 GP practices in England. TARGET POPULATION: Healthy adults 65-84 years of age. Exclusions: life-threatening illness, planning to emigrate within 5 years, known history of sarcoidosis, hyperparathyroidism or nephrolithiasis, known intolerance to vitamin D, hypercalcaemia (corrected serum calcium >2.65 mmol/l), known hepatic or renal failure, currently on cytotoxic therapy, <3 years after diagnosis of any cancer. Informed consent for blood tests (including genetic analyses) and access to all written and electronic medical records and databases, as well as randomisation and flagging for automatic follow-up. HEALTH TECHNOLOGY TO BE ASSESSED: 2.5mg (100,000 IU) vitamin D3 taken monthly for 2 years, randomised double blind v placebo (in 10 practices) or open label v no treatment (in 10 practices). MEASUREMENT OF COSTS AND OUTCOMES: Follow-up for cancer incidence and cause-specific mortality will be obtained by flagging through NHSCR. Incidence of other major diseases, including diseases of the circulatory system, will be obtained by NHS number linkage with Hospital Episode Statistics (HES). A postal questionnaire on foreign holidays, sunbathing, sunbed use and use of vitamin supplements is completed by all participants (treated and control) before randomisation. A blood sample is also taken, and corrected serum calcium is assayed before randomisation to establish eligibility. Aliquots (plasma and buffy coat) are be stored in liquid nitrogen for later analysis of 25(OH)D and (subject to additional funding) genetic studies. A pack of 12 bottles is sent to all participants except the open control group at entry and at 1 year. To minimise follow-up costs, subjects receiving medication (open label vitamin D, unmarked vitamin D, or unmarked placebo) are contacted 3-monthly by email, text message or post (patient choice of medium) requesting a short reply by the same medium to confirm medication compliance, and to report any/no suspected adverse events and any/no planned change of address. Non-compliers and those reporting adverse events or change of address are sent a short questionnaire (email or post) including validated questions on reasons for non-compliance and adverse events. All non-responders are sent one reminder a month later, then telephoned if they have still not replied. A further blood sample and questionnaire will be obtained at the final GP visit 2 years after randomisation to quantify differences in vitamin D status between the intervention and control groups. GP records for the year before entry and the 2 years on the trial will also be extracted (GP visits, prescriptions, infections) on all patients. SAMPLE SIZE: We will recruit 1,600 subjects (800 vitamin D, 800 no treatment) through 20 GP practices. We assume that 80 (~9%) of the patients aged 65-84 in each GP practice will volunteer. The principal aims are to demonstrate feasibility in a representative range of GP practices and to determine the most cost-effective randomisation and follow-up procedures for the main study.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Prevention of Falls Injury Trial
Abstract: Context: Common falls prevention strategies used in primary care settings include advice and information, structured exercise, and multi-factorial risk-reduction programmes. Little is known about the comparative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of these strategies. Objective: To estimate the comparative effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of advice, structured exercise and a multi-factorial fall prevention programme, for the prevention of fall injuries among older people living in the community. Design: A 3-arm, cluster-randomised controlled trial with economic evaluation. The unit of randomisation will be the General Practice, and minimisation will be used to ensure balance in the allocation of practices by list size and area socio-economic status. Population: 9,000 people (60 practices) aged over 70 years living in the community, including people in sheltered accommodation, but excluding people living in nursing or residential care homes. Interventions: Practices will be randomly allocated to one of the trial interventions, which they will adopt as usual care practice for the duration of the trial. The three trial arms interventions are: Advice: We will utilise evidence that, for older people, advice about the positive aspects of treatment (e.g. regaining or improving balance/mobility) as opposed to negative (e.g. falls) is a more acceptable presentation and likely to result in greater uptake. Exercise: We will use the Otago Exercise Program, delivered either on a group basis or at home. The program has a good evidence base in relation to falls, but has not been tested formally in the UK setting. MFFP. We will base MFFP on an existing programme (Tinetti et al., 1994) that is safe and feasible in the community setting. We will undertake an update and consensus building exercise (with members of the British Geriatrics Society) to ensure that the intervention is fully informed. Outcomes: The trial is powered (80%) to detect (p<0.05) a moderate difference in fracture rate, from 6% to 4% (RR 0.67). Peripheral fracture data, aggregated at the practice level, will be sourced from primary care, HES and self-report. Falls and HRQoL (secondary outcomes) will be assessed in random sub-samples of the trial population by postal questionnaire at 4 month intervals.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Observational study to estimate the changes in the efficacy of BCG with time since vaccination
Abstract: Two analytic observational studies will be conducted comparing the frequency of the BCG vaccine in people in people with and without a history of illhealth. Both studies will evaluate how the effect of BCG vaccine changes with time since vaccination. The first study will examine children aged from 0-17 years, born when BCG can be given in infancy. The second study will examine an adult age range from 23 to 37 years and aged 13-years old when the pre-2005 school aged BCG programme existed

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Electronic services: implementation and impact
Abstract: This study will: 1. Develop of a detailed narrative account of the implementation of shared electronic services for older people; 2. Establish the cost-effectiveness of shared electronic services used in hospital discharge processes for older people; 3. Evaluate the implementation of shared electronic patient records in diabetes services across NHS organizations in Yorkshire and Humber SHA. There is good evidence that partnerships involving health, social care and other organizations are difficult to establish in practice. Worse, in responding to demography, technological advances and other forces, health care is becoming ever more complex and expensive, suggesting that effective partnerships may be even more difficult to achieve in future. Electronic networks are increasingly viewed, across Government, as a key tool for achieving integrated service delivery in the face of current challenges. In the NHS the National Programme for Information Technology (IT) is in effect a major infrastructure programme, designed to ensure that all parts of the NHS - and in time social services - can communicate electronically with one another at any time. Local NHS organizations are being provided with some new electronic services, including shared electronic patient records and electronic prescribing services. They are, though, expected to pay for most elements of their local systems. GPs will continue to pay for their practice systems, hospitals for operating theatre and out-patient systems, and so on. At present there is very little empirical evidence about two key issues concerning these large scale electronic networks. The first concerns implementation. A succession of reports in 2006 highlighted the practical difficulties involved in implementation. Published studies have generally focused on specific settings (eg out-patient clinics, GP surgeries) and they do not help policy makers who are trying to understand what helps or hinders implementation. The second issue is cost-effectiveness. There have been many studies of the effectiveness of single, stand-alone systems such as GPs' computer systems. But there have been very few which capture the effects of integrated networked services on health care delivery, and so far as we are aware none at all which report high quality evidence on cost-effectiveness. This study will generate evidence in this under-researched area. A case study design will be used. The study will have three distinct components, which between them will address the key elements in the SDO brief: 1) Observational qualitative study of the implementation of shared electronic patient records across primary, community and secondary care services for older people, over a 12 month period in two sites. 2) Observational study, using qualitative and quantitative methods, to establish the cost-effectiveness of electronic services in co-ordinating hospital discharge for older people in three sites. 3) Quantitative observational study of the effects of the implementation of shared electronic patient records in diabetes care across Yorkshire and Humber SHA.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Commissioning for long term conditions: hearing the voice of and engaging users
Abstract: The aim of this research will be to examine how commissioners enable voice and engagement of people with Long Term Conditions and identify what impact this has on the commissioning process and pattern of services. It will explore the processes and mechanisms by which local patient and representative groups for people with long term conditions engage with the commissioning processes in health and social care agencies. The research will examine in depth three case studies in three long term condition groups - diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and neurological conditions. Our approach involves reviewing practice across the UK and then focussing on three geographical areas to examine practices of commissioning and purchasing health care for people with long term conditions, approaches to patient and public involvement, patterns of services for people with long term conditions and the activities of local patient and voluntary organisations for people with long term conditions. Methods of data collection will include documentary analysis, participant workshops, observation of meetings, focus groups, interviews and the collection of data on service use and patterns of service in the three localities. Our intention is to identify changes in service profiles, changes in investment, changes in service use and clinical verification of actual/potential improvements in patient outcomes. A key outcome of the research will, therefore, be to develop guidance (a ‘road map') for commissioners on the skills and expertise needed by different commissioners, what actions are most likely to lead to responsive services and the most effective mechanisms and processes for active and engaged commissioning for people with long term conditions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Commissioning high quality care for people with long term conditions - an action research study
Abstract: The overall aim of this research is to explore how NHS commissioning can improve care for people living with long-term conditions. In doing this we will examine the organisation and processes of commissioning (such as needs assessment, service planning and specification, design of incentives and performance management) and other influences that are known to shape success (such as local clinical leadership) alongside outcomes. An action research approach will be adopted, with researchers working alongside three ‘commissioning communities' (primary care trusts and other local partner organisations) with a known track record of undertaking competent and innovative commissioning work. Within the three sites, we will focus on long-term condition (LTC) sub-groups, in order to investigate how commissioning does (or does not) work in practice. We draw on three theoretical frameworks to underpin and shape this research: first, the nature and levels of commissioning organisation in the NHS, and the extent of their integration with providers (Smith et al, 2004); second, analysis of the processes of commissioning that extends Ovretveit's (2005) ‘cycle of commissioning'; and third, work by Bate et al (2008) that links descriptive accounts of factors considered to shape success in service improvement effort in health care with a chronological account of commissioning processes and the dynamics of change. Similarly, we will draw on elements of social network theory (Wasserman and Faust, 1994) when observing and mapping relationships between clinical and managerial actors within each commissioning community. The project extends for two years and has three main phases. First, initial site selection, involving identification of ‘high performers' using a set of quantitative metrics combined with seeking the views of experts and then issuing a call for applicants to be part of the study, followed by a period of orientation that takes the form of researchers shadowing key commissioning stakeholders for a period of two weeks. This orientation will inform selection of LTC-oriented sub-groups for within- and cross-case study. Second, fieldwork in the three ‘commissioning communities' will entail observations of commissioning activity, semi-structured interviews with clinicians, managers, and service user/carer representatives, mapping of commissioning relationships, and analysis of a range of routine data. Third, there will be a process of data analysis, synthesis and reporting, including site and cross-project workshops that will both provide feedback on emerging findings and inform subsequent stages of the research. In line with an action research approach, specific objectives within case studies will be negotiated with local stakeholders. We anticipate that these will focus on the research team assessing and supporting local commissioners at key stages in the ‘cycle of commissioning' - the two-year research will encompass a full commissioning cycle and its preceding and subsequent months. We will draw conclusions about how the organisation, processes and incentives within this commissioning cycle can most effectively be aligned when developing services for people with LTCs. The project report will focus on identifying lessons for the NHS and health purchasing more generally, and will include the development of good practice guidance in this area.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Understanding and improving transitions of older people: a user and carer centred approach
Abstract: Despite a series of positive changes following the 2001 National Service Framework for Older People, research and inspection reports continue to reveal that transition between services is one of the most problematic areas of policy and practice. This project seeks to investigate the information, advice and support needs of older people experiencing a transition between services, as well as conducting the research in a way that helps to embed the findings in health and social care policy and practice. Specifically it aims to: - Explore older people's experiences of moving across service boundaries, identifying positive and negative experiences, information and advice needs, access to services and needs for ongoing support. - Identify how the needs of particular groups of older people may differ from each other, and the different needs of service users and carers. - Investigate these issues over time, to illuminate how previous transitions impact on current and future needs. - Draw out policy and practice implications for the way in which services prepare and support older people and their carers for transition between services. - Support, and share the learning from, implementation of project findings in four health and social care communities. The project will be conducted across four case study areas, which will be purposively chosen to reflect different locality characteristics and focusing on different user/carer groups to include: - An area with a high proportion of older people from a minority ethnic community. - A site where the research focuses of the experiences of people with dementia and their families. - A rural area. - An area with a low proportion of older people. Following a participative action research methodology, service users and carers from each area will be recruited, trained and supported to participate as co-researchers. Working with academic project team members, co-researchers will jointly conduct two waves of in-depth interviews to explore the experience of care transitions from a user/carer perspective. In the final stage of the project, a series of feedback and change management activities will be undertaken to facilitate implementation of the research findings into practice, and support a process of learning about how to improve transitions for older people. The project team will work with local advisory groups and stakeholders to co-design the change processes, so that local capability and capacity is enhanced throughout the process and sustained beyond the research period. In addition, a local and national dissemination strategy will be developed to translate the findings into policy recommendations and usable outputs, as well as sharing learning from the case study examples. Given that poorly managed transitions can lead to a worsening of patient health, increased risk of complications and costly additional care, the study has the potential to support both economic and quality gains in the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Transitions between services at the end of life for older people - patient and provider perspectives
Abstract: More than two thirds of the UK population can expect to die when they are aged over 75 years, and the last year of life is a time of high service utilisation for older adults. The NHS End of Life Care programme acknowledges that people will be transferred many times between different settings in their final years, months, days and hours. Hence commissioners need to understand how and why older people make transitions between services, and the relationship between transitions and older people’s health and well-being. This study will consider three conditions, lung cancer, heart failure and stroke, that are the focus of current NHS policy, but differ in their disease trajectories and the provision of specialist end-of-life services. Aim: The aim of this project is to understand the patterns and causes of health service transitions and their association with older people’s experiences at the end of life. Type and location: This is a three-phase study, combining a quantitative analysis of routine linked data, interviews with carers and patients and a qualitative interview study with commissioners and providers of care. The research will take place in the North West and South Central NHS regions of England. Methods of working: Phase one will map transitions into and out of hospital at the end of life for older people in England and estimate the financial costs. Newly linked mortality data and Hospital Episode Statistics for England 2001-2005 will be analysed, identifying factors associated with frequency of admissions before death and patterns of transitions for the three disease groups. Phase two: Retrospective data will be gathered from 90 bereaved carers to explore the effect of the transitions quantified in phase one, on health status, quality of life, symptom control and satisfaction with care for individuals. Carers’ understanding of the aims, appropriateness and consequences of transitions and the decisions underlying them, will be studied using previously validated tools. Interviews with 30 patients will provide insights into their lived experiences of transitions. Phase three consists of an interview study with 40 commissioners and providers of care, selected to represent the pathway from commissioners of health and social care, through the management of services, to care delivery in the home and hospital. Data provided by participants in phase 2 will be summarised into short clinical scenarios representative of differing transition patterns. These will be used to elicit professional understanding of transitions at the end of life, the reasons behind different models of care operating, and the barriers and facilitators to delivering high quality, appropriate services. Outcomes: This study will provide the first national estimate of transitions and hospital resource use in the last year of life, enhance our understanding of patients’ experiences and the consequences of transitions, and provide insights into the perspectives of service commissioners and providers including the challenges that constrain their work. The synthesis of data from the component parts of the study will enable us to clarify the implications of our findings for the NHS, and make evidence based recommendations for change.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: An evaluation of transformational change in NHS North East
Abstract: NHS North East has embarked on an ambitious transformational change initiative known as the North East Transformation System (NETS). Designed to improve health and healthcare services for the region’s population, the NETS comprises three elements: vision, compact, method (based on the Toyota Production System as applied to the Virginia Mason Medical Center in Seattle with which the NETS approach has a close working relationship) and related Lean tools. The research will evaluate how far these elements are aligned and kept in balance to sustain lasting change. There are at least three types of system change in evidence in NHS North East: the pure version of the NETS; a mixed version where elements of the approach are being adopted alongside other quality improvement methods; and a non-NETS approach to change where completely different methods are being adopted. The study will attempt to compare and contrast these different, though overlapping, approaches. A key aim of the research is to establish how far the NETS, or any of its variants, has become embedded and is sustainable in the long term in terms of the desired changes. These include: reducing variation across services and waste, improving patient safety and quality of care, freeing up professionals to use their time where best deployed, empowering staff to take control of their own work, achieving a better work-life balance for staff thereby reducing work-related stress, securing a new compact between clinicians between managers in order to realise the vision for NHS North East. The evaluation will seek to ascertain how far NETS and its variants have improved performance, and to identify the factors making for success and, conversely, the barriers that inhibit change.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Developing and piloting a peer mentoring intervention to reduce teenage pregnancy in looked-after children and care leavers.
Abstract: This is a feasibility study of a peer mentoring intervention for Looked After Children to reduce teenge pregnancy, which will incorporate phases 1 and 11 of the MRCs original framework for the development and evaluation of complex interventions to improve health (MRC2000).Design i) Scoping Exercise and Targetted Literature Review of Interventions to reduce Teenage Pregnancy ii) Focus groups with LAC, carers, health and social staff to refine the intervention iii) a 3 month pilot of the intervention with 6 mentor-mentee pairs. Setting : 3 Local Authorities (Southend, Lambeth and Ealing) iii) Phase 1: will involve 6 mentor-mentee pairs in Ealing. The intervention will be piloted for 3 months and then refined according to feedback from mentors and mentees. Phase 11: 48 LAC aged between 14 and 18, will be recruited as mentees from the 3 LAs. They will be randomised to 24 peer mentors, who are young women aged between 18 and 24, who have themselves had experience of the care system. Half the mentees will receive peer mentoring, the other half will receive care as usual. The intervention will be for one year. Mentors will be provided with smart phones to enable them to record frequency and nature of their contacts with mentees, in diary form. The primary outcome measure is differences in pregnancy between the intervention and care as usual group. Mentors and mentees will be asked to complete a number of psychological heath measures at the beginning and end of the intervention. A detailed process evaluation will be undertaken to examine implementation and receipt of the intervention in order to assess feasibility and fidelity, accessibility and contextual factors affecting these, as well as gaining insights into the mechanism of action and developing hypotheses to guide secondary analyses. A mixture of quantitative and qualitative research methods will be used. A project coordinator will be identified for each of the Las who will assist in local recruitment of mentees and mentors and will provide local coordination and management of the project throughout the intervention. Mentor training will be led by the NCB and will run as a 3 day module at the beginning of the intervention for mentors and the local LA project coordinators. Mentors and project coordinators will also receive two followup support training session during the project.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Weight Loss Maintenance in Adults (WILMA)
Abstract: Background Studies of weight loss maintenance have had limited effectiveness with weight regain common. Reviews have identified issues important for maintenance including: physical activity; low calorie/low fat diet; self regulation; tailoring, social support, internal motivation and self efficacy. These are central to the intervention being evaluated in this trial. Aim To evaluate the impact of a 12 month multi-component intervention or a less intensive version on participants': Body Mass Index (primary outcome); waist circumference; waist to hip ratio; body composition; physical activity levels and diet three years from randomisation. Design A 3 arm (intensive, less intensive, control) individually randomised controlled trial. During the trial those allocated to the intensive or less intensive groups will receive a 12 month individually tailored intervention based on three key features; MI, peer support and self regulation. The focus will be on maintaining the gains participants have already made. The control group will receive an information pack detailing lifestyle changes for weight maintenance. Population We will recruit 950 obese adults aged 18-70 (current or previous BMI 30+) who have lost at least 5% body weight (independently verified) from community based groups, gyms, commercial weight loss groups and exercise on prescription schemes. Exclusion criteria include; pregnancy or inability to comply with study protocol. Outcome measures The primary outcome is BMI at 3 years post randomisation. Secondary outcomes include waist circumference; waist to hip ratio; body fat distribution; self report physical activity; proportion maintaining weight loss; self report dietary intake; health related quality of life; health service and weight control resource usage; binge eating, psychological well being and duration of participation and drop out from intervention. Duration and follow-up The trial will start after participants are recruited and consented. Participants will be assessed at 6 months during the intervention and followed up at the end of the intervention (one year from randomisation) and at 12 and 24 months after the intervention is complete.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: A pragmatic randomised controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of Collaborative cARE for people with DEMentia in primary care (CARE-DEM trial)
Abstract: This study will develop and evaluate the feasibility of collaborative care for people with Dementia in primary care. It will create a training programme for primary care staff to enable them to undertake case managment with patients with dementia and their families (Work package 1). The feasibility of implementing the training programme will be tested in a pilot rehearsal trial (Work package 2), which will also allow effect sizes to be estimated for a definitive main trial. Qualitative methods will be used to study the development process and implentation in the field, to inform refinement of the training programme and introduction of the case management methods into routine practice. If the intervention appears to be effective, we will seek further funding for Work package 3, a definitive main trial which will address the key research question: Primary objective: To evaluate the clinical and cost effectiveness of usual care augmented by collaborative care, compared to usual care, at reducing behavioural and psychological disorders in people with dementia in primary care. Secondary objectives of this study: 1) To develop and pilot the feasibility of a UK model of collaborative care for dementia, led by a primary-care based case manager using evidence based care pathways (Work packages 1 & 2). 2) To provide a detailed description and analysis of the case management intervention, including a description of how it works in practice, and a toolkit for its replication should the intervention prove effective (Work package 2 & Qualitative study). 3) To explore the acceptability and value of a collaborative care model in dementia, delivered by a case manager, to people with dementia, their family carers and other dementia care professionals and services (Qualitative study). Secondary objectives of the follow-on study (Work package 3) 4) To conduct a cost-utility analysis of usual care augmented by collaborative care management, compared to usual care, on NHS resource utilisation by people with dementia and their family carers. The outcome in this analysis would be change in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) derived from the DEMQOL (using an algorithm currently being developed in a study by Banerjee, Brazier, Knapp and others, funded by the HTA) (Work package 3, definitive trial).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A randomised trial to increase the uptake of smoking cessation services using Personal Targeted risk information and Taster Sessions
Abstract: Recent figures show a reduction in smoking prevalence, but there is no room for complacency, smoking remains a major cause of ill health and mortality. Most smokers say they want to quit but only a tiny proportion make use of the free Smoking Cessation Services provided by the NHS. This research will evaluate, in a randomized trial, a two-pronged intervention to increase the number of people attending the services. We will recruit 60 general practices through the PCRN in areas that are representative of the English smoking cessation service. All smokers aged 16 and over identified from their medical records in participating practices will be sent a brief questionnaire to update their smoking status and to assess their dependence, motivation to quit, previous attendance at NHS services and to seek consent to participate in the trial. Current smokers who consent and are eligible will be randomized to: a) the Control Group to receive a generic letter advertising the NHS service and inviting them to contact the service for an appointment; b) the Intervention Group to receive i) a brief personalized tailored letter from the GP, offering risk information using information about general health status and chronic conditions from the patient's medical records, and data from the assessment; and ii) an invitation and appointment to attend a 'Come and Try it' taster session to find out more about the services, run by advisors from the local service. Attendees will be encouraged to sign up to a group or one-to-one session at convenient time. Participants who fail to attend will receive a further invitation and appointment 3 months later to encourage attendance. Research interviewers will conduct follow-up interviews 6-months after randomisation, by telephone, to assess attendance at the services, current smoking status, daily cigarette consumption, reasons for non-attendance and barriers to attendance in all participants.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Improving the Quality of Dentistry (IQuaD): A randomised controlled trial comparing oral hygiene advice and periodontal instrumentation for the prevention and management of periodontal disease in dentate adults attending dental primary care
Abstract: Periodontal disease is the most common oral disease affecting adults. Effective self-care (tooth brushing and interdental aids) for plaque control and removal of risk factors such as calculus, by periodontal instrumentation (PI), commonly known as a “scale and polish”, are considered necessary to prevent and treat periodontal disease. A Cochrane review found evidence that psychological interventions resulted in improvements in oral hygiene behaviours but there is a lack of reliable evidence to inform clinicians of the relative effectiveness of different types of Oral Hygiene Advice (OHA) on the prevention of periodontal disease in adults. Similarly there is mixed evidence on the effectiveness and optimal frequency of PI. The majority of trials that have been carried out to date have been of poor to moderate quality with few conducted in primary care and a lack of patient centred outcomes and economic analyses reported. The IQuaD trial will investigate the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of the following dental management strategies in general dental practices across the UK: 1. Personalised OHA versus routine OHA 2. 12 monthly PI versus 6 monthly PI 3. No PI versus 6 monthly PI Participating dentists (60) will be cluster randomised to provide routine (current practice) or theory-based personalised (to the needs of the patient) OHA.
