Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Royal United Hospital Bath NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Optimising care, diagnosis and treatment pathways to ensure cost effectiveness and best practice in gynaecological cancer: improving the evidence for the NHS
Abstract: When the major gynaecological cancer sites are combined they have the second highest incidence of any female cancer in the UK (17,083 cases in 2007, UKCR figures) behind breast cancer and ahead of colorectal and lung cancer. Mortality from gynaecological cancer in the UK (9537 deaths between 2007-2008 UKCR figures) is only lower than lung and breast cancer. The NHS has made major improvements in gynaecological cancer care and it is one of the most integrated and multidisciplinary areas in medicine with an active Improving Outcome Guidance (IOG) programme. This is important as there are seven tumour sites with multiple complex care pathways. Theme and scope of proposed programme (1,000 characters max): Theme: to improve patient care by preparing systematic reviews to improve cost-effectiveness and best practice in gynaecological cancer and associated cancer care which will inform national guidelines and local protocols. The gynaecological oncology community has some priority issues to deal with in the near future, some of which will be addressed by the completion and publication of the reports from a study looking at screening the general population for ovarian cancer (UKCTOCS). Also, the UK CHORUS trial comparing surgery before and during chemotherapy for ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer completed recruitment in August 2010; the full results are due for publication in 2012. Another important area is the findings of the recently reported EORTC report on neo-adjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval debulking surgery for ovarian cancer. The CGCRG will also consider the recently published NHS colposcopy and European cervical cancer guidelines. Scope: Current protocols vary widely from Network to Network. As with the previous application, topics for potential reviews will be developed by a thorough prioritisation project involving Cancer Networks, to identify areas where evidence is weak or missing. Criteria for Prioritisation 1) Improving patient outcomes 2) Importance to NHS priorities 3) Achievability and cost effectiveness 4) Impact on efficacy and efficiency 5) Timeliness. For this project new strands of work (screening, early recognition, predictive factors, diagnostics and prognostic methods) will be considered, as well as generic themes such as surgery, radiotherapy, first and second line chemotherapy, combined modality therapy, communication, supportive and palliative care, organisation of care delivery, rehabilitation and complimentary therapies. . Updating reviews will form a large part of the work to ensure that the most up-to-date evidence is available. We will concentrate on those reviews on the Cochrane Library within our module which are accessed frequently and are cited most often.

Award_Title: Lifestyle and pharmacological interventions for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease
Abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is still the number one cause of death and disability in the UK. The burden of disease will increase with an aging population and increasing levels of obesity and sedentary lifestyles. Prevention of CVD by targeting modifiable factors (smoking, physical inactivity, obesity, high blood pressure, raised cholesterol levels) remains a key public health priority. Successive guidance (e.g. The National Service Framework for Coronary Heart Disease (NSF CHD, DH 2000)) has been important in reducing deaths from CVD, but has indicated that a shift in emphasis is required towards primary prevention. This shift has been further highlighted by the report Destination 2020 (Cardio Vascular Coalition), which builds on the 10 year targets of the NSF CHD and which particularly welcomes the national roll out of the Vascular Risk Assessment Programme to assess, manage and reduce risk in all those aged 40-74 (Putting Prevention First, DH 2008). NICE guidance on prevention of CVD at a population level has recently been published (June, 2010). These initiatives to prevent CVD at the individual and population level are currently ongoing and await evaluation. The programme theme is “Lifestyle and pharmacological interventions for the primary prevention of CVD”. The focus will be on modifiable risk factors in the general population and in those at increased risk of CVD. We plan a programme of work relevant to policy, organisational, public health, clinical and individual levels which will provide a strong platform for wider, more comprehensive prevention programmes including both population and high-risk strategies. Several recent publications commissioned by the Department of Health in the area of primary prevention (Statins for the prevention of CV events (NICE, 2006), Lipid modification (NICE, 2008), Putting prevention first (DH, 2008), Prevention of CVD at a population level (NICE, 2010)) have highlighted gaps in the evidence base and propose further research. A programme of over 20 new reviews and 20 reviews currently registered with the CHG will be taken forward. Planned new titles all take the form of intervention for the primary prevention of CVD as follows: Lifestyle interventions: Mediterranean diet Vegetarian diet Vitamin K Selenium Coenzyme Q10 Coenzyme Q10 in people taking statins Flavenoids Brisk walking Cycling Alternative exercise regimens (Tai Chi, Qigong, Yoga) Meditation Pharmacological interventions: Fibrates Polypill Over the counter statins Risk assessment and interventions directed at specific groups: Patient-led methods of risk assessment Financial incentives for primary care-led risk assessment Systematic vs. opportunistic risk assessment Lifestyle interventions aimed at black and minority ethnic groups Methods of risk assessment for identifying children with hypercholesterolemia Interventions to reduce CVD risk in children with hypercholesterolemia Reviews currently registered with the CHG to be taken forward/updated: Lifestyle interventions: Dietary advice Omega 3 fatty acids Reduced or modified dietary fat Wholegrain cereals Homocysteine lowering interventions Supplemental plant sterols and stanols Vitamin D Multiple risk factor interventions Exercise for people with high CVD risk Interventions for promoting physical activity (3 reviews) Pharmacological interventions: Statins Aspirin Clopidogrel plus aspirin versus aspirin alone Hormone replacement therapy Risk assessment and interventions directed at specific groups: Risk scoring Interventions for preventing obesity in children Interventions for treating obesity in children Interventions for increasing fruit and vegetable consumption in preschool children

Award_Title: A programme of high priority systematic reviews in the diagnosis and treatment of Peripheral Vascular Disease: an NHS partnership with the Cochrane PVD Review Group.
Abstract: We will focus on three main areas, each of which is associated with serious consequences such as amputation or death if left untreated. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) can cause death from massive internal bleeding. Each year 6,000-10,000 people in England and Wales are affected and in 2009 the English NHS AAA screening programme began screening men over the age of 65. 1,2,3 Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) includes deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE). These are estimated to cause 25,000 deaths annually. Many of these deaths are potentially preventable and VTE prevention is currently a top NHS priority.4,5,6,7 Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) is a manifestation of systemic arthrosclerosis. It can severely limit walking distance due to the onset of intermittent claudication (IC) and in more severe cases can lead to a lower limb amputation. PAD is also a marker of increased cardiac risk equivalent to the presence of angina.8,9,10 Our programme of systematic reviews has been designed to produce reliable information about the management of these conditions and is aimed at improving quality of patient care in the NHS. This programme of high priority systematic reviews will support the effective prevention, diagnosis and treatment of AAA, VTE and PAD for those delivering and receiving care in the NHS. Working in partnership with the Cochrane Peripheral Vascular Disease group we will produce; 1. 20 new reviews on AAA, VTE and PAD, including 13 on interventions (9 new titles, 3 completions of on-going reviews and 1 umbrella review of interventions for IC) and 7 new diagnostic test accuracy reviews 2. 20 updates of interventions for AAA, VTE and PAD, including updates which are overdue due to lack of existing resources and/or are required before the key umbrella review of all interventions for IC can be completed We have selected and prioritized new review where (i) consultation with NHS clinicians, patients and managers has identified a need for evidence on effectiveness of specific health care interventions and tests, (ii) there are no comparable reviews already available or in-progress, either within Cochrane or elsewhere and (iii) reviews will inform policy, including forthcoming guidelines planned by national bodies (e.g. NICE). Award_Title: Cost effective treatments and diagnostic approaches for people with schizophrenia within the NHS
Abstract: Schizophrenia, an illness often starting in teenage years, affects the ability to think, perceive, feel and move. With a lifetime prevalence of 1%, one person in approximately every 25 households, will either have or will develop this disabling illness. In terms of NHS economics, schizophrenia costs are second only to stroke; outweighing those associated with heart disease or cancer (2007 - £2bn). Costs to social services, voluntary sectors and the criminal justice system are also considerable (2007 - £4bn for unemployment alone). This programme aims to review key treatments/approaches that are comparatively inexpensive and universally accessible. Inexpensive treatments/techniques for schizophrenia do exist. We are less clear if good diagnostic tests are available. This work will help review diagnostic data and have the potential to offset introduction of unproven techniques to the NHS. 1. Linking Cochrane and NHS' Map of Medicine, engaging end-users, Project Ref: 10/4000/17 , DoH Ref: 006/632 Theme and scope of proposed programme (1,000 characters max): The 20 new reviews and 20 updates cover four themes linked by cost efficient use of resources. Theme A: Benchmark comparisons Benchmark treatments against which new expensive drugs are compared are often overlooked by reviewers when selecting a high-impact topic. These benchmarks are inexpensive. Theme B: Cost efficient delivery Simple, brief psychosocial packages/approaches or drug techniques have been developed that have the potential to save the NHS much compared with their longer or more sophisticated counterparts. Theme C: Diagnosis CSzG requests support to undertake the first Cochrane reviews of diagnoses in mental health to direct effort to real world NHS needs, set standards, develop skills and avoid waste. Theme D: NICE update NICE review of management of aggression due to serious mental illness will be updated 2012 and, anticipating NICE need, relevant reviews will be updated or produced. All reviews will be produced in line with the care pathway of the NHS (Map of Medicine). The diagnosis theme will involve contracting additional expertise and construction of a register of relevant studies. Contractor: South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Assistive Technology and Telecare to maintain Independent Living At home for people with dementia: The ATTILA Trial
Abstract: Design: A randomised controlled multi-centre clinical trial. We will compare the effects of an assessment followed by access to a suite of assistive technology and telecare (ATT) services with assessment and a control intervention; limited to the fitting and checking of smoke detectors; on the time that people with dementia who are at high risk of institutionalisation can be maintained in independent living. Target population: Participants will be patients with all dementia diagnoses and will include individuals with young-onset dementias. Health Technologies being assessed: Commercially available ATT devices that we and others have successfully piloted to promote independent home-living for people with dementia. All participants will undergo a full assessment of home safety and risk and the potential for ATT intervention to monitor and manage risk. Following assessment, participants randomised to receive ATT would be provided with elements from a dementia-specific menu to include: 1. Monitored sensors; including smoke detectors, gas detectors, temperature extremes sensors, carbon monoxide detectors, property exit sensors, bed exit sensors, movement detection and pager systems. 2. System to augment assessment; using Just Checking. 3. Non-monitored (stand-alone) systems; including automatic lights (motion activated or dawn to dusk, battery or mains), motion/door contact to activate previously recorded message, gas isolation switch, carer alerting devices (including stand-alone pager activated by door contacts or passive infra-red (PIR), PIR/door contacts linked to small electrical devices). 4. Peripheral systems; including a keysafe for emergency access. 5. Associated environmental adaptation; including non-toxic fire retardent spray for furniture and clothing. Participants randomised to the control arm will be supplied with battery operated smoke detectors if assessment of home safety and risk has identified that this is indicated. Measurement of cost and outcomes: The co-primary trial outcomes will be (i) Time in days from randomisation to institutionalisation and (ii) Cost-effectiveness.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Neuraminidase inhibitors for preventing and treating influenza in healthy adults and children - a review of unpublished data
Abstract: Neuraminidase inhibitors (NIs) have become global public health drugs, stockpiled against possible influenza outbreaks. Despite their popularity, the discovery of sizeable reporting bias, uncertainty over the number of trials run, ghost authorship and widespread discrepancies between published and unpublished versions of the same trials, have led to a reappraisal of the published evidence and calls for public release of hitherto confidential data. The project aims to review unpublished data on effectiveness and harms of NIs for influenza in all age groups updating and amalgamating two established Cochrane reviews on adults and children. The review will be in two stages. Stage one will identify, reconstruct and assess all NI trials conducted to January 2010 using regulatory and pharmaceutical reports. Only reliable* trial data will be included in the second phase of the review (an analysis following standard Cochrane methods). Because of the complexity of our task we have devised four additional types of tools for data management and information: a directory mapping citations to clinical trials in our data sources; its expanded version with annotations; a narrative of our review, documenting the evolution of methods and detailed summary of the regulatory documents and a reference resource holding details of all trials. In addition we have created a tool for assessing all known types of reporting bias in trials and sub-trials programmes. *Reliability is made up of 5 aspects: 1.Completeness - there is sufficient material to assess the other reliability criteria. 2. Internal consistency - all parts of the same CSR/unpublished pharma report are consistent and coherent. 3. External consistency - all versions of the various CSR/unpublished pharma reports are consistent and coherent. 4. Clarity - all parts and versions allow understanding of the design and conduct of the trial. 5. Robustness - exposure of reconstructions to regulatory comments do not lead the majority of voters (at least 4 of 7 in the team) to change the study conclusions or their trustworthiness.

Award_Title: Exercise interventions for the management of health related quality of life and fatigue in cancer survivors during and after treatment
Abstract: The summary of three Cochrane reviews will address the following questions: 1. Does exercise enhance overall HRQoL or specific HRQoL domains among cancer survivors during active treatment? 2. Does exercise enhance overall HRQoL or specific HRQoL domains among cancer survivors after active treatment? 3. Does exercise reduce CRF among cancer survivors during active treatment? 4. Does exercise reduce CRF among cancer survivors after active treatment?

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Can text messages increase safer sexual health behaviours in young people? Intervention development and pilot trial.
Abstract: Design: Part A: Intervention development. Part B: A pilot randomised controlled trial. Part C: Final modifications to the intervention. Setting: Recruitment: community sexual health clinics, general practices and pharmacies. Intervention delivery: via mobile phones in the community. Target population: Chlamydia screening programme participants diagnosed with chlamydia or gonorrhoea and/or who have had unsafe sex in the last year (more than one partner and at least one occasion of unprotected sex). Part A: Developing the intervention: Existing evidence: New results from our txt2stop trial show that text-messaging interventions can sustain health behaviour change in the long term. The text based intervention doubled biochemically verified smoking cessation at six months: 10.7% txt2stop versus 4.9% control, RR 2.20 (95% CI 1.80-2.68)(2). Mobile phones are able to provide confidential and non-judgemental support, which is essential for a sexual health intervention(3). Interactive support can be delivered at any time. Behaviour change techniques used in effective face-to-face interventions can be modified for delivery via text message(4-5). The content can be personalised for different gender and ethnic groups. Recipients referred to the text messaging support we developed as: ‘being ‘a ‘friend’ it felt like someone was holding your hand throughout.’ (Female) and ‘you’ve got someone there giving you a bit of support, which is what you need isn’t it?’ (Male). Thus, support via text message could be acceptable to young people and might increase safer sexual health behaviours. We conducted systematic reviews of interventions promoting condom use and mobile technology based interventions(6-7) and described the behaviour change techniques used in effective interventions(5-12). We developed preliminary content and conducted interviews and focus groups discussions with young people. The discussions suggested that the preliminary content was welcomed, effectively communicated sensitive issues and was effective in portraying gender and ethnic appropriate content. Theory: Sexual behaviour is influenced by motivation, capability and opportunity. The intervention aims to alter these factors to reduce sexual risk. First, by encouraging those in the target audience to use condoms. Second, by encouraging participants to obtain testing for STI for themselves and their sexual partner(s) prior to unprotected sex. Third, by urging participants to correctly follow instructions for STI treatment and informing partner(s) about infection. Text message development: To develop messages we will use the approach we used to develop our previous effective text messaging intervention(15-16). The content will be based on the content of effective sexual health behaviour change support(8-12), modified for delivery by text message. We will develop messages with the input of sexual health counsellors and young people. We will ask a panel of young people about their preferences for the intervention, the acceptability, comprehensibility and appropriateness of the text messages and suggestions for improvement. According to their feedback, we will retain, discard or modify messages and retest them. We will then ask 100 participants to score text messages regarding their acceptability, comprehensibility and appropriateness. Part B: We will conduct a pilot randomised controlled trial of the intervention in 200 participants to test all trial methods and procedures. Participants will provide written informed consent. A web-based link to an independent randomisation service will allocate participants to intervention or control groups. The system will automatically generate text messages according to allocation. Part C: We will make final intervention modifications and design the main trial.

Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Self-management support interventions to reduce health care utilisation without compromising outcomes: a rapid synthesis of the evidence
Abstract: We propose a a quantitative review to identify models of self-management which reduce health services utilisation without compromising outcomes. The literature concerning self-management support is growing rapidly and a full primary review of all models across all conditions will not be feasible in 12 months. To meet the SDO brief, we will restrict our review to the subset of studies of self-management support that report quantitative data on health care utilisation (including, but not restricted to, hospital admissions) and outcomes. We will use the studies identified in the meta-review as an initial source, complemented by our previous published review of the economics of self-management We will update these reviews as necessary with additional searches to increase sensitivity and ensure searches identify recent studies. We will extract data from each study on risk of bias, and also extract data on the effect of these self-management interventions on health care utilisation and patient outcomes. The primary analysis will consider the ability of models of self-management to reduce hospitalisation rates and costs, without compromising patient outcomes. We will present the results using a modification of the permutation matrix, plotting the effect of interventions (together with their associated confidence intervals) on utilisation and outcomes simultaneously and placing them in quadrants of the permutation matrix depending on the pattern of outcomes. This will enable the research team and commissioners to identify interventions showing different patterns of effects (i.e. to distinguish those models of self-management support that reduce costs without compromising outcomes, and those that reduce costs at some reduction in outcomes).

Award_Title: Management by geographic area or management specialised by disorder? An evaluation of effects of an organisational intervention on secondary mental health care for common mental disorder
Abstract: THEORETICAL/CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK Descriptions of the structural changes associated with the CAG program and relevant theories such as product line management provide little clear understanding of the CAG program and how its outcomes will be achieved. In particular, they fail to take advantage of the detailed contextual knowledge of stakeholders in the program and the availability of data for quantitative analyses. Our response is to perform a realistic evaluation (Pawson & Tilley 1997). Realistic evaluation aims to establish clear and measurable relationships between an intervention like the MAPCAG program and its outcomes, which are explained by an underlying theory comprising a set of context-mechanism-outcome relationships (CMOs). It ”employs no one standard ‘formula’, other than the base strategy of producing a clear theory of program mechanisms, contexts and outcomes, and then using them to design the appropriate empirical measures and comparisons” (Pawson & Tilley 1997, p.xv). In WP1, logic modelling (Ling & Scoggins 2006; Soper et al. 2008) will be used to “produc[e] a clear theory of program mechanisms, contexts and outcomes—the visual representation of key context-mechanism-outcomes functions first to orient qualitative data collection to the central task of developing and refining a theory of the program under evaluation, and then provides a visual representation of the results of the evaluation and an interpretative structure for the quantitative results. WP2 (time series analyses) will entail the design and carrying out of the “appropriate empirical measures and comparisons”, and the feeding back of these results into the logic modelling process. WP1 – LOGIC MODEL – MONTHS 1-4, 10 AND 22 Key context-mechanism-outcomes for the CAG program will be defined by the managers, clinicians, service users, family members and GPs involved, using a logic model as a diagrammatic and visual means of eliciting their professional, tacit and formal knowledge (see above). WP1 will be co-led by an external expert (Dr Bryony Soper) and by a service user researcher (Dr Diana Rose), and assisted by an additional researcher. The respondent group will comprise at least 6 clinicians, managers and GPs involved in / impacted by the MAPCAG, 3 service users and 3 relatives of service users. Professional respondents will include research team members indicated in “Team Expertise”. These “insider” team members have already identified a number of innovations of interest within the CAG—see “Background” above. Service user respondents will include and will otherwise be identified by the patient-public involvement representative for the CAG. In months 1 to 4, two user-only meetings, two meetings for relatives of service users, and two professionals-only meeting will be followed by a first joint meeting (the logic model will combine elements from each group). There will be further joint meetings in Months 10 and 22, where the logic model will be refined in the light of WP2’s results. The lead for WP2 (Dr Tulloch) will provide input regarding data availability. Data collection will be performed by Dr Soper, Dr Rose and a further service user researcher. The central output will be the final logic model for the CAG program. WP2 – TIME SERIES ANALYSIS – MONTHS 1-22 SLaM is the only NHS Trust in England that both uses a comprehensive electronic patient record and makes its contents available for research in anonymised form (the BRC Case Register—see Detailed Project Description). Data will come from this unique resource, from staff and patient surveys and by content analysis of archive materials, especially minutes of borough directorate meetings and CAG board meetings. We will define all episodes of care for depression, anxiety and personality disorder from 2009 onwards using activity data and ICD-10 codes, as well as additional text-mined diagnostic codes. We shall restrict the study to secondary rather than tertiary services and take a 10% random sample (N~2000). To each episode we will append measures determined by the logic model: outcomes of interest and mediators. From the point of view of dataset construction, much important data (e.g clinical activity, routine outcome measures such as the Health of the Nation Outcome Scales) already exists in usable structured form. Other variables, for example guideline concordance, would require manual coding. This can be facilitated, as in the Veterans’ Administration (Watkins et al. 2011), by using SAS to generate customised data displays in which the necessary free-text is selected, arranged and displayed in order to streamline coding (see the detailed project plan for screenshots from a similar project). We will measure interrater reliability of this “facilitated” coding and its validity compared to full casenote review. Cost-effectiveness is an important outcome; we will measure costs from the provider perspective by combining activity data (inpatient care, clinican contacts, medication) with appropriate unit costs (reference costs, BNF, PSSRU). Effectiveness will be measured using routine outcome measures (HoNOS/CORE). We will create a dataset of indicators from January 2009 to December 2013, aggregating data at 208 weekly timepoints. Main analyses will make use of piece-wise regression of each indicator of interest, allowing for autocorrelation, and testing for an interaction between slope and time-period that would indicate an effect of CAG implementation. We will also estimate the effects of lagged variables that are postulated mediators of the effect of CAG implementation and perform tests of Granger causality. We will test for interactions by borough and by diagnosis. In the analysis of each time-series, a sample of 208 timepoints has >99% power (at alpha 0.05) to detect a time x slope interaction that has a medium effect size (0.15). Economic analysis will compare cost-effectiveness (service cost divided by outcome change) pre- and post-CAG. Where HoNOS scores are missing we will use multiple imputation and use the imputed scores in sensitivity analyses. Potential variables included in the imputation will be demographic characteristics, previous HoNOS scores and past service history.

Award_Title: Location of care for people with serious mental illness: implications for service use and costs
Abstract: The proposed study consists of 1) a quantitative component based on routinely collected health records, 2) a qualitative component investigating users’ views and experiences, and 3) an economic modelling component. COMPONENT 1. People living in Lambeth who have severe mental illness (SMI) will be identified from SMI registers in primary care. We will produce a dataset containing information on demographic, clinical details, physical health conditions, and use of primary and secondary care services. Data on secondary mental health care use and clinical ratings will be obtained from the Clinical Record Interactive Search (CRIS) system. Primary care data will be obtained from Lambeth DataNet supplemented with specifically requested GP consultation data. The PCT is also able to link primary and acute hospital services data for the purposes of data validation and risk stratification and these can be additionally linked to CRIS. These data are encrypted but proceadures are in place to combine them by third party de-encryption/re-encryption. Data will be obtained on service contacts and clinical characteristics for the 12 months prior to the SMI register index date (January 2010). These data will be used to categorise patients as being under secondary care management or primary care management. Comparisons in terms of clinical and demographic characteristics will be made between the two groups using appropriate statistical tests. Service use data will be combined with unit cost information to generate service costs. Service use will be compared between the two groups. The proportion using specific services will be compared using logistic regression models controlling for background differences. Costs will be modelled using linear regression models in order to identify cost predictors. Separate models will be generated for each group and these will be used to ‘cross-predict’ what the costs would have been for patients with similar characteristics managed in the alternative setting. We will conduct survival analyses (using Cox’s regression) to identify demographic, clinical, and service use variables in the year prior to the index date that are associated with a move from secondary care to primary care or primary care to secondary care. Two separate models will be produced (one for each form of management) plus a combined model where the original form of care will be entered as a potential predictor variable. COMPONENT 2.This will explore the experiences/views of service users subject to the transition from secondary to primary care and receiving at least one of the health and social care interventions aimed at supporting people with severe mental illness in a primary care setting. Given the complex nature of the interventions and the fact that these are new, and potentially developing, services an exploratory qualitative approach is proposed, comprising of semi-structured interviews conducted longitudinally in order to fully explore the transition process. Interviews will begin at the point of discharge from secondary care as service users take up the new services. The same respondent will then be interviewed again at a point, up to one year after the transition from secondary care, where they can reflect on their experience of primary care. Interviews will follow a standard topic guide modified according to the type of service received and the interview stage. An important part of this component will be to achieve triangulation by collecting data from a range of sources, including: health records, the accounts of service users and also the accounts of primary, mental health and social care professionals involved in their care. While the emphasis in this part of the study would be on the accounts of the service users themselves these would be complemented by interviews with workers involved in their care. A purposive sample of 30 service users with a SMI recently discharged from secondary care and in receipt of at least one of the three specified primary care interventions will be recruited. Patients will be recruited via their GP, or one of the services being evaluated. The study will include a further sample of workers associated with the respondents’ care – comprising approximately 3 participants per intervention. A semi-structured interview will take place at a time point where participants have recently been discharged from secondary care. Participants will be interviewed again up to one year later. The emphasis in the topic guide will be on their overall views and experience of the primary care services and their reflections on the transition from secondary care. Interviews will be transcribed and analysed following a structured thematic analysis approach. Analysis will follow the constant comparison method [29,30]. That is, transcripts will be initially coded, by the researcher, using categories derived from the topic guide as a starting point with new codes subsequently added when necessary. Each category will then be compared with the rest, using an iterative process to look for patterns, differences and similarities, to further refine existing categories and create new ones. COMPONENT 3. We will produce decision models to assess the cost-effectiveness of the three interventions. Data generated in Component 1 will serve as a baseline against which the impact on costs of these will be assessed. The first stage in this will be to structure the models followed by ‘populating’ the models with local data. Finally the models will be tested using sensitivity analyses. The structuring will involve service users, clinical staff, commissioners and research staff in focus groups to ensure that the models are acceptable. The structure will map out the pathways through the care system following engagement with the intervention. It will need to include the most likely types of service use such as admission, readmission, psychiatrist contact etc. Data on the probabilities of different services being used will be largely derived from the databases described above. Changes in these probabilities will be estimated from data collected as part of the record keeping for the interventions themselves. Costs of different events occurring will be calculated again using data already described. The models, once ‘populated’, will be ‘rolled back’ to reveal the expected costs of the different interventions. One-way and probabilistic sensitivity analyses will be conducted. During the focus groups we will ask participants to complete two measures to rate their expected satisfaction (Client Satisfaction Questionnaire) and health-related quality of life (EQ-5D) following use of the interventions.

Award_Title: The effectiveness, acceptability and cost-effectiveness of psychosocial interventions for maltreated children and adolescents: An evidence synthesis
Abstract: DESIGN We will address our research objectives by searching the published and unpublished literature and conducting an evidence synthesis of i) studies of the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions provided for children and adolescents who have suffered maltreatment, ii) economic evaluations of these interventions and iii) studies of their acceptability to children, adolescents and their carers. SEARCH STRATEGY: Evidence will be identified via electronic databases for health and allied health literature, social sciences and social welfare, education and other evidence based depositories, and economic databases. We will identify material generated by user-led,voluntary sector enquiry by searching the internet and browsing the websites of relevant UK government departments and charities. Additionally, studies will be identified via the bibliographies of retrieved articles/reviews; targeted author searches; forward citation searching. We will also use our extensive professional networks, and our planned consultations with key stakeholders and our study steering committee. Databases will be searched from inception to time of search. REVIEW STRATEGY Inclusion criteria: 1) Infants, children or adolescents who have experienced maltreatment between the ages of 0 – 17 years. 2) All psychosocial interventions available for maltreated children and adolescents, by any provider and in any setting, aiming to address the sequelae of any form of maltreatment, including fabricated illness. 3) For synthesis of evidence of effectiveness: all controlled studies in which psychosocial interventions are compared with no-treatment, treatment as usual, waitlist or other-treated controls. For a synthesis of evidence of acceptability we will include any design that asks participants for their views or provides data on non-participation. For decision-analytic modelling we may include uncontrolled studies. Primary and secondary outcomes will be confirmed in consultation with stakeholders. Provisional primary outcomes are psychological distress/mental health (particularly PTSD, depression and anxiety, self-harm); ii) behaviour; iii) social functioning; iv) cognitive / academic attainment, v) quality of life, and vi) costs. After studies that meet the inclusion criteria have been identified (independently by two reviewers), data will be extracted and risk of bias (RoB) assessed (independently by two reviewers) using the Cochrane Collaboration RoB Tool (effectiveness), quality hierarchies of data sources for economic analyses (cost-effectiveness) and the CASP tool for qualitative research (acceptability). Where interventions are similar and appropriate data are available (or can be obtained) evidence synthesis will be performed to pool the results. Where possible, we will explore the extent to which age, maltreatment history (including whether intra- or extra-familial), time since maltreatment, care setting (family / out-of-home care including foster care/residential), care history, and characteristics of intervention (type, setting, provider, duration) moderate the effects of psychosocial interventions. A synthesis of acceptability data will be undertaken, using a narrative approach to synthesis. A decision-analytic model will be constructed to compare the expected cost-effectiveness of the different types of intervention identified in the systematic review. We will also conduct a Value of information analysis if the data permit. EXPECTED OUTPUTS: A synthesis of the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of psychosocial interventions for maltreated children (taking into account age, maltreatment profile and setting) and their acceptability to key stakeholders.

Award_Title: Enhanced Invitation Methods to Increase Uptake of NHS Health Checks. Randomised Controlled Trial
Abstract: Study design: Three-arm randomised controlled trial. Interventions: A, QBE questionnaire followed by standard invitation one month later; B, QBE questionnaire + financial incentive (retail voucher) to return the questionnaire followed by standard invitation one month later. An arm with financial incentive is included to assess the impact of this on the response rate; C, No questionnaire, standard invitation only. QBE questionnaires will be sent with a stamped addressed envelope one month before the standard invitation letter for health checks is posted. Participants: Participants will be patients registered with general practices in three South London boroughs, aged 40-75 and scheduled for invitation to the NHS Health Checks programme. Allocation: Randomisation of individual participants will be in blocks, stratified by general practice. Outcomes: Primary: proportion of partcipants attending for NHS Health Checks within 6 months. Secondary outcomes: proportion attending at 3 months (prior to reminder letter); cost per additional participant attending for NHS Health Checks. Sample size: To detect a minimal important difference in uptake of Health Checks between any treatment arm of 5%, 2128 participants are needed per arm at 80% power and 5% significance, with Bonferroni correction. Analysis: Intention-to-treat analyses by logistic regression, accounting for age, sex and stratification, comparing outcomes between arms A vs C, B vs C, A vs B. Secondary analyses will compare outcomes by deprivation quintile. Timetable (months): 0-6: set-up, ethics , establishing trial steering committee, research networks; 6-18: recruitment (600/month); 12-24: 6 months follow-up; 25-30: data analysis write up, dissemination. Ethics: Research ethics and NHS R&D approvals will be obtained. Initial consent will be from participating general practices. Study team: includes skills in epidemiology (Gulliford), statistics (Cornelius, Nicholas), health psychology (Burgess, Wright), health economics (Bokhari) and public health (Dodhia).

Award_Title: DeCoDer Trial Debt Counselling for Depression in Primary Care: an Adaptive Randomised Controlled Trial.
Abstract: Our proposed randomised pragmatic adaptive trial compares: debt advice counselling within a collaborative biopsychosocial approach plus NICE recommended treatment as usual (TAU); versus TAU plus a debt management advice leaflet; for patients located in Primary Care with depression or mixed depression & anxiety. Our multicentre trial will recruit populations across the range of deprivation levels & practices. We will recruit from GP lists & waiting rooms. The trial protocol will be refined with patient & public involvement (PPI) within COMET Initiative. We will co-develop the intervention with Citizen’s Advice Bureau (CAB) senior managers & PPI advisors. Our adaptive design extends the feasibility approach, to robustly monitor recruitment, test cluster versus individual randomisation, assess sample size assumptions, check treatment adherence & fidelity. We will also explore explanatory models influencing outcome using psychometrics & qualitative in-depth interviews. Design: Two phase adaptive pragmatic RCT with 1:1 allocation to intervention or control. Setting: GP practices in Liverpool, Cheshire, Plymouth & Swansea extending to neighbouring areas if required to achieve recruitment. Target Population: Patients with Depression or mixed Anxiety & Depression who are currently depressed (BDI>13) & consider themselves to be experiencing financial problems, will be recruited from practices across urban to rural areas (50% from lowest deprivation quartile) through targeted GP invitation letters from list searches, or waiting room recruitment. Health Technology being assessed: Collaborative Primary Care orientated debt counselling & advice by senior trained CAB advisors linked to practices with shared comprehensive assessment & formulation (GP/Patient/CAB worker) in addition to NICE informed TAU. Comparator: NICE informed TAU plus debt advice leaflet. Cost and outcomes: Primary outcome – depression (Beck Depression Inventory [BDI]). Secondary outcomes: wellbeing (short WEMWEBS), NHS/social services utilisation & costs (Adapted Client Service Receipt Inventory, Stanford Presenteeism scale & FitNote/absenteeism self-report), anxiety (Beck Anxiety Inventory), debt assessment & progress (measurement developed in pre-grant phase with CAB/PPI), health–related quality of life (MANSA & EQ5D5L), service satisfaction (GSQ). Life events (LED-S), Hopelessness (BHS),rumination (RSQ) & attributional style (ASQ) will be included as potential mediators for modelling & theory building. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, then 4 & 12 months post-randomisation. Qualitative design & Process evaluation: In feasibility & full RCT we will undertake baseline & post intervention qualitative interviews exploring with participants: recovery factors, biographies & ethical issues-analysed using a narrative approach; & assess adherence to intervention (staff/participants) using Normalization Process Theory (NPT). Assess commissioners' willingness to commission the service: we will recruit commissioners, providers & other key stakeholders to a 'virtual group' to advise us on cost-effectiveness measures that will most influence their decisions, & then review our findings with them at the end of the feasibility trial. Sample Size: 135 per patients/arm gives 90% power to detect a clinically meaningful difference of 3.5 BDI units between groups at 5% two-sided alpha (based on standard deviation of ~9). To allow for a cluster allocation, we would need to inflate the sample size (e.g. a design effect of 1.45 for an intracluster correlation coefficient of 0.05 (likely to be lower) & cluster size of 10). Allowing for 20% attrition & feasibility trial clustering effect, 195 patients/arm overall need to be recruited if we use individual randomisation in the full trial, but this will be 235 per arm if we cluster randomise throughout. In feasibility RCT, we propose to recruit & randomise 120 patients to intervention & control groups nested by individual or cluster randomisation. Intervention: Controls will receive NICE Guidance informed treatment for their depression from GP &/or IAPT services plus a debt advice leaflet prepared in collaboration with CAB. Intervention participants will see a Primary Care based CAB advisor & their GP who will complete a shared comprehensive assessment at their respective appointments. CAB will then offer up to 4 appointments with a debt advisor in their Primary Care-based service. Project Plan: Pre-grant -3 to 0mths: COMET Initiative-informed approach to finalising data collection packs (quantitative & topic guides) with PPI/CAB consultants including developing & adapting process measures & debt monitoring, informed by brief literature reviews; preparation of recruitment & intervention materials. Complete IRAS & governance applications. Select pilot recruitment site practices. Recruit research staff (2 years initially to end of feasibility, then review whether we proceed to full RCT), & CAB counsellors into study. Setup phase 0-4mths: Co-development of manualised intervention, GP briefing sessions about TAU & joint comprehensive assessment. Organise final permissions, service support costs & initiate preliminary list searches & mailings. Feasibility RCT 4-14mths: Allocate practices to intervention & control using cluster or individual randomisation. Participant recruitment, screening & baseline (6-mths), 7-12 from each of 4 practices in 3 areas; monitor baseline data for case mix, severity, acute v chronic/recurrent, & associated risk factors for debt & depression. Set up & test economic data collection systems. Undertake 4 month follow-ups. At the end of feasibility we will check for evidence of contamination, rate of recruitment & BDI SD in order to inform the design of full RCT, according to our Stopping & Design Change rules as outlined in more detail elsewhere. We will undertake purposively sampled qualitative interviews (~40), using narrative approach to understanding debt biographies & 'NPT' for treatment fidelity, using constant comparative data analysis, with PPI input. Full RCT: 15-39mths- All practices either cluster or individually randomised according to feasibility evidence of contamination. Recruitment (mth 15-27), data collection at 0/4/12 mths plus qual interviews. Final analyses, Knowledge Translation Events & Dissemination: 39-45mths- Statistical, economic & qualitative analyses, writing papers, presenting findings, preparing for implementation.

Award_Title: The REACH Study: Exploring patterns of Retention and Engagement Across specialised Care services of HIV
Abstract: The proposed study will systematically define the patterns of HIV health care attendance in the UK and increase our understanding of the characteristics and contextual factors that make patients more likely to disengage from care. This is essential to inform the design and implementation of effective interventions to improve patient retention. The research will be undertaken in three phases. The first phase will comprise of secondary analysis of the UK CHIC database to examine HIV out-patient attendance patterns. Group-based trajectory modelling will be used to identify clusters of individuals following similar, distinctive patterns of outpatient attendance. Logistic regression analyses will be used to predict the probability of an individual being within a particular group according to a particular set of risk factors. In this way emerging subpopulations will be identified and characterised in detail from the complex cohort. We will investigate the potential health impact of disengaging with care in terms of mortality, and disease progression, and will measure the costs associated with disengagement. A tool to predict ‘retention risk’ will be devised and tested for validity. The tool will be an algorithm for use in clinical practice. The second phase explores the patient experience and uses both quantitative and qualitative methods. According to criteria outlined during phase one of the study, HIV patients within each pattern of attendance will be recruited to participate in a questionnaire based survey. Five HIV outpatient centres across London have agreed to participate in the study. This will be followed by a nested sub study of 40 semi-structured interviews to gain in-depth contextual information on patients’ experiences, their service preferences and perceived barriers to accessing HV services. Supplementing these will be four community focus groups, used to uncover alternative perceptions that may be articulated in a different, non-medicalised setting. Within the third phase, ten service providers will be surveyed to provide their opinions on barriers to engagement, how best to adapt services to optimise patient engagement, and what service models would be operationally feasible. Throughout the study a validated framework to enable development of effective behaviour change interventions will be utilised. The outcomes will directly inform innovative service strategies, streamlining and building on current initiatives. Preliminary estimates of the costs of these interventions will be determined. The outcomes of this research will represent a tailoring of national HIV services to improve patient-centred care and health outcomes. The importance of optimising service engagement is relevant across NHS services.
