Award_Title: Public health air pollution impacts of different pathways to meet the UK Climate Change Act commitment to 80% reduction on CO2 and other greenhouse gas emissions by 2050
Abstract: 1. Design The design of the project follows the flowchart. The first steps are the identification of a series of scenarios as set out in section C3 to identify the range of options for achieving the greenhouse gas emission target with potentially large differences in public health impacts. The choice of these scenarios will be informed by published policy documents from the Department of Energy and Climate Change (DECC) such as 'The Carbon Plan' published in November 2011 and previous reports. These analyses contain only approximate assessments of air quality impacts. The national scale energy scenarios will then be translated into air pollution emissions inventories, on a finely resolved grid (approx. 9km, finer in cities)over the whole UK, based on King's expertise in building emission inventories in London and the UK. These emission inventories will then be used in a state-of-the-art air quality model (CMAQ) to produce concentrations of harmful air pollutants, notably PM2.5, ozone and NO2. There are then established methods to estimate the impacts on mortality and morbidity knowing the concentrations of these pollutants. There is some uncertainty over the health impacts for NO2 but judgements will be made based on the extensive epidemiological and toxicological expertise available at King's and in the Advisory Board so that best estimates will be made. Having established the public health impacts of a range of scenarios, further iterations may be necessary to achieve an optimal strategy, but the final stage of the project will be an identification of a strategy to achieve the Climate Change Act target in 2050 while maximising the benefits for public health. 2. Setting. DECC has recently published 'The Carbon Plan' setting out some options for scenarios to meet the 2050 target. This analysis is based on a macro-economic study using the MARKAL model to derive national-level energy demand and potential fuel use. While such studies are useful in giving an indication of the strategic needs for energy supply and demand from different sectors, the fact that they are carried out at a national scale, and that there are no specific details of implementation in terms of technologies and locations, means that the air quality impacts they quote are not accurate assessments of the impacts on air quality and public health. They are based on a 'do-it-yourself' calculator on the DECC website to allow anyone to develop their own scenarios to achieve the 2050 target. This system incorporates an option to estimate the health impacts. The estimates are based purely on national level emissions (i.e. the total amount of pollutant released in the atmosphere in the UK) rather than concentrations at ground level and inevitably make many assumptions and approximations in deriving impacts, nor would they be able to address potential health inequalities. There is therefore the need to evaluate the public health impacts of the policies in a more accurate and realistic way. This will involve modelling of air quality exposures and impacts at a detailed spatial scale using methods described above and in the detailed project description. The potential policies and scenario/pathway choices are being considered by Government now and over the next few years. There is at present no systematic or detailed analysis of possible public health impacts of these choices. There are important public health issues at stake and a careful analysis of these impacts is necessary for informed choices to be made. 3. Target Population The project covers the impacts on public health of the UK population as a whole. 4. Intervention being evaluated. The interventions are the policy and scenario options for achieving the Climate Change Act target for CO2 emissions which simultaneously minimize the impacts of air pollution on public health. 5. Measurement of outcomes and duration of follow-up. The outcome of the project will be a policy scenario or scenarios which minimize impacts on public health while attaining the Climate Change Act target in 2050, and hence are not measurable in the same sense as shorter-term interventions. However, the optimal scenarios identified by the project can be used to assess the policy options being considered by government and the relevant public health improvements achieved or even foregone, can be evaluated. 6. Sample size. As with 3 above, the sample size is not strictly relevant to a project such as this. 7. Planned analyses. These have been described in the 'Design' section above. 8. Project timetable. The project is planned to take 3 years; no recruitment is anticipated. The outline timetable is as follows Selection of scenarios (Year1:Q2) and production of pollution emission inventories, model set up (Year 1 Q4) Modelling of current and future pollutant concentrations (Year 2 Q4); Fine (20m grid) in London (Year 2 Q4) Exposure modelling; population exposures using hybrid model (Year3 Q1); assessment of exposure inequalities (Year2 Q2) Health outcomes: continuous assessment of literature on exposure response functions from start of project, final decision Year 3 Q1; life-table calculations of mortality and morbidity in all scenarios (Year3 Q2); assessment of effects of scenarios on health inequalities (Year3 Q2);cost-benefit analysis (Year3 Q3); identify optimal scenarios for climate and public health (Year3 Q4).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Preventing domestic abuse for children (PEACH)
Abstract: The study will comprise a mixed knowledge review with three phases: a systematic mixed methods literature review, a mapping study of current practice, and a consultation phase. Target Population: children and young people under 18 in the general population. Interventions: educational programmes, media and community campaigns aimed at raising young people’s awareness of domestic abuse and reducing their susceptibility to harm from domestic abuse in both their own and their parents’ interpersonal relationships. The study will have 3 overlapping phases: 1. Literature review: The applicants will harness their knowledge of work in this field to search electronic databases, key journals, reference lists and websites. A search strategy will be devised in collaboration with 3 Advisory Groups. The review will include relevant material in all languages (translation will be used where required) published since 1990 comprising meta-analyses, research reviews, controlled studies, before-and-after studies and independent case evaluations. Recent reviews of prevention of different forms of violence have identified between 16 and 52 relevant studies. These reviews have not however included ‘grey’ literature which will be included in our review (much UK material is only available in this form). In-house evaluations will be excluded. All studies meeting the inclusion criteria will be subject to quality assessment using a tool relevant to the methods used. Back-chaining of the reference lists of included studies will take place before the inclusion list is finalized Three topics will be addressed in the analysis of the included literature: study and outcome description; costs and cost-effectiveness; and views and experiences. Differences in important subgroups, such as gender, will be explicitly identified and logged A realist review approach will provide the framework for the analysis, based on the approach used by Greenhalgh et al (2007). For the study and outcome description, six intersecting narrative analyses will be performed, to include mapping of study characteristics, creation of logic models to examine the theoretical basis of each type of programme of intervention, description of the outcomes assessed across the whole dataset, narrative summary of the effectiveness of all programme types against each outcome, and of all the outcomes assessed in each programme. We will record all data on cost and cost-effectiveness identified in the literature review. Cost data are likely to include the cost of interventions, societal costs, and potential savings from the implementation of preventive interventions. Cost-effectiveness analyses may relate costs and outcomes. For comparative purposes cost will be adjusted for inflation and presented in local currency and sterling using appropriate exchange rates. The quality of economic studies will be assessed using a pro forma developed from established appraisal tools. Data describing views and experiences will be tabulated separately. Quantitative data will be summarized narratively based on a simple thematic overview of the areas covered by the data collection processes in each study and across the studies. Good quality qualitative data will be synthesised employing a meta-synthesis approach (based on meta-ethnographic techniques) using reciprocal and refutational translation, and line of argument synthesis. 2. Mapping study: to determine what preventive initiatives are currently being delivered in the UK, to which groups, by whom and to what extent and to identify any additions to the evidence base. A stratified sample of 18 local authorities will be developed using police figures for domestic abuse incidents to ensure inclusion of local authorities with high, medium and low rates of domestic abuse. In each local authority, an on-line survey will be undertaken of schools and other educational establishments (including Pupil Referral Units); sexual health services; domestic violence forums/partnerships and Local Safeguarding Children’s Boards. Key local collaborators will be identified with assistance of organisations such as the Personal Social and Health Education (PSHE) Association who will assist in distribution of the survey. The survey will address questions including: nature of preventive initiative, format, context, target group, content, structure, facilitators, uptake, funding and evaluation. 3. Consultation: Individual interviews to establish the relevance and acceptability of different approaches will be undertaken with 12/15 key informants from the policy, campaigning, education, health and voluntary sectors identified with the assistance of the advisory groups and from the researchers’ networks. Telephone interviews will be held with a small number of key informants from N America and Australia where interventions are more developed. Since the area addressed by this scoping study is broad, covering a range of professional groups and disciplines, the study will benefit from the advice of 3 advisory groups convened to provide expertise in the field, facilitate access to networks and to advise on research design. These 3 groups will be convened at 3 key stages: at the outset; at completion of the mapping study and to comment on study findings. The Advisory Group for Education will address the evidence on educational programmes and will be convened by the PSHE Association. The Advisory Group for Media and Community Initiatives will examine community education campaigns, social marketing campaigns and the media (including the internet) campaigns as well as community and social marketing initiatives and will be convened by Women’s Aid. The Young People’s Advisory Group will be recruited from an established young people’s participation group with experience of being consulted on similar issues. This group will provide young people’s perspectives on key questions to be addressed, the scope of the study and on emerging findings. Outputs: The evidence will be synthesized to create a framework of effective and cost-effective interventions that also addresses their acceptability and applicability in the UK context. The synthesized data will be mapped together narratively and graphically to illustrate commonalities and differences between the data sets and to identify where particular strategies have been used successfully with particular groups of children and young people, in the search for what works, for who, in what circumstances. The study findings will inform policy, practice and future research, addressing which interventions should be investigated and how, target population groups and potential outcome measures. In addition to a project report, papers will be produced for relevant peer reviewed journals, and findings will be presented to a range of professional, policy and research audiences. Timetable: The 3 phases of the study will run in parallel over 18 months. The 3 meetings of the advisory groups will represent key milestones at months 3, 12 and 18.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Sexual health promotion delivered by digital media: scoping review
Abstract: Aim: This work will scope, appraise and synthesise available evidence on digital interventions for sexual health for young people, integrating the findings with key informant views (both professional and lay) to produce summaries of evidence on investment in future research, development and implementation of digital interventions for sexual health. Objectives: * To appraise and synthesise evidence on effectiveness, cost-effectiveness and mechanism of action of digital interventions for sexual health * To determine optimal research methods for intervention evaluation * To determine optimal practice for intervention development and identify 'front running' interventions * To appraise and synthesise evidence on contexts for successful implementation of digital interventions for sexual health * To delineate gaps in available evidence * To provide evidence-based pointers for local and national policy in relation to the adoption and implementation of digital interventions for sexual health * To scope the future potential for sexual health promotion by digital media Study design- The work involves the integration of findings from systematic and rapid evidence syntheses with key informant views (both professional and lay). The work falls into five related research topics: A. Systematic review and meta-analyses of evidence on effectiveness of digital interventions for sexual health promotion * How effective are digital interventions for sexual health promotion? * What features of interventions, participants or settings are associated with efficacy? * What are the effects on health inequalities? - Systematic literature search for RCTs of digital interventions for sexual health promotion - Meta-analyses - Meta-regression ………………………………………………………………………………............................................. B. Optimum research methodology to evaluate digital interventions * What are the strengths of different research methods to evaluate digital interventions? * What are the challenges of conducting randomised controlled trials of digital interventions? * What are optimal comparators (controls)? * What are the best ways of measuring outcomes (including social and emotional wellbeing)? * How can we maximise the strength and quality of evidence? - Focused literature search (for qualitative and quantitative evidence on research methodology concerning digital interventions for sexual health promotion) - Review of reviews (on research methodology from other fields) - Key informant interviews (experts' health researchers’ views on optimum research methodologies) - Key informant interviews (young people’s views on suitable outcomes) - Expert symposium (to debate areas of controversy on optimal research methods) …………………………………………………………………......................................................... C. Optimum design, development and implementation of digital interventions for sexual health promotion * What are the barriers and facilitators for successful design, development and implementation? * What is best practice for sexual health digital intervention design and development? * What are the mechanisms of action of digital interventions for sexual health promotion? * Which behaviour change theory and techniques should be incorporated? * What are the merits of alternative models of intervention delivery? (e.g. direct vs. facilitated access) * What are the merits of alternative modes of intervention delivery? (e.g. different technological platforms) * How can intervention access, uptake and adherence be optimised? * Are there ‘front running’ digital interventions for sexual health suitable for further research? - Focused literature search (for qualitative, quantitative and theoretical evidence on design, development and implementation) - Review of reviews (on design, development and implementation from other fields) - Key informant interviews (experts' views on digital intervention design, development and implementation) - Key informant interviews (young people’s views on digital intervention design and implementation) - Expert symposium (to debate areas of controversy on design, development and implementation) ………………………………………………………………................................................................ D. Costs, cost-effectiveness, and optimal methods for economic measurement and modelling in sexual health * What are the costs of digital interventions for sexual health? * Are digital interventions for sexual health cost-effective? * What is the scale of possible health and cost benefits? * What are the optimal methods for economic measurement and modelling in a sexual health context? - Focused literature search (for papers which report costs, cost-effectiveness and health economic outcomes for digital interventions for sexual health promotion) - Key informant interviews (experts' views on optimal methods for economic measurement and modelling) - Expert symposium (to debate areas of controversy on optimal methods for economic measurement and modelling) ……………………………………………………...................................................................……. E. Future potential for sexual health promotion via digital media * What are the barriers and facilitators to future implementation of digital interventions for sexual health? * How should digital interventions integrate with current educational and health promotion practice? * Should sexual health promotion interventions be linked with other digital interventions, e.g. for alcohol and drug use harm reduction? * Where is this field leading? * What strategic investments are needed in future research or implementation to optimise the potential of digital media interventions for young people? - Focused literature search (for reviews, reports and opinion pieces concerning the future potential of digital interventions for sexual health promotion) - Internet search to scan the horizon on future potential - Key informant interviews (experts' views on future potential) - Key informant interviews (young people’s views on the future potential) - Expert symposium (to debate the future potential of digital interventions for sexual health promotion)

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Maximising cycling safety to improve public health: a Cochrane review to assess the effectiveness of cycling infrastructure at reducing the risk of cycling injuries in cyclists
Abstract: Methods: We will include RCTs, cluster-RCTs, controlled before-and-after studies and non randomised controlled trials. Target population and setting: Adult and child cyclists in the urban and rural environment in developed countries. Intervention being evaluated: 1. Cycling infrastructure that aims to manage the shared use of the road space for motorized vehicles and cyclists. 2. Infrastructure to separate cycle traffic from motorized traffic. 3. The management of infrastructure which aims to separate different types of traffic using direction signage which differentiates by vehicle type, or speed management by the use of physical measures such as narrowed roads or speed bumps. (See section C2 for more details). In some situations there will be more than one infrastructure feature in place and the effect of individual features will be determined where possible. Studies for inclusion must include some measure of cycling injuries, either self-reported non medically attended or medically attended. We will not include injuries sustained while racing, mountain biking or playing but we will include those sustained as a result of maintenance issues of infrastructure, such as, poor surfaces. Search strategy: Search strategies will be developed iteratively: results will be assessed to determine whether the strategy is identifying relevant papers and adjusted as required. The proposed review will include a search of the following databases, Medline, PubMed, Embase, Geobase, SIGLE, Index to Theses, SafetyLit, Google Scholar, TRANweb, TRID, the Cochrane Library, and also the database at the Transport Research Laboratory. We will systematically search the internet. We will search relevant websites such as the National Bicycle Safety Network and the Cycling Embassy of Great Britain and road safety organisations such as AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety, Australian Road Research Board, Transport Canada and Transportation Research Board (US). We will handsearch abstracts of relevant conferences, that is, the World Conference on Injury Prevention and Safety Promotion, Australian Cycling Conference, NZ Cycling Conference and the European Transport Conference. We will search reference lists of included studies. Where we are unable to find the full paper or if we require further data we will contact authors. Review Process: A two stage screening process will be undertaken. Two reviewers will independently scan titles and abstracts of articles for relevance according to pre-determined criteria for study inclusion. For those articles retained at this stage the full article will be retrieved and will be reviewed independently once again by two reviewers for relevance. Disagreement at either stage will be dealt with by deferment to a third reviewer. Papers retained at this stage will be included in the review. An initial scoping exercise suggests that approximately 30 articles will be included in the final review. Two authors will independently extract data using an extraction form designed specifically for this review and pre-tested. Reviewers will extract data on study design, country, characteristics of the intervention and control areas, nature of the intervention, length of follow up and relevant outcome data. Two authors will undertake critical appraisal of the included studies for potential sources of bias; these will be selection, performance, detection, reporting and attrition bias rated as high, low or unclear. It is anticipated that due to the nature of the intervention the majority of the studies will be non RCT and for these studies quality assessment will consider selection bias based on the degree of similarity between the control and intervention areas, performance and detection bias will be based on an assessment of whether data collection and analyses were performed by a researcher blind to location/time of data collection and attrition bias will consider length of time of data collection before and after installation of intervention. For both data extraction and critical appraisal, the findings of the two reviewers will be examined for discrepancies. Expected output of research: Where sufficient data is available a meta-analysis will be undertaken. For binary outcome measures, pooled relative risk will be estimated using random-effects meta-analysis and summary data. For outcomes measured as rates, pooled incidence rate ratios (IRR) will be estimated using summary data and a random-effects model. A fixed-effects model will be used if there are fewer than five studies. If there are insufficient clinically homogenous studies to combine in a meta-analysis, the results from individual studies will be combined in a narrative review. We will undertake statistical tests of homogeneity using chi squared tests (with significance defined as a P-value of <0.1) and the I2 statistic will be presented. Heterogeneity will be explored using subgroup analyses (these will include separate analyses of randomised and non randomised studies). If there are sufficient studies and there has been uncertainty or disagreement regarding the inclusion of studies, missing data, or in the event of one or more studies dominating the results, a sensitivity analysis will be undertaken to determine whether the findings are robust to the decisions made relating to choice of study inclusion. If appropriate, the possibility of publication bias will be assessed using funnel plots. Findings from the review will be presented in a report which will include strengths and weaknesses of the review, and implications for practice and research. We will disseminate the findings through presentations at conferences and through peer reviewed publications. Timetable. Months 1-4 Devising and running search strategies, handsearching - time required to identify studies in grey literature. Months 5-6 Initial review of titles and abstracts. Months 7-9 Obtaining copies of full papers, review of full papers, data extraction. Months 10-12 Data analyses and summarising. Months 13-15 Write up and dissemination.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: The Health Impacts of Structural Energy Performance Investments in Wales: An Evaluation of the Arbed Programme
Abstract: The research consists of 6 interlinked work packages: WP1: Secure Anonymised Information Linkage System (Lead: Lyons, Rodgers): SAIL is used to retrospectively evaluate Arbed Phase 1 with routinely collected hospital and GP consultation data. SAIL is an ethically approved tool developed and hosted by Swansea University that anonymously links individual and property-based data to objective health service data. The system ensures that individuals remain anonymous, while retaining the ability to make links between different datasets. The procedure involves the removal of names by a trusted third party, who will replace them with an unidentifiable code. This procedure ensures that no-one sees all datasets together, maintaining patient confidentiality. This WP will use multiple comparator groups, i.e.: (a) 13,000 household living in social housing in low-income neighbourhoods, and (b) the whole Welsh population. Households that received Arbed 1 improvements will be excluded from both groups. We will evaluate admission and consultation rates for cardio-respiratory condituions for the intervention and comparator groups in the same periods before and after the Arbed 1 intervention. WP2: Community-Based Health Impact Study (Lead: Poortinga, Palmer): A health impact study will be set up to evaluate Arbed Phase 2. The intervention will target private and social housing in low-income areas. In total, 500 householders will be interviewed before and after the Arbed 2 intervention that will take place in 2014. Control households (n=500) in similar low-income neighbourhoods will be interviewed in the same before and after periods. Householders will be interviewed face-to-face by trained interviewers. Participants’ self reported respiratory conditions and the MCS of SF12 are the main outcomes. Secondary outcomes include reported health-related QoL (PCS of SF12), thermal comfort, financial position, fuel poverty, and social isolation. Parts of the questionnaire are already developed as part of a health impact assessment of the Carmarthenshire Homes Standard programme, led by the Principal Applicant. Ethical approval will be sought from the School Research Ethics Committee. Welsh Health Survey data collected in 2013-2015 is used to examine if the health status of the intervention group has improved relative to the whole Welsh population. WP3: Household Monitoring (Lead: Tweed): Detailed energy consumption and internal condition data will be collected, and linked to experienced thermal comfort. The study will include a subset of dwellings undergoing Arbed improvements (n=50), a control group where no such improvements will take place (n=50). Detailed indoor temperature and relative humidity measurements will be made with Tinytag data loggers in the living room, main bedroom, and hallway. Recording will be made every 15 minutes over a 4 week period in the heating season to make a reliable assessment of average temperature and humidity. Energy use over the same period will be estimated by meter readings. The data will be adjustments for external meteorological conditions. The lead has developed a comfort survey method which allows occupants' thermal comfort to be tied directly to physical measurements of environmental conditions. This WP will show whether the intervention improves thermal comfort and indoor environmental conditions, and expands occupants’ living space, all which may be part of the pathway to improved mental and cardio-respiratory health. It will make an objective assessment of fuel poverty using income and energy bill data. WP4: Health Economic Assessment Tool (Lead: Phillips): The HEAT for Housing tool is used to provide an economic evaluation of the energy efficiency investments. HEAT was initially developed to estimate the economic savings as a result of improved health due to regular cycling and walking. In the active NIHR-PHR project, the tool is being adapted so it can be used for housing improvements. The approach will be a cost-consequences analysis (CCA) from the perspective of the public sector as a whole. The costs of delivering the Arbed programme will be compared to the cost savings associated as a result of reduced health service use. Comparisons in cost-consequences will be made between intervention and control areas; with future costs and benefits being discounted to bring them into present values. The HEAT for Housing tool is applied to data collected in the community-based study and by SAIL. Cost savings to the health service are calculated using hospital/GP admission and treatment data from SAIL, while the cost utility of the intervention is calculated using QALYs obtained from SF6D utilities calculated from SF12 responses WP5: Steering Board (Lead: Poortinga): We will convene an expert steering board for the project for advice and critical feedback on the design and direction of the research. The panel comprises both public policy and leading academics in housing and health research. The board will meet bi-annually throughout the research. Having members from Public Health Wales and the Welsh Government on board ensures that the research keeps sight of its policy relevance and the results will be directly communicated to relevant policy areas. WP6: Resident Engagement (Lead: Poortinga; Tweed): The research is informed resident engagement. Focus groups will be conducted in areas where improvements have been made i (n=2x7) and where they are expected to take place (n=2x7).Focus groups will discuss the resident experiences to improve WP2 survey design, and where possible adjust the direction of research. A number of participants will be recruited to meet 3 times in an occupants panel. Second, the results of the project will be made available to residents via presentations at central locations and an easy-to-understand key findings brochure.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Risks and benefits of psychotropic medication in pregnancy
Abstract: Longitudinal observational study of women with psychoses who are in receipt of psychotropic medication using data from The Health Improvement Network (THIN) and General Practice Research Database (GPRD). These databases include longitudinal clinical and prescribing records for more than 10% of the UK population. SETTING: United Kingdom General Practice TARGET GROUP: Women with psychosis (bipolar disorder, schizophrenia or overlap syndromes) who are in receipt of antipsychotics, lithium and anticonvulsant mood stabilisers and who become pregnant. HEALTH TECHNOLOGIES: Prescriptions of: a) lithium b) AEDs c) typical and atypical antipsychotics. OUTCOMES: Quantity of prescribed psychotropic medication before, during pregnancy and after delivery. Time to discontinuation and restarting of medication. Markers for change of severity of illness including psychiatric hospitalisation, psychosis, suicide and suicide attempts.Foetal losses, neonatal death, preeclampsia, major congenital anomalies, preterm birth, low birth weight, low weight for gestation, low Apgar scores, maternal and child renal problems.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Massage intervention for promoting mental and physical health in infants aged under six months
Abstract: Background 1.1 Infant Massage Touching is an intrinsic part of caring for an infant and, in many areas of the world, especially in the Africa, Asia, indigenous South Pacific cultures and the Soviet Union, infant massage is a traditional practice (Field et al. 1996). Infants are commonly given a massage with oil before sleep during the first few months of their lives (Field 2000). A survey of 332 primary caretakers of neonates in Bangladesh, for example, found that 96% engaged in massage of the infant's whole body between one and three times daily (Darmstadt and Saha 2002). In many areas of India, the traditional daily massage routine begins in the first few days after birth and each body part is systematically stretched and vigorously rubbed before infants are swaddled (Field 2000). The popularity of infant massage has spread to western cultures and researchers initially became interested in evaluating the benefits for high-risk infants, with the majority of studies being conducted with pre-term infants in neonatal care units where the environment is stressful and lacking in tactile stimulation (Field 2000; Vickers 2004). The introduction of infant massage into western cultures during the latter half of the twentieth century coincided with the rapid development of multi-disciplinary knowledge about infant mental health. Parenting support interventions such as Sure Start in the UK began to advocate infant massage as a way of increasing ‘bonding and attachment’ although the National Evaluation of Sure Start found the evidence to support the intervention disappointingly anecdotal. Field (2000) highlighted the importance of researchers addressing the question of whether infant massage is an effective medium for enhancing infants’ primary caregiving relationships. In 2006 Underdown et al conducted a systematic review of infant massage and this was published by the Cochrane Collaboration. This review aimed to assess the impact of infant massage on mental and physical outcomes for healthy infants in the first six months of life. A total of 23 randomised controlled trials were included but it was only possible to combine the results of the included studies for a small number of outcomes. The results of nine studies provide some evidence suggestive of improved mother-infant interaction, improved sleep and relaxation, reduced crying and a beneficial impact on a number of physiological processes. Results showing a significant impact on the number of illnesses were limited to a study of Korean orphanage infants. There was no evidence of any impact on infant growth, attachment, temperament, psychomotor or mental development. These results provided tentative evidence to support current practice with regard to the teaching of infant massage within the community during the first six months of life, but fall short of the evidence needed to recommend universal provision. The review highlighted the need for further research to identify the relative benefits of the different approaches to infant massage, the best approach to teaching parents and the optimum frequency and intensity. The popularity of infant massage is increasing and it is important that commissioners, early years’ professionals and parents are able to access the most up-to-date evidence about the effectiveness of this intervention. An update of the 2006 review is now required.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Maternal and perinatal outcomes of pandemic influenza in pregnancy
Abstract: Design: National cohort study using the UK Obstetric Surveillance System (UKOSS). Setting: All consultant-led hospital maternity units. Target population: Pregnant women. Health technologies being assessed: Pandemic influenza or other pandemic infection such as COVID-19. Measurement of costs and outcomes: The following outcomes will be compared between women with pandemic infection and comparison women, and explored in different subgroups according to management variations: maternal death, maternal level 3 critical care unit admission, other major maternal complication, preterm birth, congenital anomaly, perinatal death. Sample size: The primary objective of this study is to determine the incidence of pandemic infection in pregnancy. The study size will therefore be dependent on the infection rate among pregnant women, together with the UK maternity rate (currently approximately 750,000 maternities per year). If the patterns are similar to the 2009 influenza pandemic, we anticipate identifying 3-500 affected pregnancies during a 6 month initial study period. Information on up to 1500 comparison women is available from existing UKOSS data. A study of this size will have 80% power at the 5% level to detect a doubling of the risk of any adverse outcome (severe maternal morbidity or mortality, preterm delivery, congenital malformation or perinatal death) in women with influenza compared with comparison women. Project timetable: PRE-ACTIVATION PHASE (provisional start date 1 June 2012) January 2012 Apply for necessary approvals, develop web-based reporting systems, finalise and format data collection form and clinician information. ACTIVATION PHASE Week 1: Study information mailed/emailed to clinicians Week 3: Data collection commenced Months 2-6: Ongoing reporting of new cases, data analysis, production of management guidance and dissemination. Months 7-10: Collection of remaining pregnancy outcome data Month 12: Final pregnancy outcome analysis, production of guidance and dissemination

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Early estimation of pandemic influenza Antiviral and Vaccine Effectiveness (EAVE) - use of a unique community and laboratory national linked dataset
Abstract: • Design: Primary Research - a large national retrospective observational cohort study of patients using a unique community, hospital and laboratory linked dataset. • Setting (PR): The PTI network of 40 general practices covers a five percent representative sample of the Scottish population (n=300,000). These practices receive an annual financial incentive to record all of their practice data electronically. Using the unique Community Health Index number, general practice patient level data will be extracted and linked to the SMR01 catalogue, which comprises of death data from the General Registers Office Scotland and in-patient hospital data for the whole of Scotland and also the Health Protection Scotland (HPS) dataset consists of laboratory confirmed cases of new pandemic influenza from throughout Scotland. In addition, Scottish laboratories (West of Scotland Specialist Virology Laboratory & Regional Virus Laboratory Specialist Virology Centre) will store all biochemistry samples (n~2000) from a subset of participating practices until the beginning of a new pandemic. • Target population (PR): 300,000 people of all ages registered with participating practices throughout Scotland. • Health technologies being assessed: The new pandemic influenza vaccination and antivirals (if available). • Measurement of outcomes: • Vaccine effectiveness will be measured using: Influenza positivity from virological swab data in vaccinated and unvaccinated patients stratified by ‘at-risk’ populations, age, sex and socioeconomic status. • Consultation for influenza-related morbidity from general practice data in vaccinated and unvaccinated patients stratified by ‘at-risk’ populations, age, sex and socio-economic status; • Mortality and influenza-related serious morbidity (e.g. influenza, pneumonia, COPD and cardiac related death and hospitalisation from SMR01 records) in vaccinated and unvaccinated patients stratified by ‘at-risk’ populations, age, sex and socioeconomic status; and • For patients with stored serology (and prior to the introduction of any vaccination) whether cross-reactivity occurs due to previous exposure to A/H1N1 or A/H1N1 vaccination, other pandemic influenza or other seasonal influenza vaccination or exposure. • Sample size: We plan to recruit 40 practices with a combined list size of 300,000 patients. Approximately 5% (n=15,000) of patients will be aged 0-5 years, 15% (n=45,000) aged over 65 years, and 30% under 65 years will be deemed to be in the at-risk category on the basis of existing illnesses.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The provision of antenatal information for the NHS Newborn Bloodspot Screening Programme (NBSP)
Abstract: Design. A two phase, sequential, exploratory, mixed methods project.(1) Health Technologies Being Assessed: Current practice of providing NBSP information antenatally and associated consent. Measurement of cost and outcomes: The provision of NBSP information antenatally meets many of the criteria of the MRC’s definition of a complex intervention. At present there are insufficient data to effectively design a comparison of alternative communication models. Therefore this project focuses on providing the necessary data to facilitate such evaluation via two phases. The first will generate alternative models of NBSP communication and consent, establish costs of current best practice and examine parents understanding of NBSPs following this model. Phase 2 will quantitatively measure preference and costs of alternative models of communication and consent, with the acceptability and broader impact of the alternative models and study findings being examined through a qualitative study with parents, NBSP providers and key stakeholders. The setting, target population, sample size, research objectives [RO] answered and timeline for each study is outlined below. Phase 1: 1: A realist review to generate characteristics of alternative models of communication and consent for NBSPs [RO1; months 1-3]. 2: Interviews regarding experiences and views of current practice, and alternative models [RO2,3; months 1-14]. Service providers: Telephone interviews will be conducted with all national newborn screening co-ordinators (N=9) and purposively sampled hospital screening co-ordinators (N=18), community midwives (N=14) and hospital based midwives (N=4). Telephone interviews enable busy health professionals to participate in health service research.(2,3) Parents: Parents (N=77) from across the screening pathway and with a range of experiences and characteristics will be purposively sampled in the North West Strategic Health Authority via midwives and health visitors to participate in face-to-face interviews. Sample sizes were approximated to ensure variation in screening experience whilst permitting timely reporting of data and was based on previous experience of gathering such data (4) and consultations with our study advisors (see project description). 3: Resource use and costs of current practice [RO4; months 1-9]. Survey: A national sample of midwives (N=300) recruited via the Royal College of Midwives (RCM) register to capture resource use in current practice. Observational study: Data from study 2 and the survey will direct purposive sampling of 5-8 midwives in the North West SHA to be directly observed for one week each. This will be achievable in terms of project resources and also give a reasonable view of the breadth of current practice. Phase 2: 4: A discrete choice experiment (DCE) of preferences for alternative models [RO5; months 10-15]. A DCE will be designed, using the responses from phase 1 to define the attributes and levels regarding communication models, to elicit and quantify trade-offs for service process and outcome attributes from 250 midwives sampled and 500 current and prospective parents. The views of midwives and parents will be compared. The samples should be sufficient to estimate preferences in astudy design comprising ~6 attributes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: An evidence synthesis to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of interventions to prevent postnatal depression.
Abstract: Design: Systematic review, evidence synthesis and meta-analysis of quantitative and qualitative studies. Search strategy: We will 1. use major health-related, and health economic electronic bibliographic databases; 2. consult via the internet key health service organisations and guideline producing bodies; 3. consult national/international experts in research/practice in preventing PND; 4. search the UK CRN Portfolio Database, archive of NRR, CCT and its links, Clinical Trials.gov, HSRProj and Index to Theses to identify ongoing/recently completed research; 5. use existing systematic reviews to identify relevant studies; 6. identify Grey literature; 7. examine reference lists of included studies for further relevant references and, if appropriate, use the citation facility in Web of Science to search for specific papers/authors; 8. restrict searches to English language trials or systematic reviews, with no date restriction. For the qualitative literature synthesis we will include qualitative research which: 1. examined acceptability by reports from women who received PND preventative interventions; 2. identified promising components of candidate interventions by reports from women who did not develop PND; 3. examined how acceptability may affect clinical effectiveness using data within trial reports or process evaluations; and, 4. reported the acceptability of interventions to health care practitioners with data from separately conceived research or within trial reports. We will 1. use a three-line strategy to identify studies using wide ranging, multi-disciplinary databases, with sifting to examine title and abstract, then article full-text; 2. use complementary strategies of citation tracking, citation pearl growing, and Related Articles; 3. target Dissertation Abstracts and Index to Theses for qualitative research reports; 4. identify “sibling studies”, e.g. process evaluations, and identify mixed methods studies blending quantitative and qualitative research within a common context; to maximise external validity; and 5. track studies through citation linkage from included RCTs and follow-up of principal investigator web sites. Review strategy: We will include reports of systematic reviews, RCTs and economic evaluations of prescribed medicines, supplements, social support, “mind-body interventions”, complementary and alternative medicines, and maternity care organisation used in the prevention of PND for antenatal or early postnatal women, in all settings, using controls or specific comparators. The outcomes of interest are maternal, infant and family. We will assess the quality of the quantitative and qualitative studies. Data will be extracted using a standardised data extraction tool then double checked. Where appropriate, for cost-effectiveness modelling, clinical effectiveness estimates will be obtained by meta-analysis of available evidence, and network meta-analyses where appropriate, with the cost per QALY as the final outcome. Qualitative meta-synthesis will provide added value to the quantitative analysis. Expected output: We plan to disseminate findings in high profile journals, national/international conferences, guideline development bodies and feed results into curricula for professional education. Team expertise: The team have extensive experience in literature searches, systematic reviews, evidence synthesis, value of information analyses, Bayesian statistics in health economics, decision analytic models, health economic modelling and mapping, plus mental health technologies, mental health research, PND, clinical experience and research with antenatal and postnatal women, maternity care organisation, public health, primary care, parenting and infant outcomes. Study timetable: 15 months from 01.11.12 – 31.01.13. Search and quantitative studies review; then Critical appraisal of quantitative literature; Data analysis and report from meta-analysis; Search and review qualitative studies; Dissemination of reviews, Decision Analysis, Cost-effectiveness modelling, Final Value of Information analyses; Final report and continuing dissemination.

Contractor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A clinical and economic evaluation of screening and diagnostic tests to identify and treat women with gestational diabetes: association between maternal risk factors, glucose levels, and adverse outcomes
Abstract: Gestational diabetes (GDM) affects a significant proportion of women each year, the incidence is increasing globally and is associated with a range of adverse perinatal and longer term health outcomes which may repeat across generations. Various strategies are used to identify women with GDM [1] with no clear evidence of superiority for any one method over another and there also remains uncertainty how GDM is best identified and at what glycaemic threshold treatment should begin. This uncertainty partly reflects lack of clarity around glycaemic thresholds for diagnosis. Recent evidence shows a graded positive linear association between fasting and postload glucose level and adverse outcomes [2]. This research will use systematic reviews, analysis of new individual participant data and contemporary modelling techniques to identify the most cost and clinically-effective strategies for identifying GDM and for preventing associated adverse health outcomes. More specifically, the objectives will: (1) determine adverse outcome incidence rates associated with incremental increases in maternal glucose level, including: large for gestational age, operative delivery, birth injury, maternal postnatal length of hospital stay, admission to neonatal unit and perinatal death (2) estimate the incidence of GDM in the contemporary UK obstetric population and in subgroups of the population, for example by ethnicity and by BMI category; (3) compare the characteristics of screening tests and (4) compare the characteristics of diagnostic tests in relation to key perinatal and longer term maternal outcomes and (5) determine the most cost and clinically-effective methods to treat GDM to reduce adverse outcomes. The objectives will be accomplished using relevant data from studies identified through systematic searching carried out by a team of information specialists; included studies will be quality assessed and analysed by the research teams at Bradford and York and evidence synthesised as appropriate to produce ranges of estimates of the key parameters. A new analysis of individual participant data from cohort studies will be undertaken using the Born in Bradford (BIB) cohort. Comparisons will include (a) universal non-blood based risk factor screening followed by selective 75g OGTT; (b) universal fasting glucose screening followed by selective 75g OGTT; (c) universal random glucose screening followed by 75g OGTT; (d) universal HbA1c followed by 75g OGTT and (e) universal diagnostic testing with 75g OGTT. We will extend our recent systematic review [3] and compare how outcomes differ for OGTT undertaken at different times in pregnancy and with different doses and types of glucose load. Incidence of GDM and associations between incremental increases in maternal glucose levels and adverse outcomes including macrosomia, birth injury and instrumental birth and long-term health outcomes (maternal insulin and glucose dysfunction) will be examined. The costs of treatment for GDM will be estimated from previous economic evaluations and from routine UK data sources (for example the British National Formulary). The health consequences for the population of untreated/treated GDM will be identified from the reviews and new analyses and their associated costs will be estimated from previous economic evaluations and routine UK data sources (e.g. NHS reference costs). Estimates obtained from the literature reviews and the new analyses of individual participant data from BIB and other studies will be used to populate a decision analytic model for the cost and clinical effectiveness analysis [4]. Alternative screening and diagnostic strategies are expected to differ in terms of costs of identifying women with GDM, and the proportion of women identified in whom appropriate treatment can be provided. The decision analytic model will allow differences to be translated into differences in total costs and health outcomes from the perspective of the UK NHS [5]. Cost-effectiveness analysis divides the overall participant population into sub-groups of women who would be identified as being at similar baseline risk of adverse events from GDM and similar in terms of response to treatment. Treatments for GDM recommended by guidelines in the UK [6] and their cost-effectiveness will be characterised within the decision analytic model in order to predict, for a woman diagnosed with GDM, what would be the expected costs and health outcomes in terms of quality adjusted life years. The decision analytic model produced will not only be able to inform policy and practice on screening for GDM, it will also identify any key underlying uncertainties which may be worth addressing through further research. The model will be available to the NHS to update in the future as new data emerge and so be a useful resource for NHS decision makers. 1.
