Contractor: South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Preventing blood borne virus infection in people who inject drugs in the UK: the development and feasibility of psychosocial interventions
Abstract: DESIGN Mixed methods project with 6 complementary phases. AIM 1) To develop an evidence based psychosocial intervention to reduce transmission risks among IDU at risk of acquiring or transmitting blood-borne viruses(BBV) (target group) 2) conduct a feasibility randomised controlled trial(RCT) of the intervention. PHASE 1. DETERMINING THE EVIDENCE BASE A systematic review of efficacy of psychosocial interventions to reduce Hepatitis C risk behaviours conducted in 2012 by PI Gilchrist for the REDUCE project will be updated to include HIV & Hepatitis B. Medline, CINAHL, PsycINFO & Cochrane databases will be searched. Trials will be assessed using Cochrane risk of bias tool & reported using PRISMA statement. A scoping review of UK grey literature will also be conducted. UK commissioning drug partnerships (previously Drug Action Teams) will be contacted to source available interventions. All interventions will be reviewed. PHASE 2. UNDERSTANDING IDUS' INFLUENCES ON BEHAVIOUR & VIEWS ON PSYCHOSOCIAL INTERVENTIONS Indepth interviews with a purposive sample of 60 IDU (15 from London, Yorkshire, Glasgow & North Wales) from needle exchanges & drug treatment will elicit the influences on risk behaviours & determine the content & preferred mode of intervention delivery. PHASE 3. KEY STAKEHOLDERS’ VIEWS ON THE DELIVERY & EFFECTIVENESS OF PSYCHOSOCIAL INTERVENTIONS 40 national & local stakeholders including service providers, policy makers & commissioners with responsibility for BBV will be interviewed indepth by telephone (10 from Scotland, England, Wales & Northern Ireland) to determine their views on whether psychosocial interventions are effective & how they should be delivered. All interviews will be recorded & transcribed verbatim. A qualitative research framework approach will be used for analysis. PHASE 4. INTERVENTION DEVELOPMENT Informed by Phases 1-3, previous effective interventions & the REDUCE intervention will be adapted where possible. The intervention will be brief & contain core sessions with optional sessions for specific high risk IDU–including the homeless, prostitutes, women & BME groups. A working group of clinical experts, interventionists & service users will develop the intervention. PHASE 5. FEASIBILITY RCT A feasibility RCT will be conducted in 4 regions (London, Glasgow, Yorkshire, North Wales) among 128 IDU to determine whether the study can be done & inform parameters for a definitive RCT & economic evaluation. In each region 16 IDU from drug treatment services & 16 from needle & syringe exchanges will be randomly allocated to receive the intervention or an information leaflet. A mix of NHS & 3rd sector services will be recruited. Differences in number of risk events in past month will be assessed pre, end & 1 month post intervention using intention-to-treat analysis. Focus groups will examine IDU & staff experience of receiving/delivering the intervention & identify issues to its uptake & delivery. PHASE 6. PREPARATION FOR MULTISITE TRIAL Discussions with additional UK regions regarding a future multisite trial will ensure any challenges to implementation in other regions/communities are considered. EXPERTISE Team includes addiction & BBV experts in systematic reviews, intervention development, clinical trials & health economics. Service users, providers & academics will be members of intervention development & project steering groups.

Award_Title: Seasonal Influenza Vaccination Effectiveness II (SIVE II): Use of a large national primary care and laboratory-linked dataset to evaluate live attenuated and trivalent inactivated influenza vaccination effectiveness
Abstract: Design: A national longitudinal retrospective observational study. Vaccine effectiveness will be derived from linked virological swab data, using a nested case-control study design (test negative) and adjusted for covariates including comorbidities, healthcare utilisation (i.e. any cause primary care and hospital consultations – including out-patient attendance and admission) and previous vaccination. Setting: A national laboratory and hospital/mortality linked primary care database. Strategy for reviewing literature (Primary or Modelling): A structured literature review using Pubmed, Medline, Embase, Scopus and Google Scholar (all articles published to January 2013). The search terms include “live attenuated influenza vaccine, trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine, and effectiveness”. Target population: Primary analysis will be performed on children and young adults between two and 17 years (targeted for live attenuated influenza vaccine), registered with 500 primary care practices (including all sentinel influenza surveillance practices) in Scotland. Data from 2013 to 2015 (two pooled seasons providing one million patient years of data) will be linked to the Health Protection Scotland virology database (Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction [RT-PCR] tests collected in influenza season) and national hospital/mortality datasets using the Community Health Index number. Health technologies being assessed: We will evaluate the live attenuated influenza vaccine. Measurement of outcomes: Primary outcome is RT-PCR laboratory confirmed influenza (cases sub-typed as A(H1N1)pdm09, A/H1N1, A/H3N2 or B). Sample size: Using data generated from the SIVE project [09/200/37] we estimate a vaccination rate of 40% amongst children targeted for receipt of LAIV and a swab positivity rate of 20% among the unvaccinated. This gives an 80% power to detect a VE of 21% based upon 3000 swabs over two seasons (NB additional funding has been released to increase swabbing in children). Project timetables including recruitment rate: Month 12 – Governance and ethics approvals, practice recruitment, data specification, statistical modeling, drafting of methods protocol. Month 13 – Publication of protocol. Month 20 Test data collection and linkage. Month 20 – Draft early estimates of LAIV uptake/vaccine effectiveness available. Month 25 – Full data extraction, statistical analysis. Month 30 – Final report completed. Expertise in team: Our team, which includes experts in medical statistics, data linkage, epidemiology with a proven track record in carrying out vaccine effectiveness studies. The PIs Dr Colin Simpson and Dr Nazir Lone have considerable expertise in the use of primary care data and data linkage and has successfully led previous NIHR projects in evaluating vaccine programmes. Ms Ehrlich is a retired teacher and experienced public and patient involvement lead. Dr Jim McMenamin and Professor Chris Robertson have considerable expertise in the evaluation of vaccine programmes. Professor Sir Lewis Ritchie has led the implementation of several new national immunisation programmes. Professor Aziz Sheikh is a Professor of Primary Care Research & Development is a methodologist has long-standing expertise in the use of linked primary care based datasets for undertaking epidemiological and public health research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The Filter FE Challenge: pilot trial and process evaluation of a multi-level smoking prevention intervention in further education settings
Abstract: Aim: To evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of implementing and trialling a new multi-level smoking prevention intervention in FE settings. Design: Pilot cluster RCT and process evaluation. Intervention: “The Filter FE Challenge” is a universal, multi-level smoking prevention intervention that is intended to be adaptable for use in all FE settings (i.e. general FE colleges/campuses, sixth form colleges, etc.), delivered by trained staff, using resources developed by ASH Wales for “The Filter” youth project. Informed by evidence of effective smoking prevention methods and approaches, the intervention aims to prevent the uptake of smoking among FE students aged 16-18 at multiple levels via: (1) restricting the sale of tobacco to under 18 year-olds; (2) implementing tobacco-free campus policies; (3) training FE staff to deliver anti-smoking messages and support institutional change; (4) publicising “The Filter” youth project’s online social marketing campaigns, advice and support services; and (5) youth work activities to provide credible educational messages, modify perceived norms,and promote social/situational resistance skills, as well signposting cessation services if necessary. Control group: Standard practice. Setting: Six FE settings (purposively sampled for a pilot trial to examine delivery and trial methods in a range of institutional contexts). Target population: FE students aged 16-18 Objectives of the pilot trial: (1) examine the feasibility, fidelity and acceptability of delivering and trialling the intervention according to pre-specified progression criteria; (2) explore student, staff and intervention team experiences of implementing and trialling the intervention, and how this varies, in order to refine the logic model, intervention and methods prior to progressing to any subsequent evaluation phases; and (3) pilot the primary outcome measure (transition to smoking weekly or more), secondary outcome measures (ever smoked, frequent cannabis use, high risk alcohol use, health-related quality of life, and cessation/reduction in smoking), process measures (community-level tobacco availability, institutional environment, students’ knowledge, attitudes and skills) and economic evaluation methods. Data sources: New students enrolling at the participating FE settings for the 2014-15 academic year (approx. 2500) will complete an online survey at baseline (September 2014) and 1-year follow-up (September 2015). Other quantitative (process) data will be collected via: structured observations; intervention team delivery checklists; ‘mystery shopper’ audits of local shops; analysis of college policy documents; and a staff training evaluation survey. Qualitative data will be collected via: interviews with FE college managers (n=12/2 per college) and the delivery team (min. 6); focus groups with intervention college students (n=12/4 per college) and staff (n=6/2 college). After the follow-up survey, 200 students will be recruited via stratified, random sampling to provide a saliva sample for cotinine testing to examine the validity of the self-reported smoking outcome. Governance: A trial steering committee (TSC) will be established, including South East Wales Trials Unit (SEWTU) representatives. A study protocol and pre-specified trial progression criteria will be agreed by the TSC, the NIHR, ASH Wales and the investigators.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The effectiveness of adjunctive Medication Management and Contingency Management to enhance adherence to medications for relapse prevention in alcohol dependence
Abstract: Design: 3-arm, pragmatic, randomised controlled, parallel group clinical trial of strategies to enhance adherence to acamprosate (AC) for alcohol dependence. Standard support (SS), SS with adjunctive medication management (SS+MM), SS and MM with adjunctive contingency management (SS+MM+CM). Outcome assessment will be at 3, 6 and 12 months post randomisation. Setting: 5 NHS trusts (London (South and North-West), Humberside, Southampton and Birmingham) and community pharmacies. Population: Detoxified alcohol dependent adults, suitable for prescription of AC, willing and able to provide informed consent. Inclusion: Aged >=18, ICD-10 alcohol dependence, completed medically assisted alcohol detoxification, commencing a prescription for AC. Exclusion: Severe physical/mental illness identified by the treating clinicians, current dependence on other substances (except nicotine), participation in another trial, current use of other relapse prevention medication. Heath technologies: MM provided by community pharmacists (weekly for 6 weeks and then fortnightly for 6 weeks and then monthly up to 3 months). MM+CM: Small incentives (vouchers) will be provided to reinforce adherence with MM contingent on attendance at appointment with the community pharmacist. Primary outcome: Percentage of prescribed medication taken estimated using Medication Events Monitoring System (MEMS) and verified using pill count and self-report at 6 months post randomisation. Secondary outcomes: Percentage of prescribed medication taken, estimated by self-report at 12 month follow-up. Alcohol consumption measured by TLFB-90: % days abstinent; units of alcohol per drinking day; time to first drink; relapse to any drinking; and relapse to heavy drinking (8+/6+ UK units (1 unit = 8g alcohol) for males/females on a single occasion). Alcohol related problems (APQ), alcohol craving (AUQ), Participants beliefs about medications (BMQ), the therapeutic relationship with the care giver (STAR), health related quality of life (EQ-5D-5L), Adult Service Use Schedule, costs of control and trial interventions, adverse events. Economic analysis: Analysis of the costs and effects of MM with or without CM for alcohol dependence compared to SS. The primary economic perspective will be the health and social care provider perspective. Broader perspectives will be considered in sensitivity analyses (i.e. criminal justice contacts and criminal activity, productivity losses, patient and family costs). Sample size: Differential allocation of the order of 2:1:1 with twice as many being allocated to the SS group than the intervention groups. A clinically important difference in adherence to medication is estimated as an effect size of the order of 0.3. To estimate this difference using power of 80%, alpha 0.05 with a 2 sided test requires 524 analysed at 6 months across the three groups. Allowing for attrition of 30%, less than observed in other trials in similar populations, requires a total sample size at allocation of 748; 374 allocated to SS, and 187 each to SS+MM and SS+MM+CM. Timetable: Months 0-8: Ethical, R&D, regulatory approvals, adaptation of CM procedure, staff training. Months 9-11 Pilot study. Months 12-33: Recruitment for main trial (average 6 participants/centre each month), Months 12-36: 3 month follow-up, Months 18–42: 6 month follow-up, Months 24–45: 12 month follow-up, Months 46-48: Analysis, report writing, dissemination.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Development and feasibility cluster randomised control trial evaluation of a Peer-Led physical Activity iNtervention for Adolescent girls (PLAN-A)
Abstract: Physical activity (PA) is associated with positive cardio-metabolic, psychological and social outcomes during adolescence. However the majority of adolescent girls are insufficiently active to confer such benefits. As the influence of peers on PA increases during adolescence, interventions which harness the power of peers present an un-tested opportunity. The proposed research is the development and two-arm cluster-randomised controlled feasibility trial of a school-based peer-led intervention to increase PA among 12-13 year old girls. The study will inform the design of a definitive trial. The intervention builds on a successful adolescent peer-led smoking cessation intervention (ASSIST), based on Diffusion of Innovations Theory. Phase 1 will comprise public involvement to adapt the intervention to target PA and pilot testing in one school. Formative and evaluative qualitative research comprising focus groups and interviews with participants and training deliverers will address how to adapt the peer-led intervention model to target PA promotion among girls aged 12-13. Phase 2 comprises a two-arm cluster-randomised controlled feasibility trial of the peer-led intervention conducted in six schools identified as above the local median for deprivation (Pupil Premium). Participants will be entire Yr 8 female cohorts (approximate N=660). Two control schools will receive no intervention. In the four intervention schools, at least 15% of Yr 8 girls, nominated by their peers, will be trained as peer-supporters in a two-day, off-site interactive education programme. Peer-supporters will then diffuse messages about PA to their peers through informal conversations for 10 weeks, supported by a mid-point training day. Peer-supporter training will be based on Self-Determination Theory and will be delivered by individuals educated in PA/public health and experienced in working with young people (Diffusion of Innovation will remain the theory which informs the overall intervention). The feasibility trial will answer two questions: 1) Is it feasible to conduct a cluster RCT evaluation to investigate the effectiveness of the intervention? 2) Does the intervention show evidence of promise to increase the moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA) of 12-13 year old girls? The outcome variables will be the acceptability of the peer-supporter training, recruitment, retention and data provision rates. Data will be collected to allow the intervention costs to be estimated and to examine the feasibility and appropriateness of the methods that would be needed to calculated cost-effectiveness alongside a definitive trial. The feasibility of collecting the data necessary to link study data to pupils’ academic achievement and health records will also be tested to allow the examination of broader long-term intervention effects in a definitive trial. PA and psychosocial variables will be assessed at baseline (T0), immediately post-intervention (T1) and 12 months post-baseline (T2) and the adjusted between-groups difference in accelerometer-determined minutes of MVPA per day at T1 and T2 will be estimated with a focus on 95% CIs. A process evaluation will be conducted to assess delivery, implementation, mechanisms of impact and context using qualitative and quantitative approaches among peer-supporters, non-peer supporter pupils, parents, training deliverers and school contacts. Intervention costs will be funded by Wiltshire and South Gloucestershire Councils.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Enhancing Social-Emotional Health and Wellbeing in the Early Years: A Community-based Randomised Controlled Trial (and Economic) Evaluation of the Incredible Years Infant and Toddler (0-2) Parenting Programmes
Abstract: Background: Behavioural and mental health disorders have become a public health crisis and by 2020 may surpass physical illness as a major cause of disability. There is a strong causal link between parent and child wellbeing. Incredible Years (IY) group-based parent programmes aim to promote social & emotional wellbeing in children aged 0-12 years (http://incredibleyears.com/).Robust evidence for IY with parents of children aged 3+ years demonstrates increased child social and emotional wellbeing, fewer behavioural difficulties, and importantly, a positive impact on parent wellbeing - a major risk factor for healthy child development. Few programmes, and little evidence, currently exists for ehancing social emotional wellbeing in the 0-2 year age range. Two newly developed IY programmes for parents of 0-2 year-olds, IY-Infant (IY-I) and IY-Toddler (IY-T),have not been rigorously evaluated in targeted large-scale randomised controlled trials. We propose delivering IY as a proportionate universal intervention based on assessment of risk/need, to include, prior to IY programme delivery, a low-level universal dose comprising of the IY-I book. Main research question: Are the IY-I book,IY-I and IY-T programmes, when delivered in a dose proportionate to need,and when compared to services as usual, effective and cost-effective in enhancing child social and emotional wellbeing at 20 months of age? Setting: The intervention will be delivered in community settings,such as children or community centres,by local children and family service and health staff across four Local Authorities (LAs). Participants: Parents of children aged 0-2 months at baseline, will be identified by children centre staff, self-referral,Health Visitors,with additional research awareness activities being conducted by our parent committee. Primary carer level of need will be assessed by completion of a mental health questionnaire. Co-parents/significant carers will be included in measure completion (and intervention levels if primary carer is allocated to intervention condition). Design: An 18-month internal randomised pilot study,leading to a definitive 30-month randomised controlled trial. The Trials Unit will randomise participants following baseline assessments, to intervention or control on a 2.9:1 ratio (respectively), stratified according to level of need based on primary carer depression scores, and gender of child and primary carer. Intervention parents will receive an IY-I book (universal level), followed by an IY-I (8-10 weeks, 2 hours/week),and/or IY-T (12 weeks, 2 hours/week) dependent on level of need at data collection points 2 and 3. Control parents will receive services as usual (SAU).IY-I and IY-T will not be SAU in participating LAs. Outcomes: Primary outcomes assessed at final follow-up when child is 20 months old: 1. child social and emotional wellbeing using a validated assessment tool (e.g. Ages and Stages Questionnaire - Social Emotional version). 2. Primary parent depression/wellbeing levels using a validated assessment tool (e.g. PHQ9). Measures will be administered during home, or community-based, visits at four intervals, baseline and 3 follow-ups (2, 9, 18 months post-baseline). The IY interventions (IY-book, IY-I, and IY-T) will be delivered in the interim periods between data collection points. Implementation fidelity and cost-effectiveness will also be evaluated. Intention to treat (ITT) and per protocol analyses will be conducted. Clustering and hierarchical effects (e.g. LA) will be accounted for using linear mixed models. Potential confounding factors (demographic variables) will form co-variates in the analysis. Timetable This is a 4.5 year project,including a 1.5 year internal pilot.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Long term weight loss trajectories in participants in a randomised controlled trial of a weight management and healthy lifestyle programme for men delivered through professional football clubs: the Football Fans in Training follow up
Abstract: The prevalence of obesity is increasing, and at a faster rate in men than in women in the UK. Men’s tendency to carry excess fat abdominally may make them more vulnerable to the adverse health consequences of obesity than women, with those who are less affluent and less well educated at increased risk of ill health. The problem is compounded because: men are under-represented in commercial and NHS weight management programmes; and, whilst behaviour change techniques that are effective in helping people initiate weight loss are well-described, evidence on what helps people maintain weight loss for longer than 12 months remains limited. The potential of professional sports clubs to engage men in weight management is now recognised. Football Fans in Training (FFIT) is a group-based, gender-sensitised, weight management and healthy lifestyle programme delivered over 12, weekly sessions by community coaches at top professional football clubs across Scotland. Each week includes ‘classroom activities’ on healthy eating and behaviour change techniques, and a physical activity ‘training’ session. The 12 sessions are followed by a light touch weight maintenance phase with regular email prompts and a club-based reunion meeting at 9 months. In 2011-12, 747 men aged 35-65 with BMI at least 28kg/m2 enrolled in an NIHR PHR-funded randomised controlled trial (RCT) of FFIT at 13 top football clubs in Scotland. They were randomly allocated either to start FFIT immediately after baseline measurements in Autumn 2011 (intervention group N=374) or to wait 12 months until Autumn 2012 before attending the programme (waitlist comparison group N=373). FFIT attracted men across the socioeconomic spectrum whose excess weight put them at higher risk of ill health than the general population. Retention was excellent, 92% of men attended 12 month measurements. Mean 12 month between-group weight loss difference was 4.94 kg (95% CI 3.95, 5.94, p<.0001) in favour of the intervention group, with 39.3% of the intervention group achieving a weight reduction of at least 5%, compared to 11.3% of the comparison group. FFIT has now been delivered to over 2500 men and has been extended to over 20 clubs across Scotland (delivery funded by the Scottish Government). However, crucial questions around long term weight loss outcomes remain unanswered. We propose a longitudinal follow up cohort study of men in both RCT groups 3.5 years after baseline measurements (3.5 years since the intervention group, and 2.5 years since the waitlist comparison group, began the FFIT programme). We aim, first, to investigate differences in long term weight loss trajectories from baseline to 3.5 years between and within the intervention and comparison groups. We will use a mixed methods approach including: re-administration of the RCT outcome measures; assessment of potential predictors of long term weight loss; and qualitative accounts of men’s (varied) experiences of long term weight control. Second, to investigate medium and longer term cost-effectiveness; and third, to investigate the potential of long term, low cost, passive follow up through linkage to routinely-collected NHS data by: conducting an exploratory analysis of hospitalisation, death, cancer, diabetes and blood test data in previously-consented RCT participants (utility); and asking men enrolling in FFIT in Spring and Autumn 2015 to consent to data linkage (feasibility).

Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: An Evaluation of Alcohol Treatment Centres: Implications for Service Delivery, Patient Benefit and Harm Reduction
Abstract: Welfare Centres, Safe Havens and Alcohol Treatment Centres are designed to receive intoxicated patients who would normally attend Emergency Departments (ED), to lessen the burden that alcohol-misuse, an avoidable healthcare cost, places on unscheduled care and care for those who have become vulnerable. They are typically located close to areas characterised by excessive intoxication and are open at times when levels of intoxication peak. They therefore offer the potential to mitigate some of the pressures on ED at times when it is experiencing a sustained increase in demand. The need to reduce pressure in ED is clear. Most admissions to ED are alcohol-related at peak times and they cause the ED clinical environment to suffer, as well as staff morale. Staff become stressed causing a detriment to care and patients can become aggressive or fearful. This project aims to estimate the effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, efficiency and acceptability of centres in managing alcohol-related ED attendances. The proposed evaluation method, organised into three work streams (WS), is that of a natural experiment, comparing areas in which centres have been implemented or are planned to control cities matched using Home Office iQuanta “similar families”. Mixed methods are used to address specific research questions. WS1 will use ethnographic studies; interviews with stakeholders, policy makers and practitioners; interviews with patients attending centres and surveys of ED and centre users. In WS2 routine data will be analysed to quantify the effect of centres in respect of key performance indicators and in WS3 an economic evaluation will consider the cost of centre implementation. WS1 will consider the impact of centres on working practices of front-line professionals in the emergency care system, with particular reference to well-being. Interviews with centre users will inform the development of a survey for this group to assess the acceptability of centres. Surveys will assess the impact of centres on ED users’ perceptions of the ED environment, compared to control EDs where there is no centre implementation. The inter-agency relationships between the police, health, ambulance and the broader community, required for successful implementation, including opportunities for shared funding, will be scrutinised. WS2 will assess any improvements to effectiveness across partners (e.g. ambulance handover times, patient episode duration in ED, police resource effectiveness measured through a reduction in city centre violence) and explore whether the effects of improved capacity (e.g. fewer police and ambulance resources in ED bottlenecks) due to centre provision impacts on community safety and therefore alcohol-related violence. In WS3 we will ask what are the costs of setting up and running centre and what cost savings may be realised elsewhere? In addition, the project will seek to capture the variability that exists in night time economy provision for managing the intoxicated. The research will inform local and national decision makers on opportunities for a national roll-out across UK cities and will share what is known about what works through the study of effectiveness, efficiency, processes, barriers and opportunities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Factors influencing the utilisation of free-standing and alongside midwifery units in England: A Mixed Methods Research Study
Abstract: Government policy for maternity care in England since the early 1990s has promoted women’s choice of place of birth. These choices are hospital obstetric units (OUs), midwifery units (MUs) and home. MUs are classified in two ways: either attached to OUs, alongside midwifery units (AMUs) or geographically separate, free standing units (FMUs). MUs are only recommended for low risk women who constitute approximately 50% of all pregnant women (Dodwell, 2012). In 2012, only 11% of women gave birth in MUs, with 87% in OUs and 2% at home (NAO, 2013). This is despite strong evidence that MUs reduce caesarean section rates by two thirds, are very safe, improve patient satisfaction and are 20% cheaper than OUs (Brocklehurst et al, 2011; Schroeder et al, 2012). The reasons why most low risk women give birth in OUs when there is no clinical indication and where care is more expensive require investigation. Place of birth choices are affected by the lack of MUs across England, where a third of all maternity services have no MU of any kind. Even in maternity services with MUs, they are underused. In some maternity services, 20% or more women deliver in MUs whereas in other services the figure is 10% or less (NAO, 2013). In addition, some services have opened MUs that have subsequently closed. Identifying the barriers and facilitators to high percentage MU births and developing guidance for developing and sustaining MUs, would improve women’s clinical and psychological outcomes and be more cost effective for the NHS. Based on the Birthplace study (Brocklehurst et al, 2011), we estimate that by increasing provision so that an additional 10% of all women give birth in MUs, (to 20% overall), the caesarean section rate for these women should reduce by approximately 7% and normal birth rates increase by nearly 20%, resulting in a significant cost saving (approx. 3% of total maternity care budget) with no reduction in standard of care. The research therefore aims to investigate the barriers and facilitators to provision of MUs across England, to identify interventions to increase MU provision and uptake and to develop service guidance for commissioners and providers. The project will adopt a mixed method design, incorporating a Comparative Case design. This will draw on Damschroder et al’s (2009) Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to identify constructs which help explain cross case variations in the degree of implementation, combined with consideration of salient institutional factors shaping the broader context of change (Currie et al, 2012). Stage 1 will map the existing national configuration, organisation and operation of MUs. Stage 2 will purposively sample 6 case study sites, and investigate the complex interrelation of variables of potential importance in understanding the provision of MUs in England (Anderson 2005). Using documentary analysis, focus groups, interviews and analysis of local media coverage of local maternity care provision, these in-depth case study data will provide not only detailed context dependent knowledge but also identify what can be transferred to other NHS sites (Payne & Williams 2005). There will be extensive user involvement throughout. The final phase will include a multidisciplinary stakeholder workshop to collaboratively generate interventions and to develop service guidance to support future maternity service commissioning and provision and commence the dissemination process (Minkler, 2005).

Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Improving NHS Quality Using Internet Ratings and Experiences (INQUIRE)
Abstract: AIM: To improve NHS capability to interpret online feedback from patients and the public, and to understand whether and how to act on this to improve services. RESEARCH QUESTIONS: 1. What is current knowledge on using online feedback on patients experiences and what do experts and stakeholders in the field (including patients and public) consider the most important related issues for the NHS? 2. Why and how do people choose whether to provide feedback, who are these people and what is the risk of biased conclusions? 3. How do NHS staff and organisations interpret social media and ratings sites amongst other indicators of patient experience ? What are the barriers and facilitators to using online feedback to improve NHS quality? What skills and capacity are required to draw benefit (eg immediacy, efficiency, transparency) and avoid harm (eg bias, confusion) BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE: As the NHS embraces a responsive, patient-centred, listening culture, it is important that it is listening, interpreting and responding to the right signals. As in many sectors, these ‘signals’ are increasingly coming from online content as patients use the internet to read and share their experiences of the NHS. We need to establish whether this online feedback is (or could be) credible and useful for NHS service improvement. RESEARCH ENVIRONMENT: The research is based in the Oxford University Health Experiences Research Group (HERG), part of the Oxford University Nuffield Department of Primary Care Health Sciences. RESEARCH PLAN: Five interlinked projects of applied health services research, each delivering NHS benefit and academic outputs in their own right, and adding value to each other. Project-1 What is known regarding online feedback from patients? A stakeholder/expert consultation and scoping literature review. Project-2 Population survey to identify the extent of the use of online feedback and public characteristics and attitudes towards it. Project-3 In-depth qualitative work to explore the motivations and actions of people who choose to create or use online feedback. Project-4 What are the attitudes and behaviours of frontline NHS staff to online feedback? Surveys and focus groups of health professionals to understand use of and attitudes to online feedback. Project-5 NHS case studies to capture the views of other staff groups (NHS managers, and other non-clinical workers) and understand organisational practices in relation to online feedback.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Screening Strategies for Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
Abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common cardiac arrhythmia. The prevalence of AF is at least 1.8% in the adult population and roughly doubles with each decade of age, with over 6% prevalence in those over 65 years, and almost 9% in people aged 80-90 years. On average, people with AF are five times more likely to have a thromboembolic stroke and are at increased risk of premature death. More than 20% of the 130,000 annual strokes in England and Wales are attributed to AF. Warfarin is an effective oral anticoagulant for the prevention of stroke in patients with AF2, although newer oral anti-coagulant treatments (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, otamixaban and betrixaban) are becoming available, which avoid the need for therapeutic drug monitoring. AF is asymptomatic in up to 20% of cases. Furthermore, symptoms may be intermittent (paroxysmal), making detection challenging. It is estimated that 7000 strokes and 2000 premature deaths could be potentially be avoided every year through effective detection and treatment of AF3. This project aims to identify whether it is cost-effective to screen for AF in the UK, and if so what is the most cost-effective screening, testing, and primary preventative treatment strategy. We will search for published cohort evidence to estimate prevalence and incidence of different forms of AF, according to key risk factors, including age. We will use the forthcoming update of the NICE clinical guideline1 for risk prediction equations for stroke, mortality, and bleeding risk. We will update the recent Cochrane review4 for randomised and quasi-randomised controlled trials of screening strategies for AF, comparing systematic screening (for given age-range) with the current practise of opportunistically testing for AF (given a consultation, age range, and AF risk-score). We will also systematically review the literature to identify evidence from diagnostic test accuracy studies to estimate sensitivity and specificity of diagnosing AF, depending on risk-of-stroke score. Diagnostic tests considered will include: 12-lead ECG (gold-standard), 6-lead ECG, pulse palpation, single-lead ECG, sphygmomanometers, finger probe. Prophylactic anti-coagulation treatment options include warfarin, and the newer oral anti-coagulants (dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban, otamixaban and betrixaban). The relative effects, adverse event profiles, costs, resource use, and utilities of these drugs will be taken from the economic evaluation to be conducted by our NIHR funded project HTA 11/92/17 “What is/are the best oral anticoagulant/s for primary prevention and treatment and secondary prevention of venous thromboembolic disease, and for prevention of stroke in atrial fibrillation?” (due to complete 31/12/14). The primary outcomes are stroke and mortality. The primary safety outcomes are major bleeding and major haemorrhage.

Award_Title: The RESPECT Study (Randomised Evaluation of Sexual health Promotion Effectiveness informing Care and Treatment): a feasibility study of an intervention aimed at improving the Sexual Health of People with Severe Mental Illness
Abstract: There is evidence to suggest that people with Serious Mental illness (SMI) (e.g.schizophrenia and bipolar affective disorder) experience poor sexual health including greater levels of violence, sexual exploitation, sexually transmitted infections, and low rates of contraception. Reviews of interventions which aim promote sexual health have concluded that there is currently no reliable evidence on which to base interventions in the UK. Therefore the overall aim of this study is to assess the feasibility and acceptability of an intervention delivered within mental health services, as well as the feasibility and acceptability of conducting a randomised trial of this intervention. DESIGN: A feasibility study with randomisation; parallel arm individual randomised controlled trial comparing usual care alone, with usual care plus an adjunctive intervention to promote sexual health SETTING: Community mental Health services in 4 NHS Trusts: Leeds and York; South West Yorkshire, Camden and Islington; and Sussex NHS Trusts. TARGET POPULATION: People with serious mental illness using secondary community mental health teams and in receipt of Care Programme Approach (CPA) (excluding cognitive disorders). HEALTH TECHNOLOGY BEING ASSESSED :A manualised behavioural intervention (co-produced by clinicians, people with lived experiemce and academics in stage 1) which is designed to promote sexual health by assessing need and targeting specific needs (including referral to appropriate sexual health services) OUTCOMES: The main outcome is to establish the feasibility and acceptability of the intervention and the trial methodology. We will use a battery of quantitative outcome measures (to be specified in stage 1) related to sexual health knowledge, motivation, sexual behaviour, sexual stigma, violence in relationships, service use, and quality of life. In addition we will interview a sub-sample of participants in both arms to gather qualitative data on the acceptability of the outcome measures and the intervention itself. We include both arms as we are interested in whether the outcome measures in themselves led to greater interest in, and uptake of sexual health and family planning services and other related services, and whether involvement in the study has increased the likelihood of their conversations with their case manager being related to sexual health and relationship issues. ANALYSIS: All data will be presented descriptively with no formal statistical analyses undertaken. Recruitment rates, attendance data, withdrawals and outcome completion rates will be compared between study arms at each stage of the trial. HEALTH ECONOMICS: The economic analysis will evaluate the feasibility and challenges of measuring costs and outcomes in the target population to inform the choice of effectiveness and resource use measures for the full-scale study. OUTPUTS: The findings from this study, whilst not definitive in terms of clinical and cost effectiveness, will inform the parameters required to undertake a fully powered trial. We will publish in peer reviewed journals, produce a range of summaries to a variety of audiences and use social media to increase reach and impact.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Vaccines for preventing influenza in healthy adults (A060)
Abstract: Influenza occurs globally with an annual attack rate estimated at 5% to 10% in adults. Illnesses can result in hospitalisation or complications mainly among high-risk groups. In the UK, about 600 people a year die from a complication of seasonal flu. Pregnant women have a high chance of developing complications particularly in the later stages of pregnancy. Present national policy recommend immunisation of pregnant women, elderly, people with serious medical condition, healthcare workers, people living in a residential or nursing home. The annual vaccination program costs more than £100 million. The available evidence on immunisation of pregnant women suggests that this intervention has a very modest effect in preventing infection of new-borns and it is not protective against symptoms. The extension of the programme to other age groups is unlikely to be cost effective, but it is worth monitoring all new evidence on the issue. Decisions in this field are really controversial (North American guidelines include vaccination of healthy adults while most European countries do no) and possible changes in vaccine effectiveness could easily lead to policy changes. On average, with each update, searches provide about a thousand citations; around 20 papers need to be evaluated for inclusion. Some studies have been performed on thousands of particpants. In this update we will consider adding to the existing body of evidence test-positive studies, a frequently adopted method to evaluate the efficacy of seasonal immunisation. This implies an adaptation of the tools used for methodological quality assessment. On many of the 90 already included studies, we are planning to perform a separate analysis relating to the definition of the outcomes “influenza” they use. The updating process is always lengthy - a lot of literature has been published and few review authors are actually working on this update.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: RISKIT-CJS Pragmatic randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of a multi-component intervention to reduce substance use and risk-behaviour in adolescents engaged with the criminal justice system.
Abstract: Aim: Mixed method, two-arm randomised controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the RISKIT-CJS intervention in reducing substance use in young people in criminal justice settings. Setting: Youth Offending Teams in 3 geographical locations; South-East, London, North East England. Participants: Adolescents aged 13-17 years engaged with youth offending teams who score 2 or more for substance use on the ASSET tool. Intervention: RISKIT a multi-component intervention that addresses substance use and risk-taking behaviour including both group and individual work components. The intervention is delivered by trained, experience young peoples' substance use workers. The group intervention is provided in addition to treatment as usual and delivered in two half-day sessions over consecutive weeks and the combination of individual and group interventions is delivered over a four week period. Control: Treatment as usual as provided in the participating YOT. This will range from no intervention to referral for intervention from specialist services. Outcomes: Our primary outcome is percent days abstinent from substance use, 12 months after randomisation assessed using the Time Line Follow Back Method. Secondary outcomes include mental health wellbeing (WEMWBS), Strengths and Difficulties (SDQ) readiness to change (RCQ-TV), self-efficacy (SCQ) and criminal activity. Economic outcomes will be assessed using costs of intervention delivery and resources used from a health, social care and criminal justice perspective. Process will be assessed through recording interventions delivered and an assessment of intervention fidelity. Qualitative outcomes will be assessed through a combination of telephone semi-structured interviews with service providers and commissioners. Participant experiences will be explored using a purposive sample of participants at the end of the intervention and by employing participatory research approaches to enable participants to explore, analyse and interpret elements of intervention delivery. Assessments: Assessments will be conducted at baseline and then again at 6 and 12 months, face to face, with a trained researcher. Sample size: In order to maintain the efficiency of the study and minimise the associated costs we plan to allocate participants to control and intervention groups differentially, with twice as many participants allocated to the control arm as to the intervention arm. We aim to recruit 567 participants over a 12-month period with the aim of assessing at least 396 of these at the 12-month assessment. This will provide allow us to assess for an effect size difference of 0.3 or more between the groups in terms of percent days abstinent and mental wellbeing with 80% power within 95% confidence levels.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: SOLID (Supporting Looked After Children and Care Leavers In Decreasing Drugs, and alcohol): a pilot feasibility study of interventions to decrease risky substance use (drugs and alcohol) and improve mental health of Looked After Children and Care Leavers aged 12 -20 years
Abstract: Young people looked after by the Local Authority (Looked After Children –LAC) are four times more likely to misuse drugs and alcohol compared to their peers. We do not know the most effective intervention to decrease substance misuse in this vulnerable population. The SOLID pilot trial (Supporting Looked after children In Decreasing Drugs, and alcohol) aims to assess the feasibility and acceptability of a definitive multi-centre randomised controlled trial (RCT) of two behaviour change interventions to reduce substance misuse, and improve mental health in LAC aged 12-20 years. We will undertake a two-phase formative study and pilot feasibility trial in 3 sites in the North East of England which will include: Phase 1: The formative study will use qualitative methods to adapt and integrate two evidence based interventions: Motivational Enhancement Therapy (MET) and Social Behavioural Network Therapy (SBNT) into care pathways for LAC. MET is a concentrated form of motivational counselling where young people are encouraged to discuss the pros and cons of specific behaviours, which are fed back to increase motivation for change. SBNT in contrast uses methods to identify and enhance the social network around the young person to support behaviour change. This is particularly salient for LAC as they are often away from parental support. Qualitative interview data will be collected from a purposive sample of LAC aged 12-20 and their carers to assess the needs of potential service users in relation to the delivery and content of the interventions. Focus group discussions will be held with drug and alcohol and social workers to consider barriers, facilitators and feasibility of intervention delivery. Thematic data analysis will be based on the constant comparative method. Key findings will be shared and the intervention finalised with participants in two workshops. The adapted interventions will be integrated into LAC care pathways. An online survey will also be conducted with named paediatric and local government leads for LAC in each Local Authority in England (n=152) to map models of ‘usual care’ for LAC with drug and alcohol misuse, and identify potential collaborative centres for a definitive trial. Phase 2: In the three arm pilot feasibility randomised controlled trial (RCT), LAC aged 12-20 years will be screened for risky drug and alcohol use by their social worker using the CRAFFT, a validated and extensively used drug and alcohol screening tool. Young people who screen positive for Mirza’s ‘at risk for substance misuse’ stage (= 2 on the CRAFFT) will be consented for individual randomisation to MET or SBNT delivered by drug and alcohol workers, or usual care (control). The intervention arms will each involve 6, 1:1, 50 minute sessions. LAC enrolled into the trial will be followed up after 12 months to assess recruitment and retention, self-reported drug and alcohol use, mental health and wellbeing, sexual behaviour, quality of life, antisocial behaviour and placement stability using validated tools. The pilot evaluation will give insights into the acceptability of the interventions and feasibility of a definitive multicentre RCT. Specifically, the mixed methods process evaluation will provide rich data on both interventions including “dose” delivered (how many sessions taken up), its fidelity (assessment of content and interaction), acceptability (LAC and practitioner perceptions about receiving and delivering the actual interventions) and the potential “mechanism of change” from both the perspective of the service provider and LAC (service user). These data will allow us to assess if either of the interventions is clearly more acceptable to both service users and providers, is most likely to be integrated into routine service delivery, and to elicit behaviour change in the young person. These data along with feedback from LAC and practitioners will be used to draw element of the interventions together into a single ‘optimised’ intervention if appropriate to take forward as an enhanced treatment intervention, designed for LAC, to a definitive trial. The team will develop economic evaluation tools and complete a value of information analysis to inform a definitive study. Stop:go criteria, based on recruitment, retention and acceptability of the intervention, will inform a recommendation regarding a definitive multicentre RCT.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Optimisation, feasibility testing and pilot randomised trial of Positive Choices: a school based social marketing intervention to promote sexual health, prevent unintended teenage pregnancies and address health inequalities in England
Abstract: A) With the National Children's Bureau, a secondary school and other stakeholders, to optimise Positive Choices, a school-based social marketing intervention to promote sexual health, prevent unintended teenage pregnancies and address health inequalities in England. B) To conduct a formative feasibility assessment and refinement of the intervention in collaboration with the secondary school involved in optimisation. C) To conduct a pilot RCT (4 intervention, 2 control schools) to determine the feasibility and utility and of conducting a phase III trial of effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. D) To answer the following research questions: a) Is it possible to optimise Positive Choices? b) Is it feasible and acceptable to implement each component of this intervention in some school, and what refinements are suggested? c) In the light of a pilot RCT across 6 schools, is progression to a phase III trial justified in terms of pre-specified criteria? d) Are secondary outcome and covariate measures reliable and what refinements are suggested? e) With what rates are schools recruited to and retained in the trial? f) What level of student reach does the intervention achieve? g) What do qualitative data suggest in terms of intervention mechanisms and refinements to programme theory and theory of change? h) How do contextual factors appear to influence implementation, receipt and mechanisms of action? i) Are any potential harms suggested and how might these be reduced? j) What sexual health related activities occur in and around control schools? k) Are methods for economic evaluation in a phase III trial feasible? Objectives 1. To optimise Positive Choices. 2. To assess the feasibility and acceptability of implementing each component of the intervention in the school involved in optimisation, and to make any necessary refinements in the light of the feasibility assessment. 3. To recruit 6 schools for the pilot RCT, undertake baseline surveys of students at the end of year 8 (age 12/13 years) and randomise schools. 4. To implement the intervention to students in year 9. 5. To conduct quantitative and qualitative elements of the process evaluation. 6. To undertake follow-up surveys at 12 months post baseline. 7. To link self report data to routine administrative data on teenage pregnancies 18 months post baseline. 8. To conduct data analysis addressing all of the above research questions and draft a report of the pilot evaluation. 9. To disseminate findings and determine whether progression to a phase III trial is justified. Design and methods After optimising the intervention and assessing its feasibility in one school, we will conduct an external pilot cluster RCT with integral process evaluation and economic evaluation feasibility study. We will purposively select schools varying by local deprivation and attainment. After baseline trial surveys, schools will be randomly allocated 2:1 to intervention/control, stratified by attainment. The intervention will be delivered for 1 school year (2 in full trial). Follow-up survey (secondary outcomes) and data linkage (primary birth/termination outcomes) will respectively occur 12 months and 18 months post-baseline to test feasibility (24 and 48 months in full trial). Process evaluation will draw on audio-recordings, observation and interviews. Analysis will assess criteria for progression and address our other research questions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Tees, Esk and Wear Valleys NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Community pHarmaciEs Mood Intervention STudy (CHEMIST). Feasibility and Pilot Study
Abstract: FEASIBILITY STUDY DESIGN: A before and after observational/qualitative study. SETTING: UK community pharmacy settings (Durham/Teesside). POPULATION: People with long term health conditions who screen-positive for depression but who do not reach the threshold for DSM IV Moderate Depressive disorder. INTERVENTION: Enhanced Support Intervention (ESI) delivered by an appropriately trained community pharmacy team member of 4-6 follow up sessions over 4 months. ESI is a modified form of collaborative care for sub-threshold depression validated in previous studies in UK primary care which appears suitable for dissemination to community settings. Defining features are a brief psycho-social intervention (behavioural activation based on goal orientated activity scheduling) using facilitated self-help developed and tested in previous studies in comparable populations. Pre-existing training, intervention and self-help materials (developed by co applicants) will be adapted for use in community pharmacy in consultation with PPI and stakeholder groups. SAMPLE SIZE: 20-30 OUTCOMES: As we are assessing feasibility we will assess study implementation (recruitment and attrition rates), quality of data collection at baseline and 4 months and ESI adherence (number of contacts, DNA and drop out). QUALITATIVE EVALUATION: In depth interviews with up to 10 patients and 4 ESI facilitators and one focus group (range of pharmacy staff n=8-10) will be conducted to explore feasibility and acceptability of the training, intervention and study procedures. Findings will inform adaptations prior to pilot trial. PILOT STUDY DESIGN: Pilot randomised controlled trial, including a prospective economic and qualitative evaluation. SETTING As above incorporating North Yorkshire POPULATION: As Above INTERVENTION: As above with adaptations post feasibility study. COMPARATOR: Usual care SAMPLE SIZE: 100 participants. OUTCOMES: Data will be used to estimate recruitment, intervention delivery and study completion rates. We will not make definitive estimates of the effectiveness of ESI. PRIMARY OUTCOME: depression severity (Patient Health Questionnaire 9) at 4 months. SECONDARY OUTCOMES: Patient acceptance, uptake and attrition. We will also measure ICD10 depression status; anxiety at 4 months (GAD 7); health related quality of life (SF-12); health-state utility (EQ5D) at 4 months. ECONOMIC EVALUATION: The incremental cost per QALY will be calculated from both the NHS and societal perspective. PROCESS EVALUATION: Using mixed methods we will examine potential mediators/moderators of the intervention, the acceptability (to participants and pharmacy staff), barriers and facilitators to the use of ESI in community pharmacy, and impact on usual practice. Qualitative interviews with up to 20 patient participants, up to 10 pharmacy staff and up to 10 GPs will be used. HEALTH INEQUALITIES: We will prospectively sample pharmacies from a range of socio economic areas and explore potential benefit of the intervention though quantitative, economic and qualitative analysis. PROJECT TIMETABLES. Project set up/intervention refinement meetings (mnths -6-2). Feasibility study recruitment and intervention delivery (mnths 2-8), analysis/write up (mnths 9-12). Pilot study site set up (mnths 10-12), recruitment/intervention delivery (mnths 12- 19), follow up (mnths 20-24) and analysis/write up (mnths 24-28).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Evaluation of legislation to reduce the drink drive limit in Scotland: a natural experiment
Abstract: Background: It is well recognised that drink driving is a leading cause of road traffic accidents (RTAs). The British Road Safety Act introduced a legal blood alcohol concentration (BAC) limit of 0.08 g/dL in 1967 which is still in place today, with the exception of Scotland where the BAC limit was reduced to 0.05 g/dL on 5th December 2014. Aim: The overall aim of this research is to evaluate the change in drink driving legislation in Scotland. Research questions: 1) Has the change in drink driving legislation in Scotland been effective (reduction in RTAs)?; 2) Has the change in drink driving legislation in Scotland led to a reduction of inequalities associated with socio-economic deprivation?; 3) Has the change in drink driving legislation in Scotland led to a reduction in population alcohol consumption?; 4) Has the change in drink driving legislation in Scotland provided good value for money (been cost-effective)? Research design: we will employ a natural experimental design and analytical approaches to measure the causal effect of the change in BAC legislation in Scotland. Our control group will be England and Wales, the other countries in GB that still have a 0.08 g/dL BAC law. The data for the intervention and control groups used to measure effectiveness comes from the same data source and covers the same study period (four years in duration, two years pre- and post-legislation change - 5th December 2012 to 5th December 2016). We will follow MRC guidelines on best practice for conducting natural experiments Outcomes: The primary outcome measure for the effectiveness study is weekly rates of all RTAs. The secondary outcome measure of effectiveness is alcohol consumption per capita. For the economic evaluation, outcomes are weekly rate of RTAs (for a cost-effectiveness analysis); years of life lost and quality adjusted life years (for a cost-utility analysis); and contingent valuation values related to prevented fatalities as well as human injuries (for a cost benefit analysis). Impact: The scientific quality of the studies in the existing evidence base evaluating a change of BAC legislation from 0.08 g/dL to 0.05 g/dL is poor. Our study will directly address the methodological shortcomings of previous research and enrich the evidence base. It will be the first study to evaluate whether socio-economic deprivation influences the magnitude of the intervention effect, and the first to evaluate whether a reduction in BAC limit (for a whole country) has led to a reduction in that country’s population drinking.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Identifying nurse-staffing requirements using the Safer Nursing Care Tool. Modelling the costs and consequences of real world application to address variation in patient need on hospital wards
Abstract: The quality of nursing care and the potential for inadequate nursing to harm patients has emerged as a factor in many reports on failings in NHS hospitals. Reports often cite inadequate nurse staffing as a causal factor in these failures. NICE has recently issued guidance on determining safe staffing for hospital wards which endorsed using the Safer Nursing Care Tool (SNCT) to indicate the number of nurses required on a ward to meet patient need, based on a patient acuity/dependency measure. Our review for NICE found little evidence about the costs or consequences of tools used to determine staffing levels based on assessed patient need, or the extent to which different staffing policies, based on using the tools are affordable, effective or feasible. [6] Our proposed study examines how patients’ needs for nursing care, as measured by the SNCT, vary from day to day. This will allow us to determine how often staffing shortfalls occur, whether there may be excess staff on other wards who could make up a shortfall, and to model the costs and consequences of different strategies for using the tool and deploying nursing staff to meet varying need. We will collect data on ward nurse staffing, validated nurse reported measures of staffing adequacy, and SNCT measures of patient acuity/dependency from all adult medical / surgical wards of three general and one specialist hospitals daily over a period of 1 year. The daily nursing hours (RN, HCA, all nurses) available per patient will be compared to: • the required nursing hours (derived from daily SNCT acuity/ dependency assessment) • planned staffing for that day and professional judgment of staffing adequacy. We will assess the association between periods of understaffing identified by the tool and nurse reported staffing adequacy and use computer modelling techniques that account for variability in patient acuity, length of stay, admissions and workforce availability to compare the recommended strategy (staffing based on mean patient acuity/dependency) with: • a maximum staffing strategy (staffing set to meet maximum patient acuity dependency) • a flexible staffing strategy (regular staffing set to meet minimum patient acuity/dependency with shortfall met by redeployment from other wards or bank/agency staffing) • other staffing policies, as determined by an expert reference group. For each strategy, we will assess the proportion of shifts with a critical shortfall of nurses, using criteria derived from NICE guidance. We will model the staffing costs and consequences of each strategy with varying approaches to filling critical staffing shortfalls. Costs will include costs of any ward nursing staff and bank/agency staff deployed to meet shortfalls. Consequences will be modeled using regression coefficients from robust studies showing the association between nurse staffing and outcomes. Feasibility of flexible strategies will be assessed by examining data to identify when staffing shortfalls can be met by surplus on other wards and the required availability of bank/agency staff. The study will provide evidence for the usefulness and accuracy of the SNCT, which is widely used in the NHS. It will be the only study to have explored costs and consequences of the SNCT. The results of the study will give guidance on the feasibility and relative costs and consequences of a variety of staffing policies aimed at addressing fluctuations in demand, including flexible staffing

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Optimum ‘Hospice at Home’ Services for End of Life Care
Abstract: Evidence has shown that the number of patients wishing to die at home is increasing [1,2,3]. Providing patients with choice about where they receive their care at the end of life is central to UK policy [4]. Much effort has been invested in health services to support care in this setting, including services called Hospice at Home (HAH) which aim to offer the quality and ethos of hospice care at home. There is minimal consensus regarding what constitutes or defines a HAH service and a lack of evidence on what HAH features promote better care and outcomes at the end of life. The James Lind Alliance has identified this topic as a priority in its work: Palliative and end of life care Priority Setting Partnership: Putting patients, carers and clinicians at the heart of palliative and end of life care research [5]. Our aim is to investigate the impact of the organisation and delivery of different models of HAH services on patient and carer outcomes and experiences of end of life care. Our research question is: What are the features of HAH service models that work, for whom, and under what circumstances? The study objectives are to: 1. Identify the range and variation of HAH models operating across England. 2. Categorise the models by type, key features and setting. 3. Assess the impact of each model type on patient and carer outcomes. 4. Investigate the resource implications and costs of patient care in each model. 5. Explore the experiences of patients, family carers, providers and commissioners of the different HAH models. 6. Identify the enablers and barriers to embedding HAH models as part of service delivery. Our research design is informed by realist evaluation [6]; it will be used to identify candidate programme theories that will be tested and refined throughout the proposed research in order to address our objectives. The research will be conducted in 3 phases: 1:Survey. A national telephone survey of all known HAH services in England to map the range and variation of HAH services to develop a typology of models. The analysis will be used to develop a sampling framework to identify case study sites and to inform phase 2 data collection. 2:Case studies. We will purposively select up to 6 case studies of HAH services that vary in type and location. Sixty six (66) patients per case study will be recruited and tracked over time. The primary outcome will be Quality of Dying and Death (QODD), a validated interview instrument conducted with bereaved carers [7-9]. Secondary outcomes will include holistic patient assessment (iPOS) [10], bereaved carer assessment of care (VOICES) [11] and service use (ACHR) [12]. Regression methods will be used to isolate the impact of each service model on quantitative outcomes. An embedded economic analysis will capture resource use and calculate costs. Barriers and enablers to service provision will be explored through in depth interviews with carers, commissioners and providers. Analysis will be iterative with the aim of testing and refining programme theories and to develop provisional context-mechanism-outcome (CMO) configurations. Normalisation Process Theory (NPT) will be used to understand why a model has or has not been embedded within a whole system of care [13]. 3:National consensus workshops. Provisional CMO configurations will be presented and discussed with stakeholders in two workshops to validate interpretation of the data and to refine our understanding of what works, for whom, and under what circumstances. Guidelines will be developed for services/commissioners to help develop HAH services to match their local needs. References 1. Sheppherd S, Wee B, Straus SE. Award_Title: Stroke Sentinel Audit Programme: Investigating and Evaluating Stroke Therapy (SSNAPIEST)
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Stroke is the UK’s greatest cause of severe adult disability. Physical, occupational and speech therapy (known collectively as ‘the stroke therapies’) are a cornerstone to effective stroke care but many patients receive sub-optimal amounts of therapy and little is known about cost-effectiveness. AIMS AND OBJECTIVES: We want to improve this situation. To do so, we need to understand WHY insufficient therapy is provided. We plan an in-depth analysis of data from the national stroke register to investigate the effectiveness of UK stroke therapies by • Identifying different therapy pathways • quantifying variation in therapy provision and the contributing organisational and patient related factors • Relating variation of therapy to care quality, outcome, and cost to identify the most clinically and cost-effective stroke therapy pathways • Explore optimal resource use for each pathway from the NHS perspective focusing on direct costs. Secondarily, we will identify patient sub-groups (defined by patient and stroke related characteristics), examine the therapy they receive and the association with functional recovery to inform future development of stratified stroke therapy pathways DATA SOURCE: The Sentinel Stroke National Audit Programme (SSNAP) database which records stroke related problems, recovery and treatment received for 95% of all stroke patients admitted in England and Wales. PARTICIPANTS: adult candidates for stroke therapy using in-patient or community stroke services. STATISTICAL ANALYSIS: Descriptive statistics will identify therapy pathways and quantify variation in therapy provision. Mixed effect regression modelling will account for patient-related factors influencing therapy provision. The regression models will be extended by linking them with SSNAP’s organisational data to determine the organisational factors influencing therapy provision. This process will be repeated for the factors influencing the quality of therapy (using data from the processes of care). Then all (patient, organisation and therapy related) factors will be modelled to explore their contribution to patient- and service-related outcomes. The processes of care, patient and organisational factors and outcomes are detailed in the ‘detailed project plan’. For the secondary aim: we will tabulate the co-morbidity of stroke related physical and psychological impairments and other patient characteristics using standard regression methods to identify how stroke characteristics relate to therapy input and outcomes HEALTH ECONOMIC ANALYSIS: The cost of each therapy pathway will be ascertained from NHS and Personal Social Services Research Unit costs resource utilization data linked with Hospital Episode Statistics data. Defined pathways will be compared with incremental cost effective ratios estimated in terms of cost per improved mortality, reduced length of stay. The cost/ effect optimal model will be derived from the cost effectiveness modelling using standard dominance strategies. NHS cost savings will be estimated by attributing cost of improved outcomes to the cost of ‘standard’ stroke care. The impact of patient characteristics and organisational features will be modelled using econometric modelling techniques allowing us to separate effects for each therapy pathway. We will assess the impact of different resource use on efficiency of outcomes using data envelopment analysis or stochastic frontier modelling

Award_Title: Stand Out in Class: Restructuring the classroom environment to reduce sedentary behaviour - a pilot cluster randomised controlled trial
Abstract: Background: Sedentary behaviour (sitting and expending <1.5 METs) is an important and highly prevalent negative health behaviour, accounting for >70% of wake time (~10 hours/day) in samples of Bradford primary school children. Adverse associations between sedentary behaviour and cardio-metabolic health risk markers have been reported in children. As sedentary children are highly likely to become sedentary adults the reduction of sedentary time in young people is pertinent for the primary and secondary prevention of chronic diseases that result from excessive sitting in adulthood. Classrooms are conducive to high volumes of sitting, therefore changing the classroom environment through the provision of sit-stand desks appears to be a feasible way of reducing children’s sedentary time in the short term. Classroom-based interventions are accessible to all children, providing a suitable environment for targeting health inequalities. Feasibility study: We have demonstrated the feasibility of incorporating sit-stand desks in the classroom over a 9-week period in a sample of Bradford primary school children. A reduction of 80 mins/day in daily sitting time was achieved. Behavioural improvements in class and no perceived negative effects on teaching and learning were observed. However, the longer term acceptability of this intervention in UK primary schools is yet to be established. Aim: The aim of this study is to undertake a pilot cluster randomised controlled trial (RCT) of an 8-month sit-stand desk intervention in primary school classrooms to inform a future fully-powered trial. Research plan: Year 5 children from 8 participating Bradford schools (4 intervention and 4 control, stratified by ethnic mix of pupils) will be invited to participate. We estimate that at least 120 participants will enrol into the study, which will provide estimates of the variation in the outcome measures, informing a sample size calculation for a full trial. Sit-stand desks (provided via an in-kind donation from our industrial partners) will replace 6 to 8 standard desks in the intervention classrooms. In consultation with teachers, we will ensure all pupils are exposed to the sit-stand desks for at least 1 hour/day. An advantage of this intervention is the minimal human resources needed for successful implementation after desk installation. Schools assigned to the control arm will be asked to continue with their usual lesson delivery, no environmental changes will be made to their classrooms. Measurements will be taken at baseline (October/November 2016) before desk installation and at the end of the school’s academic year (June/July 2017). In this pilot study, the primary outcome will be the acceptability of the long-term use of sit-stand desks and outcome measures proposed for inclusion in a full RCT (objectively measured total daily sitting time, physical activity during and outside school hours, adiposity, blood pressure, cognitive function, academic progress, engagement and behaviour). Acceptability of the trial will be assessed by monitoring recruitment uptake, compliance and attrition rates. We will conduct a full process evaluation and an exploratory economic evaluation to further inform a full trial. Impact: The primary output of this pilot study will be acceptability data to inform the development of a full, multi-site RCT designed to examine the efficacy of this intervention on health and education related outcomes in UK primary school children.
