Contractor: Manchester Mental Health and Social Care Trust
Award_Title: A Community-Based Intervention to Improve Health-Related Quality of Life in Children and Adolescents of Parents with Serious Mental Illness: Feasibility Study
Abstract: Children of Parents with Mental Illness (COPMI) have an increased risk of maltreatment and neglect, behavioural, social and educational difficulties, and mental and physical health problems (Diggins, 2011; Stanley, 2003). The problems arise not only because parents with serious mental illness find it difficult to manage their role as children's carers, but also because they often live in deprived conditions and have the ongoing stressor of their children potentially or actually being removed from home (Park, Solomon, Mandell, 2006).Evidence-based interventions to improve these children’s quality of life are scarce (Bee et al, 2014). Further intervention development and evaluation should focus on improving the children’s coping mechanisms and mental health literacy and should use measures that capture their specific needs (Bee et al, 2013). Family SMILES (Simplifying Mental Illness + Life Enhancement Skills) is a 3-month family-centred intervention delivered in few parts of the UK by the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) to 8-13 year-olds who have mentally ill parents. Family SMILES comprises children’s group sessions, parents’ one-to-one sessions and joint parent-child sessions, with the aim of enhancing the children’s resilience and self-esteem, reinforcing their parents’ protective function, and improving parent-child communication and family relationships. Our 3-year research project will adapt the NSPCC’s Family SMILES programme to produce a new manualised intervention, called Young SMILES, which focuses on improving the children’s health-related quality of life (HRQoL). We will evaluate the feasibility, acceptability and outcomes of Young SMILES for children and families who see or receive support from the NHS. Families whose children aged 6-16 have at least 10 hrs/week contact with a seriously mentally ill parent/carer will be invited to participate. The intervention will include children at risk of maltreatment or neglect and those with childhood mental health problems as well as children without any current or emerging health or social problems. Phase 1 (months 1-9) will draw on focus groups and individual interviews with stakeholders (children and parents/carers with severe mental illness, adults who grew up with mentally ill parents, professionals from health and social care, education, and the voluntary sector) to co-produce Young SMILES and determine optimal age-clustering for the children’s groups as well as optimal duration, interval, format, content and delivery mode for both the children’s and parents’ sessions. Phase 2 (months 10-30) is a feasibility Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT), which will determine rates of recruitment, randomisation, intervention adherence and retention to follow up, describe the outcomes and costs of the intervention added to usual care against usual care alone, and indicate optimal outcome measures and costing methodologies for a future definitive RCT. A maximum of 60 families will be recruited over 15 months across the North East of England, with two hubs in Middlesbrough and Newcastle. Practitioners from the NHS, Social Care and the Voluntary Sector will deliver the intervention in a combination of community settings and family homes. We shall collect data at baseline (randomisation) and at months 3 (primary endpoint), 6 and 12 post-randomisation, on children’s HRQoL, mental health literacy and problem-solving, depression and anxiety, family functioning and parent-child relationship, health and social care utilisation. We shall use two standardised child-rated questionnaires to measure child HRQoL: the PEDQOL (Calaminus et al, 2000) and the KIDSCREEN (Ravens-Sieberer et al, 2007). Both measures have been validated for our population’s age group (6-16 yrs) and show sensitivity to change in quality of life domains such as physical/ mental/ emotional health and social/school functioning. Outcome measures will include the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ, Goodman et al, 2000), which is routinely used by IAPT-CYP and NSPCC services, and the Revised Child Anxiety and Depression Scale (RCADS, Chorpita et al, 2005). We shall use relevant case vignettes with follow-up questions similar to Jorm et al (1997) to assess the children’s mental health literacy and problem-solving skills. We shall measure parenting skills and child-parent relationships using the Arnold-O’Leary parenting scale (Arnold et al, 1993) and the Parenting Stress Index Short Form (Abidin, 1979). For the economic analysis, we shall use the CHU-9D (Stevens, 2012), which has been validated for children aged 7-17, to estimate incremental health gain in quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). Resource use will be assessed using a modified version of the Adult Service Use Schedule (Ad-SUS) (Byford et al, 1999) which will be revised and piloted for use with our participating families. Phase 3 (months 31-36) will be for data analysis and reporting of the study’s findings. We shall also prepare a protocol for a definitive RCT, should our findings warrant it. Our team of co-applicants and collaborators includes adult and young service users as well as professionals with expertise in child and adult psychiatry, third sector organisations, social work and family law, nursing, psychological therapies, NHS service delivery and management, statistics, qualitative methods, health economics and user-led research. We shall work with the NSPCC as part of our dissemination plan to draw up an open IP licence agreement which will enable the large-scale use of Young SMILES on a not-for-profit basis. We shall work with national and local service user groups and agencies, such as Rethink Mental Illness and Young Carers, to communicate and discuss our findings.

Award_Title: An online randomised controlled trial to evaluate the clinical and cost effectiveness of a peer supported self-management intervention for relatives of people with psychosis or bipolar disorder: Relatives Education And Coping Toolkit (REACT)
Abstract: We propose a single blind 2 arm pragmatic online RCT to compare “REACT (including Resource Directory) +Treatment As Usual ” versus “Resource Directory +Treatment As Usual“. REACT is an online self-management intervention for relatives (defined as family or friends) of people with psychosis/BD, supported by Expert Relatives. The Resource Directory (RD) provides information on how to access all currently available online support. Eligibility criteria are as inclusive as possible and require relatives to be over 18, living in the UK, supporting someone with psychosis/BD, distressed, help seeking, and connected to the internet. Recruitment will be national through a wide range of routes including NHS services, third sector organisations, and self-referral. Following online consent relatives will complete baseline measures prior to individual randomisation. Three and 6 months after randomisation, relatives will be invited to repeat the measures and analysis will be a direct comparison under the intention to treat principle between the 2 arms adjusting for baseline scores. The primary outcome is relatives’ distress (GHQ-28) and secondary outcome is carer well-being and support (CWS). An adapted version of the Client Service Receipt Inventory (CSRI) will assess treatment as usual, and inform a cost effectiveness analysis. Cost utility using quality adjusted life years will be assessed using the EQ-5D-5L. Based on feasibility data, and accommodating for design adaptations, we estimate the mean difference between arms to be 5.0 units (s.d. 16.60). A conventional power calculation shows us that a total sample of 466 participants would give us 90% power to reject the null hypothesis (p<.05) when the true effect size is 5.0 units. Based on a review of online trials [17] we allow for a 30% dropout rate, although we describe a number of strategies we will employ to reduce this. Our total sample size becomes 666. Our estimated total population size of relatives of people with psychosis/BD (total 750,000), regularly using the internet (76%), and showing significant levels of distress (approx. one third) is 190,000 relatives. Our recruitment strategy is broad and over 18 months so, based on recruitment rates from other online trials, we are confident we can achieve this. Our team has extensive methodological experience in conducting large RCTs (Liverpool CTU, Hollingsworth) specifically in mental health (Lobban/Jones/Johnson) and in online trial methodology (Murray). We include a relative with expertise in using her lived experience to inform research, and clinical service development (Minns).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Improving health, under community supervision, with the support of a Health Trainer: Developing and evaluating a pilot randomised controlled trial
Abstract: Target population: People under community supervision who express a desire to receive support, from a Health Trainer, to do things that make them feel better about themselves and improve their health, supported by the ‘5 Ways to Wellbeing’(5WWB)(19,32) and/or working towards one of the four target health behaviour changes (smoking reduction, alcohol consumption reduction, increasing physical activity or improving healthy eating). The proposed study will involve a developmental Phase 1, and a pilot RCT in Phase 2 with a focus on exploring the feasibility and acceptability of the intervention and trial methods to support progression to a definitive trial. Intervention: In Phase 1 we will develop and manualise an intervention building on existing training for Health Trainers (HTs) and for promoting the 5WWB to people receiving community supervision. HT support will be up to a maximum of 12 client centred one-to-one sessions: But we have planned for a mean of 6 sessions which could be sufficient to impact on the planned outcome measures and allow us to assess the possible mechanisms and component interactions through process evaluation. HTs will draw on motivational interviewing techniques and principles to support engagement in positive behaviours (e.g. such as physical activity, volunteering, creative pastimes) and growth in core human needs (competence, autonomy and relatedness). HTs will also help participants to self-monitor and set goals to achieve health behaviour change and link participants to other existing community resources and services. In Phase 2 we will further assess the acceptability and feasibility of the intervention (vs usual care) in a pilot randomised controlled trial, through indicators of engagement, interviews with health trainers, and assessing intervention fidelity from recorded sessions. Outcomes: In Phase 1, we will develop the methods for delivering a pilot trial, including refining our planned recruitment and randomisation procedures and assessments. In the pilot trial we will assess recruitment and retention rates at 3 and 6 months post-baseline. At the end of the study we will assess the trial procedures against proposed progression rules to support a bid for completing a definitive trial. Our primary interest will be in assessing subjective well-being (WEMWBS), with assessment of other behavioural outcomes (e.g. self-reported alcohol consumption, smoking, diet, physical activity, substance use), quality of life (SF36 and EQ-5D-5L), depression (PHQ-9), and various process measures and health care and related utilisation costs. We will also estimate the resource use and costs associated with delivery of the intervention, and pilot methods for determining future cost-effectiveness analyses. Process evaluations: Mixed methods (1:1 interviews with HTs, participants, decliners and justice staff; audio recorded intervention sessions; participant case report forms; and engagement monitoring database). Formative evaluation (1-8 months) to ensure components of the intervention work together coherently and understand how to deliver intervention components effectively, for the target population and setting. Process evaluation (months 9-21) to identify mechanisms by which things did, and did not change for participants. We will also explore the utility of our logic model underpinning the intervention. Sample size: In the pilot trial we aim to recruit 60 participants per arm (i.e. 30 in each arm per site).

Award_Title: Multi Centre RCT of a group psychOlogical intervention for poStnatal depression in britisH mothers of south asiaN origIn - ROSHNI-2 (The word Roshni means ‘light’ in Urdu/Hindi)
Abstract: Design: A multicentre Randomised Control Trial with a partially nested design to compare Treatment as Usual (TAU) plus the Positive Health Programme (PHP) with TAU in British South Asian (BSA) women with postnatal depression. There is a built in 18 months internal pilot phase with clear stop/go criteria to prove viability to proceed to a full trial across all the study sites. Setting: Participants will be recruited from general practices and children centres in areas of high BSA density in North West, East Midlands, Yorkshire, Glasgow and London. Target Population: Self-ascribed British South Asian women meeting DSM V depression criteria, aged 16 years or above, and having an infant up to 12 months of age. Health Technologies Being Assessed: A culturally adapted group intervention, based on the principles of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT). The manual-assisted intervention has been designed to be delivered by non-specialist mental health professionals. The intervention has 12 sessions, approximately 60-90 minutes each, and its feasibility has previously been established. Measurement of Costs and Outcomes: The primary outcome is recovery from depression (Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD) score less than 7) at 4 months (end of intervention). The analysis of the primary outcome and the long-term follow-up (at 12 months) will use a logistic random effects model to estimate the odds-ratio of caseness between treatment, adjusting for severity of depression, parity, and education at baseline. Cost data will be collected using an Economic Patient Questionnaire (EPQ). Economic analysis will estimate the costs of health and social care and quality adjusted life years (QALYs) from a societal perspective. Qualitative methods will be employed to explore patient and professional experiences. Sample Size: With 40 groups of size 9 and 360 control subjects the trial will have 90% power to detect a clinically important difference between a 55% recovery rate in the intervention and a 40% recovery rate in the control assuming an ICC for group treatment of 0.05, a 75% follow-up and a 5% significance level. We believe that an ICC for group treatment of this magnitude is plausible, but the trial is robust to larger values. If the ICC for group treatment is as large as 0.1, the power is still greater than 86% We will use an established approach in order to understand what factors block and facilitate successful delivery of the programme. EXPERTISE: We have a strong multidisciplinary team. NH, NC, AR, CW, NA, KB, KL. NSi, AB, FN, CB, DW, PB, CR, IB, JKa CCG, RR, JM, WW, TB, RM with experience of conducing trials of CBT in primary care and recruiting BSA participants. A strong health economics team LD and SM. The trial statisticians have expertise in trials of psychological interventions (CR, BT). NS and JK are experts by experience. Add on study - The existing cohort of 4,319 participants on the ROSHNI-2 trial in the five study centres (Northwest, Yorkshire, East Midlands and London) have been invited to participate in the add-on study. In addition, the study is inviting BSA mothers beyond the ROSHNI-2 participants via existing contacts and through social media campaigns, GP's and BSA community organisations. Methodology - For data collection, we are using a mixed-method approach including online survey and one-to-one interview and focus group discussion. The COVID-19 impact survey will be completed by the participants via an online link (Qualtrics - available in Urdu, Punjabi, Gujarati, Hindi, Bangla, Tamil) or over the telephone and will include questions related to mental health, isolation, education, relationships, child development, views on the vaccination, and wider impacts. In addition, the study will also explore the nature and intensity of breastfeeding problems encountered, help seeking behaviour, and sources of support for the mothers during the pandemic.The screening tool for Interpersonal Violence (IPV) -HITS (Hurt, Insult, Threaten, and Scream will be integrated within the survey and participants who score on this will be approached to complete further assessments specific to IPV. Similarly, during the one-to-one interviews and focus group discussion, questions will explore IPV, and anyone indicating experience of IPV will answer further questions to understand their experiences in more detail. The qualitative interviews will be conducted with participants and key stakeholders including mid-wives, health visitors, general practitioners, and third sector organizations to understand from their perspectives the experiences of BSA women related to the pandemic and in accessing support services and the wider impact of the pandemic, including what future programs on IPV should include. We will be interviewing a total of 70 participants (35 BSA women and 35 health care professionals and representatives from third sector organisations). Research significance: This study will identify difficulties, barriers, and consequences of COVID-19 in BSA women and suggest key recommendations to inform the NHS England and NHS Confederation. The study will also inform the design of future IPV-related mental health interventions and inform the training roles of health professionals and key stakeholders working with BSA survivors of IPV.

Award_Title: BRIGHT Trial: Brushing RemInder 4 Good oral HealTh: the clinical and cost-effectiveness of a Short Messaging Service behaviour change programme to improve the oral health of young people living in deprived areas
Abstract: BACKGROUND: Dental caries affects 1 in 3 UK 12 year-olds and is closely linked to deprivation. Brushing with fluoridated toothpaste is a highly effective preventive measure. The Keep on Brushing SMS programme in New Zealand increased self-reported toothbrushing in unemployed young people (aged 18-24 years) over 10-weeks. AIM: The BRIGHT trial will evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of a SMS behaviour change programme with a classroom-based session to improve the oral health of young people living in deprived areas. DESIGN: Multi-centre, school based, assessor-blinded, two-arm cluster-randomised controlled trial with an internal pilot trial. Internal Pilot Trial: Aimed to randomise 1,200 young people (aged 11-12 and 12-13 years) from 10 schools at the year-group level to intervention or control group. Key progression criteria: 1) An indication of a positive effect of the intervention on self-reported frequency of tooth brushing at approximately 3 months using an 80% one-sided confidence interval approach; 2) Engagement with 80% of the schools required for the main trial and obtain agreement to participate, in principle; 3) Recruiting an average of 48 young people per year group from the 10 schools included in the pilot trial; 4) Minimum 80% response rate to questionnaires completed by young people; A mixed-method process evaluation will complement the outcome evaluation and examine implementation, mechanisms of impact and context, as per Medical Research Council guidance. SETTING: 42 Secondary Schools (with an above average percentage of pupils eligible for free school meals) across England (South Yorkshire and West Yorkshire), Scotland and South Wales. TARGET POPULATION: 5040 young people (11-13 years at trial entry) attending school in UK deprived areas. HEALTH TECHNOLOGIES BEING ASSESSED: The BRIGHT intervention, based on the New Zealand Keep on Brushing programme, comprises a curriculum-embedded classroom-based session (CBS) and a series of follow-up text messages for young people living in deprived areas, and is compared to routine education and no text messaging. SAMPLE SIZE: Based on the pilot trial, it was estimated that approximately 5040 young people from 42 schools would be required in total across the main trial and internal pilot, using within-school cluster randomisation (year group level, where schools are randomised to deliver the intervention to either 11-12 year olds [Year 7/S1] or 12-13 year olds [Year 8/S2], with the other year group allocated to control). This sample size would give 90% power (5% two-sided a) to detect an 8% absolute reduction, from 34% to 26%, in the proportion of young people with ’obvious decay experience’ and is based on a conservative assumed intra-cluster correction coefficient of 0.02, an average of 60 young people per year group and 20% attrition at follow-up. MEASUREMENT OF COSTS AND OUTCOMES: Primary outcome • Caries prevalence for ‘obvious decay experience’ at approximately 2.5 years: Presence of at least one treated or untreated carious lesion in any permanent tooth, measured at the young person-level at the 2.5 year follow-up using the permanent tooth index ‘DMFT’ (Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth), where decay is measured as carious lesions extending into dentine - International Caries Detection and Assessment System (ICDAS) levels 4-6 (‘obvious decay experience’). Secondary outcomes • Self-reported frequency of twice-daily toothbrushing at time of CBS (pilot only), between CBS and 12 weeks (pilot only), 6 months, 1 year, 2 years (pilot only) and 2.5 years; plaque levels and gingivitis at 2 (pilot only) and 2.5 years). • Caries prevalence for all carious lesions at 2 (pilot only) and 2.5 years - Presence of at least one treated or untreated carious lesion of any severity (ICDAS levels 1-6) in any permanent tooth at 2 (pilot only) and 2.5 years clinical follow-up. • Number of treated or untreated carious teeth (using the DMFT) at 2 (pilot only) and 2.5 years (ICDAS 1-6), and caries into dentine (ICDAS 4-6) at 2 (pilot only) and 2.5 years follow-up. • Caries prevalence for obvious decay experience at 2 years (pilot only) - Presence of at least one treated or untreated carious lesion in any permanent tooth, measured at the young person-level using DMFT where decay is measured as caries into dentine (ICDAS levels 4-6), at 2 years follow-up (pilot only). • Child health-related quality of life and oral health-related quality of life (Child Health Utility-9D and CARIES-QC at 1, 2 [pilot only] and 2.5 years). • School Attendance at 1, 2 (pilot only) and 2.5 years. Cost-effectiveness • Resource use will be assessed via parent questionnaires at 1, 2 (pilot only) and 2.5 years and may be estimated from routine data sources. Quality adjusted life years will be calculated using CHU-9D data from young people via questionnaires. Cost-effectiveness will be calculated over 2.5 years and modelled to a child’s lifetime. PROJECT TIMETABLE: Start date: 01/01/17; pilot recruitment start: 01/08/2017; Main trial recruitment start: 01/07/18; follow up over 2.5 years; final report submission: 31/07/22. EXPERTISE IN TEAM Child oral health, secondary education, trial methods, trial statistics, health economics, digital technology, process evaluation, behaviour change, patient/ public involvement.

Award_Title: A randomised controlled feasibility trial of a tailored digital behaviour change intervention with e-referral system to increase attendance at NHS Stop Smoking Services: The MyWay Project
Abstract: Smokers are four times more likely to stop smoking with help from a NHS Stop Smoking Service (SSS). Service uptake has been in decline in recent years (especially in lower socio-economic status (SES) groups). This may be explained, in part, by the rising popularity of e-cigarettes. Other barriers include negative assumptions about what is offered. Given the proven effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of SSS, and the continuing pressure on public health budgets, the importance of ensuring that SSS are fully utilised, especially by low SES communities, remains. Recent research suggests that smokers who report higher motivation to quit, and who self referred to SSS had the highest quit rates. StopApp is a brief, tailored, evidence and theory-driven digital behaviour change intervention with the potential to reach greater proportions of the smokers making quit attempts each year and support self-referral to SSS. It is designed to increase motivation to attend SSS and includes the facility to instantly book an appointment at a location and time of choice, with reminders to attend. Although a number of digital interventions support smoking cessation, none have explored them as a method of increasing uptake at SSS. Therefore this intervention is, to the authors knowledge, the first to target booking and first attendance at SSS. With its built in capacity for scalability via the system it connects to, it could have significant benefits for improved smoking outcomes and cost savings to services in reduced administrative burden and wasted appointments. StopApp can be delivered to users via personal mobile phone or desktop computer, or via tablets in NHS and community settings, as part of 'Making Every Contact Count' (MECC). Because of the novelty of this intervention and general concerns around the potential for digital interventions to contribute to health inequalities a feasibility trial is required to assess whether it is possible to recruit the numbers required for a future potential RCT from a sufficiently representative sample of the smoking population. Objectives: To conduct a feasibility randomised controlled trial (RCT) to i) assess recruitment and attrition rates in primary care, community and online settings; ii) assess any differential recruitment and attrition by SES, age and gender; iii) assess acceptability of proposed outcome and health economic analysis measures; and iv) assess SSS attendance rates in control vs. intervention groups to support future trial effect size and sample size calculations. Methods: We will conduct a two-armed parallel group feasibility RCT. All smokers over the age of 16 years, identified from practice records in 4 GP practices, will be invited to participate. Smokers in community and online settings can opt to participate by following web links. Baseline data will include demographic information, current smoking status, use of SSS and motivation to stop. Participants will be randomised into one of two groups. Both groups will be sent an email or text with near identical content. The control group will be asked to link to an online leaflet about SSS. The intervention group will follow a web-link to the StopApp. At 2 month follow-up questionnaires will be sent to assess smoking status, booking and attendance at SSS, quit dates set and 4-week abstinence. Objective data will be accessed from services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Reduced noise Impacts of Short-Term Aircraft Noise and Cardiovascular Outcomes (RISTANCO)
Abstract: In areas affected by aircraft noise near major airports, relief periods of lower or absent aircraft noise are valued by residents whether in relation to deliberate flight path changes or weather variations especially wind direction. However, the impact of short-term changes in aircraft noise on physical health is unclear. Investigations, including from the HYENA study (Jarup, Environ Health Perspect 2008), have established associations between chronic exposure to aircraft noise and hypertension and with long-term average aircraft data and cardiovascular disease (Hansell, BMJ 2013; Vienneau Environ Res 2015). Short-term effects on cardiovascular outcomes have been little studied, in part due to lack of availability of relevant exposure data. However, recent experimental studies have documented short-term rises in blood pressure and cardiovascular risk markers in the blood in association with aircraft noise exposure during sleep (Schmidt F 2015) and short-term associations of road traffic noise with cardiovascular mortality (Walker ED, 2016, Tobias A, 2015). It is therefore possible that there are short-term as well as chronic effects of aircraft noise exposure on cardiovascular health, as is the case for particulate air pollution. This study proposes to utilise variability in night and daytime aircraft noise related to flight path trials, and operational and weather-related (e.g. easterly/westerly wind) changes in flight paths in the area around London Heathrow airport. This forms a ‘natural experiment’ to examine for short-term effects of reductions in aircraft noise on cardiovascular disease in the general population around London Heathrow airport affected by aircraft noise numbering >3 million (Hansell, BMJ 2013). We will use flight track movements 2011-15 to generate daily noise metrics for night-time and daytime noise and number of events. These will be used to examine potential associations between daily hospital admissions and mortality from cardiovascular disease in relation to variations in population exposures. Statistical analyses using a case-crossover approach (statistically equivalent to a time-series but able to take into account space as well as time variability) will compare noise exposure on the day of the event with 'control' days (e.g. past two days and following two days, same day in the fortnight either side). Analyses will take account of other factors that might influence cardiovascular disease on a day-to-day basis such as temperature, other meteorological factors and air pollution. Factors that might interact such as ethnicity and deprivation will also be investigated. Smoking habits do not change on a day to day basis so would not affect the analyses. Interaction terms in the statistical model will be used to determine whether areas with higher noise shows high daily variability have different risk estimates from those where noise levels are more constant. This will also be one of the first studies to examine short-term associations of aircraft noise with cardiovascular outcomes. The results will allow us to infer (i) whether interventions that reduce aircraft noise levels reduce cardiovascular disease outcomes in the short-term (ii) whether areas with relief periods show reduced risk of cardiovascular admissions with implications as to whether these should be regularly scheduled (respite periods).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: A network meta-analysis of complex interventions to prevent mental-ill-health in children and young people: evaluation of effective and cost-effective intervention components.
Abstract: Lifetime trajectories of mental ill-health are established early in childhood. 10% of young people aged 5-16 have a clinically-diagnosed mental health disorder. For some, mental health problems continue into adulthood; half of adults with mental ill-health report their first symptoms occurring before age 14. Young people with mental ill-health are at greater risk of suicide, self-harm, substance mis-use, risky sexual behaviour, anti-social behaviour and experience poorer educational outcomes. The mental health of young people has been the focus of multiple preventative interventions which have been compared in systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Many systematic reviews do not provide a quantitative assessment of effectiveness. Those that do suggest modest effects of prevention programmes for young people, however statistical heterogeneity is high and comparisons are restricted to direct, head-to-head evidence alone (e.g. “targeted prevention intervention” vs control). This ‘lumping’ over diverse interventions in meta-analysis can conceal the complexity of mental health interventions which are usually made up of multiple, well-defined components. Knowledge of the effect of specific components is important for practitioners when commissioning, or designing, an intervention, since identifying ‘key’ components enables locally adaptive implementation and value for money. To date, no review has quantified the effectiveness of specific intervention components for use in economic evaluation. The effect of intervention components (individually or in combination) can be modelled in meta-analysis using meta-regression methods. In our research we will identify the most effective and cost-effective intervention component(s), or combination of components, for universal and targeted prevention of mental health problems in children and young people. We will produce a taxonomy of components to characterise the preventive mental health interventions identified by the systematic review. We will work with third sector representatives, clinical and public health experts to ‘sense-check’ the identified intervention components. The analysis will use a random effects, component-based network meta-analysis (NMA). A network meta-analysis is an extension of standard meta-analysis which enables the simultaneous comparison of multiple interventions in a single model, whilst retaining the distinct identity of each intervention analysed. Economic evaluation will be conducted to determine the most cost effective component, or combinations of components, for common mental ill-health problems in young people. All analyses will be conducted in a Bayesian framework using OpenBUGS software. Three population age groups will be distinguished and evaluated separately: primary, secondary and university-aged children and young people. Eligible interventions are those which are primarily school- and university-based. We will work with young people, their parents, service commissioners and third-sector representatives to identify outcomes of interest. This feedback will also inform the economic evaluation. Using an established methodology, these outcomes will be mapped to those reported in the literature. Primary outcomes identified in scoping searches include self-report depression, self-report anxiety, self-report emotional well-being, suicidal ideation and behaviour; self-harm and inequalities in mental health.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Assets-based feeding help Before and After birth (ABA): feasibility study for improving breastfeeding initiation and continuation
Abstract: The feasibility trial aims to test the approach, recruitment, delivery, retention and acceptability of a feeding helper intervention; additional aims will test the fidelity of proposed intervention delivery, protocol and data collection for a definitive RCT. INTERVENTION: Feeding helper service applying a proactive, assets-based, woman-centred, non-judgemental approach, delivered antenatally and postnatally tailored through face-to face contacts, telephone and SMS texts. Texts will be co-produced with mothers at start of study. A face-to-face contact at 28 to 30 weeks of pregnancy will be followed by monthly texts during pregnancy tailored to the mother and linked to a menu of social network/local/national assets (e.g. family member who has breastfed, breastfeeding support groups). After birth, a telephone call within 24 hours of hospital discharge will offer a further meeting. For breastfeeding mothers, brief daily calls/texts will be offered for 2 weeks, then reducing until 8 weeks with further texts at 3, 4 and 5 months. Intervention will aim for continuity of feeding helper. For women who ultimately choose to formula feed, the feeding helper will go through how to prepare bottles safely. DESIGN: Feasibility RCT with 100 first time mothers recruited from scanning clinic and randomised (stratified by site) 1:1 to intervention (see above) or control group (usual reactive feeding support). Mixed methods will include qualitative interviews with mother/partners (intervention and control), interviews with feeding helpers and health service staff; feeding helper logs to assess fidelity of intervention delivery. Outcome collection by SMS texts and email will take place at 3 days, 8 weeks and 6 months postnatal. SETTING: Home and community. Two areas of low breastfeeding prevalence, in different UK regions, with a high proportion of disadvantaged women. Eligible areas provide standard breastfeeding peer support only postnatally and reactively following request from the mother. TARGET POPULATION: All women pregnant with their first baby, regardless of feeding intention. Willing to provide contact details to feeding team. FEASIBILITY OUTCOMES: Ability to deliver intervention, with recommended intensity and duration to disadvantaged women (e.g. teenagers, low income); acceptability to women, feeding helpers and professionals; recruitment rates, willingness to be randomised, follow-up rates at 3 days, 8 weeks and 6 months and level of outcome completion. OUTCOME MEASURES TO INFORM FULL TRIAL: Proposed primary outcome of full trial: any breastfeeding at 8 weeks. Breastfeeding initiation; any and exclusive breastfeeding and maternal wellbeing at 8 weeks and 6 months. Quality of life measures and costs to women and service to inform future economic study. PROJECT TIMETABLE: Duration: 24 months. 4 months to optimise feeding helper training, map local assets and complete regulatory permissions; 18 months feasibility trial and mixed method process evaluation; 2 months write-up. TEAM EXPERTISE: Leading researchers in breastfeeding; considerable experience of designing, delivering and evaluating complex interventions using RCTs, qualitative and mixed methods research. Service users will link to a PPI group and we are collaborating with the NCT which trains breastfeeding peer supporters. A Clinical Trials Unit will provide randomisation and support the trial.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: How do smoking cessation medicines compare with respect to their neuropsychiatric safety: a systematic review, network meta-analysis and cost effectiveness analysis.
Abstract: Design: This is an evidence synthesis study and will include systematic reviews and network meta-analyses (NMAs) of the safety and effectiveness of the pharmacologic interventions for smoking cessation in addition to economic decision modelling. Strategy for reviewing the literature: Details of our search strategy are provided in Section 12 of the Detailed Project Description. We will search a range of databases and manually search the reference lists of relevant research articles and previous reviews and communicate with authors to identify unpublished information. We will also record information on the risk of bias for each trial; the Cochrane tool for assessing the risk of bias will be used (see Section 15) (46). Target population: All adult smokers who are seeking to quit smoking using prescribed smoking cessation therapies in NHS and primary care settings in the UK. This includes adult smokers accessing local authority stop smoking services. Health Technologies being assessed: These will include varenicline, bupropion, nicotine replacement therapy as monotherapy and in combination treatment (i.e. varenicline combined with NRT, varenicline combined with bupropion and bupropion compared with NRT). For NRT, combinations of different formulations given concurrently, for example patch and gum, will also be assessed. Different dosages of treatments will also be examined. Measurement of Costs and Outcomes: We will also update a previously reported economic model, created by the University of Sheffield, which is based on the Benefits of Smoking Cessation on Outcomes (BENESCO model), to assess cost-effectiveness of treatments for smoking cessation (13), and adapt it to incorporate adverse effects of treatments. A UK NHS perspective will be taken, with future costs and benefits discounted at a rate of 3.5% per year. Sample Size: Not applicable Project timetables including recruitment rate: The total project time is 26 months. Total time to conduct the systematic reviews including the retrieval of economic analyses, data extraction and preparation will be 14 months. Statistical analyses for the NMAs and the health economic analyses will be carried out in the final 12 months, together with writing of the project report and dissemination of the project’s findings to the general public, healthcare practitioners and clinicians, academics (via peer reviewed publications and presentations at conferences), industry and policy makers including the MHRA and NICE. We will involve patients and the public throughout the project via members of the UK Centre for Alcohol and Tobacco Studies (UKCTAS) Smokers’ Panel and the Elizabeth Blackwell Institute’s Public Advisory Group. Expertise in team: We are a multidisciplinary team of epidemiologists, biostatisticians, public health clinicians, health economists and biological psychologists based within the University Of Bristol- School Of Social and Community Medicine, the Centre for Public Health, the Tobacco and Alcohol Research Group, the Centre for Research Synthesis and Decision Making (CReSyDa) and the University of Sheffield- School of Health and Related Research (ScHARR). We have a track record of collaborating and publishing research of the highest quality and impact. Please see Section 21 for a detailed description of the team members, their contributions and responsibilities and how this project will fit within the core aims of each of the centres.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Innovation to enhance health in care homes: Rapid evidence synthesis
Abstract: The NHS Five Year Forward View identified a need for flexible, integrated models of service delivery to meet the changing demands of an ageing population. Six locations (vanguard sites) in England have been selected to lead on service transformation to enhance health in care homes. Critical summaries of the research evidence are now needed, so that ongoing development of innovative models of care has a robust basis in the international empirical literature. In this proposal we will focus exclusively on care homes, where the mixed economy of care poses particular challenges for service development. We will investigate four specific areas, identified as key enablers for the vanguard programme, where an understanding of the current evidence base is needed for care home sites: use of technology, workforce, communication and engagement and evaluation. Service integration and other cross cutting themes for all vanguard settings will be the subject of a separate application for funding by some of the co-applicants. Aim: To identify and synthesise evidence underpinning new models of care to enhance health in care homes. The focus will be in four key areas: technology, workforce, communication and engagement, and evaluation. Objectives - 1) To determine the potential uses, benefits and challenges of technology in care homes, and for enhancing communication between care homes and partner organisation; 2) To identify flexible uses of the nursing and support workforce and innovative ways of working to benefit resident care; 3) To identify and critically describe the key characteristics and benefits of effective engagement between care homes, communities and other health related organisations, including barriers and facilitators to relationship initiation and maintenance; 4) To summarise existing evidence on approaches to evaluation of new models of care in care homes, including assessment of the quality of care received by residents. Methods Four linked rapid critical reviews of the available evidence will be undertaken, using systematic, transparent and well established methods. Systematic searches of health, social care and technology related databases will identify English language publications from 2000 to 2016. Citation searching, reference list checking, expert and stakeholder recommendations will identify additional and forthcoming evidence, including reports and guidelines. Narrative and quantitative syntheses will be produced where data are available. As descriptive studies and opinion pieces will form a substantial section of the literature in some areas; they will be retrieved and the findings synthesized using content analysis. Outputs This work will provide evidence for innovation in four areas of particular importance to care homes. We will provide a concise overview of the evidence underpinning innovative health and social care, highlighting the potential barriers and enablers. Dissemination of the findings will be tailored to stakeholders, so that local commissioning can deliver effective and cost effective services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: An evidence synthesis of the international knowledge base for new care models to inform and mobilise knowledge for Multispecialty Community Providers (MCPs)
Abstract: Health and social care economies face the challenge of designing care models to deliver better value in a climate of increasing financial pressures. This is resulting in a shift towards whole system working (Ham and Walsh, 2013) and NHS England (2014) has formally introduced a programme for new models of care (Vanguards) to improve quality, outcomes and patient satisfaction. Within this, the Multispecialty Community Provider (MCP) models of care aim to provide wrap-around and coordinated services for patients, which whilst following some standard principles, will adapt to local context. The evidence base on integration of local health and social care services is variable, characterised by a lack of consensus on definitions, models and approaches; this is evident in the models developed in the 14 MCP demonstrators. Our rapid desk-based analysis of the demonstrators suggests various interventions and mechanisms at different levels (micro, meso and macro) within the system, e.g.: extensivist primary care; multidisciplinary community teams; social prescribing (interventions); community assets and social capital (mechanisms). The evidence base will provide important lessons regarding what might be considered the “active ingredients” for MCP models (Naylor et al., 2015; Cameron et al., 2014; Association of Directors of Adult Social Services, 2013; Goodwin et al., 2014; Ling et al., 2012; NHS England, 2015c). Our aim is to provide decision makers with a practical evidence base on the MCP model of care. The synthesis will develop a conceptual framework which articulates what works, why and in what circumstances, to inform design and implementation of future iterations of the model. We will: • articulate the underlying programme theories behind MCP models, mapping the logic models of MCP demonstrator sites; • identify evidence to test programme theories; • appraise, extract and analyse evidence; • develop the synthesis, producing a “blueprint” to explain how the mechanisms used in different contexts contribute to outcomes; • consult with key stakeholders to validate findings and test applicability; • disseminate findings via a series of practical tools to support knowledge mobilisation. The synthesis will use an innovative combination of two synthesis techniques that have the potential to be harnessed together to yield unique insights: best fit framework synthesis and realist synthesis. “Best fit” framework synthesis is a rapid tool by which to facilitate the data extraction and analysis process and is “especially suitable in addressing urgent policy questions where the need for a more fully developed synthesis is balanced by the need for a quick answer” (Dixon-Woods, 2011). Best fit framework synthesis will be combined with realist synthesis principles to maximise the value of the interpretative process resulting in practicable and feasible recommendations for practice. The realist approach acknowledges that interventions do not necessarily transfer easily from one setting to another and offers deeper insights into the contextual factors involved in change. Recently methods have been proposed for rapid approaches to realist synthesis (Saul et al., 2013) and the methods proposed in this review (i.e. synthesis and analysis of logic models developed by the Vanguards and use of a best fit framework) offer an alternative systematic route to harnessing the exploratory potential of the realist lens within an accelerated timescale.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: From Programme Theory to Logic Models for Multi-specialty Community Providers: A Realist Evidence Synthesis
Abstract: Background The study will produce more strongly evidence-based logic models to inform the development of Mutli-Specialty Community Providers (MCPs). Current NHS policy on MCPs implicitly assumes that: 1. Repeated unplanned admissions of older people with multiple morbidity make disproportionately heavy use of NHS hospital bed-days. 2. Reducing these admissions would substantially reduce cost and access pressures on NHS hospital services. 3. A substantial proportion of these admissions are preventable. 4. 'Integrated' (better-coordinated) care will reduce these admissions by partly replacing hospital care with non-hospital care, hence raise the quality and reduce the cost of NHS care. 5. MCPs will promote the 'integration' of care for these patients. To varying extents the first four of these assumptions have been tested through research but not yet assumption (5), about which the present study would synthesise existing evidence. Research Questions 1. How do policy makers and top NHS managers predict MCPs will generate the outcomes stated in 5YFV? What variants of MCP are they creating? 2. Internationally (including the UK), what equivalents to MCPs, or components of MCPs, exist? 3. How do they compare to those proposed for MCPs? 4. What policy outcomes are they reported to produce? 5. What is the evidence about the ways in which these mechanisms of action depend upon specific contexts? 6. What do the answers to the above questions imply for the organisational design (logic models of governance structures, internal management and working practices) of MCPs? Methods Realist evidence synthesis and 'logic analysis' through the three main methods, applied in the following sequence: 1. Discourse analysis (cognitive frame analysis) eliciting policy-makers' initial assumptions ('programme theory') about what structures, working practices and services ('mechanisms') the MCPs (or each main variant of MCP) will contain, and how these mechanisms are expected to produce the outcomes stated in the NHS Five Year Forward View. 2. Realist review, finding and synthesising existing international evidence about what effects are likely to be produced by the kinds of structures, working practices and services ('mechanisms') which MCPs will contain. Search terms will be derived from: (a) the discourse analysis above. (b) existing studies, especially systematic and realist reviews, into the effects of different organisational structures, coordination methods and working practices upon the integration of care. Data-base searches will be supplemented with hand searches of key journals. 3. 'Logic Analysis', A. Comparing the policy-makers' initial programme theory with the findings of the realistic review. Depending on what these findings are, we will elaborate and/or qualify and/or revise the initial programme theory so as to synthesise a set of more strongly evidence-based logic models for MCPs. B. Assembling the set of logic models into a coherent whole. Besides peer-reviewed publications and final report to HSDR, the study will yield a set of more strongly evidence-based logic models to guide MCP formation and early operation. We will consult stakeholders (primary care clinicians including GPs; NHS managers from vanguard sites) to establish what foci, forms of presentation and dissemination media are most useful and interesting to NHS managers and clinicians working in MCPs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: What are the health and health inequalities impacts of the Big Local community empowerment initiative in England?
Abstract: We propose to investigate health and social outcomes at the population level and amongst engaged residents of the community engagement approach adopted in an area-based empowerment initiative. The initiative, Big Local (BL), being implemented in 150 relatively disadvantaged areas across England, is funded by the Big Lottery Fund. It is noteworthy in its attempt to create empowering conditions, rather than engaging communities for health promotion purposes. In theory, such an initiative has potential to improve health via several pathways. First collective action by communities may improve local social determinants of health e.g. by improving transport, quality of green spaces, and reducing place-based stigma.. Second, collective action by residents may reduce social isolation and improve mental health. Third, feeling more in control over decisions that affect your life may have direct health benefits. An evaluation of BL offers a unique opportunity to generate much needed evidence on how best to design and implement community empowerment initiatives to maximize positive impacts on health and health inequalities. The proposal builds on our current research on BL funded by the NIHR School for Public Health Research (SPHR. We developed a novel systems approach for this evaluation and collected base-line data for the longer term follow up that we now propose the objectives of which are to: (1) Investigate longer-term health and social outcomes of BL's approach to community engagement at population health level; (2) Investigate impact of active involvement in BL on health and well-being of engaged residents (3) Assess changes in collective control amongst BL residents and identify any resulting improvements/deteriorations in social determinants of health. (4) Illuminate pathways to changes in collective control by BL residents and to health and social impacts, including dampening/amplifying processes (5) Conduct an economic evaluation of BL (6) Draw out policy/practice and research implications for future community engagement strategies. We propose four work packages (WPs). WP1 uses a difference-in-differences design to investigate the impact of BL on population outcomes in all 150 BL areas compared to matched comparator areas (created by propensity score matching). The primary outcome is mental health measured by self reported anxiety from the ONS Annual Population Survey. The secondary outcomes include antidepressant prescribing, rates of hospital presentation for self harm and rates of recorded crime. WP2 assesses impacts of active engagement in BL on health and social outcomes. The primary outcomes are mental wellbeing, plus changes in perceived control using secondary data from a biannual longitudinal survey conducted by Local Trust of all BL partnership board members in all 150 BL areas. WP3 will conduct qualitative research in 15 BL neighbourhoods to understand pathways to impact using a systems change framework. A central focus of this fieldwork will be investigation of 15 Critical Collective Control episodes exploring how residents act together to improve their neighbourhoods and identifying positive and negative impacts. WP4 assesses economic impact of Big Local, comprising assessment of: costs of changes in mental wellbeing amongst BL residents compared to matched comparitors; any spill over effects areas; cost-benefit analysis in15 fieldwork neighbourhoods ; and any costs savings to the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Integrated evidence synthesis for joint appraisal of tobacco and alcohol tax interventions for harm reduction in the UK
Abstract: Background == Tobacco and alcohol are major risk factors for cancers, respiratory and cardiovascular disease, causing substantial hospital admissions and mortality and around £6 billion per year of National Health Service (NHS) costs in England. Taxation is one of the most effective interventions for reducing consumption, but UK impact assessments for tax interventions do not currently examine the effect of tax changes on tobacco and alcohol in an integrated way. The reason for investigating tobacco and alcohol together is that they are correlated behaviours that together generate multiplicatively increased risks e.g. for head, neck and esophageal cancers, and therefore the evidence on the effects of changes to the tax on tobacco and alcohol would be incomplete – especially on differential social impacts - if considered singly. Aim == To provide evidence and tools to inform the potential scale of effects of taxation across tobacco and alcohol as an intervention to improve public health and reduce health inequalities in the UK. We will produce evidence on effectiveness and inequality of effects that integrates qualitative research on stakeholder views with quantitative research on health and economic outcomes. Methods == Work package 1. Qualitative research to define and understand relevant tax interventions -- The reason for our qualitative research in workpackage 1 is to ensure that we model relevant tax interventions across tobacco and alcohol, that we understand the rationale of different stakeholders for these interventions and in doing so explore the challenges for tax as a tool to improve health. We will take a structured approach that involves conducting expert UK stakeholder interviews, informed by a rapid review. WP1 aims to define a set of 'candidate' alcohol and tobacco tax interventions relevant to the UK context that will be modelled, and to provide a grounded understanding of the policy effects valued by stakeholders, of mediating factors they perceive as affecting deliberation and implementation, and evidence gaps in relation to both separate and joint tobacco and alcohol taxation intervention options. These interviews will enable the project team to gain a rich understanding of the complex policy space in which tobacco and alcohol taxation changes take place, co-exist and interact. Work package 2. Analysis of social patterns in spending on tobacco and alcohol -- WP2 aims to describe the socio-demographic variation in patterns of spending (product type and price) across the spectrum of tobacco and alcohol products. We will combine consumer spending data on tobacco and alcohol from the Living Costs and Food Survey (LCFS) with market research data on retail prices. We will conduct descriptive and statistical analyses of how spending varies by demographic (age, sex, family status) and socio-economic group (education, social class, employment status, income, index of multiple deprivation), and we will assess this expenditure in the context of household budgets. Work package 3. Analysis of industry and consumer responses to tax changes -- WP3 aims to estimate the responses of industry and consumers to changes in taxation. We will develop evidence to investigate tax pass-through (how taxes are passed-through to the prices faced by consumers) across the product and price spectrum for tobacco and alcohol products (using a consistent approach for tobacco and alcohol). We will also harmonise estimates of the price elasticities of demand across tobacco and alcohol in terms of how retail price changes affect participation in tobacco use, participation in alcohol use, quantity of tobacco products purchased and quantity of alcohol products purchased including the interactions between these behaviours. We will look to develop new price elasticity of demand estimates based on the LCFS to quantify effects of price changes on demand for different sub-types of tobacco and alcohol products including participation elasticities and purchase volume elasticities. We will consider how uncertainty in elasticities should be accounted for in WP4. Work package 4. Population modelling to appraise the health and economic outcomes of tax interventions -- WP4 aims to conduct a prospective long-term health economic assessment of the taxation interventions for tobacco and alcohol. We will build on prior modelling for alcohol and combine workpackage outputs to model the effects of tax interventions defined as relevant by stakeholders in WP1. Outcomes will be the overall and social differentials of effects on: i) hospitalisations and deaths; ii) NHS treatment costs; iii) tax revenue; iv) work absence; v) consumer spending. We will forecast 30 years from our baseline year. Our comparator will be the estimated effects of continuing the current tax regime. We will estimate uncertainty through sensitivity analysis, particularly in terms of uncertainty around industry modification of tax pass-through and consumer price elasticities of demand. Outputs == Use of evidence to support decisions -- Our outputs will provide an objective comparison of alternative tax changes across tobacco and alcohol. We are aiming for our outputs to inform decisions about changes to tax on tobacco and alcohol e.g. through submission to government consultations and a continuation of the research team's engagement with decision-makers. Scientific understanding of tax as a public health intervention -- Our technical contribution will be in developing methods that allow the fair comparison of interventions and outcomes across risk factors. Our outputs in conferences and peer-reviewed papers will cover the qualitative comparison of stakeholder perspectives (WP1), the use of national-level data on consumer behaviour (WP2), the behavioural economics of industry and consumer responses to tax change (WP3), and the synthesis of evidence using mathematical modelling to provide evidence that is effects at decision-support (WP4). Informing public debate -- In producing media we will look to partner with stakeholders and consumers from our public involvement panels to present and explain our findings in an engaging accessible way and with a consumer focus.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: NHS priorities in the management of chronic respiratory disease
Abstract: NHS priorities in the management of chronic respiratory disease Background: This programme of work focusses on strengthening the evidence-base for interventions to improve the health of people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) through the production and publication of Cochrane Reviews. We will also update two key asthma reviews. The systematic reviews will be produced by Cochrane Airways in collaboration with national and international author teams and will be published on the Cochrane Library. Lung diseases are responsible for 115,000 deaths in the UK each year, and represent some of the most burdensome long-term conditions, not only for individuals and carers but also for the NHS. COPD is a progressive condition affecting primarily the lungs leading to increasing breathlessness, reduced quality of life and intermittent flare-ups (exacerbations). It is a major cause of death and disability and a considerable cost to the NHS, affecting over one million people in the UK alone. COPD accounts for approximately 1 million inpatient days and £1 billion in direct healthcare spend. There is also a considerable burden on the public, with around 24 million working days lost annually due to this often debilitating condition. Respiratory disease is an active research area and new, often expensive, treatments become available while others go out of date. There is an urgent need to provide health care providers, policy makers, patients and carers with the most up to date and comprehensive synthesised evidence available to allow them to make evidence-informed decisions. In planning this programme of work we have we have consulted guideline producers, clinicians and patients and have scoped the relevant topics to prioritise titles which will address the most important issues currently facing the NHS. Theme and scope: Our programme focusses on three key areas; systematic review of these topics have strong potential to bring about changes in practice: 1. Effective treatment and prevention of COPD exacerbations and hospital admissions: Around 50% of patients with moderate-to-severe COPD have at least one exacerbation per year and around 22% have more than two exacerbations per year. Increasing exacerbation frequency is associated with accelerated decline in lung function, impaired physical activity and quality of life, and early death. COPD exacerbations are responsible for approximately 100,000 hospital admissions and 1 million bed days in the UK annually. The National COPD Audit programme reported a large increase in re-admissions for COPD since 2008. Inadequate treatment is common and may delay or prevent recovery. Hospitalisation impairs physical function, which can accelerate physical decline and increase dependence. Effective treatment and prevention of exacerbations and related hospitalisations are therefore key goals. 2. Improving self-management, quality of life and care pathways: This area of the programme was developed in conjunction with our COPD patient advisory group and focusses on measures that they felt to be important, including those with potential to increase activity and independence and improve coordination of healthcare. 3. Safe and effective prescribing: The NHS spends around £1 billion annually on respiratory inhalers. In the last few years there has been rapid proliferation of inhaled drugs and devices. Clinicians advise us that this has made it very difficult to select the most appropriate medicine for their patients. In this climate of uncertainty, our proposed new network meta-analysis (NMA) will be important to direct effective clinical practice. Updates of our existing long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) safety overviews will ensure clinicians and guideline producers have the most up-to-date information about safe use of this class of inhaled drug in asthma. Project outline: During this three year programme grant we will complete 15 reviews (eight new reviews; three review updates; two overview updates; one NMA; and one prognostic review). We will actively disseminate these reviews via guideline bodies and clinical networks to optimise their impact on patient care in the NHS. We will recruit an experienced full time systematic reviewer to lead the reviews from the editorial base. We will seek external methodological support for the NMA, prognostic review and any review that requires the inclusion of non-randomised studies. We will set up a Steering Group which will include health care providers, researchers and a patient representative to monitor progress and provide advice. We will collaborate with local clinicians, the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE), the National COPD Audit programme, the NIHR Complex Review Support Unit and Cochrane Pain, Palliative and Supportive Care Group. Planned reviews: 1. Effective treatment and prevention of COPD exacerbations and hospital admissions: •Long term antibiotics: use is increasing to prevent COPD exacerbations and is a concern due to limited evidence and antibiotic resistance •Vitamin D supplementation: our recent high impact review shows vitamin D can reduce asthma exacerbations; this may also apply in COPD •Targeted management: exacerbation management by ‘phenotype’ (e.g. by measurement of procalcitonin, CRP, blood eosinophils) •Long term non-invasive ventilation: may reduce night-time hypoventilation, hypercapnia, and hospitalisation. New trials have recently been published •Prognostic indicators: symptom control and place of care are essential priorities towards the end of life and are poorly addressed in COPD •Interventions to improve adherence to therapy: adherence to treatment is suboptimal in many people with COPD •Pharmacotherapy in people with frequent exacerbations: stratification of treatment according to exacerbation status is increasingly important 2. Improving self-management, quality of life and care pathways: •Interventions to increase physical activity and exercise capacity: patients prioritise being able to do more •Telehealth for COPD: a developing field, but with potential harms as well as benefits •Strategies/care pathways for multimorbidity: common in people with COPD, burdening individuals and costly for the NHS •Use of weather forecasting/air pollution monitoring for self-management: a priority for patients to whom we spoke 3. Safe and effective prescribing: •Long acting inhaled therapies for COPD: we will update our existing NMA of inhaled therapies for COPD to reflect the rapid expansion of new drugs •The safety of LABAs in asthma: an ongoing controversy and is a patient priority. Three large new trials mandated by the Food and Drug Administration will be incorporated into existing evidence Dissemination and knowledge translation: The output of our programme will be a series of high-quality systematic reviews. These will synthesise the best available evidence to determine which therapies are most effective and which are ineffective or may cause harm. A key feature of our programme is the engagement of patients, clinicians and guideline developers, which creates a direct pathway for our output to be embedded in clinically - and cost effective services. NICE is currently updating its guidelines for COPD management and we have agreed a timeline to ensure that our long term antibiotic reviews are considered in the process. NICE guidelines are widely adopted into the NHS, so this is an effective way for our programme to make an early contribution to clinical practice. Grant co-applicants contribute to clinician networks, such as the British Thoracic Society, National COPD audit programme and national respiratory specialty interest group. These networks will be used to disseminate programme outputs to respiratory specialists and encourage uptake into clinical practice. Patient networks will approached (e.g. British Lung Foundation) to disseminate information to patients and participants from a local COPD patient advisory group will form a Patient Steering Group.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of 'Strengthening Families, Strengthening Communities': a community led parenting programme (TOGETHER)
Abstract: Background Between 10-20% of UK children experience socio-emotional difficulties which can have serious implications for themselves, their families and society. Stark socioeconomic and ethnic inequalities in children’s well-being exist. Giving every child the best start in life is a key strategy to reduce inequalities. Supporting parents to develop effective parenting skills is an important preventive strategy. A range of group-based parenting programmes have been delivered in the UK and evidence from recent reviews showed these can be effective. However most parenting interventions have focused on early childhood (0-5 years) and have failed to engage with families from ethnic minority groups and those living in poverty. A parenting programme for families with children aged up to 18 years (Strengthening Families, Strengthening Communities - SFSC) has been designed by the Race Equality Foundation, a charitable community organisation focused on promoting race equality, and has been delivered across the UK for over 10 years. Small pre-post studies have produced encouraging results but no randomised controlled trials have been undertaken so far. This study aims to address this knowledge gap. Aim To assess the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the SFSC parenting programme in enhancing parental mental well-being and children’s social and emotional well-being at 6-months follow-up. Design This multi-centre waiting list control randomised controlled trial will evaluate the SFSC programme. The study will be conducted in 2 phases. Participants will be randomly allocated to intervention or control arms. Phase 1 will comprise of a 6-month internal pilot to determine the feasibility of the trial. Should progression criteria be met, phase 2 will comprise the main trial. A nested process evaluation will also assess the fidelity and acceptability of the intervention. Setting participants The study will be conducted across 7 urban English areas with ethnically and socially diverse populations where the programme is currently being delivered. Participants (n=676) will be parents of children aged 3-18 years who either self-refer or are referred by health/social care professionals to attend the programme. Intervention and comparator Based on social learning theory, the 13-week programme aims to develop parents’ confidence, competence and skills through interactive group based activities. Local authorities in the 7 areas will supply staff, community venues, resources and other costs associated with delivering the intervention through existing contracts. Participants randomised to the control arm will be offered the intervention after approximately a 10-month wait. Outcomes The primary outcome will be parental mental well-being (assessed by the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale). Secondary outcomes will include child socio-emotional well-being, parenting practices, family relationships, parenting stress, quality of life, and community engagement. Outcomes will be assessed at baseline, post intervention and 6 months follow-up. Potential impact If this trial demonstrates beneficial effects on both parental and child outcomes, then the potential impact, both immediate and longer term, is potentially significant. As the intervention focuses in particular on supporting families living in poverty and those from minority ethnic communities, the intervention should also ultimately have a beneficial impact on reducing health inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A three arm cluster randomised controlled trial to test the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the SMART Work & Life intervention for reducing daily sitting time in office workers
Abstract: Background: Office-based workers spend 70-80% of working hours sitting and typically spend large proportions of their time sitting during leisure time. High levels of sitting have been linked to poor health including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, some cancers and mortality. Current evidence shows a need for fully powered randomised controlled trials (RCTs) with long term follow up to test the effectiveness of interventions to reduce sitting. Previous Work: Our group spent 18 months developing and testing a multi-component (organisational, environmental and individual strategies) intervention (delivered with the provision of a height-adjustable workstation), to reduce workplace sitting in NHS office workers (SMArT Work). SMArT Work has now been refined and extended based on a full process evaluation, our collaborators’ experiences in Australia, and recently published research - now called SMART Work & Life. To address gaps in existing interventions, SMART Work & Life will go beyond sitting in the workplace by also focusing on behaviour change outside of the workplace to emphasise a ‘whole-of-day’ preventive approach as well as enhancing behaviour change maintenance. Aim: To determine the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the SMART Work & Life intervention, delivered with and without a height-adjustable workstation, for reducing daily sitting time, compared with control. Research Plan: A 3 arm cluster RCT will be conducted. A powered sample of 33 office clusters (660 office workers who spend the majority of their waking hours sitting) will be recruited from councils in 2 areas in England– Leicester and Manchester). Upon completion of baseline measures, office groups (clusters) will be randomised to receive the multi-component SMART Work & Life intervention delivered with (intervention group 1) or without (intervention group 2) a height-adjustable workstation or a usual care control group (group 3). SMART Work & Life (guided by the Behaviour Change Wheel) includes organisational (e.g., management buy-in, provision for standing meetings, competitions), environmental (e.g., relocating waste bins, printers) and group/individual (education, action planning, goal setting, addressing barriers, coaching, self-monitoring) level behaviour change strategies, driven by workplace champions within the council. Baseline, 3, 12 and 24 month measures will be taken. Primary outcome: Objectively measured daily sitting time. Secondary outcomes: objectively measured sitting, standing, stepping and prolonged sitting time and number of steps at work; objectively measured daily standing, stepping, prolonged sitting time, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and sleep (wrist accelerometry). Adiposity, blood pressure, and glycated haemoglobin, cholesterol (total, HDL, LDL) and triglycerides will be assessed from finger prick blood samples. Questionnaires will examine dietary components (alcohol, snacks, sugary drinks), vitality, fatigue, musculoskeletal issues, job performance and satisfaction, work engagement, presenteeism, stress, anxiety and depression. Health related quality of life and resources used (e.g. GP visits, outpatient attendances) will also be assessed. Sickness absence data will be collected from organisational records. We will conduct a full process evaluation and cost-effectiveness analysis. Impact: The results of this RCT will provide evidence for policy guidelines around population and workplace health and well-being.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Combined diet and exercise interventions for preventing gestational diabetes mellitus
Abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) affects a significant and increasing number of women (3-18% of UK pregnancies), and is associated with adverse perinatal and longer-term outcomes which repeat across generations. Preventing GDM can reduce serious complications, leading to benefits and savings (e.g. NHS average daily unit cost of neonatal intensive care admission: £1,118; pre-eclampsia management cost: £4,300). There is great uncertainty regarding how to prevent GDM; no recommendations were made in recent NICE ‘Diabetes in pregnancy’ guidelines. This review is in the top 5% of outputs scored by Altmetrics, indicating wide interest in the area. In the previous version (13 trials, 4983 women), 16 ongoing trials were identified; many have been completed, and there has been an ‘explosion’ of new research, making an update challenging but imperative. These trials assess complex interventions and mixed populations, thus careful analyses are essential. The CRG and lead author have excellent track records in delivering reviews within timeframes (previous Inventive Award: 13/101/04); no financial support is available for this update. The review needs to be up-to-date to include in a Cochrane Overview ‘Interventions for preventing gestational diabetes’.
