Both reviews will inform consumers, policy and practice (including NHS decision-making and NICE guidance), and identify key uncertainties.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Identifying models of care to improve outcomes for older people with emergency and urgent care needs
Abstract: Introduction Emergency and Urgent care (EUC) is a major international issue. Older people with EUC needs, in particular those with frailty, are especially vulnerable to harms that can arise in this care pathway. The first hours of an EUC episode can have a powerful influence on patient outcomes. We will undertake a series of linked studies, with a focus on implementation, which will provide robust, practical and focussed guidance about how best to organise care pathways in Emergency Departments, so as to improve outcomes for older people with EUC needs. Methods Workpackage (WP) 1 Identifying best practice WP1.1 Review of reviews of EUC interventions for older people, their outcomes and costs and any implementation factors identified. WP1.2 Interviews of older people and their carers with recent experience of EUC, using the findings to ensure that the patient’s voice is at the centre of this study. WP1.3 Clinician interviews about emerging interventions and key elements of high quality care. WP2 Qualitative study of delivery of exemplar EUC pathways Qualitative fieldwork (interviews, ethnography, documentary analysis) in 4-6 sites exemplifying promising pathways, to identify aspects relevant to transfer and adaptation of these models to other settings. Elements of this work were undertaken remotely during COVID-19. WP3 Individual patient level data analysis to describe EUC pathways and outcomes Analysis of linked databases to describe EUC pathways experienced by people aged 75+ across the Yorkshire and Humber region, 2010-2017. The aims are to assess which pathways deliver better patient outcomes and lower costs than others, how pathways have changed over time, and what patient characteristics, demand factors and supply factors explain differences in outcomes and costs between patients, from place to place, and over time. WP4 Modelling changes to EUC pathways We will develop a family of System Dynamics (SD) computer simulation models representing patient flow through the entire care process (attendance through to transfer home) for different EUC pathways, using evidence from WP1 and WP2 and data from WP3. We will use these models to evaluate different EUC interventions in different settings, in terms of their impact on patient outcomes and their knock-on effects in the wider care system. PPI PPI input will include high level strategic oversight of the study progress, assured by quarterly briefings to the PPI leads at the Executive Management Team meetings, complimented by ‘deep dive’ reviews of specific aspects of the project, and quarterly consultations with the broader Leicester PPI forum to bring wider perspectives to the research. Dissemination A comprehensive dissemination strategy (evidence summaries, high impact papers, press releases, and national dissemination events) will be developed and targeted to key audiences who will be interested in the findings of this research. Impact The primary output will be a validated, patient-centred, SD model with guidance adaptable to health care systems through an easy to use interface, allowing modelling of emergency department interventions on the whole system. We will provide outputs relevant to teams planning and delivering EUC for older people, and to academics. These will include a user-friendly classification of the different types of care pathway, summarising the strengths and limitations of different approaches and key points of information about optimising their delivery.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: How general practice team composition and climate relate to quality, effectiveness and human resource costs: a mixed methods study in England
Abstract: Background: General practice is under pressure: General Practitioners’ (GPs’) workloads are increasing while recruitment and retention problems have reduced the number of GPs per capita, and shortages of primary and community nurses have exacerbated staffing problems. New roles, organisational forms and contractual models of primary care are emerging. Effective and efficient use of the GP workforce is important, but evidence on how practice organisation, skill mix and team climate influence performance is scarce. Aim: To explore how organisation, skill mix and climate in GP teams relate to quality of care, clinical effectiveness and human resource costs. Design: Concurrent, parallel, multistage, mixed methods in 7 work packages (WPs): WP1: Overview: (i) policy review; (ii) new practice models; (iii) construction of a ‘Practices Database’ covering, for all English practices (n~7600): skill mix (NHS Digital primary care Minimum Data Set), other practice characteristics (routinely available data), and model type, (iv) workforce costs WP2: Systematic review of impact of team composition and climate on staff and patient outcomes WP3: Practice-level modelling (using Practices Database) of associations between skill mix (e.g. % of total FTEs GPs / other care staff) and quality of care (QOF clinical summary score, CQC inspection rating, patient experience survey indicators), controlling for practice characteristics. Production function approach to identify the output contribution of different staff, substitution possibilities and cost savings. WP4: Patient-level modelling of association between practice skill mix and clinical effectiveness (hospitalisations for ambulatory care sensitive conditions e.g. diabetes complications, asthma), controlling for patient level confounders. Patient outcomes from linked primary and secondary care data (n=546 practices, Farr Institute), merged with Practices Database for analysis. Economic analysis to identify savings from clinically effective staff deployment. WP5: In-depth qualitative analysis. a) focus groups (8) with service users for perspectives on how teams affect care; b) survey of staff in a sample of practices (n~240) to explore team climate and burnout in relation to workforce and performance indicators; c) case studies in 12 varied practices (traditional model, with task substitution and role creation, and new models), using staff interviews, observations and patient survey, to assess how skill mix and team climate are associated with effectiveness and patient experiences. Synthesis using receptive contexts for change and interactionist theory. WP6: Knowledge transfer. Two groups (GP primary care practitioners, commissioners) in 4 regions, total of 144 participants, score potential components of implementation guidelines (developed from findings of WPs 2-5) over two rounds, to reach consensus on final guidance to support future decision making (RAND/UCL Appropriateness Method). WP7: Active dissemination strategy to engage commissioners, primary care providers, statutory and non-statutory bodies. Benefits and potential impact. The research will produce evidence about which skill mix and team climates work best in primary care, and role and task substitutions that reduce costs while maintaining or improving outcomes. This will enable GP partners, managers and commissioners to make informed decisions that address current staffing problems and future workforce requirements.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: The immunogenicity and efficacy of pneumococcal vaccines: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of individual participant data
Abstract: Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus) is a leading cause of bacterial pneumonia, meningitis, sepsis, and otitis media in children.(1) Pneumococcal disease can be prevented by vaccination. In the UK, infants are vaccinated against pneumococcal disease using a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine containing 13 serotypes (strains) of pneumococcus (PCV13, “Prevenar 13”, Pfizer). Public Health England estimate that pneumococcal vaccination has prevented 40,000 cases of invasive pneumococcal disease in England and Wales.(2) There is a different pneumococcal vaccine used in many countries that contains 10 serotypes (PCV10, “Synflorix”, GSK). It is important that policy makers know whether one vaccine is superior to the other when deciding on the right vaccine for the UK. If both vaccines are equally efficacious then the vaccine tendering process can be opened up to both suppliers, likely resulting in competition in the market and cost-savings to the NHS. Very few studies have directly compared these two vaccines so data are limited. Trials that have compared them have only looked at immunogenicity (antibody production induced by vaccination) which is not the same as comparing efficacy (actual disease prevention). However, large randomised efficacy trials with a placebo control are no longer possible now that licensed vaccines are in routine use. Previous reviews to determine which vaccine is more immunogenic only looked at published estimates and only for trials that directly compared the two licensed vaccines. No meta-analyses were possible in these reviews. We will conduct a wider systematic review and an individual participant data network meta-analysis to fully answer the question of which vaccine has better immunogenicity, as well as superior efficacy. We will incorporate additional trials published since the last review as well as unpublished data that is available on company websites. We will access the individual participant data rather than relying on published estimates alone, and use novel methods to derive estimates of efficacy based on the individual infant’s serology data (‘sero-efficacy’). Our methods for determining sero-efficacy have successfully been used before to estimate the efficacy of vaccines for which no large randomised trials have been completed. Our review will be substantially larger than previous reviews as we will not only include direct head-to-head studies of PCV10 vs PCV13 but also include a large number of trials that compared one of the two vaccines to the older vaccine (PCV7) that is no longer in use. The studies of these three vaccines form a ‘network’ that can then be analysed together. The additional trials and the connections within the network will add a large amount of statistical power and precision to the analysis and enable us to fill in the gaps where data are limited for the direct comparisons of PCV10 vs PCV13. Our results will provide robust estimates of the comparative immunogenicity and efficacy of licensed pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, enabling economic modellers and policy-makers in the UK and worldwide to make informed evidence-based decisions to protect the population from disease.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: The SAFEST Review: The Shock-Absorbing Flooring Effectiveness SysTematic Review including older adults and staff in care settings
Abstract: Aims of the research: We aim to summarise what is known about shock-absorbing flooring in hospitals and care homes, with regards to reducing injuries from falls. We want to help people decide whether or not to invest in using shock-absorbing floors. We will see if shock-absorbing flooring can: (1) reduce injuries from falls; (2) increase the chances of someone falling over; and (3) lead to injuries in staff who may find it harder to move equipment across a softer floor. We will also summarise any research on the economic costs and savings of shock-absorbing floors. Finally, we will look at any practical issues people had when installing the new floors, and explore the experiences and attitudes of people who have used the floors (staff, residents/patients, and visitors). Background to the research: Falls and fall-related injuries are a major problem in hospitals and care homes. Older people are more at risk of falling, and more at risk of injuring themselves if they do fall. Injuries from falls can lead to loss of independence and mobility, shorter lives, and lower quality lives. Shock-absorbing flooring is one potential solution to help reduce the impact of a fall. Researchers from different countries have been studying the use of shock-absorbing floors in hospitals and care homes, but nobody has brought all of these studies together to summarise their findings in a systematic way. Design and methods used: We will carry out a thorough search to identify all the studies we can find that have looked at shock-absorbing flooring use in hospitals and care homes. We will assess these studies for quality, and gather data on what they did, who they involved, and what they found. We will summarise the information we find, to make it more easily understood. Where appropriate, we will combine the data from different studies to produce an overall result. We will explore the differences between studies, to help us understand which factors might influence whether shock-absorbing flooring works, and to determine how trustworthy the findings are. We will use the findings from studies included in the review to produce recommendations that can guide end-users of the review. Patient and public involvement: Our patient and public members will be involved throughout the project. They will help make sure our findings are easy to understand, and include all the important information. They will check the judgements we make about the quality of the research we find, to make sure we are being fair and clear. They will be involved in meetings to help guide us and make decisions. They will help us make a short video, which explains the findings of our research through patient experiences. Dissemination: We will share our findings in different ways to suit different people. We will publish our report in an academic journal, with universal free access. We will present our findings at two conferences (one in England and one abroad), which have a focus on caring for older people, and online in a webinar. We will hold a half-day workshop, to which we will invite people who may find our review useful. We will produce short reports to give to people who make decisions about which flooring to use in hospitals and care homes. Finally we will make a short online video which tells the findings of the review through the views and stories of patients. This is because many people like to make decisions when they hear patients’ or residents' views.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The STanding up fOR Myself (STORM) psychosocial group intervention for young people and adults with intellectual disabilities: Feasibility study
Abstract: Background: Adults and young people with intellectual disabilities (ID) are at increased risk of mental health problems, due to biological, psychological, and environmental factors; one important environmental factor is stigma: negative stereotypes, which lead to prejudice and discrimination. Despite many positive changes, prejudice and discrimination are still a reality for many young people and adults with ID and render them vulnerable to low self-esteem, mental health problems, and poorer quality of life. Whilst psychosocial interventions for the general population have been adapted for digital delivery, no interventions for adults with ID have been digitised, creating a digital divide. With the Covid-19 pandemic preventing adults with ID accessing services in the community there has been a shift to groups instead meeting online. Our group intervention (Standing Up for Myself-STORM) seeks to enhance the capacity of young people and adults with ID to manage and resist stigma, a need which is ever present during the pandemic, however STORM is has not been designed for digital delivery, thus requires adaptation and piloting. Aims: To adapt STORM for digital delivery via online meeting platforms and carry out a pilot study with four groups to assess feasibility and acceptability. We will assess the feasibility of recruiting and retaining participants, of collecting proposed outcome measures via online methods, and consider the fidelity of Digital STORM delivery. A process evaluation using mixed methods will examine delivery and acceptability of the intervention and factors that may affect future implementation and a future feasibility trial. Intervention: STORM is a manualised psychosocial group intervention delivered over four 90-minute sessions (plus one follow up session) to established groups of people with ID by group facilitators who are familiar with group members. During STORM sessions, prompted by first-hand filmed testimonials by people with ID, participants discuss what ID means to them, experiences of negative interactions with others, different possible responses to negative interactions and their consequences, and plan ways of dealing with stigma in future. Intervention adaptation: An intervention adaptation group will be established to adapt the original STORM materials for digital delivery. This group will include people with ID and facilitators from third sector organisations. Inclusion Criteria: Individuals aged 16+ with mild to moderate ID who are in receipt of specialist services for people with ID within the education, social care or third sector will be recruited through community organisations and education providers who work with groups of people with ID. They will be members of established groups for people with ID run by such organisations, and will have verbal and cognitive abilities sufficient to provide informed consent, complete the outcome measures, and engage in a discussion-based group programme. Participants will need access to a device and internet connection to enable them to connect to an online meeting platform to take part in Digital STORM. Exclusion Criteria: severe ID, unable to communicate in English, lack of capacity to consent to participation. No devices or internet connection with which to join the online meetings. Study procedures: 4 groups with an average 5 participants (N=20) will be recruited to take part in the pilot of Digital STORM. Outcomes: Feasibility of recruitment and retention; acceptability of digital intervention delivery; feasibility of collecting secondary health-related outcome data using virtual methods: mental wellbeing, self-esteem, self-efficacy in rejecting prejudice, negative reactions to discrimination, sense of social power, and health economic data, assessed at baseline and end of intervention(4 months. Trial progression criteria: Criteria regarding feasibility and acceptability of digital delivery of the intervention, and feasibility of digital collection of outcome data defined using a traffic light system will inform a decision whether to progress to a feasibility trial and whether the design would be two-arm (STORM and treatment as usual or Digital STORM and treatment as usual) or three arm (STORM x Digital STORM x treatment as usual). This decision will also need to be informed by the evolving picture in relation to the Covid-19 pandemic.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Optimisation, feasibility testing and a pilot randomised trial of SaFE: a sexual health and healthy relationships intervention for Further Education
Abstract: Background: Dating and relationship violence (DRV) includes threats, emotional abuse, controlling behaviour, physical violence and forced sexual activity and is reported by over half of further education (FE) students. The median age for most recent occurrence of non-volitional sex (sex against one’s will) is 18 among men and 16 among women. The UK also has the highest rate of under-18 births in Western Europe, 21% of unplanned pregnancies occur among 16-18 year-olds and 16-24 year olds account for over half of chlamydia and gonorrhoea diagnoses. Improving sexual health and reducing DRV in young people is a UK public health priority. In England, there are 1.2 million 16-18 year olds studying in FE with participation across social groups. FE provides a scalable setting for intervention as most students are aged 16-24. However intervention in this setting is virtually non-existent. Aim: To optimise, feasibility test and pilot ‘SaFE,’ a sexual health and DRV intervention for FE settings. Objectives: 1) Convene a network of stakeholders to optimise the intervention materials. 2) Assess the feasibility and acceptability of implementing SaFE in two FE settings. 3) Conduct a pilot cluster randomised controlled trial (cRCT) in six FE settings to determine whether a Phase III cRCT assessing effectiveness and cost-effectiveness should be conducted. Methods and timelines: Phase 1) Intervention optimisation (Jan–Apr20) Informed by existing literature and the MRC PHIND funded Phase I intervention development “SaFE Project” [MR/M026272/1], the intervention components are: 1) onsite access to sexual health and relationship services; 2) publicity of onsite services and signposting to educational resources; and 3) FE staff training to promote sexual health and recognize, prevent and respond to DRV and sexual harassment. Existing literature and materials will be reviewed, adapted and refined, and draft staff training and publicity materials will be produced. Stakeholders, FE students, staff and the ALPHA youth advisory group will be consulted and the intervention materials refined. Phase 2) Intervention feasibility testing (Apr–Aug20) Intervention components will be tested for feasibility and acceptability in two FE settings; one 6th form and one college (one in England, one in Wales). Refinements will be made based on feedback. Phase 3) Pilot cRCT (Aug20-Mar22) A pilot cRCT will be conducted (4 intervention, 2 control settings) with integrated process and economic evaluations. Following baseline surveys (Sep 2020), clusters (settings) will be randomly allocated to 2 arms: SaFE in 4 settings and usual practice in 2. Allocation will use a 2:1 ratio in favour of the intervention, stratified by country and setting. Follow up surveys will be 12 months post-baseline (Sep 2021). A process evaluation will explore intervention feasibility, acceptability, fidelity, sustainability, reach, mechansisms of action, contamination, and scalability. Impact and dissemination: As well as the NIHR monograph, we will submit two open access papers to high impact journals on the implementation of SaFE and the pilot trial results. Findings will be presented at academic conferences and two stakeholder meetings with practitioners and policy makers (one England, one Wales). We will disseminate our findings to participating FE settings, and use DECIPHer and Centre for Trials Research blogs, Twitter and infographics to maximise public awareness.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Clinical and/or cost-effectiveness of first trimester ultrasound screening for fetal anomalies: Is a prospective study an efficient investment?
Abstract: Fetal anomaly screening is routinely performed in the second trimester. Our group has recently published a systematic review and meta-analysis of first trimester anomaly screening. This shows that the sensitivity for the detection of major anomalies in a low risk unselected population (19 studies, 115731 fetuses) was 46 % (95% CI, 36.88–55.46%), representing just over half of all abnormalities detected prenatally. We also showed a significant association between the sensitivity of first-trimester ultrasound and the use of an anatomical protocol for screening. These findings suggest that first trimester anomaly screening has the potential to be a valuable addition to prenatal care for all women. However, a trial assessing this in practice would be very large and expensive. This study will establish the current clinical and sost effectiveness of such a first trimester scan; and whether further study of this would be feasible and cost effective. In order to define, justify and protocolise the 12 week detailed anomaly scan we will undertake: - Systematic review and meta-analysis of literature to establish screening characteristics of the first trimester anomaly scan, and in particular measure uncertainties regarding the existing data (effect of gestational age at the scan; preferred route (transabdominal vs transvaginal); what specific anomalies detectable and at what false positive rates). - Systematic review of the detection rates of fetal cardiac abnormalities specifically; this is done separately as fetal cardiac defects are the most common congenital abnormality, frequently remain undeteceted and have major impact on neonatal morbidity and mortality, while there are specific details that make these studies too heterogenous to combine with the systematic review above. - Nationwide survey of all maternity units to establish current practice; the choice that women are offered; and what impact a suspected abnormality has in changing a woman's care from the standard NICE antenatal care pathway. - Analysis of National Congenital Anomalies Disease Registry (NCARDRS) to determine the impact of first trimester screening policies (from the survey) on the timing of diagnosis. - Prospective survey to understand parental opinions of an early anomaly scan. - Consensus procedure to develop a protocol for the first trimester scan will be undertaken, taking into account acceptability of this amongst pregnant individuals. To derive an economic model and conduct a value of information (VOI) analysis, we will develop a decision analytic model to determine the expected cost and outcomes associated with current practice and with each of the discrete protocols defined above. This will be populated with evidence from the systematic reviews and assessment of dataset of detected anomalies, above. Evidence gaps will be noted and “plugged” by systematic review findings and evidence from expert panels. A de novo probabilistic decision analytic model to estimate the cost-effectiveness of implementing first trimester anomaly screening based on current evidence will be undertaken. VoI analysis to ascertain the degree of decision and parameter uncertainty; the need for further research, which will include cost modelling for the resource of sonographers required. Based on this information we will outline the design of plausible prospective studies. Candidate study designs will be discussed in workshops of health care professionals and focus groups including patients and the public.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Exploring the uptake and use of electronic cigarettes provided to smokers accessing homeless centres: a feasibility study
Abstract: Smoking rates in the UK are at an all-time low, at 15.8% of the adult population. However, this masks considerable inequalities; prevalence amongst adults who are homeless, for example, remains four times higher than the national average. Homeless smokers make fewer quit attempts, are less likely to stop smoking, and are at risk of poor physical and mental health outcomes including other addictions. As such, this is a difficult to engage population, however, not tackling smoking in this population will only increase health inequalities. E-cigarettes (EC) are now the most common method of stopping smoking in the UK, used in over one third of quit attempts. There is emerging evidence of cessation efficacy but initial start-up costs may deter those on lower incomes from purchasing. Supplying free e-cigarette starter kits at a location already being accessed by homeless smokers may therefore facilitate behaviour change and smoking cessation. Our aim is to undertake a feasibility cluster randomised controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of supplying free e-cigarette starter kits for smoking cessation to smokers accessing homeless centres. The study will take place in four homeless centres (who will serve as clusters) across the UK: two in the intervention (e-cigarette) and two in the control (usual care) arm; each control and intervention centre matched for accommodation provision. 120 participants (30 at each centre) will complete questionnaires measuring smoking behaviour and general health and provide a breath carbon monoxide (CO) sample at baseline. Those in the e-cigarette arm will be provided with an e-cigarette starter kit including 4 weeks supply of e-liquids and support to use them. Follow up assessments including smoking behaviour, quit rates, CO levels, health-related quality of life and e-cigarette usage patterns will be conducted at 4, 12 and 24 weeks. Centres in the control group will be provided with information on smoking cessation and how to access their local stop smoking service and will be followed up at the same time points. Qualitative interviews with 24 participants (12 in each arm) including completers and non-completers, and 12 service centre staff (6 in each arm) will be conducted between weeks 4 and 8. The feasibility study will inform the design of a future trial. Specifically, we will assess: willingness of smokers to participate; retention in the intervention and control groups and the percentage that are still using e-cigarettes at each follow up time point; unintended consequences; preliminary evidence of the effectiveness of supplying free e-cigarette starter kits; the feasibility of collecting data on contacts with health care services within this population as an input to an economic evaluation in a full RCT; the cost of providing free e-cigarettes on a per person basis. We will monitor engagement with the study through quantitative measures and qualitative interviews with completers, non-completers and staff to assess facilitators and barriers to comply with the study. If successful, findings from this feasibility study will be used to inform the design of a fully powered cluster randomised controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of providing free e-cigarette starter kits to homeless smokers for smoking cessation. If the main trial is effective, the service delivery model has the potential to be rolled out nationally across homeless centres.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Feasibility study and pilot trial of an evidence-based low intensity psychosocial intervention delivered by lay therapists for asylum seekers and refugees (PROSPER)
Abstract: Asylum seekers and refugees (AS&Rs) experience reduced mental health and wellbeing, related to stresses in their country of origin, experiences in transit and reception on arrival, including exclusion from mainstream services such as income support, housing and healthcare. Their contact with healthcare is often crisis-driven and mediated through non-governmental organisations (NGOs), whose staff lack knowledge and skills in the management of distress. This study will test the feasibility of a randomised controlled trial to evaluate an intervention based on Problem Management Plus (PM+), a psychosocial intervention recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for adults impaired by distress in communities exposed to adversity. PM+ provides clients with skills in managing practical problems and mental health problems. In this context, is proposed that an adapted PM+ will be delivered by lay therapists with lived experience as AS&Rs, through NGOs working with AS&Rs in Liverpool City Region. Research question. Is it feasible to undertake a randomised controlled trial of PM+, delivered by lay therapists in NGOs, for distressed and functionally impaired asylum seekers and refugees? Methods. The research will be undertaken in Liverpool City Region over 24 months. First, we will refine and adapt PM+ to suit local context. We will do this by a) systematic review of barriers and facilitators to psychosocial interventions led by lay therapists to improve migrant health and wellbeing, and in parallel, b) focused inquiry with local stakeholders to ensure acceptability, linguistic and cultural relevance to target populations. Second, we will assess the feasibility of the proposed training procedures. These will involve master training and supervision in PM+ provided to a counselling NGO who, in turn, provide training and supervision for lay therapists in NGOs in contact with AS&Rs. Then we will undertake a pilot randomised controlled trial of five 90 minute sessions of PM+ delivered individually or in groups by lay therapists to AS&Rs with emotional distress and functional impairment, compared with usual peer support offered by the NGOs. Distress and impairment at baseline will be measured by Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) and WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHO-DAS). For this pilot trial we will aim for three arms (individual, group and control) with 35 participants per arm. Primary health outcomes will be anxiety and depressive symptoms at 3 months, measured by HADS. Secondary outcomes will include subjective wellbeing, functional status, progress on identified problems, post-traumatic stress disorder, depressive disorder and service usage. Longer term impact will be assessed at 6 months post baseline assessment on the same parameters. We will assess the feasibility of conducting a randomised controlled trial in relation to the following elements: * adaptation of PM+ to local context; * recruitment, training and retention of lay therapists; * delivery model: participant recruitment and retention; acceptability and fidelity; * outcome measures: acceptability and suitability. We will use these findings to specify the parameters for a full randomised controlled trial to test the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of PM+ in reducing emotional distress and health inequalities, and improving functional ability and wellbeing, amongst asylum seekers and refugees.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health protection
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: How can e-health interventions reduce the ‘syndemic’ of HIV/STIs and sexual risk, substance use and mental ill health among men who have sex with men? Systematic review and evidence synthesis
Abstract: Background MSM in the UK experience disproportionate burdens of HIV and other STIs, alcohol and drug use, and mental ill-health, which inter-correlate at the level of both the individual and the sexual event. Existing reviews focused on general populations suggest e-health interventions are effective in addressing alcohol consumption and common mental illness symptoms and are promising approaches for addressing sexual risks and drug use. But intervention effects may differ for MSM because of their greater use of social media and greater exposure to homophobia and other structural risk factors; and higher exposure to social norms supportive of alcohol and drug use. Despite the existence of a sizeable primary literature, there are no adequate existing reviews of e-health interventions targeting these outcomes singly or in combination among MSM. Aim To search systematically for, appraise the quality of, and synthesise evidence to address the following research questions: RQ1. What approaches and theories of change do existing e-health interventions employ to prevent HIV, STIs, sexual risk behaviour, alcohol and drug use, or common mental illness symptoms among MSM? RQ2. What factors relating to interventions, providers, participants or contexts promote or impede delivery or receipt of such interventions? RQ3. What are the effects of such interventions on HIV and STIs, sexual risk behaviour, alcohol and drug use, and depression and anxiety, overall and by intervention and client sub-group? RQ4. Are such interventions cost-effective in reducing these outcomes? RQ5. Does the existing evidence overall suggest that these outcomes can coherently, feasibly and effectively be addressed by a single, joined-up e-health intervention targeted UK MSM and if so what might such an intervention look like? Objectives a) To conduct electronic and other searches by Feb 2019. b) To screen found references and reports for inclusion in the review by May 2019. c) To extract data from and assess the quality of included studies by September 2019. d) To develop a typology of interventions and synthesise theories of change and process evaluations by January 2020. e) To consult with policy/practice and community stakeholders on the typology and theory of change/process synthesis by February 2020. f) To synthesise outcome evaluation and cost-effectiveness data by May 2020. g) To draw on these syntheses to draft a report addressing our research questions by July 2020. h) To consult with policy/practice and community stakeholders on the draft report (to inform amendments and dissemination) by September 2020. i) To submit the final report to NIHR by October 2020. Design and method We propose a multi-component systematic review. Included studies must address our research questions. Outcome evaluations must be randomised or quasi-experimental in design. We will search via databases and other methods. References will be screened first on title/abstract and then on full report. Two reviewers will extract data and assess the quality of included studies using existing tools. Syntheses of intervention descriptions, theories of change and process evaluations will employ thematic synthesis. We will narratively synthesise evidence of effectiveness and conduct meta-analyses. We will use an ‘equity lens’ to examine subgroup effects to assess impacts on health inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Programme: Health and Social Care Delivery Research
Award_Title: Meeting the transgender challenge: improving the experience of health services for gender diverse young people and their families
Abstract: Gender Identity Services provide advice and help for people who find themselves distressed by their natally defined gender and who experience themselves as living with a wrongly gendered body. Demand for gender identity clinics is increasing; the Tavistock and Portman Gender Identity Development Service for young people (which is the only NHS funded clinic for gender diverse young people) has an estimated waiting list of 1400 people. This can mean lengthy waits for young people and their families who are likely to have questions, concerns and support needs during this period. Finding balanced online information can be challenging as views about transgender issues vary widely. Little is known about the experiences, information and support needs of young people waiting for gender identity clinic services. Our proposed research will help address this shortfall through a nationwide collection of narrative interviews with gender diverse children, young people and adults, and families. Our aim is to improve the care and support for young people and their families before and after referral to specialist gender identity services. Our objectives are to: •Develop a 360 degree understanding of the perspectives and experiences of young people, families and “gateway” professionals (GPs, CAHMS, gender identity clinic clinicians) in gender identity health services. •Identify ways in which specialist gender identity services can be improved and develop resources to help achieve these improvements. •Support young people and their families through the development of two new sections on Healthtalk.org. •Evaluate these Healthtalk sections with patients and their families on the waiting list for services. Methods. To meet our objectives we will: •After updating our literature and field review, we will conduct video and audio recorded in-depth narrative interviews with a diverse nationwide sample of 40 gender questioning young people (up to the age of 25 years ), 10 adults over the age of 25 years, and 20 (non-paired) family members. We will audio record interviews with 20 “gateway” professionals (GPs, Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service professionals). (Months 1 to 21) •Hold a national networking event to present key findings from the research, explore best practice and potential for service improvements and recommendations to help health and care staff to respond effectively to young people and their families. (Month 24) •The interviews will be used to develop an online resource (as part of the well-established, public facing Heathtalk.org) featuring analyses and balanced video and audio extracts from the interviews, to improve the care and support of patients and families. The material will also be made available to train staff, inform service improvements and develop resources for relationship and sex education in schools. (Month 28) •Conduct a mixed methods formative evaluation of the new Healthtalk sections, using a validated questionnaire, to assess its role as a source of information and emotional support for people waiting for specialist services. (Months 26 to 27) Anticipated impact: specialist service providers have identified the need for a reliable resource, featuring an appropriately wide range of experiences, to prepare, inform and support those on the waiting list, currently estimated to be 1400 people at the GIDS. Specialist staff, GPs, CAMHS, Relationship and Sex Education (RSE) teachers will all potentially benefit.

Award_Title: An evaluation of the implementation of national school food standards in secondary schools and their impact on the school food environment and pupil intake of free sugars: a mixed methods study
Abstract: BACKGROUND National School Food Standards were introduced in 2006 and are a legal requirement for most state schools. In 2013, the School Food Plan, a wider set of voluntary recommendations for schools, was developed, and subsequently updated standards were introduced in 2015. There is little information on the impact of School Food Standards on school food provision and pupil food intake in secondary schools, and the impact of the updated standards and the School Food Plan recommendations has not been explored. The way in which the School Food Standards legislation has been introduced means that all academies and free schools set up between 2010 and 2014 are not obliged to meet the standards. This gives an opportunity to examine the influence of a legal requirement to meet the standards by comparing schools which are, versus those that are not required by law to meet them. Specifically, we want to assess whether the standards influence pupils' sugar intake, as adolescents have high levels of sugar consumption, which can lead to obesity and poor dental health. AIMS We aim to make comparisons between secondary schools required to meet the standards and those who are not required to meet the standards. We will compare: the food provided and sold in schools; the school eating environment and ethos; the healthy eating and cooking skills curriculum; the cost to schools of measures to improve healthy eating and food provision; the consumption of foods high in sugar, other elements of the diet and dental health in pupils. We will also explore the extent to which schools vary in how the School Food Standards and School Food Plan are implemented. DESIGN We will recruit 44 secondary schools in the West Midlands to take part (22 who are required to adhere, and 22 that do not have to adhere to the standards). We will examine whether a requirement to adhere to the standards policy is associated with the provision, sale and consumption of healthier foods (focusing on sugar intake) in schools, and whether and how requirement to adhere relates to the implementation of the School Food Plan. This will be done through collation of data from a variety of school documents (including relevant school policies, food and catering contracts, relevant curricular teaching), researcher observations (to ascertain the school environment and culture including the food on offer and the eating spaces in schools) and questionnaires to key staff members, governors and parents to gain their views and experiences of the food standards, the school eating environment, culture and curriculum. We also aim to recruit around 1980 pupils from years 7, 9 and 10 from the 44 participating schools. In school time we will ask them to complete an online survey including a 24-hour recall tool, and questions about the food they eat and the health of their teeth. We will compare the average sugar intake, tooth decay symptoms and treatment, and intake of other food types among pupils in the two school groups. We will compare information on school food sales across the two school groups. We will use the above information to identify 4-8 schools with varying levels of provision and sale of healthy foods, in which we will collect more in-depth information through interviews with key staff members and small discussion groups with pupils. We will explore whether consumption of sugar and other foods is influenced by how well the School Food Standards and School Food Plan are implemented. PUBLIC INVOLVEMENT Secondary school pupils, parents and teachers in senior management positions have contributed to the study design. We have convened a panel of parents, governors, and teachers to consult with at key points during the project. We will also regularly consult with a secondary school council of pupils. DISSEMINATION We will communicate the findings to key health and educational organisations nationally and locally. Findings will help shape future school food policy.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Long-term follow-up of ARTISTIC cervical screening trial cohort
Abstract: In the ARTISTIC Trial 24,510 women undergoing routine screening by liquid-based cytology were also tested for HPV (Hybrid Capture 2, with HPV typing if positive) and randomised for the HPV result to be concealed or revealed. Women were followed up until 2009 (6-8 years after entry) via two cytology laboratories in the Manchester area. Any women moving out of the area were lost, and these laboratories have now been restructured to cover a different geographical area. We shall extend follow-up of the ARTISTIC Trial cohort until December 2015 (up to 14 years from entry) through the NHS Central Register (cancer incidence and mortality) and the Open Exeter national screening programme database (cervical screening records), and review all histopathology reports for CIN3 and cervical cancer held by cancer registries. The Open Exeter database includes all cervical screening records regardless of the Health Authority in which the woman resides. The introduction of primary HPV testing in the NHS cervical screening programme will require several practical decisions on test method and frequency with large effects on costs, staff time and patient acceptability, as well as on effectiveness of cancer prevention. 1. The role of HPV typing. HPV typing provided by different tests ranges from none (HC2) to partial (COBAS) or full typing (several systems). Possible follow-up policies include immediate referral of HPV16/18 and delayed retesting for other types, immediate cytology of all HPV positives, and a delay of at least a year before retesting, then treating all women with type-specific persistence. 2. Age at first HPV test. NHS CSP sentinel sites will implement HPV testing beginning at age 30, when most infections acquired before age 25 will have disappeared. Starting screening as early as age 22 could be cost-effective if HPV positive results were followed up (say) 3 years later without intervention. At the next screening round at age 25 women with type-specific HPV persistence over 3 years would be treated, and new infections would be followed up 3 years later. 3. Test specificity. If a quantitative test such as HC2 is used, the conventional cutoff (RLU = 1) gives a false positive rate of about 2%, which in older women is about a third of all positive results. We shall analyse age-specific effects of different cutoffs. 4. Age at last HPV test, and test sensitivity. An attractive cost-saving possibility is to stop screening at age 50 in women who are HPV negative. A final HPV test at age 50 might require a more sensitive test than at younger ages. Two women in the ARTISTIC trial have already developed invasive cervical cancer after a negative HC2 sample that was HPV16 positive when retested by PCR. ARTISTIC over-recruited older women, and 43% of women in the trial will be aged over 55 years by 2015. 5. Screening interval. The screening interval after a negative test can be much longer with HPV testing than with cytology. Long-term data are limited, but the cancer risk may be negligible up to 10 years after a negative test. Extending follow-up to 2015 will increase the median follow-up from 7 to 13 years from entry and from 4 to 10 years from round 2, providing a basis for evaluating policies in relation to HPV clearance, acquisition and persistence. For the purpose of modelling an established programme using HPV screening an important group are women who were negative at their previous test. This analysis must begin at the 2nd screening round, when these women can be identified.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Developing LifeLight: A contactless vital signs monitor for CVD screening
Abstract: Research question: Is Lifelight® technology clinically efficacious and safe? Background: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the most common cause of mortality with 28% of UK deaths attributed to it. CVD risk is highly modifiable however steps to reduce CVD risk can only be made if these individuals are detected. The leading risk factor for CVD is hypertension and hence Public Health England aims to diagnose an additional 3.7 million cases of hypertension by 2029. Lifelight® is the world s first contactless method for measuring vital signs, including blood pressure. The contactless and software nature of this CE marked technology means it overcomes issues of conventional methods for measuring vital signs that make hypertension screening unfeasible. Its advantages over traditional methods means it could also be useful for helping people with hypertension to keep their blood pressure at safe levels. Aims and Objectives: Collect clinical data to improve Lifelight® accuracy for measuring blood pressure and other vital signs. Trial primary endpoint is progression of the technology s performance closer to standard-of-care efficacy levels (e.g. automatic blood pressure machine). Collect data and patient feedback and strengthen strategic relationships with NHS and PHE to prepare for real-world implementation. Methods: Prospective multi-centre trial conducted at Portsmouth Hospitals NHS Trust and Barts Health NHS Trust collecting artificial intelligence training and testing data from 10,000 people. Collection of vital sign measurement timing data to assess cost-saving opportunity of CVD screening use case and patient feedback on the concept. Timelines for delivery: 24-month project incorporating a 12-month trial. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination: Project outputs include publications in The Lancet, attendance at major clinical conferences, and health economics model. If future real-world implementation is successful and rolled out nationally, application of the technology for CVD screening and hypertension monitoring could save UK health and social care £210 million over 10 years.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: The Newcastle Upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Delivering the first evidence based lifestyle service pathway for people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
Abstract: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) represents a spectrum of liver conditions ranging from hepatic steatosis through steatohepatitis to cirrhosis. Its prevalence has been estimated at between 1 in 5 and 1 in 3 of the adult population depending on country and diagnostic criteria used. Prevalence increases with degree of obesity, and is very common in those with Type 2 diabetes. Rising prevalence of obesity and Type 2 diabetes, particularly in younger people, will ensure that NAFLD remains a growing clinical concern for the future. Lifestyle modification, which encompasses diet, weight loss, physical activity, and/or exercise related behaviours, is the primary recommended therapy for NAFLD, especially in the absence of approved pharmaceutical agents. Despite the prevalence and importance of NAFLD in developing more advanced clinical presentations, pathways for the clinical management of NAFLD are poorly defined. The lack of a defined care pathway essentially leaves patients unsupported until they present with more advanced conditions before they are actively engaged in care.This research will define the current lived experience for people diagnosed with NAFLD and their care teams, both in Primary and Secondary Care. Furthermore, the treatment algorithms and treatment trajectory (i.e. who gets referred to Secondary Care and how the condition is monitored) will be defined alongside how patients perceive the condition / service and feel about the care pathway.On this foundation, I will refine the service pathway for people with NAFLD by actively engaging patients and healthcare professionals to deliver a streamlined and practical service pathway based on current evidence for disease management. The focus of this refinement will be on the delivery of lifestyle interventions. Refining this service will involve creating new tools to aid service delivery which will be developed with all relevant stakeholders (to include patients, medics, nurses, allied health professionals (AHPs) and exercise specialists) to allow a consistent approach to disease management. This research will deliver patient benefit by creating a new lifestyle service which has been developed and designed in consultation with both patients and care teams. By doing so this pathway will, for the first time, deliver a consistent level of care across the NHS, regardless of whether they are being managed in Primary or Secondary Care for patients with NAFLD. Healthcare professionals will also be able to provide lifestyle interventions based on the most up-to-date scientific evidence and will have extensive knowledge with regards to the supporting infrastructure/services available in the area to support physical activity/exercise. This service, if proven to be effective, could not only potentially create a step change in the management of NAFLD but also in the prevention of conditions associated with NAFLD such as Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

Award_Title: Parental and home environment influences on youth physical activity and screen-viewing: Identifying factors to increase physical activity and decrease screen-viewing as a means of preventing childhood obesity
Abstract: Objective: The objective of the proposed research is to identify the parental and home environmental factors that influence children’s physical activity (PA) and screen-viewing (SV). Design: Research involves analysis of existing and new datasets. PA will be assessed via accelerometer and SV by parent self-report. Paths of association between variables and children’s PA, SV and BMI will be examined. Parental and home environment strategies to change SV and PA will be developed and piloted. Outcomes and benefits: The study will highlight key variables that could be changed to reduce SV and increase PA as a means of preventing childhood obesity.

Abstract: This research will identify and begin to evaluate methods for supporting the maintenance of weight loss through changes in diet and physical activity. Literature reviews and stakeholder meetings will identify evidence-based strategies for intervention that may be effective and deliverable in NHS primary care. To address key questions about how much intervention is needed to achieve maintenance of weight loss and whether providing more intensive interventions would increase or decrease costeffectiveness (value-for-money), intervention materials will be developed for delivery at 3 different levels of intensity. A pilot study will assess the feasibility and acceptability of the interventions and provide data for planning a large, definitive trial. The results will inform commissioning of NHS weight loss services. The intervention/training materials will be published online for use by NHS staff and funding will be sought for a full-scale trial and related research.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine
Award_Title: Assessing metabolic profiling strategies for nutritional management of cardiovascular disease risk
Abstract: A cornerstone of governments' policies to reduce cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk is to encourage population change towards healthier diet and lifestyle. However, monitoring dietary changes in response to policy recommendations is based on self-reported dietary assessment tools, which are known to have high misreporting rates. This makes it difficult to understand if poor response to policy recommendations is due to lack of physiological effect of a diet, poor compliance to recommendations and/or variation in individuals' response to dietary changes. I previously developed an analytical pipeline to accurately classify metabolic profiles in healthy individuals according to dietary type and to assess adherence to diet, independently of dietary recording based on NMR urine spectra. I now want to focus on developing a method that effectively reflects adherence and variability in response to dietary changes in people at risk of CVD in order to implement metabolically-personalised nutritional advice to increase participants' compliance to dietary recommendations that will result in reducing CVD-risk factors (e.g. high cholesterol, BMI, blood pressure). I will achieve this by expanding coverage of the metabolome to incorporate plasma lipids and urine/plasma markers of gut bacterial modulation, using a multiplatform (NMR, LC-MS, GC-MS) approach.Research question Can metabolically-informed personalised dietary advice be used to more effectively change dietary habits of CVD-risk participants in comparison to traditional dietary advice? Specifically I aim to: - Build a multiplatform mathematical model to establish the level of adherence of individuals to dietary recommendations based on comprehensive molecular phenotyping of urine and blood plasma and to ascertain whether metabolic patterns at baseline are predictive of an individual's response to diet in terms of changes in metabolism. (Study 1) - Establish the response of free-living individuals at risk of CVD to dietary interventions by determining the relationship of the metabolic profiles with traditional CVD-risk metrics including cholesterol, BMI and blood pressure and evaluate the clinical benefit of incorporating this information into nutritional management programs compared to standardised clinical advice (Study 2). A further objective is to establish whether metabolically-tailored strategies can improve compliance to dietary recommendations and reduce misreporting.Investigation planStudy 1: 1H-NMR-spectroscopy, lipidomics and mass-spectrometry of urine and plasma will be used to generate a comprehensive metabolic profile of volunteers at risk of CVD based on an in-patient randomised cross-over clinical trial (CCT) to follow either a healthy dietary intervention, compliant with current dietary guidelines for risk reduction of CVD or a diet associated with high risk of CVD according to current UK dietary intake. Study 2: Mathematical models from the in-patient study will be used to objectively assess dietary intake, monitor adherence to diet and responses to dietary changes in free-living people at risk of CVD. Participants will follow a randomized CCT for 12-weeks, in which a dietitian will provide personalised dietary advice based on knowledge of urine and plasma metabolic profiles from samples collected at clinic every 2-weeks in addition to 24-h food diaries. A control group will mirror the intervention group but will receive standard NICE-guideline dietary recommendations. The changes in CVD-risk factors will be compared between the intervention and the control group.Furthermore, the 24-h food diaries of the intervention and the control groups will be assessed against objective measurements of their dietary habits using the metabolic profiles and the mathematical models from the in-patient study. The success of this project will facilitate improved measurement and monitoring of dietary intake in free-living people. This Fellowship will support a major step forward in improving British clinical nutritional practice by introducing new strategies to provide personalised advice, patient education and improve compliance to dietary advice for people at risk of CVD.

Award_Title: Exercise programmes for hip control to protect lower limb joints during recreational exercise in adolescents: a proof of concept and feasibility trial
Abstract: Background Arthritis is the biggest cause of pain and disability, with musculoskeletal conditions costing the NHS £5 billion per annum in England. Known risk factors for osteoarthritis (OA) include excessive activity, abnormal loading and obesity, which could be prevented. Moderate exercise is beneficial for joint cartilage and we need ways of exercising safely to prevent joint damage and subsequent OA. The hip is one of the most common sites for OA and Femoracetabular Impingement (FAI), a strong biomarker in the young for later OA, provides a useful model for developing prevention programmes. In FAI, altered bony geometry of the femoral head and acetabulum causes jamming within the hip. FAI occurs in 14-35% of the general population, 24% of military recruits, 39% of hockey players and 72% of footballers, who have a high incidence of OA and hip replacement surgery. The government's drive for a more active nation has increased uptake of football, so preventive programmes to protect joints are needed urgently. This project builds on laboratory studies of academy footballers and school children that identified movement patterns associated with FAI and abnormal loading on joints. Functional assessments were developed to identify abnormal movement patterns to inform exercise programmes, which will be finalised in collaboration with international experts in movement control. The next stage is to test the proof of concept (PoC) and feasibility of evaluating exercises in recreationally active adolescents in the general population.Research Questions: 1) 'Does a movement control exercise programme improve movement patterns?; 2) Is it feasible to conduct a clinical trial of preventive exercises in recreationally active adolescents?' Aims and Plan of Investigation: 1.Determine interrater and test-retest reliability of movement control tests 2.Finalise development of an exercise programme to improve hip movement control 3.Provide PoC that exercises improve hip control and movement patterns to reduce abnormal loading during functional tasks (by validation in a related biomechanical study) 4.Examine feasibility of conducting a full clinical trial in a community setting 5.Measure the rates of non-contact lower limb injuries 6.Examine post-study adherence to the exercise programmeParticipants will be assessed by a Physiotherapist using the movement screening tool and will complete the Hip and Groin outcome score pre and post intervention. The exercises will be taught to coaches who will instruct participants to conduct them as part of their warm-up programme to 'pre-activate' muscles prior to training and matches for 12 weeks. Feasibility of recruitment, acceptability and compliance will be examined. The findings will underpin a cluster randomised controlled trial with internal pilot to test the effectiveness of exercises targeted at improving control of hip movements, to reduce abnormal lower limb joint loading and prevent damage that leads to OA. Engagement with PPI representatives of players, coaches, parents and people with FAI and OA is key to this research, which will also be overseen by the PPI community within the Arthritis Research UK Centre for Sport, Exercise and Osteoarthritis. Potential Benefits to Patients and the NHS Effective targeted exercises would ensure correct use of muscles to avoid abnormal loading of lower limb joints, improving conservative evidence based treatment. Including programmes in school physical education lessons would ensure quality of movement to protect joints during development, particularly in very active or obese children. The exercises may help those with OA to be more active and limit further damage and avoid surgery. Ensuring safe exercise to prevent obesity would have direct impact on the government 'Get Active to Get Healthy' initiative. Prevention of recurrent joint problems would improve efficiency, saving NHS resources, in accordance with the Quality, Innovation, Prevention and Productivity (QIPP) Agenda.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Evidence based prevention, identification and treatment of chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS/ME) in children and young people
Abstract: Background: Chronic Fatique Syndrome (CFS/ME) is a common childhood condition with potentially serious consequences for those affected. The proposed research has 3 projects. Objectives: Project 1- Use population-based data to determine the prevalence of CFS/ME at age 13 and investigate risk factors for paediatric CFS/ME; Project 2- Investigate outcomes of care and compare three care models; Project 3-Develop a school-based early intervention to prevent development of CFS/ME and test its feasability and acceptability. Design: Project 1 Analyses of existing data from the ALSPAC birth cohort study Project 2 Expansion of existing longitudinal patient cohort to two additional paediatric clinical services using different models of service delivery; Project 3 Qualitative research followed by pilot intervention study Approaches: Project 1 Linear and logistic regression analysis, incorporating methods allowing for missing data; Project 2 Expansion of database, Linear and logistic regression models controlling for case mix; Project 3 Nurse-Led screening of young people with unexplained school absence, focus groups of parents professionals and children, development of tools to measure the economic impact of school absences Outcomes: Project 1 Novel and reliable estimates of prevalence of and risk factors for CFS/ME; Project 2 Improved understanding of outcomes of care based on the worlds largest paediatric cohort, credability to apply for further reading to create a national database; Project 3 An early intervention ready for testing using a full scale cluster RCT.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Precision antibiotic prescribing for urinary tract infection in hospital
Abstract: Background: Reducing inappropriate antibiotic prescribing to tackle antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global health priority. This is widely acknowledged, yet physicians continue to prescribe antibiotics for patients in whom bacterial infection is unlikely. Antimicrobial stewardship is the only approach with potential to immediately impact on AMR by preserving the lifespan of existing antibiotics. The major burden of drug-resistant infection is in hospital, but antibiotic prescribing in this setting is poorly understood due to lack of individual-level prescribing data. Without this information we cannot estimate the number of patients who could be safely treated without antibiotics, or devise evidence based stewardship initiatives to improve prescribing quality. Aims: I propose a novel, precision medicine approach to antibiotic prescribing in hospital, using high resolution electronic health records (EHRs) and host transcriptomic bio-signatures to guide prescribing decisions. I propose to test the safety and acceptability of this approach in a proof of concept study. I focus on urinary tract infection (UTI) syndromes as an exemplar of antibiotic overuse in hospital. Plan of investigation: I will analyse electronic health records (EHRs) from more than 9000 patients at University Hospital Birmingham to describe the clinical course, management and outcomes of patients with suspected UTI syndromes in order to estimate antibiotic overuse. Applying conventional statistical and machine learning approaches in parallel to these EHRs, I will develop a series of risk models to predict each patient's need for antibiotic treatment. For individuals who require antibiotics, I will predict the choice and duration of antibiotic treatment based on the patient's clinical syndrome, their risk of drug-resistance and the severity of their illness. In order to determine whether inclusion of omic data can improve predictive accuracy, I will collect RNA samples from peripheral blood from 300 patients with UTI syndromes. I will investigate whether previously defined host transcriptomic bio-signatures can discriminate between patients with different UTI syndromes which merit different types and duration of antibiotic treatment. Provided my models can adequately discriminate patients who are unlikely to require antibiotic treatment for UTI, I will use them to identify a target population of patients for inclusion in a proof of concept study. This trial will be designed in collaboration with patients, members of the public and healthcare professionals to test the safety and acceptability of an intervention (such as antibiotic discontinuation at 24 hours following hospital admission) to reduce unnecessary antibiotic prescribing. If this study suggests the intervention is feasible, my work will lay the foundation for a future randomised controlled trial of risk-assessed antibiotic prescribing beyond this fellowship. Benefits to patients and the NHS: This work will inform the development of novel diagnostic and risk prediction tools to reduce inappropriate antibiotic prescribing in hospital. It will benefit patients by reducing the number of people who get side effects from unnecessary antibiotics and will benefit society by reducing antibiotic resistance. In addition, we will develop a unique resource of clinical samples linked to high-quality electronic health records as the basis for a future program of research on infection and AMR in hospital.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Deprivation, difference and early development: Healthy societies for healthy families
Abstract: This proposal consists of a programme of research designed to test an integrated explanation of the social determinants of population health and health inequalities. One of the key problems in this area has been to understand the importance of the direct effects of material factors on health, compared to the psychosocial effects of social status differentiation. However recently,research on the effects of income inequality on health is providing strong evidence for the damaging effects of greater social differentiation. The research programme will involve testing the primary of social differentiation versus material factors by studying group density effects - where members of particular groups are healthier when the live in areas with higher concentration of people like themselves (Projects 1a and 1b). Another factor to bear in mind from research on health inequalities is that group who suffer from a wider set of problems linked to their low social status, such as low educational performance, and a range of behavioural and social problems that increase the risk of poor health. The clustering of ill health and other social problems seems to be confirmed by recent work showing that income inequality is not only associated with worse physical health but with a broad range of other problems, such as mental illness, teenage births, low education and obesity. The precursers of many of these problems seem to lie in early childhood. A second set of proposed projects focuses on child development. I will examine family and neighbourhood social contexts in relation to developmental markers determined before adulthood (Project 2); and study international differences in child poverty in relation to development precursers of low social morbidity and later poor health (Project 3). The proposed programme of research will have important implications for policy on child poverty and family support

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Effective ways of communicating NSAID related risks with brief information at the point of prescribing. Conjoint analysis to identify doctors’ and patients’ preferences, and randomised controlled study to determine whether prescribing behaviour is influenced by the use of information at the point of decision making
Abstract: The aim of this project is to find better ways of presenting the risk of serious side effects when prescribing painkillers called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. We want to know what doctors and patients prefer in terms of how risks are presented, and whether they like similar types of information. Participants will be asked to choose between different options, a method that is called conjoint analysis. The preferred type of risk information will then be tested in written prescribing scenarios to find out if it will make a difference to doctors’ prescribing decisions. The prescribing support developed in this study can be used in medical computer systems to help doctors and patients with better decision making.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A Pilot Randomised Controlled Trial of Retraining for Attentional Bias in Cigarette Smokers Attempting Smoking Cessation
Abstract: There are effective treatments to help smokers quit, but no interventions are effective beyond a few months after quitting. The majority of initially successful quitters resume smoking. There is evidence that environmental cues create urges to smoke and prompt smoking resumption. A translational pilot study is proposed here to examine the effectiveness of a computer programme to change the automatic processes in response to smoking-related cues. The trial will randomise 200 smokers to either attentional retraining or a sham procedure completed in a clinic on a laptop computer, while standard smoking cessation medication and NHS behavioural support is provided.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Managing Resources in NHS Dentistry: Using health economics to inform commissioning decisions.
Abstract: The research will develop a unique economics-based framework to guide decision-makers in their management of devolved, finite resources for NHS dental services. The aim of the research is to maximise oral health from the available resources for patient and public benefit. The study will use an action research approach involving local patients, dentists and NHS staff in focus groups and interviews across several Primary Care Trusts and a dental hospital. The research intends to develop dental commissioning through decision-making based upon pragmatic economics-based principles. Evaluation of the framework will involve qualitative methods and consideration of ethical issues including equity (fairness).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A sociological exploration of the use of alcohol by women as a stress coping strategy – towards the development of an appropriate self care intervention for stress management
Abstract: Heavy drinking by women is a significant public health problem. Recent surveys have linked increased drinking with stress. Such cross-sectional data cannot show causation and this link needs further elucidation. Stress can arise due to adverse life-circumstances including multiple societal roles. A lack of recent research on stress and lifestyle behaviour requires an in-depth exploration of this complex issue. This research proposes a systematic review of current research on stress and alcohol use, a gendered critique of stress management interventions and qualitative health diary interviews with women. The data will be used to develop a self care stress management intervention.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Sudden Unexpected Death in Infancy in the West Midlands: an Evaluation of the Joint Agency Approach to Investigating Unexpected Infant Deaths. (The West Midlands SUDI Project).
Abstract: Despite overall reductions in infant death rates, 300-400 infants each year die suddenly and unexpectedly in England and Wales. Many of these deaths remain unexplained and the unexpected nature of the deaths necessitates the involvement of the coroner and a police investigation, adding to the grief suffered by the parents. The West Midlands SUDI (sudden unexpected death in infancy) project aims to assess the impact and outcomes of a new national approach to investigating sudden infant deaths, where police, health and social services work jointly following a set protocol. It will assess if the new approach, which has not previously been evaluated, is more effective than previous approaches at determining causes of death and factors contributing to those deaths. It will study in detail the parents’ experiences of support to determine which aspects of the new approach are most beneficial. It will evaluate the views of professionals following the introduction of the new approach. The project will take place in the West Midlands, recruiting up to 100 families whose babies die suddenly and unexpectedly in the years 2010-12, and following them for the next 2 years. The research will use a variety of methods including analysing case notes, structured interviews and open ended interviews with parents and professionals. Eventually it is hoped that this research will result in improvements in the care and experience of parents whose infants have died suddenly and unexpectedly and contribute to a fall in infant mortality.

Award_Title: Fluoride interventions to prevent dental decay in care home residents: A randomised feasibility study.
Abstract: Background: The oral health profile of our aging population is changing. Improvements in oral health, namely through the widespread availability of fluoride toothpastes, has resulted in a shift from an older population, which was largely edentulous (had no natural teeth) to one which is dentate. This shift in oral health means we now have an older population that can benefit from prevention, restoration and maintenance of the dentition. In care homes, this presents a particular challenge. A greater proportion of older people with natural teeth, but limited self-care abilities and increased vulnerabilities mean care home residents are at significantly higher risk of dental decay. This is further compounded by frequent sugar intake, poor carer attitudes to oral care [16] and reduced salivary flow due to medications.
