Research has shown people in care have significantly higher level of dental decay and fewer teeth than their free-living peers [39,44], and care home residents report that oral health impacts their ability to eat, type of diet, social interaction and quality of life [32]. Dental decay is entirely preventable. There is a strong body of evidence linking the use of fluoride to a reduction in dental decay in children and adults [29, 30, 31]. Usual toothpaste contains 1450ppm (parts per million) fluoride and widespread evidence has shown a dose related response between decay reduction and fluoride concentration. As a result, higher dose fluoride interventions (toothpaste doses 2800ppm or 5000ppm, or professionally applied varnish) are recommended as part of usual care in dental practice [19] and are widely delivered as part of community based public health programmes for children and adults. There is emerging evidence on the clinical effectiveness of professionally applied fluoride varnish [46], and high dose (5000ppm) fluoride toothpaste [9] on older people in care homes. However, there is no study showing the effectiveness of 2800ppm sodium fluoride toothpaste, nor any evidence directly comparing this to a professionally applied fluoride varnish intervention in older people in care homes. Rationale: Fluoride delivery as part of daily brushing and professional applied varnish are simple and effective methods to prevent tooth decay. For older people in care, this would help support maintenance of the dentition for function and prevent pain and so improving quality of life. This would also offer NHS cost savings from dental care. However, decision-making on which intervention would be most suitable is hindered by the limited research comparing fluoride programmes in the care home setting. Aim: The aim of this randomised feasibility study is to establish the acceptability, compliance and fidelity of residents and care staff to fluoride programmes for the prevention of tooth decay. Plan of Investigation: This study will be a randomised feasibility study to be conducted in 6 care homes. The trial will be an individually randomised, assessor blinded, 3-armed trial (1450ppm toothpaste, 1450ppm toothpaste with quarterly fluoride varnish application, and 2800ppm toothpaste) . Delivery of the intervention will be over a period of 12 months. As high dose fluoride toothpaste (Duraphat 2800ppm) is a licensed product in the UK, this trial is a CTIMP. As the product will be used in this study for the purpose it is licensed for, it has been deemed a low risk trial, and all legislative requirements will be met accordingly. This is a mixed methods study. Qualitative and quantitative research methods will be used to assess the outcome measures, as well as economic assessment of costs. The outcome measures will be measurement of study recruitment, consent and attrition, compliance and acceptability to trial processes, fidelity to intervention delivery in care home and assessment of resources and costs utilised.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Models of maternity care for women living socially complex lives: What works, for whom, and in what circumstances?
Abstract: What are the aims of this research?To explore what models of maternity care are effective in improving clinical outcomes for women and infants living with complex social risk factors, and how. Based on the findings, a feasible model of care will be developed for formal evaluation in future research. Why is it important?Many women and children in the UK who live in poverty and face difficult social circumstances struggle to engage with maternity services. These circumstances can include social isolation, young motherhood, homelessness, difficulty speaking or understanding English, domestic violence, women with mental illness and substance abuse problems. The most recent national surveillance reports of infant and maternal mortality (MBRRACE 2015, 2016) found that pregnancies to women living in socially deprived areas are over 50% more likely to end in stillbirth or neonatal death, and were associated with an increased risk of maternal death. This group of women also report worse experiences of maternity care than any other group of women in the UK. The reasons for this are not fully understood but it is likely to be partly due to inequality of access to services and education, discrimination within the system, and how maternity care is perceived by different groups of women. A recent national maternity review has prioritised a reduction in the poor outcomes experienced by socially disadvantaged populations and women with socially complex lives.Standard maternity care in the UK usually involves pregnant women seeing a number of different healthcare professionals. Care is fragmented and women have often never met the midwife looking after them in childbirth. Although there is high quality evidence that relational models of midwifery care improve outcomes and experiences, there is a significant knowledge gap around the mechanisms, including their effectiveness for women with social risk factors. Identifying what models work in improving outcomes, for whom, in what context, and how, will enable the development of safe maternity care for this at risk population. How will the research be carried out?• A realist review of current literature and expert opinion around maternity care for women living socially complex lives. The aim of this review is to conduct an analysis of programme theories and key principles informing specialist models of care and to identify what works, for whom, in what circumstances. A programme theory and logic model will be developed using the findings of the review to guide the realist evaluation.• A realist evaluation of two different models providing maternity care to women with complex social risk factors will be carried out using the findings of the review. Through immersion in the two settings this research will take an ethnographic approach and include following the cohort through their pregnancy journey, conducting in-depth interviews with the women, their families, and the care providers. A full analysis of each setting will be carried out to examine the mutual influence of the context and care delivered in each model, its impact on practitioner-mother interactions, women's experiences, clinical outcomes and cost effectiveness. How will the findings be used to improve services for women and their infants?This research will be concluded by developing a theoretically informed model of care aimed at reducing health inequalities for women with complex social risk factors. Using implementation science methods, this model would be formally evaluated as a future project in order to have impact on patients and the public within 5 years. The findings will be disseminated to service users, providers and commissioners. The cohort studied will be followed up to explore future health outcomes, engagement with early year's services and subsequent pregnancies through post-doctoral life course work.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: The relationship between general practice funding, staffing and healthcare outcomes
Abstract: Background Primary care is often described as the cornerstone of a strong healthcare system. It has been demonstrated across a wide range of international settings that greater investment in primary care is associated with improved population health outcomes. At a practice level, healthcare outcomes for patients are determined by a variety of factors including resource allocation (staffing and funding) and registered patient characteristics. Data which are available on healthcare outcomes in general practice include secondary care usage, patient satisfaction, health-related quality of life, Quality and Outcomes Framework achievement, practice-level mortality, vaccination achievement and Care Quality Commission ratings. Primary care funding data was first made available in 2015 for the 2013/14 financial year. Outcome achievement and allocated funding varies widely across practices in England, raising the consideration that healthcare outcomes might be optimised for a given level of funding. Aims Using general practice funding data for the four years 20013/4 to 2016/7, I will address several research questions related to understanding the association between general practice funding, staffing and healthcare outcomes in England. These are divided into three distinct studies: Study 1 1. To determine the relationship between general practice funding, staffing and healthcare outcomes. Study 2 2. To identify the barriers and facilitators to delivering efficient primary healthcare. Study 3 3. By achieving aims 1 and 2, I will develop a general practice 'Performance Improvement Tool' to measure practice performance based on the difference between expected costs and actual costs of healthcare outcomes. Methods Study 1 will use quantitative methods to address the following research questions: What is the relationship between general practice funding and healthcare outcomes? What is the relationship between workforce mix e.g. the ratio between nurses and general practitioners, and healthcare outcomes? I will construct a dataset containing practice-level data by linking a number of NHS administrative data sets (NHS payments to general practice, General Medical Statistics, Quality and Outcomes Framework, Hospital Episode Statistics and Primary Care Mortality) with small area census and socio-economic data from Neighbourhood Statistics. The sample includes all general practices in England (n=7900). All data are routinely collected and non-patient identifiable. Study 2 will use qualitative methods to identify the barriers and facilitators to delivering efficient primary healthcare. The Normalisation Process Theory may provide a helpful framework in orienting Studies 2 and 3 in the development, implementation and evaluation of a Performance Improvement Tool for general practices. Semi-structured interviews will be conducted with 39 general practice staff members from six practices across two Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs). Additionally, I will also complete 24 semi-structured patient interviews. Study 3 includes developing and piloting a Performance Improvement Tool to improve general practice delivery of healthcare outcomes, informed by Study 1 and 2. An individualised practice report will be prepared for each practice previously visited in Study 2. I will also work closely with the two CCGs to test the feasibility of using this tool at CCG-level. Potential benefits to patients The potential benefit to patients includes utilisation of the Performance Improvement Tool in each practice to deliver high quality patient care for a given level of funding. This tool can be used to maximise clinical achievement, patient satisfaction and health-related quality of life scores. The findings from this proposal may be used to shape national policy by contributing to the development of the proposed new funding allocation formula contained in Sustainability and Transformation Plans and included in general practice contract negotiations, therefore promoting cost-effective models of primary care. Furthermore, with the acquisition of practice-level mortality data, this proposal provides the first primary care analysis of the association between mortality reduction and investment in general practice.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Disparities in detention: An investigation into relationships between sociodemographic status and compulsory psychiatric care among children and adolescents
Abstract: Background The number of people, including children and adolescents, being detained in psychiatric units under the Mental Health Act 1983 (MHA) is growing. This has become a high-profile issue as compulsory care contradicts the ethos of modern medical ethics, can be associated with poor long-term mental health outcomes, and diverts significant funds from community services. It has been identified as a priority for urgent change by the Care Quality Commission (CQC), and there is an imperative to reduce the rate of detentions through early community intervention, targeted at those groups most at risk of detention. While inequalities in use of the MHA are well documented in adults, we know very little about the factors that may increase the risk of detention among children and adolescents. Understanding the disparities in risk and experiences of compulsory admission among children and adolescents is needed in order to identify modifiable causes and highlight where preventative interventions should be targeted.Aim To undertake a linked quantitative and qualitative investigation of disparities in risk and experiences of compulsory psychiatric care among children and adolescents, in order to identify modifiable causes and expose potential targets for preventative intervention.Plan of investigation This study is a two-phase mixed-methods sequential explanatory design.Phase 1: Quantitative The world's largest database of child and adolescent mental health service (CAMHS) records that can be used for research purposes, the Clinical Record Interactive Search system (CRIS) established by Kings College London and South London and the Maudsley NHS Trust (SLaM) has recently been linked to the National Pupil database (NPD). This highly novel UK linked dataset will be exploited to identify young people aged 10-17 detained under the MHA over an 8 year period from the population of four boroughs in South London (over 155,000 young people). The in-depth clinical information within CRIS linked with the census data within the NPD will enable modelling of the associations between individual-level sociodemographic factors (eg. ethnicity and looked-after-child status), clinical factors (eg. diagnosis, previous treatment) and risk of a compulsory admission.Phase 2: Qualitative Building on the findings from phase 1, the views and experiences of key stakeholders will be sought to explore factors underlying the reasons for their detention. Semi-structured interviews will be carried out with 20 adolescents who have been detained and ten of their parents/guardians. Purposive sampling will be used to ensure to offer demographic and phenomenal variation, led by the findings of Phase 1, and interviews will be flexible but cover perceptions of the detention, circumstances leading to it, experience of the MHA assessment and inpatient care. The interviews will be analysed using thematic analysis. The views of healthcare professionals involved in decisions to detain children and adolescents will be sought through two focus groups.Summary of potential benefits to patients and the NHS This research will identify any disparities in the use of the MHA in young people, which could be contributing to life-long inequalities of access to mental health services, and repeated compulsory admissions among certain groups. It will be the UK's first large scale investigation into the compulsory care of minors, and the first time that the combined narratives of young people who have been detained, their parents/guardians and healthcare professionals will have been heard and used to explore experiences of detention and pathways to care. Improving our understanding of young people's risks and experiences of detention will provide an evidence-base to inform service improvement, address staff training and support needs, and guide the implementation of targeted community support to reduce the need for coercive inpatient care. This will offer obvious benefits to the NHS, including significant economic savings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Application anD Development of Statistical Methods to model complex Associations in meta-analysis for intervention and Risk predicTion research (ADDSMART)
Abstract: BackgroundCombining evidence from multiple clinical studies can give a wider and more complete picture of the body of evidence. Studies are usually identified through systematic reviews, where the investigator methodically searches previous research on a pre-specified question. Combining the results from individual studies statistically is termed aggregate meta-analysis. Limitations of this approach could be addressed by retrieving and re-analysing the original datasets.Sharing datasets has become increasingly popular and is often expected by funders or journals. Combining and re-analysing shared datasets at the patient level is called Individual Participant Data (IPD) meta-analysis. IPD meta-analysis is superior to standard meta-analysis in its ability to address confounding. It is possible to link participants' individual characteristics with the outcome and therefore investigate potential effects in patient subgroups that might be missed used standard meta-analysis. Despite the advantages shown and attention, this relatively novel study design has received in previous years, there is still uncertainty around the conduct of such in IPD and there are recognized limitations with the statistical methodology used for IPD in both intervention and prognostic research.Most clinical studies ignore complex associations when investigating effects, as they lack the power to do so. Complex relationships arise in intervention and prognostic research; including interactions, effect modifiers or non-linear terms. For example, risk of preterm delivery is highest among underweight and obese women (at BMI extremes). Ignoring complex associations means that potential effects are only assessed for an average patient, and ignores the possibility that different patients might experience differing intervention effects. Grouping patient populations and investigating subgroup effects has been shown to have serious limitations, such as a reduction in statistical power and an undue dependence on the actual cut-offs chosen to define subgroups. Applied medical research such as IPD meta-analysis should allow for more accurate modelling of complex associations, however methodology is currently lacking.Aims and objectivesTo identify and improve IPD meta-analysis methods, enabling the effective assessment of complex associations in intervention and prognostic research. Identify methods to assess complex associations Evaluate the methods identified using three databases Confirm that identified methods are valid under different assumptions and how they might be improved Identify approach to combine complex methods when using IPD in prognostic research Plan of investigationThrough a systematic review I will identify methods for modelling complex associations in IPD meta-analysis. This will include how to examine and estimate non-linear terms and interactions in an IPD project, and how to examine non-linear associations within treatment-covariate interactions (such as treatment-effect modifiers). Using three datasets as well as simulations, I will assess the performance of published methods and then suggest improvements.Benefits to patients and the NHSIn an environment of limited resources health interventions need to be increasingly targeted to the specific patient populations where they provide the greatest gain and are therefore most cost-effective. Assessing complex associations in applied medical research allows a more precise identification of such populations and provides more accurate estimations of risk in a prediction model.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Award_Title: Testing the feasibility and acceptability of an intervention to improve first time fathers’ transition to fatherhood focusing on the role of mental health and wellbeing.
Abstract: Background: CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Promotion of mental health and wellbeing, and prevention of mental illness is a priority for the UK (DH, 2011a) and European government (European Commission, 2008). Poor mental health impacts on individuals, their families, and is a major burden for society, accounting for 23% of all ill health in the UK (WHO, 2004). While the estimated cost of treating mental health problems is likely to double over the next 20 years, there are also wider societal impacts; loss of productivity, reduced levels of education and increased crime (DH, 2011a). This therefore is a major public health issue. A meta-analysis reported postnatal depression in about 10% of fathers after birth (Paulson and Bazemore, 2010). There is a lack of preventative interventions focusing on fathers' mental health and wellbeing, highlighting the need for research to establish efficacious and cost-effective mental health interventions for men in the postnatal period (Wee et al, 2013). The proposed intervention is the Promotional Guide system, which is the most established and evidence-based parenting intervention used by many health visiting services in England and is underpinned by the Family Partnership Model. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Research Questions: What is already known about men's mental health and wellbeing during their transition to fatherhood? How do first-time fathers perceive their mental health and wellbeing needs during this transition? What is the feasibility and acceptability of the Promotional Guide system on first-time fathers' mental health and wellbeing? Plan of Investigation: CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)This study is designed around the Medical Research Council (2008) framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Theoretical phase (April 2016 - November 2016) The first research question will be addressed in this phase through a systematic qualitative synthesis review of the literature, using meta-ethnography, which will then inform the qualitative interviews in the modelling phase of the study and allow exploration of the unknown aspects relating to men's transition to fatherhood. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Modelling Phase (December 2016 - September 2017) CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)The second research question will be answered in this phase through qualitative interviews with 15-20 first time fathers, 3-6 months after birth of their child, which will be analysed using framework analysis. This will create wider understanding of first-time fathers' mental health and wellbeing needs, by clarifying the findings and exploring the unknown aspects of the first phase. Findings from these qualitative interviews will inform the process evaluation in the third phase of the study.CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Exploratory Evaluation Phase (October 2017 - December 2018) The third research question will be addressed through a feasibility evaluation study, incorporating quantitative and qualitative data collection. This will determine whether the intervention achieved the changes in mental health and wellbeing outcomes anticipated, and enable a process evaluation of every aspect of acceptability, feasibility and fidelity of program delivery. Fathers receiving the intervention from two London sites will be asked to complete a questionnaire containing a range of outcome measures and baseline information during the antenatal Promotional Guide contact and again after the delivery of the postnatal Promotional Guide. Data will be collected over six months and analysed using statistical methods suitable for paired data. In-depth qualitative interviews will also be conducted with 15-20 of these fathers and 15-20 health visitors delivering the intervention. Potential benefits This study will increase the understanding and knowledge of fathers' mental health and wellbeing needs during their transition to fatherhood and test the feasibility and acceptability of the Promotional Guides. It has the potential to inform healthcare practice to: ensure the best start in life for every child, improve understanding of fathers' mental health & wellbeing, improve public health, and drive quality improvement in relation to this parenting intervention (Promotional Guides) and the related process.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Award_Title: Increasing the uptake of cardiac screening and/or predictive genetic testing for inherited cardiac conditions utilising a psychoeducational intervention
Abstract: Background It is estimated that about 340,000 individuals in the UK are affected by inherited cardiac conditions (ICCs) and it is a major cause of sudden death in the young. At-risk family members can avail of cardiac screening and/or predictive genetic testing for ICCs, however, the Department of Health has noted that although there is wider availability of preventative therapies for morbidity and risk of sudden death in ICCs, the uptake of screening is poor and there is a significant cost to the NHS with preventable ICC episodes amounting to £20,000 per event. The negative psychosocial impact of undergoing cardiac screening and/or predictive genetic testing for patients and their families have been reported and little is known about the impact of the clinician/patient interaction on patient decision-making, coping and psychosocial well-being. Therefore, there is a need to improve the evidence-base and develop interventions for the overall care and support that these patients require. Aims and research question The aims of the fellowship include 1) to establish an evidence base for a psychoeducational intervention to support decision-making in patients undergoing cardiac screening and/or genetic testing for ICCs 2) to develop and model this intervention utilising Self Determination Theory as a theoretical framework (SDT) and 3) to undertake a feasibility study for the intervention. Thus, the main research question is: In asymptomatic patients undergoing cardiac screening and/or predictive genetic testing for ICCs, can a psychoeducational intervention to support decision-making be developed, which is feasible for use in current practice and acceptable to patients? Plan of investigation The research will be conducted in 3 phases using the methodology described in the Medical Research Council's (MRC) framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions. In Phase 1, the evidence base for the psychoeducational intervention will be established with a systematic review of the guidelines on the care of patients with ICCs. Developing and modeling of the intervention will be undertaken in Phase 2 using the evidence from Phase 1 and the analysis of the transcripts from patient focus groups/interviews underpinned by SDT. The Delphi method will be utilised to arrive at a consensus within the patient and expert advisory group to refine the intervention model. In Phase 3, a Randomised Control Trial (RCT) design will be used to test the feasibility of delivering the intervention and acceptability to patients. The expected outcomes of the fellowship include developing the evidence base and model for the psychoeducational intervention underpinned by SDT and the results of the feasibility study will inform a definitive clinical trial for the intervention. Potential benefits to patients and the NHS The findings of this fellowship will benefit patients and service delivery in the NHS by building the evidence base from which clinicians provide psychosocial care and support required by patients with ICCs and their families. A feasible and acceptable psychosocial intervention has great potential in improving the therapeutic relationship between clinicians and patients, facilitate informed decision-making and promote psychosocial well-being. This will in turn, decrease costs to the health service by improving the communication and uptake of the preventative measures for ICCs.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Funding_Stream: HEE/NIHR ICA Programme Clinical Doctoral Research Fellowship
Contractor: Birmingham and Solihull Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Improving health and facilitating desistance in offenders with personality disorder: An intervention development study to maximise participation in prosocial occupation
Abstract: Background Participation, as defined by the World Health Organisation, is a fundamental component of health (7). Participation refers to performing meaningful activities, i.e. occupations. Prosocial occupations are those activities valued by society, such as work, leisure and self-care. Antisocial occupations are those activities considered deviant, such as crime or substance misuse. Barriers to participation in prosocial occupation contribute to poor health, marginalisation and increased risk of participation in antisocial occupations (15, 17).Approximately two thirds of prisoners have personality disorder(s). Personality disordered offenders (PDOs) experience barriers to participation in prosocial occupation in custody and on release. Participation in prosocial occupation has two important outcomes for PDOs. Firstly, it improves physical and mental health (7), which enhances quality of life among this hard-to-reach group. Compared to offenders without personality disorder, PDOs have higher rates of psychotic, mood, anxiety, substance use and somatoform disorders; more frequent and severe self-harm or suicide attempts; and lower quality of life (8, 18). Secondly, participation in prosocial occupation is associated with desistance, meaning ceasing to offend (12-14). PDOs reoffend at higher rates and are overrepresented in commission of serious crimes (8, 9, 19). Financial implications of poor outcomes amongst PDOs are borne by the public through taxation to fund the NHS, criminal justice and social services. Financial costs can be calculated, but the impact on victim and public health is immeasurable (15, 16). Existing approaches have failed (20, 21), resulting in services for PDOs becoming a priority issue in which NHS England and the National Offender Management Service have invested £24 billion (19, 22). Existing approaches take a psychological perspective of PDOs needs. There remains an absence of literature pertaining to participation in occupation as contributor to health and desistance outcomes, or to interventions designed to achieve participation in prosocial occupation.This study will apply an occupational perspective, i.e. specifically focussing on participation in occupation, to the needs and experiences of PDOs, in order to identify factors that influence participation in occupation, explore how and why they impact on participation, and design interventions to improve participation in prosocial occupation. AimEnable service providers to deliver interventions that facilitate participation in prosocial occupation and contribute to improved health and desistance outcomes for PDOs.Research questionsAmong PDOs: What factors contribute to participation in prosocial occupation? How can service providers intervene to maximise participation in prosocial occupation? Objectives Focusing on PDOs, the study will: Systematically review evidence relating to Factors influencing participation in occupation Effective interventions that target these factors Understand how participation in occupation (prosocial and antisocial) occurs Identify factors that influence participation in prosocial occupation Identify interventions with potential to modify factors that influence participation in prosocial occupation, and improve health and desistance Define feasible interventions that facilitate participation in prosocial occupation Devise an intervention manual for facilitating participation in prosocial occupation Objectives will be met by completing four work packages (WPs), consistent with MRC guidelines for developing and evaluating complex interventions (23). WP1. Two systematic reviews (objective 1). WP2. Qualitative study. Narrative inquiry interviewing PDOs (objectives 2-3) WP3. Delphi study involving expert service providers and academics (objectives 4-5) WP4. Intervention manual development (objective 6) Benefits Absence of research from an occupational perspective, the high priority afforded across services, and the failure of existing approaches indicates this study from a new perspective into the needs of PDOs is timely and beneficial. An evidence-based intervention manual enables service providers to deliver interventions that increase participation in prosocial occupation among PDOs. This will potentially improve health and desistance outcomes and therefore benefit PDOs, victims, and wider society in health and economic terms.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: Understanding barriers to referral for specialist weight management services and bariatric surgery and identifying ways to improve access
Abstract: Background to the research Obesity is a major global health concern and is associated with multiple health problems, including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, certain cancers, and depression, which cost the healthcare system billions of pounds. Public health programmes are very important to prevent people from becoming obese but for those who are already obese, effective clinical treatments are needed to achieve weight loss and improve health, particularly for those with severe and complex obesity* who are at the highest risk of health problems. Weight loss surgery (bariatric surgery), combined with improvements to diet and exercise, is the most effective treatment for people with severe and complex obesity. It leads to better weight loss and improvement in some health problems (such as type 2 diabetes) than diet and exercise or medications alone. However, NHS-funded bariatric surgery treats less than 1% of those who could benefit from it, and the UK has lower rates of bariatric surgery than other countries with similar obesity rates. The reasons for the low rates of bariatric surgery in the UK are not well understood. Important factors to understand are the pathway of weight management services that patients must go through to access specialist care and bariatric surgery, and the policies which influence access to these services. Aims of the research This research aims to understand the obstacles to being referred for specialist weight management support and bariatric surgery in people with severe and complex obesity, and how access to these services could be improved. This research is essential to ensure that patients with severe and complex obesity can access treatment and support which can greatly improve their health and/or reduce their health risks. Improved access to bariatric surgery and associated specialist support will help to reduce the health burden and healthcare costs associated with severe and complex obesity. Design and methods used There are four stages to the research process which include: Reviewing and summarising current NHS policies for referral to specialist weight management services and bariatric surgery across all regions of England. Identifying how patients with severe and complex obesity move from weight management services attached to their GP surgery through to specialist weight management services in secondary care. Interviewing patients, policy makers, and health professionals to understand their views and experiences of accessing specialist weight management services and bariatric surgery. Conducting meetings with patients, policy makers and health professionals to develop recommendations about how access to specialist weight management services and bariatric surgery can be improved for people with severe and complex obesity. Patient and public involvement Patients with severe and complex obesity who have undergone bariatric surgery have contributed to the design of this research study, and will be involved in advising on the overall conduct of the research. A panel of 4-6 patient representatives will advise on the design of all patient-related material and key ethical issues. Dissemination The main outcome of this research will be the development of recommendations for health professionals and policy makers about how services and patient pathways could be improved to ensure appropriate patients are able to access specialist weight management services and bariatric surgery. Policy makers, health professionals and patients will be actively engaged throughout the research and dissemination process, and there will be a strong social media presence to encourage exchange of ideas between the public and the research team. *Severe and complex obesity is defined as a body mass index of 40 kg/m2 or 35-40 kg/m2 with another significant health problem that could be improved by weight loss.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Addressing socioeconomic inequalities in healthcare within local areas in England: mixed methods study
Abstract: Research question How can local areas address socioeconomic inequalities in avoidable emergency admissions? Background There are unfair differences (inequalities25-27) in healthcare in England; poorer access and worse patient outcomes are strongly associated with socioeconomic disadvantage28-30. Excess hospitalisations associated with socioeconomic inequality in England cost the NHS £4.8 billion per year31, much of which is due to avoidable emergency admissions (AEA). In 2015, 263,894 excess AEAs were associated with socioeconomic inequality in England32. Reducing AEAs33-35 through improving coordination of care for people with long-term conditions is a key priority for the NHS36,37. Since the burden of disease sits disproportionately with the most disadvantaged communities, controlling hospital pressures requires addressing inequality issues29,33. The NHS has a legal duty24 to consider reducing these inequalities31 and urgently requires a clearer understanding of how to do this28,29,38.Aims To identify local areas demonstrating consistently reducing or increasing socioeconomic inequalities in AEA To understand why this is the case, identifying factors explaining these variations To help local area decision makers reduce inequalitiesResearch plan An 'explanatory sequential' mixed methods study39 will be undertaken, which aims to explain quantitative findings through subsequent qualitative investigation.In consultation with patients, the public and health professionals, a logic model40-43 will be developed and iteratively refined throughout the research to explain how factors inside and outside of the health and care system may increase, reduce or maintain socioeconomic inequalities in AEA. An equity-focused systematic review44,45 of the determinants of change in socioeconomic inequalities in AEA will be undertaken. Regression analysis of linked routine data will identify local areas demonstrating consistently increasing or reducing socioeconomic inequalities in AEA and explore potential determinants of these trends38. A comparative, in-depth, multi-case study46 of four of these local areas (two increasing, two reducing) will then be undertaken, informed by the review findings and logic model. Evidence will be triangulated from documentary review and up to 60 key informant interviews47 drawing where appropriate upon realist evaluation methods48,49. Expected outcomes Analytic generalisations across all four case studies will deliver working hypotheses about why areas see increasing or reducing socioeconomic inequality in AEA. As well as generating testable hypotheses, this research will also provide methodological learning and a rigorous example of using case-studies to investigate inequality in complex systems50-52. Policy learning about what does and does not work to reduce inequalities will be summarised in a briefing co-designed with patients, members of the public, and health professionals. NHS England and Public Health England plan to share this learning with all local areas across England as part of support they provide to help address inequalities. Impact and benefit The research will help local areas fulfil their legal commitment24 to ensuring services work better together to particularly help those living in disadvantaged communities. This will not only be fairer for patients and the tax-paying public, but by reducing AEA will also reduce pressure on overburdened hospital care, a key priority for the NHS36,37.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Impact of Clostridium difficile on clinical outcomes in hospitalised infants with diarrhoea (CD-COT)
Abstract: Clostridium difficile is a bacterium that causes diarrhoea, particularly in elderly hospitalised patients on antibiotics. It is a very unpleasant condition that can be very debilitating and require nursing and medical support, which is costly to the NHS as well as difficult for the patient. Sometimes the disease is fairly mild and resolves but sometimes it can be more serious, and even fatal. Normally, the millions of bacteria in our guts prevent disease-causing bacteria like C. difficile, from causing a problem. However, antibiotics that we may take for an infection elsewhere (eg chest infection) can damage these defences, allowing C. difficile to move in, grow and produce toxins (poisons) that affect the gut lining, resulting in diarrhoea. Hospitals diagnose C. difficile infection (CDI) by detecting the toxin in faeces (poo). It is important to detect the toxin, rather than the bacteria because it can be present without producing toxin or causing symptoms. We know a lot about how and why C. difficile causes disease in adults, but relatively little about what role it plays in children, particularly infants (children under 1 year old). Although many infants may carry the bacteria in their guts, there is no clear understanding of what the presence of C. difficile toxin in infant diarrhoeal faeces means. Because of this lack of clarity, current UK guidelines discourage testing in infants and this means that doctors and nurses do not have any rules to guide them on when they should test for C. difficile toxin in these patients. In order to find out what doctors are doing at the moment with regard to these patients in the absence of guidance, I will send a survey out to all doctors involved in diagnosing the causes of diarrhoea in children . The survey will ask doctors when and how they test infants for C. difficile toxin; what they think the test results mean and how they use those results to care for the infant. This will tell us what is currently being done to diagnose and manage these patients. We will then do a study to determine what the presence of C. difficile toxin in infant diarrhoeal faeces means: does it contribute to the diarrhoea symptoms or play no role at all? We will look for C. difficile toxin in all infant diarrhoeal faeces sent to the routine diagnostic laboratory. We will compare how quickly diarrhoea gets better in infants WITH toxin compared to those WITHOUT toxin in their faeces. This will help us to build a much clearer picture of the importance of C. difficile toxin in infants with diarrhoea. We will also look at other measures of wellness (results of blood tests will also be used to see whether infants with toxin progress less well. We will examine patient notes to see if there are factors (eg an underlying condition such as cancer, being on other treatments, breast or bottle feeding) that may be linked to infants having toxin in their diarrhoeal faeces and those who do not get better as quickly. This will help us to know which infants should be tested for C. difficile toxin. Lastly, we will examine the C. difficile bacteria we recover with DNA fingerprinting and antibiotic susceptibility testing. This will tell us what types of C. difficile are present in infants, and their resistance to certain important antibiotics. I will communicate the results of the study to health professionals at conferences and through publishing in journals, and through the Paediatric C. difficile Network of health professionals, patients/carers and the public that I will establish during the course of the lectureship.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: How can NICE intrapartum guidelines recommendations on place of birth for women with uncomplicated pregnancies be implemented in practice?
Abstract: Background: There is a growing interest in developing theoretically informed strategies for implementing research evidence into practice. Poor theoretical underpinning makes it difficult to understand and explain how, when, for whom and why implementation succeeds or fails. The use of theoretical approaches offers the potential of increasing the predictability of successful implementation. Within maternity service, the community is facing the challenge of implementing NICE intrapartum guidelines for women with uncomplicated pregnancies. Despite the NICE recommendations to commissioners and providers to ensure that all four birth settings (home, alongside and freestanding midwifery unit and obstetric unit) are available to healthy women at low risk of complications, to date the majority of births in England are assisted in hospital. Many NHS services still offer obstetric unit (OU) as the mainstream option and midwifery-led birth settings as an alternative. Aims: This Fellowship aims to develop a theoretically informed knowledge implementation pathway to guide and support commissioners and service providers in implementing evidence into the NHS services, using maternity services as a case study. The primary aim of the research project will be to explore whether the development and implementation of Midwifery-led Birth Settings Pathway (The Pathway) can have an impact on the number of births outside OUs. The secondary, but equally important aim, will be to enhance understanding of how to effectively implement evidence-based service organisation and delivery type changes in complex NHS settings, in order to apply the lessons learnt to other settings and areas of healthcare. Research question: How can NICE intrapartum guidelines recommendations on place of birth for women with uncomplicated pregnancies be implemented in practice? Plan of investigation: I will conduct a Participatory Action Research (PAR) project, in four sites that form part of the same NHS Trust, each with a different history and operational management. PAR consists of a family of research methodologies, which aim to implement change with the active engagement of the co-participants. Change is implemented and evaluated at the same time in a cyclical way following a PAR-cycle (Plan, Act, Observe, Reflect). The Promoting Action on Research Implementation In Health Services (PARIHS) approach offers a theoretically informed framework to guide implementation design and evaluation. A modified version of the PARIHS will be nested and tested within a PAR project to implement and evaluate the impact of The Pathway aimed at translating NICE recommendations on place of birth for women with uncomplicated pregnancies into an actionable local plan for increasing the number of births outside OUs.Methods: Data collection will include qualitative and quantitative methods. Qualitative methods: focus groups; interviews; non-participant observation; analysis of local documents and guidelines. Qualitative data will be analysed using thematic analysis. Quantitative methods: time-series analysis of rates of births at home and in midwifery units as well as key clinical outcomes in these settings, local audits and service users surveys as part of routine service evaluation. Potential Benefits: Successful development of a theoretically informed framework could offer not only direct benefits to service users and the NHS but also lessons to be applied more widely within the field of implementation science. Service users would benefit by having access to evidence-based care, which is safe and engenders positive experiences. The NHS will benefit by providing cost-effective care, which values its staff and offers job satisfaction, as highlighted by the literature. There could be several cost savings associated with increasing birth outside OUs: direct cost savings related to the reduction of costly birth interventions, birth complications, need for medical care and length of hospital admission; longer term cost savings due to the reduction in maternal morbidity.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Towards better quality end of life care for patients and families: using ‘circles of learning’ within NHS acute hospitals and voluntary-sector hospices to mobilise knowledge about patient-level outcome measures in palliative and end of life care.
Abstract: Background:End-of-life care is reported as 'poor' for 10% of deaths across England, with poor symptom management, communication and recognition of dying in NHS hospitals. One main reason that poor end-of-life care persists has been the difficulty demonstrating systematically the quality of end-of-life care. Until recently, valid, reliable and responsive outcomes measures for this population have not been available, have not been implemented into practice, and have not been utilised to assess whether care is (or is not) meeting the needs of patients and families. Now however, there is robust evidence to change this. Valid and reliable measures - which capture what matters most to patients and families - are available. Clinicians are using these, but find it difficult to act on this information in a systematic way to improve care. Managers have service-level outcomes data, but do not know how to use this to demonstrate effective service delivery, inform quality improvement or shape service innovations. The obstacles to the use of this knowledge need to be addressed. Limited awareness of evidence is one of the problems, while developing shared understanding of the barriers and addressing these challenges collaboratively are potential solutions. Aim: To mobilise existing knowledge about patient-level outcome measures in palliative and end-of-life care, using collaborative 'circles of learning' within NHS hospitals and voluntary-sector hospices, to embed and sustain improvements in end-of-life care. Specifically, to explore: How clinicians and managers can use outcomes data to improve the care of individuals, demonstrate effective service delivery and inform quality improvement. Whether 'circles of learning' can contribute to knowledge mobilisation and support national roll-out of outcome measures in palliative and end-of-life care. Methods: Setting: Four London providers selected purposively for diversity in size, funding sources and population served. These consist of specialist palliative and end-of-life care teams within two acute NHS Trusts, and two hospice-based palliative care services. Work will be conducted in three phases: Phase 1: Knowledge mobilisation with two sites 'Circles of learning' (Horn, 2011) will be set up at one NHS acute hospital and one voluntary-sector hospice with two different groups of stakeholders (Group A: clinicians using outcome measures and Group B: clinical leads/managers/quality leads using service-level outcomes data). These 'circles of learning' will together identify best ways to utilise outcomes data to improve individual patient care, and how outcomes data can best demonstrate effective service delivery and inform quality improvement. Phase 2: Two additional sites Similar 'circles of learning' will be set up at a second NHS acute hospital and second voluntary-sector hospice, and the processes repeated. In this way, learning from Phase 1 will be brought into Phase 2. Transferability of findings beyond participating sites will be explored. The circles may combine to operate across organisations (i.e. both NHS hospitals working together and both hospices working together). Phase 3: Research Focus groups with each Level A and B 'circles of learning' (six-eight focus groups in total), will be undertaken to explore whether the 'circles of learning' approach is of value, and if could be used to support national roll out of palliative and end-of-life care outcome measures. This will be supplemented by participant observation, plus field notes, to triangulate findings. Field notes will include information on how the outcomes data is used by clinicians at each site and how the outcomes data is used to inform service delivery and quality improvement. Data from the focus groups will be recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed thematically using NVivo 10. Participant observations and field notes will be analysed alongside the focus group findings to create 'case studies' specific to each context (NHS acute hospital and voluntary-sector hospices).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine
Award_Title: Optimising knowledge mobilisation surrounding antibiotic utilisation in the community setting.
Abstract: Background: In highly professionalised organisations, knowledge mobilisation (KM) impacts only once knowledge of what is 'acceptable' practice is developed and negotiated collectively within and across professional groups, teams, or organisations. Structural and cultural environments mediate this process. Whilst the societal threat of antimicrobial resistance is recognised, to date, KM activities targeted at GP teams, community pharmacists and patients have not been evaluated from a systems perspective. Empirical research reports that up to 30% of antibiotic prescribing by GPs may be inappropriate, and roles of other healthcare professionals, public and patients in the community setting remain unexploited. Aim: To develop and pilot a user modifiable process mapping tool to refine existing, and develop new initiatives for knowledge mobilisation amongst actors that influence antibiotic use in the community setting. Research question: how to optimise knowledge mobilisation between and across the core triad (GP teams, community pharmacy, patient) involved in antibiotic utilisation in the community setting? Plan of investigation: A three phased project to develop and apply a novel software based method of systems mapping to KM processes: Phase 1: Two mixed method case studies to explore within context, KM activities that surround the triad described. Purposive sampling for level of integration of KM activities across sectors is proposed: Case study A (Manchester): vertically integrated KM activity across secondary and community care via a dual formal antibiotic specialist pharmacist - role across an acute NHS trust and Clinical Commissioning Group. Case study B (London): horizontally integrated knowledge mobilisation activity within community care. Quantitative data of demographics, process and outcome quality indicators will establish areas of sub-optimal prescribing of antibiotics to provide context for the interventions assessed. Qualitative interviews with healthcare professionals will be used to assess extent of uptake, knowledge retention and application of national level capacity building interventions for GPs [Royal College of GPs toolkit] and Pharmacists [Centre for Postgraduate Pharmacy Education programme ]. The role of local KM initiatives, technologies including electronic decision aids and near-patient testing will be examined. Phase 2: Two patient workshops (case study B) consisting of group interviews and discreet choice methods to evaluate perceived need, demand and experience of community care based antibiotic use. A dynamic systems map of sources of advice and patient health-seeking behaviour between GPs, practice nurses and community pharmacists will be developed. 'Extreme case' sampling of patients with a special interest in antimicrobial resistance/patient safety (via the Patients' Association) will capture variance in behaviour when health literacy of patients matches or exceeds that of healthcare professionals. Phase 3: The modifiable process map (using ithink software) which can test 'what-if' scenarios, based on the findings of phase 1& 2, will be piloted to refine existing KM activities and develop new initiatives with participants from the continuum of: public, patients, healthcare professional students/practitioners , educators, in the community and secondary care settings. Theoretical approaches to analysis: A deductive-inductive process using: a. the Resource Based View, that competencies confer competitive advantage to examine if/how NHS policy structures, performance measures, and definitions of success support this approach. Essential to determine differential drivers for individual and organisational learning in GP teams compared to community pharmacists. b. a sensemaking perspective ( micro-level ) to optimise KM activities particularly for public/patients. Whilst pharmacists may be physically present and more accessible than GPs (particularly in areas of high deprivation) understanding public trust and confidence in different healthcare professionals and teams is needed. Benefits to patients/NHS: This project will provide timely actionable insights and tools as NICE guidance recommends that community sector staff promote and monitor use of antimicrobials ahead of further guidelines aimed at the public.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Valuing the benefits and harms of antenatal and newborn screening programmes in health economic assessments
Abstract: Background: Cost-effectiveness assessments of many forms of screening considered by the United Kingdom National Screening Committee (UK NSC) are conducted within a cost-utility framework and expressed in terms of incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year gained. However, a number of methodological factors, compounded by ethical challenges, have constrained capacity to evaluate antenatal and newborn screening programmes using standard cost-utility metrics. The consequence is that recommendations about antenatal and newborn screening are made on the basis of differing approaches to benefit construction and valuation and without a common cost-effectiveness threshold that reflects opportunity cost in the health system. Invariably, this results in suboptimal levels of population health and wellbeing. Aims and objectives: The overall aim of the proposed programme of work is to enhance knowledge about methods for valuing the benefits and harms of antenatal and newborn screening within economic assessments and make recommendations about health economic measurement tools that should be applied in this area in the future. Methods: The programme of work will encompass four work-streams, including: 1) A systematic review of published and grey literature on methods for evaluating benefits and harms of antenatal and newborn screening programmes adopted by economic assessments; 2) A qualitative study to capture the perspectives of stakeholders (including parents/carers, health professionals and other relevant stakeholders) about the value, benefits and harms of antenatal and newborn screening that should be incorporated into future economic assessments; 3) An evidence synthesis (encompassing a results-based convergent synthesis and a narrative synthesis) of the relative merits of alternative economic methods that have been used to assess antenatal or newborn screening strategies; and 4) A stakeholder workshop leading to a set of final recommendations for outcomes measurement and valuation within future economic assessments. Patient and public involvement (PPI) will draw upon different groups of women and their partners who could potentially have diverse views and experiences of antenatal and newborn screening, and will be integrated into each of the four work-streams. Dissemination, outputs and anticipated impact: The results of the proposed research will be submitted to academic journals, and presented to UK NSC committees and at INVOLVE conferences. Bespoke strategies will be developed for dissemination to the third sector and for broader public dissemination. The findings will be used to inform methodological recommendations for future economic assessments of antenatal and newborn screening.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: PHR Public Health Review Team: The University of Sheffield
Abstract: Background The National Institute for Health Research has asked research teams to put together bids to become a public health review team. Public health evidence reviews can examine research on a wide range of topics which have an impact on the health and wellbeing of the population, either as a whole or for specific communities or groups. The job of the team will be to carry out reviews which will look for, bring together, and evaluate research that has already been carried out. Researchers at The University of Sheffield are very experienced in this sort of research and can provide expertise across a wide range of topics. Aims The aim is that findings from reviews carried out by the team, will help in the planning of future public health programmes and research. We aim that our work will be useful for everybody who has involvement in public health. Design and methods We plan to look at a wide selection of research on public health that is already available. It is important that the way we carry out the work is good value for money, and that we complete each project quickly and efficiently. To achieve this we will carry out an initial brief overview to find out what research is available. Then we will ask relevant people what might be of most interest and use, which we can then look at in more depth. In order to ensure that reviews are carried out efficiently we will use computer software to manage all the stages of the review. Additionally we plan to have several different members of the team available to work on the projects as and when needed. We will involve other people during all stages of each research project in order to ensure that we are asking the right questions, looking at a wide selection of research that is available, putting the results together in a meaningful way, and drawing conclusions that are helpful. Public involvement Members of the public will be closely involved with the work of the team. We will use our existing public panels, together with networks of voluntary and community groups who will offer expertise for particular topics. The public will be involved in roles including helping the research teams to shape the research questions, adding knowledge to help understanding of what the findings mean, give advice on sharing the findings, and contribute to production of materials to ensure understanding of the findings among the wider community. Sharing the research findings We will put in place a plan for each project, which details who the key people are that need to know about the findings of our research, and what ways we will use to inform them. It will be important to use lots of different ways of sharing the findings of our work, so that the information is in a form which is clearly understood and usable. We intend to use methods including producing written summaries of what we have found, short videos and presentations, toolkits, and will use social media to publicise findings. We have a wealth of experience in translating wide ranging reviews into useful products. For example we recently produced a widely shared poster which summarises the findings of our comparison of public health policy across the four countries of the UK. We also recently produced a checklist of factors influencing the implementation of integrated care programmes which is now being used by people engaged in service change in the NHS who have reported it has been helpful in developing local programmes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Can embedding the MapMe intervention, a tool to improve parental acknowledgement and understanding of childhood overweight and obesity, in the National Child Measurement Programme lead to improved child weight outcomes at one year?
Abstract: Research Question: Can embedding the MapMe intervention in the National Child Measurement Programme (NCMP) lead to improved child weight outcomes? Background: Childhood overweight and obesity (OW/OB) is a Public Health England (PHE) priority. Parents are key to managing children’s weight, but tend to struggle to recognise OW/OB, and so do not take action. In England, the NCMP measures the weight status of 4-5 and 10-11 year-olds and reports results to parents via letter. Parents are often surprised by, and mistrust the result. More support is required to help parents understand and act upon the letter. The ‘Map Me’ intervention includes Body Image Scales (BIS) (images of underweight to very OW children of NCMP age, to help parents recognise child weight status), and information on healthy eating, physical activity, consequences of child OW and further support. MapMe was tested in ~300 OW/OB children who showed improved Body Mass Index (BMI) Z scores after 1 year. These findings now need to be confirmed in a larger study and, if confirmed, we need to establish how the intervention works, and if it cost effective. Objectives: 1. Update MapMe 2. Assess the impact of enhanced NCMP letters including MapMe (delivered using 2 different approaches) on child BMI Z score at 1 year 3. Examine mechanisms of impact of MapMe 4. Examine the cost/benefit of MapMe 5. Assess the impact of MapMe enhanced NCMP letter on health inequalities and psychological outcomes 6. Explore the implementation and acceptability of the MapMe enhanced NCMP letters and potential for national adoption Methods: Parents and key stakeholders will be consulted on how MapMe can be improved. The improved MapMe will then be examined by a Randomised Controlled Trial across 9 Local Authorities (LAs). Schools within each LA, will be randomised to 1 of 3 groups: 1) MapMe BIS and link to web-based MapMe added to the NCMP post-measurement letter; 2) as group 1, plus an additional ‘booster’ letter with the link to web-based MapMe sent 6 months later; 3) standard NCMP letters (control). Child BMI Z score changes will be assessed at 1 year. A sub-group will be recruited for a process evaluation examining: parents’ perceptions of child weight status; changes in child food intake, activity, and parental help seeking. Child quality of life, use of NHS/LA services will inform an economic evaluation. Data on self-esteem, eating disorder risk, deprivation and ethnicity will be used to evaluate psychological impact and health inequalities. Views from NCMP teams and parents will explore experiences and implementation of MapMe. Timelines for delivery: Total study duration is 36 months. MapMe update (months 1-6); Health-related and cost impacts of MapMe, and process and acceptability evaluations (months 7-29); Analysis and dissemination (months 30-36). Anticipated impact: If found to be effective MapMe will be incorporated into routine NCMP delivery and hosted by NHS Choices: providing a minimal cost, national scale intervention capable of improving the weight status of children with OW/OB. Dissemination: A Public Health England co-hosted workshop for NCMP commissioning and delivery teams; feedback to participating families, school nursing, NCMP teams, health practitioners, local and national policy makers (informed by the public involvement panel); dissemination at conferences and in open-access academic journals.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Shared Training and Assessment of Well-Being for looked-after children (STrAWB): Feasibility study
Abstract: Background Up to 45% of looked-after children have a diagnosable mental health difficulty. Poor mental health predicts lower educational attainment and problems in adulthood; but early identification can prevent problems from escalating, reducing the risk of later difficulties. The STrAWB package for primary-aged looked-after children, their foster/kinship carers (FCs) and designated teachers (DTs), consists of: a) A training course for FCs and DTs to increase understanding of potential mental health problems, well-being, resilience and guidance on assessments b) Measures completed by the FC, DT, and child, to provide an assessment of well-being across the home and school contexts c) A mental health expert’s review of all measures, to create individual profiles of strengths and needs for feedback to FCs, DTs, and children’s social workers Aims and objectives The overall aim of the study is to determine the feasibility of an RCT of STrAWB. Our study objectives are to: 1. Test the procedure of randomisation, and its acceptability to all participants 2. Determine the consent rate and time to consent from those approached to take part 3. Test the acceptability of the intervention to participants 4. Select the most appropriate primary outcome measure for a main trial 5. Provide data to inform a sample size calculation for a main trial Methods Thirty-five looked-after children (aged 8-11), and their FCs and DTs, will receive the STrAWB intervention, and 35 will receive care as usual. We will use mixed methods (post-training and service use surveys, interviews with participants and stakeholders, documentary evidence, activity monitoring sheets, and case studies) to assess acceptability of randomisation and the intervention, recruitment and retention rates, intervention fidelity, and data completion rates. We will also test two multi-informant measures of mental health (the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire and the Paediatric Quality of Life Scale), to assess which is more comprehensible, developmentally appropriate, and useful for measuring impact in this population. Timelines for delivery Project: April 2020 to June 2022 Intervention: June 2020 to December 2020 Primary outcomes data: Time 1 (before randomisation) and Time 2 (12 months later) Feasibility data: Time 1 through to Time 2 Impact and dissemination The main role of this project is to establish whether the main trial can be done, and investigate parameters which may inform the design of that trial. Any benefits for the public can only follow after that trial has delivered its results. The 35 young people in the study will benefit directly from a process that: a) identifies earlier, and in their daily contexts, the difficulties they are experiencing and support needed to address them; and b) documents their experiences and perspectives in order to influence future support. Pupils who share a learning environment with these children will also benefit, as they are likely to see a reduction in classroom disruption. Foster carers and teachers will benefit by improved knowledge of mental health and well-being which will enable them to better support the looked-after children in their care now and in the future. Outputs will include written pieces for an academic journal, Children & Young People Now and the general media, NIHR CLAHRC East of England, and the Rees Centre website and newsletter; a webinar; and presentations at national academic and practice conferences. We will make use of existing routes of dissemination, including meetings with key groups of stakeholders, relevant organisations (e.g. NSPCC, Coram Voice) and the DfE’s Children in Care team, and ‘trade’ newsletters.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: An interactive digital behaviour change intervention (Wrapped) to decrease incidence of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) amongst users of STI self-sampling websites: A randomised controlled feasibility trial
Abstract: Research question Is it feasible to run a RCT to test the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of Wrapped (a fully automated, multi-component and interactive digital behaviour change intervention that aims to reduce the incidence of STIs through increasing correct and consistent condom use amongst users of STI self-sampling websites aged 16-24 years old)? Background Reducing the rates of Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) amongst young people is a public health priority. The best way for sexually active people to avoid STIs is to use a condom but young people report inconsistent use. A missed opportunity to intervene to increase condom use is when they access self-sampling kits for STIs via the internet; young people are increasingly being tested via this route every year in England. Aim: to assess whether and how it is possible to carry out a future full RCT to evaluate the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of Wrapped in comparison to usual care. Primary Objectives: To estimate for the main RCT: i. the rate of recruitment of eligible participants ii. the rate of participant follow-up for the main RCT primary outcome measure (cumulative incidence of chlamydia measured using biological samples) at 12 months Methods Research design: a two-arm parallel group randomised feasibility RCT of Wrapped compared to usual care (basic information on STIs and condom use), with preceding and nested qualitative studies. The preceding qualitative study will be used to develop and refine a participant recruitment and retention strategy for the feasibility RCT. A draft version of the strategy will be developed with our Participant and Patient Involvement (PPI) group and then revised/finalised following feedback obtained through a series of three focus groups with young people (16-24 years old). For the feasibility RCT, we will recruit a minimum of 230 participants (aged 16-24 years) over 3 months from an existing chlamydia self-sampling website. Participants will be randomised into one of two parallel groups (1:1 allocation). Repeated measures will be surveys at baseline (M0) and then M3, M6 and M12, and chlamydia screening at T0, T3 and T12. We will collect health economic data to compare the resource costs and cost effectiveness of delivering Wrapped compared to usual care. Nested qualitative interviews with trial participants will be used to gain insight into factors affecting recruitment and attrition. Timelines for delivery 0-6 months – development of recruitment/retention strategy and focus groups 7-9 months – recruitment to feasibility RCT 7-21 months – data collection: surveys and chlamydia screening 9-22 months – nested qualitative interviews 22-28 months – data analysis, report writing, dissemination Anticipated impact and dissemination We have a robust plan for project dissemination which we expect to lead to some short-term limited impact in terms of an increase in public engagement with research and related societal issues, and an increase in the knowledge economy. This includes multi-media communication with stakeholders, academics and the public. To ensure the potential for more long-term and meaningful impact (a reduction in STIs amongst the at-risk group and associated improvements in health/wellbeing), this project seeks to establish what evidence is required to make an economic case for investment in the intervention and make recommendations for routes to implementation and sustainability.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Community health walks: Pragmatic feasibility evaluation of an asset-based approach to address health inequalities
Abstract: Research question Is an asset-based approach to health walks an effective and cost-effective way to reach disadvantaged groups to improve their health and wellbeing and reduce health-related inequity? Background Health walks have multiple health benefits and increase physical activity. However, there is good research evidence that participation in the walks and their health benefits may not be equitably distributed between different social groups, giving a potential for health inequity. Since 2018 the health walk provider in Norfolk England have taken an asset-based approach to the walks, focusing on the strengths of pre-existing community groups and taking health walks to them. Their premise is that this targeted approach will be more effective at reaching marginalised groups and this will help reduce health inequalities. Asset-based approaches are gaining traction but their efficacy and cost effectiveness have rarely been evaluated. Aims and objectives This feasibility study will undertake preparatory work by addressing uncertainties related to the intervention and its evaluation prior to a trial. It will also assess willingness to pay for the new Asset Based approach to Health Walks. Research Question 1: What are the mechanisms in an Asset Based approach to Health Walks that enable implementation and ensure scalability and sustainability? Research Question 2: Is it feasible to undertake an evaluation of a community Asset Based approach to Health Walks that would test walking, health and well-being outcomes? Research Question 3. How willing would the public and commissioners be to pay any potential additional costs for this new approach to reduce health inequity? Methods This is a feasibility study for a cluster randomised controlled trial. Twelve organisations (clusters) will be sampled from a list of asset-based community organisations potentially interested in running walks. Six will be randomised to receive asset-based walks and 6 will form a waiting list control, receiving a pedometer and physical activity advice. A range of feasibility questions will be tested using a traffic light system for progression to a full trial and outcomes (physical activity and wellbeing) will be measured at baseline, 10 weeks and 6 months. Research question 3 will be answered using a Discrete Choice Experiment (DCE) with members of the public and those who commission health and public health services. Timelines for delivery December 2019 for 24 months. The DCE to be completed by month 12. Anticipated impact and dissemination The primary audience will be those interested in evaluating the impact of public health interventions on inequity. Disadvantaged people are under-represented in research and our study will illuminate how to increase participation and address inequity. Outputs will provide much needed evidence on how to measure and illustrate impact and benefit of AB approaches. As an adjunct to academic dissemination, we will produce a short evidence brief targeting Sport England, public health professionals and those who commission NHS and public health services. We will also produce a best practice guidance document for community groups and voluntary organisations explaining how they can identity and mobilise existing assets to support participation in health interventions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Award_Title: How effective and cost-effective is water fluoridation for adults? A 10-year retrospective cohort study
Abstract: Research question: How effective and cost-effective is 10-year exposure to water fluoridation in preventing dental treatment and improving oral health in a contemporary adult population? Background: Tooth decay can cause pain, sleepless nights, sepsis, overuse of antibiotics, embarrassment, and loss of productive workdays. It can also lead to complete tooth loss; one of the leading global causes of disability. Dental treatment can provoke severe anxiety, and is also very costly, both to the NHS and to patients.
