Award_Title: Prevention of obesity at family, community and national level and treatment of obesity in individuals
Abstract: Obesity has profound impact on both the health and wealth of the nation. “Britain is now the most obese nation in Europe. Health inequalities between rich and poor have been getting progressively worse” [HM Government, 2010]. “Overweight and obesity represent probably the most widespread threat to health and wellbeing in the country. Excess weight costs the NHS more than £5 billion year and has serious impact on economic development. The Government’s Healthy Lives, Healthy People: a call to action on obesity in England [2011] stated that to tackle overweight effectively we need to adopt a life course approach and also called for a balance of effort between prevention and treatment and support for those who are overweight or obese. The transition of Public Health in 2013 will see a step-change in public health as budgets are transferred to local government who will have powers to decide on local priorities. With the highest prevalence of overweight and obesity nationally, local government in the north east of England have this as a high priority for local action. My proposed research and leadership programme will contribute to this local action and the national public health priority. I will contribute to the evidence base on effective and cost-effective scalable interventions. This work will be in partnership with policy and practice partners both in the NHS and local government and in collaboration with colleagues in behaviour change psychology, health economics and statistics in Newcastle but with the wide expertise in the membership of new SoPHR. In 2007 Foresight estimated that by 2050 60% of men and 50% of women and 25% of children could be obese and that the financial impact to society would be £45.5 billion/year. Foresight conclude that the obesity epidemic could not be prevented by individual action alone and demands a societal approach with action at individual, family, community and national level. Healthy Lives, Healthy People: a call to action on obesity in England [2011] stated that “We have some way to go before we have convincing evidence of cost-effectiveness across a spectrum of approaches. A more concerted effort is therefore needed to both synthesise and disseminate emerging evidence about effectiveness and cost-effectiveness and to put in place rigorous evaluation of local interventions. My research and leadership plan will address these challenges. I will focus on the prevention of overweight exploring innovative approaches and scalable interventions at family, community and national level and on treatment of obesity at individual level. I bring to this work my knowledge and skills in public health nutrition, my extensive experience in policy and practice relevant research and networks in the PHRC, UKCRC Fuse and SoPHR, my track record in leading multi-disciplinary research teams and the practical perspective of an NHS practitioner as well as my proven leadership skills and potential as a future research leader in the international arena. Work Stream 1 Changing eating behaviour: prevention of obesity Contributors: National Obesity Observatory [NOO] [Public Health England], NHS choices, School Food Trust, Dept. for Education, Food outlet business partners, Nursery school practitioners, Schools, Fuse, SoPHR, PHRC. IMPORTANCE OF THE TOPIC: Changing eating behaviours is central to tackling obesity; one of today’s foremost public health challenges and requires multifaceted solutions which consider the food environment, individual skills and individual choice within that environment. Too many children begin school already overweight or obese and evidence shows that parents are often unable to identify when their child is overweight and so take appropriate action to prevent obesity [reference 7 and 10]. Prevention must begin before school and recent reviews have cited pre-school and family settings for intervention as promising but there is a paucity of evidence on which to based effective early interventions. During primary school years the prevalence of obesity continues to rise yet schools are an opportunity for intervention which has potential to impact across the social spectrum. We are living in an ‘obesogenic environment’; with multiple opportunities to consume high energy dense foods; changing the food environment is an enormous challenge but if can be achieved has high potential gain. Key questions How can help parents to recognise unhealthy body weight in their children and families to take action to prevent childhood obesity? Where and how can we intervene to change food choice? Supporting families to take action The Government are committed to the National Child Measurement Programme [NCMP] and but also to ‘empowering individuals’ by giving feedback to parents [Dept. of Health, 2011]. Yet we know that despite this feedback many parents do not recognise overweight in their children. I am PI of a MRC-NPRI study which will begin in April. This multistage study aims to address the need for improving strategies for increasing parent’s recognition of overweight in their children and informing parents about their child's weight status. It will develop and test tools to improve parents' ability to correctly assess their child's weight status (in line with NCMP criteria), offer an on-line simulation to project a child of given BMI forward as an adult, to increase their knowledge of the health consequences of childhood overweight and provide resources and signposting to support families to take action. Policy and practitioner partners in the study team will ensure that the study outputs are directly transferable to practice and that the research will support the work of the NOO and NHS Choices. Supporting individuals to take action Anecdotal evidence suggests there has been a de-skilling of the UK adult population with respect to culinary abilities, in particular resulting in a cohort of adults, many of whom are unable to cook meals from raw ingredients (‘from scratch’). Recently, a number of interventions have been developed to address this skills gap, most notably Jamie Oliver’s ‘Ministry of Food’. However, such interventions are at a relatively early stage of development with little analysis of their theoretical basis, few rigorous outcome evaluations or translational studies to support their wider implementation. Nevertheless, such interventions may have the potential for a significant population impact, have received widespread approval from the public and may be a potentially valuable contribution to tackling the obesity epidemic. In 2011 the Dept. Health commissioned a scoping exercise by me and others [Prof White and Dr Adams]. Leading from this work we propose an outcome evaluation, involving a randomised controlled trial (RCT), a process, and an economic evaluation and that this RCT is preceded by a feasibility study. Schools in working partnership with families A new Early Years Foundation Stage has requirements for Early Years providers from Sept 2012 and has focus on engagement with parents [Dept. of Health, 2011]. A study to develop and test a nursery based intervention which involves change in food and physical activity using the nursery setting to engage with parents will soon be complete [Fuse PhD studentship]. A full rehearsal pilot will be funded by the PHRC from 2013. This work will include NHS policy and practice partners from early life settings and local government partners responsible for delivery of such interventions. Changing the school food environment Schools offer an opportunity for interventions with potential to act across social spectrum and so reduce inequalities. The Government are committed to statutory nutritional standards for school meals and will work with the School Food Trust [SFT]. I have recently reported on the evaluation of the school food standards with which all schools must comply (work funded by the PHRC of Dept. of Health, report submitted Nov 2011). This work, which was presented at a SFT/WHO international meeting in January, has large policy implications showing that while the impact of standards on both school food and total diet is significant in primary school this is yet to be realised in secondary schools. Barriers exist in secondary school [reference 11] but potential solutions have been demonstrated in Scotland and could be translated to English Schools. I plan to undertake further research on the implementation of standards in secondary schools. I will work the SFT, Dept. of Health and the Dept. for Education as well local authorities to ensure the findings of this work are translated into action. Changing the wider food environment ‘foodscape’ The Foresight review [2007] highlighted the role of our environment in obesity; the ‘obesogenic environment’ has a high prevalence of high energy dense foods and makes it harder for individuals to make healthy food choices. Changing the ‘foodscape’ will be funded by the NIHR SoPHR and will contribute to the SoPHR aim to increase the evidence base for effective public health practice, with a focus on population level interventions to promote healthier diet. A range of interventions attempting to change the out of home ‘foodscape’ (ready-to-eat food provision in out of home food outlets) has been developed, but none has been rigorously evaluated. Working closely with local government, relevant commercial and public sector partners and with policy partners at the Dept. of Health this research will identify potentially effective interventions or intervention components, based on current theory or evidence, and test them for feasibility and acceptability, leading to pilot testing of effectiveness and, ultimately, the development of protocols for definitive outcome evaluations. New Responsibility Deal agreements for local businesses will be evaluated as part of this work which will provide an evidence base for local governments wishing to influence provision in local out of home food outlets. Deliverables from WS1 1. An interactive 3D body image generator with prediction of adult body size along with supporting materials and resources available on NHS choices website 2. An evidence-based scalable preschool and family partnership intervention for prevention of overweight in children 3. An evidence-based approach for effective implementation of school food standards in secondary schools. 4. Toolkit of commercially viable evidence based interventions to be applied by food outlets to improve the nutrient profile of the ‘foodscape’ WS2: Supporting individual behaviour change: treatment of obesity and maintenance of weight loss Contributors: Prof Roy Taylor [consultant endocrinologist] Dr Ruth Bell [public health & maternal obesity], Prof Patrick Olivier [Human-computer interaction], Fuse, Local Government and dietitians delivering weight management.IMPORTANCE OF THE TOPIC: There is urgent need for prevention of overweight and obesity but with almost 1 in 4 adults in England already obese treatment must also be part of the plan to combat obesity. Large health inequalities in prevalence of obesity exist with the poor having the highest prevalence. The health and social consequences to the individual and the economic burden in the treatment of obesity related co-morbidities means that successful local strategies must balance prevention with treatment of overweight and obesity but with so many in need of support to achieve weight loss innovative solutions are required. There is good evidence of effective interventions for weight loss; with appropriate intervention individuals are able to lose weight however most regain this weight and more within 12mths. Effective interventions for maintenance of weight loss are urgently needed if the investment in treatment of obesity is to be successful in reducing individual health risks and the economic benefit of weight loss are to be realised. Key questions How can e-technologies be used in primary care to support weight loss? How can e-technologies to support weight loss maintenance? How do we support patients in the ‘cure’ for T2D’? Achieving weight loss My-dietitian-on-line is an internet weight loss system which has evolved from a commercial system developed in Denmark. The unique aspects of this system is that it involves direct consultation between dietitian and patient in an on-going treatment programme; if effective this has potential to be translated into practice and could be implemented by onward referral at point of identification from primary care and delivered by dietitians commissioned to deliver services. Currently many dietetic services are unable to offer 1:1 patient service for obesity due to limited resources. Application of existing E-technologies offers a potential solution greater increasing the manageable case load of a dietitian. A PhD studentship funded by Fuse is undertaking a full rehearsal pilot of this system in primary care in north east England. The target groups for this pilot work will be obese men [a group who seldom visit their GP or take part in group-based weight loss interventions] and post-natal woman. Working closely with NHS partners in Durham and Darlington dietitians will be trained in the application of the system; patients will be recruited via primary care and will be involved in full evaluation including detailed evaluation on the process of delivery for both practitioners and patients. This work will inform development of full RCT trial in 2014-15. Currently, diagnosis of type 2 diabetes is regarded as an irreversible step on a path of steadily increasing requirement for medications. Recent work by Prof Taylor at Newcastle has established the complete reversibility of the condition by dietary means using liquid very low energy diets [VLED] to achieve dramatic weight loss. Working with Prof Taylor and Dr Sniehotta we will submit a proposal to Diabetes UK to determine the reversibility of longer duration type 2 diabetes, the optimum nature of the long-term follow-up diet, attitudinal and motivational factors which could predict response, and metabolic biomarkers of successful re-establishment of normal glucose control. Reversing type 2 diabetes in even a modest proportion of sufferers would produce enormous benefits for health and well-being. My contribution will be to identify the social and personal characteristics which can prospectively identify those people of short and longer term duration T2DM for whom a very low energy diet (VLED) will reverse diabetes and to determine the most appropriate weight maintenance diet for those successful patients. Maintaining weight loss Effective interventions to support maintenance of weight loss are needed. With recent funding from MRC-NPRI for the ‘Development and Pilot Evaluation of Scalable Interventions to Maintain Body Weight’ we will recruit patients from NHS and commercial weight loss programmes [PI Sniehotta]. The research will use innovative technologies, working with Prof Patrick Olivier [human and computer interaction], to enable real time feedback from and to patients using ecological momentary assessment [EMA]; this will include data on body weight, activity and dietary intake. Appropriate automatic interventions will be triggered if patients begin to gain weight. This work will have direct application to locally commissioned weight management services nationally and will developed working with NHS partners through Fuse and the CLRN. Deliverables from WS2 1. Outcome of a rehearsal pilot of my-dietitian on line which will lead to a RCT to contribute to the evidence-base for scalable and so transferable weight loss interventions available to local authority commissioners. 2. Screening and treatment support for patients with type 2 diabetes treated with VLCD 3. Cost-effective interventions to ‘Maintain Body Weight’ after weight loss available to all NHS patients signposted through primary care and NHS Choices. Work stream 3: Gathering the evidence: robust evaluation of dietary interventions Contributors: Dr Emma Foster, Prof Patrick Olivier Food Standards Agency Scotland, Prof John Mathers [PI LiveWell], local obesity prevention strategies Change4Life, NOO [Public Health England].IMPORTANCE OF THE TOPIC: the 2011 Public Health White papers stated the need to put in place rigorous evaluation of local interventions. To do this we need evaluation tools which are widely available and accessible by local practitioners and commissioners of public health. Characterising habitual dietary intake remains one the most challenging biological measurements. Methods for reliable but inexpensive assessment of dietary exposure in large population groups are essential to monitor change in population diet and to evaluate policy and therapeutic interventions to promote dietary change. Nationally evaluation of locally delivered interventions to improve diet is generally poor; existing methods of dietary assessment are expensive and time consuming or require expert nutritionist input making robust assessment too costly except in research settings. Key question: How can new technologies best be used to evaluate public health interventions? Funding gained to date has supported the development of improved dietary assessment systems and tools. Further research has led to development of SCRAN24 a prototype self-completion 24hr recall system which has been trialled in partnership with NHS colleagues in evaluation of local interventions. With new funding from Foods Standards Agency Scotland (FSAS) and working with colleagues with expertise in human and computer interaction [Prof Olivier] we will take SCRAN24 to the web and develop this to be used the National Survey of young people aged 11-24yrs in Scotland from 2014. Added value will be from opportunity to further develop and test the SCRAN24 system in application in on-line dietary assessment of adults as part of the MRC LLHW programme five year LiveWell Programme [PI Prof Mathers] in which I am a collaborator. LiveWell will develop scalable and transferable interventions to promote sustained behaviour change and so enhance health and wellbeing in later life focusing on the peri-retirement window; this includes a dietary intervention. The result will be an open access web-based dietary assessment system suitable for children and adults which will have wide application in NHS and public health interventions both national and locally. There remains a need for independent methods for assessing dietary intake, such as, biomarkers, which could give a comprehensive and objective assessment of dietary exposure. New technologies such as Sensecams [which produce log of daily activities as series photographs] offer opportunity to both support and validate reports on dietary intake. Work in biomarkers from easily obtainable biological samples [salvia and urine] is advancing though not yet able to be used to assess all aspects on intake. Prof Mathers is at forefront of research on use of metabolomics approaches in this area. There is excellent opportunity through the Human Nutrition Research Centre to bring these two streams of work more closely together in development new dietary assessment methods and testing of new dietary biomarkers. An example of this in a clinical setting is current collaboration with Prof Kamali [NuTH] seeking to find a non-invasive method of assessment of Vitamin K intake in children on warfarin therapy [reference 9]. I have existing links with researchers at forefront of dietary assessment in children in US; there would be opportunity to extend this collaboration and explore use of biomarkers both in UK and US. Deliverables from WS3 1. Open access web-based individual level dietary assessment tool available for use for population monitoring and for evaluation of local and national level interventions 2. Progress on the integration of biomarkers into routine dietary assessment

Award_Title: Improve outcomes from oesophageal cancer through innovative screening and surveillance tests
Abstract: The future plans can be divided into two main components. The first is to extend the application of the Cytosponge collection device to the early detection of squamous cell cancer of the oesophagus (ESCC), which accounts for 50% of oesophageal cancers in the UK and is responsible for 90% of oesophageal cancer cases in the developing world. If a screening test for oesophageal cancer was introduced into the UK it would be ideal for this to detect the precursors for both of the main subtypes of oesophageal cancer, not just Barrett's oesophagus. The second is to take the proof of concept ex vivo work on molecular imaging, designed to highlight areas of dysplasia for biopsy and endoscopic therapy in Barrett's oesophagus, into the clinical setting. These two areas will synergise with the programme of work on early cancer detection in my laboratory. Ongoing research is focussed on addressing more basic research questions: i) the molecular triggers for the development of Barrett's metaplasia; ii) characterising the genomic aberrations in Barrett's dysplasia and adenocarcinoma as a prelude to identifying prognostic and therapeutic targets and iii) discovering and performing retrospective validation of risk stratification biomarkers for Barrett's oesophagus. These discoveries need to feed into clinical studies so that their potential for patient benefit can be realised. The ongoing BEST2 Cytosponge study described earlier is a good example of laboratory research being moved into a clinical study. The two projects described here are other examples of work which needs to be done to enable translation into the clinical setting and this NIHR Research Professorship would be an ideal platform in which to maximise pull through into the clinical arena. 1) A novel approach to screening and diagnosis for squamous cell cancer using the Cytosponge and associated assays Background There have been a number of previous efforts to develop non-endoscopic screening for ESCC in the high incidence areas of China since the 1950s and 1960s. However the analysis has relied on liquid-based cytology techniques in which cells are stained, and examined microscopically for epithelial atypia, similar to the evaluation of a Pap smear, (reviewed in Nature Review Clinical Oncology Lao-Sirieix and Fitzgerald 2012). The success of the Cytosponge as a diagnostic test for Barrett's oesophagus hinges on the combination of a successful cell sampling device which is acceptable to patients, coupled with a sample processing technique in which the cells are processed to a pseudobiopsy which still retains tissue architecture. This sample can then be assayed for biomarkers, either a single marker or multiple biomarkers, which enables an objective, quantifiable measure of the disease stage. Based on this positive experience with developing an approach to population based screening for Barrett's Oesophagus the purpose of the current proposal is to develop a non-endoscopic primary screening method for squamous cell dysplasia and asymptomatic ESCC, so that we can screen for asymptomatic ESCC using similar methods. Preliminary data We have developed a biomarker pipeline to ascertain suitable biomarkers for ESCC similar to that which proved successful for elucidating TFF3 as a diagnostic biomarker for BE (Gut Lao-Sirieix 2009). It comprises 4 steps: (i) Publically available expression array data is mined to identify mRNA species differentially expressed in normal squamous tissue (NE) and ESCC tissue, (ii) The top putative biomarkers are validated in mRNA extracted from snap frozen specimens of NE and ESCC, (iii) Biomarkers successfully validated in ii) are then validated at the protein level in paraffin-embedded specimens from NE and normal gastric mucosa compared with ESCC and squamous dysplasia (iv) Validated protein markers from iii) are then taken forward to samples, collected with the Cytosponge from known ESCC patients and controls. Using this algorithm there are 80 potential targets with differential expression between disease states of sufficient magnitude to point to clinical potential. Data for 6/10 targets which have validated so far is shown in Figure 1 and immunohistochemical assays are available for all of these. Proteomics would be another discovery platform but at the moment there are no publically available datasets. From the BEST2 Barrett's trial we also have experience in assaying for specific DNA mutations as an alternative biomarker approach and this will be a possibility for ESCC if required in addition to immunohistochemical approaches.Hence the principal aims of this proposed study are: 1) To validate putative markers at the protein level on paraffin-embedded specimens from the normal squamous oesophagus-dysplasia-carcinoma sequence and to use existing Cytosponge specimens from individuals previously recruited into the BEST clinical trial without ESCC to ensure high specificity (lack of false positives). 2) To assess the sensitivity and specificity of putative markers in Cytosponge samples for identifying asymptomatic individuals with high grade oesophageal squamous dysplasia (HGD) or ESCC in an ongoing endoscopic screening programme in a high risk population in China as a prelude to a clinical trial in the UK. For aim 1 markers validated by qRT-PCR will be validated at the protein level using immunohistochemistry (existing or custom generated antibodies as required for TFF3) in FFPE tissue from normal mucosa, LGD, HGD and ESCC (n=80). Samples are available from Addenbrooke's Hospital tissue bank for this purpose. We will then apply the most promising targets to a larger cohort of ESCC samples (n=270) which will be obtained as part of collaborative bio-resource from Dr Dawsey, NIH Washington, USA. Strict automated protocols will be used for immunohistochemical staining and scoring to ensure applicability to routine clinical NHS laboratories. Markers solely expressed in the stromal compartment will be discarded since the Cytosponge samples only the epithelium. Biomarkers with promising protein expression will then be applied to a cohort of Cytosponge specimens (N=500) collected as part of the BEST study from patients without any declared squamous cell cancer to ensure that the antibody is sufficiently specific (low false positives). Markers with a specificity of >90% (from Cytosponge samples) and sensitivity of >80% (from the retrospective cohort study) for detecting ESCC or HGD compared to the normal oesophagus will be taken forward to the prospective clinical study. For aim 2 the field testing of the identified and validated protein biomarker(s) will be performed as a research component added on to an ongoing endoscopic screening program in a high-risk population in China. Dr. Wang is the Principal Investigator of the Chinese National Early Detection and Early Treatment of Esophageal and Cardia Cancer (EDETEC) Program, which now screens over 50,000 asymptomatic adults in high-risk areas of China every year. The ongoing activities in this program, supported by the Chinese government, include a short questionnaire (patient identification and demographics), a Lugol’s chromoendoscopy examination, pathology processing and reading of the biopsies, and endoscopic therapy of all lesions diagnosed histopathologically as severe squamous dysplasia or superficial invasive esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SESCC). The Cytosponge test will be performed prior to the screening endoscopy. Processing and immunohistochemical staining of the Cytosponge cell block and selected endoscopic biopsies will be performed utilising antibodies to the protein biomarkers identified in the validation step(s) described above. The screening characteristics (sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value) of the protein biomarker(s) and histopathological assessment of the H&E from the Cytosponge specimen will be evaluated versus the gold standard of the worst endoscopic biopsy diagnosis in each patient. From these 500 individuals, we expect approximately 75 low-grade (mild) dysplasia (LGD), 75 HGD, and 5 ESCC patients, based on data from Dr Dawsey obtained from previous screening studies in China (Pan et al., Acta cytol, 2008; Dawsey et al., Acta Cytol, 1994). This number of individuals will provide good estimates of sensitivity and specificity for use of the putative biomarker(s) as a primary screening test in a realistic population setting in a cost effective manner. If the diagnostic accuracy of the test appears promising, additional larger field studies will be undertaken (with separate funding from NIHR or HTA) to further evaluate its clinical utility in the UK as part of a screening algorithm to detect precursors for both squamous and adenocarcinoma by applying more than one biomarker assay. Such a successful primary screening test, combined with endoscopic confirmation and endoscopic therapy, could have a tremendous impact on the global morbidity and mortality of oesophageal cancer in the UK and globally which in 2008 accounted for 404,000 deaths worldwide. 2) Development of an in vivo molecular imaging to highlight areas of dysplasia for biopsy and endoscopic therapy in Barrett's oesophagus. The proof of concept ex vivo work performed in my laboratory has shown that the lectin Wheat Germ Agglutinin (WGA) has the potential to be used as a molecular imaging tool for Barrett's dysplasia (Nat Med 2012). However, further work is required to determine the optimal panel of lectins and to refine the endoscopic imaging technology in order to minimise autofluorescence. Furthermore, toxicity studies are required prior to in vivo use. Hence, the specific aims of this proposal are to perform laboratory and clinical studies outlined in aim i) which will enable the design of a future prospective trial (aim ii). Specifically the aims are: ia) Identification of further molecular imaging glycan targets from already available lectin array and gene expression array data. ib) Perform ex vivo validation and subsequent toxicity studies on lectins, alone and in combination, which have already been identified as interesting. ic) Adapt a novel multi-spectral imaging system developed by Professor Vasilis Ntziachristos for use with a standard endoscope for the detection of fluorophores in vivo that minimises interference from tissue autofluorescence. This will be a collaborative project and this has already been established through our mutual collaborator Professor Kevin Brindle. id) Perform a pilot molecular imaging study in patients immediately prior to oesophagectomy to establish feasibility and enable more detailed power calculations.ii) To establish a prospective in vivo molecular imaging trial in the BE surveillance population using one or more lectins to determine their sensitivity and specificity as molecular imaging tools. Experimental plans In brief, our previous lectin array data provided binding data for 78 lectins. We initially took 3 lectins which demonstrated an epithelial binding pattern forwards to histochemical studies. Additional lectins also showed differential binding in dysplasia and may also have potential as glycan probes. We therefore plan to confirm these findings on tissues obtained from Barrett’s metaplasia, dysplasia and cancer. While a single labelled lectin might be sufficient to detect dysplasia in general we expect a combination of biomarkers to give the highest sensitivity and specificity due to molecular heterogeneity of the tissue; however this requires that there is not significant competition between the lectins for binding glycan epitopes. Lectin histochemistry using lectins in combination and alone on sequential sections will therefore be undertaken on mucosal tissue from fresh oesophagectomy specimens (n=10) and the overall level of lectin binding (tagged with different fluorochromes) will be assessed using confocal microscopy prior to validation at a macroscopic level on ex vivo specimens using the IVIS 200 camera. For the whole biopsy study, fluorescently labelled lectins (Alexa 680), alone or in combination as determined from the studies above, will be applied to biopsies taken from 40 patients with varying degrees of dysplasia and binding determined using the IVIS 200 camera. The degree of lectin binding will be correlated with the degree of dysplasia from the histopathological assessment of the same biopsy. Lectins that show promise at this stage will be progressed to whole organ (at oesophagectomy) ex-vivo proof-of-principle studies to allow transition to in vivo studies. Some of the lectins are edible foodstuffs e.g. WGA. For other lectins in order to provide the necessary safety data to the MHRA toxicity studies will be performed. Increasing concentrations of lectin will be applied to an existing panel of oesophageal cell lines and the effects on morphology, proliferation, apoptosis and metabolic activity will be determined. In vivo toxicity studies would be performed in collaboration if required and Professor Duncan Jodrell, who heads the Pharmacology and Drug Development Group at the CRUK Cambridge Research Institute. Adaptation of a novel multi-spectral imaging system will be required for in vivo lectin imaging studies. Current endoscopes use cameras placed at the tip of the instrument, which limits performance (sensitivity, spectral acquisition). Professor Vasilis Ntziachristos (Director of the Institute of Biological and Medical Imaging in Munich) has developed a system that provides simultaneous colour and fluorescence images, for accurate co-registration, performs all necessary corrections by spectral decomposition, is configurable for any fluorescence range, including near-infrared and can be interfaced to a conventional clinical endoscope. Real time spectral decomposition of the fluorochrome signal is used to separate out signal from tissue auto-fluorescence and to distinguish individual fluorophores with high sensitivity and specificity. The system would be tested first on ex vivo oesophagectomy specimens. Calibration experiments would include: (i) The fluorescence of fresh (BE) biopsies (n=30, range of disease stages) following lectin labelling will be assessed using the multispectral endoscope and values compared with those measured using the IVIS 200 and using a standard endoscope. Application of the fluorochrome alone, in the absence of the lectin, will serve as a control for background fluorescence. The signal-to-background ratios for lectin binding, as measured by each of the 3 techniques, will be determined. In the oesophagectomy model biopsies will be taken from areas of low and high fluorescence (determined using the multi-spectral endoscope) and these will be sent for histological analysis to determine the presence of dysplasia. Imaging in patients immediately prior to oesophagectomy will then be performed to establish feasibility and to generate pilot data to inform design of a larger clinical study. We will recruit BE patients (n=20) undergoing oesophagectomy. In theatre, prior to oesophagectomy and while under general anaesthetic, fluorescein-conjugated WGA (5µg/ml) +/_ other lectins alone or in combination will be applied to the mucosa for 10 minutes prior to washing with lectin buffer. Binding will be determined using a standard endoscope (Lucera GIF-Q260) as well as with the multispectral endoscope. Oesophageal biopsies will be taken from areas with the highest and lowest fluorescence intensities. The areas from which these biopsies are taken will be marked on a grid to allow for subsequent correlation with the histological mapping of the oesophagus and fluorescence measured (with subtraction of signal from auto-fluorescence) using the IVIS 200 camera prior to fixation, paraffin embedding, sectioning, H+E staining and histopathological assessment. Glucosamine (1g in 10ml), which competes with WGA for binding to GlcNAc, will then be applied to remove WGA binding and a further measurement of mucosal fluorescence taken. (If other lectins are used then the specific monosaccharide which competes with their binding would be used). The oesophagus will then be photographed, fixed and sectioned into mega-blocks to allow accurate histological mapping of the entire BE mucosa. The primary endpoint will be detection of an increased incidence of dysplasia in biopsies taken from areas of low WGA binding. Secondary endpoints will be assessment (from histological mapping) of whether all areas of dysplasia were detected. Following the pilot and during the duration of the Research Professorship, we will apply for funding for a multicentre molecular imaging study in BE surveillance. If multiple lectins complete this pilot phase, we will take forward the lectin with the greatest signal-to-background ratio, or, depending on the results of our preliminary work, a group of lectins that can be applied in combination. The primary endpoint will be to ascertain whether targeting biopsies in this manneris associated with a higher rate of dysplasia detection than the standard protocol and to determine the sensitivity and specificity of the targeted technique. The sample size and duration would be informed by the studies described above. This trial would enable a clinical evaluation of the molecular imaging technique, with the goal if successful, of introducing it into clinical endoscopic surveillance programmes for high risk patients with Barrett's oesophagus.

Award_Title: The REFINE (REducing Falls in IN-patient Elderly) Study
Abstract: BackgroundFalls are common among elderly hospital in-patients. These lead to injury, impaired rehabilitation, increased hospital stay and large costs to NHS organisations. Preventing patients from falling particularly within the first few days of admission remains challenging, even if the patient is identified as being at high risk. Elderly patients have to rapidly adapt to changes in their mental function, strength and mobility, both as they become ill and as they recover. Therefore, these patients need to be supported during this early phase of hospitalisation as the effects of treatment, rehabilitation and multifaceted falls assessment / intervention measures are undertaken.AimsThe hypothesis to be tested is that bedside chair and bed pressure sensors, incorporating a radio-paging alerting mode to alert staff to patients rising from their bed or chair, in the early hospitalisation phase, will reduce inpatient bedside falls, associated morbidity and be cost effective. The aims are to:1. Evaluate the effect of this health technology upon falls in elderly hospital in-patients and on other health outcomes.2. Estimate the cost-effectiveness of the pressure sensors, compared to usual care from a NHS perspective.3. Identify groups of patients in whom the health or economic benefits are greatest.4. Examine issues of compliance, acceptability to staff/patients and systems implementation to enable replication of the findings of this study to other hospital settings.Plan of InvestigationA 3 year randomised controlled trial. All consenting patients (except the long-term bed bound) admitted to 5 elderly-care medical wards will be randomised to bed and bedside-chair pressure sensors or standard care. The primary outcome measure will be the rate of in-patient bedside falls per 1,000 bed days. Secondary outcomes will include the rate of injurious in-patient falls per 1,000 bed days, and at discharge: transfer and mobility score, fear of falling, length of hospital stay, discharge destination, quality of life and health service resource use. Participant and staff experiences of using bed and chair sensors will be explored by an integral qualitative study and the fidelity of the intervention will be assessed by an observational study. Potential ImpactPreventing patients from falling particularly within the first few days of admission remains challenging, even if the patient is identified as being at high risk. Therefore, these patients need to be supported during this early phase of hospitalisation as the effects of treatment, rehabilitation and multifaceted falls assessment / intervention measures are undertaken. Bedside chair and pressure sensors have the potential of doing this and thus making a huge difference to the management of inpatient falls, that particular occur within the first 3-5 days of being admitted to hospital. In addition they can address a major clinical governance and risk management problem together with a potential cost saving related to treating patient injuries and reducing falls-related hospital bed days.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Evaluation of screening for depression in patients with coronary heart disease and diabetes in primary care.
Abstract: BackgroundChronic physical illness is associated with a high prevalence of depression; 33% in coronary heart disease (CHD) and 24% in diabetes. This co-morbidity can make depression hard to recognize and worsen the prognosis of both conditions. Thus NICE guidance suggests that screening should be undertaken for high-risk groups and the Quality Outcomes Framework (QOF) for general practice rewards screening for depression in all patients with a diagnosis of CHD or diabetes. Routine data indicate high levels of screening nationally; 93% of identified patients were screened in 2008-9. However screening alone does not improve recognition or management of depression. Our initial analysis of local data suggests QOF-associated screening does not lead to increased treatment or referral of depression.AimsWe wish to understand current practice in relation to QOF-based screening for depression and assess its impact to inform the development of effective strategies to detect and treat depression associated with chronic physical disease.Aim: To evaluate screening for depression associated with a chronic physical illness undertaken for QOF.Objective 1: To assess the impact of QOF-driven screening for depression associated with chronic physical illness, by analysing routinely-collected data to determine trends in diagnosis, treatment and referral rates for depression before and after the introduction of QoF.Objective 2: To investigate the process of depression screening during routine patient reviews, and its relation to subsequent clinical management of patients with depression.Plan of InvestigationObjective 1: Interrupted time series analyses to determine whether the introduction of the QOF incentive for depression screening has affected trends in diagnosis, treatment and referral for depression. We will use routinely collected clinical data from electronic records in general practice within one primary care trust. We will compare trends for incentivised conditions (diabetes and CHD) with those for non-incentivised chronic conditions (e.g. heart failure, asthma) and actively identify alternative explanations for observed trends.Objective 2: Ethnographic study of purposively sampled practices to observe how patients are screened during consultations to review diabetes and CHD, with follow-up interviews to examine their experience. We will observe 40-60 consultations in 16 practices.Potential ImpactThis study will show whether the investment of NHS resources in screening for depression as part of QOF is associated with any change in detection and treatment. We will also improve understanding of the inter-personal dynamics and process of screening during chronic illness reviews. This will help explain any impact or lack of impact of depression screening on management of depression. Given the high prevalence and healthcare and societal costs of chronic physical illness, especially when associated with depression, it is critical that we understand the advantages and disadvantages of current clinical practice. This study will inform quality assurance processes in primary care and further guideline development and hence improve patient outcomes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The Development of a Parental Suicide Bereavement Training Pack for Health Professionals
Abstract: BackgroundIt is estimated between 6-10 `significant others' are affected by each suicide and are themselves between 80-300% more likely to commit suicide than the general population. Parental suicide bereavement is considered to be the most distressing form of loss and our understanding of how to assist survivors is far behind our understanding of other `at risk' populations. Similarly, there are no specialist provisions for treatment within the NHS. Whilst studies have focused on the psychological distress health professionals experience when meeting bereaved families, less attention has been paid to their responses and intervention approaches and the way these are perceived by those bereaved.AimsAim:To develop a training pack for health professionals to support them in dealing with a parent bereaved by suicide (BBS) Objectives:1. To explore parents experiences of contact with health professionals whilst caring for their (suicidal) child and after the child's death. 2. To investigate barriers to access to good quality health services for parents bereaved by suicide, including those caring for siblings of the deceased child. 3. To investigate health professionals' views of difficulties in providing care for parents bereaved by suicide, including their views of training needs 4. To develop a training pack to provide health professionals (HP) with knowledge, skills and a framework in which to guide them on how to respond and care for parents BBS.Plan of InvestigationQualitative methods will be used. Participants will include parents BBS and HP responsible for their care. Parents of offspring, aged between 16-35 yrs, who have had either a suicide or open verdict returned, will be identified from the deceased's inquest file.The deceased will have died in Greater Manchester (GM) during 2009-2010 and will be identified by the National Confidential Inquiry which records suicides. Parents will reside and service providers will serve those in the GM area. The bereaved parents and HP who come into contact with parents will be asked to take part in semi-structured interview which will explore parents’ perception of HP responses to them and HP perception of caring for the bereaved parents. Transcripts of the interviews will be analysed using Framework AnalysisPotential ImpactSuicide bereavement (SB) is associated with psychological problems and an increased risk of suicide . It is estimated that up 50,000 people are BBS annually. An essential element of good practice is the alleviation of distress and morbidity amongst this vulnerable population. It is recognised that health professionals are often uncertain how to respond to those BBS [1] and have no specific model to help guide their response when caring for them. The findings from the study will be used to develop a training pack to inform and guide health professionals on how to respond to bereaved parents. This study would advance our understanding of suicide bereavement and would be a development from the Department of Health's SB pack which provides practical advice and guidance for bereaved families[2]

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Investigation of screening tools for amnestic mild cognitive impairment (a-MCI)
Abstract: Background: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is an emerging clinical syndrome and has been identified as a potentially effective time point for interventions to prevent or slow the decline into dementia. The commonest subtype, amnestic-MCI (a-MCI), characterised by cognitive impairment primarily in the memory domain, is associated with a high risk of Alzheimer s disease and has therefore received clinical and research interest. In order to conduct large scale, population based intervention studies in people with a-MCI, an important first step is to develop an approach to identify people with a-MCI which is reliable and efficient. A widely used and internationally accepted diagnostic standard for a-MCI is the Petersen criteria. However, these require a complex and specialist-based assessment procedure that is very time consuming. Shorter, less arduous cognitive testing procedures would provide a more resource efficient and feasible method to identify people with probable a-MCI for participation in large scale, pragmatic a-MCI intervention studies. Two candidate cognitive assessment instruments are the Memory Alteration Test (M@T) and the Test Your Memory (TYM) test. Aims: To evaluate the clinical utility and sensitivity/specificity of the M@T and TYM for identifying people with probable a-MCI in a primary care setting by addressing the following research questions: Are the M@T and TYM sensitive and specific in detecting a-MCI in community-based populations? Are the M@T and TYM reliable measures? Are the M@T and TYM feasible for use in community based populations? Plan: Participants will be recruited from NIHR research-ready GP practices in Bradford. Eligible participants will be selected via electronic record screening, followed by a screening letter and finally telephone enquiries. Participants with subjective memory impairment, no depressive symptoms, and who have a potential informant will be invited to consent to study participation. Participants will first be visited at home and asked to complete either the TYM or M@T. They will then be invited to attend the Bradford Clinical Research Facility and asked to complete either the M@T or TYM (the alternative to that completed during the home visit). Following this, the cognitive assessment questionnaires/tests for the operationalised Petersen criteria will be conducted with the participant and their informant. Scores from this will be used to classify participants as cognitively normal, a-MCI, possible early dementia or other (including people with non-amnestic MCI). A sample of participants will be visited at home again to complete either the M@T or TYM to enable the test-retest reliability of the instruments to be investigated. Using recommended cut-off scores, the sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values and likelihood ratios will be calculated for the M@T and TYM for differentiating a-MCI from cognitively normal, and for differentiating a-MCI from possible early dementia. Reliability will be assessed for both the M@T and TYM by comparing scores for the two assessments. Clinical utility of the M@T and TYM will be assessed by examining administration times, missing items and completion rates. Benefits: Identifying a screening instrument for the detection of people with probable a-MCI will facilitate research aimed at developing, testing and implementing drug, lifestyle and carer interventions to prevent or delay the decline into dementia. Additionally, management plans and care pathways for people with a-MCI can be developed. If a-MCI interventions prove successful, a reduction in the economic burden of dementia which, in the UK, currently exceeds that for stroke, heart disease and cancer combined, might be expected. Moreover, the identification of a simple instrument may allow GPs at a future time to routinely screen for a-MCI, allowing the timely referral of patients for further cognitive assessment if requir

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Using expressive writing interventions to promote health in women after birth
Abstract: Background Promoting postnatal health is a recognised clinical priority. National Service Frameworks state improving the health and welfare of mothers and their children is the surest way to a healthier nation [1]. Psychological problems such as postnatal depression or anxiety disorders can have profound effects on women and families. NICE guidelines therefore emphasise the need for intervention but draw attention to the lack of evidence-base[2]. Disclosing personal thoughts and feelings through expressive writing is associated with improved health in many other groups. Reviews show expressive writing can have positive effects on psychological and physical health, general functioning, health service use, and is beneficial during periods of stress[3,4]. Expressive writing may therefore be particularly helpful after birth but it is important this intervention is tailored to postnatal women, properly evaluated, and problems of uptake in hard-to-reach groups identified before such interventions are implemented. Aims Our research aims to evaluate expressive writing intervention for postnatal women using a randomised controlled trial to compare an expressive writing intervention, a control intervention, and normal care for postnatal women. This study aims to: 1. Evaluate the effect of expressive writing on postnatal psychological health, physical health and quality of life. 2. Evaluate the effect of expressive writing on use of healthcare services and satisfaction with healthcare services. 3. Evaluate the acceptability of expressive writing to postnatal women. 4. Examine the effect of socio-demographic factors and ethnicity on uptake of the intervention. Plan of investigation This project will determine the efficacy and acceptability of expressive writing to promote health in postnatal women using a randomised controlled trial. The sample will consist of 321 women recruited six weeks after having a baby. Women will complete baseline measures then be randomly allocated to an expressive writing group, control intervention group, or normal care. The expressive writing group will write about stressful issues that arose during or after birth. The control intervention group will write about time management. In both these groups women will be expected to write for 15 minutes a day on three consecutive days. The normal care group will receive postnatal medical care with no psychotherapeutic intervention. Primary outcomes are changes in psychological and physical health and quality of life. Secondary outcomes are changes in healthcare service use and satisfaction. These outcomes will be measured before, 1-month after and 6-months after the intervention. Women in the expressive writing group will be followed-up at the end of the study to obtain their views and evaluations of expressive writing. Potential impact This study potentially has a wide-ranging impact on health and healthcare. Unlike interventions that have to be delivered by healthcare practitioners, expressive writing interventions can be adapted to be freely provided and widely accessed via the internet. Obviously such interventions need to be adapted to the target population and properly tested before such wide-spread implementation. However, if proven to be of benefit to women this intervention could have a marked effect on maternal mental health in the UK, and subsequently on healthcare service use. Through these factors, the potential economic impact of the expressive writing intervention is also significant. From the NHS perspective, this type of intervention is simple, cost-effective, low-risk and can be incorporated into normal postnatal care through the provision of workbooks or information on the internet. The provision of preventative or low-level treatment via the internet reduces cost and pressure on services. Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Prevention of major depression in at-risk adolescents: a pilot randomised trial of a screen-and-intervene program
Abstract: Background Depression is common among adolescents, and associated with academic and social impairment, family burden, and high rates of attempted and completed suicide2. Few adolescents with depression have any contact with mental health services3, 4. Many cases of adolescent-onset depressions continue into adulthood, typically with a remitting and relapsing course5. Each episode of depression substantially raises the risk of a subsequent episode, and repeated episodes of depression are increasingly hard to treat2. In this context, recent efforts have been made to prevent the onset of depression in adolescence6-11. Large scale, high-quality, universal prevention programs have failed to demonstrate effectiveness6, 7. In contrast, targeted approaches, in which only youth at high risk of developing the disorder are offered an intervention, have been shown to be effective in several RCTs8, 9. However, no study of targeted depression prevention programs has yet been completed in the UK. Further development of targeted prevention programs in a UK NHS setting has potential to benefit patients, improve NHS provision, and to markedly reduce the burden of depression in youth and adults. Aims The proposal addresses two main questions: is it feasible and acceptable to identify youth who are at-risk of developing depression; and is it possible to reduce incidence of depression in this at-risk group? Adolescents whose parents have a history of depression, and who themselves have a history of depression or currently show elevated but sub-syndromal symptoms of depression, are at substantially higher risk of developing major depressive disorder than community samples. The proposal therefore has two main aims: among offspring of parents who have a history of depression, to investigate the feasibility and acceptability of a screening program to identify youth at-risk of depression; and to determine acceptability, feasibility, and preliminary clinical-effectiveness of a group CBT program to prevent onset of depression in youth identified as being at high risk of developing the disorder. Plan of investigation A 2-stage investigation is proposed. In Stage 1, offspring (10-17 years) of 190 adult patients with a history of depression will complete a depression screening questionnaire. Based on responses, they will be divided into three groups (Low-Risk, High-Risk, In-episode). A randomly selected sample of parents and youth from each group will be interviewed about the acceptability of screening and service provision. Data will be analysed using qualitative methods. In Stage 2, High-Risk young people will be offered further detailed clinical assessment. Those with elevated but sub-syndromal symptoms of depression, or a history of >=1 previous episode of depression, will be randomly allocated to CBT (8x 90 minute group sessions) or to usual care. Depressive symptoms and episodes of depression will be assessed at post intervention and at 6 month follow up. Clinical data will be analysed using survival regression models and hazard ratios. Young people will be interviewed to elicit their views on the intervention. Potential impact Expected outcomes include: data on the feasibility of screening at-risk youth within existing NHS structures; patient views about the value and shape of targeted “screen-and-intervene” prevention programs; and preliminary findings on feasibility and effectiveness of a novel prevention program. Potential benefits for young patients and their families include a reduced likelihood of developing a depressive disorder. Potential benefits to the NHS include the development of cost-effective and clinically-effective services for vulnerable young people, with consequent reduced burden on NHS services in the medium to long term. If this intervention is evaluated positively, data from the current study will be used to inform a future definitive trial, for which funding would be sought.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: An exploratory randomized controlled trial of brief alcohol advice delivered in general dental practice.
Abstract: Alcohol misuse is a significant public health problem in the UK. A strong evidence base exists demonstrating the effectiveness of brief alcohol interventions delivered in primary care settings. No trials have however been undertaken to evaluate the effectiveness of brief interventions delivered by dental teams in general dental practice. Excessive alcohol consumption is a major risk factor for oral cancer, oro-facial injury and dental erosion, and is therefore an important and highly relevant health promotion issue for general dental practitioners. The majority of the UK adult population visits a dentist within a two-year period. This provides a unique opportunity to deliver preventive advice to dental patients to promote both their oral and general health. Increasingly general dental practitioners ask their patients about their tobacco and alcohol habits but few dentists offer brief alcohol advice to patients who are drinking excessively. This study addresses a key public health problem where a major gap in the evidence currently exists. The aim of the study is to assess the acceptability and feasibility of delivering brief alcohol intervention to adults attending general dental practices across North Central London (NCL). Initially exploratory qualitative research (focus groups) will be undertaken with separate samples of general dental practitioners and dental patients to explore their views on the salience and relevance of providing alcohol prevention in dental practices. An exploratory randomized controlled trial will then be conducted to determine the feasibility, practicality and acceptability of delivering brief alcohol interventions in general dental practice. The pilot trial will be conducted in 10 general dental practices (randomized to 5 intervention and 5 controls) from across NCL. The primary outcome will be the score on the Extended Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) questionnaire. Baseline and 6 month follow-up outcome measures will be collected from the sample of 200 participants. A process evaluation will also be undertaken to assess the acceptability of the intervention. The findings of this study will be used to inform the conduct of a definitive RCT of brief interventions in primary care dental settings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The impact of an investment based intervention on weight-loss and beliefs about food in patients post bariatric surgery.
Abstract: Background: Obesity is a major health problem that is becoming increasingly common. Although the majority of people try to lose weight through changes in diet and exercise, the most successful treatment for obesity is weight loss surgery. Not all patients, however, lose the desired amount of weight; some regain weight and some have the surgery reversed. Research by the present author has explored why the outcome of surgery varies between patients and has highlighted the role for a number of psychological factors. In particular, research indicates that successful weight loss is related to the sense of investment that the patient has made in their operation. For example, if a person feels that the operation (or operations) has involved financial cost, has disrupted their work and family life and has been painful and difficult then studies indicate that they will be more likely to lose weight and keep this weight off. Furthermore, a recent pilot study asked patients to focus on the investment they had made in their operation which resulted in increased weight loss by follow up. This study, however, was only small scale and the follow up was only 3 months. Aims: The present study aims to evaluate an investment based intervention on a larger sample with a longer term follow up to determine the impact of such an intervention on weight loss and patient beliefs and behaviours up to 12 months following surgery. Method: Patients from UCH will be recruited 2 weeks before their operation. Measures will be taken at baseline (2 weeks pre operation) then 3, 6 and 12 months post surgery. Half will receive the investment intervention and half will receive usual care. For the intervention, patients will be asked to rate and describe the impact of the operation on their lives in terms of financial factors (eg. Did the operation cost you money? ), social factors (eg Did the operation interfere with your social life? ), physical factors (eg. How painful was the operation? ) and personal factors (eg. Did the operation influence your family life? ). This will involve a simple paper and pen questionnaire and will be given at baseline and 3 months, tailored to the experiences of the patient at that time point. It is predicted that this focus will raise the salience of patients investment in weight loss surgery thus encouraging them to feel more motivated to lose weight and make the surgery a success. The intervention will be evaluated in terms of weight loss. In addition its impact on beliefs about food, eating and exercise behavior and intentions to change behavior will also be assessed. Impact on the NHS: Obesity is a risk factor for illnesses such as heart disease, diabetes and cancer. If effective, obesity surgery improves a patient s health and reduces their need for NHS care. If unsuccessful then the costs include not only subsequent NHS costs due to these other illnesses but also the costs of the unsuccessful operation and the emotional cost to the patient. The investment based intervention should help to improve the effectiveness of surgery which in the longer term is likely to be cost effective. How the results may affect treatment of patients: This research is based upon a small scale pilot study that showed that a simple investment based intervention which encouraged patients to consider their personal investment in having weight loss surgery, improved weight loss by 7kg by 3 months follow up. If this is reproduced in the current larger scale study and persists into the longer term then such a simple, easy to adminster and low cost intervention could become routine practice for bariatric patients.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Swab-yourself trial with economic monitoring and testing for infections collectively (SYSTEMATIC): A study comparing clinician-taken versus self-taken rectal and pharyngeal samples, and separate versus pooled specimens, from each individual
Abstract: Background Current screening for chlamydia (CT) and gonorrhoea (GC) in the community outside clinical settings (not in a hospital, clinic or surgery) is with self-taken urogenital samples only. Yet these infections are also commonly found in extra-genital (pharynx and rectum) sites so are not detected by these samples. In men who have sex with men (MSM) the majority of infections are extra-genital and so are missed by current screening. The use of self-taken swabs from extra-genital sites would allow full screening to be introduced into community settings, thus identifying all infections and contributing to control. Tests for GC and CT using nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) are easy to use in all settings as they do not require incubation, but they are expensive. If rectal and pharyngeal specimens are processed in addition to the routine urogenital area, the diagnostic cost is trebled, making it too expensive for most NHS services. If all samples taken from a person (urogenital tract, rectum, pharynx) could be pooled and analysed together, the cost of the diagnostic analysis would be the same cost as current screening but without missing any infections (assuming the same sensitivity and specificity of the tests). Aims and objectives Improve detection of GC and CT by: Comparing sensitivity and specificity of pooled self-taken samples with individually analysed clinician-taken samples Comparing sensitivity of individually analysed self-taken swabs of rectum and pharynx with individually analysed clinician-taken swabs Comparing sensitivity and specificity of pooled self-taken samples with self-taken samples analysed individually Calculating and comparing the cost-effectiveness and cost per infection found by self-taken swabs versus clinician-taken swabs in pooled versus individually analysed samples. Plan of Investigation Women and MSM, attending for sexual health tests, will be recruited. Each will have three sets of samples taken. In women these will be: clinician-taken rectal and pharyngeal swabs to be processed separately; self taken rectal and pharyngeal swabs plus VVS to be processed separately; self-taken rectal, pharyngeal and VVS samples to be processed as a pooled specimen. In MSM these will be: clinician-taken rectal and pharyngeal swabs to be processed separately; self taken rectal and pharyngeal swabs plus FPU to be processed separately; self-taken rectal, pharyngeal and FPU samples to be processed as a pooled specimen. The order the samples are taken in will be randomised. The sensitivity of self-taken rectal and pharyngeal swabs tested for GC and CT by NAATs will be compared with clinician-taken rectal and pharyngeal swabs. The sensitivity and specificity of the pooled rectal, pharygeal and urogenital samples (FPU in men, VVS in women) tested for GC and CT by NAATs will be compared with (a) individually analysed self-taken samples, and (b) individually analysed clinician-taken samples. The sensitivity and specificity will be presented with 95% confidence intervals, and any differences will be assessed using Chi-squared tests or Fisher s Exact Test as appropriate. The number of additional infections identified or missed will also be calculated. Summary of Benefits If self-taken pooled-samples detect more people with infections and do not reduce the sensitivity and specificity of the FPU/VVS, it would mean extra-genital swabs could be incorporated into community screening, and the cost of their analysis would be the same as the current urogenital screening. This will prevent false reassurance of the individual, and the public health consequences, of negative urogenital community screening where extra-genital infections have been missed, yet at the same cost as current screening. Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Co-production and evaluation of an e-learning resource to improve knowledge about schizophrenia and engagement with services in African Caribbean families
Abstract: In the UK, African Caribbeans relative risk of schizophrenia in is 9.1 (IRR 6.6-12.6)2 9. In Manchester, African Caribbeans account for less than 2% of the population but 16.5% of in-patents. They access care later in their illness, presenting with more severe symptoms. Community-level misinformation and negative, stigmatising attitudes to mental illness are powerful barriers to help-seeking10 11. Untreated illness exacerbates family tensions and worsens perceptions of the burden of care12. Escalating family hostility, often resulting in police involvement, increases patients risk of estrangement from their families, relapse and social isolation6. Improving families attitudes and knowledge about schizophrenia positively affects carers perceptions and family tension13 14. However, these data relate to White families. There is little/no evidence about family educational interventions in ethnic minorities in the UK2. Aims We aim to co-produce, with African Caribbeans, a culturally-appropriate e-learning resource to improve attitudes and knowledge about schizophrenia and engagement with services in this high-risk group. We shall assess acceptability, resource-use monitoring methods and outcome measures and pilot data collection methods for outcomes relevant for a future RCT. Research questions (1) Can an e-learning resource (co-produced with African Caribbean community members) improve attitudes and knowledge in families of African Caribbeans with schizophrenia? (2) Can this e-learning resource positively impact engagement and perceived experiences of schizophrenia services? (3) Will the resource be acceptable to the families of African Caribbean people with schizophrenia? Plan of investigation This is a mixed-methods study in four phases using MRC s Complex Interventions Framework 15. Phase 1 There is little information about psycho-education in African Caribbeans. We will undertake a realist literature review16 to inform focus groups and our intervention. Phase 2 To identify culturally-salient issues for resource-development, we will conduct 3 focus groups with African Caribbean stakeholders: ex-service users, families, and community members (6-10 in each group, 18-30 in total). Phase 3 In digital storytelling workshops, using creative multi-media, we will co-produce an e-learning resource comprising: 6-8 digital stories (each focusing on a key aspect of schizophrenia), factual information and short multiple-choice quiz about issues raised by each story (e.g. hearing voices). We will produce web-based and DVD versions to enable people without internet access/computer literacy to participate. Phase 4 Participants will be 20-30 African Caribbean community recruits with family members diagnosed with schizophrenia. Using a test-retest design, we will assess their attitudes and knowledge about schizophrenia pre- and post-intervention. Pre-test, we will collect basic demographic data, test attitudes and knowledge to schizophrenia, perceptions of illness and participants own health before issuing link to on-line resource or providing the DVD. We will repeat measures 2 weeks and 6 months post-intervention, collect qualitative data (on acceptability and accessibility), and pilot recruitment, data collection, and outcome measures to inform future studies. Potential benefits for patients and NHS We anticipate the following short and longer term benefits to patients, families and the NHS Short term: 1. Improved attitudes and knowledge about schizophrenia and its management 2. Better understanding of the disorder thus more sympathetic family environments and less family tension, which reduces risk of relapse 3. Better engagement and experiences of schizophrenia services for African Caribbean families Long term: 1) Reduced delays in help-seeking 2) Better care pathways 3) Reduced relapse rates 4) Reduced rehospitalisation rates Wider potential future Public Health and NHS bene

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Feasibility of MAPS (Medication Adherence for Patient Support): A highly tailored text and voice messaging intervention to support medication adherence among patients with type 2 diabetes and/or hypertension in primary care
Abstract: Background Adherence to medication can prevent complications, disability and premature death in people with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) and/or hypertension. However, substantial proportions of people with these conditions do not take their medications as prescribed. Primary care practitioners have limited time to support medication adherence in people with long-term conditions, and the NHS is currently under financial pressures. There is a need for low-cost interventions that support medication adherence between primary care consultations. In the proposed study we will develop and assess the feasibility of a new intervention that uses individually-tailored text messaging (SMS) and interactive voice response (IVR) to provide ongoing support for medication adherence to people with T2DM and/or hypertension, as an adjunct to the primary care consultation. During the consultation (e.g. an annual review), the practice nurse gives the patient information about the intervention and how to register (by sending a text message to the system). Based on information obtained from the participant on a baseline questionnaire and from query calls and messages sent to the participant during the intervention period, the participant will receive individually tailored messages designed to address both intentional and non-intentional non-adherence. The intervention is automated and interactive and relatively inexpensive to deliver. It could potentially provide a cost-effective way of delivering support for medication adherence to a large number of people, including those with limited access to health care. Aim: To develop and assess the feasibility of an automated, interactive and highly tailored SMS&IVR intervention to support medication adherence in people with T2DM and/or hypertension as an adjunct to primary care consultations. Objectives: Phase 1: To develop the intervention and finalise the design of the feasibility study. Phase 2: To assess the feasibility, acceptability, cost and potential efficacy of the intervention. Plan of investigation This study is informed by our ongoing developmental work, which includes: a systematic review of trials of interventions that have used text messaging (SMS) or interactive voice response (IVR) to support medication adherence in people with T2DM or hypertension; and face-to-face interviews with patients and nurses recruited in primary care. In Phase 1 of the proposed research, we will develop the intervention and finalise the design of the feasibility study, using stakeholder consultations and focus groups with patients to address key uncertainties about the intervention, design of the feasibility study, and recruitment, uptake and retention. In Phase 2, we will conduct a feasibility study in 100 people with T2DM or hypertension. The focus of this study is on feasibility (both of the intervention and of conducting an effectiveness trial with economic evaluation) rather than on efficacy. This will include estimating recruitment, intervention uptake and retention/attrition rates. However, we plan to measure relevant outcomes (self-reported and objective medication adherence; clinical outcomes: blood pressure and HbA1c; resource use and costs) and to randomise participants to intervention versus usual care. This will provide additional information on the feasibility of measuring these outcomes, the feasibility of the randomisation method and the potential efficacy of the intervention, all of which will inform a full trial of effectiveness and cost-effectiveness. Potential benefits to patients and the NHS Currently there are more than 10 million people in England with T2DM or hypertension. The annual cost attributed to medication non-adherence in these two conditions is estimated to be £490 million. If effective, this intervention could yield the following benefits: 1. Increase the number of patients who take their medications as prescribed in the long t

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Central and North West London NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Low-intensity intervention for people with personality disorder: development of a practice-based protocol and feasibility study.
Abstract: Background to the research Personality disorders are long-term mental health conditions which can lead to social exclusion, suicidal behaviour and impaired quality of life. Costs of caring for people with personality are high as a result of attendance at emergency departments and inpatient treatment during emotional crises or following deliberate self-harm. No drugs are licensed for personality disorder; instead current national guidelines recommend intensive psychological treatments delivered over a 12 or 18 month period.
