Few people are able to access these treatments and many of those that do, drop out of them before they have been completed. In recent years evidence from other countries has suggested that less intensive interventions based on psychoeducation, psychological support and promoting self-management can help people with personality disorder. Mental health services in the UK have started to deliver less intensive interventions but it is unclear what the optimal content of these are, and evidence to support their delivery in the NHS does not exist. Study aims (the questions to be addressed) This study will examine the optimal form and content of a low-intensity intervention for people with personality disorder and examine the feasibility of conducting a randomized trial to examine the clinical and cost effectiveness of this intervention. The study will generate information about what works best for people with personality disorder who are referred to mental health services and will provide data needed to design a future trial of this promising approach to helping people with this condition. Plan of investigation A researcher with lived experience of using services for people with personality disorder will collect data from staff, patients and carers at four different Trusts in London that are already delivering low intensity interventions for people with this condition. We will present these data alongside the results of extant research to an expert panel of patients, carers and front-line staff who will develop consensus-based recommendations on the optimal form and content of a low-intensity intervention for people with personality disorder. In a subsequent feasibility study, six mental health teams will be randomized to an active (low-intensity intervention) or control (usual care) arm of the trial. Staff who are already working with people with personality disorder will be trained to deliver the low-intensity intervention. Patients meeting study inclusion criteria will be assessed at baseline and three and six months later using measures of mental health, social functioning, health-related quality of life and service utilisation. Qualitative and quantitative data collected during the trial will be used to examine the acceptability of study methods and the feasibility of the study design. Summary of the potential benefits to patients and the NHS This study will generate a practice-based protocol for a low intensity intervention for people with personality disorder that builds on the best features of existing interventions. The study will also establish the feasibility of a randomised trial of this intervention. If the feasibility study achieves pre-specified progression criteria we will seek funding for a full-scale trial of a promising intervention which has the potential to increase the proportion of people with personality disorder who receive an evidence based intervention that improves mental health and quality of life and reduce costs of care for people with this long term condition.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: A systematic review of physical activity for alcohol and substance use disorders: evidence synthesis with stakeholder engagement to formulate practical recommendations.
Abstract: Background Alcohol use disorders (AUDs) and substance use disorders (SUDs) have significant avoidable global human and economic cost. In the UK, AUDs and SUDs cost the economy £21bn (£3.5bn in healthcare) and £15bn (£488m in healthcare), respectively. Pharmacological interventions inherently have complications, and alternative therapies for treatment and prevention are needed. There is a growing interest in the possible role that physical activity (PA) may offer to reduce AUDs and SUDs with minimal or no adverse effects. Little is known about the best way PA can be promoted to both prevent and reduce AUDs and SUDs and NICE guidelines currently make minimal and vague reference to its role1–7. Aims To systematically review the evidence to date in order to describe and quantify the effects of PA on AUDs and SUDs and understand how it is best delivered or promoted, in what setting, and among which populations, to encourage the prevention, reduction, and abstinence from AUDs and SUDs. In the final phase of the study our aim is to elicit the views of service leads and users on how the findings can be used to guide future funding and interventions for reducing progression, use and post-treatment relapse. Plan of investigation A wide selection of electronic databases will be searched based on a list of key words to generate a list of published research (including grey literature and qualitative investigations) which will then be screened independently by two researchers according to a predefined checklist. Eligible studies will be rated for quality and risk of bias, and data on study details, participant characteristics, AUD/SUD related factors, intervention details and setting, control conditions, and outcomes will be extracted by one researcher and checked by another. Data across similar studies will be synthesised in a meta-analysis. Moreover, we will provide a detailed narrative synthesis using tables, diagrams and narrative texts across the studies, interventions, outcomes, populations and settings. Potential benefits to people and NHS The proposed review will present the evidence to date on the role of PA in the prevention, harm reduction and treatment of AUDs and SUDs. After summarising this literature service leads and users will have the chance to reflect on and add further guidance on how PA interventions can be designed to have greatest reach and effectiveness. They will also add to recommendations on how support for PA can be offered within the NHS, and other public health services, and appropriate third sector and charity organisations, with implications for funding. The review will examine the many aspects of PA in how it is delivered, to whom, by whom, and in what setting to present the potentially most effective services. It will provide information for those involved in the treatment and prevention of AUDs and SUDs as to the most effective and cost-effective applications of PA. It will also highlight potential research gaps to allow for future research planning within the NHS. The review will also be presented to the appropriate NICE Guidelines review panel with ideas on how the findings could be incorporated into future revisions of guidance on effective interventions. Should there be a need for further research on the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of PA interventions for specific groups then we will present the findings to the appropriate NIHR prioritisation panel, and other funders (e.g., National Lottery awards).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Modelling Sexual Healthcare for Substance Misusing Women
Abstract: BackgroundInjecting drug users and sex workers are 2 target populations for sexual health and HIV prevention and treatment (National Strategy for Sexual Health and HIV, 2001)but since that date no research has addressed sexual healthcare needs and optimal service delivery for substance misusing women (SMW) in the UK. The few outdated and low quality existing studies of SMW suggest: • high rates of sexually transmitted infections, unwanted pregnancy and sex work• low rates of cervical screening and condom use• negative perceptions of family planning servicesThe proposed study will address the evidence deficit around sexual healthcare for SMW; and model effective, acceptable services which directly improve the sexual health of this vulnerable population.AimsPrimary Research AimTo define a model for optimal sexual healthcare delivery for SMWSecondary Research AimsTo identify type and frequency of sexual health risks and morbidities among substance misusing womenTo identify levels of sexual health service use (ie. family planning, STI and HIV testing and treatment, cervical smear testing, abortion)To identify the enablers and barriers to effective uptake of sexual health servicesTo collaborate with service users in the research process and evaluate the impact and contribution of that collaboration on research methodology and findingsPlan of InvestigationStage 1Data on type and frequency of sexual health risks and service use will be collected by structured questionnaire, from SMW attending Hastings Addaction, Substance Misuse Service (SMS) and from snowball sampling.A qualitative interview study with 20 SMW will explore enablers and barriers to sexual health service uptake. Stage 2Informal stage of model development using Stage 1 data and key guidance documentsTwo stakeholder focus groups to test the model and identify and resolve problematic elements3 SMW (identified through SMS/Addaction as stable to participate without compromised care or health) will join the research team to inform decisions regarding recruitment and data collection, and will contribute to the model’s development.Potential ImpactThis study is unprecedented in its comprehensiveness. The model will inform how sexual health services are shaped to improve uptake and ultimately the sexual health of SMW. By following the MRC framework on complex interventions (1), the model will also then be suitable for RCT evaluation.Estimation of type and frequency of sexual health risks and morbidities will inform NHS commissioners in allocating monies and services; and will guide professionals working with SMW in identifying and addressing individuals’ needs.This study will incorporate user involvement in study design, contributing to the evidence for public involvement in research and facilitating further research with SMW. It will also reflect on the modelling methodology- about which there is a paucity of literature.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: An Evaluation of Rheumatology Practitioner Clinics held in Primary Care
Abstract: BackgroundRheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic destructive arthritis affecting 1% of the population. The delivery of care for RA patients has changed over the past two decades. Rheumatology nurse practitioners (RP) have become an integral part of the multidisciplinary team. RP services in Norfolk have evolved uniquely to include clinics led by RPs in primary care, which are independent of consultant care. There are also traditional consultant and RP clinics held at the Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital.What is not known is the clinical and cost effectiveness of independent RP services in primary care compared with conventional hospital based services. Existing data suggests that consultant care in the community is associated with better access but at higher cost.AimsThe unique presence of multiple models of rheumatology care in Norfolk provides the opportunity to compare directly their clinical and cost effectiveness for patients with RA.The aim of this study is to evaluate the health benefits, costs, and processes of rheumatology services held in primary and secondary care. In particular, we wish to evaluate the clinical and cost effectiveness of independent RP clinics in primary care in comparison with RP clinics held in the DGH and with traditional consultant clinics. We also wish to evaluate patient perceptions of the quality of care in these settings.Plan of InvestigationConsecutive patients with RA will be recruited from RP and consultant clinics in primary and secondary care. Self-administered questionnaires will be used to evaluate clinic process, patient perception of service quality, personal costs and health status. Process details will include clinic size, waiting times, outcome, investigations and procedures performed. Health status will be assessed using EQ-5D, SF-36, HAQ and RA activity measures. Resource utilisation will be assessed using standard questionnaires including staff costs (salary, travel), overheads, patient’s treatment and personal costs.Focus groups with patients will ensure that all aspects of care are covered by the questionnaires. Face-face interviews with staff will establish their attitudes to outreach clinics.Potential ImpactThis project will for the first time by exploiting the unique presence of multiple different models of care in the same community provide detailed data on the relative clinical benefits and resource utilisation of caring for patients with RA in a variety of different care models. In particular we will be able to compare the resource utilisation, cost effectiveness and clinical benefits of the independent RP in primary care model with the conventional hospital based care model. We will also be able to assess the model of care which provides the best experience for the patient. This will enable clinical practice and service provision to be redesigned around the most clinically effective, cost effective and patient friendly model.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: East and North Hertfordshire NHS Trust
Award_Title: Planning for End-of-Life Care in Dialysis Patients: Attitudes and Perceptions
Abstract: BackgroundThe number of patients undergoing kidney dialysis who are elderly, dependent and have multiple co-morbidities is growing. Such patients are confronted not just with the demands of dialysis but also with the reality of failing health and the prospect of impending death. The NSF for Renal Services states that patients and families should receive information to enable informed choices about end-of-life care. Department of Health policy also emphasises the importance of Advance Care Planning as part of a cohesive end-of-life management plan. However, achieving these aims presents difficulties, including the extreme sensitivity of the subject, identification of at-risk patients, and differences in the way patients, families and clinicians perceive and communicate about end-of-life issues.AimsResearch question: How do dialysis patients, their families and clinicians perceive end-of-life issues? Aims:1. To identify a cohort of haemodialysis patients whose need for end-of-life planning is imminent.2. To establish patients’, families’ and clinicians’ attitudes and perceptions of dialysis, future care and death, and to establish likely reasons for any differences in perceptions. 3. To assess the effectiveness of communication between patients, families, and clinicians about end-of-life issues.4. To incorporate the above into an ‘advance care planning’ framework that harmonises the perceptions of patients, families and clinicians, facilitates effective communication and allows the development of effective end-of-life care planning.Plan of InvestigationPhases: 1. Identification of patients at-risk by clinician review of 400 dialysis patients, using the question –‘would you be surprised if your patient were to die in the next year?’ 2. Questionnaire administration to at-risk patients to ascertain their perception of current health and prognosis, attitudes to advanced care planning, end-of life care, and withdrawal from dialysis. 3. 12 patients, and a family member and clinician for each, will be selected for in-depth study using a qualitative research methodology. 4. Analysis of interviews and construction of ‘advanced care planning’ framework. A focus group comprising patients, families, public and clinicians will inform the clinical review process, questionnaire design and validation, and in-depth interview schedule.Potential ImpactThe framework generated from the study will have an immediate impact on the ‘cause for concern’ initiative running at the Lister aimed at improving end-of-life care for those with kidney disease. It will give insight into the disparities between the perceptions of patients, families and clinicians with respect to end-of-life issues and help staff and patients to open channels of communication to allow appropriate care plans to be put in place. The framework will be useful generally and facilitate implementation of both Renal NSF recommendations for end-of-life care and Department of Health initiatives around advanced care planning.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Successful self-monitoring of oral anticoagulation therapy
Abstract: "BackgroundThe management of anticoagulation therapy is problematic with 40% of international normalised ratios (INRs) found to be outside target ranges. Despite this over 1million patients are currently receiving anticoagulation therapy in the UK. Self-monitoring of oral anticoagulation therapy (OAT) has been shown to be effective in clinical trials but its safety and cost-effectiveness in an unselected population needs to be established. In the UK 2000 patients a year start self-monitoring of OAT but trial evidence suggests that many will not succeed without adequate training and support, with consequent morbidity and NHS cost implications. Errors made during the failed self-monitoring period have the potential to cause patients serious morbidity or death.Aims1) To estimate the current levels of INR control, efficacy and adverse events in patients who commence self-monitoring of oral anticoagulation therapy (OAT) in the UK2) To explore the factors which predict success and failure in self-monitoring of OAT3) To ascertain whether the success in INR and level of side-effects reported from RCTs by self-monitoring for OAT are translated to a non-selected population4) To estimate the adequacy of existing patient training and QA arrangements by measuring the proportion of individuals currently achieving safe self-monitoring in routine clinical practice5) To collect data to allow us to set minimum criteria for self-monitoring, define minimum training, and recommend quality assurance arrangements during the initial monitoring period.Plan of InvestigationThree year prospective cohort study of 360 individuals in routine care who are starting self-monitoring of OAT, with a nested in-depth study to explore reasons for success and failure. All participants will receive baseline phone interviews and questionnaires and will be re-contacted by phone at up at 3, 6 and 12 months for additional interviews. INR data will be collected at 12 months for all participants as well as clinical data on adverse events. In-depth interviews will be conducted with a maximum variability sample of participants who ""fail"" at self-monitoring at different stages. Work completed on a series of systematic reviews will be integrated with the results of the cohort study to construct a complex intervention to increase the safety and success of self-monitoring of OAT.Potential ImpactThis research will underpin the development of an intervention to ensure that self-monitoring of INR can be introduced safely to NHS patients and with minimal waste of resources. It will assess the potential to improve safety of self-monitoring through pre-selection of individuals
Funding_and_Awards_Link: and adoption of quality assurance procedures. As a result of the study we will be able to set minimum criteria for self-monitoring
Award Budget: define minimum training

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Keeping warm at home in later life: a study to develop social marketing interventions that promote engagement of older people in keeping warm behaviour and access to anti-fuel poverty services.
Abstract: BackgroundIt is a public health priority to reduce health burden of individuals and the health service due to cold housing. Cold, damp housing and fuel poverty link to chronic health problems, excess winter deaths and impaired quality of life. 7.7%of Yorkshire and Humber households are fuel poor. This is due to an aging population, barriers to accessing energy efficiency and increases in fuel costs. This translational study uses social marketing and lay epidemiology to explore the issue and develop interventions. Social marketing is an approach to promote healthy behaviour change (e.g. keeping warm) and overcome barriers to healthy behaviour e.g. tools to identify those at risk and increase access to services. Lay epidemiology (knowledge, beliefs and values) provides a theoretical framework.AimsThis qualitative study aims to i) examine older person’s lay epidemiology, this is the network of empirical beliefs, values and non-rational factors that influence their health-affecting choices regarding keeping warm at home ii) develop a package of social marketing products PCTs can adopt to promote keeping warm at home in later life that is informed by the lay epidemiology identified. These are:? Brief intervention training materials for health and social care staff. ? A risk assessment and referral tool? The insight required for PCTs to commission a social marketing public campaign. The study results and user informed outputs can be readily adopted by PCT’s. Their impact on patients and NHS efficiency can be measured using routine audit and evaluation.Plan of InvestigationA qualitative study using in-depth semi-structured individual, group interviews, social marketing and framework analysis techniques. The study has three stages. Triangulation of methods adds to the rigor of the findings:1. Individual interviews and room temperature measurement with 50 older people and interviews with 25 health and social care professionals to explore the lay epidemiology of older people regarding keeping warm at home. 2. 6 focus groups with older people and professionals to verify, challenge and expand upon findings from the individual interviews.3. A structured social marketing consultation of up to 50 key stakeholders to examine the findings and shape the study outputs including education materials, an assessment/referral tool and social marketing insight.Potential ImpactThe study findings and outputs aim to improve the health and wellbeing of older adults and improve NHS efficiency and interagency working through: • Increased understanding of factors influencing older people keeping warm at home, and ways to overcoming barriers to keeping warm• Social marketing interventions i.e. • Brief intervention training materials for health and social care staff. • A risk assessment and referral tool• The insight required for PCTs to commission a social marketing public campaign. Study outputs can be applied across relevant health and social care sectors. Outputs lend themselves to routine audit and evaluation as well as future funded studies. The study equates to the first 2 phases of the MRC framework for complex technologies i.e. theory and modelling.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Bradford Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Antenatal mental health in a bi-ethnic population - understanding and responding to emotional and somatic distress in pregnancy.
Abstract: BackgroundAntenatal mood disorders are not uncommon yet are relatively neglected compared to postnatal mood disorders. They are often an antecedent to postnatal depression and have an impact on birth outcome and child development. Individual differences in the relationship between life events, somatic distress and emotional distress in pregnancy have not been explored yet may contribute significantly to our understanding of antenatal health. Cultural differences in the expression of emotional distress, subjective experiences of somatic distress and life events are also relevant to the mental health needs of women during and after pregnancy.This project builds on our current work that provides descriptive data on the emotional and somatic distress of a sample of pregnant women in Bradford.Aims[1] To describe the nature and prevalence of emotional and somatic distress in pregnancy.[2] To investigate the relationship between life events and somatic and emotional distress in pregnancy.[3] To explore how pregnant women perceive the relation between somatic distress and emotional distress in pregnancy and the association of either of these with life stress. Throughout the project we also aim to create working partnerships with relevant practitioners and consumers of maternity services.Plan of Investigation[1] Systematic reviews will provide data on the prevalence of somatic and emotional distress as well as data on physical and emotional distress and their relation to life adversities.[2] A descriptive retrospective study using standardised interviews will investigate life-events experience in pregnant women with and without high levels of emotional distress and somatic distress, as measured by the GHQ-28.[3] Semi-structured qualitative interviews and thematic framework analysis will be used to explore the subjective experience of somatic distress in pregnancy in women with a range of emotional and somatic distress.This project will be embedded in the Born in Bradford (BiB) cohort study and is linked to work we are currently carrying out in BiB..Potential ImpactThis project on antenatal mental health will help to identify the mental health needs of pregnant women in Bradford. We will have an indication of the value of using somatic distress as a gauge of maternal emotional well-being. Our study will have greater impact since it will specifically look for cultural differences in a bi-ethnic community and these findings will be relevant to other UK communities. Local partnerships will ensure that there is a meaningful dissemination strategy with greater opportunity to inform local practice. The study findings can be used to inform national guidelines and practice relevant to antenatal healthcare.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: An exploratory randomised controlled trial of guided self-help for women with chronic pelvic pain (CPP) in primary care
Abstract: Backgroundi) Approximately 38 per 1000 women attend primary care services each year with CPP, a rate comparable asthma and back pain. ii) The NHS Improvement plan promotes a model of care whereby patients are encouraged to self-manage their condition, alongside medical management and support.iii) Laparoscopy fails to identify pathology in 35% of women. Many women enter a cycle of re-investigation and re-referral in a search for an explanation for their pain. Resulting economic costs to the NHS are high. iv) CPP has a deleterious effect on women’s quality of life, affecting work, personal and sexual relationships. v) Interventions are not well developed, with current emphasis on symptom control. This study will provide a valuable resource to support self-care for women who suffer CPPAimsWe aim to assess the effectiveness and cost effectiveness of delivering an evidence-based self-help guide to women with CPP in primary care. Specifically 1. To develop an intervention package based on the draft materials created by the research team2. Within a pragmatic randomised controlled trial to assess whether use of this guidea. reduces the levels of pain experienced by the womenb. improves quality of life, self-efficacy and psychological well beingc. reduces the number of primary and secondary care consultations and other resource used. provides a cost-effective intervention3. To assess the acceptability and feasibility of the guide to women and health professionals within a real-life setting4. To understand facilitators and barriers to using the guidePlan of InvestigationWe will undertake a pragmatic exploratory individually-randomised trial comparing GP-facilitated use of the guide to standard care over a 6 month period. 140 participants will be recruited from GP consultations and advertisement. Participants allocated to the control arm will be offered the guide after the end of the 6 month randomised period. The study will be performed in approximately 8 to10 GP practices and participating GPs will be trained in the use of the guide. Prior to the start of the trial the current pilot guide will be refined using a nominal group methodology including both professionals and patientsFollowing the treatment period we will conduct semi-structured interviews with women participants and GPs to assess the feasibility and acceptability of the intervention.Potential ImpactWomen with chronic pelvic pain (CPP) maybe entered into a cycle of re-investigation and re-referral, many become dissatisfied and disengage from care. GPs recognise the need for a self-management but feel they have nothing in their armoury to help women with CPP. This study will benefit patients by providing an evidence-based self-help resource to help support women in the self-management of their condition. The guide will have the capacity to modify experience of symptoms, reduce psychological distress. If the trial demonstrates that the guide is effective it can be made available for clinical use almost immediately.General practitioners will benefit from the guide, as it will be a useful adjunct to the prescription of analgesic medication, currently the primary treatment.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Telephone consultation as a substitute for routine out-patient face-to-face consultation for children with inflammatory bowel disease: randomised controlled trial and economic evaluation
Abstract: BackgroundCrohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis, collectively known as inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), are chronic bowel disorders characterised by recurrent relapses alternating with periods of remission. The annual UK incidence of IBD in people AimsThe proposed study will test the hypothesis that telephone consultation is effective, safe, and a cost-effective alternative to traditional routine face-to-face consultation for children and adolescents with IBD. The specific aims are to determine whether routine out-patient review by telephone would:1. have a positive impact on patients’ quality of life2. have no adverse effects on patients’ disease course 3. have no adverse effects on patients’ growth4. have a positive impact on patient/carer satisfaction with out-patient consultations5. reduce out-patient non-attendance rate6. reduce IBD-related costs incurred by patients and their carers and7. be cost-effective for the NHSPlan of InvestigationThe study will be a randomised controlled trial. There are approximately 250 patients aged between 8 and16 years who attend the regional paediatric IBD centre in Manchester. They will be invited to participate until we have recruited 92 patients. Allowing for an attrition rate of 20%, this should enable us to reach our target of 74 evaluable participants. After providing informed consent, participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups: telephone consultations or usual face-to-face consultations. Outcomes that will be assessed over the 2-year follow-up period include quality of life, relapses, anthropometric measures, patient satisfaction, NHS resource use, and costs to the NHS and to patients/carers. Data will be analysed on an intention-to-treat basis.Potential ImpactThe study will provide the NHS with good quality evidence that will guide decisions on the use of telephone consultations in paediatric IBD. If telephone consultations prove to be effective, children with IBD could be offered the choice of either telephone consultation or face-to-face consultation for their routine out-patient follow-up. Those who are doing well would not have to make unnecessary journeys to hospitals. This is likely to reduce DNA (did not attend) rates. By freeing up out-patient clinic spaces, access for patients in relapse and for newly referred patients could be improved, thus reducing waiting times for appointments. The findings of this study could also be applicable to the routine follow-up of children with other chronic diseases.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Delayed antibiotic prescribing for respiratory tract infections - an evidence synthesis of individual patient data
Abstract: "Background: Between 2010 and 2013, antibiotic prescribing in primary care rose by 4.1%. Antibiotic prescribing in primary care for respiratory tract infections is common, and mostly unjustifiable since most infections are self- limiting, symptomatic benefit from antibiotics is modest and complications are rare. With major public health concerns about anti-microbial resistance and calls to prevent the overuse of antibiotics, suitable strategies are needed to reduce especially antibiotic use in primary care which is where most antibiotic are prescribed. Delayed prescribing can be a useful strategy, as it allows the patient to collect an antibiotic prescription if their symptoms do not improve in the days following the consultation. This “wait and see” approach can strike a balance between reducing antibiotic prescribing and providing a safety net for those patients who do not improve or worsen. A recent Cochrane review concluded that a delayed prescribing strategy was not significantly different to immediate prescribing in terms of clinical outcomes for cough and cold. For acute otitis media and sore throat immediate antibiotics were more effective than delayed for fever, pain and malaise in some studies. But the review noted a high level of heterogeneity between studies made combining them in a meta-analysis difficult and did not allow sufficient power for the examination of subgroups (Spurling et al). Moreover the review included only randomised trials, not observational studies. An individual patient data (IPD) meta-analysis is considered the ""gold standard"" for meta-analysis and undertaking such an analysis would allow questions to be answered that cannot be answered using aggregate data or any single dataset. Design: Individual patient data meta-analysis of both randomised controlled trials and observational studies. Objectives: 1) To use individual patient data from both RCTs and observational studies to calculate key outcome measures (duration of illness
Funding_and_Awards_Link: probability of developing complications/requiring reconsultation side effects and patient satisfaction)
Award Budget: giving more robust estimates of the clinical effectiveness of a delayed prescribing strategy. 2) To explore whether there are interactions between the treatment group and certain key subgroups

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Before Arrival at Hospital: Factors affecting timing of hospitalisation for children with serious infectious illness. An exploratory study. (The BeArH project).
Abstract: Background Infection is a major cause of childhood deaths in the UK and globally, particularly in the first 5 years of life, yet little is known about factors influencing children s journeys to hospital with serious infectious illness (SII). Many of these deaths are avoidable as infections such as pneumonia and meningococcal disease are amenable to treatment, if provided in time [5]. Given the lack of research exploring the pre-hospital pathways of children with SII, identification of all modifiable steps in the child s journey to hospital admission is urgently needed so that evidence based solutions can be developed. Aim To retrospectively identify organizational and environmental factors and individual child, family and professional factors affecting timing of admission to hospital for children with serious infectious illness in Leicestershire and East Northamptonshire. Methods A mixed methods grounded theory design [6-9] will be used in two stages and two geographical areas (a District General Hospital and a Teaching Hospital and their catchment areas). Stage 1: Anonymised documentary analysis of existing evidence: child death reviews, critical incident reports for all child deaths under 5 years of age in two study areas; hospital and ambulance data on service use; and a mapping exercise to detail services for sick children in each area. Stage 2a: Individual children s journeys to hospital admission between November 2017 and March 2018 inclusive focusing on the child s journey from becoming ill to being admitted to hospital with a SII. Parents will be recruited in the hospital setting no less than 48 hours post-admission, then interviewed after discharge or death of the child. Parents will be asked to identify health professionals involved in their child s pre-hospital care and asked for permission for the researchers to contact these professionals to interview them about their involvement in the child s care. Stage 2b: Past experiences of parents and professionals of children s journeys. This stage will focus on parents who have had at least one child who has had a SII and health professionals who have had experience of caring for such children in first contact services between 2011 and 2016. Focus groups will be conducted with parents recruited through our charity partners and separately, with professionals recruited through the Clinical Research Network, local medical committees and snowballing through existing contacts. Data from Stage 1, 2a and 2b will be subject to constant comparative analysis in line with grounded theory methodology. Cycles of data collection and analysis will be used to generate an emerging theory at which point existing knowledge will be examined for its explanatory contribution. The result will be a grounded theory explaining the positive and negative factors influencing children s journeys to hospital when they have SII. Potential benefits to patients and the NHS The primary outcome will be a grounded theory which: identifies child, family and professional factors affecting the timing of admission to hospital for children with SII in two contrasting areas; explains family and professional decision making for children with SII pre-hospitalisation; identifies human factors influencing families and professionals in primary/secondary first contact health services for children with SII; and identifies environmental and organisational modifiable factors. These findings will form the basis for intervention design and the feasibility study to follow, designed to optimise the timing of presentation to hospital of children with SII. Effective interventions would be expected to reduce morbidity, mortality, family distress, NHS costs associated with treatment, hospital admissions and litigation (estimated cost of failure/delay in diagnosis was over £20m in legal settlements in the 12 years up to 2011 [5]). Supported by the UK Sepsis Trust, Meningitis Now, the Meningitis Research Foundation and t

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The practicality, acceptability and impact of self-consent procedures for the schools-based HPV vaccination programme
Abstract: BACKGROUND. High coverage of Human Papillomavirus vaccination (HPV) programmes, administered in early adolescence, can substantially reduce cervical cancer incidence and mortality. However, research suggests lower socio-economic status (SES), some ethnic groups, and not attending mainstream school are all associated with lower uptake of HPV vaccination. Lack of written parental consent is a key reason why some young women do not receive the vaccine. The national legal framework allows girls to be vaccinated without parental consent provided they are deemed Fraser competent, but there is some reticence about vaccinating without written parental consent. AIM. To examine the implementation, acceptability and impact of self-consent procedures for HPV vaccination. PLAN OF INVESTGATION. The study comprises: a systematic review; process evaluation, and; statistical analyses of routine data concerning HPV vaccination uptake in two local authorities with low uptake (Bristol and South Gloucestershire). 1] The systematic review will include quantitative and qualitative studies relating to adolescent self-consent for vaccines. A comprehensive search strategy will be implemented across all relevant databases from inception to the present. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, assess relevant full texts, and extract information about study characteristics, methodology and findings. For quantitative studies, meta-analysis will be undertaken if appropriate, but if heterogeneity is strong the studies will be presented as a narrative review. For qualitative studies, results from individual studies will be extracted, interpreted and combined through identifying key themes across the studies. 2] For the process evaluation, a logic model will be developed, in consultation with relevant stakeholders, to show the links between inputs (self-consent procedures) and short- and medium-term outcomes (HPV vaccine implementation and uptake) that may lead to desired longer-term outcomes (increased uptake, reduced health inequalities). Context will be examined through stakeholder questionnaires, observations and field notes. The implementation of self-consent, and response to it, will be explored through observations and audio-recorded interviews/focus groups with young people, school nurses, school staff and parents in eight schools purposively selected in relation to the SES and ethnicity of students, and type of school. Thematic analysis of the qualitative data will employ the Framework method. 3] We will examine routine Public Health England (PHE) data on HPV vaccination uptake by geographical area, and data from the Child Health Information System (CHIS). Data fields extracted will include: ethnicity, postcode (to assign area deprivation score), and school. We will test whether there has been an increase in HPV vaccination uptake in two ways. First, is there an increase when comparing before and after the change in our intervention sites? Second, is there evidence that the % change in our intervention sites is different from comparison sites (similar to our intervention sites in terms of initial HPV uptake, ethnicity and deprivation levels) in England where no such intervention took place? DISSEMINATION. We will produce a report with findings and recommendations about self-consent to present at events/workshops with healthcare professionals. Two papers will be written for peer-reviewed journals, and conference presentations. A summary of results will be shared with school nurses, school staff, young people and parents/carers as requested. School nurses will be encouraged to contribute to dissemination activities. Findings will also be disseminated through appropriate websites and social media. POTENTIAL BENEFITS TO PATIENTS AND THE NHS. Increasing uptake of HPV vaccination has the potential to reduce cervical cancer incidence, saving lives and reducing costs to the health service. The research results will be shared with NHS

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The effectiveness of interventions to promote patients' and families' involvement in adult intensive care settings: a systematic review.
Abstract: Background: Despite increasing concern from policymakers and the public over a number of years (IoM 2001, NHS FYFV 2015) for greater patient and family member involvement (PFMI) in healthcare, this aspiration has not yet been met. Intensive care units (ICU) are a case in point, where PFMI can have profound consequences for care decisions, delivery and outcomes. Family members/carers have a special role since ICU patients are rarely in a position to communicate directly with clinicians, recollect their ICU experience and engage fully with the complexity of their condition. Studies have confirmed that family members can have a positive influence on a patient s care and recovery from ICU (Bench et al. 2016, Liput et al. 2016); but also that family members themselves can be adversely affected by an ICU stay even after discharge (Azoulay et al. 2014). The past decade has witnessed different, mainly local attempts at promoting PFMI in ICU; however, these lack a standard approach, which contributes to great variation in family satisfaction across UK ICUs (Wright et al. 2015). As an initial stage in a longer-term programme of research that aims to improve healthcare outcomes for intensive care patients as well as experiences for their families, this project will complete a systematic review of interventions designed to promote PFMI in adult intensive care settings. Aim: We aim to answer the following question: What are the available interventions, and which are most effective, for including patients and family members in the care processes and decisions made in adult intensive care settings? In doing so, we will develop a classification matrix of interventions, known as a typology, that takes into account their effectiveness and quality of their evidence base. Plan of investigation: We will employ well-recognised methods for searching, screening, abstracting, quality assessing and synthesising the included literature. A review protocol will be registered with the PROSPERO database. We will search a series of sources selected with the purpose of ensuring comprehensive coverage of the literature on PFMI, including the MEDLINE, EMBASE and CINAHL databases; as well as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Joanna Briggs and Cochrane Library with no date restriction. Manual searches of recent back issues of leading ICU journals will also be undertaken, as will the reference lists of included studies. Unpublished literature will be sought through grey literature databases. All evaluation studies that consider interventions to promote PFMI in adult ICUs will be included. All research designs will be eligible. Abstracts and papers will be independently screened by at least two members of the team to determine their inclusion. Included papers will be assessed for methodological rigour using a standard rating approach, which assesses quality of study and quality of information . Quality assessment will be completed by at least two members of the team. Data on interventions, evaluation methods and outcomes will be collated using a predetermined extraction table. These are likely to be heterogeneous in nature, which will mean that the review will follow a narrative approach to synthesis. Potential benefits to patients and the NHS: We will develop a typology of interventions that promote PFMI in ICU that takes into account their effectiveness, quality of their evidence base and factors that support or impede involvement. This will be made available for use by ICU clinicians to inform their decision-making for adopting particular approaches to PFMI for their units; and considered by ICU patients and their relatives/carers who may wish to be more involved in their care. Our team will draw from this typology to inform the development of a follow-up study to empirically validate and contextualise this typology in NHS settings.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Creating and validating a tool for identifying and addressing unwarranted variation in GP prescribing behaviour
Abstract: Research question We aim to develop new methods to identify CCGs and practices that are outliers in prescribing behaviour; validate these methods; implement them as a tool on the OpenPrescribing site; then further iterate on the tool following clinician and user feedback. Background Our previous research has highlighted substantial variation in prescribing beghaviours, across various different areas of medicine. Variation is sometimes partially explained by demographic changes, or by Clinical Commissioning Group (CCG) policy, but much of the remaining variation is unexplained. OpenPrescribing is an openly accessible online data tool, used by 80,000 people in the past year including clinicians, pharmacists and medicines optimisation teams. Having developed a large body of standard measures driven by clinical evidence and experience, we are now using innovative data science techniques to identify and validate new signals suggestive of unusual prescribing. This innovative approach can help identify problematic prescribing across all drugs and GP practices in England, in order to target work to improve quality of care. Aims and Objectives Our aim is to develop new computational approaches that will identify unwarranted variation in prescribing behaviour, and help clinicians and medicines optimisation teams to explore and address that variation. Specific objectives to achieve this are: Develop and refine new methods of outlier detection Implement these new methods as tools on OpenPrescribing.net Validate and iteratively improve the tool with clinicians and users. Methods Our pilot work using data-driven approaches to discover unusual prescribing has uncovered numerous promising methods for identifying outliers in both cross-sectional and time-series data. For example, we have run analyses looking for prescribing behaviours with unusual distributions, such as those with extreme values of skew and kurtosis, to identify prescribing behaviours exhibited by only a small number of practices; and examined practices that are unusually fast or slow at responding to safety alerts, price changes, or guidance. We will further refine the methods we have piloted, add additional methods as appropriate, then use our software engineers to implement the methods into a freely accessible tool for the use of GPs, medicines optimisation teams, policy makers and other users. Feedback from users will then be used to iteratively refine the tools. Timelines for delivery We will have a working prototype of the tool available within 9 months of the start of the project. This will give us ample time to improve the tool by adding additional methods of outlier detection, improving features in response to feedback, and optimise the tool to ensure it is fast and reliable. Anticipated Impact and Dissemination All tools developed will be implemented on the freely and openly accessible OpenPrescribing site, which had 80,000 unique users last year. We expect user numbers will continue to rise with the inclusion of additional features. We will also seek to actively promote the new tools with site visits at CCGs, engaging with policy makers, conventional academic publications, conference presentations, and our substantial social media following.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: South Tyneside and Sunderland NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Barriers to uptake of colorectal cancer screening: a qualitative study to understand non-participation in the Bowel Cancer Screening Programme.
Abstract: BackgroundThe national bowel cancer screening programme (BCSP) commenced in England and Wales in 2007. Uptake of BCS is 52%, lower than for breast (75%) or cervical (80%) screening. BCSP uptake is lower in men and people of certain ethnicity and from lower socioeconomic groups. Variation may be explained by social patterning (Crockett 2008) and models of health behaviour. Non-participation reasons include palatability; fear of investigations; fear or a lack of fear of cancer (Van Ryins 2008). A meta-analysis of interventions to increase uptake concluded that it is most likely achieved by organisational change in staffing and procedures (Stone 2002). The need to understand population beliefs and behaviour prior to developing interventions has been repeatedly stated (Pasick 2004, Rabeneck 2007).AimsThis study will explore reasons for non-participation in BCSP and identify interventions to improve uptake. Our initial objectives will be to develop an understanding of the beliefs and health behaviours of non-participants in BCS. Systematic review of the evidence regarding non-participation in screening will inform an interview schedule for a qualitative study of people living in North East England who have declined BCS. We will explore reasons for non participation in BCSP and seek suggestions regarding strategies that might have inclined them to participate. The study findings will be used to develop specific strategies to increase BCS participation. Subsequent work will study the effectiveness of these interventions in increasing participation and reducing inequalities in BCSP uptake.Plan of InvestigationBCSP non participants will be invited to participate in semi-structured interviews undertaken by an experienced qualitative researcher. Data collection and analysis will be carried out using strategies consistent with grounded theory (Strauss and Corbin, 2008). Open-ended questions will cover beliefs associated with the FOB test and BCS as well as reasons for non participation. Data collection and analysis will take place concurrently. Analysis will be based on the constant comparative method. Development of initial categories and assumptions will be challenged by deviant case analysis and use of additional theoretical sampling. Data will be coded into themes and indexed using the computer programme Nudist NVIVO. Results will be used to develop interventions to improve BCS participation.Potential ImpactSeveral non UK studies have identified factors involved in decision making regarding BCS. UK strategies may differ due to differences in health policy & cultural factors. Several studies have examined barriers to BCS uptake (O’Sullivan and Orbell, 2004) and have helped us understand underlying reasons (Chapple 2008; Jepson 2007). The majority of participants from these studies were, however, BCS participants. This study will uniquely focus on individuals who declined BCS and they will be able to reflect on their decision making, reasons for non-participation and factors that might have inclined them to undergo screening. The data will be used to develop specific interventions to improve BCS participation & reduce inequalities. Further work will evaluate the impact of these strategies.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Feasibility Study of a Cognitive Behavioural Suicide Prevention Intervention for Male Prisoners
Abstract: BackgroundIn 2007, there were 22,459 recorded incidents of suicidal behaviour in prisons in England and Wales, resulting in 92 suicidal deaths – a rate 5 times greater than for the general population. Coping with a prison environment that embodies fear, distrust, and a lack of control, can leave prisoners feeling overwhelmed and hopeless, leading some of them to choose suicide as a way to escape. We have developed and manualised a new talking therapy intervention for suicidal behaviour (Cognitive Behavioural Suicide Prevention, CBSP). Our individualised treatment offers a structured, theoretically-based, psychological intervention designed to address and amend the specific psychological architecture responsible for suicidal behaviour in prisoners, using established cognitive-behavioural techniques.AimsThe aim of this study is to demonstrate the feasibility of delivering our existing CBSP intervention in a prison environment. We will also investigate how best to adapt the delivery of CBSP for prisoners. To address these aims, Work Package 1 will be a randomised controlled trial (RCT) with 30 prisoners at risk of suicidal behaviour receiving CBSP plus usual treatment. Another 30 prisoners, also at risk, will receive their usual treatment alone. The RCT will be nested within Work Package 2, which will inform and subsequently assess the delivery of CBSP to prisoners. Prisoner interviews and a staff focus group will examine views on how CBSP should be modified for the prison environment. Work Package 3 will be a 6-month follow-up study of the longer-term impact of the intervention.????Plan of InvestigationThis study will take place in a male closed training prison in the northwest of England (HMP Wymott), that holds prisoners who have typically received a sentence of 2 or more years. Participants will be prisoners identified by staff as at risk of suicidal behaviour.Work Package 1: We will conduct an exploratory RCT of the CBSP intervention with a sample of 30 prisoners, compared to treatment as usual.Work Package 2: To address potential contextual issues, enhance and subsequently evaluate the delivery of CBSP, we will use qualitative methods to explore prisoners’ and staff’s experiences of the intervention. Work Package 3: To investigate the longer-term impact of the CBSP intervention, participants will be invited to assessment interviews as part of a 6-month follow up study.Potential ImpactThe costs of suicide to society are high, especially once indirect costs are included, e.g. lost productivity. Nevertheless, the economic costs can seem small in comparison to the ‘intangible costs’; the grief, anger and abandonment of family and friends, and the lost potential of lives cut short. Prisoners are from marginalised populations that have poor access to health care in the community. Therefore, periods of incarceration offer important opportunities for treatment interventions that stand to benefit not only the prisoners themselves, but also the larger public health with potential downstream savings in other publicly funded services. Furthermore, the improvement of prison healthcare, including prisoner mortality, has now become the responsibility of NHS services.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: The NHS Health Check (vascular risk assessment and management programme): predictors of the uptake of screening and the adoption of successful self management behaviour at 12 months.
Abstract: BackgroundThe NHS Health Check Programme is to be rolled out across England. By 2013, every practice will be inviting 20% of their patients each year to have their risk of developing a vascular disease assessed and receive appropriate lifestyle advice or medication. The programme has two aims: to reduce the incidence of vascular illness and to reduce health inequalities. Recent editorials have suggested that the non-White British and socially deprived populations may find ‘the offer’ less acceptable and have greater difficulty complying with advice. If the Health Check Programme reduces vascular risk to a lesser degree in those groups, who are already at higher risk of developing a vascular illness, it may not achieve its aims and may have the effect of increasing health inequalities.Aims1 to understand, at an early stage, how the Health Check programme is impacting on health and inequalities 2 characterise the groups that are taking up and benefitting from the programme3 determine which, if any, demographic groups are benefitting disproportionately4 elicit patient and NHS staff perspectives on the barriers and facilitators of uptake and health behaviour change5 synthesise quantitative and qualitative data to create recommendations to improve uptake and outcomes 6 check and refine those recommendations with frontline staff and disseminate widely to inform others establishing a Health Check ProgrammePlan of InvestigationUsing biomedical and process data from five pilot Health Check practices we will map uptake and health benefits across demographic groups to examine equity of uptake and benfit and the strategies that appear more sucessful. In a qualitative arm, we will interview attendees and non-attendees, to discover reasons for accepting or refusing the offer and, in those attending, their initial reaction and intentions to change. Twelve months later we will re-interview those who attended to explore the barriers and facilitators of health behaviour change and how they perceive themselves, their health and the programme. With frontline clinical staff we will explore the findings and formulate recommendations to disseminate to those establishing the programme acoss England.Potential ImpactIf we can discover why people do and do not benefit, especially those in ‘hard to reach’ groups it should be possible to develop strategies to improve uptake and outcomes. PCTs around the UK are uncertain how to deliver this mandatory programme in an effective and equitable fashion and will welcome the information. Around the world, in reaction to a ‘tsunami’ of chronic illness and health system costs, there is a movement to promote both prevention and better self-management of chronic disease and an awareness that these programmes often fail to reach the socially disadvantaged and those at most need. The information we seek is likely to have a wide audience and an impact far beyond the NHS Health Check Programme.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Graded Exercise Therapy guided SElf-help Treatment (GETSET) for patients with chronic fatigue syndrome: a randomised controlled trial in secondary care
Abstract: BackgroundThe chronic fatigue syndrome, also known as myalgic encephalomyelitis (CFS/ME), is characterised by chronic disabling fatigue and other symptoms, which are not explained by an alternative diagnosis. The prognosis is poor and patient management consumes significant NHS resources. NICE recommend graded exercise therapy (GET) as one of two effective and safe treatments (cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) being the other). But surveys of ME charity members suggest that GET is unacceptable and harmful, and that they prefer self-help. GET and CBT are also therapist intensive and thus expensive. Self-help based on CBT seems helpful, but GET self-help has not been tested.AimsThe main aim of this pragmatic two arm trial is to determine the acceptability, efficacy and safety of specialist medical care (SMC) supplemented by Graded Exercise Therapy guided SElf-help Treatment (GETSET), compared to SMC alone, for patients diagnosed with CFS/ME attending secondary care specialist CFS/ME clinics.The secondary aim is to determine whether GETSET is as cost-effective as having SMC alone. The tertiary aim is to examine moderators of efficacy.Plan of InvestigationThis is a pragmatic, two arms, observer blinded, randomised controlled trial of patients with a clinical diagnosis of CFS/ME, attending two specialist CFS/ME clinics who have been referred for practitioner delivered therapy. Trial follow-up will be 12 weeks after randomisation or at the start of therapy, whichever is sooner. We will compare SMC plus Graded Exercise Therapy guided SElf-help Treatment (GETSET) to SMC alone. GETSET will consist of a booklet describing a six-step programme of graded exercise self-help, and two telephone consultations with a GETSET-trained physiotherapist. The control group will continue to receive SMC. The primary outcome will be self-rated physical disability. Secondary outcomes will include overall change, symptoms, global function and healthcare costs.Potential ImpactThis will directly benefit patients who, once diagnosed, often spend many months waiting for rehabilitative therapy with little or no progress being made during that time. A clinically useful self-help approach provides advantages to both the patient and the NHS, since patient outcomes will improve while healthcare costs are reduced. If this trial shows GETSET to be acceptable, safe and comparatively effective, then the GETSET booklet could be made freely and publically available by website with the knowledge that clinics can recommend it with minimal guidance. The pragmatic approach (almost all clinically diagnosed patients being eligible) in this trial mean that GETSET will be generalisable to usual NHS practice.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Women Offenders Repeat Self-Harm Intervention Pilot II (WORSHIP II)
Abstract: BackgroundOnly 5% of the prison population is women, but they account for almost half of self-harm (SH) incidents in prison. This is a rate of 333 per 100,000 compared with a rate of 62 per 100,000 for men.The extent and seriousness of SH in women’s prisons is increasing and is a serious health concern. Rates of suicide are also far greater in women in prison. Services are required to develop close partnerships so prisoners have access to healthcare as the general population. A recent review in 2010 highlighted a need for development of evidence based SH prevention strategies for female prisoners; currently few exist, none are women-centred and none has been evaluated.There is an urgent need to develop targeted interventions to enable shared understanding and approaches to SH in female prisoners.AimsExamine efficacy of Psychodynamic-Interpersonal Therapy (PIT) versus an Active Control (AC) for repeat self-harm (SH), measured by suicidal ideation, thoughts of SH, repetition & severity of SH in women prisoners. Objectives. Immediately post therapy & 6 months post randomisation measure: 1) suicidal ideation & thoughts of SH 2) number of SH events, time to next event, severity of event (fatal, near fatal or not) and method 3) undertake process evaluation to assess factors associated with adherence and acceptability of the intervention (participant perception of usefulness, on-going skill usage & satisfaction) 4) assess feasibility of following women prisoners 6 months following randomisation 5) pilot methods for collection of prison resource allocation data incurred as a result of SH.Plan of InvestigationIn months: 0-3: Form Trial Management Group (TMG) & Trial Steering Group (TSG); recruit research assistant; update literature review; ethical, managerial and governance approvals; coordinate and publicise project in the two prisons; PIT training of TW and Therapists. 3-26: Recruitment amd randomisation of 120 particpants; deliver interventions; develop follow up methodology to access women at 6 months; blinded assessments completed before and post therapy and at 6 months follow-up; co-ordination of TMG and TSG meetings; continued contact with prisons; develop process evaluation interview and interview 20 prisoners and 20 prison staff. 26-32: Transcription of qualitative data and thematic analysis of interviews; quantitative data analysis. 32-36: Write, submit, disseminate report.Potential ImpactRecent government policy highlights the need for evidence based SH prevention strategies for women in prisons. Engagement of women offenders in a targeted, women-centred, short-term intervention for SH, we anticipate a reduction in the level of thoughts of SH, in repetition and severity of SH, and in the risk and therfore rates of suicide in this high risk group. Relationships between prison staff and women may also improve and rehabilitative work within prisons is also likely to benefit from reduced intent to SH and reductions in SH behaviour by female prisoners. Prison resources are diverted at great cost to staff and women in order to manage repeat SH.These will be able to be employed again more appropriately in rehabilitative work.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A feasibility study of a self-management stroke programme (SMP) : a cluster randomised controlled trial
Abstract: BackgroundThe incidence of stroke in the UK is high, 6000 people every year in London are left with a disability. People with stroke are high users of the NHS, annually PCT’s in London spend £1.7 million on community care and rehabilitation. Despite improvements in stroke care across the NHS, stroke survivors can feel ill-prepared to cope with discharge from rehabilitation. The UK Stroke Strategy emphasised a need to expand self-management programmes (SMPs) for people with stroke. To date few programmes have been developed for the stroke population and no study has tested the feasibility of training the community stroke team to deliver a SMP integrated within usual practice. AimsThe aim is to determine the feasibility of integrating and evaluating the delivery of a self-management programme included within a current stroke rehabilitation programme. The findings of this study will inform the next stage of research which will test the clinical effectiveness of a self-management programme in a fully powered cluster randomised controlled trial. The study also aims to monitor fidelity of the SMP according to pre-determined quality markers, explore contextual factors associated with variation between cluster sites; acceptibility of the SMP to patients, carers and clinicians, impact on quality of life, function and mood and cost effectiveness. Plan of InvestigationThe study will be conducted over 22 months with 5 phases. Community stroke teams n=4, will be recruited and randomly allocated to control or intervention (2 per group). Intervention teams will undergo training to use the SMP. 80 stroke participants will be recruited over 11 months (20 each site). An embedded process evaluation will be completed by month 19, including an economic evaluation and qualitative research. Participants, carers and clinicians will be interviewed in intervention and control sites. Clinical outcomes e.g. quality of life, function and mood will be collected at 3 time points by outcome assessors masked to allocation, by month 17. Analysis of process and clinical data completed by month 20. Reports and dissemination of findings will be completed by month 22. Potential ImpactAn integrated SMP will offer the opportunity for stroke rehabilitation and post hospital care to align more closely to policy and research on other long term conditions which advocate a person-centred approach through self-management. A SMP which can be successfully integrated into rehabilitation practice in stroke teams across the UK has the potential to improve patient care. It could decrease dependency on professional input after stroke reducing use of NHS resources. A SMP which enables stroke survivors to gain greater confidence to self-manage could also impact on health outcomes such as quality of life.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Birmingham and Solihull Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A pilot study of a social network intervention for heroin users in opiate substitution treatment
Abstract: BackgroundHeroin addiction causes a huge burden on society, with a treatment budget of £400 million/year. Opiate substitution treatment (OST) is an effective harm reduction measure, but more emphasis needs to be given to moving people away from drug use and into healthy and productive lives. NICE has highlighted the evidence for psychosocial treatments for heroin dependence, and family/social network interventions are promising for two reasons: (i) by involving family and friends in the treatment process there are opportunities for generalization of the effects beyond an episode of professional treatment (ii) treatment may reduce the considerable physical & psychological health burden of drug misuse on family & friends. Despite this, the vast majority of NHS treatment is individually-basedAimsIn order to prepare for a definitive trial of a social network intervention for heroin addiction this pilot study will test 5 elements: (1) feasibility of training NHS clinicians with no past experience of working with family members/friends to deliver an evidence-based intervention (Social Behaviour and Network Therapy, SBNT) (2) feasibility of recruiting patients engaged in drug treatment services for at least a year but still reporting heroin use to a trial of SBNT, with a 12 month follow-up (3) whether SBNT reduces heroin use 3 and 12 months after treatment, and potential mediating factors (4) methodology for evaluating quality of life measures that move beyond purely health outcomes (5) feasibility of measuring changes in health and functioning of network members before and after SBNTPlan of InvestigationAll patients engaged in OST but still using heroin in two NHS community drug treatment teams (Solihull & Leicester) will be invited to take part. Two clinicians per team will be trained in a 4-session manual-driven intervention (SBNT), and a further 2 in a 4-session case management intervention. Participants will be randomised to one of the two interventions or treatment as usual. Forty patients will be recruited to each of three arms, and interviewed at baseline and 3 and12 months after the start of the intervention. The primary outcome will be illicit heroin use (urinalysis & self-report), but secondary outcomes will include physical & mental health, crime, quality of life and social network composition. The impact of the treatment on family and other network members will be evaluatedPotential ImpactShort-term impact: we will have tested the ability of NHS clinicians to deliver SBNT in routine practice, going some way to overcoming traditional resistance to working with and supporting family and other network membersLonger-term impact: information will be gathered about the feasibility of a larger multicentre trial. In particular this will include whether the participants in the target population can be recruited in sufficient numbers, the utility of the measures used (including health economic instruments and methods), the size of any reductions in heroin or prescribed opiate use, and the feasibility of evaluating the impact of treatment on the participant’s social network members

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Rotherham Doncaster and South Humber NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Preventing unplanned repeat pregnancy in teenage mothers: a qualitative study of patients’ and professionals’ experiences of nurse led home based sexual health care.
Abstract: Background There is a very high risk that one unplanned teenage pregnancy will result in another. Around 30% of babies born to mothers aged 16-19 are second children - this compounds the well know social, economic and health problems caused by unplanned teenage pregnancy. Efforts to prevent this and promote sexual health with teenage mothers is a vital element of sexual health work. There is some evidence that home based inteventions can contribute to this goal but the evidence base for how young mothers experience this type of care and how professionals see their role in providing this care is lacking. A novel home care contraceptive service, P2P, currently helps 200 teenage mothers in Doncaster every year and a detailed understanding of how patients and other stakeholders view and experience this type of care will help improve the benefits of this care to patients. This type of patient care was pioneered in Doncaster and is the longest running NHS service in the UK of its kind. Other, emerging services exist in the NHS, but they are modelled on the P2P approach to patient care. No guidelines for the delivery of this type of patient care exist and, as this type of care is mainly in its infancy in the UK, drawing on the patient experience will contribute significantly to the development of similar services elsewhere in the NHS. Aims of the project The specific aims of the study are to: Explore new young mothers' (16-19 yrs) experiences of nurse led contraceptive home care and how does this affect their future sexual and reproductive health and behaviour. Explore the views and experiences of professional stakeholders who work with this group of women. Develop guidelines for the development of nurse led home based contraceptive care for new teen mothers. Research plan This qualitative study will conduct in-depth interviews with 20-25 teenage mothers who have recently experienced P2P care and also 20-25 interviews with women who have recieved home based sexual health care in the previous 2 years. We will also conduct 3 focus groups with P2P health professionals. Data will be analysed using a 'Framework' approach and findings will be used to gain an in-depth understanding of how teen mothers experience this type of care in order to inform the development of this type of patient care both locally and nationally through the development of care guidelines, reports and publications. Benefits to the NHS The prevention of a repeat teenage pregnancy has numerous benefits. It improves the health and life chances of the child and also the mother. It also reduces the risk of mental and physical health problems in the new mother. It removes the risk associated with a termination of the repeat pregnancy - which has mental health benefits for the woman and also has an economic impact on termination services. Undertaking research to address the current gaps in the knowledge base about home based sexual health care will help improve this type of health care for the 200 new teenage mother seen in Doncaster every year - it will also inform the development of this type of care throughout the NHS. Why we are well placed to do this study The project team is comprised of researchers with experience of qualitative projects related to the sexual health of young people as well as project management expertise. The team contains experienced NHS clinical staff with experience of sexual health work with young people and the delivery and management of NHS sexual and reproductive health services. Inclusion of service users on the project advisory group also adds strength to the team.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A pilot study to investigate improvements in physical fitness and quality of life resulting from a 9 week structured responsive endurance training programme (SRETP) following neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy prior to elective rectal cancer surgery
Abstract: BACKGROUND Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (NACRT) for advanced rectal cancer is associated with better local disease control, with minimal impact on survival (4,5). Exercise improves bowel cancer outcome. Stated by the BBC (August 2011) “The risk of dying from bowel cancer can be reduced if physically activity” (11,12). Cancer and chemotherapy are known to cause fatigue via oxidative stress, leading to muscle weakness and poor quality of life (6). Moreover, aerobic exercise, decreases oxidative stress (14). We have pilot data showing that NACRT reduces physical fitness in upper and lower GI cancer surgery (8,9). The literature shows that low fitness (high-risk patients) is associated with a higher risk of adverse outcome (death and serious complication) after major surgery (13-16,21,22). Exercise training improves HRQL, reduces complications and is safe in elderly cancer patients (15-20).We have feasibility data showing that the reduction fitness caused by NACRT can be improved. AIMS This proposal therefore outlines a study to explore: PRIMARY HYPOTHESIS A 9-week SRETP compared with a control group (no training) will result in a clinically significant difference in physical fitness (2.0ml/kg/min VO2 at LT) in patients who have had NACRT prior to cancer surgery. SECONDARY OUTCOMES A 9-week SRETP compared with a control group (no training) will result in a clinically significant difference in physical fitness (2.0ml/kg/min VO2 Peak) post NACRT prior to cancer surgery SRETP following NACRT and prior to cancer surgery will provide psychological health benefits and improve patient s HRQL (assessed by semi-structured interviews and questionnaires -EORTC QLQ-30 and EQ-5D). EXPLORATORY OUTCOMES 1. To investigate whether SRETP following NACRT and prior to cancer surgery is associated with a change in physical activity (assessed by the number of steps while active using an accelerometer) 2.
