To investigate whether there is a change in the day 7 surgical morbidity (using POMS) and mortality. 3. The effect of SRETP on cancer downstaging post-NACRT (TNM staging). PLAN OF INVESTIGATION (See Annex 1) We propose a prospective, parallel group, RCT using a 9-week SRETP in patients undergoing NACRT prior to cancer resection in two NHS hospitals. Physiological data will be analysed by an investigator blinded to study group allocation. Physical fitness before and at intervals (0, 3, 6, 9 and 14 weeks) after NACRT measured using CPET. Block randomization by centre carried out post-NACRT to an exercise (SRETP) and control group (no training) in a 1:1 distribution. The SRETP will have 3 sessions per week for 9 weeks, whilst the negative control group will be given general exercise advice. At week 9, both groups will undergo standard care cancer staging scans and a CPET. CPET is also performed at weeks 14. Activity monitors (SenseWear Pro Accelerometer) will be fitted pre-, during and post-NACRT (week 3 and 9) to measure change in physical activity. HRQL questionnaires (EORTC-QLQc30v3, EQ-5D) will also be carried out on activity monitoring sessions as above, as well as 6 weeks post-operatively. HRQL semi-structured interviews will be carried out by a psychologist at the end of the SRETP. Postoperative outcomes will be objectively recorded using POMS (Day, 5, 7 and 14). PATIENT BENEFIT If the hypotheses are supported by the study results, patients: - Will improve baseline fitness and regain control of their pre-operative management. - Reduce post-NACRT fatigue levels, - Improve HRQL, - Instigate behavioural changes in the short term, with potential long-term benefit. - Improve surgical outcomes (longer survival, fewer post-operative complications) - Improve cancer downstaging post-NACRT (Tumour, Node and Metastasis Staging – TNM). - Reduce hospital resources (reduction in patient length of stay, reduced demand for post-operative high dependency care

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Deriving evidence-based clinical criteria to aid classification of diabetes
Abstract: There are two main subtypes of diabetes: Type 1 diabetes (~15%) and Type 2 diabetes (~83%)[1], in addition to rare monogenic or secondary forms of diabetes. The type of diabetes a patient has is determined by their clinician at diagnosis. Clinical management of the two types is very different in terms of the treatment for the diabetes, the education provided, and monitoring required, so a correct classification is vital for appropriate patient care. These differences are due to the presence (Type 2) or absence (Type 1) of endogenous insulin secretion. However, measures of insulin secretion are seldom carried out in practice, and there are no clear clinical criteria to aid classification decisions. Recent studies in general practice suggest 13-16% of patients with diabetes are misclassified, so there is a clear need for evidence-based clinical guidelines to aid classification. We aim to derive a set of clinical diagnostic criteria that reflect a patient s underlying endogenous insulin secretion, which could be used to aid classification of diabetes. To achieve this, we propose three stages of work: 1) A systematic review will be undertaken to identify, critique and synthesise the evidence on clinical criteria to predict absolute insulin deficiency, that could be used to classify Type 1 diabetes (with Type 2 diabetes being defined on the basis of exclusion of Type 1). A set of criteria will be derived based on the synthesis of the results from the scientific literature. Age at diagnosis of diabetes and BMI are likely to be identified as the most discriminatory characteristics, but we will investigate all those in the literature that are relevant. We will evaluate the diagnostic performance of characteristics using hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, as proposed by the Cochrane guidelines for systematic reviews of diagnostic test accuracy. We will also incorporate any other clinical features identified as useful either using linked ROC curves or on a rational basis. 2) We will then test the criteria established in part (1) in 1600 patients recruited through primary care, on which we have measures of clinical characteristics and insulin deficiency. This will provide evidence of sensitivity and specificity of the criteria for correctly identifying insulin deficiency in a community-based cohort. This will form a validation step to determine the discriminative ability of the criteria for correctly classifying diabetes. We will also test whether there is a small subgroup of patients in which criteria are not helpful, in which it would be useful to advise direct measurement of insulin deficiency. Finally, we will assess the improvement in diagnostic accuracy using the new criteria compared with current practice. 3) We will disseminate the validated criteria through regional, national and international meetings, and submit the evidence to Diabetes UK, NICE and WHO for incorporation into their patient and professional guidance and guidelines for classification of diabetes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Who knows best? Older people’s contribution to understanding and preventing avoidable hospital admissions.
Abstract: Every year, the NHS experiences more than 2 million unplanned admissions for people over 65 (accounting for 68 per cent of hospital emergency bed days and the use of more than 51,000 acute beds at any one time) (Imison et al., 2012; Poteliakhoff and Thompson, 2011). With an ageing population, a challenging financial context and major structural upheavals throughout the health service, such pressures show no sign of abating – and the NHS is having to find ways of reducing emergency hospital admissions (in situations where care can be provided as effectively elsewhere). In the past, this issue has been researched in terms of formal tools which judge whether or not an admission was appropriate – but more detailed approaches are needed to understand the views of different professionals and of older people and their families. As previous pilot work has suggested, the latter are often best placed to take a more holistic view of what has happened to them and identify earlier scope for preventative approaches (see also Lawrie and Battye, 2012 for a rare example of more user-focused research into such issues). One of the reasons why it has proved so difficult to tackle the issue of emergency hospital admissions is that it is so complicated and multi-faceted. In this proposal, we argue that only an equally multi-faceted response will suffice – and that we therefore need to understand scope for prevention in the round. With this in mind, our research will review the formal evidence about the rate and cause of potentially avoidable admissions. However, we will supplement this with original research to explore older people s experiences of emergency admission and their ideas for more preventative approaches. Where the older people and their families would like to, this will also include consideration of a family/carer perspective. In addition we will work with local health and social care professionals to examine their ideas about the scale and cause of potentially avoidable admissions, and any service developments that could prevent admissions altogether. Overall, the study will include: A review of the literature on the appropriateness of emergency admissions identifying the rate and cause of potentially avoidable admissions and any potential solutions proposed. Interviews to identify clinical and managerial views on actions being taken locally to reduce the number of admissions (20 individuals per site in 2 case study sites). Detailed insights into the cause and experience of admission from older people and their carers (50 people per site in 2 case study sites). Additional information from a lead medic, GP and social worker about whether or not the admission could have be avoided (for each of the older people interviewed above). A focus group with professionals in each site which will comment on vignettes derived from the interviews with older people and develop practical service/policy responses. The research will be overseen by a national sounding board of researchers, professionals, managers and older people s organisations, who will help us to integrate insights from these different perspectives. We have also included as partners several leading national organisations who will help us share any lessons learnt through a good practice guide that will be sent to all hospitals across England and through a short video on Social Care TV . The research will also be informed by an older people s reference group, who will help us design material that is as accessible as possible for older participants and identify key themes emerging from the study.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Will a dedicated service improve medicine administration in older persons with dysphagia – a pilot study?
Abstract: BackgroundAdministration of oral medicines to patients with dysphagia (PWD) is difficult, results in inappropriate formulation alterations and on the ward is frequently unstandardised thereby increasing medication administration errors (MAEs). Additionally PWDs may be discharged unsure as to how best to take their medicines. Standardising care by the introduction of a specific medication administration chart for PWDs based on locally agreed best practice should reduce the likelihood of MAEs on the ward and better inform patients on discharge. A pilot study is required to determine the level of randomisation, the potential size of effect and identify which outcomes are the most appropriate to measure. An early stage economic evaluation will be included allowing the feasibility to be assessed.AimsTo determine the design of a randomised controlled trial in which a dedicated pharmacist trained in the management of dysphagia and enteral nutrition (via naso-gastric and percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tubes) promotes best practice in relation to medicine administration to PWD on care of the elderly / stroke wards.•To estimate:o The likely effect of a dedicated pharmacist’s input on MAEs (primary outcome measure) and on patients’ health-related quality-of-life, post discharge adherence and hospitalization (secondary outcome measures).o Whether randomization for such a trial should occur at ward or hospital level.o The most efficient method of patient recruitment, the likely ‘drop out’ rate, the best outcome measures, and the feasibility of a full cost-effectiveness analysis..Plan of InvestigationPhase 1:1) Literature review update & pharmacist training2) Multi-disciplinary agreement on administration protocol and charts3) Measure MAEs for PWDs on all wards for 1 month prior to and post interventionPhase 2:4) Recruit all PWDs over 6 month period5) Provide administration charts on admission intervention wards, and give to patient, general practitioner and community pharmacist on discharge6) Measure and compare between intervention and controlo MAEso Resource useo Health-related Quality of Lifeo Satisfaction with medicine informationo Patient reported adherence and ill health events8) Identify the level of ‘washover’ between intervention and control via nurse interviews on control wards. Triangulate with any identified change in MAEs.Phase 3: DisseminationPotential ImpactThe Lead Applicant has carried out in-depth interviews with PWD together with a focus group with healthcare professionals working with PWD. Both have identified that administering medicines to PWD is complex and health professionals are not fully cognisant with the best evidence-based methods of administering drugs to this client group. This pilot study will provide preliminary information regarding the value of a dedicated pharmacist and the development of individualised medicines administration charts to improve administration of medicines to PWD. It will help to identify a sound methodology to prepare an application for a large multi-centered trial, it will inform current practice and in the long term this study could lead to improved care for PWD.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Pragmatic Obesity Web management for Efficient Routine practice (POWER)
Abstract: BackgroundObesity is a major public health threat. Recent NICE guidelines documented key limitations in extrapolating trial findings to primary care settings - where neither the training nor the time permit implementation of intensive behavioural programmes for the thousands of patients with obesity in an average practice. A NICE research priority was to rigorously assess less resource intensive methods of intervention in primary care. We have experience of a small pilot trial of a manualised behavioural intervention and also of the Counterweight Programme which suggests that converting our written manuals into web format could be a highly cost-effective intervention, using web programming infrastructure already supported by a major ESRC grant as part of the National Centre for e-Social Science.AimsPhase 1. To further develop our existing structured manualised materials, convert them into web format, elicit and analyse the views of patients and nurses, and refine the website based on this feedback. (0-12m)Phase 2. To carry out a pilot study of the website intervention to estimate effect sizes, feasibility, and support required from practice nurses (12-24m).Plan of Investigation0-11 mths Website development, refine study procedures and materials, recruit GP practices. Patients with obesity, GPs and expert clinicians will be involved throughout.12-24 mths Pilot RCT among 50 patients per group to estimate the impact on weight of a) web only b) minimal support (3 follow-up appointment, and then help on request), and c) more intensive support (6 follow-up appointments over 6 months), compared with normal care. The pilot will confirm the likely relationship of intensity of support to weight loss, the estimates of variance, and inform the most likely groups for a definitive trialPotential ImpactGiven the limitations of the generaliseability and implementability of existing trials to primary care settings, the proposed package has the potential to allow dissemination of an intervention consistent with NICE guidance but requiring significantly fewer resources. The use of the web for both patients and for nurse training will also ensure the possibility for rapid dissemination and implementation. Population web access is rapidly increasing and it is likely that this intervention will be able to reach 80%+ of the population by the time the study finished. For those without web access the materials could be converted for use in CD format. Also by requiring fewer resources this intervention will potentially free up resources for the management of patients who do not have web access.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Investigating the performance of newly qualified doctors with reference to patient satisfaction and patient safety
Abstract: BackgroundThe literature indicates that junior doctors are inadequately prepared for practice on starting their post-graduate work and training. Additionally, we have identified weaknesses in the skills of year 1 Foundation doctors (F1s) through direct clinical workplace experience, and a pilot study investigating their views as to how well their undergraduate training prepared them for practice. Weaknesses in F1s’ competencies to perform key skills have direct patient safety implications and, as such, must be dealt with urgently. However, the GMC QABME reports on Medical Schools have shown no evidence of deficiencies in the educational programmes. Consequently, the factors that affect the new doctors’ performance in the workplace need further exploration so that patient safety is not compromised.Aims1. To identify areas of poor performance in newly qualified F1s, which raise issues of patient safety.2. To identify the factors which give rise to that poor performance.3. To produce recommendations that can be implemented locally to improve the competence of newly qualified F1s and, thus, directly benefit local patient safety. This will include recommendations for an evidence-based transition programme between the final undergraduate year and the first year of the Foundation Programme.4. To disseminate these recommendations to undergraduate and postgraduate medical training institutions across the UK.Plan of InvestigationSetting: 13 Acute NHS Trusts in the East Anglia Foundation School.Method: Junior doctors’ readiness for practice will be assessed by:1. Patient surveys2. Review of patient notes and prescriptions3. Direct observation of the outcome of specific procedures by a trained observer4. Collection of data from F1 doctors and clinical supervisors5. Audit of critical incidentsOn the basis of the findings recommendations for a transition programme will be developed.Potential ImpactAn effective transition programme should lead to improvements in the competence and confidence of Foundation doctors. These, in turn, should lead to an improvement in patient safety with a reduction particularly in prescription errors and the complications from practical procedures. Dissemination of the solid evidence-base for the transition programme should lead to rapid adoption of the recommendations in other Foundation Schools.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A comparison of community based preventative services to improve child dental health
Abstract: BackgroundChildren in the north-west have the highest prevalence of tooth decay in England; and Salford has the sixth highest in the north-west. More than half of all Salford children have decay experience by age 5. Every month about 19 children in Salford are admitted to hospital to have teeth extracted under general anaesthesia which is the principal reason for planned hospital admissions for children under 10. Salford PCT and Salford City Council have produced an oral health strategy with 8 aims. This study is addressing 4 of those including reducing the prevalence of dental decay in young children in a partnership with Children’s Centres, parents, general practitioners and the health promotion team to provide and evaluate new preventive dental services.AimsTo compare the costs to the NHS and the benefits to child dental health of three new dental services. Working in partnership with Children’s Centres in Salford, a new dental service will be established of linking a local dental practice to each Children’s Centre and offering dental care to the families using the Centre (Control Group). This service will be compared to one that delivers in addition, a Centre-based preventive programme to families to support establishing two key dental behaviours: a sugar-free bedtime routine and twice daily brushing with fluoridated toothpaste (Test Group 1). The new service will also be compared to one that delivers in addition, a Centre-based dental professional-applied series of fluoride varnish applications (Test Group 2).Plan of InvestigationThis study is a randomised clinical trial to compare costs to the NHS and benefits to child dental health of three new dental services. Parents of babies will be recruited at 8-10 months and will be randomly allocated. Those in the new standard service (Control Group) will be offered dental care at a practice local to their Children’s Centre. Children in Test Group 1 will additionally attend 10 group sessions from age 12 to 30 months to support establishing toothbrushing and a sugar-free bedtime routine. Children in Test Group 2 will additionally to control group attend individual sessions at their Children’s Centre to apply fluoride varnish. Dental health at 3 will be measured and economic analysis undertaken. Parents and general practioners will inform design and delivery of services.Potential ImpactReducing the prevalence of dental caries in young children leads to a reduction in the numbers of children with the disease and in the severity of the disease for those affected. Either intervention has been shown in trials of school-aged children to reduce decay by 30 to 60%. As over half of all children in Salford have decay experience by 5, many hundreds of children can benefit within a single PCT. Establishing healthy behaviours in young children can last for many years leading to significant savings in dental acre and enhanced quality of life.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Patient Experience and Public Engagement Blogs (The PEBL Project) - piloting new ways of capturing experiences and views from the community and integrating these into Primary Care Commissioning
Abstract: BackgroundA key challenge facing the NHS is how best to integrate the priorities and experiences of diverse communities into commissioning processes. Healthcare policy at local and national levels requires close and cohesive relationships between the NHS and the communities it serves. PCT’s must commission services which cater for the expressed needs of local populations, responding to the perceptions and experiences of current and potential service users. The methodologies required to achieve these policy goals are, however, under-developed. The PEBL project will draw upon qualitative methodologies in order to explore the feasibility, practicality and effectiveness of new and innovative ways of capturing patient and community data and integrating these experiences into commissioning processes.AimsThe PEBL project has three specific aims. 1) To pioneer and evaluate the use of web-based communications technology to collect ongoing narratives of patient experience and their reflections on the quality of existing Primary Care services. 2) To initiate and evaluate the development of an on-line community of ‘rapporteurs’ who will regularly reflect on (and report) their concerns, needs and perceptions of healthcare issues and those of the communities in which they live. 3) To develop and evaluate the practicality and effectiveness of a streamlined thematic analysis methodology that will allow rich and complex qualitative data to become an integral part of PCT commissioning through the production of a patient experience and community perception monthly ‘barometer’.Plan of InvestigationPEBL will involve two panels of local volunteers; a ‘pathway specific panel’ (people currently using local health services) and a ‘community panel’ (people not necessarily using a service but who can reflect and report on their perceptions and those of their communities). Both panels will provide comment and reflection, in their own words and at their own speed, via a dedicated PEBL internet site. We will use computer-assisted thematic analysis to produce a brief monthly patient experience ‘barometer’. As well as being publicly available, this document will be distributed to key figures in the commissioning process. Assessment of the impact on decisions and actions of the PEBL project will be evaluated through interviews with community representatives, PCT managers and clinicians.Potential ImpactMeasures of patient experience, quality and public consultation tend to be dominated by metrics and quantitative survey approaches. It is widely recognised, however, that key issues such as communication, compassion, care, dignity, and respect are all related to individual perceptions, specific contexts and particular cultural sensitivities. As such, there is a widespread recognition at the ‘front-line’ of the NHS that quantitative survey data and metrics have serious limitations and that proven and reliable qualitative approaches are required to complement them if we are to achieve the ambitious goals of world class commissioning. If the PEBL pilot works, a dependable, consistent and highly useable method of permanent community involvement will be available for roll-out to the whole NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The East Cambs and Fenland Diabetes Integrated Care Initiative
Abstract: BackgroundDiabetes underlies a burgeoning toll in premature morbidity, reduced quality of life and financial and social costs. While the evidence supports intensive management of diabetes, particularly from diagnosis, the means to achieve this are unclear. Questions remain around how to deliver services more effectively to assist and support patients in maintaining their routines of metabolic control, and effective self-mangement. East Cambs and Fenland includes some of the most deprived areas in Cambridgeshire and is served by a range of separate diabetes services. Cambridgeshire PCT are funding new services which allow integration of primary, secondary and community services and a focus on those at high risk of hospitalisation, including those with co-morbid chronic conditions.AimsOur aims are to describe the transition to, and impact of, a new whole system approach to diabetes care. In the transition phase we will use an action research framework to document the extent of diffusion of the innovative service to practices & patients, and its usability throughout the local health care system. We will document service evolution/integration, explore patients/staff perceptions/experiences of helpful/unhelpful attributes of services provision & identify key factors to guide further development and expansion of services to other areas.In the impact phase we will compare changes (before/after and with other parts of Cambs) and in hospitalisation/service use, medication use, metabolic control,quality of life. We will establish a cohort for long term follow upPlan of InvestigationThe new, population based, integrated approach for diabetes management includes primary care decision support and training, enhanced general practice-community-specialist service communication & operation, and strategies to address psychosocial barriers to self-care and co-morbidities. It is based on the successful ADDITION trial established locally, the barriers to care approach pioneered by the PI and local service changes. Pre, 12 & 24 month post-intervention evaluation among the expected 8000 patients will take place using utilization, payment and cost data from participating services, lab and clinical record data (eg QoF), patient and health professional surveys and face to face interviews, and cross PCT data where available. Cost data will be used to model future costs/savings.Potential ImpactThis research evaluates an approach likely to reduce morbidity, hospitalisation and improve quality of life for many with diabetes. If it reduces the risk of diabetes complications largely within existing resources, it will help reduce the predicted long-term diabetes costs. The approach is likely to be of use in other areas and for other long term conditions. Novel aspects include a roll-out of an intervention (ADDITION) already positively evaluated locally in an RCT, integrated within a whole system approach incorporating more structured diabetes specialist, community and social service involvement. The study is framed to deal with barriers to care systematically including psychosocial and health systems issues, co-morbidities and the challenges associated with social deprivation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Identifying trajectories of progression of frailty in elderly individuals
Abstract: The aim of the work is to better identify those elderly individuals in the community whose level of frailty is increasing, and for whom, it would be appropriate to target potentially resource intensive interventions such as nutritional and exercise advise, with other guidance and support. The goal would be to reduce the risks of unplanned admissions to nursing homes and acute admissions to hospital. Our research aim is that elderly individuals can be grouped into those with different time courses (or trajectories ) of becoming increasingly frail with sufficient precision to be achieve the targeting goal above. The methodological background is the recent development, and introduction into primary care, of a frailty score based, the electronic frailty index, eFI, derived from counting deficits ascertained from the accumulated health record from primary care. We believe that by taking a longitudinal approach to determining frailty would offer a robust but practical approach to identifying those most at risk. We aim to test three specific hypotheses: That there are specific clusters of trajectories of development of frailty over five years based on the changes in eFI score. That these clusters are associated with differences in the one and three-year adverse outcomes of mortality, unplanned hospitalisation and admission to care home. That these clusters add more prognostic value of adverse outcome than the current use of eFI We plan a retrospective cohort study using up to eight-year routinely collected data from two large primary care databases which link to subsequent health and social outcomes. The work comprises 3 phases: Anonymised primary care electronic health record data from the ResearchOne database of 249,000 participants with available data from January 1 2009, aged 65+ will be analysed to calculate the cumulative crude number of deficit variables based on the eFI rules. In each of the successive four years, the cumulative number of the deficits will be increased based on the new recording of any previously unrecorded variable and hence 5-year trajectories derived. As part of the analysis, to address the impact of variability in consultation behaviour on deficit recording, Age UK will lead on establishing a PPI working group to derive a consensus view on the real-life consultation patterns for the individual deficits and agree about the cut off period of the time to last mention. A patient s crude and modified frailty trajectories hence comprise the counts of both crude and modified deficits for five years, respectively. The trajectories will be tested in a second primary care database to examine their reproducibility and the fit of individual patient profiles to these We will explore the association between distinct frailty trajectories and adverse outcomes of mortality, unplanned hospitalization and care home admission using both cohorts over the next three years of follow-up. The starting time for follow up will either be the end of the fifth year or the year of the first outcome, whichever occurs first.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: The NeSCi Study - Neonatal unit Smoking Cessation intervention development
Abstract: Research Question: Is it feasible and acceptable to adapt standard smoke-free home interventions to neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) settings? Background: Smoking severely affects parental and child health and is a risk factor for low birth weight (1) and preterm birth (2). The risk of NICU admission for infants of smokers is increased by at least 20% compared with non-smokers (3). Stopping smoking is the most important health behaviour change parents can make to improve their health and minimise long-term disease risk, especially lung and other cancers, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart disease. Smoking cessation has substantial benefits for infants through reducing second-hand smoke exposure. Infants of smokers are more likely to suffer serious respiratory, and other, infections (4–9). These risks are higher for babies born prematurely or suffering other health conditions. In 2007 prices, the smoking attributable cost per child exposed to indoor smoke was 144euro (10). PPI demonstrates that parents would welcome discussions on smoke-free homes whilst their baby is on NICU. Aims: To adapt existing smoke-free home interventions to develop a specific package of support for parents of babies on NICU, including advice, guidance and support towards a smoke-free home, implementing smoking cessation guidance and policy. To be achieved by: 1. Revising a generic systematic review of smoke-free home interventions, to identify effective interventions that may be adapted to NICU. 2. Qualitative work with parents, NICU and community health professionals to ascertain views on intervention components, targeting, timing and intensity. 3. Working one-to-one with the target population to pilot the modified intervention. Methods: Phase 1 Update and extend a systematic review of smoke-free home interventions in the general population (11), in order to assess: 1.) intervention effectiveness, using data from controlled trials 2.) what works, for whom and in what settings, synthesising process evaluations, and 3.) identifying potentially effective intervention components, using analysis of behaviour change techniques. Outputs will inform adaptations of interventions for use in NICUs. Phase 2 Qualitative focus-group study, purposefully sampling parents (smokers/ex-smokers quitting for pregnancy/never smokers living with smokers) of NICU babies to gather feedback on potential intervention components from phase 1, and to discuss tailoring, timing and intensity for optimum delivery. We will also seek views of NICU staff and health professionals. Data will be collected across two sites with diverse populations: Norwich and Leicester. Analysis will take an inductive-thematic approach (11). The outcome will be a co-produced prototype intervention. Phase 3 Person-based intervention refinement(12). We will work closely with postpartum women and their families (smokers/ex-smokers, in Norwich and Leicester, with maximum variation in age, ethnicity and socioeconomic status) to refine and test the prototype intervention. Data will identify particularly salient or problematic intervention elements and consider intervention dose, targeting, acceptability and feasibility. Timeline: 18 months Impact and Dissemination: We will gather sufficient developmental and feasibility data anticipating designing a definitive randomised controlled trial with in-built pilot study, to evaluate intervention effectiveness within the NHS. Ultimately this will result in significant health benefits for parents, family members and babies.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Improving the detection of alcohol related liver disease
Abstract: BackgroundLiver deaths have increased 8 fold in 30 years and nearly all these deaths appear to be alcohol related. Cirrhosis develops silently and presents late; up to 50% of subjects die before they have a chance to stop drinking. Most patients are heavy social drinkers and able to stop drinking when faced with the harsh alternative of a progressive and uniformly fatal illness. Blood tests in routine use do not detect cirrhosis and diagnosis requires a liver biopsy – impractical for the 2 million UK residents drinking at levels that may result in cirrhosis. Newer blood tests detect fibrosis or cirrhosis at an early stage and, combined with alcohol screening, could greatly improve detection and management of these patients, reducing morbidity and mortality.AimsThe long term aim is to improve the earlier detection and treatment of alcohol induced liver disease, and thus to reduce liver related mortality. This study is the first phase to 1) Assess feasibility of screening a primary care population for hazardous drinking using the FAST questionnaire. 2) Assess practicality of screening heavy alcohol users for liver disease using a simple new blood test. 3) Assess the resource implications of assessment and follow-up of subjects identified by the twin screening protocols.Plan of InvestigationScreen subjects aged 25 – 55 in three general practices using a validated test for hazardous levels of drinking (FAST). Screen hazardous drinkers using a simple blood test to assess liver fibrosis. Offer a full liver work-up to subjects with evidence of significant liver fibrosis / cirrhosis. Subjects with portal hypertension will be offered primary variceal bleeding prophylaxis with propranolol / banding. All subjects found to be drinking hazardously will be given standard written information - those with liver disease will receive further verbal interventions and follow up. Subjects will be followed at one year, and drinking reassessed, and the liver cohort will be studied long term.Potential ImpactScreening for liver disease is not performed in primary care and existing blood tests do not detect cirrhosis. Our new fibrosis test has been fully evaluated in an out patient population, and detects 95% of subjects with cirrhosis or severe fibrosis but has not been used in primary care. We need to prove that our screening concept is effective, and to find the prevalence of hidden severe liver disease in hazardous drinkers in the community With this preliminary data we would then be in a position to seek funding for a larger scale project in which the reduction in mortality and morbidity are the main outcomes, together with cost/benefit analyses. If these later studies are positive we will have a stepped screening/intervention methodology that can be extended to other areas in the UK.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Ready, willing and able? Enabling patients & carers treated with elective coronary angioplasty to self manage
Abstract: BackgroundIn the UK over 34,000 people with coronary heart disease (CHD) are treated annually with coronary angioplasty. Although all patients with CHD are eligible for cardiac rehabilitation, those receiving angioplasty are not routinely seen within community cardiac services and as a result experience health inequity. Self management (SM) defined as 'the sum of activities that a patient undertakes to control the symptoms & progression of chronic disease', underpins rehabilitation. Lifestyle change & adherence to medications are key SM activities that slow the progression of CHD, thereby reducing death and disability. But little is known about how cardiac patients SM, despite effective rehabilitation being identified as a priority area in the (2007) CHD NSF Progress Report.AimsThis 3 year study aims to:1) Explore the SM experiences of patients & carers living with cardiac conditions, including factors that enable or constrain SM;2) Explore the SM experiences of patients & carers treated with angioplasty with a focus on lifestyle change & medication management;3) Develop a prototype SM support 'tool' (using findings from 1 & 2) for patients & carers treated with coronary angioplasty.Plan of InvestigationA 3 year NHS led study, using mixed methods, conducted in 3 phases. Phase 1: Existing qualitative evidence (1985-current) reporting cardiac patients' & carers' SM experiences will be pooled using a meta ethnographic approach. Phase 2: A 12-month longitudinal interview study will be conducted by recruiting 40-50 patient/carer dyads treated with first elective coronary angioplasty. Four interviews will be conducted with each (at 7-10 days, 6-8 wks, 4 & 12 months) after angioplasty, & data analysed using a Framework approach. These data will be supported by objective measures of health resource use, SM engagement, medication adherence, demographic & coronary risk factor data. Findings from Phase 1 & 2 will inform the design of a prototype SM support 'tool' in Phase 3 for future testing.Potential ImpactThe NSF for CHD (2007) clearly identifies rehabilitation for patients with CHD as a priority for improvement. Patients treated with coronary angioplasty are neglected & 'fall' through available systems. This is made worse, by their frequent failure to recognise the chronic nature & severity of their condition, leading to a lack of success in their SM of lifestyle change & medications. By exploring SM experiences & developing a prototype SM support 'tool', this study will address i) health inequity in a large, somewhat neglected group; ii) build theory & potentially iii) reduce cardiac death & disability in line with NSF targets; iv) improve patient satisfaction & quality of life; & v) reduce health resource use (consultant follow up, GP visits, hospital admissions).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Diabetes self management strategies for long-term biomedical outcomes and quality of life: a synthesis of longitudinal quantitative and qualitative research
Abstract: BackgroundFor the 2.5 million people in the UK with diabetes, remaining as healthy as possible over many years is crucial. In order to translate evidence-based interventions into good patient outcomes it is necessary to close the gap between what health professionals advise and what people with diabetes actually do. Medical prescription and advice is based on quantitative evidence of the long-term benefits of good clinical outcomes such as blood sugar and blood pressure. However, qualitative research indicates that patients are often focused on maintaining their current quality of life. Consequently, to engage patients in sustaining good outcomes, diabetes care must focus on both clinical outcomes AND current quality of life. The long-term relationship between these outcomes is poorly understood.AimsA. To synthesise published quantitative and qualitative research evidence to address the questions:1. For adults with Type 2 diabetes, how are biomedical outcomes (such as HbA1c) and quality of life (as assessed by quality of life measures or reported in patients’ own words) related to each other over periods of a year or more? 2. What, if any, diabetes self-management factors are associated with improving or maintaining good long-term biomedical outcomes and quality of life, in what circumstances and why? 3. Are there particular concerns reported in specific patient groups (for example, socially disadvantaged groups, ethnic minority populations) reported in this literature? B. To engage stakeholders in translating the synthesis findings into practical advice and interventionsPlan of Investigation1. Systematic search of the major biomedical and nursing databases from 1990 onwards. Search criteria will be predefined for quantitative and qualitative methodologies and include: adults with Type 2 diabetes; longitudinal outcome data > 1 year. We will use standard appraisal methodology and involve at least two researchers.2. Using a narrative synthesis approach, the quantitative and qualitative evidence will be synthesised separately and then brought together into a coherent whole. We anticipate developing a conceptual model that depicts long-term change in outcomes and the self-management related factors.3. Two workshops (patients, professionals, NHS managers) will help ensure that the synthesis is a guide to action and of benefit to patients.Potential ImpactType 2 diabetes (90% of all diabetes) is increasing rapidly. More effective support of self-management is the key to cost-containment (current NHS costs > £9 billion a year) and to reducing complications and associated disability. The strength of this synthesis is that it addresses the long-term progression of outcomes and both medical and lay agendas. By bridging the gap between these agendas, and the related ‘target-driven’ and ‘personalised care’ policies, it aims to benefit patient care at the level of the consultation and patients self-management. Our multi-disciplinary team and workshops will use our findings to provide clear guidance to:• improve provider knowledge and communication behaviour• improve patient knowledge and confidence• inform service managers and commissioners

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: An exploration of self-care in chronic low-back disorder from the perspectives of practitioners and patients: a Q methodological study
Abstract: BackgroundChronic low back pain (CLBP) is a condition of medical and socio-economic importance. NHS policy encourages patients' active involvement in self-management as a key factor in improving quality of life in long term conditions. But, there is evidence that lack of appropriate support from health professionals is a barrier to supported self-management in low back pain. Clinical experience shows that treatment such as physiotherapy, for chronic low back pain can reduce symptoms and signs, but longer term the condition will often recur if patients do not engage in behavioural change in a self-managed way. Therefore systematic examination of stakeholders' perceptions of self-management is fundamental in optimising the quality and extent of healthcare provision for chronic low back pain.Aims•Identify the range and diversity of perceptions of patient partnership and supported self-management held by patients, health, social care and voluntary sector practitioners involved in management of patients with CLBP.•Gain insight into how practitioners can effectively facilitate patients to take an active part in their own care.•Utilise the emergent viewpoints to improve the quality of shared decision-making and self-management strategies in CLBP.•Use research findings to refine local CLBP management strategies.Plan of InvestigationA research method called Q-methodology will be used. This examines how people think about a topic. Here it will used to understand and describe patients' and health professionals' subjective viewpoints on self-management. Participants will be recruited from an acute and 2 primary care NHS Trusts in the South of England to maximise breadth of cultural and demographic representation and facilitate inter-group comparisons. Stakeholder perceptions of self-management will be examined in the context of non-specific CLBP. The study findings will be presented at a consensus conference of stakeholders. Potential actions and practices will be proposed. These will be rated by delegates, with the intention of reaching consensus on the most important issues to inform subsequent recommendations.Potential ImpactThe socio-economic impact, chronic course, and uncertain causation, makes chronic low back pain an important issue. The findings of this research will be used to•enhance self-management of CLBP by increasing understanding of associated factors. •contribute to practitioner development and service user initiatives to improve long-term management of CLBP, through training events and related education packages. •influence and refine CLBP management strategies in participating Trusts in the short, medium and long-term•in the longer term successfully implemented self-management programmes may reduce recurrent episodes of CLBP.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Understanding hospital-level variation in outcomes for patients admitted for acute coronary syndrome: a qualitative study
Abstract: BackgroundHospital-level factors have been identified that affect the standard of care and outcomes for patients admitted with acute coronary syndromes (ACS). These include patient volume, hospital type and the make-up of multi-professional teams. Variation in 30 day mortality between UK hospitals can be seen in data from the Myocardial Ischaemia National Audit Project (MINAP). Using MINAP data, Hemingway, Timmis and Feder are engaged in quantitative modelling of hospital-level structures and processes to explain inter-hospital variation. Building on this work we propose a qualitative study that will provide a more detailed understanding and concrete examples of hospital processes that impact on and lead to variation in performance. AimsThe study will provide an analysis of organisational factors responsible for inter-hospital variation in outcome for patients admitted with ACS. The focus will be on hospital practice, using an ethnographic perspective that integrates diverse forms of data. The in-depth qualitative analysis will be synthesised with the quantitative modelling of hospital-level factors that have been identified as having an impact on patient outcome. Actionable factors associated with variation will be highlighted, and barriers and facilitators to implementing any such changes explored. Knowledge transfer for the synthesised results will be conducted through focus groups and workshops for key professionals. The multi-disciplinary team will reach consensus on recommendations for policy and practice.Plan of InvestigationData from MINAP will provide a sampling framework for this qualitative study. Based on 30 day outcomes for patients admitted with ACS, a sample of nine hospitals will be chosen: three hospitals with poorer outcomes, three with better outcomes and three with above average missing data. The qualitative researcher, blinded to hospital performance, will conduct fieldwork at each site, using observation in hospital departments and wards following a sample of patients admitted with ACS through to discharge. Diagnostic and treatment procedures, decision-making, communication, paperwork and processes of admission/discharge will be investigated. Interviews will be carried out with professionals and patients. The detailed, in-depth analysis will be synthesised with quantitative modelling.Potential ImpactThe study will identify organisational, clinical and administrative processes that will be amenable to change. When synthesised with the quantitative data, this will provide a unique opportunity to make recommendations on how to reduce unnecessary variation in care of patients with ACS and improve 30 day outcomes. It will provide short, accessible reports and presentations by the research team to participating hospitals and nationally, identifying actionable reasons for inter-hospital variations in patient outcome. Action by cardiac services nationally on recommendations from this study (and the parallel quantitative modeling study) has the potential to improve survival for ACS patients, improve overall care in all hosptials and reduce inter-hospital variation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Camden and Islington NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Shape Up-LD': Piloting a manualised weight management programme for overweight and obese persons with mild-moderate learning disabilities
Abstract: BackgroundObesity rates have dramatically risen in the UK over the last decade (1). Being obese significantly reduces life expectancy, increases the risk of a range of diseases, and compromises quality of life (2, 3). Costs to both the NHS and society are high (4). An increased prevalence of obesity in people with learning disabilities (LD) has been demonstrated (5). The consequences of obesity are particularly relevant to people with LD who are already confronted by health and social inequalities (6). In order to provide healthcare for all, and ensure equality of treatment for people with LD, services must be developed specifically with this population in mind.AimsThe aim of this project is to assess the feasibility of evaluating a manualised weight management programme for overweight and obese persons with mild-moderate learning disabilities ('Shape Up-LD') through a single-blind, pilot, randomised controlled trial (RCT) comparing 'Shape Up-LD' versus usual care, for people with LD and their carers. Issues including acceptability of the intervention and outcome measures, compliance, recruitment and retention, will be explored. Qualitative interviews will also be conducted with both service-users, their carers, and service-providers. We intend to use this pilot data to prepare for a definitive RCT, with the intention of applying for funding from HTA.Plan of InvestigationSixty people with mild-moderate LD and a BMI >25, and their carers will be recruited to a two-armed RCT and receive either 'Shape Up-LD' or usual care. The manualised 'Shape Up-LD' intervention will involve 12 weekly sessions, which include healthy eating messages and teaching people new behaviours to manage their weight with the support of their carer. Assessments with users and their carers will be conducted at baseline, 12 weeks and 6 months, to detect changes in weight, body fat, waist circumference, blood pressure, blood cholesterol/ LDL/ glucose levels, mental health, quality of life, self esteem, knowledge and behaviours. Service users, their carers and service providers will also give their perspectives on the experience of the intervention in qualitative interviews at 12 weeks.Potential ImpactWe will refine the 'Shape-Up LD' materials in line with the findings from this study. These materials will be available through Weight Concern, enabling widespread use by LD service providers within the NHS. The findings from this study will also inform our preparation for a definitive RCT to test the efficacy of the programme with respect to weight loss and maintenance in this population. Weight loss through 'Shape Up-LD' could lead to improvements in health and quality of life. Costs to the NHS might be reduced through decreased overall service use due to improved health. The programme would also ensure a more equitable service for overweight LD patients and fill the current gap in weight management services for this population.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Preventing obesity in young people attending primary dental care settings: an exploratory randomised controlled trial.
Abstract: BackgroundObesity is a significant public health problem in the UK. Amongst young people obesity rates have risen dramatically in recent years. The health, social and economic consequences of this epidemic are significant. Overweight and obesity is caused by a complex interplay of metabolic, behavioural, social and environmental factors but ultimately results when a sustained energy imbalance occurs. Recent NICE guidance has highlighted the need for effective preventive interventions. Epidemiological and intervention studies have highlighted the important role that sugars consumption, particularly from soft drinks has on the development of obesity. A high proportion of young people attend dentists routinely. This provides a unique opportunity to develop and test an obesity prevention intervention.AimsAim:To develop and test the feasibility of an obesity prevention intervention targeting 12-14 year olds attending general dental services in Islington and Camden PCTs.Specific objectives:1. To assess dental teams experience, motivation and training needs in providing preventive care for both oral and general health improvement2. To assess the acceptability to young people and their parents of the proposed intervention3. To develop a motivational interviewing intervention and training programme specifically designed for dental teams working with young people to prevent obesity4. To conduct an exploratory randomised controlled trial of the obesity intervention5. To make recommendations on conducting a definitive randomised controlled trial of the obesity interventionPlan of InvestigationBased upon the MRC framework for developing and evaluating complex interventions this study will use qualitative and quantitative methods in the following stages:1. undertake a quantitative survey of dentists across 2 London PCTs to assess their experience, motivation and training needs in prevention2. conduct qualitative focus groups with young people and, separately their parents to determine the acceptability and salience of the proposed obesity intervention3. develop a motivational interviewing intervention and training programme specifically designed for dental teams working with young people to prevent excess weight gain4. conduct an exploratory trial to assess the feasibility and acceptability of the intervention and trial methods for a later definitive RCTPotential ImpactTreatment options for childhood obesity are limited and frequently fail to achieve long term success. Effective and innovative preventive inteventions are therefore urgently required. This study will provide detailed information on the feasibility, acceptability and practicality of implementing a theoretically innovative obesity intervention. Contractual and commissioning arrangements now enable dentists to become more actively engaged in health promotion activity. This study will explore the potential role dentists may play in preventing a significant public health problem. The findings from this study will then be used to apply for funding for a definitive RCT. This study will therefore have potentially significant policy and practice implications.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: Camden and Islington NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A mixed methods investigation of the impact of introducing Individual Placement and Support to a catchment area
Abstract: BackgroundEmployment rates among people with severe mental health problems in the UK are currently low and seem to have fallen over the past few decades (Marwaha and Johnson, 2004). Individual Placement and Support (IPS) is an approach that involves helping people find work and then offering them the support they need to keep their jobs rather than engaging them in a vocational rehabilitation programme. Results from randomised trials indicate that IPS improves employment rates and other outcomes for those who engage with it in trial settings. However,some implementation difficulties have been reported in the UK. Evidence is now needed on how much difference this approach makes in everyday clinical settings and on factors promoting or impeding its success.AimsOur aims are: - To investigate the impact on employment rates and on costs of introducing the Individual Placement and Support (IPS) model to three community mental health teams (CMHTs) in a London Borough- To assess predictors of engagement with IPS, including investigating whether there are ethnic differences in rates of engaging with IPS workers and of getting employment - To investigate service user experiences of IPS and reasons for engaging or not engaging with the programme. - To explore the vocational and activity needs of those who do not engage with IPS. ???- To explore from service users', employers', and clinicians' perspectives the factors that impede or promote success in finding and keeping a job among those who engage with IPS.Plan of InvestigationThe investigation will have two components: (a) Natural experiment: Anonymised sociodemographic, clinical and employment data will be collected from staff regarding all patients on caseloads of care coordinators in the London Borough of Camden, where IPS will be introduced to 3 of the 6 CMHTs. Follow-up data will be collected over 2 years regarding their employment patterns and service use. Associated costs will also be assessed. (b) Qualitative methods will be used to explore service users', employers' and clinicians' views about IPS and the factors influencing whether people engage with it and find and keep jobs. ?Potential ImpactThe impact of this study will be in allowing an assessment of how far availability of the IPS approach makes a difference in practice to rates of employment among people with severe mental health problems. It will also allow us to assess within a very multicultural area which groups of patients make use of this approach and which do not, focusing especially on whether it engages a range of ethnic groups. A preliminary assessment of the impact on societal costs will also be made. Finally, difficulties in recruiting to IPS have been reported in the UK: better understanding of potential barriers to engagement and gaining work through IPS may allow development of ways of facilitating entry to IPS services and/or of alternatives to IPS that meet the needs of some who do not engage.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: RApid Primary care Initiation of Drug treatment for TIA (RAPID-TIA) – a pilot trial
Abstract: BackgroundPeople who have a transient ischaemic attack (TIA) or minor stroke are at high risk of a recurrent stroke, particularly in the first week after the event. The National Stroke Strategy recommends that people with a TIA are seen by a specialist urgently – within 24 hours to one week, depending upon clinical features. Draft NICE guidelines for management of a suspected TIA are that patients should be given aspirin immediately and that other secondary prevention drugs be given as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed. Recent data suggest very early initiation of secondary prevention drugs leads to an 80% reduction in risk of stroke recurrence. This raises the question as to whether these drugs in addition to aspirin should be given before being seen by a specialist – i.e. in primary care.AimsTo determine the feasibility of a randomised controlled trial and cost effectiveness analysis to ask: Should general practitioners (GPs) initiate secondary preventative measures in addition to aspirin in people they see with suspected TIA or minor stroke at the time of referral to a specialist?Questions to address:1. What should be included in guidance to GPs on diagnosis of TIA?2. What are patient and primary health care professional attitudes towards GP initiation of therapy and on how consent should be obtained?3. Is randomisation at the individual patient level possible? 4. What is the recruitment rate of patients to the trial?5. Are there any adverse events in patients who receive secondary prevention drugs prior to specialist diagnosis?6. How accurate is GP diagnosis of TIA?Plan of InvestigationA pilot trial will recruit patients with symptoms suggestive of TIA in practices from the catchment of two hospital TIA clinics (Birmingham & Oxford). The GP will record whether TIA is probable or possible. All will be referred to a TIA clinic. Probable cases will be invited by the GP to enter the trial, possible cases to enter a study of accuracy of GP diagnosis. Patients will be randomised by telephone, stratified by TIA clinic and stroke risk, to pre-TIA clinic drug treatment or referral with post-TIA clinic drug treatment. The TIA clinic will record final diagnosis and adjust treatment accordingly. The primary outcome will be stroke at 90 days. Preliminary qualitative interviews with patients and primary care professionals will explore attitudes towards the trial and design issues.Potential ImpactRapid administration of secondary prevention in people who have had a TIA or minor stroke might reduce the overall incidence of stroke by about 5% and save about £90m per annum nationally (National Audit Office). The current management of TIA largely by referral to a specialist TIA clinic, leads to undue delays in patients receiving preventative treatments. The proposed trial will investigate the role GPs might play in ensuring rapid treatment – should they give immediate therapy, or simply ensure prompt referral? This will be important and timely as the NHS seeks to implement the National Stroke Strategy. The pilot work for the trial will also develop material of immediate NHS relevance – guidance to GPs on how to diagnose TIA and data on accuracy of GP diagnosis.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Improving the Wider Determinants of Health
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Impact of low health literacy on older patients with chronic illnesses - a systematic review and focus group study
Abstract: BackgroundChronic illnesses are huge burden on the NHS and older people are particularly affected. Efforts to improve care may be significantly hampered by low health literacy, whereby individuals lack the skills to access, understand, and act on information for the promotion and maintenance of their own good health. Particular problems include limited self-management skills and difficulty adhering to medical advice, thus leading to poorer outcomes and higher costs. Functional health literacy declines with age. A high proportion of older patients have low health literacy, which is further complicated by poor visual acuity and co-morbidity. There is a clear absence of high quality research and systematic evaluations of health literacy issues surrounding older patients in the UK.AimsWe will perform a systematic literature review and focus group study to analyse current data on the impact of low health literacy on older patients with chronic illnesses and to identify areas for the improvements of patient care and further research. We will focus on the following aspects of health literacy research and on issues that are particularly relevant to current practice in the UK.• The prevalence of low health literacy• The impact of low health literacy on health outcomes and healthcare requirements• Acquired low health literacy due to co-morbidities and ageing• Special requirements in relation to the assessment and intervention of low health literacy• The relative benefits of any strategies or interventions aimed at improving health literacy in older peoplePlan of InvestigationWe will retrieve randomised and non-randomised controlled trials, ‘before-and-after’ studies, and observational studies (including qualitative evaluations) on the impact of low health literacy on older patients with chronic illnesses. Only articles written in English will be reviewed. Data extraction and quality assessment will be independently conducted by two reviewers using data abstraction forms specially designed. Meta-analysis will be used where this is appropriate.A focus group study among purposively selected service users, their carers and practitioners will be conducted towards the end of the project, to feed findings back to patient and practitioner groups, to get their views and to ask them to identify & prioritise areas for the improvement of patient care and for research.Potential ImpactThis project will provide up-to-date information and new data on health literacy research of older patients with chronic illnesses and its relevance to current practice in the UK. The results may have impact on the improvement in the delivery of patient care and on further health literacy research from organisations and health professionals involved in the care of older patients. The findings may also help to drive further, targeted research for improved care to older patients with low health literacy. Furthermore, this project may provide key data for the NHS and other health policymakers to allocate resources for the care of chronic illness and older patients, which are two key areas in the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Understanding factors leading to low uptake of diabetic retinopathy screening in Primary Care
Abstract: BackgroundDiabetic retinopathy (DR) is the leading cause of preventable vision loss in the working-age population. A national screening programme established in 2003 requires annual retinopathy screening to be offered to 2 million people with diabetes. Recent work has shown screening non-attendance is a risk factor for sight threatening retinopathy, and screening attendance in different General Practices in Gloucestershire varies between 55% and 95%. A recent review for the National Screening Committee showed limited primary research in this area, with much drawn from overseas and the research available focussing on population characteristics. There has been no qualitative work published relating to uptake in diabetic retinopathy screening.AimsThe aims of this research are 1) To understand the needs of people with diabetes in relation to the invitation, and attendance and receiving results and treatment options associated with diabetic retinopathy 2) To understand why people with diabetes who have been invited for retinopathy screening do not attend 3) To understand the information, educational needs, beliefs, attitudes of primary care and screening professionals in communicating the importance, consequences, investigations, results and treatment options to their patients 4) To understand the different pathways to screening and how this might influence uptake. 5) To understand and disseminate the findings of this research to enable screening programmes and primary care to change their service provision to improve uptake.Plan of InvestigationWe propose a qualitative case study design using individual and joint interviews. We will invite GP practices in three PCTs, Gloucestershire, Warwickshire and Birmingham to participate. Each practice represents a case and we will interview 2/3 professionals and 4 people with diabetes from 10 purposively selected GP practices. We will recruit 5 practices located in areas with high health needs and within those, practices with high and low uptake. An iterative approach will be used to identify a further 5 practices following analysis of early data. People with diabetes will be purposively recruited from these practices according to age, gender, type of diabetes, ethnicity, time since diagnosis, socio-economic status and previous and recent screening uptake.Potential ImpactThe national role of the applicants in relation to retinal screening will enable the findings from this research to have a high impact across the NHS to inform screening programmes. Facilitators and barriers to uptake at both patient and professional levels will be identified and the factors found to be associated with high uptake can be disseminated by the communication strategy and network of the English National DR Screening Programme. This will lead to increased screening levels in groups where uptake is low, hence identifying more individuals with sight threatening diabetic retinopathy. This will enable referral and treatment at an appropriate stage of the disease process and prevent visual loss and blindness in this high risk population.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Exploratory RCT of a group psychological Intervention for Postnatal Depression in British Mothers of Pakistani Origin
Abstract: BackgroundIn the UK, the rate of postnatal depression is reported to be 10-15% in the general population . In our MRC funded study we have found the rate of depression during pregnancy in mothers of Pakistani origin to be 17% and in the postnatal period it increased to 19%. These mothers have particularly severe social difficulties in the realms of marriage, housing, health and finances and they lack supportive relationships. Some of these difficulties are similar to those found in white Europeans but many family factors are unique to this population. A number of individual and group interventions targeting maternal depression have been developed and tested, largely in the majority white population.We are not aware of any such trials in the ethnic minorities.AimsThis is an exploratory trial of a complex intervention and the aim is to refine a culturally appropriate psychological l group intervention and to pilot test its feasibility and acceptability for postnatal depression in women of Pakistani origin in Manchester and East Lancashire. In this phase we shall test our ability to run a series of groups in the local Sure Start community centres. Hypotheses: Our hypothesis is that depressed British mothers of Pakistani origin who receive the group intervention will show significant improvements in terms of severity of depression, parental stress and social support compared to the TAU group.Plan of InvestigationThe proposed project consists of two phases1) Phase 1: Intervention refinement2) Phase 2: Randomised Control TrialThe project will take advatage of a) PhD project of developing and testing this CBT based interventionb) Wellcome Trust funded research undertaken in developing mental health interventions for maternal depression in Pakistan c) Our MRC funded epidemiological and d) MRC Trial platform study on women of Pakistani origin using social support groups to treat depression. The proposed intervention will be further refined and it will be assessed using a prospective randomised controlled design, using two groups: Psychological group intervention (PGI) and treatment as usual group (TAU).Potential ImpactImpact on service users:Mental health literacy of the participants is expected to improve. Reduction of over all morbidity and better quality of life, increased awareness and higher satisfaction.Impact on services:Improvement in the quality of mental health services. The process of culturally tailoring interventions and research may be a generalizable process or method and we intend to document this process in detail. Impact on policy:The NSF for Mental Health reaffirms the issue of inappropriate services for black & ethnic minority communities & addressing the needs of this group is a priority (See appendix) .

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Recognition of and consultation for memory problems among South Asian elders: a literature review and face to face interviews to study explanatory models
Abstract: BackgroundThe proportion of South Asians (SA) elders, Indian and Pakistani being the largest two groups, in the United Kingdom is expected to rise over coming decades. Memory problems are not uncommon among older people but SA elders with memory problems often do not access health and social services. This may in part be a result of a lack of knowledge about causes and treatments of memory problems and stigma in SA community. Also, the lack of knowledge about cultural factors among health professionals may affect their ability to assess these problems among SA elders. These patient and doctor factors, together, may lead to under-diagnosis and under-treatment of two main causes of memory problems, depression and dementia.AimsThe overall aim of this proposal is to improve our understanding of the factors that determine the recognition of and consultation for memory problems among SA elders. First, we aim to conduct a literature review to summarise current knowledge about why SA elders may not use their local services. Second, we aim to study explanatory models (EM) about causes and consequences of memory problems among Indian and Pakistani elders. We will compare EM between ethnic subgroups, those with and without memory problems, and those who use and do not use local services. We also aim to find out whether EM for memory problems are any different among middle aged SA people, who are often the gatekeepers for access to services and who themselves will form the next cohort of SA elders.Plan of InvestigationFirst, we will conduct a literature review to summarise the factors that determine recognition of and consultation for memory problems among SA elders (first 6 months). Second, based on the literature review and development interviews, we will adapt and validate the Barts Explanatory Models Inventory self report Check list (BEMI-C) to suit the assessment of EMs for memory problems among 30 SA people (7-12 months). Third, we will interview further 150 SA participants to explore EMs for memory problems and preferred treatments. The participants will included approximately equal proportions from Indian and Pakistani communities, both with and without memory problems, those who did and did not consult their General Practitioners for their memory problems, and both middle age and older people.Potential ImpactOlder people from ethnic minorities, including those with memory problems, need accessible and appropriate NHS services (DH, 2001). Depression and dementia are major challenges to the NHS in terms of numbers affected and cost (NAO, 2007). The National Dementia Strategy (DH, 2009) recommends increasing public and professional awareness, improving early diagnosis, and the need for an informed and effective workforce. This research will help to understand factors that act as barriers to the use of local services, especially the views of SA elders about causes and consequences of memory problems. The dissemination of study findings may reduce stigma, encourage early recognition and consultation, and will inform the development of services (DH, 2001, standard 7.3).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: A randomised controlled trial of patient directed self management of pain (PaDSMaP) compared to treatment as usual following total knee replacement
Abstract: BackgroundOver the last 4 years the numbers of primary total knee replacements (TKR) operations have increased by 163% to 73,455 in England and Wales, and are expected to continue increasing due to the ageing demographic of the UK population and increasing confidence of a good outcome from the surgery by surgeons and patients. However patients experienced substantial pain post-operatively which can reduce the time taken for patients to mobilise and return to normal activities and may predispose patients to develop chronic pain and adverse events. A patient’s level of pain and satisfaction with care may be influenced by who delivers pain control medications i.e. whether it is patient-directed self management of pain (PaDSMaP) or under nurse control (treatment as usual, TAU).AimsThis pragmatic randomised controlled trial (RCT) will evaluate the efficacy and cost-effectiveness of patient-directed self management of pain (PaDSMaP) compared to nurse-controlled analgesia (TAU) in patients who have undergone a primary TKR. The primary outcome will be to compare the patient’s levels of pain at three days after a primary TKR operation in the 2 groups. It will also compare the two groups up to 6 weeks post-operatively with respect to satisfaction with pain control, quality of life (QOL), activities of daily living (ADL), adverse effects and time to mobilisation. Further, it will determine the acceptability of PaDSMaP to patients and the multidisciplinary surgical and ward teams. Finally it will determine the interventions’ relative costs and cost effectiveness.Plan of InvestigationA prospective, randomised, parallel-group, single blinded, active-control study of PaDSMaP (patient-directed self management of pain) compared to TAU (nurse-controlled analgesia) for patients undergoing a primary unilateral TKR at a district general teaching hospital the Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital Foundation Trust (N&NUHFT).
