The data analysis will be blinded.A sample of 72 patients per arm is sufficient to detect a between-group difference of 0.5 standard deviations (approximately 12 points) in the primary outcome measure, a 0-100 visual analogue scale pain score at three days after a primary TKR operation, with 80% power and allowing for 10% drop out. Secondary outcomes will include satisfaction with pain control, QOL, ADL, adverse effects, time to mobilisation, and costs.Potential ImpactIt is hoped that the results of this study will allow the NHS to improve post-operative pain control after TKR. Hopefully it will also improve patient’s satisfaction with their pain control, reduce time to mobilisation, and reduce the incidence of adverse events. It is likely that the information from this study will be relevant to post-operative analgesic care in general for all patients capable of managing oral analgesics.In addition to the funds requested here the patients entered into this study will form a cohort that will be audited for up to 5 years to determine the impact of pre-operative characteristics (anxiety, depression, pain levels) and post-operative pain control on the long-term success or failure of TKRs as defined by the development of chronic pain, ADL and QOL.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Opportunistic brief intervention to reduce alcohol consumption in a high risk group attending a genito-urinary medicine clinic:a pilot study to assess feasibility, acceptability and effectiveness.
Abstract: BackgroundThere is national concern about the alcohol consumption of young people. Opportunistic brief interventions (BIs) by trained health professionals have been shown, largely in general practice, to reduce consumption in people drinking at hazardous levels. There is less evidence of effectiveness in young people. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are rising, and commonest in young people. Attenders at genitourinary medicine (GUM) clinics are mostly young, with a high prevalence of problem drinking which is associated with risky sexual behaviour. They may be highly motivated to change their consumption but less likely to attend general practice for BI. BIs are not used systematically in GUM clinics and their effectiveness on alcohol use and sexual health is unknown.AimsThe long-term aim is to evaluate the cost effectiveness of BIs in GUM clinics on reducing alcohol consumption, and improving sexual health. This is the first phase to guide design of a multi-centre RCT. It is set in one inner-city GUM department. The pilot study aims are to: i) assess the feasibility of identifying hazardous alcohol use; recruiting and randomising subjects to a BI by trained sexual health clinicians, with integrated advice on alcohol and sexual health; implementing it within the GUM clinic; and attaining a high degree of follow-up. ii) estimate effectiveness compared to usual care, measuring changes in alcohol consumption and sexual behaviour.iii) determine the acceptability of the BI to staff and patients and identify the resource implications.Plan of InvestigationAttendees to Portsmouth GUM Clinic will complete a validated screening tool for hazardous drinking (FAST). Those drinking at hazardous levels (FAST>=3) will be referred to a researcher. Study information will be given and consent obtained, baseline information on alcohol use and sexual behaviour collected, and randomisation to BI at the clinic appointment by trained sexual health clinicians (motivational interview, feedback on drinking and high risk situations, with a single reinforcement) or control (standard leaflet). We aim to randomise 100 to each group. Follow-up at 6 weeks and 6 months; primary outcome alcohol consumption and secondary outcome sexual behaviour. Qualitative research with health professionals and participants will assess the acceptability of and barriers to BI.Potential ImpactAlcohol history is noted in GUM clinics but there is little structured intervention. There is an opportunity to intervene with this hard to reach, high risk young population to reduce alcohol consumption and improve sexual health. With the preliminary data obtained here we would seek funding for a larger multi-centre study. If this was positive there would be a pragmatic cost-effective intervention which could be offered in all GUM clinics in the UK, tackling two major public health problems: alcohol related harm and poor sexual health. It would contribute to the evidence for the effectiveness of BI for young people and help guide commissioning decisions.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: Evaluation of Stroke Services in Anglia Stroke & Heart Clinical Network using patient-centred approach
Abstract: BackgroundStroke is the third leading cause of death in developed countries and the leading cause of long-term disability worldwide. A series of national stroke audits in the UK highlighted the differences in stroke care between hospitals. Recent initiatives by the Department of Health have aimed to improving stroke care in the UK, including Stroke Clinical Networks to support NHS trusts in England. This study will examine how variations in provision of NHS stroke services in the East of England affect patient outcomes and health care costs.AimsThe proposed study aims to describe variation in outcomes following stroke and to identify the characteristics of services that are associated with better outcomes, after accounting for case mix differences and individual prognostic factors. This observational study will identify areas of clinical practice which merit future randomised controlled trials (RCTs) to identify best practice in improving stroke care which will be of maximum benefit to patients, NHS and society. We also aim to obtain preliminary data to estimate sample sizes and conduct value of information analyses to design future pragmatic RCTs of innovative ways of delivering stroke care.Plan of InvestigationWe propose a 3 year cohort study in eight acute NHS trusts within East of England, with at least one year of follow-up after stroke. The study population will be a systematically selected random sample of patients admitted with stroke during the study period, recruited within each hospital. We will collect individual patient data on prognostic characteristics, health care received, outcomes and costs of care and we will also record relevant characteristics of each provider organisation. The determinants of one year outcome including patient reported outcome will be assessed statistically with proportional hazards regression models. Self (or proxy) completed EuroQol (EQ-5D) questionnaires will measure quality of life at baseline and follow-up for cost utility analyses.Potential ImpactThis study will provide observational data about health service factors associated with variations in patient outcomes and health care costs following hospital admission for acute stroke. This will form the basis for future RCTs by identifying promising health service interventions, assessing the feasibility of recruiting and following up trial patients, and provide evidence about frequency and variances in outcomes, and intra-cluster correlation of outcomes, for sample size calculations. The results will inform clinicians, public, service providers, commissioners and policy makers to drive further improvement in health services which will bring direct benefit to the patients.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Contractor: Lancashire Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
Award_Title: ASTUTE: Acute Stroke Telemedicine: Utility, Training and Evaluation
Abstract: BackgroundPatient outcomes are improved by reducing time to, and increasing accessibility of, stroke-specialist consultation and treatment, through facilitating initial diagnosis and appropriate delivery of time-dependent treatments. Telemedicine may facilitate earlier and wider access to stroke-specialist consultation and enhance emergency assessment and treatment. However, factors facilitating implementation are complex. We will explore what has worked well in existing networks, to develop standardised systems for new networks. Our aim is to optimise the reliability and acceptability of telemedicine with staff, patients and carers.AimsThis 2 year programme of research will utilise the principles of the new MRC framework for Development and Evaluation of Complex Interventions. We will develop and pilot a Standardised Telemedicine Toolkit (STT) for use in acute stroke, to determine if it can enhance time to, and accuracy of, clinical decision making. The STT will include standardised operating procedures (SOPs - patient assessments and a clinical care checklist), a training needs assessment and a training programme.We will assess if the components of the STT are aligned with the needs and expectations of patients, carers and health professionals, and explore how telemedicine can be made workable in clinical practice.We will develop a preliminary STT, which will be honed in a series of iterations to deliver a final STT.Plan of InvestigationFour phases in centres with prior stroke telemedicine experience with and without video, and centres intending to use telemedicine.Phase 1: Develop STT: evidence synthesis (Cochrane methods) of telemedicine interventions to manage acute stroke; and interviews with telemedicine experienced end users (patients, carers, staff) to identify barriers and facilitators to its use and training needs.Phase 2: Introduce and refine STT by using it in a centre and interviewing stakeholders on real time acceptability.Phase 3: Test feasibility of clinical decision making using videos from Phase 2, by a range of staff. Discuss modes of introduction locally and nationally.Phase 4: Finalise STT and pilot test in 2 centres.Potential ImpactThis project will assist in implementing the recent National Stroke Strategy, aiming to treat stroke as a medical emergency and gain rapid access to the right care, namely:• Earlier and equitable access to stroke-specialist assessment and treatment• Improve patient outcomes, experiences and satisfaction• Stroke care at a local hospital for duration of admission• Service tailored to patient and carers needs• Service delivered by staff confident with new technology• Opportunity for supervision and mentoring of new staff, facilitating delivery of stroke-specialist services and new treatments• Standard toolkit, usable in other settings• May reduce costs to NHS and society• May inform future use of telemedicine in other areas requiring stroke-specialist diagnosis eg. assessment of TIA

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Contractor: NHS Bristol, North Somerset and South Gloucestershire CCG
Award_Title: Processes of change in a group intervention for domestic violence perpetrators: a secondary qualitative analysis
Abstract: Research question Are there discursive strategies in a behaviour change programme for domestically abusive men that are useful for understanding and reducing abuse? Background Domestic violence and abuse (DVA) damages health and wellbeing, with social, public health and clinical consequences, impacting on the lives of both adults and children. It increases the risk of long-term health conditions, especially mental health problems, and causes immense human misery as well as significant financial costs. Group-based domestic violence perpetrator programmes (DVPPs) have been developed to help perpetrators (mainly men) address and change their abusive behaviour. However, encouraging perpetrators to acknowledge abusive behaviours, and how best to change such behaviours, is poorly understood. Aims To understand how men make sense of, account for, and seek to change their abusive behaviour; how group facilitators seek to engage participants to adopt alternative ways of thinking and behaving; and to consider how these insights might be applied in a range of settings. Objectives 1. To examine how men make sense of, account for, and seek to change their abusive behaviour in the context of weekly DVPP groups 2. To examine how men position themselves both in relation to women and other men during the weekly DVPP groups 3. To identify examples of facilitators engagement which elicit a move towards alternative, non-abusive ways of thinking and behaving, plus examples of facilitation which reduce engagement 4. To formulate the findings to inform improvement of DVPP group delivery, training of group facilitators and the wider identification and engagement of DVA perpetrators. Methods This is a qualitative study using critical discourse analysis combined with ethnography. The data for the study will be videos of a community-based group DVPP recorded in the course of a pilot trial of DVPP effectiveness (REPROVIDE). It is standard practice for DVPP sessions to be videoed and we have permission from participating men and facilitators to analyse the videos. Working closely with DVPP and mental health experts, we will review the videos and analyse up to 40 selected video excerpts. Supplementary information from REPROVIDE such as participants educational background and mental health status will inform the excerpt selection. Timelines for delivery Pre-study: Approvals. Months 1 – 2: PPI meetings, refine sampling strategy, review video collection, agree initial sample, coding. Months 3 -6: Discuss emerging findings with stakeholders and PPI groups, agree second sample, coding. Months 7 – 13: Final analysis, feedback, synthesis with REPROVIDE. Write-up, dissemination. Anticipated impact and dissemination The findings of this study will help to improve the identification and engagement of perpetrators of DVA, delivery of DVPP groups and training of facilitators. This study will contribute to the interpretation of the main REPROVIDE trial findings; how and why DVPPs work (or fail to work) and will inform effective implementation of DVPPs if the main trial shows cost-effectiveness of the intervention. Dissemination will be to practitioner, commissioner (e.g. Respect conference) and academic audiences (e.g. European Network on Gender and Violence and Medical Sociological Association conference).

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Development and use of performance measures in mental health care services
Abstract: Performance measurement is used to promote understanding of how to manage and improve what organisations do. There has been very little research on performance measurement of mental healthcare organisations in the UK. Despite consensus on the need to prioritise mental healthcare, the performance focus has remained on the acute sector. This research will develop the evidence in this area by examining the concept of performance in mental health and the challenges of measurement, in order to produce appropriate, robust measures. It will explore 5 key questions: 1.) What is the relationship between different performance indicators in mental health? 2.) What is the degree of variation in performance between mental health provider organisations over time? 3.) What are the differences in performance across settings (e.g. primary versus secondary care)? 4.) What is the relationship between the performance of mental health provider organisations and their commissioners and what are the main commissioning patterns over time? and, 5.) What is the impact of socio-economic deprivation measures on the performance of mental health providers? These questions will be examined by constructing a comprehensive longitudinal dataset of mental health performance for the Mental Health Trusts and PCTs who provide mental health services across England. The analysis will use various multivariate multi-level statistical techniques to address each of the questions. The work will focus on performance incentives in mental healthcare at a system level and will therefore be policy relevant to the NHS.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Towards earlier diagnosis of colorectal and ovarian cancers in Primary Care.
Abstract: This programme of research aims to expedite diagnosis of colorectal and ovarian cancer in primary care in three studies, all of which have been adopted in to the National Cancer Research Institute portfolio. The research journey is at different stages for the two cancers: in ovarian cancer we know very little about the risk of symptoms so study this: in colorectal cancer we have a tool that may speed up the diagnosis, and test it out. For colorectal cancer, I have developed a clinical prediction rule - the CAPER score. This is being tested in two ways. First, the score is being used in a pre-existing dataset (the General Practice Research Database) to validate whether it does actually identify those at higher risk of cancer. This is a cohort study, examining all patients over 40 who presented to their GP with one of constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or loss of weight, and calculating a CAPER score on them. This will then be compared with their actual outcome. The study is already funded by Cancer Research UK. The second colorectal study is a cluster randomised trial of 2480 patients in 100 general practices in the UK, evaluating the clinical and economic worth of the CAPER score. The primary clinical outcome is the time to diagnosis of colorectal cancer (or polyp) after initial presentation to primary care with any of diarrhoea, constipation, abdominal pain or loss of weight Secondary outcomes include an economic analysis. This is a major trial drawing on strong collaborative links within the National Cancer Research Institute. The third study is a case-control study of 225 ovarian cancers in Devon, and compares their symptom reporting in the year before diagnosis with 1100 age-sex and practice matched controls. The main output from this will be positive predictive values for each symptom (and symptom pairs) for patients attending general practice: this will help to inform referrals for investigation.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Applied mathematical and economic modelling for the evaluation and optimisation of the effectiveness of public health interventions against sexually transmitted infections.
Abstract: Gonorrhoea and chlamydia present a significant public health burden, and are the leading cause of preventable infertility. Mathematical models, economic analysis and parameter estimation will be used to address questions relating to sexual health service provision: 1) What is the probability of progression from chlamydia infection to complications? 2) What is the effect of heterogeneity in sexual behaviour and health care access on chlamydia screening? 3) What are the cost and reliability implications of dual testing (chlamydia/gonorrhoea)? The applicant will develop skills in economic analysis and public health commissioning and delivery while integrating into the existing STI research programme.

Contractor: London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine
Award_Title: Promoting active travel in the UK: effectiveness and equity of individual and infrastructural interventions
Abstract: Promoting active travel (walking and cycling) is a public health and environmental priority, but little is known about how to achieve this or how effects vary by socio-economic position. I will jointly lead a large randomised controlled trial promoting active travel among NHS staff. I will also examine the physical activity, travel and carbon impacts across of large-scale infrastructure projects aiming to encourage active travel. In both studies I will examine whether the effects vary by socio-economic group. This cross-disciplinary program will contribute high-quality evidence about what works in promoting active travel, and how promising interventions may affect health inequalities.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Does physical activity protect against CVD, diabetes and disability in later life? a study of objectively measured physical activity in older adults.
Abstract: The proportion of older adults (over 60 years) in the UK is growing and bears a high burden of morbidity and mortality, primarily from cardiovascular disease (CVD), stroke, type 2 diabetes, and mobility limitations. Although physical activity can protect against onset of these outcomes, evidence about the dose-response associations with the different dimensions of activity (including frequency, amount, intensity and type) is incomplete in older adults and will be studied here. The health consequences of taking up activity in older adulthood will be studied. Year on year continuities in activity will be evaluated in the first prospective large-scale study using actigraphs in older adults.

Award_Title: Understanding how changes to the environment may promote walking, cycling and physical activity
Abstract: Guidance from NICE suggests that supportive physical environments encourage walking and cycling; however few studies have shown that changing the environment actually changes behaviour. This project aims to investigate the short and longer term effects of environmental changes on walking and cycling, the impacts on physical activity, and the mechanisms by which behaviour change is brought about. These aims will be achieved by conducting new analyses of existing data, and by combining evidence from these and other studies on how specific environmental changes are linked to specific behavioural changes and impacts on physical activity, for whom and in what circumstances.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Evidence to improve the quality and safety of midwifery-led care
Abstract: Aim Using national data on perinatal deaths and two studies involving primary data collection through a pioneering midwifery research and reporting system, this research programme aims to provide evidence and a research infrastructure to strengthen the development of safe, high quality midwifery-led care and improve outcomes for mothers and babies.Objectives To describe labour and delivery complications, mode of birth and causes of death in intrapartum stillbirths and early neonatal deaths occurring in births planned in midwifery units and at home, and compare with a sample of similar perinatal deaths occurring in births planned in obstetric units in the same NHS trusts/health boards To develop and establish a new national midwifery reporting and research system (UKMidS) To use UKMidS to estimate the current prevalence of obesity in women planning birth in alongside midwifery units (AMUs) and describe their maternal and clinical characteristics, management, labour complications and outcomes compared with women of normal weight To use UKMidS to determine the incidence of and risk factors for neonatal unit admission in births occurring in AMUs To use UKMidS to describe management of labour in the mothers of babies admitted to neonatal care following birth in an AMU, with particular reference to national clinical guidelines To develop a funding system and structure to ensure further development and sustainability of UKMidS to include other midwifery-led settings for birth Objective 1: Understanding and comparing cause(s) of perinatal death in births planned in different settings Methods Using national data on perinatal deaths submitted to MBRRACE-UK for 2013-14, I will use conditional logistic regression to compare labour complications, mode of birth and cause(s) of death in babies of women planning birth in midwifery-led settings with a frequency matched sample of deaths in planned obstetric unit births in the same NHS trusts/health boards. Outcomes and benefits Identification of possible risk factors, complications or causes of death for investigation in future studies. Objectives 2 & 6: A new national midwifery reporting and research system (UKMidS) Methods As an extension of the UK Obstetric Surveillance System (UKOSS) I will set up a national midwifery reporting and research system (UKMidS) for monthly prospective data collection in AMUs in England. Reporting midwives in each AMU will notify cases for each UKMidS study and complete study-specific data collection forms for cases and comparison women where required.Outcomes and benefits A research infrastructure to generate robust, promptly reported evidence on incidence, risk factors, clinical practice, management and outcome for uncommon conditions, events and outcomes, to support the development of midwifery research capacity and enable further high quality, clinical and policy-relevant research in this area. Objective 3: Obesity in women planning birth in AMUs Methods I will carry out a national cohort study, using data collected through UKMidS, to identify the current national prevalence of obesity in women planning birth in AMUs and use logistic regression to compare the progress and management of their labour and their outcomes with women of normal weight planning AMU birth. Outcomes and benefitsEvidence on safety of planned AMU birth for obese women to strengthen clinical guidelines and AMU admission criteria, improve outcomes and inform women's decision-making. Objectives 4 & 5: Neonatal admission following birth in an AMU Methods I will carry out a national case-control study on cases of neonatal admission following birth occurring in an AMU, identified using UKMidS, to calculate the national incidence of neonatal admission and use logistic regression to investigate potential risk factors for admission and adverse outcome, including progress and management of labour. Outcomes and benefits Evidence to inform clinical practice, strengthen evidence-based guidelines and ultimately improve outcomes.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Brief interventions to reduce hazardous and harmful drinking in parents of children referred to children's social care: a pilot feasibility study
Abstract: Around 30% of children under the age of 16 years in the UK are living with at least one parent with an alcohol use disorder (AUD). As well as being a risk to the health of the parent, parental AUDs have been found to be associated with adverse experiences and outcomes in their children. As such, addressing parental AUDs is both a public health and safeguarding priority. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)There is a wealth of high quality evidence supporting the effectiveness of alcohol screening and brief interventions to reduce risky drinking in primary health care and a range of other settings. However, to date, there has been no research examining the feasibility of alcohol screening and brief interventions in a social work setting or with parents of children referred to children's social care due to a concern about the well-being of the child. Intervening early has the potential to reduce the risk of harm to both parent and child. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)This research programme seeks to determine the feasibility and acceptability of embedding alcohol screening and brief interventions within children's social care. There are three workstreams to the research programme: a systematic literature review, a pilot feasibility cluster randomised control trial (cRCT) of alcohol screening and brief interventions and a qualitative study. Workstream 1: The systematic literature review will review the international literature on the effectiveness of interventions for parental substance use. The evidence will provide valuable intelligence, that will inform the extension of brief interventions to the parental context. In addition, the systematic review will inform which parental and child outcomes are measured within workstream 2 as well as the tools used to measure outcomes. The brief intervention will be piloted during the pilot feasibility cRCT.Workstream 2: The pilot feasibility cRCT will establish the feasibility and acceptability of conducting a trial of alcohol screening and brief interventions to reduce risky drinking in parents of children referred to children's social care due to concerns regarding the well-being of the child. Social workers within children's social care will conduct alcohol screening with parents. Following a positive alcohol screen, consenting parents will receive one of three intervention conditions: a control condition of an alcohol information leaflet, brief advice delivered by the social worker or extended brief intervention (brief advice delivered by the social worker plus a referral to a health practitioner for behaviour change counselling). CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)Workstream 3: Building upon workstream 2, parents, social workers, social work managers and health practitioners will be interviewed to evaluate factors that impact upon the implementation of alcohol screening and brief interventions with parents with AUDs whose child is referred to children's social care due to concerns regarding the well-being of the child. The acceptability of outcome measures relevant to a future trial of alcohol screening and brief interventions with parents with AUDs will also be determined. CHAR(13) + CHAR(10)The research programme will ultimately inform the development of a contextually relevant protocol for a full trial of brief intervention to reduce alcohol intake in parents within this setting. As such, the research will directly impact on parents referred to children's social care, the children and upon service provision within health and social care.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health improvement
Award_Title: Mindfulness-based interventions for mental health promotion: an individual participant data meta-analysis to assess comparative effects and predictors of differential response
Abstract: Mindfulness: Helping people to feel good Public health organisations in the UK are interested in finding ways to improve the mental wellbeing of the general public, as mental wellbeing is linked to better health. One way of doing this is to offer techniques to the public that are effective in promoting mental health and preventing mental problems. One set of techniques that many people find helpful is mindfulness training. Mindfulness training is about learning to pay attention to what is happening at the present moment with an attitude of curiosity and kindness. Some mindfulness courses are specifically designed for people who are clinically unwell, but mindfulness practices were traditionally intended for anyone to improve their mental wellbeing. Mindfulness courses to increase wellbeing and reduce stress have become very popular. Many organisations in the UK now offer mindfulness training, including universities and civil service departments. If preventative mindfulness courses are found to be effective for most people, and people are interested in learning mindfulness, then there are good grounds for offering these courses as part of public health programmes. However, the research evidence for offering mindfulness courses in this way is weak: While many studies show that preventative mindfulness training is beneficial, most are poorly designed so that you cannot be sure of the results. There are concerns that studies showing no benefit have not been published in prominent scientific journals and so few people know about them. This could give an overly optimistic picture of how helpful mindfulness is. Mindfulness courses come in different 'shapes and sizes', and we don't know which ones work best, for whom and in which circumstances. When mindfulness training is compared with other feel-good practices such as physical exercise, it is not clear which one is best. Even less clear is who benefits most from each. There is evidence that not everyone benefits from mindfulness training. It may even be harmful for some people, but at present this is poorly understood. Policy makers need high quality reviews and analyses that systematically take all of these factors into account before deciding whether or not to offer preventative mindfulness training to the public at large. In 2015 an All-Party Parliamentary Group recommended that the National Institute of Health Research invite bids for research to explore the potential of mindfulness as a public health preventative intervention. Finding out what works for whom I propose to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis of all the studies that I can find on mindfulness training for mental health promotion. Systematic review is a research technique that uses clear methods to identify and critique studies. Meta-analysis is a statistical method of combining the data from these studies to show an overall effect; a kind of average result. I plan to do the most refined and reliable type of meta-analysis, one where all the data from each individual in each study is combined. This approach enables researchers to ask questions that cannot be answered by a single study, such as which groups of individuals are more likely to be helped by mindfulness training. This complex type of meta-analysis is called an individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis. I propose to train in IPD meta-analysis statistical methods, and to conduct an IPD meta-analysis to study the following: Comparative effects: To determine whether mindfulness training reduces distress, anxiety and depression, and improves mental wellbeing, self-care and performance among adults living in the community, compared with no training at all or with other feel-good practices. Predictors of differential response: To find out which types of people benefit from the different types of mindfulness courses available. I will invite members of the public interested in mental health promotion or mindfulness, health service managers, and mindfulness teachers to get involved early on in the research. Their experience will help to understand aspects of mental health promotion in daily life and society, how different mindfulness courses work for different types of people, and what effects to look out for in this research. Together we will work on all aspects of the project. For example, we will train together in effective communication, and then make a plan to share information about the research and findings with various audiences using academic, stakeholder and public networks. This study will determine whether preventative mindfulness courses really help people to feel better and avoid mental health problems, or whether they are 'just a fad'. It will also help to understand who to offer mindfulness to, and in what ways.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Planning for pregnancy: an integrated pathway to plan or prevent pregnancy and mitigate the adverse health effects of unplanned pregnancy to improve outcomes for women and their families
Abstract: Aim To provide the research and practical evidence base to deliver quality improvement in preconception care, to prevent unplanned pregnancies and abortion, and to mitigate the adverse impacts of unplanned pregnancies.Background Preconception care has been overlooked at every level of the NHS, despite a strong evidence base for the benefits to women and their children. Only 55% of women planned their last pregnancy, and most will have done so with little or no help from the NHS. To improve pregnancy planning and the uptake of preconception care, clinicians need a rapid, low-cost way of assessing a woman's prospective pregnancy intentions. If she wishes to become pregnant in the next year, preconception health advice can be given. If not, discussion can focus on contraceptive needs to prevent unplanned pregnancies and abortions, of which nearly 200,000 take place in the NHS each year. Unplanned pregnancies are a marker of, and contribute to, health inequalities and are associated with adverse outcomes, such as low birthweight, preterm birth and postnatal depression. However, women with unplanned pregnancies are not identified during antenatal care, unplanned pregnancy is not recognised as a risk factor for adverse birth outcomes, and services are not offered to these women to mitigate their risk.Methods I will refine and field-test the 'Desire to Avoid Pregnancy' (DAP) scale, a set of questions that assesses a non-pregnant woman's stance towards future pregnancy. This can be used to triage women to preconception care or contraception advice. For this 1000 women will complete the DAP at baseline and I will follow them up for one year to determine the predictive value of the DAP. Simultaneously I will work with women and clinicians to design the implementation of the DAP in a range of primary care settings.To detect women with a current unplanned pregnancy, I will pilot the London Measure of Unplanned Pregnancy (LMUP) in antenatal care at University College London Hospital. The LMUP is a psychometrically validated measure of pregnancy intention, using six questions to score a pregnancy from zero (most unplanned) to twelve (most planned). Building on my PhD research, I will map the causal pathways from unplanned pregnancy to maternal behaviours and adverse outcomes to understand how unplanned pregnancy leads to adverse outcomes. I will then work with women, midwives and clinicians to design referral pathways to mitigate the impact of unplanned pregnancies.Benefit to patients and NHS Patients will benefit from this work because NHS services will be better equipped to meet their reproductive needs regarding pregnancy planning and prevention. Women will be in better health prior to pregnancy, increasing their chances of a healthy pregnancy and better health outcomes for mother and baby in the short and long-term. Women receiving personalised contraceptive care will be at lower risk of an unplanned pregnancy and abortion, but those who do experience an unplanned pregnancy will be identified and supported to reduce the associated adverse outcomes.The NHS will benefit from this work through savings from the unplanned pregnancies and abortions avoided, estimated to cost ~£200,000,000 per year. The DAP will result in a more efficient use of clinician time. Using the LMUP in routine antenatal care will provide a public health surveillance system which can be used to estimate the incidence of (un)planned pregnancy, monitor health inequalities, determine which groups of women are most at risk and tailor services accordingly. Overall the research will lead to a package of services that will contribute to national targets related to reducing health inequalities, preventing unplanned pregnancy and improving pregnancy outcomes, including perinatal mental health, birthweight, stillbirth and neonatal and maternal death.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Protection
Award_Title: Maintaining public confidence and informing vaccine policy: Using clinical and sero-epidemiological data to predict risk of rotavirus disease in older children and adults in the UK
Abstract: Understanding how immunity to rotavirus and the risk of disease changes as vaccinated children ageBackgroundIn July 2013 the UK introduced rotavirus vaccination for infants at 8 and 12 weeks of age. Before this, rotavirus was estimated to be responsible for 80,000 GP consultations and 45% of acute gastroenteritis hospitalisations in children under 5 years old.Early impact studies have shown reduced incidence of rotavirus hospitalisations and healthcare use for acute gastroenteritis in children since vaccine introduction. However, the long-term impact of vaccination is not fully understood. This is crucial in the assessment of any vaccine programme. To achieve this aim, we need to understand rotavirus transmission, herd immunity, and changes in infection risk that occur as vaccinated cohorts age.I hypothesise that in the UK, rotavirus disease burden will shift from being endemic in young children to epidemic in older children and adults as a consequence of infant vaccination.Objectives To evaluate the impact of rotavirus vaccine 7-years after introduction. To assess how vaccination changes immunity in children as they age. To understand and predict changes in the epidemiology of rotavirus infection from childhood to adulthood. MethodsMy fellowship will be split into three workstreams:One: Epidemiological study Vaccine impact and effectiveness in England will be assessed 7-years post-vaccine introduction using large anonymised databases of laboratory-confirmed rotavirus infections, hospital admissions, emergency department attendances, and GP consultations for acute gastroenteritis. Novel methods employing interrupted time-series analysis will be used to assess vaccine impact across all outcome measures, in the context of vaccine uptake and socioeconomic deprivation.Two: Seroepidemiology For the first time in the England, rotavirus serology will allow us to assess changes in the force of infection with rotavirus over time, pre- and post-vaccine introduction. Using a collection of serum samples representative of the general population of England, rotavirus-specific IgG and IgA titres will be measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays and titres will be compared between the pre- and post-vaccine age-groups.Three: Mathematical models I will modify previously developed mathematical models describing the transmission dynamics of rotavirus strains by fitting these to laboratory-confirmed rotavirus cases in England and the serological analysis from workstream two. The fitted models will be used to generate testable hypotheses regarding changes in the age and strain distribution of rotavirus cases following vaccine introduction, at different levels of vaccine uptake and socioeconomic strata. Model predictions will be validated by using the observed data.Summary of BenefitsBy understanding changes in rotavirus epidemiology we can assess whether a booster dose of vaccine may be needed. Data from this study will enable us to understand the economics and social cost of rotavirus disease, including that borne by parents/carers identified through the consultation group. The long-term analysis of equitability of vaccine uptake and impact will inform public health efforts to efficiently target vaccine promotion. To summarise, these data will have implications for clinical management, diagnostics, health protection preparedness and economics, and will support vaccine programme policy and public confidence in the vaccine programme.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Developing sexual and reproductive health interventions for young people of Pakistani origin based on improved understanding of sexual attitudes and behaviours
Abstract: The NHS needs to take account of cultural, linguistic and faith diversity. This is particularly important for sexual health services where for some communities faith and culture play a central role in shaping sexual attitudes and lifestyles. Using quantitative analyses of available data sets and in-depth community based research, this project aims to provide detailed information to inform the development of sexual and reproductive health interventions/services tailored to the religious and cultural needs of young Pakistanis in the UK. These data will inform more culturally sensitive NHS services in London and will be a resource for the development of future sexual health service provision throughout the country.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Health Improvement
Award_Title: Understanding women’s perspectives on alcohol consumption before and during pregnancy: towards the design of a health promoting intervention for primary care.
Abstract: Risky drinking in women of child bearing age has increased significantly over recent years and there are a range of problems associated with this, including unplanned pregnancies. Risky drinking around the time of conception can adversely affect child development. However, there has been little research in the UK on reducing alcohol consumption in pregnant women. By undertaking a literature review and interviews with pregnant women this study will design an appropriate intervention aimed at reducing alcohol related harm in pregnant women and their babies.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Transfer from midwifery unit to obstetric unit during labour: rates, process, outcomes and women’s experience.
Abstract: This study will provide information to improve the care and experience of women who plan to give birth in midwifery units by exploring the factors associated with transfer during labour to an obstetric unit. Data from a large funded prospective study of women planning to give birth in midwifery units in England will be analysed to find out why and how many women are transferred and whether transfer is safe. In addition, transfer protocols and policies will be collected and analysed to examine the transfer decision-making process. Women’s views and experiences of transfer will be explored in qualitative interviews.

Public_Health_Outcomes_Framework: Healthcare Public Health and Preventing Premature Mortality
Award_Title: Missed opportunities to improve care for people with musculoskeletal disorders in primary care
Abstract: Primary care provides first contact, patient-focused healthcare in the community, with more than 70% of people consulting their general practitioner (GP) every year. Over 90% of all NHS contacts (including>300 million GP consultations) take place in primary care, through a range of health professionals including GPs, nurses and physiotherapists. This volume of demand creates key opportunities for primary care, including the efficient delivery of accessible services, the provision of comprehensive and continuous care throughout life, and the co-ordination of services for people with multimorbidity. 1 in 6 general practice consultations are for musculoskeletal problems. The commonest musculoskeletal conditions seen in primary care are osteoarthritis in older adults, and back pain in working age. However, primary care, is also the first point of contact for patients with early inflammatory rheumatological disorders and the main setting for the management of some of these, notably gout. Primary care, therefore, provides unique opportunities for improving the diagnosis and management of these conditions, and to significantly improve the health and well-being of patients, and reduce the health and economic impact of these conditions on individuals and society. This Fellowship focuses on two musculoskeletal conditions which pose significant, but different challenges for primary care diagnosis and management, namely osteoarthritis and gout. For both of these conditions, my prior research and that of others already provides considerable observational evidence on patterns of suboptimal management in primary care and existing opportunities for improvement. This Fellowship represents a concerted approach to intervention to address these. It consists of two distinct but complementary themes. The first theme 'Missed opportunities in the management of Osteoarthritis' is concerned with improving care for patients with the most common and disabling musculoskeletal complaint seen in older adults. Theme 2 addresses the primary care management of chronic gout: chosen because it illustrates challenges that GPs face when managing a relatively uncommon (in terms of day to day workload) yet serious and potentially curable condition, and one which we know is currently poorly managed resulting in long term morbidity and increased mortality. This research focuses on clinical studies that have the potential to rapidly impact on improving patient care by enhancing the use of effective but underutilised interventions and by taking novel technology into the consulting room. The first workpackage in theme 1 takes advantage of the fact that many patients with osteoarthritis already attend primary care for the management of other comorbid long-term conditions. Practice nurses will be trained to opportunistically identify people who are struggling with osteoarthritis-related pain, and to identify those with concurrent anxiety or depression: comorbidities which are known to contribute significantly to increased disability. A pilot trial will evaluate the feasibility of this approach. Workpackage 2 will 'plug identified gaps' in the current evidence base, developing and testing interventions to address these, thus improving care for patients with osteoarthritis. The first funded trial in this workpackage will investigate the effectiveness of corticosteroid hip injections for patients with hip osteoarthritis with other clinical trials being developed over the duration of the fellowship. Theme 2 is based within a programme of research aimed at optimising the management of chronic gout by addressing key questions highlighted by the European League Against Rheumatism gout guidelines group. Two clinical trials will be developed addressing the role of self-management/self-titration of urate lowering therapy in the management of chronic gout; and investigating whether prophylaxis against acute attacks of gout is needed when initiating urate lowering therapy in primary care settings. The evidence generated by this fellowship will directly impact on patient care, inform new commissioning pathways for musculoskeletal problems and influence clinical guidelines for primary care.

Award_Title: Accelerating the Elimination of Hepatitis C in the UK
Abstract: AimTo bring advances in experimental medicine to the clinic to accelerate the elimination of hepatitis C in the UKThe objectives of the work are to:1) Identify ongoing transmission of HCV through implementation of routine next generation viral sequencing in NHS services 2) Develop a clinical network to improve identification and treatment of recent HCV infection and underserved populations 3) Develop diagnostics for rapid delivery at point-of-care to improve linkage to care 4) Combine clinical and sequencing data to identify networks of transmission for targeting interventionWork planned as part of this application will :- Compare two methods for next generation sequencing (NGS) of hepatitis C (those developed by the STOPHCV and ICONIC consortia), against a standardized panel of isolates and existing methods of genotyping and, for the first time, implement one method into NHS practice for routine diagnosis to support identification of transmission networks. - Provide support to other centres wishing to introduce NGS sequencing into their service to develop capacity throughout the NHS. - Establish a multi-centre network to describe the cascade of care of individuals with recent hepatitis C infection. This will initially focus on People living with HIV (PLWH) where there is evidence of ongoing transmission driven by an overlap of high-risk sexual behaviour and injecting drug use. Detailed data will be collected to understand transmission risk behaviours (including sexual behaviours, use of recreational drugs, geographic location, barriers to treatment, linkage to care and treatment and outcomes of therapy, risks of reinfection). - Establish the feasibility of recruiting hepatitis C infected individuals presenting to secondary care into a clinical cohort to identify the proportion of those who are homeless or vulnerably housed and the barriers to accessing care and treatment - Develop new methodologies to diagnose active infection in seropositive individuals to address the challenges in linking newly diagnosed patients to care - For the first time in the UK, use a combination of data from above to describe networks of hepatitis C transmission across different areas and investigate whether transmissions are more likely to be detected at single centres or between centres to inform future interventions.Potential benefits to patients and the NHSThe harmonization of approaches in different clinics towards recent hepatitis C infection will provide a standard of care which will be able to assess the performance of services and ensure the best care for individual patients. There has not until now been a unified effort to bring together clinical and epidemiological data and sequence across a network of clinics to understand transmission of hepatitis C. The information collected has the potential to provide important insights to inform policies for control where data is currently lacking and provide a rational basis for future intervention studies. During the period of this fellowship the relative importance of the marginalised populations that are the focus of this work will increase as hepatitis C treatment become more affordable and it become possible to cure all those individuals engaged in care. There will be a need for a better understanding of where new infections are happening and how to best prevent them. The information generated will provide evidence for new interventions to intervention. Despite scaling up access to treatment for hepatitis C, new infection rates have yet to fall and preventing further infection will save the costs of care and treatment to the NHS. This Professorship will enable the world leading scientific advances made by the UK HCV community to benefit all those with hepatitis and accelerate the elimination of HCV in the UK.

Abstract: eRAPID (electronic patient self-Reporting of Adverse-events: Patient Information and aDvice) is a research program aiming to develop, introduce and evaluate in cancer care a system for patients to self-report adverse events (AE) during and after cancer treatments. The system will be:- suitable for patients receiving chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy- electronic, allowing AE reporting from home or hospitals- integrated in routine care by documenting AE in existing electronic records and generating clinicians’ alerts for severe AE- providing patient advice on self-management of mild AEeRAPID aims to improve and unify current standards of AE monitoring and documentation across treatments to enhance care and improve patient experiences. We expect eRAPID will encourage self-management of mild AE and reduce hospital visits, whilst providing rapid alerts for urgent management of severe AE.In this application we use the accepted term Adverse Events (AE) to indicate side-effects, symptoms and toxicities of cancer treatments. In clinical practice the distinction between cancer symptoms and treatment side-effects is not always clear. We expect the self-reporting AE system to capture a range of cancer/treatment-related symptoms and provide a fuller picture of patient experience.The program development grant focuses on 3 components: 1) selecting/adapting/evaluating AE items for patient self-report; 2) delivering information technology required for patient-reported data management; and 3) reviewing patient care pathways and health economic measures for implementation of eRAPID in NHS practice.Outcomes from the full program will be:1. A pool of clinically valid items suitable for patient self-reported AE during cancer treatment, plus patient advice related to the AE reports facilitating self-management of mild AE.2. Flexible electronic platform for patients to report AE from clinic and home; clinician alerts to severe AE; real time AE documentation in electronic patient records. 3. Integration of eRAPID patient pathway in current clinical practice including staff training/guidelines.4. Feasibility/pilot study of eRAPID in clinical practice.5. Large scale trial evaluating outcomes during chemotherapy (reduced patient morbidity/mortality, better quality of life; improved process of care; health economic evaluation).II. BackgroundMost cancers are treated using multiple modalities, such as surgery, radiotherapy (RT), and systemic drug treatments (chemotherapy, hormonotherapy, targeted agents). All treatments are associated with acute and long term AE which are formally recorded in clinical trials, but rarely systematically documented in routine care. Improving AE reporting can improve care. In systemic treatments significant AE will prompt changes to drug doses or hospitalisation for potentially life-threatening infections. In RT AE detection can implement appropriate treatments (rectal incontinence, altered sexual function). Post-surgery AE monitoring can prompt investigations for recurrent disease or post-operative functional problems. In all treatments addressing AE can improve patients’ quality of life.III. Many patients delay seeking emergency care especially out of hours (4, 5). Abstract: Briefly describe the context of your proposal based on the following subheadings:I. Background to the proposed research programme, including NHS context and relevant literatureThe last 20 years has seen a major change in the provision of emergency vascular surgery from general surgery to those consultants with a specified interest in vascular surgery. Abstract: I. Aims: The proposed research programme aims to: • evaluate the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of providing choice and control in health and social care through personalised care (i.e. personal budgets, direct payments and self-directed support) for people with psychosis or severe mood disorder • understand and engage with organisational cultures which mitigate against the introduction of personalised care in mental health services • evaluate how contextual variations in the use and management of personalised care influence outcomes for people with psychosis or severe mood disorder • evaluate the experience of personalised care for people with psychosis or severe mood disorder with different needs and its impact on their well being • assess the extent to which personalised care can support the management of fluctuating mental health problems and promote recovery II. Background The Department of Health (DH) is committed to providing people living with enduring mental health problems greater choice and control over the health and social care services they receive (1-3) in line with the Independent Living Strategy (4). Local authorities are required to offer personal budgets to all people eligible for ongoing social care by April 2013 (1). Personal budgets provide service users with more freedom to purchase care and support from people they feel comfortable with, such as friends or family; or to fund activities to enhance well-being and promote social inclusion such as a gym membership, a college course or a taxi fare to a local library, for example. Direct payments are an alternative funding mechanism for personalising care and these are frequently used for one-off payments for specific items or services (5, 6). However, only 6.5% of adult social care users received a personal budget or direct payment in 2008-9 (7) and the take-up is particularly low among people with mental health problems (8, 9). Self-directed support is an integral component of personalised care and is the mechanism through which personal budgets are being delivered (10). It involves supporting service users, their carers and families to design and purchase a personal package of care and support, to help them achieve chosen outcomes. This requires professionals starting with the service user rather than the service when planning care (10) and will require a culture change in both professionals and services to fully implement (11-13). 75 Primary Care Trusts are currently piloting personal health budgets for people with long term conditions such as mental health problems to explore how the principles of personalisation may be extended into the NHS (14). This builds upon earlier initiatives which provided patients with some choice in hospital appointments, elective surgery and which hospital to attend (15), for example. The Government aims to introduce personal health budgets throughout the NHS in 2012 and to explore merging them with personal social care budgets (1, 2). Community mental health services are arguably well-placed to provide merged health and social care personal budgets as they have a long tradition of multidisciplinary team working funded by the NHS and local authorities (6). III. No other health area combines frequency of occurrence with persistence and breadth of impact to the same extent, making mental health problems the largest single cause of disability in the UK (17). Mental health has been a priority of the NHS in the last decade (18) but mental health service costs, estimated at £22.5 billion in 2007, are expected to rise to an estimated £32.6 billion in 2026 (19). Abstract: Timeline: March 2013 – May 2014 The Programme Development Grant work plan has three Stages. We will also search the web sites of dental regulatory bodies, professional associations, specialist societies in the UK and internationally. 3. Award_Title: Managing uncertainty to reduce emergency bed days in older patients
Abstract: The Programme Development Grant will include three phases of work, aimed at answering the following research questions: 1) What are the defining characteristics of those older patients for whom the decision to admit to hospital may be unclear i.e. who are those 'at the margin of the admission decision? 2) How should the study population be refined for the Programme Grant for Applied Research 3) How should patients and the public be involved in the co-research of interventions to inform decisions about avoidable admissions in older people? 1) Evidence synthesis Objectives: a) To conduct a systematic review to identify studies in people over 65 years of age who are at risk of potentially avoidable hospital admission that describe place of delivery of care (intervention), risk factors and outcomes of care b) To review current guidance around emergency admittance decisions for people over 65 years of age c) To synthesise the evidence from both academic and grey literature to inform selection of a population for the PGfAR and the risk factors associated with patient outcomes in different care setting Eligibility criteria: Inclusion criteria: Types of studies Randomised controlled trials and other controlled studies (controlled trials, controlled before-and-after studies, analytic cohorts) clearly or potentially about outcomes in people over 65 years of age who are at risk of potentially avoidable hospital admission that describe place of delivery of care, risk factors and outcomes of care. Only full study reports will be included but authors of studies reported only as abstracts will be contacted to ask if full study reports are available. Study population Studies that include people over 65 years of age of either sex living in OECD countries as these countries have comparable patterns of health status, health care provision and health spend as a proportion of GDP. Definitions for the terms used to describe populations at risk of avoidable admissions will be based on ambulatory care sensitive conditions (ACSCs) building on existing work by the PI and others (Purdy, Public Health 2009). Interventions Interventions in this instance will be construed as admission to hospital, using definitions developed for previous studies (Huntley, Family Practice 2013). Comparators will be alternatives to admission including but not limited to: hospital at home, virtual ward, rapid response nursing, care at home, admission to a care home, usual care. Risk factors Risk factors that may be associated with outcome will be included e.g. co-morbidities, age, gender, social circumstances e.g. living alone, disease severity, availability of other services. Other criteria We will include studies written in any language. Exclusion criteria: We will exclude studies that only report admission for elective or planned health care and studies of hospital or ED visits for planned diagnostic services only. We will exclude case reports, case series, letters, editorials, or expert opinions only Outcomes of interest: Patient outcomes of care (including mortality, quality of life, length of stay, readmission, adverse effects of intervention) Grey literature e.g. NICE and other clinical guidelines relevant to ACSCs will be searched for guidance on which patients over 65 years of age should be admitted and what factors should be considered in decision making Search: Databases and registries An electronic search in MEDLINE, Centre for Reviews and Dissemination (CRD) databases, York, and the Cochrane Database will be composed to identify any relevant systematic reviews and their references will be checked A search strategy for primary studies will be developed using keywords for the electronic databases according to their specific subject headings or searching structure. The search strategy will be tested for citations from 1985 – 2014 on the OVID databases - Medline®, Excerpta Medica Database (Embase), Cumulative Index

Award_Title: Understanding and improving the outcome of viral encephalitis
Abstract: Aims? To determine the clinical predictors of viral encephalitis, and poor outcome ? To better understand those outcomes in terms of cognitive function, quality of life, and cost? To develop the means of intervening to improve the outcomeBackgroundViral encephalitis (inflammation of the brain substance) is one of the most important types of brain infection because of its devastating impact on those affected. It has a disproportionately large burden on the NHS and community through high health and economic costs, but this has never been quantified. In terms of research, viral encephalitis is relatively neglected, because it is not easily funded from other sources, e.g. major charities.Patients with encephalitis have difficulties at all stages of the patient journey, including:? Difficulty in accessing appropriate health care when they become unwell, because of the non-specific nature of their early symptoms? Shortcomings in the initial management, so that there are delays in investigation and treatment? Poor understanding about the neuropsychological and social sequelae, and effects on carers, so that long term planning is difficultHerpes simplex virus (HSV) is the most common cause, and is treatable with aciclovir, but delays in treatment are associated with poor outcome. There has been little research into how and why delays occur. There are no health economic data from the UK, but typical medical negligence settlements of £1-2 million for a single encephalitis case where the management was negligent give some indication of the overall costs to society. The proposed research programme builds on pilot data from previous work by the Liverpool Brain Infections Group, the Encephalitis Society, and preliminary findings from the HPA Cohort studyResearch Plans (SEE APPENDIX 1 & 2 Programme Overview, and Gantt chart).? Establishing a new prospective multi-centre cohort of patients with encephalitis across the UK (for brevity, referred to as the Enceph-UK cohort study)? Capitalising on a patient cohort established through the Department of Health (DH)-funded Health Protection Agency (HPA) study on the Aetiologies of Encephalitis (the HPA cohort study)? Developing an intervention based around Management Guidelines, and examining its role through a cluster randomised trial.Studies1. Determination of the clinical features predictive of viral encephalitis, and of outcome, with a prospective cohort study.2. Examining experiences of end users in relation to acute management (from the Enceph-UK study) and long term care (from the HPA cohort).3. Investigating the effects of encephalitis on quality of life4. Determining the total costs of viral encephalitis.5. Award_Title: Improving the effectiveness and reach of NHS support for smoking cessation in pregnancy
Abstract: Aims and Objectives: To increase the uptake and effectiveness of NHS Stop Smoking Services for pregnant women (SSSP) by determining when and how NHS cessation support is best offered in pregnancy, refining and testing ‘self-help’ cessation methods which are attractive to and, therefore, likely to be used by the vast majority of mothers who do not currently access SSSP and investigating how ‘self-help’ support is best delivered by the NHS. Background: Maternal smoking in pregnancy is the biggest avoidable cause of fetal harm in the UK with 255,000 pregnancies exposed annually in England. Infants and children of smokers suffer higher morbidity and mortality and are more likely to become smokers themselves. Pregnancy motivates many women to try stopping smoking but very few use the effective NHS SSSP; most try to stop without help. ‘Self-help’ cessation methods are effective in pregnancy but are not systematically delivered by SSSP. Research Plans:We propose to: Survey all English SSSP, determining use of self-help, referral pathways / methods of engaging with smokers and principal models and costs of service provision; combining these with routinely available data on SSSP effectiveness to determine service design factors which most influence (cost) effectiveness.Survey a cohort of pregnant women to identify i) times in pregnancy when they are most receptive to and ii) predictors of propensity to engage with SSSP support (inc. self-help). Conduct phase II studies investigating the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of two different strategies for identifying, referring and engaging pregnant smokers for SSSP support.Use a linked mother / infant primary care medical records cohort to monitor national trends in nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) use in pregnancy, compare women prescribed / not prescribed NRT and investigate impacts on infrequent fetal outcomes of NRT use in pregnancy Refine and estimate the likely uptake and effectiveness / cost-effectiveness of an interactive, SMS ‘text’ messaging ‘self-help’ intervention for smoking cessation in pregnancy delivered in routine NHS ante natal care settings. Research Team:We are academics from most UK research teams working on smoking in pregnancy, colleagues from NHS Nottingham City who commission and manage Nottingham’s NHS SSSP. Five team members are academics within Centres of Public Health Excellence centred on Nottingham (UKCTCS; - www.ukctcs.net) and Cambridge. We already collaborate substantially and are sufficiently integrated to implement our programme across dispersed research centres.Programme management:Strategic management will be from quarterly Steering Committee (SC) meetings of all applicants chaired by the Principal Applicant (PA). The SC will review progress across all worksteams, directing resources, as appropriate to ensure objectives are met. A Programme Manager (PM) will ensure efficient, operational management, integration of workstreams and optimal resource use. SC subgroups, convened by the PM, co-opting team members, as appropriate will manage workstreams. Research Environment: Our strong track record of delivering smoking cessation research in obstetric environments includes sucessfully blending expertise to implement complex NHS research projects. We have strong links with relevant speciality groups of Collaborative Local Research Networks and in addition to the two Public Health Centres mentioned above, where further support is needed, we be able to access this through memberships of the NIHR School for Primary Care (Nottingham) and Public Health Research Consortium (York).Outputs and impact:The programme will deliver peer-reviewed publications and related outputs from year 3; findings could be implemented immediately increasing uptake of SSSP, providing support to thousands of extra women annually and helping many pregnant women to permanently stop smoking who would not otherwise have done so. Award_Title: Development and evaluation of interventions for the prevention of childhood obesity in a multi-ethnic population: the Born in Bradford NHS Research Programme.
Abstract: Aims. To study the patterns and aetiology of childhood obesity in a multi-ethnic population and use this evidence to develop a tailored prevention intervention. Background. The obesity epidemic is one of the most daunting public health threats facing the UK. Contemporary data indicate that this epidemic begins in early childhood and that children from South Asian origin are at particular risk. Epidemiological evidence has highlighted the importance of a number of early life factors for the development of obesity but there are gaps in our knowledge about the impact of potentially important exposures in pregnancy and early life. Early childhood provides a unique and circumscribed opportunity to promote health and prevent obesity. However there is a disappointing lack of evidence for effective interventions in pre-school children and in children of South Asian origin. Research plan: Enrolment and data collection for the Born in Bradford cohort (10,000 babies ~ 5000 of South Asian origin) began in March 2007 with over 80% recruitment rates. Objective 1. Measuring child growth. This study will establish research-calibre routine data collection on growth monitoring in a deprived, biethnic population through strengthening routine surveillance and monitoring growth trajectories. A 10% sub-sample of the cohort (n=1080 with ~ 50% European and 50% South Asian origin) will be selected for more intensive follow-up to augment and validate data collection.Objective 2: Identifying modifiable risk factors for childhood obesity. The focus for this objective will be to identify modifiable behaviours and environmental risk factors that can be targeted in future interventions. Data will be collected in the 10% sub-sample through home visits by bilingual researchers who will administer survey instruments for behavioural measures and undertake anthropometry assessments. Objective 3. Reviewing the evidence of effectiveness of obesity prevention interventions in pregnant women and/or children up to the age of 5 years of South Asian origin.Objective 4: Determining appropriate intervention targets. Qualitative interviews, observational methods, geospatial mapping and nutritional audits will be undertaken to explore determinants of feeding practices; cultural and social differences in feeding practices; influence of key stakeholders; beliefs, attitudes and practices in relation to obesity, diet and exercise; perceptions in the South Asian community about childhood obesity; access to food retrailing; eating patterns.Objective 5: Field-testing implementation methods and potential intervention components. Evidence from current and previous implementation methods will be supplemented by a survey of nationally relevant work. Field testing of candidate components for an intervention strategy will be undertaken to test their feasibility and acceptability in small scale action research cycles.Objective 6.Feasibility of implementation and evaluation of intervention to prevent obesity. The ultimate aim of the programme is to design an innovative community/family-based intervention to improve modifiable behaviours in both parent and child. The exploratory trial will to inform a definitive (phase 3) cluster randomised trial which can be implemented within the NHS. Early evaluation will help to refine and optimise the interventions in partnership with families and professionals. We will describe the process of implementation and assess: the feasibility and acceptability of the interventions for different communities; eligibility, consent and recruitment rates; acceptability of randomisation process; follow up rates. The outcomes will inform the components and delivery of the interventions, estimate the effect size and test and validate outcome measures. Research team. Abstract: Primary aim and objectives (8)The aim is to develop and evaluate novel services delivering specialist co-ordinated multi-disciplinary care to frail older people presenting with or at risk of medical crises.
